## Volume Front Matter

## Series Title Page

**Complete Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III; a Chronological Reprinting of all the Monuments of Catholic Tradition that existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, diligently corrected by comparison with one another and with several manuscript codices; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority and weight in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is readily apparent to the reader which Fathers commented on the texts of each book of Scripture, and in which places of their works they did so.**

**The most accurate edition, and one easily preferable to all others if the following are taken into account: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection, a single, methodical, chronological gathering of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but now for the first time assembled in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the universal library of the clergy, or of the complete series in each branch of ecclesiastical learning. The Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition sells for 1,200 francs; the Greek-Latin edition for 1,800. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# In the Year of the Lord 900. Fulco, Archbishop of Reims

## Historical Notice

*(Gallicia Christiana, volume IX.)*

[Col. 0009]

[Col. 0009A] Flodoard briefly touched upon Fulco’s beginnings; nevertheless, he records him as very noble and accustomed to palace offices, and also related to Guido and Lambert, dukes of Spoleto, whom the supreme pontiffs attempted to raise to the imperial dignity. From being a canon of Saint-Omer, he became a monk in the abbey of Saint-Bertin, of which he was elected abbot in 877. After Hincmar’s death, he was chosen by both clergy and people as archbishop of Reims in 883 and was consecrated at the beginning of March.

When Hildebold, bishop of Soissons, and the other suffragans of the metropolitan see complained that this had been done without awaiting the visitor’s arrival, letters of excuse were sent to them from Reims concerning the matter, stating that the election had not taken place before the visitor’s arrival.

After his consecration, Fulco, entrusting the account of his faith to Pope Marinus, received from him, Flodoard says, the pallium in the customary manner of his predecessors. He also sent him letters requesting confirmation of the privilege due to the Church of Reims and commending King Carloman. In these he indicated that he had long been known to the same pope, from the time of Pope John, when Fulco himself had been at Rome with Emperor Charles.

Since barbarians were invading from every side, he surrounded the city of Reims with a new wall, the old wall having previously been used by Ebo for the construction of the greater basilica. A little later he utterly demolished the church of Saint Denis, since it obstructed the fortification. He also built several castles from their foundations, namely Altimont in the district of Dulcom, and another near Sparnacum, which King Odo, because it had rebelled against him on account of the elevation of Charles the Simple, destroyed in order to resist the Normans.

After the city had been strengthened with new defenses, the same bishop brought the body of Blessed Remigius back to Durocortorum from the monastery of Orbais, to which it had been carried from Sparnacum, in the first year of his episcopate, passing through Culmiciacum, with his fellow bishops and clergy assisting.

At about the same time, he transferred part of the body of the blessed martyr Nicasius, together with the body of his blessed sister Eutropia, from the church of Saint Agricola into the city newly enclosed by walls; behind the altar of Mary, Mother of God, he placed them near the relics of Blessed Pope Callistus, which had recently been brought there because of pagan attacks.

In 884, having heard of Adrian III’s elevation to the supreme pontificate, he hastened to visit him by letter, rejoicing in his honor and indicating that he wished to go to Rome if he were able, with God granting peace. Meanwhile, he asked him to strengthen and enlarge the privileges granted to the Church of Reims by Popes Leo, Benedict, and Nicholas. He again commended King Carloman, as well as Frotarius, formerly bishop of Bordeaux and then archbishop of Bourges.

When Carloman was taken from the living in the same year, Fulco undertook the guardianship of his younger brother, Charles the Simple.

[Col. 0009B] But soon such confusion overtook affairs, with the Normans invading in bands the dioceses of Reims, Soissons, and Noyon, that the nobles of the whole kingdom, at Fulco’s request, entrusted the care of the entire realm to Emperor Charles the Fat.

[Col. 0009D] In 887, or perhaps 888, [Col. 0010A] on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, he consecrated Dodilo bishop of Cambrai. Dodilo later incurred his displeasure because he favored Baldwin, count of Flanders. In 888 he subscribed the privilege of immunity granted by Lindbert, bishop of Mainz, to the monasteries of Corvey and Herford.

In 888, after the emperor had been removed and Odo, son of Robert the Strong, had been hailed king of the Franks, Fulco gradually came to regard him as reigning with hostility, and finally, at a council convened at Reims in 893, attempted to drive him from the throne. In the same year he crowned Charles the Simple in his metropolitan church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February.

At that council he made many complaints against Baldwin, count of Flanders, an invader of ecclesiastical property; the assembled bishops threatened that, unless he repented, he would be struck with perpetual anathema. At about the same time Fulco consecrated Mancio as bishop of Châlons; for this he was rebuked by Pope Formosus.

In 890 he presided over a synod convened at Vangiones, and in 892 he transferred the relics of Saint Rigobert to his metropolitan church. In the same year he obtained from Pope Formosus a privilege that, while the see of Reims was vacant, no king, bishop, or any Christian should convert the revenues of the Church of Reims to his own use, but that everything should be reserved for the future bishop, to be elected within the time established by the canons—that is, within the space of three months—so that the metropolis might not remain without a shepherd longer than was fitting.

In 896, after peace had been established between Odo and Charles the Simple, he was summoned to the Roman council that Pope Stephen VI had announced for September of that year. Labbé thinks, however, that it was not held until 897, while Marlot assigns that synod to the year 898. Fulco, who could not attend it, sent his suffragans, Honoratus of Beauvais and Rodulf of Laon.

In 898 and the following year he held the office of chief chancellor of France. From that time, our Mabillon notes, the archbishops of Reims began to perform the duties of chancellor.

[Col. 0010C] “It happened,” says Flodoard, “that King Charles took away from Count Baldwin the abbey of Saint-Vaast, which he held together with the castle of Arras, because of Baldwin’s infidelity, and granted it to Bishop Fulco. A certain count named Altimar held the abbey of Saint-Médard; Fulco thought it advantageous to exchange it with that same count, and he did so in the year 900.

“In that same year, perhaps, Fulco crowned Charles the Simple once more in the city of Reims—although, while Odo lived, only a few regarded Charles as king. Thus Fulco received the abbey of Saint-Médard from Altimar and gave him the abbey of Saint-Vaast, after taking the castle of Arras from Baldwin by force of siege.

“Inflamed by anguish over this, Baldwin and all his retinue, while seeking a way to avenge themselves, pretended to renew their friendship with the bishop, looking for an opportunity for revenge and observing how he usually traveled from his residence to an audience with the king, surrounded by guards.

“One day, when he was traveling with only a very small escort to seek an audience with the king, they attacked and intercepted him on the road, under the leadership of a certain Wincmar. At first they addressed him as though discussing friendship and the recovery of Baldwin; but then they suddenly attacked him with lances, struck him down, and killed him on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July. Some of his men, overcome by their great love for him, threw themselves upon him and were pierced and killed together with him.

“The other survivors carried this news of their greatest grief to those who had remained at the lodgings. Struck by the unprecedented deed and armed, they attempted to attack the bishop’s murderers in revenge. When they could not find them, they lifted up the lifeless body, lamenting with immense cries of grief, and brought it to the city of Reims amid the great mourning of all his people. There at last it was washed, honored with fitting funeral rites, and committed to a suitable burial.”

His epitaph is as follows:

> This tomb covers the limbs of great Fulco,  
> the distinguished bishop of the see of Reims;  
> whom France brought forth, sprung from noble stock,  
> and whom the court took from the schools and cultivated.
>
> From there God appointed him, proven in virtue,  
> a mirror of the Church and a devout pontiff;  
> over whom he presided for seventeen years in all,  
> three months, and additionally ten days.
>
> He greatly enlarged the bishopric, adding many things,  
> and restored the walls of this city.  
> The honor of the world, protector of his homeland, lover of piety,  
> he was pierced by spears for his devotion to peace.
>
> June had already reached its seventeenth day,  
> and, struck down by a dreadful death, he departed.  
> May the piety of the Mother of the Lord, and likewise of the blessed bishop  
> Remigius, obtain rest for him.

Fulco was indignant with Charles the Simple because he had made a treaty with the Normans, and, with episcopal authority, rebuked him in a letter reported by Flodoard in harsher language, so that these words might penetrate more deeply into the king’s mind. On that letter, see our Rivet, *History of French Letters*, volume V, page 692.

He is also believed to have written to Alfred, king of the West Saxons; on this matter, see the Bollandists, July, volume I, page 651.

“This bishop also accomplished many good works in this see of Reims,” says Flodoard. “For he enlarged the episcopal residence with many acquisitions, both the monastery of Avenay and possessions obtained from kings and various persons, and he adorned this Church of Reims with various gifts and ornaments.”

In his time, in the year 893, as Mabillon conjectures, the relics of Saint Gibrian were transferred from the district of Châlons to the basilica of Saint Remigius.

Finally, the aforementioned bishop, diligent concerning the worship of God and ecclesiastical order, and also ardent in his love of wisdom, restored his schools at Reims—the schools of the local canons and of rural clerics—which had almost fallen into decay. Having summoned Remigius of Auxerre as teacher, he had the young clerics trained in the liberal arts, and he himself devoted himself with them to reading and the meditation of wisdom.

He also summoned Hucbald, a monk of Saint-Amand and a man nobly trained in the learned disciplines, and illuminated the Church of Reims with distinguished teachings. Mabillon assigns the establishment of these schools to approximately the year 893.

Regino counts Fulco among the martyrs who died bravely for ecclesiastical liberty; and we formerly did not deny him the name of saint, although he has not yet been proclaimed one by public decree. Molanus thinks that he rests at Saint-Omer near Blessed Bertin; but it is more certain that he was buried in the church of Blessed Remigius at Reims, as the verses of his later epitaph clearly indicate.

The Ignacian Codex reports that Fulco made a testament, in these words:

> But the aforementioned Fulco, being a wise man who feared God, had long before arranged a testament so that he might distribute certain parts of his patrimony by right to various churches. Among them, for the remedy of his soul, he gave to the Church of Reims the estate of Nemincum, which is situated in the diocese of Noyon. Its revenues are divided annually among the canons of Reims so that his memory may be commemorated. From the revenue of the aforesaid estate, the canons of Noyon receive sixty solidi each year in that currency.

# Letters of Fulco, Archbishop of Reims

*(Province of Reims, volume I, page 520.)*

## First Letter: To Stephen V, Supreme Pontiff

*(Year 885.)*

[Col. 0011D] I have received the letter of your predecessor, binding me, together with my entire province, by almost infinite obligations to render heartfelt thanks. For he deigned, in wholly apostolic language, to comfort us amid the storms of the Normans’ afflictions with words more penetrating than any two-edged sword, and to address me by the title of brother and friend, although I am scarcely worthy to be trodden by the papal shoe.

I long with every desire to hasten to him, and now to you, most holy father; but I am prevented by the incursions of the Danes, by whom we are surrounded and harried. For eight years now they have so ravaged this kingdom that only those who could defend themselves in castles were blessed—and these attacks also prevented me from breaking up the ambushes which these pestilential men were preparing against the pontiff of blessed memory.

[Col. 0012D] If, nevertheless, the prayers of a wretched little man could accomplish anything, I certainly did not fail him. How could I fail one who had adopted my relative Wido, in a manner of speaking, as his son? When I announced this to my kinsmen, they immediately devoted all their service and reverence to the Apostolic See.

And I, together with my fellow bishops—even though some of them, such as the bishop of Morini, have been forced for a time to abandon their burned city—will persevere in devotion to the Roman See until death. Whatever the Church of God requires, we shall accomplish even at the cost of our property and our bodies, as is fitting for a man of Reims, whom your predecessors, considering him above all the Gallic bishops, honored with primacy.

[Col. 0013A] Sixtus I, the first bishop of the whole region, was sent here by Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. Pope Hormisdas also wished Remigius to exercise his vicariate throughout all Gaul. These matters now seem to require addition, lest perhaps our Reims, buried beneath the ruins of the Normans—may God avert it—should also be buried in the oblivion of the pontiffs.

For this reason, I ask that you commend the privileges which I humbly proposed to Marinus and Adrian, as well as the generous donation of my brother Rampon for the foundation of a monastery. Since Bruinifidus does not cease appropriating what has been given, let him finally be struck with anathema. There are also others who consume the property of the Church of Reims; if Emperor Charles is warned by a word from the pontiff, he will easily take notice of them.

## Second Letter: To Emperor Charles the Bald

*(Year 894.) On the treaty made with the Normans.*

Who, being faithful to you as he ought to be, would not be terrified that you wish to befriend the enemies of God and, to the destruction and ruin of the Christian name, accept pagan arms and detestable treaties? For it makes no difference whether someone associates himself with pagans or, having denied God, worships idols.

For if, as the Apostle says, “bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Corinthians 15), how much more is the chastity of a Christian soul corrupted by the counsels and companionship of pagans? A person cannot fail to imitate what he constantly sees; rather, he will gradually become accustomed to it and, as though drawn by a bond of evil habit, will be dragged into wrongdoing.

Certainly, your royal ancestors, having abandoned pagan error, submitted themselves nobly to the worship of God and always sought help from him. For this reason they ruled successfully and transmitted the inheritance of the kingdom to their descendants.

You, on the contrary, now abandon God. I shall say it, though unwillingly: you abandon God when you join yourself to his enemies. Therefore that prophetic word is rightly directed at you which was once directed against a king of Israel who acted similarly: “You give help to the wicked and join friendship with those who hate God” (2 Chronicles 19).

And certainly, when you ought to put an end to past evils, renounce the robberies and plundering of the poor, and do penance for all these things, you now unite yourself with those who do not know God and trust in their own savagery, thereby provoking God to still greater anger.

Believe me: by acting thus you will never attain the kingdom; rather, God, whom you provoke, will swiftly destroy you. Until now I had hoped better things of you. Now I see that you will perish together with all your kinsmen, if you truly wish to act in this way and heed such counsels.

In truth, those who give you such advice are shown to be not faithful but altogether unfaithful. If you are willing to listen to them, you will lose both the earthly and the heavenly kingdom.

Therefore I beseech you by God to abandon such counsel, and not wish to plunge yourself into eternal destruction or bring the loss of eternal sorrow upon me and the others who are faithful to you according to God.

For it would have been better for you not to be born than to wish to rule by the protection of the devil and to help those whom you ought in every way to oppose.

Know this: if you do this and heed such counsels, you will never have me as a faithful man. Rather, I shall recall from your allegiance as many as I can, and, together with all my fellow bishops, I shall excommunicate you and all your people and condemn you with perpetual anathema.

Because of the fidelity I preserve toward you, I write these things with groans, since I desire that you should always be honored both according to God and in the world, and that, with the help not of Satan but of Christ, you should ascend to the royal height due to you.

For the kingdom that God gives has a firm foundation; but what is acquired through injustice and plunder is unstable and quickly falls, nor can it long endure.

# In the Year of the Lord 902. Riculfus, Bishop of Soissons

## Historical Notice

*(From the Gallia Christiana.)*

[Col. 0013D] Of the judges who, at the court held at Vermer in 892, asserted the cell of Alfa for the monks of Adremar, Riculfus was one. He attended the Synod of Reims in 893, at which Charles the Simple was anointed. In 900, at the Synod of Reims, he consecrated Herveus as archbishop of Reims; at that synod he cursed with terrible imprecations the men of Baldwin, count of Flanders, who had killed Archbishop Fulco.

He issued a constitution in 889, which is preserved in volume IX of Labbé’s *Councils*, page 416. It contains many points worthy of attention.

In section 3, concerning the canonical hours, it reads:

> “We ask you to be diligent in singing the psalms, in reading the divine books, in observing the canonical hours—that is, Prime, Terce, and Sext; also in the daily celebration of Mass; in chanting None, Vespers, and Compline, as well as the morning office. Invite your parishioners, so that, if they are unable to come to the other offices, they may at least strive to hear Mass more frequently, and may not neglect to attend Vespers, Matins, and Mass on Sundays and other feast days.”

From section 8 of this constitution, examinations were to be conducted throughout the baptismal churches at the appointed time during Lent, and those who had been baptized were immediately after baptism to receive the Eucharist, that is, Holy Communion.

Section 20 decrees:

> “On the Kalends of every month, let the priests of each deanery meet together; and when they meet, let them not devote themselves to feasting or drinking, but let them converse about their ministry, religious conduct, and the things that occur in their parishes.”

Riculfus is believed to have died in 902.

# Statutes of Riculfus

*(Province of Reims, volume I, page 525.)*

[Col. 0015B] I, Riculfus, humble bishop of Soissons, having considered the needs of the parish divinely entrusted to us and having taken suitable account of our fellow ministers, with the Lord inspiring and assisting us alike, have decided to treat, modestly and usefully according to my ability, certain matters that seemed relevant either to the admonition of our priests or to the instruction of the common people.

Although the rule of the whole Christian life is sufficiently and more than sufficiently contained in the pages of Sacred Scripture, I nevertheless thought it not inappropriate to record in brief and clear chapters certain matters suited to the observance of simple people, and to entrust them to you, my fellow priests and co-workers, to be kept and read frequently. Thus, if you are not able to turn over such extensive volumes of divine and canonical authority, you may at least frequently use these very brief and perfectly clear instructions as a handbook, and, warned by these admonitions, set before the peoples entrusted to you a wholesome rule of life.

For in this way, with the Lord’s cooperation, you will be able both to free yourselves from the danger of your ministry and to hasten, together with the peoples subject to you, toward the joys of the heavenly kingdom.

## I

Pay attention, therefore, because you have shared with us the care of the Lord’s flock and hold, in the priestly ministry, a place of the second order and dignity. Just as we, although unworthy, must act in this church in the place of the apostles, so you also must exercise with us in this parish of the Lord the ministry of the seventy-two disciples.

For in the old law Moses and Aaron held the position of high priest, and the sons of Aaron likewise received the priestly office in the second rank.

The care and concern of the parishes belong to you, and upon you depend their salvation, welfare, and progress in virtue. For it is written concerning you: “The lips of the priest shall preserve knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2).

In Latin speech, *angelus* means “messenger.” You indeed fulfill the ministry of angels when you instruct and teach your parishes. But first it is necessary that you yourselves learn the reading of the sacred writings through diligent study, since afterward you must teach it to others; for no one can communicate to others what he does not know.

Indeed, we do not wish you to be unaware that, concerning those priests who are idle and slow to learn, the chapters of the kings and emperors, with the consent of many bishops, enacted the following decree:

> “If any priest, frequently admonished by his bishop to take care concerning his learning, neglects to do so, he shall without doubt be removed from office and shall lose the church which he holds. For those who are ignorant of the law of God cannot announce or preach it to others.”
>
> [Note: [Col. 0015D] *Capitularies*, XVI, year 769.]

To prevent this from happening to any of you, we warn you with fraternal affection.

## II

Therefore every priest ought, with God’s help, to excel the people entrusted to him and all his subjects in life, morals, and good works, so that in him they may see what they can imitate and follow by doing good. By the gift of divine grace, he should offer an example of chastity, humility, moderation, and the other virtues, so that, in accordance with the Apostle’s words, he may “adorn the doctrine of God our Savior in all things” (Titus 2).

## III

We ask you to be diligent in singing the psalms, reading the divine books, and observing the canonical hours—that is, Prime, Terce, and Sext; also in the daily celebration of Mass; in chanting None, Vespers, and Compline, as well as the morning office.

Invite your parishioners, so that, if they are unable to attend the other offices [Note: [Col. 0015D] That is, the office], they may at least strive to hear Mass more frequently and may not neglect to attend Vespers, Matins, and Mass on Sundays and other feast days.

## IV

Know, therefore, that the following has been said to you: “Cleanse yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isaiah 52).

You should not think that this is to be understood only of the chalice and paten [Note: [Col. 0016D] That is, the corporal], on which the body and blood of the Lord are consecrated, but also of bodily cleanliness and purity of mind.

For, as blessed Gregory says when interpreting the parable of the ten virgins:

> “Our little vessels are our hearts, in which we carry everything that we think. We therefore have a fragile vessel, namely our body, which we must always keep supremely clean, so that, while we present pure offerings to God, we too may become acceptable victims before his holy altar.”

## V

We likewise admonish each of you to strive to know by heart, faithfully, accurately, and correctly, the psalms; the discourse of the Catholic faith [Note: [Col. 0017D] This concerns the Creed attributed to Saint Athanasius], which begins, “Whoever wishes to be saved”; the canon of the Mass; and the chant, or computation.

You should also have written out distinctly and faithfully the consignation of infants, both boys and girls, whether one or several; the consecration of the font and of water to be sprinkled through the houses; the commendation of the soul; and the prayers for burying the dead. You should meditate on these frequently in practice, so that you may know how to recite them correctly and irreproachably over both a male and a female.

We wish you to divide the aforementioned consignation of infants into four forms in writing: one for a single boy, one for a single girl, one for several boys, and one for several girls, just as, with Christ’s favor, we shall provide them to you in written form.

## VI

We further admonish each of you to strive to possess a corrected and properly arranged Missal, Lectionary, Gospel book, Martyrology, Antiphonary, Psalter, and the book of the forty Homilies of blessed Gregory, according to our books, which we use in Holy Mother Church.

Do not dispense with whatever divine and ecclesiastical books you are able to possess. From them you will receive food and seasoning for souls, as the Lord says:

> “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4).

If anyone is unable to possess all the books of the Old Testament, let him at least work especially diligently to copy correctly the first book of the whole divine history, namely Genesis, by reading which he may come to know the creation of the entire world.

## VII

You must also strive to have your ecclesiastical vestments prepared suitably and honorably: namely, one or two clean albs for the divine mystery, with oraria—that is, two clean stoles—and two clean amices, as well as an equal number of clean corporals; likewise two belts, that is, cinctures, and an equal number of clean maniples. You should also have clean altar linens and a silk chasuble in which Mass may be celebrated.

[Col. 0017D] We expressly prohibit anyone from using in the sacred mysteries an alb that he wears in daily or ordinary external use [Note: [Col. 0017D] This concerns clerical clothing, the ankle-length garment, and the chasuble mentioned in the ancient canons].

You should also have clean and suitably arranged places where, after receiving the sacred mysteries, you may wash your hands and mouths [Note: [Col. 0018D] Bishops and, in the Church of Reims, priests retained the practice of washing after the sacred synaxis. See the Statutes of Hincmar].

If possible, each of you should have a chalice with a silver paten, or one made of any very pure metal. Thus, when we order each of you to bring these vessels, or the other things belonging to the priestly ministry, to our synod, or when we pass through your parishes, you may not incur our displeasure should we find these things prepared in an unseemly manner.

At Mass and Vespers also, if you are able, offer God frankincense or incense in a thurible. We further expressly command you to keep your houses clean and free of dirt and foul smells, so that you may approach the altar of the Lord from them more pure.

## VIII

We also earnestly admonish that examinations be conducted generally throughout the baptismal churches at the appointed time during Lent.

We urgently command you to take care that those who have been baptized receive the Eucharist, that is, Holy Communion, immediately after baptism. For the one who said, “Unless someone is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 5), himself also said, “Unless you eat the bread of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (ibid.).

[Col. 0018B] IX. Priests must diligently strive to care for public penitents, to know how to recite correctly the prayers for visiting the sick, male and female, and to take the greatest care that, just as no one dies without baptism, so no one dies without the provision of viaticum; nor should a public penitent, if he becomes ill, be left without it. Let them carefully consider and diligently beware lest, through such negligence, they incur grave danger. Let them also take care that they do not become like Simon Magus and Judas the traitor if, for payment or because of familiarity or kinship, they bring penitents to reconciliation before the proper time and give them a testimonial of reconciliation; or if, with bitterness—or, God forbid, hatred—or because they receive nothing from them, they cause penitents pursuing their penance with fervor and diligence to be suspended from reconciliation. For priests have been appointed by God as fellow ministers and likewise as co-workers with bishops in the divine ministry. If, however, public penitents are reconciled before the years prescribed by the canons because of a definite necessity or reason, then, just as before reconciliation they cared for their penance according to the penitents’ capacity and condition, so after reconciliation they must not neglect their life and conduct until the appointed period of penance has been completed, but must diligently examine and observe them. They should know that what is said applies not only to bishops but, according to their own measure, also to priests: “I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezek. III); and concerning each person entrusted to him it is said again through the prophet: “I shall require his blood from your hand” (ibid.).

[Col. 0018D] X. Priests must also anoint their sick parishioners with holy oil after confession and reconciliation, and then give them Communion. But if, before they arrive, the sick person has become unable to speak, and reliable witnesses attest that he showed such a sign—that he asked for penance, which the priest’s delay prevented him from receiving—then they should provide him with the aid of viaticum.

XI. Apart from these matters, you should know that, by canonical authority, the resources of the Church are divided into four parts. One is, if he wishes, for the bishop; another is for lights and repairs—that is, the restoration of the church; the third is for the priest and his household; and the fourth is assigned to guests (Council of Worms, 868, canon 7). Therefore, from the portion owed to the church’s buildings, we wish either through ourselves or through our fellow ministers to learn what is provided each year both for oil or wax for the lights, and for repairing the roofs, or for whatever furnishings are supplied from it for the church. It is also fitting that you have one, two, or three clerics who celebrate Mass with you, whom you greet and by whom you are greeted in return, because the Lord says in the Gospel: “Where two or three have been gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matt. XVIII). No one among you, however, should presume to celebrate Mass alone. In the matter of the sacred rites, you must observe this in every way: mix water with the wine in the chalice, because the bread is understood as the body and the wine as the blood; the water that flowed from the Lord’s side on the cross most certainly signifies the faithful people joined to their head, which is Christ. When these things have been observed with the greatest devotion, the true body of the Lord is undoubtedly made in truth. And whoever, purified in heart and body and renewed by faith through it, undoubtedly obtains in it the remission of sins.

XII. Strive to receive guests as far as possible and, according to your means, cheerfully provide them with what they need. Exhort your people even more earnestly to do the same and to wash the feet of the poor, knowing that if one of the poor asks for lodging and cannot obtain it, and, lying outside [Col. 0019C] the house, is either eaten by beasts or dies from cold or some other harshness of the air, the one who denied him the assistance of human kindness will be held accountable for him. Nor will the priest be free from this guilt if he failed to urge his helpers to love hospitality. For we know that great is the virtue of hospitality, through which very many have pleased God and been deemed worthy to receive angels as guests, as we read happened to Abraham, Lot, Tobit, and many others. You must always remember how great is the reward of hospitality, as the Lord says: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me” (Matt. XXV). Recall frequently to memory also the words of the Apostle, who says: “Do not forget hospitality” (Heb. XIII), so that with blessed Job you may be able to say: “My lodging was open to the traveler” (Job XXXI).

[Col. 0019D] Frequently turn over in your minds also the saying of St. Gregory in his exposition of the Gospel, where he says that guests should not only be invited but even drawn in. Once guests have been received, provide them with the service of human kindness according to your ability, in accordance with what is written: “If you have much, give abundantly; if you have little, share even that most willingly” (Tob. IV). Reflect also on the Gospel saying: “Whoever gives even a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple, amen I say to you, he shall not lose his reward” (Matt. X). And since it commonly happens that those who are received may inflict some harm on those who receive them, if you take in people about whom you have doubts, place them in a remote house, lest they find an opportunity either to sin themselves or to cause you loss.

XIII. We urgently admonish that priests or clerics must not go to taverns for the purpose of dining, nor allow wine to be sold in churches except in a case of necessity. Nor should they permit sellers or buyers to linger in the churches themselves in the manner of people feasting. This is prohibited in the Council of Carthage as follows: “Let no bishops or clerics feast in the church, unless perhaps travelers, because of the necessity of lodging, refresh themselves there; but let the people be prohibited from such banquets as far as possible” (Council of Carthage, 397, canon 30).

XIV. We also admonish that priests or clerics must not live together with women, nor give occasion for detraction. On this matter Clement, prelate of the holy Roman Church, instructs as follows: “A cleric,” he says, “must not approach or hasten to a woman’s lodging.” Nor should a priest converse alone with a woman alone, as the holy Council of Nicaea decreed: neither a bishop, nor a priest, nor a deacon, nor any cleric at all may have a strange woman living with him.

We further say that even mothers, aunts, sisters, or female relatives must be treated with caution, lest what is read in Holy Scripture concerning Tamar, the sister of Absalom, come to pass: her brother Amnon violated her through wicked desire; or lest the similar corruption committed by Lot against his daughters through the vice of drunkenness be repeated. If any one of you invites his mother, sister, or aunt to eat with him, then, once the meal is over, he must have them return to their own homes or to lodgings remote from the priest’s house while daylight remains. It is dangerous for them to live with you, and therefore this has been prohibited by the holy Fathers. Apart from the opportunity for sin mentioned above, a woman who enters together with a mother, sister, aunt, or niece is not thereby a close relative; and unless this is handled carefully, the priestly order may fall into the devil’s snare.

Priests who are invited by religious persons in memory of their dear ones must not become drunk, nor presume to sing amid their cups. Nor should they perform drinking prayers under the names of the saints. Rather, they should dine religiously, drink soberly, speak of matters conducive to edification, and return to their churches in good time, while daylight remains [Col. 0020D].

XV. Priests must not become stewards—that is, administrators of estates—nor act as agents for widows; nor may they be tenants of secular lands or seek their livelihood or profit through any shameful or dishonorable business. Nor should they take such care of widows’ company as to damage their own reputation or give occasion for detraction. They must also take care that public officials—that is, vicars and centenarii, or other collectors—do not oppress strangers and the poor. If they cannot correct this themselves, they should make it known to us or to our fellow ministers.

XVI. We further admonish that priests should serve rural—that is, agricultural—and other occupations only to such an extent that they do not neglect the divine office. They must discipline their pupils moderately, nurture them chastely, and so instruct them in letters that they do not destroy them by bad conduct. They must never receive girls into their school to study with their pupils, and they must not devote themselves to shameful profit or commercial dealings.

XVII. We judge that this too must be admonished: all must withdraw from usury. If, according to the Lord’s commandment, we must love our friends in God and our enemies for God’s sake, and freely give them our goods, which he himself has bestowed on us undeserving, how can we demand from those who are our brothers in Christ—as he himself says, “For you have one Father, and you are all brothers” (Matt. XXIII)—what we did not lend, and reclaim what we did not provide?

[Col. 0021B] Therefore, let each person receive only as much as he has provided, and the same kind and measure of grain, wine, silver, or indeed some other equivalent value, according to what they have agreed between themselves; but in such a way that it is neither multiplied nor increased. We likewise decree that the following must be observed concerning travelers: no other measure may be given them when selling than the one by which you yourselves receive or purchase your goods, because it is written: “Do not defraud your brother in business” (1 Thess. IV); and, “With the measure with which you measure, it shall be measured back to you” (Luke VI); and, “You shall not have diverse weights, greater or smaller, but you shall have a just bushel and an equal sextarius” (Deut. XXV).

XVIII. We prohibit in every way those commercial dealings that are forbidden by divine and human laws and are now again practiced by certain wicked men on Sundays; and we decree, by canonical authority, that you must prohibit them with every effort. For it is improper that any Christian should conduct secular business or trade on the day on which the memory of the Lord’s resurrection and our redemption is renewed—a day he ought to devote entirely to divine praises, offices, and offerings for his own salvation, that of all who belong to him, and the stability of the whole Church.

XIX. Each priest must arrange the burial of the dead with ecclesiastical decency and piety, and must not demand gifts for burying the dead. Accordingly, blessed Gregory speaks as follows to those who presume such things (Letter to Januarius): “It is exceedingly grave and far removed from the office of a priest to seek a price for earth granted to corruption and to wish to make profit from another’s grief. This vice, after, by God’s authority, we had attained the honor of the episcopate of the Roman See, we resolved entirely to eradicate from our Church, and we do not permit the perverse custom to be practiced again in any way. If, however, the devout freely offer something to the church or to priests for their dead, we do not prohibit priests from accepting it.”

We teach through many authorities, and especially through that of blessed Gregory, bishop of the holy Roman See, that you must not bury anyone inside a church. For when his disciple Peter asked him whether it benefited souls in any way if the bodies of the dead were buried in churches, he answered in these words (Letter 55):

“When grave sins do not weigh them down, it benefits the dead if they are buried in churches in this respect: whenever their relatives come together in those sacred places, seeing the tombs of their own people, they remember them and pour out prayers to the Lord for them. But those whom grave sins weigh down are not placed in churches for release, but rather for a greater accumulation of condemnation. We shall show this more clearly,” he says, “if we briefly recount what happened in our own days.

“There was a man of venerable life, Felix, bishop of Porto, born and brought up in the Sabine territory. He testified that a certain consecrated woman had lived in that same place. She had bodily continence, but did not avoid boldness of tongue and foolish talk. After she died, she was buried in a church. That same night the church’s custodian saw in a revelation that she had been led before the sacred altar and was being cut in half; one part of her was consumed by fire, while the other part remained untouched. When he rose in the morning and told the brothers what he had seen, and wished to show the place where she had been consumed by fire, the burning of the flame appeared on the marble before the altar as though that woman’s body had actually been burned there.

“From this it is plainly understood that those whose sins have not been forgiven here cannot escape judgment by being assisted after death in sacred places. John also, a distinguished man who held the prefecture in this city, whose truthfulness and seriousness we know, testified to me that a Patrician named Valerian had died in a city called Brescia. The bishop of that city, having accepted payment, granted him a place in the church where he was to be buried. This Valerian had remained frivolous and morally slippery into extreme old age and had refused to put an end to his depravity.

“On the very night on which he was buried, blessed Faustinus the martyr, in whose church his body had been buried, appeared to the custodian and said: ‘Go and tell the bishop to throw out from here these stinking meats which he has placed here, because if he does not, he himself will die on the thirtieth day.’ The custodian was afraid to confess this vision to the bishop. When he was warned again, he avoided doing so. On the thirtieth day, however, the bishop of that city, having returned to bed healthy and unharmed after evening prayer, died a sudden and unexpected death.

“From this, Peter, conclude that those whom grave sins weigh down, if they cause themselves to be buried in a sacred place, must also be judged for their presumption, so that sacred places do not free them but rather their guilt of rashness accuses them.”

Strengthened by these authorities, we have judged that you must be earnestly admonished to guard against such presumption among yourselves, and that when people irrationally request such burials, you should take care rationally to refuse them after setting forth these authorities.

XX. We have also decreed that it is close to reason for priests in each deanery to meet together on an appointed day every month—that is, on the Kalends of each month. When they meet, they should not devote themselves to eating or drinking, but should discuss their ministry and religious conduct, as well as what occurs in their parishes; and they should consider together how they ought to pray for the king or the rulers of the Church, and for their own relatives, both living and dead.

XXI. Teach your parishioners also that, whenever they come together at church, they should strive to pray for themselves and for others with sighs and tears and withdraw from idle words. For when our Savior entered the temple and drove out those who were selling and buying in it, he immediately said: “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer’” (Matt. XXI). If any people there are at odds with one another, recall them to concord through pious admonition and priestly exhortation [Col. 0023B]. But if, after being admonished by you once and twice, they refuse to listen, let them be excommunicated from the Church according to the authority of the Council of Agde. For in that council, concerning those who do not return to peace because of hatred, it is written in chapter 31: “If they wickedly refuse to lay aside their enmities, let them be expelled from the assembly of the Church by the most just excommunication.” Likewise, in the Council of Carthage, chapter 93: “The offerings of brothers who are at odds with one another must be received neither in the sacristy nor in the treasury.”

XXII. Whenever a fast is imposed on you by our unworthiness or by our fellow ministers, ask the people to come to church; and, after the litany has been performed and Masses celebrated, [lacuna].

ANNO DOMINI DCCCCII. MANTIO, BISHOP OF CHÂLONS.

[Col. 0023]

## LETTER OF MANTIO TO FULCO, BISHOP OF RHEIMS

*(Province of Reims, vol. I.)*

[Col. 0023C] To the lord Father Fulco, venerable archbishop, and to all the bishops who are his suffragans, and to all their clergy—priests, deacons, and every order, both canons and monks—Mantio, humble bishop of Châlons: faithful service and devoted prayers.

We beg that your holiness may know that a certain priest named Angelricus, from the village of Wasnau, belonging to the church of Saint Lupus, came before us in the presence of our synod held at Châlons on the Nones of May. Convicted, he confessed with his own mouth that, together with his parishioners, he had betrothed, or contracted marriage with, a certain woman named Grimme, with the consent of her relatives [Note: [Col. 0023] This is the first one recorded who, wearing the priesthood, conceived the idea of entering into marriage]. As he was proceeding to take her as his wife, good, pious, and faithful men, together with others, resisted his most wicked attempt through God’s merciful regard [Col. 0023D].

Since we all grieved over this action for a long time, we agreed not to deliberate further about it before writing to your fatherhood through this same priest, asking to be instructed about what we ought to do and not to punish through correction the evil presumption which we seek to have made known through you. Therefore, we all entreat your holy fatherhood to receive in the Lord this same brother who bears the letter and, through him, instruct our ignorance by your desired letter. Carefully consider how this presumption may be expelled from the Church. It was thus agreed among us that he should remain separated from our fellowship until we are consoled by your reply. Farewell; we beg you to pray for us.

ANNO DOMINI DCCCCVI. MARTINIANUS, MONK

[Col. 0023]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(In Mabillon, Annales, vol. III, p. 324.)*

[Col. 0023D] At the beginning of the tenth century there flourished the monk Martinianus, whose writings—some of them, as I think, previously unknown—we found in the Resbach codex. In it are contained four books of his Exercises: two addressed to the monks of his time, one to clerics, and one likewise to laymen.

He was sent, for the sake of regular discipline, to a certain monastery. From there his abbot and priors ordered him to move to another monastery, which is said to have flourished in ancient times under earlier men with the greatest abundance—namely, in wealth and land, gold and silver, and every sort of innumerable ornament. That monastery was governed by a regular abbot, whom two hundred and sixty brothers obeyed there.

“There,” he says, “when I had arrived with other brothers more subtle and noble than I, having been sent to restore” *(sic; I read this nearly effaced word in this way)*, “I endured many adversities from envious and false brothers.” Consequently, compelled to withdraw from the place, he retreated into solitude. There he composed two books of monastic Exercises or exhortations, which he dedicated to the most reverend Father, lord J., in whose monastery he had stayed for some time—perhaps the abbot of the monastery of Resbach, where this codex, which I believe to be the only one, was found by us.

In the first book he attacks monks who love more expensive clothing, contrary to what Saint Benedict commands concerning the holy and humble garment which the holy Fathers instituted to signify humility, dishonoring it with dyes and shears. He then reproves them because prayer is entirely neglected among them, and because under the pretext of teaching they leave the cloister, aspiring to be teachers before they are perfect disciples. He also reproves them because they seek honors and dignities.

In the second book he teaches that the coenobitic life is to be preferred to the eremitical life; then he gives various admonitions to coenobites. Later he introduces certain brothers complaining about themselves in this way: “Why is observance of the rule imposed on us here more strictly than in other places? For in one monastery people live in one way, and in another they live in another way; and they are without murmuring and dissension, as Saint Benedict commands. These are superstitious practices which this impostor forces us to perform.”

To them he replies that he demands nothing more than what is read in the Gospel, in the Apostles, and in the Rule. He also teaches that silence must be maintained in the church, dormitory, refectory, and kitchen. “Therefore,” he says, “if one of us pollutes with idle talk those holy places perpetually dedicated to silence, or does anything contrary to the precepts of the Rule in any place whatsoever, he cannot be cleansed except through pardon and satisfaction.” For this reason, he says, a place for conversation was established among the monastery’s workrooms, where necessary speech might take place.

The third book of the Exercises, published by Martinianus against the transgression of clerics, is entitled as follows: “To my most noble and distinguished lords, namely, the foster-sons of Saint Martin: Brother Martinianus, least of all monks, in the pious Redeemer, [wishes you] a noble triumph over hidden enemies.”

First he reproves clerics because they wore weapons rather than clerical dress, because they lived with women, went hunting, and were merchants. Then he recalls them to their duty by reflection on death. Finally, he identifies three principal vices among them: pride, avarice, and lust. These are the very vices which the monk Abbo of Prüm, as we saw above, reproved in the people of his own age.

Martinianus’s fourth little book, addressed to laymen, aims to deter them from carnal pleasures, love of ruling, and vain hope. The period in which this author lived is inferred from the Resbach codex, written seven hundred years ago; from the scarcity of monasteries in which monastic discipline is said to have flourished at that time; from the custom of carrying weapons, which he reproves in clerics and which was customary toward the end of the ninth century; and finally from the fact that the foster-sons of Martinianus—that is, the canons of Saint Martin at Tours, to whom he dedicates the second book concerning clerics—had already discarded the cowl.

It is therefore highly probable that Martinianus wrote at the beginning of the tenth century, and indeed before the rise of the Cluniac congregation, through which regular discipline flourished again in many monasteries during that century. Perhaps the monastery to which he was sent for restoration was the Maius Monasterium, once highly celebrated, which in about the tenth century had been reduced almost to a wilderness and to a few clerics.

[Col. 0025]

## PROLOGUE OF MARTINIANUS TO THE MORAL BOOKS

*(In Mabillon, Annales, vol. III, Appendix.)*

[Col. 0025C] To the most reverend Father, lord J. . . .: Brother Martinianus, lowest of all monks in Christ Jesus, [sends] the gift of happy perseverance and the prize of eternal reward.

After my unhappy and foolish mind had separated me bodily from you, my Father, though it could not separate me in thought, I came to your monastery and resolved, according to the purpose of the monastic order, to live and serve there. After a short interval, however, my abbot and priors discussed my moving to another monastery. This monastery is said to have flourished in ancient times under earlier men with the greatest abundance—namely, in wealth and land, gold and silver, and every sort of innumerable ornament. It was governed by a regular abbot, whom two hundred and sixty brothers obeyed there.

When I had arrived there with other brothers far more subtle and noble than I, I endured many adversities from envious and false brothers. Nor was this without reason. For that cunning serpent who, through the taste of the forbidden fruit, expelled the first man from paradise was shamefully and miserably mocking me through his assaults, so that I often walked about as though drunk and came to delight in disdaining holy things and thinking slippery thoughts.

At last, by God’s gift, when I returned to myself, I exclaimed: “Let God arise and let his enemies be scattered” (Ps. LXVII), and so forth. Then, groaning, I said: “If the Lord had not helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell” (Ps. XCIII). No one saw this battle except God, my deliverer. If the envious men who thought something of me and insisted that I was good for nothing had seen it, what do you think they would have done against me? Certainly, the mere fact that sin reigned in me would have been enough for them to tempt and disturb me. But the merciful God did not permit this.

Finally, whenever, by God’s generosity, that temptation disappeared, I immediately felt the devil withdraw and my God draw near. Then, having invoked Christ’s aid, I would take a tablet and a stylus and try, poor as I was, to write something against that temptation, so that the writing itself, seen and read frequently, might offer me assistance, however small and unpolished it was [Col. 0027A].

Thus, my Father, I began and completed this little work. From you I desire to receive it; I long for it to be read by you; I ask that it be corrected by you; and I request that it be strengthened by you, so that if someone like me should find it after my death and prefer to read it and rise from it to something better, his progress may benefit me. Thus, though I am dead, let even my tiny work live, and, while I am silent, may my most impoverished speech cry out in the service of the Creator.

For the rest, I ask that attention not be paid to the wretched appearance of the tree, but to the honey-sweet taste of the fruit of the best kind—namely, that fruit through which the force of death introduced by tasting the forbidden tree is emptied.

[Col. 0028A] Here ends the prologue.

One day, then, when I had left the chapter meeting exceedingly distressed by the quarrelsome, boastful, or worldly speech of certain brothers, it occurred to me that, setting aside those exercises, I should go to the estates for the sake of quiet. When I had done this and was sitting more peacefully, I took tablets and a stylus and began to dictate in this manner:

“I know, and I know truly, that what my brothers accuse me of is true, though they are also deceiving themselves: the word that I report to their ears from the divine readings I do not utter sweetly or gently, but harshly. I too judge that this is so—but why? Because the divine word cannot enter a malicious soul, that is, a secular mind, and so forth. I am not speaking of everyone, and so forth.”

ANNO DOMINI DCCCCV. POPE JOHN IX

[Col. 0027]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(In Mansi, General Councils, vol. XVIII.)*

[Col. 0027B] John IX, a Tiburtine by nationality, born of a father named Rampoaldus, a monk by profession and a deacon by order, became pope after the death of Theodore in the year of our Lord 901 [Note: [Col. 0027B] More correctly, 808. See Pagi on this year], under the emperor Louis IV.

When Berengar, duke of Friuli, had deprived the captured emperor both of his eyesight and of his imperial power, and, having marched to Rome with an armed army, had violently extorted the imperial crown from this pope and tyrannically claimed the name of emperor for himself, John, after Berengar’s death, summoned Lambert, son of Guido, to Rome. Lambert had been invested with the imperial crown by Pope Formosus eleven years earlier. There John ordered, by synodal judgment, that the coronations of Berengar and Arnulf be declared null and illegitimate, since they had been wholly extorted by force and therefore ought to be annulled; but that Lambert’s coronation, in whose favor the free votes of Pope Formosus and his successors had agreed, should be regarded as legitimate and valid [Col. 0028B].

On this occasion the princes of Italy, abandoning Berengar, recognized Lambert as king and emperor. Since many Romans favored Berengar and adhered to him against Lambert, Pope John, judging himself insufficiently safe if he remained in Rome, departed for Ravenna. There he invalidated through a synod the acts of Stephen against Formosus. In these most turbulent times, like another Jeremiah sent by God, he uprooted, scattered, and destroyed all the things that his predecessor Stephen had wrongly planted and most wickedly built.

He sat for three years and two days [al., five]; he died in the year of our Lord 905. He was buried at Saint Peter’s, before the doors and in front of the gate called Guidonea. On his tomb was carved an epitaph, which Baronius reproduces under the year 905.

[Col. 0027]

## LETTERS OF POPE JOHN IX

*(Mansi, same work.)*

### FIRST LETTER. TO HERIVEUS, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS

Reply of Lord Pope John to the inquiries of Heriveus, archbishop of Rheims, concerning the Northmen recently converted to the faith, some of whom had been baptized and rebaptized and had lived as pagans after baptism: how they should be advised; at the end, absolution is granted to him and his people.

[Col. 0027C]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend brother Heriveus, archbishop of the Rhemans.

[Col. 0028C] We most willingly receive and most carefully consider the honey-sweet letters of your fraternity and your revered holiness; we have been exceedingly sorrowful and also exceedingly joyful. We grieve over the many calamities, pressures, and distresses occurring in your regions, not only among pagans but also among Christians, as the testimony of your letters informs us. We rejoice, however, over the very people of the Northmen, who, converted to the faith by the inspiration of divine mercy, once delighted in raging with human blood but now, through your exhortations and with the Lord’s cooperation, rejoice that they have been redeemed and given to drink by the ambrosial blood of Christ [Col. 0029A].

Therefore, we offer abundant thanks to him from whom every good thing proceeds, humbly beseeching him to confirm them in the solidity of the true faith, make them recognize the glory of the eternal Trinity, and lead them into the indescribable joy of his vision.

As for what your fraternity has made known to us concerning them—what should be done because they had been baptized and rebaptized, had lived as pagans after baptism, killed Christians in the manner of pagans, slaughtered priests, and, while sacrificing to idols, had eaten food offered to idols—indeed [al., and indeed. HARD.], if they were not beginners in the faith, they would be subjected to canonical judgments [Col. 0029B]. Since they are inexperienced in the faith, however, we entrust them to your judgment and your discipline for examination. You, who have that people living near your borders, are better able than others to observe carefully and to understand all their customs, actions, and manner of life.

Your diligence knows well what the sacred canons decree: that one must deal more gently with them, lest perhaps, bearing burdens unfamiliar to them, they should—God forbid—find them unbearable and, through the ambush of the ancient adversary, fall back into the old way of life and the former self they cast off. If any among them are found who prefer to discipline themselves through penance according to canonical institutions and to expiate such great crimes with worthy lamentation, do not refuse to judge them canonically [Col. 0029C]. In all things, however, remain watchful over them, so that, coming before the tribunal of the eternal Judge with abundant fruit of souls, you may deserve to attain eternal joys with blessed Remigius.

As for the gift which your holiness deigned to send us, we have received it with the same love with which it was sent by you. May divine majesty grant that you and all subject to you live in this world in such a way that, through the intercession of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he may loosen the bonds of all your sins and lead you without offense to the glory of the heavenly kingdom. We wish your holiness good health and ask that you intercede for us with pious supplications before the most merciful Lord.

### SECOND LETTER. TO STYLLIANUS, BISHOP OF NEOCaesarea

He denies him the permission he had requested to communicate with those whom Photius had ordained.

[Col. 0029D]

We give your love, honored brother, the thanks that are due because you never wished to depart from your mother, the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church. For neither tortures, nor exiles, nor the frauds of adulterous men could tear you away from your mother. I nevertheless hope that the favor of your prayers will soften the hardness of the hearts of those who ought to be saved, and that the desired peace will return. This appears likely from clear indications, and the schism of almost forty years will return to its former health.

Whatever your mother rejected, you too have rejected until now; and whatever she approved, you too have approved. Therefore, we wish that even now, according to the same rule, the decrees of the most holy pontiffs, our predecessors, should remain unshaken. Accordingly, Ignatius, Photius, Stephen, and Antonius—as the most holy Pope Nicholas, John, Stephen VI, and the whole Roman Church have maintained until now—we too receive and maintain in the same order; and we urge you to extend your hand in the same agreement to those who remain from their order. We grant them unity of peace and communion, provided that they themselves observe the rules in the same manner. As for the document in your own hand which you gave us, although we have searched for it extensively, we have been entirely unable to find it.

### THIRD LETTER. TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF LANGRES

He restores Bishop Argrinus to them.

[Col. 0030B]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of the holy Church of Langres, beloved sons.

We have received from the Lord, founder of this holy see and of the Apostolic Church, and from blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, such great confidence that we labor with tireless devotion for the Church redeemed by the blood of Christ in its universality, and hasten to the aid of all who serve the Lord; that by apostolic authority we offer assistance to all who live piously; and that, with the Lord’s help, we do not delay correcting and amending whatever is harmful. For this purpose divine providence has established distinct grades and different orders, [Col. 0030C] so that, while those of lower rank show reverence to their superiors, and those of higher rank extend love and assistance to their inferiors, one bond of concord may arise from their diversity, and the administration of the duties of each may be properly conducted.

We have gladly received the letters of your affection, which you sent to the see of blessed Peter the apostle on behalf of your affair not once only, but also a second and a third time, together with the documents of our beloved son, King Berengar. But we have been greatly saddened by the afflictions and troubles which, as you lamentably complained, you have endured for so long—namely, that your Church, worn down by many calamities, has been deprived of all pastoral consolation ever since the venerable Bishop Argrin was removed from it through the deceit of certain persons. You testify that you all unanimously elected, received, and acclaimed him, and that after him you voluntarily received no other bishop, as is more fully contained in your written protest.

Long ago we had learned this very thing through Count Anscharius, our beloved son, who humbly confessed that he had gravely erred in this matter. Therefore, since we bear the care and solicitude of all the Churches of God, and wish and are bound to preserve inviolably for every Church its unimpaired right and canonical authority, we will by no means permit you to suffer such things any longer. Rather, sympathizing with your fraternity and approving your tearful complaint, by truthful assertions, [Col. 0031A] together with the college of our brother bishops and the ministry of the remaining orders, we canonically restore to you our aforementioned brother, the venerable Bishop Argrin, and authorize him to undertake the reform of his Church—not condemning the sentence of our predecessor Pope Stephen, but canonically changing it for the better on grounds of usefulness and necessity, just as we readily know that our predecessors acted in many matters.

For this reason we admonish you, exhort you by this letter of our pontificate, and command you by the authority of God and our own, that you receive without any hesitation the same Bishop Argrin, whom we have restored to your unanimity as you requested, with kindly love and united devotion; and that, obedient to him in all things, you honor and cherish him as the pious shepherd of your souls, [Col. 0031B] observing in every respect his canonical commands. But if any one of you should presume to act against this apostolic judgment and decree of ours, or to minister in his Church of Langres without the consent of Bishop Argrin himself, and should refuse to receive him according to our decree, let him know that by our authority he is excommunicated and condemned. Farewell.

Written by the hand of Samuel, notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, in the second indiction.

## LETTER IV. TO CHARLES THE SIMPLE, KING OF THE FRANKS

He urges him to support the restoration of Argrin, bishop of Langres.

[Col. 0031C]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son Charles, glorious king.

Because we know from the report of many that, following the custom of your predecessors as kings, you act manfully for the defense and welfare of the holy Church of God against the fury of wicked men and even of pagans, we rejoice exceedingly and reverently embrace your sonship in Christ. We exhort you as a father to strive always to advance toward better things, to love peace, justice, and truth, and in no way to deviate from the straight path, so that you may obtain the blessing of our most merciful Lord Jesus Christ, and also of Peter, prince and keeper of the keys of his apostles, for whose love you strive to do such things. [Col. 0031D]

Finally, we wish your sonship to know that the tearful groaning and lament of the Church of Langres has reached the ears of our clemency not once only, but also a second and a third time, concerning the removal of its shepherd, Bishop Argrin. They testify that they all unanimously elected, sought, and acclaimed him, but that he was separated from them through the deceit of certain persons. As a result, the Church itself has been deprived of pastoral consolation and is constantly harassed by various disturbances and troubles, to such an extent that [Col. 0032A] it now appears almost reduced to nothing.

After weighing this matter carefully with the college of our venerable bishops, investigating the truth of what occurred, and mercifully coming to the aid of their misfortune, we canonically decreed that his Church should be restored to him by our authority, changing the sentence of our predecessor Pope Stephen for the better on grounds of necessity and usefulness, just as we readily know that our predecessors acted in many matters.

Therefore we have foreseen this and admonish your glory and piety: since we have canonically restored him to his aforesaid Church of Langres, always extend to him the hand of assistance, consent to our decree, and wherever appropriate be his helper and defender for love of almighty God, in reverence for the blessed apostles, [Col. 0032B] and in virtue of our apostolic fatherhood. Thus, under your royal protection, he may be able to govern that Church peacefully and worthily, so that he may preside over and benefit those whom he ought to lead. Farewell.

Written by the hand of Samuel, notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Ides of May, in the second indiction.

## LETTER V. OF MATTO, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, AND HIS SUFFRAGANS, TO POPE JOHN IX

Concerning the death of [Note: [Col. 0031D] Arnulf the emperor, whose death is announced here: he died on 20 November in the year 899, during the pontificate of Stephen VI. Nevertheless, this letter was written not to him but to his successor John, as is readily understood from the complaint concerning the archbishopric of the Moravians, [Col. 0032D] which the following letter declares to have been established by John. Why these bishops write so late, they explain in the letter itself. GABRIEL COSSART.] Emperor Arnulf; concerning his seven-year-old son Louis, hailed as king of Germany; concerning an archbishopric established among the Moravians.

To the lord pope of the holy, apostolic, and universal Roman Church, Hatto, unworthy prelate of the Church of Mainz, together with all the suffragans associated with our lowliness, offers the service of due prayer [Col. 0032C] and faithful obedience.

Let your holy sublimity know, then, that no fellowship of brothers subject to the authority of the holy Roman Church appears more faithful, devoted, and submissive than we do, for we submit with the full intention of our minds to your lordship and to the head of all the Churches. We rejoice greatly in the Lord and in the gift of his grace, because through your holiness and wisdom the see of that Church is being magnificently and most extensively enlarged in divine religion. For this we devote ourselves most earnestly to prayer, beseeching divine clemency to grant that you may always ascend to higher things and pursue and accomplish better things from day to day.

Furthermore, we make known to your clemency that our elder, Emperor Arnulf, has departed from the exile of this life. But so long as we remain in this world, we are carried along amid uncertainties, not knowing where the souls of certain people receive their dwelling after this light. Therefore, as though prostrate at your feet, we earnestly beg you to release his soul from the bonds of sins by the power of your authority, because whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven (Matthew 16).

After losing such a lord, ruler, and governor, the ship of the Church in our regions began to waver. For a short time it remained uncertain whom it should choose as king; [Col. 0033A] and because there was great fear that the united kingdom might be divided into parts, it came about, as we believe, through divine inspiration that the son of our elder, although still very young, was raised to the kingship by the common decision of the princes and the consent of the entire people. Since the kings of the Franks had always proceeded from one lineage, we preferred to preserve the ancient custom rather than introduce a new institution.

But we do not doubt that your prudence understands why this was done without your command and permission. Clearly, no other reason is evident except that, because pagans dwell between us and you, our journey to our holy mother, the Roman see, was obstructed, so that messengers could not be sent from our lowliness to your dignity. But since at last an opportunity and time have come [Col. 0033B] when our letter could be presented to your sight, we ask that our common decision be strengthened by your lordship’s blessing.

Moreover, we inform your piety that our brothers and fellow bishops of Bavaria, complaining among us and drawing deep sighs, lamented that the Moravian peoples, rebels against the power of the Franks, boast that they have separated themselves from their fellowship and glory in having been elevated by your grant to a metropolitan of their own, although no metropolitan see had ever existed among them, but they had always belonged to their province and diocese.

They also complained to us that, through the machinations of certain persons, they had been marked by great infamy in your sight—namely, that they had entered into a treaty and peace with the pagans, and that those pagans had undertaken so many wicked and unlawful acts at their counsel. When the Bavarian bishops sought our advice concerning all these matters, we replied that it was just always to cleave to the assistance of one’s brothers, because the Prophet says: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together” (Psalm 132 [Vulgate 131]). Those who withdraw themselves from the support of their brothers, or prepare ambushes for their brothers, do not dwell together.

Sympathizing with their sorrow, we did not wish to offer them counsel concerning such accusations before coming by our letter to seek your judgment. We know that the carnal always persecute the spiritual, and that the malicious weaken and tear apart the benevolent. Therefore all who persecute the priests of the Lord, secretly or openly, must take the greatest care lest what the Prophet said apply to them: “They devised wickedness in their heart; all day long they prepared battles. They sharpened their tongues like a serpent; the venom of asps is under their lips” (Psalm 140 [Vulgate 139]). And shortly afterward: “Coals shall fall upon them; you will cast them into the fire” (ibid.). And again: “A man of many words shall not prosper on earth; evil shall hunt the unjust man to destruction” (ibid.).

And through Jeremiah the Lord says: “All are judged in blood; each one oppresses his neighbor. All prepare their hands for evil.” For outsiders ought not to become either the accusers or the judges of bishops. Hence it is written concerning Lot: “You have come as a stranger; will you also act as a judge?” (Genesis 19.) [Col. 0034A] Let no servant or freedman be an accuser of bishops; let every suspect or infamous person be rejected, and let all laymen be excluded.

These brothers and fellow bishops of ours in Bavaria, true worshipers of God and good shepherds, guard the flock entrusted to them with sleepless vigilance, lest the fury of wolves seize any little sheep of the holy flock as its prey. They stand as a wall before the house of Israel, lest any hostile force destroy the stronghold of the Church. Whoever disturbs such men and attacks them through his wickedness will not escape punishment in the future, even if he escapes it in the present, because it is written: “Whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye” (Zechariah 2 [Vulgate 3]).

We have sent all these things to you because you are the head of the whole holy Church spread throughout the world, and the consolation of the sorrowful—whatever sad things have befallen your members—[Col. 0034B] since the most holy shepherds of Christ mentioned above, deviating in no respect from the Catholic faith but adorning it with holy works and ecclesiastical duties, complained to us and asked that we make their situation known to you. They also promised that, if their lives were spared, they would make the same things known to you personally.

Therefore we ask that your consolation restore their sorrow to joy, and that such members may always rejoice in cleaving to their supreme Head, which is yourself. But those Moravians, as has been reported to our ears, take as an occasion for their pride the claim that they receive a metropolitan by your grant, and, living apart, reject the fellowship of the other bishops. If they continue to swell with this confidence, they will, as many believe, advance even to the shedding of blood. As far as our authority extends, we admonish you that, before this occurs, your authority should correct them and bring them down to the way of humility, so that at last they may recognize whose dominion they ought to obey.

We acknowledge that we are debtors to inform you if anything should escape from the holy mother, the Roman Church, so that your power may bring it back to the line of rectitude. But if your admonition does not correct them, whether they wish it or not, they will submit their necks to the princes of the Franks; and we believe that this may then occur successfully without bloodshed or mutual slaughter on either side.
