Again and again we repeat to the ears of your dignity that the Bavarian bishops and laymen alike are proved inferior to no people in Christian religion, nor have the Franks ever accomplished anything worthy of mention or renown, either in ecclesiastical affairs or in military matters, without their aid. Nor have those men accomplished anything without these.

[Note: [Col. 0033D] Cordesius published this letter together with the works of Hincmar, but wrongly attributed it to John VIII. For it is clear that it was sent to John IX from the age of the bishops who wrote it, as may be learned from Hundius’s *Metropolis Salisburgensis*, vol. I. Gevoldus had previously published this letter, and another which immediately precedes it, in an appendix to the *Chronicle of Reichersberg*. GABRIEL COSSART.]

## LETTER VI. OF THEOTMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF JUVAVUM, AND OTHER BISHOPS, TO JOHN IX

They complain that one archbishop and three bishops have been created in the lands of the Slavs, formerly subject to the bishop of Passau.

To the supreme pontiff and universal pope—not of one city but of the whole world—the lord John, illustrious governor of the Roman see: the most humble sons of your fatherhood, Theotmar, archbishop of the Church of Juvavum; Waldo of Freising; Erchenbald of Eichstätt; Zacharias of Säben; Tutto of Regensburg; and Richarius, bishop of the Church of Passau. Also, the entire Christian clergy and people throughout Noricum, which is also called Bavaria, wish you prosperous advancement in our Savior, an increase of Catholic peace, and an eternal kingdom.

We are fully instructed by the decrees of your predecessors and the ordinances of the Catholic Fathers that, in all matters obstructing or opposing our priestly ministry, we are to appeal to the Roman pontiff, so that whatever concerns the unity of concord and the preservation of discipline may not be violated by any disagreement, but may be determined by him with supreme foresight. For we by no means believe [Col. 0035B] that anything perverse has flowed from that holy and apostolic see, which is the mother of our priestly dignity and the source of the Christian religion, as we are compelled to hear every day; rather, we believe that ecclesiastical teaching and authoritative reason have flowed from it.

But, as they themselves have proclaimed, three bishops came from your side—namely, John the archbishop, and the bishops Benedict and Daniel—into the land of the Slavs, who are called Moravians. This land had been subjected to our kings, our people, and also to us together with its inhabitants, both in the worship of the Christian religion and in the payment of secular tribute, because there they had first been instructed and had been made Christians from pagans.

Therefore the bishop of the city of Passau, in whose diocese those peoples had been from the beginning of their Christianity, entered there whenever he wished and ought to do so, without anyone opposing him. He held a synodal assembly with his own people and with those whom he found there, carried out with authority everything that had to be done, and no one resisted him to his face.

Our counts who bordered that land likewise continued to hold secular courts there, corrected what needed correction, collected tribute, and met no resistance—until the devil stirred their hearts. Then they began to abhor Christianity, reject every form of justice, challenge us to war, and resist us with extreme violence, to such a degree that the bishop and preachers no longer had access to that land, while the inhabitants did whatever they wished according to their own desire.

Now, what seems grievous and incredible to us, they boast, to increase the injury, that they accomplished this by the greatness of their money—things such as we have never heard came from that apostolic [Col. 0035D] see, nor have the decrees of the canons sanctioned, so that one Church should suffer so great a schism. For one bishopric has been divided into five.

The bishops mentioned above entered, as they themselves said, in your name, and established within one and the same bishopric one archbishop—if, indeed, an archbishopric [alternate reading: an archbishop. HARD.] can exist within another bishop’s bishopric—and three suffragan bishops, without the knowledge of the archbishop and without the consent of the bishop in whose diocese they had been.

Yet the Council of Africa, chapter 20, decreed that the communities held by bishops within their dioceses, which had never had bishops, should receive their own pastors—or [that is, according to another reading, “and”] bishops—only with the consent of the bishop by whom they were held. Likewise, in the same council, chapter 65, it was decreed that communities which had never had their own bishops should receive none except by the decision of the full council of each province, with the consent of the primate and of the bishop to whose diocese that community belonged.

In the decrees of Pope Leo, chapter 15, it is written: “No principle permits those to be regarded as bishops who are not consecrated by the provincial bishops with the judgment of the metropolitan.” Likewise, chapter 49: “If pastoral rank and the government of a Church are given to persons who are unworthy and far below priestly merit, this is not to provide for peoples but to harm them; it is not to furnish governance but to increase danger.” And in the same chapter, shortly afterward: “It is difficult for things to reach a good outcome when they have been begun with a bad beginning.”

And in the decree of Pope Celestine, your predecessor, chapter 17, it is stated that no place is to be granted to any priest to the injury of another.

Your predecessor, at the request of Duke Zuentibald, consecrated Withing as bishop. He did not send him to that ancient bishopric of Passau, but to a certain newly converted people whom the duke had subdued by war and made Christian from pagans.

When, however, those Slavs were granted a place of intimacy with your legates, they accused and defamed us in many matters and pressed us with lying words, because no one was answering them truthfully. They said that we had been at odds and in conflict both with the Franks and with the Alemanni; yet the falsity of this is proved by the fact that they are our very good friends and cooperate with us affectionately. They also accused us of being at odds with themselves.

We admit that this is so—not because our fault required it, but because of their insolence. For when Christianity began to become contemptible to them, and they further refused to pay the tribute owed to our elder kings and princes, resisted by war, and began to harass our people, sedition arose among them. Since they defended themselves against them by arms and brought them into servitude, they therefore ought, and still ought, by right to have them as tributaries; and whether they wish it or not, they will be subjected to our kingdom.

[Col. 0036D] Therefore you must watch from on high and maintain moderation above all, lest the worse party be strengthened and the better weakened. For the ancestors of our most serene elder, namely Emperor Louis, and the kings, came from the most Christian people of the Franks. But the Moravian Slavs came from pagans and heathens. The former exalted the Roman commonwealth by imperial power; the latter condemned it. The former strengthened the Christian kingdom; the latter weakened it. The former appeared renowned throughout the world; the latter remained hidden in retreats and cities. By the counsel of the former the apostolic see flourished; through the persecution of the latter Christianity suffered.

In all these matters our young king, inferior to none of his predecessors, wishes to be the strongest helper of the holy Roman Church and of you, the supreme pontiff, together with all the princes of his kingdom, according to the strength granted him by God. For he wills and works that the whole kingdom divinely entrusted to him be devoted to the service of God and to his own assistance. Hence he flourishes in peace, rejoices in concord, and is glad to recognize that he belongs to your fatherhood, as his fathers did.

What those Slavs accused us of—namely, that we had violated the Catholic faith with the Hungarians, made treaties and peace through a dog, or a wolf, and other most abominable pagan objects, and given money so that they might cross into Italy—if the matter were argued before you in God’s presence, he who knows all things before they occur, their falsehood would be exposed and our innocence proved.

For since the Hungarians were always threatening our Christians who lived far from us and were afflicting them with excessive persecution, we gave them no treasure of precious money, but only our linen garments, so that we might soften their ferocity to some extent and obtain relief from their persecution.

They interpreted such acts, as we have described, according to the malice of their hearts and incited your bishops [manuscript reading: “our bishops”] against us, to such a degree that, in a letter sent to us as though from the apostolic see, they reproached us for all these things, inflicted various injuries upon us, and, among other accusations, declared us worthy of being struck by the divine sword.

Indeed, what a certain wise man said is fulfilled in us: “The just man bore the crime of the wicked.” For they themselves have committed for many years the crime which they once falsely attributed to us. They took a considerable number of the Hungarians into their service, completely shaved the heads of their pseudo-Christians according to their custom, and sent them against us Christians. They themselves then followed, taking some captive, killing others, destroying others through the bestial hunger and thirst of prisons, consigning countless others to exile, reducing noble men and honorable women to servitude, burning the churches of God, and destroying all the buildings.

Thus, in our entire great province of Pannonia, scarcely a single church is to be seen, as the bishops sent by you, if they are willing to admit it, can recount. They passed many days and saw the whole land laid waste. [Col. 0037D–0038A]

When we learned that the Hungarians had entered Italy, we greatly desired, with God as our witness, to make peace with those same Slavs. For the sake of almighty God we promised to forgive completely all the evils committed against us and our people, and to restore everything that it was established that our people possessed from them, provided that they would make us secure from them and grant us enough time to enter Lombardy, defend the property of Saint Peter, and, with divine assistance, redeem the Christian people.

Yet we could not obtain even this from them—that after so many crimes they should receive benefits. They are false accusers who have always been persecutors of Christians. If anyone in the whole world attempts to prove that we have wandered in another direction or resisted justice, let him come in person; then you will find that we have exposed his deception and that we are utterly pure in this matter.

Therefore, as we admonish you all and each of you, we ask that you in no way believe anyone who reports any suspicion against us falsely, before circumstances require that a messenger sent from your eminence to us, or one dispatched from our lowliness to you, should appear for this purpose.

A common groaning and universal sorrow oppress all whom Germany and the whole of Noricum contain, because the unity of the Church is divided by a fissure. For, as we have stated above, one bishopric has been divided into five. Therefore, if anything the fraud of the wicked [alternate reading: wickedness of the. HARD.] Slavs has brought about through cunning, let justice reverse it.

And you, clothed with strength from on high and armed with apostolic power, apply to them the words of the prophet: “Bind up what is broken; strengthen what is weak; bring back what is cast away,” so that thereafter the people may rejoice in the integrity of the faith and the holy Church may rejoice in tranquil devotion.

Theotmar, unworthy archbishop and most zealous administrator of apostolic affairs.

The money owed to your jurisdiction I was unable to send either through myself or through others because of the hostile violence of the pagans. But since Italy has been liberated by the grace of God, I will send it to you as soon as I can. Our humility asks that your sublimity deign to answer each of the matters sent in a letter.

Gracious father of the world, worthy of Peter’s name,

May you follow in virtue the name that you bear,

And may you be a true and mighty protector of your servants,

Commending them to the Lord who presides over the high heavens.

[Col. 0038D]

## CANON OF POPE JOHN IX ON THE ELECTION OF THE POPE

(According to Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*)

[Col. 0037D] Because the holy Roman Church, over which by God’s authority we preside, suffers very many acts of violence when a pontiff dies—because the consecration of the pontiff takes place without the emperor’s knowledge and without the presence of his legates, and because the envoys whom the emperor has sent according to canonical rite and custom are not present to prevent violence and scandals from occurring at his consecration—we wish this practice henceforth to be abolished.

The pontiff to be appointed shall be elected by the assembled bishops and the entire clergy, with the senate and people requesting the man who is to be ordained. Thus, after being solemnly elected by all in the sight of everyone, he shall be consecrated in the presence of the imperial legates. No one shall dare, under penalty of danger, to extort from him by any novel invention an oath or any promises except those required by ancient custom, lest the Church be scandalized or the honor of the emperor diminished.

## ADDRESS OF POPE JOHN IX AT THE COUNCIL OF RAVENNA

(According to Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XVIII)

[Col. 0039B] Address of the pontiff.

Since, by the inspiration of divine mercy, your fraternity has joined with us, so that, by the will of the Holy Spirit, who is never absent from his faithful, we may, with the common counsel of all of you, dearest brothers, together with our spiritual son, the most glorious Emperor Lambert, and your holy college, take forethought for those things necessary to the holy Church of God, and strive with the canonical hoe to uproot from the field of the holy Church whatever was attempting to sprout as a harmful shoot, let the matters noted under separate headings be read in the presence of all, if they please everyone; let them be examined; and, once examined, let them be confirmed by the hands of all for future memory, so that no one may ever violate them without danger to his position, but so that they may remain ratified and firm forever [Col. 0040B] for the order and defense of the holy Church of God, and for the salvation of all the faithful, by God’s mercy.

### Response

We return immense praises to God our Savior, who placed you over his Church at such an opportune time that you strive to uproot all the weeds from it, as is openly demonstrated to all nations by the clear evidence of this holy synod. If it pleases your piety, let the chapters also be read which have been written for the general security, strength, and defense of all, so that through them we may all be taught what we ought to observe and what we ought to avoid, lest we be found in any respect to have deviated—God forbid—from the rules of the holy Fathers.

## In the Year of the Lord 905. Pope Benedict IV

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(According to Mansi, *The Most Extensive Collection of Councils*)

[Col. 0039C] Benedict IV, a Roman by nationality, was appointed after a one-day interregnum in succession to John IX in the year of Christ 905, during the reign of Emperor Lambert. Most generous toward the poor, widows, and orphans, he shone among the pontiffs of those times like a brilliant star. In the third year of his pontificate, which was the year of Christ 907, he departed this life and was buried at Saint Peter’s near the entrance leading to Saint Gregory. There his tomb was also adorned with an epitaph, which Baronius transcribed from Manlius at the place mentioned above.

## LETTERS OF POPE BENEDICT IV

### LETTER I. TO THE BISHOPS, PRINCES, ETC. OF GAUL

He restored Argrin, bishop of Langres, to all the rights of his Church.

(From Mansi’s *Councils*)

[Col. 0039D]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend [Col. 0040D] and most holy brothers, the archbishops and bishops of Gaul, or to the most glorious kings, dukes, and counts, sons and faithful members of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church.

How great is the grace of piety, and how greatly the holy mother Roman [Col. 0041A] Church excels and shines forth among all who dwell in the unity of faith through the sublimity of her compassion and condescension, instructed as she is by apostolic exhortations, is clearly evident, since all mercy shines forth from God, just as she has drawn it from the drinking of the most sacred fountain. Therefore we wish it to be known to all who abide in the bosom of holy conduct that envoys of our venerable fellow bishop Argrinus approached our apostolic office, humbly entreating us to apply, according to the practice of our predecessors, the balance of justice and the scales of equity, both for the love of God and for reverence toward blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to attend to the order of his election and the decree drawn up by the people and clergy of the Church of Langres, which they held before them. This we did, taking care to preserve in every respect what was to be preserved, [Col. 0041B] namely, how, after the departure of Gerlo, formerly bishop, the aforementioned Church of Langres unanimously desired, concordantly elected, and acclaimed him by clergy and people; how he was canonically consecrated by his own metropolitan, Aurelianus, together with his suffragans, and by Bernuinus, archbishop of Vienne; and how he was enthroned in the see of Langres by common vote and desire; and how for the space of two years and three months he governed that same Church with pastoral direction, as best he could. But afterward, through the insolence and subterfuge of certain men, he was separated from his own Church during the reign of the emperor Wido, who at that time ruled the Romans.

After some years had elapsed, he frequently visited this holy Roman Church because of his misfortune, always tearfully begging that she might deign to open to him the bosom of her mercy. He came before our predecessor Pope John, of pious memory, accompanied by the tearful complaints of his Church, whose members mourned his absence both by word and letter: after his departure they had been worn down by various and excessive hardships and deprived of all pastoral consolation, so that neither chrism had been prepared nor infants confirmed in that Church of Langres, and no episcopal ministry had been properly performed. Therefore that most holy Pope John, kindly receiving his complaint concerning his Church, carefully investigated the matter with his college of bishops and the attendance of the remaining orders, and canonically determined that, by apostolic authority, his Church should be restored to him, as is more fully recorded in the archive of the holy Roman Church.

We, having heard these things and carefully weighed them, and desiring in every respect to preserve the decrees of our predecessor Pope John, since this account of the matter, being unexamined and requiring an irrevocable determination, could not attain its consummation without the counsel of the reverend bishops, convened a holy synod in the Lateran palace. Having thoroughly established that all these things were true, with the counsel and exhortation of the reverend fathers assisting us, we granted him his ecclesiastical rights: namely, since he had been unjustly deprived of his Church, that it should also be restored to him by just governance; and, solemnly fortified by our apostolic privilege, that he should thereafter canonically hold the Church of Langres without anyone’s opposition, govern it pastorally, and dispose of it according to God’s ordering. We do not thereby condemn the judgment of our predecessor Pope Stephen, but canonically change it for the better on grounds of necessity and utility, just as it is evident that our predecessors acted in many cases.

For this reason we ordered a privilege of our authority to be issued to him, in which we granted him the use of the pallium on the consecrated days appointed for the solemn celebration of Mass, which he had formerly received from our most holy predecessor, Pope Formosus. Therefore, by the power of the Holy Spirit and by our apostolic authority, we command that no royal power, and no person of any status or order, [Col. 0042B] sex, or condition, dare rise against this apostolic privilege of ours or in any way attempt to oppose our commands. Rather, let it be permitted to him, with the Lord’s help, to govern his Church in peace, so that he may be able to benefit those over whom he ought to preside.

But if anyone should prove to be a rash transgressor of this privilege of ours, fail to observe it in every respect, invade anything belonging to the aforesaid Church of Langres that it has justly acquired, or attempt to diminish it, let him know that he is excluded from the life-giving body and blood of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, separated from the fellowship of the Christian faithful, and, unless corrected, makes satisfaction, condemned to perpetual anathema. Farewell.

Written by the hand of Sergius, scriniary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of August, in the third indiction. [Col. 0042C] Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, by the hand of Leo, primicerius by the mercy of God of the apostolic holy see, in the first year of the lordship of Pope Benedict. In the eleventh year after the death of the emperor Landebertus Augustus, in the third indiction.

## LETTER II. TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF LANGRES

*(In the same source.)*

[Col. 0042C] BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of the holy Church of Langres.

Apostolic and evangelical institutions continually admonish us that we must diligently care for all the Churches. Truth itself instructs us and commands us in blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, [Col. 0042D] when it says: “Simon, son of John, do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John 21). Relying on his authority and, by divine disposition, exercising his vicariate, we are prepared both to rejoice with all in prosperity and to offer assistance in times of need.

And because the law of God given through Moses commands: “If,” it says, “you see your neighbor’s donkey lying beneath its burden, you shall not pass by, but shall lift it up with him” (Exodus 23), when we examined your calamity and your continuing afflictions, we received with no small grief and astonishment the news that, throughout so many days and periods of time, the vigilant concern of men had not at all disclosed your injury to us.

Now, therefore, since, as we have learned from your letters, Teutbald was neither desired by you, nor elected, nor acclaimed, [Col. 0043A] and was not even advanced to any sacred order in your Church, as you are able to prove by true evidence—and the matter is indeed as you had long ago made known to our predecessor, Pope John, of pious memory—it does not seem to us incongruous, but rather fully supported by every sacred and canonical authority, to change the former judgment for the better, following the practice of our predecessors, as we can prove by many most evident examples.

Therefore we permit Argrinus, your pastor, unanimously elected and desired by you, to preside over you canonically. As you state, it is plainly evident that he was rashly expelled from you through subterfuge. We command you to receive him with fitting and appropriate reverence and, obeying him in all things as your own bishop, [Col. 0043B] to enjoy, by our authority, both his address and our consolation, and, as though such a great pastor had been restored and received by you, to rejoice with you in the Lord.

Indeed, because we wish the inviolate right and canonical law to be preserved for all Churches without violation, we neither ought to inflict force upon your Church nor seek to impose any prejudice upon it; rather, we decree that canonical authority and the ancient election remain unaltered in every respect. Farewell.

Given on the second day before the Kalends of September, by the hand of Sergius, scriniary of the holy Roman Church, in the third indiction.

## LETTER III, AN ENCYCLICAL

It commends Bishop Malacenus and his companions, who were ill-treated by the Saracens.

*(Mabillon, Vetera Analecta, p. 428.)*

[Col. 0043C] BENEDICT, servant of the servants of God, to all most reverend [Col. 0044A] and most holy bishops and archbishops, and likewise to abbots and counts, or judges, and also to all orthodox worshipers of the Christian faith.

We wish it to be known to your holiness and to the religious devotion of all Christians that this present venerable bishop Malagenus of the Church of Jerusalem, together with his faithful companions, was plundered from his Church by the Saracen peoples; moreover, some of his men were killed by that most wicked Saracen nation because they utterly refused to celebrate their faith.

Accordingly, when this most reverend bishop Malacenus had been plundered by those same Saracens, he was purchased by certain Christians who feared God; and thirty other Christians [Col. 0044B] who were plundered with him are being held by those same Saracens in custody. Therefore we command you, for love of Almighty God, insofar as the Lord grants you the strength, to provide them assistance, and to allow them to travel safely and peacefully, without anyone’s oppression. Through your help and assistance, let them remain safe from city to city, so that no one may dare to plunder them or do them any harm. Rather, for the love of God and in reverence for the blessed princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, to whose threshold these men have come, receive them kindly, send them safely from city to city, and prepare lodging for them.

For we believe that whatever good you do to them will be repaid to you by God, the Creator of all things, and that from this you will receive your reward. [Col. 0044C]

## PRIVILEGE OF POPE BENEDICT GRANTED TO HUOGGI, ABBOT OF FULDA

*(From Dronke, Codex Diplomaticus Fuldensis, p. 298.)*

[Col. 0043C] BENEDICT, servant of the servants of God, to Huoggi, abbot of the venerable monastery of the Lord Savior, and through him to his successors, the abbots of that same venerable monastery, forever.

[Col. 0043D] Since we bear the greatest concern for all venerable places, we strive, insofar as the possibility granted by divine assistance allows, to promote their stability. Through this endeavor divine mercy is appeased and praise is secured for the Church of Christ. For this reason we dare with greater confidence to implore eternal mercy for the obtaining of pardon for our sins.

Therefore your reverence petitioned us that the aforesaid venerable monastery of the Lord Savior, constructed by Archbishop Boniface at the place called Boconia beside the bank of the river Fulda, should be adorned with the protection of a privilege of the apostolic see, so that, established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve, it might not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other Church.

Favoring this pious desire, by this apostolic authority of ours we commit to effect what has been requested, according to the wording of the privilege which you have endeavored to show us as having been permanently issued there by our predecessor, Marino, of blessed memory, bishop of this life-giving see. Therefore we prohibit every priest of any Church from exercising any authority or jurisdiction in the aforesaid venerable monastery, except the apostolic see and the bishop in whose diocese that venerable monastery is known to have been constructed. To the latter we grant permission only when the occasion for consecrating an altar arises. We further prohibit anyone from presuming to celebrate the solemnity of Mass there unless he has been invited by the abbot of the monastery.

Thus, in accordance with the fact that it remains subject to the apostolic see through the firmness of this privilege, it shall remain securely endowed and shall enjoy perpetual stability, without opposition from any person, both in the places and possessions which it now holds or possesses and in those which divine mercy may in future wish to increase within the rights of that monastery through the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful.

Furthermore, after deliberation, we decree that at suitable times a report be made to our ecclesiastical care concerning the manner in which the monastic life is directed according to the rule and entrusted to suitable harmony with ecclesiastical observance, lest—God forbid—under cover of this privilege the mind and steps of your rectitude should in any way be turned aside from the norm of justice.

Nor shall it be lawful for a king, any bishop, count, or any other person, great or small, to inflict any force or raise any dispute concerning the property or dependents of the same venerable monastery. By our authority we forbid any woman ever to presume to enter there. No one shall hold a public hearing in that venerable monastery or in any of its other places. No one shall compel its servants or tenant-farmers to perform any service, except those persons to whom the abbot has given consent for the useful fulfillment of his needs.

Whenever necessary, the brothers shall have full power among themselves to choose an abbot according to the rule of Saint Benedict, without opposition from any person. And to you, beloved son Huoggi, because we know you to be a well-educated and eloquent man, we both grant and command, by the authority of Saint Peter, that you preach the word of God.

Therefore, establishing this by apostolic care, we decree by the page of this document that if any prelate of any Church, or any person endowed with whatever dignity, should presume to violate this authority of our privilege, which we confirm by the prerogative of the prince of the apostles, let him be anathema unless he quickly repents; incurring the wrath of God, let him be expelled from the assembly of all the saints; and nevertheless let the dignity of the aforesaid monastery remain unquestioned by us. But whoever proves to be its guardian shall receive blessing and grace from the Lord. [Col. 0046B]

Written by the hand of Leo, scriniary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, in the fourth indiction. Farewell. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, by the hand of Anastasius, primicerius of the defenders of the holy apostolic see, while our most pious lord Augustus, Louis, crowned by God, the great and most holy emperor, was reigning.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 905. CHRISTOPHORUS, INVADER OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON CHRISTOPHORUS

*(From Mansi, Councils.)*

Christophorus, the invader of the apostolic see, was likewise driven from the pontificate by the invader Sergius, just as Christophorus had removed his predecessor Leo V, legitimately elected, from his see. For after he had held the papal see for seven months, Sergius violently expelled him from the see, bound him in chains, and thrust him into prison; by force he was induced to assume the monastic life and habit.

## CHARTER OF CHRISTOPHORUS

For the confirmation of the privileges of the Abbey of Corbie in the diocese of Amiens.

[Col. 0045C] CHRISTOPHORUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops of Gaul.

Since it is established that the pontiff of the Roman see is the head of all the Churches of Christ, acting as the representative of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom Christ said, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,” no one should hesitate that we ought to provide for the peace, salvation, and tranquility of all the Churches, but especially for those who wish to bring the causes of their necessity before us.

Therefore let the most beloved fraternity of all the holy bishops of Gaul know that the venerable man Franco, abbot of the monastery of Corbie in the province of Gaul, constructed in the district of Amiens beside the river Somme, approached us through our venerable fellow bishop Orgarius. He requested that by a privilege of our authority we confirm the commands or edicts granted to that place by kings and emperors in ancient and modern times, as well as the privileges of bishops: one issued by Bertefridus, bishop of Amiens, to whose diocese the place itself belongs, together with his fellow bishops, and granted at the time when his monastery was first built; another written much later, during the reign of Charles, by Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, and the universal council of the bishops of Gaul; and, in addition, the privileges of our predecessors, Benedict and Nicholas, of blessed memory. In all of these it was decreed that the aforesaid monastery of Corbie [Col. 0047A] should freely possess dominion over its property and should always have the power to choose an abbot for itself from among its own members, while those who opposed or resisted this sanction were to be condemned by anathema.

Concerning this matter, let the entire assembly of the bishops of Gaul know that we strengthen, by an edict of our authority, the privileges granted to the aforesaid monastery of Corbie by the holy bishops of Gaul and by the Roman see, over which, by God’s authority, we preside; and we declare that everyone who resists them is to be condemned by divine judgment.

Moreover, the aforesaid abbot Franco, together with the congregation entrusted to him, earnestly begs that, since by the decree of divine justice the ferocity of pirates is so devastating the maritime regions of Gaul, in which the monastery itself is situated, that no place is left secure for anyone remaining outside fortifications, and since, compelled by the force of this devastation, the aforementioned monastery has been fortified by a wall, [Col. 0047B] it should remain forever, as before, in the power of the abbot and brothers. Thus neither a count nor any judge should dare presume to exercise authority there, whether to reside or to do anything against the will [Col. 0048A] of the abbot and brothers, lest the privileges granted from the beginning be violated.

Judging their petition just and appropriate to the circumstances, we decree that no ecclesiastical or secular person dare act against the privileges confirmed by our authority; rather, just as they have remained secure until now, so they shall remain undisturbed thereafter and into the future. Since the events of the past make us cautious for the future, we decree that anyone who resists this holy authority, unless he has made worthy satisfaction to those whom he has injured, is to be regarded as alien from the fellowship of the faithful both here and hereafter. But may the Lord deign to fill with the abundance of his grace all who favor these decrees of ours, those of the holy successor of Peter.

Written by the hand of Sergius, scriniary of the holy Roman [Col. 0048B] Church, in the month of December, [Note: [Col. 0047B] In Dacherii, who published this charter in the *Spicilegium*, the seventh indiction is given; this is the year of Christ 903, whose September Kalends had begun the seventh indiction. [Col. 0048B] At that time Christophorus was in fact seated in the Roman chair, according to the reckoning of Pagi.] in the eleventh indiction, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, while our most pious lord Augustus Louis, crowned by God, the most holy emperor, was reigning. Farewell.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 908. REMIGIUS, MONK OF SAINT-GERMAIN OF AUXERRE, OF THE ORDER OF SAINT BENEDICT

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON REMIGIUS

*(From Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina medii et infimi aevi*.)*

[Col. 0047C] Remigius, a monk of the monastery of Saint-Germain of Auxerre, of the order of Saint Benedict, was summoned after the year 882 by Archbishop Fulk of Reims to direct the school there, according to Flodoard, *History of Reims* IV.9. The *Literary History of France*, vol. VI, p. 99, treats him at length. He published the following works:

1. An *Exposition of the Mass*. This little work was attributed to Alcuin, since it forms chapter 40 of his book *On Divine Offices*, as Eckhard observes, *On Frankish Affairs* XXVII.26. Bulaeus notes that he borrowed much from Marcus Florus, *History of the University of Paris*, vol. I, p. 635. Possevinus mentions a book *On Divine Offices*, printed at Cologne in 1536; I do not know whether it is the same as this *Exposition of the Mass*. It is found in vol. XVI of the *Maxima Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 883.

2. An *Exposition of the Eleven Minor Prophets*, which appeared together with Oecumenius and Arethas at Antwerp in 1545.

3. *Commentaries on the Psalms*, compiled from Ambrose, Augustine, and Cassiodorus. Cologne, 1536, folio. These three works are found in vol. XVI of the Lyon *Bibliotheca Patrum*. [Col. 0047D]

4. A *Commentary on the Epistles of Paul*, commonly attributed to Remigius of Reims or to Haymo [Note: [Col. 0047] For in the Casinensis manuscript, according to Possevinus, it is written “Raimo.”], belongs rather to our Remigius, since Gregory the Great and Bede are cited in it, and mention is made of the Saracens. Cave reports that it appeared under our author’s name in the Cologne *Bibliotheca Patrum*, but this is far otherwise. For in volume V, part three, there is expressly found, from the edition of Joannes Baptista Villalpandus, *Remigius, Bishop of Reims: Explanation of the Pauline Epistles*. Rome, 1598, folio; Mainz, 1614, folio. In the Lyon *Bibliotheca*, however, vol. VIII, p. 883, it is attributed to Remigius of Lyon. See the *Literary History of France*, vol. III, p. 162.

5. A *Commentary on the Apocalypse*, commonly attributed to Haymo, belongs to our author. For out of a certain modesty he did not add his name to his writings, or appended the abbreviated name Reymonis or Raymonis; those insufficiently familiar with the matter consequently made Haymo out of it. The style is that of our Remigius, as Abbot Lebeuf observes, vol. I of his *Dissertations Relating to French History*, p. 279; he also promises a separate dissertation on the matter. To add this in passing, the abbot just mentioned is there concerned to claim for Germany Honorius, whom until now they have called of Autun, so that he should rather be assigned to Augsburg, Vindelica, or Raurica.

6. An *Epistle to Dado, Bishop of Verdun*, in which he explains what is to be understood by Gog and Magog in Ezekiel and recounts certain matters concerning the origin of the Hungarians, is found in the *Most Ample Collection* of Edmond Martène and Ursin Durand, vol. I, p. 230. Although only the initial letters R. and D. appear in the Floreffe manuscript, the dates nevertheless agree, and near the end of the letter he calls the congregation of Saint-Germain “his brothers and lords.”

7. A *Commentary on Genesis* was published by Bernhard Pez [Col. 0049A] in the *Newest Treasury of Anecdotes*, vol. IV, part 1, near the beginning.

8. A vast *Commentary on Matthew* is preserved in manuscript at Munich in the library of the Most Serene Elector of Bavaria, according to the Reverend Bernhard Pez, *Introductory Dissertation to Volume I of the New Treasury of Anecdotes*, p. 23; also in the Vienna Library and in the Library of Saint George Major at Venice, according to Possevinus, *Apparatus*, vol. II, p. 320.

9. Bulaeus mentions one book *On the Feasts of the Saints*, addressed to the Bishop of the Aedui.

10. Thirty sermons occur in the lectionary of the monastery of Medianensis, written more than seven hundred years ago; from these, Hyacinthus Alliot copied several concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist. This is reported by Theoderic Ruinart in the *Alsatian and Lorraine Journey*, vol. III of the posthumous works of Mabillon and Ruinart, p. 441. Whether Alliot published them, however, is not known to me.

11. Unpublished *Commentaries on Martianus Capella, Donatus, and Priscian* are preserved in various libraries. See the catalogue of Bernard de Montfaucon. It should be investigated whether the titles include Remigius’s *Grammatical Works*, published at Cologne in 1500, folio, according to Maittaire, vol. I of the later edition of the *Annals of Typography*, p. 728.

12. A *Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict* may be his. It is found in Florence, in the Medicean Library and the Camaldolese Library. The same author, pp. 413, 430.

[Col. 0050A] 13. A *Reply to Gualo, Bishop of the Aedui*, concerning Michael’s battle with the devil, the body of Moses, and Behemoth, which Possevinus mentions.

14. He wrote *On the Manner of Governing the Church*, as Eisengrein teaches, cited by the same Possevinus.

15. An *Interpretation of Hebrew Names* in alphabetical order, commonly attributed to Bede, whose works contain it in vol. III, p. 371. Oudinus, however, testifies that it is attributed to our Remigius in manuscripts of the finest quality. Add Meric Casaubon’s notes on Optatus, p. 49.

I believe that certain homilies to be read in a manuscript homiliary of the library of the canons of the major church of Lucca belong to this Remigius of Auxerre. They are as follows: a homily of Saint Remigius on “Therefore keep watch, because you do not know,” beginning, “Here, therefore, clearly”; another on “But concerning that day,” beginning, “Arius rejoices”; another by the same author on “Nothing is covered,” and so forth, beginning, “Why ought you to fear?”; another on “You are the salt of the earth,” beginning, “Because the Lord had said”; also a tract on “You know that after two days,” beginning, [Col. 0050B] “And it came to pass,” and so forth, with this sentence; also a homily on “But on the evening of the Sabbath,” beginning, “Matthew, on the one hand”; another on “Master, I brought my son to you,” beginning, “He turns the blame”; and another on “Explain the parable to us,” beginning, “But it must be asked.” The manuscript is, I believe, from the twelfth century.

## NOTICE ON THE WORK THAT FOLLOWS

*(From Pez, *Newest Treasury of Anecdotes*.)*

[Col. 0049B] Ancient as well as recent writers have praised Remigius, monk of Saint-Germain of Auxerre, in many places and with great commendation. Above all, Frodoard must be heard concerning him in *Chronicle* IV.9, where, speaking of the restored and flourishing schools of Reims under Archbishop Fulk, he writes:

“Finally, the aforementioned honorable bishop Fulk . . . restored the two schools at Reims, namely that of the canons of the place and that of the rural clergy, which had almost fallen into ruin; and, having summoned Remigius of Auxerre as master, he had the adolescent clerics trained in the study of the liberal arts, and himself devoted his efforts with them to reading and meditation. He also summoned Hucbald, a monk of Saint-Amand, a man nobly trained in the sophistical disciplines, and enlightened the Church of Reims with distinguished teachings.”

The author of the *Life of Blessed John of Gorze*, in Labbe, vol. I of the *New Manuscript Library*, p. 744, [Col. 0049D] praises Hildebold, who, as one of the disciples of the learned master Remigius, the most learned man of that age—that is, around the year 890 of the Lord—had schools in Lotharingia.

The necrology of the cathedral church of Auxerre, written around the year 1100 and formerly preserved in the Thuanean Library, announces Remigius’s death on the second of May in these words: “Remigius, monk and outstanding teacher, died.”

It is remarkable and worthy of notice that Bernard of Montfaucon, in his *Italian Diary*, chapter 3, records from an almost contemporary manuscript of the monastery of Saint Benedict at Polirone near Modena a testimony concerning both Remigius’s learning and his modesty. For after certain little works attributed to Saint Ambrose, he says that there follows “a treatise of the venerable monk Lord Remigius, the most learned commentator, on Mark.” Then the copyist adds: “In all things he concealed his name, so that together with the summit of wisdom he might also attain the height of humility.”

I pass over in silence the honorable testimonies concerning Remigius by Sigebert of Gembloux, Trithemius, and others, whom in a long succession are followed by Antonius Possevinus in the *Sacred Apparatus*, vol. II, p. 319; Bellarmine and Labbe in the works which both composed on ecclesiastical writers; Du Pin in the *Ecclesiastical Library*; Cave in the *Literary History*; Gottfried Olearius, vol. II of the *Library of Ecclesiastical Writers*; and most recently Casimir Oudinus, a Premonstratensian apostate, vol. II of the *Commentaries on Ecclesiastical Writers and Writings*, col. 329 and following. Oudinus also appears to have treated most carefully all the surviving monuments of Remigius’s genius, although he does not mention in a single word the *Commentary on Matthew*, which I noted in the *Bavarian Journey* as existing in the library of the Most Serene Elector of Bavaria at Munich, and which, as I learned from an anonymous author, is also preserved at Vienna in Austria, specifically in the Imperial Library at Vienna, and at Venice. That anonymous author recently published a little work on the tradition of the Church of Auxerre concerning the Quesnellian Propositions, condemned by Pope Clement XI with an anathema.

Nor will you find in the same Oudinus anything more concerning Remigius’s *Commentary on Genesis*, which we are now publishing for the first time from manuscript copies. The Anonymous of Melk, who wrote on ecclesiastical writers in the twelfth century, expressly mentions this work. His sixty-sixth chapter reads as follows:

[Col. 0051A] “Remigius, a distinguished man, sufficiently instructed in both divine and secular letters, wrote, among other works, an *Explanation of Genesis*. He also composed a notable commentary on the Psalter. There is nevertheless another commentary of his, which he wrote on Donatus.”

The manuscripts of Tegernsee and Garsten agree with the Anonymous of Melk; both are approximately from the twelfth century. These same manuscripts also present, under Remigius’s name, a *Commentary on the Pentateuch* beginning: “Deuteronomy is called the second law,” and so forth. We observed the same thing in a manuscript of the Cistercian monastery of Baumgartenberg in Austria, although it is scarcely older than the fourteenth century.

In fact, we later discovered that this work belongs not to Remigius of Auxerre but to Rabanus Maurus, archbishop of Mainz, among whose printed works it also appears. Therefore, setting it aside, we decided to devote our efforts solely to publishing Remigius’s *Commentary on Genesis*.

In this undertaking I was greatly assisted by the kindness of the Reverend Fathers Adalbert Düstl, ascetic of Tegernsee, and Peter Oberhueber, superior of Garsten. The former copied the entire work from an elegant manuscript of his monastery; the latter supplied a second copy from his library, written much more accurately than the Tegernsee manuscript. We have therefore chiefly prepared our edition according to the latter.

Remigius’s own work is weighty, concise, and elegant, and is composed altogether in the manner which Sixtus of Siena long ago observed in Remigius’s *Commentary on the Psalms*: namely, that Remigius so transferred the opinions of the ancient Fathers that he also added certain things of his own. This was in accordance with the custom of his age, when the practice of plundering the commentaries of earlier writers was widespread.

It was recently announced publicly that there is an educated man in Italy who is preparing for the press Remigius’s commentaries, happily discovered, on nearly all the books of divine authority. We sincerely hope that this is true.

One thing is entirely certain: the Reverend Father Felix Würtenberger, a most learned man of the Order of the Servants of the Blessed Virgin Mary, is now wholly occupied in recovering the very serious and elegant homilies of Herricus, a monk of Auxerre. I mention this here all the more gladly because Remigius was once a diligent auditor and noble disciple of that same Herricus. But we shall find another opportunity elsewhere to say more about these matters.

## FIRST PART OF THE WORKS OF REMIGIUS, MONK OF SAINT-GERMAIN OF AUXERRE, OF THE ORDER OF SAINT BENEDICT—EXEGETICAL WORKS

## COMMENTARY ON GENESIS

Recovered from the manuscript of the illustrious monastery of Garsten, of the Order of Saint Benedict in Austria, by Father Bernard Pez, collated with the Tegernsee manuscript by the Reverend Father Adalbert Düstl, Benedictine ascetic of that place.

## IN THE NAME OF GOD BEGINS REMIGIUS’S EXPOSITION ON *BRESITH*, THAT IS, ON GENESIS

[Col. 0051C] [Note: [Col. 0051] The text of Saint Jerome’s preface to the Pentateuch, which is explained in what follows, is absent from the manuscript.]

A certain bishop named Desiderius, a familiar friend of blessed Jerome, to whom he writes this preface, was called Desiderius.

“Preface” is said in Latin; in Greek, *prologos* or *prooemium*, that is, an abbreviation. In Greek, *Ymen* means in Latin “way.”

“By augury,” that is, by foreknowledge or a sign of future things.

He shared a name with Daniel, who likewise was called “a man of desires.” And just as Daniel desired to know future things beforehand, so this man desired to possess knowledge of the Scriptures.

“Pentateuch”: *penta* means “five,” and *teuchos* means “[a] book”; that is, the five books of Moses.

“Of detractors,” that is, of the envious.

[Col. 0052C] “By reproach,” that is, by criticism. At that time everyone was reading the Septuagint and receiving it with great veneration.

“To forge new things in place of the old,” that is, the Hebrew truth in place of the old version, namely, the Septuagint translators.

“Thus testing genius as though it were wine.” For just as wine is tested by smell or taste, so they tested his genius when they said that Jerome did this in criticizing the Septuagint.

“By a portion,” that is, for something worthless.

[Col. 0052D] “Because of my poverty.” In another preface he says that, in the tabernacle of God, some offered gold, onyx stones, linen, scarlet, and purple; for himself it was enough if he could at least offer goat hair. He calls this a worthless portion, humbling himself, although he himself was offering great things in the tabernacle of God, that is, in the Church.

“To the ancient edition,” that is, to the translation of the Septuagint.

Theodotion was a Jew who translated the divine Scriptures, but in many places he erred by Judaizing. Origen inserted his translation into the translation of the Septuagint.

“An independent composition,” that is, a composition of his own.

“If,” he says, “I were to gather together everything found in the Gospels or Epistles, and everything that is in the Septuagint, I could compose a book of my own. Many ignorant people, not knowing that these things are absent from the Hebrew truth, pursue the ravings of the apocrypha.”

The Greeks call *apocryphon* “secret.” Hence books that possess no authority and are not to be read publicly are called apocryphal. Hence also *apocrypharius*, “a messenger of secrets.” “Ravings,” [Col. 0053B] that is, vanities, or insanities and absurdities. For *lira* means “a furrow” made by a plow. Hence oxen are said to “go astray” when they veer out of the furrow. From this we call insane people “deranged,” as having departed from reason and understanding.

“Iberian trifles,” that is, Spanish vanities. Properly speaking, *naeniae* are things written upon the tombs of the dead, than which nothing is more vain.

“Authentic books,” that is, books full of authority.

Ptolemy, king of Egypt. He had become a worshiper of the one God, instructed by the Platonist philosopher Aristaeus. The Jews therefore say that the Septuagint concealed the mystery of the Holy Trinity for this reason: lest Ptolemy, who worshiped one God, should discover the divinity of the Father and the Son. Thus they did this not through error but by prudent counsel.

[Col. 0053C] I do not know what first author fabricated, by his lie, the story of the seventy chambers at Alexandria. Alexandria is the capital of Egypt. Josephus reports that King Ptolemy sent messengers with great gifts to the Jewish priest and asked him to have the books of the divine Scriptures translated from Hebrew into Greek, because he himself was Greek and did not know the Hebrew language. Then the priest sent him seventy [Col. 0054A] highly learned men. When they came to Alexandria, they assembled in one basilica and translated the Scriptures from Hebrew into Greek, comparing their work with one another. But those who venerated the Seventy excessively invented the story that they had been separated into individual chambers and had written the same things under the dictation of the Holy Spirit.

**YΠepictec** [Note: [Col. 0053C] Thus in the manuscript], that is, “faithful protector,” who protected Ptolemy with the shield of his wisdom.

Unless perhaps Tullius is to be regarded as an *oeconomicus*, that is, a steward, since an *oeconomus* is called a steward; he translated this book from Greek into Latin, but he did not prophesy, because he was an interpreter, not a prophet.

Plato’s *Pythagoras* [*Protagoras*]. Plato wrote a book which he called *Pythagoras*, because he wrote it to Pythagoras [Col. 0054B], his philosopher and friend. Tullius likewise translated this work.

And Demosthenes’ *Against Ctesiphon* [Note: [Col. 0053C] Both manuscripts read *Prothesifontem*, here and below]. Demosthenes was a Greek rhetorician who wrote a book *Against Ctesiphon*, because he wrote it before Ctesiphon.

*History*. “History” is said to derive from *apo tou historia*, that is, “from seeing.” There is a distinction between histories and annals, because histories concern things that we see or can see, whereas annals concern things that we do not see.

“Among spiritual gifts,” that is, gifts or the grace of the Holy Spirit.

“In the Apostle,” namely Paul, where he recalls the gifts of the Spirit, saying: “To some, he says, he gives the rank of apostles, to others prophets,” and so forth. In these gifts interpreters held almost the lowest rank; and this is also found in the same Apostle Paul’s Epistle, where he says: “To one is given through the Spirit a message of wisdom,” and so forth, until he concludes by saying: “To another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues.”

And the Latin copies are more corrected than the Greek, and the Greek more than the Hebrew. For each thing, the more often it is translated, the more securely it is corrected.

# THE TEXT OF BRESITH BEGINS

[Note: [Col. 0053D] This title is absent in that manuscript.]

[Col. 0053]

# CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0053D]

**Verse 1. “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”** The author of this work, as the holy teachers have handed down, is known to have been Moses, who learned through God’s revelation about the creation of the world; nevertheless, in the manner of Scripture, he speaks of himself as though of another.

At the beginning of this volume the philosophers are refuted. They attempted to discuss the creation of the world: Plato, for example, said that there were three principles—God, the exemplar, and matter—and that God had not created all things from nothing as their author, but had supplied matter as an aid to the craftsman in creating things. Aristotle, however, said that there were two principles, namely matter and form; wishing to mention a third element of some kind, he called it the operative principle [Col. 0054D]. Opposing these errors, Moses, chosen by God, is said to have demonstrated the truth, showing that God formed all things simultaneously from nothing—not in time, but at the beginning of time. When he says, “In the beginning,” “of time” is understood; and it is unquestionably clear that time then began, since previously it did not exist at all.

“For he created heaven and earth.” We should not understand “heaven” as this visible firmament, but as that empyrean, that is, fiery, or intellectual heaven [Col. 0055A], which is called fiery not because of heat but because of splendor. It was immediately filled with angelic spirits, concerning whom it is said in Job: “When the morning stars praised me together and all the sons of God shouted for joy” (Job 38:7). Note that three elements are mentioned here. By “heaven,” understand the air; by “earth,” the earth itself; and also fire, which lies hidden in its depths. The fourth element, water, is mentioned below.

**Verse 2. “But the earth was formless and empty.”** That is, useless, fruitless, and unformed. All the elements had been mixed and confused, and the entire expanse of air extending from earth to heaven was filled with waters. Yet they did not have the quality they now possess; rather, they were thin, like clouds [Col. 0055B]. The waters above the heavens still retain this quality. “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.” Just as the mind or wisdom of a craftsman is borne over the work he is about to make, so that he may fashion it as he wishes, so the Holy Spirit was borne over the waters, foreordaining and, as it were, arranging what he wished to make and how he wished to make it.

**Verse 3. “God said.”** Not with a fleshly voice or by movement of the lips, but “said,” that is, “willed.” For his willing is his speaking. Hence it is written: “He spoke, and they were made” (Psalm 148:5). Or “he said” means that he begot the Son, through whom all things were made. “Let there be light.” Light is said to derive from *luere*, that is, “to cleanse,” because it cleanses away darkness. That light, however, was not of the kind that now exists when the sun is above us, but like the light that appears either before sunrise or after sunset.

[Col. 0055C] **Verse 4. “And God saw that the light was good.”** This does not mean that he then saw for the first time something whose goodness had always been present to him. Rather, “he saw” means that he wished us to see that the light was good. “And he separated the light from the darkness.” Darkness is said to derive from *tenere*, “to hold,” because it holds the eyes so that they cannot see. God made both things—the light and the darkness—so that human beings might work in the light and rest at night. Therefore darkness too is God’s work. Hence, in the hymn of the three young men, in which every creature is invited to bless God, darkness is placed together with light.

Allegorically, what is said—“In the beginning God made heaven and earth”—may suitably be understood as referring to the Son of God under the name “beginning,” just as he himself said to the Jews: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8:28). For the Son of God is the beginning, but not from a beginning, because he was not made or created by the Father, but begotten. Through this beginning God the Father created heaven and earth, that is, heavenly and earthly beings. “Heaven” signifies heavenly beings or those who lead a heavenly life; “earth” signifies those intent on earthly affairs. Both were created through the beginning, because, when Jesus Christ was born, it became evident who were heavenly and who were earthly.

“But the earth was formless and empty,” that is, the human body was empty of heavenly meditation and empty of the fruit of good works. “And darkness was over the face of the abyss,” because the darkness of unbelief and ignorance covered the abyss of the human heart. “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters,” because divine foreknowledge was borne over the fluid and fruitless hearts of human beings, foreseeing and arranging in which hearts it could worthily dwell. “Let there be light.” By the word “light,” faith is understood. Therefore light was rightly made on the first day, because faith is commended in the first commandment of the Law, which says: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God.”

**Verse 5. “There was evening and there was morning, one day.”** By “morning,” the beginning of faith is understood; by “evening,” the perfection of good works. The morning of that day is brought to evening when the beginning of faith is perfected through the completion of good works.

**Verse 6. “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters.”** By this firmament the waters above were divided from the waters below, and the upper portion was frozen into the form of crystal, while the lower portion was turned into the sea. This was done on the second day. The work of this day is not said to have been good, as the work of the other days is, where it says, “God saw that it was good.” This is not because what was made was not good and beautiful, but because of the number two, which is a transgression of unity and has an evil significance. Hence the holy Fathers dedicated it to discord. It also signifies bigamy. In the same significance, two animals of each unclean kind were sent into the ark.

**Verse 11. “Let the earth bring forth green vegetation and fruit-bearing trees.”** All things were known by God in their perfection. Hence human beings were created at a perfect age, and the trees were created simultaneously with their leaves and fruit. Therefore he says “fruit-bearing tree,” each one possessing its seed. *Sementis* is the seed of crops and trees; *semen* is that of human beings and animals; *seminium* or *sementum* is the beginning of any thing.

**Verse 14. “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven.”** By the lights we understand the sun, moon, and other stars. In truth, however, the sun, moon, and seven planets are not placed in the firmament but hang in the ether; for that reason they are said to have been placed in the firmament. “And let them divide the day and the night.” The sun rules the day, and the moon the night. “Let them be for signs.” This is said either because of the date of Easter, since the moon marks the date of Easter, which is celebrated only after the fourteenth day of the moon, or because the stars are signs for sailors traveling across the sea or for travelers passing through Libya, where the trace of the route is scattered by the movement of the wind.

Among the Hebrews the moon is called by three names: *Lare*, *Lavana*, and *Mavors*. It is called *Lara* from the number of days in the month; *Lavana* from its whiteness; and *Mavors* from its waning, because it decreases each month.

**Verses 20–21. “A moving creature with a living soul.”** Here understand fish as the creeping creatures. He calls the soul of animals mutable [Vulgate: “mobile”] in comparison with the human being. For although a human being is mortal in comparison with God, he is nevertheless immortal in comparison with the other animals, insofar as he retains the image of God.

**Verse 26. “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness.”** Whereas he made the other things by command, when God was about to make what was, as it were, the greatest thing and what was to be preferred above all that he had made, he said, as though in counsel: “Let us make.” Although some say that this should be referred to the angels, it is better referred to the Holy Trinity.

**Verse 27. “In his image and likeness.”** *Imago* is said as though from *imitago*, “imitation.” There is a distinction between image and likeness. Image exists in reason and immortality; likeness, however, in holiness of conduct and justification. By sinning, therefore, he lost the likeness but did not lose the image.

Nor should we heed those who say that the human being bears the image of God in the body. In this respect we have the body in common with animals, for just as they have five bodily senses, so do we. It is in the soul that we have the image of God. What God does in the greater world, the soul does in our body [Col. 0057B]. Hence it is called in Greek *microcosmos*, that is, “a small world.” God, though placed outside the world, is not excluded from it; within the world, he is contained in it. By presiding he sustains, by sustaining he presides; by surrounding he fills, and by filling he surrounds.

So too the soul, though it is not placed outside the body, is not excluded from the body; nor is it enclosed within the body. Rather, it is wholly everywhere and everywhere entire.

“Male and female.” The two were not made at the same time in outward appearance, but all things are said to have been made simultaneously in the presence of God. Hence the saying: “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclesiasticus 18:1).

Mystically, the firmament signifies Holy Scripture, as is said in its symbolic meaning in the Apocalypse: “And heaven departed like a scroll being rolled up” (Apocalypse 6:14). The many waters are peoples. The firmament was therefore made in the midst of the waters when divine Scripture became known to the peoples. The waters above the firmament signify the angelic hosts, who are rightly said to be above the firmament because, always having God before their eyes, they do not need legal instruction or evangelical commandments. The waters beneath the firmament signify human beings, who are taught by divine commandments and without them cannot reach the heavenly kingdom.

On the third day the waters were gathered into one place, and the dry land appeared. By the dry land are signified the hearts of the elect, thirsting for the water of baptism and the fountain of heavenly teaching. When the waters were gathered into one—that is, when the reprobate were separated from the righteous—the saints appeared, divided from the bitterness of unbelief and strengthened by the unshaken firmness of faith.

On the fourth day the lights were made in the firmament. As we have said, the firmament may suitably be understood as Sacred Scripture; by the lights we understand the evangelists, teachers, and preachers, who, illuminated by the grace of the Holy Spirit, turn others to the light of faith through their preaching. To such men Peter [Paul] says: “Among a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life” (Philippians 2:15–16). The lights are rightly placed or established in the firmament so that they may always cling to it, because teachers ought to contemplate and adhere to Sacred Scripture.

This was aptly prefigured by the poles placed in the four rings of the ark, which were never removed from it (Exodus 35). By the four rings, the four books of the Gospels are prefigured; by the poles, the teachers, in whose hearts the ark—that is, the divine law—is carried. The poles were therefore never removed from the rings of the ark, because preachers and teachers must never have an empty meditation on the law of God.

On the fifth day the waters brought forth moving creatures with living souls. By these animals, formed from the waters and living in the waters, the order of the baptized is signified. Like fish, they cannot live without the waters of Christ’s baptism. The flying creature likewise preserves the type of the saints, who strive to hasten toward heavenly things on the wings of virtue and contemplation.

By the cattle, which were created on the sixth day, teachers and all ecclesiastical men are represented. Though less capable, they strengthen others in the firmness of faith through the assistance of their preaching. The beasts, however, prefigure the powerful or proud, who, like beasts, display the savagery of their cruelty toward whomever they can. By the serpents, which in this passage are understood in a good sense, the prudent and shrewd saints are signified, who beware of the devil’s deceits. To them the Lord says: “Be wise as serpents” (Matthew 10:16).

On this same day the human being was made, that is, Christ was born through the Virgin as the second Adam, who would remove the sins of the first human being.

Nevertheless, the works of these six days may also be referred to the six ages of the world [Col. 0058C]. On the first day, therefore, God made light. In that same age he created the rational human being in his likeness. The human being is called “light,” as it were, in comparison with irrational animals; concerning him it is said: “He was the true light which enlightens every human being” (John 1:9). On this day he divided the light from the darkness, because in this age the sons of God—that is, the sons of Seth—were separated from the impious generation of Cain. The evening of that age was the multiplication of human iniquity, so that God brought about the Flood.

On the second day the firmament was made, because in this age the ark floated through the Flood, and, after the entire human race had been condemned, only eight souls were saved in it. The evening of that age was prideful presumption, because human beings wished to build a tower, and the confusion of languages took place.

On the third day the waters were gathered together, because in this age the people of God were separated from the other nations through Abraham. While the others were gathered or confined in the bitterness and volume of their sins, these people were established in the worship of the one God, so that they might produce the green vegetation of virtues and bring forth the fruit of good works. The evening of that age was the destruction of Saul and Jonathan on Mount Gilboa, when they were killed by the Philistines.

On the fourth day the lights were made, because in the fourth age royal dignity shone forth in David, Solomon, and the other kings and prophets who flourished especially in this age. Its evening was in Zedekiah, whom the king of Babylon punished by putting out his eyes; after Jerusalem had been overthrown and the temple destroyed, he carried him away to Babylon.

On the fifth day animals were brought forth from the waters, because in this age the Jewish people lived among the nations as captives, as though in the waters, and nevertheless did not depart from the worship of God. Many of the saints were already lifted toward heavenly things through contemplation, like birds—for example, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Nehemiah, and others. The evening of this age was the unbelief and great sin of those who, seeing the Christ promised to them, refused to receive him.

On the sixth day the human being was made. In this age Christ was born through the Virgin. He was set above the beasts of the earth, the fish of the sea, and the birds of the heavens, because he subjected all nations to the yoke of his faith. The evening of this age will be the end of the world.

On the seventh day God rested, because the seventh age is the rest of souls resting in Christ and awaiting the general resurrection of bodies.

# CHAPTER TWO

**Verse 4. “These are the generations of heaven and earth.”** This is a recapitulation of God’s creation. He calls the adornments of heaven and earth their “generations.” The adornments of heaven are angels and stars; the adornments of earth are human beings and cattle, together with the varieties of trees and flowers.

“In the day,” that is, “in time.” Here he uses “day” for “time,” as the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation!” Here the error of the philosophers vanishes. They said that the world was coeternal with God; or, even if it had been made by God and without a beginning, they claimed that it consisted of matter that had not been created by God. Both claims collapse when it says: “In the day he made heaven and earth.” When he says “in the day,” he shows that the world is not coeternal with God. When he adds, “he made heaven and earth,” he reveals that the world was founded by God.

If, however, we understand “day” as referring to one day, it should be understood according to the sense expressed by the prophet: “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclesiasticus 18:1). In accordance with this interpretation, blessed Gregory says: “The nature of things was created together in substance, but was not created together in form.”

**Verse 5. “Every shrub before it arose, and every herb before it sprouted.”** When he says “before it sprouted” or “before it arose,” it is plainly evident that they were not then produced in the way in which trees and herbs now arise from seed or root, or through human cultivation. Rather, they burst forth suddenly at God’s will and command, with leaves, fruit, and every perfection.

“It had not rained upon the earth.” This refers back to what was said above. It had not rained so that shrubs and herbs might grow through the increase of rainfall. For how could it have rained when the entire expanse of air was filled with extremely thin waters, like mist, as was stated above? But after those waters had been gathered together into one place and the dry land had appeared, no rain is recorded as having fallen until the Flood.

[Col. 0060A] **Verse 6. “But a fountain rose from the earth and watered its entire surface.”** That fountain either flowed upward through hidden passages in the earth in order to water the surface of the earth, like the Nile, which, overflowing the boundaries of its bed, waters the plains of Egypt; or it watered the entire surface of the earth—not by covering the whole surface of the earth, but by branching out in streams through various places, as rivers do.

Or, as is more agreeable to the manner of Sacred Scripture, a singular was used for a plural: “fountain” for “fountains,” just as “fly” is used for “flies” and “frog” for “frogs.” Or perhaps “fountain” is used because of the totality of all waters, which exist together and are, as it were, one fountain in the womb of the abyss.

**Verse 7. “God formed the human being.”** Here we must avoid the poverty of human understanding, lest we imagine that God worked with hands to form the human being or spoke with fleshly lips, or anything of that sort, which it is impious to conceive or understand of God. God is spirit, and therefore is not distinguished by bodily members or burdened by bodily mass, so that we should imagine or understand anything fleshly concerning him.

When it says, “He formed the human being from clay,” this means that by willing and commanding he brought him forth externally. “And he breathed.” When it says that he breathed, this should not be understood to mean that he blew or infused this corporeal air into the human being. Rather, “he breathed” means that he animated him with rational life, which he subsequently called the breath of life.

In comparison with the other animals, whose souls die, the human being received a rational soul. Hence the Greeks, making a distinction among animals that live only without reason, call them *zōa*, because *zōē* means “life”; but those that participate in reason they call *psychika* [Note: [Col. 0059] The Garst. manuscript reads *Yki Psiche*. The Teg. manuscript reads *partic. Psiche quia*, etc.], because *psychē* means “soul.”

He is said to have breathed into the human being’s face because all the senses are especially active in the head, although one of them—that is, touch—is distributed throughout the entire body.

**Verse 8. “He had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning.”** That is, a garden of delight. In Greek, *paradeisos* means “garden”; in Hebrew it is called *Eden*. “From the beginning,” that is, at the beginning, after the waters had been removed from the surface of the earth and gathered into one place.

Where we read, “a paradise from the beginning,” some manuscripts read, “Eden toward the east.” From this we may infer that paradise was situated in the East. Whatever part of the world it occupies, we know that it is earthly and extremely far removed from our world, with the Ocean and intervening mountains lying between. It is situated in a very high place, reaching as far as the lunar sphere. Hence it is also said that the waters of the Flood did not reach it.

“Where he placed the human being.” From the fact that the human being is said to have been placed in paradise, it is understood that he was not created there, but on this mortal earth of ours, since God’s foreknowledge knew that he would sin and therefore be driven from that holy land into this valley of misery.

**Verse 9. “And he brought forth from the earth.”** “Of paradise” is understood. “The tree of life,” and so forth. The tree of life was a particular kind of tree, so called because it had naturally received the power that, if anyone ate its fruit, he would be strengthened with perpetual solidity and clothed with blessed immortality, thereafter to be oppressed by no illnesses or anxieties and weakened by no weariness or frailty of old age.

The tree of the knowledge of good and evil should not be understood as a definite species of tree. Rather, its name was assigned in view of what would later occur, according to the character of obedience or disobedience. For the obedient person it would produce knowledge of good; for the disobedient person, knowledge of evil, and thus of sin, would arise in the one who incurred it.

Obedience alone is the virtue that reconciles the human being to God; conversely, swelling pride—that is, disobedience—separates him far from God. For what is disobedience other than refusing to be subject to God and wishing instead to belong to one’s own power?

[Col. 0061B] **Verse 10. “And a river went out, which is divided into four heads. The name of one is Pishon.”** It is interpreted as “change of mouth.” Coming out of paradise and running through our world, it changes the beauty and pleasantness of its appearance. This is the Ganges. “It encircles the whole land of Havilah,” that is, India, drawing along golden sands. Havilah is a region of India, named after Havilah, the son of Joktan, the son of Eber, from whom the Hebrews are named. These rivers do have definite sources. Pishon rises in the Caucasus Mountains; Gihon near Mount Atlas in Mauritania; the Tigris and Euphrates in Armenia.

**Verse 12. “And there bdellium is found.”** Bdellium is an aromatic tree the size of an olive tree, with an oak leaf and the scent of the wild fig tree. Its tear or gum is bright and somewhat white, like *manna*. Hence it is said in Exodus: “The manna was like white coriander seed, having the appearance of bdellium” (Exodus 16:31).

“And the onyx stone.” In Greek, *onyx* means “fingernail.” Hence the onyx stone is marked with white spots resembling a human fingernail.

Gihon itself is the Nile, which flows through Mauritania. It is interpreted as “precipitous” or “precipice.” Falling from extremely high cliffs [Note: [Col. 0061D] The Garst. manuscript lacks “cliffs”], it produces such a powerful sound that it condemns its inhabitants to deafness. The place from which it descends is called Catadupa.

The Tigris runs through Armenia. It is called Tigris after an extremely swift animal whose speed it imitates.

Euphrates is interpreted as “fruitful,” because it makes the land through which it flows fruitful.
