Allegorically, paradise signifies the present Church, which is rightly called a garden of delights, since spiritual delights are provided for us in it. The tree of life in the midst of paradise is Christ in the midst of the Church. Concerning him a certain wise man says: “He is a tree of life to those who grasp him” (Proverbs 3:18). He is also the fountain that, descending from the substance of the Father, came to water his holy Church. Concerning it the prophet Zechariah says: “There shall be an open fountain for the house of David for the washing of the sinner and of the menstruous woman” (Zechariah 13:1).

The house of David is the holy Church, for whose salvation the fountain—that is, Christ—is open as a washing for the sinner. The sinner is one who carries out in deeds the evil he conceives in his mind. The menstruous woman is one who does not touch another’s flesh but is defiled by her own. She signifies the sinful soul that does not bring to completion in action the evil it conceives. Therefore she is not defiled externally, as though by another’s flesh, but internally, like one defiled by her own flesh, through her thoughts.

From this one and singular fountain four rivers emerge: that is, from him proceeds the teaching of the four Gospels, or the four virtues in which the Church excels.

**Verse 15. “He placed the human being in paradise, to work and to guard it.”** That work was not for labor or weariness, but rather for delight. We often see people taking pleasure in certain activities, and if they are forbidden to engage in them, they become considerably saddened.

“And to guard it.” Not from thieves, since at that time there were none, but he was to keep it for himself, so that he might delight in it.

**Verse 17. “You shall surely die.”** He is not speaking of bodily death, but of the death of the soul. For as soon as he ate, he did not die bodily, but he died in soul through sin. Yet because of the death of the soul—that is, sin—bodily death, the punishment of sin, followed later in its appointed time.

**Verse 18. “Let us make him a helper.”** That is, a woman, so that herbs and shrubs might be propagated—not, however, so that the procreation of children would be as it is now, namely, so that children would succeed their parents after their death. Rather, it was so that parents, seeing children born from them, might rejoice and, living happily with them for a long time, await that blessed state and angelic life to which they were to be transferred at the end of the world—not through death, but through a certain imitation of divine virtue.

When the full number of all the elect had been completed, and no reprobate would be born, all would taste from the tree of life and thus be transferred from this intermediate state into that blessed state, where they would neither wish nor be able to sin.

**Verse 19. “When they had been formed,” and so forth.** Above it was said that the flying creatures were produced from the waters. Now, however, it says that they were formed from the earth together with the other living creatures. This can be resolved in two ways: either, when it says, “when the animals of the earth and the birds of the sky had been formed from the ground,” we are to understand, with respect to the birds, “formed from the water”; or the waters that are in the earth are also universally included under the name “earth.”

Likewise, in the Psalm the prophet includes together with the earth the things that exist in the air and in the waters, saying: “Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all abysses, fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy wind” (Psalm 148:7–8), and so forth.

“And he brought her to Adam.” Not as a shepherd drives his flock, but “he brought her,” that is, he caused her to come by the sign of his disposition, just as in the Flood he caused all the living creatures to be gathered into the ark.

“Whatever Adam called it, that was its name.” In Hebrew Adam imposed names on all things. But after the division of languages, the various nations called everything according to their own usage and preference. The Lord therefore caused all the living creatures to come to Adam so that he might impose names on them according to his own judgment, and thereby recognize that he was held dearer and more worthy than the other things, since the Lord granted him such authority.

Mystically, Adam signifies Christ, who descended from the bosom of the Father’s majesty and appeared to human beings so that they might see him. He imposed a name on the whole creation—that is, on human beings, whom he transferred through regeneration into a new creation—because he wished them to be called Christians from his name, as was said through the prophet: “He will call his servants by another name” (Isaiah 65:15).

**Verse 21. “The Lord cast a deep sleep upon Adam, and he took one of his ribs.”** Could the Lord not have removed Adam’s rib while he was awake and without pain, rather than taking it while he slept, as is said? Certainly he could. But this should rather be understood as having occurred in a mystery, so that at the beginning of the world the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion might be prefigured—something that would take place in its own time, that is, in the final age of the world.

Adam’s sleep signifies Christ’s death on the cross. While he hung upon the cross, the mysteries of blood and water flowed from his side; by these the holy Church is constituted and from them receives strength. Hence it is rightly said that he did not “form” the rib but “built” it, as though prefiguring the house of the Church, which is built from living and chosen stones.

And what he said above briefly—“Male and female he created them”—he now explains more fully, showing how he created the woman herself:

[Col. 0063C] **Verse 23. “This now is bone of my bones.”** When Adam saw a woman like himself in every respect, he recognized that she had been formed from the substance of his flesh. Or, as blessed Augustine says, Adam, having entered into ecstasy of mind and being filled with the spirit of prophecy, knew that the rib had been taken from him and the woman formed.

“She shall be called woman.” *Virago* is derived from *vir*, “man,” just as in Hebrew *ish* means “man,” and from it *ishshah* is derived, meaning “woman.” From this, *Israel* is also formed.

**Verse 24. “Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother.”** Explaining this passage, the Apostle says: “This mystery is great, but I speak in reference to Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5:32).

“Man” is understood as Christ because of the humanity he assumed. He left the Father when, descending from the Father’s bosom, the new man appeared visibly to the world—not by abandoning the Father, with whom he always remained inseparably in divinity. He left his mother, that is, the synagogue, from which he also assumed flesh. He adhered to his wife, that is, he joined to himself the Church, which has neither spot nor wrinkle. “And the two became one flesh,” that is, Christ, who is the head, and his members, namely the Church, just as he prays to the Father for his primitive Church, that is, for his apostles, saying: “I desire that they may be one, just as we are one” (John 17:21).

**Verse 25. “They were both naked, and they were not ashamed.”** What cause for shame could there have been in those whom no dishonorable movement and no sensual stirring of the flesh impelled? For if the human being had not sinned, he would never have been driven by the heat of desire. Rather, just as we turn our eye here and there without any injury or wantonness, or as we extend a finger, so we would have used the genital members not for pleasure but for producing offspring.

It is therefore rightly said that they were not ashamed to be naked, since they were more beautifully clothed with the garment of innocence and the delight of immortality.

# CHAPTER THREE

**Verse 1. “But the serpent was more crafty.”** Or “wiser,” as Theodotion says—not by its own nature, since it does not possess a rational soul capable of wisdom, but because it was filled with a demonic spirit, which the evil spirit used as a kind of instrument.

Therefore that craftiness or wisdom did not belong to the serpent but to the demon who spoke through the serpent, just as evil spirits commonly speak through the possessed, the frenzied, and the prophets of demons. The serpent itself did not understand what it was saying, just as the possessed do not understand what the hostile or evil spirit speaks through them.

It is characteristic of an evil spirit that, once it has invaded someone, it weighs him down with the burden of its assault, takes away all understanding and reason from him, and renders him entirely unaware of the things he says. The Holy Spirit, by contrast, makes those whom he has deemed worthy through his favor and filled with his grace into people who see—that is, understand—so that through the Spirit they know not only present things but also future things. Hence the Apostle says: “The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets” (1 Corinthians 14:32).

“Why did God command you?” and so forth. The crafty enemy questions the woman for this reason: so that after the transgression she would not be able to offer an excuse for her guilt. For perhaps she could have said: “I forgot God’s commandments, and therefore I sinned.” To remove every such excuse, he repeats God’s commandments, impresses them upon her, and recalls them to her memory.

**Verse 4. “You shall certainly not die.”** The devil deceitfully urges the human being to despise God’s commandment, so that he would refuse to be subject to God and instead wish to belong to his own power.

Verse 5. “For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, you will be like gods.” Many ask: If God foresaw that the human being could be deceived, why did he permit him to be tempted? But, as blessed Augustine says, it would not have been a matter of great praise if he had lived well in paradise without anyone persuading him. For, as the Apostle says, “he will not be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (II Tim. II, 5). And certainly he possessed free choice, so that, if he had wished, he could have resisted the tempter. If he had done so, he would deservedly have been rewarded.

With artificial and clever contrivance the devil composed the deceit of his persuasion, saying, “You will be like gods,” so that, if he could not overthrow the human being through the contempt of disobedience, he might at least boast of victory in corrupting his faith and persuading him toward idolatry. But if he had led him into disobedience and contempt of God, he would have been victorious in both respects.

Verse 6. “So the woman saw that the tree was good for eating.” Here it is openly shown that the woman was without excuse. For under such deliberation she could have noticed the enemy’s deceit. She considered the beauty of the tree and that it was pleasant to eat. “She gave it to her husband.” It is not expressly said that she persuaded him to eat, but in the statement “she gave” it is understood that she urged him to eat—although there was no need for her to persuade him, since, when he saw that she had eaten and had not died at all, he too ate without fear.

Verse 7. “And their eyes were opened.” Why is it said, “their eyes were opened”? Had God established them in paradise without sight? Certainly not. Rather, their eyes were opened to desire and to the knowledge of the bestial impulse, which they had previously not known within themselves at all. There is a certain kind of blindness which in Greek is called *aorasia*, that is, “inability to see,” by which some things are seen and others are not. The two disciples who were traveling with the Lord to Emmaus were held by this blindness, concerning whom it is said: “Their eyes were held, lest they should recognize him” (Luke XXIV, 16).

“And when they had realized that they were naked.” They realized that they were naked in that they felt the bestial impulse which they had not felt before. Hence they also fled to the fig tree, because perhaps, as blessed Augustine says, they found this tree first after the transgression; and from its leaves they made themselves *perizomata*, that is, coverings or breeches, and placed them over their sexual members, namely around the loins, in which the generative power is recognized to reside. Appropriately, they are said to have made themselves coverings from fig leaves, which are known to possess a certain irritant quality. This signifies the irritation of the flesh and the burning of the kindling of lust, concerning which blessed Ambrose says:

> “Blessed are those who tie their horses to the vine of the olive, to the trees of joy and peace, not to the fig tree, which is low in height, soft for labor, and barren for fruit.”

Verse 8. “And when they had heard the voice of the Lord God.” God spoke to the first human being through a subordinate creature, that is, through an angel appearing in human form; hence he is said to have heard the voice of the Lord. Nor is it without significance that he is said to have perceived the same voice after midday, when the day was already growing cool after its heat: for by then the fervor of charity and the light of truth had failed in him. Hence he gave up his spirit at the ninth hour, although he had been crucified at the sixth hour. And rightly was this accomplished in such an order, so that at the hour when the human being was expelled from paradise, he might at that same hour be restored there.

Verse 10. “I heard your voice and hid myself.” Like a madman and one terrified by excessive fear. He hid himself, not so that the Lord would fail to see his crimes, but so that he might show himself to have become unworthy of the Lord’s sight. They were constrained by a twofold shame: either because they felt in their members that obscene impulse which they had never before experienced, or because they understood that this had happened to them because of their transgression of God’s command.

“Adam, where are you?” He did not ask as though ignorant, since nothing can be hidden from him; rather, when he said, “Adam, where are you?” he expressed the misery of the transgression. That is: “How miserable have you become! You were created immortal, yet you are held under the penalty of death and deprived of the blessedness of innocence.”

Or, as blessed Gregory says, the Lord asked him not so that God might learn what he did not know, but to provoke him to humble confession, so that he might erase by confessing what he had committed by transgressing. But he wished to shift his sin onto another, saying:

Verse 12. “The woman whom you gave me.” As though by this he were casting blame upon God, who had given him the woman through whom he had been deceived. Likewise, when questioned, the woman redirected the blame to the serpent, saying: “The serpent deceived me.” The human race suffers from this disease even to the present day. Finally, the serpent is not questioned, because the devil, who had spoken through the serpent, had sinned irrecoverably.

And Adam is rightly questioned first, because God had given the command to him, and through the man the command came to the woman; conversely, through the serpent sin came to the woman, and through the woman to the man.

Verse 14. “And the Lord said to the serpent: Because you have done this, you will be cursed among all living creatures.” What is said to the serpent must be referred to the devil.

“You will walk upon your breast.” The devil walks upon his breast because, carrying deceit and ambushes in his heart, he attempts to deceive human beings. Hence he is rightly called a serpent, because he creeps secretly. “You will eat earth,” because he feeds upon and delights in earthly works.

Verse 15. “I will put enmity between you and the woman and between your seed and her seed.” Here he calls the Church “the woman,” since the devil is opposed to her. The woman’s seed is the Church’s good works; the serpent’s seed is every work of iniquity. For this is that woman of whom John says in the Apocalypse that the dragon persecuted her, wishing to devour her, after he had also cast a river from his mouth (Apoc. XII, 13), because he stirred up the persecution of the nations against the Church.

“She will crush your head.” That is, the Church will crush your head, meaning the beginning of evil will, before it breaks out into action. Hence blessed is he who, in the psalm, is said to have seized Babylon’s little ones and dashed them against the rock (Ps. CXXXVI, 9). Babylon’s little ones are the beginning of sin and the origin of evil will. These are the little ones of confusion, who must be dashed against the rock, that is, Christ, before they grow strong.

Verse 16. “And you will lie in wait for her heel.” The heel is the end of the body. Therefore the devil lies in wait for the heel because he especially wishes to deceive human beings at the end.

“And to the woman he said: I will multiply your troubles; in pain you will bear children.” Because, if she had not sinned, she would have given birth without pain, this punishment is imposed upon her after the sin, so that she now bears children in pain.

“And you will be under the power of the man, and he will rule over you.” Even if she had not sinned, she would have been under the man’s power. But that submission would have been less punitive, because it would have proceeded from love; now it is imposed upon her as a punishment, so that even unwillingly she is subjected to the man.

Morally, the woman is placed under the man’s power because the flesh must be subjected to the spirit, lest it resist, but rather obey.

Verse 17. “But to Adam he said: Cursed is the earth in your work.” The earth is cursed, not Adam himself, so that the others, for whom these things had to be written, might be frightened lest they do similar things and suffer a similar punishment. But Cain, because he added parricide to the first transgression, is himself cursed, for it was said to him: “You will be cursed upon the earth” (Gen. IV, 11).

“Your earth will produce thorns and thistles.” Thorns already existed, because God created thorns among the other trees and plants, but not so that they would cause labor for the human being. After the sin, they were given for labor and affliction to the human race; likewise, serpents and all harmful things existed before the sin but were harmless.

Mystically, the earth produces thorns and thistles because our flesh does not cease to produce the pricks and barbs of vices. And this should be noted: punishment is imposed externally upon Adam when it is said, “Cursed is the earth in your work,” but internally upon the woman when it is said, “I will multiply your troubles,” and so forth. Because the woman, having been seduced, deceived the man, a heavier punishment is imposed upon her.

Verse 21. “The Lord God made tunics of skin for Adam and his wife.” Skins are taken from dead animals. Through the tunics of skin, therefore, it was shown that they had become mortal from being immortal; and they had not only lost the blessed state into which they could have been changed had they not sinned, but had also lost the very happy life in which they could have lived blessedly in paradise.

They themselves made coverings for themselves in order to hide their sin from God. But God made tunics of skin for them and clothed their entire bodies with them, because by a just judgment he condemned them in body and soul: in soul because of the sin of transgression, and in body because of the punishment of sin.

It is a foolish question if someone wishes to inquire how, or through what agent, the skins were stripped from the animals. God, who created everything from nothing, did this also in whatever manner and fashion he willed.

Verse 22. “Behold, Adam has become like one of us!” God repeats, mocking their pride, the words that the persuader had spoken as the crowning point of their condemnation, saying, “knowing good and evil.” It is as though he were saying: “Adam not only could not attain what he sought—namely, to become like God—but also lost what he was. He desired to be like God, not by humbly imitating God, but by becoming proud and rejecting his dominion.”

In what follows—“like one of us”—a mention of the Holy Trinity is reiterated.

“Now therefore, lest he perhaps stretch out his hand.” The words “lest he perhaps stretch out his hand” are God’s words. What follows, finally:

Verse 23. “He cast him out of paradise.” The act itself is meant, and this is a defective expression appropriate to one who is angry or disturbed—not that any movement of anger or disturbance can arise in God, who is perfect tranquility, but because Scripture, speaking in our customary manner about God, attributes to God what belongs to human beings.

“Take from the tree of life and live.” As we have already said, when the number of the elect had been completed, all were going to taste from the tree of life and pass into that blessed state. Since he had made himself unworthy of that state, a guard was rightly placed over him, so that he could no longer touch the tree of life.

Verse 24. “And he placed before the paradise of delight the cherubim and a flaming sword.” That is, through angelic ministry he established a fiery guard. The flaming sword signifies the tribulations and labors of this age, through which the saints are exercised in the present life; or the flaming sword signifies the sentence of just condemnation that was given to the human being. Yet he was condemned in such a way that he could be redeemed through Christ’s suffering. Hence the sword is rightly called “turning,” since it could at some point be removed.

It was removed for Enoch, for Elijah, and for the Lord after his baptism, and for all the faithful each day, when they pass from this life to that heavenly blessedness. And he does not say “flame and sword,” but “flaming sword,” because whoever desires to return to paradise must burn away all the desires of this life with the fire of the Holy Spirit and cut off with the sword of God’s word whatever harmful and useless thing he sees within himself.

Another translation has “opposite the paradise,” because a violent opposition came upon Adam. For blessedness and misery are not slightly opposed. The one who had previously been blessed became miserable, and the one who had originally been created immortal became mortal.

“Cherubim” is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” Therefore the cherubim and the flaming sword are placed before paradise, so that it may be understood that we can return to paradise through knowledge of heavenly discipline and through the tribulations and labors of the present life.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0068C] Verse 1. “Now Adam knew his wife.” He is not said to have known his wife while placed in paradise, but only after he had been expelled from paradise. Because he was going to sin and beget mortal children, no one from his offspring was born in paradise, which is the place of life.

“She conceived and bore, saying: I have acquired a man through God.” In Hebrew, *Cain* is said to mean “to possess.” Therefore, since the mother said, “I have acquired a man,” he was called Cain, meaning “possession.”

Verse 2. “And again she bore his brother Abel.” Abel is interpreted as “mourning” or “vapor.” There was mourning for his parents when he was killed by his brother, and he quickly perished or disappeared like vapor.

Verse 4. “The Lord looked upon Abel and upon his offerings.” In what way did the Lord look upon Abel’s offerings? By sending fire from heaven, evidently, by which the sacrifice was consumed. The translation of Theodotion shows this when it says: “The Lord set fire upon Abel, but upon Cain he did not set fire.” In this way it is proved that the offering pleased God.

But it may be asked why God looked upon Abel’s offerings, but did not look upon Cain’s offerings. Is an animal offering more pleasing than a sacrifice to God from the fruits of the earth? It must be understood that God pays more attention to the minds of those offering than to what is offered. Therefore he looked upon it—that is, he accepted it—and Abel’s offering pleased him.

Another explanation may also be given: he detested the greed in Cain’s labor. There are some who toil more than is right in their work, not merely so that they may have enough, but so that they may amass every surplus and everything less necessary. God saw this excessive labor in Cain, and therefore did not look upon his offering. The pastoral art, however, is simple and harmless; the holy Fathers are read to have possessed it after Abel.

Verses 5–6. “And his face fell to the ground. And the Lord said to him: Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen?” That is: “Why are you tormented by envy and not covered with a good shame?” For as Wisdom says: “There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings glory” (Eccli. IV, 25).

Verse 7. “Sin will immediately be present at the door.” That is, it will be open to everyone, and you will be accompanied by it as though by a doorkeeper. “But it will be under you,” that is, its desire will be under your power, “and you will rule over it.”

The meaning is: Because you are capable of reason and know what is good and what is evil, you ought to rule over sin, so that evil will does not proceed as far as wicked action. This is what the Septuagint says: “You have sinned? Be quiet.” That is: “Have you sinned in your will? Cease from evil action.”

Another translation has: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, the Lord says: You have sinned.” Cain offered rightly, since he offered to God, who alone is to be worshiped and to whom sacrifice is to be made. But he did not divide rightly, giving what was his to God while giving himself to himself, although God desires us rather than what is ours. For everyone who offers something must consider to whom he is offering, what he is offering, when he is offering, and who he himself is who offers.

Verse 8. “And Cain said to his brother Abel:” [Col. 0069C] But [Note: [Col. 0069D] Both manuscripts have this; perhaps it should read *scilicet*, “namely.”] what he had heard from God: for it is superfluous.

“Let us go outside.” For there was not yet a house or temple in which sacrifice could be offered to God.

“And Cain rose up against his brother and killed him.” According to tradition, with a shepherd’s staff.

Allegorically, the malice of the Jews is represented in Cain’s crime. Cain killed his younger brother Abel, and the Jews killed Christ, the head of the lesser people, that is, of the Gentiles, just as he himself had said to the Father through the Psalmist: “You will appoint me as head of the nations” (Ps. XVII, 44).

Verse 9. “And the Lord said to Cain: Where is Abel your brother?” The Lord asks, not because he was learning what he did not know, but to provoke him at least in this way to confession, or to condemn him, if he denied it, with a just punishment.

But he, multiplying sins, replied proudly, saying: “I do not know. Am I my brother’s keeper?” As though his crime could be hidden from God, before whom all things are naked and open (Hebr. VI, 13).

Verse 10. “Behold, the voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth.” Because he refused to confess, he is now rebuked with a just reprimand when it is said: “What have you done? Behold the voice,” and so forth. The voice of Abel’s blood is the power of great justice, which was seeking vengeance and retribution for the blood of the innocent.

Verse 11. “Now therefore you will be cursed upon the earth, which has opened its mouth.” In Adam’s transgression, as we have already said, the earth was cursed, not Adam himself. But in Cain’s sin Cain himself is cursed, because although he knew of the guilt of the first transgression, he did not fear it, but in addition committed the crime of homicide, or rather fratricide.

Allegorically, we have already said above that Cain signifies the Jews and Abel Christ. In this passage the earth signifies the Church, which receives the blood of Christ poured out with an open mouth—that is, with the desire of great devotion—for eternal salvation.

Verse 12. “You will be a wanderer and a fugitive upon the earth.” This is plainly true of those who are wanderers and fugitives throughout the entire Roman world and have no fixed dwelling anywhere.

Verse 13. “And Cain said: My iniquity is greater than that I should deserve pardon.” Adding sins to sins, he despaired and did not believe that he could be saved or obtain forgiveness. This is the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit that will be forgiven neither here nor in the future (Luke XII, 10). For one who despairs either thinks that God does not wish to forgive or that he cannot. If he cannot, he is not omnipotent, because there is something he cannot do. But if he does not wish to forgive—which it is also impious to think—then he begrudges salvation to the human race.

Verse 14. “Behold, you cast me out today from the face of the earth.” That is: “You judge me unworthy in your sight. And from your face,” because, hating my own life, I will withdraw myself from your presence.

“Everyone who finds me will kill me.” Because, from the trembling of my body and the agitation of my frenzied mind, whoever finds me will recognize that I deserve to be killed.

Verse 15. “By no means will this happen.” That is, “You will not die quickly, as you wish.”

“He will be punished sevenfold.” That is, fully and completely. The number seven is customarily used to signify perfection. Hence the Lord often threatens: “I will strike you seven times” (Lev. XXVI, 24), that is, completely.

Accordingly, according to the Septuagint, it is read: “Whoever kills Cain will pay seven retributions.” The meaning is: It will not happen as you wish, namely, that by a swift death you should escape the torment of a long life. Rather, by living for a long time, until the seventh generation, whoever kills you will finally pay—that is, bring to an end—the seven retributions that are upon you. This does not mean that the person who killed him would be punished sevenfold, but that by killing him he would bring to an end those seven retributions, that is, the complete retributions by which Cain was tormented while living for a long time. This is according to the Septuagint.

But according to the Hebrew truth, “he will be punished sevenfold” means fully and completely; by this he warns lest anyone dare to repeat homicide.

“The Lord placed a sign upon Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him.” This was because he was a wanderer and a fugitive upon the earth—or, according to the Septuagint, “groaning and trembling.”

Allegorically, God placed a sign upon the Jews so that no one would kill them, namely, the very law that they carried for their own condemnation and our deliverance. Because of this sign no one killed them. For neither pagan persecution nor even the tranquility that now exists under Christianity prevented them from using their own laws and living according to their own custom.

This is what the Son says to the Father through the Psalmist: “Do not kill them, lest they at any time forget my people; scatter them by your power” (Ps. LVIII, 12).

Verse 16. “And Cain went out from the face of the Lord and dwelt as a fugitive in the land east of Eden.” Eden is interpreted as “feasts” or “delights.” The Septuagint says: “He dwelt in the land of Naith.” But Naith is not the name of this place. It is interpreted as “unstable” or “wandering,” and therefore he is said to have dwelt in the land of Naith because he wandered about unstable and wavering.

Verse 17. “Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch; and he built a city and called its name after the name of his son Enoch.” Because he was in fear and trembling, perhaps he built a city so that he might be protected there in hiding.

But it may be asked with whom he built it, if there were no more human beings than those whom Scripture mentions. It must be understood that many more already existed at that time, because by living for a long time they begat many children. Nor is this surprising, since the children of Israel are also read to have multiplied so greatly during forty years that their army could not be numbered.

“He built a city,” it says, “which he called Enoch after the name of his son.” Enoch is interpreted as “dedication.” It should be noted that in the first generation Enoch, that is, “dedication,” was born from Cain, because the people of the reprobate dedicate themselves in the first generation—that is, in the present life—adding themselves to this world and wishing, if it were possible, to remain in it forever.

Hence he also built a city, because the reprobate have their happiness and, as it were, their foundation here, whereas the Apostle says of himself and those like him: “We do not have here a lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come” (Hebr. XIII, 14).

From Seth, however, Enoch [elsewhere Enos or Henos] was born in the seventh generation, because the saints who belong to the city of God dedicate themselves to another life, that is, to the future life, which will be revealed after the six ages of the world in the seventh generation, that is, in the assembly or resurrection of the righteous.

Lamech was the first to commit bigamy, because he had two wives, and for this reason he perished in the Flood.

Verses 19–21. “The name of the one was Ada, and the name of the other Sella. And Ada bore Jubal. He was the father of those who play the cithara and the organ.”

Concerning him Josephus says:

> “Jubal loved music; he praised the psaltery and the cithara. And lest what he had discovered should ever slip from human memory, he inscribed it on two columns, one of brick and the other of stone, after he had heard Adam proclaim that there would be two floods and the destruction of all things.”

Verse 22. “Sella bore Tubal-cain.” Josephus also says the following about him:

> “Tubal-cain practiced the arts of war with distinction and taught the art of working iron; he also invented certain things that pertain to the desire of the eyes.”

“The sister of Tubal-cain was Noema.” It should be noted that no woman is recorded as having been born in the generation of Seth; but in Cain’s generation the sister of Tubal-cain is recorded as having been born. By this is signified the wantonness and recklessness that dominate the reprobate in the present life.

Verse 23. “I have killed a man for my wound, and a young man for my bruise.” The Hebrews explain this passage as follows. Lamech, having lived for a long time, had developed dimness of the eyes and could not see. He had a certain young man who guided his steps. One day, while he was engaged in hunting, he directed his weapons toward the place indicated by the young man. By chance he struck Cain, who was hiding among the bushes, because the young man had pointed him out, and Lamech had thought that he was a wild animal. But when he realized that he had killed a human being, he became angry with the young man and killed him as well.

This is what follows: “I have killed a man,” that is, Cain, “for my wound,” because I too will be wounded and killed on his account; “and a young man for my bruise,” because I will also be condemned on his account.

Verse 24. “Sevenfold vengeance will be exacted for Cain, but for Lamech seventy-sevenfold.” As sin increases, so too does vengeance. There were seventy-seven souls from Lamech’s line whom we read perished in the Flood.

Allegorically, Lamech represents this world, whose sin, through Adam’s transgression, was so great that it could not be expiated except in the seventy-seventh generation, when Christ came through the Virgin.

Verse 25. “Adam knew his wife again, and she bore a son and called his name Seth.” Seth is interpreted as “placing,” which in Greek is called *thesis*, an etymology derived from what the father said: “God has placed another seed for me in place of Abel.”

In another sense, Seth is interpreted as “resurrection,” because he arose in the place of his murdered brother.

Verse 26. “And to Seth also a son was born, whom he called Enos.” Enos is interpreted as “human being.” This man began to invoke the name of the Lord, that is, to worship God and implore him, although the opinion of the Hebrews is different. For they say that idols were first made at that time and worshiped as God.

## CHAPTER V

Verse 5. “And all the days that Adam lived were nine hundred and thirty years.” They report that after Abel’s death Adam vowed never again to know his wife or beget a son. But the word of God came to him so that he might break this vow, because the Son of God could not assume flesh for the redemption of the human race [Note: [Col. 0071D] Both manuscripts read: “and assume flesh.”]. Cain was unworthy for God to be born as a human being from his line. Hence he is not read to have begotten anyone before Seth; after Seth, however, he is said to have begotten sons and daughters.

[Col. 0072D] Verse 22. “Enoch walked with God.” That is, he imitated God.

Verse 31. “Now Noah, when he was five hundred years old, begot Shem, Ham, and Japheth.” Here we must contemplate a profound mystery. Noah is tenth from Adam after Seth. For the number ten signifies the perfection of the elect, because it is the number of the first counting-board, that is, four, and counting cannot proceed beyond it unless one returns again to unity.

Therefore, if we add Noah’s two sons, Shem and Ham [Note: [Col. 0072D] Perhaps *Ham* should be deleted], and Japheth, with Ham rejected, they become twelve. The number twelve is sacred in the twelve patriarchs and especially in the twelve apostles. It consists of the parts of seven, which are three and four. This is the perfection of the righteous, preserved in the line descending from Seth.

Let us consider the imperfection of those who descended from Adam through Cain. From Adam to Lamech there are six generations; if we add his three sons and his fourth daughter, they become eleven. The number eleven signifies sin, because it is a transgression of ten. Behold, here the imperfection and wickedness of Cain’s generation shines forth.

“And all the days of Lamech were seven hundred and seventy-seven years.” This is according to the Hebrew truth. But according to the Septuagint there is a very great error in the number, since Lamech is found to have lived fourteen years after the Flood.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0073B] Verse 1. “And when human beings had begun to multiply upon the earth, the sons of God, seeing the daughters of human beings, saw that they were beautiful.” He called the sons of Seth “sons of God,” because, as long as they preserved themselves uncorrupted in their father’s holiness, they deserved to be honored by this name, so that they might be called sons of God. But after they joined themselves, overcome by the pleasure of the flesh, to Cain’s condemned stock, they began to imitate its wickedness.

Some have wished to interpret the sons of God as evil angels. For there are certain wicked demons associated with women. But it is better, as we have said, to understand the sons of God as the sons of Seth.

Verse 3. “And God said: My Spirit will not remain in human beings forever, because they are flesh.” Another translation has: “My Spirit will not judge human beings forever, because they are flesh.”

According to this translation, the meaning is as follows: Because human beings are fragile and clothed in mortal flesh, I will not judge them forever so that they should perish eternally; rather, in the present I will render to them what they deserve. From this we understand that there is great mercy when he does not allow sinners to act according to their own decision, but recalls them to himself by chastising them.

Hence he also threatens certain sinners: “I will not visit your daughters when they commit adultery” (Hos. IV, 14). And elsewhere: “Let each one walk after the perversity of his heart” (Jer. XIII, 12). Hence also the Psalmist says: “The sinner has provoked the Lord; according to the abundance of his anger he will not seek” (Ps. X, 4).

Conversely, concerning those who are acceptable to God it is said: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 33).

“And their days will be one hundred and twenty years.” Some think that the human lifespan was reduced to one hundred and twenty years after the Flood. But this should not be understood in that way. For we read that many people lived for more years after the Flood.

This should therefore be understood as follows. Wishing to bring the Flood upon sinners, God gave them a period of one hundred and twenty years in which to practice repentance. But since they refused to repent and persisted in their wickedness, God did not wait for them until the allotted period of one hundred and twenty years; rather, the Flood occurred in the hundredth year.

Verse 4. “Now there were giants upon the earth in those days.” He calls “giants” those who were born from the mixed stock of Seth and Cain: monstrous in body, proud in strength, and uncivilized in character. He calls such people giants, that is, “sons of the earth.”

Verse 5. “And God, seeing that the wickedness of human beings was great upon the earth and that every thought of their heart was directed toward evil, repented that he had made human beings.” No repentance falls upon God. For God once and firmly and steadfastly arranges all things. But Scripture, speaking in our manner, says that God repented, because he appears to change his work, while his unchangeable will and disposition remain.

For however things may turn out—whether they remain as they were created or are changed—God foresaw this before the ages by an unchangeable reason.

Verse 8. “But Noah found grace before God.” Noah is interpreted as “rest.”

[Col. 0074B] Verse 9. “He was righteous and perfect.” If no one can live without sin, how is Noah said to have been righteous and perfect? The saints of God are perfect according to a certain measure of their own, but they are not yet perfect in the way in which they are to be perfected. Hence it is rightly said: “in his generations.” In the present life they can be perfect according to their measure, with the grace of God assisting them. In that blessed life, in which they will neither wish nor be able to sin, they will be perfect in a very different way.

Verse 11. “The earth was corrupt.” That is, every human being. Because everything was created for the sake of the human being, when the human being sinned, everything is therefore said to have been corrupted.

Verse 12. “All flesh,” that is, every human being, “had corrupted its way.” That is, it had perverted its actions.

“And I will destroy them together with the earth.” Why does he say “together with the earth,” since the earth was by no means destroyed in the Flood? The teachers say that after the Flood it was no longer of such strength and fertility as it had been before the Flood. Hence the eating of meat was also granted to human beings after the Flood. Before the Flood they ate fruits and vegetables. Therefore human beings were destroyed with the earth because its former strength and grace had been lost.

Verse 14. “Make yourself an ark from smoothed wood.” That is, from strong and imperishable wood. This is also what the Septuagint says: “From squared wood,” that is, strong wood.

“You will make compartments in the ark.” He calls “compartments” those in which the various kinds of animals would be received. The Septuagint says: “You will make the ark two-chambered and three-chambered.” The two-chambered part was in the lower sections, and the three-chambered part in the upper sections.

Therefore the ark was divided into five compartments. The first compartment, that is, the lowest, was for dung, where the animals’ excrement flowed away, so that those in the ark, especially the human beings, would not be harmed by the stench. The second was a storeroom, where various foods for the animals were kept. The third was for wild and savage animals and serpents. The fourth was for beasts of burden and tame animals. The fifth, that is, the highest, was for human beings and birds.

The door that is later described as having been in the side of the ark is believed to have been located where the two-chambered and three-chambered sections joined, between the storeroom and the dwelling of the wild animals.

“And you will coat it with bitumen.” Bitumen, which in Greek is called *asphaltos*, from which the Asphaltite Lake takes its name, is an extremely adhesive substance. Whatever it touches never becomes worm-eaten, nor can it be dissolved by any force of rains or by the blowing of winds.

Verse 15. “Three hundred cubits.” We should not be surprised at this if we know that it was measured by a geometrical cubit which, as Origen says, contains six human cubits.

The shape of the ark was as follows. Its foundation was square, though its length and width were unequal; gradually rising from the corners, it was elevated upward into a narrow form until its top was completed in a cubit of width and length. It was ten times as long as it was high, and six times as long as it was wide, in the likeness of the human body.

For if we measure a human being lying face down or face up, he will be ten times as long from head to feet as he is high from back to abdomen, and six times as long as he is wide from the right side to the left.

Verse 16. “You will make a window in the ark.” A window was made at the top of the ark so that Noah would have an opening through which he could send things out, as he later did when he sent out the dove and the raven. The Hebrews report that this window was made of crystal.

Mystically, Noah, a righteous and perfect man in name and deed, signifies Christ. For his name is interpreted as “rest,” because Christ will lead his elect, when the labors of this age have ended, into eternal rest. He alone is truly righteous and perfect, concerning whom the Apostle says: “So that he himself might be just and justifying the one who is of faith” (Rom. III, 26).

Noah may also represent those placed over the Church, or even the entire household of Christ, namely, his members, who are saved through the wood of the cross and the water of baptism.

The ark is the holy Church, constructed from smoothed wood—that is, from the saints who will live forever. And just as there were different kinds of animals in the ark, so there are different kinds of human beings in the Church.

The door in the side signifies the wound in Christ’s side, from which the Church itself is constituted together with the sacraments of blood and water.

Verse 19. “Of all living creatures you shall bring two into the ark.” A question is raised concerning the small animals—not only such as mice and lizards, but also such as flies, beetles, scarabs, and fleas—whether this number could be preserved among them. But it should be understood that those creatures which are not generated by mating, but arise from the moisture of the earth or from the decay of corpses or of other [Col. 0075D] things, did not need to be kept in the ark. This is also suggested by the wording: “Of the birds according to their kind, and of the beasts according to their kind.” Nor was it necessary to observe this number in the creatures that live in houses, such as fleas, mice, and flies, which are understood to have been more numerous in houses at that time. Likewise, it must not be said that the animals born from the mingling of different kinds, such as mules, hinnies, and other creatures of this sort, were in the ark. Again, a question is raised concerning those living creatures that live commonly both in water and on land: whether they are believed to have been in the ark, or, if they were not, how they could have survived—for example, otters and sea calves. But concerning these it can be believed that they were outside [Col. 0076A] the ark; nevertheless, they had prepared enclosures outside the ark into which they could withdraw, as though into dry places. The same should be thought concerning sea- and river-birds, since at times they were in the water and then again withdrew into prepared little shelters outside the ark.

Verse 21. “You shall take food of every kind.” Here a question is raised concerning animals that eat meat: how did they live in the ark for an entire year, since meat could not have been preserved unspoiled for so long? The answer is that there are certain animals that eat meat but, when necessity requires it, can live on fruits and produce of various kinds, especially figs and chestnuts.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0076B]

Verse 2. “Of all living creatures take seven.” When he says “seven and seven,” we should understand not a doubled seven—that is, fourteen—but only seven. Similarly, where it says “two and two,” we should understand not four but two. “Male and female.” Here it should also be noted that clean animals are brought into the ark in an odd number, that is, seven, whereas unclean animals are brought in an even number, because an odd number presents a certain appearance of virtue, while an even number is a sign of weakness and vice. The clean animals are said to have been brought in greater numbers, namely seven, so that when Noah came out of the ark he would have some to sacrifice to the Lord and some for himself and his sons to eat.

Verse 7. “And Noah and his sons entered the ark.” It should be observed that when he entered the ark, he and his sons entered separately, and their wives separately. For it says: “He entered the ark, he and his sons”; then: “his wife and the wives of his sons.” But when they came out, the men are read to have come out together with their wives. For it says: “Noah came out, and his wife.” This is what Solomon says: “A time for embracing, and a time to be far from embraces” (Ecclesiasticus III, 5). They entered the ark at God’s command, evidently without human agency.

Verse 11. “In the six hundredth year, in the second month.” That is, in the month of Nisan, which the Latins call May. For among them the first month is April. “The floodgates.” That is, the windows of heaven. The windows of heaven are called clouds, which were opened so that unusual and heavier rains might be poured down from them. For “floodgates” properly refers to the mouths of the Nile, but the word is used figuratively for all windows. “The fountains of the great abyss were also broken open,” so that they did not flow gradually in their customary manner, but covered the surface of the earth with a sudden inundation.

Verse 16. “The Lord shut him in from outside.” What the hand of man could not do, divine power accomplished by shutting him in from outside and not allowing the waters to enter.

Verse 20. “The water was fifteen cubits higher than the mountains.” Some say that this could not have happened literally, but that it was written on account of some symbol or mystery. They say that it could not have happened for water of such a dense nature to rise to the upper region of the air, especially because of Mount Olympus, whose height is so great that no winds are able to blow there and no clouds can cover its summit. But those who admit this do not consider that the mountain itself is earth. We know that earth is more massive than water. Therefore, if heavier earth could rise, why could lighter water not do so?

## CHAPTER VIII

Verse 1. “He brought a spirit.” That is, a wind; or, as some wish, we should understand the sun, or the Holy Spirit, of whom it is said at the beginning: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters.” For he who in the beginning was borne over the waters in order to gather them together so that dry land might appear was now, by his own will and that of the whole Trinity, brought over the earth, so that he might rescue it from the invasion of the waters and restore to it its former beauty [Col. 0077B] and fertility.

Verse 8. “He sent out the raven, and the dove after it.” The Septuagint says that the raven, once sent out, did not return to the ark. Either it was caught by the waters and killed, or it clung to a corpse floating on the waters and perished because of its greed. For the earth was not yet dry, since it is said of the dove that it did not find a place where its foot could rest.

We have said above allegorically that the ark signifies the Church, which was three hundred cubits long, because the holy Church is saved through faith in the Lord’s cross and Passion. The length of three hundred cubits signifies the Lord’s Passion. For the letter Tau, which expresses this number, also has the shape of a cross. The width of fifty cubits signifies the glory of Christ’s resurrection, which was proclaimed through the apostles on the fiftieth day, Pentecost; through hope in it the Church is enlarged. The height of thirty cubits signifies that the same Church would be spread through the three parts of the world, Africa, Asia, and Europe. For ten multiplied three times rises to the number thirty.

This Church contains together both the raven and the dove, that is, the good and the wicked. But the raven, sent out from the ark, does not return, because the reprobate, although they are held within the bosom of the Church through faith, nevertheless perish by clinging to the desires and allurements of the world. But the dove, returning to the ark, carries in its mouth a branch of an olive tree with green leaves, because the saints, rejoicing in simplicity, carry the hands of peace in their mouths, and say with the Psalmist: “With those who hated peace I was peaceful” (Psalm CXIX, 7).

Verse 14. “In the second month.” That is, in May. “On the twenty-seventh day of the month.” Let us examine this passage more carefully. We said above that Noah spent a year in the ark and came out on the same day on which he had entered. He entered on the seventeenth day of the second month; now it says that he came out on the twenty-seventh day of that same month. But it should be understood that if you add eleven days to the present day, the moon will be in the same phase on that day after a year. Therefore, when Noah entered on the seventeenth day of the moon, it was the seventeenth day of the second month; and so, after a year, when eleven days had been added, it was the twenty-seventh day, or the twenty-seventh day of the moon.

[Col. 0078A]

Verse 22. “They shall not rest.” Rather, they shall serve man.

## CHAPTER IX

Verse 2. “Your terror and dread.” God did not place man over man, but over the living creatures. For he did not say, “Let your terror be upon human beings,” but “upon the animals of the earth.” Therefore, as Blessed Gregory says, it is excessive pride to wish to be feared by one’s equal. Nature created all human beings equal, but by the difference of their merits, according to God’s just yet hidden judgment, it subjected some to others. “All the fish have been delivered into your hand.” That is, into your power. “And everything that moves shall be food for you.” After the flood, the eating of meat was permitted. Previously they had fed on fruits and vegetables. But because in the flood the earth had lost the power of its fertility, God, taking human weakness into consideration, permitted man to eat meat.

Verse 4. “Except that you shall not eat flesh with its blood.” Here, as also in the law of Moses, the eating of blood is prohibited. In the Acts of the Apostles, too, the Gentiles were forbidden fornication, things sacrificed to idols, what was strangled, and blood (Acts XV, 20), because the seat of the soul is in the blood; therefore the eating of blood is prohibited.

Verse 5. “I will require blood from the hand of beasts.” He calls cruel and savage people “beasts.” “From the hand of a man and of his brother.” He calls every human being a brother because of their common nature.

Verse 13. “I will set my bow.” The bow has two colors: blue on one side and fiery on the other. By this, two floods are signified: one of water, which has already passed, and the other of fire, which is believed to come at the end of the world. Thus the blue color is seen on the outside, while the fiery color is on the inside. Mystically, the bow, which is formed when the sun illuminates a cloud, signifies that the one who has seen the true Sun, Christ, through the cloud can be saved from the flood—that is, from eternal condemnation. This means the one who has believed in his Passion and resurrection, foretold through the prophets.

Verse 18. “Therefore there were three sons of Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.” Shem is interpreted as “name” or “named”; Ham as “cunning”; Japheth as “expanse.” Mystically, Shem and Japheth signify the faithful from both peoples who believe in Christ. Ham signifies heretics, and thus he is rightly interpreted as “cunning.” Heretics are cunning not through wisdom but through wickedness, because they seek to deceive the simple in the Church.

Mystically, Noah, whose name is interpreted as “rest,” signifies Christ, who was made drunk with the cup of his Passion. He was stripped, because then the weakness of his mortality was revealed, and, as the prophet had foretold, “there his strength was hidden” (Habakkuk III, 4).

Verse 21. “And he was uncovered in his tent.” That is, among the Jewish people, among the members of his own household. Ham, his son, who reported his father’s nakedness to his brothers, designates the Jews, who read in the prophets long beforehand about Christ’s Passion and announced that it would come. But when they saw fulfilled what they had long foretold, they preferred to mock rather than believe.

Shem [Col. 0079A], the firstborn, and Japheth, the youngest, signify those who were in the primitive Church—namely, the apostles and those who believed from the Gentiles. Ham, in the middle, signifies the Jews, who refused to receive faith in the Lord either first with the apostles or later with the Gentiles. Shem and Japheth, however, did not wish to look upon their father’s nakedness when it was reported to them, but covered him with a cloak, because the faithful do not despise the mysteries of Christ’s Passion together with the Jews, but honor them with due reverence. And rightly do they carry the cloak on their shoulders, because they do not await that Passion as something still to come, but believe that it has been fulfilled.

Verse 24. “When Noah awoke from his wine, having learned”—that is, through the prophetic spirit—“what his younger son had done to him, he said: ‘Cursed be Canaan.’” It should be noted that he does not curse Ham himself but his son Canaan. The name is interpreted as “their movement”; from him the Canaanites were later named, whom the Lord drove out before the face of the children of Israel. Therefore, the cursing of Canaan was a prophecy, because that nation was to be expelled from the place of its habitation.

Verses 26, 27. “Blessed be the Lord God. May God enlarge Japheth.” From Shem came the patriarchs, the prophets, and the other Fathers of the Old Testament; from Japheth came the multitude of the Gentiles who believe in Christ. Japheth was enlarged because the multitude of believers from the Gentiles grew within him. He dwelt in the tents of Shem because the Gentiles who believe in Christ followed the grace possessed by the earlier Fathers and now rest with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob by imitating their faith and good works.

“And let Canaan be his servant.” That is, the Jews now serve the faithful from both peoples, because they preserve the books of the divine Scriptures not for themselves but for those faithful, and are, as it were, their scribes.

## CHAPTER X

Verse 2. “The sons of Japheth.” He now mentions the seventy-two nations that were spread abroad from the three sons of Noah after the flood. First he speaks of Japheth, the younger, from whom seven sons were born who occupied the northern region from the Taurus and Amanus [Note: [Col. 0079D] Codex Tegernseensis reads “Taurus, Etham, and Eidon.” Perhaps read “Amanus.”] mountains of Cilicia and Assyria.

Gomer, as Josephus says, refers to the Galatians, who in Latin are called Gallo-Greeks. Magog, whom some think to be the Massagetae. Madai, the Medes. Javan, the Ionians, who are also the Greeks; from them come the Ionian Sea and the name “Ionic” for the fifth of their languages. Tubal, the Iberians whom we call Spaniards. Meshech, the Cappadocians, whose capital city is still called Mazaca. Tiras, the Thracians.

Verse 3. “The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz.” These are whom the Greeks call the Rheginians. “Riphath,” the Paphlagonians. “Togarmah,” the Phrygians.

Verse 4. “The sons of Javan” [Note: [Col. 0079D] Both codices read: “Laban, son.”] “Elishah,” from whom came the Elishans, that is, the Greeks, who are also called Hellenes. “Tarshish,” the Cilicians, whose city is the famous Tarsus, the birthplace of the apostle Paul. “Kittim,” the Citians, whose city is still called Citium. “Dodanim” [Note: [Col. 0080D] Codex Garsten reads: “Dodamin. Tegerus. Dodamim.”], the Rhodians.

Verse 5. “Each according to his language.” This must be understood by prolepsis, that is, by anticipation. For the division of languages had not yet taken place.

Verse 6. “The sons of Ham: Cush.” This is Ethiopia. “Mizraim,” Egypt. “Put,” Libya; from this the river of Mauretania is also called Put, and the whole region is called the land of Put. “Canaan,” from whom came the Canaanites.

Verse 7. “The sons of Cush: Seba.” That is, the region of Arabia that produces incense. “Havilah,” a part of western Ethiopia. “Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca.” Their names have fallen out of use, and we do not know what places now bear them. “The sons of Raamah: Sheba.” This Sheba is different from the one mentioned above, and the distinction appears in Scripture. For the former is written with Sin, while this one is written with Samekh. Indeed, in the psalm where we sing, “The kings of Arabia and Sheba” (Psalm LXXI, 10), the Hebrew has: “The kings of Sheba and Sheba.” “Dedan” [Col. 0080B] is the farthest region of Ethiopia.

Verse 8. “Cush begot Nimrod” [Note: [Col. 0080D] Both codices read: “Menroth.”] Josephus says of him that, from a new desire for kingship, he seized tyrannical power, worshiped fire as a god, and himself became the originator of the building of the tower whose summit would touch heaven.

Verse 9. “And he was a mighty hunter before the Lord.” For he hunted souls to destruction, making man worship fire. Another translation says: “against the Lord.”

Verse 10. “Babylon” is interpreted as “confusion,” because the confusion of languages took place there. “And Harath” [Vulgate: Arach]. This is Edessa, a city of Mesopotamia. “Archath” [Vulgate: Achad], which is now called Nisibis. “And Calneh.” This is Seleucia, named after Seleucus, king of Asia. “In the land of Shinar.” That is, in Babylonia, where there are bitumen wells.

[Col. 0080C]

Verse 11. “From that land.” That is, from Shinar. “Asshur went out.” That is, the Assyrian empire, which first existed under Ninus. “And he built Nineveh.” Nineveh is a city of the Assyrians. Ninus, the son of Belus, built Ninus, which the Hebrews called Ninniveh. It is interpreted, on account of repentance, as “beautiful.”

Verse 13. “But Mizraim begot the Ludim.” Ludim is Libya, which was previously called Put.

Verse 15. “Canaan, the son of Ham, begot Sidon.” From him came Sidon, a city of Phoenicia.

Verse 18. “The Arvadites.” These are the people who held the island of Aradus.

Verse 19. “Sodom and Gomorrah.” These cities are known for the destruction of their overthrow. “The Samaritenes.” From them came Samaria, which is called by this name both among the Assyrians and among the Hebrews. [Col. 0080D] It was also called Antioch or Epiphany. “The Hamathites.” These names are unknown, either because these peoples were destroyed in the Ethiopian war or because it is unknown what names they now bear.

Verse 21. “From Shem also were born those whom we shall now mention.” He was the father of all the sons of Eber and the elder brother of his younger brother Japheth. He is spoken of last because the account was about to speak of his descendants and follow his line.

Verse 22. “The sons of Shem: Elam.” From him came the Elamites, that is, the rulers of Persia. “Asshur.” It was said above of him [Col. 0081A] that he built Nineveh. “Arphaxad.” From him came the Chaldeans. “Lud.” From him came the Lydians. “Aram.” From him came the Syrians.

Verse 23. “The sons of Aram: Uz.” From him came the land of Uz mentioned in Job, which the Septuagint calls the land of Ausitis, that is, the southern land. “Hul.” From him came the Armenians. “Gether.” From him came the Acarnanians. “Mash.” The Septuagint calls them Mosoch, that is, the Maeonians.

Verse 25. “Two sons were born to Eber.” Eber means “one who crosses over”; from him came the Hebrews, those who cross over. The true Hebrews are those who pass from present things to future things and from transient things to things that endure. “Peleg,” meaning “division.” In his time the division of languages took place.

## CHAPTER XI

Verse 1. “The earth was of one language.” That is, of the Hebrew language, which is believed to have remained after the division of languages in the family of Eber. In this language also the Son of God preached when he came to human beings. For it was fitting that in the same language in which Adam had heard the devil’s persuasion, he should receive the Savior’s preaching. Nor should it be said that God did something new when the division of languages took place; rather, he divided modes and forms of speech according to different understandings. Hence the same words are found with different meanings among different nations. For *alma* means “secret” among the Hebrews, but “holy” among the Latins. Stars are called *stellae* by the Latins and *ferrea* by the Greeks. The Greek reads: *rhabdo sidera* (the sense of this corrupt or transliterated phrase is uncertain).

Verse 4. “Let us make a tower for ourselves.” They feared that another flood might occur, and therefore, under the leadership of Nimrod, they wished to build a very high tower in which they could be saved if the flood happened again. For bitumen could not be dissolved by water. Indeed, nothing can dissolve it after it has dried except menstrual blood.

Verse 5. “He descended to see.” God is said to descend when he accommodates himself to human perceptions or actions, as he said to Moses: “Seeing, I have seen the affliction of my people, and I have descended to deliver them” (Exodus III, 8). And it was said concerning the Sodomites: “I will descend and see whether they have completed in action the outcry that has come to me” (Genesis XVIII, 21). Note also that in what follows the mystery of the Trinity is commended when he says: “Let us descend and confuse.”

Mystically, this tower signifies the pride of the world, or also the arrogance of heretics who wish to build against God a tower of perverse doctrine. It is rightly called the tower of Babel, that is, of confusion. They set out from the East because they abandoned the true Sun. They found the plain of Shinar, which is interpreted as “stench” or “shaking off of the teeth,” because the doctrines of heretics do not possess the good fragrance of Christ but stench, and they lost the teeth with which they might have ground the food of the word of God.

Verse 28. “Haran died, and Terah, in Ur of the Chaldeans.” The Hebrews relate that Abraham and Haran were brothers and, because they refused to worship fire, were thrown into the fire. Through God’s mercy Abraham emerged unharmed. Hence God often says to him: “I am God who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans.” Haran, however, was consumed by the fire. Therefore Ur is not the name of a place.

Verse 29. “They took wives.” Abraham took Sarai; she is the same as Jescah. For she had two names, that is, she was binominal. Her sister was Milcah, whom Nahor took as his wife.

## CHAPTER XII

Verse 3. “I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse those who curse you.” Two promises were made to Abraham. One was earthly, by which the land of Canaan was promised to him when it was said: “Go out from your land and from your kindred,” and so forth. The other, which is greater and spiritual, was expressed when it was said: “I will bless you,” so that he would be the father of Christ and of all who believe in Christ.

It should also be noted that he had already gone out from his land when it was said to him: “Go out from your land.” But in the earlier instance he went out bodily, whereas here he went out in mind and will. Perhaps he still retained a desire to return there when it was said: “Go out.”

“In you all your kindred shall be blessed” [Col. 0082B], because Christ was to be born from him, through whom all generations were to receive blessing.

Verse 4. “Abraham went out, and Lot with him.” That is, he determined in his mind never to return there. Earlier he had gone out bodily; now he went out in mind, at the Lord’s command.

Verse 6. “He passed through as far as the place of Shechem.” Shechem is a city that some incorrectly call Sichar. It is interpreted as “shoulder.” “The notable valley of the Pentapolis” refers to the region that is now the Salt Sea and is called the Dead Sea, as well as the Asphalt Lake and the Salt Lake.

Verse 7. “And the Lord appeared to Abraham.” The Lord rightly appeared to him who, renouncing idolatry, built an altar to the Lord.

Verse 8. “Having Bethel on the west and Hai on the east.” Bethel is a city in the tribe of Benjamin that was formerly called Laza, that is, “almond.” Hai is a city situated in the tribe of Judah. Bethel is interpreted as “house of God,” though later it was called Beth-aven, that is, “house of an idol.” Hai is interpreted as “eye” or “spring.” Therefore the patriarch, journeying toward the promised land, pitched his tent between Bethel and Hai, because all the saints, regenerated by the fountain of baptism and conducting the course of this life with vigilance, hasten toward God’s tabernacle and the heavenly city.

Verse 13. “Say, I beg you, that you are my sister.” Some ask why the holy patriarch wished to lie by saying that Sarah was his sister, rather than entrusting the matter to God, who could preserve both his life and her chastity. The point is that, as long as we have something that reason enables us to do, we should not tempt God but provide for our own salvation. He would in a certain way have tempted God if he had confessed her to be his wife, entrusting two things to God: his own life and her chastity. Therefore he did what he could for his life; what he could not do he entrusted to God, certain that, if God willed, he could preserve her modesty even before Pharaoh.

Verse 15. “She was taken into Pharaoh’s house.” Sarah may be excused in that she was taken into Pharaoh’s house unwillingly or under compulsion—not only because the body is not defiled without the consent of the mind, but also because this happened with the connivance and permission of her husband.

A further question is raised: how could she have remained untouched before Pharaoh for so long? For it says: “They treated Abraham well on her account, and he had cattle, sheep, and household servants.” But the account in the book of Esther is also useful for resolving this question, since the girls who were brought to King Ahasuerus were not immediately introduced to the king, but were kept for a year; for six months they were anointed with myrtle oil and for another six months with various perfumes (Esther II, 12). It could therefore have happened that Sarah remained undefiled during this long delay, while the Egyptians treated Abraham well, until God struck Pharaoh and, having learned that she was Abraham’s wife, restored her to him untouched.

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0083B]

Verse 1 and following. “He went up from Egypt, and he was very rich.” Another translation says: “He went up from Egypt, very heavily laden,” which agrees well with the mystery. For the riches of Egypt are burdensome to a holy man. Egypt is interpreted as “darkness” or “sorrow.”

Verse 8. “For we are brothers.” In sacred Scripture people are called brothers in three ways: by nature, as Jacob and Isaac; by kinship, as Abraham and Lot—for Lot was the son of Abraham’s brother Haran; and by nation, as all Jews are called brothers, as the law says: “If your Hebrew brother, being weakened, sells himself to you” (Leviticus XXV, 25).

It should also be observed how carefully the holy man pursued harmony, for the sake of preserving which he gave Lot the choice either that he himself should go one way while Lot remained, or, if Lot wished to withdraw elsewhere, that he himself would remain there.

Verse 10. “It was watered”—the verb is understood to mean “by the Jordan”—“like the paradise of the Lord.” From this we learn that paradise is earthly, since an earthly region is compared with it. This region was level and plain; it was watered by the river Jordan, just as Egypt was watered by the Nile. “And Lot chose for himself the region around the Jordan,” and so forth.

Allegorically, Lot with his shepherds represents heretics who, having abandoned the truth of ecclesiastical doctrine, choose for themselves beautiful and low-lying places because they do not think rightly about the truth of faith and do not ascend the mountain to God with Moses. Sodom is interpreted as “silent livestock.”

Verse 13. “The men of Sodom were very wicked and sinful before the Lord.” For they were also very wicked before human beings. Before God, the sinner is one who appears, in some fashion, just before human beings. Hence it is said of Zechariah and Elizabeth: “They were both righteous before the Lord their God” (Luke I, 6).

Verse 14. “Lift up your eyes.” That is, “look.” By these four regions of the earth the promised land is promised to him. When in some passages the sea is placed in the west, this is because the promised land lies by the western sea.

Verse 18. “Beside the valley of Mamre.” This is in Hebron. Hebron is a city in the tribe of Judah, which is also called by another name, Kiriath-arba, that is, “city of four.” For *kiriath* in Hebrew means “city,” and *arba*, “four.” There lie Adam the great, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The valley of Mamre was named after one of Abraham’s friends, who was called Mamre.

## CHAPTER XIV

Verse 1. “It happened at that time that Amraphel of Shinar,” and so forth. Four kings entered into war against five. Mystically, these four kings signify the hostile powers that seek to dominate the five senses of the body through the flesh, which consists of four humors.

Amraphel is interpreted as “he said that he should fall.” He is king of Shinar, which, as we said above, is interpreted as “shaking off” or “stench of the teeth.” He signifies heretics who deliberately sin and fall against God, speaking perversely and emitting the stench of obscene doctrine.

Arioch is interpreted as “drunk” or “drunkenness.” He signifies the Gentiles, who, drunk with the cup of error, worship creation instead of the Creator.

Chedorlaomer is interpreted as “beautiful” or “sheaf.” He is taken as signifying hypocrites who, although full of wickedness, are commonly thought beautiful because of their supposed virtues. He is king of the Elamites, that is, of the world or the globe.

Tidal is interpreted as “knowing the yoke.” He prefigures greed, whose yoke the greedy know how to bear willingly. He is king of the nations because greed rules the nations above all.

Verse 2. “They entered into war against Bara.” Bara is interpreted as “wickedness” or “creation.” He is king of the Sodomites, that is, of “silent livestock.”

Bera is interpreted as “in distress.” He is king of Gomorrah, which is interpreted as “a fearful people.”

Shinar [Vulgate: Sennaab] is interpreted as “shaking off” or “stench of the teeth,” and is the proper name of a man. He is king of Admah, which is interpreted as “earthly.”

Semeber is interpreted there as “destruction.” He is king of Zeboiim, which is interpreted as “bond of sorrow.”

Bela is interpreted as “little city,” “abyss,” or “precipitation.” It is also called “the terrified heifer.” The Hebrews relate that it collapsed in a third earthquake. It is the same as Senor, that is, “little.”

Verse 3. “The valley.” He calls it the wooded valley of Sodom, which is now the Salt Sea, namely a lake. After the burning by heavenly fire, it was turned into a lake; the Jordan falls into this lake and there loses its praiseworthy waters.

[Col. 0084D]

Verse 5. “They struck the Rephaim.” That is, the giants, for Rephaim is interpreted as “giants.” Carnaim and Guttim [Vulgate: Zuzim] are names of places and peoples. Seir is said by prolepsis, for that place was not yet called by this name. Seir is Edom, which is also the name of Esau and is interpreted as “hairy” or “shaggy,” because he was born like a hide; from him the region he possessed was called Seir.

Verse 7. “To the spring of Mishpat, which is Kadesh.” Kadesh is interpreted as “judgment.” There the murmuring people were judged. It is also interpreted as “holy” by *cata antiphrasin*, that is, by contrariety. He calls it the spring of the rock from which Moses brought forth water. “They struck the Amorite who dwelt in Hazazon-tamar.” Hazazon-tamar is interpreted as “city of palm trees.”

[Col. 0085A]

Verse 13. “In the valley of Mamre, the brother of Aner and Eshcol” [Note: [Col. 0085D] Both codices read: “brothers.”] Mamre is a proper name. These three had made a covenant with Abraham.

Verse 14. “He numbered his unencumbered household servants.” “Unencumbered,” that is, without wives. “He pursued them as far as Dan.” Dan is a spring from which the Jordan is formed. For there are two springs at the roots of Mount Lebanon, Jor and Dan, which, joined together, form the Jordan. Dan is interpreted as “judgment,” and Jor as “stream.” “As far as Phoenicia.” He means Syria by Phoenicia.

Allegorically, this war of Abraham against the four kings signifies the war between virtues and vices. Therefore Abraham, the father of faith and the first path of belief, fought and conquered the four kings for his brother Lot—not with a multitude of soldiers, but with three hundred and eighteen unencumbered household servants. In the same way, each of us should wage a spiritual war for his soul, as for his brother Lot, against the four kings—that is, against the spiritual forces of wickedness—with three hundred and eighteen unencumbered household servants, that is, with the help of the holy cross. This number is expressed in the letter Tau, which has the form of Christ.

Verse 18. “Melchizedek brought forth bread and wine.” They relate that this Melchizedek was Shem, the son of Noah, and, calculating the years, say that he lived until the time of Isaac. Salem itself is the city of Jerusalem, which has three names: Salem, Jebus, and Jerusalem. The Jebusites held it and called it Jebus; thus, with the names joined together, it was called Jerusalem.

“He was the priest of the Most High God.” All the firstborn from Noah onward were priests until Aaron, who was the first lawful [Col. 0085C] priest.

Mystically, Melchizedek, whose name is interpreted as “king of righteousness” or “king of peace,” signifies Christ, through whom we have been reconciled and who will justly judge the world at the end of time. The Apostle recalls his mystery when he says: “Without father and without mother, without genealogy” (Hebrews VI, 3).
