Melchizedek did have a father and mother, but Christ, whom he signifies, was without a father according to his humanity and without a mother according to his divinity. He was born from the Father without a mother and from his mother without a father.

“He brought forth bread and wine.” Here the change of the legal priesthood was already prefigured. For in the New Testament the sacrifice of victims has been transferred into the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood. Therefore this true priesthood of Christ is older than the legal priesthood. Melchizedek, like Abraham, was a Gentile, while Levi, the head of the legal priesthood, was still in Abraham’s loins; and he who later received tithes from the people was himself tithed in Abraham, while those who later blessed were blessed in Abraham by Melchizedek. The lesser is always blessed by the greater.

Verse 22. “Give me the souls.” That is: “Return the captives to me.” “The rest”—that is, “take the spoils for yourself.”

Verse 23. “From the thread of the warp.” We call the threads standing in the loom the warp, and the woof the thread that runs across the loom; it is also called a small strip of cloth.

## CHAPTER XV

Verse 2. “The son of the steward of the house.” That is, of the manager or administrator. Eliezer is interpreted as “my God is my helper.” They say that the city of Damascus was built by him.

Verse 3. “A servant born in the household.” This is a diminutive derived from *verna*, that is, “servant” or “household-born.”

Verse 5. “Count the stars. So shall your offspring be.” A twofold kind of offspring of Abraham is shown. Above he said: “Your offspring shall be like the sand of the sea.” Here he says: “So shall your offspring be like the stars of heaven,” because among that people some were to be carnal and earthly, compared with sand—dry and unproductive in good works—while others were spiritual and heavenly, shining with the splendor of virtues, whom he compares with the stars of heaven.

Verse 8. “How may I know that I shall possess it?” He asks for a sign, not as one doubting God’s promise, but asking in what manner this could happen. From this the custom arose among the Jews always to seek signs, as the Apostle says: “The Jews ask for signs” (I Corinthians I, 22).

Verse 9. “Take a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, and a three-year-old ram.” These things are clear according to the literal sense. Mystically, these animals designate the Jewish people, which traces its origin from Abraham. It is signified by the heifer because it bore the yoke of the law; by the foul-smelling and fetid she-goat because it was to become sinful; and by the ram, which is the leader of the flock, because at another time it held royal power with great strength.

When he says that the she-goat, heifer, or ram must be three years old, he shows that this people advanced to royal dignity through three periods of time under David. The first age was from Adam to Noah, the second from Noah to Abraham, and the third from Abraham to David.

The division of the animals, while the birds were not divided, signifies that all carnal people are subject to division. For they are divided by the scandals of sects. But spiritual people, signified by the birds, remain undivided because they suffer no corruption of faith.

Verse 11. “The birds that descended upon the carcasses” signify demons, who seek a kind of food for themselves from the division of carnal people. The fact that Abraham drove them away with his hand signifies that the holy Fathers, by the hand of holy action, protected that people from the attacks of spiritual or bodily enemies.

Verse 12. “When the sun was setting.” The setting of the sun signifies the end of the world, when through Antichrist a dark terror—that is, persecution or disturbance—will come.

Verse 13. “They will afflict them for four hundred years.” They were afflicted by the Egyptians, but only during the final part of that period.

**Verse 16. “In the fourth generation they shall return here.”** Moses says: “In the fifth generation the children of Israel came out of Egypt.” Here, however, he says: “In the fourth generation.” Both statements are true. For if you count through Levi, you will find the fourth generation as follows: Levi, Kohath; Kohath begot Amram; Amram begot Aaron; Aaron begot Eleazar; Eleazar begot Phinehas. Kohath entered Egypt with his father Levi, whereas Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, entered the promised land.

But if you wish to know how this happened in the fifth generation, you must count through Judah. Judah begot Perez; Perez begot Hezron; Hezron begot Amminadab; Amminadab begot Nahshon; Nahshon begot Salmon. Judah entered Egypt with his son Perez. Nahshon, however, was the leader of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness, and his son entered the promised land. [Col. 0087A]

**Verse 17. “When the sun had set.”** The setting of the sun signifies the end of the age; the dark gloom signifies the tribulation and distress that were to come. The furnace or fiery lamp passing through the divided pieces signifies the judgment to be carried out by fire, by which the elect are to be separated from the reprobate. [Col. 0087B]

**Verse 18. “From the river of Egypt.”** We should not understand the river of Egypt to mean the Nile, but rather the small river Rhinocolura, which divides Palestine and Egypt.

## Chapter 16

**Verse 1. “Now Sarah, Abraham’s wife, had not borne children.”** How can Abraham be excused for adultery, since he joined himself to a slave-woman while his wife was alive? But the law of the Gospel concerning one wife had not yet been promulgated. He had also heard that his offspring would be multiplied like the stars of heaven, but he did not know through which woman, since he knew Sarah to be barren. Therefore, it was not lustful pleasure in intercourse, but a devout love for the propagation of offspring. It must also be said that he did this at the urging of his excessively insistent wife, who, since she could not have children herself, desired to receive them through another woman. [Col. 0087C]

**Verse 2. “Perhaps I shall receive children through her.”** That is, when she gave birth to a son, he might receive him and adopt him in place of a child of his own.

**Verse 9. “You shall call his name Ishmael.”** This name is interpreted as “hearing.” Since the angel said, “Because the Lord has heard your voice,” the name Ishmael was taken from this etymology, meaning “hearing.”

**Verse 12. “He shall be a wild man.”** That is, rustic and uncultivated. In place of this, the Septuagint says: “He shall be Phara.” *Phara* is interpreted as “wild ass.” It signifies the Saracens, who trace their origin to Ishmael and, wandering through the broad desert with no fixed settlements, attack all the inhabitants of the surrounding wilderness and are attacked by all.

Allegorically, these two women signify the Synagogue and the Church, as the Apostle explains (Galatians 4:22 and following). Hagar signifies the Synagogue, which gives birth in slavery to the Jewish people, who are wild and uncultivated, unwilling to receive the Lord’s easy yoke and his faith. Therefore they are scattered and wandering throughout the whole world and are especially hostile to all Christians. Sarah, however, signifies the Church, which was at first barren and unfruitful but afterward gave birth to the catholic people in the freedom of faith and grace. [Col. 0087D]

**Verse 13. “You are the God who saw me.”** That is, “who had mercy on me.” For God’s seeing is his showing mercy. What he says here—“I have seen the back of him who sees me”—agrees with the passage where the Lord said to Moses: “For man shall not see me and live.” And afterward: “There is a place with me; you shall stand upon the rock. When I pass by, I shall take away my hand, and you shall see my back” (Exodus 33:20 and following).

That Wisdom which is God, being invisible to every creature, certainly cannot be seen by anyone. The back of God, however, is the mystery of Christ’s incarnation, through which he could be seen by human beings. Hence he also rightly said, “When I pass by,” for passing by belongs to a human being. [Col. 0088A]

## Chapter 17

**Verse 5. “You shall not be called Abram, but Abraham.”** Abram is interpreted as “exalted father,” whereas Abraham means “father of many nations.” The Hebrews relate that, from the name of God written with four letters—hence it is called the *tetragrammaton* and is said to be ineffable—God took the letter *he* and added it to Abraham’s name. Similarly, from the name Sarai he took the letter *yod* and added that same *he*. It is not surprising that we have *a* in place of *he*, since the Hebrews write *he* but pronounce it as *a*.

Abraham is called “father of many,” with “nations” understood, because all nations were to believe in his seed, that is, in Christ. Sarai is interpreted as “my princess”; Sarah, absolutely, means “princess,” with all the souls who believe in Christ understood. [Col. 0088B]

**Verse 7. “By an everlasting covenant.”** Many ask how it can be called an everlasting covenant when it plainly did not last forever. But here “everlasting” is used for “worldly” or “age-lasting,” which in Greek is called *aionion* (*αἰώνιον*). For the Greek word *aion* can signify both “everlasting” and “worldly” or “temporal.” Or, better, the covenant is called everlasting because of its spiritual meaning: the covenant of Christ and the age of the faithful believers who are Abraham’s spiritual children will have no end. [Col. 0088C]

**Verse 10. “Every male among you shall be circumcised.”** This law was rightly established for Abraham because, since the first man had displeased God by transgressing his commandments, Abraham was to be a sign of the covenant between God and humanity. [Note: [Col. 0087] Codex Teger., “and Abraham.” The same was written by the first hand in Codex Garst., but another ancient hand corrected it to “humanity.”]

Second, it was so that through this sign they might be distinguished bodily from the other nations. Third, it was so that, receiving it on the member over which lust usually exercises dominion, they might learn to preserve chastity for themselves and to cut away every form of impurity. [Col. 0088D]

**Verse 12. “Both the homeborn and the purchased servant.”** That is, both slaves born under their master’s authority and those who came through purchase. And because the Lord is the creator of all, he excludes no one from salvation and accepts no one’s person, but has mercy on all.

**Verse 14. “From his people.”** That is, from the assembly of the saints. Hence we also read: “But you shall go to your people,” because he made my covenant void. The covenant meant is the one given to Adam in paradise, in which all sinned (Romans 3:12). For we were all causally present in Adam, and therefore we are guilty of original sin. [Col. 0089A]

This circumcision, which was performed on one member, signifies the spiritual circumcision that must be displayed in the heart and in all the members. The heart must be circumcised of harmful thoughts; the eyes must be circumcised so that they do not see vanity; the ears must be circumcised—that is, stopped up—so that they do not hear bloodshed; and thus circumcision must be practiced in all the senses.

**Verse 17. “He laughed.”** He did so not from doubt, but believing the promise of God with joy. Hence his son Isaac was also called “laughter.” Sarah, however, later laughed out of unbelief, and therefore deserved to be rebuked.

**Verse 20. “I have heard you also concerning Ishmael.”** We said above that Ishmael signifies the Jews, who were increased through carnal generation into an immense multitude. Hence it is said through the prophet: “His glory is from the womb, and from the vulva, and from conception” (Hosea 9:11). [Col. 0089B]

**“He shall beget twelve leaders.”** That is, the twelve apostles, the greatest leaders of the Church, who were born from that people. Or by “twelve leaders” he means the twelve tribes of that people itself.

**Verse 21. “I shall establish my covenant with Isaac.”** Because his mercy and grace are in the Christian people.

**Verse 23. “He circumcised Ishmael and all the males.”** It may be asked: if males were saved by circumcision, how were females saved, since they were not circumcised? Certainly by faith and the offering of sacrifices, just as holy men were cleansed through the commandment of circumcision mentioned above, in accordance with what Paul says: “Purifying their hearts by faith” (Acts 10:9). [Col. 0089C]

## Chapter 18

**Verse 1. “The Lord appeared to him in the valley of Mamre.”** Literally, it may be asked whether Abraham understood that those who appeared in human form were angels. If so, why did he prepare for them the services appropriate to mortals? Perhaps he first believed them to be human beings, but later understood from what they said or did that they were angels.

He understood that they were angels when he saw them return to heaven, just as we read in the Book of Judges about Manoah, who at first, on seeing the angel, thought him a man and said: “Are you the man who spoke to the woman?” (Judges 13:11). And when he wished to prepare a kid for him as a human courtesy, the angel said to him: “If you force me, I shall not eat it. But if you wish, offer it to the Lord.” When he had done this and the flame of the sacrifice rose up, the angel also ascended in the flame.

As for Sarah, there is no doubt that she thought they were human beings. For she even dared to deny what the angel had said to Abraham: “Why did your wife Sarah laugh?” She denied it and said: “I did not laugh.” [Col. 0089D]

Mystically, Abraham bore a threefold figure: namely, that of God the Father, in that he offered Isaac. He also bears the figure of the Son, in that he went out from his house and kindred. Here, however, he signifies every holy soul that joyfully receives God as a guest in the lodging of its mind.

Some interpret the three men who appeared to him as Christ, Moses himself, and Elijah, who also appeared with him on the mountain at the Transfiguration. The Lord therefore came when he displayed to Abraham the mystery of the incarnation, because the law given through Moses and the prophecy represented by Elijah always foretold his coming. [Col. 0090A]

**Verse 6. “Hurry, three measures of fine flour.”** A *seah* is a kind of measure. The three measures signify the three sons of Noah, from whom the whole human race was spread after the flood. Through the three measures the Church and the evangelical teaching, which were to be spread through the three parts of the world, were signified.

Hence in the Gospel a woman—that is, the Church—is also said to have taken leaven, the evangelical teaching, and hidden it in three measures of flour (Luke 13:21), that is, in the three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe—until the whole was leavened, that is, until the entire world believed.

The bread signifies the unity of believers, because bread is made from many grains. They were unleavened, because the unity of the holy Church is incorrupt. They were baked under the ashes, because the saints, thoroughly prepared by the power of the Spirit’s fire, make themselves an acceptable sacrifice or food for God. The calf from the herd is Christ according to his humanity from the fathers, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “He shall be pleasing to God as a young calf” (Psalm 68:32). [Col. 0090B]

**Verse 8. “He took butter and milk.”** Milk is the food of infancy, and therefore signifies the old law. Butter, however, being rich and congealed, is the evangelical teaching, which restores the saints with solid food. The cooked calf signifies the suffering Christ. “He was standing beneath the tree.” The tree signified the cross, beneath which Abraham stood because, inspired by God, he was already contemplating the mystery of Christ’s passion.

[Col. 0090C] **Verse 9. “Behold, she is in the tent.”** Abraham was outside with the angels, while Sarah was hidden in the tents, because it belongs to the wise and to teachers to preach openly and to instruct others by their example. The weak and the less learned, however, ought to remain within themselves and submit to teachers.

**Verse 11. “They had ceased.”** That is, they had stopped. “For Sarah the things belonging to women had ceased,” that is, her menstruation; when this happens to a woman, she is no longer capable of bearing children.

**Verse 20. “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has been multiplied.”** As blessed Gregory says, sin accompanied by a voice is sin in action, whereas sin accompanied by a cry is sin committed openly. Since the Sodomites practiced every impurity openly and shamelessly—indeed, they rejoiced and exulted in the worst crimes—their cry is therefore said to have reached God. [Col. 0090D]

**Verse 21. “I shall go down and see whether they have completed in deed the cry that has come to me.”** The cry had indeed reached God, but they were not punished immediately, unless the angel had descended and seen whether they had actually committed these things. As soon as this was discovered, they were consumed without delay by fire sent from heaven.

Here we are taught not to believe too readily what we hear concerning someone’s crimes; but as soon as the matter has been proved, vengeance follows immediately. When it is said, “I shall go down and see,” God speaks in our manner, as though doubting and ignorant, although he himself possesses complete and certain knowledge. [Col. 0091A]

**Verse 26. “I shall not destroy it for the sake of fifty.”** The number fifty is dedicated to repentance. Hence the fiftieth psalm is sung in repentance. When he says, “I shall not destroy it for the sake of fifty,” he shows that they could have been freed from the impending destruction if they had wished to flee to repentance.

That he gradually descends and reaches ten shows that no one can be saved unless he strives to bear the cross of Christ and follow him, and fulfills the ten commandments of the law. For the number ten signifies the cross of Christ, because the tenth letter, by which the number ten is expressed, has the form of a cross.

## Chapter 19

**Verse 1. “He went out to meet them.”** From this and many other passages of Scripture the virtue of hospitality is commended. Concerning it blessed Peter [Paul] the Apostle also says: “Do not forget hospitality. For through it some, having received angels as guests, pleased God” (Hebrews 13:2). [Col. 0091B]

**Verse 8. “I have two daughters.”** It is commonly asked whether this kind of compensation ought to be made: namely, whether we should permit a lesser sin in order to avoid a more serious offense. For Lot wished to hand over his daughters to incest so that the greater sin against nature might not be committed against the men.

But this must be attributed to a mind thrown into confusion. Not knowing what he was doing, or where to take his guests, whom he thought to be human beings, he must be believed to have acted in this way. [Note: [Col. 0091D] Codex Teg., “whom he thought to be guests.”]

**Verse 11. “They struck them with blindness.”** There is a kind of blindness called in Greek *aorasia* (*ἀορασία*), that is, “invisibility,” by which some things are seen and others are not seen. Thus the Sodomites saw other things, but they could not see Lot’s door.

Morally, Lot signifies the righteous, while the Sodomites represent the envious and the slanderers. In a certain sense they seek a door through which they may break in upon Lot when they wish to criticize people’s good deeds, but they cannot find an entrance for criticism because, with that fortress of virtue secured, the corrupters of minds have nothing to criticize. [Col. 0091C]

**Verse 14. “He spoke to his sons-in-law.”** Some think that Lot had daughters who already had husbands, whom he called sons-in-law, and that these daughters remained in Sodom with their husbands, while two other daughters, who had no husbands, went out with their father.

But another translation says explicitly: “He spoke to the betrothed men who were going to receive his daughters.” Therefore they were not yet sons-in-law, but wished to become so. [Col. 0091D]

**Verse 17. “Save your life.”** Allegorically, Lot’s flight from Sodom—which according to another interpretation means “blindness”—signifies the renunciation of the desires and enticements of the world.

Lot is therefore commanded to flee from Sodom’s fire and not to look back, because everyone who, after receiving grace, has entered the ways of life ought not to return again to the things he abandoned, in accordance with what the Lord commands in the Gospel: “On that day, whoever is on the roof or in the field must not return backward” (Luke 17:31).

He also recalls the example of Lot’s wife, who, when she looked back, remained transformed into a pillar of salt. She signifies those who, after professing the service of God, fall back into the desires of the world. [Note: [Col. 0092D] So both codices.] Hence she is rightly said to have been changed into a pillar of salt, because by her example, like a seasoning of salt, she teaches the minds of readers or hearers not to suffer such things. [Col. 0092A]

**Verse 20. “There is a small city.”** That is, Zoar, which was formerly called Bela, according to the statement: “There is a small city which is called Zoar,” that is, “little.” Mystically, the mountain signifies the height of the virtues, to which the angel exhorts us when he says: “Save yourself on the mountain.” An example is the contempt of all possessions.

The Lord invites us to this perfection when he says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matthew 19:21).

But whoever sees that he cannot climb this mountain should remain in Zoar—that is, in what is small—content with the lay life and ordinary conduct, rather than, after taking up the mountain of virtue, return to lower things, that is, to worldly matters. [Col. 0092B]

Virginity also is a very lofty mountain, to which the teacher of the nations exhorts us when he says: “It is good for a man if he remains as I also am” (1 Corinthians 7:8).

The angel therefore urges Lot to climb this mountain while fleeing the fires of lust. But whoever sees that he cannot preserve this should descend to Zoar—that is, should make use of lawful marriage—because it is better to use a moderate good than to be hurled headlong over the precipices of lust.

Hence, when the apostles said, “If such is the situation of a wife, it is not expedient to marry,” the Lord replied: “Not all accept this word, but those to whom it has been given. Whoever can accept it, let him accept it” (Matthew 19:10 and following). And the Apostle says: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife” (1 Corinthians 7:2). [Col. 0092C]

**Verse 24. “The Lord rained fire and sulfur from heaven.”** Fire has heat, and sulfur has stench. Since these people had burned with the flame of lust and had lived in the stench of the flesh, they rightly perished together by fire and sulfur.

It should be considered here that the first sinners were destroyed by the water of the flood, because they too had offended God through the desire of the flesh. The Sodomites, however, perished by a more severe punishment, namely, a flood of fire and sulfur. For although the former exceeded the proper measure, they nevertheless sinned naturally with women; the latter, however, sinned irrationally and against nature, and therefore were condemned as the gravest example of punishment. [Col. 0092D]

**Verse 29. “Abraham remembered.”** These words show that Lot was delivered through Abraham’s merits, although Scripture calls him righteous. But it should be understood that he was not perfectly righteous, but righteous in a certain respect. Or he is called righteous in comparison with the Sodomites among whom he lived, who were filled with every impurity and iniquity.

**Verse 30. “Lot went up from Zoar.”** It must be asked why, when he himself had requested to live in Zoar and the angel had urged him to be saved on the mountain, he again left Zoar and climbed the mountain.

From this the opinion of the Hebrews appears to be true: they say that the city collapsed in a third earthquake. Knowing this, Lot feared to remain there, reasoning with himself that if it had fallen while the others were still standing, it could now much more easily perish along with the others as they perished. And because of this sin of unbelief, since he did not believe the angel, they say that the crime of incest happened to him. [Col. 0093A]

**Verse 31. “Our father is old.”** Lot’s daughters thought that the whole human race had perished everywhere and that no men remained except their father. Therefore they conceived this plan in order to preserve offspring through their father.

Origen excuses their adultery in many ways, because they did not act from lust but from the desire to restore the human race. Lot, however, is inexcusable: first, because he did not believe the angel; then, because he became drunk on wine. Thus a lesser sin became for him the cause of a greater crime.

**Verse 35. “He did not know when she lay down, nor when she arose.”** The Jews reject this so completely that whenever they read this passage they are distressed. For they say that it cannot happen that a man has intercourse without perceiving it. [Col. 0093B]

**Verse 37. “The elder bore a son and called his name Moab.”** Moab is interpreted as “from the father.”

**Verse 38. “The younger also bore a son and called his name Ammon.”** Ammon is interpreted as “son of my people,” or “son of my kindred.” These are the fruits of drunkenness: the Moabites and Ammonites, that is, those who are from the father, the devil, in accordance with what the Lord says to such people: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8:44). They are also the children of a people that envies and persecutes the saints.

## Chapter 20

**Verse 1. “He journeyed in Gerar.”** Gerar is the land of the Philistines. [Col. 0093C]

**Verse 2. “Abimelech sent for her and took her.”** It may be asked how Sarah could be loved at that age, since she was an extremely old woman. But it is more a matter for wonder than for inquiry that she possessed such great beauty of appearance that even her old age could not diminish it.

**Verse 6. “I protected you, so that you would not sin against me.”** When the Lord said, “I protected you, so that you would not sin against me,” he showed that those who commit such acts sin against God, although among worldly people the sin of adultery is considered either slight or nothing at all.

**Verse 12. “She is the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother.”** Another translation states this more clearly: “From my father, but not from my mother.” For she had been the daughter of Haran, Abraham’s brother, and the sister of Lot. [Col. 0093D]

**Verse 16. “This shall be a covering for your eyes.”** That is, “in the provision of the gift”; and, “Remember that you have been exposed.” He says this as though joking, affectionately warning her not to dare to do such a thing, lest she likewise appear to have been discovered.

Mystically, Abraham here signifies Christ, while Sarah signifies the Church. Abraham was honored on account of Sarah’s beauty, and Christ is praised and honored in the world through the Church, because, as the Psalmist says: “God is wonderful in his saints” (Psalm 17:36).

Sarah had a husband, but he was hidden; the Church also has Christ, but in the present he is understood to have been received into the hidden realms of heaven.

## Chapter 21

**Verse 4. “He circumcised him on the eighth day.”** Although circumcision was commanded for many symbolic reasons, it particularly prefigures Christ, who in the present strips us of the old man through baptism and in the future, through the resurrection, circumcises from us all mortality and corruption.

The fact that Isaac was circumcised on the eighth day also signified the eighth age of the world, when the resurrection of the dead will be celebrated universally. [Col. 0094A]

**Verse 8. “He held a great feast.”** Literally, it would have been more fitting for Abraham to prepare a banquet on the day of Isaac’s birth or circumcision. But the man filled with a prophetic spirit preferred to do this on the day of his weaning.

This signified that we celebrate a kind of festival for God and the angels whenever, having laid aside the milk of infancy, we grow into a mature man and already make use of solid food.

**Verse 9. “Playing.”** The Hebrews relate that he made idols as though playing, by which he might deceive Isaac in his infancy. Blessed Jerome also says that, as though he were the elder, he presumptuously claimed the firstborn’s privileges through play.

More simply, we may say that he wished to make him slippery and wanton, as he himself was. Hence the Apostle calls this play persecution, saying: “But just as then the one born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the spirit, so also now” (Galatians 4:29). [Col. 0094B]

**Verse 11. “Abraham took this very hard.”** Although he understood that these things were taking place in a mystery, he was nevertheless moved by paternal affection toward his son.

**Verse 14. “Beersheba”** is interpreted as “the seventh well” or “the well of the oath.” But that place did not yet have this name. Therefore it must be understood by anticipation. [Col. 0094C]

**Verse 13. “Hagar cast the boy aside.”** This does not mean that she carried him on her shoulder—for when he was circumcised he was thirteen years old—but that she cast him out from her mind and rejected him from her care. For we commonly speak in this way: “I have cast him out of my mind.”

**Verse 17. “The Lord heard the voice of the boy.”** Although the mother was weeping, it is said that he heard the boy’s voice because she was weeping for him and not for herself; thus the mother’s voice was in a certain sense the boy’s voice.

Typically, Hagar signifies the Synagogue and Ishmael the Jewish people. Ishmael is carried by Hagar, and the sinful Jewish people press the neck of their mother, the Synagogue, with the heavy burden of a curse.

The bread she carried signifies the bread of the Presence, which had been sanctified on the table. The water that failed them signifies legal purification, or also the carnal teaching of the scribes and Pharisees, which was contained in a dead skin—that is, in carnal observance—and killed those who observed it according to the letter because it did not possess the life-giving Spirit.

That Hagar cast the boy under a tree signifies those among that people who believe in Christ and are protected by the shadow of his passion and cross. [Col. 0094D]

**Verse 18. “Rise, take the boy, and hold his hand.”** That is, “Join yourself to him and walk with him.” This is what people do when they walk together.

Literally, we understand that the mother had hidden herself when she said, “I shall not see the boy dying.” The angel therefore urges her to return to the boy and take him—not by raising him from the ground or carrying him, but by receiving him into her care and providence. [Col. 0095A]

**Verse 23. “The land in which you have lived as a stranger.”** That is, in Palestine. Abraham was living as a foreigner in Gerar. Gerar is the place now called “Salvific Palestine,” where Isaac was born, although some assert that he was born by the oak of Mamre.

**Verse 31. “The place was called Beersheba.”** “The Seventh Well,” because six ewe-lambs were sacrificed there; or “the Well of the Oath,” because both men swore an oath there. *Sabee* has both meanings: “seven” and “oath.”

Here it must be asked why we read above that Hagar stood at the well of the oath, when this happened only later and after a long period of time. It did not yet have that name. Therefore it must be understood by prolepsis, that is, by anticipation. This manner of speaking is extremely common in the divine Scriptures, although the well may already have existed at that time. If this is so, then this passage must be understood by recapitulation. [Col. 0095B]

**Verse 33. “He planted a grove at Beersheba.”** Above it is said that God did not give him an inheritance or even “a foot’s breadth” (Acts 7:5), as the Apostle Paul says. But we understand that there was some area of land around the well which, together with the well, passed into his possession.

## Chapter 22

**Verse 1. “God tested Abraham.”** There is a testing that proves, not one that condemns. He therefore tested Abraham, not because he himself learned anything—for all things are naked and open to him—but so that Abraham might show himself to himself and recognize how great his faith in God was. [Col. 0095C]

**Verse 2. “Upon one of the mountains.”** The Hebrews relate or suppose that this mountain was Moriah, on which the temple of God and the *Dabir*, that is, the oracle, were later built. Hence Mount Moriah is interpreted as “light” or “illuminated.”

**Verse 12. “Now I know.”** That is, “I have caused it to be known.”

**Verse 13. “Caught by its horns in the thicket.”** Another translation preserves the Hebrew word itself, saying: “Caught in the thicket of Sabee.” *Sabee* is interpreted as “dense” or “thick,” signifying the density of the shrubs and thorns in which the ram’s horns were caught.

Literally, holy Abraham gives us a great example of great obedience. Although he had one son and had heard from the Lord, “In Isaac shall your seed be called,” he nevertheless did not hesitate to offer him to God, believing—as the Apostle also says—that God could raise him from the dead (Hebrews 11:19).

Allegorically, Abraham here bears the person of God the Father, and Isaac that of the Lord Jesus Christ. Isaac’s sacrifice signifies Christ’s passion. It is rightly said: “He himself carried the wood of the burnt offering,” because Christ carried his own cross, as it is said of his passion: “And carrying his cross, he went out to the place called Golgotha” (John 19:17).

The two men who accompanied Abraham signify the Jewish people. They are two because after Solomon’s death that people was divided into two kingdoms: ten tribes, over which Jeroboam ruled, called Israel; and two other tribes, Judah and Benjamin, over which Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, ruled, called Judah. The priestly tribe, Levi, was also with them. [Col. 0095D] [Col. 0096A]

The ass that they led with them signifies the foolishness of the Jews. For the ass did not know what it carried, and the Jews read Christ in the prophetic books but did not understand him when he came. Hence it is rightly said to them: “Wait here with the ass.” Even to this day, and until the end of the age, they are as though waiting for Christ with their foolishness, as the Apostle says: “A hardening has come upon Israel in part, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25).

What he says—“After we have worshiped, we shall return to you”—signifies that, when the passion has been fulfilled, God will return in the final age of the world and be reconciled to believing Jews.

[Col. 0096B] When it says that on the third day he lifted up his eyes, the three days signify the three periods of the world: before the law, under the law, and under grace. The Son of God is also said to have come to the wedding on the third day and to have changed water into wine, because in the third period of the world he came to join the Church to himself and to transform the letter of the law into spiritual understanding.

The ram that appeared to Abraham signifies the humanity of Christ. It is rightly said to have been caught by its horns in the thicket, because Christ was fastened to the cross, with his hands caught on the horns—that is, the arms—of the cross. Or it was caught among the thorns because he was crowned with thorns.

The fact that the ram was sacrificed while Isaac escaped signifies that Christ could suffer according to his humanity, but remained incapable of suffering according to his divinity. For there are two substances or natures in Christ.

Literally, because the ram was caught by its horns in the thicket, the Jews therefore customarily sound horns at their solemnities, so that by this God may remember them and be reconciled to them on account of Abraham’s great obedience. [Col. 0096C]

**Verse 14. “On the mountain the Lord will see.”** This became a proverb among the Jews, so that whenever they are held by some necessity or distress they say: “On the mountain the Lord will see,” or, as it is found in Hebrew: “On the mountain the Lord will be seen.” That is, “He will have mercy and deliver us.”

**Verse 16. “By myself I have sworn, says the Lord.”** Every human being swears by one greater than himself, as the Apostle says. But God, since he has no one greater than himself, is said to swear by himself (Hebrews 6:13 and following). [Col. 0096D]

**Verse 20. “Milcah, Sarah’s sister.”** Abraham took Sarah as his wife, and Nahor took Milcah.

**Verse 21. “Uz,”** from which the land of Uz is named in Job; **“Buz,”** from whom came the Buzite called Elihu [printed *Elia*], whom the Hebrews also suppose to have been Balaam. **“Kemuel, the father of the Syrians.”** The statement that he was “the father of the Syrians” should not be referred to those who reported this, but rather to the person who wrote it long afterward.

## Chapter 23

**Verse 3. “Heth,”** from whom the Hittites are named.

**Verse 7. “He rose and worshiped.”** Since the Lord says in the law, “You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone,” what does it mean that Abraham is read to have worshiped human beings?

It is one thing to worship God in the manner in which he alone is to be honored and worshiped; it is another to honor and welcome holy people mutually, even though he did not say, “You shall worship the Lord your God alone,” as he said, “You shall serve him alone.”

There is a service owed to God alone, which in Greek is called *latria* (*λατρεία*). Hence those who abandon the Creator and serve the creature are called idolaters. But when the Apostle says, “Through charity serve one another” (Galatians 5:13), he speaks of that service by which holy people anticipate one another and attend to one another. In Greek this is called *dulia* (*δουλεία*), and hence we call servants *douloi* (*δοῦλοι*).

When the angel in the Apocalypse prevented John, who wished to worship him, saying, “See that you do not do this,” perhaps John had suspected something divine in the angel and therefore wished to worship him as God; for this reason he was prohibited. [Col. 0097A]

[Col. 0097B] **Verse 17. “The field of Ephron was confirmed.”** At first Ephron is named, meaning “confirmed” and “perfect.” But after he received payment for the burial, although Abraham compelled him to do so, his name was changed and he was called Ephran, meaning “weak” or “imperfect.”

Let those who sell burial places for the dead hear this. If the man who, although unwilling, could nevertheless be induced to accept payment for a burial was condemned by the change of his name, then much more will those who are not compelled but themselves demand payment be condemned and not be counted among the perfect. [Note: [Col. 0097D] Both codices: “sell.”]

**“In which there was a double cave.”** Mystically, the double cave signifies right action and contemplation, namely, the active and contemplative lives. Sarah is therefore buried in a double cave when the faithful soul, dead to the desires and longings of the world, is hidden beneath the shelter of good works and contemplation.

Hence the Apostle Paul also says: “You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” [Col. 0097C]

## Chapter 24

**Verse 2. “Put your hand under my thigh.”** The Jews say that Abraham swore by his sanctification, that is, by circumcision. But it is better to refer this to the incarnation of Christ.

The holy patriarch, foreseeing that Christ—perfect man and perfect God—would be born from his descendants, commanded him to put his hand beneath his thigh and swear. Because he foresaw that a human being would be born from his flesh, he said: “Put your hand under my thigh.” But because he recognized that he was God, he added: “Swear to me by the God of heaven,” that is, by the divinity of the one who was to be born from my flesh. [Col. 0097D]

### Verse 13

“Therefore I am standing near the spring of water.” Blessed Augustine asks here, in the literal sense, whether we ought to do this—namely, to seek a sign from God. For it seems scarcely different from augury. But it is one thing to seek God’s will through some sign in which there is a miracle, and another to seek divination in the calls of birds or dumb animals, although even the former should not be presumed upon except in the greatest necessity.

Allegorically, Abraham’s servant signifies the company of holy teachers. He is that servant who was sent by his master in the Gospel to make those who had been invited come to the prepared banquet. Abraham’s servant placed his hand beneath the thigh of his master because teachers receive Christ’s incarnation with the highest reverence. He places his hand not upon the thigh but beneath the thigh, because they understand Christ’s flesh to be far different from the flesh of other human beings. For Christ’s flesh was born from the Virgin without the stain of sin.

Rebecca, whose name is interpreted as “patience,” is the Church from the Gentiles, which preserves its virtues through patience. The spring at which the servant stood signifies the streams of evangelical teaching, or also the sacrament of baptism toward which Rebecca—namely, the Church—was already hastening, with a water-jar, that is, with the measure of the Word.

It is rightly said that she lowered the water-jar from her shoulder onto her arms. By the shoulders, good will is understood, in which she first received faith. By the arm, however, is understood the activity that follows faith.

The ornaments with which the servant adorned Rebecca are the virtues and commandments of teachers. The earring signifies the humility of a good hearer, by which he advances in the love of God and neighbor. Hence she is said to have had two shekels’ worth of earrings. The bracelets signify the obedience of a good hearer, or good activity. They weighed ten shekels, because all our activity consists in the ten commandments of the Law.

### Verse 22

“After the camels had drunk.” The fact that Rebecca gave drink not only to the man but also watered the camels signifies that the Church must withhold the word of preaching from no one, but must proclaim it alike to the wise and the foolish. Hence Paul says: “I am a debtor both to Greeks and to barbarians, to the wise and to the foolish” (Romans L, 14).

Or otherwise: by the camels we ought to understand our flesh. The camels are watered when care is taken for the body—not in desires, but in necessity—so that Rebecca, or the soul, may be able to bear it.

### Verse 25

“A spacious place for staying.” The spacious place for staying that Rebecca says is with her is the natural law, which the holy Church possessed before it came to Christ, by which it is said: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matthew VII, 12). Thus, through this law of nature, entry into the evangelical law was being prepared.

### Verse 29

“Rebecca had a brother named Laban.” Laban represents carnal people. This man calls the husband “lord” and calls him “blessed of the Lord,” because carnal people admire the virtues of holy teachers and honor them, but do not rise to imitate their perfection.

### Verse 50

“The word has gone forth from the Lord.” Because they knew that Abraham was a prophet, they therefore said that what Abraham had spoken had come forth from the Lord. Or else, because Abraham’s servant had sought a sign from the Lord and a sign had immediately been given to him, they said for that reason that God had spoken.

### Verse 61

“Therefore Rebecca and her maidens.” The maidens who accompanied Rebecca to Isaac signify faithful souls who conduct themselves simply in the Church, but do not reach the bridal chamber of contemplation.

### Verse 62

“He lived in the southern land,” that is, in Gerara.

Mystically, the well of the one who sees and lives (Jeremiah XXII, 24) is Holy Scripture, through which we receive knowledge of God. He himself is the living and seeing one who speaks through the prophet: “As I live, says the Lord.” “All things are naked and open to his eyes” (Hebrews IV, 13).

The road that leads to the well of the living and seeing one is Christ’s Passion, which leads us to an understanding of the Scriptures. For we could not otherwise have understood the things written in the Old Testament, unless they had become clear when they were fulfilled in the Passion.

It should also be noted that it says, “he was walking along the road”; it does not say, “he was walking,” but “he was walking back and forth.” For to walk back and forth is to travel a road repeatedly, going and returning. Thus Christ’s Passion was repeatedly encountered in different ways and at different times. At one moment he was attacked by the Jews with blasphemies and insults, at another he was struck on the cheek, and again he was spat upon; in this way and in such forms he walked back and forth along the road of his Passion.

The fact that Rebecca found Isaac in the southern land signifies that the holy Church, having abandoned the coldness of unbelief and been kindled by the warmth of faith, came to Christ.

### Verse 63

“He had gone out to meditate in the field.” Some manuscripts have, “to exercise himself in the field.” Another translation says, “to speak in the field.”

“When the day was already declining.” The holy man had gone out alone, already after the ninth hour of the day, when it was declining toward evening, in order to offer spiritual sacrifices to God—that is, to offer prayers and hymns.

Allegorically, the field is the world, as the Lord explains his parable: “The one who sows is the Son of Man; the field, however, is the world” (Matthew XIII, 38). Isaac therefore went out into the field to meditate when the day was already declining, because the Son of God came into the world in the final age of the world, according to what had been said through the prophet: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, with your Christ” (Habakkuk III, 13)—that is, in order to exercise himself and complete the contest of his Passion.

“And when he had lifted up his eyes, he saw camels coming from afar.” By the camel, a twisted animal weighed down by its hump, the Gentile people are signified: twisted by corrupt customs and burdened by idolatry. Since it found among itself objects of worship, it carried them on its back like a humped animal burdened by a swollen growth.

Rebecca came to Isaac seated upon a camel, because the holy Church, still relying upon and as if supported by the error of paganism, was called to the grace of Christ.

### Verse 64

“Rebecca, having seen Isaac, descended from the camel.” Because the Church, having recognized Christ, humbled itself in shame for its errors. Hence it is rightly said that she covered herself with a cloak, because she covered herself with the shame and embarrassment of her error. Thus Paul also speaks to certain people: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Romans VI, 21). The Psalmist likewise says: “Shame covered my face” (Psalm LXVIII, 8).

### Verse 67

“He brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother.” Because Christ established the Church in the place of the Synagogue, from which he had assumed flesh.

“He took her as his wife.” Because he bestowed upon the new bride the grace that the former had once possessed, betrothing to himself one who had neither stain nor wrinkle.

“To temper the grief that had arisen from his mother’s death.” The mother’s death is the unbelief of the Synagogue, for which Christ grieved greatly. Hence, during his Passion, he also said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew XXVI, 38). For he was not sorrowful on account of the Passion itself, but on account of the destruction of the Jews.

He therefore tempered this grief through his love for Rebecca, because he compensated for the loss and rejection of one people by the faith and salvation of all the nations.

## CHAPTER XXV

### Verse 1

“Abraham took another wife, Keturah.” Her name is interpreted as “joined” or “united.” Hence the Hebrews relate that she was Hagar, the mother of Ishmael, who had previously been a concubine but, after Sarah’s death, was lawfully united to Abraham. They invent this story in order to excuse Abraham, so that, already old and weakened, he would not seem to have indulged in new marriages.

### Verse 2

“She bore.” Those who were born from Keturah occupied the land of the Trogodytes and Arabia, which is called Eudemon, as far as the Red Sea.

Allegorically, just as the Jews born into slavery are represented by Hagar and Ishmael, so heretics are represented by Keturah and her sons. In the New Testament, under the pretext of Christ’s name, they have held an erroneous opinion concerning the truth of the faith in him.

Hence it is rightly said afterward that Abraham gave gifts to the sons of his concubines, but that Isaac alone received the inheritance. For in the present Christ grants heretics the benefits of knowledge and understanding, but only the Catholic Church is led to the kingdom.

### Verse 3

“Assurim” is translated as “merchants.”

“Latusim,” as “those who beat bronze or metals.”

“Lomim,” as “phylarchs,” that is, “leaders of tribes.”

### Verse 8

“Having failed, he died.” Blessed Jerome says that this was wrongly added through the error of copyists. For decline or diminishment does not suit a righteous man, since he ought rather to increase and multiply, as the Psalmist says: “The righteous will multiply like the cedar of Lebanon” (Psalm XCI, 13).

“Full of days.” Fullness is ordinarily found in the birth, conduct, and death of the saints. Therefore Abraham is rightly read to have died full of days: he was complete and perfect in every virtue. By contrast, in the reprobate everything is marked by a certain imperfection. Hence the Psalm says: “Men of blood and deceit will not halve their days” (Psalm LIV, 24).

“He was gathered to his people,” that is, to the multitude of the fathers who had gone before.

### Verse 13

“The firstborn of Ishmael, Nabaoth.” From him the whole region from the Red Sea to the Euphrates is called Nabataea.

### Verse 18

“From Hevila,” that is, from India.

“He died before all his brothers,” that is, in the hands of his brothers, while all were still alive and none had been taken before him by death. He calls them brothers instead of sons, just as in the place where Jacob later said to Laban: “What have I done wrong to you, that you pursued me? Set it before my brothers and your brothers.” For Jacob had no other brothers there than his own children.

### Verse 20

“From Mesopotamia.” Mesopotamia is a very fertile region, which is called by this Greek name because it lies between two rivers, namely the Tigris and the Euphrates. For *mesos* means “middle,” and *potamos* means “river.” Hence *hippopotamos*, “river horse.”

[Note: [Col. 0101] The manuscript has *apotamos*. The word is missing, together with what follows, in the Tegernsee manuscript.]

### Verse 21

“He prayed for his wife.” The Lord had promised Abraham that he would multiply his offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea. This multiplication was to take place through Isaac, according to what was said to Abraham: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called.”

What, then, is the meaning of Isaac’s receiving a barren wife, if Abraham’s offspring was to be multiplied through him? We must understand that the things the saints obtain through prayer have been predestined in such a way that they are obtained through prayers. Thus Abraham’s offspring was to be multiplied through Isaac, but he obtained this very thing by praying.

Likewise, the kingdom of God has been prepared for all the righteous before the ages, but in such a way that they reach it in its appointed time through prayer and labor.

### Verse 22

“They struggled.” The Septuagint says: “They played and kicked.”

“And she went to inquire of the Lord.” It is asked where she went to inquire of the Lord. The tabernacle had not yet been built, nor the temple of God. Perhaps she went to the place where Abraham had built an altar to the Lord; or, as some think, perhaps Melchizedek, the priest of God, was still living at that time. It may also be believed that there was then some holy man whom they customarily visited to seek counsel.

It may likewise be said that she went to God in mind and thought, and, having presented her petitions, slept in that place and received a divine response there through a vision.

### Verse 23

“Two nations are in your womb.” Literally, he speaks of two nations, the Idumaeans and the Jews. When he says afterward, “The elder shall serve the younger,” he refers to the time when Esau, the elder among the Idumaeans, served Jacob, that is, the Jews. For David made them tributary, and they served under tribute until they rebelled, according to what is read in the Book of Kings: “Edom withdrew, so as not to be under Judah” (IV Kings VIII, 20).

Mystically, these two twins signify two peoples: Esau, the elder, the Jews; Jacob, the younger, the Gentile people. The elder therefore serves the younger, because the Jewish people, scattered throughout the whole world, serve the nations—not only in bodily servitude, but also because they preserve the Law and the Prophets for the benefit of the nations.

This quarrel between two peoples also takes place within us, when the law of the flesh resists the law of the mind, and when vices oppose virtues. Vices are represented by the elder, because they are more numerous than virtues, and the wicked are always more numerous or earlier in number than the good. But through God’s help the wicked are overcome by the good, and vices yield to virtues.

### Verse 25

“He who came out first was called Edom or Rufus.” *Edom* is interpreted as “red” or “ruddy,” from which the Idumaeans are called by that name.

“Hirsute,” that is, “hairy,” which in Hebrew is called *Seir*, from which Mount Seir received its name.

Thus we know that he had three names, for he was called Esau, Edom, and Seir.

Jacob is interpreted as “supplanter.” Mystically, Jacob—namely, the Gentile people—supplanted the Jewish people, that is, placed them beneath his foot, because he rose, as it were, above them when he received their dignity.

### Verse 27

“Esau became a man skilled in hunting.” By Esau the hunter, people who seek earthly things and pursue the profits of the world as though they were hunting are signified.

He is also rightly said to have been a farmer, because the more worldly people neglect their inner selves, the more they occupy themselves with cultivating and pursuing present things.

“Jacob, however, was a simple man and dwelt in tents.” Every saint who is less occupied with earthly things dwells within the house of a holy conscience and does not scatter himself through external matters.

Literally, instead of “simple,” another translation has “without deceit,” which in Greek is *aplastes*, that is, “not feigned.” But how was he without deceit, when he deceived his brother by deceit? This must be referred to the mystery, not to his wickedness, because everything happened in figure (I Corinthians X, 11).

### Verse 31

“Sell me your birthright.” Birthrights are called all things that open the womb of the mother, and these were especially owed to firstborn sons. Some say that “birthright” refers to the garment worn by the firstborn, by which they became priests.

This dignity, which Esau as firstborn ought to have received, he sold to his younger brother after being overcome by his appetite.

In what ways are we tempted by the vice of gluttony? We should know that we are tempted by gluttony in five ways:

1. When someone wishes to eat before the appointed time or before there is a need.
2. When someone seeks more luxurious foods.
3. When someone wants ordinary foods to be prepared with excessive care.
4. When someone exceeds the proper measure in eating.
5. When what is eaten is contemptible.

Yet when someone receives something worthless with great desire, he reveals himself even more in the heat of that desire. Esau’s food was displeasing and rejected in this respect.

Hence blessed Augustine says: “I do not fear the uncleanness of the food, but the uncleanness of desire.”

Mystically, the Jews, who are signified by Esau, devoted to the pleasures of their flesh and occupied with earthly works, abandoned not only the dignity they then possessed but also the blessedness that had been promised to them. All their dignity was transferred to the Gentile people.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### Verse 10

“Why have you imposed this?” That is, “Why have you deceived?” From this impostors receive their name.

### Verse 18

“Again he dug other wells that the servants of his father had dug.” Allegorically, Isaac signifies Christ, who, when he came through the mystery of the Incarnation to the torrent of our mortality, dug wells—that is, opened the knowledge of the Scriptures—which the servants of his father Abraham had dug, namely Moses, David, Solomon, and the great-voiced prophets.

For these were servants of Abraham, that is, of almighty God, whose figure Abraham bore. But the Philistines, envying these wells, filled them with earth. The Philistines signify the Jews, alienated from God, who had corrupted the Scriptures through an earthly understanding. For *Philistines* is interpreted as “alien.”

### Verse 19

“They dug in the torrent and found living water.” Isaac’s servants found living water in the torrent. Who are Isaac’s servants except Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, together with the other apostles, who found the water—that is, evangelical teaching—and handed it on to believers?

But again the Philistines quarreled, because the Jews resisted evangelical teaching, neither permitting anything new to be established nor wishing the old things to be cleansed.

### Verse 22

“They dug another well, over which they did not contend.” Having already been defeated, they did not contend over the third well, because after the faith of the Holy Trinity began to be preached throughout the world, the adversaries, overcome by the patience of the saints, ceased their opposition.

Hence the well was rightly given the name “Breadth.” For the true Isaac—that is, Christ—was enlarged through the faith of all believers. God, who had previously been known only in Judea, is now said to be known in this way: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm XVIII, 5).

Morally, we dig wells when we understand or penetrate the depths of divine knowledge. Yet the allophylists—“foreign peoples”—filled those wells with earth, because when we investigate the depths of the Scriptures, demons often heap earthly thoughts upon us in order to take away from us the water of divine knowledge.

### Verse 26

“Abimelech and Ochoza.” Ochoza was Abimelech’s marriage attendant. The Septuagint uses “company” in place of Ochozath, so that it is not the name of a man but designates a multitude of friends, one of whom was Phicol, the commander of the army.

### Verse 33

“Bersabee.” This does not mean, as above, “seventh well” or “well of the oath,” but “well of holiness.” For the Hebrew letter *sin* has been changed into *samekh*.

## CHAPTER XXVII

### Verse 1

“When Isaac had grown old and his eyes had become dim,” and so forth. We said above that Isaac represents God the almighty Father, while Esau the firstborn represents the Jewish people, of whom he himself said to Pharaoh: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exodus IV, 22).

Isaac desired to eat the food of his son, and God the Father desired to be nourished by the good works of that people. But while that people neglected him and, as though hunting, was occupied with external matters [Note: Both manuscripts read “from internal matters.”], Rebecca—that is, motherly grace—substituted the younger son, namely the Gentile people, and seized the place and dignity of the former.

The fact that Isaac, with dim eyes, foretold future things to his son Jacob but did not see him signifies that God the Father foretold the calling of the nations in many ways through the prophets, but in a certain sense did not see them—that is, did not show them mercy—and allowed them to enter their own ways and wander through the five ages of the world.

The fact that Jacob prepared food for his father not from hunted game but from domestic animals, namely young goats, signifies that the Gentile people did not strive to please God through external things or through the letter of the Law, but offered in themselves an acceptable burnt offering through faith and love, saying with the Psalmist: “In me are your vows, O God, which I shall repay to you in praises” (Psalm LV, 12).

The garments of Esau with which Rebecca clothed the younger son are the adornments of divine commandments, with which that former people was once adorned. But after it was rejected through unbelief, the nations believing in Christ are clothed with them, the Lord saying: “The kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew XXI, 43).

The fact that she protected his hands and the bare parts of his neck with the skins of young goats signifies that the nations coming to faith are not ashamed to confess the sins of their deeds. For the young goat signifies a sinner, the Lord saying: “He will set the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left” (Matthew XXV, 33).

When he says, “It was God’s will that what I wanted should quickly come to me,” he signifies the swift conversion of the world. For, in a manner almost beyond belief, the faith of Christ was proclaimed throughout the whole world within a very brief period.

### Verse 27

“He approached and kissed him.” The father’s kiss, with which Jacob kissed him, signifies the reconciliation of the world, which the Church desired when speaking in the Song of Songs: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song of Songs I, 1).

“Behold, the scent of my son is like the scent of a full field.” The scent of the garments is the fragrance of virtues. That scent is rightly compared with a full field, because the world has been filled with the virtues of the saints.

Hence Paul also said: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (II Corinthians II, 15). The full field is the world, filled with the good works of the saints. There the roses of the martyrs give off their fragrance, the lilies of the virtues exhale perfume, and the violets of the continent breathe forth their scent; there also the flowering vineyards of the apostles spread their fragrance far and wide.

### Verse 28

“May God give you of the dew of heaven.” Dew falls gently and almost imperceptibly, and therefore signifies subtle contemplation. The richness of the earth signifies good works.

Jacob—that is, the Gentile people—is therefore blessed so that he may abound in heavenly contemplation and good works.

“An abundance of grain, wine, and oil.” In grain and wine, charity and the fervor of a new way of life are signified; in oil, works of mercy. Grain and wine may also be understood as the mysteries of Christ’s body and blood; oil as the mercy of God, by which the human race has been saved, according to what was said through the prophet: “The yoke will decay before the face of oil” (Isaiah X, 27), that is, the yoke of sin will decay in the presence of God’s mercy.

### Verse 29

“Be lord of your brothers.” By “brothers” or “sons of his mother,” he means heretics or Jews, who are brothers through the invocation of Christ’s name and through the same sacraments that they share with us.

Concerning them the Church speaks in the Song of Songs: “The sons of my mother fought against me” (Song of Songs I).

### Verse 30

“After Jacob had gone out, Esau came.” The fact that Esau returns to his father signifies the conversion of the former people at the end of the world, concerning which the Psalmist had said: “They will return toward evening and suffer hunger like dogs” (Psalm LVIII, 15). And the prophet says: “They opened their mouths like a poor man eating in secret.”

### Verse 39

“In the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven.” Although every blessing came to Jacob, Esau is not sent away empty. He is blessed in the richness of the earth, that is, in the abundance of all things, and in the dew of heaven from above, that is, in knowledge of the Scriptures, because that people is still sprinkled with it, although without cause.

### Verse 40

“You shall live by the sword.” By this he signifies that the Jews would cruelly persecute Christ and all the prophets and apostles.

“You shall serve your brother.” For the Idumaeans were tributary to Israel, who was called Jacob.

“And the time will come.” That time signifies the period when they rebelled, so that they would no longer be under Judah.

### Verse 42

“These things were reported to Rebecca.” Who reported them, when he had said it in his heart? Certainly she learned this through the spirit of prophecy, through which she had also learned that he was to be placed before his elder brother.

### Verse 43

“Haran.” In Hebrew, Syria.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### Verse 2

“Go and depart.” Another translation has, “Flee.” From this we understand that he too had learned through the spirit about his brother’s threats.

### Verse 10

“Therefore Jacob went out from Bersabee.” As we have said, Jacob signifies Christ, who, leaving his parents—that is, the Jews from whom he had assumed flesh—and leaving also his house, that is, Jerusalem, and leaving his homeland as well, that is, Judea, went to the nations, where he would receive the Church as his bride.

### Verse 11

“He took one of the stones.” Jacob’s sleeping on the journey signifies Christ’s death or Passion on the cross.

The stone that he placed beneath his head is Christ according to his humanity. Jacob anointed it, so that Christ might thereby be plainly indicated. For *Christus* is Greek and is translated into Latin as “anointed.”

The Apostle says: “The head of Christ is God” (I Corinthians XI, 3). Therefore the stone placed beneath Jacob’s head signifies the humanity joined to God who assumed it.

The ladder that he saw in his sleep, which was a way to heaven—that is, from flesh to soul or spirit—is Christ, who, by raising his chosen ones through various stages of advancement, makes them spiritual from being carnal.

The angels whom he saw ascending and descending are the holy evangelists and the other preachers. They ascend by the ladder, so to speak, when they proclaim Christ’s divinity, saying: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I, 1). They descend when they describe the lowliness of his incarnation, saying: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid., 14).

Paul was a supreme angel who ascended when he said: “We preach Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Corinthians I, 24). He descended when he said: “I judged that I should know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Corinthians II, 2).

Morally, to sleep on a journey is to rest, along the road of this world, from the hindrance of worldly matters or activities. Jacob, while sleeping, saw angels, because those behold divine things who close their eyes to the desire for temporal possessions.

The devil opened these eyes, rightly closed, when he said: “On whatever day you eat, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods” (Genesis III, 5).

### Verse 14

“You shall spread out toward the east and the west.” The fact that the land is promised to Jacob signifies the possession of the Church promised to Christ.

By the west, the killing of the righteous is signified; by the east, the beginning of a good way of life; by the north, the destruction and mortification of sinners; by the south, the fervor of divine charity. Christ reigns in these things and rejoices to possess this inheritance.

### Verse 17

“This is nothing other than the house of God.” He calls it the house of God because through the spirit of prophecy he foresaw there the future tabernacle of God. He calls the gates of heaven the entrance to divine hearing.

Or mystically, he calls the gate of heaven the departure through the incarnation and the return from it.

It should be noted, in the literal sense, that this was not idolatry. He did not call the stone itself God, nor worship it with any sacrifice, but used it only as a sign and memorial that God had appeared to him and that the tabernacle of God would be there.

### Verse 18

“He raised it up as a monument.” The raising of the stone signifies Christ’s resurrection.

## CHAPTER XXIX

### Verse 2

“He saw a well in the field.” This well figures the knowledge of the Scriptures.

The three flocks lying around the well signify the simple and gentle, who desire to be satisfied by the mysteries of Holy Scripture.

The stone placed over the well signifies the covering of the letter, by which the spiritual water was concealed. But our Jacob—that is, Christ—removed the stone, because he dispelled the surface of the letter and opened the spiritual understanding in the Scriptures.

We may also, without impropriety, understand the well as the font of baptism. The three flocks lying there signify those who, through humility and faith in the Holy Trinity, seek to be cleansed by the water of baptism.

### Verse 10

“When Jacob saw her and knew that she was his cousin.” It may be asked how he knew that she was his cousin, since he had never seen her before. We can understand that he learned this from the shepherds with whom he had previously spoken. Therefore, as soon as he saw her, he rushed confidently to kiss her.

### Verse 20

“The days seemed few.” Why does he say, “The days seemed few,” when even a short time seems long to a lover? He says this because of the servitude, which, although harsh, seemed easy to him because of the greatness of his love.

### Verse 27

“Complete the week of this union.” Here “week” means seven years. A week may mean seven days, seven years, or seven times seven years.

Allegorically, these two women signify two ways of life, the active and the contemplative.

Leah is interpreted as “laboring”; she signifies the active life. She is rightly said to have weak eyes but to be fruitful, because the active life sees less through contemplation, but bears spiritual children to God through preaching and the examples of good works.

Rachel, whose name is interpreted as “ewe” or “beginning of sight,” signifies the contemplative life, simple and rejoicing in quiet. It sees that Beginning who speaks in the Gospel: “I am the Beginning, who also speak to you” (John VIII, 25).

She is beautiful but barren, because the contemplative life is comely and pleasing to God, unstained by any dust of earthly contagion, devoted to God alone and seeking to please him alone; nevertheless, it does not beget spiritual children through preaching.

Jacob loves Rachel but receives Leah at night, because every saint desires to enjoy the rest of the contemplative life, but first must be exercised, in the night of this world, by the labor of the active life.

### Verse 28

“When the week had passed.” It must not be thought that he married Rachel after seven years of service. Rather, after Leah’s wedding, he completed seven days, and after those days he served another seven years.

### Verse 29

“Her father had given her Bala as a maidservant.” Leah had earlier been given a maidservant named Zilpah, while Rachel was given one named Bilhah.

Zilpah is interpreted as “a speaking mouth”; Bilhah as “aged” or “old.”

These two maidservants signify those who perform good works either in the active life or in the contemplative life without right intention, and who preach without right purpose—that is, not for God but for popularity or worldly advantages. Concerning such people the Apostle says: “There are those who preach Christ not sincerely” (Philippians I, 1). And shortly afterward: “Whether from occasion or for truth Christ is proclaimed, in this I rejoice, and I shall also rejoice” (ibid., 18).

Hence Zilpah is rightly interpreted as “a speaking mouth,” because such people have preaching on their lips, not in their hearts. Of them it is said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matthew XV, 8).

Bilhah is called “aged,” because such people, although they bring forth the fruits of good works as though they were good children, nevertheless, because they do this without right purpose, continue in the conduct of their former error.

### Verse 32

“She called his name Reuben.” Reuben is interpreted as “vision of a son” or “seeing a son.”

Simeon means “hearing” or “being heard.”

### Verse 34

“My husband will be joined to me.” Another translation says, “My husband will follow me.” The meaning is: Because I have borne him three sons, he will love me most ardently and will be joined to me, so that he will never leave me.

Hence the name Levi, that is, “taken.”

### Verse 35

“I will confess,” that is, “I will praise the Lord.”

Judah means “confession.”

## CHAPTER XXX

### Verse 6

“God has judged for me.” That is, he has rendered judgment for me, making me equal to my sister. Therefore she called his name Dan, that is, “judgment.”

### Verse 8

“Naphtali,” “comparison.”

### Verse 11

“Gad,” “happiness” or “fortune,” which in Greek is called *tychē*.

In the interpretations of Hebrew names, blessed Jerome says that Gad is interpreted as “armed” or “arming.”

### Verse 13

“Asher” is interpreted as “blessed” or “rich bread.”

### Verse 14

“He found mandrakes.” Mandrakes are fruits that are indeed beautiful and fragrant, but hairy.

[Note: [Col. 0107D] The Tegernsee manuscript has *odora*, “fragrant,” instead.]

### Verse 18

“Issachar” is interpreted as “reward.”

### Verse 20

“Zebulun” is interpreted as “dwelling of strength.”

### Verse 24

“Joseph” is interpreted as “increased” or “blessed.”

### Verse 33

“My righteousness will answer tomorrow.” “Tomorrow” is used here for a future time.

### Verses 37–38

“Taking poplar rods, so that they might conceive at the sight of them.” When Laban had proposed that Jacob should have the animals with varied offspring as his wages, Jacob, with the prudence of a clever man, partly peeled poplar and almond rods, and rods from plane trees, while leaving part of them intact. He placed them in the channels into which the water from the well flowed, so that the sheep coming to drink would be held by a double desire, to mate and to drink. In the heat of mating they looked at the rods and thus conceived varied offspring.

This refers to the final stage of the act, when the whole body of the animal is already trembling and the climax of pleasure is imminent. No one should find this incredible, since even today, it is said, the same thing is done with mares in Spain.

Blessed Augustine also says that it is written in the book of the physician Hippocrates that, when an Ethiopian woman had given birth to a most beautiful and exceptionally white child, and was therefore being led to death as though guilty of adultery, the physician Hippocrates arrived and explained that a woman can conceive from looking at something, or from holding it in her mind. He therefore ordered that a search be made in her house to see whether there was any image or likeness that the woman had seen or kept in mind while lying with her husband. When such an image was found, the woman was freed from the danger of death.

[Note: [Col. 0108D] The Garst manuscript has *Hippocras*.]

Allegorically, the rods signify the teachings of the holy Fathers, which they cut from the body of divine Scripture as from a tree. Because they are straight, they are called rods.

We partly peel these rods and partly allow the bark to remain when we treat the divine Scriptures partly historically and partly allegorically. Where we follow the historical sense, we leave the bark. But where, fleeing the historical sense, we devote ourselves to allegory, we uncover the brightness of spiritual understanding as though the bark had been removed.

To place these rods before the eyes of the sheep is to set examples from the Scriptures before the minds of the faithful, so that they may live according to what they find there and bring forth spiritual offspring of good works.

## CHAPTER XXXI

### Verse 7

“He changed my wages ten times.” “My” is understood. For when Laban saw the varied offspring increasing, he changed the agreement and said: “I want the varied offspring to belong to my share, while the single-colored animals belong to your share.” Again, when he saw the black animals multiplying, he changed the agreement again and claimed these for himself. In this way Jacob says that he changed his wages ten times.

Typologically, Laban, whose name is interpreted as “whitening,” signifies the devil, who, although dark by his own merit, nevertheless transforms himself into an angel of light.

Verses 11–12. And the angel of God said: “Jacob!”—“I have seen everything that Laban has done to you.” From this passage we learn that what Jacob did, he did neither by deceit nor by fraud, but by divine dispensation; or else because these things were being enacted figuratively, which is why he deserved to be strengthened by an angelic vision.

Verse 31. “Toward Mount Gilead.” Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony.” But that place was not yet called by this name; it was given the name later, when Jacob and Laban swore an oath to one another and gathered a heap of stones as a testimony. Therefore this place must be understood by prolepsis—that is, by anticipation.

Verse 35. “I cannot rise before you.” Nature teaches that children should rise before their parents and honor them. Since Rachel was sitting and did not rise before her father, she excused herself by saying, “Let my lord not be angry.” She also discreetly indicated the reason why she could not rise, saying that her menstrual period had come upon her. For this is what she means: “It has happened to me according to the custom of women.”

Allegorically, Laban signifies the devil or the world, which is whitewashed and beautiful to its lovers. Laban’s idols signify avarice. For the Apostle says: “and avarice, which is the service of idols” (Ephesians 5:5). Laban sought these from Jacob when the devil showed Christ—which Jacob signifies—the kingdoms, glory, and honor of the world, supposing that he might find in him some trace of avarice. But Jacob did not know the idols, because Christ possessed no desire for the world.

Rachel stole the idols and, hiding them beneath the bedding, sat on them, because the Church, coming to Christ, recognized that the desires of the age, which she had formerly served, were contemptible; and by sitting upon them—that is, by humbling herself—she hid them through repentance. Sitting signifies humility. Hence the Psalmist says: “Rise up after you have sat down” (Psalm 26:2).
