Verse 37. “Set it here before my brothers.” In the manner customary in Scripture, he calls his sons “brothers.”

Verse 40. “I was scorched by heat and frost.” With one word—*urebar*, “I was scorched”—he answered for two opposites, heat and frost, because heat and cold produce one and the same effect.

[Column 0109D] Verse 42. “The Fear of Isaac”—the one who must be feared by every creature.

Verse 50. “No one is a witness to our speech except God.” That is, there is no witness among outsiders. Or, “no one except God,” because no one can be compared with his testimony.

CHAPTER XXXII

Verse 2. “These are the camps of God”—that is, the angelic hosts. And rightly, as Jacob was journeying to meet his brother, the angels of God came to meet him, so that he might be strengthened by this and not fear his brother, secure in angelic assistance.

Verse 7. “He divided them into two companies.” He divided the people not into three companies, as some think, but into two. The first company consisted of the two maidservants, Zilpah and Bilhah, with their sons. The second company consisted of Leah and Rachel and those who were with them.

But one may ask here: Since God had promised Jacob his help, saying, “Do not fear; I am with you, and I will multiply you,” why did Jacob fear and take measures for his safety, rather than entrust himself to God’s protection? By this example, however, we are warned not to tempt God when we have something we can do for our own safety. Indeed, although Jacob took precautions for himself, let us nevertheless hear what he said in prayer.

Verses 9, 11. “God of my father Abraham, deliver me from the hand of my brother.” Thus, while taking precautions for himself and praying to God, he gives us an example: we should provide for our own life, yet also ask that divine help be present to us.

Verse 24. “And behold, a man wrestled with him.” This man who wrestled with Jacob was an angel. He wrestled not by an embrace of the arms, but by persistent prayer, in which Jacob entreated him to bless him. The prophet Hosea also shows this when he says: “He prevailed against the angel and was strengthened. He wept and entreated him” (Hosea 12:4).

Mystically, Jacob, both lame and strong, signifies the two divisions of the Jewish people, namely the faithful and the unfaithful. Jacob was lame in the unbelieving, but sound and strong in the faithful. The fact that the angel touched the sinew of his thigh and it withered signifies, in the moral sense, that whenever God deigns to bless someone, he causes every carnal pleasure in that person to wither.

Verse 28. “But Israel shall be your name.” The change of name was a blessing. Although Israel is commonly interpreted as “a man seeing God,” it is better interpreted as “a prince with God.” The meaning is: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name”—that is, “Just as I am a prince, so are you, since you were able to wrestle with me.”

Verse 30. PHANUEL is interpreted as “the face of God.” Because Jacob said, “I have seen God face to face,” he therefore called that place Phanuel.

CHAPTER XXXIII

Verse 10. “Thus I have seen your face, as though I saw the face of God.” He said this either as flattery, or rather because his mind was disturbed by fear of his brother. It may also be understood that he used “God” for some great man. Holy men are often called gods, as it was said to Moses: “I have appointed you god of Pharaoh” (Exodus 7:1). For in the Greek there is not *tou Theou* with the article, by which the divine substance is understood, but simply *Theou*, in which a human being is signified.

Verse 28. “He passed over to Salem, a city of the Shechemites.” Blessed Jerome says that *Salem* has been corruptly substituted for *Shechem*. It may also be understood that there were two cities with related names: Salem, the city of the Jebusites, in which Melchizedek reigned; and another, Sale, a city of the Shechemites. Among the Hebrews, however, they are written with different letters and have different interpretations. The former is called Salem, “the city of peace”; the latter, Sale, is interpreted as “completed.”

CHAPTER XXXIV

Verse 1. “Dinah went out.” Allegorically, Dinah signifies a soul that neglects its own concerns and investigates the deeds of others with excessive zeal. It goes out, as it were, to see the women when it abandons its inner life and occupies itself with external matters. As soon as she thus goes out from Shechem—that is, from the devil—she is oppressed and defiled. Hence Dinah is appropriately interpreted as “judgment.” For this is the judgment: because she wanders away of her own accord through negligence, she is immediately corrupted by the devil.

Verse 3. When he says that Shechem’s soul “was joined to her,” this signifies that through an evil habit the soul is united with the devil, so that it not only sins but is also held captive by the deed and pleasure of sinning. Yet if, at some point, she comes to her senses and is grieved through repentance, the devil proposes empty hopes in order to take useful sorrow away from her: at one moment saying that God is merciful, at another recalling the worse deeds of others; now saying that what she has done is practically nothing, now promising a long span of life in which to perform repentance. This is what is meant by saying that “he soothed her sorrow with flatteries.”

But the shepherds of the Church, like the sons of Jacob, ought to avenge the sin of the flesh or of the soul and punish it with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Ephesians 6:17), always ready, according to the Apostle, “to avenge every disobedience” (2 Corinthians 10:6).

According to the literal sense, one may ask how the sons could have done so great a deed, since Jacob himself had earlier called them little ones when he said to Esau: “You know that I have little ones with me.” But it must be understood that Jacob did not remain there for a short time. He fixed his tent there, built an altar, and bought a portion of a large field for one hundred lambs. This shows that Jacob lived there for a long time, during which his sons grew and Dinah became mature.

The fact that only Simeon and Levi are mentioned in the crime should be understood to mean that they had several companions, but these two were the leaders of the slaughter, and Dinah was their uterine sister.

CHAPTER XXXV

Verse 4. “And the earrings that were in their ears.” Earrings pertain more to adornment than to idolatry. Earlier, Abraham’s servant is also said to have put earrings on Rebecca to adorn her face. Therefore we should understand that the objects placed upon idols were called *phylacteria*—amulets.

Verse 5. “The terror of God fell upon all the surrounding nations.” In order that God might fulfill the promise he had made to Jacob, he struck the inhabitants of that land with divine terror. Otherwise Jacob could not have passed unharmed through the midst of those nations.

Verse 10. “You shall no longer be called Jacob.” The Lord said almost the very words that the angel had spoken. Yet Jacob was not then called Israel; rather, it was foretold to him that this would be his name. What was foretold there, therefore, is fulfilled here.

Verse 11. “Grow and multiply.” This is better referred to the spiritual Israel, which grows and multiplies in virtues. For everyone who is a supplanter of vices and contemplates God in his mind is rightly called Jacob or Israel.

Thus, when he says, “You shall no longer be called Jacob,” this does not refer to that one man but to Jacob’s spiritual offspring. Jacob himself was called Jacob afterward. But all the saints—that is, the true Israel—after laying aside all corruption and decay, will not be called Jacob, that is, “supplanter,” since there will be no vices for them to supplant. Rather, they will be called Israel, because they will see God as he is, and the vision of the Creator will be their highest blessedness.

“Kings shall come from your loins”—that is, those who are truly kings, governing themselves well according to God’s will; they are sons of Israel by imitation.

Verse 14. “He erected a stone monument.” Observe that it does not say that he poured a libation over it, but “upon it.” He did not sacrifice to the stone, as idolaters do; rather, he sacrificed to God upon the stone.

Verse 16. “Ephrathah.” This is Bethlehem, and it is interpreted as “land of fruit”; Bethlehem, however, is interpreted as “house of bread.”

Verse 18. “The father called him Benjamin.” The mother, who was dying on his account, called him “son of sorrow.” This was a prophecy concerning the Apostle Paul, who was from that tribe and who, by persecuting his mother—the Church—caused her great sorrow.

But the father, foreseeing through the prophetic Spirit that Paul would be converted, called him “son of the right hand,” because he was to be transferred from the left hand of unbelief to the right hand of faith and preaching.

Allegorically, Benjamin here signifies the city of Jerusalem, most of which lay within the tribe of Benjamin. Jerusalem afflicted its mother—the Synagogue—with grief unto death when it demanded the death of the Redeemer of the world, crying: “Crucify him, crucify him!” (John 19).

[Column 0112C] Verse 21. “Beyond the Tower of the Flock.” He calls it “the tower of the flock,” that is, of the flock itself. The Jews relate that the Temple of God was later built there; hence it was called the Tower of the Flock—that is, of the multitude, congregation, or assembly.

Blessed Jerome says that the Tower of the Flock means the tower of the shepherds, which lies beyond Bethlehem, where the holy shepherds learned through the message of an angel that the Lord had been born, and where the bodies of those three shepherds also rest. Concerning this tower it had been foretold through the prophet: “And you, O misty Tower of the Flock, to you shall come the first power of the daughter of Zion” (Micah 4:8).

Verse 22. “He went and lay with his father’s concubine.” According to the literal sense, Reuben’s crime is described. Allegorically, however, Reuben, the firstborn, signifies the Jews, to whom knowledge of God was first given, and concerning whom it was said: “Israel is my firstborn son.”

Bilhah the concubine signifies the Law. The Apostle Paul shows that the Law is signified by a concubine when he says that Hagar, Abraham’s concubine, represents the Law given on Mount Sinai (Galatians 4:24). Reuben lay with his father’s concubine because the Jewish people corrupted the holy and just Law through false traditions and lost the dignity of the firstborn.

Verse 26. “These are the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Mesopotamia.” One may ask why he says that all of them were born in Mesopotamia, since Benjamin was not born in Mesopotamia. A simple answer may be given: it was said by synecdoche—that is, the whole is used for a part. Or all are said to have been born in Mesopotamia because, although Benjamin was not born there, the circumstances of his birth originated there. He was conceived there but born within Canaan.

Verse 27. “Mamre, Arbe, and Hebron.” They are one city.

CHAPTER XXXVI

Verse 6. “He went into another region.” Here one may ask why Esau is said to have gone to Seir and withdrawn from his brother after their father’s death, when he is said to have been living in Seir already when Jacob arrived.

It may have happened that, while Jacob was fleeing to Mesopotamia, Esau, grieving and angry because the blessing had been taken from him, withdrew from his parents and lived in Seir during the twenty years of Jacob’s absence. After Jacob returned and was reconciled with his brother, Esau again lived with his brother away from Seir for as long as their father lived. When Isaac died, as this passage says, Esau took the substance of his household and withdrew from his brother. They were exceedingly wealthy and could not live together.

Verse 10. Eliphaz. This is the Eliphaz the Temanite who is mentioned in the Book of Job.

Verse 20. “The sons of Seir the Horrite.” The Horrites are interpreted as “free.” As is recorded in the Book of Chronicles, these people first lived on Mount Seir; the Idumeans drove them out and settled there in their place.

Verse 24. “This is Ana, who found hot springs.” This passage is explained in various ways by the Hebrews. Some say that he discovered a pool in the desert, since such a thing is easily found in those regions. Hence another translation says: “He found *jamim* in the wilderness.” In Hebrew, *jamim* means “seas,” that is, a collection of waters.

Others say that he caused wild asses—that is, wild donkeys—to mate with she-asses, so that exceptionally swift donkeys might be born from them. Some say that he made asses mount a herd of mares, so that mules might be born from such intercourse. Others simply say that he discovered hot waters in the desert, which we call thermal springs.

Verse 31. “The kings who reigned in the land of Edom.” It must be understood that he does not mention all the kings who existed before the children of Israel had a king, the first of whom was Saul, but only those who reigned while Esau himself was alive.

Verse 32. “Balaach” [Note: Thus both manuscripts; the Vulgate has *Bela*.], son of Beor. This is not the Balaach mentioned in the Book of Numbers, who hired Balaam the diviner. That man was king of Edom; this one was king in Seir. The former was the son of Sephor; this one was the son of Beor.

Verse 33. Jobab. Some think that this was Job, but it is more suitably believed that he belonged to Job’s lineage, as was stated above.

CHAPTER XXXVII

Verse 2. “He accused his brothers before their father of a very serious crime.” Some think that he accused them because they were coupling with livestock. So Alwinus says in his *Questions*. Others say that he accused Reuben alone because of his father’s concubine. If this is so, we should understand it by synecdoche—that is, the whole is used for a part. For he did not accuse all his brothers, but only one.

Verse 3. “A many-colored tunic.” That is, one joined together or decorated with circles, distinguished by beautiful variety. Another translation has: “He made him a full-length tunic,” which in Greek is called *poderis*. Symmachus, however, has “a tunic,” that is, one varied with marvelous beauty by the hands of an artisan, or “a sleeved garment,” that is, one having sleeves. At that time people chiefly wore *colobia*, garments without sleeves.

The history of Joseph is clear according to the literal sense; now let us investigate its mystery. Allegorically, Joseph signifies Christ according to his humanity. Jacob loved Joseph more than his other brothers; and God the Father loved Christ his Son in a unique way, above all the Jews, who were his brothers according to the assumption of flesh.

He made him a many-colored tunic—that is, he surrounded him with a multitude of believers from every nation, saying through the prophet: “You shall clothe yourself with all these as with an ornament” (Isaiah 49:18).

“And his brothers hated him.” When the Jews saw Christ declared to be the Son of God through signs and miracles, they envied him and often spoke with him deceitfully and treacherously.

When he says that Joseph’s sheaf stood upright and that his brothers’ sheaves worshiped his sheaf, this signifies that after the resurrection he would be worshiped by all believers with the fruit of good works. He is the grain of wheat which, sown through death, sprouted through the resurrection and thus produced throughout the world sheaves of faith and good works.

When, relating another dream, he said that the sun, moon, and eleven stars worshiped him, one may ask according to the literal sense where or when he was worshiped by his father, represented by the sun, and by his mother, represented by the moon. For Jacob is not recorded as having worshiped him when he descended into Egypt, and his mother had died in Bethlehem.

Therefore, since this cannot stand according to the literal sense, let us turn to allegory. This vision was plainly prophetic concerning Christ, whom the sun, moon, stars, and every creature worship. Mystically, the sun—that is, the excellence and brightness of the saints—worships him; the moon—that is, the Church—worships him; and the stars—that is, each individual believer—venerate him as God.

Verses 13 and following. “Joseph was sent by his father to find out what his brothers and their flocks were doing.” The Son of God was likewise sent by God the Father into the world, so that he might gather to faith, like sheep, the people whom God had destined for himself and lead them to eternal pastures.

Verse 19. “He found them at Dothaim.” Dothaim is interpreted as “defection.” And truly, they were in a great state of defection, since they were contemplating fratricide.

Verse 24. “Joseph was thrown by his brothers into a cistern after being stripped of his full-length tunic.” Christ, having laid aside the tunic of flesh through death, descended into hell. The full-length tunic morally signifies a good work brought to completion. For in God’s sacrifice the tail of the victim was also commanded to be offered (Leviticus 7:3). The tail is the end of the body. The tail of the victim is offered when an initial virtue is brought to perfection.

Verse 25. “They were carrying storax into Egypt.” Storax is a drop of the myrrh tree, although the substance itself is also called myrrh. Joseph’s extraction from the cistern signifies Christ’s resurrection.

Verse 27. “Joseph was sold to Ishmaelite merchants at the advice of Judah the patriarch.” Christ was sold at the counsel of Judas Iscariot, and afterward was purchased by the Gentiles for the price of faith [Note: Thus the Codex of Tegernsee; but Garst., “bought with silver, for the price of faith.”]. In the Septuagint it is given as “gold pieces,” but in the Hebrew truth it is better given as twenty silver pieces. For a servant ought not to be sold for a price in a more valuable metal than the Lord.

But this concerns the literal sense. We must ask what is meant by the fact that above it says, “They saw Ishmaelite travelers coming,” whereas here it says, “They sold him to the Midianites.” Ishmael was descended from Hagar, Midian from Keturah. Therefore the opinion of the Hebrews is true: they say that Hagar and Keturah were one woman.

It may also be said that earlier we read that Abraham gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and separated them from his son Isaac toward the east. At that time these two—namely Ishmael and Midian—began to live together and formed one nation.

Verse 31. “They took his tunic.” Joseph’s tunic is the flesh of Christ, which he took from the Virgin and adorned with various forms of virtue. They dipped it in the blood of a kid when they attempted to attribute the guilt of sin to him, accusing him before the governor as a revolutionary who was stirring up the people.

Verses 32–33. “We found this,” up to “a savage beast has devoured him.” This lament of Jacob is prophetic: he grieves more over the destruction of the Jews than over the death of his son Joseph, as he supposed it. The savage beast was the Jewish people, concerning whom the Psalmist once said: “The sons of men, whose teeth are weapons and arrows” (Psalm 56:5).

Verse 35. “Mourning into hell.” From this passage blessed Augustine asks whether only the wicked descend into hell, or whether the wicked and the good descend together. Or perhaps these are simply the words of a troubled mind.

It is nevertheless credible that before the Lord’s Passion there were in hell certain more secluded and less painful places, to which the saints also descended, since no one could enter Paradise and no one could enter the gate of the heavenly kingdom until Christ removed the flaming sword.

Verse 36. “To Potiphar the eunuch.” Another translation calls him not commander of the army but *archimagirus*, that is, chief of the cooks. He is also said to have been a priest of Heliopolis.

Here one may ask how he could have been a priest while having a wife. For the Egyptian hierophants could be neither anything but chaste nor attached to wives. The Jews relate that Joseph was extremely handsome and was therefore purchased for an indecent service; but God caused his genitals to wither so that he could not corrupt the chaste boy. He then became a priest of Heliopolis, whereas previously he had been a layman.

CHAPTER XXXVIII

Verses 3–10. “He called his name Er. Again, after conceiving a child, she called his name Onan,” and so on up to “the Lord killed him, because he had done a detestable thing.”

Judah here is a type of the royal line that descended from Judah. Judah’s two sons signify two kinds of evil people: those who do harm, signified by Er, of whom it is said, “Er was wicked before the Lord, and he was killed by him.” Hence Er is interpreted as “skin” or “leathern.” Skin signifies sins; for our first parents are read to have had tunics of skin after the sin.

The other kind consists of evil people who are unwilling to provide a benefit—that is, to do good—and these are signified by Onan. His name is interpreted as “their sorrow,” with “their” understood to mean those to whom he refuses to provide a benefit. Of him it is said that he spilled his seed upon the ground, unwilling to raise children for his deceased brother.

Divine vengeance therefore condemns both those who do evil and those who refuse to do good.

“And she bore a third.” The third son, who was unmarried and was called Shelah, signifies the period when the Jews were without a king, without a priest, and without a sacrifice. Hence Shelah is interpreted as “his division.”

Verse 14. A *theristrum* is a type of garment worn by Palestinian women, especially Arabian women. It is called *theristrum* because they use that covering in *theri*, that is, in summer. From this passage we learn that even at that time widows had one kind of clothing and prostitutes another.

Verse 23. “Let her keep them; certainly she could not accuse us of falsehood.” In Judah’s deed, not justice but faith is apparent. If he had been just, he would have preserved his chastity. His faith, however, consisted in this: he sent back the kid that he had promised.

Mystically, Judah here represents Christ. Tamar, whose name is interpreted as “bitterness” or “changed,” is a type of the Church, which had been involved in the bitterness of idolatry.

But Judah sought her with his shepherd, the Adullamite called Hiras. Hiras is interpreted as “the vision of my brother,” signifying John the Baptist, whom Christ sent before him as a herald. He was an Odollamite, which is interpreted as “testimony,” because he bore testimony to the Lord in the waters of the Jordan.

Judah came to shear the sheep. Christ came to human beings to relieve them of the fleeces and filth of their sins. Then he saw Tamar—that is, he had mercy on the Church—and, changing her name and her appearance, he made her from a Synagogue into a Church, from a prostitute into a bride.

The statement that he did not recognize her means what he himself says through the Psalmist: “A people whom I did not know served me” (Psalm 17:44).

He gave her a ring, a staff, and a bracelet as a pledge: a pledge of calling, justification, and glorification, as the Apostle says: “Those whom he called, these he also justified; and those whom he justified, these he also glorified” (Romans 8:30).

Verse 26. “She is more righteous than I.” Because I did not give her to my son Shelah. Another translation says: “She has been justified in comparison with me,” that is, “in relation to me.” For she did not do this out of a desire for wandering lust, but from the love of producing offspring.

Verse 29. “Why has the barrier been divided because of you?” He calls the membrane of the afterbirth a “barrier.” Phares is interpreted as “division”; from him come the Pharisees.

Verse 30. Zara is interpreted as “Rising” or “East,” either because he ought to have come out first or because many just and wise men arose from his family.

Allegorically, these two sons of Judah represent two peoples. Through Zara, who first extended his hand, the Jewish people are signified. It stretched out its hand, as it were, when it showed itself prepared to fulfill God’s commands. The midwife wished to tie scarlet around it—that is, to mark it with faith in the Lord’s Passion and Cross. Scarlet, having the color of blood, indicates Christ’s Passion.

But he withdrew his hand stained with the blood of the prophets and of the Lord himself, because he refused to accept faith in his Passion. While he delayed, his younger brother came out: that is, the Gentile people, by believing in Christ, prepared themselves to obey his commands.

CHAPTER XXXIX

Verse 6. “Joseph was beautiful in appearance.” We have said that Joseph signifies Christ, whose beauty surpasses every form of loveliness. Concerning this the Psalmist says: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 44:3). And the Apostle says: “Into whom angels long to look” (1 Peter 1:12). He truly prospers in all things, and everything is directed by his hand.

Verses 7–20. “After many days, the woman cast her eyes upon Joseph.” This woman represents the Synagogue, which had a husband—namely the Law itself, by which it was ruled and taught. [Note: Column 0117D. Codex Garst. has the abbreviated reading *vol. aevi leg.*—apparently “wished … law”; its expansion is uncertain.]

She wished to deceive Christ, appearing as a man, through seduction, because the Synagogue wanted to observe his Law carnally, fulfilling according to the letter the Sabbath and everything else that had been given to it in figures.

When Christ refused to obey her, he left his cloak with her, because he left her the covering of the legal letter. Hence, as the Apostle says, “to this very day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart” (2 Corinthians 3:15).

Thus the Lord abandoned that people, saying: “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matthew 23:38), and he passed to the Gentiles with the spiritual understanding of the Scriptures.

The woman accused him, displaying the cloak to her husband as evidence, because the Synagogue accused Christ of destroying the Law and of making himself equal to God by saying that he was God.

Joseph was sent to prison: Christ descended into hell. Joseph was brought out of prison: Christ rose from the dead. But the one who had been sent into prison alone was not brought out alone. For he brought out the chief official who offered the cup and restored him to his former rank. Thus Christ, rising again, freed his own from the prison of hell.

CHAPTER XL

Verse 1. “Cupbearer.” A wine-servant who offered or poured the cup to the king. That this office was not insignificant among the ancients is shown by the poets’ myths, in which it is related that Jupiter appointed his beloved Ganymede cupbearer of the gods.

Verse 17. “And in one basket, which was higher, I carried for me all the foods made by the baker’s craft.” In the Greek it says that he carried *chondriton* [Note: Codex Garst. has *contiton*; Codex Tegernsee, *dontiton*], that is, a food-loaf or bread for nourishment. But this does not suit Pharaoh, as though he were eating ordinary food-bread. Nevertheless, as blessed Augustine says [Note: *Book I of the Questions on Genesis*, question 131], it could have been that the basket appeared to contain food-loaves at the bottom, above which were all the things made by the baker’s craft.

Mystically, these two men are two peoples, both of whom sinned gravely, as the Apostle says: “There is no distinction between Jew and Greek; all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Romans 10:12).

But when the true Joseph appeared, the one—that is, the Jewish people—was condemned because it did not believe in the wood of the Cross, on the wood of transgression.

Verse 20. “The third day,” on which one was restored and the other hanged, signifies the Lord’s resurrection, which took place on the third day.

CHAPTER XLI

Verse 1. “After two years Pharaoh had a dream,” and so forth. The seven years of abundance, signified by seven fat cows and an equal number of full and beautiful ears of grain, mystically signify the fullness of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, which was manifested in the earliest times among the apostles and other believers.

The barrenness of the following seven years, displayed by seven emaciated cows and an equal number of thin ears of grain struck by scorching heat, signifies the time when, at the end of the age, love will grow cold and iniquity will abound, and there will be a famine of the word of God. The Lord foretold this through the prophet: “I will send a famine upon the land—not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God” (Amos 8:11).

Verse 14. “Immediately, after they had brought Joseph out of prison, they shaved him.” Joseph’s being brought out of prison is Christ’s resurrection, through which he cast off all mortality and weakness, as though they were the growth of hair, and received the garment of immortality and joy.

Verse 42. “He took the ring from his hand.” The ring on Joseph’s hand signifies the priesthood of faith, which has been placed in the hand—that is, in the power—of Christ. For he became a priest according to the order of Melchizedek.

The linen robe signifies his holy flesh, which arose from the earth of virginal flesh and, like linen, having been worn down by various sufferings, attained the whiteness of immortality and eternal glory.

“And he placed a golden chain around his neck.” The golden chain with which Joseph’s neck was adorned signifies heavenly wisdom, which, like a circle, has neither beginning nor end. The golden chain may also be understood as good will and the simplicity of good people.

[Column 0119A] Verse 43. “And he made him ascend into a chariot.” Joseph ascended into a chariot because Christ, adorned with divine gifts, returned to heaven.

“While the herald was proclaiming.” The herald who announced his glory is John the Baptist, who proclaimed his first coming; or the angelic trumpet, which will precede him when he comes for judgment.

Verse 45. “He called him savior of the world in the Egyptian language.” That is, *Phontophones*. Another edition says: “He called him tender father”—“father” because of his wisdom, and “tender” because he was a young man.

Verse 46. “He was thirty years old.” This is the perfect age in a human being. At this age David was appointed king, and Ezekiel began to prophesy. The Lord of all was also baptized at this age and began to preach.

“He stood before Pharaoh.” Because he presented himself to the world by preaching and performing miracles.

Verses 51–52. Manasseh is interpreted as “forgetfulness”; Ephraim as “growing” or “fruitful.”

Verse 56. “Joseph opened the storehouses and sold grain to the Egyptians.” Christ opened the storehouses of the divine word throughout the whole world and sold them the grain of the divine utterances, receiving from them the price of their salvation.

CHAPTERS XLII–XLIII

Verse 1. “Jacob said to his sons: ‘Go down to Egypt.’” Jacob here bears the figure of God the Father. The grain is Christ, who compared himself to a grain of wheat. Jacob sends to Egypt for grain, and God the Father called the Son back from Egypt, saying: “Out of Egypt I have called my Son” (Matthew 2:15).

The ten older brothers who were sent signify the more mature people from the Jewish community, who knew how to fulfill the Decalogue of the Law spiritually.

Verse 7. “He spoke harshly to them, as though they were strangers.” It should not be attributed to cruelty that he afflicted his brothers in this way or delayed revealing their mutual relationship for so long. He did this because he wished to test whether they had abandoned the wickedness through which they had sold him, and whether they would prove toward their brother such as he knew them to have been toward himself when they sold him into foreign lands.

Verse 9. “He remembered the dreams that he had once seen”—namely, that the sun, moon, and stars would worship him. And truly, every creature worships Christ; spiritually, the perfection of the saints, the splendor of the Church, and the entire multitude of the elect worship him—young men and virgins, old men together with the young.

Verse 24. “He turned away for a little while and wept.” Joseph rightly signifies Christ, who shines forth with so many virtues: with chastity, by which he regarded the wickedness of the loving woman as nothing; and with wisdom, by which he interpreted the secrets of dreams and foretold the future.

He was also severe in correcting his brothers and compassionate in comforting them. He not only did not avenge their injuries, but even wept for them.

Verses 8–9. “Judah also said: ‘Send the boy with me,’” up to “I shall be guilty of sin against my father forever.” Let us consider Reuben’s words, given above. He said: “Kill my two sons if I do not bring him back to you.” Yet although he proposed so great a pledge, namely the death of his sons, he did not obtain what he wanted.

Let us also consider Judah’s words, by which he bound himself on behalf of the boy: “If I do not bring him back to you,” he said, “I shall be guilty of sin forever.” And he obtained what he wanted, for Benjamin was entrusted to his care. Let us therefore consider whether it is worse to be guilty of sin than to kill someone bodily.

Verse 11. “A little resin.” We call resin *gummi*, a name generally applied to all trees; but here a species is meant that is called by its proper name *Stiracis* [Note: Thus both manuscripts]. *Stiracis* is a kind of resin. In place of storax, the Septuagint has *thymiama*, which in Hebrew is called *NECHOTA*. Storax is a drop of the myrrh tree. The terebinth is a tree whose resin is likewise called—

Verse 23. “As for the money that you gave me, I have it tested.” It is not a lie when he says that he has the money they found at the tops of the sacks. He was a wise man, being the steward of a wise master; therefore he did not speak of silver as money, but of that which is always given and never diminished. Hence he called it “tested,” in accordance with what the Psalmist says: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire” (Psalm 12:7).

Verse 32. “Joseph separately, and his brothers separately,” as strangers; the Egyptians separately, as natives.

Verse 34. The greater portion fell to Benjamin. As we have often said, Benjamin signifies the apostle Paul, to whom the greater portion fell because he labored more than the others in preaching and filled the Gospel of Christ from Jerusalem to Illyricum.

## CHAPTER XLIV

[Col. 0120C]

Verse 2. “Put my cup in the mouth of the sack of the younger one.” Allegorically, Benjamin designates the apostle Paul, as we have often said. He is called younger, or least, because he had not yet attained manhood in Christ; in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter VII) he is called a young man. He also says of himself: “I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15:9).

The silver cup is the splendor of the divine utterances, which were entrusted especially to Paul. For he had a greater gift of knowledge than the others, in accordance with the testimony given by blessed Peter, who says: “Our brother Paul, according to the knowledge given to him [Note: [Col. 0119D] Codex Tegernsee has ‘wisdom’], wrote to us.” He had a silver cup—that is, divine knowledge—but it was hidden inside the sack, that is, within the usefulness of the legal letter [Note: So both codices; perhaps read “worthlessness”]. But the steward came and tore open the sack. Ananias, sent by Christ, came and dissolved the thickness of the legal letter, that is, its blindness. Immediately the cup shone forth, because Paul at once began to act boldly in the synagogues, preaching Christ and transferring the letter of the Law, which kills, to its spiritual meaning.

Verse 13. “He returned to the town.” Literally, he was not cruelly troubling his brothers, but cleansing the sin of the sale which they had committed against him; at the same time, he wished to discover whether they were toward their brother as they had been toward him.

## CHAPTER XLV

[Col. 0121A]

Verse 17. “Loading the animals, and so forth.” In this passage Pharaoh represents the gentile people, who will rejoice at the conversion of the Jews at the end of the age and will promise them an abundance of the divine Scriptures and “the marrow of the earth,” that is, the sweetness of spiritual understanding.

Verse 21. “And the sons of Israel did as they had been commanded.” Joseph’s brothers are the apostles, the brothers of Christ—Peter, Paul, and the others.

Verse 22. “Benjamin gave three hundred pieces of silver.” This signifies the mysteries of the faith of the Holy Trinity and of the cross of Christ, which are to be preached. For the letter tau, which has the shape of a cross, signifies the number 300. The apostle Paul says: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2). [Col. 0121B] He also commands his beloved disciple: “Do not be ashamed of the cross of Christ, nor of me, his prisoner” (2 Tim. 2:8).

He also received five excellent garments, that is, wisdom and moderation in the five senses; all these qualities were greater in Paul than in the others. The other brothers received two garments each, so that they might preach Christ as God and man, and preach that love of God and neighbor must be maintained.

Verse 23. “The asses that carried bread and grain on the journey” signify the gentiles converted to Christ. Previously they were foolish and of low status, but after their conversion to Christ they carried the nourishment of the word of God.

Verse 27. “His spirit revived.” Here Jacob represents the Israelite people, which through unbelief was wasting away in a kind of old age and was already almost dead. [Col. 0121C] But when it heard the preaching of the apostles, whom Jacob’s sons represent, and when it saw the miracles and the gifts of divine power that Christ—who was the son of that same people according to the flesh—had performed, it revived and prepared to go to meet him.

## CHAPTER XLVI

Verse 7. “Daughters and all his offspring together.” Since he uses the plural, “daughters,” we must understand a part from the whole. He had only one daughter, Dinah.

Verse 26. “All the persons who entered Egypt were seventy.” This is the Hebrew truth. For what is read in the Septuagint—“All the persons were seventy-five”—is plainly shown not to agree when Jacob’s sons are counted. Those who entered Egypt with Jacob were sixty-six; if Joseph himself and the sons whom he had fathered in Egypt are added, there were sixty-nine. If Jacob himself, the father of all, is added to these, the total is seventy.

When Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles, “Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy-five persons” (Acts 7:14), this is a similar error. But because at that time the Septuagint had greater authority than the Hebrew truth and was read by all the churches, holy Luke wrote seventy-five.

“All the persons who came forth from Jacob’s thigh.” Certain heretics have twisted this passage to support their error, saying that souls, like bodies, are born from the father’s seed. But the truth is otherwise. God creates souls from nothing—not from bodies, nor from other souls—and gives them to bodies when and as he wills. Therefore, when it says, “the souls who came forth from Jacob’s thigh,” by “souls” we must understand the whole human being, taking the whole from the greater part. So also the whole human being is sometimes understood from the lower part, as when John says, “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14), designating the whole human being by “flesh.”

Verse 28. “He sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph.” Judah, whose name is interpreted as “confession,” is sent ahead to Joseph, that is, to Christ, because confession precedes the grace of faith. After the confession, Joseph himself comes to meet them, because Christ’s mercy follows.

[Col. 0122B]

Verse 34. “We are shepherds, both we and our fathers.” This is the proper order of servitude: that human beings rule over animals and animals serve human beings. Human servitude, however, is produced either by iniquity or by adversity. By iniquity, as when Noah cursed his son and said: “Cursed be my son Canaan; he shall be a servant to his brothers.” By adversity, as in the case of Joseph, who was sold and became a servant.

“The Egyptians detest all shepherds of sheep.” Egypt rightly signifies this world, in which iniquity has abounded. The Egyptians abhor shepherds of sheep because every unrighteous person hates the righteous.

“In the land of Goshen.” He says that Goshen is the region of the Thebaid, which is called Gosen by the Septuagint [Note: So both codices].

## CHAPTER XLVII

Verse 9. “The days of my pilgrimage.” Notice that holy men confess themselves to be strangers and pilgrims, because they have no abiding city here but seek the one that is to come. Ramesses is a part of the Thebaid, a district now called Arsinoite [Note: So both codices].

Verse 12. “And he fed them, and so forth.” People usually ask in this passage how the animals and cattle could have survived when famine pressed upon the whole land for seven years, especially since Jacob’s sons had earlier said that there was no fodder for them in the land of Canaan because there was no rain there. But it must be understood that the Nile in Egypt forms enormous marshes, in which abundant grass grows for the animals; the fodder for the cattle is more fertile the drier the Nile has been. In these places, therefore, the animals and the other creatures—which were extremely numerous in Egypt—were fed.

[Col. 0122D]

Verse 19. “Buy us into royal servitude.” Allegorically, all Egypt is a slave, and all the more so because it surrenders itself voluntarily. The sons of Israel, too, had been slaves in Egypt, but not voluntarily. The Egyptians, however, willingly undertook servitude, signifying those who exclude God from their minds and surrender themselves to serve impurity and iniquity, unto iniquity.

Verse 22. “Except the land of the priests, which had been given to them by the king.” The land of the priests is the holy Church, in which there are true priests who possess true freedom and suffer no lack from spiritual hunger, because they are nourished by Christ the King with the food of the divine word.

Verse 23. “Take seed and sow the fields.” Our Joseph, that is, Christ, urges the faithful to receive the seeds of evangelical preaching and sow the fields—that is, the hearts of their hearers—so that they may receive from them the fruit of good works.

Verse 24. “You shall give a fifth to the king.” The fifth part, which was paid to kings, signifies the guardianship of the five senses, which must be consecrated to Christ. For the Law also commands that every firstborn male be redeemed for five shekels of silver (Exod. 13:15). The permission to retain the other four parts signifies that each person in lay conduct—that is, in active life—is permitted to live according to his purpose or ability.

Verse 29. “Put your hand under my thigh and swear to me by the God of heaven that you will not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan.” Jacob showed that he was the son of holy Abraham not only in the flesh but also in his conduct. Abraham had adjured his servant in these words: “Put your hand under my thigh; swear to me by the God of heaven that you will not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan.” Here Jacob similarly adjures his son Joseph not to bury him in Egypt. Both men foresaw and faithfully believed in the future incarnation of Christ.

It may be asked why the holy patriarchs took such care concerning the burial of their bodies, since they knew that corpses buried in sarcophagi and those left beneath the open sky could decay equally. The poet also says:

> He is covered by the sky who has no urn.

But they did this not because they were concerned about the corpses themselves, which in any event would return to the earth, but so that they might leave their memory to others and thus urge them to imitate them. The Lord also says to Job: “It will be restored like clay beneath a seal, and it will stand like a folded garment” (Job 38:14). The seal—that is, the human being made in the image of God—is restored like clay through death; yet he is not cast away recklessly or carelessly, but is placed safely, like a folded garment, so that he may be clothed again through the resurrection.

Verse 31. “Israel worshiped God, turning toward the head of the bed.” Augustine: What certain Latin codices have—“And he worshiped over the head of his staff,” or “at its head”—misleads them. The Greek word is written with the same letters whether it means “his own” or “his,” but the accents differ; and those who know these matters do not disregard the difference in manuscripts [Col. 0123D], for it is important for distinguishing the meanings.

Accordingly, the question arises concerning what was said. It would easily be understood that the old man worshiped the top of his own staff, which he carried in such a way that, bending his head over it, he worshiped God. But when the text says “his,” the reference is different: after his son’s oath, he again leaned upon the staff taken by his own son and worshiped its top—or his son’s top. This holy man, devoted to God and weighed down by old age, had arranged the bed on which he lay so that, with his head turned toward the east, he could immediately turn to prayer without difficulty if he wished.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

[Col. 0124A]

Verse 5. “They shall be reckoned to me as Reuben and Simeon.” That is, they will individually constitute their own tribes, so that it will no longer be called the tribe of Joseph, but the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh. Just as Simeon and Reuben each constitute a single tribe, so Ephraim and Manasseh will be two tribes; thus thirteen tribes will be completed, with the tribe of Joseph divided into two parts.

Verse 14. “Joseph brought his two sons to his father,” so that he might bless them. He placed his firstborn, Manasseh, at his father’s right hand, and the younger, Ephraim, at his left. Filled with the prophetic Spirit and foreseeing what was to come, Jacob placed his right hand on the head of the younger Ephraim and his left hand on the head of Manasseh, who was older, crossing his hands in the form of a cross. He saw that Ephraim would multiply and that Jeroboam would become king from the tribe of Ephraim.

Mystically, these two sons of Joseph signify two peoples. Through Manasseh, whose name is interpreted as “forgetfulness,” the Jewish people are understood, because they forgot the Lord their creator. Through Ephraim, whose name is interpreted as “fruitful” or “fruitfulness,” the gentile people are represented, because by believing in Christ they offered the fruit of faith and good works to the Lord and multiplied through spiritual fruitfulness. Although this people received knowledge of God later, it was placed before Manasseh, because after the Jews were rejected it received the grace, the mysteries of the Scriptures, and all the dignity of the divine Law that the Jews had possessed [Note: Both codices read “because once they had”].

[Col. 0124C]

Verse 21. “He will bring you back to the land of your fathers.” The patriarch Jacob was held by a great desire, longing to be buried in that land where he knew that Christ would suffer and redeem the human race. Indeed, as experts in the holy places report, from the place called the Abramium, where Abraham and Isaac are buried, to the place of the Lord’s Passion there are approximately thirty miles, so that by this very number, which is contained in the letter T, the mystery of the Lord’s Passion might also be revealed.

Verse 22. “Beyond your brothers.” That is, beyond the portion that he will receive with the other brothers when the possessions are divided. When he says, “which I took from the hand of the Amorite with my sword and my bow,” he calls his justice his sword and bow, by which, after the slaughter of the Shechemites, he was able—under God’s protection—to escape from the surrounding nations. Another translation says, “which I took in my strength.” He calls the money or wealth that he possessed his strength, since he acquired it through his own sweat and labor.

## CHAPTER XLIX

Verse 1. “In the last days.” By saying this, he shows that he is going to speak prophetically. Although these words with which he blessed his sons pertain to the division of the possession they received in the land of Canaan, they must nevertheless be referred especially to Christ, who was incarnate at the final time of the age.

[Col. 0125A]

Verses 3–4. “Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my sorrow.” What he says, “the beginning of my sorrow,” signifies literally that every firstborn is the beginning of sorrow, since at his birth the father’s and mother’s inmost parts are first shaken. The sense of these words is as follows: “O Reuben, who were my firstborn, to whom all firstborn privileges and priestly and royal dignity were owed, who were first in gifts and greater in authority—yet you lost all these things, because you poured yourself out like water through the force of evil desire. Therefore do not increase, or do not multiply and grow.”

In this sense Moses also says when blessing him: “Let Reuben live and not die, and let him be few in number,” and “do not increase”—or, “that you may repeat your crime.” This is the literal interpretation.

Allegorically, Reuben signifies the Jewish people, of whom it was said: “Israel is my firstborn son.” He is called “strength” because he understood the mysteries of the Scriptures. He was also the beginning of God’s sorrow, because after promising to serve God, he frequently provoked him to anger by murmuring and despising his benefits. He was first in gifts because the faithful mysteries were entrusted to him, and greater in authority because, so long as he served God, he ruled many nations faithfully.

But he poured himself out like water—that is, he lost all these things very quickly, as water is quickly poured out when it cannot be contained in a vessel. And why? “Because you went up,” he says, “onto your father’s bed.” The bed of God the Father is Christ according to his humanity, in whom the fullness of divinity rests. The wicked people went up onto this bed when they rose up against Christ and demanded his death. It also stained God’s couch when it called Christ a sinner, a Samaritan, and one who had a demon. Therefore it deserved to hear: “Do not increase, but rather diminish, and be diminished among all the nations.”

Verse 5. “Simeon and Levi, warring vessels of iniquity.” These two brothers of Dinah, enraged because of their sister’s violation, destroyed the allied city after killing its inhabitants. He calls them “warring vessels of iniquity,” that is, instruments of iniquity. “Let my soul not enter into their counsel.” By these words he shows that it was not his will that Hemor and Shechem, though innocent, should be killed with the others. “Let not the soul enter”—that is, let not the will and counsel enter.

[Col. 0125D]

Verses 6–7. “They killed a man.” That is, Hemor and Shechem. “They undermined a wall,” namely, the wall of the hospitable city. When he says, “I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel,” he signifies that the tribe of Levi did not possess an inheritance with the other tribes, but received small cities among the other tribes for habitation. Concerning Simeon, too, it is written that he had no allotted portion of his own, but received something from Judah’s possession.

Mystically, Simeon and Levi signify the leaders of the Jews, who fought against Christ, inflamed by the torches of envy. They are rightly called “vessels of iniquity,” because just as vessels are filled with liquid, so the scribes and priests of the Jews were filled with deceit and malice. Therefore, foreseeing their wickedness, the patriarch prays that his soul—that is, his will—may not enter into the counsel they formed against Christ.

“They killed a man,” that is, Christ. “They undermined a wall,” that is, they fastened his body with nails and opened it with a lance. He calls the body of Christ a very strong wall, built in the Virgin’s womb over forty-six days, just as the Lord’s Temple was built or constructed over forty-six years.

“I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.” Division and scattering must not be understood in the same sense. Division is understood in a good sense, while scattering is understood in an evil one. God divided those from that people who believed from the unbelievers and joined them to the body of the Church. But those who persisted in unbelief he scattered throughout all the nations.

Verse 8. “Judah, your brothers will praise you,” and the rest, “your father’s sons will worship you.” Under the name Judah, this blessing is understood literally of David, who belonged to the same tribe and was a most powerful king. His brothers—that is, the remaining tribes—will praise him. “His hand was on the necks of his enemies,” that is, he possessed the power and strength to humble the might of the other nations. He humbled and made tributary nearly all Syria and Palestine and the remaining surrounding nations. Therefore his father’s sons—or brothers, that is, the entire Jewish people—will worship him, seeing that the Lord is with him.

Mystically, Judah signifies Christ, who is the true confessor, as he says to the Father in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. 11:25). His brothers praise him—that is, the entire multitude of the righteous—not with ordinary praise, but with a special and divine praise, as their God and Lord. His hand is on the necks of his enemies, to humble them and subject their necks to his faith. His father’s sons will worship him—that is, the saints, whom he made sons of God and his own brothers.

Verse 9. “You have gone up to seize the prey, my son.” What is handed down here pertains both literally to David and spiritually to Christ, whom the patriarch addresses by apostrophe: “You have gone up to seize the prey, my son.” Christ went up to seize the prey because he came to fight against the devil and rescue those whom he had taken captive.

When he says, “you have gone up,” he shows the Creator’s confidence and security. He reclined and rested like a lion because, in the firmest hope of the resurrection [Note: Both codices have “of the firmest”], he accepted death, over which he had power. He rested like a lion’s cub because he lay in the tomb for three days. Physicists report that a lion’s cub sleeps for three days after it is born and is finally awakened on the third day by its father’s great roar. So Christ also slept in the tomb for three days and was finally raised by God the Father on the third day. The Psalmist describes his roar, saying: “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp” (Ps. 107:3). And he himself answered: “I will awake at dawn.” Who raised him? No one, clearly, except the Father and the very divinity with which his humanity was filled.

Verse 10. “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor the ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent.” It is evident to everyone that this is said of Christ, until whose coming rulers from the tribe of Judah existed among the Jewish people. For Herod, under whom the Lord was born, was a foreigner and a proselyte. The one who was to be sent had already come. “And he will be the expectation of the nations,” namely, of those who were to be redeemed by his precious blood.

“Tying his foal to the vine, and his donkey, my son, to the vine.” Here it is plainly shown that these words are spoken not of Judah but of Christ. For although he seems to be speaking about Judah, he turns to Judah himself as though speaking about another and says: “tying his foal to the vine.” He calls the choir of the apostles a vine; they had grown like branches from one true vine, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the vine; you are the branches.”

The foal signifies the gentile people, whom he tied to the vine when, through apostolic preaching, he subdued the people so that they might follow the apostles’ faith and teaching. The donkey, however, is the Church gathered from the gentiles, once foolish and weighed down by the burdens of sins, but after receiving the faith of Christ it cast off the devil’s yoke in exchange and took upon itself Christ’s easy burden. He tied this donkey to the vine because he joined the Church from the gentiles to himself by the bonds of love.

“He will wash his garment in wine.” Christ’s garment is his flesh, which he washed with the wine pressed from the cluster hanging on the cross, because he drenched his flesh with the blood of his Passion.

The cloak signifies the nations, with which Christ is clothed, in accordance with what was said to him through the prophet: “With all these you shall clothe yourself as with an ornament” (Isa. 49:18). He therefore washed his cloak in the blood of the grape, because he redeemed the gentile people with his blood. Hence John says: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1:5).

Verse 12. “His eyes are more beautiful than wine.” Christ’s eyes are the apostles and evangelists, who poured spiritual knowledge into us. Wine signifies the austerity of observance under the Law. Christ’s eyes, therefore, are more beautiful than wine because evangelical teaching is clearer than the tradition of the Law.

His teeth are the holy preachers, who, like teeth breaking down food, break unbelievers out of their hardness so that they may be received into the body of the Church. Milk is the tradition of the Law, by which the Jews were nourished like infants, unable to receive solid food. His teeth are therefore whiter than milk because the preachers of the New Testament surpass the teachers of the Law. They are rightly called white, because those who teach others must themselves be pure and free from every stain of sin.

Verse 16. “Dan will judge his people.” Some understand these words, spoken under the person of Dan, of Judas the traitor, who is rightly called a serpent and a cerastes—that is, a horned serpent—because of the deceits and poisons of his malice. They understand the horse, or its rider, as Christ according to his humanity. The serpent or cerastes bit his hoofs when it laid snares for his death, so that its rider might fall backward—that is, so that Christ through death might be reduced to dust like other human beings. They fall backward, as it were, when through death they return to the earth from which they were taken.

But because he foresaw by the prophetic Spirit that Christ would rise on the third day, he said: “I will await your salvation, Lord.” Yet it is better to refer these words to the Antichrist, who is to be born from the tribe of Dan. Hence we rightly read that the tribe of Dan camped in the wilderness on the northern side, indicating the one who said: “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north.”

[Col. 0128B]

For this reason Dan is called a serpent and a cerastes: a serpent because of deceit, and a cerastes because of power. The Antichrist will strive to subjugate those whom he cannot deceive by fraud through the power of the world, like a horned serpent.

It must be observed that he says, “a serpent on the road, a cerastes on the path.” No one is unaware that a road is broader than a path. Therefore the road signifies those who walk the broad ways of the world; the Antichrist will secretly bite and deceive them like a serpent. The path signifies the saints who proceed toward life by the narrow way; the Antichrist will oppress them by his power like a cerastes.

“Biting the horse’s hoofs.” Here the horse signifies the world, which foams with pride and ambition in the course of passing time. The hoof is the extremity of the foot, and the foot is the extremity of the body. Since the Antichrist seeks to seize the final times of the world, he is therefore said to bite the horse’s hoofs. The rider of this horse is everyone who takes pride in the world’s dignities and power.

Thus the cerastes, that is, the Antichrist, bites the horse’s hoofs so that its rider may fall backward, because he occupies the world’s final times in order to drag the reprobate with him into eternal damnation. Falling backward belongs to the reprobate, just as, conversely, falling on one’s face belongs to the elect. To fall on one’s face is to blush with shame over the evils one has committed, because one who falls on his face falls where he can see; but one who falls backward falls where he cannot see. Thus to fall backward is to plunge unknowingly into the pit of eternal damnation.

Some understand this passage, under the person of Dan, literally of the very strong Samson, who belonged to the same tribe and judged Israel for many years. He compares him to a serpent and a cerastes. Just as serpents lie in wait for travelers, so Samson allowed no enemy to pass through his territory or do any harm there. And if anyone, relying on agility or strength, came against him, Samson bit that man’s hoofs—that is, overcame him by great force and compelled him to flee backward, as though making a rider fall backward from a horse.

But when he says, “I will await your salvation, Lord,” the sense is this: “When I saw Samson, so strong, accomplishing such great deeds and conquering the Philistines, who then ruled the Israelites; when I saw him kill a thousand men with the jawbone of a donkey, carry the gates of Gaza on his shoulders to the mountain, and kill a lion as though it were a kid; when I saw him doing these and similar things, I thought that he was the Christ. But when I saw him again deceived by the love of a prostitute, and when I saw him killed without rising again, I understood that he was not the Christ promised to us. Therefore I will await your salvation,” that is, Jesus, whose name is interpreted as “saving” or “salvation.”

Verse 13. “Zebulun will dwell on the shore of the sea.” Literally, the patriarch foretells the possession held by the tribe of Zebulun. It possessed the shore of the Great Sea, extending as far as Sidon, a maritime city.

Allegorically, Zebulun signifies the Church, which, rescued from the waves of the world, enjoys the stability of the shore and is a station for ships, because the Church is spread among the peoples of the gentiles, whom Sidon—whose name is interpreted as “hunting”—signifies.

Verse 14. “Issachar,” he says, “is a strong ass.” He calls him a strong ass literally because he labored in carrying merchandise to the sea. “He lies down between the boundaries,” namely, beside the territory of Naphtali. The Hebrews say that the men of that tribe continually occupied themselves with meditation on the divine Law, and that therefore he is called a strong ass because of his constant effort in seeking wisdom.

“Issachar is a strong ass.” Since he had spoken of Zebulun’s possession as being in maritime regions, he returns to the inland territories and foretells the possession of Issachar, which would be exceedingly fertile and rich in commerce.

Mystically, Issachar signifies the gentile people, once foolish and of low status, weighed down by the burdens of sins. But after it came to know Christ, it began to lie down “between the boundaries,” that is, to rest in hope of the promised blessedness, which it awaits at the boundary—that is, at the end of the age. It saw that the resting place was good, namely, the one promised to all the saints in the next life. It saw that the land was excellent, the land of which the Psalmist says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13). Therefore it placed its shoulder under the burden, because for the sake of attaining the heavenly homeland it willingly endures all the adversities of the world. It became a servant to tribute, because it renders to Christ the tribute of faith and good works.

Verse 19. “Gad, girded, will wage war.” In Deuteronomy we read that the tribe of Gad, together with the tribe of Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh, received possession beyond the Jordan. Moses granted it to them on the condition that they would not return to their homes before their other brothers had received their possession. Thus these men, girded—that is, equipped or prepared for war—went ahead of their brothers.

When they returned after the war had been completed and peace restored, they found that their sons, whom they had left as children in their possession, were being attacked in a very serious war by the surrounding enemies. It was therefore necessary for them once again to gird themselves and prepare for battle. This is what is meant by: “Gad, girded, will wage war before him,” that is, before the people; “and after he has returned, he will gird himself again behind,” against the nations.

Allegorically, Gad signifies Christ. At his first coming, when he came in hidden form, he was girded to fight against the devil; and he will gird himself again behind, at his second coming, when he will arrive openly to judge the world and repay each person according to his merits [Note: Codex Garstenensis has “he would be girded”].

Verse 20. “Asher’s bread is rich.” Literally, these words pertain to the fertility of his possession. Allegorically, however, Asher—whose name is interpreted as “blessed” or “rich bread”—designates the same Christ, whose bread is rich, that is, his body, by which we are refreshed for eternal life, as he himself said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven, and I give life to this world” (John 6:35).

He provides delicacies for kings, that is, for the saints, who know how to govern the movements of their bodies well. To them he provides delicacies—that is, the sweetness of the word, or even himself, since Asher is interpreted as “delicacies.”

Verse 21. “Naphtali is a released stag.” He is called a released stag because of the seasonal fruits, which ripen more quickly in that region; therefore he is called a released stag, that is, swift or fleeing. Another translation says: “Naphtali is a watered field.” This signifies the hot springs found in that tribe, or perhaps it refers to the lake of Gennesaret, which is located there.

The Hebrews report that the city of Tiberias is in this tribe and that teachers of the Law are found there. This is what is meant by “giving beautiful utterances.”

Mystically, Naphtali signifies the apostles, who were chosen by the Lord from the tribes of Naphtali and Zebulun, in accordance with what had been foretold through Isaiah: “At the first time he made light the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali” (Isa. 9:1). The Lord first preached in these regions, and then their land was made light by the removal of the devil’s exceedingly heavy yoke.

Therefore Naphtali is called a released stag because the apostles traveled with great speed throughout the whole world. They are the sons of those who have been shaken free, sent from the hand of the Lord like arrows from the hand of a mighty man (Ps. 127:4). They give beautiful utterances, that is, the words of divine preaching.

Verse 22. “Joseph is a growing son, Joseph is a growing son.” Joseph is interpreted as “increased,” that is, multiplied in virtues and worldly dignity. For he was beautiful in appearance, and therefore he was bought by the ruler of Egypt.

“Daughters ran upon the wall.” The Hebrews say that when Joseph was being led for sale through the Egyptian city of Heliopolis, the daughters—that is, the girls of Egypt—ran along the city wall, admiring his beauty. We may infer what he was like from the fact that women, whose particular quality is beauty, admired it in Joseph.

Verse 23. “But they provoked him, and quarreled with him.” Because of the dreams he had seen, they said: “Will you perhaps be our king?” They envied him, having arrows. Wounded by the arrows of envy, they envied him. Therefore they sold him into Egypt.

[Col. 0131A]

Verse 24. “His bow remained in the strong one.” That is, his strength and his hope remained—were established—in the strong one, that is, in Christ. “And the bonds of his arms were loosened by the hands of the mighty one of Jacob,” that is, of almighty God.

From him—that is, from Jacob’s offspring—the stone went forth, that is, Christ. The shepherd went forth, that is, Christ, who is also the stone of Israel, the firmness and strength of all who contemplate God.

### Verse 25

“With blessings of heaven above.” By saying “with blessings from above and from the abyss,” he signifies through these two the abundance of all things—namely, the fertility of the earth and the moderation and yield of heaven, that is, of the air. By “the blessings of breasts and womb” he indicates the multiplication of his offspring, especially on account of Ephraim, whose multitude increased to an immeasurable extent. [Col. 0131B]

Allegorically, Joseph signifies Christ. He is called “increasing” because he grew through the faith of the nations. For he is “beautiful in appearance,” because he is “fairer in form than the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV, 3). The daughters who ran along the wall, admiring his beauty, are the souls of the saints, established upon the solidity of faith. They admire the beauty of Christ and love him all the more because they are conscious of their own greater frailty. They run along the wall—that is, upon the solidity of faith, or upon the unconquerable firmness of the divine Scriptures—so that there they may behold Christ’s beauty.

“But they embittered him and quarreled with him.” This is said of the Jews, who embittered Christ by calling him a Samaritan and one possessed by a demon. “Having darts of envy,” with which they wounded themselves. Hence the Psalmist also says: “Their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. LVI, 5).

“He sat upon his strong bow.” That is, the hope of his strength remained in God the Father. “And the bonds of his arms were loosed.” For he was brought bound before the governor. Or by “the bonds of his arms” he means the blasphemies by which they tried to obstruct his works of power, saying that he cast out demons by Beelzebub. And this happened “through the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob,” that is, through the operation of almighty God.

“The God of your father is your helper.” The patriarch speaks to Christ according to the fact that he is human. “God,” he says, “of your father”—that is, the God whom your fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob worshiped. “And the Almighty will bless you,” namely, with a singular blessing above the other saints. [Col. 0131D]

By “the blessing of heaven above and of the abyss lying beneath” is signified that all things were subjected to Christ—namely, the angels in heaven and human beings on earth. Of this blessing the Apostle says: “And God exalted him and gave him a name,” and so forth (Phil. II, 9).

By “the blessings of breasts” he means the two Testaments, one of which announced that Christ would come and the other that he had come. The infancy of the Church is nourished by these breasts. Or by “the blessings of breasts” he means those of the blessed Virgin Mary, who bore Christ as an infant, and from whose undefiled womb he was born. Hence in the Gospel a certain woman cried out: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked” (Luke XI, 27).

“The blessings of your father have been strengthened by the blessings of his fathers.” That is, those blessings with which God the Father blessed the Son have been strengthened and have prevailed over the blessings of all the holy Fathers. For none of the righteous could be made equal to Christ, because he is by nature the Son of God, whereas the other saints are so through the grace of adoption.

“Until the desire of the eternal hills should come.” By the eternal hills he means the patriarchs and prophets, who do not lie among earthly things but are lifted up toward heavenly things. Their desire was the longing with which they desired to see Christ’s coming.

“Let these blessings be upon the head of Joseph.” That is, let them be fulfilled in Christ. “And upon the crown of the Nazarite.” That is, of Christ, who is the true flower of purity. In him the blessings were first made, and from this crown they descended through all the members of the Church [Col. 0132B] down to the hem of his garment, that is, down to the last of the elect.

### Verse 27

“Benjamin is a ravening wolf.” The Hebrews explain this passage in the following way. The altar that was in the Lord’s temple stood in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. Therefore he calls this altar a bloodthirsty and ravening wolf, because the victims offered there in the morning were devoured by the fire that was always burning on the altar. This is what he says: “In the morning he will devour the prey.” What follows—“In the evening he will divide the spoils”—refers to the priests, who divided among themselves in the evening whatever they had received from the people during the day from the sacrifices of the altar. This is according to them.

We, however, understand it as having been spoken of the Apostle Paul, who was from the tribe of Benjamin and, like a ravening wolf, persecuted the Church at first. Hence it is also said in the Psalm: “There is Benjamin, in an ecstasy” (Ps. LXVII, 28). He therefore devoured the prey in the morning when he was mangling the saints and, having received letters from the rulers, pursued them even to foreign nations. In the evening, however, he divided the spoils, when, having already been converted, he distributed the teaching of the Gospel to the faithful with great discernment.

It should also be noted that, together with those brothers who were born of free women—that is, Leah and Rachel—the sons of the maidservants were also blessed. By this it is shown that with God there is no acceptance of persons: he wills all to be saved and does not distinguish between degrees of birth, which one faith makes equal.

### Verse 32

“And he was gathered to his people.” This is often read in the divine Scriptures: “He was gathered to his brothers,” and “he was gathered to his people.” Therefore we must ask of what people this is said. There is no question concerning the fathers, since he was gathered together with Abraham and Isaac. But concerning “the people” there is doubt, because a people is a multitude. Yet those men were still so few that they could not be called a people.

Let us therefore understand that this was said not only of holy human beings but also of the angels, to whose company the saints departing from the world were added. Paul speaks of this people: “You have approached Mount Zion and the heavenly Jerusalem and the assembly of angels” (Heb. XII, 22).

## CHAPTER L

### Verse 3

“Forty days passed.” This number is appropriate to repentance and humility. Hence it was observed in the Law, in the Gospel, and by the Lord himself.

“For seventy days.” The pagans—that is, the gentiles—mourned their dead for nine days. Hence the ninth day was called the novendial day, when the dead person was buried. Our people, however—that is, worshipers of God—celebrate the funeral rites of the dead for seven days. Thus it is written: “The mourning for the dead is seven days, but the mourning of a fool is all the days of his life” (Ecclus. XXII, 13).

The number seven signifies rest; hence the seventh day is called the Sabbath, that is, rest. They therefore celebrate the seventh day for the dead, wishing them to rest with the Lord from the labors of the present age. Here, then, he says: “Egypt mourned him for seventy days,” which is the tenfold seven. For seven times ten is seventy.

This may also be said: just as the third day of the dead is observed by the faithful so that the soul, which has a threefold nature, may rest, so the seventh day is celebrated so that the soul may be reconciled to the body, since it sinned through the enticement of the flesh. For in seven there are three and four. The number three, as has been said, pertains to the soul, which is irascible, concupiscible, and rational; the number four pertains to the body, which consists of four elements.

### Verse 10

“And they came to the threshing floor situated beyond the Jordan.” The Seventy say, “to the threshing floor of Atad,” which is a place beyond the Jordan and many thousands of paces distant from Abramium—that is, from the place where Abraham was buried. Thus they passed beyond the place where Jacob was to be buried, and afterward, having crossed the Jordan again, they returned to the place of the double cave.

One may therefore ask why they did this. Perhaps someone will say that they feared wars might arise against them, just as the children of Israel were led around for forty years through the desert until, after the fortieth year had passed, they crossed the Jordan and came into the land of promise. But let us understand that this was done for a more significant reason.

For in this place, which is called the threshing floor of Atad, a multitude of the children of Israel later murmured against the Lord and was consumed by divine fire. That vehement mourning therefore prefigured this: it was not so much Jacob’s death as the destruction of that people, which was to occur there, that was being lamented.

### Verse 21

“He spoke to his brothers: ‘After my death, the Lord will visit you,’ and so forth.” Joseph, therefore, who, like his father Jacob, desired the promised land with his whole mind and detested his sojourn in Egypt, morally instructs us that, as long as we are in this world, we should always desire to enter the land of promise—that is, the land of the living—and wish to rest there. This is rightly accomplished if we imitate the number of his years in our conduct.

### Verse 25

“Thus, after completing one hundred and ten years of his life, he died.” Let us also strive, through the number or observance of the Decalogue, to attain eternal blessedness, which the number one hundred signifies.

“Joseph himself was embalmed with spices and placed in a coffin in Egypt.” A coffin is a storage vessel in which something entrusted for safekeeping is preserved.

O happy soul, which, embalmed with the spices of the virtues, dwells in this little body and, making daily progress, is reserved for eternal life! Without doubt, if it is embalmed with such a preparation and kept in faith, hope, and charity, it will deserve, through the grace of Christ, to reach the vision of divine contemplation. Its attainment is perfect joy, which the Psalmist, beholding it with his eyes, says: “You will fill me with joy in your presence, O Lord; delights are in your right hand forever” (Ps. XV, 11). Amen.

The Commentary on Genesis ends. [Note: [Col. 0133C] Thus the Tegernsee manuscript.]

[Col. 0133]

## ONE BOOK OF THE EXPOSITIONS ON THE PSALMS BY REMIGIUS, MONK OF THE ANTISSIODORAN ORDER OF SAINT BENEDICT (G)*

### VARIOUS PREFACES BY VARIOUS AUTHORS TO THE PSALMS

(From the *Bibliotheca Maxima Veterum Patrum*)

[Col. 0133]

### What “To the End” signifies, which is frequently found in the titles of the Psalms

[Col. 0133D]
