We understand “end” in two ways. The first is common and moral: when something has been brought to its limit and has arrived at the extremity beyond which it cannot proceed, and is shown to have reached the termination of its movement.

Thus we speak of food as finished when it has been consumed by careful eating; of money as finished when it is declared to have been spent; and similarly of other things that are expressed in this way.

The second is called the perpetual and perfect end, which is what we are now seeking. This end begins to be extended and enlarged for us when the mind has devoutly reached it. The end, therefore, and fullness of the Law is Christ, as the Apostle says (Rom. X): “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.” When we have reached him, we shall seek nothing further; but, drawn into that end of blessedness, we shall enjoy the fullest delight. Its love advances as far as our understanding, by the Lord’s gift, grows bright. Therefore, whenever you find “the end” in the titles of the Psalms, direct the attention of your mind toward the Lord our Savior, who is the end without end and the contemplative perfection of all good things.

### Why they are called “Psalms”

It is a kind of musical instrument, namely a cithara having ten strings, to which the name psalterium was given because its strings are struck from above with a plectrum. When it is touched from below, it is called a cithara. From this you should understand that the psalterium, sounding from above, gives voice not to carnal or earthly things but to spiritual and heavenly things.

Why, then, were the Psalms sung through these instruments? Because the people were carnal and had been corrupted into idolatry through such pleasures; therefore it was necessary to recall them to God by a similar sweetness. They did not wish to be healed by harsher admonitions. For when they gathered, as though to hear songs and melodies, the words of God were sown in their minds with a salutary and familiar sweetness. Whatever is gladly heard is held more firmly. At the same time, this was so that they might learn to sing these things rather than shameful ones.

[Col. 0135C] For this reason David is read in Chronicles to have appointed eighty-eight singers with their leaders, so that the greatness of the sound of the instruments and voices of the people might pierce the heart with a pleasure mingled with awe.

### How is the statement “David’s praises have ended” reconciled with the fact that David’s Psalms are later found?

It is resolved as follows. We should know in which Psalm they end: namely, in the seventy-first, which is entitled “of Solomon” but does not pertain to Solomon at all, rather to Christ. Therefore David’s praises rightly ended in the praise of Christ, because the Law and the Prophets preached until John (Matt. XI).

One Psalm is likewise entitled “A Prayer of Moses, the man of God,” that is—[Note: [Col. 0135D] Something is missing.]—or twelve, [Col. 0135D] according to the Hebrews, who say that the following Psalms, up to the ninety-ninth, which have no titles, should be joined to the eighty-eighth, just as in the book of the Prophets, whose times are not marked.

### What is a diapsalma?

Wherever the Seventy placed *diapsalma*, the Hebrew does not have *diapsalma* but *sela*, that is, “forever.” *Diapsalma* is interpreted as “a musical interlude.” The Seventy themselves translated the word *sela* as “to the end,” in the seventieth Psalm, saying: “For the Lord will dwell to the end.” Thus they too did not understand *sela*.

Some indeed think that *diapsalma* means a cessation of the Holy Spirit. But since at the end of the third Psalm the Hebrew has *diapsalma*, it is superfluous to speak of a cessation of the Holy Spirit. Even if this name were used, no one would doubt that there had been a cessation “to the end.” But in the ninth Psalm a song is called “diapsalms,” which is plainly impossible. Who could cease by singing, or sing by ceasing?

Concerning those Psalms that have no titles, there is also this tradition: when the inscription of an author has preceded, the others that follow without a title are believed to belong to that author.

It should nevertheless be known that among the Hebrews all the Psalms were mixed together and disordered. Ezra was the first to gather them into one volume, arrange them in order and number, and add titles. By this means he placed some before others according to the hidden mystery of the sacrament. The order is beautiful and wondrous, bounded indeed by a mystical number but infinite in sacred virtues.

This entire order of the Psalms, insofar as human ingenuity has been able to investigate it, is known to proceed according to a twofold mystery.

First, as the authority of the Fathers has stated, it embraces the mysteries of the New and Old Testaments. Seven decades refer to the Sabbath, which undoubtedly pertains to that first worship; the eight decades that follow are assigned to our time, since we venerate the Lord’s resurrection with pious devotion on the eighth day.

Second, just as the earth was cleansed of its crimes when the flood covered it for fifty days, so the spiritual abyss of the Psalms purifies hearts polluted by sins through a perpetual inundation until the time of judgment.

[Col. 0136C] All the Psalms that are inscribed “of David” pertain to the mystery of Christ, because Christ is called David. Finally, the Psalms that explain David’s flight and suffering reveal the Lord’s flight and suffering. Those inscribed “to the end” disclose the perfection of good works, because this end differs from other ends: in it there is fulfillment. “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10).

“Of the winepresses”: a hymn concerning the fruits of eternal gifts.

“For those who will inherit”: the reward of the saints, or the Church, which is Christ’s body and will receive the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven.

“For the eighth.” Some assign this number to the Gospels, because they contain the beatitudes through which one enters the kingdom of God; or to the eight souls of that ark.

“In the dedication,” or “in the completion,” of the tabernacle: the perfection of the Church is understood.

“For those who will be changed”: it provides for the change of the Jewish people and the gentiles, or of the Synagogue and the Church.

“For hidden things”: it announces the coming of the Son of God, who was hidden from the Jews.

“A song of resurrection”: the truth of the Lord’s resurrection itself.

“A prayer of Moses, the man of God”: it returns to the Law of God, since it declares that the Law itself satisfies us through the resurrection of the Redeemer.

“A Psalm concerning Solomon,” that is, “the peaceful one,” which is in Christ, who is our peace.

“In confession”: it teaches that a person should continually acknowledge God both with voice and with heart.

Those who narrate historical events according to the letter are nevertheless understood to possess the summit of spiritual understanding.

The Psalm of the sons of Korah prefigured the people to be redeemed through Christ’s passion, because Korah is interpreted as “baldness,” since our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified at the place of Calvary.

“Concerning the words of Cush the son of Jemini.” This refers to Cush, who abandoned David and went over to Absalom, who was the enemy of his father, just as Judas was the enemy of Christ.

[Col. 0137B] “At the morning assumption.” Because, rising in the morning, the Lord took captivity captive, bringing it with him from the underworld.

“On the first day of the Sabbath”: in the resurrection itself.

“Before he was anointed”: before he was glorified through the resurrection.

“Upon the recompense of sins,” namely, his own. “A Song of Ascents” signifies the heavenly ascent.

Therefore the Psalm that stands in the middle of the Songs of Ascents is placed like a most beautiful tower.

Nor do I think it is without a mystery that this book is composed in three groups of fifty.

The first grants remission of sins. The second invites us to hope for the heavenly kingdom. The third sends us into the kingdom of eternal blessedness.

[Col. 0137C] The *diapsalms*, which are always interpreted as “forever,” teach that the faithful mind should always exercise itself in these things.

In the First Book of Chronicles (I Chron. XXV) it is read that, when David the prophet had grown old in devoted service to the Lord, he chose four young men from the people of Israel, who caused the Psalms that he himself had produced under the inspiration of the Lord to resound with great joy of heavenly grace on instruments—organs, citharas, nabla, tambourines, cymbals, trumpets—and with their own voices.

That sweet joining together consisted of three parts. The rational part belonged to the human voice; the irrational part to the musical instruments. The common part was fashioned from both, so that the human voice might be produced in measured melodies and the music of the instruments might be joined with harmonious delight.

Thus that sweet and pleasing music proclaimed the Catholic Church, which, composed of diverse languages and varied harmonies, was, by the Lord’s gift, to believe in one concord of faith. From this number we often find names inserted in the titles, such as Jeduthun, Asaph, the sons of Korah, and similar names—not because they themselves, as some wish, were the authors of the Psalms, but because, having been assigned to the musicians, they proved to be suitable administrators of those matters, so that those who served in the sacred office with devoted minds might receive honor from such remembrance. This is especially so because their names are also known to indicate appropriate interpretations of the matters concerned.

[Col. 0138A] For the men mentioned above were not chosen to compose Psalms; we read only that they were gathered together to sing. No history testifies that they were psalm-writers, and it is presumptuous to assert what cannot be established by any authority. The Psalms, however, are shown by certain indications to belong to the prophet David alone.

Finally, in the Apocalypse, wishing this work to be understood, he mentions David alone, saying: “Thus says the holy and true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens” (Apoc. III). In the Gospel also the Lord says to the Pharisees: “How then does David, in the Spirit, call him Lord, saying: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand’?” (Matt. XXII.) Hence it is proved that all the Psalms belong not to many but only to the one whom it is evident was named by the Lord.

The practice of the Catholic Church, also, by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, generally and immutably holds that whenever one of them is to be sung—one that is identified by a differing inscription—the reader must not proclaim anything other than “A Psalm of David.” If they belonged specifically to Jeduthun, the sons of Korah, Asaph, or Moses, their names would certainly be proclaimed, just as in the Gospels they are announced under the names of Mark, Luke, Matthew, or John. Following this as well, Father Augustine appropriately says that all the Psalms are Davidic.

The psalterium, as Jeremiah says, is a resonant hollow of wood formed in the shape of the letter Δ, having a swollen belly above, where the strings are fastened; when struck rhythmically with a plectrum, they are said to produce the sweetest melody. Its position appears contrary to that of the cithara, since what the latter contains at the bottom, the former carries at the top in reversed arrangement.

This kind of singular and musical instrument is adapted to the body of the Lord Savior. For just as this instrument sounds from higher places, so the other celebrates from above the glory of his institution, as he himself says in the Gospel: “He who is of the earth is of the earth and speaks of the earth; but he who comes from heaven is above all, and what he has seen and heard, this he testifies” (John III). Hence some define this work as Davidic and say that the Psalms are so called because they are known to resound from the heavenly summit. Understand, therefore, that only those contained in this volume are called Psalms on account of their excellence.

*Psalterium* is a Greek word, and in Latin it is called an instrument or an instrument of praise, because the Hebrews call it *nablum*. *Psalmus* derives its name from playing, or from *psalterium*, or ἀπὸ τοῦ ψάλλειν—that is, “from touching.”

A psalm is produced when a certain sweet and tuneful melody is poured forth from the musical instrument alone, that is, from the psalterium. A song is what is sung in honor of God when someone uses the freedom of his own voice and is not joined in harmonious melody to any speaking musical instrument; this is also what is now performed in divine praises.

A “psalm of a song” occurred when, while a musical instrument played the prelude, a singing chorus acclaimed with joined voices, attending exclusively to divine words. A “song of a psalm” occurred when, with the chorus singing beforehand, the art of the musical instrument was adapted in common to a single harmony, and the words of the divine hymn resounded in a sweet union.

### On the manifold inscriptions of the titles

It is clear that certain superscriptions of the Psalms should be contemplated spiritually through similar allusion. For if you consider the letter, the matter is foreign, since you do not find in the Psalms the things contained in the titles. If, however, they are drawn toward typological interpretation, they appear exceedingly appropriate.

Thus there is the title in which historical events are signified: “When he fled from the face of Absalom”; one in which a place is indicated: “When he was in the desert of Idumea”; one in which a day is indicated: “On the first day of the Sabbath”; one containing Hebrew names: “Jeduthun”; one in which a comparison with events is made: “He changed his countenance before Abimelech”; or one referring to a similar kind of thing: “For the winepresses.”

Therefore, whenever in the superscriptions of the titles you find “psalm,” “song,” “psalm of a song,” “song of a psalm,” “to the end,” or anything belonging to the sixth category we mentioned—or when you recognize one, two, three, or four of these inserted together—apply them to the virtues that we say are present in each one. For the commemoration of these matters is subtly placed in the likeness of hidden understanding.

They unfold before the doors of the Psalms like sacred veils, through which, if you direct the attention of your mind, certain threads becoming thin, you can easily behold their inner chambers. For through the title of each Psalm its meaning is obtained. Who would think that so many causes and so many varieties of names were pointless, when it is impious to believe that the divine Scriptures contain anything superfluous, since it is written: “Amen, I say to you, not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law until everything is fulfilled” (Matt. V)?

For what is a title except a key? And just as no one enters a house except by a key, so the meaning of each Psalm is not understood except through its title. For it is understood according to whose person it is sung: whether in the person of Christ, the Church, or the prophet.

Among the interpreters of the Psalms, a certain difference of opinion concerning this name is known to have arisen. Jerome, the most learned investigator of the Hebrew language, affirms that it is a continuation of the Holy Spirit, saying: “Some have said that *diapsalma* is a change of meter or a pause of the Holy Spirit; others, the beginning of another sense or a division of rhythm; and, because at that time the Psalms were sung with joined voices to an instrument, a sign of some musical variation.”

None of these interpretations seems correct to us, since Aquila, who is the most diligent interpreter of Hebrew words, always translated the Hebrew word *sela*; the Seventy Interpreters, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated it as *diapsalma*. We find *diapsalma* placed at the end of certain Psalms, as at the end of the third Psalm and at the end of the twenty-third; and it is entirely absent from many Psalms. From this we observe that this word joins what comes before and what follows and teaches that the things spoken are eternal, so that we may know that they pertain not only to the present time but also to eternity, whether to what follows or to what preceded.

[Col. 0140A] It should be known, however, that among the Hebrews it is customary at the end of books to append one of three things: *amen*, *sela*, or *shalom*, which expresses peace. Just as we usually insert, to mark the distinction of a subsequent matter, *explicit*, *feliciter*, or something of that kind, so the Hebrews strengthen what has been written. They write *amen*; or they place *sela*, recalling what has been written and what is to be written as being “forever”; or, testifying that what has been completed has been completed happily, they mark peace at the end by writing *shalom*.

Such is Jerome’s view. This is Augustine’s.

The blessed Augustine, however, the most subtle investigator of obscure matters, moving without stumbling among difficult subjects, is known to have preferred this interpretation: that it should rather signify a division. He examines the character of the word itself. For *sympsalma* is called a joining together of voices, whereas *diapsalma* is a broken continuation of discourse, indicating that wherever it is found there is a change either of persons or of matters. Such a name is rightly inserted wherever either meanings or persons are shown to be divided. Therefore we too shall appropriately make divisions wherever *diapsalma* occurs in the Psalms.

The Psalms speak of the person of the Lord Jesus Christ in three ways for the instruction of the faithful.

First, they speak according to what is known to pertain to his humanity, as in the second Psalm: “The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together as one”; and in the twentieth Psalm: “You granted him the desire of his soul,” and so forth.

Second, they speak of him as equal and coeternal with the Father, as in that same second Psalm: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you”; and in the hundred and ninth: “With you is the beginning on the day of your power.”

Third, they speak from the members of the Church, whose leader and head is Christ, as in: “Far from my salvation are the words of my sins”; and in the sixty-eighth: “O God, you know my foolishness, and my offenses are not hidden from you.” We should understand this as having been said on behalf of each of the faithful. The offenses themselves, however, are proved to be utterly foreign to Christ.

Whether the head speaks or the shadow, there is one Christ, and it belongs properly to the head to speak even in the person of the members. Consider our own ordinary experience: first, how can any of our members speak except through the head? Now consider how our head speaks in the person of all the members. Someone steps on your foot in a tight place? “You are stepping on me,” says the head. Someone wounds your hand? “You have wounded me,” says the head.

Thus let us hear Christ speaking, but let each person recognize his own voice there, as though clinging to Christ’s body. For it is said of him and the Church: “The two shall be one flesh,” that is, in one body.

At times he speaks words in which none of us finds his own person, because they pertain to the head alone. If we keep this in mind, we shall not be led into confusion. For if he had spoken in only one way, who could have recognized his twofold substance, when even now, despite the most evident distinction, some strive through sacrilegious intent to confuse the divine and human nature of the Lord Christ?

He also teaches many things according to the letter and commands many things spiritually. He suddenly changes persons appropriately, so that now Christ, the Word of God incarnate and made human, the head of the Church, seems to speak; now the Church herself; now a righteous person; now a penitent. In this way he touches upon and embraces everything necessary. Everywhere the sacred eloquence of heavenly fullness flashes forth, and through a manifold diversity of virtues the merciful Redeemer intimates the mysteries of his kingdom for the salvation bestowed upon the human race.

We have prefaced these remarks so that, when the reader comes to such passages, he may be able without fear to hear what he recognizes as having been taught profitably concerning himself.

The order of the Psalms is arranged not according to the succession of times but according to the character of what is said. For, as the history of Kings testifies, David’s third Psalm, composed when he fled from the face of his son Absalom, is later in historical event than the fiftieth Psalm, since Absalom’s persecution of his father is known to have occurred after David’s adultery and murder. Yet the Psalm is shown to have been assigned the third place because of its appropriate spiritual power.

It was fitting that it hold the third place, since it contains the power of the Holy Trinity and the mysteries of the Lord’s three-day resurrection. For David’s deliverance aptly signifies the Lord’s resurrection. We confess that it is difficult for us to discover such a rationale for the order of all the Psalms, since the authority of the Fathers left this matter both determined and unresolved.

Throughout the entire Psalter there are four Psalms that are shown to contain the complete alphabet in Hebrew: the hundred and tenth, the hundred and eleventh, the hundred and eighteenth, and the hundred and forty-fourth. These indicate praises of the Lord to be sung through the devotion of merits, which he himself grants.

There are three Psalms that, with certain letters omitted, do not contain the complete alphabet: the twenty-fourth, which lacks the sixth and nineteenth letters; the thirty-third, which lacks the sixth letter; and the thirty-fifth, which lacks the sixteenth letter. These show that there are people in the Church whose integrity in all good works is not especially pleasing.

For just as those Psalms with all their letters complete appear to indicate the merits of excellent righteous people, so these, having certain letters missing, designate those who are not filled with every merit, but are nevertheless known to dwell in the second rank. Since all the letters among the Hebrews have their own significations, it may perhaps be considered worthy of belief that the person lacking a particular element also lacks its significations.

The text of the entire Psalter is concluded in twelve parts according to the number of the Apostles, so that we may recognize that what the Apostles accomplished is contained here.

For in the Psalter the Lord’s carnal life is described. First, the nature of his divinity; second, the multitude of those striving to extinguish the Lord; third and fourth, the Prophet’s admonition that the Jews cease from doing evil; fifth, Christ’s prayer to the Father, so that the world may advance through his resurrection; sixth, the words of the penitent; seventh, Christ’s appeal that the Father come to their aid; eighth, everything is referred to Christ through allegorical likeness; ninth, the Lord’s praises through the alleluiatic titles that signify “Praise the Lord”; tenth, the Songs of Ascents, so that they may lead us to the Savior; eleventh, we praise the Holy Trinity with hymn-like exultation; twelfth, seven Psalms remain at the end, which celebrate together the whole glory of the Trinity.

## Jerome’s Letter to Pope Damasus

Jerome to the most blessed Pope Damasus, of the apostolic see of the city of Rome.

I, your servant, humbly beg that this utterance be sung by those who chant in the Roman see, day and night, at the end of every Psalm, whether at Matins or at Vespers. That is, command them always to say:

“Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit; as it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, throughout the ages of ages. Amen.”

Command that this song of praise be joined to all the Psalms, so that the faith of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers of the Council of Nicaea may be proclaimed with equal fellowship by our mouths. Let “Alleluia” always be attached to all the Psalms and commonly answered everywhere during the night.

In the Church, however, from the resurrection at Easter until Pentecost, let the Psalter be brought to an end. During the span of the fifty days, because of the newness of holy Easter, let this voice of praise be sung in *Aleph*, which is “Alleluia.”

## Sayings of Saint Augustine: How Many Are the Virtues of the Psalms?

> “The singing of the psalms adorns souls, invites angels to our aid, drives away demons, dispels darkness, [Col. 0142C] produces holiness. For the sinful person it is refreshment of the mind; it wipes away sins, is like the alms of the saints, gives birth to faith. Like the sun, it illuminates; it reveals God, offends the devil, extinguishes unlawful desire. It is the oil of mercy, the portion of joy, the chosen share of the angels; it softens harshness, suppresses every rage, breaks anger. It is continual praise of God, like honey. The singing of the psalms is a chosen song before God. It drives out every sin and commends the bond of charity. It accomplishes everything, endures everything, fulfills everything, teaches everything, signifies everything; it magnifies the soul, purifies the mouth, gladdens the heart, builds a lofty tower, glorifies the human being, opens the understanding, destroys every evil, equips one for perfection, points out the heights, gives the desire for the heavenly kingdom, [Col. 0142D] and makes peace between body and soul. It kindles spiritual fire in the heart, removes anxiety about all vices. It is the contest of the good; daily it drives out the root of all evils, and it defends like an armor worn and like a helmet. It is the hope of salvation, consolation in grief, completion of labor, knowledge of the true light, fountain of holiness; it chastens the young person, gives the kingdom of God upon earth, removes weariness from the soul, and is a wondrous trumpet. Whoever continually loves the singing of the psalms cannot commit sin. Whoever has the praise of God in his heart will at last rejoice before God and glorify his soul in heaven. The psalms pray for future things, groan over past things, rejoice over benefits, hope in mercy, fear because of guilt, and draw tears from [Col. 0143A] a stony heart. They are the work of angels, the perfect praise of Christ; they announce Christ’s coming, the hope of the incarnation and resurrection, and warn of fear of punishments. They are the promise of glory, the revelation of mysteries; they bestow eloquence and happiness, honor and glory, instruction and understanding. The singing of the psalms is to be loved by all, because it multiplies every virtue: all virtues are found in the psalms. If you wish to practice confession and repentance, sing these two: ‘Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger’; and these two: ‘Lord, hear me.’ ‘Blessed are those whose …’ ‘Have mercy on me, O God.’ ‘Out of the depths.’ If you wish to pray, say: ‘To you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul.’ ‘In you, Lord, I have hoped.’ ‘Incline, Lord God, to my help.’ ‘O God, in your name …’ ‘May God have mercy on us.’ ‘Hear, Lord, my justice.’ [Col. 0143B] If you wish to praise God, say the psalms entitled ‘Alleluia,’ and those beginning: ‘Give thanks,’ ‘Praise,’ ‘Bless.’ If you are afflicted by human or spiritual trials and temptations, and seem to yourself abandoned by God, sing: ‘O God, my God, look upon me.’ ‘Hear, O God, my prayer when I plead.’ ‘Save me.’ ‘How long, Lord God, [shall this be] to our ears?’ ‘Have mercy on me, O God.’ ‘Hear, O God, my prayer, and do not despise [me].’ ‘In you, Lord, I have hoped.’ After these, when rest has been received: ‘I will bless the Lord.’ ‘Bless, my soul [the Lord].’ If life becomes wearisome to you and you already desire to see your heavenly homeland, sing: ‘As the deer longs …’ ‘How beloved are …’ ‘O God, my God, to you I keep watch from the dawn.’ If you wish to exercise yourself in divine praises and heavenly commandments, sing: ‘Blessed are the undefiled.’ And although, even at the hour of death, you may have fulfilled the power of this hymn, you will never, I think, be able to understand it perfectly, since there is no verse in it that does not contain either the way of the Lord, or God’s commandment or precept, or words, law, justifications, discourses, or judgments. At every time, whether of prosperity or adversity, sing the hymn of the three children. In the Psalter all the divine books are found in part.”

It should be known that the psalms were not previously provided with titles as they are now, but were first joined together by the Seventy translators and afterward, following the migration from Jerusalem, were arranged and titled by the prophet Ezra, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, in the order in which they now stand. Although Saint Augustine asserts that the Seventy were enclosed in individual cells [Col. 0143D] when they translated them, Saint Jerome, by no means accepting this, says: “If they had been enclosed, they would have been called prophets rather than translators.” It is also known—so the authorities say—that they did this under compulsion, because King Ptolemy himself worshiped one God, as the Hebrews did, and therefore, out of love for him, ordered the Scriptures of the Hebrews to be translated into his own language.

The title is the key of grace. Just as we enter a house by means of a key, so through the title we understand a psalm.

The purpose of this prophecy is to console the human race, which had been cast down from the greatest blessedness into the greatest misery by the sin of its first parent and could not rise from it except through the mercy of God. Or, alternatively: the prophet intends in this work to invite all his contemporaries [Col. 0144A] and those to come to place all their hope of eternal blessedness in Christ, by conforming themselves to him insofar as members are able to imitate the head.

The first psalm has no title because it is itself, as it were, the title of the whole book, dealing with the one to whom the purpose of the entire book must be referred. The purpose of the first psalm is to point out the one through whom we may rise from the misery into which we were cast.

If it is asked why this prophecy is recited in the Church more frequently than others, I answer: because the entire dispensation is demonstrated here more fully than in the others; because its words can be enlarged so as to apply to every just person or sinner, so that each may use them as though they were his own; and because it moves the human mind with greater devotion and compunction than the others. Here some things are ascribed to Christ [Col. 0144B] according to his humanity, some according to his divinity, and some according to both. Those things that belong to his human nature according to his humanity are set forth so that, by conforming ourselves to him in certain respects, we may hope in him. Those things that belong to him according to the sublimity of his divinity, or according to both natures, are referred to this end: that through conformity to him we may not hesitate to serve one who is so great that he cannot repay us according to our vice.

Just as in secular books, so also in divine books one may ask to which part of philosophy a work belongs. Ecclesiastes tends toward physics, since it investigates the beginning and end of all things that are in the world and shows that all things are subject to vanity. Proverbs, however, tends [Col. 0144C] toward ethics. The Song of Songs tends toward the theoretical, that is, toward contemplation of divine things.

Wherever something is lacking in the Greek in comparison with the Hebrew truth, Origen added here from the translation of Theodotion a sign, placing an asterisk *, that is, a star, which illuminates what previously seemed hidden. Wherever something is found in Greek that is not in Hebrew, he placed before it an obelus, ÷, that is, a lying or horizontal stroke, which we Latins may call a spit; by this sign it is shown that what is not in the authentic books ought to be pierced through.

## Letter of Blessed Jerome to Paula concerning the Hebrew Alphabet

[Col. 0145A]

The day before yesterday, when I was trying to explain to you Psalm 118 and said that every moral subject was contained in it, you diligently asked what the Hebrew letters seemed to signify that were inserted in the psalm we were reading. I replied that it had been composed according to the order of the letters: namely, eight verses began with the first letter, which among the Hebrews is called *Aleph*, with the same letter inserted at the head of each verse. Then the same number of verses began with the following letter, *Beth*; afterward the same number was completed with *Gimel*; and so the psalm was written all the way to *Thau*, which among them is the final letter. [Col. 0145B] According to their interpretation, what follows is to be understood from each individual element.

You also requested that I state the interpretations of the individual letters. I did so, I admit. But because, owing to the barbarity of the language, everything we said slips from memory, you desire a commentary to be made, so that if you should happen to stumble over anything, reading may console your forgetfulness.

Before I discuss the individual letters, you should know that four psalms begin according to the order of the Hebrew letters: the 110th, the 111th, this one about which we are now writing, and the 144th. In the first two, individual verses, consisting of an iambic trimeter, are attached to the individual letters; the later ones consist of an iambic tetrameter, just as [Col. 0145C] the song of Deuteronomy is written (Deut. 32). In Psalm 118, eight verses follow each individual letter. In Psalm 144, a single verse is assigned to each letter. Some think that other psalms also begin in this order, but their opinion is false, for they do not contain the complete alphabet.

Now what you requested must be completed, so that the attached interpretation may indicate the meaning of each element:

*ALEPH* is interpreted as “teaching”; *BETH*, “house”; *GIMEL*, “fullness”; *DALETH*, “of tablets”; *HE*, “this”; *VAU*, “and”; *ZAIN*, “these”; *HETH*, “life”; *THET*, “good”; *IOD*, “beginning”; *CAPH*, “hand”; *LAMED*, “of discipline” or “of heart”; *MEM*, “from them”; *NUN*, “everlasting”; *SAMECH*, “help”; *AIN*, “fountain” or “eye”; *PHE*, “mouth”—understand *os* as “mouth,” not “bone,” so that you are not deceived by the ambiguity of the letters; [Col. 0145D] *ZADE*, “of justice”; *COPH*, “calling”; *RES*, “of the head”; *SIN*, “of teeth”; *THAU*, “signs.”

After the interpretation of the elements, the order of their meaning must be stated.

The first connection is: “teaching, house, fullness of tablets,” because the teaching of the Church, which is the house of God, is found in the fullness of the divine books.

The second connection is: “this; and, these, life.” For what other life can there be without knowledge of the Scriptures, through which Christ himself is also recognized, he who is the life of believers?

The third connection is: “good beginning.” For although we now know all that has been written, we know only in part and prophesy in part, and now we see through a mirror in an enigma. But when we have deserved to be with Christ and have become like the angels, then the teaching of books will cease, and we shall see face to face the good beginning as it is (1 Cor. 13).

The fourth connection is: “hand, of heart or of discipline.” We understand “hand” in relation to work; “heart” and “discipline” are understood in relation to understanding, because we can do nothing unless we first know what must be done.

[Col. 0146B] The fifth connection is: “from them, everlasting, help.” This needs no explanation; it is clearer than daylight from the Scriptures that eternal assistance is supplied through them.

The sixth connection is: “fountain or eye, of mouth, of justice,” according to what we explained in the fourth number.

The seventh connection is also the final one. There is a mystical meaning in the number seven itself: “calling, of the head, of teeth, signs.” Through the teeth articulated speech is expressed, and by these signs one reaches the head of all, who is Christ.

I ask you: what is more sacred than this sacrament? What pleasure is sweeter than this? What foods, what honeys are sweeter than knowing the wisdom of God, entering his courts, contemplating the Creator’s meaning, and learning full of spiritual wisdom the words of the Lord your God, which are mocked by the wise men of this world? Let others have their riches, if they wish; let them drink gems, shine in silk, delight in the applause of the people, and through various pleasures fail to surpass their own wealth. Let our riches be to meditate on the law of the Lord day and night, to knock at a door that is not open, to receive the bread of the Trinity, and, with the Lord going before us, to tread upon the waves of the world.

Greet Blaesilla and Eustochium, our beginners. Greet Feliciana, truly blessed in the virginity of flesh and spirit. Greet the remaining choir of chastity and your household church, for I fear everything—even what is secure—lest, while the father of the household sleeps, the enemy sow weeds over it (Matt. 13). Although they may dare to say, “I am a strong city, a city that is not attacked” (Isa. 27, according to the Seventy), no one is secure when an enemy army is besieging him. No one, as blessed Cyprian says, is sufficiently safe when near danger.

Give a copy of the letter, if our most industrious Marcella (Greek *philoponotatē*) wishes to receive it, and remember me, praying that our Lord Jesus Christ may swiftly crush Satan beneath our feet (Rom. 16). Amen.

## Preface of Remigius

[Col. 0145]

[Col. 0145D] Prophecy is divine inspiration or knowledge of mysteries [Col. 0146D] of God, and it occurs either through hidden inspiration or [Col. 0147A] through angelic administration. Through angelic administration it occurs in three ways: by words, by deeds, or by vision.

By words, as in: “Hail, Mary, full of grace” (Luke 1).

By deeds, as when Gideon doubted whether to lead the children of Israel against the Midianites and asked for a sign. A sign was given to him: on the first night the fleece spread upon the threshing floor was wet while the floor was dry; on the following night the floor was wet and the fleece dry (Judg. 6). The fleece, wet first, signified the Jewish people, previously watered by the teaching of God’s word. The dry floor signified the Gentiles, upon whom the Lord had not yet rained the teaching of faith. The floor afterward wet, with the fleece dry, signified that the word of God would pass over from the Jews to the Gentiles. Hence: “It was necessary that the word of God be preached to you first, but since you reject it, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” [Col. 0147B] (Acts 13).

By vision, as with Paul, who was caught up to the third heaven (2 Cor. 12), and John in the Apocalypse. Since there is only one heaven, Paul does not seem to have been physically caught up to a third heaven. It therefore appears more suitably understood in this way: the first heaven, that is, the first form of knowledge, is sensation; the second is reason; the third is understanding. Caught up to this, he heard secret words that it is not permitted to a human being to speak.

Through hidden inspiration prophecy occurs in three ways: concerning the past, the present, and the future.

Concerning the past, as with Moses: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1).

Concerning the present, as with Elizabeth addressing blessed Mary: “And from where is this granted me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1). And John: “Behold, the Lamb of God” (John 1).

Concerning the future, as with this entire prophecy of David, which is called the Psalter.

[Col. 0147C] There is a certain musical instrument called in Hebrew *nablath*, in Greek *psalterion*, and in Latin *organum*. With this instrument David played the praises of the psalms, which one hundred and fifty men sang around the ark of the covenant when he brought it back from Shiloh to Jerusalem. After the ark had been brought back, he appointed three hundred singers to accompany the psalmody continually in the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem. Over them he placed four leaders of the singing: Heman, Ethan, Asaph, and Jeduthun. From this instrument he named the prophecy of the psalms the Psalter—not without reason, because it seems mystically to bear the form of that instrument.

The Psalter, as we have said, is a musical instrument, triangular, with ten strings stretched across it; when struck below, it gives forth a sweet sound above. Thus, if we wish to sing psalmody, that is, a sweet melody, to God, we must strike the lower part of ourselves not only with our voice but also with our heart—that is, afflict the flesh. For the more we afflict the flesh, the more our higher part, namely the spirit, pleases God.

[Col. 0147D] We cannot play this instrument worthily for God if faith in the Holy Trinity is absent, because without faith it is impossible to please God (Heb. 11). In the ten strings we understand the ten words of the law. By observing them, mortifying the flesh, and persevering in faith in the Holy Trinity, we make the pleasing instrument of the Psalter resound above in the Holy Spirit.

It is titled in these three ways: “The Book of Psalms begins”; or “The Book of Hymns begins”; or “The Book of the Soliloquies of God begins.”

“Of psalms,” that is, of divine works.

“Of hymns,” that is, of the praises of God. A hymn is praise of God composed metrically. Hence Arator:

> “The feet of lyric verse composed the Psalter.”

“Of the Soliloquies of God”: either because here he prophesied about Christ better, more familiarly, and more worthily than the other prophets, as one to whom the Holy Spirit had shown that Christ would be born from his lineage; or because this prophecy must be referred especially to Christ.

Now the prophets sometimes relate future things by means of the past, sometimes past things by means of the past, sometimes future things by means of the future, and sometimes present things by means of the past. This is not surprising, because for the Holy Spirit, who speaks through the mouth of the prophets, nothing is past or future, since eternity is present reality for him—that is, the present state of all things. Therefore he sometimes announces things according to the way they are with him, and sometimes according to the way they exist with us.

Just as in secular books, so also in divine books each person may ask to which part of philosophy a work belongs. But just as among the former, so also among the latter, some belong to physics, such as Ecclesiastes—in which the beginning and end of all things in the world are sought and all these things are shown to be subject to vanity—and Genesis; some belong to ethics, such as Proverbs and, in part, the Gospels; some belong to the theoretical, such as the Song of Songs and, in part, the Gospels, which lead us to the contemplation of divine things. In the divine writings logic is not present; instead of logic, the theoretical is present.

It should be known that all the psalms were composed by David, although not all are titled with his name. Ezra the scribe, who added the titles, titled some under David’s name and others under the names of various persons, such as Asaph, Heman, and others. This was either because of a mystery or because of the interpretation of the names, which suits the psalms to which such titles were attached.

The purpose of this prophecy, as also of the others, throughout the whole book is to console the human race, which by the sin of its first parent was cast down from the greatest blessedness into the greatest misery and cannot rise from it except through the mercy of God. Nevertheless, the particular purpose of each psalm must be sought.

The prophet’s purpose in this first psalm is to show how and through whom the human race can rise from that fall and that misery in which it lies and moves about: namely, through Christ, by imitating him. For through ourselves we fell, but through ourselves we cannot rise.

Now, with God’s help, let us approach the exposition of the first psalm.

# Expositions on the Psalms

[Col. 0149]

## Psalm One

[Col. 0149A]

> “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, who has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the seat of pestilence; but his will is in the law of the Lord, and he will meditate on his law day and night. And he will be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which will give its fruit in its season. And its leaf will not fall, and everything whatever he does will prosper. Not so the ungodly, not so; but they are like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth. Therefore the ungodly will not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the counsel of the righteous, because the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the path of the ungodly will perish.”

[Col. 0149B] **Exposition**

“Blessed is the man.” It is as though he were saying: Long ago someone came into this world who was not a man, but without strength, because he succumbed to the incitements of vice. Therefore he was unhappy, because through the pleasure of forbidden things he departed from the law of the Lord his God; he stood through consent, he sat through action and habit. For this reason he fell from the highest blessedness into the deepest misery, from life into death, from immortality into mortality, and with himself, like a root, cast the whole human race down into the depths like branches.

But someone will come who is a man—and rightly a man, because he is strong, because he is unconquerable. “Blessed,” as though “well increased,” namely, the perfect man, because although the gifts of the Holy Spirit are given to others according to measure, in him the entire fullness of divinity dwelt bodily (John 3; Rom. 12; [Col. 0149C] Col. 2), that is, completely and solidly, as the prophet says: “And the Spirit of the Lord will rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding,” and so forth (Isa. 11).

“Who has not gone.” He will not depart from the law of the Lord his God, unlike that unhappy one who perished through the pleasure of sin, namely, in the counsel of the ungodly. The counsel of the ungodly was that of the serpent and Eve. Counsel is a devised plan. Since the serpent could not seduce Adam by himself, he seduced Eve, and through Eve, Adam—very skillfully, through the vice that is closest to virtue, through the desire for honor—saying: “You will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3).

Hence it is also said that the devil seduced Adam and Eve in the form of a serpent, because no vice creeps more easily into the human mind than ambition—not because he assumed the form of a serpent, since he could have deceived a human being more easily in human form.

Alternatively, “in the counsel of the ungodly”: the counsel of all the ungodly is to seek their own things, not the things that are God’s. The desire for exaltation did not steal into Christ’s mind. He “did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” and so forth (Phil. 2). He had no pleasure in any sin, nor did he seek his own things, but those of God the Father.

Here the prophet speaks of Christ the head, and therefore what he has said seems sufficient. “Who has not gone.” For if he did not take pleasure, much less did he consent; if he did not consent, much less did he act.

But in order to show that we must rise from the threefold death of the soul in the contrary order to that in which we fell, and that in Christ we have the pattern of rising, he attributes this to him.

It can also be read in another way, so that this division suitably applies to different persons and shows the ways of rising:

“Blessed is the man who had no pleasure in sin,” such as Mary and John; and blessed also is the one who, although he took pleasure and although he consented, nevertheless did not carry it into action—although he is not as blessed as the former.

“And who has not stood in the way of sinners.” The way of sinners is every unlawful thought in which we stand when we give consent. But Christ, who never even thought an unlawful thought, much less consented. Here “sinners” and “ungodly” are understood as the same.

“And who has not sat in the seat of pestilence.” That is, he did not bring sin into action. For whoever neither thought nor consented much less committed sin. The seat belongs to kings or teachers. This means that he did not desire an earthly kingdom.

When people saw that he had fed five thousand men with five loaves and two fish, they, longing for earthly advantages, thought of offering him a kingdom. He countered their thought in this way: “Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which remains unto eternal life” (John 6). They wanted to make him king so that he might provide them with necessities.

He did not reject earthly power because he could not possess it without sin, but because mortals do not know how to possess it without sin and without harm to others. So that he might not give them an occasion and example of destruction, he did not desire an earthly kingdom, which is always pestilential because it leads to exaltation.

Whoever sins out of habit sins as though from necessity. Such a person scarcely afterward attacks the sinner, and it often happens that he draws toward harmful things those whom, while they are already sinning, he strives to protect. Thus he sits in the seat of pestilence, that is, of destruction, not only destroying himself but—what is worse—becoming, insofar as he can, the author of others’ destruction. Both “being an author” and “sitting” belong to the seat.

Christ, however, always stands as the author of good action by word and example, and therefore he did not sit in the seat of pestilence.

[Col. 0150D] The three falls of Adam, according to Augustine, prefigured the threefold death of the soul. Just as death is the separation of the soul from the body, so death is the separation of the soul from God. For just as the body lives by clinging to the soul, so the soul lives by clinging to God.

There is an Eve within us, and there is also an Adam. There are two powers of the human soul: one by which the body is given life, which may be called animality, because of its affinity with the body; and reason, which restrains animality from extending itself toward unlawful desire. For, as the Apostle says, “the head of the woman is the man, the head of the man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11).

If reason does not restrain itself as a man but consents to carnality by taking pleasure, consenting, or acting, then, in the likeness of Adam, it produces three falls by departing from its head, Christ, and clinging to its wife.

These three deaths of the soul are signified by the three dead persons whom Christ raised.

The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, whom he raised in the house, signifies the soul dead within through the pleasure of sin (Matt. 9; Mark 5). “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5). But this death of the soul is not very strong, because she is signified by a young girl: she is, as it were, still chaste, since she has not yet been polluted by consent, and she can easily rise from it, namely, through the Lord’s Prayer. This is shown by the fact that the Lord stretched out his hand and raised her.

The son of the widow whom the Lord raised at the gate (Luke 7) signifies the soul dead through consent to sin. When sin has proceeded as far as consent, it is not far from action.

This death, which is outside, is strong, and we cannot rise from it except through worthy repentance. This is signified by the fact that he was a young man. And the Lord said to him: “Young man, I say to you, arise” (John 11).

Lazarus, already stinking, whom the Lord nevertheless raised from the tomb, signifies the soul that brings sin as far as action and, through long habit and the excessive stench of vices, has already fallen into despair of its restoration.

“When the sinner has come into the depths, he despises” (Prov. 18). The Lord deigns to raise such people, but only through the greatest repentance and great labor. This is signified by the fact that the Lord cried out in a loud voice: “Lazarus, come forth.”

Blessed is the man who did not think evil, did not consent to it, and did not teach it by acting or teaching. And because it is not enough to turn away from evil unless one strives to do good, he adds:

“But his will is in the law of the Lord.” This one statement refers to those two: “he has not gone” and “he has not stood,” because both concern the will. It is one thing to be in the law and another to be under the law.

Those who do not wish to sin because of their love of virtue are with the law and in the law, because “the law is not laid down for the righteous” (1 Tim. 1). But whoever observes the law through fear of punishment is under the law, [Col. 0151D] because he does good from necessity, not from willingness. Fear belongs to slaves, love to children. Therefore the will of the Son of God was in the law of the Father.

“And in his law he will meditate day and night.” To increase the good, he adds diligence to the will. Above, where he said, “he has not sat in the seat of pestilence,” this also is referred to it: “day and night,” that is, at all times, whether in prosperity or adversity.

Christ’s prosperity was his resurrection and ascension; adversity was before the Passion and during the Passion. Prosperity did not exalt Christ so that he would depart from the law of the Lord, nor did adversity disturb him in this way.

Thus far the prophet has spoken about Christ the head. It can also be understood as though Christ himself were saying all these things about himself, as John says: “This is the disciple who bears witness concerning these things and wrote these things” (John 21), because people ordinarily speak more familiarly about themselves and to themselves.

It can also be understood as referring to three periods: before the law, under the law, and under grace. Thus it may be said:

“Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly,” namely, the one who before the law did not depart from God his creator by serving the creature rather than the creator, as Abel (Gen. 4) and others before the law. He calls idolaters “the ungodly”; their counsel is to despise the creator and worship creatures.

And blessed is the one “who has not stood in the way of sinners.” He calls those who transgress the law sinners, namely the Jews under the law; their way is carnal understanding. That is: blessed is the one who understands the law spiritually.

And blessed is the one “who has not sat in the seat of pestilence” during the time of grace. Heretics sit in the seat of pestilence because through perverse teaching they lead many astray. And blessed is the one who teaches the way of God in truth.

“But in the law of the Lord”—this remains unchanged up to: “And he will be like a tree.” This blessed man will be like a tree, that is, conforming himself to Christ.

And thereafter the text refers to Christ: “And he will be like a tree.” Because he will never depart from the law of the Lord his God, he will be like that tree which is planted beside streams of water, that is, in a watered place.

Such a tree puts forth leaves, flowers, and fruits at the proper time. So does Christ. Christ himself called himself a tree, as in: “If they do these things in the green tree, what will be done in the dry?” (Luke 23).

Here “tree” is not simply stated, but “planted tree,” that is, a tree. The Lord also called himself a tree to the Jews who received his deeds and words but rejected him himself, saying: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad” (Matt. 12).

And that tree which was planted in the middle of paradise prefigured Christ.

In divine Scripture, waters are understood in three ways: as the gifts of the Holy Spirit, as the flow of carnal desires, and as peoples. Therefore this may be understood in different ways.

“And Christ will be like a tree,” that is, he will be such—so kind, so effective—as this tree ought to be, the tree planted beside streams of water. That means: the man who was conceived in blessed Mary not according to carnal desire, but beside streams of water, that is, according to the abundance of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, as in: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1).

[Col. 0152D] The Holy Spirit, coming upon blessed Mary, protected her from every heat of unlawful desires and directed all her love toward God. And because he who was born from such an operation was so pure, he could commit nothing unlawful.

“Streams” is appropriate, because the Holy Spirit came upon her; and because nothing can obstruct his operation, he removed all unlawful thoughts from Mary.

That tree, namely Christ, “will give its fruit,” that is, its faithful people, his Church, in its proper time. Every time is its own, but that time especially seemed to belong to it in which he became more widely known and glorified, namely when he was thirty years old and began to teach, and after the coming of the Holy Spirit, when the sound of the apostles went out into all the earth. Hence it is said: “Jesus was not yet glorified, because the Holy Spirit had not yet been given” (John 7).

Or “in its proper time,” that is, at the consummation of the age, when he will hand over the kingdom to God and the Father, when death, the last enemy, will be destroyed (1 Cor. 15).

Or: “He will be like a tree,” that is, like the man who came into this world not in sinful flesh but in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. 8), because he was conceived and born without sin. Nevertheless, he was like sin in its punishment, because he was mortal and capable of suffering.

Or: “beside streams of water,” that is, beside the nature of peoples, in which some pass away and others come after them.

The Holy Spirit is called water because, just as water washes away external filth, so the grace of the Holy Spirit washes away internal filth.

Nor is it surprising that he will give his fruit, because “his leaf will not fall,” that is, his words will not be ineffective. Even if they do not operate in some people, it remains true that they are not ineffective, because such words are not words to those who do not perceive them with the ear of the heart.

Therefore the words of God are compared with leaves: just as leaves adorn trees, so teaching adorns Christ; and just as the fruit lies hidden among the leaves, so the blessedness of the faithful is governed within Christ’s teaching.

“And everything whatever he does will prosper,” whether in himself or in his own people: in himself, whether in words or deeds; in his own people, whether circumstances are prosperous or adverse. In this the providence of God is wondrous, because he uses even the evils of his own people for good.

Some he permits to fall so that they may rise stronger, as Peter in his denial and Thomas in his doubt; or even for their own benefit and that of others, as Peter, who through his own fall learned with what gentleness the life of subordinates ought to be corrected. Not so the ungodly—that is, not so that all things work together for their good—for even what seems good to them works together for evil, as it is written: “The prosperity of fools will destroy them” (Prov. 1).

He calls those who do not know God ungodly, such as Jews, Gentiles, and heretics. They will be like dust not compacted by rain, which the wind drives away from before it—that is, from the surface of the earth—because, lacking the moisture of God’s word on account of their ungodliness, they will be driven away by the wind, that is, by the devil or by the first suggestion, from the knowledge of God, who is the land of the living—that is, from his presence. “Presence” is understood as knowledge, because from a person’s face we ordinarily gain knowledge of him. [Col. 0153C]

Therefore the ungodly—that is, idolaters—do not rise in judgment, that is, so as to judge or to be judged, because they have already been condemned. Of those who rise, some rise for judgment, while others do not rise for judgment. Those who rise for judgment will either be judged for salvation, having already been purified in purgatory, or for condemnation, like those whose destruction was not manifest in this life. Of those who do not rise for judgment, some will not be judged because they will judge others, such as the holy apostles and other perfect members of the Church. Others will not be judged because they have already been evidently condemned, not only before God but also before the Church, such as Gentiles, Jews, and heretics, and those who end their present life in grave sins without confession and worthy penance, even if this is unknown to the Church. Nor do sinners—namely, transgressors of the Law, Jews and false Christians—rise in order to be in the council of the righteous, because here they refused to be in the council of the righteous. [Col. 0153D]

He says this so that they would not presume upon the sacraments, imagining that they would either judge or be judged for good, any more than the ungodly would. For only the godly will rise in judgment, either to judge or to be judged for good. This is because the Lord knows the way of the righteous—that is, he has approved and loved their way, meaning their good life. The ungodly and sinners will not rise in this manner because the way of the ungodly—that is, the life which they themselves chose for themselves—will perish from God’s favor.

Alternatively: the ungodly will be scattered like dust, because idolaters will be carried about by every wind of doctrine (Eph. 4), or by the breath of pride, like the one who said, “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). “From the face of the earth” means from the vision of God, who is the land of the living. As it says: “Let the ungodly be taken away, lest he see the face of God” (Isa. 26). This will happen because the ungodly—that is, idolaters—do not rise from the fall of the first parent and from their own fall in judgment, namely, so that in this life they may weigh by just judgment how just it is that the lesser should serve the greater: the servant, the Lord; the creature, the Creator; and that one should withdraw from him without whom one cannot exist and should venerate a creature. [Col. 0154A]

Nor will sinners—that is, transgressors of the Law—rise in the assembly of the righteous. The assembly of the righteous consists in seeking the things that belong to God, not the things that belong to oneself; in pleasing not oneself but God. Therefore the way of the ungodly will perish, that is, their life and labor will be without reward. [Col. 0154B] For whoever has no part in the first resurrection will have no part in the second resurrection (Rev. 20). That the way of the ungodly will perish he demonstrates by contrast, because the Lord knows the way of the righteous not only by knowledge but also by favor: their life and conduct. [Col. 0154C]

## PSALM II. A PSALM OF DAVID

“Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate on futile things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ. Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke away from us. He who dwells in the heavens will mock them, and the Lord will deride them. Then he will speak to them in his anger, and in his wrath he will trouble them. But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming his command. The Lord said to me: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession. You will rule them with an iron rod, and like a potter’s vessel you will shatter them.’ And now, kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling. Embrace discipline, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the righteous way. When his anger suddenly burns, blessed are all who trust in him.” [Col. 0154D]

## EXPOSITION

“Why did the nations rage?” Some say that from “Blessed is the man” through “Blessed are all who trust in him” there is one psalm. Jerome gives this reason for considering it one psalm: it begins with blessedness and ends in blessedness, and blessed Paul demonstrates its unity in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 13). Those who regard it as a separate psalm give it the title: “A Psalm of David.” “Psalm” means an action. [Col. 0155A]

For this reason, throughout the psalm “psalm” is understood as action, because the psalter is touched by the hand in order to produce sound. By the hand we understand action. David is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable in appearance.” This signifies Christ, who is strong of hand because he conquered the devil and distributed his spoils. “Some he gave as apostles, some as prophets, and others as teachers” (Eph. 4). He is desirable in appearance because not only human beings but also angels desire to see him. He himself is the food of angels and human beings; for human beings to eat the bread of angels, the king of angels became human. [Col. 0155B]

Let us therefore say this: the action understood in this psalm is Christ’s action, and its purpose is to show that whoever wishes to reign with Christ must not refuse his persecutions, because “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (Rom. 8; Titus 2). Whether this is one psalm together with the preceding one or distinct from it, it is read as spoken in Christ’s voice and is connected with the preceding psalm in this manner:

“I came into this world to save sinners. I did no evil, nor did I teach evil. Therefore, why did the nations rage?” That is: for what advantage to themselves? Certainly none, but rather for their own condemnation and for my glory. The nations—that is, the Gentiles—Pilate and Herod raged; that is, without reason, like lions they roared against me. By “nations” are understood the pagans, who were born but not reborn. [Col. 0155C]

“And the peoples”—that is, the Jews—“why did they meditate on futile things?” That is, on things ineffective and empty of truth. For they gathered a council, saying: “If we let him go on in this way, everyone will believe in him.” “From that day they planned to kill him” (John 11). These plans were futile because Christ’s death was his exaltation. And now the whole world has gone after him.

“The kings of the earth stood forth.” This can be read in two ways. It is as though he said: not only did the nations—that is, the lesser Roman soldiers—stand against me, but the greater ones, the kings, also stood with them, that is, helped them against me. “Kings of the earth” means earthly kings, lovers of earthly things and despisers of heavenly things. And not only the people of the Jews—that is, the lesser ones—but also the rulers of the age, Annas and Caiaphas. [Col. 0155D]

Both groups gathered together in one council against the Lord, who is Lord of lords—that is, against the Father. It is said to be against the Father because it is also against his Christ, that is, against his will, since the Father’s Word is his will.

Alternatively: “The kings of the earth stood forth.”

They did not merely rage with their voices; they stood forth, that is, they drew near through action. One draws near to do harm when he labors to accomplish it. The Jewish people not only meditated on futile things but also all came together in one determination against their Lord and creator, and against his Christ, the mediator between God and human beings, saying: [Col. 0156A]

“Let us break their bonds”—those of Christ and Christians. The bonds are the arguments and teachings by which they wish to draw us under the yoke of faith. “And let us cast their yoke away from us,” that is, the faith; or the yoke is the Law by which they wish to restrain us from pleasant custom: “You shall not commit adultery”; “You shall not steal” (Exod. 20; Matt. 19).

By “bonds” understand the gentle teaching by which they attract people to the faith. By “yoke,” the severe Law imposed upon Christians after faith. They thought to break Christ’s bonds and cast his yoke away from themselves, but in vain, because he who dwells in the heavens—that is, in his preachers, namely the Holy Spirit—will mock them. The holy preachers are called heavens because they rain down words, flash with miracles, and thunder with threats. [Col. 0156B]

“He will mock them.” Divine Scripture often attributes to God what he effects in others. He will mock them, that is, he will show them to be worthy of mockery when they are unable to accomplish what they desired. Thus it is written: “All will begin to mock him, saying: ‘This man began to build and was unable to finish’” (Luke 14).

And he will not only mock them but, more seriously, he will deride them, when he not only shows them ineffective in their perverse will but also makes them follow him; thus one who was previously a persecutor of Christ later becomes a preacher of Christ. Mockery is made with the mouth; derision with the nose contracted into wrinkles.

Alternatively: he will mock them by giving them over to a reprobate mind, that is, to inner darkness; afterward he will deride them by sending them into outer darkness. [Col. 0156C]

Alternatively: “Let us break their bonds.” This is spoken in the person of Christ. It is as though he said: They gathered together against the Lord and against me, his Christ. But we, O my preachers, shall break their bonds—those of Jews or Gentiles—that is, their flattering arguments by which they wish to draw us back from preaching the faith; and we shall cast their yoke away from us, that is, we shall despise their threats. And rightly can we do so, because he who dwells in us, his heavenly preachers, will mock them. This interpretation remains unchanged.

“Then he will speak in his anger.” “Then,” that is, after mocking and deriding some by converting them, he will speak in his anger to the unbelieving, to whom previously he spoke in mercy: “Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. 33). He will place the unbelieving on his left and say to them: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food” (Matt. 25), and so forth. He will say these things then in his anger, that is, in just vengeance. [Col. 0156D]

After this, “in his wrath he will trouble them,” saying: “Depart from me, you accursed, into eternal fire” (ibid.). Neither anger, nor wrath, nor any disturbance of mind belongs to God; rather, these things appear to be attributed to him because of their effect.

“But I have been appointed king by him.” They gathered together against the Lord and against me, his Christ, saying: “Let us eradicate him from the earth” (Jer. 11). But in vain. Through that passion and death I have been appointed king, not over straw but over grains, that is, over Zion.

Zion is interpreted as “watchtower” and signifies those whose manner of life is in heaven (Phil. 3), who forget what lies behind and stretch forward toward what lies ahead. Such people are also called mountains because of the excellence of their virtues and the stability of their faith: “his holy mountain,” that is, the mountain which he himself made holy. “Holy” has been added so that that mountain might not be understood to be the literal Mount Zion. [Col. 0157A]

And because that place too was called holy, since it was near Jerusalem, he therefore added: “proclaiming his command.” He proclaims this so that the nations may be given to me as an inheritance and the ends of the earth as a possession.

This can be read in two ways. “For this purpose I preach, so that the nations may be given to me as an inheritance.” And because this could be understood in various ways by some, he specifies: “and the ends of the earth,” that is, all the nations.

Alternatively: “so that the nations may be given to me as an inheritance.” An inheritance is cultivated so that it may provide food; likewise Christ preaches to his Church so that he may refresh her, as it is written: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4). The Church is Christ’s inheritance, which nourishes him, and Christ is likewise the Church’s inheritance, refreshing her. [Col. 0157B]

And not only the nations, that is, the lesser ones, but “the ends of the earth”—that is, those who have already withdrawn themselves from love of earthly things, namely perfect men—will be given to me as a possession. A possession is usually understood as something within the house, something nearer and more beloved. Likewise, those who have already renounced the world are dearer to God.

“Truly I will give them to you,” because the Lord—that is, God the Father—“said to me,” that is, arranged this with me. “Ask of me,” that is, make yourself such that you can ask; take on a lower condition so that you may become lesser, because asking is spoken only of one who is lesser in relation to a greater. Unless he had become human, he could not have asked on our behalf.

“And I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.” This has been explained. [Col. 0157C]

And rightly will I give them to you as an inheritance because you are my Son—that is, my will—for I begot you, that is, caused you to proceed from my essence. And this was not done temporarily, but “today,” that is, eternally. The Son always proceeds from the Father, yet never abandons the Father, because his will never dissents from him as ours does. This was not said with reference to the Son’s humanity but to his divinity.

Alternatively: I have been appointed king not only over Zion—that is, over the Jews—but also over the nations. He proves this not by some ordinary authority but by the greatest authority, namely that of God the Father: “You are my Son,” not merely by grace or adoption, but by nature. The nations will rightly be given to you because you are suitable for this.

“You will rule them with an iron rod,” that is, with inflexible justice, not with human justice, which is easily changed. What is once just before him will never become unjust, and what is unjust will never become just. [Col. 0157D]

“And like a potter’s vessel you will shatter them.” In this way you will rule them—those, I mean, who were formed by the first parent, earthen vessels made not for honor but for dishonor. You will shatter them by taking away what is earthen in them so that they may be reformed for the better.

Alternatively: “You will rule them with an iron rod,” that is, those who obey you; but the disobedient you will shatter like a potter’s vessel, easily, because such people are fragile when they oppose you.

“And now, kings, understand.” Since I have been appointed your king, and you are my inheritance, you have thereby become kings, although previously you were servants of sin. [Col. 0158A]

You are called kings because you are able to rule what is earthen in you by reason and command of mind. Now be shattered like a potter’s vessel. “Understand,” that is, act rationally, lest being called kings lift you up into pride, since pride must be guarded against even in good works.

“Be instructed by me”: when I was in the form of God, I did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but rather humbled myself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death (Phil. 2), because to be humbled under him is to reign. “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (2 Tim. 2).

“You who judge the earth,” that is, you who, having now been made kings by grace, judge—that is, condemn—what is earthly in you, namely the vices of your flesh.

Alternatively, by “kings” we understand those who are lower in the Church; by “those who judge the earth,” we understand the prelates.

He expands upon what he said: “Understand.” “Serve the Lord in fear.” To understand is to act intelligently, to weigh by just judgment how fitting it is that the creature serve its Creator and the servant his lord. [Col. 0158B]

Serve in fear of mind: fear lest your mind become proud because you have been justified and made kings. Rather, serve him for whom to serve is to reign. And lest service humble and sadden you, rejoice, because in this way you reign.

“Rejoice in him,” that is, serve him joyfully—not with carnal joy in gluttony and drunkenness, but with trembling in the affliction of the flesh, because this is joy of mind. Trembling belongs to the body; fear to the mind.

“Embrace discipline.” He expands upon what he said: “Be instructed.” Embrace—that is, take up and love with great desire—discipline, meaning my chastisements. Whoever wishes to follow Christ must walk as he walked (1 John 2). “No one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. 2). [Col. 0158C]

Therefore love the discipline of the Father, because “the father chastises the one whom he loves” (Heb. 12). Embrace it, lest the Lord become angry because you have not embraced his discipline (Wis. 12). As has been said, anger does not belong to God. Hence the prophet says: “But you, Lord of hosts, judge all things with tranquility” (Jer. 11).

“He becomes angry,” that is, appears to be angry, when he justly condemns you. “And you perish from the righteous way,” from the teaching of the righteous by which all will be justified, having been handed over to inner darkness, that is, to a reprobate mind.

Alternatively, “lest you perish from the righteous way” means lest you fall away from Christ, who is the way that leads to life (John 14), because you do not wish to endure his discipline. [Col. 0158D]

It is as though he said: What harm does it do us to perish from that way? In the end you will come to eternal misery. He shows this by contrast, because blessed will be all who trust in him. This will happen when his anger, which now burns in you by giving you over to inner darkness, blazes forth—that is, burns intensely—by sending you into outer darkness.

## PSALM III. A PSALM OF DAVID WHEN HE FLED FROM THE FACE OF ABSALOM HIS SON

“Lord, why have those who trouble me become so numerous? Many rise up against me. Many say to my soul: ‘There is no salvation for him in his God.’ But you, Lord, are my protector, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head. With my voice I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain. I slept, and I was overcome with sleep, and I rose, because the Lord received me. I will not fear the thousands of people surrounding me. Rise up, Lord; save me, my God. For you have struck all those who oppose me without cause; you have crushed the teeth of sinners.
