Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people.” [Col. 0159A]

## EXPOSITION

“A Psalm of David when he fled from the face of Absalom his son.” The historical account says that Absalom persecuted his father David, wishing to take his kingdom from him. He took away a part, namely the Israelite tribe (2 Sam. 15), and Judas, together with part of the Jewish people, persecuted Christ (John 18). With reference to this persecution the psalm says of Christ: “Lord, why have they become so numerous?” Therefore this title was appropriately placed upon the psalm by Ezra, because what happened there historically in the carnal David happened here figuratively in the spiritual David, that is, Christ. [Col. 0159B]

Absalom is interpreted as “peace of the father,” not because Absalom had peace toward his father, since he constantly persecuted him, but because the father had peace toward him, as far as he himself was concerned. Whenever his men directed their attack against him, David asked them to take care that Absalom not perish. Even after Absalom’s death he mourned him for a long time with great weeping.

So too Christ had peace toward Judas. On the night when Judas betrayed him, Christ did not send him away from the supper; he gave him the sacrament of his body and blood along with the other disciples and did not deny him a kiss (Matt. 26). He was a son because he was one of the disciples of whom the Lord said: “The sons of the bridegroom cannot mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them” (Matt. 9). [Col. 0159C]

“A Psalm of David,” that is, the action understood in this psalm is that of the spiritual David, Christ, prefigured in the historical David when he fled from the face of his son Absalom. David fled Absalom, and Christ fled from Judas, because after rising from the supper he withdrew from him to the Mount of Olives to pray; Judas, however, went to the Jews to betray him (John 18). Or Christ withdrew from Judas’s heart so that the devil might enter, because God’s dwelling was not worthy to remain with a thief who carried the contents of the money box, which were put into it (John 12).

The purpose of this psalm is to encourage its members by Christ’s example not to fail amid many and great tribulations, even if they suffer persecution from those who are within, if they wish to attain the same glory to which he also attained. This purpose differs from that of the preceding psalm because that psalm dealt with persecution inflicted by those who are outside, whereas this one deals with persecution inflicted even by those who are within, that is, by false brothers. It encourages us by his example in tribulations and teaches us to whom we should flee. [Col. 0159D]

The voice of the head:

“Lord, why have those who trouble me become so numerous?” “Why,” that is, to what extent? So that even from the number of disciples the number of persecutors would increase. Or “why,” that is, for what purpose? For their own confusion and my glorification. This is spoken for the encouragement and consolation of his own.

Indeed they trouble me, that is, afflict me in the flesh, because “many rise up,” that is, rise up deliberately, “against me,” not in order to follow me but to persecute me. [Col. 0160A]

Truly against me, because “many say to my soul,” that is, to my life—or not merely to my body but also to my soul: “There is no salvation for him in his God,” not even resurrection; nor is there any salvation in his God, whose Son he claims to be.

It is as though they said: God has abandoned him. Because they thought this, they persecuted him. “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2). But they lie.

“But you, Lord, are my protector,” that is, my defender. A protector is one who undertakes another’s case in order to defend him; one who is protected is the person received into protection. Or “protector” refers to the one who protects my humanity.

Here it appears that in this psalm Christ’s humanity speaks to his divinity. [Col. 0160B]

“My glory,” that is, the glorification of my humanity. For I, insofar as I am human, am my own disgrace; or, “my glory” is the one in whom alone glorying is proper. “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord” (Jer. 9; 1 Cor. 1). Therefore he is my glory because he is “the one who lifts up my head,” that is, my mind, which is the head of carnality, raising it up so that it may not fail in tribulations.

And rightly do you lift me up, because I prayed in such a way that I was worthy to be heard. “I cried,” that is, I worked good without ceasing. “With my voice,” that is, in harmony with my heart, because I did good works for the Lord out of great desire, asking for no other reward than him. For if someone does good and seeks something other than the Lord, he will not be heard by the Lord: “Truly I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6). [Col. 0160C]

And because I cried out so worthily, he heard me “from his holy mountain,” that is, from me, who am a mountain because of the excellence of virtues and the stability of faith. “Holy,” that is, anointed with blood. Properly speaking, only martyrs are called holy; others are called blessed or righteous.

Or “from his holy mountain,” that is, from the one whom he consecrated with the blood of his martyrdom.

Or “from his holy mountain” means from the justice he gave me in a special way, since justice is a mountain: “Your justice is like the mountains of God” (Ps. 35). True innocence is the highest justice. Innocence by nature is that which harms neither itself nor another, and this was found in Christ. This was also the reason why he was heard.

Indeed he heard me: “No one will take my life from me” (John 10). Rather, I willingly slept by suffering. [Col. 0160D]

Sleep is a passage from wakefulness to slumber, just as awakening is a passage to wakefulness. “And I was overcome with sleep,” that is, I died voluntarily, “and I rose when I wished.” And just as I desired, so also pray, my faithful ones, that you may be heard.

“Some say: If Christ died voluntarily, then what sin did those who killed him commit? But one must consider not only what is done, but how it is done.” For every sin is in a certain respect good and in another respect evil. It is good with respect to God’s justice, in whose perfectly ordered household nothing happens unjustly. It is evil with respect to the will of the one who commits it. Whoever sins because of a preceding fault suffers this punishment; the punishment itself proceeds from God’s justice, even as it did in the first sin. But the act proceeded from freedom of choice.

“Therefore I rose, because the Lord received me.” The one who received me from the tomb is the one who received me in the Virgin’s womb. Or “he received me” because I am his received one. And because the Lord received me, “I will not fear the thousands of people surrounding me,” the head and the members. [Col. 0161A]

He says rightly “surrounding,” because true Christians are few in number compared with unbelievers. And because I, the head, do not fear, “rise up, Lord,” that is, complete what you have begun; cause my preachers to rise from fear of mind so that they may preach with confidence. “And thus save me” in the future, that is, save my members. And you ought to do so because you are my God.

Everyone makes a god for himself according to what he loves most: the lustful man makes Venus his god, the drunkard Bacchus, Epicurus his belly. But I and mine both love you alone and have you as God.

Or “rise up, Lord,” that is, give knowledge of yourself to those who love you. The more people are converted, the less the preachers will fear. Christ rises every day when his resurrection is made manifest to those who do not know it. [Col. 0161B]

“For you have struck all those who oppose me without cause.” Therefore I will not fear the thousands of people surrounding me, because you will strike them and eventually separate them from your Church as you separate straw from grain in judgment.

And how do I know this? Because you have already struck all those who oppose me without cause. The fact that they oppose me without cause indicates that they have been struck by you, that is, handed over to a reprobate mind.

“You have crushed the teeth of sinners,” that is, the malicious words with which they tear us apart; you have reduced them to nothing. “There is no salvation for him in his God.” They have already been reduced to nothing.

Or “teeth” means the authors of their destruction, who devour them, as it were, when they incorporate them into themselves and make them become what they are. Thus it was said to Peter, with respect to good things: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10). [Col. 0161C]

“Salvation belongs to the Lord.” I rightly said, “Save me,” for salvation belongs to the Lord, not to me. And because salvation is yours, O Lord, “your blessing is upon your people.” “Blessing” means an increase of virtues and good works upon your people, as in: “May God, our God, bless us” (Ps. 66), that is, may he multiply us.

## PSALM IV. FOR THE END, IN SONGS. A PSALM OF DAVID

“When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me. In tribulation you enlarged me. Have mercy on me and hear my prayer. Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood? And know that the Lord has made his holy one marvelous: the Lord will hear me when I cry to him. Be angry and do not sin; for what you say in your hearts, be pierced with remorse in your chambers. Sacrifice the sacrifice of righteousness and hope in the Lord. Many say: ‘Who will show us good things?’ The light of your countenance, Lord, has been marked upon us; you have given gladness in my heart. From the fruit of their grain, wine, and oil they have been multiplied. In peace I will both sleep and rest. For you, Lord, have established me uniquely in hope.” [Col. 0161D]

## EXPOSITION

“For the end: a psalm of David, a song, or in songs.” By “song” we understand joy. In the titles of the psalms one often finds “song” attached to a psalm, or “in songs.” Therefore it has been asked whether every psalm is a song, or conversely whether certain psalms are songs, or the reverse.

But it has been discovered that in some psalms “psalm” precedes and “song” follows, while in others “song” precedes and “psalm” follows. This signifies that the earlier parts of the psalm console us for labor, while its later parts console us through joy; the earlier parts invite us to glory, while the later parts exhort us to labor.

In the psalm in whose title “psalm” precedes and “song” follows, its earlier parts exhort us to labor, while its later parts invite us to glory.

So also in this psalm: “When I called, for the end, a psalm of David.” That is, the good action understood in this psalm belongs to David. And because there is a carnal David, there is also a spiritual David; therefore “for the end” specifies that this action is to be understood as belonging to David in such a way that we understand the one who is the End.

This is so for two reasons: either because he is the fulfillment, not the destruction, of the Law and the Prophets; or because he is the perfection of all good things, since all imperfect good things tend toward him who is the supreme good. Everything incomplete is destined to be perfected. [Col. 0162A]

And it is “a song,” that is, it shows us joy and the reward of labor after good action. Here both good action and the reward of action are shown to us through the example of the head. The title itself reveals the purpose.

The voice of the head:

“You, my faithful ones, who through many tribulations are making your way toward the kingdom: if you wish to arrive, call upon God,” that is, call him inwardly in your heart, not merely with your voice. Or call God into yourselves, so that you seek no reward for your labor except him himself. Then he will hear you, because in this way he heard me, the head.

And this is what he says:

“When I called, God heard me.” I call him “the God of my righteousness,” that is, the one who taught me how to ask justly, because he himself gives both the will and the ability according to his good will (Phil. 2).

Or I called God, and no other, because all righteousness comes from him, not wealth or anything of that kind.

But because it seems sweeter and more intimate to speak with God than about God, after speaking about God to his faithful ones for their encouragement, he turns his speech to God himself. [Col. 0162B]

Truly you have heard me, both in me and in mine, because “in tribulation you enlarged me,” that is, you gave me an enlarged heart rather than a constricted one, so that I would love not only friends but also enemies. “Narrow is the way that leads to life” (Matt. 7), and yet no one runs along it except with an enlarged heart. [Col. 0162C]

The head speaks of himself in this way, but of his members as follows: “You enlarged me,” that is, you enlarged my members in tribulation, so that tribulation itself would not seem narrow to them, but you enlarged their joy, because “tribulation and anguish are upon every human soul that does evil” (Rom. 2).

Hence the Apostle says: “Not only this, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces testing, and testing produces hope; but hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5).

“Have mercy on me.” Here it becomes clear that in this psalm Christ does not speak only about himself. “Have mercy on me,” that is, complete what you have begun. Glorify me in yourself, and glorify some among mine in hope, namely the perfect. Have mercy on those who are still weak, so that you may enlarge and perfect them, and hear my prayer.

“Hear,” that is, fulfill my prayer, which is for the increase of virtues, so that they may grow in virtues.

We pray that good things may come; we plead that evil things may be turned away.

Alternatively: “The God of my righteousness heard me.” He heard me in this way, by giving me the righteousness I was asking for. Truly, O God, you gave me righteousness, because in tribulation you enlarged me. And because you heard me by justifying me and preserving me in misery, you did so so that I would pray for nothing except what is worthy. [Col. 0163A]

This was the case with Paul, who prayed for what he ought not to have prayed for; therefore it was said to him: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness” (2 Cor. 12).

And because God heard me when I called upon him, he will also hear you if you call upon him. For this reason I say:

“Sons of men”—that is, sons of Adam and Eve, persisting in old age and original vices, unwilling to become God’s sons—“how long,” that is, how long a time? The Son of God has already come, seeking to make you his sons. Until his coming you were, in a certain sense, excusable on account of ignorance; now, however, you are not excusable at all.

“Will you be heavy of heart?” How long will you love earthly things? As blessed Gregory says, they are a burden, not a support, because they draw you back from true blessedness rather than lead you to it. [Col. 0163B]

“Why do you love vanity?” “Why,” that is, to what extent do you love vanity, meaning these temporal goods, which are vanity—that is, merely the shadow of true good? And not only do you love them, but you also seek falsehood, namely these same earthly things. Although they are only the shadow of true good, they lie because they do not fulfill what they promise. Wealth does not provide sufficiency; honors do not bestow power; and so it is with the rest. Yet they seem to promise these things.

Why, then—that is, for what advantage—do you love vanity and seek falsehood?

Alternatively: “Sons of men,” as though he were saying: It is not surprising if others do not call upon God, since they are not sons of men but rather sons of those after whom they have been named. But you Jews, who are sons of men—that is, sons of the patriarchs and prophets through their teaching, men who truly were human because they used reason and who in many ways instructed you in the worship of God—“how long will you be heavy of heart?” What more are you waiting for? [Col. 0163C]

The one whom your fathers foretold has already come—namely, me. “Come, children, listen to me” (Ps. 33). Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood, saying, “The Messiah has not yet come”? [Col. 0163D]

It is as though he said: Do not love vanity and do not seek falsehood, and the Lord will make you marvelous.

And that you may believe this more firmly, know—that is, do not doubt—that the Lord has glorified me: that is, in a wondrous manner he has made me, his holy one, immortal from mortal—holy in this respect, that is, pure, because I did not love vanity and did not seek falsehood. Thus you also, if you do not seek these things, will be glorified. “The Lord will hear me.” As if he were saying: Imitate me, because I am for you not only an example but also a helper. Because I called upon him—that is, called upon God worthily—he will hear me, because he has already glorified me; and he will hear me when I cry out to him, even on your behalf.

As if they were saying: What shall we do so that we too may be heard? Be angry over past sins, and do not sin, because it is not enough to lament the sins we have committed unless afterward we do not admit sins to be lamented. “What you say”—that is, what you think in your hearts—say only in your hearts, and let what ought not to be thought not burst forth into action. And yet, because there is sin in the heart even when it does not proceed to action, “in your beds”—that is, in your hearts—be pierced with remorse: that is, amend even the consciousness of sin through repentance; in other words, let it grieve you that you even thought of it.

Alternatively: “Be angry,” that is, let anger shake you; let it be only this, and not an agitation of the mind that also becomes an action—and do not sin. And because anger alone does not drive us to sin, he adds: “What you say,” that is, whatever other vices besides anger you utter in your hearts, vices worthy of repentance: say them only in your hearts—that is, think of them—and do not let them pass into action. Yet concerning these vices, which exist only in thought, even if they are slight, “in your beds”—that is, in your hearts—be pierced with remorse for them. That is: crush the head of the serpent, as was said to Eve and to the serpent: “You shall crush his head, and he shall lie in wait for your heel” (Gen. III). The serpent’s head is the beginning of sin, that is, the devil’s suggestion. We must crush it through remorse and prayer while it is still small, lest it grow into action. Hence the saying: “Blessed is he who will seize and dash his little ones against the rock” (Ps. CXXXVI). By the heel the completion of sin is understood, because the devil watches especially for this: that we should bring sin to completion. For this he lies in wait; for this he labors.

It should be noted that he does not say, “Do not be angry,” because this is not within our power. As punishment for sin, we have received the condition that our flesh should be subject to various desires.

But we possess the mind’s reason, which restrains these desires so that they do not burst forth into actions. For the Apostle says: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Rom. VII).

And if they are carried through to action, how are they to be corrected? In this way, as was said above: “Sacrifice the sacrifice of righteousness,” namely, by punishing anger and the other vices in yourselves. For each vice, slaughter a separate victim for God: by cutting off pride, sacrifice a bull; by cutting off wantonness, a kid; by cutting off lust, a he-goat—and so likewise with the others. This is the sacrifice of righteousness: when we ourselves punish our vices, established as judges within ourselves. And thus, by sacrificing, hope in the Lord. For whoever does not sacrifice should not hope.

Here the psalm’s song is unfolded.

Alternatively: “Be angry,” by taking vengeance upon sins already committed, and do not sin further. After renouncing the vices, sacrifice the sacrifice of righteousness—that is, live rightly. And thus hope for the reward of your labor, yet in the Lord, so that he himself may be the reward and nothing else. You who live in this way, hope for eternal rewards.

For there are many who do not hope, saying: “Who will show us good things?”—namely, the good things that you promise. Who has ascended into heaven, seen them, and reported them to us? Or who will show us evil things—namely, the torments that you say exist in hell?

They say this in vain, because you, Lord, have shown them to us by giving us reason according to your likeness. For “the light of your countenance, Lord,” has been stamped—that is, sealed—and within that seal is the Holy Spirit, upon us: that is, the light which causes your image to appear in us.

Alternatively: “the light of your countenance,” that is, the radiance of your image which was obscured in Adam—namely, true reason, by which we are like you—has been re-formed in us, preceded by the seal of the Holy Spirit. And this is what follows: “You have given gladness,” that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, in my heart, because “the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. V).

Alternatively: “You have given gladness in my heart,” by sealing “the light of your countenance,” that is, reason, upon us—namely, in our higher part, the soul. You have given—that is, you have shown me—your gladness, namely eternal blessedness, not to be sought outside but in my heart, that is, in hope alone and not yet in possession.

Those who say, “Who will show us good things?” are therefore ignorant of this blessedness because they have been multiplied—that is, because they are entangled in many things and troubled by many cares. “From the fruit,” that is, from the usefulness, of their grain—not yours, namely Christ’s, of whom it is said: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone” (John XII); and, “I am the living bread” (John VI). From their wine, not yours. The Lord’s wine is imitation of Christ’s Passion, of which the body of the faithful bears witness, as did the body of blessed Lawrence and of many others. “For how excellent is the Lord’s cup which intoxicates!” (Ps. XXII). And from their oil, not yours. The Lord’s oil is the grace of the Holy Spirit; the oil of sinners, however, is the delight or flattery of the flesh.

Through these three—grain, wine, and oil—which are opposed to the precipitous impulses of the flesh, all other carnal things are understood.

But I, the perfect Church, because I do not seek my blessedness in these things, “will sleep” in this life, in forgetfulness of all temporal affairs. “In peace,” that is, in desire for eternal goods, which are peace, because there no vices are in turmoil; a desire, I say, tending toward it, namely, where nothing follows except peace itself. And afterward I shall rest in holy eternal repose, when this mortal nature puts on immortality, when at last death, the enemy, is destroyed (I Cor. XV).

The reason why I shall sleep here and afterward rest is this: “For you, Lord, have established me uniquely in hope,” that is, in hope alone of my inheritance, so that I should not seek my blessedness outside, in these transitory things.

# Psalm V. To the End, for Her Who Receives the Inheritance. A Psalm of David

> “Give heed to my words with your ears, O Lord; understand my cry. Attend to the voice of my prayer, my king and my God. For to you I shall pray, O Lord; in the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I shall stand before you, and I shall see that you are not a God who wills iniquity. The wicked shall not dwell near you, nor shall the unjust remain before your eyes. You hate all who work iniquity; you will destroy all who speak falsehood. The man of bloodshed and deceit the Lord will abhor. But I, in the abundance of your mercy, shall enter your house; I shall worship toward your holy temple in your fear. O Lord, lead me in your righteousness because of my enemies; direct my life in your sight. For there is no truth in their mouth; their heart is vain. Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they acted deceitfully. Judge them, O God. Let them fall from their thoughts; according to the abundance of their ungodliness drive them out, for they have provoked you, O Lord. And let all who hope in you rejoice; they shall exult forever, and you will dwell in them. And all who love your name shall glory in you, for you will bless the just. O Lord, with the shield of your good will you have crowned us.”

## Commentary

“‘To the end, for her who receives the inheritance. A psalm of David.’”

In this psalm it is figuratively understood what was once enacted historically in Sarah and Hagar, one free and the other a slave (Gen. XXI; Gal. IV): the free woman received the inheritance with her son; Hagar the slave was deprived of the inheritance with her son.

By Sarah the free woman and her son, the Catholic Church is signified; by Hagar the slave and her son, the church of the malicious—that is, of false Christians and heretics—is signified, together with her offspring. Although they have been generated from Abraham—that is, from Christ—according to baptism and certain other sacraments, they will nevertheless not obtain the inheritance, since, because of the demands of their wicked merits, that generation tends more toward slavery than freedom.

The title is explained as follows: This psalm—that is, the present exhortation to good action—is David’s, that is, Christ’s, directing toward the end, that is, toward perfected goodness, those whom he exhorts, for her—that is, the Catholic Church—which receives the inheritance, from which inheritance the opposing party will be expelled.

The purpose of this psalm is to set forth an example of those who attain the inheritance and of those who are deprived of it, so that those who are called to the inheritance may learn whom they ought to imitate, whom to flee, and how to arrive there.

The Catholic Church, advancing toward the promised inheritance—that is, toward eternal blessedness—and seeing many obstacles on the way, namely, in this life, fears that it may not arrive and invokes the help of him who is the way there, the guide, and the inheritance itself (John XIV).

“Give heed to my words with your ears, O Lord.” In order to be worthy of being heard, he prays with as much feeling as he can. O Lord, this is because I am your servant. “My words,” therefore, because they accord with my heart, namely, because they are perfect: “give heed to them with your ears,” that is, do not disdain to hear them.

This is not said as though God were bounded by bodily limitations. For God’s hearing is nothing other than his clearly displaying the inclination of his will. Rather, it is said according to human custom, since people show that words to which they lend their ears are worthy of being heard.

Alternatively: “Give heed with your ears,” that is, you who possess the power of perceiving sensible things, judge whether my words are worthy of being heard.

“Understand my cry.” The greater a cry is than words, the greater understanding is than hearing with the ears. As if he were saying: May my forceful petition incline you to mercy, namely, so that you may accomplish what I ask, because for you to understand is to act.

He asks for something still greater: “Attend to the voice of my prayer.” Because I cry out intensely and without interruption, so do you attend—that is, hear me without remission.

Alternatively: Because without your help I can do nothing, “attend to the voice of my prayer,” that is, make it unremitting, so that you too may hear it unremittingly. For you command what you will and accomplish what you will.

“My prayer,” which concerns progress in the virtues. Through this we can also understand the earlier “cry” as a groaning.

You are my king because you rule me; or because, by my own will, I do not wish to have another king except him whom I have as God by nature, lest I turn aside from the way of righteousness. And you are “my God,” that is, my strength. God is strength, and whoever prays—that is, whoever seeks the virtues—seeks God. And he is rightly called God from the Greek word δέος, “fear”: hence “God,” because fear causes one to know God.

Alternatively: “My king,” Christ; “my God,” the Father, that is, my Creator.

And truly you will attend, because I have cried out and shall always cry out, in myself and in my descendants, until the consummation of the age. And this is why: “I shall pray,” O Lord, “and to you,” so that my entire prayer may be directed toward you, so that you may be the measure of my petition. And because I shall pray to you and toward you, “you will hear my voice,” not at night but “in the morning.”

This whole life is like night, because it is enveloped in many and great darknesses of ignorance and vices. When this corruptible life has passed, when this mortal nature puts on immortality (I Cor. XV), morning will come—that is, the beginning of a day that never fails. Then “the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII), radiant with the splendor of the virtues and possessing no stain of corruption.

In this way you will hear me, because in the morning—that is, when the darkness of ignorance and all corruption has been removed, and I am radiant with the light of virtue and immortality—“I shall stand before you”: I shall stand continually with you. This is not the case here. Here we stand with God, but we do not stand before him, because by living well we draw near to him, while by living badly we withdraw from him.

Alternatively: “I shall stand before you,” that is, I shall stand close to the knowledge of you. For now I know in part, but then I shall know as I am known (I Cor. XIII). And then, when I am wholly luminous, having neither stain nor wrinkle, “I shall see” clearly. For now “we see through a mirror in an enigma,” but then “face to face” (I Cor. XIII).

Alternatively: “In the morning,” that is, promptly and without delay, you will hear my voice in this life, advising me through your commandments and supplying strength lest I fail on the way. And rightly you will hear me promptly, because “in the morning I shall stand before you,” that is, promptly, like one eager for labor who begins at daybreak. “In the morning I shall begin and stand before you,” that is, I shall be constant.

Truly, “in the morning I shall stand before you,” because not at night: “for you are not a God who wills iniquity.” And this is what he says: “The wicked shall not dwell near you.”

As if he were saying: Only the righteous will obtain this inheritance, because the unjust will be deprived of it (Deut. IV; Heb. XII). “The wicked,” that is, the unclean detractor, the hateful person, in whose heart malice alone dwells. He will not dwell near you so as to possess the inheritance, because darkness cannot remain near light. And since you are a consuming fire, he cannot cling to you. For “if anyone builds upon this foundation wood, hay, stubble, the fire will test what sort of thing it is” (I Cor. III).

Nor will “the unjust,” that is, workers of iniquity—namely, Jews, heretics, and other false Christians—remain before your eyes. You mercifully await their repentance, because you allow them to share in faith and the sacraments with your faithful; but they will not remain.

Alternatively: By “the wicked,” we may understand a Jew who uses the Law wickedly; by “the unjust,” false Christians. Or by “the wicked,” the devil; by “the unjust,” his members.

And lest anyone despair because he has deprived the wicked and the unjust of the inheritance, although scarcely anyone in this life is entirely free from vice, he therefore specifies whom he is speaking about, while consoling the righteous: “You hate all who work iniquity.”

Great is God’s mercy: he does not hate those who have worked iniquity, but those who work it—that is, those who persist in it. “You hate” is appropriate, because whoever hates something either withdraws from it or separates it from himself. So too God separates the ungodly—not because hatred exists in him.

It can also be understood in this way: by “the wicked,” let us universally understand every unrighteous person, whether pagan, Jew, or false Christian, all of whom are as one in iniquity. To these the statement refers: “all who work iniquity.”

By “the unjust,” we may understand heretics, who are introduced in the plural because of their various sects. And concerning these it is said: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood,” not those who have spoken falsehood.

Just as destroying is greater than hating, so lying is a greater sin than merely doing evil—not every kind of lie, but the lie that is always active, as in the case of heretics. God may hate someone who nevertheless remains alive; but whoever he destroys is reduced to nothing.

There are certain lies that are fairly pardonable, such as those told in play, to preserve another’s life, and in many other circumstances. Yet however it is done, it is sin. He rightly says “you will destroy,” because God is true Being. Whoever lies says what is not, and wholly destroys being by asserting non-being.

He shows how great the sin of heretics is by calling the heretic “a man of bloodshed.” Rightly so, because he pours out the blood of souls—that is, the faith by which the souls of the righteous live: “My righteous one shall live by faith” (Rom. I; Heb. II).

Therefore the falsehood of heretics is greater than other sins, because other sins kill only the person who commits them, whereas this sin kills both the one who lies and all those whom he leads into error.

He calls the man of bloodshed the same man as “the deceitful man,” for two reasons. Either because he has one thing in his heart and another on his tongue: although he knows that what he says is not true, he nevertheless tries, with a kind of presumption, to assert it as true. For it is not ignorance that makes a heretic, but boastfulness.

Or he is called deceitful because he mixes truths with falsehoods, so that he may deceive more easily.

Alternatively: “The man of bloodshed and deceit the Lord will abhor.” If we understand the earlier statement universally—“You hate all who work iniquity”—there will be a particular confirmation of it, since the Lord will also abhor the man of bloodshed, that is, a murderer.

“You will destroy all who speak falsehood,” because he will destroy not only the deceitful man who lies, but also the man who speaks the truth in order to deceive—for example, one who shows a level road in order to send someone into a band of robbers. All such people will be disinherited.

“But I,” the Catholic Church, “shall enter your house,” the heavenly Jerusalem, namely the fellowship of the citizens above. “I shall enter” like a stone into a building, “in the abundance of your mercy,” that is, not through my own merits.

He says “in the abundance” because entering is a great thing, or because I shall enter together with the many whom your mercy will cause to enter. I shall enter because I shall first worship. Here he explains “I shall worship,” namely, “toward your holy temple,” or so that I may arrive there, “in your fear,” namely, chaste fear, not adulterous fear, which love casts out (I John IV).

In this way I shall pray: “O Lord, lead me in your way,” because I am on the way—that is, in progress. Make me go from virtue to virtue. This is “in your righteousness,” not in my substance. Direct my way—that is, my life—in your sight, so that it may be worthy in your eyes.

Or: Make your way—that is, your commandments—clear to me, so that I may understand them correctly. And do this “because of my enemies,” the heretics, because they set ambushes for me on that way.

Therefore direct my ways, “for there is no truth in their mouth,” that is, in their words. There is no truth in their words because “their heart is vain”: they do not possess the truth. Or it is vain because, through pride, it has been reduced to nothing, drawn from smoke, which grows more insubstantial the higher it rises. As it is written: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and they vanished in their thoughts” (Rom. I).

“Their throat is an open tomb.” Their doctrine is like a broad and deep tomb which, after receiving one corpse, is not closed but remains open to devour; it continually emits a harmful stench.

“With their tongues they acted deceitfully,” not with yours, O God, because you gave them tongues for the purpose of speaking the truth. He says “their” because they use them for falsehood. “They acted deceitfully,” that is, they acted as deceivers.

He rightly says “they acted,” because they act imperfectly, sometimes producing truths and sometimes falsehoods.

And because they are such, “judge them, O God.”

This can be understood for good or for evil.

For good: “O God, judge them,” that is, condemn them as they have made themselves; condemn their vices in them. “Let them fall from their thoughts,” that is, let their own conscience accuse them, or let them be separated from their wicked thoughts. “According to the abundance of their ungodliness drive them out,” because they have provoked you, O Lord—that is, according to your many mercies, may the multitude of their sins be erased.

Let them fall from their thoughts because those thoughts are wicked; they have provoked you, O Lord, that is, they have treated you as null while attempting to destroy your law. Or they have provoked you in the sense that they have made you—the sweetest food by nature—tasteless to themselves and to others. For to a fevered palate sweet food becomes tasteless.

“And first let all who hope in you rejoice” at the conversion of their enemies. Let them rejoice here in hope, and afterward “they shall exult forever,” that is, they shall rejoice fully, when they receive the double garment of immortality.

He rightly says first “let them rejoice” and afterward “they shall exult,” because joy belongs to the mind, while exultation belongs to the body. From *salto*, “I leap,” comes *exsulto*, “I exult.” The faithful first rejoice over the resurrection of the soul, which is the first garment, and afterward rejoice fully over the resurrection of the body, which is the second garment.

And rightly shall they exult, because you will dwell in them.

The statement “Judge them, O God” can also be understood in an evil sense. Because they are incorrigible and greatly harm your faithful, O God, judge them—that is, condemn them; separate the chaff from the grain.

The Church does not say this as a wish but as a prophecy. “Judge” means condemn them both here and in the future.

“Let them fall from their thoughts” in this life—that is, let them fall because of the wicked thoughts into which they have fallen through their preceding wicked merits. Let them fall—that is, let them descend into worse things, falling from error into error. And in the future drive them out from your inheritance according to the abundance of their ungodliness—that is, drive them out greatly, because their ungodliness is great.

“For they have provoked you,” that is, they have despised you as something worthless, O Lord, who are Lord of all.

And after the chaff has been separated from the grain, and darkness from light, let all who hope in you—not in another—rejoice because they have obtained the inheritance. And rightly let them rejoice, because they will exult forever, as was said above.

They will exult because you will dwell in them. At present you dwell in them through active grace; then you will inhabit them according to your presence and manifestation of yourself.

And, what is greater, “they will glory in you,” that is, they will see themselves to have attained perfect glory in you, the highest good. All those who now love your name—that is, “Lord,” for “Lord” is his name. Those love this name who willingly serve God.

They will therefore glory because “you will bless the just.” He rightly says “the just,” for we are all one in Christ. You will increase and multiply every grace and all virtues, because what they now possess in hope they will then possess in reality: now in part, then perfectly.

Truly they will glory in you, O Lord, and not in another, because “you have crowned us,” that is, surrounded and fortified us like a crown of soldiers, with a shield—that is, with the protection of your good will.

Or you have crowned us after victory, not because of our merits, but because, like a shield of your good will, you preceded our will: for you gave the will, and you gave the accomplishment. You work in us through your grace, and you crown in us the work of your mercy.

# Psalm VI. To the End, with Songs, for the Eighth. A Psalm of David

> “O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger. Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak; heal me, O Lord, for my bones are troubled. And my soul is greatly troubled; but you, O Lord—how long? Turn, O Lord, and deliver my soul; save me because of your mercy. For in death there is no one who remembers you; but in hell, who will confess to you? I have labored in my groaning; every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall water my couch. My eye has been troubled by fury; I have grown old among all my enemies. Depart from me, all you who work iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping. The Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord has received my prayer. Let all my enemies be ashamed and greatly troubled; let them turn back and be exceedingly and swiftly ashamed.”

## Commentary

“A psalm of David for the eighth, to the end, in hymns.”

The eighth is understood as the day of judgment. Some, understanding the matter perversely, took seven thousand years for the seven days, followed by the eighth day, that is, the day of judgment; thus they thought they had discovered the fixed date of judgment. The Lord’s words contradict them: “It is not yours to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in his own authority” (Acts I), along with many other passages.

It can, however, be understood in this way: from the time when all things subject to change began, the whole period revolves through seven days. Therefore this entire life can be understood in relation to the number seven. When this revolving course of things has passed, the eighth follows, in which there will be no need for changing times, because that day will not vary or turn into darkness.

Alternatively: The Lord worked for six days. In the creation of each thing, one may understand a span of one day in which work is permitted. The seventh day is understood as that interval which lies between the passing of this life and the general resurrection. The eighth day is the resurrection.

Alternatively: There are two generations, one carnal and the other spiritual. The carnal generation extended from the first man to Christ. This was the first generation, and it lived carnally, although some spiritual persons existed within it, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who served God in the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, they were called carnal because they received carnal observances and lived in the shadow.

The spiritual generation is understood as the generation of the faithful from Christ’s coming to the end of the age. It is called spiritual because it lives in the name of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter (I Cor. XV). This is the second generation. “First the carnal, then that which is spiritual” (Rom. VII).

These two generations are related to the number seven, which consists of four and three. Four refers to the first generation, because it lived carnally, and the flesh consists of four elements. Three refers to the soul’s three powers. The soul is rational, irascible, and concupiscible.

It possesses reason in order to distinguish between things to be desired and things not to be desired; then concupiscence, so that it may know how to desire good things; and anger, so that it may know how to be angry at evil things.

But because, through their affinity with the body, these powers are often dulled, instruction is applied to illuminate reason, and virtue to restrain excessive anger and excessive desire.

After this number seven, the eighth day will come, on which each person will be rewarded according to whether he has used this sevenfold structure well or badly: the one in body and soul unto glory, the other unto punishment.

The psalm—that is, the good action expressed by this psalm—is David’s, that is, Christ’s, in his body. David, I say, directs toward the end, and this action is for the eighth, that is, for expectation of judgment. It is to be received in hymns, because the faithful soul hymns well to God when, through repentance, it afflicts itself.

“For there is joy among the angels of God over one sinner who repents” (Luke XV).

In this psalm there is the voice of every weak believer who considers that eighth day, namely the dreadful day of judgment, to which all will come to be judged: some to blessedness, others to punishment. By his example he exhorts others to repentance and to calling upon divine mercy.

Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger. I call upon you, who are Lord of all. I know that you will come to judge some in fury and others in your anger; I ask you to judge me here, while it is the time [Col. 0172B] of mercy and the day of salvation. Just as fury is greater than anger—for anger is brief, whereas fury is prolonged—so to rebuke is greater than to correct. Often those who are rebuked are accused; condemnation follows accusation, whereas correction is made for amendment. And because at the future judgment some are rebuked in fury—not that fury falls upon God, for fury is a great agitation of the mind toward vengeance—that is, because of severe punishment, for they will be crushed with double contrition (Jer. XVII), while others are rebuked in anger, such as those who built wood, hay, and straw upon the foundation of faith and will nevertheless be saved, yet as through fire (I Cor. III): O Lord, before you come to judge, while it is the time of mercy, have mercy on me; that is, correct me here mercifully. And this is necessary, because I am weak.

The sin of the first parent [Col. 0172C] brought upon all his descendants the punishment of great weakness. For I do not do what I want, but I do the evil that I hate (Rom. VII).—I am weak not only in body but also in soul. And this is what he says: Heal me, O Lord, who are the physician of souls, because my bones are troubled—that is, the virtues that are the soul’s strength, or the forces of carnality, are troubled, that is, confused and darkened by that weakness which I contracted from the first parent. And lest anyone understand “bones” corporeally, he explains what he means by bones. And my soul is greatly troubled. Alternatively: because I am weak in the flesh and weak in the virtues, therefore my soul is greatly troubled toward compunction and lamentation. And because I am troubled toward repentance, are you, Lord, [Col. 0172D] troubled forever? And how long do you delay healing? A physician ought not to deny medicine to a sick person who confesses his weakness. Do not be troubled any longer—or do not delay showing mercy—but rather turn, Lord; just as you turned away from one who turned away, so turn toward one who turns toward you. God neither turns away nor turns; rather, his turning is the showing forth of mercy, just as his turning away is when he withdraws the hand of mercy.

And rescue my soul, which clings to the thorns of carnal pleasures. And having rescued me, make me safe—that is, grant perseverance in the good, like a good physician who preserves the one he has healed by showing what ought to be avoided and what ought to be taken. Because of your mercy, not because of my merits. I have no other price to offer. Therefore rescue me, therefore save me, so that [Col. 0173A] I may remember you—that is, so that I may praise you. For if you do not do this, I shall not praise you. For I shall be in death, because there is no one in death who remembers you (I Pet. II).

Alternatively: Therefore rescue my soul from carnal desires, which wage war against it; for if you do not rescue me, they will kill me—that is, they will separate me from you, who are my life. And if I am dead, I shall not remember you, so as to return to repentance through confession. Therefore, after instruction—that is, after repentance—preserve me, lest, having fallen again, I return to the depths of vices, where there is already despair. And this is what he says: But in hell, who will confess to you? Alternatively: Rescue my soul, but do so now, while it is the time of mercy, lest I die in sins, because in death there is no one who remembers you for repentance. [Col. 0173B] But in hell, who will confess to you in such a way that you will hear? No one. For there repentance is fruitless, as in the case of that rich man: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me” (Luke XVI). Or “will confess” means: no one will praise you.

Alternatively: Rescue me, make me safe, because I am not in death—that is, in perseverance in sin and contempt of you. The sinner, when he has come into the depths, despises (Prov. XVIII). I demonstrate this by the fact that I remember you—that is, because I pray to you. I demonstrate it by its opposite: “For there is no one in death who remembers you.” I say that I am not in death because I remember you; therefore I am much less in hell. Hell means despair, which is lower than all sins. I demonstrate this by the fact that I confess to you my misery and my sin, [Col. 0173C] not yours. For who among the despairing will confess to you—that is, for your honor—by removing you from blame, as I do? Those in despair sometimes confess their sins, but not to you; rather, they confess against you, when they say that they ought to have been created by you in such a way that they could not sin. Thus, in a certain way, they judge themselves righteous and accuse you.

Alternatively: Rescue me, free me, because I am not in death—that is, I am not a dead member for whom medicine is useless. Because I remember you—that is, I recognize you as merciful, I recognize you as a physician. I said, “Free me, make me safe because of your mercy,” and yet, insofar as I am able, I wish to merit your favor. Because I labored in my groaning—that is, I groaned diligently—and not only did I labor, but I will wash my bed every night [Col. 0173D]. I will wash it—that is, I will purify through groaning my bed, that is, my conscience; namely, I will amend everything I have committed inwardly. “Conscience” is understood as “bed” because there each person rests—that is, consents either to the law of God or to the law of sin—or because there is the rest of the righteous. For this purpose it is cleansed of the filth of vices, so that there may be a peaceful and pure rest of the soul there.

“Every night” means through every evil thought; or “my bed” means carnal pleasures. “Every night” means through every vice in which I have taken delight. And not only will I water with my outward tears my conscience, or the pleasure to which the spirit consents, but also my couch—that is, my lower self, which ought always to lie beneath the mind—[Col. 0174A] like a garden, so that it may become fit to bear fruit for God. Or the body is called a couch because it is turned about in various ways by the weakened soul. “You have turned all his couch in his sickness” (Ps. LX).

He adds the cause of so great a labor: My eye is troubled—that is, reason or the mind, that eye which is more worthy than many bodily eyes. For reason enables one to distinguish evils from goods and condemnation from salvation. It is troubled when it foresees future condemnation and considers that we have deserved it. By fury—that is, by the condemnation of the future judgment on the eighth day; or by fury, that is, by the punishment which we received in the first parent; or by fury, because I do not judge either myself or others in gentleness and patience, but in anger. Therefore the inner eye is troubled, [Col. 0174B] seeing your fury that is to come on the eighth day.

Because I have grown old among all my enemies. He does not merely say “I have grown old,” but “I have become exceedingly old,” that is, I have become very old through the habit and persistence of sins among all my enemies, so that I have become a participant in all their sins. Or “I have grown old” means that I, who had begun through faith and innocence to be a member of the new human being, have been reduced among all my enemies to a member of the old human being, so that I am one of all the sins that were previously my enemies. Or “I have grown old” means that I have become like a very old garment, suitable neither for use nor for adornment—for my own use or for the Church’s adornment through teaching.

The faithful soul, considering the great mercy of God, who says, “I do not desire the death [Col. 0174C] of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live,” and, “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. XVIII), does not doubt, after a true confession of sin, that it has been heard; and so it says exultantly: The Lord has heard the voice of my weeping. So you also, whoever wish to be heard, give voice to your weeping. But you who practice iniquity—that is, who do not wish to confess them but persevere in them—depart from me, here in affection and afterward also in body, namely, on the eighth day.

Let him show how he has been heard: The Lord has heard my supplication, which was for sins, as in the words, “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury.”—The Lord has received my prayer, namely, the prayer that was for perseverance in the good, as in the words, “Save me because of your mercy.”—[Col. 0174D] Let all my enemies be ashamed and greatly troubled.

This can be understood either for good or for evil. For good, as follows: because I have deserved to be heard through shame at my sins and worthy compunction, I therefore urge all my enemies to recognize their sins and the end toward which they are heading. For their end is death (Rom. VI). Let them be ashamed that they have committed these things, and after their shame let them be troubled toward compunction and repentance; let them turn, that is, toward the Lord. And let them be ashamed not after some delay, but very quickly.

For evil, as follows: Let all my enemies be ashamed and troubled, now already judged, blinded, and given over to a depraved mind; or let them be ashamed on that eighth day, rather than merely “be ashamed.” This is not a wish [Col. 0175A] but a prophecy and a rejoicing in the divine sentence, when they see us to be in glory and say, “These are the ones whom we once held in derision” (Wis. V). And they will be troubled with great fear, that is, exceedingly. Let them afterward turn to see their torments, and then let them be ashamed with eternal shame—and let this happen very quickly, that is, without delay.

## PSALM VII. TO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID, WHICH HE SANG TO THE LORD BECAUSE OF THE WORDS OF CUSH THE SON OF JEMINI

> “Lord my God, in you I have hoped; save me from all those who persecute me, and deliver me. Lest he seize my soul like a lion, while there is no one who redeems or saves. Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is iniquity [Col. 0175B] in my hands, if I have repaid evil to those who repaid me with evil, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies. Let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it, trample my life into the earth, and bring my glory down into the dust. Arise, Lord, in your anger, and rise up at the boundaries of my enemies. And arise, Lord my God, according to the commandment that you gave, and the assembly of the peoples will surround you. And for this reason return on high: the Lord judges the peoples. Judge me, Lord, according to my righteousness and according to my innocence, which is in me. Let the wickedness of sinners come to an end, and you will direct the righteous, O God who searches hearts and kidneys. My just help is from the Lord, who saves the upright in heart. God [Col. 0175C] is a just judge, strong and patient; will he be angry every day? Unless you turn back, he will brandish his sword; he has bent his bow and prepared it. And in it he has prepared instruments of death; he has made his arrows burning. Behold, he travails with injustice, has conceived pain, and has given birth to iniquity. He opened a pit and dug it out, and he fell into the pit that he made. His labor will return upon his head, and his iniquity will descend upon his crown. I will confess to the Lord according to his righteousness, and I will sing psalms to the name of the Lord Most High.”

## EXPOSITION

“To the end, a psalm of David, which he sang to the Lord because of the words of Cush the son of Jemini” (II Sam. XVI and XVII). When Absalom was persecuting David, there was a certain Ahithophel [Col. 0175D], whose plots instructed him in every evil. But a certain Cush, David’s friend, went over to Absalom in order to investigate all the counsels of Ahithophel and report them to David, so that he might make him cautious concerning that persecution. This psalm does not seem to concern those counsels; therefore they are recalled from history to mystery.

Ahithophel is interpreted as “the ruin of a brother.” He signifies Judas, who plotted Christ’s ruin—that is, his death—and who called himself the brother of all the apostles: “Go, tell my brothers” (John XX). Cush is interpreted as “silence,” signifying that dispensation which God the Father used through his Son for the redemption of the human race. When this was happening, it was unknown, and it remains unknown [Col. 0176A] except to those to whom the Lord has wished to reveal it, as in the passage: “God revealed through his Son to the apostles the mystery hidden from the ages” (Col. I, Eph. III). This is that silence: “A partial blindness has happened in Israel, until the fullness of the nations should enter” (Rom. XI). And what Judas and the Jewish people contrived for the ruin of one person was made to result in the salvation of many. Jemini is interpreted as “right,” signifying that the right—that is, the propitious—God brought about this silence.

The psalm—that is, the good action about which this psalm speaks—is David, that is, the perfect faithful person who belongs to the body of David, namely, the one who presses toward the end, that is, toward Christ. He sang this psalm—that is, he performed this good action and, as it were, gave thanks—exultantly to the Lord, that is, for the Lord’s honor [Col. 0176B], because of the words—that is, the revelation—of Cush, that is, of silence. For the Lord graciously revealed to him how, through humility and obedience, he crushed the pride of the one who through pride cast the first parent out of paradise. How he should sing and give thanks for this revelation is shown by what follows in the psalm, where he shows that he imitates Christ’s humility and patience, saying: “If I have done this,” and so forth.

Because Cush was the son of Jemini—that is, because silence proceeded from the propitious God—he rightly gives thanks to him. The Prophet’s purpose in this psalm is to show how every perfect person ought to guard himself. For the more perfect someone is, the more cautious he ought to be, namely, never to act negligently. Even if he has already conquered external enemies, he must nevertheless beware of the inner enemy, [Col. 0176C] lest he fall through pride. This vice must also be guarded against in good works. The psalm also shows how he should offer himself as an example of patience and humility to others, by invoking God’s help and imitating God’s humility and righteousness.

## The voice of the perfect person before Christ’s coming
Lord, whose servant I present myself to be, I have hoped in you, not in myself and not in anything else—because you are my God, and not I, like that wretched first parent—and because I have hoped in you, save me from all who persecute me. Having overcome all vices, save me, that is, guard me now placed in the stronghold of the virtues. Having overcome all carnal vices, in mind I serve the law of God, but in the flesh the law of sin (Rom. 7). The flesh always desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh (Gal. 5). Good people are never without battles. Therefore, O Lord, I do not ask that there be no tinder of sin in my body, but I pray that sin may not reign there. Save me, so that my mind may command and the flesh serve; or, save me from all who persecute me. All who wish to live devoutly in Christ Jesus suffer persecution (2 Tim. 3); therefore save me, that is, make me steadfast in the virtues, so that I may be able to disregard both their threats and their flatteries.

And deliver me—not from those whom he has already overcome, but lest he ever seize my soul like a lion. This prayer belongs to the perfect, who fear only the devil’s ambushes. Even after all vices have been overcome, he must still be feared in good works, lest through pride he cast one down from the summit of the virtues: lest he ever seize my soul as something alien [Col. 0177A] and not his own, but your sheep—the one who is like a lion, namely, strong and unconquerable except by you. Hence the words: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. 5). “Since there is no one who can redeem except you”—this pertains to the words, “Deliver me.” “Nor anyone who can save”—this pertains to “Save me.” Lord my God. This repetition arises from great affection.

“If I have done this.” As though he were saying: You ought to redeem me, as you ought to save me, because I have perceived what you revealed to me and, insofar as I am able, strive to imitate it. You were obedient to the Father; you patiently endured your persecutors; you returned good for evil. And if I have not observed all these things, may I not be worthy of redemption by you.

Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is any iniquity in my hands—that is, in my works; that is, if I have provoked them to persecute me by any iniquity of mine; namely, if I did what I ought not to have done; if I returned evil to those who repaid me with evil for good; that is, if I did what even seems just among mortals, namely, to return evil for evil. As though he were saying: If I did not return evil to those who persecuted me without any preceding fault—which was a great act of patience; that is, if I did not do what I ought to have done.

“If I, a human being, have overcome another human being in anger, may I fall empty”—that is, emptied of glory and victory, overcome by my inward enemies. For as blessed Gregory says: “While we seek to take vengeance outwardly, we are grievously wounded inwardly.” Everyone sins first against himself rather than against another; for before he harms another outwardly, he has already lost innocence inwardly. Thus, while he thinks he has gained victory outwardly, what is more grievous is that he has been overcome inwardly—and rightly so. For what does a human being claim for himself when, while he takes revenge on another human being, he is himself conquered by the devil? Therefore, vengeance should rather be taken on the devil than on a human being.

That is: “Let the enemy pursue my soul,” by suggesting evil, “and seize it,” by binding it through consent; and thus “let him trample my life upon the earth”—that is, by trampling it down and subjecting it to himself, let him make my life earthly, so that I may become his food. For it was said to the sinner: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3), and to the serpent: “You shall eat earth” (ibid.).

“And let him bring my glory down into the dust”—that is, the testimony of my conscience. “Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (1 Cor. 1). “Let him bring it down,” that is, let him lead it from the conscience into the dust among those who are dust, so that I may seek to glory outwardly before human beings; or “into the dust,” that is, into earthly things, which are dust, so that I seek glory in nothing but them. Here lies the whole force of the statement. This is the essential point.

As though he were saying: But there is no iniquity in my hands, nor have I returned evil to those who repaid me with evil; therefore, “Arise, O Lord, in your anger”—a good vengeance, worthy of a perfect man. As though he were saying: I shall not be overcome by the enemy; rather, let the enemy be overcome by you, and take away his spoils.

“Arise, O Lord,” through knowledge—you who now seem to lie among my persecutors because of their ignorance. Make them know you, so that they may follow you. And do this “in your anger,” by showing them your anger, that is, the future condemnation and punishment of their impiety.

“And be exalted”—that is, be glorified—so that you may be praised “in the territories of my enemies,” that is, among those who are now the possession of demons, or among those who are the territories, that is, the stronghold, of all enemies—namely, among the worst of them, as in Paul.

And so that you may be exalted in the territories of your enemies, “arise, O Lord my God, in the commandment that you commanded”—that is, appear and manifest yourself in the commandment that you gave to the first parents, namely, in obedience and humility, so that through these you may turn them back to yourself. Let them learn through humility to conquer him who through pride overcame the first parent.

And when you have appeared in this way, “the assembly of the peoples will surround you”—that is, the congregation of the faithful and the unfaithful will surround you: the former for imitation, the latter for destruction. And on account of this assembly—namely, of the faithful and the unfaithful—“return on high,” that is, return to the heights.

On account of the assembly of the faithful, return to heaven, so that it may now recognize you as more than merely human, and so that you may send the Holy Spirit, who will strengthen it. Thus Peter, who had previously denied the Lord before a servant-girl, after the coming of the Holy Spirit, being strengthened, did not fear to confess him before a king.

On account of the assembly of the unfaithful, return on high, so that their blindness may increase. For although they saw through many signs that the one whom they handed over to death was God, they did not dare to confess it, lest innocent blood be demanded from them.

This may be read in the favorable sense, beginning with “Arise, O Lord, in your strength” and continuing through “Judge me, O Lord, according to my justice.”

It may also be understood in an unfavorable sense, with the same continuation as above:

“Arise, O Lord”—that is, O Christ, ascend on high; withdraw from their knowledge. “Make darkness your hiding place,” and do this in your anger, being angry at their refusal to be corrected. “And be exalted in the territories of my enemies.” This is a repetition. Or “be exalted,” that is, exercise your greatness and power even upon them; make them your scourge; use them for the salvation of your faithful and for their own condemnation. “Assyria is the rod of my anger, but he did not understand” (Isa. 10).

“Arise, O Lord”—that is, make yourself lofty, inscrutable, and unknowable to them. “In the commandment that you commanded”—that is, let them see you humble in humility, and not recognize God. For if they had recognized him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2).

“And the assembly of the peoples will surround you.” This is explained as above.

“The Lord judges the peoples.” This can be understood in two ways.

In one way: I said, “Return on high”—that is, ascend to the Father, from whom you came. But I, to whom you have already revealed your secrets, see that what brings salvation to some brings condemnation to others. Therefore I say: The Lord judges the peoples by a hidden judgment. For this reason I ask you to judge me for salvation.

In another way: Appear in humility and return to heaven; afterward you will come only to judge openly. And this is what “The Lord judges the peoples” means: he will judge them.

It should be noted that he says, “Return.” Divinity, which is everywhere, neither descends nor ascends. Humanity did not descend, because it was assumed from the Virgin, although it is said: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven” (John 3). But it must be said that the divinity of the Word was seen to have descended in this manner: when it manifested itself to us through the flesh of the Lord’s humanity. It returned when it withdrew itself from us.

And because in the future you will judge openly, before I come there, judge me here first. Scourge me, burn me, test your gold.

Or, because here too you judge by a hidden judgment—making some into scourges and others subject to scourging—judge me, O Lord; punish and scourge me according to my justice, that is, for testing. For my justice demands this. Whoever is just has nothing that needs to be cleansed; just as pure gold has nothing to lose in the fire, so the just person is scourged and judged for this purpose: so that his justice may increase.

“And according to my innocence.” Justice consists in doing good; innocence, in abandoning evil. Neither of these comes from me, but from above—that is, from on high.

And because this is my testing, not my condemnation, “the wickedness of sinners will be consumed in me”—that is, it will be brought to perfection. Let them exercise their iniquity against me as long as they can; for the more they become filthy, the purer I become. Just as fire, the more filth it draws from gold, makes the gold purer, while losing nothing of its own nature.

“The impious lives for the pious,” and in this way “you will direct the just”—that is, the justice of the just person will grow. For just as the wicked, by exercising wickedness against the unjust, becomes more wicked, so the just person becomes more just through patience. And this is the direction of the just: that he proceed from virtue to virtue.

You, God, will do this, for you are the perfect physician, who know what you should punish in us; because you are God, examining hearts—that is, the counsels of hearts, which are upright—and kidneys, that is, desires, which are perverse. For in the kidneys is the seat of lust in a man; that is, you know (*tu scis*) when the mind consents to the pleasure of the flesh, or when the flesh obeys the spirit.

Or, “hearts” means intentions, and “kidneys” means the ends of intentions, because every intention tends either toward good pleasure or toward evil.

“My just help is from the Lord.” As though he were saying: I do not fear the torments of the impious, since I am just, because my just help is from the Lord. “For he saves all the upright in heart.”

Or: I do not fear that the Lord will judge me at the future judgment, that is, openly, because now, in the hidden judgment, my help is justly from the Lord, while he temporarily scourges me who temporarily sin, as an example of his just judgment—namely, so that through this he may show how justly he will eternally punish the one who sins eternally, so that he who does not spare the Son may not spare the servant.

He sins temporarily who voluntarily ceases to sin; he sins eternally who would sin forever if he lived forever.

And because he saves the upright in heart, do not fear, then, you who are just. But you, impious ones, beware, because God, who now judges you secretly by blinding you, will brandish his sword—that is, his Son, whom he mercifully sent to you, concealed by the sheath of flesh.

“He will brandish it,” that is, he will uncover it, when he judges through him openly. For “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). And this is because God is a just judge. No lack of power hinders his judgment, because he is strong.

As though he were saying: If he is just and strong, why, then, does he not continually judge the sinner?

Because he is patient. And he demonstrates this: “Will he be angry every day?” He does this so that you may be converted. For “he does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted” (Ezek. 18). And the Apostle says: “Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance?” (Rom. 2).

But if, because he delays punishment, you think that he will not judge, and therefore sin securely, “you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the just judgment of God.”

And this is what follows: “Unless you are converted, he will brandish his sword.”

Truly he will judge in the future openly, because now he judges secretly. “He has already bent his bow.” The bow is divine Scripture, which he has already bent, because the harshness of the Old Testament has been flexed by the cord of the New. There it says: “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Exod. 21); here, however: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live” (Ezek. 18).

Or it has been bent in this way: it has been inclined to the capacity of the faithful through holy interpreters and preachers; and by bending it, he prepared it so that it would be suitable for understanding.

And in it—that is, in the bow—“he prepared vessels of death,” namely, holy preachers, who receive from it a life-giving liquid and pour it into the sick and wounded minds of human beings, so that they may drive out the deadly poison of the dreadful serpent.

Or “vessels of death” may be understood negatively of those same apostles, who become vessels of death for those who despise their teaching, while becoming vessels of life for those who receive it. “For to some we are an aroma of death unto death, and to others an aroma of life unto life” (2 Cor. 1).

And this is what follows: “He made his arrows burning.” He made those same preachers his arrows, which spur the hearts of the faithful toward the love of God; and he made them so by making them burn with charity.

Alternatively: “In it he prepared vessels of death”—heretics, who take from it the poison of distorted understanding and, by teaching others perversely, bring death both to themselves and to others. And he made those same people his arrows, that is, goads for those burning with love of God and neighbor.

For they aroused many to examine and open divine Scripture, as the Apostle says: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Cor. 11).

He said, “God will brandish his sword”—that is, he will send his Son openly to judge. And this can be known from the fact that he already judges secretly in sacred Scripture, blinding some unto death and enlightening others unto life.

And to show that that manifest condemnation will not arise from the cruelty of the judge but from the impious’ own merits, he adds:

“Behold, he labors with injustice and has conceived pain.”

As though he were saying: Do you not see how he stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath?

Or this may be said of heretics, as follows: Truly they are vessels of death. “Behold, he labors with injustice and has conceived pain.”

If we speak of all the impious, the meaning is this: Behold, he has conceived pain, just as a woman conceives seed with pleasure, from which she later experiences great pain. So this person conceives in his heart delight in those things that will cause him great pain, since they can neither be abandoned without the greatest pain nor retained.

And therefore “he labors,” that is, he meditates giving birth to injustice through consent, while he thinks about completing evil. For from the fact that he has conceived evil, he meditates becoming a liar, perjurer, unjust, and other such things.

“And he has given birth to iniquity”—that is, he has brought it into action.

“He opened a pit.” The comparison is this: the one who opens a pit and digs it, making it deep, later falls into the pit that he himself made for others, and falls into it first, because in the very meditation he has already sinned against himself. For everyone sins first against himself rather than against another; and the only thing that harmed the other excessively was that he wished to do so.

Or he explains what he said, “Behold, he labors with injustice and has conceived pain,” by adding, “He opened a pit,” which pertains to “he conceived pain.” He opened a pit when he consented to evil. He dug it when he devoted himself to fraud, or when he labored to bring it into action; this pertains to “he labors with injustice.” And “he fell into the pit that he made” pertains to “he gave birth to iniquity.”

“His pain will turn back upon his head.”

If this is understood as a comparison, the meaning is as follows: just as one who prepares a large pit eventually falls into it, and whatever he has gathered, collapsing upon his head, crushes him, so whatever evil the impious person has built throughout his entire life will fall upon him when he is finally condemned.

Alternatively: “His pain will turn back upon his head” when he has thought about outwardly doing evil to his neighbor. Before he harms his neighbor outwardly, it will turn inwardly upon his own head—that is, his mind—in order to strike it first. And not only upon his head, that is, his mind, but “his iniquity will descend upon his crown,” that is, upon his discernment, so as to destroy it. For discernment is the crown of the mind, that is, its highest part.

This is said by way of comparison, because at the crown the hair is parted and descends toward different parts of the head.

If we understand it of heretics alone, we shall say: Behold, see how they become vessels of death. This person has conceived pain from that bow—that is, a poisonous interpretation—and therefore “he labors with justice,” while attempting to assert his distorted interpretation to others. For one who speaks the truth does not labor.

“And he has given birth to iniquity,” when he persuaded others; “he opened a pit,” by preaching error for the downfall of many. As there is darkness in a deep pit, so there is darkness in the doctrine of heretics. And he dug it with great labor and many assertions, confirming it; and he fell into the pit that he made—not only to be condemned for it at the future judgment, but already beforehand in the hidden judgment, when he is permitted to live in his blindness.

He shows how he fell into it: “His pain will turn back upon his head.” The unbelievers and heretics are judged secretly, and afterward openly.

But I, your servant, who understand that your hidden judgment is now being carried out for this purpose—that the just person may be justified and grow from virtue to virtue—“will confess to the Lord,” and give thanks and praise according to his justice, by which he chastises me as a father chastises a son. And I will not praise with my mouth alone, but will sing psalms—that is, perform good works—because “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15); “to your name,” that is, for your praise, not mine.
