Alternatively: Jerome says that Chusi was not the son of Jemini but of Arachi, and according to him Chusi is interpreted as “Ethiopian.” Through him the devil and his members may be understood, namely, all persecutors.

“He who is Chusi is the son of Jemini.” Jemini was descended from Benjamin, as were Saul and Shimei, who, with his head sprinkled with dust, insulted David, calling him “a man of blood” and “a man of Belial” (2 Sam. 16). All those persecutors of David were descended from Benjamin.

Accordingly, this may be read as spoken in the person of the prophet David, or of some perfect person from the earlier people.

“He sang it”—that is, he performed it joyfully—“on account of the words,” that is, on account of the threats or flatteries, “of Chusi,” that is, of the persecutor, the son of Jemini.

In the person of those people the psalm may be read, just as above at the beginning:

“Lord my God, I have hoped in you; save me.” As though he were saying: Come, Lord, and do not delay.

Alternatively, in the person of the Head:

“Psalm of David”—that is, of Christ the Head—“which he sang,” that is, joyfully fulfilled, “to the Lord,” that is, for the Lord’s honor, “on account of the words of Chusi,” that is, on account of the manifestation of that secret which he arranged through David; “I say, of the son of Jemini,” that is, of the propitious God.

It is not that he spoke the words that are said in the psalm, but that the manifestation of the matter shows that this could have been done and said, as must be understood in all the psalms.

Voice of the Lord’s humanity:

“Lord my God, I have hoped in you,” insofar as concerns the humanity. “Save me”—the Head and the members—from all my persecuting Jews, and deliver me from the Jews who persecute me, so that through me my people may be saved.

“Lest the Jewish people seize my soul like a lion”—“soul,” that is, life.

“Since there is no one who redeems, nor anyone who saves, if you do not redeem.”

“Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands”—that is, if I have not fulfilled the obedience and humility enjoined upon me by you, and so forth, as above—“may I deservedly fall from my enemies,” the Jewish persecutors, “empty,” that is, emptied of the glory of the resurrection.

In this way: “Let the enemy pursue my soul”; let the Jewish people pursue it in order to kill me. “And let him trample my life upon the earth,” by handing me over to death. “And let him bring my glory”—the glory of me, the Head, and of my members—“down into the dust,” so that only my body may be dissolved into dust and not rise again.

But if I have done what you commanded, becoming obedient to you unto death, and have returned not evil for evil but good for evil, “Arise, O Lord”—that is, withdraw from them. Blind their hearts so that they may persecute me. For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. Unless you were angry with them, you would not have withdrawn from them so greatly.

“And be exalted in the territories of my enemies”—that is, let the greatness of your power appear not only in the good but also in the evil. Use them for good; make them your scourge. Let them crucify and kill me for the life of my people and their own destruction.

“Arise, O Lord my God”: withdraw from them, but arise for my people—that is, grant them knowledge of you. Or “arise,” that is, make me rise, so that I may ascend into heaven and send them the Holy Spirit, who will fill their hearts with charity.

“In the commandment that you commanded”—that is, in charity. “This is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you; and by this they will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13, 15).

“And the assembly of the peoples will surround you”—that is, the congregation of the faithful for imitation. And because in this assembly of the faithful there will be some who bear the Christian name but not the works, he therefore adds also: “On account of this”—not only on account of the assembly of persecutors—“return on high”; withdraw from them.

This is what the Apostle says: “In those days perilous times will come, and people will be lovers of themselves” (2 Tim. 5), and: “The love of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24).

He then adds for what purpose all these things will occur:

“The Lord judges the peoples”—those who are to be saved and those who are not to be saved. Those who are not to be saved he blinds here, on account of their preceding merits, so that they may be condemned in the future. Those who are to be saved he judges by justifying them, so that they may be crowned in the future.

And because you, Lord Father, judge the peoples—these for salvation, those for destruction—“judge me according to my justice,” and so forth to the end, as above.

# PSALM VIII. FOR THE END; FOR THE WINEPRESSES. A PSALM OF DAVID

[Col. 0183B]

“Lord, our Lord, how admirable is your name in all the earth! For your majesty has been exalted above the heavens. From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise because of your enemies, so that you may destroy the enemy and the avenger. For I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars that you founded. What is man that you are mindful of him, or the son of man that you visit him? You have made him a little lower than the angels; you have crowned him with glory and honor, and set him over the works of your hands. You have subjected all things beneath his feet: all sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field; the birds of heaven and the fish of the sea, which travel along the paths of the sea. Lord, our Lord, how admirable is your name in all the earth!”

[Col. 0183C]

## EXPOSITION

“A Psalm of David for the winepresses.” This psalm says nothing about winepresses, and therefore this title is not understood literally. “For the winepresses,” then, means for the churches, in which it is now brought about that the worthy are separated from the unworthy in disposition and in deed, just as wine is separated from grape-skins in winepresses and grain from chaff on the threshing floor. Nevertheless, such coverings were necessary both for the wine and for the grain, so that they might reach maturity. For “the impious lives for the pious.”

Alternatively: “For the winepresses” means for the martyrs, whose soul is like wine and whose body is like grape-skins. Just as in winepresses wine is separated from the grape-skins, and the wine is carried into storerooms for preservation while the grape-skins are thrown out to be eaten by pigs, so here the souls of the martyrs are separated from the body through the pressure of martyrdom and sent into eternal rest, while their bodies are cast out to be eaten by the earth.

Alternatively: The Word of God is like a grape. When it reaches human ears through preachers, it comes like a grape to the winepress. There the Word remains like the covering, while the understanding, like wine, is stored in the memory and does not turn sour, but is poured out into moral discipline and the disposition of the mind.

In this psalm the Prophet speaks, foreseeing the Son of God who would come into this world in human form for the redemption of human beings and the building up of his Church. The intention is this: because we believe what we have not seen, more numerous testimonies are needed for faith; therefore so many prophecies concerning Christ were also given.

The exposition follows:

Lord, our Lord: you who by nature are God of all, became our God by grace, because when he deigned to disclose his will to the Jewish people through the Law, he became, as it were, spiritually their God through grace. How wondrous is your name—your fame—throughout all the earth, you who were formerly known only in Judea (Psalm 75). Properly does he say, “throughout all the earth,” because there is no nation from which some people are not in the Church.

Here the title is disclosed: “For the winepresses,” that is, in the churches. Truly wondrous—that is, greatly worthy of praise—because your majesty has been exalted above the heavens. This can be understood in three ways. “Your majesty,” that is, your majestic Christ, who may emphatically be called “Majesty itself,” has been exalted above the heavens [Col. 0184B]. This is understood materially, because he ascended as far as the eighth heaven.

Alternatively, “above the heavens” means above all the prophets and apostles. They are indeed great, but Christ is greater than all of them, because “God anointed him with the oil of gladness above his companions” (Psalm 44), who are called “heavens,” as in, “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 17).

Alternatively, “above the heavens” means above the proclamations of the divine Scriptures. They proclaim you as great, but your glory is greater than their fame. These Scriptures are called “heavens” because they conceal the divine mysteries, or because various forms of sacred meanings—history, morality, and mystery—have been engraved in them by the finger of God, that is, by the Holy Spirit. Heaven is also an iron instrument suitable for engraving, that is, for carving; or it is so called because the pattern of the lives of all human beings has been impressed in them. [Col. 0184C] In this sense we may say: “Your majesty has been exalted above the heavens,” because whatever has been raised up and formed in those Scriptures through the engraving of the Holy Spirit appears far less fully there than in Christ, who is the truth and the consummation of all the Scriptures. In this respect, O Christ, my glory is greater than the proclamations of the Scriptures concerning you.

“For from the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise”—that is, you made your praise perfect—in choosing to proclaim your name not through the powerful of this age, nor the rich, nor the wise, but through the lowly and the poor (1 Corinthians 1), and through “infants,” that is, those without eloquence as measured by worldly eloquence, so that the faith of believers might appear to rest purely on your power, not on rhetorical grandeur.

And “nursing children”: they were so much infants that they suckled milk, that is [Col. 0184D], your simple teaching, not yet able to receive the solid food of your divinity, before they grew through the instruction of the Holy Spirit into a mature man.

Alternatively, “nursing children” means that although they were infants with respect to human eloquence, they were nevertheless nursing children, that is, capable of nourishing the little ones of the Church. And in choosing such people, you acted “because of your enemies.” The enemies of God are all who seek their own glory rather than God’s.

He explains what he meant by “because of your enemies”: “to destroy the enemy,” namely, the enemy of your praise and the avenger of his own praise—that is, the philosopher, the Jew wise according to the flesh, and the heretic. For “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and the lowly, to confound the noble; and he chose the things that are foolish to confound the wise” [Col. 0185A] (1 Corinthians 1).

Alternatively: “From the mouth of infants”—those who were crying out “Hosanna” (Matthew 21)—“you perfected your praise,” because there it became evident how great your praise and power are, when they too praised you. And when you made them proclaim you, you did so because of the enemy, the Jewish people who denied you, and because of the avenger of his own law, so that through the wisdom of children you might condemn the foolishness of the elders.

“For I shall see your heavens.” This is connected with what was said above, where we understood “heavens” as the faithful saints or as Holy Scripture, in this way: It is true what I said, that your majesty surpasses the heavens. This will be clearly proved because in my descendants I shall see your heavens, namely, the faithful saints, flashing with miracles and pouring forth words. If the reference is to Holy Scripture, I shall see those heavens made from your engraved Scripture [Col. 0185B]: “the work of your fingers,” that is, those whom your fingers made into heavens; and therefore your majesty surpasses them.

Through the diverse gifts of the Spirit, holy men were made into heavens. These gifts are assigned to the fingers because no bodily member has as much differentiation as the hand through its fingers. The Spirit is one, but the gifts are diverse.

“The moon and the stars”—these he calls heavens. “The moon” means the universal Church, which is compared to the moon because it receives its brightness from elsewhere; or because it has perfection now in the soul but imperfection in the body; or because it possesses fullness in the perfect, while it is diminished in the imperfect.

“The stars” mean either the individual churches or the individual faithful within the Church. They differ from one another in the beauty of their lives, as “star differs from star in glory” (1 Corinthians 15). These churches and faithful you founded—or “which you founded”—on the foundation of faith [Col. 0185C], so that they could be moved neither by any wind of temptations nor by any storm of tribulations, for they have been founded upon the rock (Matthew 7).

“What is man, that you are mindful of him?” This should be read with wonder and joy. I see that through your majestic one you make human beings into heavens; you make the moon and the stars. What is man—what greatness or worth does he possess before you? For I see him as fragile, worthless, and unworthy of your regard, but this is because of his fault, not his nature, since you created him in your image and likeness (Genesis 1).

From this it is evident that man is something great before you, since you are mindful of him. Properly does he say “mindful,” because through disobedience he had withdrawn from you and had entered “a distant region” (Luke 15). But you, in your mercy, remembering that he had been created like you in reason, summoned him through the obedience of your Son [Col. 0185D].

“Or the son of man, that you visit him?” It should be noted that he says “man” and “son of man.” By “man” he wishes every sinner to be understood: Adam, who was made from the earth and bent himself entirely toward the earth, and everyone who is born and remains in his oldness. “Son of man” is rightly understood as Christ and everyone who bears his image.

Christ is “son of man,” not “son of men,” because he was born from the Virgin alone, without male involvement and without carnal desire. Everyone bears his image who puts off the old man with his deeds, laying aside that nature which he contracted from Adam, and puts on the new man, who was created according to God in holiness (Colossians 3).

Alternatively, “Son of man” means Christ, the Son of the Virgin [Col. 0186A]. And what is he with respect to his human nature? I do not say that you are mindful of him, because he did not withdraw from you; but that you visit him. Properly does he say “visit,” as a physician comes to a sick person, because the sick person cannot come to him. Thus the divinity of Christ visited his humanity, which could not raise itself up, and lifted it to the things above.

You bestowed great glory on man through the Son of man. Truly, it is a great thing before you that you visit him. He shows how he visited him: “You made him a little lower than the angels,” with respect to his human nature, because you made him mortal and capable of suffering—but nevertheless, only a little lower. He says “a little lower” because he was not mortal or capable of suffering from necessity, as were the rest of human beings, who are far inferior to the angels, but by his own will.

And because he was weak, you therefore visited him [Col. 0186B]. This is clear from the fact that you crowned him with glory and honor: with the glory of resurrection and the honor of ascension, because you made him sit at your right hand.

Alternatively: You crowned him with glory—that is, in the darkness of hell, where there is neither place nor distinction, you surrounded him with great light—and with honor, when he returned surrounded by a multitude of angels ministering to him. Many bodies of the saints also rose with him (Matthew 27).

“And you established him over the works of your hands”: after the ascension, that is, over the orders of angels, who may rightly be called the works of his hands by reason of their dignity, since in comparison with other creatures they appear to have been created with greater care. This is said by analogy, because we customarily apply our own hands to those works that we wish to make more perfect.

And you established him not only over the higher creatures [Col. 0186C], but also subjected the lower ones to him. “You subjected all things to him,” namely, everything except the angels, “under his feet,” that is, under the sacraments of his incarnation, so that through them creatures might either be saved by believing and preserving them, or perish by despising them.

“All things”—except him who subjected all things to him—namely, “sheep,” that is, the simple in the Church, and “oxen,” that is, the preachers, who thresh in the Church as in a threshing floor. For with their feet, that is, with their teaching, they separate the grain from the chaff when they make righteous people out of sinners, stripping them of the chaff of their sins, or separating the faithful from the unfaithful. Of these it is said: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is threshing” (Deuteronomy 24; 1 Corinthians 9).

Note that he uses “oxen” in the feminine gender, referring to those suited for bearing offspring. So too the apostles, although they thresh among those who are lesser [Col. 0186D], also beget other oxen, so that the leaders of the churches may never fail. As it is said: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you” (Psalm 44). Therefore he also added “all.”

“Moreover, the cattle of the field.” He says “moreover” because those who persecute differ from the preceding groups in their manner of life. “The cattle of the field” means the pleasure-seekers, those who flee arduous things and are devoted to gluttony and lust.

“The birds of the heavens” means the arrogant, who investigate heavenly things and attribute this to themselves through pride, like astrologers. Alternatively, “the birds of the heavens” means the powerful of this age, who blaspheme God through pride.

“And the fish of the sea” means the curious people of this age, “who travel along the paths of the sea,” that is, who in their thoughts pursue things that are transitory and soon fade away [Col. 0187A], like the paths of the sea.

Note that he says “of the sea,” not “of a river” or “of a stream.” By this he shows that their investigation is excessively broad and is not confined by any measure.

In these three classes—the beasts of the earth, the birds of the heavens, and the fish of the sea—the three temptations of the devil by which the Lord was tempted may be signified: gluttony in the beasts of the earth, pride in the birds of the heavens, and vainglory in the fish of the sea.

And because of all these things: “Lord, our Lord, how wondrous is your name throughout all the earth!”

## Psalm 9. To the End, for the Hidden Things of the Son. A Psalm of David

[Col. 0187B] “I shall confess to you, Lord, with my whole heart; I shall recount all your wonders. I shall rejoice and exult in you; I shall sing to your name, O Most High. When my enemy turns back, they will be weakened and perish from your presence. For you have carried out my judgment and my cause; you have sat upon the throne, judging justice. You rebuked the nations, and the impious person perished; you erased their name forever and ever. The swords of the enemies have failed completely; you destroyed their cities. Their memory perished with a crash, but the Lord remains forever.

“He prepared his throne for judgment, and he himself will judge the world in equity; he will judge the peoples in justice. And the Lord became a refuge for the poor, a helper in times of need, in tribulation. And let those who know your name hope in you, for you have not abandoned those who seek you, Lord.

“Sing praises to the Lord who dwells in Zion; proclaim his purposes among the nations [Col. 0187C]. For when he sought their blood, he remembered them; he did not forget the cry of the poor.

“Have mercy on me, Lord; see my humiliation because of my enemies. You who lift me up from the gates of death, so that I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion. I shall rejoice in your salvation: the nations are fixed in the destruction they made. In this snare, which they concealed, their foot has been caught. The Lord will be known as one who executes judgments; the sinner has been caught in the works of his hands.

“Let sinners be turned into hell, all the nations that forget God. For the poor will not be forgotten forever; the patience of the poor will not perish forever. Arise, Lord [Col. 0187D]; let man not prevail; let the nations be judged in your sight. Appoint, Lord, a lawgiver over them, so that the nations may know that they are human beings.

“Why, Lord, have you withdrawn far away? Do you despise us in times of need, in tribulation? While the impious person exalts himself, the poor person is set on fire; they are caught in the schemes they devise. For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked person is blessed.

“The sinner has provoked the Lord; according to the abundance of his anger he will not seek him. God is not before his eyes; his ways are defiled at every moment. Your judgments are removed from his presence; he will dominate all his enemies. For he said in his heart: ‘I shall not be moved from generation to generation, without evil.’

“His mouth is full of cursing [Col. 0188A], bitterness, and deceit; under his tongue are toil and sorrow. He sits in ambush with the rich in hidden places, in order to kill the innocent. His eyes look toward the poor; he lies in wait secretly like a lion in his den. He lies in wait to seize the poor; he seizes the poor while he draws him to himself. He will humble him in his snare; he will bend down and fall when he has gained mastery over the poor.

“For he said in his heart: ‘God has forgotten; he has turned away his face so that he may not see forever.’ Arise, Lord God, and let your hand be exalted; do not forget the poor. Why has the impious person provoked God? For he said in his heart: ‘He will not require an account.’

“You see, for you consider toil and sorrow, so that you may deliver them into your hands. To you the poor person has been abandoned; you will be the helper of the orphan. Crush the arm [Col. 0188B] of the sinner and the malicious person; his sin will be sought, and it will not be found.

“The Lord will reign forever and ever. You will perish, nations, from his land. The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; your ear has heard the preparation of their heart, to judge the orphan and the humble, so that man may no longer presume to exalt himself upon the earth.”

## Exposition

“A psalm of David, to the end”: that is, this is the work of Christ directing things toward the end, that is, toward consummation, “for the hidden things of the Son.” Since he stated simply “of the Son,” a mode of expression demanded by the excellence of Christ, it is understood in the sense of: “If the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8).

His hidden things are many, but above all these: his earlier coming in humility, which is followed by his manifest coming [Col. 0188C]. It was also hidden that the wild olive shoot was grafted in (Romans 11), for which purpose Christ used Israel’s blindness as an instrument.

It is also hidden that in this life God judges in three ways: a person is either exercised by scourges, as are perfect men, who have no need of correction; or is warned by punishment so as to turn back; or, if he despises the warning, is prepared for punishment.

“Therefore, for the hidden things of the Son,” that is, for his own hidden things. This is the voice of Christ the Head, giving thanks and urging his members to praise God for all his benefits by his example.

I will confess to you, O Lord—that is, I will proclaim praise to your name. There is a confession of praise, and there is also a confession of sin. With my whole heart—that is, fully, contradicting your disposition in nothing. Or, “with my whole heart,” that is, having in no part of my heart anything except what pertains to your praise, [Col. 0188D] and giving myself wholly to you. And while others praise you, I will recount all your wonders—that is, those things which you willed and ordained to be recounted through me. Or, “I will recount,” that is, “I will make manifest,” because God made all things through him, all wonders, visible and invisible (John 1). The Son of God performed many miracles, both by himself and through his own, secretly and openly. Secretly, by making a godly man out of an ungodly one, and a disciple out of a persecutor. Openly, by healing the sick and raising the dead; yet this is less than what he did secretly, for raising a soul is greater than raising a body. It was greater to convert Paul the persecutor (Acts 9) than to raise Lazarus from the tomb (John 11). Hence the Lord says: “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, [Col. 0189A] and will do greater works than these” (John 12). Everything that God the Father ordained to be done for the restoration of the human race, he displayed through his Son. Therefore the Son rightly says, “I will recount all your wonders.”

And while praising you, I will rejoice perfectly, because I will rejoice both in soul and in body: I will be glad in soul and exult in body, in you, not in myself and not in anything else. And so that I may do this, I will sing psalms: I will make myself into a psaltery, and by gladly receiving the striking of the lower part, I will sound forth from above a sweet melody in the spirit of humility. And I will do this for your name—that is, for your praise—so that your praise may increase through me, O Most High. For who has known the mind of the Lord? (Romans 11). Or, “in this, O Most High”: when you turn my enemy backward, I will praise you and give thanks, not only in the past or in the present, but always [Col. 0189B] in me and in mine, when you turn my enemy backward.

Therefore I always give you thanks, because the enemy of the human race, who first overcame the first man and made him follow after him, having become the ruler of this world, and also testing me—for “the ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14)—has been driven backward, so that he rules only over those who are backward in earthly things and unwilling to reach forward to what lies ahead (Philippians 3). For he who was the leader of death for the human race has now gone backward, testing and persecuting like a dog.

Alternatively: You will turn backward each of my enemies who is unbelieving, one who at first, not recognizing his weakness, thought that he did not need a physician, so that he may follow after me and seek me as his physician. According to this interpretation, “they will be weakened” follows rightly. [Col. 0189C] They will be turned backward because they will be weakened—that is, those who formerly seemed strong to themselves will recognize themselves as weak, and thus will perish as what they had been. As it is said: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2). “From your face”—that is, from knowledge of you, after they recognize you as their God and creator.

Because that one enemy is singular in himself but many in his members, the singular is followed by the plural. According to the earlier interpretations, this is how the passage is fitted together: “They will be weakened” in this way: you will turn the enemy, head and members, backward, because they will be weakened; they will become ineffective here and afterward will perish—that is, they will withdraw completely—from your face, that is, from your presence. “Let the ungodly be taken away, so that he may not see the face of God” (Isaiah 26).

Therefore they will perish because you have made—that is, will make, O Father—a judgment which they thought was theirs; you will make it [Col. 0189D] mine. As it is said: “It is better that one man should die for the people than that the whole nation should perish” (John 11). Just as a sailor calls the wind his own because he uses it, so you made the cause—the judgment—which they thought was theirs, mine. What judgment was this? “Lest perhaps the world should follow after him.”

And so that this judgment might become mine, you sat upon the throne—that is, you judged rightly. The throne is the seat of judgment. A judge is said to sit upon the throne when he does not misuse that seat.

Alternatively: You sat upon the throne, judging justice—that is, my humanity; you prepared for yourself a judgment seat, so that from it you might judge the world. As it is said: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5). And again: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” What the Son judges, [Col. 0190A] the Father and the Spirit judge also; but judgment is attributed to the Lord’s human nature, because if he judged human beings solely by the power of his divinity, they could in some way excuse themselves on the ground of weakness and inability. But now, with the Son’s humanity set before us—the humanity in which he did the good things required of us and avoided evil—all will be judged according to his example.

He shows how they will perish. Sitting upon your throne, you rebuked the nations; through me and my apostles you convicted them of unbelief and ungodliness. And the ungodly perished, having become faithful. And this was not for a time only, but you erased their name forever—that is, for the age, for eternity and the end of this age, which is called time, the age of this revolving world. Nor is it surprising that the ungodly perished, because the enemies’ [Col. 0190B] weapons—that is, opinions of error, or those persecuting Christ—failed against the two-edged sword of God, namely, against the truthful judgments of the New and Old Testaments.

“Unto the end”—that is, to Christ, who is the sword of God; namely, against the preaching of Christ. Or, “unto the end,” that is, completely. And after the opinions of error had been destroyed, you destroyed cities—that is, the associations and gatherings of evil people—in order that they might become your cities.

Or we may understand “cities” as the breasts of the malicious, where there are both a deceitful senate-house and counsels. The prince of that senate-house is the enemy of truth; its most destructive attendants are the senses and limbs of the body; and the populace consists of various carnal desires in tumult. You destroyed these cities when you directed all their counsels toward good. And in this way their memory perished [Col. 0190C]—that is, the reputation they had acquired for themselves in earthly things, so that they might be remembered after this life with great noise and great tumult, after they learned that there was nothing in these things in which to glory.

Or, “the memory of the ungodly,” so that sin might no longer reign in their body (Romans 6); and this “with noise,” that is, with the great outcry of the whole world.

Or in this way: “with noise,” because they could not put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new (Colossians 3) without great tumult and great conflict.

Alternatively: “When you turn my enemy backward,” namely, the devil, who tested Christ in order to seduce him, just as he had done with the first man (Genesis 3). The Lord said to him: “Go away, Satan; you shall not test the Lord your God” (John 10). And not only he, but also his ministers, the Jews who persecuted [Col. 0190D] Christ, will be weakened, being unable to accomplish in me what they desired, because “no one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (ibid.).

Here they will be weakened, and afterward, at the future judgment, they will perish from your face when they see the one whom they pierced; for then they will clearly recognize that I was not merely a man. Therefore they will be weakened because you made the judgment by which they judged me my judgment, so that they might secretly serve me, giving the judge of human beings something to suffer.

For although they judged outwardly in the body, you nevertheless sat with judicial power upon the throne—that is, upon my soul, which you made your seat, and upon my flesh, the footstool of your feet. Therefore Christ’s soul is called the seat of divinity, because although it is superior to other souls, it is nevertheless inferior to the Godhead. [Col. 0191A]

“You who judge justice.” It is as though he said: You sat in my soul, not to be judged, as I am as a human being, but to judge, you who always judge justly. Therefore you also executed my judgment, because I was judged justly.

In the condemnation to death you did this. Afterward you rebuked the nations through preachers, sending the Holy Spirit after my ascension, to teach them discipline and wisdom, as I myself said: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to resist” (Luke 21). You rebuked the nations: the Gentiles for idolatry, the Jews for unbelief. And the ungodly perished, the devil, the leader of death; their name—that is, the name of unbelief—you erased from your book, which is the book of life and death (Revelation 20), that is, from your memory. And you wrote them in the book of life—that is, in Christ, namely, in the faith [Col. 0191B] of Christ—so that they might be called faithful and Christians forever and throughout the age of the age.

“When the ungodly turns away from his ungodliness which he has committed, I will remember none of all his iniquities any longer” (Ezekiel 18). And thus those who formerly were the enemies’ weapons—that is, the devil’s weapons, through whom he slaughtered Christ and his own—fell away from the enemy, because they abandoned him for the end, that is, for Christ. They abandoned him for this purpose: to follow Christ.

“And you destroyed cities”—that is, all the disturbed movements of the soul. Not only were they all destroyed, but their memory also perished, so that they would no longer remember their idolatry and ungodliness: “with noise,” that is, with irrational tumult; or “with noise,” that is, with the great fame and wonder of the whole world.

The enemy of the human race, who was not lord but [Col. 0191C] tyrant, perished, because “a slave does not remain in the house.” But the Lord, who was judged to death, remains—that is, he lives—because “the son remains in the house forever.” And he not only remains, but also prepared his throne in judgment—that is, in the fact that I was judged and condemned by human beings, I was appointed judge by the Lord.

Or he prepared his throne in the hidden judgment—that is, the heavenly seat—because through the humility of his first coming that man merited heaven. Or “his throne,” that is, his Church, from which he judges the nations.

And because he was appointed judge, he himself—so humble, so just—will judge the world, that is, the perfected members of the Church who made themselves into a world, who joined the beginning to the end: “in equity,” that is, in himself, who is equity, perfection, [Col. 0191D] wholly smooth and rounded, against whom ever-maimed Fortune crashes; namely, he will give them perfect blessedness. “Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known” (1 Corinthians 13).

But he will judge the peoples—that is, unbelievers—in righteousness, condemning them according to their merits.

Or he will judge “the world,” that is, the whole world, in equity, repaying each according to his works (Matthew 16). In equity, because in justice, not in mercy: for now is only the time of mercy, but then will be the time of justice.

And the Lord became a refuge for the poor. It is as though he said: While he waits for the judgment, he became a helper for the poor—that is, for the one who in this life desires to possess nothing that either abandons him while he lives or is abandoned by him when he dies. He became for him like a fortress to which he may flee in mind. [Col. 0192A]

Hence Boethius: “Our leader gathers his forces into the fortress. But from above we laugh at those occupied with useless bundles.”

He rightly became a refuge, because his humanity is humility and patience; and from humility comes the glorification of his faithful, and in great tribulation there is consolation.

It is as though he said: If he is their refuge, why then does he permit them to suffer tribulation? For their benefit, like a good physician: he heals some and preserves others who have been healed. And this is what he says: he is a helper in tribulations, not one who abandons them in times of need. He permits the body to suffer outwardly, which, by permission, usually burdens the soul (Wisdom 9). But in this way he helps the soul inwardly, and this for its protection. As it is said: “A thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to strike me” (1 Corinthians 12). And afterward: “For [Col. 0192B] power is made perfect in weakness” (ibid.).

Alternatively: The poor of Christ, so that they may become lovers of God, in whom is the highest good, must be recalled from love of the world. This cannot be done more advantageously than through tribulations. In this way he is a helper in times of need, in tribulation. For “he scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12).

And because they made themselves poor, abandoning the things that are not, they must hope in you—that is, in the one who is—those who know your name. Not others: these are the true poor. “I am who I am” (Exodus 3); and, “He who is has sent me to you” (ibid.). Only those who despise the things that are not love this name.

Alternatively: “The Lord” is his name. The one who does not show him the service he deserves does not know that name.

Therefore let them hope, because even if they are afflicted, [Col. 0192C] you have not abandoned those who seek you, O Lord—you, I say, not fleeting things, not transitory things.

And because you have not been abandoned, “sing praises to the Lord who dwells in Zion,” that is, to the one who makes you a watchtower by dwelling in you, so that from the watchtower you may come to vision. Here we are a watchtower; that is, we live in hope. For “we do not have here a lasting city, but we see and greet it from afar” (Hebrews 13). Therefore it is not surprising if in this homeland, which is foreign to us, we suffer tribulation.

And therefore, so that you may reach the homeland, sing praises to the Lord—that is, do good works. It is as though he said: Serve the Lord. And not only perform works, but also proclaim among the nations—not in one place, but among the peoples, in the midst of a crooked generation that fears no one—his purposes, that is, his wishes: how, for the salvation of human beings, he wished to become human, to suffer, to die, and to rise again.

And [Col. 0192D] do not fear those who kill the body (Matthew 10), because you will not suffer these things without great reward. For the Lord whose purposes you proclaim, seeking their blood in judgment in order to avenge it, has remembered them. Because he delays until the future judgment the crowning of those who suffer and the condemnation of those who inflict suffering, he appears to have forgotten them. Therefore he says, “he has remembered,” that is, “he will remember.” But because he has not forgotten, he corrects himself: indeed, he has not forgotten the cry of the poor.

Alternatively: Proclaim his purposes among the nations, for if you do not proclaim them, he will seek their blood—that is, their destruction—from your hand. The Lord says: “If you do not warn the ungodly of his iniquities, he himself will die in his sins, but I will require his blood from your hand” [Col. 0193A] (Ezekiel 3; 33).

But if you suffer from the world because of righteousness, you will be blessed (1 Peter 3), because he has remembered and has not forgotten the cry of the poor.

Alternatively: Proclaim his purposes among the nations, namely these: “Because, seeking their blood, he has remembered and has not forgotten the cry of the poor.” Understand this as referring to those who say: “Have mercy on me, O Lord”—that is, make these scourges serve not for punishment but for testing.

Or “have mercy” in this way: See my humility—that is, my rejection and oppression; that is, show that you see it by granting me a reward and them punishment. Or “my humility,” that is, my degradation, which has come upon me from my enemies, the serpent and Eve.

Alternatively: “See my humility,” that is, my devotion, rejected by my enemies.

Another continuation, namely [Col. 0193B] in the voice of the head, connected with what he said above, “For you have not abandoned those who seek you, O Lord”: and so that you may not abandon them, “have mercy on me, O Lord,” in my members, because they are members; “sing praises to the Lord.”

Interjection: You have mercy because you can—you who exalt, that is, raise up and free me from the gates of death, that is, from evil desires, through which there is an entrance into death.

Or “from the gates of death,” that is, from the five bodily senses, through which the soul goes out to destruction by consenting to them; or from false preachers; or from human judgments, which are often unjust.

This is taken from the fact that ancient judges judged at the gate, so that those entering and leaving might see, for terror, the punishment of the wicked and the reward of the good.

You exalt me for this purpose: so that I may proclaim all your praises, visible and invisible, “in Zion,” that is, in the daughter of the Church, to whom [Col. 0193C] great care must be devoted for the protection of chastity. And I will make that proclamation “at the gates,” that is, in the virtues, so that the teacher’s word may be preceded by the example of a good life.

Alternatively: “at the gates of the daughter of Zion,” that is, in the ecclesiastical sacraments, or beginnings of faith, or in pure senses, or openly.

And I will do this confidently. For although I suffer tribulation outwardly, I will exult inwardly: “You have put gladness in my heart” (Psalm 4), “in your salvation,” that is, in your saving work. For “the father chastises the son whom he loves” (Proverbs 3).

Alternatively, in the voice of the head: “Let them hope in you, because you have not abandoned those who seek you, O Lord.” And let them do this according to my example, because although I, the head, suffer tribulation outwardly, I will exult inwardly in your salvation—that is, in salvation hidden here and manifest in the future. And rightly so: for the nations will not only be condemned openly in the future, but have already been condemned now in the hidden [Col. 0193D] judgment.

“They are fixed”—that is, fixed inwardly in the heart—the nations, all unbelievers. In the destruction which they themselves caused, namely, by killing our body outwardly, they killed their own soul.

He shows how they are fixed: “In this snare,” that is, in a deceitful plan, “which they hid,” that is, secretly devised, “their foot was caught,” that is, their love. In this way they are secretly condemned and prepared for punishment.

Love is like the foot of the soul. If it tends toward evil, it is desire; if toward good, it is charity.

And because God judges so powerfully that he uses neither iron, nor stone, nor wood, nor anything of this kind for the judgment of the wicked, as earthly [Col. 0194A] judges do, but only withdraws from them the hand of his mercy and does not correct them, the Church, rejoicing with him, says: “The Lord will be known as one who executes judgments”—namely, judgments of this kind.

The Lord will be known, not as just any lord, but simply as the Lord of lords. At last he will be known when the sinner unwillingly pays for what he willingly committed.

He shows what these judgments are: “The sinner was caught in the works of his hands,” that is, captured like a mouse in a mousetrap. And because their evil works and their deceits capture them, not your servants, “let sinners be turned into hell”—that is, let all transgressors [Col. 0194B] of the law, falling from sin into sin, descend into the depths of sins. This is rejoicing in the divine sentence, not a wish.

And not only the transgressors of the law, but also all the nations that forget God—that is, who do not have God before the eyes of their mind, sinning securely—will be turned.

“For the poor will not be forgotten to the end,” because even before the end—that is, before the manifest judgment, which will occur at the end—he will secretly judge the ungodly, giving them over to a debased mind.

Alternatively: “There will be no forgetting of the poor,” namely of Christ, who, “though he was rich, became poor for our sake” (2 Corinthians 8), “to the end,” that is, until his labor and patience come to an end, that is, are brought to nothing.

But because there are many in the body of that poor man, he says: “The patience”—that is, the perseverance of the poor in tribulation, which serves for the palm of those who are killed and the condemnation of those who kill—“will not perish to the end.”

And so that their patience may not perish, [Col. 0194C] “arise, O Lord,” that is, bring help, you who seem to lie fallen and defeated in your own people. In the very thing by which they think us defeated, let them rather be defeated themselves.

“Let man not be strengthened”—namely, the old man; rather, let the new man, the Son of Man, be strengthened. Rise in this way.

“Let the nations be judged in your sight,” that is, inwardly in the soul, where you alone see. While they judge outwardly, let them be judged inwardly.

Alternatively: So that the patience of the poor may not perish, “arise, O Lord,” in the manifest judgment. “Let that sinful man not be strengthened,” the man who is now strengthened by afflicting your poor, while he does not know that he is thereby being punished secretly. Let him openly know that he is being punished when he unwillingly pays for what he willingly committed; and yet inwardly let him not be without punishment.

“Let the nations be judged in your sight” in this way: Establish, O Lord, a lawgiver over them.

The order seems to proceed well: after introducing the members, he brings in the head. For they will reach such an accomplishment of their iniquities that, having despised Christ the Son of God, they will choose the Antichrist, so that under his leadership they may go into eternal punishment.

Because they did not wish to have me as the bearer of your law, [Col. 0194D] let them have over themselves the bearer of their own law, namely, the perverse law: the Antichrist and his ministers. Let them heap up for themselves teachers who itch in their ears.

“Let the nations know”—namely, that one lawgiver alone. And this because they are human beings, that is, sinners and grown old.

It is as though he said: Let them suffer this blindness of mind, so that they love only the bearer of the law of death, because they rejected the bearer of the law of life.

Alternatively: “Let the nations know,” that is, those living like Gentiles, “that they are human beings”—because, [Col. 0195A] in Greek, ὅτι means “that” or “because.” Let them know—that is, let them come to know—in the future condemnation: for the fact that they are now handed over to a debased mind is a kind of preparation for future punishment.

When he says “establish,” he speaks according to the order of events, not of creation, as in: “Making good and creating evil” (Isaiah 45).

And because he foresees the future excessive persecution under that lawgiver, so great that those poor whose is the kingdom of heaven appear to have been abandoned, he says for their consolation, with a kind of astonishment: “Why, O Lord, have you withdrawn far away?”

O Lord, “why”—that is, insofar as—you seem to have withdrawn from us while we suffer excessive outward tribulation and you do not openly avenge us. “Why”—that is, for what reason—have you withdrawn? He adds the cause for consolation. This rhetorical figure is called subjection.

“You disregard” them “in tribulation”—that is, you seem to disregard [Col. 0195B] your own while you do not immediately rescue them. But you do this “in times of opportunity,” that is, for great benefits, namely these: while the ungodly man grows proud, the poor man is inflamed.

Once bitterness has been tasted, sweetness is desired more strongly. The more the tribulation of this life irritates the godly, the more they desire that life where there will be no persecution. For if they were always in joy here, they would not desire it so earnestly. This is the benefit that affliction produces in the faithful.

But the ungodly are secretly condemned by no persecution, because they are caught in the counsels which they devise—that is, their evil counsels become chains for them, drawing them into destruction.

And it is not surprising, because, by God’s anger, there is no one to correct them. Indeed, the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul—that is, in his sins—and the unrighteous is blessed. [Col. 0195C] Therefore no one considers a person sinful if he is not corrected; rather, he is praised as one who is unpunished, because the tongue of flatterers binds souls in sins.

“The sinner has provoked the Lord.” It is as though he said: It is evident in this way that, according to his impenitent heart, he has stored up God’s wrath for himself, because God does not correct him as a father. And that he has provoked him is shown in this: “According to the multitude of his anger he will not seek him”—that is, he will not visit him with fatherly correction, but will hand him over into his hands.

If God were to take away your bodily eye, you would think him angry. When he closes the eye of your soul so that you do not see him, when prosperity in sin carries along polluted thoughts and counsels, do you not think him angry? Let no one, therefore, rejoice in the impunity of sin.

“God will not seek him,” or, “he himself will not seek God.” The word “seek” is fitting, as though he had been [Col. 0195D] lost.

He shows how the sinner provoked the Lord: “God is not before his eyes.” He sins so securely that he has no regard for divine judgment. Therefore his ways—that is, his thoughts—are polluted with the filth of vices at all times.

“Your judgments are removed from his sight.” This explains how God is not before his eyes. For a mind conscious of evil, while it is lifted up by the impunity of sin, forgets that God will judge.

And this is because “he will rule over all his enemies.” For “the prosperity of fools will destroy them” (Proverbs 1).

This is said spiritually of the Antichrist himself, the head of all the ungodly. All the friends of Christ will be his enemies, and he will rule them with respect to the body, because he will be permitted to rage against [Col. 0196A] them without opposition, for their salvation and his own destruction.

Alternatively: “He will rule” not in reality but in his own opinion, made proud by impunity. Hence it also follows: “For he said in his heart: I shall not be moved from this prosperity of mine; I shall be without evil”—that is, without any disadvantage—from this generation into the future generation. “If I were not pleasing to God, I would not prosper in everything in this way.”

Alternatively: “I shall not be moved”—that is, I shall not be advanced to the Lord from one generation to another without their evil.

Alternatively, in a good sense, as though Christ were saying out of compassion: O Father, when the sinner is permitted to sin, he is not unpunished; rather, he is punished by a hidden judgment which he does not know. Therefore I ask: Let sinners be turned into hell—that is, let attention be directed, with a certain agility of mind, to the punishments that follow [Col. 0196B] their impunity, and in this way let all be turned away from their evil way, both sinners—that is, transgressors of the written law—and the nations. Let them attend to this.

“For the poor will not be forgotten to the end,” because the Lord will avenge him. Therefore let them turn away from persecuting him, namely Christ, who suffers in his members.

This patience of the poor, who are members of that poor man, will not perish to the end—that is, until they come to an end, that is, are annihilated.

And so that they may be converted, “arise, O Lord,” you who now lie as though dead in their hearts; rise for them through knowledge.

“Let man not be strengthened,” namely the old man, that is, the flesh. Make them recognize their weakness, so that they may put down their pride and seek you as their physician.

And so that man may not be strengthened, let the nations be judged here, before that manifest [Col. 0196C] judgment. “In your sight”—that is, inwardly in the heart, where you alone see—let vices be condemned and virtues assumed. Rise in this way.

“Establish, O Lord, a lawgiver over them,” namely your lawgiver, Christ. Make them believe in him and wish to have him as their ruler. Establish him in this way: Let the nations know that he alone is the lawgiver.

And this is fitting, because they are human beings—that is, rational beings.

And because he delayed so long to recall the nations, he says with astonishment: “Why, O Lord, have you withdrawn far from them?” That is, for so long a time? I see why: you disregard them, not helping them in tribulation, allowing them to be tested and overcome by the enemy. And you do this “in times of opportunity,” namely these:

While the ungodly man grows proud—while the sinner, who is ungodly because he does not honor you as his creator, grows proud, that is, boasts of his ungodliness, by which he has merited God’s wrath [Col. 0196D] and condemnation—the poor man, recognizing his poverty and misery, and that he cannot rise except through the mercy of the one whom he formerly despised, is inflamed with sorrow of heart toward repentance, or is inflamed toward the love of God. “For he to whom more has been forgiven loves more” (Luke 7).

But those who do not wish to become poor are caught in the counsels which they devise. This does not change, and so on to the end. Now let us return to that passage.

His—the Antichrist’s—mouth is full of cursing, that is, slander, and bitterness against God, and deceit against his neighbors. Under his tongue—that is, in his heart—are labor and pain: love of those things which will be labor for him and pain for others.

He shows [Col. 0197A] what those things are which are labor and pain. “He sits in ambush,” that is, he remains and diligently lays snares with the rich—that is, the proud, who arrogate everything to themselves—in hidden places where it is not easy to discern what ought to be held fast, as in: “Spare your youth”; “Look to your wife and children”; “Consult your parents.”

He prepares these snares in order to kill the innocent, separating him from Christ, his life, and making him guilty. These are the snares.

“His eyes look upon the poor” with a certain false compassion: You are young; at present you cannot fast, keep vigils, or endure such things. Their time will come.

And through that feigned compassion he lies in wait secretly, that is, in the heart, like a lion in its den. Just as a lion hides in a den so that the beasts outside will not fear it, and thus approach it while its terror is nowhere apparent, until [Col. 0197B] it comes out and openly devours them, so the cruelty of the Antichrist will deceive many through a kind of flattering preaching and certain miracles.

Those whom he cannot deceive in this way [Col. 0197C] he will attack violently with various punishments, like a lion.

He describes all these things so carefully concerning the Antichrist and his members in order to make his own people cautious. Arrows that are foreseen wound less deeply. Hence elsewhere: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matthew 7).

There have been two persecutions in the Church: open and violent; violent at the first time, fraudulent in the middle period, as through heretics and false brothers; and at the end, in the time of the Antichrist, the most powerful persecution, joined from both kinds. Those whom he cannot attract by miracles, he will compel by threats.

Because he lies in wait like a lion in a den, the text appropriately adds: “He lies in wait”—namely, with flattering words—so that, if he cannot prevail by flattery, he may seize the poor by a kind of violence.

“He lies in wait to seize the poor” while he draws him to himself. And so that he may draw him more effectively, “in his snare he humbled him”—that is, he will make him contemptible to those who will be stupefied by his miracles.

But not without punishment, because “he bowed himself”—that is, he will collapse inwardly, having been handed over to a debased mind—by the very act through which he inflicts punishments outwardly.

He shows that indignation: “He will fall when he has ruled over the poor.” His very condemnation will be his downfall and a kind of preparation for punishment. This is the most miserable bending of the mind: when one who is blinded inwardly and reserved for the final judgment is not punished openly for his sins, believing God to be powerless [Col. 0197D] or unjust.

Powerless in this way: “For he said in his heart: God has forgotten, and therefore he does not punish.” Unjust in this way: “He has turned away his face so that he will not see to the end”—that is, to the earth, which is the last of all the elements. It is as though he said: God does not care about mortal things.

And because by the impunity of his crime—as it seems to him—he despises you, he says: “Arise, O Lord God.” O Lord, arise for the manifest judgment. And you can, because you are God.

“Let your hand be exalted,” that is, let your Son, who first came in humility and mercy, now appear exalted in the manifest judgment—that is, as God.

“Do not forget the poor”—that is, let it appear that you have not forgotten.

And rightly you will not forget. “For what reason has the ungodly provoked God?” Truly, he provoked him without cause. [Col. 0198A] For he said in his heart: He will not call my sins to account for punishment, because he does not see them; for if he saw them, he would already have punished me.

But he said this in vain, because you see them now and delay judgment, preparing them for punishment, in order afterward to hand them over into your hands—that is, to punish them more severely afterward. Therefore you consider—that is, see together—the labor of those who inflict punishments and the pain of those who suffer them.

And rightly so: for the poor has been left to you, the one who abandoned everything in order to cling to you.

“You will be the helper of the orphan.” There are many poor who are not orphans. A ward is one who has been deprived of his father; an orphan is one deprived of both father and mother. That one is an orphan whose world is dead, and who is himself dead to the world, seeking no consolation from this world.

And therefore “break the arm of the sinner and the malicious,” that is, reduce his strength to nothing. [Col. 0198B]

And truly you will break it, because his sin will be sought and will not be found. Nothing is sought except in a place. His sin had a place here, because the ungodly man lives alongside the godly. As long as gold has something that can be purified, the furnace is useful, just as the file is useful for iron.

So the ungodly had a place in the Church as long as it could not exist without offense. For they were God’s scourge. His sin will be sought where it has a place, and it will not be found; therefore it will no longer be sin in them.

This was the reason why the ungodly were among the godly.

The Lord will reign forever and throughout the age of the age. You will perish, O nations, from his land—that is, you will be separated completely from his Church. He speaks of the land because it is stable in him.

Alternatively: “Break the arm of the sinner”—that is, condemn the work of the sinner, [Col. 0198C] that is, of the one who acts wickedly. Take away from him the power to sin.

“And of the malicious”—that is, of the one who is always thinking evil, such as heretics—because they will no longer be necessary. His sin will be sought, namely the sin of the poor man, and will not be found, because after the judgment he will be without stain before the throne of God (Revelation 14). He will have nothing that can be purified, because the Lord will reign in him.

Therefore you, O Gentiles, will perish from his land, because the Lord has heard the desire of the poor, namely, that they should be judged.

And not only may they be judged, but also your ear, O God—that is, your clemency—heard the preparation of their heart, that is, the kingdom which they prepared for themselves through patience and expectation; or “the preparation,” that is, their meditation.

This desire is “to judge the orphan,” the one whose world is dead.

But because they seek [Col. 0198D] empty glory from this, he defines who the true orphan is: “and the humble,” the one who seeks no lofty things.

You judge them for this purpose: “so that man may no longer set himself to magnify himself”—that is, the sinful Antichrist—“upon the earth,” that is, over the Church. He “sets himself [to it]” when he deceitfully seeks to magnify himself over the Church; he “adds” when he tries to subject it to himself by threats and tortures.

# PSALM 10. A PSALM OF DAVID, UNTO THE END.

«In the Lord I trust; how can you say to my soul, “Migrate to the mountain like a sparrow”? For behold, sinners have bent the bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, so that they may shoot in the darkness at the upright in heart. For they have destroyed what you established: [Col. 0199A] but what has the just man done? The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord’s throne is in heaven. His eyes look upon the poor; his eyelids examine the children of men. The Lord examines the just and the wicked; but whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul. He rains snares upon sinners: fire and brimstone and the spirit of storms are the portion of their cup. For the Lord is just and has loved righteousness; his face has seen equity.»

## EXPOSITION

A Psalm of David, directed to the end. “Psalm,” that is, a good exhortation, is understood in this psalm to belong to David—that is, to the prophet directing it toward the end, namely Christ, in whom is the perfection of every good. This, then, is the purpose of this psalm. The prophet David, foreseeing [Col. 0199B] through the Spirit that certain people would arise in the Church, like stiff-necked bulls through their pride, unwilling to preserve the unity of the Catholic faith with the other faithful, nor to ask God for understanding of the Scriptures, but attributing everything to themselves and striving, through a perverse interpretation of them, to appear to be the only ones who know and the only ones who are just; and while seeking their own glory rather than God’s, striving to separate the little ones in faith from the breasts of Mother Church and make them follow the tracks of their error, professing the hope of religion in words but wholly denying it in deeds—he, considering that Christ’s little ones must be helped and showing by his own example how the assailants of the sacred faith must be resisted, says:

### “In the Lord I trust.”

All my faith is in Christ; through him alone I believe that I am justified and saved. He is my mountain; he is my refuge. For he is my Lord, who is God by nature. But you, who are human beings as weak as I am, how can you say to my soul, “Migrate to the mountain”? It is as though he said: How dare you persuade my soul, which is so well placed and trusts in no one other than the Lord, to “migrate to the mountain”—that is, to cross over to us, where the mountain is, where Christ is—as though from the valley and from a lowly place, from the simplicity of that faith which you hold, in which you can easily be deceived?

With us you will be well instructed, where the mountain is—that is, the height of virtues and the perfect life—where no one can lead you astray. Faith does not belong to everyone; we alone possess it; we alone can justify, because we are just. “Migrate,” I say, “like a sparrow,” that is, like a small bird which, unable to resist predators, climbs to high places and nests there; or also, guarding itself on level ground from snares and from the crowds of men. So you, too, cautiously cross over to us, who will be your protection. Jerome says that all small birds are called sparrows.

Alternatively: How can you say to my soul that it should migrate to you, as though there it should take on wings, since it is like a sparrow—namely, feathered with the wings of virtues—so that it may be fit to fly to the kingdom of heaven?

Alternatively: How can you say to my soul, “Migrate to us,” when this is not for my good, but so that I may be like a sparrow—that is, wandering and unstable in faith, to my destruction?

### “For behold, sinners have bent the bow.”

This can be read in two ways: either in the person of the prophet or in the person of the heretics. In the person of the prophet, as follows: Because he is speaking for the instruction of the little ones, he turns toward them and says: They say, “Migrate to us,” but one must not migrate there. Here is the reason why.

“For behold”—that is, see that it is nothing other than deception: sinners who make themselves just and call themselves mountains have bent the bow—that is, they have curved the rigor of sacred Scripture through the sinew of a perverse interpretation. They have prepared their arrows—that is, poisoned doctrines—through a perverse understanding, in the quiver, that is, in the heart, so that they may shoot at the upright in heart—that is, at the simple and those directed according to the rule of faith—who are placed in darkness, that is, in ignorance, and are not yet able to examine those higher matters.

Truly I know that for this purpose they have prepared their arrows—that is, their perverse doctrines—so that they may shoot [Col. 0200B] at the upright in heart.

### “For they have destroyed what you established.”

Those commandments which you, O Lord, established—that is, wrote with your finger—unchangeable and indissoluble, because what is once just before you will never become unjust, and conversely: they have destroyed those commandments—not with respect to the commandments themselves, for you said, “My words will not pass away” (Luke XXI), but with respect to their own error and perverse understanding.

In the person of the heretics, it is understood thus: “Migrate to us; cross over here, where there is height, where only the perfect and only the just are. Like a sparrow”—for you are dwelling dangerously below, living among sinners who wrongly interpret sacred Scripture for you and in this way wish to deceive your simplicity.

Then again the prophet: They appear to say these things under the appearance of piety, but they must not be believed. [Col. 0200C] Why? “For they have destroyed what you established, O Lord.” You established your praise in the little ones, but they destroyed them by turning them away from you and saying that only the just are in the Church.

### “But what has the just man done?”

O heretic, you who say that we are sinners and therefore are not part of Christ’s body, and that no one can be incorporated into Christ through our ministry, tell me: What has the just man—namely Christ, who alone is just and justifies all—done?

What do you charge against him, when you tear his body apart and separate it from him, although no one is justified except through him, whether he receives the sacraments of faith through the ministry of a sinner or through the ministry of a just man? You, however, say that no one can be justified except through the ministry of some just person. Do you not thereby separate Christ’s body from him [Col. 0200D] and usurp his power for yourselves?

Alternatively: “But what has the just man done?” It is as though he said: You despise sinners and separate them from Christ’s body. Do you imitate Christ in this? Did he not himself associate with sinners? Did he not know that Judas was a thief and had the money box? Yet he sent him to preach with the other apostles; and at that supper at which Judas betrayed him, he gave him, together with the others, the Eucharist of his body and blood, prepared by his own hands and commended by his own mouth.

He did this in order to show that God’s gift does not arise from the merit of the giver but from the faith of the recipient; nor does the gift become invalid even when it is administered by someone such as Judas.

Truly you are lying, because you say that among you alone is the faith of Christ, and that through you alone human beings can be incorporated into Christ. For the Lord—namely, the God of all—is Lord, not you.

### “In his holy temple.”

Not in your temple, because he alone is the one who justifies. “For God’s temple is holy, and that is what you are” (II Corinthians III). “But if anyone destroys this temple, God will destroy him.”

But what has the just man—namely Christ—done? In what has he offended you, that you tear his body apart? You do not do this with impunity. “For the Lord is in his holy temple.” “But if anyone destroys this temple, God will destroy him.”

### “In heaven is his throne.”

That is, in those whom he has made heavens because of the eminence of their virtues. He calls the faithful both a temple and heavens; but the lesser may be called a temple, and the greater, heavens.

### “His eyes look upon the poor.”

It is as though he said: He does indeed sit in heaven—that is, in the saints—but in those whom he himself has made heavens through consideration of his mercy, not through their merit and not through yours.

Or, his eyes look upon the poor in order to avenge him—that is, the humble person who presumes nothing of himself. And his eyes do not look only upon the poor; his eyelids also examine the children of men.

His eyelids—that is, the opening or closing of his sacred Scripture. This is said by comparison, because eyelids sometimes open the eyes and sometimes close them.

They examine the children of men—that is, those regenerated and renewed from the old state of the first human beings. They examine, that is, they inquire into and scrutinize who are those who approach impatiently and despise, and who are wearied rather than exercised by obscurities; and who are those who approach patiently and are not wearied by obscurities, but are exercised by them so that they may discover.

They also examine who are those who are puffed up by the opening of Scripture rather than enlightened, and who are those who are not puffed up by it but nourished by it.

He explains what he has said: “The Lord examines,” namely, through his eyelids, “the just and the wicked,” as has been said. The just man answers him according to his capacity: he is humbly exercised when the eyelids are closed, but he is enlightened when they are opened, and therefore he will be saved.

But whoever loves iniquity—that is, when the sacred Scriptures are closed to him, he despises them, and when they are opened, he is puffed up—will be condemned. The text says this more forcefully, showing him already slaughtered by his own sword, through *apolophasis*, when it says: “He hates his own soul.”

It is as though he said: The little ones of the Church must beware of such people, because in this way he rains snares upon sinners.

### “He rains.”

Well said, “rains,” because preachers are called clouds, whether good or evil, as in: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon her” (Isaiah V).

“He rains snares upon sinners,” that is, he sends the teaching of his error—not upon the hearts of the just, whom he cannot deceive and upon whom the Lord rains the early and latter rain, but upon sinners, that is, upon those whose hearts are dry from the rain of God’s word.

Therefore both the teacher of error and those ensnared by his errors will be condemned, both here and in the future.

Here there will be fire—that is, the fervor of desires consuming them—and brimstone—that is, foul conduct—and afterward, at the future judgment, the spirit of storms: evil spirits bringing upon them storms and the whirlwind of punishments. These will be the portion of their cup—that is, the punishment given to them by means of the cup, according to measure.

For just as the good will receive their reward according to measure, as each has deserved, so also the wicked will receive punishment according to measure.

Alternatively: “But what has the just man done?” It is as though he said: Those seducers prepared their arrows for them—that is, they caused them to shoot at the upright in heart—and this because they destroyed the words which you established. With respect to your truth, those words are indissoluble; they destroyed them only with respect to their own perverse understanding.

But the just man—that is, your Son, to whom you have given all judgment, and who judges all things justly—what has he done? He poses this question for the consolation of the good and just and for the terror of the wicked.

He has acted so that those who are just may become still more just, and those who are filthy may become still more filthy (Revelation XXII): the former for a greater reward, the latter for a greater condemnation.

And this is what he says first concerning the just:

### “The Lord is in his holy temple.”

That Lord who is Lord of all by nature is properly Lord by grace in those whom he cleanses from the filth of vices, making them his holy temple, because he possesses them and cultivates them so that grace may increase in them.

The Lord is in those who are his temple—that is, in the lesser ones, who hear God’s commandments and keep them in the sanctuary of the heart.

### “In heaven is his throne.”

That is, he sits in those whom he has made heavens through the eminence of their virtues, so that through them he may judge or take delight in them.

### “His eyes look upon the poor.”

Those who are heavens—that is, teachers enlightened by him and made his eyes, as in: “If your eye causes you to stumble” (Matthew V), and so forth—look upon the poor, that is, the simple faithful person who is not yet rich in knowledge, in order to instruct him how to guard himself against the snares of the living.

“His eyelids,” as above, “examine the children of men,” that is, all human beings.

It is as though he said: I said “eyelids.” Rather, the Lord examines through those eyelids the just and the wicked; that is, through them he inquires who is just and who is wicked. He inquires in order to reward the one and condemn the other.

But whoever loves—that is, reads in everything—iniquity hates his own soul, as above.

As has been said, this is what the just man did: the Lord is in his holy temple, and his eyes look upon the poor. In this way he rains his mercy upon his own.

But he rains upon sinners—that is, upon those who persevere in wickedness and perversely receive his teaching. For just as from the same earth grain is produced for making fine flour and chaff for burning, so from the same teaching some are saved through sound understanding, while others are condemned through perverse understanding.

“Snares,” that is, errors by which they are dragged toward condemnation. And because they are bound by the snares of errors and dragged along, therefore there is a portion—that is, a share—of the cup, that is, of the reward which will be given to them by the cup: as above, fire, brimstone, and the spirit of storms.

He adds the reasons why rewards are imposed upon the just and punishments upon sinners. “For the Lord is just,” and therefore he loved righteousness; and because he loved righteousness, he will crown the just.

But his face—that is, his knowledge—did not love the unjust; rather, it saw equity, that is, judgment. He sees them for this purpose: so that he will not leave them unpunished.

## PSALM XI. A PSALM OF DAVID, DIRECTED TO THE END, FOR THE EIGHTH

[Col. 0203A]

«Save me, O Lord, for the holy man has failed, for truths have diminished among the children of men. Each has spoken vanity to his neighbor; with deceitful lips and a double heart they have spoken. May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the tongue that speaks great things. They said, “We will magnify our tongue; our lips are our own: who is our lord?” Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord. I will place him in salvation; I will act confidently toward him. The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver tested by fire, proved by the earth, purified sevenfold. You, O Lord, will preserve us and guard us [Col. 0203B] from this generation forever. The wicked walk around; according to your exaltation you have multiplied the children of men.»

## EXPOSITION

A Psalm of David directed to the end, for the eighth: that is, the good work understood in this psalm belongs to David—namely, to the prophet—and to every perfect faithful person from the former people, moving through the Spirit toward the end, that is, toward Christ, and sighing for him with the whole of his desire.

“For the eighth,” that is, for perfect salvation, which is necessary for those born into the course of this corruptible life, which revolves in a cycle of seven.

Every faithful person from the former people, to whom the saving advent had been made known through the Spirit, seeing that perfect salvation could not be given through laws and carnal observances, because “the law was given through Moses, grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John I)—and yet that former people, still immature, had to be led through carnal institutions from visible things to invisible things—invokes the one in whom, through the Spirit, he foresees that perfect salvation will arrive, saying:

### “Save me, O Lord.”

You who are the Lord, come, so that you may save me with perfect salvation, namely that which will not change. For your servant-prophets could not do this, nor could the carnal observances imposed only until the time of correction.

Save me by conforming me to yourself in the newness of the spirit. And there is need of this, because the holy man has failed with respect to that holiness and perfection of virtues in which the human being was created and from which he fell.

Or: Come now, because it is the time for mercy, because no holy person is found. “All have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Romans III). Or, no other person is found suitable for this purpose.

The holy man has failed, and rightly so: “For truths have diminished among the children of men,” that is, because your commandments, true and holy in themselves, have not been fulfilled through disobedience—not only by human beings, namely Adam and Eve, but also by the children of men, that is, by their descendants.
