Alternatively: Not only by those who have dehumanized themselves by worshiping the works of their hands, but also by those who are children of men—namely, patriarchs and prophets.

Before Christ’s coming there were many just people and many truths; but they were diminished because the head—that is, the truth—had not yet come. For all were descending to the underworld. As many images come from one mirror, so truth is one in itself but many in the saints.

They were diminished in this way:

### “They have spoken vanity.”

They spoke God’s commandments with their mouths but denied them by their deeds. This is said concerning the Jews.

But if the text concerns everyone, then each person—not a few, but all—persuaded his neighbor, whom he ought to love as himself, by voice and life in earthly things, possessing deceitful lips ready to deceive.

### “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips.”

This can be understood in two ways: for good, by changing them for the better; or for evil: “May the Lord destroy”—that is, that Lord whom they previously despised as his servants—“all deceitful lips” of all who flatter themselves and presume upon themselves, and the boastful tongue, which presumes and excuses sins.

Or “the boastful tongue” may be understood in this way:

### “They said, ‘We will magnify our tongue.’”

That is, “We will acquire great eloquence for ourselves.”

“Our lips”—that is, the utterances which we have acquired for ourselves—“are our own,” that is, they defend our side and attack our adversaries.

Or “are our own” means: We ourselves have devised them through our own diligence; we do not need other commandments or other defenders. Therefore, “Who is our lord?” Whose other commandments shall we accept to rule over us, or who prevails over us in any matter? No one.

It is as though he said: These are the presumptuous words of philosophers, scribes, and Pharisees, who said, “Moses gave us the law,” and many similar things—things which the servants of Christ who were sent beforehand were unable to destroy.

Their Lord—that is, Christ—coming in the flesh, will destroy them [Col. 0204C] in various ways, namely through himself and through his apostles. Or “he will destroy” means that he will refute them through various arguments, while choosing foolish and contemptible people to preach.

I said, “May he destroy them,” and indeed he will do so. For that Lord who previously sent servants says through the Spirit:

### “Now I will arise.”

It is as though he said: I appeared to lie inactive in my servants whom they despised; now I will arise by sending the Son, and I will make them recognize my power through him.

And I will do this because of the misery of the needy—that is, of the Gentiles, who possess no help of their own or from anyone else—and because of the groaning of the poor—that is, of the Jews, who are not destitute but poor, because although they are poor in themselves, they nevertheless possess the help of God’s commandments.

### “I will place him in salvation.”

That is, in Christ, I will place what I did not place in the servants: perfect and abiding salvation. Nor did I place it in carnal institutions.

And just as earlier I acted through servants as though with restraint, in him I will act confidently—that is, reproving everyone without fear and sparing no one. Hence the saying: “He was teaching them as one having authority, and not as their scribes” (Matthew VII); and: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV).

And rightly will he act confidently. For that perfect one says:

### “The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances.”

Pure in themselves, by comparison: just as a chaste woman always conducts herself in the same way toward her husband, so Christ’s utterances are unchangeable. What is once just in them will never become unjust, and conversely.

Alternatively: “The utterances of the Lord are pure” because they were preached faithfully and sincerely, without charge, in both the Old and the New Testament. This is the doctrine being commended here.

Alternatively: “Pure,” like pale death—not that it is pure, but that it makes pure; and likewise these utterances are pure because they make people chaste.

The same point is expressed through another comparison:

### “Silver tested by fire.”

For just as silver cooked by fire is better extended in length and breadth, so these utterances, received purely and worthily through the grace of the Holy Spirit, extend the faithful in length—that is, in perseverance in good works and hope of eternal life—and in breadth, because in tribulation they are enlarged in charity, so that they love not only friends but also enemies.

### “Proved by the earth.”

That is, by the Church—not proved by it, but proving it.

Or “proved by the earth” may be taken as a confirmed name.

### “Purified sevenfold.”

That is, because they purify the hearts of the faithful through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.

The prophet places this commendation of Christ’s preaching beforehand so that it may afterward be believed more truly.

And because the Father will act confidently in you, you, O Lord, and no other, will preserve us, whom the first parent lost, by conforming us to yourself. And, once preserved, you will guard us from this generation, so depraved, lest we be led astray by it, forever—that is, into eternity—transferring us, namely, into the eighth, the perfect blessedness.

But the wicked will not arrive there. They walk around—that is, within the seventh, in which all this time revolves—bound to these perishable things that turn like a wheel.

But you have multiplied the children of men—that is, the faithful who imitate the faith of the patriarchs and prophets. You have multiplied them, that is, enriched them in many ways, according to your exaltation—that is, according to heavenly glory—counting them as the spiritual seed of Abraham, not his carnal seed.

To the spiritual seed it was said: “I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven” (Genesis XXII); this refers to the spiritual seed, while “like the sand of the sea” refers to the carnal seed.

Or: You have multiplied the children of men—that is, enriched them—not from the fruit of their grain, wine, and oil, but according to your exaltation, raising them from virtue to virtue.

Alternatively: “The wicked walk around,” that is, they will walk around, because they will not enter into that eighth, while they continually revolve in misery.

Yet you have multiplied them—that is, made them many more than your own—because “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew XX).

And you did this according to your exaltation—that is, according to your inscrutable counsel.

Or, if this is the question, “Why, then, do they live?”: You have multiplied the children of men according to your exaltation.

## PSALM XII. A PSALM OF DAVID, DIRECTED TO THE END

«How long, O Lord, will you forget me forever? How long will you turn your face from me? How long shall I place counsels in my soul, sorrow in my heart by day? How long will my enemy be exalted over me? Look upon me and hear me, O Lord my God. Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death; lest at some time my enemy say, “I have prevailed against him.” Those who trouble me will rejoice if I am shaken; but I have hoped in your mercy. My heart will rejoice in your salvation; I will sing to the Lord, who has bestowed good things upon me, and I will sing psalms to the name of the Most High Lord.»

## EXPOSITION

A Psalm of David directed to the end. This psalm can be read as spoken by the same person as the preceding psalm, and continued in this way: Because you, O Lord, will preserve us, and no other.

### “How long will you forget me?”

That is, How long will you confound me through the delay of your coming? He says this because of an excessive desire, not because of any doubt.

“Forever,” that is, eternally.

Or: I know how long it will be—“forever,” that is, until the time predetermined by the Father.

### “How long will you turn your face from me?”

That is, your Son, in whom you are known, as in: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV).

Forgetfulness and turning away do not occur in God; rather, he is said to have forgotten and turned away when he delays what is desired, in human fashion, because prophets commonly speak through comparisons.

In the same way the text continues: “Forever”; or “forever” may be taken without interrogation.

And while placed in that expectation:

### “How long shall I place counsels in my soul?”

That is, the consolations and arguments of the prophets in my soul, which languishes with desire for you. I would rather see you than hear promises.

Or “counsels” means deliberations: what I should do and what I should avoid, so that I may be able to wait so long.

Or: “Shall I see you? Shall I endure?”

### “How long shall I place sorrow in my heart?”

The sorrow I have because of your absence. Yet I have this counsel and this sorrow only “by day,” that is, through your illumination.

Or “by day” means through each individual day.

Or: This will last as long as I place counsels in my soul.

### “How long will my enemy be exalted over me?”

That is, the devil with his members. How long will he mock me as I wait alone, saying each day, “Where is your God?”

Do not turn away, but look upon me; do not forget, but rather hear me, O Lord my God.

Hear me in this way:

### “Enlighten my eyes.”

The eyes of my mind, that is, right thoughts. These eyes were blinded—or rather, darkened—in our first parent.

Enlighten them through the true light, that is, your Christ, who will be the book of life for us. Send him, so that through his conformity I may be able to know you and love you.

Do this so that I may never sleep in death—that is, sleep against that light in sins, ceasing from virtues.

May I not sleep so deeply that, gradually closing my eyes in lesser sins, I descend from the sleep of virtues into death—that is, into mortal sin, which separates us from God, our life.

Hence the saying: “There is sin unto death; concerning this I do not say that one should pray” (I John V), namely, because it cannot be cleansed by prayer alone.

Lest at some time my enemy say, “I have prevailed against him”—that is, “I have overcome him,” because he withdrew from his God and consented to me.

How can that enemy prevail over you? If I am shaken—that is, shaken away from you—those who trouble me will rejoice.

Or, if I am shaken from my good purpose, they will rejoice.

But I will not be shaken, and I do not have this confidence from myself; rather, I have it because I have hoped in your mercy.

Therefore I will not sleep in death. Rather:

### “My heart will rejoice in your salvation.”

That is, in the salvation of your Christ, who will truly come.

My heart will rejoice not only in its own salvation but also in the redemption of my body. For the body’s rejoicing consists in this: that I may deserve to attain to that rejoicing.

Meanwhile I will not be idle. For I will sing—that is, I will frequently and without interruption of heart praise him—to that Lord who, by creating me good, has bestowed good things upon me, namely mercy, and not to him who gave me evil, namely the one who cast me down through pride.

And so that my praise may be perfect, I will sing psalms—that is, I will chastise my body and bring it into servitude.

I will do this not for my own praise, but for the name of the Most High Lord, so that when others see my goodness and steadfastness, they may glorify God, who possesses such servants.

Alternatively, this may be understood in the person of every perfect person who, after Christ’s first advent, longs for his second advent, in which true peace and perfect salvation will be given, when death will finally be destroyed. One of these was the person who said: “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians I).

### “How long, O Lord, will you forget me forever?”

That is, How long will you delay bringing me to the end of this misery and this struggle which exists between the inner and outer person?

### “How long will you turn your face from me?”

That is, your presence and your truth from me. For now I see you through a mirror, but then face to face; now in part, but then perfectly, just as I have been perfectly known by you (I Corinthians XIII).

And while you delay coming to judge:

### “How long shall I place counsels in my soul?”

That is, How long will I remain in adversity and struggle, where counsel is necessary? Namely, how long will the law of the flesh struggle against the law of the mind? When will the labor be removed from this body of death?

### “How long shall I place sorrow in my heart?”

The sorrow I have because of your absence by day, as above.

Alternatively: I will suffer these things as long as I place counsels in my soul—that is, as long as there is struggle between body and soul, namely, as long as I remain mortal.

Therefore I cry out to you: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans VII).

And, “How long shall I place sorrow in my heart by day?” as above.

### “How long will my enemy be exalted over me?”

The enemy—that is, the devil—who labors to devour me. How long will he reign in this mortal body, raising the flesh against the spirit, and the servant against the Lord?

The rest is as above.

## PSALM XIII. A PSALM OF DAVID, DIRECTED TO THE END

«The fool has said in his heart, “There is no God.” They are corrupt and have become abominable in their pursuits; there is no one who does good, not even one. The Lord has looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God. All have turned aside; together they have become useless. There is no one who does good, not even one. Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they acted deceitfully; the poison of asps is under their lips. Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood. Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace. There is no fear of God before their eyes. Will all who work iniquity not understand—those who devour my people as though they were bread? They have not called upon the Lord; there they trembled with fear where there was no fear. For the Lord is with the just generation; you have confounded the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his hope. Who will grant salvation to Israel from Zion? When the Lord has turned back the captivity of his people, Jacob will rejoice and Israel will be glad.»

## EXPOSITION

A Psalm of David directed to the end, belonging to David himself. That is, the reproach made in this psalm is directed toward this end: that it may be directed toward the end, namely perfect blessedness, attributing it to David—that is, to Christ—not to the body but to the head itself.

Therefore, in this psalm there is the voice of Christ reproaching the hardness of the Jews’ hearts, because they did not recognize the time of their visitation (Luke XIX), and showing what punishment follows unbelievers and what glory follows the faithful. According to this reading, there is a certain transposition, so that what is said may appear more forcefully, in the following manner.

The fool said. The order of the narrative, however, begins with that verse: “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the sons of men.” The Lord—that is, God who by nature rules over all—from heaven—that is, from me, Christ as man—looked down, that is, inclined the eyes of his mercy from afar. For he could not otherwise have manifested his knowledge to human beings more suitably than through human nature, [Col. 0208C] upon the sons of men—that is, the Jews, sons of the patriarchs and prophets—who may be called “men” because of their excellence in comparison with others.

This is spoken by way of comparison. Powerful men and army commanders customarily climb to more elevated places and look down to see who are ready for battle and who are not; who conduct themselves bravely and who, through cowardice, are unable to hear the sound of the trumpet. Those commanders, placed on high, are usually seen partly and partly remain unseen. So too the divinity of the Word was hidden in Christ through his humanity, but appeared through his divinity, performing works that no one else performed.

For this purpose you appear to display, through my humanity, the divinity that was itself invisible and incomprehensible: so that he may see—that is, make it possible to see and test—whether there is among that people anyone who understands God, namely, by conforming himself through faith to me, the Lord’s human being. Or not merely one who understands, but also one who seeks him, namely, in action. For this reason he set his humanity before human beings as an example, so that through him they might know whether human beings could understand the divinity and seek it through their works. What Christ as man did, he showed to be possible for a human being.

But he found no such person, because that foolish people said in their heart—that is, thought, which was more serious than saying it with their mouth—“There is no God.” Some of them did not even believe that he was a prophet. For one said: “If this man were a prophet, he would certainly know what sort of woman is touching him” (Luke 7). It is as if he were saying: “And in this matter the author cannot be accused,” because they had been corrupted—that is, by their own fault, away from the integrity of a good nature.

And to such an extent they became abominable—that is, hateful and disinherited—in their pursuits, that is, in their own inventions, not God’s. This is clear from the fact that there is no one—that is, among them—who does good, that is, God’s will, for the doing of which they were created. So completely, that there is not even one.

“Up to one” may be understood inclusively or exclusively. “Up to one” means “not even one”: here it is inclusive. Or “up to one” means “until they reach the unity of my body, where there is one faith and one baptism.” For those outside that unity can do no good. Hence the saying: “The water was stirred, and one was healed” (John 5).

Or it may be understood comparatively: there are so many who do evil that, in comparison with them, those who do good cannot even be called one. Thus it is said: “Oholibah, you have justified your sister Sodom” (Ezekiel 16), because your iniquities are so numerous and so great that Sodom, previously ungodly, may seem righteous in comparison with you. Likewise: “This man went down to his house justified rather than the other” (Luke 18).

“There is no one who does good.” For they do evil, as follows: “All have turned aside from the Lord’s will”—not only the nations, who did not receive the law, but also the Jews—“together,” namely with the nations; that is, the Jews became like the nations. This was said to heighten the crime: they became useless to others, like a person who, useless and harmful to himself, is nevertheless maintained as a citizen of his country.

“There is no one who does good,” as above. In this way they are useless.

“Their throat is an open tomb.” It is always open for this purpose: to emit the harmful stench of evil persuasion, or to swallow the dead—that is, those separated from God.

“They acted deceitfully with their tongues.” “Teacher, we know that you are truthful” (Matthew 22).

Or this may be said of everyone: “The poison of asps is under their lips,” that is, in their heart, that malice which is incurable, like that poison.

Alternatively: the asp, fearing the incantation of a Marsian, who wishes to possess its poison against other poisons, has this nature: if it finds other poisons in an animal, it drives them out; if it does not, it kills the animal suddenly. So that it may not hear, it applies one ear to the earth and presses the other with its tail. In the same way, these people, so that they may not hear God’s commandments, fasten the ear of their heart to present goods as though to the earth, while others turn over the pleasures of their former life.

And therefore: “Destruction and misery”—destruction in the body, misery in the soul.

Or, “miserable destruction,” namely, the supreme condemnation, “is in their ways,” that is, in their works. Hence the saying: “Whoever stumbles over this stone will be shattered; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him” (Matthew 21). For whoever offends the Son of God by not believing is shattered inwardly, because he loses all strength of spirit. Christ falls upon him whom he crushes at the final judgment with a twofold destruction.

And this is because they did not know “the way of peace,” that is, Christ, who says: “Come to me, all you who labor” (Matthew 11). For if they knew God, they would fear him. Hence: “There is no fear of God before their eyes,” that is, in their mind.

It is as if he were saying: Now they do not wish to know the way of peace—that is, me—through mercy, but at some time they will know it through punishment.

He adds this by way of a question: “Will not all those who work”—not those who have worked—“iniquity know this?” Namely, those “who devour my people as they eat bread,” that is, continually, because bread is the daily means of sustenance. By saying “my people,” he shows that this psalm must be read as spoken in the voice of the head.

They devour them because they did not call upon God—namely, God himself and concerning God—but something else, namely earthly things. “For they loved darkness more than light” (John 3), and therefore “they trembled with fear where there was no fear.” They feared losing the world, but did not fear losing God (John 11): “If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him.”

Truly you will know me, the way of peace, through punishments.

“For the Lord”—namely, I, Christ—“is in a righteous generation,” that is, among his people whom you devour, [Col. 0210B] a people that is righteous because it serves its Creator and loves light more than darkness.

“But you have confounded the counsel of the poor,” that is, you regarded as confused and indiscriminate the counsel of the poor—one who presumes nothing of himself—because the Lord is his hope. This was because you did not see in him the pomp of this age.

And he did not hope in him in vain, because he himself will give the salvation of Israel.

He proves this as if saying: “It is evident to you, Jews, that someone—that is, some person—coming from Zion, namely from the Jewish tribe, will give the salvation of Israel,” that is, to the faithful people who see him through faith. Who else will give it, if not the Lord, whose humility you despised? Either this one or another. In truth, it is this one.

And when will this happen? “When the Lord turns away”—that is, removes—“the captivity,” that is, the capacity for suffering and mortality [Col. 0210C] by which it is held captive, “of his people.”

This removal of captivity will occur as follows: “Jacob will rejoice,” that is, that same people will rejoice in hope, having become Jacob—that is, progressing from virtue to virtue. Jacob had this name when he was living as a pilgrim and was advancing. On his return to his homeland, when he wrestled with the angel, he was named Israel (Genesis 35). And after becoming Israel—that is, seeing God—he will rejoice fully, seeing face to face the one whom he previously saw through a mirror (1 Corinthians 13).

Or, having become Jacob—that is, “supplanter”—he will receive the firstborn status of the Jewish people, namely the inheritance that had been promised to it.

## Psalm 14. A Psalm of David

> “Lord, who will dwell in your tabernacle? Or who will rest upon your holy mountain? The one who enters without blemish and practices righteousness; who speaks truth in his heart and has not acted deceitfully with his tongue; who has done no evil to his neighbor and has not accepted reproach against his neighbors. The wicked person is brought to nothing in his sight, but he glorifies those who fear the Lord. The one who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive; who has not given his money at interest and has not accepted gifts against the innocent. Whoever does these things will not be moved forever.”

## Exposition

The psalm beginning “Lord, who will dwell” is connected with the preceding one as though he were saying: “I said that he will then give the salvation of Israel, when the Lord turns away the captivity of his people. But let no one applaud himself for this, because not everyone is to be counted among that people. Whoever wishes to belong to his people should hear the description of Christ’s soldiers.” To make this statement more authoritative, the Son asks the Father who they are who conduct themselves bravely here in the tabernacle—that is, in the military camp where rewards will be given.

“Lord,” to whose authority the matter must be entrusted, since many possess only a temporary dwelling—for they believe for a time, but withdraw at the time of temptation (Luke 8)—“who will dwell,” that is, remain continually, “in your tabernacle,” that is, in this temporal Church?

“The life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7). This is the dwelling of those engaged in warfare, namely, in ecclesiastical institutions. Hence it is also called a *contubernium*, as though it were a *contubernium*, a fellowship of the tabernacle.

Or: “Who will rest after the labor of the present life upon your holy mountain?” That is, in the elevated dwelling, in the palace of the heavenly Jerusalem, where there is great height and great fortification; where no enemy is enclosed and no friend is excluded. It is called holy because only holy people dwell in that city, namely the citizens above.

The appropriate ordering of these soldiers follows. First the strong and armored are placed; afterward, the common soldiers.

The response of the Lord the Father is: “The one who enters without blemish,” that is, the one who lives without a grave sin that stains the soul, though not without a blemish, that is, a lesser fault. Hence the saying: “The lamb shall be without blemish” (Exodus 12).

Note that “enters” may mean either entering inwardly into knowledge, or entering this tabernacle so as to live there innocently.

And because it is not enough to cease from evil, it follows: “And practices righteousness,” that is, strives to fulfill the edict of his king, leaving aside the other virtues. He places “righteousness” first because it is the mother and the greatest of all the other virtues: the others delight only the person who possesses them, whereas this one benefits others as well.

This may be the heading for what follows: “The one who speaks truth in his heart,” because it is not enough to speak the truth unless it is also present in the heart. The devil spoke the truth: “What have we to do with you, Son of God?” (Matthew 8), and yet he did not dwell in the Lord’s tabernacle.

And that person also who “has not acted deceitfully with his tongue,” that is, who has not spoken for the purpose of deceiving others.

And that person who “has not done evil to his neighbor.” Augustine: Understand every human being as one’s neighbor, namely one of the same nature and the same creation. “Evil” means some injury to the body, or to the soul, or to external possessions. This entire requirement belongs to the perfect.

Nor merely has he not committed reproach; “he has not accepted reproach against his neighbors,” that is, he has not readily or recklessly believed an accuser or slanderer—or, he is not accused as guilty by his neighbors.

“The wicked person is brought to nothing in his sight,” namely the person who loves the creature more than the Creator—gold and silver.

Or otherwise: “The wicked person,” that is, the devil, “is brought to nothing in his sight,” that is, in his understanding; “he is brought to nothing,” that is, he is regarded as nothing, because, having been made from nothing, after losing the goodness of his nature he was reduced to nothing. And since he is nothing, the strong man does not fear him.

Alternatively: the wicked one, that is, the devil, is brought to nothing when he has prevailed over the strong man in no suggestion, “in his sight,” that is, in the vigilance of his mind.

Alternatively: “in his sight,” that is, in his knowledge. The wicked one, namely the devil, who seems able by himself to prevail, is brought to nothing—that is, to the creatures that were created from nothing. The strong man recognizes that the devil can conquer only those whom he turns from the true and eternally unchanging form toward the creature and changeable desire, so that they submit themselves to money or to some other thing belonging to this world. In this way he brings him down as though above himself.

“But he glorifies those who fear the Lord.” In contrast to “the wicked person is brought to nothing in his sight,” he glorifies those who serve the Creator rather than the creature.

Here he passes to the common soldiers. The person who “swears to his neighbor, a human being, and does not deceive by lying” will dwell in the tabernacle and afterward rest in the palace.

Augustine: In human contracts it is permitted to swear, but it is prohibited for this reason: lest continual swearing lead to perjury.

And the person who “has not given his money at interest,” but has lent it freely, expecting a reward from God. The Father is speaking here of lesser matters. “Money” includes all other things; it is especially money that is customarily lent at interest.

“And has not accepted gifts against the innocent,” that is, the person who, corrupted by money, has not suppressed a just cause. Hence the prophet’s saying: “Woe to you who justify the wicked by gifts and take away the righteousness of the righteous from him” (Isaiah 5).

Whoever does not merely do the things mentioned above but also these lesser things “will not be moved,” that is, will not be separated forever, either from the tabernacle or from the palace.

This psalm may also be read in another way: “The fool said,” still under the same speaker and with the same intention as before, namely, according to Augustine, in this order. First it is said concerning the nations: “The fool said in his heart, ‘There is no God,’” namely, in reality. “They were corrupted and became abominable,” as above. “In their pursuits,” worshiping the works of their hands, and the rest as above, up to: “The Lord looked down from me, his Son,” that is, showed that he looked down also upon the sons of men.

Here it concerns the Jews: “so that he might see,” that is, make it known, “whether there is among them one who understands,” that is, one who is faithful, “or who seeks God through his works.” Or “from heaven,” that is, from the patriarchs and prophets.

But even among these no one was found who understood or sought God, although according to the flesh they were sons of men, that is, of the patriarchs and prophets, and although they had received the law and commandments, receiving everything according to the letter.

If, however, some were found seeking God in the law or in the time of grace, they are no longer called sons of men but Christians. For those who said, “We are disciples of Moses” (John 9), were sons of men and did not understand or seek God. “Seeking” is rightly said, as though he had been lost in the first parent.

The rest is as above, up to: “The counsel of the poor,” that is, of Christ, “who, though he was rich, became poor for our sake” (2 Corinthians 8). His counsel was that he might redeem you and teach you humility and patience. “You have confounded it,” that is, you regarded it as contemptible, counting it among contemptible things, because the Lord is his hope—that is, because you did not see him as like yourselves.

## Psalm 15. The Inscription of the Title: To David Himself

[Col. 0213A]

> “Preserve me, Lord, for I have hoped in you. I said to the Lord, ‘You are my God,’ for you have no need of my goods. He has made all my desires wondrous in his saints who are in his land. Their infirmities have multiplied; afterward they hastened. I will not gather their assemblies from blood sacrifices, nor will I remember their names with my lips. The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and my cup; you are the one who will restore my inheritance to me. The measuring lines have fallen for me among excellent things; indeed, my inheritance is excellent for me. I will bless the Lord, who has given me understanding; moreover, even until night my kidneys have reproved me. I kept the Lord always before my eyes, for he is at my right hand, so that I may not be moved. Because of this my heart rejoiced and my tongue exulted; moreover, my flesh also will rest in hope. For you will not abandon my soul in the underworld, nor will you allow your Holy One to see corruption. You have made known to me the ways of life; you will fill me with joy in your presence. Delights are at your right hand forever.”

## Exposition

“The inscription of the title: A psalm to David himself.” Jerome: There are three kinds of inscriptions that are written: one above the tombs of the dead, another on the thresholds of cities or houses, and a third in connection with the victory of a king.

The inscription of this title concerns the victory of Christ, King of the Jews—that is, King of all who confess: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.” This psalm is said to be his inscription because it contains the written cause of that victory. For it deals with Christ’s obedience, on account of which God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name (Philippians 2).

The title continues: “A psalm to David himself.” For in this psalm there is the voice of the head himself. It also treats the transformation of carnal observances, the rejection of the Jews, the reception of the nations, Christ’s resurrection, and his final glorification—all for the instruction of the faithful.

## The Voice of Christ in the Passion

Lord Father, preserve me, just as until now you have preserved my soul inwardly, free from every sin, giving me patience and steadfastness. So now preserve me—that is, preserve my body together with my soul, lest it descend into corruption. Or: preserve me, the head, together with the body, because in my resurrection lies their redemption.

And you ought to do so because I have hoped in you, not in another, as that wretched first parent did. Whoever wishes to be preserved should hope in you.

I show this in what follows: “I said to the Lord,” namely, in the Holy Spirit, in the manner in which it was necessary to speak. For no one can say “Lord Jesus” except in the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12). This is what I said: “You are my God,” that is, my special God—not “I,” as to those to whom it was said, “You will be like gods” (Genesis 3).

Let others make other gods for themselves, to their own confusion; I desire nothing other than you, to my glory. Therefore I offer you this price of my salvation, and nothing else, because you, Lord of lords, do not need anything, unlike other lords who need the goods of their servants. The servant needs you, not you the servant.

This is what follows: “For you have no need of my goods,” whether this means my incarnation, death, and resurrection. This, however, is for the sake of its fruit.

“He has made all my desires wondrous in his saints who are in his land,” that is, in those whom I made holy, because they are already in the land of the living through hope. He made all my desires wondrous—that is, made them desirable—by showing their crooked desires and my upright ones, their foul desires and my honorable ones, so that they might be in them, that is, so that they might possess them in action.

I also made known to them how both the humanity of my divinity and the divinity of my humanity benefited them. The humanity of my divinity benefited them because I died for our sins; the divinity of my humanity benefited them because I rose for our justification (Romans 4).

He made this wondrous to the saints, that is, to all the faithful of every nation who are in the land of the living through faith and hope.

Alternatively: “The Lord has made all my desires wondrous in his saints who are in his land,” because I called upon him in the manner in which he must be called upon, namely because I said to the Lord, “You are my God.” It is evident from this that he made my desires wondrous for them, because “their infirmities have multiplied.”

The infirmities that had previously lain hidden—or iniquities that had seemed nonexistent—multiplied, that is, appeared in many forms. As it is said: “Sin revived, and I died” (Romans 7), because previously I had in some sense been alive.

And this also happened: through me they came to know their book. For, seeing my upright life, they recognized their own crookedness.

“Afterward,” that is, after they recognized their infirmity, “they hastened,” namely to the physician. Hence the saying: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7).

I say that they hastened, but not in the way they had previously done, namely so that their assemblies would be different. For there will be one assembly, because in the faith of Christ there is neither slave nor free, neither male nor female, neither barbarian nor Scythian (Colossians 3).

Or “from blood sacrifices,” namely from many victims, because I will call them to one sacrifice and to my one blood. This is what he says: “I will not gather their assemblies from blood sacrifices.” “I will not gather” means “I will summon.”

For I will not receive Jews alone, whose synagogue is interpreted as “assembly.” These assemblies of the Jews—such as the house of Jacob and the house of Levi—were small in comparison with all the nations, as it is said: “All the nations will come to it” (Isaiah 2; Jeremiah 16).

“From blood sacrifices,” namely of bulls, calves, and goats, which were effective only for the cleansing of the flesh. I will summon them to my own blood, which will cleanse their conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9).

“Nor will I remember their names.” They will no longer be enemies, nor servants, nor merely righteous, but friends, free, and righteous—“with my lips,” that is, through my heralds, the prophets, because I myself, who spoke in them, will be present.

Alternatively: those assemblies and blood sacrifices existed “through my lips,” that is, I myself commanded them. And if they observed what I commanded to be done through servants, much more will they observe what I myself command.

“I will not remember their names with my lips,” that is, through my peace and reconciliation. For he himself is our peace, who made both one, reconciling what is in heaven and what is on earth (Ephesians 2; Colossians 1); for with the lips we give the kiss of peace.

Alternatively: “I will gather them through my lips,” not through another’s. I myself will show them the true sacrifices, because my flesh is truly food and my blood is truly drink (John 6). For they will find nothing in me that is not to be consumed.

“The Lord is the portion of my inheritance.” As if he were saying: “I will summon them all to one gathering for this reason: they themselves will not separate themselves. For they will ask for one thing alone, not many—namely, the Lord.”

“The Lord is the portion of my inheritance,” that is, of my Church, which is my inheritance, because it feeds me and delights me. Everything has been divided into two: creature and Creator. Others establish their portion for themselves in creatures, namely in things that pass away; my inheritance, however, is the Lord alone.

“And he will be the portion of my cup,” namely of the same Church, which is my cup because it refreshes me. For this reason I said on the cross, “I thirst” (John 19).

Alternatively: “of my cup” through imitation, as in the saying, “They drank the Lord’s cup and became friends of God.” The Church is called both inheritance and cup by way of comparison.

This inheritance and cup is mine, not from myself but from you, because “you are the one who will restore my inheritance to me,” which was lost in Adam—not I, the Lord’s human being, but you, God.

Alternatively: “I will not gather their assemblies from blood sacrifices,” because the Lord will be the portion of my inheritance through the man whom I assumed; he will be the portion of my body. He himself gives my people to eat, not the blood of victims. Hence the saying: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6).

“And he will be the portion of my cup,” that is, of the same body. It is called Christ’s cup because, while the fullness of divinity dwells perfectly in him (Colossians 2), it is given to his body according to measure.

Alternatively: “You are the one who will restore my inheritance.” The Jewish people was my inheritance. I lost it because my chosen vineyard was turned into bitterness (Isaiah 5; Jeremiah 2), so that it crucified me: “Branches of the olive tree were broken so that the wild olive might be grafted in” (Romans 11). But you, Lord, will restore it, because a remnant will be saved.

And lest anyone applaud himself in that inheritance without reason, he defines who those are whom he wishes to call his inheritance.

“The measuring lines,” that is, the measures and boundaries of that inheritance. And rightly “measures,” because the Lord knows who are his (2 Timothy 2). This is spoken by comparison, because fields are measured with ropes.

“They have fallen to me,” that is, by your grace they have fallen to me by lot, “among excellent things,” that is, among bright things, having neither blemish nor wrinkle: the blemish of unbelief, the wrinkle of heresy.

Or “among excellent things,” that is, in victory. For those are mine who have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires (Galatians 5). But because they did not appear so to the world—in fact they appeared ragged and contemptible, as in the saying, “We have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings, the refuse of all even until now” (1 Corinthians 4)—he adds:

“Indeed, my inheritance is excellent for me.” And through that inheritance I will bless the Lord, who gave me understanding to know it, namely to preserve or distinguish my own from those who are not mine.

Moreover, I will bless the Lord for this because “even until night my kidneys reproved me.”

“Kidneys,” that is, my lower part, namely the flesh, “reproved,” that is, instructed me. For instruction often comes through reproof. “Until night,” that is, until the darkness of death. In all the things that I endured in the body, I learned obedience, humility, and patience.

Alternatively: “Moreover, I will bless the Lord because my kidneys,” namely the Jews, from whose kidneys I was born, “reproved me,” that is, sternly accused me, even unto death, because there I offered my own an example of humility and patience.

Alternatively: “Moreover, I will bless the Lord because my kidneys,” that is, my weaker parts, “reproved me even unto death,” and I died in weakness. But “my kidneys” were also my delights; that is, I bless you not only because the spirit was willing, but also because the flesh took delight in it. “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover” (Luke 22).

I rightly bless him because, in the passion, so that I might not fail, I “kept before me”—that is, looked ahead toward—the Lord as rewarder or as one assisting me, “in my sight,” that is, inwardly in my heart, where true vision exists, “always,” both in the passion and in death.

And rightly I kept him before me, “for he is at my right hand,” that is, among the things of greater worth, or as my supporter and gracious toward me and mine, “so that I may not be moved,” namely away from him together with those who try to devour me, whose feet have been moved.

Or I will bless him, and no other, for this reason: “he is at my right hand,” that is, I regard him as preeminent.

“Because of this,” namely because I will not be moved, “my heart rejoiced,” that is, I rejoiced inwardly, although I suffered outwardly.

Or “because of this,” namely because you will restore my inheritance to me in this way.

“And my tongue exulted,” that is, my tongue gave thanks to you with exultation, as in the saying: “Father, I thank you” (John 11).

“Moreover,” that is, not only will my soul rejoice, but “my flesh also will rest,” that is, will lie in the tomb, “in this hope”: “for you will not abandon my soul in the underworld, nor will you allow your Holy One to see corruption,” namely the corruption of my body.

Christ’s flesh did lie in the tomb, but it was not corrupted, because he rose on the third day.

Alternatively: “Moreover,” that is, not only I, the head, but also “my flesh,” namely the Church. Hence the Apostle says: “The two will be one flesh. Now I speak of Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5). It will rest in death from the labors of this life, “in the hope” of resurrection.

And rightly so, because “you will not abandon my soul in the underworld.” What is seen to have preceded in the head does not lead those members attached to him to despair concerning themselves.

It should be noted that elsewhere he says: “What profit is there in my blood, when I descend into corruption?” (Psalm 29). But this was said of the wound in his side and the piercing of the nails, not of corruption of Christ’s body in the tomb.

Truly you will not allow him to see corruption. Rather, “you have made known to me”—that is, through me to my people—“the ways of life,” namely humility, patience, and perseverance, so that by imitating me they might return to life through humility, from which they had fallen through pride.

Or “the ways of life,” that is, the commandments. Hence it is said: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matthew 19). You did this beforehand.

“But you will fill me with joy,” that is, fill me completely, “with your presence,” that is, when I and all who belong to me with me enjoy the joy of your presence. Then you will fill me, although now you have filled me with the joy of my resurrection.

You will fill me in this way: “Delights,” not one delight but many. For you will be all things in all (1 Corinthians 15). “At your right hand,” that is, among those who will be at your right hand, in the more worthy portion, or in your favor, “forever,” that is, always, with those delights extending toward their end and never arriving.

## Psalm 16. The Prayer of David

[Col. 0217B]

> “Hear, Lord, my righteousness; attend to my supplication. Receive with your ears my prayer, not spoken by deceitful lips. Let my judgment come forth from your presence; let your eyes behold equity. You have tested my heart and visited it by night; you have examined me by fire, and no iniquity has been found in me. So that my mouth may not speak the works of men, because of the words of your lips I have kept hard ways. Perfect my steps in your paths, so that my footprints may not be moved. I cried out because you heard me, O God; incline your ear to me, and hear my words. Make your mercies wondrous, you who save those who hope in you. Guard me from those who resist your right hand, as the pupil of the eye. Protect me under the shadow of your wings from the face of the ungodly who have afflicted me. My enemies have surrounded my soul; they have enclosed their fat; their mouth has spoken pride. Having cast me down, they have now surrounded me; they have fixed their eyes to cast me down to the earth. They seized me like a lion ready for prey, and like a lion’s cub dwelling in hiding places. Arise, Lord; go before him and supplant him. Deliver my soul from the ungodly; deliver my sword from the enemies of your hand. Lord, divide them from the few of the earth in their life, and their belly has been filled from your hidden things. They are filled with children, and have divided their remnants among their little ones. But I shall appear before your presence in righteousness; I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.”

[Col. 0217D]

## Exposition

A prayer to David himself. This psalm is a prayer to be attributed to David, that is, to Christ—not to the body, but to himself—although both are prayer. Jerome says that in this passage *oration* and *supplication* have this distinction: prayer is for the obtaining or perseverance of good things; supplication, that evils may not come, or may be removed.

Therefore Christ prays in this psalm that his judgment, which was for the salvation of human beings, may be revealed to the world, so that believers may be saved. He also prays that his faithful may be protected from the ungodly, lest they be led astray.

Hear, O Lord, my righteousness, which stands opposed to Adam’s righteousness. As though he were saying: Since it is your will that the author of human salvation [Col. 0218A] be brought to completion through suffering, it is right that I obey you; and because I am obedient, my righteousness pleads for me and for my own before you. Attend—that is, consider without ceasing—my supplication, that is, my prayer for the sins of humanity. For this reason the whole psalm is entitled “prayer,” since it consists either in petition or in supplication; and both are prayer.

And not only does my righteousness pray, but also hear my prayer with your ears—that is, hear it mercifully—which is on lips free from deceit, that is, worthy of your ears because it agrees with the heart. For not everyone who says, “Lord, Lord,” is worthy of being heard (Matt. VII). This is what I ask; in this hear me: Let my judgment proceed from your presence. “Judgment”—that judgment by which I was judged to suffer for the salvation of the world; “my,” that is, useful to me and [Col. 0218B] to my own—let it proceed, that is, let it be shown to have come forth from your presence, that is, from your will, not from the Jews’ plan. Let this be made manifest.

Your eyes—that is, the preachers whom you make the eyes of the Church—let them see, that is, understand, equities, that is, equalities, in my glorification and in their condemnation.

Alternatively: Let my judgment, by which I offered myself as a sacrifice for the sins of humanity, proceed—that is, appear to have come forth—from your disposition, not from my rashness. Let your eyes, which cannot be deceived, see and make known the equity, namely, mine, since it was equitable that, sent by you, I should obey your command.

Alternatively: Let every judgment, that is, all my discernment, proceed—that is, go forth—from your presence, that is, from your watchfulness. And not only I, but also my eyes—that is, the preachers through whom I provide for my own [Col. 0218C]—or your eyes in the same way—let them see equity, that is, understand that it is just that they fulfill in deed what they teach in word. And they do this by imitating my example.

For you tested my heart and made it upright and steadfast; and you visited it, as though it were infirm, in order to strengthen it, at night—that is, in tribulation. It is called “night” by comparison, because it causes confusion. With fire—that is, with severe tribulation, which is called fire because it burns—you examined me, that is, you confounded the sins of humanity in me. And iniquity was not found in me, because in none of these things did I depart from your commandments.

Thus act so that in them also no iniquity may be found: namely, cause my mouth—that is, my teachers—not to speak of human works, that is, the vanities of this age which people love, but rather of your works and your victories. Let them do this by imitating me, because, for the sake of the words of your lips [Col. 0218D]—because you commanded your commandments to be kept with great care (Ps. CXVIII)—I kept difficult ways.

Alternatively: Truly your eyes will see equities, because you tested my heart and visited it at night, as above. With fire you examined me, and iniquity was not found in me. In all these things they will recognize and imitate my obedience and humility. I preserved equity so completely in that examination that, even in the greatest tribulation, my mouth did not speak anything foolish against you, just as it is said of Job: “In all these things Job did not sin with his lips, nor did he speak anything foolish against God” (Job I, II). And Christ, “like a sheep led to slaughter, did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII).

Human works, namely the worst works, were committed against me, because they condemned me to the most shameful death. [Col. 0219A] By saying simply “human works,” he indicates their enormity. And yet, for the sake of the words of whose lips—that is, in order to fulfill what the prophets, who were my lips, foretold about me—I kept difficult ways.

In Hebrew, David says “the ways of robbers,” that is, “the ways of all flesh,” concerning death. The way of robbers was the death of the cross, which was assigned to robbers and sacrilegious criminals. The Lord kept the ways of robbers when he was crucified between two robbers (Luke XXIII); although such a death was undeserved by his deeds, he nevertheless endured it patiently.

Alternatively: Just as he says, “Let my mouth not speak of human works,” so “iniquity was not found in me,” so that nothing other than your praise might proceed from my mouth. For if I said this to my own praise, I would speak of human works, not yours.

Alternatively: The tribulation is so great that my mouth does not speak of human works [Col. 0219B], that is, it is not necessary for me to speak, because the human works committed against me—foul and exceedingly cruel as they are—speak sufficiently for themselves.

“For the sake of the words of your lips,” that is, because you commanded it, “I kept difficult ways,” that is, many torments.

Alternatively: “For the sake of the words of your lips,” that is, for the sake of the peace and reconciliation which you promised the world through me, since with our lips we give the kiss of peace, “I kept difficult ways,” that is, your difficult commandments—not difficult for me, but for beginners.

Jerome? How are they difficult, when it is said: “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. XI)? Light for those who are willing, but heavy for those who are unwilling.

Alternatively: “For the sake of the words,” that is, the threats of future condemnation, “of your lips,” that is, of the heralds, apostles, and prophets—as in: “Brood of vipers, who will free you from the coming wrath?” (Luke III)—“I kept difficult ways” [Col. 0219C], that is, great torments in my own, so that I might escape those future torments.

And because I kept difficult ways, iniquity was not found in me. But you, Lord, complete what you began in me and in my members. Complete my steps, that is, all the affections and intentions of my preachers, in your paths, that is, in your narrow commandments. Complete them in such a way that my footprints—that is, the examples of my humility and patience—may not be moved from them.

Complete this in my members, because in me you have already completed it, since you have heard me, O God. You heard me because I cried out, that is, I openly proclaimed your faith; or I cried out in the manner in which one ought to cry out to you, that is, I acted without ceasing; or I directed prayers to you with free and powerful intention.

Therefore now incline your ear to me as I pray for those [Col. 0219D] who will also be mine in the future. Incline your ear like a physician to the sick, who cannot rise by themselves because they lie in the bed of sins, whose infirmity I have taken upon myself.

In this way hear my voice. Make your mercies, displayed to the world through me, marvelous—that is, make them desirable to them or show them to be marvelous—so that they may not become despised, by declaring them through your teachers. Make them marvelous for this purpose: that they may hope in you and, by hoping, be saved; for you save those who hope in you.

And because you save those who hope in you, preserve me from those who resist your right hand, that is, from those who resist me, the head, and mine. Preserve me like the apple of the eye, by comparison.

Alternatively: The pupil is that part through which the eye sees and distinguishes; so Christ is the pupil of his Church, because he alone distinguishes his own from those who are not his. He therefore says [Col. 0220A]: Cause your preachers, who are the eye of the Church, to imitate my humility, without which they cannot understand or see what must be seen, just as an eye cannot see without the pupil.

Preserve me in this way: Protect me under the shadow of your wings. Let the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit come upon me through the two wings, that is, love of God and love of neighbor, and protect me from the harmful heat of every incitement. Hence the saying: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I).

Alternatively: Protect me through the understanding of the two Testaments in my body, just as a hen protects her chicks under her wings, lest a hawk—that is, the devil—snatch them away.

Protect me from the presence of the impious who afflicted me, that is, from the image of the Jews and heretics, lest in my body I be drawn away from your image [Col. 0220B] and likeness and be conformed to theirs.

And it is necessary that you protect me. My enemies have shut in my soul. The Jews shut in Christ, and the impious heretics and others shut in the Church—not in order to imitate it, but in order to destroy it. They surrounded my soul with many deceits, threats, and flatteries; for whatever they did to the body, they contrived against the soul, so that they might draw it away from you.

They enclosed their own fat, that is, they bound and wrapped themselves in wickedness and temporal joy, so that they would not eat me, the living bread, who descended from heaven in the likeness of manna. [Col. 0220C] By “fat,” wickedness is signified; in the old Law they were forbidden to eat it, because their heart had been made fat with wickedness (Matt. XIII). Therefore it is said in the Song of Deuteronomy: “The beloved kicked, grew fat, became thick, and grew broad” through wickedness (Deut. XXXII). He kicked because he did not wish to observe the commandments. He was beloved because manna rained down upon him from heaven.

And because they had grown fat with temporal joy, their mouth spoke arrogance: “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke XIX).

“Casting me away” previously in my own—that is, first rejecting my teaching—or casting me outside the city as though I were polluted, as though the city would be polluted by my death—or now, namely, after these things have been set forth: “now they surrounded me,” that is, at last they completed their wickedness, spitting upon me, striking me with blows, and finally condemning me to a shameful death.

[Col. 0220D] And it is no wonder that they did these things to the author of life, because they fixed their eyes—that is, the mind by which they ought to have seen the divinity working in me—and firmly resolved to turn them downward, that is, to incline them toward the earth, namely, toward my body. They wished to believe that I was merely human and not God.

Or alternatively: They turned the love of their heart toward earthly things, so that they loved the world more than God.

Or alternatively: They surrounded me with complete determination in order to destroy me; this was shown by the fact that they fixed their eyes on the earth.

They received me—either the Jews from the disciple, or Pilate and his servants from the Jews—like a lion prepared for prey: those exceedingly fierce leaders who crucified me; and like a lion’s cub: the Jewish populace or its offspring, dwelling in hidden places [Col. 0221A], that is, consenting as though secretly. For the lesser ones, even though they did not openly condemn him, nevertheless sinned secretly because they consented to his death. For not only those who do evil are guilty, but also those who consent (Rom. I).

Rise up, Lord; bring help, you who appeared to lie in my humiliation. Go before him, namely, the devil, at whose instigation they do these things. Let him come to me and find nothing in me [John XIV]. Or let him himself be caught in the snare of death which he prepared for me: “O death, I shall be your death” (Hos. XIII).

And trip him up, so that in my death, through which he believed himself to be exalted, he may be humbled. Or he himself lies in wait for my heel, but you crush his head (Gen. III).

Rise up in this way: Rescue my soul from the impious, so that he may not hold it among the dead; or the souls of my own, who are being held captive, undeserving, among the dead [Col. 0221B].

Rescue your sword—that is, me, your sword, by whom the enemy must be slain—from the enemies of your hand.

Alternatively: Go before him, the Jewish people; let its wickedness be blinded within, so that vengeance may precede its deed. And afterward, when it believes that it is exalted through me, trip it up, that is, cast it down. For it believed that through my death it would retain its place and nation (John XI), but through that death let it lose both. The one who is crushed is like someone who has something placed beneath his foot in order to be raised up, and then has it withdrawn so that he may fall more heavily. The weakness of my flesh was placed beneath them, and they were exalted; afterward it was withdrawn when I rose again, and they fell.

Trip them up in this way: “O Lord, divide them from the few of the earth.” Although in the land of the dying the weeds and the wheat grow together until the harvest (Matt. XIII), nevertheless you will eventually divide them [Col. 0221C] from the few, that is, from the elect of the land of the living.

“In their lifetime,” namely, in the lifetime of the few, when the rich will rise with the few to life and the many to disgrace: for their belly—that is, their memory—has been filled with your hidden things, that is, with iniquities which you do not know, or with ignorance and forgetfulness of you.

Alternatively, according to the historical sense: “In their lifetime,” namely, this life, which alone they love, divide them from their land. This happened in the time of Titus and Vespasian, when they were captured, sold, and scattered into captivity. “For their belly has been filled with your hidden things,” as above.

As though he were saying: Why this downfall of the Jews? “A partial blindness has happened in Israel, so that the fullness of the nations might enter, and thus”—corrected by this example—“all Israel might be saved” (Rom. XI).

They were filled [Col. 0221D], that is, they were full of joy at my passion and death; and not only were they filled for themselves, but also for their sons, so completely that they gave a portion to their sons: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII).

And they left their remnants—that is, the surplus of their condemnation—to their little ones, that is, to their descendants, so that the blood of Christ might be reckoned against the third and fifth generation.

Alternatively: They were filled, that is, they satisfied their perverse will, not their own advantage but that of their sons. Their sons, recognizing their condemnation and God’s glorification in the death, were converted to the faith; and they left their remnants, that is, spiritual understandings which they themselves considered superfluous, to their little ones, that is, to the humble among their descendants, the apostles and the remnants [Col. 0222A] who will be saved at the end.

Alternatively: They were filled with the Lord’s death. For just as Jonah was in the whale’s belly for three days and three nights, so Christ’s death was in the heart of the earth, that is, among the earthly Jews (Matt. XII; John II). For they thought about it throughout Thursday and the following night; on Friday they crucified him; on the Sabbath he was taken down from the cross and lay buried in the earth, until he rose again after three days, that is, on the morning of the first day after the Sabbath.

And they left their remnants, that is, the resurrection, to their little ones, who in his resurrection rose together from the death of unbelief.

[Col. 0222B] With reference to mortality, this may also be read in the following way: “Lord, divide them from the few before they are entirely divided from your earth; let them also be separated here in their lifetime, though not in the flesh, yet in affection, from the few,” that is, from the elect. Let them not be here with them in the first resurrection, so that afterward they may not have fellowship with them in the second resurrection.

But I shall appear in righteousness before your presence. As though he were saying: They cast me outside the city and judged me unworthy of their fellowship; but I have not been rejected by you, because I shall appear before your presence in the glory of the Ascension. In righteousness, because it is just that the righteous man be justified.

There they were filled with swine’s flesh, that is, with wickedness; but I shall be filled there, having now, as it were, dined, in my glorification. I shall be filled, that is, I shall have complete joy, when your glory appears, that is, when I present your Church to you, when I hand the kingdom over to you, God the Father, in which your glory will appear.

Or when that glory is manifested in reality which is now hidden in [Col. 0222C] hope: for they will see you as you are, whereas now they see through a mirror (1 Cor. XV).

# PSALM XVII

**For the end; for David, the servant of the Lord, who spoke to the Lord the words of this song on the day when the Lord rescued him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul; and he said:**

> “I will love you, O Lord, my strength.  
> The Lord is my firmament and my refuge, and my deliverer.  
> My God is my helper, and I shall hope in him.  
> My protector and the horn of my salvation, and my receiver.  
> Praising, I shall call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies.  
> The pains of death surrounded me, and torrents of iniquity troubled me.  
> The pains of hell surrounded me; [Col. 0222D] the snares of death overtook me.  
> In my tribulation I called upon the Lord, and I cried out to my God.  
> And he heard my voice from his holy temple, and my cry entered his ears in his presence.  
> The earth was shaken and trembled, and the foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken, because he was angry with them.  
> Smoke rose in his anger, and fire blazed from his presence; coals were kindled by him.  
> He inclined the heavens and descended, and darkness was beneath his feet.  
> And he mounted upon the cherubim and flew upon the wings of the winds.  
> And he made darkness his hiding place; around him was his tabernacle, dark water in the clouds of the air.  
> Before the brightness of his presence the clouds passed by, [Col. 0223A] hail and coals of fire.  
> And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave his voice; hail and coals of fire.  
> And he sent forth his arrows and scattered them; he multiplied lightning and troubled them.  
> And the springs of waters appeared, and the foundations of the world were revealed.  
> At your rebuke, O Lord, at the breath of the spirit of your anger.  
> He sent from on high and took me, and received me from many waters.  
> He rescued me from my strongest enemies and from those who hated me, because they had grown stronger than I.  
> They overtook me on the day of my affliction, and the Lord became my protector.  
> And he led me out into a broad place; he saved me because he desired me.  
> And the Lord will reward me according to my righteousness, and according to the purity [Col. 0223B] of my hands he will reward me.  
> For I kept the ways of the Lord and did not act impiously against my God.  
> For all his judgments were before my eyes, and I did not reject his righteousnesses from me.  
> And I shall be blameless with him, and I shall keep myself from my iniquity.  
> And the Lord will reward me according to my righteousness and according to the purity of my hands in the sight of his eyes.  
> With the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent.  
> And with the elect you will be elect, and with the perverse you will deal perversely.  
> For you will save the humble people, and you will humble the eyes of the proud.  
> For you illumine my lamp, O Lord my God; illumine my darkness.  
> For in you I shall be rescued from temptation, and in my God I shall leap over a wall.  
> My God—his [Col. 0223C] way is undefiled; the sayings of the Lord are tested by fire; he is the protector of all who hope in him.  
> For who is God besides the Lord? Or who is God besides our God?  
> God who girded me with strength and made my way blameless.  
> He made my feet like those of deer and set me upon high places.  
> He teaches my hands for battle, and you have made my arms like a bronze bow.  
> And you gave me the protection of your salvation, and your right hand received me.  
> And your discipline corrected me to the end, and your discipline itself will teach me.  
> You enlarged my steps beneath me, and my footprints did not become weak.  
> I shall pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I shall not turn back until they fail.  
> I shall crush them, and they will not be able to stand; they will fall beneath [Col. 0223D] my feet.  
> And you girded me with strength for battle; you cast down beneath me those who rose up against me.  
> And you gave me the backs of my enemies, and you destroyed those who hated me.  
> They cried out, and there was no one to save them; they cried to the Lord, and he did not hear them.  
> And I shall crush them like dust before the face of the wind; like the mud of the streets I shall wipe them away.  
> You will rescue me from the contradictions of the people; you will establish me as head of the nations.  
> A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear it obeyed me.  
> The sons of strangers lied to me; the sons of strangers grew old and limped from their paths.  
> The Lord lives, and blessed is my God, and exalted is the God of my salvation.  
> God who gives me vengeance and subjects peoples beneath me, my deliverer [Col. 0224A] from my angry enemies.  
> And from those who rise up against me you will exalt me; from the unjust man you will rescue me.  
> Therefore I shall confess to you among the nations, O Lord, and I shall sing a psalm to your name.  
> Magnifying the salvations of his king and showing mercy to his anointed, to David and to his seed forever.”

## EXPOSITION

“For the end; for David, the servant, who spoke to the Lord the words of this song on the day when the Lord rescued him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.”

“I will love you, O Lord.” According to the historical sense, David sang this psalm when, after Saul and his other enemies had died, he was freed from their persecutions. But he did not sing these praises [Col. 0224B] to God only on his own behalf; he sang them on behalf of that true and perfect redemption which he saw would come in the true David, Christ, and in his members. For this psalm treats of the victory of Christ’s passion, the glory of his resurrection, the establishment and shaping of his body, and how and through whom these things were accomplished.

The title is constructed and explained as follows: The words of this song, that is, of exultant praise, are to be referred “to the end,” that is, to Christ, and are to be attributed to David, the servant of the Lord. After Saul had been rejected, it was said by the Lord: “I have chosen a man after my own heart” (Ps. LXXXVIII). Therefore that man was rightly called David, “the servant,” that is, the chosen one of the Lord.

And Christ, who sings these praises to God the Father, is called the servant of the Lord, as in: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. III), and: “A child is born to us” [Col. 0224C] (Isa. IX). And truly he is a child, because he is pure and without blemish.

These are the words which he spoke to the Lord, that is, in contemplation of that day on which the Lord rescued him from the hand of all his enemies. This happened in the head itself, who rose again and ascended into heaven. And “from the hand of Saul,” that is, from death.

According to the interpretation of the name, Saul signifies death. For Saul is interpreted as “desire,” because the children of Israel desired him as king for themselves against the will of God. And concerning death it was said: “God did not make death” (Wis. I); but the impious summoned it upon themselves with hands and feet.

This perfect rescue will not occur until death is destroyed for the last time, when Christ hands the kingdom over to God the Father (1 Cor. XIII). Then at last the whole Christ, that is, in head and members, will be rescued [Col. 0224D] from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.

## VOICE OF CHRIST

“I will love you, O Lord.” Because I see that at last you will rescue me from the hand of all my enemies and from Saul, I will love you. I do not say “I loved” or merely “I love,” because charity will never fail, while faith and hope will be abolished when that rescue comes, when what is partial is abolished; but love will increase. And rightly so, because you strengthen me in that love: you are my strength. Through you I deliberately undertake dangers and endure my labors.

To exhort his own also to praise God, he turns to them and says: “The Lord is my firmament,” because in the first parent I was weakened through pride [Col. 0225A] and was not strengthened through his grace. “And my refuge,” to whom one securely flees inwardly when one cannot resist outwardly. “And my deliverer”: at last he delivers not only from enemies but also from mortality.

Because of his excessive joy, he multiplies his praises: “My God” by nature, “my helper” by grace, lest I fail under the burden. And therefore I shall hope in him; I shall not be like the one who hoped in himself and fell. In this way he became a helper by grace.

“My protector,” and not just any protector, but “the horn of my salvation,” that is, the one who makes me spiritual and strong from what is carnal and fragile, and makes me, as it were, surpass my own nature. As it is said: “Although we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh” (2 Cor. X). Just as a horn, though it is made of flesh, is nevertheless transformed into hardness, surpasses flesh [Col. 0225B], and passes into another nature.

Alternatively: Since different animals protect themselves with different weapons—the wolf with its tooth, the horse with its hoof—you are a horn to me, because you give me firm reason by which I can scatter enemies, especially heretics.

Alternatively: I do not raise a horn of pride against you; rather, you are the horn, that is, the firm height of my salvation, raising my hope toward you.

And you are not only my protector and horn, but, what is greater, you have become my receiver, that is, of my weakness. This concerns the body. Or “my receiver,” that is, of my cause.

In this way he received me. God the Father sent his Son, coeternal with himself, from on high, that is, from the Father’s bosom. He sent him, that is, he caused him, who was invisible in his own being, to appear in humility. “And he took me,” namely, the form of a servant, not an angel, nor any nobler kind of being. For nowhere did he take hold of [Col. 0225C] angels; and “he assumed me,” that is, my body, which is the Church, “from many waters,” that is, from many peoples, because he gathered it not only from Judea but from all lands.

Waters are called peoples (Rev. XVII) by comparison, because through departure and succession they are always in flux, like waters.

Or “from many waters,” that is, from the flow of carnal pleasures, or from many baptisms. For although baptism is one, and all past vices are drowned there, just as the Egyptians were drowned in the Red Sea (Exod. XIV), so that not one remained, the Red Sea signifies baptism, which, sanctified and reddened by Christ’s blood, is powerful for drowning vices. Yet it is divided according to the subsequent merits of those baptized.

Some are baptized in such a way that they remain in [Col. 0225D] that purity, so that they are entirely clean and need only wash their feet from dust (John XIII), that is, their thoughts from unlawful things. Others add certain crimes, but venial ones. For others it profits nothing, because by living wickedly they return completely to their former state, as it is written of that sea: “He divided the Red Sea into divisions” (Ps. CXXXV).

For as many tribes as Israel had, so many divisions was it divided into. And because it received me as its head, and assumed me in its members, I will call upon the Lord while praising him. I will not merely call upon the Lord, but invoke him—that is, call him into myself—so that he may be both what I ask and the one from whom I ask. And I will do this while praising him, that is, by living in a praiseworthy manner. For by such people God is made propitious.

And in this way [Col. 0226A] I shall be saved from my enemies—namely, from these: “The pains of death surrounded me,” that is, those in whom the pains were present, those who lead to death, namely, the sufferings of envy. For they begrudged me life. “And torrents of iniquity,” that is, the sudden assaults of the wicked, which quickly pass away, like water suddenly stirred by an increase of rain and quickly subsiding; “troubled me,” that is, for a short time they grieved me with death, for after three days I rose again. For disturbance is a sudden movement that quickly passes away.

It is as though he said: Their envy alone was the cause of my death, but it profited them nothing, because their assault suddenly increased and suddenly ceased, like water stirred by rain. For I lay dead in the tomb, but only for three days.

“The pains of hell,” that is, those grieving over the loss of earthly [Col. 0226B] things. Just as there are heavenly pains—namely, those arising from the loss of heavenly things—so also there are infernal pains, arising from the loss of earthly things and leading to hell. “Iniquities and pains” is said emphatically. For the lovers of this world heard: “The world and its desire are passing away” (I John II). “You shall accuse no one”; “You shall do injury to no one.”

“They forestalled me,” as though I were unaware, according to their opinion, of how far they were proceeding: “the snares of death,” that is, causes intertwined with causes and tending toward my death. Or: Their plots prepared death for me as though I did not know it.

“I shall be saved from my enemies.” And salvation is necessary, because “the pains of death”—that is, those sufferings which I possess through my mortality—“surrounded me,” that is, my flesh. And therefore “the torrents of iniquity,” as above, “troubled me”; for this reason they wanted to trouble me.

“The pains of hell,” that is, the pains of my lower part, namely, my flesh, which is my lower part, “surrounded me,” that is, they embraced me more forcefully. And no wonder, because “the snares of death” forestalled me in my first parent, namely, in the mass. From that mass I contracted not guilt, but punishment.

I, however, did what belonged to me: I fled for refuge to prayers.
