Or: “I invoked,” that is, called into myself, the Lord who rewards, “in my tribulation”—in mine, not in theirs, because it profited them nothing. “I invoked the Lord,” that is, called him inwardly into my heart, where the voice is free and the hearing prompt.

Which Lord? “And to my God I cried,” that is, I acted without ceasing. Or: I invoked him on my own behalf, and cried out on behalf of my people.

“And he heard me from his holy temple,” because I invoked him, not another; “my voice,” made on my own behalf, not for human approval; “and my cry,” made on behalf of my people, “in his sight”—that is, made in the heart or through unceasing action, where it is always before his sight—“entered into his ears,” that is, it merited being heard. The effect demonstrates this hearing.

When the old law had been given or received through a servant, the earth was shaken. At the Lord’s resurrection—through whom the law was to be fulfilled and invoked—it was shaken materially, and likewise the hearts of earthly people were moved from unbelief to faith, which the earthquake signified. And not only the earth, but Judaea also trembled—that is, together with Judaea the whole earth trembled, namely, the earth of the Gentiles; that is, all earthly people were afraid.

He adds afterward why they were afraid: [Col. 0227A] “And not only the lesser ones, but also the foundations of the mountains”—that is, the greater princes, such as Gamaliel, a teacher of the law, and Joseph of Arimathea, in whom the lesser princes placed their confidence—“were troubled” because of sins and “shaken” from unbelief to faith.

Or: “the foundations of the mountains,” that is, the hopes in earthly things in which the mountains—that is, the proud—trusted, were troubled, because people no longer trusted in them as before, after they had heard: “All flesh is grass” (I Peter I), and: “The world and its desire are passing away” (I John II). Hence the saying: “The Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt, and the idols of Egypt will be shattered” (Isaiah XIX). And the Apostle says to Timothy: “Command the rich of this world not to trust in uncertain riches” (I Timothy VI).

Alternatively: “The foundations of the mountains,” that is, the idols in which the mountains—that is, demons—were worshiped; or: the mountains, that is, the things in which the mountains, namely the proud of this world, trusted, were troubled—that is, confused or scattered—and shaken from the hearts of human beings, or from that former honor.

Whether they are understood in this way or in that, they were both troubled and shaken, because he was angry with them, namely the Lord; that is, he made known to them his anger and their future condemnation. Hence the saying: “Brood of vipers, who will deliver you from the coming wrath? Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke III). In this way they were shaken.

“Smoke ascended,” after they had recognized their sins—that is, tearful supplication—“in his anger,” that is, in their knowledge of his anger. Smoke is produced from two things, fire and water. By fire is signified remorse, by water tears, and by smoke, as is fitting, supplication. Thus: “And the smoke of the incense ascended” (Revelation VIII); and afterward: “which are the prayers of the saints” (Revelation V).

And after the smoke, “fire blazed,” that is, charity, “from his face,” that is, from knowledge. For the knowledge of God kindled them to his love.

“Coals were kindled by him,” that is, those in whom the love of God had been extinguished in the first parent were now kindled and illumined by the grace of God, having received the light of truth. Hence the saying: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Romans III).

If we refer what has been said to Christ’s incarnation, we read the following in this way: “He inclined the heavens.” But how were the coals kindled? “He inclined the heavens,” that is, he humbled those exalted by virtues so that they might descend to endure all things. And because the Lord is in them, he himself descended with them.

Yet “darkness”—that is, those who were dark—was “under his feet,” because although they trampled them outwardly, inwardly they were trampled by them.

Alternatively: He inclined the apostles, making them condescend to our capacity. In this way “darkness,” that is, those who were dark, was “under his feet,” that is, under his affections, and became good. Or: “darkness,” that is, the devil, was trampled underfoot.

“And he ascended upon the cherubim,” although he descended, because what was thought to be a descent was rather an ascent.

But if we read the preceding verses in sequence, saying: “My protector and the horn of my salvation and my receiver,” and because he is my receiver, “I will call upon the Lord while praising him,” and so forth up to this point, “He inclined the heavens,” we shall refer this to Christ’s incarnation and show in what order the preceding events occurred.

God the Father “inclined the heavens,” that is, joined the highest things to the lowest, heavenly things to earthly things, divinity to mortality. And “he descended,” that is, he diminished himself in this manner, “taking the form of a servant” (Philippians II).

And “darkness,” that is, the obscurity of the Scriptures which was in the prophets, was “under his feet,” that is, under the apostles. As it says: “Then he opened their minds so that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke XXIV).

Or: “darkness,” that is, those who had previously been wrapped in the darkness of sins, recognized him and were “under his feet,” that is, under his affections; in other words, they venerated him. Or darkness was under his feet because “the world did not know him” (John I).

Alternatively: “and darkness,” that is, obscurity and incomprehensible light, was “under his feet,” that is, hidden in the flesh—namely, the divinity of the Word.

However this following statement is understood, namely, “And he ascended upon the cherubim,” the sequence is as follows: “I said, He inclined the heavens and descended; and yet, although he descended in his humanity, through his divinity he ascended upon the cherubim,” that is, he was exalted and incomprehensible. And he was inaccessible light to those who were cherubim, that is, full of knowledge. For the closer one approaches him, the farther he withdraws; the more he is known, the more he is unknown.

“He ascended upon the cherubim,” that is, he transcended all the knowledge and thought of the perfect. And to show how inaccessible was his withdrawal, he says: “He flew,” that is, he raised himself on high—not once, but, so that it might be said how often and how far, “he flew upon the wings of the winds,” [Col. 0228C] that is, above the agility of all spirits. For no spirit is so swift that it can comprehend him, whether it be a soul or an angel.

Alternatively: He was exalted above the fullness of knowledge, so that no one reaches him except through charity. For “the fullness of the law is charity” (Romans XIII).

And lest anyone wish to represent him through bodily images, he presents him as incomprehensible. “He flew,” I say, “upon the wings of the winds,” that is, upon the twin wings of charity or of the virtues of holy souls. Although these are lifted into the airs of freedom, the knowledge of the Godhead remains incomprehensible to them. For his charity surpasses the charity of all, and his virtue surpasses every virtue.

“He made darkness his hiding place,” that is, he made them dark so that he might secretly work the salvation of his own within them. Thus: “Assyria is the rod of my fury” (Isaiah X), yet it did not know this.

And although he worked secretly in those who were dark, nevertheless “his tabernacle is around him,” that is, those who tabernacle with him and serve as his soldiers are around him; that is, they know that he works openly, and through them he himself works openly.

And it was necessary that he work openly through those who tabernacled with him, that is, through the apostles, because “the water in the clouds of the air was dark before the brightness in his sight.” That is, obscure doctrine was present in the prophets who contained the air—that is, the apostles. For the apostles stand within their doctrine.

The doctrine of the prophets was obscure in comparison with the brightness in his sight, that is, in comparison with that splendor and manifestation which occurs for those who are in his sight, that is, for those who saw and knew him, such as the apostles.

Alternatively: He made human hearts, which are dark because they are not seen, his hiding place, so that he might lie hidden in them through secret hope. And therefore “his tabernacle is around him,” that is, those who tabernacle with him serve him openly.

Alternatively: He made darkness his hiding place, that is, he wished to lie hidden in the obscurities of the mysteries. Yet “his tabernacle is around him,” that is, those who tabernacle with him turn toward him and recognize that he is truly present in those mysteries, or that he truly works in them through those mysteries.

And because he said, “His tabernacle is around him,” lest anyone suppose that he would obtain no other clarification than this—namely, that he possesses God through the mysteries—he adds: “The water in the clouds of the air is dark,” that is, also in the air, namely the apostles, and in the clouds of the air, namely the prophets.

“The water is dark,” that is, doctrine. For no one is able to praise or explain him in words as he truly is. It is “before the brightness,” that is, in comparison with that brightness, namely the splendor that will be in his sight, that is, in the vision of him, when “we shall see him as he is” (I John III), and when “the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew XIII).

According to the earlier interpretation, where we said that “he inclined the heavens,” that is, the heavenly things, and that God, having become human, descended, we can say: “He made darkness his hiding place,” that is, the obscure Scriptures. “His tabernacle is around him,” that is, those who were around him and saw him, such as the apostles, were his tabernacle; that is, they served him openly and taught him openly.

It is as though he said: This incarnation and manifestation of his did not occur suddenly, because the water—that is, the doctrine—of this manifestation was in the clouds of the air, even though it was dark, that is, obscure. For in this saying there is truth: “One is he who sows, and another who reaps” (John IV). “Others have labored, and you have entered into their labors.” The prophets sowed Christ and the institutions of the Church; the apostles, however, reaped.

“The clouds passed over.” It is as though he said: Through those who tabernacled with him, that is, through the apostles, “the clouds passed over,” that is, the prophecies were transferred from the Jews to the Gentiles. Or: “the clouds passed over,” that is, the obscurity of the Scriptures was revealed.

Jerome: “Before the brightness in his sight,” that is, before the splendor of the Spirit whom they received when they saw him. “The clouds,” that is, the apostles, “passed over” from the Jews to the Gentiles, with the Holy Spirit leading them.

“There was hail in them,” that is, terror and a threat of future punishment, crushing human vices. “And coals of fire,” that is, those who were burning, setting human hearts aflame toward remorse for lower things and desire for higher things.

It is as though he said: This did not come from the apostles themselves, because “the Lord thundered from heaven,” that is, from the apostles. He explains what he meant by “thundered”: “And the Most High,” namely, he who flew upon the wings of the winds, “gave his voice,” not theirs. For “it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew X). He “thundered,” that is, preached with terror. In that voice there were hail and coals of fire.

He himself gave his voice. “And he sent his arrows,” that is, the apostles or evangelists. [Col. 0230A] He himself sent them, not they themselves. Or “arrows,” that is, his words. “And he scattered them,” namely, those to whom they were sent. For some were pierced by arrows unto death, others unto life: “To some we are the aroma of death unto death, to others the aroma of life unto life” (I Corinthians II).

Or: “He scattered them,” namely, those whom he sent. For he sent them throughout the whole world (Mark XVI).

“He multiplied flashes of lightning,” that is, miracles, as in: “God working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (ibid.). And he troubled those to whom they were sent, that is, he moved them to remorse and repentance.

“And then the springs of waters appeared,” that is, the apostles and evangelists, in whom there were waters, namely the various gifts of the Holy Spirit. They appeared, that is, they preached openly concerning Christ. And through them “the foundations of the world,” that is, the writings of the prophets on which the whole world—that is, the Church—was founded, were revealed, that is, uncovered and opened.

Or: “hidden waters,” namely the writings of the prophets; “springs of waters,” their interpreters, appeared at that time, such as Augustine, Jerome, and others. And through them “the foundations of the world” were revealed, as above.

Or: “springs of waters,” that is, those reborn through the waters of baptism.

And all these things, O Lord, were done “at your rebuke,” for you rebuked them with a salutary rebuke: “O foolish ones and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken” (Luke XXIV)!

Alternatively: I said that the Lord sent his arrows and troubled them; he multiplied flashes of lightning and troubled them. But this was done “at your rebuke,” O Lord—not by the arrows, not by the flashes of lightning, but by [Col. 0230C] the inspiration of the spirit of your anger, because you inspired them with that Spirit who would make your anger known to them, so that they might begin from fear: “Lord, from fear of you we have conceived” (Isaiah XXVI).

“He sent from on high and took me.” If we understand there the dispensation of Christ’s incarnation, where it says, “He inclined the heavens and descended,” let us understand this in the following way, as though all these things were accomplished in this manner.

God the Father sent the Holy Spirit from on high, that is, from heaven or from his exaltedness, “and took”—that is, my body. And in this way he assumed me, that is, my people, “from many waters,” as above.

This is how he assumed me: “He rescued me from my strongest enemies”—from the Jews in the Passion, and from the devil and his angels in hell. They were “strongest,” because they handed me over to death. Strong is he who takes away what belongs to us; stronger, he who wounds us ourselves; strongest, he who kills.

“And from those who hated me,” in the body, namely those who persecuted many out of hatred for me. For many hated me even though they had not seen me.

And it was necessary that he rescue me, because “they were strengthened against me,” that is, they prevailed over me in the flesh.

If we refer this to Christ: “from those who hated me,” that is, from those who had no other reason to be my enemies except hatred alone. That they hated me is shown by this: “they were strengthened,” that is, they rose up against me with one accord.

He shows how they were strengthened: “They forestalled me,” that is, they prevailed over me outwardly, “on the day of my affliction,” that is, at the time appointed for my Passion, which was useful to me, not to them.

They forestalled me on the day of affliction, but they will not forestall me on the day of glorification.

And this is because “the Lord became my protector” (Psalm LXXV), in the head and in the members. By protecting me, he led me, the head, into breadth—namely, the breadth of the Gentiles—because I was previously known only in Judaea, but after death in all the nations. Or he protected my members in this way, so that they would not be called away.

He led me in them, and me in them. He led me—that is, he led me beyond the narrowness of the flesh, through hope, into the breadth of future recompense, where there will be no narrowness. Or here he led me into the breadth of charity, so that I might even love my enemies.

In this way he led me, the head, into the breadth of the Gentiles: “He saved me,” by raising me from the dead.

Or he led my members into breadth in this way: he saved me as their head, because he willed it, not because of my merit. For he loved me when I was ugly, in order to make me beautiful. His will preceded mine.

And yet, although everything was theirs by grace, “the Lord will repay me on the day of glorification according to my righteousness,” that is, according to my humility and obedience, although it is nevertheless not my own. “And according to the purity of my hands he will repay me,” that is, according to the innocence of my works. That is true innocence which harms neither itself nor anyone else.

He demonstrates that righteousness: “For I have kept the ways of the Lord,” that is, his commandments, “and I have not acted impiously against my God.”

I kept them in this way, by contrast. I kept them because “all his judgments were before my eyes,” that is, in my mind. In all my works I always considered his judgments, which are four: two concerning the present and two concerning the future—chastisements for those being corrected, temptations for those being tested, rewards for the righteous, and punishment for the wicked.

And it is evident in this way that I kept his righteousness, that is, his commandments: I did not reject them from myself.

The righteousness of Christ is one thing, and that of human beings another. Christ’s righteousness is to suffer for others, as it says: “It was fitting that he who was to lead many sons into the glory of the Father, the author of their salvation, should be perfected through suffering” (Hebrews II).

Up to this point Christ has spoken only about himself, beginning at the words: “And the Lord will repay me.” Now he speaks about the members.

“And I shall be in my members with him in this way: because I am immaculate.” Note that he did not say “without sin,” but “immaculate,” that is, without criminal sin. Whoever commits such sin is not with him.

And this is not merely for a time, but “I shall keep myself from my iniquity,” that is, I shall persevere in my innocence. [Col. 0231D] And therefore “the Lord will repay me in my members according to my righteousness,” as above.

“In the sight of his eyes.” This righteousness and purity were not for human praise, but in God’s sight, so that he alone might see their extent with respect to merit. Or: “He will repay me in the sight of his eyes,” that is, when I shall see him face to face, not through a mirror (I Corinthians XIII).

And truly you will repay, because “with the holy you will be holy”: you, holy by nature, will be holy with him who will be holy by grace. Your holiness precedes his holiness in him and works in him. Therefore I know that you will crown the work of your mercy. The same interpretation applies in the other cases, up to: “And with the perverse you will act perversely”—not that you make him perverse, but his perversity, namely his turning away from you, will cause you to turn from mercy to judgment, as in Leviticus: “If you walk perversely against me, I also will walk against you with a perverse fury” (Leviticus XXVI).

Alternatively: Truly he will repay me—that is, my members—with their merit according to my righteousness, and this in the future, that is, in your sight. For here “with the holy he will be holy,” that is, the holy one will have you as holy; and “with the innocent” he will have you as innocent. And “with the one first chosen by you,” as in: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John XV), “you will be chosen,” that is, he will choose from among all.

“With the perverse you will act perversely,” that is, the perverse person will have you as perverse—especially the Jewish people. Although they worshiped one God and had received his commandments, when they saw a Gentile being admitted, who had always worshiped idols, they said: “The way of the Lord is not fair” [Col. 0232B] (Ezekiel XVIII).

Therefore the perverse Jewish people regard you as perverse, because you will save the humble people and humble the eyes of the proud. That is, because you resist the proud, as in the case of the Jews, and give grace to the humble (James IV), as in the case of the Gentiles, you will humble the eyes of the proud, because they see nothing except through another.

Or it appears perverse to the perverse, that is, to those who are ignorant of true righteousness, that you will save those who confess their sins, whom they customarily condemn.

And because you will save the humble people—namely, those who confess their sins to you and accuse themselves, setting you forth as just—therefore, O Lord my God, “enlighten my darkness,” that is, make me see and recognize my sins and ignorance with my inner eye.

For this reason I ask this of you and not of another, because you enlighten “my lamp,” that is, the eye of the inner person, namely the intellect. For just as a lamp does not shine by itself but receives light from elsewhere, so the inner intellect does not see what is right unless it receives it from your light.

According to another interpretation, the sequence is as follows: Because “with the holy you will be holy,” that is, no one can be holy without you, the Holy One, therefore, O Lord my God, “enlighten my darkness,” that is, the Gentiles, who are still darkness. Through my predestination, enlighten them; by calling them to faith, give them knowledge of you. For you, and no other, enlighten “my lamp,” that is, those who have already been enlightened, the apostles and the other faithful.

Therefore I ask this of you because it belongs to you to accomplish it—namely, because you will save the humble people, specifically the Gentiles, who humble themselves and confess their sins.

It should be noted that he uses “lamp” in the singular but “darkness” in the plural. This is because all who shine shine by one light, whereas those who err err through different errors.

Therefore I ask you to enlighten the eyes that are still in darkness, or to make them recognize their sins, because through you, O God, and not through another, I shall be delivered from temptation, that is, from the spirit of lust and avarice.

“And in my Lord,” not in idols, “I shall pass over a wall” in my members—the wall which pride has erected between the creature and the Creator by adding sins to sins. I shall cross it through humility, submitting myself to my Creator.

“No one comes to me unless my Father draws him” (John VI).

Or: I, the head, shall be delivered in you, the Father, from the temptation of the Jews; and in my God, that is, in my Creator, not in gods made by human hands, I shall cross the wall in those who are destined to be mine.

And this is what follows: “My God the Creator,” who alone can, “will rescue me from the contradictions of the people,” namely the Jewish people, which always contradicted me: “This man is not from God” (John IX); and: “You have a demon” (ibid.). Some said, “He is good”; others said, “No” (John VII).

“And you will establish me as head of the nations,” so that they may have me as their head. In place of one Judaea, O God, you will give me the nations.

And you who hear me call him my God, make him your God as well. Therefore his way is undefiled—the way by which he came to you, that is, through my incarnation without the admixture of a man; or the faith by which one comes to him, which is undefiled because it makes people undefiled.

“And because the words of the Lord are tested by fire,” that is, pure and cleansed by the Holy Spirit, because he produced words that make those who receive them tested, that is, purified; and because he is the protector of all who hope in him, therefore hope in him.

This too can be read in sequence, so that it is said thus: Truly I shall cross the wall in my God—God by nature, mine by grace—because my God is the protector of all who hope in him, that is, of those who have him as their God.

It is rightly in him that one must hope, because his way is undefiled, whether the way by which he came to us, namely charity, or the way by which one comes to him, namely faith. It is not defiled, as is the way of false gods. “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Romans VI).

And because “the words of the Lord are tested by fire,” that is, pure and true—as the words of false gods are not—for the Holy Spirit is a consuming fire which tested them: “Discipline will flee deceit” (Hebrews XII; Wisdom I).

Or “tested by fire,” that is, tested in tribulations. In this way he is the protector of all who hope in him. And he can rightly do this.

For what other God is Lord by re-creation besides the Lord—the one by whose grace we were reborn? Or what other God is God by creation besides our God? Is it this one or another? But there is no other, as I show by the following:

“The God who girded me with strength” is Lord by re-creation; he girded me, the head, with strength, that is, with virtuous apostles. “I live,” says the Lord, “because you will be clothed with all these things as with a garment” (Isaiah XLIX).

“And he made my way immaculate,” that is, without crime—namely, the way of my people.

Alternatively: “He girded me with strength,” that is, my members, who were unstable through various errors of unbelief or through carnal pleasures. He girded them with strength, that is, with sobriety, which restrains these things.

Alternatively: In addition to the other virtues he was going to give, “he girded me,” that is, my members, “with strength,” namely faith, which must be called strength in a singular way because of its excellence and dignity, since it is the foundation of the other virtues.

Or: He girded me with that strength which was singularly necessary for such a girding. For it belongs principally to faith that those who are unstable through various errors of unbelief should be confined by it. Hence elsewhere: “Faith shall be the girdle of his loins” (Isaiah XI).

“And he made,” that is, established in an orderly and firm manner, “my way immaculate,” that is, charity, which does not admit within itself the stain of any grave sin, which excludes all vices and admits all virtues, and by which I might come to him securely. Hence in the Song of Songs: “He ordered charity in me” (Song II).

Or: “with strength,” that is, continence, which would restrain the broad folds of desire, lust, and the other vices. In this it appears that he alone is God by re-creation, and therefore rightly to be loved.

And he is my God who “made my feet perfect,” that is, made my apostles perfect in virtue and knowledge. Of them it is said: “Blessed are the feet that carry peace” (Isaiah LII). He made them “like the feet of deer,” so that they might leap over the mud and thorns of this life, as the Apostle says: “I consider all things as refuse” (Philippians V).

“And establishing me upon high places,” that is, he made my apostles such that it was not enough for them to have neglected all earthly things and to live a heavenly life; but, what is greatest, with the gaze of their reason fixed upon the highest good, they looked upon it with unshaken eyes. Thus blessed John, leaping beyond all things, said: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I).

Or: He “made my feet perfect,” that is, the affections of my members, in virtues, so that they might be like the feet of deer, as above. “And establishing me upon high places,” that is, he fixed their anchor of hope in heavenly things.

And he is the true God who “teaches my hands for battle,” that is, my workers, namely my apostles, who serve as my soldiers. Those whom he calls feet he calls hands as well, using a different comparison, as in: “Be strong in battle, and fight against the ancient serpent” (I Peter V; Revelation XX).

“And you made my arms like a bronze bow,” that is, inflexible and unyielding—the same teachers, who may be called arms because by preaching they embraced the whole earth.

Sacred Scripture often takes its comparison from what is impossible, as here: a bronze bow is not found, but if one could be found, such would they be.

Alternatively: “He who teaches my hands,” that is, the works of my people, “for battle,” that is, who teaches my members to act in such a way that they can fight against the devil’s snares: “For our struggle is not against flesh and blood” (Ephesians VI).

Hence he teaches them in this way: “Stand therefore, girding your loins with charity and putting on the breastplate of righteousness” (ibid.).

“And you made my arms like a bronze bow,” that is, you made the good intentions of my members unyielding, by comparison, because arms are extended, and so are intentions.

And so that I would not fail, you gave me the protection of your salvation—namely in this way: “Your right hand received me in my members.”

“Your right hand,” that is, your dignity and propitiation, assumed my humanity; or “right hand,” that is, your help. This is apparent because “your discipline corrected me unto the end,” that is, your chastisement and scourging—your rod or staff, namely the removal of possessions, illness, or tribulation inflicted by others—corrected me, that is, my members, whenever they withdrew from your commandments, “unto the end,” that is, unto me, who am their end, namely the completion of their life, so that they might learn to be conformed to me.

Or he corrected my members unto the end, lest by living wantonly and wickedly they should fail to reach that appointed prize. “For whom the Father loves, he disciplines” (Proverbs III).

Hence the Apostle says: “All discipline at the present time seems not to be of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, it yields the most peaceful fruit” (Hebrews XII).

And your discipline itself will teach me to persevere and to reach the appointed end. Note that not only your right hand—that is, your clemency—teaches me to reach the appointed end, but scourging does so as well.

And in that discipline “you enlarged my steps,” that is, the apostles, through whom I walk into the knowledge of human beings. You enlarged them, that is, you placed them inwardly in such breadth that they even loved their enemies or rejoiced in tribulation.

Yet they were “beneath me,” that is, they had me as their teacher and predecessor, just as when Peter wished to go ahead and said to his teacher Christ, who foretold his Passion, “Lord, let it be far from you,” the Lord answered him: “Get behind me, Satan” (Matthew XVI).

And because they are beneath me, “my footsteps were not weakened in them,” because they imitated me in all things: “As the Father sent me, I also send you” (John VI).

Alternatively: “You enlarged my steps beneath me,” that is, you placed the carnal affections of my members in such breadth—that is, in such joy—that in tribulations they rejoiced with their superior, so that neither the flesh resisted the spirit nor the spirit the flesh. And in this way “my footsteps were not weakened,” that is, my imitators, or my commandments, did not fail.

“And through them I shall pursue my enemies,” namely unbelievers, with a good persecution, or carnal affections. “And I shall seize them so that they may follow me,” although previously they wished to go ahead.

“And I shall not turn back until they fail,” that is, until carnal affections are subjected to the spirit, or until persecutors become imitators.

“I shall crush them”—the persecutors: I shall kill what they are and make them what I am. Or I shall crush carnal affections, that is, by afflicting the flesh I shall diminish it so greatly that they will be subjected to the affections of the spirit.

“They will fall beneath my feet,” either because persecutors will be trampled by my members, or because they will be under their dominion.

“And you will trample the lion and the dragon,” or carnal affections will be subjected to reason.

And this is not from me but from you, because “you girded me with strength for battle.” Strength—that is, with the virtuous; or: you girded me, that is, my members, with strength, namely temperance, which above all restrains carnal affections.

And through them, or in this way, “you gave me the back of my enemies,” so that those who refused to be converted might become turned away, or a back—that those who previously wished to go ahead might follow.

“And you destroyed those who hate me,” that is, those unwilling to be converted and remaining in their wicked hatred. Or outwardly, in the time of Titus and Vespasian; or inwardly, so that none of their desires would be fulfilled.

This is evident from the fact that “they cried out, and there was no one who saved them.” For the Jews cry out daily with intense desire for salvation, but they are not saved because they do not believe in the Savior.

They cried out to God the Father, and he did not hear them because they do not cry out through the Mediator.

Or they will cry out in the future, placed in punishments, to be delivered, but they will not be saved, because the Savior cried out to them here and they refused to hear.

“Whoever is ashamed of me before human beings, I also will be ashamed of him before my Father” (Luke IX).

“And I shall crush them,” namely those who were not heard, “like dust before the face of the wind.” Their pride will destroy them. Or, dry and deprived of the rain of the word of God, I shall hand them over to the winds, that is, to various pleasures, so that whatever solidity was in them may be reduced by those winds.

“Like the mud of the streets I shall wipe them out.” I shall wipe out those who have been so crushed, like the mud of the streets. Just as mud lying in the streets, that is, on broad roads, is trampled by people and gives off a stench, so I shall cause them to be trampled by everyone.

And I shall be able to do this, for “you will rescue me from the contradictions of the people” and “establish me as head of the nations,” as above.

And rightly so, because “the people whom I did not know served me”: the Gentile people whom I did not know—that is, whom I did not cause to know me through bodily presence or instruction in the law—obeyed me.

“By the hearing of the ear they obeyed me,” although they had seen neither miracles nor my presence.

By comparison he shows that these are to be chosen and those rejected. “But the sons”—the Jews, whom I had as sons and to whom I promised an inheritance—were “aliens,” that is, of the devil. Of them it was said: “You are from your father …”

You are of the devil (John VIII). They lied when they said, “This is the son of Joseph” (Matthew XIII; John VI), or, “The disciples came and stole him” (Matthew XXVIII)—for me, that is, for my advantage.

The sons of strangers have grown old: that is, they remained in the oldness of the first man, unwilling to be conformed to my newness. They have grown old because they have limped from their paths, that is, they have limped through their own wicked devices, having neither a right foot, nor spiritual understanding in the Law, nor Christ in faith in the Trinity. They limped, and they thought to destroy me; but the Lord—that is, I—lives. [Col. 0236C] Hence the Apostle says: “He died through the weakness of the flesh, but he lives through the power of God” (II Corinthians XIII).

Therefore, “Blessed be my God”—that is, may he be increased through me and thus exalted through me, that is, may he appear great—the God of my salvation. In this manner let him be exalted: “He who magnifies the salvations of his king,” that is, he who causes the salvations granted through me, his king, to increase, in this manner: “And who shows mercy to his anointed one, David,” by raising him, “and to his seed,” that is, his imitators, by raising them and inwardly leading them from this resurrection even unto eternity (II Samuel XXII).

Rightly, then, you are to be blessed by me, because you are the God who gives me vengeance against the Jewish people by subjecting them to me; or, you are the one who gives mine the power of binding and loosing, as in: “Behold, I give you power [Col. 0236D] to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke X).

You are my deliverer from my enraged enemies: from the Jews crying out to me, “Crucify, crucify!” (Luke XXIII); the Church, from heretics; and each member of the Church, from vices. And you not only deliver me, but you exalt me above those who rise up against me, placing me at your right hand, where they can do nothing. Finally, you will rescue me from the wicked man, that is, from the devil—that is, you will rescue my people—by turning them from unbelief to faith.

Therefore I will confess to you, namely, on account of that deliverance; I will praise you, or I will make confession of sins to you, in those who are still nations—that is, born, but not reborn. And I will sing a psalm, that is, I will devote myself to good works, to your name, that is, for your praise, not [Col. 0237A] mine, because you give both the willing and the doing according to good will (Philippians II).

“He who magnifies the salvations” continues through that verse: “May the God of my salvation be exalted,” as was said above.

# Psalm XVIII. For the End. A Psalm of David.

> “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands. Day pours forth the word to day, and night makes knowledge known to night. There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard. Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. In the sun he has placed his tabernacle, and he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber, rejoiced like a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the summit of heaven. [Col. 0237B] And his circuit reaches to its summit, and there is no one who can hide himself from his heat. The law of the Lord is spotless, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to the simple. The ordinances of the Lord are right, gladdening hearts; the commandment of the Lord is radiant, enlightening the eyes. The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever; the judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves. More desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. Indeed, your servant keeps them; in keeping them there is great reward. Who understands transgressions? Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others. If they do not rule over me, then I shall be blameless, and I shall be cleansed from the greatest transgression. And the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart shall be pleasing [Col. 0237C] in your sight always. Lord, my helper and my redeemer.”

## Exposition

“For the End. A Psalm of David”: that is, this good exhortation, which is understood in this psalm, belongs to David the prophet directing unbelievers, especially the Jews, to the End—that is, to the grace of Christ, who is the end and consummation of the Law and the Prophets. The Prophet’s purpose in this psalm is to commend to everyone, and especially to the Jews, the grace of the New Testament, brought to completion through Christ: “For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1). Thus believers may be saved, while unbelievers are condemned all the more severely the more fully it has been made known to them. He commends this grace by its preachers, by the distinction within its preaching, and by the breadth of that preaching, since it is in all languages and throughout the whole earth. He also commends it by amplification, comparing it with the old law administered through a servant.

“The heavens declare the glory of God.” As though he were saying: The outward heavens declared it when a new star appeared at the Lord’s birth (Matthew 2), and when the heavens were opened above him and a voice was heard: “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3). To you Jews they declared the glory of God—that is, the Son of God, in whom God the Father appeared glorious. And not only those outward heavens, but also certain inward heavens, whose soul is the seat of God, who [Col. 0238A] will have been raised in mind from earthly things to heavenly things. Such heavens declare—that is, they will clearly proclaim—the glory of God, namely this: that he saved us not on account of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy. And this is the great glory of God. “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely” (Romans 3). This, then, is what it means to declare the glory of God: the mercy displayed through the Son, in which God is to be glorified.

“And the firmament proclaims the work of his hands.” What above was called “glory” is here called “work”; what above was called “heavens” is here called “firmament,” by a different comparison. That is, they are the same preachers of the New Testament, confirmed in heart by the Holy Spirit and made a firmament against the attacks of those who rage and reject this glory. They proclaim the work of his hands—that is, God’s own works, works that no one could perform except God alone.

And they make this proclamation with great discrimination, because “day pours forth the word to day.” That is, the perfect proclaim the divinity of the Word to the perfect with great meditation—that is, wisdom. Now “day” means those who have been enlightened by Christ, the true sun, as in the saying: “The sun of righteousness has risen for us” (Malachi 4). One day pours forth the word to another, because pouring forth proceeds from the inward parts and signifies teaching produced with great meditation and inward reflection. “Pour forth” is rightly joined to “the Word,” that is, to divinity, specifically to wisdom, because wisdom is knowledge of divine things. Hence the Apostle says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Corinthians 2). One of those who poured forth this wisdom was the man who said: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1).

“And night makes knowledge known to night.” That is, the imperfect reveal Christ’s humanity simply to the imperfect. It is called “knowledge” because knowledge concerns human things. Hence the Apostle says: “For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2). The imperfect are called “night,” because the true sun has not yet risen upon them; they are not yet able to grasp the height of divinity. Such people do not pour forth the word, but they make knowledge known—that is, they display it in simple words: the incarnation of the Word.

Alternatively, it may be said that those same people who, as day, pour forth the word to day, accommodate themselves to the little ones of the Church and, having become night, make knowledge known to night. Hence the saying: “I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able to receive solid food” (1 Corinthians 3).

They make this proclamation in the fullness of all languages. “There are no languages”—that is, tongues—“or speeches”—that is, varieties within those languages—whose voices are not heard by the preachers of the New Testament. More precisely, their speeches appear to be their own, not foreign languages. Each of the apostles possessed all languages. This signified that the one whom they preached, the one Christ, was to be gathered from all peoples speaking all languages.

And because they knew all languages, “their sound”—that is, their preaching—“has gone out into all the earth,” that is, throughout the whole extent of the earth. It rightly says “has gone out,” because they first preached in Judaea. Hence the saying: “Beginning from Jerusalem, which is in the middle of the earth” (Luke 24). For there he was born, there he suffered, and there he was first preached.

“And to the ends of the world,” that is, to the neighboring islands, “their words.”

Alternatively: “There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard.” As though he were saying: They did not declare those languages, or the glory of God in those languages, only where they had learned them after being taught by the Holy Spirit, who appeared to them in the form of fire, intending to consume the hay of their flesh and test their gold. Rather, “their sound has gone out into all the earth.”

Alternatively: “Into all the earth,” that is, into all who have been called and initiated into the Church’s sacraments. “Their sound has gone out,” that is, the preaching which was sound to them, because they received it only with the bodily ear and not with the ear of the heart, which is the ear for hearing. Such people are called merely “earth.”

And not only “throughout the world,” that is, to the perfect, who have already withdrawn in mind from earthly things, but also “to the ends of the world,” that is, to the more excellent, to the more excellent. Their words became words to those who received them with the ear of the heart and fulfilled them in action.

I say “their,” meaning those who say: “God has placed his tabernacle in the sun,” that is, his flesh, in which for a time he served God the Father. He placed it “in the sun,” that is, in the manifestation of good works, because he healed the weak, raised the dead, and justified sinners. Hence, by contrast: “Whoever loves darkness hates the light.” Or “in the sun,” that is, in labor, as an example to his followers.

Alternatively: the “tabernacle,” that is, the Church in which he serves, he placed “in the sun,” as above.

And, in order to provide his Church with an example of good works and labor, “he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber.” He resembles a bridegroom who, coming out of his bridal chamber—that is, his marriage bed—walks forth adorned with various ornaments. So Christ came forth from the womb of blessed Mary, in which, by assuming our flesh, he joined to himself his bride, the Church, adorned with every virtue and especially with humility, by which he was to destroy the enemy’s pride.

Thus adorned, “he rejoiced,” that is, he went forth joyfully, “like a giant,” that is, like a strong man, “to run his course,” not to be held back on the way. In humility through love he was beneath all; in majesty, however, he was above all. His love and humility did not allow him to be delayed, so that he would disdain to suffer the body’s indignities and degradations. But the power of his divinity did not permit him to be held in death or to fear any adversity. Therefore he ran along the way; he was not detained on the way.

He then adds what this way was: “His going forth is from the summit of heaven,” that is, the Word proceeds from the Father, who may be called the highest heaven—not in the essence of majesty, which is one in the three persons, but in the order by which he wished to make himself known to human beings.

The first heaven is the Father, and the highest, because from him proceeds the Son—that is, the will through which he works all things. This will is not something other than the Father in essence, for in God there is no diversity and no accident.

The second heaven is the Word proceeding from the Father.

The third heaven is love, that is, the affection and concord of the Father’s will, because his will is never changed or opposed to him.

“And his circuit reaches to its summit.” Thus the Word itself, in a certain manner, proceeded from the Father when, in the flesh he assumed, he manifested himself, so that he found nothing meeting him—that is, equal to him—except his summit, from which he had gone forth, namely the Father.

“His going forth is from the summit of heaven,” that is, from the Father, “and his circuit reaches to its summit,” that is, he found nothing that could meet him until he returned to the equality of the Father. He returned, however, having appropriately received what was proper to him.

Alternatively: “The heavens declare the glory of God.” What glory? “In the sun he placed his tabernacle.” The passage may also be connected in this way: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” Therefore it is clear that he placed his tabernacle—that is, his Church—in the sun, that is, in the open and in the broad expanse, not in some hidden corner of the earth, not in secret, as certain heretics say.

This is directed against certain heretics who say: “Look, Christ is with us; come over to us.” This interpretation is according to Augustine.

“And there is no one who can hide himself from his heat.” Up to this point the words were those of the apostles; now the Prophet returns to his own words. As though he were saying: Because he is so powerful and has been preached so openly, there is no one who can hide himself—that is, excuse himself—from his heat, that is, from knowledge of him or from his gift.

Just as a great fire is hot and shines, so Christ is hot, because there is no one who does not possess some gift of his grace by which he can recognize him—not even a pagan. No one can excuse himself concerning knowledge, because no one is empty of a gift. “For his invisible attributes may be perceived through the things that have been made, being understood by the reason given to human beings” (Romans 1).

And it is no wonder that no one can excuse himself regarding this glory or claim that he cannot understand or observe it, because “the law of the Lord”—that is, the law of grace, which is Christ and his commandments—has been given. “For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1).

That law of the Lord is “spotless,” that is, it makes people spotless, whereas the law of the servant was stained because, through its difficulty, it made people transgressors. It could command, but it could not give assistance for fulfillment. Here, by amplification, he commends the new law by comparing it with the old.

It is truly spotless because it converts souls from slavery to freedom, from fear to love: “I will no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15).

Alternatively, the law of the servant converted the hand or eye through fear; this law converts souls from illicit love.

“The testimony of the Lord is faithful,” because it does not deceive. For it bears witness to nothing that is not true. The testimony of the servant was unfaithful because it often deceived—though this resulted from a carnal misunderstanding of the Old Testament. For that law in itself is from the Lord, holy, spotless, and does not deceive.

“I will give you this land and your offspring” (Genesis 15): they understood this carnally, and therefore were deceived. Many of them did not see it, and many other such things happened.

He calls the same thing both “law” and “testimony”: it is law because it restrains; testimony because of its promises. In this way it is faithful.

“Giving wisdom to the simple,” that is, teaching them to know and wisely perform all that I have heard from my Father and made known to them. “No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matthew 11). “To the simple” means to the humble.

“I confess to you, Lord Father, because you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to the simple” (Luke 10). The testimony of the servant was unfaithful because it hid these things from the simple. Hence the Lord says: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who possess the keys of wisdom; you yourselves do not enter, nor do you permit others to enter” (Matthew 23).

“The ordinances of the Lord are right”: his justifications, which he teaches, are right, because whatever he commands others to do, he himself does; he commands by word what he urges by example. But the servant often teaches what he either cannot or does not wish to do.

“For they bind heavy and unbearable burdens and place them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves are unwilling to move them with their finger” (ibid.).

“Gladdening hearts,” because they teach people to perform good works through love, not through fear.

“The commandment of the Lord”—that is, the New Testament—“is radiant,” without the veil of carnal observances. Hence the saying: “And not as Moses, who used to veil his face” (2 Corinthians 3). It enlightens the eyes of the inner person.

“The fear of the Lord is chaste”: it does not fear approaching him as a servant, but fears departing from him as a son. It is “holy,” that is, sanctifying.

The fear of the servant, however, inflicts punishment. “Enduring for ever and ever”: it does not perish like that punitive fear which love casts out.

“The judgments of the Lord are true,” assigning to each according to his works. For what is once just with him is never changed; and conversely, what is once unjust never becomes just. They are therefore true—that is, unchangeable—because they are justified in themselves.

Human judgments are often unjust because they are justified by something external. Often one person judges something unjustly, and another, who knows better, corrects it. But the Lord’s judgments are always true because they are not justified by anything external.

“For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Romans 11). “Or who has first given to him, so that he might be repaid?”

Those judgments are desirable above much precious gold and much precious stone, or above many desirable things; and they are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. That is, they are better than all the precious and pleasant things of this world.

Alternatively, if we wish to dwell on the matter more deeply: Blessed Paul says, “If anyone has built upon this foundation with gold and precious stones, he will be saved” (1 Corinthians 3). These are the gold and precious stones that, having been purified and tested, await being carried into God’s treasury.

These people desire the judgments of God above gold and precious stone, that is, they love God’s will more than their own, because they prefer his will to their own.

Those are “honey” who, released from the bonds of the flesh—not in reality, but in mind, as in the saying, “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1)—await the day on which they will be carried into God’s banquets.

Those are “the honeycomb” who, surrounded by flesh but not fused with it, await the pressure of the hand of God—not a hand that crushes, but one that presses out—so that they may be drained from temporal life into eternal life. These people have already been so purified inwardly that, although they still live in the world, they can nevertheless easily be separated from its love. They do not need to be pressed in the winepress—that is, under severe affliction—in order to learn to abandon the world.

These people desire the judgments of the Lord above honey and the honeycomb, that is, more than themselves. Or they desire that those judgments come upon them, because they await the Judge without fear.

“These things are desirable by nature to your servant.” Indeed, “your servant keeps them,” that is, the righteous person. Whoever does not keep them does not love them: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John 14).

And rightly so, because “in keeping them there is great reward,” not only in the future but also in the present. Virtue is never without reward, just as vice is never without punishment. One person has here the reward of a good conscience, while another has the punishment that comes from the reward of vices. Either virtue is an empty name, or a man who tests it rightly seeks its reward.

And the Apostle speaks of “thoughts accusing or even defending” (Romans 2). That reward is great, since it exists both here and in the future.

“Your servant keeps them.” And rightly so. For “who understands transgressions,” namely, transgressions that must be guarded against? No one, because even the person who is not your servant does not understand them.

Alternatively: “Your servant keeps them because he understands them.” For “who understands transgressions?” No one. If darkness is seen, then transgressions are understood. To see is to withdraw from darkness; to understand is to withdraw from transgression. I speak of those who are in transgressions, just as of those who were in darkness.

Alternatively: “Your servant keeps them.” But those who can understand transgressions and keep your judgments are few. For “who understands transgressions” as they ought to be understood—that is, so as to avoid them? Few; indeed, no one by his own power. Therefore: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults.”

Alternatively: Since your servant keeps them, or since there is great reward in keeping them, “cleanse me from my hidden faults,” that is, from original transgressions, which secretly descend from parents as though by hereditary right. “And from those of others”—that is, from those I did not contract from my parents, namely, from those I later added—“spare your servant,” who did not spare your freedman.

Alternatively: The sin was hidden when the devil sinned, because he possessed pride secretly and from himself. The sin by which Adam fell was “of another,” because Adam had been alien to the devil.

He therefore says: “From my hidden faults”—that is, from evil thoughts—“cleanse me,” that is, cleanse my heart. “And from those of others”—that is, from the evil persuasions of others—“spare me, lest I consent.” “Your servant” means my people, who do not wish to depart from you through pride but wish to submit to you through humility.

Therefore spare your servant, because you did not spare your freedman—that is, Adam—from another’s persuasion. He refused to obey your commands, wishing to be free: “You will be like gods” (Genesis 3).

Therefore I ask you to cleanse me from what is my own and spare me from what belongs to others, because “if they do not rule over me, then I shall be blameless,” that is, free from the criminal sin that stains.

Notice that he does not say, “If they are not in me,” but adds, “rule over me.” For as long as we are in this corruptible body, it is impossible for sin not to be in us. But it rules when we consent to it and subject our will to it. Hence the Apostle says: “Therefore let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Romans 6).

For this reason cleanse me and spare me: so that neither my own evil thoughts may subject me nor the persuasions of others.

“And I shall be cleansed from the greatest transgression,” that is, from pride, which is the greatest transgression. While the other sins are to be feared only in evil deeds, this one must also be guarded against in good deeds. It first thrusts itself upon those who are departing, and it also thrusts itself upon those who are returning.

“And the words of my mouth shall be pleasing,” namely, when I have been cleansed from pride. Then I shall strive to please you with mouth and heart, and not human beings. Pride seeks human glory.

And this is what he says: “And the meditation of my heart in your sight always,” so that you alone may see it and be pleased by it.

“Lord, my helper and my redeemer.” This verse is joined to the words “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, Lord, my helper”; the other words are inserted between them.

He is “helper” in good things and “redeemer” in evil things. Or, he is redeemer through faith and helper by justifying.

# Psalm XIX. For the End. A Psalm of David.

> “May the Lord hear you on the day of tribulation; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you. May he send you help from the sanctuary, and from Zion may he guard you. May he remember all your sacrifice, and may your burnt offering become fat. May he grant you according to your heart, and may he confirm all your counsel. We shall rejoice in your salvation, and in the name of our God we shall be magnified. May the Lord fulfill all your petitions. Now I know that the Lord has saved his anointed. He will hear him from his holy heaven; salvation is in the mighty deeds of his right hand. Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we shall call upon the name of the Lord our God. They are bound and have fallen, but we have risen and stand upright. Lord, save the king, and hear us on the day when we call upon you.”

## Exposition

“For the End. A Psalm of David.” In the preceding psalm the Prophet commended Christ’s passion, by which believers are saved. In this one he commends Christ’s resurrection, by which believers are justified. In the former it is shown what benefit the mortality of divinity brought us; in this one, what benefit the divinity of mortality brought us. For “Jesus Christ died for our transgressions and rose for our justification” (Romans 4).

Foreseeing through the Spirit the future glory of Christ’s resurrection and the resurrection with Christ of all believers, the Prophet pours out prayers to God the Father in the form of a wish—not from any doubt, but from an exceeding desire—speaking as follows:

“May the Lord hear you,” namely, O Christ, because you are my helper and redeemer. May the Lord Father, to whom you display complete obedience, hear you by raising you “on the day of tribulation,” that is, at the time appointed for the Passion.

“May the name of the God of Jacob protect you,” that is, may the invocation of the name of the God of Jacob protect you. Jacob is the younger people, the one who wrestled and seized the birthright from the earlier people, that is, from the Jewish people, namely, the dignity and honor promised to the Jewish people, who were the firstborn because they were chosen before the Gentiles.

“The name of the God of Jacob” means the invocation of the name of the God of Jacob, and not of the God of Esau, who said: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated,” and “the elder shall serve the younger” (Genesis 25; Romans 9). He casts down the powerful and exalts the humble (Luke 1). May he protect you, humble and invoking his name, from the persecution of the proud Jews, just as he protected the humble Jacob, who invoked his name, from the persecutor Esau.

“May he send you help from the sanctuary.” To you—that is, to your people—may he send help from you who are holy.

Or, to you the head may he send help from the sanctuary, that is, from your people, making them holy and sanctifying your members; may he increase your helpers, just as hands and other members are helpers to the head.

“And from Zion”—that is, from the watchtower, namely, from hope of heavenly joys—“may he guard you,” that is, may he watch over you, that is, over your people. Just as there were watchmen of Jerusalem in Zion, so may the hope of heavenly joys be a fortification for your people, from which they may take precautions for themselves.

“May he remember all your sacrifice,” that is, may he cause your people to remember all the injuries you suffered before the gallows of the cross, injuries that were an acceptable sacrifice to God for human sins.

“And may your burnt offering”—by which you wished to offer your entire self to God on the altar of the cross—“become fat,” that is, be changed into the joy of the resurrection, so that just as you died for our sins, you may also rise for our justification.

*Holon* means “whole”; *causton* means “burned.” Hence *holocaust* was the name given to a victim that was entirely burned.

“May he grant you according to your heart,” that is, according to your will, so that you may be able to lay down your soul when you wish and take it up again when you wish—not according to the heart of your enemies.

“And may he confirm all your counsel,” both concerning the rejection of the Jews and the salvation of the Gentiles.

Suppose someone says: Why do you ask so earnestly for Christ’s salvation? The answer is: “We shall rejoice in your salvation.” I and those like me shall rejoice in the salvation of your Christ, because death will no longer rule over him. Here we rejoice in the hope of that same resurrection, already saved inwardly through faith.

“And we shall be magnified” by complete salvation, when this mortal nature has put on immortality. Yet first we shall be magnified “in the name of the Lord our God,” namely, when conformed to him, called Christians from Christ, and made his body.

“May the Lord fulfill all your petitions.” The preceding verse was inserted between the clauses. The present verse contains the wishes.

May the Lord fulfill all your petitions, both those you pour out as a mortal for us and those you will pour out after becoming immortal, seated at the right hand of the Father.

And truly he will fulfill them, because “the Lord will hear him for himself and for his people from his holy heaven,” that is, from the power of his divinity, which is his holy heaven, namely, from the divinity of the Word.

And truly he will hear him, because “the Lord will save his anointed.” And truly this will happen, because I now know—long before it happens—that “the Lord has saved his anointed.”

This is evident from the fact that “the salvation of his right hand”—that is, the salvation to be given to humanity through his right hand, namely through his divinity—“will be in mighty deeds,” that is, exceedingly powerful; it will never be changed into weakness.

And in this way we who are saved will be magnified in the name of the Lord our God. Those who are saved only through the left hand glory in the riches and powers of this world; therefore they are bound in their desire for those things.

Alternatively, according to the order of the text: “May the Lord fulfill all your petitions.” And truly he will fulfill them, because I now know, before it happens, through the Spirit—or “now,” when it was especially needed on the day of tribulation—that “the Lord has saved his anointed,” raising him and placing him at his right hand.

He will also hear him who sits at his right hand “from his holy heaven,” that is, from the sending forth of your Holy Spirit, who is his heaven.

He was heard on earth, so that he might be raised; he was heard in heaven, so that the Holy Spirit might be sent.

And this will be evident from the fact that he will hear him from his holy heaven: “For salvation is in the mighty deeds of his right hand,” that is, the salvation given to us through the Son, who is at his right hand, will be powerful for us—an eternal and unfailing salvation, which is neither afflicted by diseases nor wounded by sorrows.

Or “in mighty deeds” means that even when we are weak, we may then be powerful; the salvation of the right hand is eternal. As it says: “In her right hand are peace and security” (Proverbs 3). The salvation of the left hand is temporal, as in the saying: “In her left hand are riches and glory.”

By saying “He will hear him from heaven,” he shows that the preceding wishes arose not from uncertainty but from the greatest affection.

“Some trust in chariots, and some in horses.” As though he were saying: Those whose salvation is in the left hand glory in the movable things and powers of this world.

“Some call upon you in chariots,” namely, they come to invocation while trusting more in the movable things of this world than in you. Therefore their salvation is not in power but in weakness, not in the right hand but in the left.

“And some in horses,” that is, in pride and dignities. This is drawn from those who, from all Israel, went up to Jerusalem three times a year to pray.

“But we,” to whom you will give the joy of your salvation, “shall call upon the name of the Lord our God,” not upon those things, so that the name of the one who is God by creation and Lord by re-creation may be glorified in us.

Alternatively: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses,” as Esau and his people did. “But we,” namely, the Jacobites who seize their birthright, “shall call upon the name of the Lord our God,” as Jacob did; we shall place our trust in no other.

And rightly so, because “they are bound”—to chariots and horses—by their evil desires or by the ends of their vices.

“And they have fallen,” away from that salvation, because, bound and bent toward earthly things, they cannot raise their minds to heavenly things.

“But we,” who invoke the name of the Lord our God, “have risen,” that is, we shall rise from that inclination of mind—from unbelief to faith—“and we stand upright” through our works.

And, O Lord, so that we may rise and be made upright, “save the king,” raising him and placing him at your right hand. Thus, just as in his Passion he gave us an example of fighting, so at your right hand he may intercede for us, himself both victim and priest.

“Hear us on the day,” that is, in purity of mind, or in the light of faith, on which we call upon you. For you do not hear us in the night.

# Psalm XX. For the End. A Psalm of David.

> “Lord, the king will rejoice in your power, and he will exult greatly in your salvation. You granted him the desire of his heart, and you did not deprive him of the request of his lips. For you came before him with blessings of sweetness; you placed upon his head a crown of precious stone. He asked life from you, and you granted it to him: length of days for ever and ever. Great is his glory in your salvation; you will place glory and great beauty upon him. For you will make him a blessing for ever and ever; you will gladden him with joy in your presence. For the king hopes in the Lord, and through the mercy of the Most High he will not be shaken. Let your hand be found by all your enemies; let your right hand find all who hate you. You will set them like a furnace of fire at the time of your presence; the Lord in his anger will trouble them, and fire will devour them. You will destroy their fruit from the earth, and their offspring from among the children of men. For they have turned evils against you; they have devised plans that they could not establish. For you will make them turn their backs; among the rest you will prepare their faces. Be exalted, Lord, in your power; we shall sing and psalmodize your mighty deeds.”

## Exposition

“For the End. A Psalm of David.” The purpose of this psalm is the same as that of the preceding one. There the Prophet dealt with the resurrection by way of a wish; here, however, he commends the resurrection itself as something that rightly took place. It is joined to the preceding psalm in this way:

I said: “Lord, save the king”—and rightly ought You to save him, because, O Lord Father, the king will rejoice in Your strength, that is, in the Word united to him, which it has from You. He is the King over all kings, who alone rules and alone directs all things, attributing everything to You and presuming nothing of himself, unlike wretched Adam. He will first rejoice in his salvation, and will greatly exult with complete exultation in Your saving work, that is, in the salvation of the human race entrusted to him: joy belongs to the soul, exultation to the body.

And rightly will he exult, because You granted him the desire of his heart. This was his laying down his life when he wished and taking it up again (John 10); or, that he should die because of our sins and rise because of our justification (Romans 4). And You did not deny him the will of his lips, that is, the will for peace and reconciliation given through him to the world. For he made peace between the things in heaven and the things on earth. Hence the Apostle says: “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2). Hence the angels, our fellow citizens—previously enemies, as though transferred into the kingdom of another Lord when he was born who had come to give peace to the world—sing together: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2).

By “lips,” with which we give a kiss—which is a sign of peace—we understand peace. Alternatively: “By the will of his lips,” that is, by his heralds, You did not deny him those who would have the same will toward his Church as he had: to preserve it, to suffer, and to die for it. Hence the Apostle says: “Every day I die for you, brothers” (1 Corinthians 15). Or: “By the will of his lips You did not deny him,” namely, by refusing him the desire of his lips that he should have such heralds as he wished, or that his heralds should attain the same glory in which he is. “Father, I desire that where I am, there my servant also may be” (John 17). Truly, You will not deny him.

For You went before him—or, You will go before him—in blessings of sweetness, that is, in freedom from sin. In Adam all were preceded by the curse; he alone was free among the dead (Psalm 87). You went before him, that is, You first bestowed on him the gifts of grace, so that he might be “the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8), with respect to the younger people of the New Testament. You joined that people to the Head as a body after his experience of death, like a victorious crown upon the head after victory.

Truly he was preceded by these blessings, because he was conceived by the Holy Spirit. Adam was preceded by the fullness of bitterness, in whom all die (1 Corinthians 15); Christ was preceded by blessings of sweetness, in whom all will be made alive. Or, You went before him because no one preceded him who was not previously under the curse; but he was the first in the human race to be free from it, and alone free from every sin.

“You placed upon his head a crown of precious stone.” Because he was preceded by blessings of sweetness—that is, because he overcame the bitterness of death—you placed upon his head, after the victory, a crown of precious stone: that is, You surrounded him with the illustrious order of the precious apostles.

He had said above, “You granted him the desire of his heart,” and he demonstrates this by saying: “He asked life of You, and You granted it to him.” Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more (Romans 4). “Length of days” in this age and in the age of the age—that is, You granted enduring life in his members. Or, You granted length of days in his members because “his kingdom will have no end” (Luke 1).

And in that life “great is his glory in Your salvation,” because You made him sit at Your right hand. Or it is great in this way: not only has he been glorified, but “You will place glory and great splendor upon him,” that is, You will add to him faithful people, glorious through miracles and splendid through virtues. For whoever wishes to remain in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked. Or, You gave him—namely, to the Lordly Man assumed by the Word—the power to glorify his own and to adorn them: to make them glorious in victory and splendid in triumph. In this way You will place these things upon him.

“For You will make him a blessing for ever and ever,” so that through him blessing may be given to all, that is, an increase of every good. For this is not for a time, but for ever and ever. “And at last You will gladden him with joy,” namely, complete joy, when his body is joined to him, “with Your countenance,” that is, when Your presence is made manifest.

And rightly will You make him a blessing, because “the king,” namely, the Lordly Man, hopes in the Lord, not in himself, like Adam, who was given over to the curse. “And in the mercy of the Most High”—that is, he hopes in such a way, both in himself and in his members, that he attributes everything to the mercy of the Most High—and therefore “he will not be moved,” namely, from that hope.

It is as though he said: Those, however, who do not hope in the mercy of the Most High will be moved from that hope, and therefore they will be made not a blessing but a curse. And therefore, O Lord, out of compassion for those who have been moved away from hope and from Your mercy, I desire that Your hand—that is, the help of Your mercy—may be found by all Your enemies, both Jews and Gentiles. Let them seek Your mercy, and they will find it. Hence the Apostle says: “Who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2).

But if they are unwilling to seek You, may Your right hand—that is, vengeance—find all who hate You. And this is spoken prophetically, not as a wish. In this way Your right hand will find them at the future judgment, those who here, in the day of salvation, were unwilling to find the hand of Your mercy.

“You will place them like a furnace of burning fire within their consciences,” when they will see the glory of the children of God and their own disgrace. “Behold, they have been counted among the children of God” (Wisdom 5). Woe to us! What did riches profit? What did boasting profit? “A furnace of fire,” that is, something ignited. A furnace is an oven whose opening is closed so that it may burn within.

“In the time of Your countenance,” that is, of Your presence, which will terrify them. At the time of judgment they will fear Your countenance, those who in the time of grace despised Your hand. And afterward “the Lord, in His anger”—namely, in the great anger proper to Him—“will trouble them,” saying: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25).

And then He will devour them, that is, He will utterly absorb them—not merely inwardly, but soul and body. And not only them, but “You will destroy their fruit,” that is, their works, “from the earth,” from the land of the living. Their works, which had a place here in the land of the dying, will be removed from the land of the living, because the saints, shining like the sun and like pure gold received into God’s treasury, will have nothing that requires purification.

“And their seed,” that is, their imitators, “from the children of men,” that is, from the imitators of those who did not name themselves after them.

And rightly so. “For they turned evils upon You”—the evils they feared, namely death and the loss of their place and nation. They turned these away from themselves and upon You, saying: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish” (John 18).

This may also be referred to all—both Jews and Gentiles—and to the members of Christ, because it was said to everyone: “The world and its desire are passing away” (1 John 2). Fearing that they would lose the world they loved, worldly people killed the preachers of this teaching.

“They devised plans which they could not establish”—all of them, both Jews and Gentiles—because, while killing the body of Christ, they thought they would destroy them; but they themselves were preserved, passing from death to life. Or, specifically concerning Christ, the Jews said: “We remember that that deceiver said, ‘After three days I will rise again.’ Therefore command that the tomb be guarded” (Matthew 27), and so forth. This was not established, because, against their will, he rose.

It is as though he said: And from where did those wretched people get the result that they turned their evils upon You? By the hidden judgment of God they will be handed over to a depraved mind, their evil merits having gone before them.

“For You will make them a back”—so that those who were unwilling to turn toward You may be turned away from You, because they hated the light; turned away from it, they love darkness. Or, “You will make them Your back,” namely, so that because of their excessive impiety Your mercy may not look upon them.
