And therefore “in what remains of You You will prepare their countenance,” that is, You will reveal their perverse and shameless will in what remains of You, namely, in Your lower part, in Your flesh, against which they raged so greatly. The highest part of Christ is divinity; next is the soul; the lowest and, as it were, rejected part is the flesh.

Alternatively: “In what remains of You,” that is, in these earthly things which You left behind, “and in Your own,” You will prepare—that is, prepare greatly—their countenance, that is, their will, so that by loving these things they may despise heavenly things.

Alternatively: “I said, ‘You will make them a back,’” that is, You will reject them; yet not entirely, because “their countenance,” that is, the benevolence owed to those who have been made a back, You will prepare—that is, reveal—in what remains of You, namely, in those who at the end will remain from the people, because “a remnant will be saved.” Or, You will prepare that countenance in what remains of You, namely, in Elijah and Enoch, by whose preaching the remnant will be converted.

And so that Your hand may be found and Your right hand exalted—namely, so that Your enemies may either be converted or judged—“Exalt Yourself, O Lord.” Rise again; exalt Yourself from mortality into immortality. “In Your strength,” that is, in the power of Your divinity. I desire this for the following reason: in Your resurrection we will sing in our hearts and make melody in our deeds of Your powers, that is, we will imitate Your humility, obedience, and other virtues by which You overcame all Your enemies. Or, we will sing with the mouth and make melody through our deeds.

# PSALM XXI. FOR THE END, FOR DAVID, FOR THE MORNING ASSUMPTION

> “God, my God, look upon me; why have You forsaken me, far from my salvation are the words of my sins? My God, I will cry by day, and You will not hear; and by night, and it will not be counted folly for me. Yet You dwell in the holy place, the Praise of Israel. In You our fathers hoped; they hoped, and You delivered them. They cried to You, and they were saved; they hoped in You, and they were not put to shame.
>
> “But I am a worm and not a man, a reproach of men and an outcast of the people. All who saw me mocked me; they spoke with their lips and shook their heads. He hoped in the Lord; let Him deliver him; let Him save him, for He desires him.
>
> “For You are He who drew me from the womb; my hope from my mother’s breasts. Upon You I was cast from the womb; from my mother’s belly You are my God; do not depart from me. For tribulation is near, because there is no one to help.
>
> “Many calves surrounded me; fat bulls besieged me. They opened their mouths against me like a lion seizing and roaring. I have been poured out like water, and all my bones have been scattered. My heart has become like melting wax in the midst of my belly. My strength has dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue has clung to my jaws; You have brought me down into the dust of death.
>
> “For many dogs surrounded me; the assembly of the wicked besieged me. They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. But they themselves looked upon me and examined me; they divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots.
>
> “But You, O Lord, do not remove Your help far from me; look upon my defense. Deliver my soul from the sword, O God, and my only one from the hand of the dog. Save me from the mouth of the lion and my humility from the horns of the unicorns.
>
> “I will proclaim Your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will praise You. You who fear the Lord, praise Him; all the offspring of Jacob, glorify Him. Let all the offspring of Israel fear Him, for He has not despised or scorned the prayer of the poor. Nor has He turned His face away from me; and when I cried to Him, He heard me.
>
> “With You is my praise in the great Church; I will fulfill my vows in the presence of those who fear Him. The poor will eat and be satisfied, and those who seek the Lord will praise Him; their hearts will live for ever and ever. All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord. And all the families of the Gentiles will worship in His presence.
>
> “For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and He will rule the Gentiles. All the fat ones of the earth have eaten and worshiped; in His presence all who descend into the earth will fall. And my soul will live for Him, and my seed will serve Him. The coming generation will be proclaimed to the Lord, and the heavens will proclaim His righteousness to the people who will be born, whom the Lord has made.”

## EXPOSITION

For the end, for the morning assumption: a psalm of David.

This psalm is to be attributed to David, that is, to Christ directing it toward the end, that is, toward perfection, “for the morning assumption,” that is, for His resurrection, which took place very early, while it was still dark (John 20), when mortality assumed immortality, after the likeness of the sun, which gradually gathers strength as it rises and drives away the darkness.

So, when Christ rose again, He gradually enlightened the minds of the faithful. In the Hebrew, *a hind* appears instead of “for the morning,” which has the same force by analogy: just as a hind rejoices in the light at the first dawn and climbs to high places, so human nature will rejoice in its resurrection.

Christ, our Head, speaks in this psalm according to His humanity with the Father concerning the glory of His resurrection, the fruit of that resurrection, the glory of the righteous, and the blinding of the wicked. His passion is set forth first, so that His resurrection may appear the greater, because the greater the struggle, the greater the joy of victory. And in the struggle of His passion He prays to be delivered, speaking in the person of the old human being as follows:

God, who are God of all by nature, my God in a special sense through grace or through singular obedience, look upon me—that is, come to the aid of my own—whom until now you have despised. Here it becomes clear that Christ does not pray here in his own person, since he is free from sin, but that he took upon himself our offenses in order to bestow upon us his justification. He therefore prays in our place:

“Look upon me”—that is, deliver me. You are far from my salvation, as it seems to those who say, “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross, and let him deliver him if he wishes” (Matt. XXVII), because, if you do not deliver me, you appear to have abandoned me. “Why have you abandoned me?”—that is, why do you permit me to appear abandoned by you, since you do not deliver me in the manner in which my persecutors say I should be delivered? He makes this inquiry in order to disclose the reason carefully.

This is the reason why you do not wish me to come down from the cross, but to rise from the tomb: “The words of my offenses are far from my salvation”—those poisoned words of the ancient serpent, “You shall be like gods” (Gen. III). These were the words of offenses, that is, the words of disobedience and of every sin. “My offenses”—that is, of all those for whose sake I came to suffer in order to deliver them—“are far from my salvation,” namely, from that salvation by which I might descend alive from the cross. For they do not ask that I come down from the cross, but that I die upon the cross; this alone is, in their view, the price of redemption.

Alternatively: “Why have you abandoned me?”—that is, why do you appear to have abandoned me, since you do not look upon me by delivering me from the cross? Therefore “the words of my offenses”—that is, the pleas of my people, which are offenses, or which are made on account of offenses—are far from my salvation; that is, they do not ask that I descend from the cross, because then my people, those predestined for me, would not be delivered.

Alternatively: “Why have you abandoned me?” As though he were saying: These words that I utter—“look upon me” and “you have abandoned me”—are far from my salvation, that is, from me, who am free from every sin. They are not my words, that is, they are not spoken on my behalf, since you never despised me and never abandoned me. Rather, they are “the words of my offenses,” that is, spoken on account of the offenses of my people, which I bear; as it is written: “He himself bore our iniquities, and he himself took away our illnesses” (Isa. LIII). Or: I may rightly appear abandoned, and you have abandoned not only me from such salvation, but also my people.

“My God, I shall cry to you by day”—that is, through those who, in the perfection and brightness of their virtues, may be called day. “And you will not hear,” as through Paul, who three times entreated the Lord that the thorn of the flesh might be taken from him, and was not heard. For it was said to him: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness” (1 Cor. XII). “And I shall cry by night”—that is, through those who may be called night because of their ignorance of the mysteries of God—“and you will not hear.” You teach that one must not cry out with the words of offenses.

Alternatively: “I shall cry to my enemies by day”—that is, for the prosperity of this age, that they may remain—and “by night”—that is, in adversity, that they may prosper—“and you will not hear.” And the fact that you do not hear will not be for my folly, but you will do it for wisdom: namely, so that my people may learn that you know better, or provide for them more wisely, than they themselves do. You are a physician: you do not act according to the will of the sick, but according to their recovery. You show that, when you do not grant what they ask with the words of offenses, this is not punishment leading to condemnation, but medicine leading to salvation.

Alternatively: I say, “Look upon me,” because, “Why have you abandoned me?”—that is, “Why do you appear to have abandoned me?” I shall cry by day, namely, with the words of offenses, and you will not hear. And the fact that you do not hear you do for me not unto folly, so that I might become foolish, but unto great wisdom—namely, so that my people may learn that one ought not to pray with the words of offenses.

Alternatively, in the person of the Head: “My God, I shall cry by day”—that is, throughout the entire period of the Passion that preceded the night, that is, the death of the cross—“and you will not hear,” because you permit me to be spat upon, mocked, beaten, and to suffer many indignities. “And by night”—that is, in the punishment of the cross, when the sun will be darkened—“and you will not hear,” because you permit me to die upon the cross. And you will do this for me not unto folly, but unto great wisdom. For it was necessary that the author of their salvation, who was to bring many sons into the glory of the Father, should be perfected through suffering (Heb. II).

“But you dwell in the holy place.” As though he were saying: You appear to have abandoned me because you permit me to suffer so many indignities and do not deliver me outwardly. Yet you do not abandon me, because you dwell in the holy place: namely, in me, the assumed man, whom by dwelling in him you make holy, working salvation secretly while not saving me outwardly.

“O praise of Israel”—that is, you who never abandon your own, through whom all Israel is praiseworthy; that is, everyone who sees you through faith and hope. “O praise of Israel,” whose dwelling makes Israel praiseworthy; or, whom Israel alone rightly praises, because he has never been abandoned. And he demonstrates this in detail.

“In you our fathers hoped.” Moses, Aaron, and many others hoped in you, and you delivered them from the hand of Pharaoh and the Egyptians, and from the hand of all their enemies. “They cried to you,” as in the wilderness, “and they were saved”: you sent them manna and gave them water from the rock. “In you they hoped, and they were not put to shame,” because they were saved both inwardly and outwardly. You gave them what you had promised—namely, the promised land, long life, and the begetting of children.

“But I am the reproach of men”—of the Jews who said as an insult, “You are his disciple; we are disciples of Moses” (John IX). And not merely of men, by whom greater persons may be understood, but also “the outcast of the people,” that is, of the vilest members of that people. For they cast me outside the city, spat in my face, and struck me with blows.

As though he were saying: All those who hoped in you were not abandoned by you, whereas I appear to have been abandoned, although I am greater than all of them. For I am a worm, namely, born of a virgin mother without a father, just as a worm comes from wood or earth alone; and I am a man above men, since I am free from sin. And although I am a man above men, I am not merely a man, because I am God, since “the Word became flesh” (John I). The prophet calls him a worm when he says: “Do not fear, O worm of Jacob” (Isa. XLI).

“All who saw me”—that is, my humility, my patience, and that I had no helper—openly mocked me, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews.” They spoke with their lips the evil that they held in their hearts, and they shook their heads in derision. In every kind of mockery they ridiculed me, saying: “He hoped in the Lord; let him deliver him, since he made himself the Son of God. Let him rescue him from our hands; let him save him by making him come down from the cross, since he desires him,” that is, to save him (Matt. XXVII).

As though he were saying: They think that I have been abandoned because you do not openly deliver me by the deliverance in which they suppose I should be delivered, if you were with me.

“But you, Lord, do not depart from me”—namely, give me steadfastness in suffering and raise me from death, because there is no one who can deliver me except you. For you are the one who drew me from the womb, when no human being conceived me or opened the way. By your operation alone I assumed human nature; I belong especially to you alone. Therefore do not depart from me, because you are my hope.

Yet “from the breasts of my mother”—namely, from the weakness by which I sucked my mother’s breasts—I have hope in you, not from the power of divinity; or, from the very childhood that is usually more inclined toward evil. And rightly are you my hope, because “upon you I was cast from the womb”—that is, I was set far apart from all the others who were cast into Adam. Moreover, I was cast upon you because I was born in your image and likeness, as the Apostle says: “Put on the new man, who was created according to God” (Eph. IV).

And truly I was cast upon you, because you are my God—not I, as unhappy Adam was. And that I have you as God comes from my mother’s womb: that is, from the nature that I received in my mother’s womb. For you are not my God from yourself, but my Father.

Alternatively, according to the order of the words: “They mocked me,” and this because you are the one who drew me from the womb; that is, because you wished me to become mortal and capable of suffering for their sake, and to become one in whom all these things could take place—one who, though equal to me in divinity, became my hope through humanity. And because you humbled me so greatly, do not abandon me.

Alternatively: For this reason they persecuted me and for this reason they mocked me, because I was unlike them, and for no other reason. This is what he said: “For you are the one who drew me from the womb”—that is, from the shadow and obscurity of the Law, which is like the womb of the Synagogue. In this way you drew me out, becoming my hope “from the breasts of my mother”—that is, from the carnal observances of the Law in which I was born—so that I might trust in your righteousness, not in the righteousness of the Law, because no one is justified by works of the Law, but by your grace (Rom. III).

For the carnal observances were given not in order to justify, but to educate that crude people through certain elementary lessons, so that at last they might pass from carnal things to spiritual ones. And rightly are you my hope, because “upon you I was cast from the womb”; on you alone I placed my hope when I came out of the womb—that is, from the shadow of the Law—into the Law of grace. And because I was cast upon you, you are my God, namely, my hope from my mother’s womb, from which you drew me. Therefore do not depart from me. Show now that you are with me by raising me from the dead, just as you were with me when you drew me from my mother’s womb. And it is necessary that you not depart, because “tribulation is near,” since there is no one to help except you.

He shows how it is near: “Many calves have surrounded me”—namely, the wanton Jewish populace, not for imitation but for persecution. “Fat bulls have encircled me”—the rulers of the Jews, bulls because of their pride, fat because they were made sleek with wickedness. “They opened their mouth against me,” saying, “Crucify him” (John XIX); or, they pronounced death sentences against me. Their sentences were their own, that is, arising from falsehood, not truth, like a lion that tears its prey, when they seized me with swords and clubs (Matt. XXVI), roaring and shouting against me.

“I have been poured out like water,” shamefully and without any loss, as it seemed to them. “All my bones have been scattered”—that is, my strong men, namely, the apostles. For just as flesh is strengthened by bones, so the body of Christ, which is the Church, is strengthened by the apostles. They were scattered—that is, they fled in different directions.

“My heart has become like melting wax in the midst of my belly”—that is, in the midst of the sacred Scriptures, in which my will lay hidden. They were weakened in the midst of my belly—that is, in the hearts of my weak members.

“My strength has dried up like a potsherd”—that is, the strength of my people dried up in them, that is, failed, just as moisture fails when a potsherd is dried by fire. Thus the strength of my people gradually began to vanish as the fire of the Passion approached.

“My tongue has clung to my jaws.” All my people, who had previously been my tongue—that is, my preachers—became as though mute. “And you have brought me down into the dust of death”—that is, you permitted me to be enclosed in the tomb, as though I were to dissolve into dust.

Alternatively: They surrounded me, pronounced death sentences against me, and shut me in the tomb, but in vain, because I was poured out throughout the whole world like water: for some unto ruin, for others unto salvation—for unbelievers unto ruin, and for believers unto the washing away of sins. Hence the saying: “Behold, this one is appointed for the ruin and resurrection of many” (Luke II).

And in order that I might be poured out, “all my bones have been scattered”—that is, my preachers, strengthened by the Holy Spirit so that they might be like the bones and strength of my body, were scattered in order to preach throughout the whole world.

“My heart has become like melting wax in the midst of my belly”—that is, after the fire of the Passion, the hardness of the Scriptures was opened and manifested in the midst of my belly—that is, in the firm memory of my people. This is by analogy, because what is in the middle usually adheres more firmly. Memory is called belly by analogy, because just as many things are stored in the belly, so they are stored in the memory.

“My strength has dried up like a potsherd.” In the fire of the Passion my strength was not weakened, as they supposed, but it dried up—that is, it was strengthened like a potsherd. For I was changed from passible to impassible, from mortal to immortal, just as a potsherd, at first moist and fragile, hardens when placed in fire.

“And after the Passion my tongue”—that is, the tongue of my people—“has clung to my jaws,” that is, my people have not ceased preaching. The tongue appears to cling to the jaws when one is constant in speaking.

“And through them you have brought me down into the dust of death”—that is, you have led me into the hearts of the Gentiles, who previously were the dust of death: dry and without the moisture of the word of God. That dust is called dead which is without moisture and is easily carried away by the wind.

Alternatively: “You dwell in the holy place,” something those who say the following do not believe: “In you our fathers hoped; they hoped, and you delivered them.” Nothing is changed here except that these words are spoken in the person of the persecutors up to “But I”—namely, I do not appear worthy of your salvation to them, because I am so vile and appear so fit to be trampled upon that I am like a worm. I do not appear to them to be a man, and therefore I am “the reproach of men,” as above: “They spoke with their lips”; “Ah, you who destroy the temple of God” (Matt. XXVII). “And they shook their heads” in derision.

And rightly did they shake their heads outwardly, because inwardly, in their hearts, they had removed Christ, the true Head, and had taken many heads of enemies for themselves. And the rest as above, up to “and you have brought me down into the dust of death.” And rightly did you bring me down, for they could not kill me except by permission.

Here the transition is made to the verse: “But you, Lord, do not distance your help from me.” Since you permit me to be handed over to death, do not delay my resurrection until the general resurrection, but look upon my defense—that is, having seen my death, consider my resurrection—or, look upon my defense by giving me strength, lest I fail amid the torments.

And your defense is necessary, because “many dogs have surrounded me,” fawning upon the enemy and barking against the author of salvation: “Not this man, but Barabbas” (John XVIII).

“They have pierced my hands and my feet,” fastening them with the nails of the cross. “They have counted all my bones”—that is, they stretched me out upon the cross so that all my bones might be broken and counted.

“But they,” namely, so blinded and so cruel—for others showed compassion—“looked upon me crying, ‘Eli, Eli’” (Matt. XXVII; Mark XV), and despised me.

Alternatively: They remained unchanged and were not moved to pity. They looked upon me—that is, carefully observed everything I suffered, with no one coming to my aid. “They looked upon me,” that is, they looked only downward and did not consider me from above as a man, nor recognize me as God.

“They divided my garments among themselves, and over my robe they cast lots.” There was one garment among the Lord’s garments that the soldiers did not divide as they did the others, namely, the tunic. Because it was not sewn but woven from above, they did not wish to tear it, but cast lots for whom it should fall. Thus cruelly did they act toward me.

“But you, Lord, to whom I obeyed in all these things, do not distance your help from me,” because their assault will draw very near. They looked toward my attack; you look toward my defense—namely, raise me from the dead.

Alternatively: “Many dogs have surrounded me among my own,” tearing my people with a dog’s teeth. “The assembly of the wicked has besieged me”—that is, my people—as it is written: “Princes sat and spoke against me” (Ps. CXVIII).

“They have pierced my hands and my feet”—that is, they craftily plotted to overthrow my works and my affections, as in the saying: “Lord, we remembered that that deceiver said, ‘After three days I will rise again’; therefore command that the tomb be guarded” (Matt. XXVII). In the same way they pierced the works and wills of my people when, by killing them, they wished to destroy the salvation of human beings that they were working for and desiring.

“They counted all my bones,” just as they carefully sought out my preachers in order to condemn them, so that they might know their exact number.

“But they looked upon me and inspected me”—that is, they made me and my people a spectacle for themselves, as their mockery, according to the saying: “We have been made a spectacle” (1 Cor. IV), like captives being led to a public show.

“They divided my garments among themselves.” Some of that people divided my apostles, who are my garments, as in the saying: “I live, says the Lord” (Isa. XLIX), because you will clothe yourself with all these as with a garment. They divided them, supposing that there was a different faith among them, as in the saying: “I am of Paul, but I am of Cephas” (1 Cor. I).

Or, “my garments” means the sacraments of the Church with which I am clothed. Some thought that one immersion ought to be made in baptism, others two, and likewise in other matters.

“And over my robe they cast lots.” This is by analogy with the soldiers who did not divide the robe woven from above and not sewn by hand, but cast lots for it. Some, unable to divide charity as they divided the other things, cast lots for it: they understood that it came to them by the grace of God, as though by lot. Charity is said to be woven from above because God’s charity precedes our charity, as in the saying: “Beloved, let us love God, because God first loved us, and God is love” (1 John IV).

“But you, Lord, do not distance your help from me; look upon my defense.” This does not belong with the present interpretation, but with the earlier one.

In this way: “Look upon me. Deliver my soul from the sword”—that is, from death, naming the cause for the effect; or, deliver me from the condemnation of the Jews, according to the saying: “Their tongue is a sharp sword” (Ps. LVI). “My soul”—that is, my life.

“And from the hand of the dog”—that is, from the power of the Jewish people barking blindly like a dog—“my only one,” that is, the one who is alone without sin; or, the one who is unique to you. Or, deliver me from the hand of hell, which eagerly devours everyone in the manner of a dog. Or, deliver me from death so that in this way “my only one”—that is, the Church chosen uniquely—may be rescued from the power of the devil.

“Save me from the mouth of the lion,” whether the devil or earthly power. “And from the horns”—that is, from the pride of the Jews—“of the unicorns,” who proudly possess the Law in a singular manner and reject the admission of the Gentiles; or, they are called unicorns because, through one understanding of the Law, they drive others away; or, save me from the servants of demons who oppose my humility.

And with what benefit do you ask to be delivered? “I shall declare your name to my brothers.” Up to this point he has spoken of Christ’s Passion; thereafter, of his resurrection.

Augustine says that what follows is not so necessary, but that he introduces it for the convenience of his argument, on account of certain future heretics who would say that the Church of Christ existed only in one part of the earth. Such were the Donatists, who said that Christ was only in Africa—that is, among themselves—drawing testimony from the Song of Songs: “Where do you lie at midday?” (Song I).

“I shall declare your name”—that is, your glory—“to my brothers,” namely, the apostles. “And through them I shall praise you in the midst of the Church,” not in Judea alone, but in the universal Church, which will be joined from both walls, from the Jewish people and from the Gentiles; or, in the common Catholic Church, not in some particular part, saying:

“You who fear the Lord, praise him”—not a few, but all. Do not seek your own praise, but that of our Creator.

He shows in detail who those are who fear the Lord: “All the offspring of Jacob, glorify him”—that is, all who belong to Jacob, whether Jews or Gentiles, by giving earthly things and purchasing heavenly things, forgetting what lies behind and stretching themselves toward what lies ahead.

“Let all the offspring of Israel fear him.” Those who are advancing, or who are continually struggling, are the lesser ones; he exhorts them to glorify him. He teaches the Israelites, who are greater, to fear: those who are advancing need praise and action, lest they fail; those who are greater need fear, lest they fall through exaltation.

Therefore let him fear with chaste fear, because “he did not despise the prayer of the poor”—namely, my prayer, since, although I was rich, I became poor (2 Cor. VIII). He did not despise me when I prayed for myself, nor did he despise me when I prayed for my people, as the enemies did. “Nor did he turn his face away from me,” the poor one, though previously he had turned it away from the rich Adam, who “did not consider it robbery to be equal with God” (Phil. II). And this shows that, when I cried to him, he heard me: “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John XII).

Therefore “my praise is with you”—that is, the praise of my people with you, so that not the Jew alone may please you.

“In the great Church,” made great and increased in virtues through my resurrection, though previously it was small because of my death; or, “in the great Church,” that is, spread throughout the whole world, against the heretics.

“I shall pay my vows in the presence of those who fear him”—that is, I shall offer the mystery of my body and blood together with those who celebrate it in your fear.

“And in paying their vows the poor shall eat”—that is, the humble, who attribute everything to the Lord and presume nothing upon themselves. They shall eat me, that is, they shall receive the sacrament of my body and blood, and they shall be filled by imitating me and handing themselves over. For to eat the Lord is to desire to imitate him in all things and to be united with him.

And in that fullness they shall praise the Lord, because this is the true praise of God: to imitate Christ in all things as far as one is able.

Those shall praise him who first seek him through faith and hope; or, they seek him because they have been sought and redeemed by the Lord, and they ask for him with their whole desire, putting everything else aside so that they may cling to him.

And rightly will they praise him, because their hearts—that is, the desires of their hearts—shall live for ever and ever.

And not only the poor from the Jewish people, but also the Gentiles shall remember the Lord, though previously they had forgotten him. “And they shall turn to the Lord,” though previously they had turned away, giving creatures the honor they owed to the Creator: “all the ends of the earth,” that is, people from the whole earth.

And when they have turned, “they shall worship in his presence”—that is, in a pure heart, where he alone sees—or, in his presence and not in the presence of human beings—“all the families of the nations,” that is, people from every family of the Gentiles. This is again directed against the heretics.

This whole passage can also be understood of the Gentiles, just as what was said earlier was understood of the Jews, that is, of the apostles and the other believers.

“My vows”—that is, the same vows that I fulfilled, namely, the vows constituting the price of their redemption, which I paid by my death—“I shall pay the same vows,” not I myself in myself, but “in the presence of those who fear him,” that is, in the understanding of those who recognize the mercy of God displayed through me and fear him with chaste fear.

And not only the faithful Jews, who had previously been rich in knowledge of God’s commandments, but also the poor—that is, the Gentiles, impoverished in mind with regard to knowledge of God—shall eat and be filled, and thus shall praise the Lord who seek him.

These are the poor who shall eat, namely, those who seek him. This is how they shall seek him: “They shall remember and turn to the Lord.”

And not only people from all the ends of the earth, but “all the families of the nations” shall worship in his presence—that is, in a manner worthy of his acceptance—both greater and lesser.

And rightly so, “because the kingdom is the Lord’s”: they have now become the kingdom of the Lord through the victory of the cross, though previously they were the kingdom of the enemy. And he, who is Lord and not a tyrant, shall rule the nations with a merciful dominion, though previously they had been under a cruel tyrant.

“All the fat ones of the earth have eaten and worshiped.” This may be read as referring to what he said about “all the families of the nations,” and truly to all, since they include the poor and the rich. The poor have been discussed; he now adds what concerns the rich.

Alternatively: It was said that the poor would eat—that is, those poor both in circumstance and in spirit. They shall eat the Lord because in this world they will desire no other food for their soul. And those who eat him here will be filled, because the love of God will refresh their soul in such a way that they will desire nothing further, since at last God will be all in all (1 Cor. XV).

And not only the poor, but also “all the fat ones of the earth”—those fat in every way, whether rich in earthly possessions or fattened by wickedness—have eaten the Lord, not with the heart but with the mouth, and have worshiped outwardly, not inwardly.

And although such people eat and worship outwardly in the presence of human beings, and thereby suppose themselves to stand in the Lord, nevertheless they will fall in his presence—namely, inwardly in the soul, where he alone sees—all those who descend into the earth. Their heart is not lifted upward by desire through that bread; rather, they descend toward earthly things through illicit desire.

For whoever eats and drinks the body and blood of the Lord unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself. “Let a person examine himself” (1 Cor. XI).

The fat ones of the earth will eat and will not be filled. Rather, through that eating they will fall—that is, they will be condemned—because they desired earthly things more than God.

“And my soul”—that is, the soul of my people—“shall live,” clinging to him and not to earthly things. For this is eternal life: “that they know you, the true God” (John XVII).

Those who have left everything and followed his will, such as the apostles and other perfect men, may be called the soul of Christ.

“And my offspring”—that is, my imitators—“shall serve him,” imperfectly, so that from servitude they may eventually come into freedom.

Alternatively: “My soul,” that is, the soul of my perfect ones, shall live for him, having died to the world; it shall live for God alone and serve him alone. “And my offspring,” that is, the imitators of my people, who nevertheless are counted as belonging to me, shall serve him, not human beings.

And this will not be for a short time, “for the coming generation shall be announced to the Lord.” He touches upon what was prefigured in the Old Testament, when it was said: “If someone’s brother dies without an heir, the surviving brother shall take his widow and raise up offspring for his brother” (Deut. XXV).

Thus, when Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church, had died according to the flesh and afterward had been taken from the sight of his brothers, as though without an heir because so few of his own remained that they appeared almost nonexistent, the brothers of the deceased—that is, the apostles—took her to themselves and begot many children through the word of faith, not for themselves but for the Lord.

Hence it is said: “It shall be announced”—that is, it shall be attributed—to the Lord, not to the preachers of the New Testament: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Cor. III).

And this happens because “the heavens shall announce”—that is, the preachers, exalted in virtues and miracles—“his righteousness,” not their own, to the people who will be born through grace.

Who is this people? The people “whom the Lord made.” He made the old people through Adam’s conformity to himself, namely, as servants; but the new people the Lord himself made, because he justified them freely, without preceding merits. We made ourselves sinners, but God’s mercy alone made us righteous.

Alternatively: “Because tribulation is near”—that is, because the matter is being carried out not in external things but in me myself—“therefore help me in my suffering, lest I fail.” For there is no one to help: the enemies have surrounded me, and the friends have fled.

“They have besieged me with counsels and accusations.” And not only this, but “they opened their mouth against me.” He shows how: “Like a lion tearing and roaring”: “Crucify, crucify” (John XIX).

“I have been poured out like water”—that is, killed so shamefully as water is poured out.

“And now all my bones have been scattered”—that is, the disciples, who ought to have been strong in faith, fled, according to the prophet’s saying: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zech. XIII; Matt. XXVI).

He explains why they fled: “My heart has become,” and so forth; that is, my teaching was destroyed in them. Although they should have been firm, they became belly—that is, weak. And this is not surprising, because “my strength”—that is, my power—“dried up like a potsherd,” since it appeared fragile to them.

And therefore they despaired, because “my tongue clung to my jaws,” since I contradicted nothing. And because “you brought me down into the dust of death,” they thought that I had been brought down into death in such a way that I would become dust like the others.

“My tongue”—that is, the tongue of my people—“clung to my jaws,” that is, they will cling to the Scriptures, which are my mouth. And thus through them you will bring me to the knowledge of those who were the dust of death, namely, the dry, lacking the dew of the Holy Spirit.

“My praise is with you in the great Church.” Where you are praised, I too shall be praised. For “I and the Father are one” (John X). He says this so that no one might doubt that he is equal to the Father because of the humility mentioned above.

“This is how I shall praise”: “I shall pay my vows”—that is, I shall offer myself, as I was ordained with the Father before the ages. And I shall do this “in the presence of those who fear him,” so that those who fear him may understand what those vows are and for what reason they are vows—not because of diversity, but because of places and persons.

They shall understand what they are: that they are the Lord’s body, not merely a commemoration, as certain heretics wished, although the Lord plainly said: “This is my body, which will be given for you” (Matt. XXVI), and, “This is my blood, which will be poured out for you” (Mark XIV). Thus the sentence that follows—“Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke XXII)—leaves no room for doubt.

[Note: Against the heretics, especially the Sacramentarians.]

Bread and wine are spoken of according to Christian truth, not because they retain within themselves the nature of bread and wine after consecration, except with respect to appearance, taste, and odor. For the one who was able to unite personally and ineffably to his Word the flesh assumed in the Virgin’s womb, and who by the power of his command will also make our mortal bodies immortal, is able to transfer the matter of bread and wine into the nature of his body and blood.

These mystical signs are also called sacraments by analogy, not because they signify Christ, but because they signify us. For great signs and mysteries are contained in them.

The matter—namely, the bread from which the Lord’s body is prepared through priestly blessing and with God’s cooperation—is joined together from many grains ground by the mill and mixed with water. The wine that is transferred into blood is made from many grapes through the pressure of a winepress or some other weight. The grains and grapes, in turn, are produced through the labor of cultivators assisted by God.

So we too, generated in faith through the cultivation of preachers, mixed with the water of baptism, afterward devoted to good works, and crushed through the exercise of afflictions, become many yet one body. Hence the Apostle says: “So we, though many, are one body in Christ” (Rom. XII).

The flowing water is mixed with the wine for the confection of the sacrament, as a figure of us. Thus we too, flowing downward like running water into deaths, are joined to Christ through the mystery of the Lord’s Passion, which effects this, by the grace of adoption.

When this body is received by the faithful, it is a sign that our bodies, still mortal, are to be restored through Christ’s Passion. Through the reception of the blood, we understand the restoration of souls, since the soul dwells more especially around the blood.

Although this sacrament is received by many, it is not divided into portions, as it might seem; rather, it is wholly present in each person and remains undivided. The Apostle Andrew bears witness to this: “The Lamb, though sacrificed, remains whole and alive.”

It is received for sustenance and imitation in the present, and finally for the reward that is to come. Hence it is also called viaticum, provisions for the journey.

And the poor of Christ, understanding this in the proper way, shall eat that sacrifice and shall be filled—that is, they shall imitate, if necessary. In this way those who seek him shall praise him—not something else—through that sacrifice. And at last their hearts, that is, their souls—for the soul exercises greater rule in the heart—shall live.

And not only the poor, but also the rich of the earth shall eat and worship that sacrifice, through which they shall also be filled. If only the poor were to worship and be saved, Paul would certainly not have admonished his disciple in order to instruct them: “Command the rich of this world not to be proud in their thinking” (1 Tim. VI).

## Psalm XXII. A Psalm of David

> “The Lord governs me, and I shall lack nothing. In a place of pasture he has settled me. Over the water of refreshment he has led me; he has restored my soul. He has led me along the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake. For even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evil, because you are with me. Your rod and your staff have themselves comforted me. You have prepared a table before me in the presence of those who afflict me. You have anointed my head with oil, and how exceedingly splendid is my inebriating cup. And your mercy shall pursue me all the days of my life. And I shall dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days.”

## Exposition

A psalm of David. In this psalm the voice is that of the Church, recalling the misery into which it fell through the fault of the first parent, but now recognizing its salvation, accomplished through Christ in that morning assumption. It therefore gives thanks to God by enumerating his benefits and urges others to love God. It says:

[Col. 0261A] The Lord shepherds me. The Lord of all things, whom I rightly serve. Adam, the transgressor, twisted me away and unhappily recalled me from the pasture of life, that is, from the commandments of God. The Lord Christ, the true shepherd who gave his life for his sheep (John 10), now shepherds me, that is, directs me by the teaching of life. In Hebrew it reads “he pastures”; this has the same meaning, because the soul’s food is the teaching of God. And because such a shepherd feeds me, I shall lack nothing that pertains to salvation and true refreshment. For he himself directs my mind in the sacred Scriptures. Therefore I shall lack nothing, because, like a good shepherd, he has placed me in a pasture, that is, in the understanding of sacred Scripture, in which there is great refreshment for the soul, or in the hope of future blessedness. There he has placed me, that is, in such certainty and such complete abundance, having settled me [Col. 0261B] there, whereas previously I wandered, seeking pasture—that is, blessedness—now here, now there: now in riches, now in honors, and in other such things.

And as a good shepherd, after placing me through faith and understanding in a pasture, he did not abandon me there, but led me out, that is, nourished me, beside the water of refreshment, that is, the teaching of the New Testament, which says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11).

Alternatively, the Church, placed in a pasture—that is, in the hope of future blessedness—shows how it arrived there, namely through grace. “Beside the waters of refreshment he led me out,” that is, he laid for me the foundation of the water of baptism, that is, the faith received in baptism as a foundation, because “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11). [Col. 0261C] And upon that water he led me out.

In this way he converted my soul, previously turned away from the Creator toward creatures, from the unchanging toward changing things. And after converting my soul through faith, he led me along the paths of righteousness, that is, he made me proceed from virtue to virtue. This is drawn from shepherds, who lead their flock from place to place, that is, from one pasture to another. And he did this in order that his name might be glorified in me, not because of my merit.

It should be noted that he says, “upon the paths of righteousness,” as if to say: He taught me not only to keep the easy commandments, which may be called a road because many frequent them on account of their ease, but also the narrow ones, which may be called paths because few follow them on account of their difficulty. It is evident in this respect that he led me upon the paths of [Col. 0261D] righteousness: for even if I move amid the obstacles of this age, I shall walk securely under his guidance, not fearing that I will fall into any crime that might separate me from him. This is what he says:

“Even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death”—that is, even if I live among those who in this life overshadow others with riches, power, or honors, not for salvation but for destruction—“I shall fear no evil” because of their superiority, namely, I shall not be seduced by them. And this is not from myself, but because you are with me, such a provident shepherd, watching so carefully over his flock.

Or, “in the midst of the shadow of death,” that is, in the common condition of this life, which is not true death but a shadow, that is, an image of the final darkness, namely, the darkness outside. [Col. 0262A] “I shall fear no evil”: I shall not fear falling into vices that may be called criminal evils. Of these it is said: “Let sin not reign in your mortal body” (Romans 6). “There is sin unto death; concerning that I do not say that one should pray” (1 John 5), namely, only for this.

Or, “in the midst of the shadow,” that is, in the common ignorance that belongs to death, that is, which I possess because of mortality and susceptibility to suffering. “I shall fear no evil,” just as a flock with a good shepherd fears no evil, whether attacks by wolves, the seizure of thieves, or anything of that kind.

Therefore I shall fear no evil, because “your rod and your staff, they have comforted me.” As a discerning shepherd, you have a rod with which you gently correct wandering sheep and lambs; you have a staff with which you restrain larger and stronger animals from wandering. [Col. 0262B] “Your rod,” that is, mild discipline by which you rebuke me when I go astray, namely illness or some such adversity; “and your staff,” that is, severe tribulation—they have comforted me.

It is as if he said: You console me not only in sparing me, but also in chastising me, because “the one whom the Father loves he disciplines” (Hebrews 12).

Alternatively: “Your rod,” that is, your chastisement, whether small or great; “and your staff,” that is, your support: “God is faithful, who will not let you be tested beyond what you can bear” (1 Corinthians 10)—they have comforted me.

For I sought another consolation. In this way they have comforted me: although the bitterness of tribulation is outside, you nevertheless prepared a table, that is, refreshment, before me, that is, before the eyes of my soul, according to the saying: “For when I am weak, then I am strong and powerful” [Col. 0262C] (2 Corinthians 12). And in the Song of Songs: “I am black, but beautiful” (Song of Songs 1).

“Against those who afflict me”: you did this contrary to what they think. For to them your discipline in the present appears not joy but sorrow (Hebrews 12).

Alternatively: Your discipline not only comforted me, but you also prepared a table before me, that is, the teaching of your law, by which I am no longer nourished as a child with milk, but, instructed as a perfect man, chewing its meanings with a spiritual tooth, I can resist the perverse. This is the table that refreshes me after labor.

And in this way “you anointed my head,” that is, my mind, “with oil,” that is, with spiritual joy; and your same teaching is the oil of my mind, because it makes it glad through the promise of reward after labor.

“My cup is intoxicating,” filling my mind with such spiritual joy that I do not feel external evils. In this way my cup has become intoxicating; how splendid it is for me, even if it does not appear so to others.

Alternatively: The imitation of your Passion has become for me an intoxicating cup, that is, a sweet drink, causing me to forget all torments. How—meaning, how greatly—splendid it is, even if to others it appears obscurity and disgrace, while to me it appears great glory. “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6).

It is as if he said: Your teaching not only consoles me, but also the imitation of your Passion.

“And your mercy will follow me.” It is as if he said: Your mercy went before me, calling me through faith; it followed me [Col. 0263A] in the keeping of the commandments; and it will follow me all the days of my life. It will follow me until I dwell in the house of the Lord, that is, until I come from this tabernacle, in which I serve for a time, to Jerusalem—that is, to the vision of peace—in which the Lord dwells. There I shall remain for length of days, that is, in glory that never fails.

PSALM XXIII. A PSALM OF DAVID FOR THE FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK.

“The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness; the world and all who dwell in it. For he founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the rivers. Who will ascend the mountain of the Lord? Or who will stand in his holy place? One innocent in hands and pure in heart, who has not received his soul in vain, nor sworn deceitfully to his neighbor. He will receive a blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his Savior. This is the generation of those who seek him, who seek the face of the God of Jacob. Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle. Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts—he is the King of glory.”

ENARRATION.

“A psalm of David for the first day of the week.” Among the Hebrews, the whole week is called the Sabbath, named from its final day. “The first day of the week” is the day of the Resurrection, [Col. 0263C] before whose dawn the Lord rose.

The whole period of the Lord’s time before the Resurrection, from Adam’s fall onward, can be called night because of the darkness of sins in which the human race was enveloped, and because of the blindness of the mind. But the whole period from the Lord’s Resurrection until the end of the age can be called “the first day of the week,” that is, the first day of the week, in which Christ, the true sun, having assumed immortality, gave the world light that never fails.

This psalm, then, is of the prophet David in contemplation of that day on which Christ, victorious over the dead, rose from the dead, having defeated the prince of death and stripped him of his kingdom. It exhorts all the princes of this world, especially rebellious and unbelieving Jews, to rejoice with Christ the victor and receive him triumphantly with joy, after the manner of the rulers of this age who receive their returning victors with great joy and enlarge their gates so that nothing may obstruct those entering and leaving in triumphal procession. Therefore he said:

Princes of this age, “lift up your gates,” that is, remove from yourselves your desire and fear, through which there is an entrance into death. These are the principal gates to every sin that leads to death. He exhorts everyone, but especially princes, because they descend to hell most of all through these gates.

And, O eternal gates—love of neighbor and pure fear of God—be lifted up, you who until now lay prostrate, cast down by the fall of our first parent. Now appear in human beings, so that through you Christ may enter the hearts of the faithful. And the King of glory will enter, not the king of disgrace.

Earthly kings are kings of disgrace: from disgrace, that is, from the defect of virtue, one human being made another his king, to restrain him from unlawful acts. For “the law is not laid down for the just but for the unjust” (1 Timothy 1). If human beings had remained as they were created by God in our first parents, one would not have been inferior to another.

Christ is the King of glory, because by ruling he makes people glorious; to serve him is to reign.

The response of the princes: “Who is this King of glory?” Although these words are not spoken, the Prophet is nevertheless apparent in the evidence of events: the Lord is strong in suffering and powerful in rising again. Or, he is strong because he overcame death; powerful, namely, powerful in battle against the devil, defeating him and distributing his spoils; [Col. 0264B] or strong in the flesh, powerful in divinity; or strong because he conquered the strong one, that is, the devil; powerful because he stripped hell.

“The Lord mighty in battle”: this repetition is an expression of rejoicing.

Then he turns to the princes of darkness, who had erected those gates to be removed from human beings, and says: O princes—that is, demons—who until now held dominion over human beings, “lift up your gates,” namely, the vices through which you enter human beings.

And, O eternal gates—that is, virtues—be lifted up in human hearts, you who were previously cast down. “For when you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to righteousness” (Romans 6).

The demons’ response: “Who is this King of glory?” Answer: “The Lord of hosts,” the Lord of angels—he himself is the King of glory, no other.

It can also be read as an address first to the good angels, in this way: O princes, namely, citizens of heaven who hold authority among your fellow citizens, lift up your gates in human beings; that is, help so that your virtues, which you have never abandoned, may be raised up in human beings, though until now they have lain cast down.

And, O eternal gates, that is, angelic virtues, which have always been and always will be in them, be lifted up in human beings. And the King of glory shall enter, as above.

The angels’ response: “Who is this King of glory?” We have always seen the Father and the Son together; who is this King of glory? Those spirits who have always been with God and were never sent to know Christ’s humanity can say this: “The Lord strong and mighty,” as above.

Then the speech turns to the evil angels, as above: “Lift up your gates, O princes.” [Col. 0264D] This is not changed. It is as if he said: I exhort you, O princes, to rejoice with Christ the victor, the King of glory, and open yourselves to him.

And rightly so, because “the earth is the Lord’s,” though previously it was the enemy’s earth, that is, all those who, having been initiated into the ecclesiastical sacraments and cultivated in this way, can be called earth.

“And its fullness”—namely, it is the Lord’s: the perfection of that earth, namely, the Church; that is, those who are full of faith and good works.

And this earth is not his in some particular part of the world, as some wish, but throughout the world. And lest anyone understand “the world” to mean good and evil human beings alike, when he said “the world,” that is, throughout the whole world, he specifies whom he says were acquired in that victory. [Col. 0265A] In this way:

I said that the world is the Lord’s, namely, all who dwell in it—not those in whom the world dwells, who have subjected the world to themselves, but those who are not subject to the world.

It can also be read so that “the world” explains what he said, “its fullness.” It is as if he said: This is the fullness of that earth which was made the Lord’s: the world, that is, those perfect people who can be called “the world,” that is, the extremity of the earth, because they have entirely withdrawn themselves from the vices and desires of this age, “whose citizenship is in heaven.” And all who dwell in heaven, that is, all who remain firmly in those perfect people through imitation.

As if he said: Perfect men and their imitators are the fullness, and this fullness is the Lord’s.

And rightly is the world the Lord’s, [Col. 0265B] because “he founded it upon the seas,” that is, upon those who were previously sea—people entirely worldly and storm-tossed, always agitated by various movements of the soul. He founded this world by making believers out of unbelievers and disciples out of persecutors, just as he made Paul out of Saul. By “seas” we may understand the greater rulers, namely, kings and tetrarchs.

“And upon the rivers he established it,” that is, he made his own out of those who were the satellites of the princes of this age, converting them.

Alternatively: “He founded it upon the seas,” that is, upon the disturbances of this world, by which it had been enveloped from the beginning. He established his Church in faith, so that now the world might be trampled underfoot and despised by it. For the faith of Christ is like a mountain upon which it has been founded, so that the storms of this age cannot move it, since it has been founded upon a firm and lofty place. [Col. 0265C]

“And upon the rivers he established it,” that is, upon the powerful or greedy people of this age, as Solomon says: “All the rivers enter the sea, and the sea does not overflow” (Ecclesiastes 1). So also the powerful of this age, although they acquire many things, are never satisfied. The Church has been established upon these rivers so that it may preach to them and convert them.

And because it has been said, “The earth is the Lord’s,” lest anyone falsely applaud himself, thinking that he is the Lord’s earth when he is not, he describes who constitute his earth, prefacing the question.

It is as if he said: I said that the Lord’s earth is founded upon the seas and raised up. “Who will ascend the mountain of the Lord,” or to Christ, who is the mountain prepared at the summit of the mountains? Who will ascend by the steps of virtues [Col. 0265D] so as to be his earth?

Or “the mountain,” that is, the Church raised from earthly things to heavenly things by faith and hope.

I said, “Who will ascend?” Or rather I say, “Who will stand in his holy place?” That is, who will persevere? For many ascend and do not persevere. They approach the faith, which is a holy place, sanctifying those who rightly believe, but they do not stand in it while living idly; for faith without works is dead (James 2).

The one who ascends is the one who will stand here: “Innocent in hands,” that is, in works—the one who harms neither himself by doing evil nor another.

“And pure in heart,” that is, free from every evil thought.

He shows who is pure in heart: “The one who has not received,” that is, who has not made his soul received and pleasing “in vain,” that is, in transitory things—who has not made any offense pleasing to himself, not even in his mind. [Col. 0266A]

And for this reason he has not sworn deceitfully to his neighbor, that is, for the purpose of deception. Often those who make the vanities of this age pleasing to their minds, in order to obtain them, fall into perjury.

This one, and no other, will receive a blessing from the Lord: such a man will be that earth which the Lord blesses, according to the Apostle’s saying: “The land that receives rain and produces suitable vegetation for those by whom it is cultivated will receive blessing” (Hebrews 6), that is, an increase of virtues.

And such a man will be in an increase of virtues because he will receive mercy from God, who gives both willing and accomplishing according to his good will (Philippians 2). “From his Savior,” that is, from the one by whom alone he desires to be saved.

“This is the generation.” It is as if he said: This alone, which lives so innocently, and no other, is the generation of those who seek the Lord through faith and good works in this life. And after “those who seek his face,” that is, his presence, “the face of the God of Jacob,” that is, of those who imitate Jacob, despising temporal things and desiring eternal things, who seek no other reward for their innocence than the face of God.

Or: “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord,” that is, those who are generated as seekers of the Lord in the manner I have described.

PSALM XXIV. A PSALM OF DAVID.

“To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul; my God, in you I trust; I shall not be put to shame. Nor may my enemies mock me; for all who wait for you shall not be confounded. Let all who act wickedly in vain be confounded. Show me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths. Direct me in your truth and teach me, for you are God my Savior, and I have waited for you all day. Remember your mercies, O Lord, and your compassion, which are from of old. Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances. According to your mercy, remember me, you, for your goodness, O Lord. The Lord is sweet and upright; therefore he will give a law to sinners on the way. He will direct the gentle in judgment; he will teach the meek his ways. All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, for those who seek his covenant and his testimonies. For your name’s sake, O Lord, you will be gracious to my sin, for it is great. Who is the one who fears the Lord? He has established a law for him on the way that he has chosen. His soul will dwell among good things, and his offspring will inherit the earth. The Lord is a stronghold for those who fear him, and his covenant, that it may be revealed to them. My eyes are always toward the Lord, for he will draw my feet out of the snare. Look upon me and have mercy on me, for I am alone and poor. The troubles of my heart have multiplied; deliver me from my necessities. See my humiliation and my labor, and forgive all my sins. Look upon my enemies, for they have multiplied, and they hate me with unjust hatred. Guard my soul and deliver me; I shall not be put to shame, for I have hoped in you. The innocent and upright have clung to me, because I have waited for you. Deliver Israel, O God, from all its troubles.”

ENARRATION.

A psalm of David. In this psalm there is the voice of those who consider their misery and their frailty to be so great that even any tiny worm could harm them.

Or it may be understood of a person who presumed too much upon himself and recognizes that what he lost through pride and disobedience cannot be recovered except through humility and obedience, by imitating Christ.

The first and second verses can be read as spoken in the person of Christ, in this way:

“To you, Lord Father, I have lifted up my soul”: with my entire desire I directed it toward you; I did not cast it down toward earthly things. “My God, I shall not be put to shame” by not rising, since I said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” [Col. 0267B] (John 2), because I trust in you, not in myself, not in another.

“Nor may my enemies mock me,” the Jews, saying: “This man began to build and was unable to finish” (Luke 14). And truly I shall not be put to shame while I wait for you and keep your commandments.

“For all who wait for you shall not be confounded.” Up to this point it is spoken in the person of the Head.

The whole psalm can also be read as spoken in the person of every faithful person acting in this way with the Lord their God:

“To you, O Lord”—namely, in order to possess you—“I have lifted up my soul”: with my entire desire I lifted it from earthly things to you, not against you, as unhappy Adam did.

And rightly so, because you are my God, not I, and not anything else. And because you are my God, Lord, “in you I trust”: I cast all my confidence upon you. “Cursed is the man who trusts in man” (Jeremiah 17).

And because I trust in you, not in myself, like unhappy [Col. 0267C] Adam, who considered it robbery to be equal to God, “I shall not be put to shame,” as I have been until now, having been made by my presumption so weak that the most worthless little worm can afflict me. Restore to me, humbled and trusting in you, the strength that I lost through pride.

“Nor may my enemies mock me,” because I trust in you. Let neither carnal nor spiritual enemies, who do not trust in you, mock me as one overcome and seduced away from you.

And truly I shall not be confounded, because I have waited for you, that is, I have borne the burden of your commandments; or I have patiently awaited your rewarding me. “For all who wait for you shall not be confounded,” namely, in their expectation.

Let those who act wickedly be confounded instead. Let those be ashamed who are acting wickedly in vain, that is, with excessive ineffectiveness, namely, hating your servants who love them.

If this is understood in the person of Christ, we may take “those who act wickedly” to mean the Jews, plotting death against God, the author of salvation, in vain, that is, ineffectually.

And so that I may not be confounded, so that my enemies may not mock me, “show me your ways, O Lord,” that is, show me your commandments, which do not permit me to go astray. “And teach me your paths,” that is, your narrow and difficult commandments; teach me them clearly, so that I may not be deceived in them.

Teach me, I say, not merely so that I may know them, but so that I may fulfill them in practice. For perfect teaching consists in this, namely, in those commandments.

“Direct me in your truth,” that is, in your commandments, which are true, because I am crooked in my falsehood. And in this way teach me.

I ask you to teach me because you [Col. 0268A] are God my Savior, that is, powerful to save me. And therefore I have waited for you, that is, for your commandments, or for you as the one who will reward me; I have waited patiently all day, that is, continually—or in prosperity and adversity.

Lord, direct me. And do this by remembering your mercy and forgetting my sins.

“Remember your mercies, O Lord, and your compassion, which are from of old.” From the beginning of the world you have been merciful: you did not permit sinful humanity to fall into corruption and depart from you without the hope of forgiveness. In mercy you formed humanity outwardly; in mercy you reformed it inwardly. You recalled me when I was lost; mercifully preserve me once recalled.

Compassion and mercy are different. Compassion is the manifestation of mercy, whereas mercy is fellow-feeling.

“Do not remember the sins of my youth [Col. 0268B] and my ignorances.”

The sins of youth are grave sins, because the young are reckless, and what is committed recklessly becomes more serious. “And my ignorances,” that is, lighter sins, because we sin less when we commit something unknowingly.

Or, “sins” means original sins, which I contracted from my parents at the very beginning; and “ignorances” means actual sins, which I committed unknowingly after I became young, that is, after I was renewed from the old condition of my first parent.

“And my ignorances”: these are the sins of youth, because someone renewed through faith has promised and strives faithfully to fulfill that promise. He guards against future sins and, cleansed from past sins, commits only certain slight sins through ignorance—sins from which scarcely anyone is so perfect that he can guard himself.

Do not remember these sins, that is, do not preserve them for punishment at the end, but mercifully erase and forget them here. [Col. 0268C]

And so that you may not preserve them for judgment, “remember me,” because I forgot myself when I departed from your commandments. Remember me “according to your mercy,” which I have not deserved, not according to the anger that I have deserved. And do this not because of my merit, but for your goodness, O Lord.

But let no one who hears this applaud himself in his sins, secure in forgiveness because of your goodness. For the Lord is sweet in mercy, calling to repentance and forgiving sins. And after mercy he is upright, because he repays each person according to his works. And because he is upright, because he is incorruptible, after mercy he will leave nothing unpunished.

This is what he says: “He will give a law,” that is, scourges and corrections, “to sinners on the way,” that is, in the commandments of the Lord, which are the way to life. Or “on the way,” that is, in Christ, who is the way to life, he will give a law to sinners, because Christ is the law, that is, a book and pattern for the good to imitate what he did and taught, and for the wicked to avoid what he himself avoided and forbade.

Alternatively: Because he is upright, he will give a law, that is, scourges, to sinners on the way, that is, in this life, so that by punishing temporal sinners temporally he may show that he will punish eternal sinners eternally. One sins temporally if, were a long life granted, he would cease sinning; but one sins eternally when the opportunity is removed but not the will.

“He will direct the meek in judgment”: in such judgment, that is, through such a law, he will direct the meek. For he will not direct the harsh; rather, he will disturb them. This is drawn from animals: [Col. 0269A] when they are tame, if they go astray, they are brought back onto the road by being beaten; but if they are untamed and unbroken, the more they are struck with whips, the more they stray and become fierce.

And by chastising in this way “he will teach the meek his ways,” for in this manner he will remove the harsh from his ways.

He shows what those ways are: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.” All those ways by which he comes to us are mercy and truth. Mercy is that by which he grants forgiveness without preceding merits. Truth is that, after the mercy of calling and forgiveness, he examines each person’s merits at the final judgment.

His first coming was in mercy; his second will be in truth, that is, in incorruption, at which time he will seek only merits. And he will teach these ways to the meek, so that they may recognize God’s mercy, not their own merits, [Col. 0269B] and therefore not become proud but humble themselves, according to the saying: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4).

And after the mercy granted beforehand, let them attend to the future judgment, at which he will repay each person according to his works (Romans 2), and therefore let them strive to do good.

Mercy and truth do not belong to everyone, but only to those “who seek his covenant,” that is, who earnestly strive to become his inheritance, and who seek the testimonies of his covenant, that is, who diligently seek the proclamations of the prophets who bore witness to that covenant.

Jerome: He is merciful who seeks his New Covenant and its testimonies, that is, the prophets and apostles, by whose testimonies the Church has been gathered.

He returns to what he said: “Remember me for your goodness, O Lord.” The rest was an interpolation.

Therefore I asked you to remember me, not according to merit but according to mercy, because “for your name’s sake, O Lord”—namely, so that it may be glorified—“you will be gracious to my sin.” And truly you will be gracious: “for it is great,” that is, it seems great to me.

It is as if he said: I have now prepared a place for your graciousness.

Augustine: God forgives to the extent that you recognize; hence the Lord says to Saul: “When you were small in your own eyes, you appeared great in my eyes; but when you became great in your own eyes, you were small in my eyes” (1 Kings 15).

Lest anyone applaud himself over the saying, “You will be gracious to my sin, for it is great,” saying, “He will be gracious to me because my sin is great,” he shows who it is to whom it seems great, namely, the one who fears the Lord.

And therefore he asks: “Who is the person who fears the Lord?”

Since there are many who say that they fear the Lord but do not fear him with enduring fear—for one who says that he fears the Lord but does not keep his commandments is a liar (1 John 2)—and according to the saying, “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he will greatly delight in his commandments” (Psalm 111), he therefore adds definite signs by which the one who fears the Lord with chaste fear may be recognized.

Namely, “he establishes a law for him,” that is, a firm resolve, not turning aside to the right or left, “on the way that he has chosen,” that is, righteousness.

Jerome: “He establishes a law on the way,” so that he may not turn aside from the things he has chosen, as in Moses: “Today I have set before your eyes fire and water, good and evil, life and death; choose life and you will live” (Sirach 15). This is what he says: He sets before him and indicates what must be chosen.

Another sign: “His soul,” that is, his heart, “will dwell among good things”: he will always persist in good, turning away from evil; or he will desire only those things that are truly good, namely, eternal things.

And therefore his offspring will inherit the earth: his good works will cultivate him so that he becomes the Lord’s inheritance. “Will inherit,” that is, will make him an heir; or through works of righteousness he will receive as an inheritance the land of the living.

And a third sign: “The Lord is a stronghold for those who fear him.” Fear of human beings weakens; fear of the Lord strengthens.

But it is so that he may finally be revealed to them, so that they may not fail before they see him. And because he is a stronghold for those who fear him, therefore my eyes—the eyes of the heart, by which God is seen—are always toward the Lord, my deliverer.

And rightly so, for he will draw my feet out of the snare, that is, he will rescue all my affections from the anxieties of this age, so that my soul may move freely toward him; or from the snare, that is, from the devil’s ambushes.

And so that I may be rescued, look upon me, humbled, whom you previously despised when I was proud; look upon me, that is, upon my help. And have mercy on me, that is, make me persevere in that deliverance.

It is necessary that you rescue me because I am alone and poor. The order is inverted: I am poor, that is, I am not sufficient for myself; and I am alone, that is, I have no one besides you whose help or example I might rely upon. Truly, I cannot rescue myself.

“For the troubles of my heart have multiplied”; they have grown beyond measure. Prosperity troubles me, adversity troubles me, and various suggestions of mind or body trouble me.

It is rightly with many troubles that one must be supported, lest one fall. How many and how great are the weaknesses and susceptibilities to suffering of the flesh—in hunger and thirst, cold, standing, sitting, and many other things? By these we need to be supported daily, lest we fall. In all these things the heart is troubled, lest they hinder and devour us.

And therefore “deliver me,” that is, free me from my necessities, that is, grant that this mortal nature may put on immortality and this corruption incorruption (1 Corinthians 15). He calls necessities the wants and susceptibilities to suffering that one necessarily endures while remaining in this corruptible body as in a prison. Sufficiency and want, mortality and immortality, had been set before it; turning away from immortality and sufficiency, it necessarily begins to experience their opposites.

And so that you may deliver me, I strive, insofar as I am able, to earn your favor: see my humiliation, which I endeavor to display before you, [Col. 0270D] and my labor, that is, the perseverance with which I labor continually to humble my flesh before you, so that I may receive you as my rider. For “I discipline my body and bring it into subjection” (1 Corinthians 9).

And “forgive all my sins,” namely, my ignorances, which I commit because of the necessities of the journey. For no one is so washed that, traveling after washing, he does not have dusty feet. So no one is so purified by the water of baptism that he is not sprinkled with lesser sins on this way, that is, in this corruptible life.

And so that you may deliver me from my necessities, not only forgive my [Col. 0271A] sins, but also look upon my enemies, so that you may convert them. Thus I shall serve you securely if there is no one attacking me.

“For they have multiplied”: they are enemies because they have been diverted toward many vanities from the fruit of their grain, wine, and oil (Psalm 4). And because they have multiplied, they hate me—not because I seek many blessed things, but because I seek one [Note: [Col. 0271D] The passage is corrupt.]: they hate me with unjust hatred because I love their salvation.

There is also a just hatred, as in: “With perfect hatred I hated them” (Psalm 138).

And because they hate me with unjust hatred, guard my soul, namely, from conformity with them, even if you do not guard my flesh. And finally deliver me, completely separating me from them and placing me at your right hand.

“I shall not be put to shame” at last, namely, in my expectation, because I have hoped in you, namely, as the one to be earned; or in you as my helper, and in no other.

Alternatively: Deliver me from the perplexity of this life after you have guarded me from conformity with my enemies. These perplexities are many: the persuasion of friends, the delight of children, the love of parents. Deliver me, entangled and impeded in these things, so that I may not be seduced. “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10).

Therefore guard me also, because “the innocent and upright have clung to me.” The innocent, those turning away from evil; and the upright, those persisting in good, have clung to me through imitation and conformity, so that through me they may be joined to you. Just as limbs are joined to the head through the neck, so lesser people are joined to Christ through preachers and perfect people by imitating them.

They clung to me because I waited for you, that is, I kept your commandments; or because I patiently awaited you as the one who would reward me. And therefore [Col. 0271C] deliver me, lest, when I fail, these who seek you also fail.

And so that they may cling to you, O God, “free Israel,” that is, those desiring to see you, “from all its troubles,” carnal and spiritual, lest they be seduced by them. “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you preserve them from evil” (John 17).

PSALM XXV. A PSALM OF DAVID.
