«Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence, and, hoping in the Lord, I shall not be shaken. Test me, O Lord, and try me; assay my kidneys and my heart. For your mercy is before my eyes, and I have pleased myself in your truth. I have not sat with the council of vanity, and I shall not enter with those who practice iniquity. I have hated the assembly of the malignant; [Col. 0271D] and with the ungodly I shall not sit. I shall wash my hands among the innocent, and I shall surround your altar, O Lord, so that I may hear the voice of praise and recount all your wonders. O Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where the glory of your dwelling resides. Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, nor my life with men of blood, in whose hands are iniquities; their right hand is filled with gifts. But I have walked in my innocence; redeem me and have mercy on me. For my foot has stood on level ground; in the churches I shall bless you, O Lord.»

ENARRATION.

A Psalm of David. This psalm is attributed to David, that is, to every perfect person belonging to David. It is the voice of the perfect person praying and acting with his God, so that, just as in this mortal life he is separated from the ungodly in body, so in the future he may be separated from them in place; or so that here he may be burned, cut, and scourged temporarily, lest at last he be condemned with the ungodly.

“Judge me, O Lord.” I do not fear your judgment; rather, I ask that it come and separate me from the company of the ungodly, with which I share not in mind but in body. This is a difficult and especially fearful prayer: to ask for the judgment of the one before whose sight the heavens are scarcely found clean (Job XV), if the other merits did not follow, on account of which the perfect man, confident in his merit, adds: “For I have walked in my innocence”—that is, since, after the innocence you bestowed on me through your glory, I remained in it in such a way that I hope to have some merit in it. He lives innocently who harms neither himself nor another.

“I have walked”—that is, I have lived in this life, which is, as it were, an entrance into the future life. I say, “I have walked.” “And I shall not be shaken”—that is, I shall persevere in that innocence, yet not presuming on myself but hoping in the Lord. In this hope I dare to make this promise concerning myself.

And so that I may not be shaken, “test me, O Lord”—that is, lead me into the experience of labors; and thus “try me”—that is, show me, once tested, to be firm. For many seem to themselves tested who do not know themselves; but they are proved in temptation, as Peter, who seemed sufficiently steadfast to himself when he said: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matt. XXVI).

The passage may also be connected in this way: I said that I shall not be shaken; nevertheless, lest any of my hidden faults escape me, show me to myself—namely, “test me, O Lord, and try me,” that is, make it so that I neither delight in vanities nor think about earthly things. And so that, once tried, I may be proved: “assay my kidneys and my heart.” If there is anything in the pleasures of my flesh or in the thoughts of my heart that ought to be consumed, apply the fire of your love, which may consume it all and render me tested like gold in a furnace (Wis. III). Let your love cut away all earthly things from my pleasures and all vanities from my thoughts; or, in the heat of temptations, make it so that my pleasures and thoughts are not consumed.

And rightly I ask you to burn and cut me; or rightly I ask you to test me and lead me into combat, because I know that your mercy is present in this, by which, like a father, you scourge every son whom you receive (Heb. XII). I know that this is for my completion, not my destruction. [Col. 0272D] This is what he says: “For your mercy is before my eyes”—before the eyes of my heart. And therefore “I have pleased myself in your truth”—that is, in your commandments, which are true; or in the faith of your Christ, in whom I first displeased myself in my falsehood; or in your truth, which you taught me—namely, that you are my God, not my appetite, not my belly, not any creature. In this truth I have pleased myself.

“I have not sat with the council of vanity”—that is, I have not delighted in the entertainments of this age or in meditation on earthly matters. “And with those who practice iniquity I shall not enter”—that is, with the irreligious and those who do not fear God I shall not conceal my conscience, because “I have hated the assembly of the malignant”—that is, the gathering of those who plot evil. [Col. 0273A]

“And with the ungodly”—that is, those who love neither God nor their neighbor—“I shall not sit,” delighting in their ungodliness. These are the heretics.

“But I shall wash”—that is, purify—“my hands,” that is, my works, “among the innocent,” that is, by imitating the innocent; and by being among them in this way, I shall resemble the priest who first washes himself and then approaches the altar.

And after washing my hands, “I shall surround your altar, O Lord”—that is, I shall adorn your faith, which you gave me and in which the place of the true sacrifice is found, with good works, just as an altar is adorned with hangings and other ornaments. Or, “I shall surround your altar”—that is, I shall adorn the altar of my heart with various virtues, where vows, whether already made or still to be made, are both offered and fulfilled.

Therefore I shall adorn either my faith with good works or my heart with virtues, so that I may hear—from the Spirit presiding within me—the voice of praise; so that with the ear of my heart I may hear, that is, understand, what that voice is which praises you: a good life and good conduct. Or I shall hear the voice of praise, true and consonant with the heart. We understand the voice of praise when we understand that the voice proceeds from a pure heart.

What is that voice of praise? This: “and I shall recount all your wonders,” both inward and outward: that you wonderfully create the human being outwardly, but more wonderfully recreate him inwardly. For it is greater to make Saul the persecutor into a disciple than to raise Lazarus from the tomb. Whatever good I have, I shall attribute to you; whatever evil, to myself. Or I shall understand how you are to be praised and recount it to others.

Therefore I shall wash my hands among the innocent, or therefore I shall surround your altar, because, O Lord, “I have loved the beauty of your house”—that is, the perfect people who are the ornament of your Church, who are precious stones. “And the place where your glory dwells”—that is, those in whom your glory dwells, who attribute nothing to themselves but everything to your mercy.

And therefore, because here I have been morally separated from the ungodly, “do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, O God.” Since they were not with me in the first generation, may I not have a share with them in the second generation. “With the ungodly”—that is, with those who never withdraw from their ungodliness.

“And with men of blood”—that is, with those who hate their brother, namely, heretics. “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John III). Do not destroy my life—that is, do not condemn me.

Those who have iniquities in their hands, that is, in their works, are rightly condemned: they never do anything except injustice. “Their right hand”—that is, if any of their works seem good—“is filled with gifts.” There is a gift from the hand, a gift from the tongue, and a gift from office. Such people think that piety is a means of gain; they do not wish to do anything except for human praise. [Col. 0273D]

“But I have walked”—that is, I have lived in my innocence, which was bestowed on me; that is, I acted perseveringly in it, not superficially. And therefore “redeem me” for conformity with them. For as long as I am in this tabernacle, I am entangled in their perplexities by living among them. And finally, “have mercy on me”—that is, rescue me from the misery of this life, making me immortal instead of mortal, impassible instead of passible.

And you ought to have mercy, because “my foot”—that is, the whole inclination of my heart—“has stood on level ground”; that is, it has perseveringly acted according to your commandments, which are upright. Or, “on justice,” or “on level ground”—that is, in you—because the foot of my soul has not slipped into evil; this is your mercy.

And therefore “in the churches I shall bless you, O Lord”—that is, I shall increase your praise, adding love of neighbor to love of you.

PSALM XXVI. A PSALM OF DAVID, BEFORE HE WAS ANOINTED.

«The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life; from whom shall I tremble? When evildoers draw near against me to devour my flesh, those who afflict me, my enemies, they themselves were weakened and fell. If armies should encamp against me, my heart will not fear. If battle should rise against me, in this I shall hope. One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, so that I may see the delight of the Lord and visit his temple. For he hid me in his tabernacle on the day of evils; he protected me in the secret place of his tabernacle. He exalted me upon a rock, and now he has lifted up my head above my enemies. I went around and sacrificed in his tabernacle a sacrifice of shouting; I shall sing and make melody to the Lord. Hear, O Lord, my voice with which I cried to you; have mercy on me and hear me. My heart said to you, ‘My face has sought you’; your face, O Lord, I shall seek. Do not turn your face from me; do not withdraw in anger from your servant. Be my helper; do not abandon me or despise me, O God my savior. For my father and my mother abandoned me, but the Lord received me. Establish a law for me, O Lord, in your way, and guide me on a straight path because of my enemies. Do not hand me over to the desires of those who afflict me, for unjust witnesses have risen against me, and iniquity has lied against itself. I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, and endure the Lord.»

ENARRATION.

A Psalm of David, before he was anointed. David is recorded as having been anointed three times: first in his father’s house by Samuel, sent by the Lord after Saul was rejected (1 Kings XVI); second in Hebron; third in Jerusalem, when he was established as king over Israel [Col. 0274D] (2 Kings II and V). Before this final and perfect anointing he sang this psalm to the Lord.

Previously, however, these two persons were anointed: king and priest. In them Christ was prefigured, the true King and true Priest, anointed not with corruptible oil but with the fullness of the grace of the Holy Spirit. He was made immortal King and, standing before God the Father as true High Priest, always interceding for us (Heb. VII).

His body, that is, the Church, is first now anointed before baptism and afterward in baptism, foreshadowing that third and true anointing which has already been completed in its head, Christ, and which will finally be completed in his members when this mortal nature puts on immortality and this corruptible nature puts on incorruption (1 Cor. XV). Then we shall be true kings, because then the spirit will truly rule and dominate the flesh; and true priests, offering ourselves to God as a living, holy sacrifice, pleasing to God (Rom. XII).

Thus in this psalm there is the voice of Christ’s body, laboring and praying before we arrive at that eternal anointing, which is now temporally prefigured through sacraments, and acting with its God:

“The Lord is my light.” I am darkness to myself; I am blindness to myself. But the Lord has enlightened me through faith, so that here I may contemplate him in hope and finally in reality. Here he has given knowledge of himself; there he will give contemplation of himself.

“And my salvation.” Apart from him I am weakness to myself, but he himself is my salvation: now inwardly for the present and finally outwardly; now in part, then perfectly. And therefore, “whom shall I fear?” Who will be able to take him away from me? No one.

Therefore I am secure, because “the Lord is the protector of my life; from whom shall I tremble?” It is as though he says: Inwardly I shall not fear being led astray, because the Lord is my light. Nor shall I fear external enemies, because the Lord is the protector of my life. A mortal protects a mortal and is secure; the Immortal protects me, a mortal. From whom shall I tremble? Trembling belongs to the body; no place has been left for trembling.

Therefore I shall not tremble in the flesh, because, although evildoers draw near against me, having become superior to me externally or for the purpose of overcoming me, they do not overcome or harm me. They draw near in order to “devour my flesh”—that is, to consume the carnal affections within me and test me like gold. Therefore I shall not tremble.

Those who afflict me, my enemies, externally, have themselves been weakened, unable to lead me astray. “And they fell”: inwardly condemned by blindness of heart. For if they had first been weakened and fallen inwardly, they would not have taken such great pains to afflict me.

And therefore, because they are weakened, not I—or because the Lord is my shield—“if armies should encamp against me, my heart will not fear.” That is, if the plans of the ungodly, or the multitude of conspirators who contradict me—for both are usually found in armies—should stand not with me but against me, my heart will not fear, even if my body fears: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear” (1 Cor. X).

“Even if battle should rise against me”—that is, the gravest persecution—“in this I shall hope”: the battle itself will be my hope. Or the following may be understood as a comparison with someone who invades another’s land: after the invasion he establishes an encampment, and after establishing the encampment he attacks him with the most serious battle. That person, then trusting in someone powerful, would have no concern for himself. Therefore I shall not fear, and in this I shall hope, because I ask for what cannot be taken from me.

“One thing I have asked of the Lord”: one request, not many; or one thing, which is always one and never changes. “This I shall seek without remission”: it is this one thing, “that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.” I who am now in mourning and in the tabernacle shall finally dwell in the house of the Lord, that is, in heavenly blessedness, in which there is rest and true peace as in a house. “All the days of my life”—that is, in that eternity which will be without both night and death.

And not only that I may dwell there, but also “that I may see the delight of the Lord”—that is, that I may be filled with it; or that I may see the face of the Lord with my face, that is, in his presence. Or: What did the Lord intend by enlightening me, and what did he prefigure temporally in the ecclesiastical sacraments?

“And that I may visit”—that is, perpetually see—“his temple,” that is, Christ, already anointed with the perfect anointing and already made immortal, in whom, as in a sanctuary, “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II). I, having already been made his temple, that is, conformed to the body of his glory, have already become his true body.

Alternatively: This is the one thing: “that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life”—that is, that throughout this entire life no tribulations and no adversities may remove me from the number of those who hold to the unity and truth of Christ’s faith. And afterward, “that I may see”—that is, understand—“the delight of God”: that I may share in the counsels of the Lord; or “delight,” that is, the love of God. “And that I may visit”—that is, frequently see—“his temple,” that is, the holy place which he himself frequents. This is said by way of comparison. For it seems a great thing to be present at the counsels of someone powerful in his house.

And truly I shall dwell there, because I have a certain pledge of it: “for he hid me in his tabernacle.” That is, he placed my life, hidden and unknown to my enemies, in his tabernacle, that is, in the ecclesiastical sacraments, in which their malice is exercised. “On the day of evils”—that is, in the time of tribulation; or in his Church, in which Christian warfare is found. He hid me—that is, he protected me—separating me from sinners.

And he not only hid me, but, as a good commander, he protected me from the attack of enemies. Or: “In his tabernacle he hid me”—that is, he made me the body of Christ, who is the tabernacle of his divinity. “In the secret place of his tabernacle”—that is, in Christ, who is the hidden place of this tabernacle, either because he was taken up into heaven or because he is understood secretly in the ecclesiastical sacraments.

In this way he hid us in Christ, because he took our nature with him into heaven. Where the head is, there too are the members. In the words of the Apostle: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III). And this great hope is our protection against the savagery of enemies. Just as he was below with us in human nature, which is hidden from us, so we shall also be above with him.

Or: “He protected me in the secret place of his tabernacle”—that is, in the heart that believes unto righteousness. He made me so steadfast in faith that I cared nothing for torments. What is that hidden place? The rock. Hence the Apostle says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. X).

“Upon that rock he exalted me through hope,” because, since I am a member of his body, where he is, there someday I also shall be. And he not only exalted me through hope upon the rock, but even now, among enemies, “he lifted up my head above my enemies,” so that although they are superior in my flesh, I may then prevail over them in my mind.

Or: “He exalted me upon the rock”—that is, in Christ. He exalted me in this way because “now he has lifted up my head”—that is, Christ—above my enemies, making him superior to all his enemies; in him he has also exalted me through hope.

Or: “Upon the rock”—that is, in the faith of Christ—“he exalted me,” giving me steadfastness in preaching and confession. “For one believes with the heart unto righteousness, but confession is made with the mouth unto salvation” (Rom. X).

“I went around and sacrificed.” It is as though he says: In all these things he carried out in me the office of a good commander. What did I do? I followed the office of a brave soldier.

“I went around and sacrificed in his tabernacle a sacrifice of shouting”—that is, his grace in me was not empty (1 Cor. XV). “I went around”: I examined myself on every side, like a soldier serving bravely, adding all diligence; in my faith, virtue; in virtue, knowledge; in knowledge, self-control; in self-control, endurance; in endurance, godliness; in godliness, brotherly affection; in brotherly affection, charity (2 Pet. I). And because these things are with me and overcome evil, “I sacrificed a sacrifice of jubilation”—that is, of ineffable praise: with my whole heart I glory in you, not in myself.

Alternatively: In my mind I went around all creatures—heaven and earth, their adornments, and everything—and they all spoke your praise to me in their beauty and order. In them I found what I could sacrifice to you: a sacrifice of jubilation, that is, boundless praise and boundless joy for which no words would suffice, because jubilation is ineffable praise.

Or: I considered the faith of the whole world, in which my head was exalted above those who persecuted me; and in that tabernacle of his, that is, in the Church spread throughout the whole world, I praised the Lord ineffably.

And I did not praise him only once; I shall always praise him. “I sang a psalm to the Lord” in my heart, not to myself, directing everything toward his praise. Or: Here I rejoiced, and finally “I shall sing and make melody to the Lord.” With heart and body I shall praise him entirely when I have been made immortal and have nothing in me that displeases him.

And so that I may be able to sing and make melody to you: “Hear, O Lord, my voice with which I cried”—that is, my strong intention with which I acted unceasingly toward you and nothing else, so that you might enlighten me. “Have mercy also on me,” giving that true salvation; “and thus hear me”—that is, show that you have heard me.

And you ought to hear me because my heart spoke to you, not to another. This is what he said: “O Lord, my face”—that is, my presence—“has sought you”; it has sought your presence from among all things; it has believed that you alone are sufficient for blessedness. And it not only sought you, but “your face, O Lord, I shall seek”; I shall never cease until I reach you.

Therefore, “do not turn your face from me”—that is, while I am seeking, do not allow me to go astray and seek something else. “Nor withdraw in anger from your servant” while I am finding you, so that I may find nothing other than you, as those who are not your servants do. This is said by comparison, because an earthly lord who is angry with someone turns his face away from him.

Do not withdraw in anger; rather, “be my helper,” giving knowledge of the truth and perseverance. “Do not abandon me” in seeking and finding; grant that I may seek you alone and find you. And so that you may not abandon me, “nor despise me,” for I, a mortal, seek the Immortal. “O God, you are my savior”—that is, you alone can save me.

And it is necessary that you not abandon me, because “my father and my mother”—my carnal father and mother, Adam and Eve—“abandoned me,” that is, disinherited me. And because I had been disinherited and cast out, “the Lord received me”—that is, he made me his received and adopted child by assuming my nature.

Alternatively: “Do not despise me, O God my savior,” whom until now you rightly despised when I was a son of the devil and of Babylon; my father, the devil, and my mother, Babylon, having been abandoned by me, abandoned me.

Just as there are two generations, one of the faithful and the other of the unfaithful, so there are two fathers and two mothers. One generates for confusion, namely Babylon, which is interpreted as “confusion”; the other generates for life, namely Jerusalem. The husband of Babylon is the devil; the husband of Jerusalem is God.

“But the Lord received me.” This is an address to the hearers, urging them to rejoice together. The passage may also be connected in this way: Do not wonder if I cry out so devoutly to God, because my father and mother, Adam and Eve, exposed me to death through disobedience; but the Lord received me from the mass of the lost.

And, O Lord, because you have deigned to make me your received child, “establish a law for me”—that is, make my will steadfast as a law. Do not allow me to act superficially; and do this “in your way”—that is, in your Christ, or in your commandments.

And do not merely establish a law; “guide me on a straight path”—that is, in your stricter commandments. Make me keep your strict commandments; truly, let me yield my own will. And do this so that I may escape my enemies, both carnal and spiritual.

“Do not hand me over to the desires of those who afflict me”—that is, do not allow me, by going astray, to fall into the formation of evil things. And if you hand me over into their hands, do not hand me over to their desires.

Therefore do not hand me over to their desires, because “unjust witnesses have risen against me”—not only openly hostile people, but also those who tell me false things about myself so that I may withdraw from you, saying that blessedness consists in these superficial things and that they should not be abandoned.

“And iniquity has lied”—that is, those irreligious, wicked men lie that blessedness is to be sought here, in the land of dying people. It has lied “against itself,” that is, to its own condemnation, not mine.

Not mine, because “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord,” not the good things of this age—not superficial things, but eternal good things—“in the land of the living,” that is, in that Church which will have all its members immortal, namely, in the heavenly holy city of Jerusalem.

“Wait for the Lord,” as though he says: If this is to happen, wait for the Lord. This is an exhortation to every believer, or rather to himself. It is as though he says: I believe that I shall see such things. But no one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully (2 Tim. II).

“Wait for the Lord”—that is, for the reward; patiently persevere in the Lord’s commandments; do not fail. And in waiting, “act manfully”: do not have slack hands and weak knees, but work without ceasing. And by acting manfully, “let your heart be strengthened,” and thus let your flesh be afflicted, because the father scourges the son whom he receives (Heb. XI).

If he delays, “endure the Lord”—that is, bear the weight of the Lord’s commandments; or wait for him, because he will rescue you from the land of the dying. For your sake he deigned to assume the land of the dying and to die among the hands of the dying.

PSALM XXVII. A PSALM OF DAVID HIMSELF.

«To you, O Lord, I shall cry; my God, do not be silent toward me, lest at some time you be silent toward me and I become like those who descend into the pit. Hear, O Lord, the voice of my prayer when I pray to you, when I lift up my hands toward your holy temple. Do not hand me over together with sinners, and with those who practice iniquity do not destroy me; with those who speak peace with their neighbor but evil is in their hearts. Give them according to their works and according to the wickedness of their schemes. According to the works of their hands, repay them; render their recompense to them. For they have not understood the works of his hands; you will destroy them and will not build them up. Blessed is the Lord, for he has heard the voice of my supplication. The Lord is my helper and my protector; in him my heart hoped, and I was helped. And my flesh blossomed again, and from my will I shall confess to him. The Lord is the strength of his people and the protector of the salvations of his Christ. Save your people, O Lord, and bless your inheritance; rule them and lift them up forever.»

ENARRATION.

A Psalm belonging to David himself. In this psalm there is the voice of the head, praying to the Lord the Father, or to the Word personally united to him, so that, just as he did not depart from him but strengthened him in his passion and raised him from death, so he may not depart from his members either, giving them knowledge of himself and instructing them, so that they may not finally perish with those who do not know God but may be glorified in eternal glory with Christ their head.

“To you, O Lord, I shall cry.” O Lord the Word, I, the Lordly man whom you assumed, shall cry to you—that is, in order to merit you, not anything else. I shall direct the whole intention of my heart toward you, the liberator. For no one cries to you who asks from you anything other than you.

And rightly, because you are my God. As you are, so I make you supreme for me. And therefore “do not be silent toward me”—that is, do not separate the unity of your Word from my lowliness, but raise him from death. This is said by comparison, because the one from whom the word departs is silent.

And I pray not only for myself, but also: “lest at some time”—that is, at any time—“you be silent toward me,” that is, depart from me, namely from those who belong to me, from the condition and instruction of my people. Then “I shall become like those who descend into the pit”—that is, my people will be very like those to whom the light of your Word has not been made known, and who have consequently fallen into the greatest miseries of this age.

This is said by comparison with teachers who, when angry with their hearers, are silent toward them and thus withdraw from them the words of instruction.

Alternatively: Do not be silent toward me in my passion; do not at some time be silent toward me in death. And if you are silent toward me in death, I shall be like those who descend into the pit—not merely those who fall into a pit, but those who descend into a lower pit; that is, not merely those who fall into death, but those who descend from death into putrefaction and dissolution, which is the lower pit of misery.

And so that I may not be like those who descend into the pit, either in myself or in my members, “hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication”—the voice, that is, the strong and free intention of my supplication, which is made to remove evils.

Hear me, I say, “when I pray,” namely, I who am free from sin; and I do this toward you, that I may merit you. Yet I do not merely pray; I do so “when I lift up my hands”—that is, by extending them on the cross; or “hands,” that is, my works, I lift up, that is, magnify, doing what no human being has done.

“Toward your holy temple”—that is, toward the salvation of those who are destined to believe, your holy temple; that is, so that I may establish your Church for you.

Do not be silent toward me and do not remain silent—namely, “do not hand me over together with sinners,” that is, with the robbers with whom I endure punishment. Do not allow me to putrefy with them and the other sinners in the tomb.

Alternatively: “Do not hand me over”—that is, my people—“to a reprobate mind,” from the invisible and eternally unchangeable form to the visible and temporally changeable form, together with sinners who were handed over to the desires of their hearts in uncleanness, so that they might do things that are unfitting. Do not judge my people here and blind them as those others are blinded.

And in the future, “with those who practice iniquity do not destroy me”—that is, with those who, setting aside the fear of the Lord, are not subject to the justice of God. Do not condemn me with everlasting condemnation.

Do not destroy me only with those who sin more gravely, but also with those “who speak peace with their neighbor”—with me, Christ, who became their neighbor through the assumption of flesh and through mercy—saying: “Teacher, we know that you are true” (Matt. XXII).

“But evil is in their hearts”: “Is it lawful to pay the census to Caesar or not?” (ibid.). Or he speaks of all the enemies of Christ’s body: Do not destroy my people only with the other workers of iniquity, but, what is less, also with those who “speak peace,” that is, deceit, with their neighbor, with every human being who is their neighbor through kinship of flesh.

He shows that such people are not free from punishment; and by positing the lesser, he does not leave out the greater. For it is lawful to deceive no human being. “But evil is in their hearts”—that is, deceptions. What deceit is there when one thing is done and another pretended?

“But give them according to their works.” If this concerns the enemies of the head, that is, the Jews, then although what they did may benefit others unto salvation, nevertheless give them according to their works, that is, according to the intention of their works.

And not only according to their works, but also “according to the wickedness of their schemes”—that is, according to what they wickedly devised, even if they were unable to carry it into action. The same may be understood of those who act evilly and think perversely against Christ’s members.

This may be a rejoicing in the divine judgment, or a prophecy. Alternatively: “Give them according to the wickedness of their schemes”—that is, let what they wickedly devise against others be turned back upon them. They think outwardly of deceiving others; let them themselves be deceived inwardly.

“According to the works of their hands, repay them.” More plainly: according to those works toward which their hands were directed, and not according to what you have worked.

But if this concerns the Jews who persecuted Christ, then: according to those works which were so cruel and wicked toward me that, because of their excellence, they may truly be called the works of their hands—that is, their own works—repay them.

It is as though he says: Those who refused to receive mercy deserve to experience judgment; and this not from cruelty but from justice. They returned evil for good; let them find evil as their reward. “Render their recompense to them”—that is, because they wished to repay deceit for the truth they heard, let their deceit deceive them.

And rightly, “for they did not understand the works of the Lord,” namely, of the Father, who determined to work salvation for the world through the Son. They did not understand—that is, they did not proceed with understanding—“the works of his hands,” that is, of Christ and his preachers: the miracles which he openly performed and which his disciples performed, bearing witness to him concerning the good.

And therefore rightly, “you will destroy them”—that is, their deeds and plans, though not for their salvation—“and you will not build them up.” You will destroy their vices, because finally the capacity for doing evil will be taken away from them, and you will not build virtues in them.

But in my people, who have been destroyed in vices, virtues will be built. “Blessed,” therefore, “shall be the Lord”—that is, he shall be increased and multiplied, like a good king through the multitude of his army.

And rightly, because “he heard”—that is, greatly fulfilled—“the voice”—that is, the strong and free intention—“of my supplication,” made for the sins of those who were destined to become mine. Even if the chaff is thrown away, the grains are preserved.

In this way the Lord heard me: the Father, or the Lord who is the Word, was “my helper,” namely, of my humanity in the passion, so that I would not fail; and “my protector” in death, raising me up.

Therefore “in him my heart hoped”—that is, the hearts of my people, so that they too may believe that they will someday rise again. This is because I, their head, “was helped.”

He explains how I was helped: “my flesh blossomed again.” Mine in reality, theirs in hope; it blossomed again, that is, returned to immortality. In Adam, insofar as concerns the mass of humanity, it had withered and become almost dry.

Therefore “from my will I shall confess to him” with a confession of praise: having already been made immortal and without sin in my members, I shall do so from love, not from fear of punishment, which arises from awareness of sin. For then there will no longer be a divided will in my members, nor will the law of the flesh oppose the law of the mind; there will be one will in all.

Note that he said, “it blossomed again.” Human flesh blossomed in Adam by nature toward immortality, if it had preserved obedience; it blossomed again through grace and humility so that it might bear fruit for God, although through disobedience it had withered and become barren.

And rightly my people will praise and glorify him, because “the Lord is the strength of his people”—that is, of those who destroy their own justice and establish God’s justice in themselves, attributing no good to themselves but everything to God.

And finally he is “the protector of the salvations of his Christ”—that is, he will defend those saved and redeemed through me, his Christ, from mortality and corruption.

And, O Lord, because you alone are helper and protector, “save your people”—that is, preserve in innocence the people whom, through your grace, you made your own.

And “bless”—that is, grant an increase of virtues—“your inheritance,” namely, those whom you gave me as an inheritance, concerning whom you said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. II).

“And rule them”—that is, direct them in your commandments; and by ruling them, “lift them up”—that is, magnify them. Make them grow from virtue to virtue “forever”—that is, until they reach eternity.

PSALM XXVIII. A PSALM OF DAVID, AT THE COMPLETION OF THE TABERNACLE.

“Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams. Bring to the Lord glory and honor; bring to the Lord glory for his name; worship the Lord in his holy court. The voice of the Lord is over the waters; the God of majesty has thundered; the Lord is over many waters. The voice of the Lord is in power; the voice of the Lord is in magnificence. The voice of the Lord breaks the cedars, and the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon. And he will shatter them like a calf of Lebanon, and the beloved like the son of unicorns. The voice of the Lord cuts through the flame of fire; the voice of the Lord shakes the wilderness, and the Lord will shake the wilderness of Kadesh. The voice of the Lord prepares the stags; he will reveal the thickets, and in his temple all will say, “Glory.” The Lord makes the flood dwell, and the Lord will sit as king forever. The Lord will give strength to his people; the Lord will bless his people with peace.”

## Exposition

Psalm of David, at the completion of the tabernacle, or, “at the completion of the tabernacle.” After the ark had been brought back from the captivity of the Philistines and had been left at Shiloh, David built a tabernacle in which he urged the people to offer sacrifices to God. David signifies Christ, and the ark the Church. Just as David brought the ark back from captivity, so Christ brought the Church back from the power of the devil.

Thus, in this psalm there is the voice of David the prophet, contemplating through the Spirit the future liberation of the Church from the power of the devil, and urging the faithful people to complete—that is, perfect—the tabernacle, that is, the Church, offering themselves and their imitators for the construction of this tabernacle, taking the opportunity afforded by Christ, since he had already reckoned the expense and what was necessary for its completion by preaching and preparing human hearts. In the fact that “the voice of the Lord” is repeated seven times, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit may be signified; by their aid the breasts of the faithful are prepared to build this structure.

The psalm may be read in its proper order, but it is more conveniently begun for exposition at “The voice of the Lord is over the waters” and continued to the end, so that one may return from the end to the beginning in this way:

“The voice of the Lord”—that is, the preaching of the Son of God, who is King of kings and Lord of lords—“thundered over the waters,” that is, he preached terribly from the cloud of flesh over the Jewish peoples. In the first place, he preached terribly through himself and through his followers: “Brood of vipers, who will deliver you from the coming wrath? Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke 3).

Or, “the voice of the Lord the Father” was over the waters, that is, over Christ in the waters of baptism: “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3). Whose Lord? The God of majesty, the God of great power, thundered. “The Lord thundered over many waters,” as though he were saying: not only over the Jewish people, but over all nations, in accordance with: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28).

“The voice of the Lord is in power,” namely, power that is to be given, because he gives the power to bring the work to completion; or because he did not speak as the Pharisees did, but as one having authority (Mark 1).

“The voice of the Lord,” both in himself and in his followers, is “in magnificence,” that is, in many miracles, in accordance with: “God working with them and confirming the word through the signs that followed” (Mark 16). He shows how it is “in magnificence”: “The voice of the Lord,” I say, “breaking the cedars,” that is, humbling the proud among the nations and submitting them to the yoke of faith, breaking their pride through repentance.

And he breaks not only the cedars of the nations, but also “the cedars of Lebanon,” that is, the proud from the Jewish people, who were stronger than the other proud and resisted Christ’s preaching more intensely, armed with the divine Scriptures. We understand the proud Jews by “the cedars of Lebanon” because Lebanon is a mountain in Judea and is interpreted as “whitening”; and the Jews were white, in comparison with the nations, through the illumination of the commandments and the knowledge of God.

He says: “This is how he breaks them.” “And he will shatter them,” the proud signified by the cedars, “like a calf of Lebanon,” that is, like Christ, so that they may become imitators of Christ’s humility. Christ was born and raised in Lebanon, that is, among the Jewish people, in order to be sacrificed for the salvation of the world, just as calves destined for sacrifice were raised on that mountain.

And in this way he will shatter them like a calf of Lebanon, because “the beloved”—that is, each believer from that people—will be humbled “like the son of unicorns,” that is, Christ according to the flesh, the Son of the Jews, who are called unicorns because they have one law, by which they raise themselves up in pride; or because of the hope of earthly goods, which they alone think were promised to them.

Alternatively: as though someone were asking, “Was that calf diminished?” Indeed it was, because “the beloved”—that is, the Son of God, to whom it was said, “You are my beloved Son” (Mark 1)—“will be like the son of unicorns,” that is, like any son of the Jews, mortal and capable of suffering.

Alternatively: “The beloved,” that is, the Son of God, will be shattered—not according to his divinity, but according to the mode in which he himself was the son of unicorns, that is, according to the nature he assumed from the Jews.

And therefore he is “in magnificence,” because “the voice of the Lord” is “cutting through”—that is, dividing—“the flame of fire,” namely, the raging anger of persecutors. For he called some to his love and left others in their wickedness.

Or, he diminishes the fire of hell by withdrawing a great multitude from it and converting them to himself.

Or, he “cuts through the flame,” because his help cuts through the flame among the persecutors and comes to the aid of his own.

Or, he “cuts through the flame,” that is, the flame of greed and desires, making it so that they do not reach the completion of the burning, in accordance with: “Therefore let sin not reign in your mortal body” (Romans 6).

And therefore he is “in magnificence,” because “the voice of the Lord” is “shaking the wilderness,” that is, moving the nations toward the end, among whom there was no furrow of preaching; or shaking the soul that had previously been deserted by God, occupied by vices.

He says that “in this way also he will shake”: “The Lord will shake the wilderness of Kadesh,” that is, he will open the holy words of the Law, which had previously been deserted by understanding, bringing out from them a life-giving abundance of teaching, just as in the wilderness of Kadesh, which was deserted through lack of water, the rock struck twice with the rod produced exceedingly abundant waters, so that what had previously been deserted might be inhabited (Numbers 20). For Kadesh is interpreted as “the seed of the Law.”

“Was not our heart burning within us when he spoke on the way and opened the Scriptures?” (Luke 24).

Alternatively: “The Lord will shake the wilderness of Kadesh,” that is, he will stir those whom an evil conscience consumed and devastated inwardly, depriving them of peace—like a moth consuming garments—so as to move them away from that evil conscience, by granting people the strength and steadfastness for good works. For Kadesh is interpreted as “the shaking of the moth,” and through his preachers he will produce that shaking.

For “the voice”—that is, the Lord’s preaching—is “the voice of one preparing servants,” that is, preachers made ready to leap across the thorny growths of this age, namely, its anxieties, while consuming the poison of the ancient serpent. Through them he will “reveal,” that is, open, “the thickets,” that is, the obscurity of the Scriptures and the darkness of their meanings.

And then “in his temple all will say, ‘Glory!’” For even those who previously opposed him, like heretics, once refuted by the teaching of the apostles, will give glory to God, joined with the others in the unity of faith.

And it is no wonder, because “the Lord makes the flood dwell”: the nations, floating about amid every error, he makes stable through faith and causes himself to dwell in them.

Or, it is no wonder if all will praise the works of God, because “the Lord will make the ark inhabit the flood,” that is, his Church inhabit this world, where it will be tossed about as the ark was in the flood, yet will not be submerged.

As has been said, the voice repeated seven times signifies the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, by which the Church is constituted. And although they were a flood, the Lord will sit as king in them forever, because he will rule them and no longer permit them to drift about.

Nor is it surprising that he makes the flood dwell, because the Lord—that is, the ruler of all things, to whom everything is obedient—will give strength, that is, steadfastness, to his people, namely, the faithful. The Lord will bless his people, that is, give an increase of virtues to his people, “with peace,” that is, in the observance of a good life.

Or, he will “complete,” that is, perfect, his tabernacle when the final destruction of death takes place (1 Corinthians 15), and when “that which is perfect has come” (1 Corinthians 13): “with peace,” that is, in eternal rest.

Therefore, because the Lord has prepared servants for the building of this tabernacle, “Bring to the Lord”—namely, offer yourselves as living stones through faith and action for the completion of this tabernacle—“sons of God,” apostles received through adoption as sons.

“Bring to the Lord,” that is, for the completion of the Lord’s tabernacle, “sons of rams,” that is, your imitators. The apostles are called rams because they are leaders of flocks; or because they strike their enemies with both horns, that is, with the testimony of the Old and New Testaments; or “to the Lord,” that is, for the Lord’s honor.

Bring them in this way: “Bring to the Lord glory”; attribute your righteousness to him. And bring him “honor” by living rightly, so that those who see your good works may glorify your Father.

“Bring to the Lord glory,” not your own glory, but glory “to his name,” that is, for his praise.

And thus, not with empty hands and not with relaxed knees, “worship the Lord,” asking for nothing else but him, “in his holy court,” that is, in this temporal Church, which is the court of the Lord’s house, that is, of heavenly blessedness. The likeness is appropriate: just as a court is before a house, so this temporal Church precedes the heavenly one.

And just as in the courts of lords people stand carrying gifts, awaiting the lord’s arrival, so we too ought to wait in this temporal Church with the expectation of good works.

Or, “in his holy court,” that is, with a pure conscience. The likeness is appropriate because fragrant herbs are customarily planted in a court; so too virtues are planted in the conscience.

Or, “in the court,” that is, in faith.

It is as though he were saying: I command you to bring and worship, and you are able to do so, because “the voice of the Lord is over the waters,” if we wish to read the psalm in its proper order.

# PSALM XXIX. A SONG-PSALM AT THE DEDICATION OF THE HOUSE OF DAVID

“I will exalt you, Lord, because you have received me, and have not delighted my enemies over me. Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me. Lord, you brought my soul up from the underworld; you saved me from those descending into the pit. Sing to the Lord, his holy ones, and confess to the memory of his holiness. For there is wrath in his indignation, and life in his will. In the evening weeping will remain, and in the morning joy. But I said in my abundance: I shall not be moved forever. Lord, by your will you provided strength for my beauty. You turned your face from me, and I became troubled. To you, Lord, I will cry, and I will entreat my God. What profit is there in my blood, when I descend into corruption? Will dust confess to you, or will it announce your truth? The Lord heard and had mercy on me; the Lord became my helper. You turned my mourning into joy for me; you tore my sackcloth and surrounded me with gladness, so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced. Lord my God, forever I will confess to you.”

## Exposition

Psalm of David at the dedication of the house. This psalm contains the voice of the Head, rejoicing over the resurrection, already completed in reality in himself and to be completed in appearance in his members. Hence the Apostle says: “He raised the Lord from the dead, and he will also raise us by his power” (2 Corinthians 4). The house of the Lord was constructed when our nature was assumed by the Word of God in the Virgin’s womb. It was dedicated when, renewed, it was made immortal and incapable of suffering. This house is constructed in us when we receive the word of faith. It is now dedicated in hope, and finally in reality, when “this mortal nature puts on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15), when nothing else will be in us except the praise of God.

Thus, in this psalm our Head acts, rejoicing with the Lord his God over his resurrection, namely, that the foundation of this house has already been dedicated. He also shows how his body, which is the Church, now dedicated in hope, will finally be dedicated in reality.

“I will exalt you, Lord.” In contemplating this dedication, the prophet introduces our Head speaking both in himself and in his members: “Lord,” to whom I offer myself as a servant through obedience, “I will exalt you,” that is, I will cause you to be made known and praised through me, because “whoever honors the Son honors him who sent him” (John 5).

And rightly will I exalt you, “because you have received me.” You received me, the Head, from the tomb, having previously received me from the Virgin’s womb. “And you have not delighted my enemies over me.” You did not delight my enemies, the Jews, so greatly that they should be over me, that is, that they should overcome me. You delighted them in my death, but crushed them in my resurrection.

This is how you received me: “Lord, you brought my soul up from the underworld.” And in this way you saved me, that is, my flesh, “from those descending into the pit,” that is, into corruption; for my flesh did not decay in the tomb with the others.

Alternatively: “I will exalt you, Lord”; my people will exalt you, freely praising you in victory, when death has finally been swallowed up. And rightly so, “because you have received me,” that is, my people, from death and from the capacity to suffer—now meanwhile in hope, and finally in reality—or, here you received the cause of my people against the adversaries who attack them.

“And you have not delighted my enemies over me,” for they were not able to devour my people. They killed the body, but they could not kill the soul.

Indeed you did not delight them, because “Lord my God,” whom my people have as their chief, “I cried to you,” that is, my people acted without remission, “and you healed me,” that is, you will heal and dedicate my people by giving them immortality, now meanwhile in hope and finally in reality. This is how you healed my people.

“Lord, you brought up my soul,” that is, the soul of my people, “from the underworld,” that is, from consummate wickedness, so that they would not descend into mortal sin, which is as an underworld for the soul. “You saved me,” that is, my people, “from those descending into the pit,” that is, from conformity with those who, taking excessive delight in the stench of vices, have already come to despair, over whom the pit has closed its mouth.

Since you have such hope—that your body, wounded by mortality and the capacity to suffer, will finally be healed in the common dedication—“sing to the Lord,” that is, praise the Lord by doing good, “his holy ones,” possessing holiness through his grace, hoping in yourselves for what you believe in Christ. “And confess to the memory of his holiness,” because he remembered to restore to you the holiness you lost through the guilt of the first parent, remembering with respect to you, not with respect to himself.

This is how he sanctified you, because life was restored to you “in his will,” that is, in me, who never departed from his will. And “there is wrath in his indignation,” that is, the punishment of death in his indignation, namely, in Adam, who through disobedience became the object of God’s indignation. “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15).

“In the evening weeping will remain.” It is as though he were saying: That wrath which began in the evening, when the sun of justice and truth departed from the human race in Adam, will last until evening, that is, as long as this life lasts, which may be called evening. For after the sun of justice and truth declined from the human race, it does not return perfectly until the common resurrection.

In the present life a human being has weeping when he remembers the good things lost in Adam. “And in the morning,” namely, when the common resurrection has come and that brightness which we lost in Adam has returned, “there will be joy,” that is, the joy of immortality and incapacity for suffering. “For when Christ your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3).

Alternatively: That wrath will not harm Adam alone, but this weeping and this wrath will remain for everyone who looks toward evening, that is, toward Adam’s setting. Joy will remain for everyone who looks toward morning, that is, toward Christ, who is morning, the true sun who drove away the night of unbelief.

Or, by way of comparison: “In the evening weeping will remain”; in the evening the Lord was placed in the tomb, and the disciples wept for him, and in the morning of the third day joy returned when the Lord rose from the tomb. After Adam’s transgression the human race became mortal and was placed in the evening in the tomb, that is, when the Sun of justice and truth departed from it, and remained in the tomb—that is, in mortality—before the Law and under the Law. On the third day it rose, that is, under grace: in reality with respect to the Head, Christ, but in hope with respect to his members.

It may also be connected and stated in this way: “And life,” namely, eternal life, the only life without death, is “in his will.” And yet, although you have life in hope, “in the evening weeping will remain,” that is, throughout this present life the punishment of sin will remain in you.

As though he were saying: And whence that weeping? From guilt. Adam, created and placed in abundance and fullness of virtues, though subject to a condition, said—that is, thought—“in my abundance,” placed in the abundance which I can have through myself, “I shall not be moved from it forever.” And through this presumption he fell from that perfection, becoming mortal and capable of suffering.

But I, namely, the Lordly human being, preceded by blessings, the only one of human beings who came into the world free from sin in order to lead human beings out of this misery, said “in my abundance,” namely, in the fullness of my reason: “I shall not be moved,” that is, from the Lord’s will, by any temptations or sufferings, forever. And this was not from myself, but “you provided strength,” that is, steadfastness, “for my beauty,” that is, for my freedom from sin or my rationality.

And yet “you turned your face from me,” that is, you appeared to turn it away, although I did not turn away from you as Adam did. You appeared to turn it away because “I became troubled” in death; for you permitted me to suffer and die.

Alternatively: “Sing to the Lord, his holy ones”; return thanks to God, “because there is wrath,” that is, brief vengeance—for wrath is a brief fury—“in his indignation,” that is, in your guilt, with which the Lord was rightly indignant; namely, by temporal death you paid the debt of sin. But eternal life comes not from merit, because we were able to fall through ourselves but could not rise through ourselves; it comes from his will, that is, from mercy alone.

And therefore sing, because “in the evening,” that is, until the end of this life, which has a setting, “weeping will remain,” namely, the weeping of mortality and capacity for suffering. And “joy,” namely, the joy of resurrection and immortality, not temporal but enduring “until morning,” that is, until the light that will never fail, will come when “this mortal nature puts on immortality,” namely, in the common resurrection, when the house is dedicated and we put on the second garment.

As though he were saying: That weeping arises not from the judge’s injustice but from my merit. Here Christ speaks in the person of the old human being: for he who deigned to assume our weakness did not disdain to assume our voice.

“But I”—as though he were saying, “I deserved that wrath, because I said, in my abundance, ‘I shall not be moved forever’; I shall not be moved from this abundance. I will not obey the command of the Creator, who says, ‘On whatever day you eat, you shall die,’ but I will consent to the voice of the serpent persuading me: ‘You will be like gods’ (Genesis 3). I will be God; I will be immortal.”

“But, O Lord, you provided strength for my beauty,” that is, for me who was beautiful, “in your will,” not in my merit. That I was immortal, I had through you. From this I understood: “You turned your face from me,” that is, you withdrew your hand from me, “and I became troubled,” that is, mortal.

And because I, Adam, became troubled with respect to the human nature I assumed—for “in Adam all die” (1 Corinthians 15)—I, free from sin, was sent for this purpose: to do the will and redeem them.

“To you, Lord, I will cry,” that is, I will pray for myself with undivided and vigorous intention, so that I may rise from death. “And I will entreat my God” for the sins and mortality of my people, saying: “What profit is there in my blood,” that is, in my death, “when I descend into corruption?” That is, if my flesh decays and does not rise? What good will my death do if my resurrection does not follow? For our death profited us nothing unless redemption had profited us.

“If I do not rise, will dust confess to you,” that is, will the gentile people redeemed through me praise you? It was previously dust, that is, without the rain of the word of God, loose and driven about by every wind of doctrine and error, unable to resist the wind of pride. “Or will anyone,” namely, a preacher, “announce to that dust your truth,” which was promised in the prophets to be fulfilled through me, “if I do not rise?” No one.

Alternatively: “Will dust confess,” that is, will a dead person make confession of sins to you so that he may recover his senses? Or will dust announce—to dust, that is, will the dead announce to the dead—the truth, that is, your salvation? There is no redemption in the underworld. This must be done by the living. And therefore raise me.

The Lord heard me praying in this way, and it is evident in this that “he had mercy on me,” that is, on my people. This is how he had mercy on them: by raising me.

“The Lord became my helper” in the passion and in death. This is how he became my helper: “O Lord, you turned my mourning into joy for me,” that is, you turned the sadness of passion and death into the joy of resurrection. You did this by tearing “my sackcloth,” that is, my flesh, which was like sinful flesh, possessing not sin but the punishment of sin; you permitted it to be pierced by a lance and fastened with nails.

Sackcloth is the garment of penitents, made from the hair of goats and kids, and it stands for sinful flesh, which is, as it were, the soul’s garment. Christ had sackcloth, but he did not have the work of sackcloth, of whom it is said: “He committed no sin” (1 Peter 2).

“And you surrounded me with joy,” namely, the joy of resurrection, so that “my glory may sing to you,” that is, so that my resurrection may praise you, because in praising me all those for whom my resurrection is beneficial will praise you. And I will no longer be pierced by the sting of death, in accordance with: “Death will no longer rule over him” (Romans 6). And therefore, “Lord my God, forever I will confess to you”; once my house has been dedicated, my praise of you will not cease.

Alternatively: “You turned my mourning,” that is, the mourning of my people, “into joy for me,” by raising them inwardly in the meantime; that is, you gave them the first garment. “You tore my sackcloth,” that is, you destroyed the flesh of sin for my people in my death, in accordance with: “Jesus Christ died for our sins” (Romans 4).

“And you surrounded me,” that is, my people, “with joy,” the joy of immortality in hope, so that in my resurrection they might hope that they would finally be dedicated to immortality and incapacity for suffering, when in the common resurrection they receive the second garment.

They will be dedicated for this purpose: “so that my glory may sing to you,” that is, so that the glorious resurrection of my people may praise you. And rightly will I praise you in them, because “I will not be pierced,” that is, they will no longer be pierced by the consciousness of sin or fear of judgment.

And therefore, “Lord my God, forever I will confess to you” in them with a praiseworthy confession.

# PSALM XXX. FOR THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID, FOR ECSTASY

“In you, Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be confounded forever. In your justice deliver me. Incline your ear to me; hasten to rescue me. Be for me a protecting God and a house of refuge, so that you may save me. For you are my strength and my refuge; and for your name’s sake you will lead me and nourish me. You will bring me out of this snare which they hid for me, because you are my protector. Into your hands I commend my spirit; you have redeemed me, Lord God of truth. You hate those who observe vanities in vain. But I have hoped in the Lord; I will exult and rejoice in your mercy. For you have regarded my humility; you have saved my soul from necessities. And you have not shut me up in the hands of the enemy; you have set my feet in a spacious place. Have mercy on me, Lord, because I am afflicted; my eye, my soul, and my belly are troubled in anger. For my life has failed in grief, and my years in groaning. My strength has been weakened in poverty, and my bones have been troubled. I have become a reproach to all my enemies, and especially to my neighbors, and a fear to those who know me. Those who saw me fled outside, away from me. I have been forgotten like one dead from the heart. I have become like a ruined vessel, because I heard the reproach of many who dwell around. While they gathered together against me, they conspired to take my life. But I hoped in you, Lord; I said, ‘You are my God; in your hands are my lots.’ Deliver me from the hand of my enemies and from those who persecute me. Make your face shine upon your servant; save me in your mercy, Lord. Let me not be confounded, because I have called upon you. Let the wicked be put to shame and led down into the underworld; let deceitful lips become mute, which speak iniquity against the just in pride and abuse. How great is the multitude of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you! You have perfected it for those who hope in you, in the sight of the sons of men. You will hide them in the hiding-place of your face from the disturbance. You will protect them in your tabernacle from the contradiction of tongues. Blessed is the Lord, because he has made his mercy wondrous for me in a fortified city. But I said in the excess of my mind, ‘I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes.’ Therefore you heard the voice of my prayer when I cried to you. Love the Lord, all his holy ones, because the Lord will seek truth and will repay abundantly those who act proudly. Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord.”

## Exposition

This psalm is to be understood as “for the end,” David, that is, for the final one, Christ, who is called the end because he brings to completion, not because he destroys; in the same thing, not in another. The psalm is attributed to Christ himself, that is, it is to be read in the voice of the Head. I say, “for ecstasy,” that is, for an excess of mind.

Ecstasy is called in Greek ἔκστασις (*ekstasis*) and is interpreted in Latin as *excessus*, “an excess” or “departure.” In this place, however, it means an excess of mind. This occurs in two ways.

It occurs when the human mind raises itself toward divine things, and it is called attention to heavenly things or revelation, as when holy men are occupied solely in contemplation. One of these was blessed Paul, who, with his flesh placed on earth but with his mind flying toward heavenly things, was caught up to the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12). He also says: “Whether we were beside ourselves, it was for God; whether we are sober, it is for you” (2 Corinthians 5).

But when they see that, in that high understanding, they live for themselves alone, the love of God compels them to descend to the weakness of their neighbors, so that their neighbors too may at some time be able to ascend with them to those heights, imitating the power and wisdom of God, Christ, who, although he was rich in himself, made himself poor for us (2 Corinthians 8). He assumed our humanity so that he might grant us participation in his divinity.

Or the excess of mind occurs toward lower things, as has been said, and it is called terror. The proper state of the human mind is when it distinguishes by sense, opinion, or reason. But when it raises itself to understanding, which belongs to God alone, it exceeds itself; or when either reason or sense is alienated and disturbed by fear of lower things.

Both kinds of excess can appropriately be understood in this psalm. When “ecstasy” is placed first in the title, it warns us to expect something great and divine, as the succeeding words of the psalm extend themselves.

For only those whose conduct is in the Church can speak with God in this way. This psalm concerns the passion of Christ and the persecution of his body, and in it terror is understood—not with respect to Christ, who, even if he were only human, could not credibly have feared death, since he was so certain of the resurrection; indeed, he went to the passion exultantly, as Augustine testifies—but with respect to his members.

For he who deigned to assume our nature did not disdain to transfer our terror into himself, in accordance with: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matthew 26). And to Peter: “I am going to Rome to be crucified again.” What is surprising if the Lord did not fear in his passion? Many in his body did not fear death; indeed, they received it joyfully, like blessed Andrew, who went singing toward the cross. A soldier could do this, and an emperor could not.

This terror is useful, because it makes us fear with respect to what is ours, but hope in the gift of God. In this psalm charity is especially commended, for charity creates a joining together; joining together tends toward unity, unity preserves charity, and charity leads to glorification.

Voice of the Head transferring into himself the voice of his members.

In you, O Lord, I have hoped, not in myself, who have nothing from myself except fear and weakness. In myself I fail, but in you I advance; therefore I shall not be confounded forever, because I am confounded temporally. For otherwise I would not hope in you. He is temporally confounded who, looking back upon his past sins, shudders; shuddering, he is ashamed; being ashamed, he corrects himself. Hence the Apostle says: “What fruit, then, did you have at that time in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. VII). Those are confounded forever who reserve their sins for God’s judgment.

Confusion is spoken of in connection with sins because many things are gathered together at once and placed before the sinner’s eyes for his shame. In you there will be eternal shame of judgment, because it will be fruitless. Woe to us! What did boasting profit us? What did the pride of riches profit us? Behold, everything has passed away (Wis. V). And, so that I may not be confounded in this way, free me in your justice from that confusion. Destroy my justice in me and establish yours. My justice is to repay evil with evil; but you alone are just. You have displayed this justice toward us, repaying evil with good, making the impious pious, the unbelieving faithful, and the wolf a lamb.

And, in order that you may free me, incline your ear toward me—that is, arrange mercy concerning me, as a physician does for a sick person. Hasten to rescue me, namely, from that confusion. He does not say this in order to obtain by prayer that it happen sooner, since that is immutable; rather, for consolation he shows that this deliverance will come quickly—namely, when this temporal life has ended, which, in relation to eternity, seems scarcely to possess any duration. It is as though he said: “And I know that you will soon rescue me from the pit of that confusion.”

Meanwhile, until the time of deliverance comes, be for me a God who protects me. Be my shield against the arrows of bodily and spiritual enemies. And be a house of refuge for me—that is, be reconciled to me through mercy, so that I, who flee from you when you are angry, may take refuge in you when you are reconciled. Be a house of refuge for me in such a way that you may save me, because I am weak. Heal me, so that I may be able to come to you. For if I am not healed, I shall not be able to flee to you.

Therefore be my protector, because you are my strength: I am weakness to myself. And therefore be my refuge, because you are my refuge—not power, not riches, nor anything else, but you. It is fitting that he invoke him as protector and refuge who trusts in nothing else.

And you will lead me from the pit of sin, so that I may come to you from virtue to virtue, for the glorification of your name in me, not through my merit. And, in order to lead me out, you will nourish me—that is, you will bend your wisdom, incomprehensible to my weakness, to the capacity of my understanding. Just as a mother passes through her own flesh the same food which a child is not yet capable of eating, and gives the child milk, so the Lord, in order to make his wisdom like milk for us, came to us clothed in flesh; and thus, having led us out of the pit of sin like little children, he nourished us.

You will also lead me out of this snare which they have hidden for me. Because I am a child, lest I be deceived, you will free me from the ambushes of the enemy, the devil and his members. There are two snares by which the faithful are ambushed: terror, by which he may break them, and error, by which he may entice them. Whoever wishes to escape these must close two gates against them: fear and desire. Fear must be closed against terror, and desire against error.

This is illustrated by the example of our Head. When the devil tempted him through ambition and pleasure, saying, “I will give you all these things if you fall down and worship me,” he closed the gate of desire by saying, “Go away, Satan” (Matt. IV). It follows: “The devil left him for a time” (Luke IV). “For a time,” because afterward he attempted to conquer him through the Passion, so that he who could not conquer him through error might conquer him through terror. But the Lord closed the gate of fear against the terror of the Passion, because he did not fear to suffer for us.

In all this, as has been said, our Head speaks in the voice of his members.

You will lead me out, because you are my protector, protecting me from the ambushes of enemies who seek to devour me. And because you are my protector, into your hands I commend my spirit. I commend my life to you, so that you may preserve it in a time of necessity and danger. This expression is drawn from those who, in a time of persecution, entrust their property to a faithful friend, so that at the appointed time he may return it preserved.

Therefore I commend it because you have redeemed me—that is, you will redeem my members from the snares of enemies and, finally, from every danger. I say “you have redeemed” because I am certain that you will redeem me, for, O Lord, you are the God of truth, deceiving no one in your promises. For you promise deliverance to those who hope in you. And because you are a lover of truth, you hate liars.

You hate all who observe vanities uselessly—that is, those who hope in temporal nobility, power, and honors uselessly, that is, to no purpose, since these cannot bestow blessedness. He also observes vanities uselessly who dies through fear: that is, he who, fearing temporal death, which nevertheless he cannot escape, lies and in this way postpones death without avoiding it; by fleeing death, he dies before he dies.

But I, who do not observe vanities, have hoped in the Lord; therefore I shall rejoice in body when this mortal nature puts on immortality. And I shall rejoice in mind, saying: “Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” (1 Cor. XV). And this is in your mercy, not in my merit.

In this mercy you saved my soul from necessities. There are many necessities of human weakness: no one can see another’s heart; he wants to attain life without death, but cannot; he often loves an enemy and persecutes a friend; he sees what is good and nevertheless does what is evil. From all these things no one can be freed except through the mercy of God, because we were able to fall by ourselves, but by ourselves we cannot rise.

Hence the Apostle says: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. VII).

Therefore it follows: “For you have regarded my humility.” You cast me, proud as I was, into these necessities; having been humbled by them, you rescued me. Nor did you deliver me into the hands of the enemy—namely, so that, ensnared by terror or error and persisting in sins, I might die and thus be handed over, bound with him, to punishments.

You did not deliver me into their hands because you set my feet in a spacious place—that is, you enlarged my affections in charity. You made justice easy for me through love, whereas formerly it was difficult without charity.

Thus far the voice of Christ in his more perfect members, already secure concerning themselves. But because charity is especially commended here, since it produces a bond—and when one member is weakened in a single body, the healthy member suffers with it—the more perfect members of Christ, now secure concerning themselves, place themselves in fear of mind on behalf of their weaker brothers, whom they see straying from the unity and truth of the faith, and pray as follows:

“Have mercy on me, O Lord,” as I suffer with my weaker brothers; perfect what you have begun. Just as you have enlarged me, so enlarge them also, who are still weak and therefore in distress. For I am troubled—not for myself, but for my fellow members—seeing them standing among theatrical spectacles. Formerly I saw them in your Church delighting in your praises; now I see them fleeing labor, pursuing pleasure, scorning truth, and loving vanity.

Therefore I am troubled, because my eye is disturbed: the eye of my mind, that is, reason, is disturbed. It has not yet been blinded by anger—that is, by brief fury—nor by hatred, which I have when I see them remaining in vanity; but I fear that anger may turn into hatred, and therefore have mercy.

My soul and my belly—that is, my inward parts—are troubled. Within I am consumed; within I burn. For I may be angry, but I may not cry out. By crying out and reproving them I would not benefit those who are incorrigible; rather, I would exasperate them. Therefore I am troubled inwardly.

Have mercy on me, namely by correcting them, because my life has failed in sorrow. The life that is joyful to me in the progress of my brothers has failed in sorrow—that is, it wastes away in grief over their failure—according to the Apostle’s saying: “For now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord” (1 Thess. III).

And my years—that is, my long life—have failed in groans, not in loud cries, as I see those going perversely who would be my joy if they stood firm in the Lord. Hence the Apostle says: “My joy and my crown” (Phil. IV).

My strength has grown weak in poverty—in poverty, that is, through lack of food—for that refreshment which I ought to have had in those whom I wished to incorporate into myself is taken away from me. My strength has failed—that is, the vigor which I ought to have received from that food.

And not only am I troubled, who am an ordinary member in Christ’s body, but my bones also—that is, the firmer and more perfect members in the Church—are troubled, because the iniquities of the brothers increase my grief.

Therefore I am troubled because I have become a reproach to my neighbors—that is, to those who are already approaching the faith. They detest me and blaspheme me far more than all my enemies—that is, more than pagans or Jews—because they have seen some people from the Church living worse than pagans or Jews, who are openly enemies of the Church. For he who lives badly within is worse than he who is outside. Those who are outside are like unfruitful logs suitable for the craftsman; those who are within are branches cut from the vine, awaiting only the fire.

Note that the perfect man says, “I have become a reproach.” For this is not attributed only to those who live wickedly; rather, it is said: “See how wickedly Christians live.”

And to my acquaintances—that is, those already initiated into the sacraments of the faith—I have become a terror. All fear equally, not knowing whom they ought to imitate, since those who recently appeared religious now conduct themselves so disorderly.

And not only to my neighbors, not only to my acquaintances, but also those who saw me—that is, those who had advanced, knowing my secrets and understanding the Scriptures—have fled outside from me. That is, they have made heresies; they have gone out from the unity and truth of the faith.

And when they fled, I was given over to oblivion—that is, they no longer take care to remember me. Like a dead man, I have become, so to speak, separated from each one’s heart; I have become like a lost vessel—that is, like a broken vessel, useless and fit for no purpose. Or, just as no one uses a vessel that has been lost for the purpose for which it was especially prepared, so I, abandoned by them for whose benefit I was established, live uselessly.

It is as though he said: “This is because, by praying for many, I make progress among few.”

For I have heard the reproach of many and the praise of few.
