Few among us are praised, and many are reproached—many, I say, who dwell round about, that is, who love earthly things, which are changeable and transitory. They dwelt in that circuit when they gathered together, while all agreed on this: to love transitory things and despise eternal things. They not only agreed in this, but also conspired against me—that is, they labored to seduce those others who are still in the Church.

But I have hoped in you, O Lord. It is as though he said: “Yet I did not fail completely in that sorrow, because, observing among human perversities a few worthy of imitation and nevertheless seeking to save them, I hoped in you.” In this there is nothing at all that can offend the one who loves.

“I have hoped in you,” that is, I placed all my confidence in you. Therefore I hoped in you because, offended by the consideration of human beings and thus attending to you, I see that you are beyond humanity. A human being advances; a human being fails; you are always the same.

And therefore I said this in my heart: “You are my God,” and therefore one must hope in you. And rightly so, because in your hands—that is, in the gift of your grace—are my lots, that is, my inheritance, which has come to me from your mercy as if by lot. The fact that I seek no other portion except you, from your grace, is in your hands.

Just as, when a lot is cast, there is no regard for human merits or persons, but the one whom chance has assigned is chosen, so in God’s election there may be some order, insofar as he does everything with counsel. But because we do not know that order, we rightly call his election grace.

Alternatively: the fact that I possess that garment which is given by lot—that is, by your grace—namely, charity by which I love God and my neighbor, is in your hands; that is, it is your gift, not my merit.

And because I have hoped in you, rescue me from the hands of my enemies—that is, from wicked human beings who are the hands of persecutors, namely, spiritual enemies—and from those who persecute me, that is, the devil and his angels. Do not allow me to be captured by their snares, or rescue me from the hands of those who lie in wait for me through error. And from those who persecute me—that is, who openly attack me through error.

And at last, shine your face upon your servant—that is, show your benevolence toward me by giving me resurrection and immortality. Separate the grains from the chaff; let the grains be received into your granary. Save me in your mercy, not in my merit.

O Lord, to whom I voluntarily present myself as a servant, let me not be confounded with eternal confusion, as are those who wish to have you as Lord. For I have called upon you.

This seems a small merit in relation to what he asks, but if it is carefully considered, it is great. Many call upon the Lord not for the Lord’s sake, but for something else. If they could obtain what they desire from another, they would not pray to him or cling to him. But only those call upon the Lord who invite the Lord into the lodging of their hearts and cleanse their hearts of every stain of vice, so that the Lord may not disdain to enter such a lodging.

Let the impious be ashamed, those who do not call upon you. Let them be ashamed in this way: let them be led down into hell. Let their merits lead them away in the opposite direction, so that, while your servants are at the right hand, they may be assigned to the left—these to eternal life, those to eternal punishment (Matt. XXV). Or let them be led down here into hell, that is, into consummate wickedness.

And at last let deceitful lips be silenced: the lips of Christ’s and the Church’s enemies, who, when they see those whom they held in derision (Wis. V) in glory and themselves in misery, will no longer be able to contradict the truth.

He shows what those deceitful lips are: those which here speak wickedness against the just. The Jews spoke against Christ: “We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX). And unbelievers and heretics speak against the faithful people. These announce peace; those bring war. These announce salvation; those, death. These friendship; those hatred. They speak in pride, following what Christ showed ought to be despised. And in abuse—that is, contempt—because lovers of the world are despisers of the faith.

The Jews also spoke proudly against Christ: “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke XIX). And in abuse: “Lest the Romans come and take away our place and our nation” (John XI).

It is as though he said: “They speak wickedness against the just because they do not consider how sweet the Lord is.”

But I, who have already tasted, say: “How great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord!” “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. II). But it does not taste so to a fevered palate, nor does it appear so to bleary eyes. Here they do not receive the reward in full, but await it in the future. In God there is nothing that displeases the good, and nothing that pleases the wicked.

How great is that sweetness which you have hidden for those who fear you, so that they alone may reach it! Nothing is sweeter than the immortality of wisdom. Yet one begins from fear, and as long as one fears, one does not reach it; rather, fear preserves one so that one may reach it.

You have perfected it—that is, you have shown it perfectly—to those who hope in you, in the presence of the children of human beings, that is, of those who believe perfectly. “Whoever is ashamed of me before human beings, of him I also shall be ashamed before my Father” (Luke IX).

This is that sweetness which has been hidden from the eyes of the impious, but which will be given perfectly to those who are not afraid to confess the Lord in the presence—that is, before the faces—of the children of human beings, that is, sinners belonging to the oldness of Adam and Eve and not to the newness of Christ.

You will hide them from the eyes of the children of human beings in heaven—not in paradise, but in the hiding-place of your face, that is, in the secret place of your presence, where no impious person may rightly enter. Let everything apart from you become worthless to them; let them dwell in you, and you will dwell in them. Be his house, and he will be your house. He has prepared for you a hidden face; through its vision and presence it will protect you.

From the disturbance of human beings—that is, from the persecution of sinners—and while they strive toward that sweetness, you will protect them from the devotion of enemies. In your tabernacle—that is, in the ecclesiastical institutions in which they serve you—from the contradiction of tongues, so that they may hold to the unity and truth of the faith, avoid heresies, and contradict the tongues of heretics.

You, O Christian, flee to the tabernacle; hold fast to the rule.

Alternatively: “You will hide them in the hiding-place of your face,” that is, inwardly in the heart, where your face—that is, your presence—is hidden, “from the disturbance of human beings,” so that those who flee there may mock from above those who disturb them outside.

Just as someone who has a fortified house withdraws into it from the face of the storm, so every faithful person returns to a pure conscience in which God dwells and remains safe from the whirlwind of persecutions. And you will protect them not only within, but also without: you will protect them in your tabernacle from the contradiction of tongues.

Outside, that is, openly, you will protect them in your tabernacle—that is, in the ecclesiastical sacraments—from the contradiction of tongues, so that, holding to the unity and truth of the faith, they may not fear the perverse doctrine of heretics.

And in all these benefits—or, since we possess such hope through the mercy of God—let us say:

“Blessed is the Lord,” that is, may he be multiplied and increase among his own. For he has made his mercy toward me wondrous: that is, he has shown me his great and wondrous salvation in a fortified city surrounded elsewhere—that is, in the Catholic Church, which at first was small and confined to Judea but is now fortified by the multitude of peoples surrounding and protecting that earlier city throughout the circuit of the earth.

At first the Church existed in Judea alone, because there was the praise of God, there were the sacraments, and there, in a certain sense, some logs were kindled—that is, the apostles were set aflame by the fire of the divine Spirit. They went out and burned all the forests around it—that is, they set the Gentiles everywhere around that former city aflame with the love of God by preaching. Thus they enlarged and fortified that former city.

Or, by “the fortified city,” he means Jerusalem, placed at the center of the world. There he made his mercy wondrous, because there he was born, there he suffered, and there he ascended.

Or he calls the Catholic Church a fortified city, fortified everywhere through faith. Or he calls the heavenly Jerusalem fortified by the multitude of angels.

And in order that that mercy—that is, redemption and salvation—might be made wondrous, “I said in the excess of my mind: I have been cast away from before your eyes.” I considered myself, in my first parent, a transgressor of your commandment. You had created him like yourself out of great mercy, had made him immortal, had placed him in the glory of paradise, and intended eventually to transfer him to greater glory.

“I said,” that is, “I thought: I have been cast away from before your eyes.” My original iniquities are so great that, if you consider merits, I am not worthy for your eyes to see me—that is, to grant me mercy. I thought this in the excess of my mind, that is, in fear.

Therefore, because I humbly accused myself and acknowledged myself, you heard the voice of my prayer—that is, you mercifully heard my free and earnest intention by redeeming me. You did this while I cried out to you, and not to anything else.

This is what he says elsewhere: “If I said, ‘My foot has slipped,’ your mercy, O Lord, would help me” (Ps. XCIII). This corresponds to: “I said in the excess of my mind, ‘I have been cast away from before your eyes’”; and “Therefore you heard the voice of my prayer.”

And because the Lord is so merciful and so ready to forgive:

“Love the Lord,” not the world. Persevere in his love, for he first loved you. He loved you when you were impious, so that he might make you just; now that you have become holy, love him.

Love him for his own merit, because he first loved you without your merit. Therefore do not cease from loving him, for the Lord will require truth—that is, he will require you to persevere in goodness and in the observance of his commandments. For whoever says that he loves God and does not keep his commandments is a liar (1 John II). He will require truth in order to reward.

And he will repay abundantly those who act proudly—that is, those who persevere in sins. For those who sin abundantly will suffer abundant torments.

Therefore, certain of the reward, “Act manfully.” Do not fail in your labors, and let your heart be strengthened in hope of so great a recompense, even if the flesh grows weak—all you who hope in the Lord, not in the world, namely, you who hope that the reward of your labor will come from the Lord and from no other thing except the Lord himself.

We have expounded the psalm in the voice of the Head, under the person of the members. It may also be expounded in the voice and person of the Head himself, as follows:

“In you, O Lord, I have hoped”—I, the Lord's man, O Lord the Word. In you is the hope of my corporeality. I did not hope in myself, like wretched Adam. And therefore I shall not be confounded forever. I was confounded in the Passion, but I shall not be confounded in death, since I said, “After three days I shall rise again.”

And, so that I may not be confounded, “in your justice free me”—namely, from death, through the humility and obedience by which you justify, since you cast Adam away in his own justice. Free me in this way: “Incline your ear toward me.” Bend your divinity toward the weakness of my humanity, so that, when I die through the weakness of the flesh, I may rise again through the power of divinity.

“Hasten to rescue me”—namely, from the pit of death. Do not delay resurrecting me until the general resurrection. “Be for me a God who protects me” in the Passion, and “a house of refuge” in death.

Therefore, because you, the Word, are the strength of my humanity and its refuge. And because you are my protector and refuge, you will lead me from death into life, or from the opposition of the Jewish people, and you will establish me as head of the nations.

And you will nourish me—that is, you will adapt a perfect body from perfect members for me, nourishing them, as it were, with milk through the example of my humility—for the sake of your name, which is to be glorified through me.

In this way you will lead me out: “You will lead me out of this snare which they have hidden for me”—that is, from the death by which they thought to hold me confined, like one bound in a snare, in Judea alone, so that the gift might not go forth after me. You will free me.

“They hid it” in relation to me, as a snare in relation to themselves, but not in relation to me, because you are my protector. “Into your hands I commend my spirit”: I surrender my soul, departing from the body, to your power, so that you may restore it when I ask—that is, so that through your divinity I may have the power to lay down my soul and take it up again.

Therefore I commend it to you because you have redeemed me—that is, you will redeem me from death, O Lord, God of truth, who never deceives in your promises. Through the prophets you promised that you would raise me up. And because you are the God of truth, you hate those who uselessly observe vanities—namely, the Jews, who, so as not to lose their place and nation, killed me to no purpose (John XI).

But I have hoped in the Lord; I shall rejoice and be glad in your mercy, as above. Through this mercy you saved my soul—that is, my life—by raising me from necessities, that is, from death and suffering.

For you regarded my humility—that is, you took up my mortality. Or you regarded my obedience, since you despised Adam’s disobedience.

And in saving me: “Nor did you deliver me into the hands of the enemy,” that is, into the power of the Jewish people, so that through death they might hold me in the confines of Judea. You enclosed me in their power because I died, but you did not shut me in, because I rose again.

“My vessel of ointment was broken, and my ointment was poured out”—that is, the fragrance of knowledge of me was spread throughout the whole world. Therefore you did not confine my feet—that is, the preachers—in a spacious place, that is, throughout all the Gentiles. Torches were kindled in Judea; they went out and set the whole world ablaze.

“Have mercy on me, O Lord.” It is as though he said: “Having been resurrected and freed from all suffering, I am no longer terrified by death. But have mercy on me; perfect in them what you began in me. For I am troubled—not in myself, but in my members.”

That is, the cruelty of persecutors inspires great fear in me because my inner eye—that is, the reason of my members—has been disturbed in anger, which the first parent deserved.

The mind of my members, which ought to have been a man and to govern Eve—that is, its flesh—if it had remained under its Head, has been weakened by withdrawing from its Head, that is, from God. And my soul—that is, their sensuality—has been weakened, because the man of Eve, that is, reason, did not wish to be under its Head, nor did Eve, that is, sensuality, wish to be under her head, namely, under the rule of reason. Nor is reason able to restrain her from extending her hands toward unlawful things.

And my belly—that is, the flesh of my members—has been disturbed, unable to resist desires. Therefore I am troubled because my life—the long life which human beings ought to have had if they had not departed from the commandment of their Lord God—has failed in sorrow, that is, in that word over which one must always grieve: “You will be like gods” (Gen. III).

And my years—that is, the eternal years which belonged to my members—have failed in groans, that is, in that word over which one must always sigh.

My strength has grown weak in poverty—that is, sensuality and my flesh, which before the transgression were firm, now suffer from complete want. For it has sufficiency in nothing.

And my bones—that is, reason and understanding—are troubled, that is, confused in their knowledge of the truth.

To remove these necessities, the Lord, who came as a human being free from sin, became a reproach to my neighbors, the Jews who were neighbors according to the flesh. Above all my enemies—that is, they despised me more than any of the Gentiles whom they called dogs and unclean. It is as though he said: “I did not deem myself worthy to suffer things so many and so unworthy.”

And I became a terror to my acquaintances—that is, to the disciples. “We had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke XIV).

Those who saw me—that is, those who understood God through miracles—fled outside from me. That is, they turned from divinity toward humanity. Although previously they thought me to be God, they believed me to be merely human.

I was given over to oblivion from their hearts, as though dead—each one, so to speak, treating me as a lost vessel, that is, as a useless vessel fit for no purpose.

Therefore, because I heard—that is, patiently endured—the reproach of many who dwelt round about, that is, who delighted in earthly things, they thought me incapable of anything, because, while suffering many unworthy things, I resisted nothing.

Or “those dwelling round about” means those who seek blessedness in vanities and never reach the middle—that is, true blessedness. Dwelling in that circuit, loving those things which draw toward destruction more than those which lead toward salvation, they were united in condemning me, although I had come for their salvation. They conspired to take my life—that is, they persecuted not only me but also my members, in order to destroy them.

But I have hoped in you, O Lord. This and what follows, however, the Head says more in the person of his members than in his own.

## PSALM XXXI. DAVID'S INSTRUCTION

“Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin, and in whose spirit there is no deceit. For while I was silent, my bones grew old, while I cried out all day long. For day and night your hand was heavy upon me; I was turned in my distress, while the thorn was fastened in me. I made known my sin to you, and I did not hide my injustice. I said: ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord’; and you forgave the impiety of my sin. For this every holy person will pray to you at an opportune time. Yet in the flood of many waters they shall not approach him. You are my refuge from the tribulation that surrounded me, my joy amid those who surround me. I will give you understanding and instruct you in this way in which you will walk; I will fix my eyes upon you. Do not become like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding. With bit and bridle restrain their jaws, for they do not approach you. Many are the scourges of the sinner, but mercy will surround him who hopes in the Lord. Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you just; and glory, all you upright of heart.”

[Col. 0300C] **EXPOSITION.**

Although every psalm contains understanding, this one in particular is spiritually assigned that name, which is common, on account of its dignity and excellence. Thus, when “the Apostle” is said, Paul is understood; when “the Prophet” is said, Isaiah; when “the City” is said, Rome.

For it contains an understanding especially necessary for the salvation of every faithful person: before faith, one must not boast of merits, since there are none; after receiving faith through grace, one must not presume upon impunity, nor be sluggish in good works; and if one does anything good, one must attribute the whole thing not to oneself but to the grace of God.

The voice of the Prophet. It is as though he said: “I see people wishing to be blessed, but different people establish different things concerning blessedness. This, however, is Catholic; this is true.”

“Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven”—not those who have no iniquities, since there are none such, but those whose iniquities, original and actual, have been forgiven—namely, through the grace of God. These iniquities were formerly intense even under the Law, according to the saying: “The law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. VII). All who were saved before were saved for this reason: they believed in what we now believe has been fulfilled. According to the saying: “The saints conquered kingdoms through faith” (Heb. XI); and, “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. XV); and, “When the law came, sin revived” (Rom. VII).

Jerome says: Sins are forgiven in three ways: through baptism, through charity, and through martyrdom.

“Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven” through baptism, “and whose sins have been covered” through charity, according to the saying: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. IV). “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” through martyrdom.

Now their sins have been forgiven in the water of baptism. And blessed are those whose sins, namely those committed after baptism, have been covered. Covered, I say, not by the sick person but by the physician. The sick person covers wounds in order to worsen the disease; the physician covers them with medicines in order to heal.

He covers sins with the medicine of repentance—not so that God may not see them, but so that he may not see them in such a way as to punish them. What is covered is not seen; what is not imputed will not be punished. If you cover your sins by neither confessing nor defending them, God uncovers them. But if you humble yourself, accuse yourself, and uncover them, God covers them.

He adds how they are covered: “Blessed is the man”—that is, immortal, or praiseworthy, or glorious—“to whom the Lord has not imputed sin.” He has not imputed it for punishment, because here he has erased it through mercy.

Alternatively: It is as though he said: Blessed are those who have been saved through baptism, having received the forgiveness of sins through grace. And blessed are those who sinned after baptism because they fell into serious sins, but corrected themselves through confession and repentance.

But that man is blessed, and truly a man, because he acted bravely—and more blessed than those others—to whom the Lord did not impute sin; that is, he preserved his soul free from sin after the remission of sins, so that he committed nothing so serious that the Lord would impute it to him. For he committed only venial sins, which he was able easily to correct through the Lord’s Prayer, psalmody, litany, or almsgiving.

Therefore he did not impute it, “because there is no deceit in his spirit.” Deceit is in the spirit of the one who is one thing and pretends to be another. Within he has injustice; outwardly he cries out for justice. This can be observed in the Pharisee and the Publican.

There was no deceit in the spirit of the Publican, because he did not conceal what proceeded from himself. He humbled himself and accused himself, standing at a distance and not daring to raise his eyes toward heaven; but beating his breast, he said: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke XVIII).

The Lord did not impute sin to him, because he went down to his house justified in comparison with the Pharisee. But the Pharisee was silent about what ought to have been proclaimed, and proclaimed what ought to have been silent. He was silent about his sins and proclaimed his merits; and therefore, even if he possessed some justice and merit, he lost it through pride, attributing to himself what he had received from God.

It is as though he said: “Blessed is the one in whose spirit there is no deceit.” Conversely, he is not blessed in whose spirit there is deceit—a fact which I, having experienced it, must affirm.

“For my bones grew old while I cried out all day long, because I was silent.”

He says this in the person of anyone who belongs to the old human being: “Because through humility I did not wish to belong to the new human being, through pride I remained in the old human being.”

This can especially be referred to the Jewish people, who are signified by the Pharisee, just as the Gentiles are signified by the Publican.

“My bones”—that is, my strength, namely virtues and justice—“grew old,” that is, became weak. I was unable by myself to resist vices, as I could have done if I had trusted not in myself but in the Lord.

I, who could have been young in the Lord, have become old in myself. For I kept silent while I should have cried out: I kept silent about sins, I cried out about merits; I kept silent about what would make me advance, I cried out about what would make me fail; I kept silent in confession, I cried out in praise. All day long—that is, continually—like that Pharisee who vaunted his good deeds out of vanity. But at last I turned from that false cry to the true one: namely, so that I would not defend my sins but accuse them, nor boast of merits but condemn them. And I made this conversion in my misery, considering the great misery within me—namely, the constant tribulation of your scourges. I saw that the righteousness which had seemed easy to me was difficult without your grace. I realized that many vices were invading me [Col. 0302B] and that I could not resist them by my own strength. And this was because your hand was heavy upon me—the hand that raises the humble and weighs down the proud. Your power greatly crushed my pride, because it allowed sin to rule over me and made righteousness difficult; yet this power would have lifted all these things if I had been willing to rely not on myself but on him. By day and by night—that is, continually.

For God confined all things under sin, so that he might have mercy on all (Rom. XI). Or, “by day and by night,” that is, both in prosperity and in adversity, because I was relieved from this misery neither in prosperity nor in adversity. Or: I turned from praising myself to accusing myself. When the thorn is fixed—that is, when pride is broken and I am bent toward humility through the prohibition of the law. [Col. 0302C] A thorn is a bone that keeps an animal’s body rigid; when it is broken, the body bends. Then I turned in my misery—that is, by attending to my misery—when the thorn is fixed: that is, when my conscience, which previously applauded itself for innocence and thought that the sins that were sins were not sins, is fixed—pierced and awakened by the thorns of your prohibitions. Previously I did not know that this was sin until the law said, “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery” (Rom. VII). Or: your hand was heavy upon me when the thorn was fixed—that is, righteousness became difficult for me, although it had previously seemed easy, when your law was given and pricked my conscience, according to the Apostle’s statement: “Before the law, sin was dead, but I was alive; when the law came, sin revived, but I [Col. 0302D] died.” For I did not know that lust was sin unless the law said (Exod. XX), “You shall not covet.” Or: when I cried out all day long in desire for temporal things—and not without cause, because your hand, that is, your power, was heavy upon me, that is, it imposed a severe punishment upon me for the sin of the first parent. “By day and by night,” that is, continually. In this way I was converted.

I made my transgression known to you, whereas previously I neither considered nor defended it: I myself condemned it; I myself confessed the transgression—that is, that I had not done what I ought to have done. And I did not conceal my iniquities—namely, that I had done what I ought not to have done. For what a physician covers is healed; what a sick person covers feeds [Col. 0303A] the wound. If you do not conceal it, thereby destroying it, God conceals it by healing it. Truly I did not conceal it, because I said—that is, thought—this: “I will confess my iniquity to the Lord; I will confess to him my sins against myself,” that is, by accusing myself. I did not attribute them to God, or to fate, or to fortune, or to a constellation, or to the devil, as many do. And because I humbled myself so greatly, you forgave the impiety of my sin—that is, the defense of sin, which arose from pride. A great commendation of God’s mercy: there was not yet a voice in the mouth, and already God’s ear was attentive to the heart.

For he does not say, “I confessed”; but to have said it is to have confessed. On account of this impiety—that is, the remission of sin—which is to be remitted, or on account of this forgiveness of sins, every saint will pray to you—that is, will pray [Col. 0303B] to you so that he may reach you, and for no other reason. “Every saint,” that is, everyone who wishes to become holy. For no one will be sanctified unless you forgive his sins.

I say that he will pray in an opportune time—that is, in the time of grace, namely, in the time of Christ’s incarnation. For all who have been sanctified, whether before the coming of the Son of God or afterward, have been saved through faith in him: before his coming, by believing that what we believe after his coming has happened. The opportune time is that of which the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI).

Although I have said “in an opportune time,” nevertheless “in the flood of many waters they shall not come near him,” that is, amid the multitude of various doctrines they will not [Col. 0303C] approach his mercy—namely, by attributing their guilt to a constellation, according to certain philosophers; to fortune, according to others; or to things of this kind. Those who could come to him by a short route—that is, by confessing their sins and humbling themselves, through which they could have him appeased—go around by a circuitous route, making accusations. It is as though he said: they will not approach him through the multitude of their excuses.

But I will approach, because I will flee back to the one from whom I fled through pride by means of humility. You are my refuge: I wish to flee to you, not to accuse you. I strive to have you in my heart as a fortress of refuge—not myself, not a human being, not the world, which perishes. From the tribulation that surrounded me, it did not drown me, because I transferred my forces to the fortress above, laughing at those occupied with the cares of this age. And afterward my exultation [Col. 0303D] will be in you; even now you are my exultation, but in hope. And because tribulation still exists in reality, deliver me from those surrounding me—namely, from many waters, or from the tribulations of the flesh—so that I may not be overwhelmed by them.

It is as though he said: “I said, ‘I will confess,’ and you forgave,” saying this to me: “I will give you understanding”—the understanding, namely, that I gave you in the first creation. For when you were in honor, that is, in the dignity of rational nature, and did not understand so as to adorn yourself in conduct and cultivate your life, you were compared with foolish beasts and became like them (Ps. XLVIII), having forgotten your God, without whom you could not remain in that dignity. But now, because you return to me through humility, I will give you the understanding necessary for blessedness, so that you may know that you must presume upon nothing except the mercy [Col. 0304A] of your God alone. And in that understanding I will instruct you, so that what you rightly understand you may complete through honorable conduct: “In this way in which you will walk,” that is, in this life in which you will not be sluggish but will always advance from virtue to virtue.

Or: “In the honorable purpose that you will choose, I will establish my eyes over you,” that is, my mercy will never depart from you, because your humility will always look toward me, as it says: “My eyes are always toward the Lord, for he will draw my feet out of the snare” (Ps. XXIV).

Therefore, placed in such great honor and possessing such great hope through God’s mercy, live intelligently and rationally. Do not become like a horse, which without discrimination carries its own rider just as it carries another. And a mule likewise bears the burden of another indiscriminately, just as it bears that [Col. 0304B] of its own master. Or: do not be without a guide, lest, indulging yourselves, you fall over precipices; for horse and mule, when they are without a guide, go along byways. Or: do not presume upon your own strength, you who possess understanding, as do the horse and the mule, which have no understanding.

But, O Lord, those who prefer to be horses and mules rather than approach you—constrain their jaws with bit and bridle, that is, with great restraint and great contrition. Crush their jaws, that is, suppress their proud speech, so that they may learn not to boast of merits but to confess their sins to you in humility. Crush their pride; place the words of your law in their mouths, words that restrain them from pride and from their wandering course. For as they go around in circles, they do not approach you. If he does not wish to approach, there will be many scourges—that is, much punishment [Col. 0304C]—for the sinner, that is, for the one who persists in sin.

But mercy will surround the one who hopes in the Lord—not in his merits or in the world—that is, it will fortify him, both here through scourges and in the future through reward. And so that his mercy may surround you, rejoice in the Lord, not in the world, whose joy is transitory. Rejoice in mind and exult in body, yet in hope, you righteous; for the unrighteous exult in the world, not in the Lord.

And at last let all who are upright of heart glory with perfect glory in reality. For those whose hearts are crooked do not glory in the Lord. They say either that God is not present in things and that everything happens by chance, like the pagans; or, if they say that God exists, they say that he is unjust, like false Christians, when they see themselves in hardship and others who do not fear God at rest; themselves poor and those others rich. Or they say that he cares only for heavenly things and despises the weak. [Col. 0304D] But those are upright of heart who direct their will toward God’s will. And if human weakness troubles them, the judgment of divine equity consoles them. If things happen otherwise than they wish, they place God’s will above their own. Such people always glory in the Lord.

## PSALM XXXII. A PSALM OF DAVID, FOR THE END.

> “Exult, you righteous, in the Lord; praise is fitting for the upright. Give thanks to the Lord on the cithara; sing psalms to him on the ten-stringed psaltery. Sing to him a new song; sing well to him with a loud cry. For the word of the Lord is upright, and all his works [Col. 0305A] are in faithfulness. He loves mercy and judgment; the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord. By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host. Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin, placing the abysses in storehouses. Let all the earth fear the Lord; let all who inhabit the world be moved before him. For he spoke, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created. The Lord scatters the counsels of the nations; he rejects the thoughts of the peoples, and he rejects the counsels of princes. But the counsel of the Lord remains forever, the thoughts of his heart from generation to generation. Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom he chose for his inheritance. From heaven the Lord looked down; he saw all the sons of men. From his prepared [Col. 0305B] dwelling he looked upon all who inhabit the earth. He who formed their hearts individually, who understands all their works. A king is not saved by great strength, nor will a giant be saved by the abundance of his strength. A horse is deceptive for salvation; in the abundance of its strength it will not be saved. Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him and upon those who hope in his mercy, to rescue their souls from death and to feed them in famine. Our soul awaits the Lord, for he is our helper and protector. For our heart will rejoice in him, and we have hoped in his holy name. Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us, just as we have hoped in you.”

[Col. 0305C] **EXPOSITION.**

This psalm is joined to the preceding one, and it is the voice of the Prophet exhorting all the faithful, who have been justified freely by the grace of God (Rom. III), no longer to exult in the world, whose joy has an end, but in the Lord, in whom they will rejoice without end. Renewed, they should sing a new song, which is sung not with the voice but with a new life: namely, putting on new humility after laying aside the voice of anger, new charity, and new righteousness, putting on the new man who has been created according to God (Eph. IV). Thus he says:

“Exult, you righteous, in the Lord.” It is as though he said: Above I said, “Exult, you righteous”; again I say, “Exult, you righteous”—not in the world, which belongs to the unrighteous, whose glory has an end, but exult, that is, leap outside yourselves [Col. 0305D], rejoicing not in yourselves but in the Lord. Attribute everything to him, in whom exultation is eternal.

Therefore you righteous, exult in the Lord; in all things give thanks to God, because praise belongs to the upright and not to others. “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Eccli. XV). The sinner blesses God in prosperity and reviles him in adversity, because his heart is crooked. But those are upright who place God’s will above their own and who know that all things work together for their good. They always praise God, like Job: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job I).

You who are righteous, who have been redeemed by grace and belong to the new man, exult in the Lord—that is, walk in newness of life [Col. 0306A] (Rom. VI)—because such praise is fitting for the upright. The righteous are those who do not deny the Lord his due.

Exult in this way: “Give thanks to the Lord on the cithara,” that is, mortify your members, because the cithara sounds from below. “And sing psalms on the psaltery,” that is, strengthen the spirit, because the psaltery sounds from above.

Or: praise him on the cithara—that is, in the lower things bestowed upon you by God, give thanks to God through the six works of mercy: offer bread to the hungry and clothe the naked. Or, bless God in the prosperity and adversity of this age. And “on the psaltery,” that is, from above, sing psalms, adding love of neighbor to love of God, drawing others to the love of God by begging, exhorting, admonishing, and giving an account.

Almsgiving is performed in these three ways: in two ways [Col. 0306B] from above—first, when we offer ourselves, which is the preeminent form; second, when we draw our neighbor toward the charity of God. The third is from below, when by ministering to our neighbors in bodily matters we serve God.

“Sing to him on the ten-stringed psaltery,” that is, spiritually fulfill the ten words given from above through the law, loving God and loving your neighbor. Since there are ten commandments, three pertain to love of God and seven to love of neighbor.

A string is first stretched, then dried, and afterward twisted. So too, if we wish by analogy to become such an instrument for God, we must stretch ourselves by crucifying our flesh with its vices and desires. We must dry ourselves, that is, withdraw from carnal desires. We must also be twisted [Col. 0306C], that is, patiently endure tortures inflicted from elsewhere. Two of these things are within us, and one is outside us.

It is as though he said: “And while doing this, sing to him a new song”—namely, laying aside falsehood, pretense, hatred, envy, detraction, and every form of wickedness, which belong to the old man; like newborn infants, put on the rational, guileless virtues of the new man, who has been created according to God in the righteousness and holiness of truth (I Pet. I; Eph. IV). The old song is anger, pride, and hatred. The new song is gentleness, humility, and charity.

And do not merely sing with your mouth, but “sing well to him,” that is, praise him by good works, “with a loud cry,” that is, with every intention of the mind, or ineffably. Elsewhere: “with jubilation.” Therefore praise the Lord [Col. 0306D] and live for him.

“For the word of the Lord is upright”: every promise of his is true; he promises nothing without fulfilling it. And all his works, which he commands to be done, are in faithfulness—that is, they deceive no one. None are without recompense. He who mercifully deigned to promise a reward faithfully wishes to pay it. Let us hold fast to the most faithful debtor, because we have the most merciful promiser. He will faithfully provide it if we faithfully demand it.

Because his works are in faithfulness, let ours also be in faithfulness. We can also understand it in this way: “Sing to the Lord a new song,” that is, a song of faith, because without faith it is impossible to please God (Hebr. XI). But because faith without works is idle (Jas. II), he therefore adds: “Sing well to him,” that is, [Col. 0307A] with jubilation or a loud cry—that is, by working with great devotion. Praise him so greatly that words fail in praise, because jubilation is praise of God that cannot be expressed in words.

Therefore work in faith, because the word of the Lord is upright—namely, the word of faith. Hence the Prophet says: “The Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth” (Isa. X); concerning which the Apostle says: “This is the word of faith that we preach” (Rom. IX). That word is upright because it is present in action. Hence it follows: “And all his works are in faithfulness.” No one can work well outside faith, whether this explanation or that one is followed. What follows is connected in this way:

Truly they are in faithfulness, because all things are either mercy or judgment; and this [Col. 0307B] is in faithfulness because they are never without recompense. “He loves mercy”—therefore let us also love mercy. What greater mercy of God can there be than this: that he calls those who have turned away, forgives, and is patient with sinners until they convert? He urges the sluggish, consoles the afflicted, teaches the diligent, forgets the past, and promises the future. He does not abandon those who labor and trust in him. He gives what may be sacrificed to him and grants what may make him propitious.

Or there is another reason why he should be sung: because he loves mercy, by which he calls and justifies, and judgment, by which he scourges his own and blinds the wicked. He also loves judgment because he distinguishes between the just and the impious, giving a reward to the just and punishment to the unjust.

So let us also love judgment and judge justly. Many think that they act well when, by defending the cause of a poor person, they turn justice into injustice. This must not be done, because neither should mercy hinder judgment nor judgment [Col. 0307C] hinder mercy. If we wish to help the poor person, let us show mercy after judgment, or seek it from the source.

He proves that God loves mercy: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord,” that is, the Church, which is the Lord’s earth and inheritance, is full of workers of the Lord’s mercy.

He shows through which workers he filled this earth: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established,” that is, by the teaching and work of the Son. “The heavens,” that is, the apostles—raining teachings, thundering threats, flashing with miracles—were established in faith, hope, and charity. The Son of God is called the Word because he interprets God’s will for you.

“And by the breath of his mouth,” that is, by the Holy Spirit sent from [Col. 0307D] heaven, from his mouth—that is, from Christ, who is the Father’s mouth, because through him he spoke to us. Here he shows that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. “All their host,” namely, their power to thunder with threats and flash with miracles, comes from that Spirit. The Trinity is indicated here.

Up to this point he has shown mercy. He also loves judgment: “Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin,” that is, reserving there the surging wills of embittered persecutors and restraining them so that they may not rage unless he permits it, so that he may have material with which to educate his children and punish his servants, test the devout and condemn the impious, crown his soldiers, and blunt the fury of their persecutors.

Or: he gathered and confined the violence of persecutors, which formerly wandered openly and everywhere, into a few, so that although they have the will, they cannot [Col. 0308A] act unless permitted—just as water does not flow from a wineskin unless the one who controls the wineskin wishes it.

“Placing the abysses in storehouses”: he has not only others but even the most depraved and desperate stored in his chamber. They too are under his power, so that they can do nothing unless permitted. Thus he has material from which to bestow gifts upon his soldiers, crown the good, condemn the wicked, test his own, and consume the impious.

Therefore “let all the earth fear the Lord”—that is, let all those who have cultivated the earth, namely their body, in such a way that they may finally receive it immortal, fear him alone, to whom all things obey by necessity. The serpent rages: let it fear the Lord. The lion rages: let it fear the Lord. The tyrant rages: let him fear the Lord. For these can do nothing more than he permits.

Nor should anyone be moved by any [Col. 0308B] of these things—that is, moved away from his purpose. But “let all who inhabit the world be moved before him,” so that they may move where he commands, going from virtue to virtue. Let all the perfect who have made their field rounded, cutting away every irregularity—that is, who have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires—fear the Lord. They inhabit that world and are not themselves inhabited by it. Let them fear the Lord with chaste fear, and not the world, which can do nothing to them unless permitted.

Alternatively: “And by the breath of his mouth,” that is, by the Spirit of Christ, “all their host,” namely, the apostles. What follows is connected with this as follows: “His,” I say, who is gathering through those heavens the waters of the sea—that is, the waves and persecutions of this age—into a wineskin, so that this age may now rage in only a few [Col. 0308C], since through the apostles’ teaching the greater part has already been converted to the faith.

And lest anyone glory in reckless exultation, saying, “Then there is nothing to fear, because the waters of the sea have been gathered,” he adds: “Let all the earth fear the Lord.” Let it exult because “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord,” but let it fear sinning and departing from him. Let the Church fear the Lord alone and nothing else, because all other things are in his power and can do nothing unless he permits it.

“For he spoke, and they came to be”—namely, in the first creation. Or: “He spoke,” that is, he permitted, “and all things that come to pass came to be,” whether those he himself made or those he permits to happen; nothing happens without his permission.

And rightly, when he says “they came to be,” we understand all things, because what has come to be is something uncertain and confused, and the only thing certain about it is that it [Col. 0308D] has come to be. Therefore what he says, “he spoke,” is understood less strongly than what he says, “he commanded,” because when we command something, we wish it to be confirmed.

“He commanded, and they were created.” And whatever things were separately recreated afterward for sanctification are all from him, and neither these things nor those people can do anything except through him.

Therefore “the Lord scatters the counsels of the nations” that seek to erase his name, hand over his saints to death, and turn them away from their God. But the nations do not scatter the counsel of the Lord.

“He rejects the thoughts of the peoples,” namely, of the Jews: “Command, therefore, that the tomb be guarded, lest his disciples come and steal him and say to the people, ‘He has risen from the dead’” (Matt. XXVII). But the peoples do not reject the counsel of the Lord.

“And he rejects the counsels [Col. 0309A] of princes,” namely, of Annas and Caiaphas, who said, “It is expedient for you that one man should die for the people” (John XI); or of all princes who seek their own interests and not the things that are God’s. But the princes do not reject the counsel of God.

And this is what follows: “But the counsel of the Lord remains forever,” namely, that Christ should rise again and redeem the human race; “the thoughts of his heart from generation to generation,” because his counsel—which consisted of the ancient disposition, the new restoration, and eternal happiness—remains immutable both in the first generation and in the second generation. In the first it was prophesied; in the second it was fulfilled. Or: in the temporal generation and in the eternal generation.

In other contexts, “thought” is less than “counsel.” Counsel is considered reasoning, but in God [Col. 0309B] they are the same; therefore they are used here indifferently.

This is the counsel of the Lord: that his nation should choose God for itself unto blessedness, in whom alone true blessedness exists. For no one can have true blessedness from something inferior to himself. Everyone wishes to be blessed, but only those are blessed who seek to be blessed above themselves.

It is as though he said: Truly the counsel of the Lord remains forever, because “blessed is the nation whose Lord is God”—the Lord by its will, its God by necessity—which has chosen no other lord for itself as an inheritance, that is, the people acquired by grace.

He chose it, I say, by grace, not by merit, in this way: “From heaven the Lord looked down,” that is, from the humanity of the Word, through which the divinity bent itself toward our weakness. The Lord, who had previously rejected them in Adam, looked down and, by looking, saw—that is, mercifully chose [Col. 0309C]—all the sons of men, that is, all the future Jews who through his grace would imitate the patriarchs and prophets.

And he did not look down only from heaven, but also “from his prepared dwelling,” that is, from the apostles, whom he made by his grace such that he might dwell in them. He looked upon all who inhabit the earth, that is, he showed his mercy to all those from the nations who cultivate the earth—that is, their flesh—in such a way, cleansing it of thorns and thistles, that they may eventually receive it immortal. Such people inhabit it and are not themselves inhabited by it.

To make them fit for election, he “formed their hearts individually,” that is, he shaped and adapted their hearts by giving them various gifts of the Holy Spirit. Hence the Apostle says: “Each person has his own gift from God” (I Cor. VII). Or “individually,” that is, by sealing and imprinting [Col. 0309D] his image upon them. Or “one by one,” imprinting the Spirit’s seal upon each.

And he not only formed their hearts, but he understands all their works. Great is God’s mercy: it does not say that he makes them understand, but that he himself understands in them, according to the saying, “The Lord working with them” (Mark XVI). Or he understands—that is, he knows with what intention they are done. He understands, that is, he sees, because all things are naked and open to his eyes; and he sees them in order to direct them.

And truly these alone are blessed; these alone are saved, who are justified by grace and not by merits. The others are not. He demonstrates this from the greater, because neither the powerful, such as kings, nor the strong, such as giants, can save others—not even themselves.

“A king is not saved with true salvation by great strength.” It is as though he said: a king is saved [Col. 0310A], but not by his pomp. “And a giant,” that is, a strong man, “will not be saved by the abundance of his strength.”

They are not saved through this because “a horse is deceptive for salvation.” A horse—that is, worldly dignity and pomp—seems to promise blessedness but does not deliver it, if we apply this to the king.

But if we apply it to the giant, the meaning is this: “A deceptive horse,” that is, the human body, which is without understanding like a horse and which, without a rider—that is, without the governance of the soul—is carried over precipices. It is deceptive for salvation because it is an impediment to the soul.

Alternatively, in a good sense: “A king is not saved by great strength.” Even one who resists carnal desires or attacks the devil and his angels is not saved if he presumes upon himself, because “a horse is deceptive”—that is, a human being—for salvation if he does not have God [Col. 0310B] as his rider. “It depends not on human willing or running, but on God’s mercy” (Rom. IX).

Job said of God: “He loosens the belt of kings and binds their loins with a cord” (Job XII). This was said of those who govern illicit impulses well and presume upon themselves. He loosens their belt—that is, he permits them to fall—such as Peter, who denied; Thomas, who said, “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (John XI); and the former threw himself at his feet. John, who reclined upon the Lord’s breast at the supper (John XIII), fled naked after leaving the linen cloth behind (Mark XIV). This happened for their benefit, because afterward he would gird their loins with constancy.

A king is saved; a giant is saved also. But he will not be saved by the abundance of his strength. Where, then, is salvation? It is almost evident: “The eyes of the Lord”—that is, the regard of the Lord’s mercy—are upon [Col. 0310C] those who fear him, so that he may pull their feet from the snare, lest, while looking toward him, they fall into a pit or a snare.

And they are upon those who hope in his mercy—that is, those who fear him in such a way that they hope in no other, or those who hope in his recompense. For fear without hope is despair; hope without fear is presumption.

The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous for this purpose: that at last he may rescue their souls from eternal death and, meanwhile, feed them in famine—that is, in the time of famine—because in this time he makes them hunger for righteousness and refreshes them with it.

Therefore, because he refreshes them in the time of famine and will finally satisfy them in the days of fullness, “our soul awaits the Lord.” It has him as its most merciful promiser and awaits the most faithful debtor. If he delays for a long time, it bears the weight of his commandments. And rightly [Col. 0310D], because he is our helper in perfecting good things and our protector in evil things, so that we may not fail.

And therefore it rightly awaits him and looks for him, because “our heart will rejoice in him,” even if our flesh is afflicted. “And we have hoped in his holy name,” not in our own, like Adam, who wished to be a god for himself.

We have hoped in this name, which is “God,” because **δέος** means “fear,” and as those who fear him we have hoped in the Holy One who makes holy. Or we have hoped in this name—namely, God—by offering him worthy service and humbling ourselves.

And so that we may rejoice, “let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us,” that is, your recompense. Let it be according to the measure in which we have hoped in you: whoever hopes greatly receives great recompense, each according to his measure.

## PSALM XXXIII. A PSALM OF DAVID, WHEN HE CHANGED HIS COUNTENANCE BEFORE ABIMELECH, AND ABIMELECH DISMISSED HIM, AND HE DEPARTED.

[Col. 0311A]

> “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise will always be in my mouth. In the Lord my soul will be praised; let the meek hear and rejoice. Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together. I sought the Lord, and he heard me, and he delivered me from all my tribulations. Approach him and be enlightened, and your faces will not be ashamed. This poor man cried out, and the Lord heard him, and saved him from all his tribulations. The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and he will deliver them. Taste and see that the Lord is sweet; blessed is the man who hopes in him. Fear the Lord, all his saints, for there is no want for those who fear him. The rich have suffered want and hunger, but those who seek the Lord will not be deprived of any good. Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord. Who is the man who desires life and loves to see good days? Restrain your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it. The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth. The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them, and delivered them from all their tribulations. The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit. Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord will deliver them from all of them. The Lord guards all their bones; not one of them will be broken. The death of sinners is most evil, and those who hate the righteous will sin. The Lord will redeem the souls of his servants, and all who hope in him will not sin.”

**EXPOSITION.**
## Psalm 33

*A Psalm of David, when he changed his appearance before Abimelech, who dismissed him, and he went away.*

It is read in the Book of Kings (I Kings 21) how David killed Goliath the Philistine, and for this deed came into the favor of Saul, king of Israel, so that he even gave him his daughter Michal and made him a guest at the royal table. But afterward, when Saul heard David’s precedence in the chorus of singers—“Saul [Col. 0311D] struck down a thousand, and David ten thousand”—the king, angered at his own thousands, wanted to kill David. Fleeing from Saul’s presence, David came into the land of the Philistines, to the city of Gath, to Achish. When this was reported to Achish, he sent messengers to seize David and bring him to be killed.

But when God’s mercy intervened, the Holy Spirit fell upon him, and he changed his appearance, pretending to be possessed. For he was handsome in appearance, and he feigned madness, and beat a tambourine at the gate of the city, and was borne in his own hands, and moved toward the doorway of the gate, while saliva ran down his beard. When Achish saw him, supposing that he was insane, he said: “Why have you brought me a madman? Do I need a possessed man?” He took no further care [Col. 0312A] of him. And he dismissed David, and David went away.

Although the narrative relates that the change of appearance took place before Achish, while the title has “before Abimelech,” it may be said that Achish was the proper name of that king, whereas Abimelech was a common title of all the kings of the Philistines, just as Pharaoh was among the Egyptians and Caesar among the Romans. Or the change of names draws us toward the mystery.

In David we understand Christ; in Goliath, the devil, whom Christ, in humility, conquered—just as the small David overcame the great Goliath, who boasted of his strength and displayed his weapons to the Israelites.

“Abimelech” is interpreted as “the kingdom of my father.” The kingdom of David, Christ’s father according to the flesh, was the Jewish people. Before the Jewish people Christ changed his appearance when he transferred that sacrifice which was in [Col. 0312B] that people which existed among that people according to the order of Aaron into his body and blood according to the order of Melchizedek, who, as a figure of this sacrifice, offered bread and wine to God (Gen. XIV; Heb. VII). This change took place at that supper at which he was betrayed, when he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: “This is my body.” Likewise he took wine (Matt. XXVI; Mark XIV; Luke XXII), and by sanctifying it changed it into his blood.

When he did this, in a certain manner he was carried in his own hands. He wished that his body should be received, under the outward form of bread, rather than under any other form, because wine intoxicates the body; likewise, the imitation of Christ’s Passion so intoxicated the holy martyrs that it transferred them wholly from the human mind into the divine and made them entirely forget earthly things [Col. 0312C].

In this handing over of his body and blood, he commended to us his humility: although he was rich, he became poor for us (II Cor. VIII). The King of angels became human so that a human being might eat the bread of angels. Human pride was so great that it would deign to imitate neither a patriarch, nor a prophet, nor any other human being. Therefore, so that this pride might humble itself, God became human, so that the human being might become God. The immortal put on mortal form so that the mortal might assume immortality. He descended so that we might ascend.

In this change of appearance—that is, of sacrifice—in which God’s will was in a certain manner displayed, because through these temporal ordinances he wished to reveal realities that were true and eternal, he feigned madness. What greater feigning could there be than that the [Col. 0312D] immortal God should undergo a temporal death through many indignities and many insults, in order to rescue the human race from eternal death?

He beat a tambourine at the gate of the city because he stretched out his body, fastened with nails upon the cross, in order to close against the enemy the human hearts that had been open to the devil, and to open them to God. He fell down at the doorway of the gate—that is, he humbled himself even to the beginning of our faith, which faith is the entrance into the Church.

Saliva flowed down upon his beard. These are the saliva-drops of children, because the Lord’s words by which the commendation of his body and blood was made seemed childish to the Jews; in those words divinity lay hidden beneath humanity. For strength is signified by the beard. When he said, “Unless someone eats the flesh of the [Col. 0313A] Son of Man and drinks his blood, he will not have life” (John VI), many who heard this, not understanding that a divine work lay hidden within it, went away backward—even some of the disciples—saying: “This is a hard saying, and who can hear it?” (John VI). For they thought that he wished to give them for eating the flesh which they saw.

Then the Lord, turning to his eleven disciples, said: “Do you also wish to go away?” Peter answered for all: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (ibid.). “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is of no avail” (ibid.).

In those who went away backward, not understanding the transformation of this sacrifice, Achish is understood. His name is interpreted as “What is this?” and signifies ignorance. While he was being sought for death by the Pharisees, chief priests, and scribes [Col. 0313B], he remained at the gate of the city and beat a tambourine—that is, he produced a sweet sound from the tambourine among the apostles, who were already established in the faith, which is the entrance to the heavenly Jerusalem: namely, the teaching that his flesh must be mortified.

Because that unbelieving people did not wish to understand the commendation of the true sacrifice and did not receive the example of Christ’s humility, Christ dismissed him and went away—that is, he transferred himself to the Gentiles, so that through this they might be saved.

This psalm is the voice of Christ, commending the new sacrifice of his body and blood and setting before the human race an example of humility: although he existed in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. II).

## “I will bless the Lord at all times.”

I, who [Col. 0313C] until now blessed the Lord for a moment through legal sacrifices according to the order of Aaron among the Israelite people, will now bless him through the new sacrifice according to the order of Melchizedek, who was prior both in time and in dignity, to whom Abram gave tithes, and in whom Aaron was tithed.

I will do this among the Christian people by taking my body and blood—that is, by imitating my humility—not for a moment but at all times, because this sacrifice was not instituted only for a time. His praise, namely, will always be in my mouth—that is, both in prosperity and in adversity.

The proud, lifted up by the prosperity of this age, bless in prosperity but curse in adversity, with the mouth of the body and the mouth of the heart: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away” (Job I).

In this way I will bless: “In the Lord my soul shall be praised.” My life, blameworthy in itself, will be praised [Col. 0313D]—that is, will be praiseworthy—in the Lord, that is, in the Lord’s mercy and gifts. I will attribute nothing to myself.

Let the meek hear this humility of mine; let the humble hear and imitate it—that is, let them learn to praise their soul in the Lord and not in themselves or in the world, and let them rejoice with true joy.

Therefore let the meek hear this changed sacrifice and understand it, because the proud did not wish to hear. They said: “This is a hard saying” (John VI). Let them rejoice in my example and not be saddened like those who said: “And who can hear it?” (ibid.).

Since there is no place for envy in this joy, and every good shared in common shines forth more beautifully, I do not wish to possess it alone; I do not wish to approach alone, as lovers of the world approach what they love. Rather, I wish to draw with me as many as I can toward the love of God—by pleading, admonishing, praying, and giving an account.

O you meek, magnify the Lord with me by doing good [Col. 0314A]. Humble yourselves with me beneath the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you (I Pet. V), so that just as I live because of the Father, you too may live because of him.

“And let us exalt his name together.” Let us make him great in ourselves by living rightly and by drawing others toward his love—that is, by exultation directed toward the same thing, namely, toward God, commending his mercy in all things. Or let us bear one another’s burdens in another way, and thus fulfill the law of Christ (Gal. VI). In this regard, take me as an example, because Christ says: “I sought the Lord” [Col. 0314B]: I sought glory from all those things, but I loved him alone.

And because I sought him alone, he heard me—namely, with this hearing—and he rescued me from all my tribulations, both external and internal.

Therefore, following my example, approach him in spirit, not in place, and not in the manner of those who approached him when they crucified me. Rather, approach by taking the body and blood of Christ and imitating his humility.

Approaching in this way, be enlightened from the darkness of ignorance, so that you may not be Achish, knowing what that sacrifice is, what it signifies, and why it exists, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. V). For he is the true light; he himself is for us the book and example of life.

After his illumination, your faces will not blush—namely, your inner consciences [Col. 0314C], now cleansed—namely, your inner consciences, now cleansed; nor will your outward faces be confounded before the true Judge, nor here be ashamed of poverty and disgrace.

It is as though he says: “And so that your faces may not be confounded, imitate my humility. Although I was rich, I became poor for you” (II Cor. VIII). So you too must not seek your own glory, but God’s.

“This poor man”—that is, I, the humble man, presuming on nothing except God’s mercy alone—“cried out,” that is, raised himself toward God with complete intention; “and he was not confounded, because the Lord heard him and saved him from all his tribulations.”

Therefore he will also hear you, if you are humble, if you cry out to him. And truly you can cry out, because you have not only an example in me but also help, because the angel of the Lord [Col. 0314D]: the angel of the Lord—namely, Christ, the Angel of the Great Counsel (Isa. IX)—“will encamp,” that is, will make his encampment, meaning his help, “around those who fear him,” that is, for the defense of those who fear him. “And he will rescue them,” here from inward confusion and finally from outward confusion.

Or: “The Lord will send an angel around those who fear him, and he will rescue them,” because each believer has a good angel who guards him, as in the Gospel: “Their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matt. XVIII).

Therefore, because you have me as an example, you also have help. “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet.” Take his body and blood, and see—that is, understand—that the Lord is sweet.

It is as though he says: Take the sacrifice of my body and blood [Col. 0315A], and understand what you are taking, because you take it as an example of my humility and patience, so that just as I did not seek my own glory but the Lord’s, so may you. Take it with fear and reverence, and you will see that the Lord is sweet.

Just as I passed from death to life, from suffering to sweetness and glory, so you too, eating me—that is, imitating my Passion and humility in this life—will finally see that the Lord, who now seems bitter because of the endurance of sufferings, is sweet in his recompense.

Taste, and do not be Achish—that is, error and ignorance—so that you say: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John VI). If you are ignorant, taste and see that the Lord is sweet. But if you do not understand, King Achish changes his face and withdraws from you.

And because the Lord is sweet in recompense [Col. 0315B], “blessed is the man who hopes in him,” because although he now appears wretched, he will finally be blessed when “this mortal puts on immortality” (I Cor. XV).

And because hope without time is presumption, fear the Lord with chaste fear, fearing to offend him.

It is as though he says: By fearing him I will not lie, I will not defraud, I will not be greedy, I will not be ambitious, and therefore I will be poor. For “there is no want for those who fear him”: there is no want of the true good for those who fear him, because they possess him in whom all good things are found. Even if they appear poor, lacking these false goods, inwardly they are rich, and in time their outward need will be supplied.

Therefore do not fear becoming poor in these false goods for his sake, because the rich of this age, abounding in riches and believing themselves sufficient for themselves, nevertheless lacked that true good. Outwardly they are rich; inwardly they are poor.

It is as though he says: There is no want for those who fear God [Col. 0315C], for there is want for those who do not fear him.

Or: You Gentiles, who are poor—that is, who believe that you are insufficient for righteousness—approach him, because nothing will be lacking to you in him.

“The rich”—that is, the Jews, who thought they were sufficient for themselves in the Law and in earthly goods—“lacked the bread of the Word of God.” Hence the prophet says: “Behold, I will send among you a famine, not of bread, but of hearing the Word of God” (Amos VIII).

Although they lacked that true good, nevertheless they hungered with natural desire, because all people naturally tend toward blessedness, even if wandering error leads some astray.

“But those who seek the Lord”—that is, those who seek him inwardly with the steps of the soul, not of the body, him in whom the true and highest good exists—“shall not lack any good”; rather, they will increase, because now they possess it partially, and finally they will possess it perfectly.

They will lack no good, because they will possess him in whom every good exists [Col. 0315D].

And because there is no want for those who fear him, “come, children,” with the steps of faith. Even if I say that you fear, you are nevertheless children, according to the saying: “As many as received him, to them he gave power to become children of God” (John I).

Come by doing good. If you are children of Abraham, do the works of Abraham (John VIII). Hear me with a listening ear. “I will teach you the fear of the Lord,” that is, how you ought to fear God, so that you may lack nothing of any good.

And so that no one may say that he fears the Lord, he determines who it is that fears the Lord with chaste fear.

“Who is the man”—namely, who fears the Lord? He is the one “who desires life,” [Col. 0316A] that is, who, in devotion to God and in his work for God, strives toward this end: to cling to God, in whom true life exists.

And he desires life who loves “to see good days,” that is, who does not delight in evil days but strives with complete intention toward that life in which there will be no adversity.

Alternatively: “Who is the man who desires life and loves to see good days?” Everyone says, “I am.” Therefore do the things that follow.

“Restrain your tongue from evil,” so that, by going around accusing the Creator, you do not accuse yourself, when by accusing yourself you could appease him more directly. Restrain your tongue from evil, because the perfect person is one who does not sin with his tongue—from evil, that is, from detraction.

“And let your lips not speak deceit.” Let the lips of the heart not deceitfully circumvent a brother. “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. XVIII). And elsewhere: “The worship of justice is silence and peace” (Isa. [Col. 0316B] XXXII).

“Turn away from evil.” This is not enough, because it is not sufficient merely not to strip the poor man unless you clothe him. The rich man who was tormented in hell is not said to have lived by robbery; rather, he did not share what was his with Lazarus (Luke XVI).

Therefore it follows: “And do good,” everything you can. It profits nothing if you destroy and do not build—if you destroy vices and do not build virtues. For I have the Lord as my helper.

And when doing good, do not seek your reward here; rather, “seek peace,” that is, recompense, lest it be said to you: “You have received your reward.” “And pursue it,” that is, do not cease.

You can seek it because “the eyes of the Lord”—that is, the regard of the Lord’s mercy—are “upon the righteous,” that is, upon those who place the will of the Lord their God above their own will.

“And his ears are toward their prayers,” because they desire nothing except what ought to be desired: namely, his hearing and the disposition of his mercy toward their prayers.

Although they sometimes do not seem to be heard when they cry out [Col. 0316C], they are heard in their tribulations, because “tribulation produces patience” (Rom. V). Whatever the righteous ask that is useful to them is ready to be granted by God’s grace.

And lest some wicked person, hearing this, should say, “I shall sin safely, because God sees only the righteous, not me,” he adds: “But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil,” not to save them, but “to destroy their memory from the earth”—that is, their fame and glory, which they prepared for themselves in the land of the dying.

He will not destroy it because it exists there, but because they think they will possess it as they do here.

It was said, “His ears are toward their prayers,” [Col. 0316D] and rightly so, because “the righteous cried out”—namely, to the Lord. They directed toward him the free and powerful intention of mouth and work; that is, by acting without interruption, they made themselves suitable and worthy to be heard by him.

Therefore the Lord heard them. This is clear to me because “he rescued them from all their tribulations.”

He rescued them here, because their tribulations profited them more than they harmed them, and finally he will rescue them completely.

It is no wonder that he rescues them, because he is near. The three young men cried out and were manifestly delivered (Dan. III). The Maccabees likewise cried out as righteous men, and they were not delivered—yet both were delivered with true salvation (II Macc. VII).

“The Lord is near,” that is, the Lord’s help is at hand not for all who are afflicted, but for those who are [Col. 0317A] “afflicted in heart”—that is, for those who, in their tribulations, crush and humble their heart, meaning the pride of their heart.

He also adds: “And he will save the humble in spirit”—those who do not murmur against the Lord about injustice, but humbly receive his fatherly discipline like good children. He will save them now with inward salvation, and finally also with outward salvation.

For others who are afflicted he is not near, but far away, according to the saying: “I am God near at hand, and not a God far away” (Jer. XXIII).

It is as though he says: I said that he will rescue the righteous from all tribulations. “For many are the tribulations of the righteous.” All who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution (II Tim. III). From all these he will rescue them finally in their reward.

Meanwhile, “the Lord guards all their bones,” that is, all their virtues, which are the strength of the soul. By giving patience, he will guard them so that they do not fail in any virtue or in any good purpose.

“One of them shall not be broken” [Col. 0317B]—namely, not one of these bones. Even if the bone of the body is crushed, broken, or diminished, the bones of the soul will not merely remain unbroken; they will become stronger. For by subduing the flesh, the spirit is strengthened.

The Lord guards the bones of the righteous, but he will break those of the unrighteous.

Therefore “the death of sinners is most evil,” because they die in that which they possess that is best—namely, in the soul. For the death of the soul is separation from its God, without whom it cannot live. Even if they die amid delights, it is a most evil death, because they do not die through labors.

But because no one is without sin, lest this frighten the faithful, he adds: “And those who hate the righteous will fail.”

It is as though he says: They alone will fail [Col. 0317C] with respect to life and incur this death who hate me, the righteous one, their Savior and reconciler, who hate the sacrament of my body and blood, despising me and resembling Achish.

Because there are many kinds of sins, and it is difficult not to be a sinner in this life, he determines whose death is most evil.

This is the measure of human righteousness: however much mortal life may progress, because it cannot be without fault, it must not fail in this—that it hopes in him in whom there is forgiveness of sins.
