“The Lord will redeem”—namely, from that most evil death by which one passes from temporal misery into eternity—“the souls of his servants.” And this because they will not fail in the gravest fault, namely, by refusing to believe in him in whom there is forgiveness of sins: all who hope in him [Col. 0317D].

## Psalm 34

### “A Psalm for the end, by David himself.”

“Judge, O Lord, those who harm me; conquer those who attack me. Take up arms and shield, and rise to my help. Draw out the sword and close ranks against those who persecute me; say to my soul: I am your salvation. Let those who seek my soul be confounded and ashamed. Let those who think evil against me turn backward and be confounded. Let them become like dust before the face of the wind, and let the angel of the Lord hem them in. Let their ways be darkness and slippery ground, and let the angel of the Lord pursue them. For without cause they secretly hid destruction [Col. 0318A] for me in their snare; in vain they reproached my soul. Let the snare he does not know come upon him, and let the trap he hid seize him, and let him fall into that very snare. But my soul exulted in the Lord and will rejoice over his salvation. All my bones will say: Lord, who is like you? You rescue the needy from the hand of those stronger than he, the poor and needy from those who plunder him. Unjust witnesses rose up; they questioned me about things I did not know. They repaid me evil for good, barrenness for my soul. But when they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth. I humbled my soul with fasting, and my prayer will return into my bosom. I was pleasing to them as to a neighbor and as to our brother; I humbled myself as one mourning and grieving [Col. 0318B]. And they rejoiced against me and gathered together; scourges were gathered against me, and I did not know. They were scattered, but not pricked in heart; they tested me. They mocked me with mockery and gnashed their teeth against me. Lord, when will you look upon me? Restore my soul from their malice, my only one from the lions. I will confess to you in the great Church; in a weighty people I will praise you. Let those who oppose me unjustly not rejoice over me, who hate me without cause and wink with their eyes. For they spoke peaceably to me, but while speaking in the anger of the earth, they devised deceits. And they opened their mouth wide against me; they said: ‘Good, good! Our eyes have seen it.’ You have seen, Lord; do not be silent. Lord, do not depart from [Col. 0318C] me. Rise and attend to my judgment, my God and my Lord, to my cause. Judge me according to your righteousness, Lord my God, and let them not rejoice over me. Let them not say in their hearts: ‘Good, good, our soul!’ Nor let them say: ‘We have devoured him.’ Let those who rejoice at my evils be ashamed and confounded together. Let those who speak evil against me be clothed with confusion and shame. Let those who desire justice for me exult and rejoice, and let them say always: ‘The Lord is magnified, who desires the peace of his servant.’ And my tongue will meditate on your righteousness, your praise all the day.”

## Exposition

In this psalm the voice of our Head teaches by his example [Col. 0318D] that, in tribulations, we should pray so that we may be delivered from inward and outward enemies.

“David” is interpreted as “strong of hand,” because by his death he conquered our death; and as “desirable in appearance,” because he promised eternal life.

What, then, is stronger than that hand which touched the bier and raised the dead man? (Luke VII.) What is stronger than that hand which conquered the world and cast out the devil—not armed with iron, but fastened with nails to the wood? What is more desirable in appearance than the one whom the holy martyrs, though they had not seen him, did not hesitate to approach through every kind of torment so that they might see him?

The whole Christ speaks and prays here: first suffering in himself, and now suffering daily in his members.

### “Judge, O Lord, those who harm me.”

O Lord Father—or, O Lord Word—do what you are doing; exercise your power. Judge those who attempt to overturn your judgment by judicial authority [Col. 0319A]. Give them over to blindness of mind. For unless they had been inwardly blinded by the demands of their perverse merits, they would never have passed sentences of death against the author of their salvation: the Jews against Christ, and other unbelievers against the preachers of this salvation.

Or: Judge between me, Christ, and the Jews who persecute me—that is, distinguish between the Church and its persecutors—so that the persecution by which they persecute me and mine may be for their condemnation, but for glory to me and mine.

And judge in this way: “Conquer those who attack me.” They judge me and mine by manifest judgment, but you judge them by hidden judgment. Conquer—that is, overcome inwardly those who attack me outwardly: the Jews who attack me and my members.

Or conquer the devil and his angels [Col. 0319B], so that they may not prevail against mine.

And in order to conquer, “take up arms and shield,” that is, let your divine power sustain my soul and the souls of my people. They are arms because through them you wage war and wound the enemies; they are a shield because they protect both themselves and others.

Yet these arms are also designated by other arms, according to the Apostle’s saying: “In all things taking up the shield of faith, and the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI).

There is one meaning in divine arms and another in human arms. In divine arms, one thing is understood under different names, as faith is both shield and helmet. In human arms this is not at all the case.

Take them up, because however suitable weapons may be for battle, they accomplish nothing by themselves unless they are carried by a strong hand.

The prophet also offers the faithful a great spectacle [Col. 0319C] when he introduces God standing armed on behalf of his own.

Thus armed, “rise to my help,” raising me up and casting down my adversaries.

God is immutable, but he is said to lie down when he permits us to fail. He is said to rise when he prepares us for battle with the weapons of the virtues and makes us strong for resistance.

In this way rise to my help.

“Draw out the sword,” that is, multiply your sword—your faithful people—through whom you keep watch over my enemies.

Or: your sword, that is, me, your Christ, who am your sword—that is, your weapon. For I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword (Matt. X; Luke XI).

Draw it out—that is, bring it forth into the knowledge of the Gentiles—so that, in imitation of me, many swords may come into being.

And in this way “close ranks”: fortify me and mine. For the more numerous my armed followers become, the more strongly fortified I will be.

Or: “close ranks”—namely, the mouths of the enemies. Make the faithful, through confirmation of me, so watchful that the adversaries have nothing to say against them; indeed, through their innocence and good conduct, let them have cause to revere them, even while opposing those who persecute me.

“Say to my soul,” that is, make my soul and the souls of my people understand that salvation comes from you alone.

They tell the human heart that God is not its helper [Col. 0319D], so that, by seeking foreign aids, I may be oppressed by them. But you say to my soul: “I am your salvation.”

“Say to my soul,” that is, never cease saying it; and say it in such a way that I hear. There is no saying unless there is someone hearing. You will say it if I hear.

You did not give Adam that saying when, having taken pleasure in what was unlawful, he gave his assent (Gen. III): “I am your salvation.” Therefore let my soul consider no harm to befall it in obeying you [Col. 0320A] even unto death.

And when the sword has been poured forth—that is, when my resurrection and ascension have been glorified and proclaimed—let those who previously sought to destroy the soul, that is, my life and the life of my people, be confounded and put to shame. Let them be confounded as they consider their sins; let them blush and stand in awe, namely, of my judgment concerning those sins. And by revering my judgment, let them be turned backward, so that they may become imitators—those who previously wished to go before and defend their own error.

And thus let them be confounded—namely, with a good confusion—as they reflect that they did evil to me, and not only to me and mine. But if they do not wish to turn backward, let them become like dust before the face of the wind—that is, let them perish in eternal confusion.

Here he identifies two kinds of carnal persecutors. One consists of those who are so overcome that, through devoted piety, they pass from the number of persecutors into the number of the faithful. The other consists of those who are so overcome not that they may be incorporated into Christ, but rather that, separated from him, they may be condemned with the impious. Or this may be understood in the following way, as referring to evil.

Above he said, “Say to my soul: I am your salvation.” And when that salvation has been proclaimed to my people, let them be confounded—that is, let them be inwardly blinded—and let them stand in awe—that is, let them fear the resurrection. Those who seek my soul for condemnation, let them be turned backward—that is, let them fall backward, because that fall is the more serious. He falls backward who sins and does not consider his sins; he falls forward who sets his sins before himself.

It is as though he said: “At my glorification, let this happen to my people: let the righteous still practice righteousness; and let the one who is unclean become still more unclean” (Rev. XXII). Those who do not wish to be turned backward, let them become like dust before the face of the wind. Just as dust cannot stand against the wind, so may these people, lacking the solidity of faith, be unable to resist the wind of temptation. And let the angel of the Lord, the evil spirit belonging to the Lord by nature—or because he can do nothing unless permitted by the Lord—be one who constrains them, that is, drives them from every side toward destruction through various temptations.

Let their ways be darkness and slippery ground, and let the angel of the Lord pursue them. That is, on this journey let them resemble one traveling through darkness and over slippery ground, to whom one who causes and drives him to fall draws near. Let them be placed in darkness, that is, in ignorance and blindness of mind, and on slippery ground, that is, in lust. Let them lead a lustful life, which is prone to falling; and yet let the pursuing devil not be absent from them.

He says these things not as a wish, but as prophecy. Jerome: “Let them not know the light of truth, nor stand firm in a stable position; but let the steps of those who rage in this passion become slippery, and let them be afflicted by the angel of the Lord’s brightness.”

It is as though he said: “Let this happen to them not through divine injustice, but according to their own deserts, because they gratuitously hid from me the destruction of their own snare.” Their destruction was outwardly directed against me, but inwardly it was a snare for them; for they were caught in the very thing by which they thought to ensnare me.

Their snare has been crushed—that is, their temporal destruction—because I have risen; but they have fallen into eternal death, from which they will not rise. “Of their own snare,” because they ensnared not me but themselves as punishment. “They have gratuitously reproached my soul,” that is, they laid many insults upon my life: “Look, you who destroy the temple of God” (Matt. XXVII); “This man is not from God” (John IX). But they did so gratuitously—that is, falsely and without truth—for they could prove nothing.

Or they hid the destruction of their own snare, linking causes with causes: “their own,” namely, not founded on truth but on falsehood. Truly they prepared the destruction of their own snare, and not of mine, because the snare that the Jewish people do not know will come upon them—namely, the capture by Titus and Vespasian. Or, for the persecutors of the Church, the snare they do not know will come upon them in the very fact that they unjustly persecute her, because inwardly they are bound by the cords of their own sins, by which they are dragged to condemnation.

And the capture that he concealed—the Jewish people, that is, the death that he secretly prepared for me, for the entanglement and destruction of the whole world—will seize him, or the sinner. Let him fall into it, namely, into the snare of death that they prepared for me, or let him remain in it, so that they may always be in it, having been ensnared by it.

But the soul—that is, the soul of my Christ, that is, my life—rescued from the snare of death will rejoice in the Lord, not in the world, as those who were ensnared did. And it will delight in its salvation, that is, in the salvation bestowed from above, not in earthly things, as did those who were ensnared.

And not only my soul, the soul of Christ, but all my bones—that is, my strong ones, imitating my steadfastness—will say: “Lord, who is like you?” They will be told: “Worship the sun; worship the moon; worship the statue of Jupiter.” But recognizing that all these things are your works, they will say: “Lord, who among created things is like you?” No one, because you, and no other, rescue the poor—that is, the humble faithful person who trusts in no one’s help except yours—from the hand—that is, the power—of those stronger than he.

As to the body, you have already rescued Christ; and daily you rescue his members inwardly, not allowing them to apostatize under any temptations. You rescue the needy—that is, the one who, believing that he is not sufficient for himself, believes that he needs God’s mercy—and the poor, that is, the one who, insufficient for salvation by himself, clings to the rich God, from those who plunder him: Christ from the Jews, and the Church from her own sinners.

Those who plunder are many. For rising up—that is, raising themselves against me—are wicked witnesses, Jews and other unbelievers, giving false testimony and testimony of death against the author of life: “If he were not a malefactor, we would not have handed him over to you” (John XVIII).

And truly they are wicked witnesses, because they questioned me about things I did not know—that is, they imposed upon me by questioning sins of which I had no experience. And in that questioning they repaid me evil for good, which is utterly unjust. He who does not return good for good is ungrateful; he who returns evil for evil is wicked; but he who returns evil for good is unjust.

That is, they repaid life with death, which was evil according to their intention: these evils, namely, the barrenness of my soul—that is, of my life. I gave them abundance; they gave me barrenness. I gave medicine; they gave wounds. I gave salvation; they gave death. I gave them the rain of God’s word; but, by refusing to receive it, they made themselves fruitless, like the tree that the Lord cursed, which, though cultivated, produced no fruit but only leaves (Mark XI)—that is, they returned words without deeds: abundance in words, barrenness in actions.

Alternatively: “the barrenness of my soul.” When they would not allow themselves to be ruled in such a way as to attain life, they rendered barrenness to my soul—that is, to my desire. I, however, did what would cause them to fail and my people to advance, because their transgression was salvation for the Gentiles.

When they troubled me—that is, when they troubled me because of my miserable appearance—I was clothed in sackcloth, that is, I remained concealed within the limits of humanity, not displaying my divinity to them through miracles. For throughout the Passion he did not wish to display his power: “For if they had known, they would not have crucified him” (1 Cor. II). In this he gave us an example of humanity and patience.

“I was clothed in sackcloth,” that is, I was hidden in the likeness of sinful flesh. And yet, although they brought barrenness upon me, although they deprived me of food, I was not angry, as other masters commonly are when food is withheld from them. But in that fast I humbled my soul—that is, I showed myself humble before them: “I have no demon” (John VIII); “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”; “You have said so” (Matt. XVI).

And although barrenness was present in them, nevertheless my prayer will return into my bosom. It will return to those who were prefigured by the hand cleansed of leprosy and brought back into the bosom. For Moses’ hand, brought out of his bosom as leprous (Exod. IV), signifies those cut off from the body of Christ because of leprosy, that is, grave sins. The healed hand brought back into the bosom signifies those cleansed by repentance and recalled into the Church.

“My prayer will return into my bosom,” that is, it will be turned from the sons of wrath into sons of mercy, so that it may convert them and not be fruitless in those who have been predestined to life in the bosom of God’s mercy. For some were converted during the Passion.

Alternatively, it is as though he said: “They gave me their barrenness,” that is, they gave me themselves as barren and fruitless. But when they troubled me—that is, despised me because of my appearance as a poor man—I was clothed in sackcloth, that is, I made some of those sinners my garment and conformed them to myself.

And yet I humbled—that is, weakened and afflicted—my soul with fasting, because I did not eat as much as I wished. For I ate only the thief and a few others (Luke XXIII). Although they could have recognized in me what would become my food, my prayer would not go out to others, but would return inwardly into my bosom, to the Word personally united to me. For I did not pray outwardly to others, as other human beings do.

Or, although I was humbled and although I was not angry, nevertheless my prayer would return into my bosom—that is, I had God within me, through whom I could take vengeance upon them. But for that reason I humbled myself, because I was pleased with myself in admonishing them, just as someone rejoices in admonishing a brother or neighbor.

And yet I was so humbled by them as one mourning and grieving—that is, so that I might be compared with one who mourns and grieves. I was like one mourning and grieving because those whom I desired to save had come together—that is, had become united for this purpose—not to follow me but against me. And what is worse, they did so neither under compulsion nor through any fear, but rejoicing—that is, they did it gladly.

And when they had thus come together, scourges were gathered against me, and this without fault of mine, because I did not know—not the punishment, but the cause of the punishment, since there was no fault of mine.

They were scattered—that is, they were found to be divided among themselves. Some said, “He is good”; others, “No” (John VII). Yet they did not cease my persecution. Or they were scattered in this sense: they were divided. “Either there are two Christs, or this is he.”

Or they became fearful because of the miracles, the darkness of the sun, and the earthquake, yet they were not pierced with remorse. Rather, they tested me: “If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross” (Luke XXIII). They mocked me with open mockery: “Hail, King of the Jews” (Matt. XXVII). They gnashed their teeth against me: “Crucify him, crucify him” (John XIX).

“Lord, when will you look upon this?” He says this in the person of his people, to whom it seems that vengeance is being delayed too long, until the general resurrection. Why do you not avenge us now? Why do you not crown us now? You seemed to have disregarded us in punishment; why do you not look upon us in judgment?

It is as though he said: “I know why you delay. You do not do this out of weariness, but out of love; not from inability, but according to reason. You are powerful enough to give, but I am unable to receive. You do not do this from impotence, but at the appropriate time, so that joy may be greater at the general resurrection.”

Restore my soul—the soul of your Christ—from their wickedness at the predestined time, from the death that the wicked prepared for me; and restore my only one—that is, my Church, uniquely beloved.

Or “my soul,” because it alone, or uniquely, is free from sin. Deliver it from lions—that is, from the ferocity of the Jews. “Restore it from lions,” that is, deliver it from those who tear its flesh like lions. Or from lions, that is, from the cruelty of the devil and his ministers.

And with what benefit do I ask to be delivered? This: “I will confess to you in the great Church,” that is, the broad Church, containing good and evil, grain and chaff. “In a weighty people I will praise you,” not in the chaff—that is, not in those whom the wind of temptations lifts up and scatters—but among those who are firm and stable in faith and works, moved by no temptations. Among them I will show you to be worthy of praise.

And so that I may praise you among a weighty people, let those who rejoiced in my death not exult over me. Let the Jews who unjustly oppose me not exult over me as one who has not risen, because the weak oppose the physician, slaves their Lord, and creatures their Creator.

He shows in what way they opposed unjustly: “Those who hate me without cause,” that is, without reason, “and wink with their eyes,” that is, deal deceitfully with me, presenting peace in words but war in action.

Or “they wink with their eyes,” as Judas did: “It is he; seize him” (Matt. XXVI).

Alternatively, understood of the members: O Lord, so that I may praise you in my people, let those who unjustly oppose me not exult over me—that is, over my people. Let the chaff not prevail over the grain, namely, so that more people imitate the life of the impious than the faith and life of the saints, who possess gravity of conduct and holiness of life.

It is as though he said: “It is no wonder that they deal deceitfully with my people, since they spoke peaceably to me, who am free from sin and who came to the sick as a physician—but deceitfully: ‘Teacher, we know that you are truthful’” (Matt. XXII).

And while speaking peaceful words, they did so “in the anger of the earth,” that is, in a perverse and unjust anger arising from earthly things, because they feared losing their place and nation (John XI). They devised plots, that is, they cunningly sought causes for my death. And finally “they opened their mouth wide against me,” that is, they pronounced sentences of death against me: “He is guilty of death” (Matt. XXVI).

And they rejoiced over my death, saying: “Good, good! It has turned out well. Our eyes have seen what we previously hoped for: that the one who promised life should die. Where are your deeds now? Where are your wonders? If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matt. XXVII).

“You have seen, Lord.” It is as though he said: “They saw my Passion; they saw my death, though they can be deceived. But you, Lord, who cannot be deceived, saw the punishment and also saw its cause. Therefore do not be silent”—namely, regarding judgment—you who seemed to be silent during my punishment. Do not be silent concerning my cause; show that my cause is better than the cause of the Jews by raising me.

“If I did not descend from the cross, I will rise from the tomb.” And when you have raised me, do not depart from me—that is, from my people—giving them steadfastness through faith, hope, and charity. For you said: “Behold, I am with you all days” (Matt. XXVIII).

“Arise, Lord,” that is, show your power in my resurrection, you who seemed to lie in my death. And thus arise: “Attend to my judgment,” that is, make yourself unwavering in distinguishing my cause from theirs, with whom I share the same punishment.

And this is what follows: “My God” by necessity, and “Lord” by will. Attend to my cause. I am not distinguished from the impious with regard to punishment; but I am distinguished by you with regard to the cause. Show in my resurrection that my cause was different from the cause of the thieves, with whom my punishment was the same.

“Judge me according to your righteousness.” In this way distinguish me from the impious. The Jews judged me according to their righteousness; but you judge according to your righteousness. For I underwent death not on account of the merit of sin, but for the sake of obedience. Therefore it is just that you should raise me, O Lord, whom I serve willingly.

“My God” by creation. Judge, therefore, according to your righteousness, so that they may not exult over me. If they rejoice over my death, let them grieve over my resurrection.

Or, “Let them not exult over my people,” by devouring those who rejoice in their destruction. Let them not say in their hearts—even if they say it with their lips—“Good, good, for our soul; our desire has been fulfilled.” It is good, they think, because we have devoured him, swallowed him, and transferred him into our body, turning him away from his God and conforming him to ourselves.

Rather, let they themselves be diminished, so that they may be absorbed into the body of the holy people whom they wished to absorb into themselves. This was prefigured by the molten calf that Aaron made from the earrings of the Hebrew women while Moses was on Mount Sinai receiving from the Lord the two tablets of the Testimony. The children of Israel sacrificed to it, saying: “These are your gods, Israel” (Exod. XXXII). Moses, descending from the mountain after receiving the law, diminished that calf and reduced it to dust, then gave it to the people to drink.

In this way let them pass into the body of your people.

Let them be ashamed of their sin and stand in awe—that is, fear my resurrection—and thus be converted. Let not only those who commit these things be ashamed, but likewise those who rejoice in my evils, consenting that the whole world should follow after him.

And let them not merely be ashamed, but let them be clothed with confusion—that is, let them be covered with great shame for their sins—and with reverence, that is, with fear of the judgment, those who speak evil things against me, that is, their lies.

And let all these people of mine rejoice in the body through hope of the resurrection, and let those who desire my righteousness—that is, those who have abandoned their own righteousness and submitted themselves to the mercy of God—now rejoice inwardly in their minds, having been raised.

And let them always say: “Let the Lord be magnified,” that is, let them humble themselves and attribute nothing to themselves except evil. The Lord appears great only to those who humble themselves and recognize that they are small.

“Always,” that is, both in prosperity and in adversity. By humbling themselves, all these people recognize God’s greatness in themselves—those who desire the peace of his servant, that is, those who gladly receive the reconciliation given through me, Christ his servant, who said: “My peace I give you”; “I leave you peace” (John XIV)—an outward peace in hope, namely, an inward peace for outward warfare.

Or: “Let the Lord always be magnified, and not the servant.” Let the servant be humbled and the Lord magnified. Then the foolish tongue—that is, the tongue of the heart, not of the mouth, which previously spoke evil against me—will meditate on your righteousness, that is, proclaim throughout the world your faith, by which alone believers are justified, and your praise all day long, that is, at every time.

It may seem impossible for someone to praise the Lord without interruption, but it is possible for those who rightly pay attention. Does someone conduct a business? Let him not defraud anyone in it; in this he praises God. Does he cultivate a field? Let him not encroach upon his neighbor’s boundary; in this there is praise of God. Does he use food? Let him not do so to stretch his stomach, but to make himself more ready for labor and to restore himself; in this he praises God. Does he sleep? Let him not break his sleep by any evil deed. In all the innocence of his actions, let him prepare himself for the praise of God, and thus he never ceases from praise.

## PSALM XXXV. FOR THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID, THE SERVANT OF THE LORD

> The unjust man said within himself that he would sin; there is no fear of the Lord before his eyes. For he acted deceitfully in his sight, so that his iniquity might be found out for hatred. The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit; he refused to understand in order to act well. He meditated iniquity on his bed; he stood by every path that was not good, but he did not reject wickedness.
>
> Lord, your mercy is in heaven, and your truth reaches to the clouds. Your righteousness is like the mountains of God; your judgments are a great abyss. You will save human beings and beasts, Lord, as you have multiplied your mercy, O God. But the children of human beings will hope in the shelter of your wings. They will be inebriated by the abundance of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight. For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light.
>
> Extend your mercy to those who know you, and your righteousness to those who are upright in heart. Let not the foot of pride come upon me, and let not the hand of the sinner move me. There the workers of iniquity have fallen; they have been cast out and have not been able to stand.

## EXPOSITION

This psalm is directed against those who oppose themselves so that they may not live well—not because they do not understand, but because they do not wish to understand. For it is one thing to wish to understand and to be hindered by human weakness, because the corruptible body weighs down the soul and an earthly dwelling depresses the sense that is occupied with many thoughts (Wis. IX); and it is another thing—more dangerous—for the human heart to act against itself by refusing to understand divine commandments, as though it might excuse itself by ignorance.

Such commandments include: “What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. IV; Matt. V), and many others that are easily understood.

These are the people who do not wish to agree with their adversary while they are on the way with him—that is, they do not wish to yield to the word of the Lord, which contradicts them as long as they delight in their sins. They love their sins and do not wish to recognize them so that they may abandon them; and if they do recognize them, either by themselves or through others, they defend them.

Fearing human judgment, they sin secretly, because they fear human judgment more than the judgment of God. Against such people the prophet acts in this psalm, desiring to lead them toward better things.

Accordingly, the title runs as follows: This psalm is attributed to the prophet David, or to any perfect person in the body of Christ who is a servant of the Lord. For whoever labors to convert the impious from the error of his way “will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (James V). In this way he serves God well—the servant of the Lord who directs him “to the end,” that is, toward perfected good.

“The unjust man”—namely, the one who delights in his sins when he ought to hate them—“said,” that is, determined; he did not act in ignorance, but deliberately resolved within himself, as though by design, “that he would sin,” that is, that he would commit sin and depart from the commandment, so that a human being would not see him, since he fears human judgment more than God’s.

“That he would sin within himself,” that is, secretly, where he alone would be conscious of it. He did not wish anyone else to share in it, so that it might remain hidden; or he first harmed himself. Does God not see? “There is no fear of God before his eyes”: he does not hold God’s judgment before the eyes of his heart.

That he does not fear God he demonstrates by this: “He acted deceitfully in his sight,” or rather, where God alone sees. He acted deceitfully in this way: he preferred to be ignorant of God’s commands and act wickedly rather than understand and act well. This is deceitful conduct, because in this way he wishes to defend his offense through ignorance.

Or he acted deceitfully in this way: “so that”—that is, as though—“his iniquity might be found out for hatred.” He pretended to seek his sin so that he might cease from it and hate it once he knew it. But because he acted deceitfully, he does not hate the sin once found so that he may be healed; rather, he defends it.

For he says: “Many do what I have done,” or “Everyone does it. Will God destroy everyone? Or, if he did not wish these things to happen, would those who do them be alive?”

And because he does not hate what he has done, but deceitfully seeks to know what he should do once he has recognized his iniquity, he adds: “The words of his mouth are iniquity.” That is, after recognizing his sin and understanding how great it was, he defends it instead of condemning it.

The word “iniquity” is emphatic, that is, augmentative. His words defending sin are so perverse that they may be called not merely iniquitous, but iniquity itself.

“And deceit.” This is the way in which they are deceitful: “He refused to understand in order to act well.” He understood what was good, but he did not wish to understand it in such a way as to act well. He understood evil, yet committed it. He understood good, yet refused to do it.

And it is no wonder that there is iniquity in his words, because “he meditated iniquity on his bed,” that is, in his heart or conscience. Where he ought to have prepared rest for himself, he prepared unrest.

If someone suffers persecution outside, he flees into his house so that he may find rest there. But if he finds there a quarrelsome and contentious wife, he has rest nowhere. So if someone is afflicted outwardly, let him have a pure conscience; let wisdom dwell within, while the quarrel of vices remains outside. Thus he will be comforted and find rest for himself. Outside there will be battles; within, joy.

“Enter into your room,” he says (Matt. VI), that is, into your heart. There, lest you suffer the tumult of affairs arising from a corrupt conscience, shut the door: do not lose anything outwardly or seek anything there.

Alternatively: “He meditated iniquity on his bed,” that is, he interrupted his rest for the sake of wickedness, just as someone might interrupt it for the sake of an honorable undertaking.

“He stood by every path that was not good,” that is, he consented to another’s evil action. And he did all this not from inability or ignorance, but because he refused to understand in order to act well. He imitated and loved the sins of others.

“But he did not reject wickedness,” that is, he did not hate his own sins. He did not do what ought to have been done: even if he could not avoid sinning because of the sin that is in the flesh, he should at least have hated it.

Some fight against the devil and overcome; others fight and are overcome because they presume upon themselves; still others neither fight nor are overcome, but are handed over as captives. These are the ones who do not hate wickedness.

The order is this: His words are iniquitous because his thought is perverse; and because his thought is perverse, his actions too are evil.

“Lord, your mercy is in heaven.” It is as though he said: “Such people will not be saved, because, O Lord, your mercy—in which alone salvation is found—is in heaven,” that is, in those alone whom you make into heavens, whom you raise up and adorn with many virtues.

“And your truth,” that is, the truth of your commandments, is powerful enough to establish clouds. For the truth of your commandments not only gives light, but also advances some people to such perfection that they become clouds—that is, teachers of others, raining down instruction, thundering with warnings, and flashing with miracles.

“Your righteousness is like the mountains of God,” because of the eminence of virtues. Or it is like the mountains of God because, just as the rising sun first illuminates the mountains and then shines upon the valleys, so Christ, the true sun, first illuminated the apostles and then, through them, us as valleys—that is, their hearers.

Conversely, “your judgments are a great abyss,” that is, those who are condemned in the depth of vices are like a great abyss.

Alternatively: “Your judgments are a great abyss.” It is as though he said: “You raise some through your mercy so high that they may be called heavens, clouds, and mountains, while you permit others not to understand in order to act well,” as in: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I; Rom. IX). In this are your judgments a great abyss—that is, inscrutable: why you choose one and reject another. “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Rom. XI.)

The passage may also be connected in this way: The unjust man determined within himself to sin; that is, the unjust man sins by himself. In every heaven, however, God’s mercy is apparent: the righteous act through God’s mercy. “And your truth,” that is, the fulfillment of your mercy, is powerful enough to establish clouds.

This intention may also be given to the psalm. The prophet, or any perfect person, acts in this psalm against those who say that they sin because of the configuration of the stars, fate, or the weakness of nature. In this way they wish to excuse themselves for their sin and accuse God.

It is as though the prophet said: “The human race falsely blames its nature. People do not sin through weakness, but by their own free choice. Therefore the creator is not to be accused; they themselves are.”

“The unjust man said within himself that he would sin,” that is, by his own free choice he determined within himself to sin, compelled by no necessity.

It is as though he said: “And from what did he determine to sin?” “There is no fear of God before his eyes”: he did not consider God to be judge or creator of all things. In this the creator is not blameworthy; rather, the man himself is.

For although God had given him understanding, by which he could understand that he ought not to sin, he nevertheless sinned. This is acting deceitfully.

And the rest proceeds as above, up to “Lord, your mercy is in heaven,” which is connected with the preceding passage in this way:

It is as though he said: “The unjust man said that he would sin because of the weakness of nature.” But this is not true, because, O Lord, “your mercy is in heaven,” that is, in Christ, the heaven of heavens, the righteous one among the righteous, where your mercy is placed to forgive sins and establish righteousness. This would not be so if human beings acted from necessity in what they do.

“And your truth,” for rewarding merits, is not only in heaven but descends even to the clouds, that is, to preachers, so that they too may rain this mercy and truth upon the world.

And truly your mercy is in Christ, because those who are so raised up by virtues that they are high like mountains possess it. “Your righteousness,” that is, God’s righteousness, not something arising from their merits. “And your judgments are a great abyss,” as above.

And although some are an abyss and others righteousness, you will save both, though by different kinds of salvation, because “you will save human beings and beasts, Lord.”

You save beasts by giving them food with which they may fill the hollow of the belly and other things that satisfy the body. And human beings—that is, those who remain in the old condition of the one who was human, not a son of man, the carnal—you will count among the beasts, so that they seek no other life than this one.

“For a human being, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. XLVIII).

And, O God, in saving such people also in some manner, you act according to how you have multiplied your mercy—that is, according to the abundance of your mercy, which is not lacking here to some in temporal salvation and to others in eternal salvation.

It is as though he said: “Carnal human beings are blessed only with earthly remedies and rejoice only in them. But the children of human beings,” that is, those who belong to the Son of Man and are conformed to him in righteousness and holiness, “although they possess these temporal things, will not hope in them as those others do. They will not possess blessedness here, but will hope for it.”

“For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come” (Heb. XIII). They say: “In the shelter of your wings,” that is, under the protection of the twofold charity, or of the New and Old Testaments—not in secular power and not in riches.

“For no one has ascended into heaven by himself except the Son of Man who descended” (John III); all others are carried upward.

Moses said: “Whoever is burdened with a hump must not approach the priestly office” (Lev. XXI). Therefore they will hope, because “they will be inebriated by the abundance of your house,” that is, by spiritual gifts flowing down from the heavenly house.

They will rightly be inebriated, because just as wine taken in excess carries the mind away, so the greatness of spiritual joy carries the mind of the faithful away from the human and transfers it into the divine.

“The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. XI). For just as someone seizes something by force, so the faithful seize the kingdom of God, because they are impelled by the Spirit of God as though by force.

Truly you will give them drink from a torrent, because “with you,” and not with another, “is the fountain of life,” that is, Christ, through whom life is given.

“And in your light,” through which you illuminate the eyes of the mind, “we shall see light,” that is, you. “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV).

And so that we may see you as light—that is, understand you—this is not within our power. Rather, “send the one whom you are going to send” (Exod. IV), so that at last we may enjoy the light of your eternity.

“Extend your mercy to those who know you,” that is, to those who wish to know you. And extend your righteousness, not theirs—that is, the faith by which you justify—before those who are upright in heart, that is, those who direct their entire will toward yours.

And with your mercy extended before me, guard me, lest I lose through pride what I have from mercy. “Let not the foot of pride come upon me,” so that I may rise up against myself by attributing something to myself.

It is one foot, not two; therefore it is easily brought down. “Let not the foot of pride come upon me,” that is, let not an inclination prone to falling come upon me.

By the foot of pride one departs from you both at the beginning and at the end. For pride is the beginning of every sin, by which one apostatizes from you, Lord; and when someone has labored sufficiently in righteousness, the final destruction is to glory in himself and not in the Lord.

Adam, the first sinner, was driven into pride not by a bodily foot but by the inclination of his mind. May this beginning of sin (Eccles. X) not happen to me, the second man.

And if I do not have the foot of pride, let not the hand of the sinner—that is, the impulse of the apostate angel—move me away from you, as it moved the first parent.

For this reason I ask it: “There the workers of iniquity have fallen,” that is, all those who persist in wickedness have fallen there, that is, into pride.

First the apostate angel became proud, he who did not stand in the truth; then, at his persuasion, those whom God expelled from paradise became proud. All who work iniquity derive this from him, because they fell in Adam through pride, driven by the first sinner.

And because after the fall they were expelled from paradise, “they have not been able to stand,” that is, to rise again, although they were able to fall.

They were expelled, namely, from the inner paradise—that is, from the testimony of conscience, from which each person is first expelled through sin. Therefore they could not stand in the outer paradise either; for that reason they lost outward rest. For as long as they were in rest and remained in it outwardly—

Alternatively: “Extend your mercy,” so that we may be able to understand you as light in your light, proceeding from that light.

“Extend your mercy,” that is, your righteousness; be first to come to our aid, so that we may not slip away from you through the foot of pride and be handed over to the work of sin. Let iniquity not be first before you in doing harm.

Therefore, when the Lord made the Church cautious, he said: “She shall watch your head, and you shall watch her heel” (Gen. III).

The serpent will watch for the time when the foot of pride comes upon you—that is, the love of apostasy—so that it may cast you down; but you must guard its head: “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Ecclus. X).

By the foot of pride we may understand what was said above: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults” (Ps. XVIII). By the hand of the sinner: “And spare your servant from the sins of others.”

“There the workers of iniquity have fallen,” that is, in pride, all who work iniquity—that is, unbelievers and all who persist in sins—according to the saying: “Although they knew God’s righteousness, they did not glorify him as God” (Rom. I); and they fell because “God gave them over to the desires of their hearts” (ibid.).

## PSALM XXXVI. A PSALM OF DAVID HIMSELF.

“Do not be jealous of those who act wickedly, nor envy those who commit iniquity. For like grass they will quickly wither, and like green plants they will soon fade. Hope in the Lord and do good; dwell in the land, and you will be nourished by its riches. Take delight in the Lord, and he will grant you the desires of your heart. Commit your way to the Lord, hope in him, and he himself will act. He will bring forth your righteousness like the light, and your judgment like midday. Submit yourself to the Lord and pray to him. Do not be jealous of the one who prospers in his way, of the man who commits injustices. Cease from anger and abandon wrath; do not be jealous so as to act wickedly. For those who act wickedly will be exterminated, but those who wait for the Lord will inherit the land. Yet a little while, and the sinner will no longer exist; you will seek his place, and you will not find it. But the meek will inherit the land and delight in an abundance of peace. The sinner will watch the just man and gnash his teeth at him; but the Lord will laugh at him, because he sees that his day is coming. Sinners have drawn the sword and bent their bow, to deceive the poor and needy, to slaughter those who are upright of heart. Let their sword enter their own hearts, and let their bows be broken. Better is the little that belongs to the just than the abundant riches of sinners. For the arms of sinners will be broken, but the Lord strengthens the just. The Lord knows the days of the blameless, and their inheritance will endure forever. They will not be confounded in the evil time, and in days of famine they will be satisfied, because sinners will perish. But the enemies of the Lord, as soon as they have been honored and exalted, will fail; like smoke, they will fail. The sinner borrows and does not repay; but the just man is merciful and gives in return. For those who bless him will inherit the land, but those who curse him will perish. The steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and he takes pleasure in his way. When he falls, he will not be dashed to pieces, because the Lord supports him with his hand. I was young, and now I am old, yet I have not seen the just man abandoned, nor his offspring seeking bread. All day long he is merciful and lends, and his offspring will be blessed. Turn away from evil and do good, and dwell forever and ever. For the Lord loves judgment, and he will not abandon his holy ones; they will be preserved forever. The unjust will be punished, and the offspring of the impious will perish. But the just will inherit the land and dwell upon it forever and ever. The mouth of the just man will meditate wisdom, and his tongue will speak judgment. The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps will not be tripped. The sinner watches the just man and seeks to put him to death. But the Lord will not abandon him into his hands, nor condemn him when judgment is passed against him. Wait for the Lord and keep his way; he will exalt you so that you may inherit the land; when sinners have perished, you will see it. I saw the impious man highly exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon. I passed by, and behold, he was no more; I sought him, and his place was not found. Keep innocence and behold equity, for there are survivors for the peaceful man. But the unjust will perish; together the survivors of the impious will be destroyed. The salvation of the just is from the Lord, and he is their protector in the time of tribulation. The Lord will help them and deliver them; he will rescue them from sinners and save them, because they have hoped in him.”

## Explanation

“Psalm of David himself,” that is, this good work is to be attributed to those who are more perfect within the body of Christ and who instruct the less perfect when they perceive them going astray. Imperfect Christians are always disturbed when they see the wicked living prosperously, abounding in temporal goods, excelling in offices and honors, possessing a secure household, lacking none of their pleasures, and experiencing nothing sorrowful to interrupt their lives. They see utterly impious conduct and abundant resources, and their hearts tell them that there is no judge in human affairs, but that everything is governed by chance and accidental movements. For if God cared to govern these lower things, their wickedness would not flourish so greatly, and my innocence would not suffer so much. But because divine Scripture provides its remedy for every sickness of the soul, it prepares for those who are sick in this way and think thus within themselves a most health-giving draught, so that they may learn not to murmur against the Lord: the prosperity of the wicked leads them to utter destruction, while the adversity of the good leads them to the highest glory.

“Do not be jealous of those who act wickedly,” that is, do not envy them; or, do not become angry with those who act wickedly—that is, with the flourishing prosperity of those who behave wickedly, while you live well and yet are oppressed by labor and poverty. “Nor envy those who commit iniquity,” that is, do not imitate or love those who do evil and yet flourish. Their beginnings flourish, but their end will wither; their beginnings are expansive, their end constricted. Your beginnings are on the narrow way; your end will be in great enlargement. Rather consider their end, for “like grass they will quickly wither”: that is, their end will be empty of glory. “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field” (Isaiah 40). And “like green plants they will soon fade,” that is, like a vegetable among other herbs. A vegetable is a kind of plant that clings superficially to the soil and remains green only in winter; when the sun returns in summer, it immediately dries up. Those who rejoice in earthly things are comparable to this: they have no firm root of charity clinging in love to this world, which is comparable to winter. But when the sun rises—that is, when Christ comes for judgment—their glory will wither. “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3). “When Christ, your glory, appears, then you too will appear with him in glory.”

Rather than imitate or envy those who now flourish and afterward wither, hope in the Lord, so that your end may flourish. Do not rejoice in the world, but await joy from the Lord. And, so that you may be able to hope, do good; do not be idle. Light is unpleasant to those whose eyes are diseased, and you should not expect to find light pleasant unless you grow accustomed to leaving darkness. And by doing good, dwell in the land—that is, in the Church. Exercise yourself in ecclesiastical institutions and do not withdraw from them, because there is no place of true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church. Or, dwell in the land—that is, cultivate your body, so that at last you may attain immortality and freedom from suffering. And when you have dwelt in the Church, you will be nourished by its riches—that is, by the Lord, who is the wealth of that land. If the passage is referred to the flesh, you will eventually be nourished by its riches, when “this mortal puts on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15).

He now adds what the riches of that land are: “Take delight in the Lord, and he will grant you the desires of your heart.” Those who take delight in the world receive here the desire of their flesh: namely, a withering and quickly passing glory. But take delight in no one except the Lord, and you will receive the unfading glory that your heart desires. They love darkness; you, light. They possess things that perish; seek what is eternal.

And, so that you may be able to hope, “commit your way to the Lord,” that is, perform such works as are worthy of the Lord’s sight—not as regards his knowledge, which needs nothing, but as regards his gracious approval. Alternatively: it is as though he said, “I want to take delight in the Lord, but I cannot fulfill this.” Therefore disclose your weakness to the Lord and hope in him, because no one hopes in him except one who is doing good.

“And he himself will act.” What will he do? “He will bring forth your righteousness like the light,” that is, he will make your faith, by which you are justified and which now appears to be nothing in comparison with its reward, manifest to all when the reward is given. “And your judgment like midday,” that is, he will bring forth from the darkness of ignorance your good purpose—the purpose by which you have chosen to follow the Lord, who promises things not seen, rather than the world, which gives things that are seen but do not endure—and he will make it known to all in the reward as the light of midday is known. Therefore “submit yourself to the Lord,” serving him with complete obedience and humility. And, so that you may be able to submit yourself, pray to him for perseverance. “Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10). Let good works persevere; let prayer persevere. You have not yet received your reward. He can give it, but you are not yet able to receive it.

It is as though someone were saying: “Behold, I submit myself and pray to him, but do you not see how that perverse man, acting wickedly, flourishing, and lifted up by iniquity, does not even consider me worthy of recognition? How can I endure this?” The answer is: “Do not be jealous”—that is, do not envy the one who prospers in his way, not in God’s way, which is narrow. He prospers in the desires of his flesh, but he will be afflicted when he reaches his destination; you are afflicted on the way, but you will prosper at the destination. In this life you walk along the narrow way, while he walks along the broad one; but he will be constricted, while you will be enlarged. His way is broad and leads to death; yours is narrow and leads to life.

Do not envy the man who commits injustices—that is, the prosperity of one who loves the world more than God, and the creature more than the Creator, which is unjust. Rather “cease from anger”; do not be disturbed. Anger is a brief fury arising from the prosperity of the wicked and the labor of the good. “And abandon wrath,” that is, do not become so disturbed by the flourishing of the wicked that the eye of your mind is blinded. Rather consult the eye of faith, in which you were told to renounce these things. These things were not promised to you as a reward; eternal goods were. For it is fury, not reason, to become angry with the Lord and murmur against him. Fury is greater than anger. Abandon this fury.

“Do not be jealous so as to act wickedly.” If you have anger in your mind, never reach the point of imitating the wicked or becoming evil. Do not resent the fact that he abounds here while you do not, because these are not true goods and they were not promised to you. Rather look to your Lord, who despised such things. You suffer nothing that he did not first suffer.

“For those who act wickedly will be exterminated”—from the land of the living; they will be outside the boundaries of the inheritance of the children of God. “Let the impious be removed, so that he may not see the glory of God” (Isaiah 26). Or, they will be exterminated here because they do not cultivate their land properly and do not rule their earthly movements; therefore they will not inherit it as a land free from suffering.

“But those who wait for the Lord,” that is, those who bear the weight of the Lord’s commandments without murmuring against him in anything, or who wait patiently if he delays, “will inherit the land”—either the land of the living, or their own land, which they cultivated well here and will eventually possess as immortal and free from suffering.

“And this will happen soon: yet a little while.” Endure, for the delay of this present time is short, however long it may seem to us when compared with eternity—so short that it cannot even be called a point in comparison with it. For who could compare the finite with the infinite? We must labor eternally for an eternal reward, but God’s mercy does not demand this: for a brief period of labor he wishes to give an eternal reward. Therefore endure a little longer; that is, wait with patience for a little while.

“And the sinner will no longer exist,” that is, the sinner’s activity will no longer exist. This does not mean that he will not exist, since it is said, “These will go into eternal punishment” (Matthew 25); but that state will be more nearly nonexistence than existence. Here the sinner exists and has a place before God, who uses him to test the good, just as he used the devil to test Job (Job 1). Thus his place here is like the place of straw in a goldsmith’s furnace: the straw burns, and the gold is purified. So the impious rage, in order that the just may be purified. After the just have been purified, those who rage against them for the sake of purification will no longer exist.

Alternatively: “The sinner will no longer exist,” that is, the devil will no longer have anything in you. “You will seek his place, and you will not find it.” Sin is the devil’s place, and it will no longer exist. Or, in this sense: “The sinner will no longer exist; you will seek his place, and you will not find it.” There he will be separated from you, because he will no longer have a place; he will not be able to be useful to you as he was here, because here the impious lives for the sake of the pious.

“Those who act wickedly will be exterminated. But the meek,” that is, those who bear the Lord’s yoke, in accordance with the words, “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew 11), “will inherit the land” from which those others will be exterminated. This means Jerusalem the holy city, which will be freed from this exile. Or, the land means their own flesh, which they cultivated here and will possess as immortal and free from suffering; and these will be their delights.

“They will delight in an abundance of peace”: in God, in whom there is abundant peace, that is, perfect abundance. “He will be all in all” (2 Corinthians 15), and therefore there will be abundant peace there, because there will be no disturbance and no anxiety.

Meanwhile, however, the persecutor will not be absent. We must fight, because no one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully (2 Timothy 2). “The sinner will watch the just man,” carefully seeking an opportunity to deceive him. “And he will gnash his teeth at him,” that is, he will direct grave and biting judgments against him in order to lead him astray. But what concern is that to the just man? He will be able to do him no harm.

“But the Lord,” in whom the just man trusts, “will laugh at him,” that is, he will show him to be worthy of laughter to the just man, so that while the wicked tries to wound the just man’s garment, he pierces his own entrails. He wounds the other’s flesh but kills his own soul. Therefore the Lord will laugh at him, “because he sees that his day is coming”—the day of examination, the day of destruction. His beginnings flourish, but his end withers.

Therefore do not envy him, but look toward his day and see that either he will be converted and become yours, or he will persevere and be separated from you. He shows how the day of his destruction will come. “Sinners have drawn the sword” in order to kill the body. “They have also bent their bow,” that is, they have prepared hidden snares by which they might destroy the soul. But observe: “their sword will enter”—it will enter their own hearts. While they strive to kill the bodies of the just, they kill their own souls. “And their bows will be broken,” that is, their snares will be frustrated.

They bent the bow in order to deceive “the poor,” that is, the just man who does not presume on himself, and “the needy,” that is, the one who seeks God’s help. They drew the sword in order “to slaughter”—to kill outwardly and terribly—those who are upright of heart, directing their hearts toward God’s will.

Therefore do not be jealous of the impious or envy him, because “better is the little that belongs to the just than the abundant riches of sinners”: better to hope for things that are not seen. Even if you give what appears little and worthless to sinners, it is better for the just man than to flourish greatly in the world.

Or the passage may be connected differently with the words “their bows will be broken,” as though someone were saying: “How will they be broken? Does he not take away what belongs to me? Does he not constantly insult me?” The answer is: “Better is the little that belongs to the just,” that is, the necessities alone are more valuable to one who lives rightly than the many riches of the unjust. Nor will this harm you for long, because “the arms of sinners will be broken”—their riches and power, in which sinners trust, will be diminished. Or their strength will be diminished in hell, as happened to the rich man who feasted splendidly among the proud but was tormented in the underworld (Luke 16).

And what happens in the meantime? “The Lord strengthens the just.” Christ strengthens his soldiers by his own example, so that they will not envy the flourishing of the wicked and will not refuse to endure their oppression. What the emperor suffered, they should not disdain to suffer in a worthy manner. “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?” (Romans 8). He died for the impious; shall we not die for the just?

He strengthens the just because “the Lord knows the days of the blameless,” that is, he loves the conduct of the good. Therefore “their inheritance will endure forever.” Their well-cultivated flesh, which here was mortal and subject to suffering, will be brought to the point of being eternal and free from suffering. In this way it will be eternal.

“They will not be confounded in the evil time,” in the time of the future judgment, which will be evil for the impious. They will not be confounded in their expectation; rather, “in the days of famine they will be satisfied,” while the wicked suffer hunger. For sinners will not be satisfied, because they will perish.

Alternatively: while they are on their way to that inheritance, they will not be confounded in the evil time—that is, in this time of tribulation—because “tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, proven character produces hope, and hope does not disappoint” (Romans 5). “And in days of famine,” that is, in this present time, in which there are days of famine, when “blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matthew 5), they will be satisfied with an inward satisfaction, in accordance with the Apostle’s words, “We glory in tribulations” (Romans 5).

“For sinners will perish.” Therefore the just will be satisfied either here or in the future, because sinners alone will not be satisfied. When sinners are afflicted, they have no place of consolation, not even inwardly. Outwardly they suffer, while inwardly their conscience does not console them. Truly, they will perish.

For “the enemies of the Lord,” as soon as they have been honored—that is, after they have been honored with earthly riches and dignities—and then exalted, that is, lifted up, “will fail utterly.” This will happen quickly, because they will last only a short time. In ascending they will descend: here through inward failure, and finally through outward failure, “like smoke,” which vanishes all the more as it rises higher.

This will rightly happen to them because “the sinner borrows and does not repay.” From God he received the fact that he is a human being, not an ox or an ass; he received the ability to distinguish by the five senses, yet he does not repay his debt. He does not give thanks to God by showing mercy, living well, helping others, and giving both external and internal goods.

“But the just man,” who will not be confounded in the evil time because he will receive and repay what he has borrowed. This is what follows: “The just man is merciful,” namely, toward himself, by not polluting his soul and not departing from the Lord’s commandments, in accordance with the words, “Have mercy on your soul, and you will be pleasing to God” (Ecclesiasticus 30). “And he gives”—namely, to others, to the poor—external goods, because whatever he gives to the poor he gives to God: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25).

“If you lend, you do not hope; if you do not lend, you do not hope.” If you lend to a human being—that is, if you give your goods to a person at interest—do not hope for a reward from him. Lend to God: give your goods to God at interest; give to the poor, who cannot repay you, and take the Lord as your guarantor. Your interest will increase greatly. He will give or distribute earthly goods—namely, he will make others prosper—by setting himself forth as an example of good living.

It is as though he were saying: “The just man gives; the sinner does not give.” Why does the just man give? Because it belongs to those who bless—to those who voluntarily establish a good life—“to inherit,” that is, to cultivate their land, namely, their life, which they will eventually inherit as eternal. Those who curse—that is, those who voluntarily establish an evil life—will perish, that is, they will not cultivate their land.

This is what he says: “Those who bless him will inherit the land, but those who curse him will perish.” It is as though he were saying: They will not merely fail to inherit it; those who curse him—that is, who despise him—will perish.

And this inheritance of the land, which you will receive by blessing him, does not come from yourself but from the Lord, because “the steps of a man are directed by the Lord.” It is not for a human being to direct his own way. “The steps of the man”—the just man, that is—will be directed by the Lord: all his desires will be directed according to the example of Christ his Lord, so that they may be with the Lord, that is, according to the Lord’s will. Solomon says, “It belongs to a man to prepare his way, but it belongs to the Lord to direct it” (Proverbs 16).

Our affections were distorted; we were outside the way. But Christ came, called us, justified us, poured out his blood for us, and thus brought us back to the way. He was tempted and suffered worse things. We cannot suffer anything that he did not first suffer. “And he takes pleasure in his way.” Therefore let us follow willingly with the one who goes before us, not considering where we are going but where we shall arrive. We suffer temporary evils in order to reach eternal goods. Therefore a man should persist in the way by which Christ went.

And because he takes pleasure in that way, “when he falls, he will not be dashed to pieces.” To desire his way is to suffer tribulations without failing: to suffer outwardly without failing inwardly. Hence it is said elsewhere, “The Lord guards all their bones; not one of them will be broken” (Psalm 33). When he falls into some tribulations, he will not be shattered. That affliction will not be for his downfall but rather for his exaltation, because “the Lord supports him with his hand.” Therefore, by his help and example, he raises him up, because he himself first suffered.

Alternatively: he strengthens his hand—that is, his works. Jerome says: “The just man falls seven times and rises again” (Proverbs 24). He falls in thought, in delight, and in speech. He rises again through confession, hope, faith, and work. He is just for this reason, because “the just man lives by faith” (Romans 1). And truly the just man will not be dashed to pieces, because the Lord will not abandon him, directing his steps. Believe this from one who has experienced it.

“I was young, and now I am old.” Here the whole Church speaks. It is one in the sacraments but diverse in persons; therefore the whole Church speaks as one human being. “I was young,” that is, more fervent in charity, when I was primitive—in Abel and in the patriarchs. And truly I was young, for now I am old: charity has already grown cold. Yet neither in youth nor in old age have I seen the just man abandoned inwardly, without the Lord always directing his steps, even if many appeared abandoned outwardly.

Or, “I was young,” that is, small, because in the few who lived in the time of the just Abel I was still without fruitfulness. He demonstrates this: “For now I am old,” that is, I have grown and multiplied in old age. “And I have not seen the just man abandoned,” namely, abandoned without the bread of God’s word. For the law of God—that is, his will—never departs from his heart and mouth. Christ was never absent from his mouth.

“Nor his offspring seeking bread,” namely, the bread of life, without possessing the bread of God’s word and therefore begging for it. Or “his offspring” means the good works he sowed here without fruit, that is, without reward. The seed is said to seek bread when it does not grow into fruit.

He shows how the just man never lacks the bread of life, because he always possesses it. “All day long,” that is, continually, in accordance with the words, “He will meditate on his law day and night” (Psalm 1), “he is merciful” to himself, not allowing the sword of reason with which he is girded to be consumed by rust. And he lends that same bread to others. He does not cease begging, admonishing, exhorting, giving an account, and drawing them toward the love of God. Thus he adds love of neighbor to love of God.

“All day long he is merciful and lends,” that is, the law of God, the will of God, never departs from his heart. When he reads, he eats; when he thinks about it, he chews the cud, so that he may be a clean animal and not an unclean one that swallows what it hears—that is, forgets it—according to Solomon’s words: “An incomparable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise man, but the fool swallows it” (Proverbs 21).

Augustine says: “‘He is merciful,’ that is, he lends at interest. He gives little and receives much. So too the just man gives earthly things in order to receive heavenly ones; he gives things that perish in order to receive eternal things.” If you lend, you do not hope; if you do not lend, you do not hope. If you lend to a human being, you do not hope for a reward from God; lend to God, and you will receive a reward. Lend to the poor, make him your debtor, and take God as your guarantor. He already sits in heaven, yet he does not disdain to repay on behalf of the poor the debt he says he receives in the poor: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25).

“All day long he is merciful and lends.” Charity is never idle. If he has external goods, he gives them; if he does not have them, he gives good will. Therefore the just man is not abandoned. Rather, because God does not abandon him, he is comparable to one who, moved inwardly by mercy, brings it into action.

Or he continually has mercy on his own soul, pleasing God, so that he may make the person who accompanies him on God’s way his neighbor. “And his offspring will be blessed”: he will be comparable to one who receives back multiplied what he sows. “He will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matthew 19).

Therefore, “turn away from evil and do good.” This is equivalent to saying: Do not be jealous; do not envy the flourishing of the wicked. Rather do good, because it will not go unrewarded. You see that no envious person will be rewarded.

“And thus dwell,” namely, in your own land, “forever and ever.” In this way you will receive it as immortal and free from suffering. It is as though he were saying: “Compete lawfully, and you will be crowned” (2 Timothy 2). If you have not sown, you will not reap.

Therefore turn away from evil and do good, because “the Lord loves judgment”—namely, this discernment. Or: turn away from evil and do good, and by doing these things you will endure many evils. But do not fail, because “the Lord loves judgment”: “The one whom he loves he chastises” (Proverbs 1). And in judgment—that is, in chastisement—he will not abandon his holy ones, as it seems to the wicked; rather, through this he will preserve them. For a temporary scourging they will be preserved forever.

And even if their beginnings appear dry, their end will flourish. But “the unjust,” whose beginnings now flourish, will be punished, that is, their end will wither. “And the offspring of the impious,” namely, the evil works they sowed here, “will perish,” that is, they will not be in blessing, meaning multiplication, because they will go unrewarded.

But the just, who now seem abandoned, will inherit the land. Or they will receive as unfading the flesh they cultivated here. Or they will receive “the land of the living,” that is, eternal blessedness. And this will not be temporary: they will dwell upon it forever and ever, standing—that is, possessing it firmly and securely.

Meanwhile, “the mouth of the just man”—inwardly, his heart—“will meditate wisdom,” that is, the King and the will of God. “And his tongue will speak judgment,” that is, discernment: he will show mercy to himself and distribute that judgment to others. He will teach his neighbor what he ought to approve and what he ought to reject.

“The law of his God is in his heart.” This is the wisdom he meditates and the judgment he speaks to others. It is in his heart because he acts willingly according to the law. Therefore “his steps will not be tripped”: his thoughts will not be deceived so that he is led away toward evil. For there is no lack of those who trip others.

For “the sinner watches the just man,” that is, he diligently investigates his life—not in order to imitate it, but in order “to put him to death,” that is, to lead him away from righteousness. Yet he will not put him to death. “The Lord,” whose law he continually meditates, “will not abandon him into his hands.”

He does indeed abandon him into his external hands, because he permits him to afflict him, but he does not abandon him inwardly, because he will not be led astray according to the other’s will. In this way he does not abandon him: even if the impious condemns him here, the Lord will not condemn him at the future judgment when judgment is passed against him—namely, against the pious man concerning the impious man.

Or he will not abandon him into his hands when he is delivered outwardly into his hands, since the impious is permitted to scourge the pious as much as he wishes, even when judgment is passed against him—namely, against the impious concerning the pious man. The pious man is judged according to the impious man’s will, because that judgment will take place for the testing of the pious and the condemnation of the impious.

And because he will not abandon you into the hands of the impious, do not be jealous. Rather wait for the Lord, the one who rewards and liberates, with complete patience. Wait in this manner: “Keep his way,” the way he himself has shown you beforehand—the way of patience and humility. Act manfully; never desist from good work. “And he will exalt you from virtue to virtue,” so greatly that “you may inherit the land.”

Or you will see the land of the living in summary, when you are at the right hand and they are at the left. Alternatively: “He will eventually exalt you so that you may inherit the land,” because he will exalt you even here. Consult the eye of faith, and you will see yourself exalted—that is, lifted up and blessed—“when sinners have perished,” when they have been handed over to a depraved mind, in accordance with the words, “He will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner” (Psalm 57).

When the just man sees the impious abandoned by God because of his iniquity, he takes greater care to protect himself. And truly the impious will perish, because, observing his beginnings, “I saw the impious man highly exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon,” in riches, honors, and power. “And I passed by,” moving with the agility of the mind toward his end, from this false happiness toward the true; “and behold, he was no more”—not that he did not exist at all, but when I sought him, “his place was not found,” because once the iron has been flattened, the file is no longer needed.

Alternatively: Why do I say, “Wait”? Why do I say, “Keep”? Because I saw the impious man, who did not keep or observe, exalted here in earthly things. But when I passed on to his end, I did not find him flourishing in this way.

And because you see that the flourishing of the wicked will quickly fall and that your happiness is drawing near, do not envy the wicked because they flourish. Do not imitate them; rather, “keep innocence.” Do not harm yourself; do not murmur against the Lord. Rather “behold equity,” that is, understand God’s justice. For he does not permit the wicked to flourish here and the good to labor without reason. God’s judgments are not unjust because they are hidden. See that it is equitable to labor in the vineyard in order to receive a coin in the evening (Matthew 20).

Therefore “keep innocence,” because “there are survivors for the peaceful man,” that is, for the one who acts patiently and does not murmur against the Lord concerning temporal prosperity. There are survivors because eternal happiness is reserved for him after death—just as what remains from a rich man’s table is reserved for a poor man who possesses nothing of his own.

Alternatively: “His place was not found,” namely, the rich man’s place. Someone might say: “Then is it not permitted to abound here?” It is permitted, he says, but keep innocence. You have a little silver shrine and guard it so that it will not be taken from you, yet you neglect the loss of innocence? “And behold equity,” that is, right direction.
