Do not direct your eyes toward present things, and you will see that “there are survivors for the peaceful man”: after death he will possess life.

But “the unjust,” who do not keep innocence, “will perish.” They will be tortured by various punishments, or they will be blinded inwardly here. “And together the survivors of the impious will perish,” that is, their end also will wither. The beginnings of the just are useful to them because they humble them, and their end is useful because it exalts them. For the unjust, by contrast, both their beginnings, by which they are exalted, and their end, by which they are cast down, lead to destruction.

“The salvation of the just is from the Lord.” It is as though he were saying: The fact that the just are saved in this way—by keeping innocence and seeing equity—is from the Lord, not from themselves. He is their protector against their attackers in the time of tribulation, that is, in this life. And because he is their salvation and protector, the Lord will help them in bringing obedience to perfection. “And he will deliver them” from conformity with the wicked. Finally, “he will rescue them from sinners,” separating the grain from the straw. “And he will save them” with an enduring salvation, because they are grain and not straw.

And rightly so, because they have hoped in him and not in the world. Therefore do not be jealous; do not envy those who act wickedly. Rather hope in the Lord and do good, because he will both help you and save you.

## Psalm 37. A Psalm of David, for the Remembrance of the Sabbath

“Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger. For your arrows have been fixed in me, and you have laid your hand firmly upon me. There is no health in my flesh because of your anger; there is no peace in my bones because of my sins. For my iniquities have risen above my head, and like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me. My wounds have become foul and corrupt because of my folly. I have been made wretched and bowed down to the end; all day long I went about in sorrow. For my loins are filled with mockery, and there is no health in my flesh. I am afflicted and humbled exceedingly; I roared because of the groaning of my heart. Lord, all my desire is before you, and my groaning is not hidden from you. My heart is troubled; my strength has abandoned me, and the light of my eyes—even that is not with me. My friends and neighbors have approached and stood against me. And those who were near me stood far away; those who sought my life used force against me. Those who sought evil for me spoke vanities and meditated deceit all day long. But I, like a deaf man, did not hear, and like a mute man who does not open his mouth. I became like a man who does not hear and who has no reproofs in his mouth. For in you, Lord, I have hoped; you will hear me, Lord my God. For I said, ‘Let my enemies never rejoice over me’; and when my feet were shaken, they spoke great things against me. For I am ready for scourges, and my pain is always before me. For I will declare my iniquity and think upon my sin. But my enemies live and have grown strong against me, and those who hate me unjustly have multiplied. Those who repay evil for good slandered me, because I pursued goodness. Do not abandon me, Lord my God; do not depart from me. Attend to my help, Lord, God of my salvation.”

## Explanation
If we review all the Scripture in which David is mentioned, nowhere will we find David remembering the Sabbath. Remembrance concerns things past. Since the Sabbath returns every week, he is not found remembering it, but observing it. Here, however, someone is introduced who remembers that rest which the human race possessed in its first parent—namely, that it was created immortal and incapable of suffering by its constitution—and also that it will one day again be immortal and incapable of suffering without qualification, so that it will be unable either to die or to suffer. For “Sabbath” is interpreted as “rest.” [Col. 0341B] Here, I say, considering that rest, lost through the fault of the first parent, and considering the future Sabbath, when either rest or eternal punishment awaits each person, while he is here amid evils and fears worse things, he prays and says:

“Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury.” For it will happen that at the future judgment some will be corrected in anger, while others will be rebuked in fury: those who are in anger, nevertheless, as though through fire. But that punishment will be so severe that, even if all the torments found here among the condemned were brought together, that fire would be more grievous and more intolerable. Those, however, who are in fury will be sent into eternal fire. Therefore he implores both, as though saying to God: Since these things that I suffer are great and many, I beg that they may suffice you as vengeance [Col. 0341C] for the guilt I deserved. And he begins to enumerate them, making satisfaction to God and offering up what he suffers, lest he suffer worse things; he shows that he willingly suffers everything here in order at last to escape those things. O Lord, burn, cut, correct, rebuke me here, provided that in the end you do not rebuke me in your fury—that is, with the gravest and eternal punishment.

Nor then should you correct me in your anger, because those who will then be corrected in anger will indeed be saved, but through a most grievous punishment. These are those who built wood, hay, and stubble upon the foundation (I Cor. III): not that fury or anger falls upon God, but that it will appear so to those who suffer. But if we speak in the voice of the Head, we shall say this: Lord God, Trinity, until the fullness of time you have rebuked the human race for the most part in fury and corrected it in anger, because, after punishing all idolaters with the first death—the death of the inner person—you cast them into the death of the body. [Col. 0341D] At last, if judgment begins from your household, do not rebuke those recalled by me through love in the first resurrection in your anger; do not correct them in your fury. Even if you visit iniquities with the rod, even if you mix everything with bitterness, let these things not happen in your fury or in your anger. Even if they undergo bodily death, nevertheless let those whom your mercy has restored through me in the first resurrection, in the inner person, rejoice in the hope that they will be restored in the second, outward resurrection.

And as though you were about to ask what reason there was, Lord, for undertaking such things on behalf of your own, the answer is this: because your arrows have been fixed in me—that is, in the human race—and in me [Col. 0342A] insofar as I share that nature. “There is no health in my flesh,” that is, in my lower members, because they too experience your earth in Adam. “There is no peace in my bones,” that is, in my stronger members, because they themselves are not free from sin.

Or, in the voice of the Church: Therefore do not judge me in the future fury or in the future anger, because your arrows have been fixed in me. Let this temporal vengeance and the punishment that I now suffer suffice for you. For you are already taking vengeance: your arrows have been fixed in me, and I suffer because of the guilt of the first parent. What was punishment for him has become nature for us. Hence the Apostle says: “We too were once by nature children of wrath” (Eph. II), that is, bearing vengeance. These arrows are mortality, hunger, thirst, sleep, and other things of this kind. He calls the pains of soul and body that we suffer “arrows.” [Col. 0342B] Or he calls the words of God arrows, because they have been fixed in our hearts and cause us to remember the Sabbath. That very remembrance of the Sabbath, and our not yet having received it, prevents us from yet rejoicing and recognizing that there is no health in this flesh itself.

It is as though he said: This your punishment, by which you now take vengeance, is also great, because “you have strengthened your hand over me”—that is, you have made my punishment continuous—like the hand of a teacher whose hand does not leave the back of a boy. This is that hand; this is that misery. “There is no health in my flesh because of the face of your anger,” that is, because of the presence of your anger. From the time when you took vengeance in the first parent, the misery of the human race has been so continuous that it constantly presents your anger to us. We bear a mortal body, full of temptations, full of anxieties, subject to bodily pains, [Col. 0342C] bound to needs, changeable, weak—and even when it is healthy, only apparently so, since it is certainly not yet completely healthy. For why would he say, “There is no health in my flesh,” unless the health that belongs to this life, for those who understand rightly and remember the Sabbath, is not truly health?

If you do not eat, hunger troubles you, and there are many other things of this kind. This is a certain natural disease, which in Adam was punishment alone. And I am not weak only in the flesh; “there is no peace in my bones” either—that is, in the powers of my soul, which are bones, the strength of a person. For a person is weakened through the flesh, but strengthened through the reasoning of the soul.

And because he said, “because of the face of your anger,” lest it appear that the punishment came from the injustice of the judge, he says, “because of the face of my sins,” that is, because of their presence. [Col. 0342D] For when I constantly see the punishment, I also constantly remember the guilt. I have your anger before my eyes; I have before my eyes my original and actual sins. Therefore there is no peace in my bones—that is, no rest for my soul.

“For my iniquities have gone over my head.” That is, my sins in the first parent raised their head—that is, my mind—so that it might raise its own head against you: “And you will be like gods” (Gen. III), since “the head of the woman is the man, the head of the man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (I Cor. XI). Those iniquities have gone over my head: by raising my mind, they pressed it down, and through your vengeance they fell upon it, so that it is no longer able to use its freedom, like anger and desire, which ought to be subject to reason. [Col. 0343A] For with perfect discernment we ought to be angry at what deserves anger and desire what deserves desire. These iniquities have gone over my head—that is, they have conquered rationality. And they have not gone over it lightly; they have weighed upon me like a heavy burden.

Alternatively: “You have strengthened your hand over me,” as it is said; and after this misery I have another: “There is no health in my flesh,” that is, I am afflicted outwardly with every affliction—and this because of the face of your anger, because I fear your future anger. “There is no peace in my bones,” that is, I am afflicted inwardly with every affliction because of the future judgment, because of the face of my sins, both original and actual.

Jerome: [Col. 0343B] “For my iniquities have gone over my head: I acknowledge my great sins and that they prevail over my strength; or because my iniquities raised their head and, as though light, flew about, they received the weight of vengeance that would press them down. ‘Like a heavy burden they have weighed upon me,’ that is, they have returned upon me and become heavy.”

As though he said: And what is more grievous, “My wounds have become foul and corrupt”—that is, the sins forgiven in baptism. Having been healed in this way, I have again made a habit of them; and when this happens, the dead person must necessarily stink, just as an untouched wound becomes corrupt and putrid. In his saying “wounds,” sins are understood as though they had been healed.

Alternatively: From the burden of that most grievous weight, “my wounds”—that is, original sins erased in baptism—have been corrupted through actual sins. Thus they have become putrid, that is, they have become most grievous, because someone who comes to baptism and sins afterward is more severely tormented than one who never came to baptism. [Col. 0343C] For it is better to be ignorant of the way of truth than, after knowing it, to abandon it.

“And this because of the face of my folly,” that is, I recognize that this happened through my folly. For just as wisdom consists in guarding oneself for the future, so folly consists in failing to guard oneself afterward, once healed.

Jerome: “It is the custom of swine to use mud instead of good fragrances; I am not like that. For my wounds stink to me, and therefore I desire repentance.”

Hence, from this corruption and this putrefaction I have become wretched—that is, I have been afflicted outwardly by continual misery. “And I was bent down,” namely, inwardly, by manifold bending, because rationality is extended not only toward what is necessary but also toward what is unlawful, as far as I could be bent and brought low, or even unto death. [Col. 0343D] From that bending I entered, that is, lived, sorrowful all day—that is, continually—from the time I began to remember the Sabbath.

Hence in the Song of Songs: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; your eyes are like those of doves” (Cant. I, 4), because the dove has a lament for its song, and the perfect in the Church lament to the world that falsely and perniciously flatters, whereas others rejoice with it.

And rightly am I sorrowful, because “my loins are filled with illusions, and there is no health in my flesh.” This repetition has the same meaning as above: there is no health in my flesh; there is no peace in my bones. In the loins is delight, and in delight is procreation. From the soul all thoughts are born, and these delights are full of illusions—that is, of vanities and many phantasms—so much so that [Col. 0344A] no one can recite the Lord’s Prayer from the heart without many things interfering and distracting the mind. “And there is no health in my flesh,” as has been said.

Alternatively: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury”—that is, at the judgment, when sinners will be condemned; rebuke me here. “Fury” and “anger” are understood as the devil. That is, do not judge me through the devil, but through yourself; or rebuke me with words and correct me with scourges. “For your arrows have been fixed in me,” that is, your words have been impressed upon my mind. “And you have strengthened your hand over me,” that is, you were not powerless to bring me low.

“There is no health in my bones,” that is, my body is not pure, according to the statement: “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh” (Rom. VII). “There is no peace in my bones,” as above.

“For my iniquities [Col. 0344B] have gone over my head,” as though he said: My iniquities are so numerous that I cannot carry them; but my head, that is, Christ, made them his own, and he himself bore our iniquities (Isa. LIII). He bore them because “like a heavy burden they have weighed upon me.”

And it is no wonder, because “my wounds have become foul and corrupt.” From the first human being until Christ, the sins of the human race grew worse, until that Samaritan came who bound up the wounds, pouring in wine and oil (Luke X)—that is, the Passion and the grace of the Holy Spirit.

“Because of the face of my folly,” namely, my wounds became corrupt because I considered Christ’s weakness folly, although his Incarnation was great wisdom. “I became wretched and bent down unto the end,” that is, unto Christ. [Col. 0344C] And because “my loins are filled with illusions,” that is, because my soul and inner mind departed from the truth; and because “there is no health in my flesh,” I was afflicted in the body and greatly humbled inwardly, because I raised myself against your commandments. Hence I roared—that is, I uttered laments inwardly with great pain, so that it may be called a roar.

“Because of the groaning of my heart,” not because of the groaning of the flesh. The groaning of the flesh is for the loss of earthly things; the groaning of the heart is for the loss of rest.

“Lord, all my desire is before you.” As though he said: You, Lord, know what I desire when I groan, and why I groan, because I desire only what ought to be desired—namely, that rest and blessedness which I lost in the first parent. For this one must always pray, since it is said: [Col. 0344D] “Pray without ceasing” (I Thess. I). Whoever always cries out always desires; whoever always desires always prays. Whoever ceases from love ceases from prayer.

Who are those who cease from love? Those of whom it is said: “Because iniquity will abound, the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. XIV). For the coldness of charity is the silence of the heart, while the fervor of charity is the cry of the heart. If charity always burns, you always cry out; if you always cry out, you always desire; if you always desire, you always pray. Therefore always desire, so that you may always pray.

And because you know—that is, approve—my desire, which accords with your will, therefore my groaning is not hidden from you. Although at times I may appear to rejoice outwardly, and although my groaning does not always come to [Col. 0345A] human ears, nevertheless it is always before you.

And rightly do I groan, because “my heart is troubled.” I fear robbers; I fear temporal losses; earthquakes and anxiety from every side are inflicted upon me. And it is no wonder if the heart is troubled, because “my strength has abandoned me,” that is, my steadfastness; I have become unstable. Or “strength” means rationality.

I have been abandoned by strength because “the light of my eyes”—the light of the heart, without which the human heart is in darkness, namely God himself—is not with me, that very one without whom I cannot exist. As though he said: To restore this strength, to return this light, and to remove this disturbance, I alone among all mortals, being suited to this purpose, became obedient to the Father unto death (Phil. II).

And because they saw me so humbled, [Col. 0345B] to increase my misery, “my friends”—that is, those who ought to be friends, as the sick are friends to the physician, servants to the Lord, and creatures to the Creator—namely, the Gentiles, and “my neighbors,” the Jews, neighbors according to kinship of the flesh, drew near in body but stood against me in heart, saying: “Crucify him” (Matt. XV). And they stood—that is, against me, and therefore against their own salvation.

Just as Christ previously spoke in the Church, so now the Church speaks in Christ.

Alternatively: “The strength of my members”—that is, rationality—abandoned my members to such an extent that “the light of my eyes,” that is, the divinity united to me, without which I cannot exist with respect to true essence, [Col. 0345C] was not with me in their estimation. For they thought that I was only a human being. Therefore “my friends,” who ought to have been friends, and my neighbors with respect to the flesh, drew near not for imitation but against me.

Moreover, those who were near me—that is, the disciples who knew me—stood at a distance, as Peter did, who denied me at the voice of a servant girl (John XVIII), in accordance with the statement: “All his acquaintances stood at a distance” (Luke XXIII).

And because my friends had failed, those who sought my life—that is, my life in order to destroy it—used force; they therefore had easier access. Those who sought evil for me—that is, death—since they had no true cause, spoke vanities, that is, lies: “We heard him subverting our nation” (Luke XXIII); and, “This man said: I can destroy this temple and rebuild it in three days” (Matt. XXVI).

And because they spoke vanities, [Col. 0345D] they meditated deceit all day long.

But I, who had come for the purpose of giving an example of patience and humility, “was like one who did not hear,” and like a mute who does not open his mouth—that is, I did not answer, as though I neither heard nor could speak.

“And I became like a man who does not hear and who has no reproofs in his mouth.” He says the same thing more openly: he did not fail to rebuke them during the Passion because he had nothing with which to rebuke them, since he had often answered them: “Woe to you, scribes. Why do you tempt me, hypocrites?” (Matt. XXII, XXIII). But he remained silent during the Passion so that the Scriptures might be fulfilled: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter” (Isa. LIII), and so that he might give us a model of patience. For if he had descended from the cross, he would not have seemed to display power [Col. 0346A] but to exhibit impatience. A greater sign of power was to rise from the tomb than to descend from the cross.

Therefore I did not contradict them; I patiently endured everything, because I hoped in you, Lord, and entrusted my cause to you. Here he teaches his own what must be done in tribulations: although he could have resisted, he did not wish to do so, but hoped in the Lord.

And because I hoped in you, you will hear me, Lord my God. Therefore, faithful man, if your cause is not heard by an earthly judge, do not despair and do not give up. For if you are not heard here, you will be heard in heaven; if here you receive a sentence from an earthly judge, you will receive a crown from God in heaven.

There is another reason why I became like a man who does not hear: because I said—that is, I determined this within myself—that I should persevere in patience. Therefore, lest my enemies ever exult over me—that is, [Col. 0346B] lest the Jews insult me as I fail during the Passion, or other enemies insult my people when they fall in tribulation—and lest my feet, that is, the works or affections of my people, be moved, that is, depart from you and fail under torments, and thus the enemies speak great things against me—many and great blasphemies.

And truly I know that they will mock my people when they fall, if their feet are moved, because they have often done such things already: “When my feet are moved, they have spoken great things against me.”

And therefore I had no reproofs, because I came voluntarily to the Passion, not by necessity.

“For I am ready for scourges.” And this because my pain—that is, the pain of my people—which they have because of the transgression of the first parent and their own sins, [Col. 0346C] is always before me until I grieve, just as a wound is before a physician.

I rightly said “my pain,” because I, Christ, will proclaim their iniquity as my own. For I did not commit iniquity, but assumed it. And I will not merely announce that the iniquity is mine; I will also meditate upon my sin—that is, upon the sin of my people—by grieving for it.

So you too, every faithful person, imitate Christ. Do not merely confess your sin; meditate on it so that you may erase it. Let tears flow; let almsgiving be performed. Let the poor rejoice in what you have given, so that you too may rejoice in what God has given. You are in need, and he is in need; he needs what you have, and you need what God has. Relieve his outward need here, so that God may fill your inward poverty.

Alternatively, they spoke great things against me because I am ready for scourges, although they do not think that I am ready for them but that I have been forced into them. [Col. 0346D] If they understood that my being scourged proceeds from obedience, because “no one takes my life from me” (John X), they would not have spoken great things against me.

“I am ready for scourges,” so that I may suffer those scourges which they themselves would have had to suffer. As though he said: I am ready for scourges, but my enemies—both my own enemies and those of my people—live, that is, flourish in this life. Therefore they have been strengthened against me, that is, they have prevailed outwardly in the cause concerning me and my people. For the Jews prevailed against me in my Passion, and against my people, by scourging and killing them.

And in that strengthening they multiplied, that is, many were found; for persecutors became more numerous than imitators. “Those who hate me unjustly.” He explains how they hate unjustly: “Those who repay evil for good were slandering me” [Col. 0347A]. What could be more wicked than this? Whoever repays evil for evil is not good; whoever does not repay good for good is ungrateful; but whoever repays evil for good is unjust. Evil for good: hatred for love, destruction for salvation, death for life. They slandered me for no other reason than that I pursued goodness—that is, because I was unlike them and opposed to their deeds.

“Do not abandon me.” As though he said: But do not allow your holy one to see corruption (Ps. LI). Lord, by grace; my God, by nature. “Do not depart from me,” by failing to raise me again, as they think; or, do not abandon my people by giving them steadfastness in tribulation, and do not depart from them by freeing them from their enemies’ enticement.

And so that you may not abandon me and may not depart, “attend to my help”—that is, give assistance [Col. 0347B] to the free will that you have given. Lord God of my salvation: you are Lord God by nature, and you have become God of salvation by grace.

Or, do not merely refrain from departing from me, Christ; instead, turn your face toward me, stretched out upon the cross, giving me resurrection. Lord God of my salvation—that is, you who gave me to my people as the author of salvation.

## PSALM XXXVIII. FOR THE END, FOR JEDUTHUN; A SONG OF DAVID

“I said: I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue. I placed a guard over my mouth, when the sinner stood against me. I was mute and humbled, and I was silent from good things, and my pain was renewed. My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation the fire will blaze. I spoke with my tongue: Make known to me, Lord, my end, and what is the number of my days, so that I may know what I lack. Behold, you have made my days measurable, and my substance is as nothing before you. Surely every living human being is altogether vanity. Yet a person passes by in an image, and is nevertheless troubled in vain. He stores up treasure and does not know for whom he will gather it. And now, what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord? And my substance is with you. Deliver me from all my iniquities; you have made me a reproach to the fool. I was mute and did not open my mouth, because you did this. Remove your scourges from me. I have failed beneath the strength of your hand through your rebukes; because of iniquity you have corrected a person. And you have made his soul waste away like a spider, yet every person is troubled in vain. Hear my prayer, Lord, and my supplication; attend with your ears to my tears. Do not be silent, because I am a sojourner with you and a pilgrim, like all my fathers. Spare me, so that I may be refreshed before I depart and exist no longer.”

## EXPOSITION

Historically, nothing is done in this psalm concerning Jeduthun, who was one of the five whom David appointed as leaders of the psalm singers (I Chron. XXV). Rather, the understanding of the truth must be sought from the interpretation of his name. Jeduthun has been interpreted for us as “leaping over them.”

In this psalm there is the voice of one who leaps over them—namely, those clinging to the ground, bent toward the earth, thinking about the lowest things, and placing their hope in earthly matters. [Col. 0348A] Thus, leaping over them, despising the world and trampling upon all earthly things, he chose to live for himself in certain spiritual joys. While we remain in this life, those joys are found especially in the divine Scriptures, where useful investigation is accomplished through the labor of inquiry and the sweetness of discovery.

But after he had trampled upon all worldly things, despised all the pleasures of this world, meditated upon the law of the Lord alone, delighted in it alone, frequently spoken to others about it, and striven to benefit others through it, he understood that he must not remain there but must ascend still higher, because through his eagerness to speak he had lost his diligence in knowing.

And when he saw that there were few imitators but many slanderers and hunters of words, defending falsehood and prepared to stand against the truth, [Col. 0348B] and that, because of the continual necessity of speaking, it was difficult not to fall through the tongue—for the tongue was not placed in a human being without danger in speaking—he determined that silence was a remedy, saying to himself: The pleasure of understanding before God is enough for me. What need have I to speak for applause and to give access to slanderers?

Therefore I said: “I will guard my ways.”

The title is “For the end.” These words are put forward for Jeduthun—that is, in the person of the one who leaps over them. The Prophet’s intention in this psalm is to show how all worldly things must be leapt over by the faithful, toward whom one must strive and to whom one must come.

I said—that is, I resolved and deliberated with myself—“I will guard my ways,” that is, I will carefully watch over all my deeds and all my faculties, so as not to sin with my tongue, which is exceedingly difficult: “Everyone is perfect who does not sin in speech” (James III). “Whoever guards his tongue guards his soul” (Proverbs XXI). And: “The cultivation of justice is silence and peace” (Isaiah XXXII). And: “I regret speaking; I never regret keeping silent.”

And after deliberation I set a guard over my mouth, not on account of the good, but when the sinner stood against me—that is, when a slanderer stood with others to listen, not in order to imitate anything good he might hear, but against me, prepared to slander anything he might hear that would deserve reproach—or when, being unable to understand, he would say that I was saying nothing. I became silent.

Fearing the slander of evil people among my fellow servants, I did not distribute provisions, although the distribution had been entrusted to me. And therefore I became silent: because I did not dispense outwardly, I did not deserve to receive inwardly from the Lord. It was said to that servant who feared to distribute the talent he had received from his lord: “Bind him hand and foot, and throw him into the outer darkness” (Matthew XXV). But if this is said to one who was not a runner bent on wasting it, but a boy appointed to distribute it, what will be said to those who lose the talent they have received by living luxuriously—that is, who give over to luxurious idleness the knowledge they received from the Lord?

“And I was humbled,” that is, afflicted. And I was afflicted because I kept silent about good things, which I ought not to have done. Thus my pain was renewed: whereas previously I had grieved over the slander of evil people and therefore kept silent, afterward I grieved because I denied my fellow servants the distribution entrusted to me by the Lord.

And when I was placed between these two necessities, speaking and keeping silent—speaking, because I had received the Lord’s talent in order to distribute it according to measure; keeping silent, lest I grant evil people an opportunity to slander—“my heart grew hot within me,” that is, my heart began to be restless, inwardly torn by a double heat. Placed between those who were prepared to slander and those who desired instruction, I was afflicted in both directions: in the case of the former, lest I cast pearls before swine; in the case of the latter, lest I distribute provisions to my fellow servants.

I saw senseless people and did not rebuke them, and while I kept silent in this way, “zeal for your house consumed me” (Psalm LXVIII). And although in this heat I had already passed over many things, I nevertheless considered that I must climb still higher and seek a safer place.

And in that meditation of mine “the fire blazes”: that is, a certain desire kindled my heart to know my end. And after this desire I spoke with my tongue—not to one whom I might instruct, but to one from whom I might be instructed. “With my tongue,” that is, with the tongue of my heart, or in speech suited to me, who had already passed beyond these worldly things: I spoke as follows:

“Make my end known to me, Lord”—an end without end, not the course of my life, so that I may not look back toward the things I have already passed beyond, but look forward toward those that remain. I have already passed beyond many things and reached certain things better than those I passed beyond, but there still remains the height to which I must ascend. For no one in this life is perfect in such a way that no further ascent remains possible. Hear the Apostle: “Brothers, I do not consider that I have yet apprehended” (Philippians III). “But one thing: forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue according to my purpose toward the prize of the heavenly calling.”

Therefore this one who is passing beyond says: “Make my end known to me, Lord,” that is, make yourself known to me, beyond whom nothing remains to be desired. “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John XIV): that is, make me know you alone as the object of desire, so that all my purpose may be directed toward pleasing you and my desire may rest nowhere until it reaches you, because true and perfect blessedness is found in you alone. And however greatly a person may progress, he must never cease until that end is reached.

Or, “my end,” that is, the proper manner of speaking and the proper manner of keeping silent, because “there is a time for speaking and a time for keeping silent” (Ecclesiastes III).

“And what is the number of my days?” That is, show me—not for the sake of knowledge but for the sake of experience—the certainty of those days, that is, of that eternity which is in the end that is the number, because it belongs to those days that do not perish and do not flow away through time: it was, or it will be, but it is; it is always in those days.

Or, according to the other interpretation, in which we said that this means the manner of speaking and the manner of keeping silent: “Show me the number of my days,” that is, the comparison with that time which truly is, so that by comparison with it I may know what ought to be said, to whom, and what ought not to be said. Or, teach me always to strive toward those days that are, so that by comparing them with those days I may regard as nothing whatever I suffer in these days that are not.

Show me that number for this purpose: that I may know what is lacking in me, namely, your presence, because now “I know in part” (1 Corinthians XIII). This is what is lacking to me here in my labor; this is that denarius. And as long as it is lacking to me, I do not call myself perfect but diminished. Show it to me; direct my mind toward it. For when I attend to what truly is and compare with it the things that are not so, seeing that more is lacking to me than is present, I shall be humbler because of what is lacking than exalted because of what is present.

It is as though he were saying: “And truly, I still lack something for perfection.”

“Behold, you have made my days measurable,” that is, brief and quickly passing. “My days,” that is, days which I myself, by my fault, have made measurable, although they were given by you without measure. And not only have my days become measurable, but my substance also, which I possess here and which you gave me from nothing, is as nothing before you—that is, in comparison with that substance and that splendor which I shall possess in your presence.

“Nevertheless, every living human being is utter vanity,” that is, although he is nothing, wretched humanity does not consider this. “Every living human being,” that is, everyone who lives according to humanity—in what he is human, not in what he is the image of God—is utter vanity. That is, by laboring he incurs complete vanity of soul and body, because he thinks and labors over earthly things that tend toward nothing.

It is as though he were saying: “It would not be so surprising if a person devoted to vain things remained in them for a long time. Nevertheless”—that is, although a human being is manifold vanity—“in an image a person passes by”: that is, he abandons all these vain things so quickly that the image passes away in a mirror. “For he considered himself, and went away, and immediately forgot what he had been like” (James I).

Yet wretched humanity, not considering this, is troubled in vain. It fears not acquiring these things and fears losing them, and it is anxious in many ways on its own behalf, on behalf of its wife, and on behalf of its children. Truly in vain, because it stores up treasure and does not know for whom it will gather it, since it is uncertain about the life of the person for whom it gathers. Wretched humanity does not consider how quickly it falls away from that very vanity; indeed, it thinks about posterity.

Alternatively: Although I have passed beyond all worldly things, trampled upon the lowest things, found delight in the law of God alone, and been anxious in distributing the Lord’s talent; although I have borne fruit in that distribution, sought the end that is without end, labored to know the number of my days, and recognized where true being is—nevertheless, as long as I live in this mortal body, as long as I labor lest I fall, and as long as I possess uncertain good and evil, I am utter vanity with respect to the things I possess beneath the sun, not with respect to those above the sun.

For every person living here, whether clinging to the world or passing beyond it, is utter vanity. Ecclesiastes says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. What more does a person have from all his labor with which he labors beneath the sun?” (Ecclesiastes I). For by the merit of sin he is subject to manifold vanity. He desires to sleep and to stay awake; he hungers and thirsts, and so forth—things of this kind, all of which are vain.

Nevertheless, “in an image a person passes by”: that is, although in the things he possesses beneath the sun he is subject to vanity, in the things he possesses above the sun he is not subject to vanity. For “a person passes by”—that is, he lives or passes through this vanity—in the image, that is, in what imitates the image according to which he was created, namely reason, when he desires his proper end.

And yet, although in mind he is above the sun and in that respect is not subject to vanity, in body he is beneath the sun; therefore every human being is troubled in vain. “He stores up treasure and does not know for whom he will gather it,” as above.

“And now, what is my expectation?” It is as though he were saying: “Since I have already passed beyond all these things in my mind and have placed no hope in what is perishable, what then is my expectation? Is it not the Lord?” Namely, the one in whom there is nothing vain, nothing transitory.

Truly, it is the Lord. He who gave me the power to despise these things will give himself. It is as though he were saying: “Rightly do I await you, Lord, as my rewarder, because my substance is with you,” that is, I possess true being nowhere except in you, that is, in your presence. For you alone are, and no one exists except one who clings to you.

And so that my substance may at last be with you, “deliver me from all my iniquities”: not only from those I have already passed beyond, lest I fall back into them, but also from those that remain by the necessity of the journey. For no one is so perfect that, by virtue of the human condition, he does not contract some iniquities. “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John I).

Alternatively: I understand my perfection, and I understand my imperfection. I am imperfect because I have not yet apprehended you, in whom my perfection lies. I am perfect because I know what is lacking to me. Therefore I ask that you deliver me from the iniquities that prevent me from reaching you.

“You have made me a reproach to the fool.” Deliver me, because you have made me a reproach to the fool: that is, because I seek you and nothing else, because I hope for what is not seen. “I have become a laughingstock to the fool,” that is, to the person who rejoices only in earthly and present things and makes no provision for the future.

Or: You have permitted me sufficiently to be a reproach to the fool; let this now suffice for you. “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Philippians I).

Or, deliver me for this reason: because, in order that I might be worthy to be delivered, you made me a reproach to the fool, and I became silent, contradicting nothing.

Or, with regard to what he said, “You have made me sufficiently a reproach to the fool,” it means: “I have been sufficiently silent and have not opened my mouth to contradict, and I possessed this patience not from myself, but because you made me patient. God, therefore I became silent, because you made that reproach happen to me by your just vengeance.”

But, O Lord, “remove your scourges from me.” For I understand whatever I suffer in this mortal body to be your chastisements. Why do I call them yours? Because I failed under your rebukes, having become mortal and subject to suffering, through the strength of your hand, which was not powerless to avenge the guilt and transgression of the human race.

And this did not arise from your injustice but from my merit, because “on account of iniquity”—his own, not yours; that is, on account of transgression—“you rebuked a human being,” namely, the first human being, and me and the entire human race in him.

It is as though he were saying: “I see myself amid evils; I see myself amid punishments, and I see no iniquity in you. If, then, I am in punishment and there is no iniquity in you, does it not remain that you have rebuked a human being on account of iniquity?” And in this way you rebuked him.

“You made his soul waste away like a spider.” That is, you made human life like the spider, which, if it is touched even lightly, is quickly broken and emits decay. You made human life decay by the merit of sin, so that it may not inappropriately be said of it: “Why is earth and ash proud?” (Ecclesiasticus X).

For “in his life he casts out his inner parts,” by analogy: just as a spider, by producing its inner substance, constructs a fragile work and dies within that very work, so a human being, by casting out his inner substance—that is, by losing his rationality, his greatest possession—devotes himself to transient things, in which he soon dies.

Nevertheless—that is, although such great calamity is not hidden—“every human being is troubled in vain”: that is, he is anxiously concerned about these vain things that quickly pass away. “Every human being,” that is, one living according to humanity.

And so that I may not be troubled in this way, “hear my prayer, Lord,” made for perseverance in the virtues, “and receive my supplication,” made for sins committed. “Give ear,” that is, show that you have heard, “to my tears,” that is, to my tearful prayers.

“Do not be silent,” that is, do not show yourself angry with me, since it belongs to angry masters to be silent. Therefore do not depart from me in anger, because here with you “I am only a sojourner and a pilgrim”: that is, since I exist with you in hope, I understand myself to be a sojourner here. For “here I have no lasting city, but I seek the one that is to come” (Hebrews XIII).

And not merely a sojourner, who may be nearby, but a pilgrim, who is very far away, “as all my fathers” were—namely, as the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles understood.

And so that I may be able to be with you, “forgive me.” My sins are intense, but release them by forgiving them, so that I may be refreshed from the heat of vices in my conscience. Give me the testimony of a good conscience before I depart—that is, before I depart from this life—or before I depart from you, in whom my substance lies.

For if I depart without having been refreshed, I shall exist no longer. Just as here, temporally, I did not exist in true being, so afterward I shall not exist in true substance.

## PSALM XXXIX. FOR THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID.

“Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he attended to me. And he heard my prayers and brought me out of the pit of misery and from the mire of filth. And he set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps. And he put a new song into my mouth, a hymn to our God. Many will see and fear, and they will hope in the Lord. Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not looked toward vanities and false insanities. Many wonders you have done, Lord my God, and in your thoughts there is no one like you. I proclaimed and spoke; they have multiplied beyond number. Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but you perfected ears for me. You did not ask for a burnt offering or for sin; then I said, ‘Behold, I come.’ In the heading of the book it is written of me, that I should do your will. My God, I willed it, and your law is in the midst of my heart. I proclaimed your justice in the great assembly; behold, I will not restrain my lips. Lord, you know. I did not hide your justice in my heart; I spoke of your truth and your salvation. I did not hide your mercy and your truth from the great council. But you, Lord, do not keep your mercies far from me; your mercy and your truth have always received me. For evils without number have surrounded me; my iniquities have seized me, and I was unable to see. They have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head, and my heart has abandoned me. Be pleased, Lord, to deliver me; Lord, look upon me to help me. Let those who seek my soul in order to take it be confounded and put to shame together. Let those who wish me evil turn back and be put to shame. Let them immediately bear their confusion, those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done.’ Let all who seek you rejoice and be glad in you, and let those who love your salvation say, ‘May the Lord always be magnified.’ But I am a beggar and poor; the Lord is concerned for me. You are my helper and my protector; my God, do not delay.”

## EXPOSITION

The true David, that is, Christ our head, shows in this psalm that no one can be justified except through faith—not through works of the law, nor through free will, as Porphyry wished. He said that he had no need to receive faith in baptism because he had already been inwardly put to death.

He also indicates, by his own example, who are justified through faith, showing beforehand that patience is necessary if we are to receive the promises. He also prays for the Gentiles, who are to be incorporated with the Jews through faith, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd.

“Waiting, I waited for the Lord.” Such a doubling of words usually arises from great affection. It is as though he were saying: “I came, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John VI)—something the first human being ought to have done. “I have a most merciful promiser; I await a completely faithful fulfiller; I present myself as a humble claimant.”

“Waiting,” that is, fulfilling obedience with patience, “I waited for the Lord”: not for some ordinary human promiser, not for one lacking power, but for the omnipotent one, who, even if he delays what he has promised, does not take it away.

And because I waited patiently, “he attended to me,” that is, he looked upon me for my benefit. It is as though he were saying: “Thus patience is also necessary for you.” What he says—“to me”—is the greater thing, as though he were saying: “He attended to me,” because the face of the Lord is also upon those who do evil. And in this way he attended to me.

“He heard my prayers,” made for the sins of my people. I call them “my” prayers because of my excessive affection; this is evident in the fact that “he brought me out of the pit of misery,” that is, he brought my people out of the fall of sins through confession and repentance.

The “pit of misery” is the manifold fall and depth of sins. In that pit some are above and others below. Above are humble suppliants and tearful petitioners; below are proud despisers. The latter remain there; the former are brought out.

“And from the mire of filth,” that is, from the slippery uncleanness of this age. In “mire,” uncleanness is signified; in “filth,” slipperiness. That is, he brought my people even out of those sins into which the fall is more inclined to occur, namely ambition and luxury.

And after he brought them out, “he set my feet upon a rock,” that is, he strengthened the affections of my people in me, the rock, so that they might imitate me and become conformed to me, so that they would no longer fall back into the mire.

And after he strengthened their affections so that they would no longer love perishable things, “he directed my steps,” that is, the works of my people, which previously had been distorted.

“And he put into my mouth”—the mouth of the heart—“a new song,” that is, a new life. Those who previously sang the old song now sing the new song: “Just as you presented your members to serve impurity and iniquity, so now present them to serve justice in sanctification” (Romans VI).

That is, a hymn to our God, so that by living rightly we may attribute nothing to ourselves but everything to the grace of God. For the old song was presumption about ourselves. And for what purpose is this new song? It is of great importance, because many will see those successors singing the new song—that is, leading innocent lives and praising God—and they will fear, namely, singing the old song: living wickedly and praising the world.

And thus “they will hope in the Lord,” in whom one ought to hope. In the Lord, because they will despair of the world. No one hopes in the Lord unless he first despairs of the world. And therefore he becomes an enemy of the world so that he may become a friend of the Lord.

Such a person is rightly called a man, and blessed. And because that song is sung not with the mouth of the body but with the heart, he therefore says: “They will see and not hear.”

This order always flourishes in the Church: some go before, and others imitate them, and these are lesser in relation to those.

And hear with what fruit they will hope in the Lord:

“Blessed”—that is, well increased—“will be the man whose hope is the name of the Lord,” that is, the man who, by displaying worthy service, makes himself suitable to hope in that name which is “Lord.”

And after he fixed his hope in him, “he did not look toward vanities,” that is, he did not turn the eyes of his heart back toward transient things, because “no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke IX).

And because he did not look back, he did not look toward “false insanities,” that is, toward the games of this age and the spectacles of the theater, which make a person insane—false because they possess no truth.

It is as though he were saying: “He rightly did not look toward these things, because one ought rather to look toward the spectacles and wonders of God.”

For “many wonders you have done, Lord my God,” toward which one ought rather to look. In them there is a healthy and sober intoxication.

Did someone marvel in the theater at a charioteer guiding a chariot without injury? Let him see God specially guiding all illicit impulses, and himself guiding them with God, and let him praise God.

Did he marvel there at a tightrope walker? Let him marvel in the Church at one who walks upon the sea—not only with the feet of the body, as Peter did (Matthew XIV), but, more wonderfully, spiritually with the feet of the heart.

For this age is a sea, because it is bitter with many anxieties: winds, various temptations, waves, persecutions, conflicts, and seditions. The saints trample upon and despise all these things.

Let each person hear the Lord crying out: “I await you; struggle; I will help you; conquer; I will crown you.”

And these wonders you did by your thoughts, needing no outside assistance; therefore there is no one like you. Hope, then, in you.

Earlier he said, “Waiting, I waited for the Lord”; the intervening words were inserted. Now he shows how he waited.

Waiting for the Lord the Redeemer, I, Christ, proclaimed by my deeds and spoke with my mouth: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew IV).

“They have multiplied beyond number,” coming to the faith. They have grown beyond the number of the elect, because “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew XX). Many fill the walls of the Church, but readily fall back into the vanities of this age.

I proclaimed a new life and new institutions. This was necessary, because you no longer desired legal institutions, which had been imposed only until the time of correction.

You did not desire “sacrifice,” namely the legal sacrifice consisting in the immolation of a lamb, “or the legal offering” that was offered on the eighth day, such as the offering of a pair of turtledoves (Luke VIII), after the fullness of time had come. But you desired what these things signified: when the body arrived, the shadow passed away.

You did not desire this sacrifice, “but you perfected ears for me,” that is, you gave me and my people perfect obedience, so that through humility and obedience they might make themselves a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to God.

Nor did you desire “a burnt offering,” namely the legal sacrifice that was wholly burned, “or one for sin,” that is, the sacrifice offered for cleansing sin and called “sin”—namely, the ashes of the heifer—any longer.

“Then,” that is, after the time of correction arrived, while all things held a common silence—that is, while all philosophers remained silent about how the human race would be restored—and while the night continued on its course, that is, while this ignorance persisted, “your almighty Word, Lord, came from the royal seats”: your Son was made incarnate.

“I said, ‘Behold, I come to do your will,’” that is, I resolved to become incarnate, and this because you had so ordained.

“In the heading of the book it is written of me, that I should do your will.” According to my humanity I am the book after whose model all books are written, that is, toward whose conformity all the righteous are made. The divinity of this book is its head.

In the heading of the book, then—that is, in your will, since you are my head—it is written, that is, it is disposed and preordained concerning me, that I should do your will: that is, that I should obey you in all things, because you are my God.

And this law, namely your will, I desired “in the midst of my heart,” that is, I fulfilled it with my whole desire.

And I proclaimed your justice not only through myself but also through my heralds: that is, the faith that justifies. “My righteous one shall live by faith” (Habakkuk II; Romans I).

“In the great assembly,” that is, in the Church of the Gentiles, not only in Judea, I proclaimed and shall proclaim it.

“Behold, I will not restrain my lips,” that is, I will not allow my heralds to be restrained, because, O Lord, you knew those lips: that is, you made my heralds such that they cannot be restrained.

And therefore “I did not hide your justice in my heart,” that is, in the heart of my people—the justice that comes from faith, or the justice by which one is judged to be just—so that the one who believes with the heart may not be silent with the mouth. They may hide it for their own edification, but they do not hide it for the edification of their neighbor.

“For I spoke of your truth and your salvation,” that is, my heralds will proclaim your commandments, without which no one should presume upon his salvation. For you commanded nothing that ought not to have been commanded justly and truly.

“I did not hide your mercy,” by which you call and forgive, “and your truth,” by which you reward merits, “from the great council,” before kings and governors. “The apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts V).

It is as though he were saying: “They themselves hide; they themselves will preach; but you, God, who are able, give the increase.”

“But you, Lord, do not keep your mercies far from me,” that is, from those who are to be mine: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold, and I must bring them also” (John X). Surrounded by innumerable evils and by iniquity without number, make them recognize their iniquity and turn to the faith that justifies.

And I am certain that you will not keep them far away, for your mercy, by which you call and forgive, and your truth, by which you reward merits, have always received me—that is, my people, from righteous Abel until now. And just as you dealt mercifully with the earlier people, just as you promised, so now deliver my people, who are still in idolatry, now that I have been manifested.

And it is necessary that you not delay, because “evils without number have surrounded me,” that is, those who are to be mine. Even if some number exists among greater evils, there is none among lesser ones. Sand, although gathered from tiny stones, may nevertheless exist in such quantity in a ship that it can sink it by its weight, just as large rocks can.

“My iniquities have seized me,” that is, they are so numerous that they have covered the heart of my predestined people from the Gentiles. I call them “my” iniquities because of my great affection.

And they have seized them so completely that they could not raise their heart so as to see those iniquities. They are not sufficient unto themselves to recognize their weakness and seek you as physician, unless your help comes to their aid.

Truly they have seized them, because “they have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head,” that is, they are infinite. And therefore “my heart has abandoned me,” that is, it has abandoned my people, so that they might recognize the light of truth.

Therefore, since they cannot deliver themselves, “be pleased, Lord, to deliver me,” because it pleases me that they should be brought in. “Be pleased, Lord, to deliver my people from the blindness of heart and the darkness of sins.”

“Lord, look upon me to help me”; help the free will that you have given. Deliver in this way; help in this way.

“Let them be confounded” by the display of miracles, “and put to shame” by knowledge of the resurrection—together, that is, not only those from the Gentile people but also the Jews—who seek my soul in order to take it, namely, to destroy it, not to enjoy it.

“Let them turn back,” so that they may prefer you to themselves, those who wish me evil—that is, those who say good things with evil intent.

The Christian law is great, but who can fulfill it?

“Let them immediately bear their confusion,” that is, without delay, let them be ashamed that their deceit has accomplished nothing against me—those who say to me, “Well done, well done”: that is, those who flatter and praise my sins, who bless by cursing.

He says “immediately” because we must especially beware of those who praise us flatteringly and favor us in the worst matters.

There are two kinds of wicked people: one kind blesses by cursing; the other curses by blessing, when it praises those who act wickedly. Both must be avoided, because both speak with evil intent.

And, in contrast, “let all who seek you rejoice” outwardly, here in hope and finally in reality, “and be glad” inwardly in the first resurrection, in you—that is, strengthened by faith, hope, and charity—all who seek you for your sake and not for the sake of anything else.

And let them say, as though this were their rejoicing: “May the Lord always be magnified,” that is, may all his works be magnified for us, whether he calls sinners to forgiveness or invites the approved to the prize.

“Those who love your salvation,” that is, your salvation. Let them say this about you; let them say nothing about themselves.

They say, “Well done, well done.”

“But I am a beggar,” that is, insufficient for my own salvation, “and poor” in affection, desiring to cling to the rich God, who is powerful to give beyond what we ask.

And therefore, because I presume not upon myself but upon God, “the Lord is concerned for me.”

In this way: he is a helper in good things that are progressing, a protector in evils, lest they overthrow me. Therefore you are the helper, because I am the destroyer; you are the protector, and I am the destroyer; God by nature for all, mine by grace.

Do not delay to help; do not delay to protect.

Alternatively: Let those who love your salvation say, “May the Lord always be magnified.” And so that they may be able to say this, I, made their head, became a beggar and poor: that is, I assumed the condition of the needy and poor in order to enrich them. Therefore the Lord is concerned for me in my passion, lest I fail in death, so that I may rise again.

You are concerned for me, I say, you who are my helper, so that I may be brought to perfection; my protector, lest I fail. Therefore do not delay to raise me up and fit a body to me.

## PSALM XL. FOR THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID.

[Column 0357C]

“Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and poor; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him. May the Lord preserve him, give him life, and make him blessed upon the earth; and may he not hand him over to the soul of his enemies. May the Lord bring him help upon his bed of pain; you have turned all his bed in his sickness. I said, ‘Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you.’ My enemies said evil things against me: ‘When will he die, and his name perish?’ And if he entered in order to see, he spoke vanity; his heart gathered iniquity for itself. He went out and spoke the same things. All my enemies whispered against me; against me they devised evil for me. They established an iniquitous word against me: ‘Surely one who sleeps will not rise again?’ Indeed, the man of my peace, in whom I hoped, who ate my bread, magnified his deception against me. But you, Lord, have mercy on me and raise me up, and I will repay them. By this I know that you have willed me, because my enemy will not rejoice over me. But you have received me because of my innocence and strengthened me in your sight forever. Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, from age to age and forever: let it be, let it be.”

## EXPOSITION

This psalm belongs to the true David, that is, to Christ, who shows that no one can be saved except through faith, while by his majesty assisting and crowning his aid.

It is as though he were saying: “I, whom the prophets have previously foretold as coming for the redemption of the human race—behold, I am present.”

And blessed is the one who has not been scandalized by me (Matthew XI), that is, the one who understands that I am not only human but also God.

Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor—that is, who understands me, Christ, as poor in such a way that he also recognizes me as rich; who understands the weakness of the flesh, yet does not fail to recognize divinity in the flesh. This is that poor man who, out of great affection, though he was rich in heaven, became poor on earth (II Cor. VIII): rich as God, poor as man; highest God, humble man, whose poverty is our wealth, whose weakness is our salvation.

Blessed will be the one who now understands concerning the needy and the poor—that is, concerning the condition of the needy and poor. For if it troubles you that you attend to death, that you think upon the cross, deal with that needy and poor man—but intellectually—and recognize that Christ alone, head and body, is truly poor and needy. Apart from Christ, however, all, through the arrogance of vanity, disdain blessedness; for them the day of judgment will be evil, because they did not intellectually concern themselves with that head. For if they had concerned themselves with him intellectually, they would have adhered to him. This will be that blessedness: on the evil day the Lord will deliver him, when he comes no longer hidden in humanity but manifest in majesty.

Here, on the evil day, he will deliver you insofar as he is God; insofar as he is man, he will raise you up. Or: blessed is the one who understands—that is, who acts intelligently—concerning the needy and the poor, because if he acts concerning them, then he also acts concerning the one who said, “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. XXV). In this way he will deliver him on the evil day.

The Lord will preserve him like grain in a granary, while the chaff will be given over to burning. He will preserve him with a twofold preservation, inward and outward. And he will give him life, so that he may preserve him with a twofold preservation; he will then give life to what is now mortal. Even now he will make him blessed, namely with the first blessedness, so that he may thus come to the second blessedness, in the land, namely, of the dying. In this way: “He will not hand him over to the soul of his enemies”—and if he hands him over to their soul, that is, to their consent, so that he may be conformed to them.

So that this may be believed more firmly as something destined to occur, Christ the head desires it and prays that it may happen. That enemy is the devil, who was a lion in killing the martyrs. Seeing that he accomplished nothing in this way, because those who were killed triumphed, he became a dragon and began to act through poison; that is, he began to make suggestions through his flatteries, saying: “The Christian law is great, but who can keep it?” But Christ and his people trample both the lion and the dragon.

And to the one who understands, so that he may not be handed over to the soul of his enemies, he will bring help upon his bed of pain; that is, by his aid he will ensure that his spirit—the spirit of every human being—does not lie in the flesh like a sick person on a pallet, that is, does not take pleasure in its desires. For the flesh is a bed of pain for those who wish to rest in it, because its joy is turned amid many bitterness. But he will cause the one who has lain upon the bed of pain to carry his pallet while ruling, disciplining, and reducing the flesh to servitude, healthy rather than being carried by it like a sick person.

And it is necessary that the Lord bring aid; indeed, he truly has a bed of pain. For “you have turned his entire bed in his sickness”—that is, you have made the whole human body, in which the weak human spirit seeks to rest as though on a bed, changeable, so that there is no rest there: now sweet things are turned into bitter, now bitter things into sweet. Thus, through various tribulations, you have unsettled him because of the sin of the first man and made him like a sick person who, because of excessive illness, shakes his entire bed.

You made him sick in his sickness for this reason: he was weak and unstable in the commandment of the Lord his God.

Alternatively, let us not understand the same thing by “bed.” “His entire bed” is the bed of pain—that is, all the pleasures of the flesh in which the human spirit may take delight without sin, such as estates, houses, a wife, and children. This is his bed in his sickness, because he still bears a sick spirit; you have turned it, that is, you have caused all carnal pleasures to be mingled with bitterness, so that through the bitterness of lower things he may learn to love better things, lest the traveler journeying toward his homeland love the inn instead of his house.

For the healing of the sickness of the human race, and for the removal of that bed of pain, I came and said, “Lord, have mercy on me.” The force of the pronoun must be emphasized: “I”—namely, immune from sin, the only human being suited to this, the only one possessing such affection toward human beings—said, “Lord, have mercy.” I do not say “on mine,” although I pray for them; rather, out of great affection I say, “on me.” In this way I also offered an example of humility.

Have mercy in this way: “Heal my soul”—that is, the soul of my people, who acknowledge that they have been justly weakened by you. Man was able to fall by himself, but by himself he cannot rise again. Heal the soul of my people, wounded by many injuries of sins, so that at last you may also heal the body.

Have mercy, heal, because I have sinned against you. You alone, being healthy, heal; you alone, without sin, have mercy. Sinners and the despairing are reserved for you, as for a good physician one who is exceedingly sick.

I said, “Have mercy; heal.” But my enemies, who ought to have been friends, spoke evil to me—that is, for my glory, namely this evil: “When will he die and his name perish?”—so that he may no longer be named or proclaimed.

Alternatively: “My enemies spoke evil to me.” He describes that neediness and poverty, as though saying: Blessed are those who understand in me more than they see in me. But my enemies spoke evil to me, and therefore they are by no means blessed.

As if he were saying: What wonder is it concerning others? For even if someone entered—that is, if someone pretended to friendship and companionship, entering under pretense, that is, associating with me or with my people, like Judas and those of whom the Apostle says, “because of the false brothers secretly brought in, who slipped in to spy out our freedom” (Gal. II)—he entered for this purpose and associated with us for this purpose: to have something to betray, not something to believe. And he spoke not merely in order to see, but also vainly; he displayed love with his mouth, which he did not possess in his heart: “Good Teacher, we know that you are truthful” (Matt. XXII).

And this was not to my harm but to his own, because “his heart gathered iniquity for himself,” not for me, since, according to his iniquity and his unrepentant heart, he treasures up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and of the just judgment of God (Rom. II).

And because he was inwardly deceitful, he went out—he departed from the fellowship and bond of charity—and spoke against the same one, namely against what the others who were openly enemies were saying, like Judas and the others against the Church; or “against the same one,” that is, against the Lord.

And not only those who entered, but also all my enemies, both those entering and those departing, whispered against me: “Come, let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance” (Matt. XXI).

And it is no wonder that they whispered against me, because earlier they had devised evil against me—that is, death—while I gave them life. “Against me,” that is, to my glory; “evil” for me, insofar as their will was concerned, but for themselves insofar as the reality was concerned.

And at last, after their thought and murmuring, they established an evil word—that is, an unjust sentence—against me: “He is guilty of death” (Matt. XXVI). They condemned me to death, but what concern is that to me? Will I not rise again?

He demonstrates this by comparison: “Will not the one who sleeps add to his rising?” Certainly he will. What they thought was death was my sleep, because it was voluntary, not forced. The first Adam slept so that Eve might be fashioned (Gen. II); the second Adam slept so that the Church might be fashioned.

And how will these things happen? Or what shall I say about the others? “For the man of my peace”—that is, the one who displayed peace to me by giving a kiss (Joan. II)—“in whom I hoped.” Not insofar as I myself was concerned, for I knew what was in man, but in whom my people were able to hope because, having associated with me, he had advanced in understanding; or in whom I ought to have hoped with regard to the common grace.

“For I was hungry,” and so forth. I hoped that my food was in the one who ate my bread, who was nourished by the same teaching by which I too was nourished. Or: “the one who ate my bread with me magnified treachery against me”—that is, he betrayed me more than the others. For he said, “It is he; seize him and lead him away carefully” (Mark XIV), as though saying: Guard him diligently, lest you lose him, because I know his works and his plans.

My enemies condemned me to death. But you, Lord, to whom I obey in this matter, have mercy on me—that is, show mercy to my people by raising me up. Have mercy in this way: “Raise me up, and I will repay them,” either by turning their action to good or by judging them for evil, having been appointed judge after my judgment. Or I will repay them temporally even here, for after forty-two years they were taken captive and killed by Titus and Vespasian.

And truly you will repay them, because my enemy, who rejoiced over me when I was dead, will not rejoice over me once I have been raised up.

And in this I knew that you desired me—that is, that my obedience and my sacrifice pleased you. As if he were saying: My enemy will not rejoice, but I will rejoice.

You received me from the grave, or made me your own when you received me, because of my innocence, since I alone among the dead was free (Ps. LXXXVII); I paid what I had not stolen (Ps. LXVIII).

And you not only raised me up, but also confirmed me—that is, you established me immortal and incapable of suffering—in your sight, even though you permitted me to appear weak for a time in their sight. It is certainly preferable to be weak for a time, so that you may be confirmed forever.

Therefore, “blessed be”—that is, may he be multiplied and increased in his members—the Lord whom Israel serves. “The God of Israel,” that is, the God who brings those journeying to their destination, from this present age and unto the age to come. Let it be, let it be. May this blessing be accomplished in the former people; may it also be accomplished in the latter.

## PSALM XLI. FOR THE END; AN UNDERSTANDING OF THE SONS OF KORAH

> “As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. My soul thirsted for the strong and living God: When shall I come and appear before the face of God? My tears were my bread day and night, while it is said to me daily: Where is your God? These things I remembered, and I poured out my soul within me, because I shall pass into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God. With the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting. Why are you sad, my soul? And why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall yet confess to him, the salvation of my countenance and my God. My soul is troubled in relation to myself; therefore I shall remember you from the land of the Jordan and of Hermoniim, from the little mountain. Deep calls to deep at the sound of your cataracts. All your heights and your waves have passed over me. By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night his song. With me is prayer to the God of my life; I shall say to God: You are my protector. Why have you forgotten me, and why do I go about sorrowful while my enemy afflicts me? While my bones are broken, those who trouble me, my enemies, reproached me. While they say to me every day: Where is your God? Why are you sad, my soul? And why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall yet confess to him, the salvation of my countenance and my God.”

## EXPOSITION

This psalm is to be understood as directed toward the end—that is, toward Christ. It is, I say, a psalm of understanding, sending us toward this understanding: that we should attend to the miseries of the present life and strive with our whole desire toward the place where there will be no disturbance of joy. This understanding was set before the sons of Korah for their instruction.

Historically, nothing is being done concerning Korah or his sons, but the interpretation of the name sends us toward an understanding of the truth. For Korah is interpreted as “bald” or “skull,” in which we understand Christ, who was bald because he had nothing superfluous; in the Word or in deed he had nothing idle or unworthy of imitation.

“My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (Joan. V). We eat his flesh when, by imitating his deeds, we consider them carefully; we drink his blood when we do not fear shedding blood for him. There was nothing in him that ought not to be eaten.

Or he is called bald because he was prefigured by the bald Elisha. When Elisha was ascending the mountain, forty-two Hebrew boys mocked him, saying, “Go up, bald one!” He cursed them, and after the curse two bears came out of the forest and devoured them.

As has been said, Christ is understood through Elisha; through the mocking boys, the foolish Jews who mocked the Lord and said, “Crucify, crucify” (Joan. XIX), because he was bald—that is, free from sin and unlike their works. Through the two bears coming out of the forest, we understand Titus and Vespasian, who in the forty-second year after the Lord’s death devastated them and afflicted them in many ways. The number of the boys prefigured this.

Or he is called bald because he was crucified at the place of Calvary. That place is called Calvary because of the exposed bones of the dead who were crucified there.

And in this psalm there is the voice of Korah, our head, setting this understanding before his sons—that is, his imitators—so that whoever wishes to follow him may deny himself and learn to abandon the world, which he wrongly loves, so that he may be able to thirst for God, the fountain of life.

He introduces this by comparison, so that whoever wishes to desire God may be like a deer in swiftness, allowing nothing to detain him in this life. He should also be like the deer in this respect: it is the custom of deer to draw serpents out of their caves and devour them, and then, thirsting, to run with great desire to a spring, so that there they may shed their old age and be renewed.

So too, whoever wishes to desire God, the fountain of life, must first extinguish within himself the serpents of iniquity. Lust hisses; greed hisses; ambition hisses and urges him to abandon what is right rather than lose an advantage. You are bitten by the serpent, yet you do not kill it. Restrain greed, govern lust, curb the remaining unlawful desires of the flesh, and extinguish the serpents of iniquity. Then this understanding will truly be set before you; then these words will rightly apply to you—once the serpents have been diligently extinguished.

“As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs”—that is, the soul of my Korah, namely of Christ, once the serpents of vices have been extinguished. I assumed them, but did not possess them by nature, for I committed no sin. My soul longs for you in order to draw from you, O God.

And because a deer may desire a spring both for washing and for drinking, he specifies how he desires it: “My soul thirsted,” namely, to come to the strong God, from whom all my strength comes, through whom I become strong enough to extinguish the serpents of the iniquity of my people; “living,” through whom true life exists for me and for mine.

Jerome: “To the strong and living God,” not to dead images.

And in this desire I said: “When shall I come and appear before the face of the Lord?” I thirst in the course of my journey; I shall be satisfied at my arrival—that is, when, having been made immortal, I return to the Father at the appointed time, when my obedience has been completed. First I must sit; first I must be humbled.
