Afterwards I shall be immortal and incapable of suffering, so that I may be worthy to stand before your sight, toward which it is not lawful for impiety to aspire.

As if he were saying: Truly I shall come and appear, because “my tears were my bread”—that is, the tears of my people arising from temporal misery, which, out of great affection, I call mine—“day and night,” that is, at all times; or “day” before the Passion, “night” in the Passion.

While it is said to me daily, “Where is your God?”—that is, while I am continually held in contempt, as though God were present with no help and no raising up.

Alternatively: While I meditate, while I am on the way, before I appear, my tears were my bread day and night, because I could not yet drink from that fountain; I consumed my tears with greater eagerness. He does not say, “My tears became my drink,” lest he seem to thirst for the tears themselves.

If a thirsty person eats, he becomes still thirstier. So too, let the person who is in this desire have tears from the present pilgrimage in place of bread. But extinguish the serpents of iniquity if you wish to thirst more fully for the fountain of truth. This thirst never exists except by day and night, through the prosperity and adversity of this life.

Attend sufficiently to the present misery. Attending to it serves instead of bread for hastening that thirst.

While it is said daily to me and to mine, “Where is your God?”: “This man is not from God” (Joan. IX); “This man, though he is a man, makes himself God” (Joan. X); “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matt. XXVII).

And it is said to mine, “Where is your God?” By those who regard a creature as God, he points with his finger to his image and says, “Where is your God?” He is nowhere.

“These things I remembered”—that is, while they were speaking in this way, I kept their contempt in mind so that I might persevere. “And I poured out my soul within me,” according to Isaiah: “When you pour out your soul to the hungry” (Isa. LVIII). Remembering their contempt, I desired you more. I poured out my soul within me—that is, I humbled myself; I considered what a creature owes the Creator, what an inferior owes a superior, what a servant owes the Lord.

And I not only poured it out within me, but poured it out beyond myself toward the desire for you.

Alternatively: While they were reproaching me in this way, I remembered that these things had been ordained and imposed upon me by you. In remembering this, I poured out my soul—that is, I poured it beyond myself in order to recognize the glory soon to come as the reward of obedience. And I poured it out beyond myself in such a way that I first poured it out within me, as above.

And rightly I poured it out; rightly I humbled myself, because in this way—by completing obedience—I shall pass through to the house of God to be established, namely the Church, which is a house in comparison with the synagogue, which was transitory. In it God dwells through faith and hope.

Therefore I shall pass through, because I shall first come into the place of the tabernacle, that is, I shall fulfill the legal rites. For he was presented and circumcised in the temple (Luke II), because he did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it (Matt. V).

I speak of the tabernacle as wondrous. The legal institutions were indeed marvelous, not in their temporal arrangements but in what they signified.

Alternatively: I humbled myself and completed my obedience because in this way I shall pass through to the house of God to be restored—that is, to the heavenly Jerusalem—coming first into the place of the wondrous tabernacle. The place of the tabernacle is on earth: the faithful who serve God, in whom the obedience of the members is wondrous, because sin no longer reigns in them so that they should obey it unto iniquity (Rom. VI); rather, they obey righteousness unto sanctification.

It is also wondrous how the soul serves God by restraining desires and cultivating virtues. I shall pass through by doing good and teaching to the house of God to be established.

And I shall do this not from justice or necessity—for God loves a cheerful giver (II Cor. IX)—but “with the voice of exultation,” that is, with an exultant voice, which occurs only when joined to good works, because exultation belongs to the body; and “of confession,” that is, of your praise, attributing everything to you.

Such is the exultation that blessed Andrew is said to have expressed: “O good cross, long desired.” And blessed Lawrence said: “My body is roasted; now turn it in your heart”—that is, consider what steadfastness I possessed, and, seeing this, eat me—that is, imitate me.

So that man might eat the bread of angels, that is, be nourished by the same divine contemplation by which the angels are nourished, the King of angels became man.

And since, by humbling myself, I shall pass through to the house of God to be established: “Why are you sad, my soul?” That is, why do you display a certain sadness assumed from mortals into yourself? “And why do you trouble me?” That is, why do you display a certain disturbance?

For “Jesus began to be afraid and troubled” (Luke XXII), and “my soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. XXVI). This was not from compulsion but from willingness, not from necessity but from affection. For he who had the power, whenever he wished, to lay down his soul could also transfer sadness into himself.

And because it was not from necessity, hope in the Lord and do not be troubled. Hope for this, because “I shall yet confess to him”—that is, it will happen that those who were formerly my enemies will at last become mine and make this confession: “You are the salvation of my countenance; you are my God.” That is, they will recognize you as the true God and the one whom you sent, Jesus Christ (Joan. XVII).

Or “my God”: God by creation, mine by re-creation. He who is the being of my countenance—that is, of my nature—is salvation, that is, my Savior. Hence another prophet says: “The Spirit before our face,” that is, the invisible God made visible by assuming our nature, “and the Spirit of our nostrils, Christ the Lord” (Lam. IV).

What is said elsewhere about the Holy Spirit being incarnate is understood in this way. The Father is Spirit—that is, something invisible and incorporeal—and the same is said of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. God, insofar as he is the Word, is salvation; insofar as he is man—

“My soul is troubled within me.” As if he were saying: My soul ought not to be sorrowful for this reason, because it was troubled in relation to myself, not outside myself, since “no one will take my soul from me, but I lay it down myself” (Joan. X).

Alternatively: My soul, referring itself to myself—that is, to the mortality and capacity for suffering assumed from man—was troubled, because in myself I was capable of suffering, although I was also God. My soul was sorrowful; I began to be afraid and troubled.

But to what end do these things trouble me? So that the human race may be remembered and converted, attending first to the promises and afterwards receiving what was manifested.

Because I have the power to lay down my soul whenever I wish and to take it up again, “I shall remember you from the land of Jordan”—that is, I shall make some from the Jewish people mindful of you, humbling themselves and descending within themselves so that they may be exalted before you. For Jordan is interpreted as “descent.”

And “from the land of Hermoniim”—that is, I shall make some from the Gentiles mindful of you, cursing themselves, that is, abandoning themselves so that they may be joined to you. Hermon is interpreted as “their anathema,” and it is in the land of the Gentiles.

Namely, “from the little mountain”: I shall make those mindful of you who will be mountains because of the excellence of their virtues, yet little in humility. In this way I shall make you remembered from the land of Hermoniim.

For “deep calls to deep”—that is, their profound and great understanding from Judea calls to the deep, the understanding of the Gentiles, to conformity with itself. That is, those coming to faith from the circumcision will draw the Gentiles to faith (Joan. IV), “at the sound of your cataracts,” that is, by explaining those voices to them.

For in this saying there is truth: some sow and others reap. Cataracts are called hidden channels through which the heavenly waters flow. And rightly will teachers from the circumcision be able to draw the Gentiles to faith, or the greater ones will be able to do so, because “all your heights”—that is, the future punishments which you still suspend and now threaten against those who deserve them—“and your waves”—that is, those sufferings which now continually flow in and disturb us because of human weakness and capacity for suffering—have passed over me, having been imposed and completed upon me on their behalf.

Whatever they deserved because of guilt, I paid because of grace. The heights have already passed in reality; the waves in hope.

“Truly he himself took away our weaknesses and bore our pains” (Isa. LIII). The waves have not passed in such a way that we are no longer mortal and capable of suffering, but they have passed in this way: they do not lead us to eternal death.

And “your heights”—that is, the severe final condemnation—were considered against me by those who inflicted it, because they thought me worthy of that condemnation. They passed over me—from them, I say, not from everyone, but from those who attend “in the day,” that is, in prosperity, to the Lord’s mercy shown to them for consolation.

And “in the night,” that is, in adversity, they understand that a song of praise should be offered to him. For many fall for their own benefit and that of others, and temporal adversity becomes beneficial to many, so that they may learn to despise the world that flatters falsely and to desire God, in whom true and supreme happiness consists.

Hence Job says: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil?” (Job II). “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job I).

This mercy, which is to be sung by day, and this song by night, the Lord commanded—that is, through me. The invisible and incomprehensible God displayed it through the assumption of my flesh. By day, that is, before the Passion, I sang his mercy; and by night, that is, in the Passion, I sang his song.

Alternatively: “They have passed over me.” They passed from those to whom they were owed, having been imposed upon me. And this happened because “by day,” that is, in prosperity, namely until the time of my Passion, when it was as though prosperity were intended for me so that I might fulfill what had to be fulfilled, “the Lord commanded through me”—that is, he made his mercy known to the human race.

That is, before my Passion I made known those things that had to be made known concerning its restoration. And “by night, his song”—that is, in my Passion I set before everyone what must be done in such circumstances: namely, that his mercy must be praised in all things.

For he is merciful when he spares in prosperity, when we deserve nothing but scourges; he is merciful when he scourges for a time, so that he may preserve us forever.

And so that they may sing of mercy by day and of a song by night, I shall offer God a sacrifice. But I shall not seek it outside myself: “with me”—that is, in me—is the prayer that I shall offer to God, namely “the calf of the lips,” the praise of the mouth together with innocence of heart and purity of conduct.

To God, the author of my life—that is, of the life of my people—I shall speak this prayer: “I shall say to God: You are my protector.” I shall attribute nothing to my merits, but everything to your grace. You received me from the grave and my people from the mass of the lost.

And because God is my protector, why have you forgotten me? That is, my people. Why do you seem to have forgotten them while you permit them to fall? And why do I go about sorrowful? That is, why do my people go about fearing a fall?

While my enemy afflicts me, to such an extent that even my bones are broken—that is, my strong ones, or my endurance, are overcome and crushed by the excessive cruelty of persecutors—and when my bones are broken, those who trouble me, my enemies, reproach me.

They reproach me for my God when they say to me every day, that is, continually, “Where is your God?” As if he were saying: Although outwardly you seem forgotten, inwardly you are not; although he delays, he does not remove himself.

Alternatively, according to Jerome: While my enemies who trouble me reproach me, while I desire to please you through repentance and affliction of body and soul, my enemies, thinking that I do these things in vain, say, “Where is your God?”

They say this in view of the evident fact, while they strive to remove me from God through tortures and words, thinking me abandoned because I suffer outwardly and am not visibly delivered. They attend to what I suffer, not why I suffer.

And because such great benefits will come from my affection—or because by day the Lord commanded mercy and by night a song—“Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?” That is, why do you display a certain sadness and disturbance, not from compulsion but from willingness?

Our head repeats this so often in order to console his people and encourage them by his example, so that they may not fail amid the labors of this transitory life, placed in hope of eternal happiness, namely the vision of God.

And because it was not from compulsion, hope in God, and rightly so, because “I shall yet confess to him, the salvation of my countenance and my God.” That is, although I now suffer so much for them, nevertheless my people will yet confess with heart and mouth: “My God is the salvation of my countenance”—that is, he is man as I am.

Alternatively, in the person of the Church: “Where is your God?” They can indeed demonstrate their gods in the present, but they do not have eyes by which my God may be seen, because “his invisible things are understood and perceived through the things that have been made” (Rom. I).

The spirit, doing certain things through the services of the body, is not incapable of perceiving other things by itself. For in order to see itself, it withdraws itself from bodily senses and turns toward the interior; then the services of the body are insufficient for perceiving splendor, sound, fragrance, taste, the gentleness of virtues—or, conversely, of vices.

“These things I remembered, and I poured out my soul within me.” I resolved also to seek my God, so that I might not merely believe in him but also see something of him. I perceive that something exists beyond my soul. For if it remained within itself, without being poured out beyond itself, it would see nothing but itself.

God must be reached above it; above the soul is the house of God. In order to ascend there, the soul pours itself out beyond itself.

But this ascent occurs only by way of the Church, because the Church has in secret a very high house and has a tabernacle on earth. While you walk within it, if the tumult of worldly things does not drown out its voice, you are led into the delight of an interior and intelligible sound, so that you despise all external things, carried away toward that inward joy.

But although we may be carried there, nevertheless, as long as we are in the body, “we are exiles from the Lord” (II Cor. V). Therefore it follows: “Why are you sad, my soul? Why are you troubled?”

My soul is troubled not toward God but toward myself. Hope in God, because I am uncertain; if I appear before the face of God, there will be nothing that can trouble me.

It is rightly troubled toward myself, because it perceives mutability; it is not troubled toward God, because it perceives the immutable. God’s justice always exists; mine, if it exists today, may not exist tomorrow.

Do you wish not to be troubled? Do not remain in yourself; do not presume upon yourself. Jordan is interpreted as “descent,” because in myself there is nothing but weakness. I shall humble myself in myself and presume upon you.

This is what it means: “I shall remember you from the land”—that is, I shall descend so that I may be delivered; I shall not ascend, lest I be dashed to pieces.

Hermon means “anathema.” Therefore I shall curse what is mine, so that by displeasing myself I may please him. From the little mountain I shall breathe toward him, so that he may make me great.

“Deep calls to deep.” The deep is an immeasurable depth. Therefore this depth demands the depth of the interpreter, and this occurs through the voice of preachers. Thus the righteous wins the righteous, and thus we must not presume upon ourselves.

Alternatively: I am troubled within myself; therefore I sigh toward you, because I hear in the voice of the Scriptures that if the abyss of iniquity now possesses me, it will call another abyss—that is, from it I shall pass into the abyss of Gehenna.

“Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. XXXV), because both here you condemn by inward darkness and afterwards by outward darkness. What, then? Let its suspensions break into you—that is, the heights it threatens—and the waves, that is, the things you already feel. Or this is the same as “deep calls to deep.”

And what of these things? In prosperity the Lord commands mercy for you. While you are secure, attend to the discipline of the Word of God, and it will deliver you; but this will become evident only in adversity.

Therefore: “With me is prayer: Judge me, O God,” and so forth.

## PSALM XLII. A PSALM OF DAVID

> “Judge me, O God, and discern my cause from an unholy nation; deliver me from the unjust and deceitful man. For you are God, my strength; why have you rejected me? And why do I go about sorrowful while my enemy afflicts me? Send forth your light and your truth; they themselves have led me and brought me to your holy mountain and to your tabernacles. And I shall enter the altar of God, to God who gives joy to my youth. I shall confess to you on the harp, O God, my God. Why are you sad, my soul? And why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall yet confess to him, the salvation of my countenance and my God.”

## EXPOSITION

This psalm may be read by itself, as the voice of the head concerning his resurrection; or it may be joined with the preceding psalm in this way.

Above he said, “All your heights and your waves have passed over me”—that is, they were considered by the enemies as things to be imposed upon me, because they judged me worthy of that most severe final condemnation and of the present persecution.

Judge me, O God. The ungodly judge me unjustly; judge me according to what is just. Others judge, but do not discern: the labor is equal, but the conscience is unequal. Judge me in this way.

Discern my cause. [Col. 0368B] Although my punishment and labor are now equal to those of the ungodly, cause my case to be distinguished at the end; cause me to rise again, so that in this way the difference in my case may be recognized.

Deliver me from an unholy nation—that is, from that nation which makes itself holy but is not so—that is, from an unjust and deceitful man. This is the unholy nation. What is more unjust than for the weak to kill the physician, the servant to kill the Lord, the ungodly to kill the just? The Jewish people were likewise deceitful when they said, “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone” (John XVIII). Yet their teeth were weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword (Psalm LVI), when they said, “Crucify, crucify” (John XIX).

Therefore, deliver me and discern my case, because you are God, my strength, through whom I and my people are strong—that is, steadfast in suffering. Or, through whom I and my people shall become strong, [Col. 0368C] when we are immortal and incapable of suffering, although now we appear weak.

And since you are my strength, why have you rejected me? That is, what reason is there for your permitting me to be afflicted so greatly that I seem abandoned? And why do I go about sorrowful? That is, what purpose, what advantage is there in my soul being sorrowful even unto death?—in my trembling and grieving, by taking into myself the fear of my people? I say “sorrowful,” while the enemy, the Jewish people, afflicts me.

I and my people have been rejected for the great benefit of the human race. For this reason blindness has happened to Israel, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter (Romans XI), and so that the word of God might be sent throughout the whole world like an army.

Therefore, because the Jews rejected me, send me forth—your light—from the enclosure of the Jews into the knowledge of the Gentiles: light, that is, the divinity which illumines [Col. 0368D] the darkness of the heart. And your truth, that is, your commandments, true in every respect.

And truly you will lead me forth, because they—not, I say, “will lead,” but “have already led,” so certain is it, as though it had already happened—have led me. They, that is, your light, namely, the power of your divinity, and your true commandments, have led me, a human being, out from the Jewish people and brought me to your holy mountain, namely, to be established in your Church, exalted by virtues, so that from both walls there may be made one temple; and into your tabernacles.

He calls the mountain “tabernacles” by a different comparison. The tabernacle is the temporal Church, because those who strive toward the palm of victory fight within it. When you hear “tabernacle,” consider pilgrimage; beware the enemy; labor in the battle, so that at last, [Col. 0369A] after victory, you may rest.

It may also be read in this way: Your Word—your light and your truth—personally united to me, will make me fit—so that this may be understood from the person of the Lord as man—to enter, through the experience of suffering and by the glory of the resurrection, into the innermost regions of heaven; and thence, once the Spirit has been sent, into the tabernacles, that is, into the Church militant in time. Let what follows, “I shall enter,” belong to the preceding persecution.

But before he leads me forth, “I shall enter the altar of God” through the Ascension. What altar is this? “To God,” that is, to divine contemplation, the God who gladdens my youth—that is, me, renewed, and my people. He gladdens my youth who earlier saddened my old age.

Alternatively: after the tabernacle has been established, my people shall enter the altar of God, that is, [Col. 0369B] to behold the height of God. Well does he say, “I shall enter,” because at present we are outside, in pilgrimage.

Only the one who approaches that altar securely approaches this one securely; there he will find his life who here discerns his cause. What sacrifice is there here? The one who enters is himself taken up as a burnt offering.

Meanwhile, while I strive toward that place, I shall not be idle. “I shall confess to you on the lyre”—I, the head, and my members in me—by experiencing suffering and death; in my members, by putting to death the limbs that are upon the earth and by ministering from what is lower, so that they may render to God sweet melody from their lower state.

And rightly so, because you are God by creation, my God by singular grace, and the God of my people by their re-creation: you who make me free from sin, who have so disposed my people that they do not wish to be conformed to the oldness of Adam, but wish to follow your will.

[Col. 0369C] And since all these benefits are to come from my affliction, why are you sorrowful, my soul, and why do you trouble me? As above, not from necessity but from your own will.

And since it is not from necessity, hope in God, for I shall yet confess him—that is, my people shall confess him to his honor. “The salvation of my countenance, and my God”: that is, he is the Savior who exists as my countenance—that is, man and God.

## PSALM XLIII. FOR THE END; FOR THE SONS OF CORE; FOR UNDERSTANDING

> We have heard with our ears, O God; our fathers have declared to us the work that you worked in their days and in ancient days. Your hand destroyed the nations and planted them; [Col. 0369D] you afflicted peoples and drove them out. For they did not possess the land by their own sword, nor did their own arm save them. But your right hand, and your arm, and the illumination of your countenance, because you were pleased with them. You are yourself my king and my God, who command salvations for Jacob. In you we shall winnow our enemies with the horn, and in your name we shall despise those who rise up against us. For I shall not hope in my bow, nor shall my sword save me. For you saved us from those who afflicted us, and you put to shame those who hated us. In God we shall glory throughout the whole day, and in your name we shall confess forever. But now you have rejected and put us to shame, and you will not go forth with our armies. You have turned us backward before our enemies, and those who hated us plundered us for themselves. [Col. 0370A] You have given us like sheep for food, and among the nations you have scattered us. You sold your people without price, and there was no multitude in their exchanges. You made us a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and derision to those who are around us. You made us a likeness among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples. All day long my shame is before me, and the confusion of my face has covered me, at the voice of one reproaching and reviling, at the face of the enemy and the persecutor. All these things have come upon us, yet we have not forgotten you, nor have we acted wickedly against your covenant. Our heart has not turned back, nor have you made our paths depart from your way. For you humbled us in the place of affliction, and the shadow of death covered us. [Col. 0370B] If we have forgotten the name of our God, and if we have spread out our hands to a foreign god, will not God require this? For he knows the hidden things of the heart. For on your account we are put to death all day long; we have been reckoned as sheep for slaughter. Rise up; why do you sleep, O Lord? Rise up, and do not reject us forever. Why do you turn your face away? Do you forget our poverty and our tribulation? For our soul has been humbled in the dust; our belly has clung to the earth. Rise up, O Lord, help us, and redeem us for the sake of your name.

### Exposition

This psalm—that is, the good work of this psalm, leading to the end, namely, to completion—is set forth by the sons of Core, that is, by [Col. 0370C] imitators of the Passion of Christ. It is addressed to other, lesser sons of Core for understanding, namely, so that they may understand that when God withdraws these temporal goods and does not always grant what they ask, and often mixes sweet things with bitter, this is done for the benefit of his people.

Thus, wishing to disclose this purpose of God to the weaker, so that they may not waste away in such circumstances, the holy martyrs ask God himself what the reason is: although he filled our fathers, the children of Israel, with present consolations and will clearly free their descendants in the future, why does he now withdraw these temporal goods from his Church, so that it may be subjected to many pressures? In this way he finally revealed God’s purpose: namely, that he withdraws them from love of the world, which is falsely sweet, and teaches them to love the heavenly and eternal things promised to them in their labor.

Or they may understand that the [Col. 0370D] things which historically happened among the earlier fathers signify this spiritual victory over vices, which is truly being enacted, so that, understanding this, they may put vice to death in themselves more and more.

“We have heard with our ears, O God”—with the ears of hearing, that is, we have come to know by understanding. The holy martyrs speak as though they were saying: Lord, you who bestowed many benefits upon the former people and will bestow many upon us in the future, why do you abandon us in this intervening time?

He enumerates the benefits of the former people, then those of the future; in between, he displays the affliction and reveals its cause.

“Our fathers,” who begot us in faith—the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles—“declared to us in their writings the work that you worked in their days,” [Col. 0371A] who announced to us how one would pursue a thousand and two put ten thousand to flight. “And in ancient days,” that is, among their predecessors, namely, the same work: “Your hand”—that is, your power—“destroyed the nations,” the Egyptians, Jebusites, and Midianites.

“And you planted them”—that is, you established our fathers securely in their place.

Or morally: “Your hand destroyed the nations,” that is, vices, “and you planted them in virtues”; “you afflicted peoples,” that is, the multitude of peoples, namely, the worship of idolatry, “and you drove them out” from your own people.

Truly you did this. “For they did not possess the land by their own sword,” that is, by their own strength. “And their arm”—that is, their external power—“did not save them” from their enemies, “but your right hand”—that is, your favor—“and your arm”—that is, your strength—“and the illumination of your countenance,” [Col. 0371B] because you were present to them through such signs that you were understood to be present, or because you were visibly present with them.

And this was not because of their merits, but “because you were pleased with them”—that is, because you dealt with them in such a way that you might be praised in them.

Or morally: Truly you drove out the vices, because they did not possess their land by their own arm, that is, by their own virtue, and their inner strength did not save them from vices. But it was your right hand, that is, your Son, who is your arm; and the illumination of your countenance, that is, the visitation of your grace, through which you gave counsel against vices. And this was for no other reason than that you were pleased with yourself in them.

“You are yourself my king and my God.” What then? Then one way, now another. The times have changed, but the Creator of the times has not changed. It is therefore wondrous that the same one was then and is now, while the circumstances then were one thing and now another.

[Col. 0371C] Those benefits have passed, but you yourself, unchanged, are “my king” with regard to the human being, and “my God” with regard to the Word. “Who command salvations for Jacob”: then you commanded temporal salvation for Jacob, the former people, through an angel; now you command inward salvation for Jacob, the younger people, through the Son. “In these last days he has spoken to us in his Son” (Hebrews I).

As though he were saying: Since these things are so, why do we suffer such great evils? This concerns the past. But what of the future? “In you we shall winnow our enemies with the horn.”

A horn is made from flesh, but once hardened it surpasses the nature of that flesh. So Christ assumed our flesh, but was free from sin. “In you we shall winnow with the horn”: through him by whom we surpass all carnality, we shall finally separate the chaff from the grain—that is, [Col. 0371D] in the final winnowing we shall separate from ourselves our enemies, who are now joined together with us.

“And then in your name we shall despise those who rise up against us”: presuming in your name, that is, through the invocation of your name. Or, because we shall retain the Christian name in faith and conduct, being truly Christians, we shall now despise those who rise up against us.

And truly this will be through you. “For I shall not hope in my bow,” that is, in my moderate merits or hidden virtue. “And my sword,” that is, greater merits or manifest virtue, “will not save me or my people” from conformity to evils.

“For you saved us from those who afflicted us”: he speaks of future things as though they were past, because they are as certain as though they had already happened. This salvation will be when “this mortal puts on immortality” (1 Corinthians XV).

“[Col. 0372A] And you put to shame those who hated us”: with an evil shame, so that they will say, “We foolish ones; we considered their life madness” (Wisdom V), because our separation will be their confusion.

As though he were saying: Once they have been put to shame, we shall glory; we shall not be idle in God, that is, in the mercy of God shown to us, by which he will crown his work in us. “We shall be praised”: we shall be worthy of praise.

Or, “we shall praise one another throughout the whole day,” that is, throughout that life which will not have death. “And in your name,” namely, by glorifying your name rather than our own—or because, being Christians from Christ, we shall confess you forever, when you will be all in all. “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; throughout the ages of ages they shall praise you” (Psalm LXXXIII).

“But now,” [Col. 0372B] namely, in this intervening time, you who dealt in this way with the former people and who will finally act so mercifully in the future, “you have rejected us,” that is, you appear to have rejected us with regard to tribulation, “and put us to shame,” with regard to the defection of some. Or, rejected from invisible sublimity, we are greatly cast down in reality; we are put to shame outwardly, but not in conscience. We go out against our enemies, but are weak in body.

“For you will not go forth with our armies.” We go out against our enemies, but your power does not go forth with us or through us. This is evident in that “you have turned us backward before our enemies,” namely, certain of our own people who, overcome by excessive tribulation, have been turned aside and become followers of the enemies.

In Hebrew, “You gave our backs to the enemy.” This signifies those who, when persecution pressed upon them, fell away from the faith so as to follow their enemies, returning in their minds to Egypt and its meat-pots, [Col. 0372C] wishing to enjoy temporal pleasures.

“And those who hated us plundered us for themselves,” by conforming us to themselves. This is how they plundered us.

“You have given us like sheep for food,” in the estimation of those people: they think that we were born for this purpose, to be killed. Some sheep are reserved for breeding, others for slaughter and eating, such as rams; or, “like sheep easily led astray,” with regard to those who have defected.

“And among the nations you have scattered us,” because some, fearing defection, fled from one city to another. Or, you scattered us so that each person might seize us for himself among the nations—that is, amid the pressure of the nations.

“You sold your people without price”: you handed many martyrs over to death and converted few. We see those whom you gave, but we do not see those whom you received.

“And there was no multitude in their exchanges.” [Col. 0372D] And if you received some, they were not many. Formerly one of your people put a thousand to flight; now, conversely, one of them kills ten thousand of us. It is a great matter that you give the supreme martyr over to death, yet although he acts bravely, not many become Christians.

“There was no”—that is, as small things are customarily exchanged for many things, there was no such exchange among your people; rather, the assemblies of those who praise you will be scattered.

Jerome: “You sold your people without price,” to whom it is said, “You were sold because of your sins” (Isaiah L). No one bought them from you as you bought them with your blood. “And there was no multitude in your exchanges.” For the price was of less value—that is, no exchange was made. [Col. 0373A] The Lord purchased the people whom he bought not with gold or silver, but with his own blood (1 Peter I).

“You made us a reproach to our neighbors.” This may be read as referring to the nations up to this point, while what follows concerns the Jews; or it may be understood universally of Jews and Gentiles, all of whom are neighbors because they dwell together.

Or “neighbors” are those who have already drawn near to our faith and likeness by their will. Seeing us treated so disgracefully, they considered that we would be their greatest reproach if they converted and were likewise tortured.

And not only to our neighbors, but also “a mockery and derision to those who are around us”—that is, to those far from us, or to the multitude surrounding us, few as we are, persecuting us from every side so that we cannot escape anywhere.

“A mockery and derision,” that is, every kind of ridicule: a mockery to those who are indignant that we preach Jesus crucified, [Col. 0373B] and a derision to the wise among the Greeks, who regard our preaching as folly, according to the Apostle: “But we preach Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed a stumbling-block, but to the Gentiles foolishness” (1 Corinthians I).

“You made us a likeness among the nations.” This is that ridicule in the form of a likeness, that is, a proverb, when they reproach someone with words and say, “May you die as shamefully as that teacher of the Christians,” or “as Laurence”; or when, intending to torture someone, they imagine making him like us.

And not only a proverb, but also “a shaking of the head among the peoples”: that is, they have a reason to shake their heads because they see us tortured in such a manner. Shaking their heads, they say: “Alas, miserable people! What great madness afflicts you? What is this new insanity, [Col. 0373C] that you do not spare your youth but desire death rather than life?”

Just as they shook their heads outwardly and inwardly against you, so also against us.

Therefore, because of that defection and insult, “all day long my shame is before me,” that is, constantly before me. “And the confusion of my face has covered me”: I am entirely covered with confusion, laboring and groaning, and having no helper outwardly; and even if I have one inwardly, it is because of “the voice of one reproaching,” that is, censuring our sect, “and reviling,” that is, attacking it with words; “because of the face of the enemy,” that is, because of inward terror, “and the persecutor,” outwardly.

“All these things have come upon us, yet we have not forgotten you.” Here the understanding is opened as to why God permits all these things to happen. It is as though he were saying: You dealt thus with our fathers; someday you will deal thus with us. [Col. 0373D] But in this intervening time you deal with us according to a great purpose: you do this so that they may know that they were made freely by you and freely restored by you.

Therefore let all these things come upon us. We worship you freely; by worshiping you, we seek nothing but you. You will be all in all.

“We have not forgotten you,” namely, in seeking you and desiring you—which perhaps we would do if temporal happiness were not mixed with any bitterness.

We who are stronger have not forgotten you, even if the weak returned in mind to Egypt and its meat-pots. This is clear from the fact that “we have not acted wickedly against your covenant,” that is, against the promise we made to you. For we promised to renounce the devil and his spectacles and to follow you alone. [Col. 0374A] Although the flesh was weak, the spirit was ready (Matthew XXVI).

He acts wickedly who does not fulfill an agreement. Rational creation has, as it were, an agreement: as a faithful servant, it must set its Creator and Lord before itself, deny itself, and renounce the devil insofar as it can.

I say that we have not forgotten you, for “our heart has not turned back” from you—that is, from your commandments. Even if the flesh turned back, the heart did not turn back. We did not return to Egypt and its meat-pots; we did not look back at the things we had abandoned.

Therefore, you who are inferior, sons of Core, imitate us and pursue this way.

And certainly “you have not made our paths depart from your way”: you have not permitted our works to depart from your commandments.

Or for this reason we have not acted wickedly against your covenant: you have “made our paths hang,” that is, depend, upon your way. [Col. 0374B] Our way is a path, that is, a narrow way; for you, it is a broad and spacious way. Therefore you caused us to imitate your way in our paths.

Just as Christ first had to die, then rise again, and enter into glory, so we also preferred to be humbled first in time. For it is necessary to fight before being crowned, to be humbled before being exalted.

Our ways are one thing, yours another: ours proceed through prosperity, yours through bitterness. And you showed that our ways are different from yours when you said to us: “You wish to walk on broad ways? Do not. This way leads to life; that way to death.”

That you have not made our paths depart from your way—or that you have made them hang upon your way—is evident in this: “you humbled us in the place of affliction.”

No one will glory in the place of exultation unless he has first been humbled in the place of affliction, that is, in the present life, in which, whichever way you turn, [Col. 0374C] there is no peace and no perfection. Nor is it possible to rejoice in triumph unless one has labored in battle.

Or “in the place of affliction” means that in the body you humble us for suffering, or that you caused us to share the sufferings of those who have defected.

And truly great was the affliction in which you humbled us, because “the shadow of death covered us”: temporal death oppressed us greatly, and this is like a shadow of the future and eternal death.

Or “the shadow of death” means those who overshadow us unto death by their power, their riches, or their evil conduct. Or the shadow of death consists of those whom ignorance of the truth weighs down.

I say that our heart did not turn back; for if it had turned back, you would have avenged it. For “if we have forgotten the name of our God”—that is, if we have failed to render him his due within us, fearing him as a creature fears its Creator—“and if we have spread out our hands to a foreign god,” that is, [Col. 0374D] if we have preferred the creature to the Creator, “will not God require this?” Certainly he will require it for vengeance.

For he knows the hidden things of the heart. As though he were saying: he knows not only outward things, but also the hidden intentions of each person, with what disposition each person does or suffers something. He himself knows why we suffer all these evils: because, O Lord, for the sake of gaining you, and not for the sake of earthly things, we are outwardly put to death all day long—that is, continually.

“For we have been reckoned as sheep for slaughter”: as foolish and easily led astray, like sheep going willingly to slaughter, or easily led astray, with regard to those who have defected.

Alternatively: I say that our heart did not turn back, and this was done with a certain confidence. For if we have spread out our hands to a foreign god and forgotten the name of our God, [Col. 0375A] let all evils come upon us.

Someone might say: Is God not unjust, since he permits us to suffer so much? No. For will he not require this tribulation from the wicked? Indeed he will, because he knows the hidden things of the heart—that is, not only the heart but also the intention of the heart, which is hidden. He knows with what intention we suffer these things: because, O Lord, we are put to death for your sake.

And because we are put to death for your sake, O Lord, rise up against those who persecute us. For you still sleep with regard to those who do not believe that you have risen, who regard you only as a dead man.

Therefore, rise also into the knowledge of the Gentiles, so that defection may now cease and tribulation may cease. “I have other sheep which are not of this fold, and I must bring them also, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd” (John X).

[Col. 0375B] Why do you sleep, O Lord? Awaken in the hearts of those who confess that you died but do not believe that you rose again, so that at last, ceasing to persecute us, they may not perish in the final death.

Why do you turn your face away? It is as though he were saying: You seem to have forgotten us, while those who fear those who kill the body are lacking to us. “Do you forget our poverty?”

Our abundance is the multitude of believers; our poverty is their defection and their withdrawal, for we hunger for their salvation. It is as though he were saying: You seem to have forgotten our poverty, while you permit your people to be led astray by many tribulations, impoverishing us in this way and enriching those who persecute us.

Truly we have become poor, because “our soul has been humbled in the dust”: [Col. 0375C] those who are merely animal among us have been humbled by conforming themselves to those who are dust; or we have been trampled down like dust.

“Our belly has clung to the earth”: our weaker members have clung to earthly things.

Therefore, O Lord, rise up, that is, help us in bringing the vocation of the Gentiles to completion. And redeem us, namely, your people who are being led astray, for the sake of your name, namely, so that it may be glorified.

Or: Why do you turn your face away while you forget our poverty and our tribulation? That is, you seem to withdraw your presence from those whose tribulation is also our tribulation, and to forget them.

The poor are those who do not wish to be stripped but wish to be clothed over; the abundant are those who rejoice in tribulations.

“For our soul has been humbled in the dust.” As though he were saying: Truly you turn your face away, because our soul—that is, [Col. 0375D] those who ought to give us life—has been humbled by those who are dust.

“Your belly has clung to the earth”: our weak members have been joined to earthly things as though by glue.

## PSALM XLIV. FOR THE END; FOR THOSE WHO WILL BE CHANGED; FOR THE SONS OF CORE; FOR UNDERSTANDING; A SONG FOR THE BELOVED

> My heart has poured forth a good word; I speak my works to the king. My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe. You are beautiful in form beyond the sons of men; grace has been poured out upon your lips. Therefore God has blessed you forever. Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty. In your beauty and your loveliness, advance prosperously; go forth and reign. Because of truth and meekness and righteousness, [Col. 0376A] your right hand will lead you wondrously. Your arrows are sharp; peoples shall fall beneath you, into the hearts of the king’s enemies. Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the rod of righteousness is the rod of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions. Myrrh, drop, and cassia are from your garments, from ivory houses, by which the daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor. The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, surrounded with variety. Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear, forget your people and your father’s house. And the king will desire your beauty, because he himself is the Lord your God, and they shall worship him. And the daughters of Tyre with gifts—all the rich among the people shall entreat your face. [Col. 0376B] All the glory of the king’s daughter is within; she is clothed with golden fringes and varied adornments. Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; her companions shall be brought to you. They shall be brought with gladness and rejoicing; they shall be led into the temple of the king. In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you will establish them as princes over all the earth. I will remember your name, O Lord, in every generation and generation. Therefore peoples shall confess you forever and ever.

### Exposition

This psalm is sung concerning a holy marriage: concerning the bridegroom and the bride, the king and the people, the Savior and those being saved. It is proposed to the sons of Core, who act on behalf of those who will be changed—that is, on behalf of those who have been changed so as to receive understanding. It is also “a song for the beloved.”

Or the [Col. 0376C] words may be arranged in an inverted order so that we say: These words are a song for the beloved—words, I say, proposed to the sons of Core for understanding.

When the name “Core” is heard, we must not take it as an occasion for mockery, lest we be found comparable in childish understanding to those boys who insulted the holy prophet of God Elisha, who bore the figure of Christ, saying, “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead” (2 Kings).

These foolish, chattering boys, cursing to their own destruction, were devoured by beasts coming out of the forest. The Apostle recalls us from imitating these boys when he says, “Do not become children in your understanding” (1 Corinthians XIV), although his own teacher invites us to imitate a child when he says, “Unless you become like this little child, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XVIII).

Let each person therefore consider what the teacher invites us to imitate and [Col. 0376D] what the disciple forbids us, so that whoever delights in imitating a little child may not delight in ignorance, but in innocence.

Those boys who insulted the holy, bald prophet of God prefigured those who, from excessive childishness of understanding, stood before the sacred wood of the Lord’s cross saying, “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross” (Matthew XXVII).

They were devoured by beasts because they were inwardly put to death by the devil; or they were devoured by beasts, that is, afflicted and condemned by Titus and Vespasian, who are called beasts coming out of the forest—that is, sent by the Gentiles. The Gentiles are compared to forests because they had not yet received any cultivation.

That forty-two of those boys were devoured by beasts prefigured the forty-two years that [Col. 0377A] elapsed from the Passion of Christ until the destruction of Jerusalem.

“For those who will be changed”: everyone who has been changed can recognize this change in himself. Let him consider what he once was and what he is now; let him consider the world, formerly worshiping idols but now worshiping God.

The pagans also recognize this change when they see their temples deserted and the churches of God filled.

Or these things were proposed to the sons of Core for understanding so that they might not be blind, like those of whom it was said, “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.” Or they were proposed for understanding so that they might know to whom this change belongs: namely, to Christ, beloved above all beloved ones.

“A song for the beloved.” Learned men customarily compose a [Col. 0377B] song to be sung at weddings in praise of the bridegroom and the bride; this is called an epithalamium. In the same way, this psalm praises Christ the bridegroom and his bride, the Church.

Here the one praised is he of whom it is said in the Song of Songs, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song of Songs I).

Let the bride, the Church, therefore rejoice that she is loved by so great a bridegroom, for he loved her when she was ugly in order to make her beautiful; he washed her with his blood so that she would have no stain; he stretched her out upon the cross so that she would have no wrinkle.

In this psalm the Lord God the Father commends this bridegroom to us, so that he may possess greater authority. First, according to that ineffable generation by which the Son himself was begotten by the Father; afterward, clothing him with humanity and bringing him forward with great power, so that he might join his bride, the Church, to himself; and then [Col. 0377C] bringing forward the bride, suitably adorned and worthy of so great a bridegroom.

My heart has uttered a good word. Lest we should think that the Lord the Father needed a consort in the generation of his Son, he shows us that this generation was effected not by another but by himself, saying thus: “My heart,” that is, my inmost substance and hidden essence, “has uttered,” that is, has begotten, “a good word,” that is, a Son equal and consubstantial with me. Concerning this Word it is said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1).

But in order that by “good” we may understand the Word equal and consubstantial with the Father, the same Word made flesh intimates this to us when he says: “Why do you ask me about the good? No one is good except God alone” (Matthew 19). In this reply he did not separate himself from God, but rather united himself to him, as if he were saying: “When you call me ‘Good Teacher’” (Mark 10), “you confess that I am God, because no one is good except God alone.”

How the Lord the Father generated his Word from his heart, we can grasp a certain likeness in ourselves, just as higher things can be grasped from lower things, and the Creator from the creature. For every wise architect, when he is about to construct a building, generates from his heart a plan in which he arranges how the building is to be constructed; and the building already pleases him—not in the visible form of the structure, but in the testing and approval of the plan. Once the building has been made, it no longer pleases him alone, but also those who see it; and thus the plan in which he first arranged it is praised, because it would not appear such in the visible form of the building had it not first existed in the approval of the plan.

Just as, from the building placed before our eyes, we understand that the plan of the wise man preceded it, so, if we turn the eye of the mind toward higher things, we can understand in ourselves that the wisdom of the Father preceded us in the ordering of our creation. Let us consider ourselves, heaven and earth, and all their adornments—namely, human beings on earth, and angels, Virtues, and Principalities in heaven—and let us understand the Word necessarily, because “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1).

The Father himself testifies to this Word here in this way: “I declare that my works are for the king,” that is, for this Word made king; “I arrange my works to be governed,” because I make them known to him alone. Let this be an exposition of what precedes: “I declare that my works are for the king,” that is, I utter the Word with whom I arrange all my works.

Lest we understand that Word to be transitory, what follows is added: “My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe.” He used “tongue” for “word” and “pen” for “writing,” that is, the cause for the effect. It is as if he were saying: “My Word is not transitory, but is the pen of a writer,” that is, comparable to a written and enduring word. “Of a scribe,” I say, “who writes swiftly,” that is, who comprehends much without delay. There are certain scribes who comprehend an entire word or sentence in a single stroke; the Father’s Word is compared in a certain way to this speed, because nothing is swifter than to have said everything once.

Hence the saying: “God has spoken once” (Job 33). For he never speaks a second time: if the first utterance perishes, let him speak a second; but if the first does not perish, let him not produce a second. This utterance of the Father never had a beginning and never had an end, because that Word “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8).

Augustine says in this passage: “I fear that what I say may at some time be understood by the slower-minded; nevertheless I shall speak. Let whoever can follow, lest he who can follow fail to follow what has not been said.”

“You are beautiful in form beyond the sons of men.” It is as if he were saying: “You, O Word, you are a king beautiful in form,” that is, in your beautiful divinity, beyond the sons of men. Note that he could have said “beyond the angels,” but because he established him as a true human being, he therefore said “beyond the sons of men.”

“You are beautiful,” I say, “because grace has been poured out,” that is, will be poured out, “upon your lips,” that is, in your inmost being, or in your presence. Hence the saying: “The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1). It is the grace of the Lord because he did everything freely: he sought the lost, carried the found back upon his shoulder, forgave what was past, and promised what was to come.

“Therefore God blessed you forever,” that is, in order that grace might be poured out upon your lips, God blessed you; that is, God multiplied you—I mean, I, the Father—with a multiplication extending into eternity. He blessed the first man, but not forever, because he fell into disobedience. Or let this be the consequence of what he said: “Grace has been poured out upon your lips”; and because it will be poured out, “God blessed you,” that is, he blessed your promises forever, because they are to endure without end. The promises of the servant, when understood carnally, were shadows and transitory things.

“Gird yourself with your sword upon your thigh, most mighty one.” That is: You who are beautiful in form, in order to overthrow the aerial powers, “gird yourself”—that is, be girded—with your sword, namely, with the divine utterance, which is the sword of the Spirit; and gird yourself powerfully with this sword “upon your thigh,” that is, upon your human nature. With this sword the Lord separated son from father, daughter from mother, and daughter-in-law from her mother-in-law (Matthew 10).

This father is the devil, from whom the human race was separated through the Lord’s preaching. The mother is the Synagogue, from whom the daughter—that is, the Church gathered from the Jews—was separated. The daughter-in-law is the Church established from the Gentiles, which will stand against the Synagogue, her mother-in-law, namely, Christ’s mother, from whom he was born according to the flesh. This daughter-in-law was signified by the Ethiopian woman whom Solomon took as his queen (1 Kings 3). Thus there are two against three: father and mother against son, daughter, and daughter-in-law. For in the Synagogue the mother-in-law and the mother are understood.

“Set your attention upon your appearance and your beauty,” that is, you who are girded with the sword, be intent upon your beautiful appearance, that is, placed in an abundance of virtues. In this abundance wretched Adam had been placed, and was relaxing when he ought to have been intent. Thus, intent upon yourself, go forth prosperously to overthrow your enemies; and reign, that is, conquer, “because of truth,” namely, the Gospel that will come from you. Hence the Apostle says: “Our exhortation was not from error, nor from deceit, nor from impurity” (1 Thessalonians 2).

Reign also because of the gentleness maintained amid torments, because in your passion you will appear humble and gentle. Reign also because of righteousness, partly displayed and partly still to be displayed. It has been displayed, as in the saying: “Let the one who is righteous still be justified, and let the one who is filthy still be filthy” (Revelation 22).

What we see here has been fulfilled. In the future, however, righteousness will be displayed, when the incorrupt judge will demand what is fitting at the final judgment. Or “because of the righteousness of your people,” namely, of those who renounce worldly desires and live soberly and justly.

“And your right hand will lead you wondrously,” that is, your power will lead you everywhere into the knowledge of human beings—and wondrously, because you will be doing divine things while suffering human things.

And how will this happen? Because “your arrows are sharp,” that is, the words of your preaching are sharp, piercing human hearts and awakening divine love. Struck by these arrows, the peoples will fall beneath you, that is, they will humble themselves before you, “in the heart of the king’s enemies,” that is, they will fall in that respect in which they held a heart hostile to you as king, and they will rise again with a heart friendly toward you.

Struck by this arrow, Saul fell and Paul arose: the persecutor fell, and the outstanding preacher arose (Acts 9). And in those struck in this way there will be your throne, O God, that is, you will sit in them not temporarily but forever and ever, that is, eternally. And you will rightly reign in them, because “the rod of your kingdom,” that is, the rule by which you govern those subject to you, is a rod not of distortion but of direction. Hence elsewhere: “You will rule them with an iron rod” (Psalm 2), whereas the rule of others is pliable and distorted.

And truly the rod of your kingdom is a rod of direction, because you have loved righteousness. This is evident from the fact that you hated iniquity; and therefore—that is, in order that you might love righteousness—“God, your God,” that is, I, your Father, agreeing with you in all things, “anointed you.”

And with what anointing? “With the oil of gladness,” that is, with spiritual joy; and this was “above your companions,” that is, above all those whose companion you are in human nature. And because he said that he was anointed above all others, he shows that their anointing was great, so that from it we may understand his anointing to be wondrous, since he was anointed above them.

It is as if he were saying: “God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.” This is great, because “myrrh, drop, and cassia”—that is, every fragrance of the virtues—will breathe forth from your garments, that is, from your apostles and apostolic men. Hence the saying: “I live,” says the Lord (Isaiah 49), “because you will be clothed with all these things as with a garment.”

The saints are called God’s garments, because just as nothing is closer to a human being than a garment, so nothing is closer to God than the saints.

“From ivory houses.” The ivory houses are those whom we called garments. For the Lord also dwells in them, and they are called ivory houses because of chastity and the brilliance of their speech. The elephant, whose bones are ivory, is said to be a most chaste animal.

“From these the daughters of kings have delighted you,” that is, from those fragrances that will breathe forth from your garments, the daughters of kings will delight you. These are the apostles, begotten in faith, who subdue the flesh and strengthen the spirit. And this is in your honor: although they are begotten in faith through them, they will not be called by their name but by yours. For no one will be called a Petrine or a Pauline; all will be called Christians.

Thus, through the garments and the ivory houses, “the queen stood at your right hand,” that is, in your propitiation. Those who will be on the left will be concubines, signified by Solomon’s eighty concubines. The number of concubines, exceeding the number of queens, signified that “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 20).

The queen, then, will stand “in a garment,” that is, in doctrine “gilded,” that is, confirmed by good teachings, “surrounded by variety,” with languages understood, since the Church of Christ has been united from various languages.

Or, she will stand in a gilded garment, that is, adorned with good morals, and surrounded by variety, namely, by the virtues. Or, in a gilded garment, that is, in sound members that do not crack under tribulation.

“Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear.” He turns to the queen, as if saying: “Although you have now become queen, you have also become a daughter. Hear the promises, and understand their fulfillment.” And how do I tell you to hear? By inclining your ear, that is, hear humbly the commands of your king.

“And forget your people,” that is, carnal institutions; or the people of Babylon, whose king was the devil. “Forget also the house of your father,” namely, the devil—that is, have no fellowship with the impious. You ought to forget your people and the house of your father because “the King will desire your beauty,” that is, he will desire you to become beautiful, he who loved you when you were ugly in order to make you beautiful. Let it be a great thing for you that the King desires you, since he, namely the King, is the Lord your God.

And when you have forgotten your people and the house of your father, “they will adore him—and the daughters of Tyre also,” namely, the daughters of the Gentiles. Thus, through Tyre, which was a city near the Jews, we may understand the land of the Gentiles. These daughters of Tyre will adore him “with gifts,” that is, with generous almsgiving, through which all things become clean for them (Luke 2).

The Lord himself makes clear that he seeks these alms in the voice of the poor, saying: “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matthew 25).

Or, according to the interpretation of the name, let us again understand the Gentiles. For Tyre is interpreted as “their distress”; by this are properly understood the Gentiles, who were greatly distressed because of their sins.

“The rich among the people will entreat your face,” that is, your ecclesiastical institutions, in which your will appears. To these rich people Paul, the friend of this bridegroom, speaks, saying to Timothy: “Command those who are rich in the present age not to be proud in mind, nor to place their hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment” (1 Timothy 6). But let the rich be rich in good works, generous in giving, sharing, and storing up for themselves a good foundation, so that they may take hold of eternal life.

And because gifts of almsgiving are sometimes made to win human favor, lest this daughter of the King should glory in herself and seek praise from others, it follows:

“All the glory of the King’s daughter,” that is, of the Church, “is from within,” that is, in the conscience, because our glory ought to be the testimony of a good conscience and of our appeal to God. This glory is “in golden borders,” that is, in a good end—so that by the borders we understand finality, and by the gold, goodness. For “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24).

“Clothed all around with varieties,” that is, with various peoples, or with varieties of virtues.

Through this daughter, also, when she has been converted from the Gentiles, virgins will be brought to the King, that is, another Church. Thus we may understand the angelic Church and the other churches that were converted after the primitive Church. These virgins will be brought after her, that is, after the primitive Church, so that they may be near her, that is, imitators of her faith. Such women will be brought to you, that is, for your honor.

They will be brought, I say, not in grief and sadness but in joy and exultation. Hence the saying: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear” (Romans 8).

The virgins themselves will be brought into the temple of the King, that is, so that they themselves may be the temple.

And lest anyone should therefore think that the Church of Christ would not grow because the apostles and the first preachers no longer remain, it follows:

“Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you.” It is as if he were saying: “Although your fathers no longer remain”—that is, those established by you—“your Church will nevertheless not diminish, because sons have been born to you.” Instead of the apostles, Gregory, Augustine, and many others have been born, whom you will establish as princes over the whole earth.

And thus, through them, “I will remember your name,” that is, I will cause your name to be celebrated in every generation and generation. And truly this will happen through them, because therefore—that is, because preachers are sufficient—“the peoples will confess to you,” that is, they will have sufficient followers. And this will be forever, that is, for ever and ever.

## Psalm 45. For the End; for the Sons of Korah; concerning Hidden Things. A Psalm of David

> Our God is refuge and strength, a helper in the tribulations that have found us exceedingly. Therefore we will not fear while the earth is shaken and the mountains are transferred into the heart of the sea. Its waters roared and were troubled; the mountains were shaken by its strength. The rush of the river makes the city of God glad; the Most High has sanctified his tabernacle. God is in the midst of it; it will not be shaken. God will help it at early dawn. The nations were troubled and kingdoms were bowed down; he gave his voice, and the earth was moved. The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector. Come and see the works of the Lord, who has set wonders upon the earth, taking wars away to the ends of the earth. He will shatter the bow, break the weapons, and burn the shields with fire. Be still and see that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, and I will be exalted on earth. The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector.

## Exposition

[Col. 0382B]

This psalm is the voice of the sons of Korah, those who, when the Apostle Peter preached—as is read in the Acts of the Apostles—recognized the hidden things of the Lord, namely, how all those upon whom the Holy Spirit came spoke in every language. They also recognized how exalted and lofty before God had become the one whom they had crucified with their own hands, so that he might fill the uneducated with the Holy Spirit and make the tongues of infants eloquent. Cut to the heart, they said: “What shall we do, men and brothers?” And Peter said: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 2).

We can also understand those hidden things of which the Apostle said: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery: that a partial blindness has occurred in Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles enters” (Romans 11).

But in order that we may understand these hidden things, the sons of Korah who speak them exhort us, saying:

“Our God is refuge,” that is, God, who assumed our nature, is our refuge; “and strength,” that is, a powerful refuge; “a helper in tribulations,” that is, in a bad conscience, “which have found us exceedingly.” In this tribulation, the only helper is the one who alone forgives sins.

These tribulations find us when, through the preaching of others, we recognize our sins. We ourselves find tribulations when, without an admonisher, we weep over our sins. In either case, however, God is our helper. Therefore—that is, because, with his help, the tumult of conscience has been driven out—“we will not fear while the earth is shaken,” that is, while the nation judged to persist in earthliness is shaken.

“And we will not fear while the mountains are transferred into the heart of the sea,” that is, while the apostles are transferred from the Jews into the hearts of the Gentiles, who are compared with the sea because they were covered by the bitterness of idolatry. In comparison with them, the Jewish nation is called earth, because it was surrounded by the bitterness of the Gentiles as by the sea.

Concerning these mountains, that is, the apostles, the Lord said in the Gospel: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘To be removed and cast into the sea,’ and it will happen” (Matthew 17 and 21). He said this of himself to that mountain, which was sent into the sea—that is, into the knowledge of the Gentiles—by the preaching apostles.

“Their waters roared and were troubled.” Here he shows how the mountains are to be transferred into the heart of the sea: they will roar, that is, those mountains will utter voices; “and their waters were troubled,” that is, the teachers of the Gentiles. And not only will those teachers be destroyed, but the mountains also—that is, the earthly rulers—will be troubled by the strength of the one who will be our refuge.

And this is not surprising, because “the rush of the river makes the city of God glad,” that is, the abundant grace of the Holy Spirit will strengthen the gathering of the saints. “And the Most High has sanctified his tabernacle,” that is, those who dwell in him.

Or let us read it this way: “The mountains will be transferred into the heart of the sea,” and then, in that very transfer, that is, in that very preaching of the Gospel, the peoples themselves will roar and their teachers will be troubled, saying: “Who is this announcer of new demons?” (Acts 17). This was said at Athens.

At Ephesus, however, they caused such a tumult in their theater on behalf of their Diana that they cried out for nearly two hours: “Great is Diana of the Ephesians!” (Acts 19). And the mountains were troubled, that is, the earthly rulers who trusted in the strength of the sea.

But what did the city of God do? “The rush of the river made it glad; the Most High sanctified his tabernacle.” And how did he sanctify it? Because “God is in the midst of it,” that is, in the steadfastness of its heart. Therefore, although the sea rages and the mountains are troubled, the city itself will not be shaken from the preaching of the Gospel, because “God will help it at early dawn,” that is, without delay; “at dawn,” that is, at his resurrection, which took place at dawn; or “at dawn,” that is, when the fear of death had been consumed.

Thus “the nations were troubled and kingdoms were bowed down,” that is, the earthly rulers. And in what order will this happen? The Lord of hosts—that is, the one who accomplishes all things powerfully—will be with us. Another prophet calls him Emmanuel (Isaiah 7). “Our protector,” that is, the one who assumed our nature; “the God of Jacob,” that is, of the former people.

“He gave his voice, and the earth was moved,” namely, the earth of the Gentiles.

And because the Lord visits you, O Gentiles, come, therefore—not with the steps of your feet but with the steps of faith—and see, that is, understand, the works of the Lord. The Lord of hosts, who is with us, our protector, the God of Jacob, has set wonders, that is, things worthy of admiration, “upon the earth,” that is, among earthly people.

And what are these works? “Taking wars away to the ends of the earth,” as another prophet says: “They will turn their swords into ploughshares and their spears into pruning hooks” (Isaiah 2).

“He will shatter the bow and break the weapons.” Behold how he will take wars away. For he will burn “the bow,” that is, hidden hostility, and “the shields,” that is, the protection of vain presumption, “with fire.”

Concerning this fire it is said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12). With this fire the Lord will burn the shields, saying:

“Be still,” that is, empty yourselves of what fills you, and be filled with what leaves you empty. It is as if he were saying: “Empty your sacks of straw and fill them with grain.” And thus “see that I am God,” whom you see as a human being; “I will be exalted among the nations, and I will be exalted on earth.”

## Psalm 46. For the End; for the Sons of Korah

> All nations, clap your hands; shout to God with a voice of exultation. For the Lord is most high, fearsome, a great king over all the earth. He subjected peoples to us and nations beneath our feet. He chose for us his inheritance, the beauty of Jacob, whom he loved. God has ascended amid jubilation, and the Lord amid the sound of the trumpet. Sing praises to our God, sing praises; sing praises to our king, sing praises. For God is king of all the earth; sing praises wisely. God will reign over the nations; God sits upon his holy throne. The princes of the peoples have gathered with the God of Abraham, for the strong gods of the earth have been greatly exalted.

## Exposition

Because the grace of God has reached you, O Gentiles, “all clap your hands,” that is, practice good works. “Shout to God with a voice of exultation,” that is, with an exultant voice.

Note that God is to be applauded in both ways, with voice and with hands. If someone applauds only with the voice, it is not good, because the hands are idle; if only with the hands, it is not good, because the tongue is mute. Therefore let hands and tongue agree: let the tongue confess, and let the hands work.

“Shout to God with a voice of exultation,” because “the Lord is most high,” although here he appeared lowly; “fearsome,” although among the Jews he was despised; “a great king,” although here he appeared humble and small—over the whole earth of the Gentiles and the Jews.

“He subjected peoples to us,” that is, while we preached, he subjected Jews and Gentiles beneath our feet. And “he chose for us his inheritance to be conformed”—namely, “the beauty of Jacob,” that is, those who imitated Jacob.

And sing praises, because “God has ascended amid jubilation,” that is, amid the great joy of the apostles. For they had great joy when they saw their nature exalted to such a degree. “The Lord ascended amid the sound of the trumpet,” that is, amid an angelic voice, when they said: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven?” (Acts 1). It was as if they were saying: “See him ascending, believe in him while absent, hope for him as he comes, and through his mercy always perceive him as present to you.”

And because God ascended amid such jubilation, “sing praises to our God, sing praises”: sing praises to the Father; sing praises to our King, the Son; sing praises to the Holy Spirit. And rightly so, because God is King of the whole earth. Therefore “sing praises wisely,” that is, in your hearts, because the one who sings praises only with his voice does not sing wisely.

Sing praises because “God will reign over the nations; God sits upon his holy throne,” or upon the Church.

But in order that he might reign, “the princes of the peoples gathered with the God of Abraham,” that is, believers adhered to him. And from what did this happen? Because “the strong gods,” that is, steadfast apostles, “of the earth,” that is, chosen from the world, “were greatly exalted,” that is, glorified by signs, so that the princes might be gathered with God.

Hence the Apostle says: “Our Gospel did not come to you in speech alone, but in the Holy Spirit and in great fullness” (1 Thessalonians 1).

Or let us read it this way: “The princes of the peoples,” that is, of the Gentiles, “gathered with the God of Abraham,” having become sons of Abraham not according to generation but according to imitation.

And because they were chosen, although the Lord had not been sent to them, “the strong gods,” that is, the Jews, who presumed greatly upon their earth—that is, upon themselves—were greatly exalted by growing proud against the Lord.

## Psalm 47. A Psalm; a Song for the Sons of Korah; the Second of the Sabbath

[Col. 0385A]

> Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise in the city of our God, upon his holy mountain. Mount Zion is founded amid the exultation of the whole earth, the sides of the north, the city of the great King. God will be known in its houses when he receives it. For behold, the kings of the earth gathered; they came together as one. When they saw, they were astonished; they were troubled; they were shaken; trembling seized them.
