There were pains there like those of a woman in labor. With a violent wind you will crush the ships of Tarshish. As we have heard, so we have seen in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God; God founded it forever. We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple. According to your name, O God, so also is your praise to the ends of the earth; your right hand is full of righteousness. Let Mount Zion rejoice, and let the daughters of Judah exult because of your judgments, O Lord. Surround Zion and encompass her; tell it in her towers. Set your hearts upon her strength and distribute her houses, so that you may recount it to the next generation. For this is God, our God forever and ever; he will rule us forever.

## Exposition

We heard above what could suitably be understood by “the First of the Sabbath”; let us hear here also what the Second contributes.

It is not unknown that, among the Hebrews of old, the whole week was called the Sabbath, and that the first day and the second day were called the First of the Sabbath and the Second of the Sabbath. And because on the first day the Creator of the human race divided light from darkness, his resurrection can suitably be signified by the First of the Sabbath, because light was truly divided from darkness when immortality was divided from mortality.

The Second of the Sabbath, on which it is said that the Lord made the firmament, not incongruously signifies the Church, because she is aptly marked by the name “firmament” on account of her more worthy members, who never yield to the temptations of this world. Hence the Apostle says: “We who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak” (Romans 15).

Seeing this Church destined to be built from every race, the Prophet exhorts his descendants not to withdraw themselves from the building of this Church, but to strive to be there as gems and living stones, joined to the cornerstone, namely Christ.

Great is the Lord, and exceedingly worthy of praise in the city of our God—that is, in the Church built by God—and worthy of praise on his holy mountain—that is, in Christ. And since a great king ought to have a great city, hear how great this city is: it is founded amid universal rejoicing on Mount Zion—that is, by those rejoicing throughout Judea, which is understood by Mount Zion.

“The sides of the north, the city of the great King”—that is, those utterly despairing ones in whom charity has grown cold. Or, “the sides of the north”—that is, those who cling to him who says, “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah XIV)—are the city of the great King. By “the north” we understand the coldness of charity, since the greater cold usually comes from the north.

Or let us read “the mountains of Zion”: thus “the whole earth is founded in universal rejoicing,” that is, this city will be built throughout the whole earth. For the mountains of Zion—that is, the Jewish people—and the sides of the north—that is, the Gentiles—are the city of the great King.

“God will be known in her houses,” that is, in the houses of this city, when he receives it in order to protect it. And against whom? Consider: “For behold, the kings of the earth gathered together in council; they came together as one,” that is, with one purpose, to destroy the Church itself. But at last those kings, wishing to destroy it, “were astonished”—that is, they will be astonished—when they see the Church founded in this way, upon so many miracles. They will be troubled because of their sins and moved to repentance, for the trembling of the future judgment will seize them.

Or understand it this way: “God will be known in her houses,” when he receives the Church to be personally united to himself. And by what signs will God be known in her houses? Look: “For the kings of the earth gathered together; they came together as one,” that is, in the cornerstone, namely Christ, so that they might be joined to him through faith. And how will this happen? Because, seeing the Church founded in this way, they were astonished, troubled, and moved; trembling seized them.

This does not differ from the preceding interpretation: there, “pains like those of a woman in labor”—that is, within that disturbance and trembling—are pains that are not fruitless but destined to be turned into joy, because they are the pains of penitents who will eventually give birth to salvation. Hence Isaiah says: “Because of your fear, O Lord, we conceived and brought forth the spirit of salvation” (Isaiah XXVI).

Here the old person has conceived, and the old person is being born. “With a mighty wind you will shatter the ships of Tarshish”—that is, the pride of the nations, trusting in the prosperity of this world and carried along in it as by a wind, but to be overcome by the great fear of your future judgment.

Different people give different interpretations of what should be understood by Tarshish. Some wish Tarshish to mean Cilicia, because its metropolis is called Tarsus, from which the Apostle Paul came; and in that city maritime commerce was especially practiced. Others wish it to mean Carthage, because its beginnings flourished through navigation. For when Dido founded Carthage, she took with her in flight the ships prepared for commerce in the region from which she departed, with the consent of the leaders of that region. Once Carthage had been founded, those ships did not cease to serve commerce. Hence the city itself became exceedingly proud; and therefore the ships of Tarshish fittingly signify the pride of the nations, presuming upon the uncertainties of riches as upon the blasts of the wind.

Or we may derive the same interpretation from the meaning of the name. For Tarshish is interpreted as “exploration of joy,” by which are understood the nations that sought their joy in the voyages of this world.

“Trembling seized them,” as they said: “As we have heard it prophesied, so we have seen it fulfilled in the city of our God,” that is, in the Church. Just as we heard it in the promises, so we saw it in the fulfillment, in the city of our God.

And why do I call it God’s city? Because God founded it forever. Christ is the foundation of this city; hence the saying: “No one can lay another foundation than that which has been laid” (1 Corinthians III).

“We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple”—that is, among those who are in the midst of your temple, steadfast and well founded, so that they do not waver in faith. In name only, all who have been initiated through the sacrament of faith are called a temple. Among these, those are called “in the midst” who possess by good works the name they bear—namely, “temple.”

And lest anyone think that these “middle” ones, to whom the Lord’s mercy has been displayed, are few, what follows says: “According to your name, O God, so also is your praise to the ends of the earth”—that is, your praise will spread throughout the whole earth, just as your name has spread. For just as there is no land where your name has not been heard, so there will be none where you are not praised. Thus “your right hand is full of justice”—that is, there will be many righteous people standing at your right hand, although “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew X).

Or understand it this way: “We have received your mercy, O God”—that is, your merciful Christ—“in the midst of your temple,” that is, among the Jewish people, which is called your temple, situated in the middle and surrounded on every side by the nations. Yet he is not known there alone, for “according to your name, O God, your praise will spread to the ends of the earth”—either everywhere, or among those who have arranged themselves for the end of their earthly existence. Thus your right hand will be full of justice—that is, of your children—and will have many imitators.

Hence “let Mount Zion rejoice”—that is, Judea—and “let the daughters of Judah rejoice”—that is, the Gentiles. Judah is interpreted as “confessed.” According to this interpretation, it is fitting that the Gentiles be called the daughters of Judah, since they rejoice because of your judgments, O Lord. By these judgments they will at one time be separated locally from those from whom they have already been separated morally. Or they rejoice because of your judgments by which, through your grace, they have been taken from the mass of the *praeditorum* [reading uncertain]; or because, through the transgression of the Jews, salvation has come to the Gentiles.

“Surround Zion and embrace her.” He admonishes those initiated through the sacrament of faith, whom above he called the temple, to imitate those whom he called “in the midst.” It is as though he were saying: You who are the temple through the sacrament of faith, surround Zion—that is, those steadfast in faith—and do this not for her destruction, but “embrace her,” that is, imitate her. And what you proclaim, proclaim “in her towers”—in the faith of the apostles, who are called towers because of the eminence of their virtues: they are impregnable and provide defense for the less perfect. They are also the gate, through whom anyone may enter into life.

Paul was one of these three, commending his preaching in this way: “Even if an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel other than the one we preached, let him be accursed” (Galatians I).

If above we read, “We have received your mercy, O God,” as referring to Christ, then this is an admonition to the Church of the Gentiles to surround Zion—that is, those converted from the Jews, called Zion because they despise present things and await future ones. Thus he says: “Surround Zion and embrace her; proclaim in her towers.”

“Set your hearts upon the strength of Zion”—that is, do not proclaim these things with the mouth only, but in strength, that is, in charity, which makes everyone virtuous. “Distribute her houses”—that is, discern which house is clean and which is not. Or, “distribute her houses,” considering to whom the varieties of tongues have been given, to whom the interpretation of speech has been given, and so forth, so that from each person you may seek whatever is useful to us for imitation and knowledge.

And why do I say that you should distribute them? “So that you may proclaim”—that is, make known through your good works—not only to those who live with you, but “to another generation,” that is, through your kindred.

And what should you proclaim? That the one received in the midst of the temple, or the one who built the city, is God, our God—the one whom we see as a human being. I say that he is God, forever, that is, throughout the age of the age. And he himself, no other—neither angel nor archangel—will rule us forever.

## Psalm XLVIII, for the end, for the sons of Korah; a Psalm of David

“Hear these things, all nations; give ear, all you who inhabit the world. Both earthborn creatures and children of men, rich and poor together as one. My mouth will speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart understanding. I will incline my ear to a parable; I will open my proposition on the psaltery. Why should I fear in the evil day? The iniquity of my heel will surround me. Those who trust in their strength and glory in the abundance of their riches. A brother does not redeem; will a human being redeem? He will not give God his propitiation, nor the price of the redemption of his soul. He will labor forever and yet live on to the end. He will not see destruction when he sees wise people dying; together the foolish and the senseless will perish. And they will leave their riches to strangers, and their graves will be their houses forever. Their tents remain from generation to generation; they have called their names upon their lands. And a human being, though he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them. This is the way of those who are a stumbling block to themselves, and afterward their mouths will approve of it. Like sheep they have been placed in hell; death will feed upon them. And the righteous will rule over them in the morning, and their help will grow old in hell, away from their glory. Yet God will redeem my soul from the hand of the underworld when he receives me.

Do not fear when a man becomes rich, and when the glory of his house has increased. For when he dies, he will take nothing with him, nor will his glory descend with him. For his soul will be blessed in his life; he will praise you when you do good to him. He will enter unto the generations of his fathers; forever he will not see light. A human being, though he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them.”

## Exposition

There is great and unusual wickedness among human beings. Although they ought to live according to God’s will, they want God to live according to their will. And although they do not wish to be corrected, they want God to be corrupted. They do not consider as just what God wills, but only what they themselves will. This is what those people do who are distressed when they see the wicked prospering and the good suffering. Such people do not wish to serve God for the sake of future things, but only so that things may go well for them in the present, and therefore they murmur against the Lord.

He says the following:

“Hear these things, all nations”—that is, both Gentiles and Jews—“give ear, all you who inhabit the world,” that is, all those whom you have made round like the world by your power. Notice that he said “give ear” after saying “hear”: he said “hear” to everyone, but because he foresaw that some would hear in such a way as also to act, and others would not, he foretold what he foresaw would happen. Those hear with their ears who demonstrate in the performance of their works what they hear.

“Both earthborn creatures”—that is, you who seek earthly inheritances—“and children of men”—that is, imitators of the prophets—“rich and poor together as one,” that is, coming into the same faith, hear.

“For my mouth will speak wisdom.” And because many have one thing in their mouth and another in their heart, in order to make them more attentive to hearing he says: “And the meditation of my heart will speak understanding.” It is as though he were saying: I do not proclaim this to you deceitfully, because what sounds from my mouth has proceeded from my heart.

“I will incline my ear to a parable”—that is, so that my heart may meditate upon wisdom, I will humble my inner ear before the one who at last sees and instructs inwardly. Yet I will incline it “to a parable,” because however much someone here humbles himself to hear, and however perfectly he understands through a parable, he understands as though through an enigma. For as long as “we groan in this tabernacle,” we sigh as though in imperfection.

“I will open my proposition on the psaltery”—that is, in my work I will first show what I proclaim. For one who wishes to adhere to the proper order of preaching ought fittingly to recognize in himself through good works what he preaches to others. Hence the saying: “What Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I). This is what he means when he says that he will incline his ear to a parable and open his proposition on the psaltery, so that he may preach to others.

And behold the proposition he wishes to open on the psaltery:

“Why should I fear in the evil day?” Here he transfers to himself the person of those who desire to live piously in Christ. It is as though he were saying: Why should I and others fear on the day of judgment, when we possess in our book that by which we can avoid fear? For where a person is not offended unless he wishes to be, why should he fear there?

“The iniquity of my heel will surround me.” It is as though he were saying: It is necessary that I and others be surrounded by carnal iniquity. The heel is that part of the body which always clings to the earth; here ambition and other carnal iniquities are rightly understood, because they are always occupied with earthly things.

Or, “the iniquity of my heel will surround me”—that is, final iniquity, which must be guarded against even in good deeds, will necessarily surround me. This iniquity may be understood as pride, without which few are found. For there are not many who do not glory in themselves over their good works. This is the iniquity that first insinuated itself into those who fell away. Concerning it, it is said: “The woman will crush your head, and you will lie in wait for her heel” (Genesis III). The serpent lies in wait for the heel because it strives to mix pride into the conclusion of a good work.

Or this may be a response to the preceding question, as follows: “Why should I fear in the evil day?” Because “the iniquity of my heel will surround me,” if I fear.

“Those who trust in their strength,” and so forth. It is as though he were saying: Those must fear on the evil day who trust in their strength—that is, who presume upon their own merit—and glory in the abundance of their riches and hope in the nobility of their friends. This third point is not stated, but is understood through the proof that follows:

“A brother does not redeem; will a human being redeem?” It is as though he were saying: One must not trust in strength or abundance, because strength and abundance will not redeem. And that they will not redeem is proved from the greater case: a friend will not redeem. And that a friend will not redeem is shown as follows.

“A brother”—that is, Christ, whose brothers we are because we are his co-heirs—“does not redeem.” And since he did not redeem, will a human being redeem? No. And because Christ did not redeem, it is added: “He will not give his propitiation”—that is, he did not make satisfaction to God for his sins, so that he might be worthy to be redeemed by his brother. For God has not arranged that this redemption should benefit others except those who strive to imitate Christ. Those who do not give God propitiation for their sins do not do this.

To give God propitiation for sins means to pour out tears, give alms, and so forth. For this reason also the brother did not redeem him: he did not give “the price of the redemption of his soul”—that is, he did not confess for the salvation of his soul. Therefore “he will labor forever”—that is, he will be crushed by a twofold contrition—“and yet live,” that is, flourish, “on,” that is, for a time, though finally. For those who flourish in this life will have eternal labor, whereas those who labor will have eternal life.

“He will not see destruction when he sees wise people dying; together the foolish and the senseless will perish.” Behold why he will live to the end: he does not consider his own destruction—that is, his inner death—when he sees wise people dying outwardly. For he thinks that his evil life does him no harm, since dying outwardly is something he shares with the good. Therefore the foolish person, who does not know how to guard himself for the future, and the senseless person, who does not consider that there is nothing in this life except misery, will perish together in eternal destruction.

“And they will leave their riches to strangers.” For although they leave them to their children, they are nevertheless leaving them to strangers, since they do not spend them for their children’s salvation. Yet although those children are, as it were, strangers because they are not concerned for the salvation of their parents, they nevertheless wish to show themselves to be their children, because they think that their parents’ graves are their houses forever. This is not so, however, because if a human being always remained in the grave, the soul would not experience torment in hell.

“They have called such graves by their names”—that is, they cause their names to be called “in their lands,” that is, in their estates. The invocation of a name used to take place at a grave, because the friends of the dead customarily received bread and wine and, sitting at the grave, invoked the names of the dead, serving their own bellies rather than the spirits of the dead. For if the drunkenness of people carried on at graves were beneficial, the rich man’s tongue would not have burned in hell, since not even a single drop descended from the wine consumed at his grave onto his burning tongue (Luke XVI).

This invocation takes place not only at graves but also in “tents,” that is, in houses in which they existed temporarily, “from generation to generation.” They have called—that is, they cause to be called—their names. For on anniversaries they customarily gathered in houses, so that, once drunk, they might invoke the names of the dead.

“A human being, though he was in honor, did not understand.” Behold why the foolish and senseless person will perish: although they were in honor—that is, created according to the image of God—they did not conduct themselves intellectually. Therefore “he was compared to senseless beasts.” This was not in any sort of superiority; rather, “he became like them,” concerned only with his belly.

And what about them? “This is the way of those who are a stumbling block to themselves.” They honor God only so far as to be among those of whom it is said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah XXIX; Matthew XV). Thus their latter state is worse than their former: previously they were openly pagan, but now, hidden under the name of religion, they are worse.

“And afterward their mouths will approve of it.” For if someone reproves their life and says that earthly things should not be pursued, they themselves confess with their mouths that this is true, yet do not imitate it in their hearts.

Up to this point the Holy Spirit has described those who think there is no happiness except the honor of this world, and who after death attend to nothing except how splendid funerals may be arranged for them and their names invoked there. Now he foretells what will happen to them:

“This is the way of those who are a stumbling block to themselves, and afterward their mouths will approve of it.” Therefore, like sheep that have been devoured and cannot withstand any tribulation, “they have been placed in hell”—that is, in the blindness of the mind—and “death will feed upon them.” That is, the devil, who is the minister of death, will be their shepherd.

“And the righteous will rule over them in the morning”—that is, in the true morning that will have no succeeding night. For then “the saints will judge the nations and rule over peoples.” Or understand it this way: “Death will feed upon them”—that is, they will be food for the devil, who delights in devouring them as though in a meal. Hence it was said to the serpent: “You will walk upon your breast, and you will eat earth” (Genesis III).

Thus the righteous, who here were held in contempt by them, will rule over them in the morning. “And their help,” whose shepherd is death, “will grow old”—that is, it will be shown to have perished. I say that their help was presumed upon “because of their glory,” that is, because of the prosperity they possessed in this life. Or, “their help will grow old away from their glory,” removed from it. Or it will grow old because of the glory they had here: to the extent that they were glorious here, to that extent they will be inglorious there.

“Yet God will redeem my soul.” It is as though he were saying: The righteous will rule in the future; and meanwhile, what? Tribulation and every misery will belong to the saints. But what consolation is there? Although they are afflicted here, he will nevertheless redeem them “from the hand of the underworld”—that is, from the power of darkness—when he receives me and makes me conformable to himself.

Or: “The righteous will rule in the morning,” and yet there will be no “middle,” namely, no shadow or legal ordinances; nevertheless, “he will redeem my soul from the hand of the underworld when he receives me,” that is, when the Word assumes my nature in order to make himself visible.

“Do not fear when a man becomes rich, and when the glory of his house has increased.” It is as though he were saying: Since those who flourish in this world will ultimately be placed in hell, whereas you, who here appear despised, will rule, do not fear to hope for future things and postpone present things when a man becomes rich and the glory of his house increases. That is, do not envy the one who prospers in his way.

“For when he dies, he will take nothing with him,” because he will carry nothing away except his sins, “nor will his glory descend with him,” the glory produced for him by an ostentatious funeral.

And why will it not descend? Because “his soul will be blessed in his life”—that is, in this present life, which alone he believes to be life—by flatterers. For, to add to the height of his misery, he is not without flatterers. “And he will praise you when you do good to him”—that is, while he is in prosperity, only then will he praise you.

And what will he gain from this? “He will enter unto the generations of his fathers”—that is, he will reach the misery reached by the generations of his fathers, namely Cain and the others. And there he will not see light forever—that is, for as long as eternity endures.

And why is this? Because although he was a human being placed in honor, he did not understand. “He was compared to senseless beasts and became like them,” as stated above.

## Psalm XLIX. A Psalm of Asaph

“God of gods, the Lord has spoken and summoned the earth, from the rising of the sun to its setting. From Zion comes the appearance of his beauty. God will come manifestly, our God, and he will not be silent. Fire will burn before him, and around him a mighty storm. He summoned heaven above and the earth, to distinguish his people. Gather to him his holy ones, who establish his covenant above sacrifices. And the heavens will proclaim his justice, for God is judge.

“Hear, my people, and I will speak; Israel, and I will testify to you: I am God, your God. I will not rebuke you for your sacrifices; your burnt offerings are always before me. I will not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks. For all the wild beasts of the forests are mine, and the cattle on the mountains and the oxen. I know all the birds of heaven, and the beauty of the field is with me. If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine. Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and fulfill your vows to the Most High. And call upon me in the day of tribulation; I will deliver you, and you will honor me.

“But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my justice and take my covenant upon your lips? Yet you hate discipline and have cast my words behind you. If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers. Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue fashioned deceit. Sitting, you spoke against your brother, and against the son of your mother you placed a stumbling block. You did these things, and I was silent. You wickedly thought that I would be like you. I will rebuke you and set these things before your face.

“Understand these things, you who forget God, lest he suddenly seize you and there be no one to deliver you. A sacrifice of praise will honor me, and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God.”

## Exposition

Since there were among the former people those who understood that the sacrifice established according to the order of Aaron had to be changed into the sacrifice established according to the order of Melchizedek, it pleased the Holy Spirit that this psalm should be announced beforehand through the Prophet in the person of those people. Thus, in this psalm, they might gather their contemporaries and descendants together to understand that carnal observance had to be changed into spiritual understanding, and that this change would come through our Lord himself.

This is also indicated here so that the Jews would not be astonished at the destruction of their law: the Lord himself came and brought a new one. Asaph says the following:

“God of gods, the Lord has spoken”—that is, the God by whom all those who are gods have been deified: they were not born from pride, but justified by his grace and thus made gods. I say that it is he who gave us the law through Moses, who in earlier times spoke through servants; now he has spoken to us, not through an angel or prophet, but through himself (Hebrews II). Hence the saying: “Behold, I who was speaking am here myself” (Isaiah LII).

And what did he choose by speaking? “He summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting.” He did not summon only Africa, as some say, but as much as he created. Yet in this summons he did not separate Africa. Let Africa therefore rejoice in unity and not boast in division.

“From Zion comes the appearance of his beauty.” It is as though he were saying: Although the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting has been summoned, nevertheless the appearance of its beauty—that is, those who are called the beauty of his Gospel—will come from Zion, that is, from the Jews. For the apostles, who are called the beauty of the Gospel because they make the Gospel itself beautiful to others, were born from the Jews.

Or understand it this way: “From the rising of the sun”—that is, from those in whom the true sun has shone in some manner through knowledge of the law—“to those in whom the sun has completely set.” He summoned the earth, but nevertheless the appearance of his beauty first proceeded from Zion. Hence the saying: “Establish, O God, what you have worked in us, from your holy temple which is in Jerusalem” (Psalm LXVII).

“God of gods, the Lord has spoken; he summoned the earth,” saying: “Hear, my people, and I will speak; Israel.” For if you do not hear, then even if I speak, I will not speak to you. “And I will testify to you that I am God, the God of Abraham and Isaac, your God”—if you hear; and if you do not hear, I am God by my goodness, but because of your evil I am not your God.

“I will not rebuke you for your sacrifices.” Behold, he testifies that he no longer requires a sacrifice performed according to legal ordinances. When he says, “I will not rebuke you for your sacrifices,” he means: I will not demand them from you, even if you slaughter fat bulls and other animals for me.

What then? “Your burnt offerings are always before me”—that is, the burning of charity that sets you wholly aflame is pleasing to me. A human being is wholly set aflame when the inner person, kindled by the burning of charity, so seizes the body’s members for its own use that they never rise again toward what is unlawful.

“Nor will I accept calves from your house.” As though he were saying: These are the sacrifices for which I will not rebuke you. I will not demand calves from your house or goats from your flocks. For if I wanted such things, I would not need to demand them from you, since “all the wild beasts of the forests are mine, and the cattle on the mountains and the oxen.”

And lest, once these had been excluded, someone wish to offer birds or the fruits of the field, he removes those as well: “I know all the birds of heaven, and the beauty of the field is with me.” Therefore, “if I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine.”

“But shall I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats?” No. “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise.” Lest those whom he has contradicted should afterward wish to appear empty before him, he shows them the sacrifice by which he is pleased:

“Offer to God”—from whom you have whatever good you have—“a sacrifice of praise,” namely your good works, so that, seeing them, others may glorify “your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew V). “And fulfill your vows to the Most High”—that is, offer yourself. For anyone who rightly considers what ought to be vowed to God can find nothing more acceptable to God than to vow and give himself.

“And call upon me in the day of tribulation.” It is as though he were saying: I tell you to offer me a sacrifice of praise for this reason: if you offer it and afterward call upon me in the day of tribulation, I will deliver you from that tribulation, and you will honor me, presuming nothing upon yourself.

“But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my justice?” It is as though he were saying: Thus the Lord spoke to his people; but to one who was not his people, namely the sinner, God said: “Why do you recount my justice and take my covenant upon your lips?”

Since “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclesiasticus XV), here he hears God forbidding the sinner to preach, while elsewhere he hears him saying: “What they say, do; what they do, do not do” (Matthew XXIII). He also hears Paul saying: “Whether in truth or in pretense, Christ is proclaimed” (Philippians I), and so forth. These things were said so that those who hear would not fear that the word of God is worthless because they hear it from anyone whatsoever.

The sinner is forbidden to preach so that those who say good things but do evil will not be secure. For there are some who say: “God will not destroy us,” although through their mouths he has willed so many good things to be spoken to his people. The Lord rebukes such people as follows: “Why do you recount my justice and take my covenant upon your lips?”

“Yet you hate discipline.” It is as though he were saying: You ought not to take my covenant upon your lips, because you hate discipline—that is, paternal instruction. When I spare you, you sing and praise; when I chastise you, you murmur, as though I were God only when I spare you and not your God when I chastise you, although “all whom I love, I chastise and rebuke” (Proverbs III; Apocalypse III).

“And you have cast my words behind you,” where they cannot be seen by you, though they honor you. And how have you done this? “If you saw a thief, you ran with him,” consenting to him, although you were not physically a thief; “and you placed your portion with adulterers,” again consenting to them. In addition to these sins, “your mouth abounded in wickedness”—that is, in detraction of your neighbor—“and your tongue fashioned deceit,” that is, it brought forth deceit against your neighbor in ornate words.

And how? “Sitting”—that is, you lingered in that deliberation, as is indicated by the word “sitting.” For someone who does something while standing or passing by does not seem to have applied intention to the deed; but one who sits seeks leisure in order to act.

This is what he says: “Sitting, you spoke against your brother,” defaming him, “and against the son of your mother you placed a stumbling block.” Brothers are called those more perfect in faith, who are sons of the fathers and capable of being nourished by solid food. When these are defamed, the sons of the mother—those who are still nourished, as it were, by milk rather than solid food—are scandalized.

When Paul was defamed by certain people, who said, “His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible” (2 Corinthians X), those who were less perfect in faith were scandalized.

“You did these things”—namely, you ran with the thief and placed your portion with the adulterer—“and I was silent,” withholding my severity and delaying vengeance so that you might repent. Therefore you wickedly thought that I would be like you, forgiving your sin and leaving it unpunished. For this reason I will rebuke you for your sin and set it before your face, so that at last you may recognize that your sin is very great—something I would not do if you had previously considered it great. For to the one for whom sin is a grave matter, God grants forgiveness.

Hence the saying: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged by God” (1 Corinthians XI).

Up to this point Asaph, in an inverted order, has introduced Christ speaking—not openly, but secretly—because although Christ was strong in himself, he appeared weak in the flesh. He had to be seen so that he would not be understood; he had to be despised so that he would be killed. Thus he walked secretly among the Jews, doing wonders and enduring evil until he was hung upon the wood.

And our God, who came so secretly in his first coming, will come manifestly and will not be silent, judging those whom he then did not cease to admonish. He will not be silent in judgment, just as he was not silent in command.

“Fire will burn before him.” This fire consumes straw and purifies gold. Let us change our lives, therefore, so that we do not fear punishment, and let each person strive for this. For even if it were possible that the day of judgment would not occur, one still ought not to live badly. If no other punishment threatened sinners except separation from the face of God, nevertheless, however abundantly rich they might be, they ought to lament because they would not see the one by whom they were created and would be separated from the sweetness of his truth. Those who have begun, however imperfectly, to experience the sweetness of that truth know this.

But whoever does not desire the face of God should at least fear the fire; and those whom rewards do not invite should be terrified by punishments. Is what he promises worthless to you? At least tremble at what he threatens.

“And around him a mighty storm,” which will separate the sheep from the goats and winnow every grain, separating it from the chaff (Matthew XXV, III).

And how will this happen? “He summoned heaven above”—that is, his judges—“and the earth”—that is, those who are to be judged—“to distinguish among them his people from the people who are not his.”

And because you, O heavens, are to be summoned for this purpose, “gather to him his holy ones, who establish his covenant above sacrifices.” These are those who make his promises more worthy than sacrifices, considering that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory” (Romans VIII). Or, “who establish his covenant above sacrifices” means those who place his promises above their good works, going “from strength to strength” (Psalm LXXXIII).

And as you gather them, “the heavens will proclaim his justice,” namely this: that God is judge and renders to each according to his works.

Or understand it this way: “He summoned the earth to distinguish his people,” and rightly so, because God is judge, distinguishing all things in truth.

And since God, hidden in his first coming, will come manifest in his second, understand these words of the Lord, you who forget God: “A sacrifice of praise”—that is, good works performed not presumptuously but in praise of God—“will honor me, and there,” that is, in the sacrifice of praise, “is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God,” that is, Jesus Christ.

Or, “I will show him the salvation of God” because I will love him and manifest myself to him. Therefore understand these things, lest he suddenly seize you, sending you into the outer darkness, and there be no one to deliver you, because there is no judgment against the Lord.

# PSALM 50. FOR THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID, WHEN THE PROPHET NATHAN CAME TO HIM, WHEN HE WENT IN TO BATHSHEBA.

> Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy. And according to the multitude of your mercies, blot out my iniquity. Wash me more and more from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. For I myself know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me. Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged. For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins. For behold, you have loved truth; you have revealed to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom. You shall sprinkle me, O Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow. You shall give joy and gladness to my hearing, and the humbled bones shall rejoice. Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities. Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Do not cast me away from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a principal spirit. I shall teach the unrighteous your ways, and the ungodly shall turn back to you. Deliver me from bloodshed, O God, God of my salvation, and my tongue shall exult in your righteousness. O Lord, you shall open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise. For if you had desired sacrifice, I would indeed have given it; you will not delight in burnt offerings. The sacrifice pleasing to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise. Deal graciously, O Lord, with Zion in your good will, so that the walls of Jerusalem may be built. Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings and burnt offerings; then they will place calves upon your altar.

## EXPOSITION

In this psalm David’s sin is set before all the faithful, not as a justification for sinning but as an example of rising again, so that those who sinned with David may learn to rise again with David. What that sin was, the title of the psalm discloses: “A psalm of David, when the prophet Nathan came to him, because he went in to Bathsheba.” This title is taken from the history (2 Samuel 11). Bathsheba was another man’s wife, namely Uriah the Hittite’s. When David saw her, walking on the roof terrace after midday as she went to bathe, he was seized by her beauty. Although he was king and prophet, the woman was far away, but the enemy who attacked him was near, namely lust. In this we are warned to flee idleness. For as long as David endured Saul’s persecution, he committed nothing of this kind.

After learning who she was, he summoned her and slept with her; she conceived by him. Therefore David, wishing to conceal the crime, sent to Joab, commander of his army, asking him to send Uriah to him. When Uriah returned from battle, the king received him graciously and eventually ordered him to go down to his house, sending royal food with him. But Uriah did not go in to his wife; instead, he remained that night in David’s house with his servants. When David learned this, he asked him why he had not gone into his house to his wife. Uriah replied that it would be unworthy for his lord Joab to be in danger with the entire army while he himself indulged in pleasure. Then the king sent letters through him to Joab, instructing him to lead the army against the enemy and, wherever the fighting was fiercest, to place Uriah there so that he would be killed by the enemy. Thus adultery was increased by murder; afterward he took Bathsheba as his wife.

After this deed the prophet Nathan was sent to him by the Lord (2 Samuel 12) to rebuke him for so great a crime. Approaching the matter by means of a parable, he told the king that there were two men: one who had a hundred sheep, and another, his neighbor, who had only one, which he cherished in his bosom, drank from his cup, and ate from his bread. When a traveler came, the first man spared all his own sheep but took his neighbor’s one sheep and prepared it for the traveler to eat. Nathan asked David what judgment he would give concerning it. Not understanding the parable, David pronounced a severe sentence: the man should die and should restore the sheep fourfold. The prophet said to him: “You are the man.”

David did not try to defend his sin but humbled himself in repentance until he heard: “Do not be afraid, because the Lord has taken away your sin from you.”

We must attend to this weakness of the flesh and remember the Apostle’s words: “Therefore, let sin not reign in your mortal body” (Romans 6). He did not say, “Let it not exist,” but “Let it not reign.” Sin is present when you take pleasure in it; it reigns if you consent to it.

By David’s example we are warned not to give free rein to carnal desire; we are also warned not to become inflated in prosperity. For prosperity is more dangerous to the soul than adversity is to the body. David’s case also removes despair: although guilty of so great a crime, he did not despair. This psalm, just as it makes cautious those who have not fallen, likewise does not allow those who have fallen into despair.

### “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.”

He whose misery is great will have great mercy. Those who sinned little—that is, through ignorance—should ask for little mercy. What I bear is grave, but I flee to you, the omnipotent one. I would despair of a mortal wound if I did not know you to be such a physician.

### “And according to the multitude of your mercies, blot out my iniquity.”

Mercy is the bestowal of compassion; that is, act according to the manifold bestowal of mercy which you have shown to the human race from the beginning of the world. You attend to those who despise you, so that you may correct them; to those who are ignorant, so that you may teach them; and to those who confess, so that you may forgive them.

Blot out my iniquity, which consisted in my doing to another what I did not want done to me. Therefore blot it out here through mercy, lest you reserve it for punishment in the future.

### “Wash me more and more from my iniquity.”

Those who have sinned less need washing; but I need more, that is, much more than I know how to ask.

Or: You who wash away the sins of the ignorant, wash even more the sins of the knowledgeable.

### “And from my sin cleanse me.”

There was iniquity against the man whose wife he took; there was sin in himself, because by this he became a transgressor of the law. I know that it is a great sin to violate another man’s wife, to kill her husband without his knowledge—and therefore without his opposition. Therefore have mercy, blot out, wash.

### “For I myself know my iniquity.”

That is: Because I punish myself, do not punish me.

Someone might say: “You do not know what you are asking; you do not know whom you are invoking. He is just; you cannot take justice away from him. Because he is just, he hates your sin, and if he hates it, he will not leave it unpunished.”

“What then? Are you asking for mercy so that you may take away judgment?”

“I do not. I know that he is just, and I cannot take justice away from him. I certainly implore mercy, but I look toward justice. For this reason I do not want you to punish me: I punish my own sin. It seems to me great mercy if you permit me to punish my sin, so that it is not reserved for you.”

### “And my sin is always before me.”

I do not place it behind me so that I cannot see it, as I did when I pronounced so severe a sentence against others. Because he did not recognize his own sin, he did not forgive another’s; therefore he judged so severely. But God used his tongue as an instrument for cutting away the wounds of his heart.

You have mercy; you cleanse, because against you alone I have sinned. You alone heal; you alone forgive sins. He alone is the just punisher who has nothing in himself that ought to be punished.

### “And I have done evil before you.”

My sin could have remained hidden from others, but I could not conceal it from you, because all things are naked and open to your eyes (Hebrews 4).

So completely have I sinned against you alone, and so completely are you just, that you may be justified in your words—that is, that you may also be shown just in your words—since every human being apart from you is a liar. And you prevail over all who are judged, for all may be judged justly, however just and advanced they may be; you alone are judged unjustly, because you alone are free from sin.

### “When you are judged.”

O Father in the Son, the Word in the humanity he assumed, foresaw this future: the Son of God would come to be judged.

### “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities.”

He says, as it were: You prevail not only when judged, over all who are judged in a crime such as mine—in which they are just and you unjust—but also over all human beings, because all are sinners, whereas you alone are without sin.

And he transfers the whole human race into himself: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities.” To this he adds:

### “And my mother conceived me in sins.”

That is, she conceived me in carnal desire. This carnal pleasure, arising from the sin of the first parent, remains active in our flesh.

People are not conceived in sins because intercourse between married persons is itself sinful. This act is chaste within marriage and has no guilt. Rather, the origin of sin carries with it, as if from its root, the punishment owed.

A husband is not mortal merely because he is a husband. The Lord too was mortal, but he did not receive our guilt from sin; he received our punishment, not our guilt. Therefore rightly “all die in Adam, but all shall be made alive in Christ” (1 Corinthians 15).

So have mercy, blot out, cleanse—and this is necessary.

### “For behold, you have loved truth.”

That is, just judgment. You have loved it so completely that you spare not even those whom you forgive. Either they punish themselves, or you punish them. Therefore you confer mercy in advance so that you may preserve judgment: you forgive the one who confesses so that you do not punish him, because he punishes himself.

And because you have loved truth, because you leave no sin unpunished, you conferred mercy in advance so that you might preserve judgment.

For when you sent your prophet to rebuke me and caused me to recognize my sin so that I would punish it, you revealed to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom, so that you would not deny pardon even to those who had fallen so grievously. This you arranged through your wisdom, by which you created humanity and strengthened your creature after it had been ruined in them—things that had until then been uncertain to others.

In this uncertainty the Ninevites practiced repentance. They said: “Who knows whether God may turn and forgive?” (Joel 2; Jonah 3). These are the uncertain things.

### “You shall sprinkle me, O Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed.”

That is, he will give me humility. Hyssop is an herb that cleanses the lungs, and it is low-growing. In the lung, which becomes inflated, the swelling of pride is understood. Against this disease humility provides medicine.

That is, I shall embrace you with humility and charity, just as the herb clings to the rock. I shall confess my sin to you; I shall not defend it. I shall displease myself so that I may please you. You shall wash me by sprinkling me in this way from my sins.

### “And I shall be whiter than snow.”

Because I shall be cleansed inwardly in the soul, whose cleansing is greater than that of the body, just as the soul is greater than the body.

### Another interpretation

“You alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you.” If others sin against a king who has been appointed as judge, they sin against God as well. But if a king sins, he sins against God alone, because God alone punishes him.

Therefore have mercy on me, O Lord, so that you may be justified in your words—that is, so that you may be found truthful in your promises. Through the Holy Spirit you promised me: “I will place upon your throne the fruit of your womb” (Psalm 13). For I seem unworthy that the Son of God should assume flesh from my offspring, unless you cleanse me from so great a crime.

And you prevail over those who deny that you ought to fulfill your promises to me, since they judge me unworthy of your fulfillment because I am guilty of so great a crime.

Therefore have mercy, blot out, wash—and this is necessary. For even if this new iniquity did not exist, you would still have much from the old one to punish in me.

“For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins,” as above.

In saying that I was conceived in iniquities, I do not cast the guilt back upon the Creator; rather, I make a true confession to you, which you love.

“For behold, you have loved truth,” that is, true confession. And because my iniquity is so great, have mercy.

I know that you will have mercy, because you have revealed to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom. Through the Spirit I have learned the counsel of the ancient arrangement, the new restoration, and eternal blessedness—what is uncertain to others.

You will send your Son, in whom true forgiveness will be hidden for us.

And with that hyssop, O Lord, you will sprinkle me—that is, with the conformity to him who is signified by hyssop. For just as hyssop is effective in suppressing the inflation of the lungs, so conformity to Christ, that is, humility, is effective in depressing our pride.

Or just as a bundle of hyssop dipped in the blood of a heifer is effective for the external cleansing of lepers, so the outpouring of Christ’s blood is effective for our external cleansing.

You shall wash me externally, and I shall be made whiter than snow internally.

### Another interpretation

Have mercy because you promised the kingdom to the righteous. Therefore, unless you justify me and others, you will find no one to whom you can give it. But have mercy, justify, and in this way prevail over those who deny that restoration can take place after a fall, or who say that for the sake of one sinner you take the kingdom away from the righteous.

This is that hyssop; this is that humility.

### “You shall give joy and gladness to my hearing.”

I shall rejoice to hear your rebuke and not speak against you; I shall not defend my sin.

Hence John says: “But the friend of the bridegroom stands and listens, and rejoices with joy” (John 3).

This is true humility: to displease oneself in order to please God; to attribute every sin to oneself and every act of righteousness to God.

### “And the humbled bones shall rejoice.”

My humbled soul shall rejoice, although through pride it came into grief.

### Another interpretation

After that cleansing and washing, you shall finally give joy to my hearing, so that I may hear: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matthew 15). Then the humbled bones shall rejoice—that is, the virtues now humbled and easily overcome will there be strong and unconquerable.

### “Turn your face away from my sins.”

That is, blot out my sins so that you may not punish them afterward. Rightly he asks God to turn his face away from his sins, since he himself did not turn his face away from them. He asks that God turn his face away from the sins, not away from him.

And not only from the sins I have now committed, but blot out all my iniquities, original and actual.

### “Create in me a clean heart, O God.”

For I polluted my heart through the work of iniquity.

### “And renew a right spirit within me.”

I distorted that spirit; renew it in my inward being. It has grown old and failed within me.

And do not cast me, once renewed, away from your face; that is, do not permit me to fall into sin again.

### “And do not take your Holy Spirit from me.”

That is, the Spirit given by you, the spirit of compunction and repentance.

### “Restore to me the joy of your salvation.”

I used to applaud myself because I knew of the coming of your Son. But now there is no reason for joy while I am unjust. Therefore justify me, so that I may be able to rejoice in that coming. For he will lead his own out from the underworld, whom he will find there.

### “And strengthen me with a principal spirit.”

That is, with the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of all good spirits.

No one can be saved without that salvation. Thus the dispensation of the flesh assumed by Christ was believed by the holy fathers, just as it is believed by us.

Someone may ask: “For what benefit do you seek this?”

“For a great one.”

### “I shall teach the unrighteous your ways.”

The unjust will not despair because of my example; through me they will recognize your ways, that is, mercy and judgment.

And by my example the ungodly will turn to you.

### “And in order that the ungodly may turn to you through my example, deliver me from bloodshed.”

That is, from carnal desires, so that I may not be killed inwardly again.

### “O God, God of my salvation.”

Understand: the author of salvation.

### “And my tongue shall exalt your righteousness.”

Not mine, but the faith that justifies—or the fact that you do not desire the death of a sinner.

Truly you will deliver me. For, O Lord, you will open my lips: the lips of my heart, closed because of sin, you will open to your praise by justifying me through grace.

### “And my mouth shall proclaim your praise.”

That is, my external mouth shall proclaim your manifold praise. You create a human being so that he may exist; when he sins, you do not abandon him; when he confesses, you forgive him; and, so that he may be secure, you cleanse him.

### “For if you had desired sacrifice, I would indeed have given it.”

I would have offered sheep, oxen, and many victims—an external sacrifice. At that time David lived when animal victims were offered to God, but he was looking toward these future times.

We therefore stand within these words.

“Then shall we offer nothing?”

You have something within to offer.

### “You will not delight in burnt offerings.”

That is, in the burnt offerings of victims.

For the sacrifice pleasing to God is a troubled spirit, resisting the flesh; a heart made contrite by repentance and humbled from pride—or humbled for this purpose, so that it may always guard itself thereafter.

Jerome says: “Many have a contrite heart but not a humbled one, because they mourn what they have done and afterward return to the same thing.”

And so that the sacrifice of praise may be offered to you not only by me but by many:

### “Deal graciously, O Lord, with Zion.”

That is, send the one whom you are going to send (Exodus 4).

Zion means your Church, which, “forgetting what lies behind and reaching forward to what lies ahead” (Philippians 3).

### “In your good will.”

That is, in your Christ—or not according to its merit but according to your mercy.

### “So that the walls of Jerusalem may be built.”

That is, so that the faithful may be perfected. Through their perfection Jerusalem will be built: the city of peace, that city into which no enemy will enter and from which no citizen will be excluded.

Or: “So that the walls of Jerusalem may be built,” that is, immortality and freedom from suffering. These walls were destroyed in the first parent.

### “Then,”

that is, when Jerusalem has been built,

### “you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness.”

That is, a just sacrifice, namely the righteous themselves. Now you accept as a sacrifice for sin a troubled spirit; then you will accept praise alone, that is, you will receive it frequently and without interruption.

“Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; throughout the ages of ages they will praise you” (Psalm 84).

### “Offerings and burnt offerings.”

True offerings and true burnt offerings, when the fire of divine fire consumes the whole of these burnt offerings.

### “Then they will place calves upon your altar.”

They will place themselves as calves—that is, pure and renewed—upon your altar, that is, upon the innermost devotion of the mind.

# PSALM 51. FOR THE END. THE UNDERSTANDING OF DAVID, WHEN DOEG THE EDOMITE CAME TO HIM AND REPORTED TO SAUL: “DAVID CAME TO THE HOUSE OF ABIMELECH.”

> Why do you glory in wickedness, you who are powerful in iniquity? All day long your tongue devised injustice; like a sharp razor you practiced deceit. You loved wickedness more than kindness, iniquity more than speaking righteousness. You loved every word of destruction, O deceitful tongue. Therefore God will destroy you forever; he will tear you away and remove you from your tent, and your root from the land of the living. The righteous will see and fear, and they will laugh at him and say: “Behold the man who did not make God his helper.” But he hoped in the abundance of his riches and prevailed in his vanity. But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God; I have hoped in God’s mercy forever and throughout the age of the age. I will confess to you forever, because you have done this, and I will await your name, because it is good in the presence of your saints.

## EXPOSITION

The history is noted in 1 Samuel 21. David, fleeing from Saul, came to Abimelech the priest and received the sword kept in the temple, with which Goliath had been killed. He also received from him the bread of the Presence. Pretending to have business, he departed from him quickly.

Doeg the Edomite was there at that time, Saul’s chief shepherd, when David came to Abimelech. Saul, becoming angry, asked what the reason was that no one was informing him about David. Doeg came and said: “I saw David in the house of Abimelech.”

Saul was so provoked that he ordered his servants to kill Abimelech and the entire priestly family of that city. Doeg, still burning with wickedness, attacked him and killed Abimelech and all those priests, although none of the others dared to extend a hand against the Lord’s holy ones.

Historically nothing of this kind is enacted in this psalm; therefore we are drawn toward its mystery.

In David we understand Christ, for the reasons often stated; in Saul, the earthly kingdom.

Saul means “desire.” Against God’s will the Jews desired Saul for themselves as king, and the Lord chose him not to remain permanently but to correct that people.

By “desire” we understand death, concerning which it is said: “God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living” (Wisdom 1). But the ungodly summoned death for themselves with hands and feet, and, embracing it, slipped down through it.

Saul persecuted David, and the earthly kingdom persecutes the children of the heavenly kingdom—or death does so. For all persecution arises from the fact that we are mortal. If we were not mortal, there would be nothing for the enemy to do against us.

Abimelech means “the kingdom of my father”; Doeg means “moved”; Edomite means “earthly.”

David came into the house of Abimelech, and Christ came into the land of the Jews, which according to the flesh had been the kingdom of David his father. He came through the Incarnation.

When the earthly movement saw him—that is, those who were moved by earthly things, which Christ taught should be despised—they accused him before earthly rulers.

Saul sent those who would persecute David, but David escaped their hands, though not without blood, because the priests were killed. So too, in Christ’s persecution, the Word escaped, but his flesh was killed.

This persecution may be referred generally to the body of Christ, that is, to all those who wish to be David in David, Christians in Christ. Those who love earthly things do not cease accusing them before the rulers of this age.

Or it may refer to the persecution of Antichrist, which will be the greatest. Hence it is said: “There will come a time such as has not been since the nations began to exist,” at which time all the priests will be killed—that is, all Christians, in whose house, that is, in whose heart, David, namely Christ, will be. Antichrist will persecute him but will not be able to kill him, for he will not be able to take Christ away from Christians.

### Construction of the title

These words of the psalm are referred to the end of the ages, that is, to their fullness, so that you may understand that these events occurred historically and also possess an interpretation. For we understand through them that tribulation must come first and joy afterward, sitting first and rising afterward.

They are attributed to David the prophet—that is, to his more worthy members—or placed by the head himself before others, so that they may understand what is appointed for all the ungodly: to devour the godly.

I say “the interpretation” signified in that historical event, when Doeg the Edomite—that is, Judas and the Jews, moved by earthly concerns, namely place and nation—came to Saul, that is, to the rulers, to Pilate and the others, saying: “David came to the house of Abimelech.”

“Behold, he is living among us. If we let him go on in this way, the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation” (John 11).

Or when Doeg the Edomite came—that is, when various persecutors, moved by earthly concerns, came to Saul, that is, to secular authorities, to accuse those into whose hearts Christ has come through conformity to him.

The prophet’s purpose in this psalm is to show that one must first be afflicted and afterward glorified; one must first sit and afterward rise—just as David, after many persecutions, attained the kingdom, and Christ, the head of the martyrs, first suffered and afterward was glorified.

### “You who are powerful in iniquity.”

That is, you to whom God permits the power to exercise cruelty and hatred against his holy ones, which is iniquitous; or powerful in worldly wealth and authority.

For every rich person is either unjust or the heir of an unjust person. Such power is not power but impotence; it is not glory but disgrace.

### “Why do you glory in wickedness?”

Since the wickedness you practice is wickedness, why do you glory in it?

You glory as if someone insane were permitted the power to kill himself. You kill the bodies of the saints; this a scorpion can do, a fever can do, a little worm can do. But you kill your own soul and preserve theirs. Why, then, do you glory in these things?

“Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1).

He shows what that wickedness is:

### “All day long.”

That is, continually, without weariness or interruption. Even when you do not act, you think.

### “Your tongue devised injustice.”

It is not the tongue’s function to think but to speak. Yet the perverse person perverts it, because “the heart of fools is in their mouth” (Sirach 21)—that is, they do not think before they speak.

### “Like a sharp razor you practiced deceit.”

That is, you made your fraudulent persecution so ready for harm as a sharp razor is ready for cutting.

Or: Just as a razor, however sharp it may be, cannot cut except what is weak, so your deceit can affect the body but not the soul.

Or, if this is said of the Jews: A razor is sharpened for the purpose of preparing the brightness of the face. In the same way God had prepared the Jews through the law so that through it they might prepare the brightness of his face in others.

But just as a sharp razor, which ought to produce brightness, practices deceit by turning itself to cut the flesh, so the Jews turned themselves to kill not only servants but also the Son. And this is iniquity.

### “You loved wickedness more than kindness.”

You placed what is naturally higher below, and what is naturally lower in the place of honor.

No liquid seeks the higher places more than oil, to which works of mercy are compared. Just as they are above, so they ought always to be held above. But although both were before your eyes, you loved wickedness more—the thing that should have been placed second—than kindness, which should have been placed first.

And you did not make this perversion only in your heart; you also loved speaking iniquity to your neighbor more than speaking righteousness.

Nothing is more iniquitous than opposing one’s God, than denying God’s command in oneself and in others.

### “You loved every word of destruction.”

Whisperings, slanders, quarrels, flatteries.

You willingly listened to all these things from others. You do not give bitterness for food to the belly, but you give food of iniquity to the soul? Wretched man, you flee shipwreck and embrace lead?

I mean words existing on a deceitful tongue, on a fraudulent tongue.

Why do you glory in such things? There is no glory in them if you wish to consider not what came before your wickedness but what will follow—namely, to what evil end it will lead you.

### “Therefore God will destroy you.”

He will destroy you through manifold destruction, going toward the end—that is, always seeking an end and never finding one.

### “He will tear you away.”

As a fruitless tree from your tent, that is, from the Church.

Will you not serve here? Will you not guard against the enemy here in the tent, so that you may finally rejoice in the palace?

Everyone is in God’s tent with respect to his natural intention, because natural intention leads all of us toward the good, although misguided error leads some away.

### “And he will remove you.”

That is, he will make you emigrate from your tent. You will not remain here in the tent; you will have no share in the first resurrection.

If this is applied to the Jews, it means removal from the institutions of the law.

### “And your root from the land of the living.”

Our root is charity; the fruit is good works. It is necessary that your works proceed from charity. Then charity is your root.

Without it, they have no greenness, because they do not remain in the root of charity.

### “The righteous will see.”

This is the interpretation mentioned in the title.

He says, as it were: Their destruction will not be without great benefit for the good. For the righteous will see—that is, they will attend not only to the former things of the wicked, which now flourish, but also to their latter things, which will be dry.

They will fear lest they suffer such latter things, and here they will guard themselves against the glorying of the ungodly.

Hence elsewhere: “He will wash his hands in the sinner’s blood.”

They will understand that the glorying of the wicked is their destruction, because “the enemies of the Lord, as soon as they have been honored and exalted, will fail; like smoke they will fail” (Psalm 37).

### “And they will fear.”

They will fear lest they encounter such an end.

### “And they will laugh at him.”

He says, as it were: By understanding this, they will become above him, since they will not place their hope in perishable things but raise it toward heavenly things. In body they are beneath him, but in mind they laugh above him—that is, they rejoice—and in laughing they say:

### “Behold the man who did not make God his helper.”

This is the man who preferred to be conformed to Adam rather than to Christ. Therefore God will destroy him.

Or, finally, in the last things they will rejoice, having become superior to those by whom they were judged here. Then, judging those by whom they were judged here, they will mock them and say:

### “Behold the man who did not make God his helper.”

This is said contemptuously, like: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us” (Genesis 3).

It appears that he is a man: fragile, one who preferred to have himself as his god, like wretched Adam, rather than to make God his helper. This is the figure of sarcasm, that is, hostile mockery.

### “But he hoped in the abundance of his riches.”

Note that it does not say, “He had riches,” but “He hoped in them.”

Joseph had riches but did not hope in them; he possessed them for the benefit of others.

Let the poor man dressed in rags who has no riches not applaud himself here. For many are poor in the treasury of the body but rich in the treasury of the heart, and the reverse.

Hence it is said in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5).

### “And he prevailed.”

That is, over us. He made himself greater than us in his vanity.

Nothing is more vain than to value money more highly than God.

Because he hoped in the abundance of his riches—by riches he means wealth, powers, honors, pleasures, and other such things—he will therefore finally be destroyed.

### “But I am like a fruitful olive tree.”

He says, as it were: He hoped in the abundance of his riches; therefore his root will be torn out. But I am like an olive tree whose root is nourished and not uprooted, ultimately fruitful in the house of God, full of fruit and full of every delight, when God will be all in all (1 Corinthians 15)—even if I am now dry.

I, I say, like an olive tree, will confess to you forever in the house of God, established in the palace, I who served here in the tent. Then I will make true confession; then I will truly praise you, when there is nothing in me that displeases you.

And rightly, because you made that confession, or made me a fruitful olive tree.

Therefore I will finally confess, because here I hoped in the mercy of God that leads into eternity, into the age of the age, and not in riches.

### “And I will await your name.”

While I am in the tent, I will endure patiently; I will not act hastily like Adam, who wished to become God before the appointed time.

All the saints will indeed be gods, but they will not truly receive this name before the time when God will be all in all.

First one must strive toward obedience as a creature, so that eventually one may become God, advanced into angelic glory.

Adam, because he prepared to make himself god, was punished with death.

I await nothing else except this, because it is good in the presence of your saints, even if it is not good in the presence of the wicked.

Or: I will await your name in the presence of your saints, or in the common resurrection—and therefore, because it is good to await that name.

### Another interpretation

After the wicked have been condemned, I remain here in the house of God, that is, in the present Church, like a fruitful olive tree flowering late, because it is characteristic of the good to be dry in this age.

And this is because I hoped in the mercy of God, not in riches—in mercy, I say, which leads into eternity, that is, into the age of the age.

At last I will confess, when God will be all in all.

The remainder is unchanged.

# PSALM 52. FOR THE END. FOR MAHALETH. THE UNDERSTANDING OF DAVID.

[Col. 0406B]

> The fool said in his heart, “There is no God.” They are corrupt and have become abominable in their iniquities; there is no one who does good. God looked down from heaven upon the children of men to see whether there was anyone understanding or seeking God. All have turned aside; together they have become useless. There is no one who does good, not even one. Will not all those who work iniquity understand—those who devour my people as though they were eating bread? They did not call upon God. There they trembled with fear where there was no fear. For God scattered the bones of those who please men; they were put to shame because God rejected them. Who will grant salvation to Israel from Zion? When God has turned back the captivity of his people, Jacob will rejoice and Israel will be glad.

## EXPOSITION

[Col. 0406C]

Known is the history (1 Kings 26). David, fleeing Saul, came to Achish, king of Gath, and served under him, receiving from him Ziklag, a small city. There he settled his wife, his sons, and all his possessions. While David had been sent into battle, the Amalekite raiders came, seized David’s wife and sons, and burned the city. On returning, David pursued them, overtook them, killed them, and brought back the spoils.

“Amalek” is interpreted as “licking the earth,” and “Ziklag” as “conversion.” By David’s wife we understand holy souls; by his sons, good works; by David, Christ. David settled his wife and sons in Ziklag, and Christ settles holy souls and good works in those who have been converted, that is, in the faithful. The Amalekites—that is, those who lick the earth and love the earthly things of this world—often lead these holy souls, together with their good works, captive through many tribulations, when they draw them down and make them conform to themselves. But Christ frees his Church from the Amalekites, pursuing them with his army, that is, with his preachers, and killing them—some for good, others for evil.

The title is constructed as follows: The words of this psalm are referred “to the end,” that is, to the final David; and the psalm is the understanding of David the prophet, or of every perfect believer. I say “understanding,” meaning what is signified or possessed, “concerning Amalek,” that is, in the history which tells how David pursued Amalek; or, according to the Hebrew truth, *pro maeleth*, that is, “for the woman in labor” or “for the woman groaning,” namely, for the oppression of the Church, which is comparable to a woman in labor. For just as a woman in labor is in pain, so also is the Church in this world.

The psalm is therefore read in this way only as referring to the person of the Church; according to another interpretation, it may also be read as spoken by the Head. Although this psalm appears in its wording to be the same as the preceding one, beginning “The fool said,” it nevertheless differs in this respect: the former is attributed to Christ, whereas this one is attributed to all the faithful; the former is understood of the first coming, this one of the second. The Prophet’s intention is to show first the Church’s oppression and then its consolation, in accordance with the words: “When God turns back the captivity of his people, Jacob will rejoice and Israel will be glad.”

It may also be said that the preceding psalm was composed before this event occurred, and that, because the Prophet understood what he had narrated there historically to signify the Church’s rescue from the hand of the Amalekites, he first made this repetition. The Prophet introduces Christ speaking about the persecutors of the faithful, both Gentiles and Jews, and showing what will be the end of the persecutors and of those who suffer tribulation.

### “The fool said in his heart: There is no God.”

The foolish people who refused to receive the Son and Wisdom of God said in their heart—that is, they devised this for themselves, not on the authority of the books. “The Lord is not God,” because to the Jews he appeared a stumbling-block and to the Gentiles foolishness (1 Corinthians 1): they thought it absurd to believe that the one treated so disgracefully was God. Or whoever thinks that evil deeds please God does not think that God exists. For if God exists, he is just; and if he is just, injustice displeases him. Whoever, however, thinks that iniquity pleases him denies that God is judge in the affairs of the world.

Cassiodorus: This is the voice of the Head, spoken for the restoration of those concerning whom the Apostle says: “We know that every creature groans and labors in travail until now” (Romans 8), and for the confusion of those who afflict them, so that the afflicters themselves and their instigators may be without excuse.

The verb “to say” properly belongs to the tongue, not to the heart. But because divine power understands our thoughts, it is rightly said that the fool’s heart speaks: what can come to the Lord’s ears, not for pardon, but for judgment. It is as though he said: “From where comes such folly among them?” They are corrupt, having fallen from their good nature in the first parent, and to such an extent have they become abominable—that is, disinherited—in their iniquities, invented by themselves; and they are so corrupt that there is no one who does good.

### “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the sons of men.”

Here a question arises. If God looks down from heaven to see whether there is anyone who understands, then God does not know everything. A second question is this: If there is no one who does good, who is *maeleth*, that is, who is in labor here among the wicked?
