The first question is answered as follows. Divine Scripture very often speaks in such a way that what a creature does by God’s gift is said to be done by God. Thus: “The Lord your God is testing you” (Deuteronomy 13), “to know whether you love him,” that is, to make you know it. Again: Why “from heaven,” if human beings do these things? Hear the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3). You see with the heart, but you do not see unless you have your heart above.

It may also be explained in this way. God made the sons of men sons of God, because from the Son of God he made the Son of Man. God granted human beings the ability to do good from him, not from themselves. They are sons of men when they do evil; they are sons of God when they do good. Therefore, remove the fact that human beings are sons of God, and what remains is that they are sons of men; thus there is no one who does good.

It is as though he said: “Let those who are sons of God clearly recognize what such people are.” Or the fool said, “There is no God,” but falsely. For in truth there is one, because “the Lord looked down from heaven upon the sons of men,” that is, through the humanity of the Word he established his mercy over the sons of men, both Jews and Gentiles. Or “from heaven,” that is, from his preachers, whose citizenship is in heaven. Through them he made his mercy known to all, both Jews and Gentiles, and therefore they are without excuse.

He looked down from heaven for this purpose: “to see,” that is, to make people see, “whether there is anyone who understands,” namely, God through faith, “or seeks” him through works. Since human weakness could not grasp God, he sent his Son in human form. Through word and deed the Son undertook to recall human beings to the worship of God; among mortals he performed divine works while enduring human things. He also sent his preachers to make this known to human beings. Yet he found no one who understood God in the condition in which they were sons of men, nor anyone who sought God.

For they had all turned aside from the way of truth; together they had become useless—useless, that is, to God—both Jews and Gentiles. They had become so corrupt that no one did good of himself: “not even one,” or “no one at all.” Alternatively, they pay no attention to the fact that God is judge in human affairs, because they refused to understand God, who mercifully looked down from heaven upon them.

### “Will they not at last recognize…”

Will they not at last recognize through punishments that the one whom they thought merely a man is God, and that he is judge in human affairs—all those who work iniquity against me and who devour my people, either by devouring them or by taking away their goods? I am their Head. They devour them “as food,” that is, continually.

They will certainly recognize it, because “God despised,” that is, blinded them, for they did not call upon God—that is, they did not invoke him within themselves. A person calls upon God within himself when he makes himself God’s possession.

“There they trembled with fear where there was no fear,” as did the Jews, who feared losing their place and nation, or the Gentiles, who feared the idols they had fashioned for themselves. It is as though he said: “From where comes such blindness among them, that they feared where there was no fear?”

For God “scattered the bones of those who please men,” that is, those who strive to please human beings rather than God. Because they had poured themselves out for human favor, they were inwardly confounded, because God had despised them—that is, blinded them.

It is as though he said: “They say, ‘There is no God.’ Who, then, other than he will give salvation to Israel?” Who, coming from Zion, will give salvation to those whom he will make Israel—that is, those who see and know God—unless he himself does so? Who will separate the grain from the chaff?

Indeed, it will be the Lord, when he “turns back”—that is, turns inwardly and outwardly together—the captivity of his people. Here the second coming is indicated. Then Jacob will rejoice: Jacob, who here was still journeying onward; and Israel will be glad: Israel, having arrived at its destination.

## PSALM 53. TO THE END, IN SONGS, THE UNDERSTANDING OF DAVID, WHEN THE ZIPHITES CAME AND TOLD SAUL: “IS NOT DAVID HIDING AMONG US?”

[Col. 0409A]

> “Save me, O God, by your name, and judge me by your strength. O God, hear my prayer; give ear to the words of my mouth. For strangers have risen up against me, and the mighty have sought my life, and have not set God before their eyes. For behold, God helps me, and the Lord is the upholder of my soul. Turn the evils back upon my enemies; in your truth destroy them. I will sacrifice to you willingly, and I will confess to your name, O Lord, for it is good. For you have delivered me from every tribulation, and my eye has looked down upon my enemies.”

### EXPOSITION

This title is taken from the historical account (1 Kings 26). David, fleeing Saul, hid in Hebron. Knowing this, the Ziphites—so called from the village of Ziph—accused him before Saul, saying: “Behold, David is hiding among us.” Saul persecuted David, and the earthly kingdom persecutes the sons of the heavenly kingdom.

Ziph is a village, and its name is interpreted as “flower.” Hence the Ziphites are “those who flourish,” signifying what has been given to sinners in this world. “Our life,” says the Apostle, “is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3). Christ is hidden here insofar as his majesty is concerned, in which he will judge. He is hidden also in the labor of the godly and the flourishing of the ungodly, because the saints prefer in this world to wither, and to be poor and obscure with respect to temporal glory, rather than to flourish here.

Christ is not hidden, however, with respect to his name—even those who deny him by their deeds proclaim it. The Ziphites, that is, those who love the flower of this life, accuse David who is hidden: namely, they accuse Christians who wish to remain hidden in this life, despising the vain glory of the world. They do this especially before secular powers, whose power and honors these Christians despise.

These things are referred “to the end,” that is, to the consummation of the ages, where God is served in the spirit. They are the “understanding of David,” that is, of the faithful soul, which desires to be David in David, or to be of Christ, and which he sets before others. I say “understanding,” to be held “in songs,” that is, in exultation.

For this is what the saints must understand: that here one must rejoice in tribulation, because at last this sadness will be turned into joy. I say “understanding,” signified when the Ziphites came and said to Saul: the Jews speaking about Christ to their rulers (John 16), and other unbelievers speaking about the body of Christ to earthly rulers.

This is the voice of the Church, which understands that the flower of this life is fleeting and quickly passes away: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field” (Isaiah 40). Therefore the Church despises flourishing in this life. It chooses rather to wither here while it is winter and to conceal its flower in the root, so that in due season it may flower. For this reason it suffers many oppressions from the lovers of the world; and in these oppressions it shows what must be done: namely, that one must pray and persevere in a good purpose.

### “O God, save me by your name…”

“O God, save me by your name,” or, “save me, sent in your name,” if this refers to the Head, glorifying God; or “save me, who glory in your name,” if it refers to the members.

Others seek salvation in their own name—in riches, honors, and powers. But you save me: me, I say, who understand that salvation is nowhere except in your name, namely, in that name which is regarded as disgraceful and dishonorable by those who flourish in the world: the name of the crucified one. “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6).

Those are saved by that name who are not ashamed of Christ’s cross, for whom the world has been crucified and they have been crucified to the world (ibid.). “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Galatians 5). Hence the Apostle says to Timothy: “Do not be ashamed of Christ crucified, nor of me, his prisoner” (2 Timothy 1).

Adam gloried to his own ruin in his own name, since he wished to become God for himself.

### “And in your strength deliver me.”

They who glory in their own name wish to destroy me in my weakness. But you deliver me “in your strength,” that is, in the divinity united to me, if this refers to the Head. If it refers to the members: “Judge me,” when you come in strength—you who have now appeared despised.

At present the Ziphites have gathered against David, that is, the lovers of this age against the lovers of God. But you, O God, judge—that is, distinguish the grain from the chaff, their flower from ours.

It would be exceedingly presumptuous to ask such a great Judge for judgment—in whose sight not even the heavens are clean (Job 15)—if mercy did not precede it. It is as though he said: “Afterward I will not fear your judgment, if you save me in your name. That judgment will be for me not for punishment but for distinction.”

### “O God, hear my prayer…”

“O God, hear my prayer,” offered for the perseverance of my people, if this refers to the Head; if to the members, hear the prayer of my heart. “Give ear to the words of my mouth,” which I utter with my lips—that is, show plainly in the matter itself that you have heard them. If this refers to the Head, these are words offered on behalf of my people.

It is necessary that you save me, because strangers—not related by kinship, but by their flower—and although my prayer sounds in their ears, they do not hear, because they do not understand. Rejoicing in temporal things, they do not know eternal things. If this refers to the Head, they have become strangers who ought to have been sons.

“They have risen up,” not to defend me, but against me. “The mighty,” with respect to their reputation, or those presuming upon themselves, “have sought my soul,” that is, my life, in order to destroy it, if this refers to the Head; if to the members, they have sought my soul in order to overthrow it.

And this is because “they have not set God before their eyes.” If this refers to the Head, they did not understand what concerned the poor and needy. If it refers to the members, they did not set God before their eyes because they had the world before the eyes of their heart; they loved darkness more than light (John 3).

They have risen up, but what concern is that to me? “For behold, God helps me.” He helps in this way: even if he does not appear outwardly, he nevertheless helps inwardly. “And the Lord is the upholder of my soul,” raising it again, if this refers to the Head. If it refers to the members, he has taken up my soul so that it might not be dragged down; or Christ has undertaken my cause to plead it.

### “Turn the evils back upon my enemies.”

Turn them away from me and turn them upon them. They feared being killed by the Romans and losing their place and nation because of me, and so they planned to kill me. But let them be killed by the Romans and lose their place and nation. This is not a wish but a prophecy.

“In your truth,” that is, in your true judgment, “destroy them,” that is, scatter and divide them throughout the whole world—those who in their falsehood wished to destroy me.

If this refers to the members: they prepared temporal death for me; let them encounter eternal death. And let this occur not from cruelty but from true judgment. Or the words may be understood for the good, spoken with compassion: “O God, turn away from their hearts the evils which they themselves think good,” namely, the flower of the present life; “and in your strength,” that is, in the truth of your commandments, “destroy them.”

“Turn the ungodly, and they will be no more” (Proverbs 12). Although they may not have deserved it, nevertheless do this from your goodness.

Or: “Turn the evils back upon my enemies.” At present they flourish, but they are being kept for the fire. “And in your truth destroy them,” those whom you tolerated in your weakness.

### “I will sacrifice to you willingly.”

If this refers to the Head: they sought my soul as though I were unwilling, but I freely offered that sacrifice to you. If it refers to the members, the Lord is rightly the upholder of my soul. For, O Lord, I will sacrifice to you willingly—that is, freely, without a temporal reward—crucifying the flesh with its vices and desires.

I will not attribute this to myself, but “I will confess to your name”: I will attribute entirely to you whatever good I do, and I will attribute it to your name and not to another, because it is good, since I find nothing good in itself.

And truly, after the sacrifice, I will finally praise you because you will be all in all. I must believe that this is good because I have experienced it: “For you have delivered me from every tribulation”—me, the Head, by raising me outwardly; the members, inwardly in reality and outwardly in hope.

“And my eye has looked down upon my enemies,” at last in the judgment, when I have been appointed judge over them. It has looked down because it is as certain to you as though it had already happened. Here, reaching you through the height of the heart, I looked down upon them from there and saw that all flesh is grass. Hence elsewhere: “I passed by, and behold, he was no more” (Psalm 36).

## PSALM 54. TO THE END, IN SONGS, THE UNDERSTANDING OF DAVID

> “Hear, O God, my prayer, and do not despise my supplication; attend to me and hear me. I am saddened in my exercise, and I am troubled by the voice of the enemy and by the tribulation of the sinner. For they have turned iniquities upon me, and in anger they were troublesome to me. My heart was troubled within me, and the fear of death fell upon me. Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me. And I said: Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly away and rest? Behold, I have gone far away in flight, and I remained in solitude. I awaited him who saved me from faintness of spirit and from the storm. Cast them down, O Lord; divide their tongues, for I have seen iniquity and contradiction in the city. Day and night iniquity and toil surround it upon its walls, and injustice is in its midst. Usury and deceit have not ceased from its streets. For if my enemy had cursed me, I would surely have endured it. And if the one who hated me had spoken great things against me, I would perhaps have hidden myself from him. But you are a man of one mind, my leader and my acquaintance, who together with me used to take sweet food; in the house of God we walked in agreement. Let death come upon them, and let them descend alive into hell, for wickedness is in their dwellings, in their midst. But I cried out to God, and the Lord will save me. Evening, morning, and midday I will recount and proclaim, and he will hear my voice. He will redeem my soul in peace from those who draw near to me, for they were many with me. God will hear and humble them, he who is before the ages. For there is no change in them, and they did not fear God. He stretched out his hand in requital. They polluted his covenant; they were divided from the anger of his face, and his heart drew near. His words were softened above oil, yet they themselves are arrows. Cast your care upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you; he will never allow the righteous to be shaken. But you, O God, will lead them down into the pit of destruction. Men of blood and deceit will not halve their days; but I will hope in you, O Lord.”

### EXPOSITION

“To the end,” that is, to Christ. “The end of the law is Christ.” “In hymns,” that is, in praises. Whether we are afflicted or rejoice, he must be praised who instructs us in tribulations and consoles us in joy. We are with Christ in heaven through hope; he is with us on earth through charity.

Therefore, when we hear “the understanding of David,” let us be admonished, and let the Church understand in what evil we now are and from what evil we desire to be delivered. We must understand that we have been made in the image of God; we must understand our honor. If we understand this, we see that this region is not a place of joy but of sorrow.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, our Head, who did not disdain to assume our form—that is, the form of a servant—deigns to give us his servants both a form of prayer and an example of life, as this psalm makes clear.

Hear, O God, my prayer made for the perseverance of my people who have already been initiated into the sacraments of faith. And do not despise my petition. For it can happen that someone is heard and afterward despised; this happens to those who, despairing of the good things of this world, receive them and afterward are despised because they by no means desired eternal things.

Hear the petition made for those who have been predestined to faith but have not yet come to it, so that they may be converted from their error; or hear the prayer for these same believers, that they may persevere in their good purpose—the petition that the love of the world may be taken away. Hear in this manner: “Attend to me and hear me”; that is, in the likeness of one who turns a calm and gracious face toward someone and gives a favorable hearing. Because I make myself unremitting in prayer, make yourself unremitting in hearing.

And hearing is necessary, because “I am troubled in my exercise.” Exercise is the continuation of honorable labor. Here the course of the Lord’s human life is briefly described. His exercise was remarkable in miracles and in teaching. But when he saw that this exercise was producing no improvement, he was troubled—not for himself, but for the salvation of those whom he saw perishing, like a good physician who sees that his skill is making little progress in those whom he wishes to cure.

And lest this sadness be understood as remaining, he adds: “I am disturbed by the voice of the enemy.” One who ought to have been a friend has become an enemy, whose voice contradicts me in everything: “You have a demon” (John 8); “This man is not from God” (John 9); “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke 19).

“And by the tribulation of the sinner.” Although he is a sinner and needs my salvation, he troubles me by striking and boxing me—the sinner, that is, the transgressor. This tribulation should rather be called his than mine, because when he prepares to trouble me outwardly, he is troubled inwardly.

Why do I call it his? “Because they have turned their iniquities upon me.” They wished to turn aside death and the loss of their place and nation through my death, but by my death they incurred these things instead. Or: they placed their iniquities upon me, making me an offering for their sins, like the people of Numantia, who first treated a captive well and afterward led him outside the city, laid all their sins upon him, and stoned him, thinking that by this means they would be cleansed. The Jews thought that by Christ’s death the place and nation would be purified.

“And in the anger which they had because of the loss of their place and nation, they were troublesome to me.” They were angry with me, although they ought to have been angry with themselves. For they were taken captive by their own sin, not mine. They thought that, because he had called himself king, he would incur the anger of the Roman rulers, although he was a Jew; and for this reason they were angry with him. Therefore, because they were troublesome, because they turned their iniquities upon me, “my heart was disturbed within me.”

It was disturbed for an hour, but “within me,” not outside me. I transferred the disturbance of my people into myself by my own will, voluntarily and not under compulsion. And because I came to suffering by my will, not by necessity, “the fear of death fell upon me”: that is, death, which is fearful to others, fell upon me and died when it came upon me. For it lost the legal power it had over others when it came to the one over whom it had no power.

“O death, I shall be your death; I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hosea 13).

He shows how death came upon him: “Fear of spirit and trembling of body came upon me.” This is a true description of death. “And after death and trembling, darkness covered me,” because one who is dead possesses no light. Or “darkness”—that is, darkened and blind people, ignorant of what they were doing—covered me on every side. They thought that they were covering the light of the world when they placed me on the cross, and from the cross in the tomb, even shutting the tomb.

“There was the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world, and the world did not recognize him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1).

Augustine says:

“There is a certain city confused by all nations, possessing nothing that is not worthy of confusion. It is called a city because those who are in it make that by which they ought to have been confounded into a defense for themselves, contradicting Christ both by not believing and by living wickedly. These are the walls of human confusion, made higher by the practice of impiety. Concerning them it is often said: ‘If this man became a Christian, what pagan would remain?’ These walls will fall after the seventh circuit of the plain (Joshua 6), that is, through the work of the sevenfold Spirit. Its streets are the impious; in them are the crossroads of every desire and the marketplace of the tumult of all things—and as though someone might come upon them.

“If this is so in the city which is outside Christ, rest within, among those who are in Christ; do not seek solitude. ‘What I lament,’ he says, ‘touches the false brothers among whom I labor within, since I would endure those who are outside.’”

These words can also be referred to the members of Christ, so that Christ might speak in this way on behalf of his members: “I was troubled in my exercise,” that is, my members are greatly troubled, laboring in doctrine by imitating me and accomplishing nothing, or little.

Or “in my exercise,” because the wicked, being wicked, exercise the good. If you are good, you have no enemy except the wicked. Moreover, this rule of goodness has been set before you: imitate the goodness of your Father, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil.

But such a person, when he extends his love so far as to love even his enemies, surrounded by the rage of many, gives way through a certain human weakness. He sees himself pierced by evil demonic persuasion, so that he puts on hatred toward his enemies. Resisting hatred and striving to perfect love in the struggle itself, he is disturbed, and in this way he is troubled.

“I am disturbed inwardly while love fights on one side and hatred on the other.” “By the voice,” that is, by contradiction—and not only by contradiction, but also “by the tribulation of the sinner.”

There are two kinds of enemies: one hidden and the other open; one inward and the other outward. Each tries to take from us that by which he can be overcome. The outward enemy strives to take away our possessions, while the inward enemy strives to take away our love.

When that inward enemy stirs up the outward enemy against us, he does not do so so much to take away our possessions as to wound our love inwardly. Therefore the outward enemy must be loved, so that the inward enemy may thus be avenged. For this reason I was troubled, fearing that I might lose love and be turned into hatred.

“Because they have turned their iniquities upon me”: that is, they have placed their own iniquities upon me. Although they themselves were impious and blasphemous, they called me impious and blasphemous.

“And in anger”—that is, in unjust fury, not in a just cause—they were troublesome to me. Therefore “my heart was disturbed within me,” that is, I burned inwardly.

For this reason he adds: “And the fear of death fell upon me,” that is, I feared that through their excessive perversity I might be turned from love into hatred. Hatred is the death of the soul, just as love, conversely, is life.

He explains how the fear of death came upon him: “Fear and trembling came upon me,” as above. And it is not surprising, because “darkness covered me”—that is, I feared that darkness had enveloped me on every side. “He who hates his brother is in darkness” (1 John 2).

And I said: “Who will give me wings like a dove?” As though he were saying: Troubled and disturbed as I rebuked that people, entreated them, reproved them, and made little progress, I said: “Who will give me wings”—that is, resurrection and impassibility—“like a dove,” in simplicity and innocence; or in this respect: just as a dove, troubled by some annoyance, flies away from its nest, yet does not go far but circles around it, so I, even if I withdraw my body from them, do not withdraw my affection.

Or “like a dove,” so that I may be like that dove which, sent out from the ark, did not wish to remain in muddy places but returned to the ark (Genesis 8), where it found rest. Thus I, unwilling to remain in the muddy hearts of the Jews, will pass over to the nations, among whom I shall rest, because there I shall find humility and gentleness.

“Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble and gentle, and upon him who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66).

Wings are called *pennae* from *pendere*, “to hang”; a dove is so called as though it were a nursling of the house, that is, domesticated, according to Isidore.

“And having taken wings, I shall fly and rest.” Or: I shall ascend into heaven and sit there at the right hand of the Father. Or: I shall depart from the Jews through my preachers and rest among the nations, because, having become immortal and impassible, I was better able to come to the knowledge of the nations than when mortal.

Who will give me this, except myself? No one. And because I am weak in respect of my humanity but powerful in respect of my divinity, behold. He is saying, as it were: This shows that I took wings by my own power, not another’s, because “I withdrew far away,” fleeing from the muddy hearts of the Jews, and “I remained in solitude,” that is, in the hearts of the Gentiles, who were unproductive and uncultivated in regard to the law, the writings of the prophets, and the examples of the patriarchs.

Or: Behold, I have done what I wished. And rightly I was able to do this, because “I was waiting for him who saved me from faintness of spirit and storm.” As the Lord’s human being, fulfilling obedience with patience, I did not act hastily but waited for him—that is, for the Word personally united to me—who finally saved me because I waited for him.

He saved me “from faintness of spirit,” that is, from weakness, as happened in Peter and the other disciples, who, previously fainthearted, were strengthened after Christ’s flight—that is, after his ascension. And he saved me “from my storm,” that is, from the most savage persecution.

In this Christ gives his members an example of life and shows what they should do when they labor greatly among their subjects and make little progress: they should flee either bodily to some secluded place, or inwardly to a tranquil dwelling of the mind. Since they cannot benefit them by laboring and preaching, they may benefit them by praying, lest by associating with such people they fall into hatred, which has been forbidden them, as it is said: “Love your enemies” (Matthew 5).

And you, Lord, who saved me from the storm of the Jews because they turned their iniquities upon me, “hurl them down and divide their tongues.”

Here he touches upon three stories: the drowning that occurred in the time of Noah (Genesis 7); the division of tongues that occurred during the building of the tower (Genesis 11); and the swallowing up of Dathan and Abiram, who despised Aaron, the priest appointed by the Lord through the hand of Moses their brother. They took a censer and began to sacrifice in the tabernacle; but the earth opened and swallowed Dathan and Abiram, the leaders of that impiety. The remaining multitude who consented with them was consumed by fire coming from heaven (Numbers 16).

He does not say this as a wish, but as prophecy and as rejoicing in the divine judgment.

“O Lord, because they rose up against you, hurl them down from the dignity and height of their kingdom and priesthood. Let them be plunged into the depth of misery; let them be led into captivity and servitude among the nations.”

“And divide their tongues”: that is, let them be scattered among the nations with various languages, so that, although they are now of one language, they may become of many.

Or “divide their tongues”: let them be blinded and divided inwardly. “Some say, ‘He is good’; others, ‘No, but he deceives the crowds’” (John 7).

Divide them in this way: those who believe that they are saved through the promises—that is, through carnal observances—should not possess the things that fulfill them. Those who believe that they are to receive only the priesthood according to the order of Aaron should receive the enduring priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek, and thus finally possess neither.

For now they do none of these things according to the law. And this is not surprising, because the old cannot be fulfilled without the new: in the old are the things that promise, in the new the things that fulfill. Nor is blame in this matter to be cast back upon the author.

“For I saw iniquity and contradiction in the city.” They are worthy of this punishment, because they are citizens and do not live as citizens; therefore they ought to perish more grievously. A city is an assembly of human beings for living according to law. The Jews, in comparison with the nations, were citizens because they had received the law, which ought to have gathered them for living according to law.

In this city there was iniquity in action, corresponding to what he said, “Hurl them down”: all their works were against the Lord. There was contradiction in words, corresponding to what he said, “Divide them.”

And these things are not found only in that city, but in all the greater and lesser parts of it. Nor are they present only for a time. “By day and night,” that is, continually, “iniquity will surround it upon its walls.” It will surround it—that is, embrace the multitude of that people, which is its defense like a wall—so thoroughly that iniquity will be above those walls, rising above the head, that is, above their mind.

They are so blind that they do nothing by reason or law. Elsewhere it says: “And upon its summit its iniquity will descend” (Psalm 7).

“And in its midst”: that is, among the leading men, who are like bones placed in the middle. “Labor”—that is, oppression of subjects—and “justice”—that is, unjust judgments. Of them it is said: “Woe to you who justify the impious for gifts and take away the justice of the just from him” (Isaiah 5).

Or “upon its walls iniquity”: that is, upon the rulers who fortify it. “Labor”: war and sedition. And this is because there is injustice there.

Or “upon its walls iniquity”: that is, upon the guardianship of angels, so that the iniquity may be greater than the angelic guardianship. The good have guardian angels, but the wicked repel every guardianship from themselves.

“And in its midst,” that is, in the common people, among both rulers and populace, there are “labor and injustice,” that is, laborious injustice.

Or: they exceed proper measure in building walls, and by their zeal for wickedness surpass the walls themselves.

He shows in part what sort of injustice it is: “And usury has not failed from its streets.” In public they practice usury, which is utterly depraved. Every evil becomes more execrable when it is practiced with public presumption.

“And deceit,” that is, circumvention and fraud.

Or “from its streets,” that is, from its rulers. The comparison is this: just as we walk through streets, so the life and conduct of a ruler are an example to be imitated. From those streets that worst usury has not ceased—the person who practices it sings the Lord’s Prayer in vain, since he takes vengeance more grievously than the offense deserves, as when he responds to a blow with homicide.

And if they do not dare to do this openly, they do it deceitfully. Therefore, Lord, “hurl them down; divide their tongues,” because they live unjustly and must especially be guarded against. For no plague is more effective for doing harm than a familiar enemy.

“For if an enemy,” that is, an open enemy, had cursed me, I would surely have endured it. What is proved acceptable does indeed seem more tolerable than what is received unexpectedly. If that enemy who is not a citizen, who worships idols, had cursed me by denying his own right to his Creator, I would surely have endured it—that is, I would have spared him the present punishment, because what had not been foretold to that people would seem bearable.

“And if the one who hated me,” openly, who did not pretend to be a citizen, had spoken great things against me by contradicting me, “I might perhaps have hidden myself from him.” Perhaps—that is, I would truly have withdrawn myself from him in order thus to appease him. Or I might have hidden myself from the punishment by concealing his sin.

“But you, Jewish man”—that is, rational in comparison with the Gentiles—who have named themselves, according to the likeness; or who ought to have been of one mind; “my leader,” whom I appointed for this purpose, that you might be the leader and teacher of others, instructed through the law; “and my acquaintance,” according to kinship, who used to take sweet foods with me—that is, who used to receive the sweet commandments of God with me in the synagogue.

For Christ himself is also read to have received the book in the synagogue and read from it (Luke 4). “Together,” that is, at the same time, “we walked in the house of God with agreement,” that is, united, we attended the sacrifices in the house of God.

Where are you leading me by your crime? Certainly to say this: “Let death come upon them.”

Here he touches upon the third story. Just as fire killed those who consented with Dathan and Abiram, the leaders (Numbers 16), so let the incentives of vices devastate the lesser members of these people. And let their rulers descend alive into hell—that is, knowingly let them descend into the depths of vices.

Of them it is said: “Woe to you who have the keys of knowledge: you yourselves do not enter, nor do you permit others to enter” (Luke 11).

As the earth swallowed Dathan and Abiram alive, so let them descend, and deservedly, “because there were iniquities in their dwellings,” that is, in their body, which they contaminated by the work of iniquity; “and in their midst,” that is, in their heart.

Alternatively, in a good sense:

“O Lord, because they are citizens, because that people is my leader and my acquaintance, let death come upon them. ‘Turn the impious, and they shall be no more’” (Proverbs 12).

“And let them descend alive into hell,” that is, let them recognize their sins and erase them, so that they may be living. And this is necessary because there are iniquities in their dwellings and in their midst: they have contaminated their flesh and heart by the work of iniquity.

Everywhere an example of life is commended to us in our Head, and he shows what rulers ought to do when their subjects remain uncorrected.

Those who live in this manner will perish by a threefold condemnation. Or: these people contradict me and hate me without cause. But I did not resist them or curse them; instead, I cried out to God—that is, I directed my whole intention toward God—for perseverance. As though he were saying: You too should act in this way in such a matter.

“And he saved me as I cried out in the evening, in the morning, and at noon.” In the Passion, which began in the evening, he saved me by giving patience; in the morning he saved me by giving resurrection—the resurrection which occurred while it was still dark; and at noon he saved me by the ascension, which occurred at that time.

And in my members I shall recount my patience in the evening and announce the life of the resurrection in the morning. “And at noon he will hear my voice.” Just as he glorified me at noon, so also at noon he will glorify my members—that is, in the general resurrection, when there will be the greatest splendor of the true sun. He will hear me by glorifying them.

Or “evening and morning,” that is, in prosperity, because then the air is temperate: “I shall recount and announce,” namely, that one must cry out to the Lord. And “at noon,” that is, in adversity, because then the air is hottest. In this way he will hear.

Augustine says:

“And you, announce in the evening the patience of the one who dies, in the morning the glory of the one who rises, and at noon the eternity of the one who sits with the Father. There, interceding for his own, he will hear this voice of mine:”

“He will redeem my soul in peace”—in peace, so that he may give me love both for those who are within and for those who are outside. “He will redeem my soul in peace”: he will redeem my life from mortality and suffering, in a peace that will never admit the opposite. “My” in reality, now “of my people” in hope; or in such great peace that I will even love my enemies.

“From those who draw near to me.” And because “drawing near” can also be understood in a good sense, he determines how they will draw near. Or: he will separate me from them because, although they were many, they were with me here—that is, because here they were mixed with mine like chaff with grain, which is numerous in comparison with the grain.

Or according to another translation: “Among many they were with me,” and in this way they draw near. For they were with me in baptism, in the Gospel, and in the festivals; in a few things they were not with me. But in those few things in which they were not with me, the many things in which they were with me do not benefit them. He says this so that no one may despair. For if they wished to be changed—that is, converted—they would certainly be saved.

These many things are those mentioned by the Apostle: “If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels,” and so forth, up to “but do not have love, I am nothing” (1 Corinthians 13). Those things are greater in number; this is greater in weight. Therefore they were with me in all these sacraments, but not with me in love.

Truly he will redeem my soul from them, because he will exalt me and cast them down. God will hear me, exalting me because I have been humbled, and in the end he will humble those who have been exalted here. And he can do this because he exists before the ages—the Word personally united to me, whom they thought mortal.

Therefore they will finally be humbled because “there is no change for them.” They do not wish to be changed from death to life, because they trample upon the blood of the Just One, in which that change was accomplished.

Or they will be humbled because then there will be no change for them. “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Corinthians 15), because the impious will indeed be immortal, but they will remain subject to suffering.

And deservedly this will happen to them, because they did not fear God, whom they condemned as though he were a human being—that is, me. Therefore “he stretched out his hand” in repaying, that is, he will repay them greatly, both here and in the future. He shows this by saying:

“They contaminated his covenant.” He permitted them to contaminate the law by attending only to the promises and not to the fulfillments, receiving the Old and not receiving the New—that is, receiving the sacrifice according to the order of Aaron and rejecting that of Melchizedek. This concerns the Jews.

But if the passage concerns heretics: they contaminated the covenant of God by a perverse understanding of the sacred Scriptures. Or in this way: “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed.” He does not say “and to seeds,” as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: “and to your seed,” who is Christ (Galatians 3).

The covenant was therefore promised in this Christ: “In your seed all the nations will be blessed.” You, heretic, who have abandoned the unity of all nations and remained in a part, have contaminated his covenant.

In this way the Jews also contaminated the law of God, because they were divided in that covenant, separating the Old from the New: receiving the former and rejecting the latter; receiving the sacrifice according to the order of Aaron and rejecting the sacrifice according to the order of Melchizedek.

Or: heretics were divided from the unity of the Church, in which there is one faith and one baptism.

“Or they were divided,” that is, they will be separated from those who do not contaminate the covenant, like chaff from grain, whether they are Jews or false Christians.

“From the anger of his face,” that is, from the anger of his just judgment, which will be made manifest in the face—that is, in the presence—of God.

Or “they will be divided,” that is, separated, “from the anger of his face,” from his angry countenance. “Let the impious be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isaiah 26).

Or they were divided, as has been said: the Jews in the covenant, or heretics in the sacred Scriptures.

“From the anger of his face”: that is, they were blinded inwardly by the hidden anger of God, which is in his face, even if it is not in human faces.

“And his heart drew near.” When blindness occurred in Israel, his heart drew near—that is, the will of God drew near, so that the fullness of the nations might enter. Or, among heretics divided from sound understanding, or among Jews who did not receive the New Testament and said: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” (John 6).

They thought that Christ’s flesh ought to be cut into pieces and eaten in a sacrilegious manner, when Christ said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood” (ibid.). When they went away backward, his heart drew near—that is, his will, which was to be understood spiritually in those sacred words, drew near among those who did not contaminate his covenant.

And it drew near in this way:

“His words were made soft above oil,” that is, they became penetrable and were softened from the hardness which those people understood when they said: “This saying is hard.” This is like Peter, who spoke on behalf of the other disciples: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (ibid.).

“The spirit gives life, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26): that is, your words, understood spiritually, give life; understood carnally, they bring death.

“Above oil,” that is, more penetrating than oil, which reaches even to the bones. The words of God, however, reach to the marrow of hearts.

Or, concerning heretics who contaminate the covenant of God and divide themselves from the unity of the catholic faith: “His heart drew near,” because the divine intentions hidden in the Scriptures, previously left unexamined, became manifest. Many were stirred to investigate the sacred Scriptures, according to the Apostle: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved among you may become manifest” (1 Corinthians 11).

“His words were made soft,” that is, understood, “and they themselves are arrows.” As though he were saying: Although they are soft, they are nevertheless arrows for refuting false brothers against heretical perversity; they pierce the hearts of enemies, kindle in them the fire of divine love, kill the persecutor, and awaken the disciple.

Therefore, because the Lord has heard me, following my example, “cast your care upon the Lord”: throw all your anxiety upon him. Do not contaminate his covenant, and he will nourish you in his words, so that you may advance from virtue to virtue. And to you, the just one, “he will not give fluctuation forever.”

Even if he gives you disturbance of mind for a time, he will not allow it to remain forever, just as it did not remain in Peter.

Alternatively: “Cast your care upon the Lord.” It is as though he were saying: His words have been made soft; and, O Christian, if they are still hard for you, do not despise them and do not turn aside into unbelief. They are hard for you because you still need to be nourished with milk.

“Cast your care upon the Lord, and he will not give fluctuation forever to the just,” because he will be a harbor of salvation for you.

“But you, God, will lead them down into the pit of destruction.” As though he were saying: But those who do not wish to cast their care upon you—you, who must necessarily be the judge—will lead them from the darkness of dreams into the darkness of torments.

“Men of blood and deceit will not divide their days.”

If this is referred to the Jews, it is joined in this way to what precedes. Someone might say: Will the things prescribed by the law not benefit them? No. For those men of blood—that is, the killers of Christ—not only committed the deed but also, through a perverse understanding of the law of God, destroyed themselves and others. They “will not divide their days,” that is, they will not separate their times; they will not separate the Old Testament from the New, believing that the former should be observed and the latter not.

For the two are joined: the former contain the promises, the latter the fulfillments. Whoever wishes to follow one without the other possesses neither.

Or this may concern all, both Jews and Gentiles. As though he were saying: Truly you will lead them into the pit of destruction, because men of blood, pouring out the blood of souls and bodies, and men of deceit, that is, deceiving their brothers in their dealings, “will not divide their days,” that is, they will not separate these days from the eternal days, thinking that there is no life except this one.

Or in this way they will not divide them: they will not serve God now and Mammon now, alternately. “You cannot serve two masters” (Matthew 6), says the divine word; this cannot occur at the same time.

Gregory says: “They will by no means divide their days, because they will not change their perverse mind even at the end.”

Cassiodorus says: “He says that such people do not complete their days because, while they promise themselves a long life, sudden destruction will overtake them. For everyone’s days are known to have been fixed in predestination.”

“But I, the Head and the members, shall divide them.” And why? “For I shall hope in you, Lord.” I shall cast my care upon you, and therefore they will be led down into the pit of destruction.

## PSALM 55

**For the end; for the people that has been made far from the holy ones; in the inscription of the title; to David himself; when the foreigners held him in Geth.**

[Col. 0421A]

“Have mercy on me, O God, for man has trampled me down; all day long, attacking, he has afflicted me. My enemies have trampled me down all day long, for many wage war against me. From the height of the day I shall fear; but I shall hope in you. In God I shall praise my words; in God I have hoped; I shall not fear what flesh may do to me. All day long they cursed my words; all their thoughts against me are for evil. They will dwell and hide themselves; they will watch my heel. As they have waited for my soul, for nothing you will save them; in anger you will break peoples. [Col. 0421B] O God, I have declared my life to you; you have set my tears in your sight. As also in your promise, then my enemies will turn back. On whatever day I call upon you, behold, I have known that you are my God. In God I shall praise the word; in the Lord I shall praise the saying. In God I have hoped; I shall not fear what man may do to me. O God, your vows are upon me, which I shall repay to you as praises. For you have delivered my soul from death and my feet from slipping, that I may please God in the light of the living.”

## EXPOSITION

### Construction of the title

What is treated in this psalm is referred to the end of the ages, so that it should not be understood as history; that is, it is to be assigned to the fullness of times, to David—the Head and body, that is, to Christ, the true David. Then, when the foreigners—that is, aliens, or the Jews falling through drink, and those like them, namely unbelievers, intoxicated by the sweet fortune of this life—held him in Geth, that is, in the winepress, namely in affliction, lest the world should go after him: it was made for the people, that is, for the instruction of the people, that God might deliver him from that people which has been made far from the holy ones by the inscription of the title.

[Col. 0421C]

This is the title which Pilate wrote above the head of Jesus, written in three languages, as though confirmed by three witnesses: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.” All who humbly receive Jesus as king and live under that king receive this title. But those who do not wish to have Christ as king are made far from the holy ones by the inscription of this title—those who said to Pilate: “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews,’ but that he himself said, ‘I am King of the Jews’” (John 19). To them Pilate unknowingly offered testimony to the truth, saying: “What I have written, I have written.” As though he said: “Why do you suggest falsehood to me? I do not change the truth.”

The people made far from the holy ones is chiefly the Jewish people, which says that it has no king but Caesar; secondly, it is every people which, for the sake of an earthly kingdom, does not permit God to reign in it. A king is earthly in relation to earthly things and heavenly in relation to heavenly things. Nor did they sin in calling Caesar king, but in rejecting Christ the King. Those who do not wish to have him as king persecute his body, that is, the Church.

[Col. 0422A]

We are with Christ in heaven through hope; he is with us on earth through love, he who is daily brought forth in his members until the consummation of the age. He was already sitting in heaven when on earth he said: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9). In this psalm we are commanded to endure these persecutors and to flee to prayer. Properly, however, those are made far from the holy ones who are so in heart, not in body.

David is indeed read to have sojourned among the foreigners when fleeing Saul, not to have been held by them; nor is any inscription of the title of that David read. This recalls us from history to mystery, so that we may understand Christ in David, whom the foreigners not only held but still hold in Geth. For as long as the body of Christ is in this life, it is held in Geth—that is, in the winepress, namely in afflictions—by those who are far from Christ.

[Col. 0422B]

In the winepress, however, pressure becomes useful. Whatever pressures the saints suffer from various persons are useful, for they produce testing. Therefore let those who are in afflictions attend to this psalm, though the voice is not confined to those who are outside suffering. It is the voice of Christ, especially in the person of the members.

Attend, O Christian, to the psalm: when you are pressed, do not refuse the pressure; but, that it may become useful to you, flee to prayer, be one, and you will flow as wine worthy of the king’s cup.

Have mercy on me, O God, for I am oppressed in Geth—both the head and the members—that this oppression may become an occasion of testing, not of destruction. And this is necessary, because man has trampled me, everyone who has become distant from the saints. [Col. 0422C] How grievous and shameful is the oppression that presses me, since he even tramples me underfoot. He alludes to the title, where it says, “In the winepress.” “Me” means my members; and this is not for a time, but “all day,” that is, throughout this present life, he has afflicted me by living wickedly and rejecting instruction.

But you, Christian, do not lose heart under the trampling; attend to whom you should invoke. For Christ was like the first grape in the winepress: he was in tribulation, and from that grape flowed the cup that gives intoxication. “All day,” that is, throughout the whole period. Let no one therefore say, “There was tribulation before, but now there is none.” If you are not afflicted, you are not a Christian.

“My enemies have trampled me all day.” Since he said “man,” lest anyone understand only one individual, he determines what he means by “man”: all those who are members of the man who is the devil, concerning whom it is said, “[Col. 0422D] An enemy has done this” (Matt. XIII). The members of the devil always strive to trample the members of Christ. “All day,” that is, throughout this present life.

“And they are many who fight against me.” They fight because they fall short of the height of the day—that is, of the knowledge of the majesty of that day whose twelve hours are the twelve apostles (John XI). That day, hidden on high, has not been recognized by the people who have become distant from the saints.

“But shall I fear that height, so that I may be judged by it?” No; rather, they will fear it, according to one translation, and not I, because I will hope in you—whether in the height of that day or from the height of your day. It is as though he said: My enemies are both many and high, that is, powerful; [Col. 0423A] but shall I fear them because of their multitude or their height, when their power belongs to the day, that is, is temporal and quickly passing, like a single day? The implied answer is: No.

And he adds the reason. But I, as one who is just, gentle, and devout, hope in you, who are just, gentle, and devout.

Or: “I shall fear the height of the day,” so that I may fail under the burden at midday, like those who carry in the morning and afterward grow faint. “I,” however, will not; rather, they will fear the height of the day, that is, the true sun coming to judgment.

And so that I may be able to hope, “in God I will praise the Word,” that is, the Son coeternal with the Father. “I will praise”—I will not be like those who do not want him as king, but despise him as though he were merely a man. “In the Lord I will praise the sayings,” that is, the preaching made about him, or all the sayings.

[Col. 0423B] “For you will either regard your sayings as false, and therefore call them yours; or, if they are true, and if you think that you have them from God rather than from yourself, they will be true, but you will be a liar.”

Alternatively: Those who now are proud and now are high will eventually fear. In the meantime I will be careful to fear, lest I be forced to despair of you. And in that hope I will not be idle, but I will perform the duty of one who hopes, because, existing in God, I will “praise my sayings,” that is, I will make them praiseworthy, both by the dignity of a good life and by truth. He makes his sayings praiseworthy who first acts well and then preaches, in accordance with: “What Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I).

And therefore I do not say only, “I will hope,” but, “I have always hoped in God”; and therefore I will not fear what flesh may do to me—that is, what the carnal person may do, who quickly passes away and quickly perishes.

[Col. 0423C] He had earlier said, “Have mercy on me, O God, because man has trampled me.” How then does he now say, “I will not fear what flesh may do to me”? There he looked to the cultivation of the vine; here he looks ahead to the wine that flows from it. Therefore: “I will not fear what flesh may do to me,” because flesh can do nothing except to flesh.

And what does flesh do? “All day,” that is, continually, “they were cursing my words.” Here it becomes clear that one person is speaking. They blaspheme my words, which are praiseworthy in you—words that I call mine, yet in such a way that they have been given by you.

Augustine: “Ask, and you will not be empty; confess what is yours, and you will not be ungrateful.”

“All their thoughts are against me.” It is as though he said: They are not only voices against me, but all their thoughts as well. But since their thoughts could be against him and nevertheless for the good, he adds, “for evil.”

[Col. 0423D] He shows how all their thoughts are for evil: “They will inhabit.” Some of them will pretend to inhabit with me, receiving baptism in the Church and accepting the Christian name, like Judas, who was a false brother and belonged to the number of the disciples. “And they will hide”—they will conceal their deceits in their hearts and prepare ambushes, like false brothers who entered to spy out our freedom.

He shows how they will hide: “They will watch my heel,” that is, my fall in word or deed, so that they may have something for which to accuse me. Thus they will watch: “As they have held my soul”—that is, in the manner of those for whom my soul, meaning my life, was burdensome and troublesome to behold. For “whoever loves darkness hates the light” (John III).

Cassiodorus: “[Col. 0424A] Truly, for evil: an inward evil, an incurable wound, because the more it is covered, the more it is injured by incurable putrefaction.”

Or, according to another translation: “My soul has endured.” The meaning is: My soul endured even those false brothers, saying to me: “Bear with them; pray for them.”

“You will save them for nothing,” that is, without labor or freely. By this he teaches that such people are to be tolerated. God chose eleven disciples for testing, so that by imitating them we might be led to perfection; eleven for temptation, which is useful to the faithful. “For nothing,” that is, without their preceding merits, he will save them—as the thief who went from robbery to judgment, from judgment to the cross, and from the cross to paradise.

Alternatively: “As they have held my soul.” But I also prayed for them, knowing this: “You will save them for nothing,” that is, easily. Or: My life was burdensome to them, and this was not to their detriment, because you, O God, will save them—that is, you will raise them from death—but “for nothing,” that is, for no benefit of theirs. “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. XV).

[Col. 0424B] And truly for no benefit of theirs, because in the anger they deserved you will crush them with a double crushing.

Or this may be understood for the good: “In anger you will crush the peoples,” by emptying out wickedness and granting grace. For they will be terrified in anger, afflicted by tribulations, strengthened by faith, and saved by grace. In this way you will crush them; in this way you will save them: because I have announced my life to them—how foul and perverse it formerly was, but now how beautiful and holy through your grace—and I attribute this to you, not to myself, [Col. 0424C] so that I may be an example to them of repentance, in accordance with the Apostle, who says: “Though formerly I was a persecutor and a blasphemer, I have now obtained mercy, so that in me he might display the riches of his mercy” (1 Tim. I).

We do not announce our life to God so that he may come to know it, but so that, attending to our humility, he may forgive us. “I announced my life to them,” the life that I first announced to you.

“And you placed my tears”—that is, my tearful prayers—“in your sight,” that is, you heard them. This is also in accordance with your promise, for you promised: “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. XXXIII).

But if “in anger you will crush the peoples” is taken in the evil sense, then “O God, my life” is joined to what precedes in this way: “They will inhabit and hide. Yet I announced my life,” that is, I set myself before them as an example of a good life.

[Col. 0424D] If we read it as spoken in the person of the head, “O God, my life,” as with the other words up to this point, although some things are spoken concerning the members, we shall say it in the same way: “They will inhabit and hide. But I, O God, announced my life to them,” that is, I set it before them for imitation, for your honor.

“And you placed my tears”—that is, the tearful prayers made for my members—“in your sight,” as also in your promise. For you said: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII).

“Then,” that is, after my life has been announced to them, “my enemies will turn back,” so that those who formerly wished to go ahead may imitate me.

“And in that turning I recognized that you are my God”—the God of all by nature, mine by grace. You made yourself my possessor; you made me your possession. And not only now, but “on whatever day I call upon you.”

[Col. 0425A] And because you made me your possession, “in God I will praise the Word.” I will not be like those who do not want to have the Son of God as king. I will praise him—that is, I will show by faith and works that the Son is praiseworthy—in God, that is, in the majesty of God the Father.

“In the Lord I will praise my saying.” If it is true, it is from him. “I hoped in God,” and therefore I will not fear what man may do to me. For man can do nothing except what man can do to the body; but as for the soul, the one who is merely man can do nothing. Rather, I will fear the one who can cast both soul and body into Gehenna (Matt. X).

And in all these things I will fulfill my vows; I will not be ungrateful. But those vows are yours, because “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (James I).

[Col. 0425B] And I will not receive those vows, those sacrifices, outside myself, but where no enemy can take them away: “In me are your vows, O God,” which I will repay to you—that is, praises. If we wish to sacrifice to God, let us not seek outside ourselves what we wish to offer. In us is the incense of praise, the sacrifice of faith; whatever we offer, let it be kindled with love.

“For you have rescued my soul from death.” This is the life that he announced to them. I was dead; through you I live. In me are the vows of praise that I will repay to you. I love my God; no one takes him away from me. You have rescued my soul from the death of unbelief, or from the death of vices.

“And my feet”—that is, all my affections—from falling; or “feet,” that is, works.

“So that I may please before the Lord in the light of the living,” so that, walking before God, I may please him in the light—that is, in Christ, who is the light that enlightens every person coming into this world (John I).

Or “in the light of the living”: the light of living believers is that they worship God freely; or the light of the living is prudence, just as the darkness of the foolish is stupidity.

[Col. 0425C] If someone wishes to read the whole psalm in the voice of the head, he will say as follows:

“They will all curse my words and watch my heel, since they were those who held my soul, that is, those for whom my life was burdensome to behold. And because my life was a burden to them, and therefore they inflicted upon me the evils mentioned above, you will save them for nothing,” that is, without any preceding merit of theirs. Mercy alone will save them by forgiving their sins.

[Col. 0425D] Or: Just as they regarded my life as a burden for nothing—that is, undeservedly—so you will save them for nothing—that is, without merit. In this the greatest mercy of God is perceived.

And when you reach this point, so that you may save them, “you will crush the peoples,” that is, the vices of the peoples, “in your anger,” that is, in consideration of your future anger, in this order:

“O God, I announced my life to you; you placed my tears in your sight,” that is, those who are to become mine will announce their life to you, and you placed my tears in your sight—that is, those for whom I shed tears, as he wept at the tomb of Lazarus (John XI), not for Lazarus, but because of what Lazarus’s death signified.

“In your sight,” that is, in the good pleasure of your presence. “As also in your promise,” that is, as you promised and I promised; this is also indicated by “etc.”

[Col. 0426A] “Then,” that is, in that announcement of their life, “those who were my enemies will turn back,” so that they may become followers.

“On whatever day I call upon you.” Let no one say that this turning concerns only those who were converted in the primitive Church immediately after the resurrection. “On whatever day”—whether in the primitive Church or in the Church that followed—my people will call upon you.

Behold, all of them will immediately recognize through experience that you are their God, that is, one who acts mercifully toward them.

“In God I will praise the Word; in the Lord I will praise the saying.” After they have recognized that you are a God gracious toward them, they will make their writings, which they will send to the churches, praiseworthy; or they will make their preaching in the assembly of the faithful praiseworthy, and likewise their own discourse which they direct to someone; or “the Word,” that is, your Son, as above.

[Col. 0426B] Here the Trinity may be indicated: “in God,” “in the Lord,” “in God”; the rest is as above.

## PSALM LVI  
### TO THE END: “DO NOT DESTROY”; OF DAVID; IN THE INSCRIPTION OF THE TITLE; WHEN HE FLED FROM THE FACE OF SAUL INTO THE CAVE

> “Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me, because my soul has trusted in you. And in the shadow of your wings I will hope, until iniquity passes away. I will cry to God Most High, to God who has done good to me. He sent from heaven and delivered me; he gave those who trample me over to reproach. God sent his mercy and his truth, and he rescued my soul from the midst of lion cubs; I slept troubled. The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue is a sharp sword. Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory throughout all the earth. [Col. 0426C] They prepared a snare for my feet and bent down my soul. They dug a pit before my face and fell into it. My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and recite a psalm to the Lord. Rise up, my glory; rise up, psaltery and lyre; I will rise at dawn. I will confess to you among the peoples, O Lord, and recite a psalm to you among the nations. For your mercy has been magnified even to the heavens, and your truth even to the clouds. Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory above all the earth.”

## COMMENTARY

Christ is our head. Just as he suffered in order to teach his own to suffer in this life, and rose again in order to give the hope of rising again, so he also prayed in order to teach them to pray, as in this psalm, in which he intimates the measure of love.

[Col. 0426D] For it agrees with the words of the Gospel in which it is said: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John XV). For if you fail beneath the commandment, his example strengthens you. But if the example seems difficult to you, begin, and the one who gave the commandment will also help you.

This is the title. These words are referred “to the end,” that is, to the one toward whom all the just strive, and once he has been attained nothing further is desired—that is, to Christ. They were established for this purpose: that each believer may will, “Do not destroy the inscription of the title of David,” by withdrawing yourself from his dominion and denying him the kingship over you—which nevertheless he possesses, whether you wish it or not—like the Jews who said: “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke XIX), and, “We have no king but Caesar” (ibid.).

[Col. 0427A] Although that title had been written in three languages, as though confirmed by three witnesses, they said to Pilate: “Do not write, ‘The King of the Jews,’ but that he himself said, ‘I am the King of the Jews.’” He replied to them: “What I have written, I have written” (John XIX). It was as though he were saying: “Why do you suggest falsehood to me? I am not corrupting the truth, because this has been ordained from the ages and cannot be changed.” Truly he is king. If human beings do not want him as king, the angels nevertheless have him as such.

I say that the inscription was made at the time when David fled spiritually into the cave. David, fleeing Saul, hid in a cave: humble, gentle, and devout, fleeing from one who was proud, harsh, and impious. In that cave he also cut off part of Saul’s cloak as testimony that he could have killed him (1 Sam. XXIV).

[Col. 0427B] So also Christ, whom the pride and impiety of the Jews persecuted, hid from the Jews’ knowledge in human nature as though in a cave. He wished to be seen so that he would not be recognized, and not to be recognized so that he would be despised. He walked secretly among human beings, doing divine things and enduring human things, until he was suspended on the cross; or when he lay hidden in the tomb. For who pursued him there? Since no history is read concerning a title of David that is attached here, this draws us toward the mystery.

“Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me.”

Augustine: “He who, together with the Father, has mercy on you cries out in you, ‘Have mercy on me.’”

[Col. 0427C] This is the voice of Christ the head. “Have mercy on me,” Christ hidden in the cave, by raising me and bringing me forth into the knowledge of the nations; have mercy on my members in me, O God, that is, you who are able to do so. And you ought to, because “my soul has trusted in you”—and the same is indicated concerning my members by the prefix *con-*.

I say that it has trusted, and I will always trust. “And in the shadow of your wings I will hope,” that is, under the protection of the two Testaments, or in the twofold love; or, under the protection of your mercies, protect me from the cold of abounding iniquity. This is a metaphor drawn from birds.

“Until iniquity passes away,” that is, throughout this present life. For just as, when the just depart, others always succeed them, so in this life, when the wicked depart, others succeed them.

And rightly I will hope, because “I will cry out” in myself and in my members, as one ought to cry out, because the fervor of love is the cry of the heart. My heart will always burn with this heat.

“To God Most High,” who hears no one unless he cries out. Because he is Most High, one must not attend to this with relaxed hands or weakened knees. He is Most High and near: God far away, God near at hand.

[Col. 0427D] The exhibition of past deeds gives hope for future ones: “Salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. CXVIII); “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart” (Ps. XXXIII). And this gives great hope, because “I will cry to God who has already done good to me.” For “if, when we were enemies” (Rom. V), he did good to us, how much more now.

“He sent from heaven and delivered me.” Here Christ speaks in his human nature. God the Father sent from heaven, that is, from the seat of his majesty, not an angel, not an archangel, not any subordinate creature, as though to one in need of mercy, but he sent the Son, who serves everyone who asks.

[Col. 0428A] Therefore he sent his Word, concerning whom it is said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John I). And he delivered me from mortality and susceptibility to suffering, from the trampling of the Jews; and in my deliverance he also delivered my members in hope.

“But he gave those who trample me over to reproach,” namely, the Jews, who trampled the blood of the righteous and held it in contempt. This was a great reproach, because they lost the kingdom and priesthood in which they especially gloried. They were expelled from that great city in which they killed the Lord; and, taken captive at the same Paschal solemnity, they were scattered throughout the world and became the book-carriers of the Christians, because they preserve the books of the Law and the Prophets, by which the gentiles may be convicted and the faithful built up.

[Col. 0428B] They have become like a blind man who possesses a mirror but does not see himself in it, while offering it to others for seeing. And at last he will give them eternal reproach, making them like those who trample Christ in his members.

But what he sent, he adds: “God sent his mercy,” that is, his Word, who has compassion on human weakness. “And his truth,” and through him he sent the true knowledge of himself, by which he is known in heavenly things, so that human beings also might recognize him.

“And he rescued my soul,” that is, my life and the life of my members in me, “from the midst of lion cubs”—that is, from the common judgment of the lions, namely, the rulers of the Jews, and of the lion cubs, namely, the Jewish populace, which, by consenting to the cruelty of the rulers, became like lion cubs.

And it was necessary that he rescue it, because “I slept,” that is, I laid down my soul. But because “to sleep” is ambiguous, he determines that this is to be understood of the sleep of death by adding, “troubled.”

[Col. 0428C] “Who troubled you?” “The sons of men,” that is, the sons of the patriarchs and prophets according to the flesh, not according to imitation.

“With what weapons?” Do not attend to hands that are inactive; attend to the armed mouth, because “their teeth are weapons.” “He is guilty of death” (Matt. XXVI). “Teeth,” that is, biting words. “And arrows,” that is, hidden counsels: “Let us kill him, lest the world go after him” (John XII). “And their tongue,” that is, the sentence of death, “is a sharp sword”: “Crucify, crucify” (John XIX).

But what concern is it of mine what they plot against me? “Be exalted above the heavens, O God.” Exalt me, a human being, above angels and archangels, or above patriarchs and prophets, so that through me, your exalted Son, you, O exalted and glorious God, may be exalted.

[Col. 0428D] “And your glory”—the glory of the resurrection, from which you will be glorified—“will be exalted above all the earth.” The Jews did not want to give you glory in Judea; but manifest your glory throughout the whole world, even if not over straw, nevertheless over grain.

This was inserted exultantly; now he returns to the previous subject:

“The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows. They prepared a snare for my feet”—that is, they prepared impediments to my affection and purpose, which was that I should rise again and that the world should go after me. But they killed me, placed me in the tomb, and secured the tomb with guards.

Or, according to Cassiodorus: [Col. 0429A]

> “For my feet,” that is, for my rebuke and my promise, because by these feet I walk throughout the world into the knowledge of human beings. Rebuke concerns past or present things; promise concerns future things.

Or “my feet” means the apostles.

“And they bent down my soul,” that is, they humbled it in their estimation; or, they pressed it down by death and attempted to cast it down from heaven.

“They dug a pit before my face,” lest I should prosper; they secretly prepared death for me, as though I were unaware. But “before my face” means in my presence, since I knew and was not ignorant of their counsels.

“And they themselves fell into it,” not I, because my death was their blindness; or, they fell into eternal death.

[Col. 0429B] By these words he strengthens us, as though saying: What could those who persecuted me do to me? They condemned themselves instead. So they can do nothing to you either.

It is as though he said: They prepare a pit for me as though I were ignorant and unwilling. But “my heart is ready, O God,” for the experience of death; I obey voluntarily. “My heart is also ready,” that is, the hearts of my members, to offer you a sacrifice. Therefore “I will sing with my heart and recite a psalm in deed to the Lord,” that is, I will offer the Lord honor.

Or: “My heart is ready” because in this way I will be a song to you, that is, a delight.

And so that I may sing, “Rise up, my glory.” O my body, now my disgrace, made my glory through immortality and freedom from suffering, rise from the tomb. You are, I say, “psaltery and lyre”: doing divine things, you are the psaltery; enduring human things, the lyre.

In one instrument there are two instruments.

[Col. 0429C] And because this was said exultantly, not doubtfully, he therefore adds: “I will rise”—and this “at dawn.”

“I will rise,” I say, and for great benefit, because “I will confess to you among the peoples, O Lord.” That is, among the Jews I will cause a confession of praise to be made to you. And not only among the Jews, but “I will recite a psalm to you among the nations,” that is, among the gentile people; by acting well, I will cause you to be praised among the nations.

The Jewish people and the gentiles will rightly praise you, because “your mercy has been magnified even to the heavens, and your truth even to the clouds.”

The order appears reversed, because truth is in the heavens, that is, in the angels, in whom it excels, since there the divine will is purely and simply obeyed; whereas mercy was needed for the clouds to be established, that is, for preachers to be established.

[Col. 0429D] Nevertheless, it may also be read in this order: “O Lord, your mercy is in heaven,” because you have mercy on wretched human beings, and by showing them mercy you join them to the angels through the change brought by the resurrection. The angels are called “heavens” because of the excellence of their virtues; thus mercy is in heaven.

“And your truth”—that is, the true knowledge in which the angels excel—“descended even to the clouds,” that is, to human beings covered by the cloud of flesh, because you gave that true knowledge also to human beings.

Or: “Your mercy,” that is, your merciful one, has been magnified even to the heavens to be established. “And your truth,” in which all the promises have been fulfilled, is powerful even to the clouds to be established, so that it may make not only heavens—that is, those elevated by virtues—but also clouds, that is, preachers who rain down teachings, thunder threats, and flash with miracles.

[Col. 0430A] That this may happen: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory above all the earth.” “Be exalted”—not because God can be exalted in himself, but be exalted in human knowledge by exalting the assumed human being, so that, when you are exalted, your glory may be exalted above all the earth.

## PSALM LVII  
### TO THE END: “DO NOT DESTROY”; OF DAVID; IN THE INSCRIPTION OF THE TITLE

> “If indeed you truly speak justice, judge rightly, sons of men. For in your heart you work iniquities on earth; your hands construct injustices. Sinners have been estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the womb; they have spoken falsehoods. Their fury is like that of a serpent, [Col. 0430B] like a deaf asp that stops its ears. It will not hear the voice of the charmers, nor of the skillful enchanter. God will crush their teeth in their own mouth; the Lord will break the molars of lions. They will come to nothing like water flowing away; he has bent his bow until they are weakened. Like wax that flows, they will be taken away; fire has fallen upon them, and they have not seen the sun. Before your thorns understood the bramble; just as living creatures, so in anger he will swallow them.
