The righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance; he will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner. And the man will say: ‘Indeed there is fruit for the righteous; indeed there is a God judging them on earth.’”

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0430C] The words of this psalm are referred “to the end,” that is, to Christ, toward whom all the just strive as their end. They are proposed for this purpose: that you, Jewish people, may not destroy David—that is, Christ—in the inscription of the title, that is, in the alteration of the kingdom ascribed to him and acquired by his blood.

The Jews in particular are warned of this, and then the whole human race, so that those redeemed through Christ may not establish another king for themselves.

The Prophet foresaw that Christ would be born among the Jews in the flesh for the restoration of the human race, and that the Jews, although understanding from many proclamations that he would be born, would nevertheless not believe in him: they would speak the truth about him with their mouths, but carry malice in their hearts.

[Col. 0430D] The divine word rebukes their hardness, and that of all, both Jews and gentiles, who in this way attempt to destroy David—that is, Christ—by removing him from themselves while speaking the truth only with their lips.

It was said concerning the Jews: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX).

The Prophet therefore urges that their words be present in their life and their lips in their deeds.

If indeed people wish to speak justice, if they do not wish to drive Christ the King away from themselves, no one, when questioned about the truth, fails to answer what is true—that is, what is easy to answer—because the Psalmist’s hand has naturally inscribed the law of life upon human hearts: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. IV). The whole of justice and the whole law are contained here: not only what must be avoided, but also what must be pursued. Everyone understands this; that is, every person recognizes what displeases him: theft, murder, adultery, and whatever he does not wish done to himself [Col. 0431A]. But if some think that something is lacking, God wrote the law and placed it before human eyes, so that they might be inexcusable concerning justice, and so that each might confirm the other. Hence it is said: “Transgressors of the law, return to your heart” (Isa. XLVI).

But because it is not enough to know the truth unless one also strives to practice it, the divine word exhorts everyone in this way, and especially the Jews, instructed in both laws, presenting the matter as follows: “I know that you speak the truth about Christ, saying: ‘Teacher, we know that you are truthful’” (Matt. XXII), and: “Good Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?” (Matt. XIX). “But if you speak justice,” that is, truth, “and speak it truly,” that is, without deceit, so that what is in your mouth is no different from what is in your heart—“and if you speak it as you ought, judge rightly,” that is, rightly discern what it means to speak the truth. “For praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. XV). Let your words be consonant with your heart, sons of men—that is, sons of the patriarchs and prophets who persevered in this truth—or sons of men, that is, mortals [Col. 0431B].

It is as though he said: “I warn you of these things because inwardly you devise and carry out in action something different from what reason shows ought to be done. For in your heart you work iniquities.” It is as though he said: “You do not merely think evil in your heart; you also perform it there.” Augustine: “Whatever is thought but not carried into action, God counts as an accomplished deed, not because a person does not wish it, but because he cannot.” “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V).

It is as though he said: “You sin in your heart through both pleasure and consent, which is already the second [Col. 0431C] death.” And you do this “in the earth,” which was given to you for this purpose, so that you might preserve equity; or “in the earth,” that is, in earthly affections—in anger, hatred, and envy—or while devoted to earthly things. And it is not enough for you to work evil in your heart: you also offer your members as weapons of iniquity. “Your hands fashion injustices,” that is, they continue evil deeds. For you do not repent of your sins.

This is the fashioning of sin. Someone commits adultery; fearing that the matter may become known, he kills the person suspected of it. Perhaps someone was aware of this murder; he also considered killing that person, and did not consider freeing himself from the snares of the enemy. Hence Isaiah says: “Woe to them who draw their iniquities like a long rope” (Isa. V).

It is as though he said: “And from where do those wretched people acquire such great blindness?” “Sinners have been estranged from the womb.” Sinners—that is, transgressors of God’s law, [Col. 0431D] both the written law and the natural law—“have been estranged from the womb,” that is, according to God’s foreknowledge, they were rejected by God at conception, in accordance with the saying: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I). “They went astray from the womb,” that is, after they were born, they persevered continually in error and unbelief. “They spoke falsehoods,” that is, they revealed that very unbelief with their mouths, if the reference is to the Jews: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath,” and: “You have a demon” (John IX, VII and VIII).

Or, “they have been estranged from the womb” of the catholic mother, that is, in the very beginnings of the Church, in which they ought to have been conceived for life as though within her. They were estranged because they did not rightly receive those sacraments: the Jews, the legal ordinances; the heretics, the ecclesiastical sacraments. “And from the womb,” that is, from the [Col. 0432A] delivery of that mother, “they went astray.”

If the reference is to the Jews, they went astray from the womb of the Church, in which they ought to have been formed and instructed. If to heretics, they left her before they had been formed and taught in the womb of that mother, presuming to preach what they had not learned, and so producing a miscarriage. If you patiently endure the Church’s labor, you are formed; if impatiently, you are expelled—through the mother’s pain, but to your own harm.

“Their fury is like that of a serpent.” It is as though he said: “This kind of fury exists because they do not wish to hear the preachers of truth.” Thus we read concerning Stephen that they stopped their ears and rushed upon him with stones.

“Their fury is like that of a serpent,” whose nature he then adds: “Like a deaf asp,” not deaf by nature, but one that stops its own ears. *Obturans* (“stopping”) is derived from *ob* and *ture*.

The priests, lying in the temple and accustomed to hearing divine voices, filled the ears of their servants with incense so that they would not hear. Not everything that is introduced by way of comparison is proved to exist in the thing itself. The enchanter is not introduced here as a likeness in order to encourage people to become enchanted. For the asp is summoned by the enchanter from its dark cave into the light; refusing to hear the voices by which it feels itself compelled, it presses one ear against the earth and blocks the other with its tail.

So also the preacher enchants darkened minds in order to lead them out into the light of truth. If the present life delights you, you have fixed one ear to the earth. If you delight in your past deeds, although you ought already to turn your back on them so that we may put on what is promised to us, you have blocked the other ear with your tail.

Stephen wisely enchanted them, because the Jews could not resist the wisdom and the Spirit who spoke. [Col. 0432C] But the Jews were deaf as asps: they stopped their ears and rushed upon him with one accord (Acts 7).

Although they stop their ears, and although they speak truth deceitfully, nevertheless “God will crush their teeth in their mouth,” that is, their malicious words, with which they try to tear apart the head and its members. He will destroy them through their own arguments and their own words. Thus, when they said, “By what authority do you do these things?” the Lord replied, “You also answer me: Was the baptism of John from heaven or from human beings?” (Matt. XXI).

If they said, “From human beings,” they feared being stoned, because John was regarded as the greatest prophet. If they said, “From heaven,” he could say to them: “Why, then, do you not believe me, whom John proclaims?” And so, confounded, they went away.

Likewise: “This woman has just been caught in adultery, and the law commands that such persons be stoned” (John VIII). If the Lord said that she ought to be stoned, he would diminish the great reputation for piety that he possessed; if he denied that she ought to be stoned, he would be judged a transgressor of the law. But Jesus bent down and wrote on the ground: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.” It was as though he said: “The law has been given and must be observed, but see whether you yourselves keep it. It is shameful for a teacher to be reproved by the very fault with which he reproves another.”

Likewise: “Is it lawful to pay the census-tax to Caesar, or not?” If he said that it should be paid, they would accuse him of wanting to make them tributaries; if he denied it, they would say that he wanted them to incur the anger of the Roman rulers. But the Lord said: “Bring me the coin of the census.” When it had been brought, he asked: “Whose image and inscription is this?” They said: [Col. 0433A] “Caesar’s.” “Therefore give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s” (Matt. XXII)—that is, let Caesar’s coin be returned to Caesar, and God’s coin, which is in you, be returned to God. And so they were convicted by their own arguments.

“And the jaws of lions,” that is, violent and open condemnations such as “Crucify, crucify!” (John XIX). The Lord broke them when he rose, and death no longer ruled over him. And when the Lord breaks them, “they will come to nothing like water flowing away.” They are comparable to winter waters, which swell for a time and soon afterward disappear.

Therefore they will cease, because God “bends his bow,” that is, he directs threats through his warriors. He does this; he issues threats, but does not yet strike. He threatens for this purpose: so that those whom he threatens may recognize themselves as weak, in accordance with the saying: “Lord, what do you want me to do?” (Acts IX). This is what he means by “until they are weakened.”

But if they rise up, if they do not wish to be weakened, do not be afraid, because this is their present condemnation. “Like wax that melts, they will be taken away from their substance,” which is to cling to God. How will they be taken away, and by what fire? “Fire has fallen upon them”—the fire of pride, desire, and anger—“and they have not seen the sun.”

Great is the anger of God: that the impious are handed over to their perverse desires, so that they are unable to resist their lusts. This is the fire by which they are utterly consumed and fall away from their substance, as their desires lay them waste. Hence they are called melted and dissolved. From what, except from the fire of desire? Few pay attention to the fact that this is a punishment.

What does he say? “Therefore God gave them over to their desires” (Rom. I). He explicitly presented this as a punishment, as in the saying: “If someone commits theft, he has lost the light of his eyes.” Come, then: if he lost the light of his body, everyone would clearly understand that God did not spare him; and does he spare the one who loses the light of his heart?

“Fire has fallen upon them,” that is, it has pressed them down with great weight. Or, “fire has fallen upon them”: that fire has come from the power and vengeance of God, consuming and darkening the mind. Laid waste and blinded by that fire, they did not see the sun of justice; they did not recognize the Lord Christ, by whom they ought to have been illuminated. Hence it is said: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will illuminate you” (Eph. V). Hence they will say at the judgment: “The sun did not rise for us, and the light of justice did not shine upon us” (Wis. V).

That fire is the kindling of vices. And that fire consumes them as living persons, as though in anger. It is as though he said: “They will not feel the anger of God only after death; even now, while they are still living, it is an expression of God’s anger that the fire of desire consumes them.” It is “as living persons” because this is not true life, or because they appear to live while they are truly dead.

For God, through whom the soul lives, is not in their soul. It is “as though in anger,” because after death the anger will be fixed and true; or because it is written: “But you, Lord of hosts, judge with tranquility” (Wis. XII). God does not become angry; rather, he appears angry to those upon whom he inflicts punishment.

And because he wishes this to be understood as having been said about their temporal punishment, he turns to them in reproach and says: “Before your thorns understand the bramble.” It is as though he said: “You impious people have already been handed over to such punishments before it becomes evident through manifest torments where your temporal pleasure is leading.”

The bramble is said to be a kind of thorn that is first like a herb and afterward rises into thorns. That is, before this pleasure—which is thorny, being full of many anxieties—turns into punishment, the fire of desires falls upon them and prevents them from seeing the sun of justice. And deservedly so, because they do not desire the medicine of compunction; the punitive fire falls upon them.

How great is the fire that falls upon one who does not see the sun of justice, because, handed over by God to his desires, he has departed from God?

“The righteous man will rejoice when he sees vengeance.” It is as though he said: “He will not see it”—that is, he will not understand that punishment consists in the impunity of crimes, not in mercy. He will rejoice when he sees that this is God’s vengeance: that the wicked are handed over to the desires of their hearts.

He will not rejoice in the vengeance itself, but because “he will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner,” that is, he will cleanse his works through the sinner’s destruction. He will not rejoice in the impunity of crimes as that person did, but through compunction and repentance he will cleanse his works from sins. For the fall of the one who precedes corrects the one who follows. Hence Solomon says: “When the fool perishes, the wise man becomes more prudent” (Prov. XIX).

If he is righteous, what does he have that must be washed away? But he is righteous by faith, for the faithful person already begins to be called righteous. When he sees the vengeance inflicted upon the impious in this life, he weighs it and advances through another’s punishment.

And while washing his hands, “the human being”—that is, one who uses reason—“will say: ‘If indeed there is a reward for the righteous on earth,’” that is, in this life, as there truly is. For the righteous person has the reward of justice not only in the future life but also in the present, because he rejoices in hope. [Col. 0434C]

Or he has this reward: that he is not permitted to rejoice in the impunity of sin. Or this one: “Let the one who is righteous be justified still more” (Rev. XXII). Just as the impious person has this fruit of his injustice even in this life: “Let the one who is filthy become filthy still more” (ibid.).

It is as though he said: “If there is this reward for the righteous in this life—that he be justified still more—then it is necessary that the one who is in filth become still more filthy.”

## PSALM 58. TO THE END. “DO NOT DESTROY.” OF DAVID. FOR THE INSCRIPTION OF THE TITLE, WHEN SAUL SENT AND GUARDED HIS HOUSE IN ORDER TO KILL HIM.

> “Deliver me from my enemies, my God, and free me from those who rise up against me. Deliver me from those who practice iniquity, and save me from men of blood. For behold, they have seized my life; the mighty have rushed upon me. Neither is there iniquity of mine, nor my sin, Lord; without iniquity I ran and directed my steps. Rise to meet me and see; and you, Lord God of hosts, God of Israel, attend to visit all the nations; show no mercy to all who practice iniquity. They will return toward evening and suffer hunger like dogs, and they will go around the city. Behold, they will speak with their mouths, and a sword is on their lips; for who has heard? And you, Lord, will laugh at them; you will reduce all the nations to nothing. I will keep my strength for you, because you, God, are my protector; my God, his mercy will go before me. God has shown me concerning my enemies: do not kill them, lest my people ever forget. Scatter them by your strength and bring them down, my protector, Lord. The sin of their mouth, the word of their lips—and let them be caught in their pride. And they will be proclaimed because of their curse and falsehood, in the consummation, in the anger of consummation, and they will not exist. And they will know that God will rule Jacob and the ends of the earth. They will return toward evening and suffer hunger like dogs, and they will go around the city. They themselves will be scattered to eat; but if they are not satisfied, they will murmur. But I will sing of your strength, and in the morning I will exalt your mercy. For you have become my protector and my refuge on the day of my tribulation. My helper, I will sing a psalm to you, because you, God, are my protector, my God, my mercy.”

## EXPOSITION

Our Lord Jesus Christ, our head, prays in this psalm, and by praying teaches us to pray. He also teaches us not to despair concerning sins, but rather to be concerned about them, since many Jews, seized by such madness that they killed their physician and savior, will be saved when they do penance; and the nations, which had entirely forgotten God and worshiped things made by human hands, have not been wholly rejected.

The title shows us how we must not despair, in this manner: these words are referred “to the end,” as has often already been said, being set forth for this purpose: that you, whoever desires to be saved, may not destroy the inscription of the title of David, that is, of Christ, by denying him kingship in yourself, by not believing in him, and by living wickedly. I speak of the inscription made when Saul sent, and so forth.

It is read in the historical account (1 Kings XIX) that Saul sent men to David’s house to seize and kill him by night. But Michal, Saul’s daughter and David’s wife, rescued him by placing an idol in his place and covering it in the bed.

The title “King of the Jews” is inscribed, and this draws us from history to mystery. It was not falsified, because Christ was established as King through dying. What it says about the time when Saul sent men to guard the house refers to Christ’s body.

After Christ had died, he was placed in the tomb. Saul—that is, the kingdom of the Jews—stationed guards at it as though it were a house, so that he might be killed—not with regard to the head, which was already dead, but with regard to the body. For this was the chief way of killing Christ: to take away the glory of the resurrection, in which the Church, the body of Christ, was to be called forth.

Deliver me from my enemies, my God.

The voice of the Head. God of all by nature, my God by a singular grace, by which I am free from sin, or by a singular obedience. Deliver me, the Head, from my enemies, the Jews, who are especially hostile to me, so that when they hand me over to death I may not remain there; or deliver me from the devil and his ministers—not so that they may be afflicted, but so that [my members] may not be incorporated into them.

And deliver me from those who rise up against me, all the Jews as well as the Gentiles who persecute my members. And save me from men of blood, as though not merely from those who rise up against me, but also from those who kill—especially the Jews, who, as though they had an hereditary right, left my blood to their descendants (Matt. XXVII). They themselves killed me, the Head; those others killed my members.

And it is necessary that you deliver me, because, behold, they have seized my soul, that is, my life, according to their opinion. This is evident from the fact that powerful men rushed upon me—that is, members of him who was called “powerful,” namely, one presuming upon himself. Hence it was said: “The strong man bound the strong man” (Matt. XII). They rushed upon me, yet did not prevail, because “the prince of this world is coming, and in me he has nothing” (John XIV). Or they are those presuming upon temporal things, or, worse, establishing their own righteousness and presuming excessively upon their merits.

They rushed upon me—that is, regarding me as a kid, namely, a sinner, they killed me—and therefore they did not deserve to be redeemed by the Lamb. They rushed upon me, but in me they found no sin.

Neither my iniquity nor my sin, O Lord. “Iniquity” refers to others, “sin” to myself: I have not transgressed your law. For I did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it (Matt. V). Therefore they rushed upon me without cause.

For without iniquity I ran and directed my course. No enticement of this life detained me from running along the way of the virtues, and by my example I directed others. Christ became a sharer in our weakness and our iniquity, so that by sharing our weakness he might abolish our iniquity; and this is what he means by “I directed.”

But you, O Lord, rise to meet me—that is, let your help come forward in support of my purpose. And see—that is, make it evident what I run toward and what I direct, in accordance with what is said to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear the Lord” (Gen. XXII). Make them recognize and believe that what has been made straight by the rule of unshaken truth is not distorted.

Or, “rise to meet me” means: make your excellence understood through my resurrection, so that my equality may be understood to meet it, that is, to correspond to it. And after the resurrection, turn your attention to visiting all the nations—you who visited the Jewish nation through me. Turn your attention through your preachers, so that you may visit all the nations, as weak and unable to raise themselves up unless aided by another.

You, I say, turn your attention—you who are able, who are the God of powers, that is, of the heavenly citizens. “The same God of Israel,” that is, of those who see you. Or “God of powers” means: governing them lest they fall; he became “God of Israel” by redeeming them from sins.

And in this way visit all the nations; have mercy on all who practice righteousness. This is righteousness: that whoever commits sin and wishes God not to punish it should punish it himself; that he should judge himself. If he does anything good, let him attribute it not to himself but to God; if anything evil, let him charge it to himself and not throw the blame back upon the Creator. Whatever God hates, let him hate; whatever displeases God, let it displease him, if he desires to please God.

But do not have mercy on all who practice iniquity. Make this understood, for it is taken in two ways.

First, thus: God spares no iniquity that a human being commits. Do you commit iniquity? It will certainly not go unpunished. If you do not punish it, God will punish it. Do you wish God not to punish it? Punish it yourself.

Second, thus: there is a certain exceedingly great iniquity whose practitioner God does not pity. This occurs when sins are defended—not by saying that sin is not sin, for no one is so deprived of human nature as to say that theft or murder, and things of this kind, are not crimes—but when someone does something good and attributes it to himself, and something evil to God. When someone commits perjury, theft, adultery, and many such acts, he judges them to be evil but attributes them to God, saying: “If God did not wish it, I would not do it.”

Alternatively: “Turn your attention to visiting all the nations,” and, if not the chaff, at least the grains. But do not have mercy on all who practice iniquity, namely, that spiritual iniquity—and especially those who killed the Lord, the author of life. They killed not only servants but also the Son.

And truly you will visit all the nations, because they will be converted to you from their idols—even if at evening, that is, late, namely in the sixth age; or at evening, that is, after the Ascension and after the sending of the Word of God.

And they will suffer hunger, hunger for the word of God, according to this: “Behold, I shall bring a famine upon the earth, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God” (Amos VIII).

Like dogs—that is, like dogs that return to their vomit; or “like dogs,” that is, eagerly; or “like dogs,” that is, recognizing and confessing themselves to be sinners and unclean.

Or they will not merely be converted; they will also hunger to incorporate others into themselves, while themselves existing like dogs—that is, comparable to dogs—or like dogs, that is, keeping watch and barking, namely, teaching. With the greatest cunning and speed, dogs drive wolves and robbers away from their own feeding-troughs by their barking. So also the faithful from the Gentiles, having become preachers—Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, and many others—drive unbelievers, heretics, and false Christians away from the Church.

And they will go around the city, that is, the Church of the Gentiles, preaching and fortifying it against the attack of heretics and false Christians.

“Like dogs”: he was belching forth an evil satiety who said, “I fast twice on the Sabbath” (Luke XVIII); he suffered a good hunger who said, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (ibid.).

Behold—you should understand, “how they will go around,” namely, by preaching. For they will speak with their mouth, that is, with a fitting mouth, not ashamed before kings of the sayings of God. And they will do this with great confidence, because there is a sword in their lips.

A two-edged sword, that is, the word of God: two-edged either because it strikes through both Testaments, or because it first cuts away the author’s own vices and then those of others. Hence the Apostle says: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (I Cor. IX). This is the sword of which he says: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth but a sword” (Matt. X).

“For who has heard?” This is what he means by saying; this is what causes him indignation: “Lord, who has believed our report?” (Isa. LIII). To rely on the sword is to do this. The arm of the Lord is scarcely revealed to anyone, as regards the desire and hunger of those who preach.

And yet you, O Lord, will mock them—that is, although this may seem difficult to them, it will nevertheless be easy for you to bring about the conversion of all the nations. In this way you will show your preachers as though worthy of laughter, because you will reduce all the nations to nothing in what they live as Gentiles—that is, all those among the nations who are grains.

Or, truly, they will speak the word of God openly, and it will be like a sword in their mouth, sparing the vices of no one but cutting away everything rotten. Therefore they will act with such great confidence.

“For who has heard?” You should understand: such things as these—a virgin giving birth, a dead man giving life. These are not human but divine things, and therefore they will act with great confidence.

And you, O Lord, will mock them. It is as though he said: You will deal thus with the nations; and you, whom they despised, will mock them—namely, the Jews who practice iniquity—and in the future you will show them worthy of laughter because they rose up against you.

As regards the grains, you will reduce all the nations to nothing in what they are nations—that is, in what they live as Gentiles.

I will keep my strength directed toward you. It is as though he said: The conversion of the nations will come about through my strength and that of my people, because my strength and that of my people will expose their weakness. I will keep this strength directed toward you if I refer it to you, if I presume upon nothing from myself.

My people likewise will keep their perseverance directed toward you. The strength of the soul is wisdom and virtue; but the soul neither understands by itself nor has power by itself. There is, however, a certain region of unchangeable truth: when one approaches it, one is illuminated; when one withdraws, one is darkened.

Rightly, “toward you,” because you are my God, my protector: God of all by nature, protector of my people by grace; God of all by creation, protector of my people by re-creation; or protector of the cause of my people against their attackers.

And therefore he is “my God,” that is, I make him my God—that is, I regard him as pre-eminent. This is also apparent from the fact that he is mine, because his mercy will precede me: it will precede me so that I may begin to cling to him. It will precede me so that I may persevere. He who gave the will shall also give its completion.

Or, with reference to the Head: “he will precede me,” because he created me free from sin. He will also precede me before glorification, so that God may be recognized, as was said through the voice of the centurion: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. XXVII). Or he will precede me before glorification because he will make me steadfast in the Passion.

And this—that his mercy will precede me—God has shown to me in relation to my enemies. In those upon whom he has not had mercy, God has shown how great is what he has bestowed upon me. For the good things of the virtues are not known except by comparison with vices.

The body of Christ, having passed beyond its enemies through that superiority of God which it possesses, clearly sees how much it has received and how much they have lost. Just as the value of gold is displayed by considering lead or iron, so God shows how great a mercy he has had toward my people in those against whom he exercised his justice, making them vessels for dishonor.

And yet, O Lord, although they are enemies, although they have deserved it, do not kill them inwardly, since they have already been killed outwardly; do not wipe them from the earth.

Lest my people ever forget them—that is, lest they ever forget that people which was mine—let them always have it as an example, so that they may not grow proud. For if I did not spare the natural branches, that is, the Jews, much less will I spare the wild olive grafted in, that is, the Gentile people, if it grows proud (Rom. XI).

There are many reasons why the Jews were not immediately wiped from the earth: for the guarding of his house, that is, the tomb. They will have no refuge by which they can avoid being compelled to confess that he rose again.

Either we would not possess the prophecies and books of the old law at all, or, if we possessed them, they would not have been corrected. When blessed Jerome had corrected almost all the writings of the Seventy Translators according to the Hebrew truth, we too still have recourse to them whenever we are uncertain about any letter.

The prophecy also would not be fulfilled which says: “The remnant of Israel shall be saved” (Isa. X; Rom. IX).

And therefore do not kill them meanwhile, for that would be useless. But do what is necessary: scatter them throughout the world by your strength, since, presuming upon their own strength, they refused to be subject to your righteousness. And cast them down from the priesthood, from the kingdom, and from their pride.

You, I say, O Lord, my protector, lest I fail beneath the burden of tribulation; protector against attackers.

Do not kill them, but kill the sin of their mouth, namely this: “We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX). The word of their lips: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII).

And let them be seized—that is, convicted—in their pride. Let it be shown to them by you how great their pride was when they said and did such things against the author of life. Give life to the one whom they sought entirely to extinguish, and in this way seize them.

For they will perceive that they wished to kill life in vain and out of pride alone; thus they will realize that their deed came to nothing, while the crime remained as the product of pride, and through this they will be converted.

And from their curse and falsehood they shall be proclaimed at the consummation—that is, through proclamation and preaching they shall attain consummation, namely, the perfection of their restoration.

Some of them will be restored not on account of their merit but on account of the curse, that is, the malediction, because they crucified him as though he were accursed: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deut. XXI), that is, a human being. For he could not be crucified in his divinity.

And from the falsehood of the corrupted witnesses they will be restored to life—those who killed life. This will arise from the riches of divine goodness, namely, in the wrath of consummation.

Or, “they shall be proclaimed at the consummation,” so that they may first be proclaimed from their curse, that is, from the fact that they had previously been cursing: “Be a disciple of that man” (John IX); and from falsehood, that is, from the fact that they were previously liars, because they corrupted the guards so that they might give false testimony: that his disciples had come and stolen Jesus while they were sleeping (Matt. XXVII).

Of all these things they shall be proclaimed—that is, they shall be taught—so that they may learn not to curse the name of Christ and may learn not to lie about him, in order that they may be at the consummation, that is, among the number of the perfected, namely, the good.

“In wrath,” which he showed them inwardly to be impending over them, and by which they would be consumed in the future unless they were perfected in the present. This is “in the wrath of consummation,” that is, in the manifestation of the future wrath impending over those who are not converted—a wrath, I say, that consumes them.

And they shall not be, namely, impious and blasphemous as before. Then they shall know that God will rule over Jacob and the ends of the earth.

Concerning that wrath the Apostle says: “Where sin abounded”—that is, after they recognized themselves as sinners and weak, and therefore in need of a physician, whereas previously they had established their own merit, and had gained this recognition by understanding that God’s wrath was impending over them—“grace abounded still more” (Rom. V), that is, the free remission of sins.

Then, I say, they shall know that God, whose power they did not understand when they said, “We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX), will rule Jacob, that is, the Jewish people—and not Jacob alone, but also the ends of the earth, that is, the Gentiles.

This will be shown to them because they will be converted, you should understand, to the faith of Christ, from whom they had previously turned away, even if at evening, that is, late, after Christ’s death. Earlier they ought to have been converted, when he preached to them; or “at evening,” that is, at the end of the world, when the remnant shall be saved (Rom. IX).

And they shall suffer hunger like dogs, that is, they shall humble themselves and recognize themselves as sinners and in need of God’s mercy, like Gentiles whom they previously judged to be dogs, that is, unclean, while they presumed upon their own righteousness.

Or they shall hunger to gain others and incorporate them into themselves. Then they will be better dogs than they are now human beings, when they strive faithfully to defend the law in which they now transgress and pursue the savage beast with religious barking.

Or they will be converted at evening, that is, to the hearing of the evening death.

And they shall go around the city. Like dogs they shall go around the city, namely, keeping watch and barking—that is, teaching the Jewish people. This city is called “the surrounding region,” because this one nation has been surrounded by the whole world.

Preaching, therefore, throughout the whole world, they shall go around that city. Those who were the first to attack the name of Christ shall be scattered throughout the whole world in order to eat—that is, to gain—others.

But if they are not satisfied, they will murmur. This is that hunger: if they cannot gain as many as they wish, they will murmur against the Lord, saying: “Lord, who has believed our report?” (Isa. LIII). As though they were saying: “No one.”

It is as though he said: All this will not come about through them.

But I, namely, the Head in my members joined together from both walls, will sing of your strength—that is, I will frequently and continually preach the triumph of the resurrection, reproving, entreating, and rebuking.

And I will exalt—that is, rejoicing, I will proclaim to my people—your mercy, by which you call and justify, in the morning, that is, when they will already see you, the darkness of unbelief having been removed.

Therefore your mercy, because you have become my protector, giving me steadfastness in the Passion, and my people steadfastness in me. And my refuge, by raising me from the dead; or the refuge of my people, to whom they may flee inwardly when they are afflicted outwardly.

“In the day of my tribulation,” whether of the Head or of the members; or “my protector” is assigned to what he said, “my mercy,” and “my refuge” to what he said, “your strength.”

My helper: by giving perseverance in obedience. To you I will sing psalms—that is, I will do good works to the honor of your name.

And rightly to you, because you are my God by creation, my protector, separating me from the mass of the lost. But God is my God in that you have become my mercy through a second creation. God, because you created; mercy, because you recreated what was good.

This passage can also be read in the following way:

“Turn your attention to visiting all the nations; but do not have mercy on all who practice iniquity”—that is, on the Jews practicing a singular iniquity, killing the author of their life.

And yet they, that is, the Jews, will be converted, even if at evening, that is, late, namely after the Lord’s Ascension. For many were converted through the preaching of the apostles.

And they shall suffer hunger like dogs—that is, they shall recognize themselves as sinners and in need of God’s mercy—like dogs, that is, like Gentiles, whom they previously called dogs, that is, unclean, while they presumed upon their own righteousness and the law.

Previously these people did not believe, so that their trespass might become salvation for the Gentiles, and afterward the salvation of the Gentiles might become their salvation.

And they shall go around the city, as was previously said concerning the Gentiles.

And there is a sword in their lips, that is, the word of God in their mouth—a word, you should understand, that is a sword for killing, according to this: “To some we are the fragrance of death unto death” (II Cor. II).

Therefore it is a sword and not a medicine, because “who has heard?” You should understand: them—scarcely anyone.

And because they were unwilling to hear the word of God, you, O Lord, will mock them, examining them at the final judgment and showing them worthy of laughter because they rose up against you. For you will reduce all nations—that is, those remaining in their Gentile condition—to nothing, that is, to eternal destruction.

But I will keep my strength directed toward you, whereas they will direct theirs toward themselves, and therefore they will fall.

Yet do not kill them, namely outwardly; do not wipe them from the earth, lest that people at some time forget me—that is, my law—for not all are worthy of death.

Rather, kill them inwardly, in this way: lead them into confusion. Scatter them by your strength; kill the sin of their mouth. Let them recognize that they have sinned, and let them be seized—that is, convicted—in their pride.

Let them recognize that they have acted proudly and irrationally against you. And let them not only be seized in their pride, but from their curse and falsehood they shall be proclaimed at the consummation—that is, recognizing that what they did was a curse and a falsehood, they shall be proclaimed by teachers at the consummation, namely, at the perfection.

And this shall occur in the wrath of consummation, not of consumption, that wrath impending over them having been shown.

Then they shall know that the God whom they considered merely a man will rule Jacob and the ends of the earth, that is, over Jews and Gentiles.

And truly over the ends of the earth, that is, over the Gentiles, because they will be converted at evening, that is, in that final age.

According to this reading, the rest is to be understood in the same way as above.

## PSALM LIX. FOR THE END; FOR THOSE WHO WILL BE CHANGED; IN THE INSCRIPTION OF THE TITLE; TO DAVID HIMSELF; FOR INSTRUCTION; WHEN HE SET FIRE TO MESOPOTAMIA OF SYRIA AND SYRIA OF ZOBAH, AND JOAB RETURNED AND STRUCK EDOM IN THE VALLEY OF THE SALT-PITS, TWELVE THOUSAND.

[Col. 0441D]

“God, you have rejected us and destroyed us; you have been angry, and you have had mercy on us. You have shaken the earth and troubled it; heal its fractures, for it has been shaken. You have shown your people hard things; you have given us wine of compunction to drink.

You have given a sign to those who fear you, so that they may flee from before the bow. So that your beloved may be delivered, save with your right hand and hear me.

God has spoken in his sanctuary; I shall rejoice and divide Shechem, and I shall measure out the Valley of Tents. [Col. 0442A] Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine, and Ephraim is the strength of my head. Judah is my king; Moab is the pot of my hope.

Into Idumea I shall extend my sandal; the foreigners are subjected to me. Who will lead me into the fortified city? Who will lead me as far as Idumea? Is it not you, O God, who have rejected us and will not go forth, O God, with our armies?

Give us help in tribulation, for the salvation of man is vain. In God we shall act with strength, and he himself will reduce those who afflict us to nothing.”

## EXPOSITION

It is read in the Book of Kings that David overcame all those whom we read of in the title, but it is not found there that he set fire to anything. This addition therefore draws us toward the mystery.

“For the end,” then—that is, to Christ—these things must be referred. He is called “the end” in many ways. And they are said to be “for those,” that is, in the person of those who are changed, namely, those who become light from darkness, in the inscription of the title.

The title was written above the Lord’s cross: “This is the King of the Jews” (Matt. XXVII). They are changed in the inscription of this title who pass into the kingdom of Christ from the kingdom of the devil, who abandon the world and follow God.

It follows: “to David himself for instruction.” They are changed not so that they may live for themselves, but for him. “For instruction,” that is, they are those who neither desire an earthly kingdom nor earthly things, as he himself says: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John XVIII).

Christ effected this change by sending fire upon the earth—not material fire but carnal fire. And he struck them not with a material sword but with the divine word.

With that fire he set fire to Mesopotamia of Syria, that is, that Mesopotamia which was in Syria. “Mesopotamia” is interpreted as “the elevated calling”; “Syria” as “sublime.” Thus he set fire to the Jews called to the faith, raised up through the law, yet sublime—that is, presuming upon themselves. This was burned away in them.

“Zobah” is interpreted as “vain old age.” He therefore struck Syria of Zobah, that is, Gentiles dwelling in vain old age: in wealth, in the power of this age, and in secular learning; and in all these things they were sublime, that is, greater than the Jews, because “God chose the weak things to confound the strong, and the foolish things to confound the wise of this age” (I Cor. I).

“And he turned Joab.” Joab, that is, “enemy,” turned the enemy—that is, the devil—back, because he cast out the prince of this world. Or he turned the enemy by making the unjust just.

Or Joab is interpreted as “father,” because he made some of the converted into fathers, that is, preachers.

Therefore the earthly emperor struck with the sword of the divine word those clinging to the earth, so that they might cling to God.

And he struck all these in the Valley of the Salt-Pits. By the valley, humility is understood; by the salt-pits, savor, because those converted to Christ are wisely humbled—that is, for eternal things—not foolishly, that is, for temporal things. They do not suffer for these latter things.

Salt-pits are hollows beside the sea, where seawater is collected for making salt.

And he struck these with the sword of the divine word, that sword being administered by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. Its sevenfold division consists of three and four, which, multiplied by one another, produce twelve.

By four we understand the four parts of the world; by three, faith in the Holy Trinity. Through this faith the whole world, summoned from its four parts, has been struck by the sword of the word of God and by the administration of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.

And he struck these thousands—that is, toward perfection and unity, because one thousand is a threefold unity.

The faithful of Christ, thus joined together as has been said, give thanks to God for the benefits conferred upon them; and they give thanks all the more because they had deserved a greater downfall, from which they have been delivered. They pray for the future change and also show with what confidence they dare to pray for it.

God, you have rejected us and destroyed us. It is as though he were saying: You created us perfect, made us dwell with you, but, because we were unworthy to dwell with you as transgressors, you rejected us from the inner paradise, and therefore from the outer one as well, [Col. 0443B] because “in Adam all die, but in Christ all will be made alive” (I Cor. XV). And you destroyed us—that is, implicitly, us who had been badly built—or, having created us immortal and incapable of suffering by nature, you made us mortal and capable of suffering when sin intervened. In doing this, you were angry with our vices and had mercy on us: you were angry with what we had done, but had mercy on what you had made. For “you hate nothing of what you have made” (Wis. XI). You were angry by destroying the old condition; you had mercy by renewing it. In this way you had mercy.

You shook the earth—earthliness, that is, carnal pleasures—through your diggers, by calling us. And you troubled it in the consciousness of sin: you shook earthly people, that is, by calling them to seek mercy. You troubled them because you made them recognize their evil conscience. Therefore heal its fractures, [Col. 0443C] its mortality and capacity for suffering, or the fractures of its evil conscience. For it has been shaken—that is, toward repentance—and it would not be worthy to be healed if it had not been shaken.

You showed your people hard things. It is as though he were saying: You ought also to have mercy for this reason: since you suffered for us, you left us an example so that we might follow your footsteps. And this is what follows: You showed your people, in your own person, hard things, very difficult to imitate. By way of comparison: just as David, after historically conquering his peoples, imposed a harsh law on them and subjected them through many hardships, so you did with your people, so that they would no longer raise their necks against you. Hence Solomon says in the Book of Wisdom: “My son, draw near to the service of the Lord, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Eccli. II). And blessed Peter says: “It is time for the scourge to come forth from the house of God” (I Pet. IV): “If it begins with us, what will be the end of those who do not receive the Gospel of God? If the righteous will scarcely be saved, where will the unrighteous and ungodly appear?”

Or, you showed your people hard things that previously had seemed pleasurable. For the first labor is to become displeasing to oneself; the second is, on behalf of the one who has been changed, to endure tribulations.

You gave us to drink the wine of compunction. In this way you showed it. You gave us to drink the wine of compunction, not of destruction. Tribulation itself is refreshment for us, because it is not a ruin that destroys but a burning medicine. Just as pleasure formerly lay for us in earthly things, so compunction itself is wine for us.

Truly you gave us to drink the wine of compunction in temporal tribulation, and not of destruction, because you gave those who fear [Col. 0444A] you a sign, so that they might flee from the face of the bow. That is, through temporal tribulations you signified to your people that they should flee from the coming wrath, which, the more it is delayed, will come all the more severely—just as a bow, the farther it is drawn back, sends its arrows farther forward. You burn your people with temporal fire so that you may not reserve them for eternal fire.

Or, “so that they might flee from the face of the bow” means from the manifestation of that wrath which your bow—that is, Holy Scripture—threatens against those who are unwilling patiently to endure the tribulations they have deserved. They should flee for this purpose: so that your elect may ultimately be delivered from that wrath. Let them flee from wrath—that is, from final condemnation—having been made your elect. For they recognize that here they are afflicted only for small matters, so that they may guard themselves against greater ones, for which eternal punishment is reserved.

And because you showed this to me, because you gave these things, even if you scourge me outwardly, save me inwardly from conformity with the wicked. Save me by your right hand to such an extent that you may finally place me at your right hand. And in order that you may save me, hear me—that is, implicitly, hear me praying for perseverance, praying that your right hand may finally console those whom it has inflamed and destroyed.

And truly it will save me, because God spoke in his holy one—that is, in Christ, the Holy of holies—because “in these last days he has spoken to us in his Son” (Hebr. I), in whom he promised this salvation, according to the statement: “And I will send you a savior who will go before you and bring you into the land for which I swore to your fathers” (Exod. XXIII).

Therefore, because he who does not deceive spoke this salvation in that place, I, the Church, will rejoice—and rightly so—because “I will divide Shechem.” Shechem is interpreted as “shoulder.” Therefore I will divide those who bear the burden, so that the weight of the commandments presses down on some, while my yoke, which lifts rather than oppresses, rests upon others. The yoke of the devil presses upon some, the yoke of Christ upon others. I will divide them because I will take these and reject those.

According to the historical account, when Jacob was returning from Laban, his father-in-law, he stayed at Shechem (Gen. XXXI). There Rachel hid her father’s idols, which she had carried away with her, beneath a bundle of straw, when her father pursued her and searched for them. By the idols we may understand the nations who worship idols. The Church will divide these nations, because it will take some and abandon others in their wickedness and error. According to the interpretation of the name, by Shechem we may understand the Jewish people, placed under the yoke of the Law, as has been said.

“And I will measure the Valley of the Tabernacles.” When Jacob departed from there—that is, from Shechem—he pitched his tents in a certain valley where there were abundant pastures. He remained there for a long time, feeding his herds and sheep and refreshing himself and his household. By this we may understand the Jewish people, who were like sheep of pasture, whom God fed with the nourishment of his word in the Law. I, the Church, will measure this valley, because I will take some to spiritual nourishment and leave others in the carnal.

“Gilead is mine,” which is interpreted as “heap of testimony.” That is, the martyrs are mine. They are interpreted as witnesses, for they heap up God’s testimony within themselves, preserving the testimony of truth even to the shedding of blood.

“Manasseh is mine.” Manasseh and Ephraim were sons of Joseph. Manasseh means “forgetful.” That is, everyone is mine who now remembers no longer that former confusion [Col. 0445A] when it was a disgrace to be a Christian. These are all my confessors.

“And Ephraim is the strength of my head.” Ephraim means “fruitful.” Christ is the head of the Church, and the strength of his head is the multiplication of the faithful. Christ fell in his Passion, and fruitfulness followed in the Resurrection, because “unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it will not multiply” (John XII).

“Judah is my king,” that is, Christ, who is from the tribe of Judah. He is the head and ruler of all these.

“Moab is the pot of my hope.” Up to this point he seems to have listed his own people from the Jewish nation; now he turns to the nations. Moab means those living without the Law, namely, the Gentiles. “The pot of my hope” means a boiling pot: a people afflicting me through tribulation. It is the pot of my hope—that is, boiling for the sake of my hope—because “tribulation produces perseverance, perseverance produces testing, and testing produces hope” (Rom. V).

In Moab are understood those who misuse the natural law, namely, the Gentile people. Moab was born from Lot’s daughter, who wrongly used intercourse with her father (Gen. XIX); hence the Moabites, conceived from sin. He prefigures those who misuse the Law, who produce Moabites—that is, evil works—from which tribulation comes upon the good.

“Into Idumea I will extend my sandal.” In this way tribulation is the pot of hope, because I will extend my sandal—that is, my preachers, who protect me like a sandal; or faith, which protects the Church from the mud and thorns of this world. Or I will extend the sandal of the Gospel into Idumea, that is, into the innocence of Idumea, meaning the Gentile world devoted to earthly things, because Idumea is interpreted as “earthly.”

“Foreigners”—that is, allophyli—are subject to me. They are interpreted as “those who fall through drinking,” namely, those made drunk by the sweet fortune of this life. They too will receive my yoke.

Or, “Moab is the pot of my hope,” by way of comparison. It is as though he were saying: Even the most depraved have become for me the hope of satiety, just as a pot is ordinarily the hope of food and refreshment.

Or, “Idumea is bloody.” It is as though he were saying: I will do all these things, not by my own power. For who will lead me, from the distress of the Jewish people, into a fortified city—that is, so that I may become a great city fortified by the multitude of the whole world? It is also called a surrounding city, because it encircles the Jewish land, which is set in its midst.

Who will lead me as far as Idumea, that is, the bloody land—the Gentile world shedding the blood of body and soul? This question is not asked in doubt but in rejoicing.

It may also be understood in this way: Who will lead me into Idumea so that I may become so extensive that I may also reign over earthly things, so that even those who do not wish to advance through me may honor me? For, as has been said, Idumea is interpreted as “earthly.”

“Will it not be you, God”—implicitly, who will lead me—“who rejected us?” That is, implicitly, in Adam. And now you also seem to reject us, because you do not go forth with our armies—that is, because you do not act openly with us as you acted with our fathers, when one pursued a thousand and two put ten thousand to flight. Rather, you allow us to be afflicted outwardly so that you may free us inwardly.

And because you will not go forth with our armies, because you do not free us outwardly, give us help inwardly—that is, implicitly—from tribulation, which is outward. Make it so that through our patience and your consolation, tribulation itself may become for us a testing.

Therefore I ask for inward salvation and not outward salvation, because “the salvation of man is vain”—that is, because outward salvation is nothing. And because the salvation of man is vain, “through God we will act bravely”: we will be strong by suffering and persevering here. And finally he himself will reduce those who afflict us to nothing, either by converting them or by rendering them ineffective.

Or, save me not in your left hand—that is, in temporal things—but in your right hand—that is, in eternal blessedness. And because I ask for what ought to be asked, hear me.

God the Father will truly do this, because he spoke this—that is, he promised that he would hear those who ask in this way—in his Holy One, that is, in his Son: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John XVI).

It may also be understood in this way: Truly he will save me, because God the Father spoke in the Holy One—that is, he will speak in his Son—saying: “I will rejoice,” that is, I will joyfully fulfill obedience, “and I will divide Shechem,” in the same manner as above.

“And the Valley of the Tabernacles”—that is, I will take those who serve me humbly, or those who have the Jews as their shepherd. “And Manasseh”—that is, the people who forget what lies behind and stretch forward toward what lies ahead—“is mine.”

“Ephraim is the strength of my head,” that is, my head is strong because it is fruitful after death. “Judah”—that is, everyone who confesses—is my king; I establish him as king.

“Moab is the pot of my hope,” that is, my refreshment. I will also extend my sandal into Idumea—that is, among the bloody—my sandal, meaning my incarnation or my apostles. And thus the foreigners will be subject to me.

By whose leadership will this happen? By my leadership—not insofar as I am human, but insofar as I am God. For “who will lead me?” and so forth.

“Will it not be you, God, who rejected us in Adam, or who now seem to have rejected us with respect to outward things?” Truly you seem to have rejected us, because you do not give them outward salvation, and so forth, as above.

## PSALM LX. TO THE END, WITH HYMNS. A PSALM OF DAVID

> “Hear, O God, my supplication; attend to my prayer. From the ends of the earth I have cried to you; when my heart was troubled, you exalted me upon a rock. You led me, because you became my hope, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy. I will dwell in your tabernacle forever; I will be protected under the shelter of your wings. For you, my God, have heard my prayer; you have given an inheritance to those who fear your name. You will add days upon days to the king; you will extend his years to the day of generation and generation. He remains forever in the sight of God; and who will seek his mercy and truth? Thus I will sing a psalm to your name forever and ever; I will fulfill my vows from day to day.”

## EXPOSITION

The words of this psalm are to be referred “to the end,” that is, to him who is the end, and not attributed historically to David himself, but to David’s more worthy members; they are to be held “with hymns,” that is, with praises. Thus the Church, in its more perfect members, gives thanks to God because he made them the ends of the earth, because he exalted them upon a rock, because he led them, and because he will give them an inheritance. It may also be read as spoken by the Head, but on behalf of the members.

“Hear, O God, my supplication,” that is, my prayer made on account of my sins, which I have contracted and daily contract through the necessity of this journey; or on account of the sins of fellow members who are weaker. I regard their sins as mine, because in one body, “if one member suffers, all the other members suffer with it” (I Cor. XII).

“Attend to my prayer,” made for perseverance in a good life. And rightly will you hear me, because “from the ends of the earth I have cried to you.” Therefore, through devotion and action, I have directed all my attention toward pleasing you, from the ends of the earth—that is, bringing all earthly desires in me to an end and removing myself far from the midst of the earth.

“When my heart was troubled,” that is, when I refused to remain here without labor and temptation. For I know that no one who has not been tempted is known to himself. “No one will be crowned unless he conquers” (II Tim. II); no one will be victorious unless he has fought; and no one will fight unless he has an enemy.

“When my heart was troubled,” that is, when fear increased in me, not only concerning those things that are bitter here, but also concerning those that appear sweet. I say that it was troubled, but it was not overcome. It was not overcome because “you exalted me upon a rock”: either by conforming me to the example of the humility and patience of Christ your Son, you made me firm, so that just as he was tempted and suffered without being moved, so I too might follow his footsteps.

“You exalted me,” I say, above the whirlwind of this stormy and afflicted life. And he exalted me upon the rock: you led me along the path of justice so that by it I might return to my homeland. You led me because, as guide, you were first tempted and first suffered in yourself. And you led me in yourself because you are the way, according to the statement: “What Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I). In this way he taught the path by which one must go: first doing, and afterward teaching. And he leads to himself because he himself is the homeland. No one will reach the homeland outside him. Therefore you are my guide as I strive toward the homeland, because you became my hope.

I would despair of reaching it unless you went before me through hardships and difficulties, dying and rising again. By dying you showed labor; by rising again, reward. There are two lives: one that we possess and another that we hope for. We knew none before except this mortal and passing life, and we desired only these temporal goods. He taught that there are two lives: one of labor and another of reward; one that we possess in reality and another that we possess in hope.

Let us therefore endure the life in which we are, following his example, so that at last we may reach the life for which we hope. And you are not only hope but also “a tower of strength,” that is, a firm fortification, “against the face” of the enemy—that is, against his terror and persecution—so that they cannot harm us.

In this way he is a firm tower. Christ’s martyrs indeed suffer, but they do not fail in the contest, because they enter a fortified tower. They consider how their Lord was tempted, suffered, and died here, and finally rose in glory, and why he endured all these things. Hoping for such an end, they are not conquered by any terrors, nor can the darts of their enemies harm them. Indeed, they have from this tower a place from which to shoot darts at them.

And because you are my hope and my tower, “who will separate me from the love of Christ? Shall famine, or nakedness, or persecution, or the sword?” (Rom. VIII). Therefore “I will dwell in your tabernacle,” that is, I will serve in your Church; I will not be moved from it forever, until I reach eternity.

Or, “forever” means throughout all these times: let the lion rage openly, let the dragon rage secretly, let disturbances come, let scandals come; nevertheless I will dwell in your tabernacle, in faith, hope, and charity.

Yet this will not happen by my own power, but “I will be protected under the shelter of your wings.” I will be embraced by a twofold charity, by which I will love not only you but also the enemy for your sake.

And truly I will be protected, because you, my God, whom alone I love, to whom I cry, have heard my prayer—that is, you will hear the prayer made for perseverance. This will be certain in this respect: because you have given—that is, you will give, or have already given Christ in reality and us in hope—an inheritance, that is, immortality and incapacity for suffering, not to everyone but to those who fear your name. They fear not only you but also your name with chaste fear: namely, they fear being separated from you, who are fear, because in Greek “fear” is δέος (*deos*), from which “God” is derived in Latin, *Deus*.

Mortal children ordinarily succeed to an inheritance when their parents have died; but living children succeed you, the living one who reigns forever. This is the inheritance, namely eternity, which you will give to your people.

“You will add days upon days to the king.” To the days that bring this kingdom to an end, you will add eternal days to our king. To the days that are closed by night, you will add days that are closed by no night. Although the king will reign forever and there will be no end to his kingdom, who are those who fear the name of God?

And because it seems insufficient to say “days,” he increases the expression: “his years,” implicitly, you will add, “to the day of generation and generation,” that is, to the time of the generation that now exists and the one that will come. But whether days or years are spoken of, less is said than what exists.

He shows what that future generation is: such and so great that it remains forever in the sight of God, worthy of God’s sight. And because that king is so great and there will be no end to his kingdom, let everyone seek his mercy and truth.

But who is the one who will seek his mercy—that is, who will diligently inquire into it so as to find the mercy by which he does not consider merits but forgives sins—and the truth by which he truly and unchangeably fulfills his promises? Who will diligently seek these things?

The one who shows mercy to the needy will keep truth in his promises; or he will walk in God’s commandments, which are true. For many seek his mercy in written texts, not in deeds: they seek to know it for temporal profit, not in order to do it. Such people do not seek it—that is, they do not seek it diligently and in the manner in which it ought to be sought—and therefore they do not find it.

Nor do they seek it according to a certain translation, because they do not seek it for God’s honor but for their own advantage.

It is as though he were saying: I have said, “Who will seek it?” The one who will “sing a psalm to your name,” that is, who will understand, and who will put into good practice what he understands, so that your name may thereby be glorified, not his own.

Thus he will sing a psalm so that he may fulfill his vows—that is, himself, whom he vowed to God—from day to day, advancing from this life toward the future one.

It is as though he were saying: Whatever others may do, I will sing the psalm in this way.

Alternatively: “You have given an inheritance to those who fear your name,” that is, you have given your preachers the multitude of the faithful, whom they cultivate with the plowshare of doctrine. This is the inheritance.

“You will add days upon days to the king,” that is, to the preceding faithful of Christ, illustrious through the light of faith, you will add other faithful enlightened by the word of faith. I said “days”; rather, “his years,” that is, his multitude and successors. You will add them “to the day of the generation of generations,” that is, the number of the faithful will always increase until the day—that is, the time—of that generation which is the generation of generations.

And what does the king do? He remains in them, that is, he reigns in them forever, “in the sight of God,” that is, in the glory of God the Father.

Therefore who will seek his mercy, so that afterward he may find truth, so that where the king is, there also may his minister be? The rest is as above.

## PSALM LXI. TO THE END, FOR IDITHUN. A PSALM OF DAVID

> “Will not my soul be subject to God? For from him is my salvation. For he himself is my God and my savior, my protector; I will not be moved any further. How long do you rush upon a man? All of you kill, like a leaning wall and a tottering fence. Yet they planned to repel my honor; I ran in thirst. With their mouth they blessed, but in their heart they cursed. Yet be subject to God, my soul, because from him is my patience. For he is my God and my savior, my helper; I will not depart. In God is my salvation and my glory; God is my help, and my hope is in God. Hope in him, every assembly of the people; pour out your hearts before him. God is our helper forever. Yet the sons of men are vain; the sons of men are liars in the balances, that they may deceive; they themselves are altogether [less] than vanity. Do not hope in iniquity, and do not desire robberies. If riches flow in, do not set your heart upon them. God has spoken once; I have heard two things: that power belongs to God, and to you, Lord, belongs mercy, because you repay each one according to his works.”

## EXPOSITION

The things enacted in this psalm are referred “to the end,” that is, to Christ. The psalm is attributed to David, that is, to his more worthy members, “for Idithun,” that is, in the person of Idithun.

Idithun is interpreted as “one who leaps over,” namely, those placed in the lowest regions who love earthly things. The soldier of Christ introduced in this psalm, having despised the happiness of the world, passed beyond all who love the world and scorned all who reviled him. He withdrew to a certain lofty place from which he could look down upon them as though they were placed in the lowest regions. Yet in this one soldier of Christ many are understood.

We must therefore see how far he ascended, whom he also passed over, and where he was placed. He seems to have ascended to a certain spiritual and secure place, from which he looks upon those below—not in order to fear a fall, but to rouse others placed below to imitate him and to rebuke them for their sloth.

And he praises the place, not so that he may grow proud by showing himself to be so exalted, since he nevertheless remains subject to the Lord his God, but so that he may encourage others to ascend.

He passed beyond all lovers of the world, despising all the obstacles of those whom he passed over: the flatteries of heretics, the insults and snares of false Christians, and the open persecutions of unbelievers. He addresses them as though saying:

Why do you direct your flatteries at me? Why do you insult me? Why do you make threats? Why do you prepare death? Do you think you can devour me and obstruct my journey? Whatever you plot, whatever you carry out against me—
Will my soul not be subject to God? And, being subject to him, does it fear a fall? Certainly not. For however high I may ascend, I do not fear falling, so long as I remain placed beneath him. I shall safely rise beyond all things while I climb up to him. Truly, my soul will always be subject to him, because he has subjected the world to himself. For he has not subjected himself to God who is subject to the world. And rightly will it be subject to God, since from him comes my salvation—that is, Christ the Lord, in whom my salvation is found, in whom salvation is for me an example of patience. And truly he can save, because although he is human, he is not merely human. A human being can be another human being’s condemnation, but cannot be another human being’s salvation. For he himself, like the Father who sent him, is my God. And because he is God, he is therefore also my Savior. He is my God in this respect: he is the protector of my cause, defending it. And therefore I shall no longer be moved from my God.

Previously the hand of the sinner moved me, when I refused to be beneath him, when [Col. 0450C] I raised myself into pride. But now that I am placed beneath him, I shall not fear falling. What is said elsewhere, “Let not the foot of pride come against me” (Psalm 35), is expressed here as, “Will not my soul be subject to God?” What is said there, “Let not the hand of the sinner move me” (ibid.), is expressed here as, “I shall no longer be moved.” And because my soul rests upon God, and I shall no longer be moved: therefore, how long will you attack me, a human being, attending to my humanity and not attending to divine protection? How long—that is, to what end—will you attack me by cursing, insulting, plotting against me, persecuting me, and killing me?

The soldier of Christ is never without battles, because two cities are now mingled together: one Jerusalem, the other Babylon; one here, the other there. One king is here, another there; one people here, another there. These fight for justice, those for injustice; these for truth, those for falsehood. These seek to build up what has been destroyed, those to destroy what has been built. Yet this city is gathered from that one. For the spiritual did not come first, but the carnal; the former is first in time, while the latter is first in dignity. That this city proceeds from the other was prefigured by Jerusalem, which was built as the second city after the first had been destroyed, although the first city, which Cain built, was constructed independently.

You attack a human being in vain, because a human being endures what a human being can endure, yet with the help of him who became human for humanity’s sake. Truly you attack, because all of you kill yourselves—both those who are within and those who are mingled outside and separated: tolerated now, but to be separated at some time. You attack me; you press upon me like a leaning wall, [Col. 0450D] that is, as though I were a wall that could quickly be thrown down, leaning as if toward ruin. For because I am lower than you, I incline myself toward your salvation; and I am like a displaced stone wall. A stone wall (*maceria*) is a dry wall without mortar, which, when pushed, is easily thrown down.

Alternatively: Do not attack; do not kill. If you do not consider injustice, at least consider your own condemnation, because by killing us outwardly you all kill yourselves inwardly. By killing our body, you kill your own soul, while you press upon me like a leaning wall and a displaced stone wall. The godly person falls to the condemnation of the ungodly, just as a wall falls upon those who carelessly throw it down.

Nevertheless, they planned to repel my prize. It is as though he were saying: I confronted them concerning their innocence; I admonished them in this way. Yet when they could not move me from the course I had begun by open attacks, they envied me, because the honor of the good torments the heart of the wicked. They planned by plots to turn aside my prize—that is, my crown, my reward—while preparing to obstruct my course, reproaching it as difficult and declaring it impossible for anyone, so that I would not complete this life of mine.

Here the obstacles of false Christians are indicated. By flattering words and evil counsels they secretly prepare hindrances for the soldiers of Christ, being ashamed to attack them openly. They prepared obstacles, but I ran, held back by no enticement of this life and turned back by no threats or terrors. And I ran in thirst—that is, in the desire to transform them for myself and transfer them into the body of Christ. This thirst was prefigured in the head of that calf which Moses, descending from the mountain after receiving the Law, threw into the fire and reduced to fragments, then mixed with water and gave the people to drink (Exodus 32).

The calf’s head, which was the head of the idol, signifies the people of Babylon. This people is cast into the fire of tribulations, and through Moses—that is, through a teacher—its understanding is reduced to fragments, that is, humbled toward repentance. Afterwards it is cast into water—that is, baptized—and is thus transferred into the body of the faithful.

It was necessary that I conform them to myself, because with their mouths—deceitful mouths—they blessed, while with their hearts they cursed: with their mouths professing truth, so that they might lead more easily and secretly to falsehood, and with their hearts concealing falsity. Here the depravity of heretics is indicated.

Nevertheless—that is, although so many obstacles and so many plots are prepared for me—O my soul, endure everything. And in order that you may be able to endure, be subject to God, who gives endurance. And rightly to God, because my patience comes from him. My suffering has come; my rest will come. Gold is now placed in the furnace so that, once purified, it may come into the light: the furnace is the world; the chaff, the wicked; the gold, the righteous; the fire, tribulation; the goldsmith, God.

Therefore I do what the craftsman wishes; wherever he places me, I endure. I am commanded to endure; he knows how to purify. Although the chaff burns in order to set me aflame, it is turned into ashes, while I am freed from impurity. Why? Because my soul is subject to God, because my patience comes from him. This patience is necessary here, so that we may receive the promise.

And therefore be subject also to him, because although he is by nature the God of all, he is my God by grace: calling me, my Savior by freely justifying me, my helper by preserving me—or my helper by glorifying me—and therefore I shall not depart. I shall migrate from the tent, but I shall not depart from the palace, because then my salvation will be in God—that is, inward salvation—and my glory—that is, the honor of immortality. For he himself will be all things in all.

Meanwhile, while I am on the way, while I have not yet arrived, he is the God of my help, so that I may not fail. Therefore my hope is in God, so that I may reach the crown. So, following my example, hope in him and not in the world, every assembly of the people—whether those placed below or those outside, open enemies or hidden ones—for he himself will save you, and he himself will glorify you.

And so that you may be able to hope in him, pour out—that is, empty—your hearts before him, not before human beings. Or, “pour out before him” may mean by consideration of him, or while he receives it. Or, “go out,” “rise beyond,” your hearts, so that you may be sufficient to think about him. Whatever you conceive in your heart apart from him passes away. He remains. Pour into him whatever anxiety your heart conceives.

Then he sees when we make a true confession of sins. I say, pour out your hearts by imploring with tears, confessing humbly, repenting sincerely, and believing without deceit.
