Therefore pour them out before him, because what you cannot do by yourselves, he will do. “God is our helper here,” bringing us into eternity. He is a helper by calling, justifying, and preserving.

But although I urge them to hope in God and not in the world, nevertheless: “The sons of men are vain”—that is, devoted to vain things, namely temporal advantages; “they are liars,” deceiving others; “sons of men”—that is, imitators of the first men, with the unstated sense, “placed on scales,” or “pretending equity,” in order that they themselves may deceive through vanity, with the unstated sense “temporal,” that is, through this falsehood, “toward the same end,” with the unstated sense “striving,” that is, toward eternal vanity and eternal condemnation, from temporal darkness into eternal darkness.

“They deceive through vanity toward the same end.” Although their errors are diverse and manifold, all who belong to that city, which has the devil as king, nevertheless agree in the same thing through vanity. Therefore they are objects of pity and must always be admonished. Hence he says: Do not hope in them.

As they deceived others here, so there they will be deceived—not that the torments there are false, but that, in respect of the estimation of the good, they are worthless. Or, “the sons of men are liars on the scales,” that is, in their business dealings, using a part for the whole; for “a false weight and a false measure are an abomination before God” (Proverbs 20).

Augustine: “You pay attention to what you weigh, but not to what you are weighed against.”

“They deceive through vanity toward the same end,” that is, they all agree in vanity. Do not hope in injustice. It is as though he were saying: I have said, “Hope in him.” But if you wish to hope in him, do not hope in injustice—that is, in riches, which are the mammon of iniquity, because every rich person is either unjust or the heir of an unjust person.

Nevertheless, he inserted “the sons of men are vain” out of a certain compassion, Idithun having directed this toward the rich. But you poor: do not desire plunder. You who seize another person’s property do not know by whom you are being seized. You seize money and lose innocence; and thus inwardly that lion seizes you, the one who prowls about roaring and seeking whom he may devour (1 Peter 5).

O unjust bargain! O ruinous profit—to acquire money in order to lose justice! Therefore do not seize; do not fear poverty. For the one who feeds a robber feeds an innocent person; the one who feeds someone destined for condemnation will feed someone destined for salvation.

Or do not suppose that riches acquired through injustice will benefit you when you use them to do good. It is as though he were saying: Rich person, do not seize what belongs to others, because necessity does not compel you. Listen: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them.” That is, do not love them, do not hope in them, and do not fasten your heart there, lest you flow away together with them. For what flows in may also flow out: iniquity is vain, flourishing for a time.

The soldier of Christ, Idithun, who has spoken thus far to those whom he saw beneath him, inviting them to the course and urging all to place their hope in the Lord while dissuading them from hoping in the world, now supplies the reason for both matters and turns to God, speaking more familiarly, as though saying:

Hope must be placed in you, O Lord, and not in the vanities of this world, because you, O God, will repay each person according to his works: punishment to the unjust, a crown to the just. And you will do this by power and mercy, because power belongs to God, and mercy belongs to you, Lord: power by which you condemn the wicked; mercy by which you reward the good.

Power—that is, justice—is in him, so that you may not presume upon mercy; and so that you may not despair of justice, he is merciful. By power you humble the proud; by mercy you exalt the humble. In these two things all that the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles wrote or said is contained.

Let us therefore love mercy and fear power. Let us love mercy in such a way that we do not despise power; let us fear power in such a way that we nevertheless do not despair of mercy. Let us therefore fear his supreme power. Whatever he wishes to do, he can do; yet he does nothing except justly, even if sometimes secretly.

The devil has power, but under him. For he can do nothing unless permitted, and only as much as he is permitted, and when he is permitted. By his power God permits his own people to be afflicted; by his mercy he brings forth an outcome so that they may be able to endure (1 Corinthians 10).

And it is as though he were saying: I do not have from myself what I tell you, but I heard these two things concerning the power of God and his mercy from God, to whom my soul is subject. It is as though he were saying: By passing beyond all worldly things, I heard many things and learned many things, including these two things necessary for the human race: that God is merciful and powerful.

And it is not surprising, because I also ascended so far as to understand “what God spoke once”—that is, he begot the Word from himself, or he made all things in the Word before they existed, without beginning and without end.

Question: How “once,” if he heard two things? He certainly spoke through many people and in many ways, but all of that came from the one who spoke once, because he alone begot the Word. To this the speaker had risen beyond all else, namely, that he made all things once in the Word before they came into being. For they first existed together in the plan of his counsel before they were brought forth into their forms.

And because I heard these two things and received them from God, do not despise me, then, as I persuade you of things useful to you.

Alternatively, in the voice of the Head: Our Head teaches his members how this world must be transcended, setting himself before them as an example. [Col. 0454A] The soul of the first Adam was not subject to God, and therefore the humanity of Christ was moved by the hand of the sinner. “Will not my soul be subject to God?” It certainly will, because the foot of pride will not come against me. For from him—namely, from the Word united to me—comes my salvation, not from me as a human being: from himself, as a human being, comes condemnation for himself; but from God comes salvation.

For he himself—namely, the Word—is my God by the first creation, my Savior—that is, the Savior of my members—by the second creation, my protector, taking me from the mass of the lost or from the tomb. Therefore I shall no longer be moved. I was moved previously in the mass, but I shall not die again.

And because God is my Savior, therefore, how long will you attack me, O Jews, in order to kill me? And as though they were saying, “We are not seeking to kill you,” he replies: Certainly, all of you kill yourselves. Even if you attack me with swords, you attack me with your tongues. I am like a leaning wall and a displaced stone wall, crushing you through my death.

Nevertheless, although I warned them about my prize, so that every knee might bend in my name, with their mouths they blessed me: “You teach the way of God in truth” (Matthew 22); but with their hearts they cursed me: “This man is not from God” (John 9).

If this concerns false Christians, they confess that they know God, but deny him by their deeds. “God of help”: I am not my own help, nor am I my own glory, but God is my glory, giving help. Hope in him, having me as an example. Pour out your hearts before him; empty them of vices so that they may be filled with virtues.

“Our helper”—insofar as this concerns the mass—he says this in accordance with the Apostle: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Corinthians 11).

# Psalm 62. A Psalm of David, When He Was in the Desert of Idumaea

> “O God, my God, I keep vigil for you from the light. My soul thirsted for you; how manifoldly my flesh thirsted for you. In a desert land, pathless and waterless, so I appeared to you in the holy place that I might see your power and your glory. For your mercy is better than lives; my lips shall praise you. Thus I shall bless you in my life, and in your name I shall lift up my hands. As with fat and richness my soul may be filled, and my mouth shall praise you with lips of rejoicing. If I remembered you upon my bed, in the mornings I shall meditate upon you, because you have been my helper. And in the shelter of your wings I shall rejoice; my soul clung to you, your right hand received me. But they sought my soul in vain; they shall enter into the lower parts of the earth. They shall be handed over to the hands of the sword; they shall be portions for foxes. But the king shall rejoice in God; all who swear by him shall be praised, because the mouth of those speaking iniquity has been stopped.”

## Exposition

Idumaea is interpreted as “earthly,” and signifies human life. The desert of Idumaea is the present world, where one is subjected to many and great miseries. For what desert is greater or more dangerous than that in which, when a traveler enters, he finds no inhabitants and therefore no consolation? He cannot leave because he does not know the way. It is difficult to remain because he finds no refreshment there, since there is a lack of water.

Such was this world, and it still is, insofar as it is considered in itself, until God, having mercy on us, sent his Son into this desert. He himself dwelt there, caused his own people to dwell there, opened the way by which they were to leave, and gave water—that is, the word of his teaching—with which we might be refreshed and, speaking with God, might have consolation.

Our Head, therefore, the true David, instructs us in his own voice and in that of his members concerning what we must do while placed in this desert. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matthew 5), who will experience it in thirsting and will experience it in being refreshed. This is a place for thirsting, not for being refreshed; for growing thin, not for being fattened.

God—God of all by nature, my God by grace—I keep vigil for you, not for this desert. You alone I desire. The person who sleeps to the world keeps vigil for God.

There are two kinds of sleep, just as there are two kinds of vigilance: one of the body, the other of the soul. Sleep of the body is sometimes necessary, so that through rest it may be renewed and become sufficient for the movements of the soul, which is always active. Sleep of the soul is forgetting its Creator. Hence it is said: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Ephesians 5).

Vigilance of the soul is always to have its God in memory, to thirst for him, to desire him, and to strive toward him through good conversion and life. It is of this vigilance that he says here, “I keep vigil”: that is, through good action and every effort my heart stretches itself out toward pleasing you.

“From the light,” that is, from your illumination. You gave me this light—that is, this understanding—in accordance with the Apostle: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (ibid.).

Or, “I keep vigil,” that is, I am concerned through diligent and constant activity. “For you,” that is, to carry out your commandments. “From the light” is said by comparison, meaning diligently, like good laborers who rise at first light for their work.

Cassiodorus: The very repetition of the revered name displays the affection of devout supplication: “O God, my God.” Therefore I keep vigil for you because my soul thirsted for you. No one keeps vigil for God unless he first thirsts for him.

Thirst is the soul’s desire. “My soul thirsted for you,” that is, it desired not the goods found in this desert, but those that are in you, namely eternal rest and eternal blessedness, which exist nowhere except in you.

For the soul is subjected to many passions: it desires, fears, grieves, and rejoices. From these arise anger, hatred, envy, and countless things of this kind. Therefore my soul thirsted for you in many ways—that is, because of its manifold passion, it desires manifold healing.

And not only my soul, but also my flesh thirsted for you, awaiting the resurrection, so that the soul might receive blessedness. But the flesh thirsted “how manifoldly,” that is, much more than the soul, because the soul is impassible, while the flesh is mortal and subject to suffering.

It is not the flesh that thirsted, but the soul, considering the flesh’s manifold weakness. It keeps vigil and thereby grows weary; it sleeps and thereby grows weary; it stands, sits, eats, and hungers. In all these things there are weariness and satiety, and therefore no rest.

And I shall have this thirst in this life, where one must thirst, because it is full of needs, namely, “in a desert land, pathless and waterless.”

This way is desert, because insofar as it is considered in itself, no one cultivates it and no one inhabits it. It is pathless, because insofar as it is considered in itself, it has no way leading to life; rather, it is full of many errors. It is waterless, insofar as it is considered in itself, because it has no living water by which the soul may be refreshed—namely, spiritual grace or the teaching of God’s word.

But the Son of God came into this deserted land and cultivated it through virtues, by his work and teaching and through his own people. He showed the way by which we might leave and return to our homeland. He set before us the example of his life, so that at last we might pass from corruption to incorruption, just as he died and rose again. And he gave water with which we might meanwhile be refreshed here—that is, the teaching of his Word and his commandments, by which we might speak familiarly with him.

“Thus,” that is, thirsting for you, in the holy place—with “desire” understood—I appeared to you, that is, I pleased you and was deemed worthy for you to see me. This happens only through humility. Just as we withdraw from God through pride, so in humility we appear before God, confessing both our weakness and our thirst.

For this I appeared, so that I might see—that is, so that you might make me know—your power: the power by which my soul, thirsting and desiring you, does not depart from you. This power is yours, not mine.

“And your glory,” that is, immortality and incorruption, which I now possess in hope and will at some time possess in reality. This too is yours, not mine. Or, all my power and all my glory are from you. For “what do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4).

Alternatively, it may be understood as follows: my soul and flesh first thirsted here, and I appeared to you because “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2). You saw me so that I might see you; I appeared so that I might attribute this to you.

Let us therefore appear to him in holiness, so that we may see his power and glory—that is, Christ. “That I might see your power,” and my weakness; “and your glory,” and my disgrace. And because one must glory in you, not in myself, the text says, “your power and your glory.”

“For your mercy is better than lives.” That life of soul and body which you gave me through your mercy, without any preceding merits of mine—calling me freely, freely forgiving sins, freely justifying—is better than all those lives that mortals possess in their various pursuits.

And because that holy life which you gave me through your mercy is better than every life I could desire for myself, my lips—if Christ is speaking in the person of his members—shall praise you, not me. Let outward lips not be ashamed to confess you before human beings.

“Thus,” that is, by praising outwardly, “I shall bless you in my life,” that is, by living laudably I shall multiply your praises. And not only shall I praise you in word and deed, but for the example of others I shall lift up my hands—that is, I shall set my good works before others for imitation.

Gregory: Let your works be done openly, so that your intention may be hidden. This is followed by: “And I shall lift up others in your name,” glorifying not my own name but yours, “so that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father” (Matthew 5). This is what he asks of you: “May my soul be filled as with fat and richness.”

Fat is the richness that embraces the inward parts; “richness” is obesity and thickness around the skin. Therefore let my soul be filled—not my flesh, not with fat or richness, since it would be a base thing to ask for something you also provide to brute animals—but “as with fat,” that is, with wisdom. For when the soul lacks wisdom, it is dry and thin.

“And let it be filled with richness,” that is, with the practice of holy virtues, through which practice the soul’s wisdom may shine outwardly. Thus, once fattened, I may at last become an acceptable sacrifice to you, offering you the calf of my lips. This is what follows: “And my mouth shall praise you with lips of rejoicing.”

For now there are lips of prayer, while I am in the desert and thirst. As long as thirst lasts, prayer lasts; but when thirst ceases, prayer will cease and praise will follow. All the soul’s strength consists in these two things: wisdom and virtue.

Alternatively: “My lips shall praise you” in this way, or “I shall bless you in my life”: whatever I live and whatever adherence I have to you I shall attribute to you, not to myself, entirely to your mercy. “And in your name I shall lift up my hands,” that is, I shall pray to you with raised hands, imitating the one who, by praying for me, stretched out his hands upon the cross.

By hands we understand works, because we work with our hands. When we pray, we raise our hands so that, if our works differ from our prayer, they may be made consonant with it.

“In your name,” that is, I shall seek you principally when I raise my hands. Or, “I shall lift up in your name”: if I do something good, the good will be in you for me, not in me.

Thus—understand: I shall do these things with this intention and desire—so that my soul, which now thirsts and is now bitter, may be filled as with fat and richness, that is, with an abundance of virtues and eternal joy. And then “my mouth shall praise you with lips of rejoicing,” as above.

And truly I shall finally praise you with rejoicing, because meanwhile I shall meditate upon you in the mornings, in the diligent practice of my works. For those who are diligent rise in the morning for their work. I shall meditate upon you; I shall be constant in those works, in meditation upon you, because I shall do everything for your honor. Therefore I shall meditate upon you, because you have been my helper, enabling me to complete these things.

“In the mornings I shall meditate,” that is, in labor. “If I remembered you upon my bed”: this is from the greater, meaning, if I placed you above rest. While a person is at rest, he meditates upon Christ; when he comes to work, he remembers Christ. If I interrupted the rest I could have had for your sake.

Or, let it be spoken in the person of the Head. Then my soul—that is, the soul of my members—once filled as with fat and richness, “shall praise with lips of rejoicing,” and my mouth—that is, the mouth of my members—shall praise. In this he shows what that praise will be. They shall praise you in the mornings, that is, in their resurrections, because there are as many mornings as there are righteous people. “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13).

Then they shall meditate upon you, that is, all their thought will be in your praise, because there will no longer be anything else about which they must be anxious: “There will no longer be mourning, or crying, or any pain” (Revelation 21). Therefore they shall praise you because you have been their helper—that is, the helper of my members—so that they might reach that blessedness.

I shall then praise you in the mornings if here I remembered you upon my bed. There is no one who does not remember his bed, namely, who does not consent to the flesh. But if he remembers God upon his bed—that is, if he loves God more than carnal desires—he will praise him in his morning. Then I and my members shall rejoice “in the shelter of your wings,” that is, in your protection, or in love of God and neighbor.

There I shall rejoice in your protection because my soul clung to you—that is, here it was firmly bound to you with the glue of charity. Yet it clung “after you,” not as though it wished to go before you or go with you, like Peter, who said to the Lord: “Be favorable to yourself, Lord; this shall not happen to you.” And the Lord said to him: “Go behind me, Satan” (Matthew 16).

It is as though he were saying: You ought not to go before me, but to follow. Whoever wishes to live in Christ according to his own arrangement wishes to go before him, not to follow him. But hold fast to charity in such a way that meanwhile, amid the mixture, you follow Christ in all things, so that afterward, in the separation, you may be received at his right hand.

And so that my soul might cling to you, “your right hand received me,” that is, your favor received me from the mass of the lost. Or, if this is spoken of the Head, his divinity received me as a human being from the tomb.

Or: I shall go to the right hand; but what of the Idumaeans who killed me? “They shall enter into the lower parts of the earth,” that is, they shall plan to kill Christ for the sake of earthly things. For whoever follows earthly things against his own salvation, while making himself lower than the earth, is beneath the earth. And what happened to them? They lost their place and nation—something they killed Christ in order not to lose (John 11).

How were they given over to the sword of the Romans? Because they rejected the Lamb of God, saying: “We have no king except Caesar” (John 19). And what of the king? “The king shall rejoice in the Lord.” He will not be killed in respect of what he is as God, but his people will glory in him.

And what of his own people? Those who remain with him in life are glorious; but those who conspired against him, saying, “It is necessary for one man to die,” are confounded and scattered. Those who did not cling to him, for whom the example of right living had been set, sought my soul—that is, my life—not in order to imitate but to betray me; but they sought it in vain.

There were three principal reasons for which they sought the Lord’s life in order to destroy it, but in vain: so that his name might be erased from the earth; so that the world might not follow him—which arose from great envy; and so that they might not lose their place and nation.

But his name increased because he rose from the dead, and his fame increased throughout the whole world. The world has now followed him, while they have lost their place and nation. Therefore they sought my soul in vain.

They will seek my soul in order to destroy it because they will value earthly things more than themselves: “They shall enter into the lower parts of the earth.” The person who consents to the earth—that is, to his flesh—enters the earth. The person who values the things below more than himself enters into the lower parts of the earth.

And because they sought to destroy my soul, “they shall be handed over to the hands of the sword,” that is, to the power of the sword-bearers Titus and Vespasian. “And they shall be portions for foxes,” that is, prey for the Roman rulers, who are called foxes because of their cunning.

Among other beasts, the fox is an entirely deceitful animal. It seeks food through trickery and guards its own safety by crafty deception. Cunning people are rightly compared to these animals, since through feigned cleverness they strive to accomplish their injustices.

This is aptly applied to Herod, concerning whom the Lord said: “Go and tell that fox that he is not to apprehend a prophet outside Jerusalem” (Luke 13). And in the Song of Songs: “Catch for us the foxes that destroy the vineyards” (Song of Songs 2).

Or the Jews were portions for foxes when they said: “We have no king except Caesar” (John 19). For then they chose a fox as their king.

Or the Jews entered into the lower parts of the earth—that is, they hid themselves in the earth’s holes to preserve their temporal life—when, in order to kill Christ, they placed earthly concerns first, saying: “Lest the Romans come and take away our place and nation” (John 11).

And in this they were portions for foxes, that is, deceitful like foxes, which hide themselves in caves in the earth. Or, “portions for foxes” was a prophecy concerning Josephus and the other leaders of the Jews, who, after the burning of the city and the killing of their people, were dragged out of the caves of the earth in which they had been hiding.

But the king is Christ, whom they killed, established as king in the very fact that he was killed. He shall rejoice in God, that is, in the life given by God. And not only the king, but “all who swear by him shall be praised”: cause is stated for effect, meaning that they shall live forever, just as Christ their Head does. All those who firmly pledge their life to him, having first lived praiseworthily, do so.

Therefore these will be praised because the mouth of those speaking iniquity has been stopped. The Jews spoke iniquity when they despised their Creator and chose a fox as king, when they said, “We have no king except Caesar.”

The foxes prevailed against the Lamb, but they were defeated by the Lion. Behold, he has risen; “the Lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Revelation 5). Thus the mouth of those saying, “He is guilty of death” (Matthew 26), has been closed. For the king has risen, and the world has now followed him.

Or thus: Truly the king will rejoice, which will be completely evident to all, because the mouth of those speaking iniquity has been stopped. Those who said, “We have no king except Caesar,” have nothing to say. What the king says is greater than if he said, “I am king,” because he alone is called absolutely king, by antonomasia.

# Psalm 63. A Psalm of David, for the End

> “Hear, O God, my prayer when I plead; rescue my soul from fear of the enemy. You have protected me from the assembly of the wicked, from the multitude of those who work iniquity. For they sharpened their tongues like a sword; they bent their bow, a bitter thing, to shoot in secret at the innocent. Suddenly they will shoot at him and will not fear; they have strengthened for themselves an evil speech. They recounted their schemes in order to conceal their snares; they said, ‘Who will see them?’ They searched out iniquities; they failed while searching with a search. A human being will approach the deep heart, and God will be exalted. The arrows of children became their wounds, and their tongues were weakened against them. All who saw them were troubled, and every person was afraid. And they proclaimed the works of God, and understood his deeds. The righteous shall rejoice in the Lord, and shall hope in him, and all upright in heart shall be praised.”

## Exposition

In this psalm Christ, our Head, sets before us the endurance of his passion and the glory of his resurrection, so that by his example the holy martyrs, his members, may not be terrified or fail in tribulation, but may fight bravely and, after the struggle, reach glorification. For where the Head is, there the members will also follow.

Hear, O God, my prayer when I entreat you. God the Father, hear my prayer, because my blood, poured out on the altar of the cross, prays for my members. Such is the power of love: that we cling to those whom we love, even when they are absent, so long as neither place nor time tears away the affection implanted within us. When I entreat you, I do not ask that they not be killed, but that, once killed, they not be overcome.

That is, “Deliver my soul from fear of the enemy”: deliver the souls of my members from fear of the enemy, and subject them to your fear; freed from fear of them, let them be subjected to your service. For many of Christ’s martyrs have been killed but not overcome, because they persevered in the faith and testimony of Christ: some were swallowed up dead, others swallowed up alive. Those who were swallowed up dead are the unbelievers who trample upon the blood of the righteous; those swallowed up alive are those who believed in Christ but failed in tribulation, transferred into the body of the enemies. The former were swallowed up because they were dead; the latter died because they were swallowed up.

Therefore, “Deliver my soul from fear of the enemy,” you who command: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matthew 10). And truly you will deliver the souls of my members from fear of the enemy, because you, their head, have protected me from the assembly of the wicked. I have this as a kind of assured pledge from that event, because the chief priests and Pharisees of the Jews gathered a council, saying, “If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him” (John 11). Great envy! So they planned to kill him—but in vain, because he rose again, and the world followed him.

“From the multitude of those who work iniquity”—namely, that greatest iniquity. Although they had seen so many and such great miracles, although he had given sight to their blind, cleansed lepers, healed the sick, and raised the dead, the unbelievers killed him. This is that iniquity: “For even if they did not kill him with the sword, they sharpened their tongues like a sword.” What others did with the sword, these did with the tongue.

This was the Jews’ greatest sharpness when they said, “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone” (John 18). As though they were saying: “Let us kill him, and let us not kill him. Let us kill him in such a way that we ourselves will not be judged to have killed him.” Great folly: it is not lawful to kill, but it is lawful to hand over the one who must be killed.

From this the discrepancy can be resolved whereby one Evangelist says that the Lord was crucified at the third hour, while another says at the sixth. When the Jews cried out, “Crucify, crucify,” at the third hour, what the officers of the authorities did with their hands at the sixth hour, the transgressors of the law had already done with their tongues at the third hour (Matthew 15; Luke 23; John 16).

“They bent the bow”—that is, they prepared ambushes, saying, “Let us kill him in such a way that we do not seem to have killed him.” They pretended to be just; but simulated justice is a twofold iniquity. They pretended to be just also when they said, “It is not lawful to put it into the treasury, because it is the price of blood” (Matthew 27). What madness! It is not lawful to put the price of blood into the treasury, but it is lawful to put the blood itself into the conscience?

They bent the bow and prepared ambushes; and they bent “a bitter thing,” namely this: they subverted with money a disciple, Christ’s companion, so that through him he might be betrayed. They bent the bow so that they might shoot—that is, kill—in secret, that is, secretly kill the spotless one whom nothing escapes, namely, the one who had come to remove the stains of sins.

“Suddenly they will shoot him”—that is, recklessly and thoughtlessly, looking at the man but not looking at God. “And they will not fear.” A hard heart, which did not fear unjustly condemning the judge whom none of the judges could deceive. A hard heart, which did not fear handing over the one who had come to release the world from sins, though he himself was bound. A hard heart, which did not fear killing the one who had come to free the world from death.

[Col. 0461B] The authority was afraid, because Pilate handed him over to them after having him scourged, finding no cause of death in him—not in order to condemn him, but to satisfy their cruelty. The authority was afraid, yet the Jews’ brutality did not tremble. The authority washed its hands, while they polluted their consciences with blood.

Truly they did not fear, because “they confirmed for themselves an evil word.” That was the evil word: “He is guilty of death” (Matthew 26). They confirmed it when they said, “Crucify, crucify”; and the authority asked, “Shall I crucify your king?” They answered, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). And they confirmed it a third time when the authority said, “I find no cause in him,” and they answered, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27).

But they confirmed it for themselves—that is, to their own condemnation, not God’s. He killed death; they were themselves killed, because they refused to kill iniquity within themselves. In the Lord, death was killed; in them, the iniquity in which they died remained alive. Either you kill iniquity, or it kills you. If you wish to kill it, do not seek the enemy outside yourself: you have him within.

For the soul has two parts: one that clings to carnality, which is called spiritual, and the other sensual. [Note: Col. 0461D: Something is missing.] This is our Eve, who still stretches out her hand toward illicit things and drags us into sin, unless she is subjected to her husband, that is, to her spiritual father, who is also her head, because “the husband is the head of the woman” (1 Corinthians 11).

“They recounted things in order to conceal the snares”: that is, they entered into counsel about how, secretly so far as they themselves were concerned, they might kill him or trap him in speech, as in the saying, “This woman has just been caught in adultery” (John 8), and the other: “Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” (Matthew 22).

They said, not aloud but in their hearts, “Who will see them?” Yet they said this and plotted this against the one whom nothing escapes. O Jew, you say, “Who will see?” But he sees who made you. For he who made the human being knows what is in the human being, and no one needs to testify to him about a human being. These are the snares.

“They searched”: that is, they carefully investigated wicked plans by which they might appear to have condemned him justly. These they searched: “Let him be killed not by us, but through a disciple; let him be killed by the judge. Let us do everything and appear to have done nothing.” But “they failed in their searching out of searches,” that is, in their sharp plans.

Therefore they failed, because this was feigned innocence. For they were saying, “Crucify him.” When the soul turns away from the light of justice, the more it seeks what it might discover against justice, the more it is driven back from the light and plunged into darkness. Rightly, then, these men, departing from justice, failed.

They failed also because “a human being will approach a deep heart”: that is, my humanity will of its own accord approach their profound counsels, and God in the human being will be exalted. “And God will be exalted”: he will ascend there in exaltation, from where he did not descend in humiliation.

Or, “a human being will approach”—that is, humanity—“a deep heart,” that is, the inscrutable counsel of God, because he did not wish to be seen, so that he would not be recognized; not to be recognized, so that he would be despised; to be despised, so that he would be crucified.

Or they failed for this reason: a human being would approach their counsels. For he would not be held unless he were a human being—and not merely a human being, since “a deep heart” means God: “For I and the Father are one” (John 10).

The human being died, and God was exalted—not among human beings, among whom he was humbled in his humanity, but in that same humanity, now exalted, he was also exalted. “A human being will approach a deep heart, and God will be exalted”: the very one who was shown to be truly human in his passion appeared to be truly God in his resurrection.

For this reason God will be exalted—that is, divine power will be manifested—because “the arrows of children have become their wounds.” Everything was turned against them. Their wounds are comparable to the arrows of children because they were ineffective and weak; or because, returning upon their own heads, they were like children’s arrows recklessly shot upward.

They were the arrows of children because “their tongues were weakened against them”: the words that they themselves thought advantageous to their case were against their case, because they were especially effective in confirming it.

For Christ rose again. The guards were corrupted, because the same greed that had taken captive Christ’s companion, the disciple, also took captive the soldier guarding the tomb. They said, “While we were sleeping, his disciples came and stole him” (Matthew 28). This was a weak claim. For what? If they were sleeping, how could they be witnesses to the Jews? A witness cannot establish anything except what he has seen or heard. But if they were not sleeping, why did they not prevent it?

They arranged for them to say something by which they would be held all the more—or by which they thought they would confirm their own story more strongly—and by that very means they weakened it more. For they lost both the place and the nation.

When their tongues had been weakened, “all who saw them were troubled”: that is, those who saw—that is, understood—that they had been weakened and rendered ineffective worked out their salvation with fear; or the apostles and the other disciples, who understood that they were acting wickedly, were distressed.

“And every human being,” that is, everyone endowed with reason, feared their fellowship—or feared for them. And those who had turned, or the disciples, after their fear, announced the works of God: what God the Father accomplished through the Son for the restoration of the human race.

“And they understood his deeds,” that is, they understood these things, because it was fitting that the one who was to bring many sons into the glory of the Father, the author of their salvation, should be perfected through suffering (Hebrews 2), in accordance with the saying, “It was necessary for Christ to suffer” (Luke 24).

On the cross he bore those who insulted him; in the tomb, the guards. Why? He had to die on behalf of those who were to die, and rise again on behalf of those who were to rise again. These things were not understood beforehand.

“The righteous man will rejoice in the Lord”: the one who was righteous in the Lord’s death, like the apostles and many others, will rejoice in his resurrection. “And he will hope in him”—not in himself, not in the world, but he will hope to rise again in the one who died and rose again.

And not only will the righteous man who saw him hope to rise again, but “all upright in heart” will be praised—that is, they will live in a praiseworthy manner, so that they too may hope. They are upright in heart who govern their hearts so that God’s disposition and will please them in everything, rather than their own.

Alternatively: after they understood the deeds of God when he rose again—though previously they had not understood them when he died—they said, “What shall we do, brothers?” And they answered them, “Repent” (Acts 2), approaching the unity of faith. Those who were then present, and those who are present now, having become one through faith, will rejoice in the Lord—that is, in the Lord’s resurrection—hoping also to rise again in him.

“And he will hope in him,” because it has now been made clear why he wished to die and rise again. And so at last they will be praised: “Come, you blessed of my Father” (Matthew 25), all who are upright in heart, when those who are crooked in heart will be condemned—those who take pleasure in their own counsel and reject the counsel of God.

## Psalm 64. To the End: A Psalm of Song, a Song of Jeremiah and Ezekiel concerning the People of the Captivity, when They Began to Depart

“To you praise is due, O God, in Zion, and to you the vow will be fulfilled in Jerusalem. Hear my prayer; to you all flesh will come. The words of the wicked have prevailed against us, and you will be merciful toward our iniquities. Blessed is the one whom you have chosen and taken to yourself; he will dwell in your courts. We shall be filled with the good things of your house; holy is your temple, wondrous in justice.

“Hear us, O God our savior, hope of all the ends of the earth and of the distant sea. You prepare the mountains by your strength, girded with power; you disturb the depths of the sea, the sound of its waves. The nations will be troubled, and those who inhabit the ends of the earth will fear your signs. The outlets of morning and evening you will make delightful.

“You visited the earth and watered it abundantly; you multiplied its wealth. The river of God is filled with waters; you prepared their food, for such is its preparation. Water its streams; multiply its fruits. In its showers the sprouting growth will rejoice. You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness, and your fields will be filled with abundance. The beautiful places of the desert will grow fat, and the hills will be girded with rejoicing. The rams of the sheep are clothed, and the valleys will abound in grain; they will cry out, for they will also sing a hymn.”

## Explanation

The event is recalled in the title. It is well known how God’s people—namely Israel—were led captive into Babylon (2 Kings 25). While they were captive, Jeremiah, who belonged to the same people, foretold their return to Jerusalem after seventy years and the restoration of the temple (Jeremiah 25, 29). Haggai, moreover, assisted in rebuilding the temple upon their return, by his authority and counsel (Haggai 1–2).

These things happened to them in symbolic form (1 Corinthians 10); therefore, in them let us recognize our own pilgrimage. Those two cities were shadows of two cities that are mixed together in this present life. Babylon was an exceedingly wealthy and powerful city in the farthest regions of Persia. Jerusalem was a city in the regions of Syria, built by the Jebusites and called Jebus. After it was destroyed, Jerusalem was built.

Just as Babylon was greater and more powerful, so now the number of unbelievers is greater, because “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 20). And just as Babylon afflicted the Israelite people, so now the unbelieving people afflict God’s people, because they are now mixed together but will one day be separated.

Yet even now they are separated, although not bodily, nevertheless in affection, because two loves make these two cities: the love of God and the love of the world. Let each person therefore question his own conscience and see whom he loves. If he loves the world, he is a citizen of Babylon. Let him therefore uproot desire and plant charity within himself, so that he may pass from the people of Babylon into the people of God, because this people is gathered from that one. The former is first in time; the latter is first in dignity: first the natural, then the spiritual.

But if he loves God, he recognizes himself as a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem and understands that he is a pilgrim here. Let him therefore endure captivity and hope in this way for his return to his homeland.

Jeremiah, whose name means “exalted”—namely, the teachers of the Church, whose minds are raised toward higher things and who despise earthly things—foretells this return to us. They teach us to leave the world not by bodily steps but by the steps of the soul: that is, to withdraw our love from the world’s confusion, because Babylon means “confusion,” and to sigh for the vision of peace, because Jerusalem means “vision of peace.”

And so let us begin to depart, because gradually abandoning all the things of the world and loving heavenly things is beginning to leave captivity. By believing, let us begin to rebuild the temple of God—that is, ourselves: “You are the temple of the living God” (1 Corinthians 3).

This temple is now being built, when we begin to depart; and one day it will be completed, when we arrive, when this mortal nature puts on immortality (1 Corinthians 15). Through Haggai, whose name means “festive,” we understand Christ, the true priest, in whom we truly keep Sabbath and celebrate the true festival, abstaining from vices.

He helps us on our return, makes us living stones suitable for the construction of that temple, and, as the cornerstone, makes the two peoples one in himself.

This captivity began in Adam and was, in a certain sense, ended in Christ: “For we were saved in hope” (Romans 8). It will finally end when this mortal nature puts on immortality.

The return of the children of Israel after seventy years signifies that our pilgrimage will end after this revolving world has passed away, since it revolves in a sevenfold cycle, that is, in the number of the seven days. Or it is sevenfold in this way: the life of each single day is understood within the sevenfold number, during which it has been granted us to work.

The seventh is that span of time in which, after the passage of this life, the resurrection is awaited; the eighth is the resurrection itself. Or because the number seven consists of three and four, in the number four we understand carnal generation, since the body consists of four elements—namely, those who lived carnally before the Lord’s coming.

By the number three we understand spiritual people, who came after the Lord’s coming, because of the soul’s threefold power: rational, irascible, and concupiscible. To these are added two others: teaching and virtue.

When this sevenfold period has therefore passed—that is, when the number of the faithful who are to be taken from both generations has been completed—this captivity will end.

The construction of the title is as follows: the words of this psalm refer to the end, namely, the end of the ages; that is, they are to be understood as taking place after the fullness of time has come. “A psalm of David”: that is, the good work of each faithful person. There was one David, but he is not always understood as one person.

This work is a song, that is, rejoicing over the word of pilgrimage—namely, over the knowledge of pilgrimage. This knowledge comes when they begin to depart; or the song itself comes when they begin to depart.

The voice in this psalm is therefore the voice of all the faithful, recognizing that as long as we are in this body we are pilgrims away from the Lord. From this pilgrimage he is already departing who has fixed his heart in heavenly things by the root of charity, and in this way he sings a hymn to God:

“To you praise is due, O God”: praise truly due to you in heart and deed—not to Jupiter, not to Apollo, not to this world. To you alone a hymn is fittingly sung, not in Babylon but in Zion, that is, among the people who are watchful: those who recognize that here they have no lasting city (Hebrews 13), but seek the one that is to come, greeting it from afar.

There are two cities: one of confusion, the other of divine vision. While you are still a pilgrim among the citizens of confusion, sigh for your homeland and sing from what you possess, not with your voice alone.

“To you praise is due, O God, in Zion,” because “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Sirach 15). Therefore it is in Zion, and not in Babylon.

“And to you the vow will be fulfilled in Jerusalem.” If you are renewed, you are no longer singing in Babylon. You fulfill your vows if you persevere to the end. Here the vow must be made; there it must be fulfilled, where there will be true peace and true joy.

If anyone rightly considers what he should vow to God, let him vow and offer himself. And so that I, renewed, may finally offer myself to you in Jerusalem, hear my prayer, made for perseverance, so that I may arrive there and not remain captive in Babylon. Therefore hear me, so that I may arrive, because “to you,” in whom there is the vision of peace, “all flesh will come.”

That is, people of every human kind—male or female, free or slave, rich or poor—will come to you, both in the first resurrection here and afterward in the second resurrection, when we shall be caught up to meet Christ in the air (1 Thessalonians 4).

Or for this reason hear me: every human being will turn to you, because you alone are the Redeemer. Or because he said “in Zion” and “in Jerusalem,” lest this appear to have been spoken only of the Jewish people, he specifies whom he wishes to receive.

Or, if it is spoken in the person of the Jews, the one known only in Judea is oppressed; through this we are taken captive by the nations. But the time will come when all flesh will come to knowledge through the Word made flesh: “In you all nations will be blessed” (Genesis 12). Or both the good and the wicked will appear before your tribunal.

It is necessary that you hear us because “the words of the wicked have prevailed against us”: the words of the serpent and Eve, “You will be like gods” (Genesis 3). They ruled over us excessively because they took us captive and drove us out of paradise.

Or because everyone learns the language and customs of the homeland in which he was born, the speaker—already wishing to return from the Babylon in which he was born to Jerusalem—says: “Our fathers truly cultivated falsehood” (Jeremiah 16). They taught us wicked things: to abandon the Creator who made us and worship what we ourselves made; to abandon the Creator and worship the creature; or to follow the doctrines of philosophers and the folly of the Gentiles.

“They prevailed,” I say, but they did not drown us, because “you will be merciful toward our iniquities.” He speaks to Christ as to a priest. Mercy is compassion shown after a sacrifice. Thus Christ, wishing to show mercy to his people, became a priest, praying to the Father with hands raised on the cross, so that you may say, “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Psalm 140).

He offered a sacrifice because he sacrificed himself on the altar of the cross: he himself the high priest, he himself the victim; he himself the one who shows mercy, he himself the mercy shown.

And those toward whom you show mercy will be blessed. But because he chose unity rather than multiplicity—not heretics, not schismatics—he fittingly says:

“Blessed is the one whom you chose by grace and took to yourself according to the rule of justice,” because those whom you call by grace you afterward take to yourself through justice. Or, the one whom you, Father, chose by calling and took from the mass of the lost through your Word.

And truly he is blessed, because “he will dwell in your courts”: that is, he will not be driven by any adversities from this temporal Church. Whoever dwells in the court will not be excluded from the palace.

He says “will dwell” because many inhabit this temporal Church but do not truly dwell in it: they believe for a time, and in the time of temptation they withdraw. A court is a suitable place in front of a house; likewise, in the adornment of virtues, this temporal Church precedes the one that will remain forever.

“He will dwell in your courts”: that is, he will persevere in this temporal Church. And finally “we shall be filled with the good things of your house,” so that we may understand many people in that blessed one. He says “we shall be filled” because, although there is unity in charity, there is nevertheless distinction among persons.

At first we are full of the good things of God’s house—that is, angelic virtues—but we emptied those good things. Finally, however, we shall again be filled with those good things with which your house is full: the angelic creature that you inhabit.

Or with those good things with which your house is full—that is, Christ, specifically his immortality and freedom from suffering; or with the virtues of your Christ; or with those good things with which those whom you inhabit are full.

And lest anyone think that these good things are gold, silver, and costly garments, with which the houses of mortals are adorned, he adds: “Holy is your temple.” That is, those who are your house are your temple. This temple is wondrous—that is, desirable and lovable—not in riches, not in gold or silver, but in justice.

For if justice were not wondrous in them, many saints—ragged, decrepit old men, seemingly contemptible—would appear unworthy; yet because of the beauty of justice they are held in honor.

Or, “we shall be filled with the good things of your house,” that is, of the Church, which keeps watch over the good things of various spiritual gifts, if we wish to receive present blessings.

“Holy is your temple.” If we understand Christ, the temple in which “the whole fullness of divinity dwells” is holy (Colossians 2), so that the house is the Church and the temple is Christ.

And so that we may be filled with those good things, or because blessed is the one whom you have taken to yourself, “hear us, O God our savior.” “Send the one whom you are going to send” (Exodus 4), our savior, by taking up our nature.

Hear us, you who are hope not only of Judea but “of all the ends of the earth”: that is, in you are all the nations of all the ends of the earth, namely, those who live at the ends of the nations, on the islands of the sea. For knowledge of you has reached even to them.

Or “of all the ends of the earth,” that is, of the Gentiles who surround our cultivated land.

Or “of all the ends of the earth,” that is, of all those who have withdrawn themselves from earthly things, not bodily but in affection.

“And hope in the distant sea”: that is, even those who are the sea—that is, bitter and immersed in the depth of this age, and therefore far from you—will hope in you.

Or “in the sea” explains “of all the ends of the earth”: he means not only the ends of the earth, that is, the sea and its islands, but also the distant sea, namely remote islands.

He shows how you will become the hope of the nations: by sending your teachers even to the ends of the earth, so that they may bring knowledge of you to all nations.

In this way God became the hope of all the ends of the earth: “preparing the mountains,” that is, the apostles, first illuminated by you and then transmitting your light to others, “by your strength,” not by their own, because they were weak in themselves but strong in you.

“God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Corinthians 1). Yours, I say, “girded with power,” that is, with those powerful ministers.

Alternatively: “Preparing the mountains by your strength”—that is, in Christ your strength was manifested. Christ will be “girded with power,” that is, with powerful flesh immune from sin. Through those mountains, by virtues and miracles, you disturb the depth of the sea for good: even the deep hearts of the impious, embittered by the depth of their sins.

According to this interpretation, you also disturb “the sound of its waves,” that is, you make those who contradict and persecute afraid.

Or “you disturb the depth of the sea,” that is, the devil; “the sound of its waves,” that is, the murmurs and disordered roarings of prophets and philosophers. Therefore they will be troubled when they see their holy men and prophets powerless and numerous.

Or “the sound of its waves” means the visions of rulers. And because they will see these things in the greater ones, “the nations will be troubled,” that is, the lesser ones.

“And those who inhabit the ends of the earth will fear”: those who are neither carnal nor entirely righteous—or, in a negative sense, those who are neither fully wicked nor fully righteous.

“You disturb through those mountains the depth of the sea,” that is, the deep hearts of the impious, so that they are stirred up against the mountains.

They will truly be troubled. For, when he says “the sound of its waves,” we should supply: who could endure it by himself when something great overtakes him? Words are often left incomplete.

“Unless the Lord had been with us when people rose up against us, they would perhaps have swallowed us alive” (Psalm 123). “The sound of its waves” means the threats and terrors of the persecutors of that sea.

He explains what he wishes to be understood by “sea”: “The nations will be troubled.” But what concern is that? Finally, not only those who are nearer, but also those who inhabit the ends of the earth—that is, the most remote—will fear.

Or those who, after fear, will make themselves inhabitants of the ends of the earth will first fear.

They will fear, I say, “because of your signs,” that is, miracles—not the signs of the mountains, but yours, as the Lord works with them and confirms the word through accompanying signs (Mark 16).

What follows from this—that they will fear and believe? “You will make the outlets of morning and the outlets of evening delightful.” That is, you will make them pass out through prosperity, signified by morning, and adversity, signified by evening, so that they are neither lifted up by prosperity nor broken by adversity.

If departure does not delight you, you will not labor to depart. What profit is there if you yourself gain but are condemned?

Consider the word of the Lord that should delight you, by which you are drawn not to consent to the one who promises you something in order that you may abandon justice or commit fraud. That is your morning: what flatters you with profit is a snare. You have a way out, a way of escape: return to the word of God.

“What does it profit a person to gain the whole world but suffer the loss of his soul?” (Matthew 16).

But if you are not being enticed to commit some offense and instead are being troubled, that is your evening; as though night were rushing upon you, you are weighed down. Yet here too you have a way of escape: the word of God. “Do not fear,” he says, “those who kill the body” (Matthew 10).

And thus “you will make the outlets of morning and evening delightful,” because he will make you despise both. In this way you will make them delightful.

“You visited the earth”: those who were formerly morning, made into earth and prepared for cultivation. You will visit them by justifying them and preparing their hearts for the furrows of your word.

“And you watered it abundantly; you multiplied its wealth”: that is, you enriched it with spiritual grace and manifold gifts.

Through which ministers will he visit it? “The river of God is filled with waters.” As though he were saying: that earth must be plowed, and first watered. But first the river of God—that is, the primitive Church of the Jews—from which streams flowed out, watering the whole earth.

That river is filled with waters, that is, with spiritual gifts and the preaching of truth. Thus that earth was watered, and by watering the earth through that river, “you prepared their food”: you gave them the bread of life and understanding. Those who had formerly been sea have now become cultivated land.

This food is not chewed by the teeth but devoured by the soul’s eagerness. Of it it is said, “Humanity ate the bread of angels” (Psalm 77). You prepared it, “for such is its preparation”: by grace, not by merit.

And because they have everything from you, O Lord, so that that river might be filled with waters, “water its streams”: the apostles, through whom that river may grow more and more. And through those streams “water its fruits”: multiply successors within the same people.

Thus afterward the Gentile people, sprouting from the showers of that same river—that is, from lighter teachings—will grow, in accordance with the saying, “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Corinthians 3). “It will rejoice,” that is, it will succeed the Church from the Jews with joy.

Alternatively: “You multiplied its wealth” means that you determined to enrich that earth with manifold gifts. Someone might ask: From where do those manifold gifts come? “The river of God”—that is, the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son—is filled, that is, is abundantly full, with waters, namely spiritual gifts. It is full not from another but from itself.

And you, God, by sending the Spirit through that river and watering hearts, “prepared the food of those who became your earth,” giving each person gifts appropriate to his capacity.

You do this, “for such is its preparation”—the preparation of the earth. Without you it could not be prepared.

“Water its streams”: elsewhere he calls them furrows, that is, fill the hearts of that earth, cut open by the plow of preaching, with the graces of the same river.

“And multiply its fruits”: that is, multiply those generated in Christ throughout the world.

Then “the sprouting growth”—that is, what is still inexperienced as it approaches the faith—“will rejoice in the showers of that river,” seeing the world already filled on every side with believers.

And thus, by restoring it, “you will bless the crown of the year of your goodness.” The year of goodness is the time of restoration. The years had been years of barrenness.

“The crown of the year”: glorious victors triumphing with Christ over the devil. You will bless those crowns—that is, those victors who will exist in the year of goodness, the time of restoration.

“You will bless”: that is, you will cause the number of your faithful to multiply.

“And your fields”—that is, the humble people represented by the crown, whom you made your own by grace—“will be filled with abundance,” with an abundance of virtues.

By these fields we understand the Jews, now humbled. “The beautiful places of the desert will also grow fat”: the Gentiles, who formerly were uncultivated, made beautiful by fear of the word of God, with the thorns of vices uprooted from them. They will grow fat with virtues and with the richness of good works.

“And your hills”—that is, those who stand out among others, namely their teachers—“will be girded with rejoicing”: they will be surrounded on every side by a rejoicing crowd of the faithful.

He explains what he said: “The hills will be girded with rejoicing.” “The rams of the sheep are clothed”—we should supply, with abundant fleece—that is, the preachers, the leaders of Christ’s flocks, will everywhere be covered with the multitude of the faithful like wool.

“And the valleys will abound in grain”: that is, they will abound in virtues and good works—not in barley, which is covered on the outside and hidden within. They will perform good works openly, so that others, seeing them, may glorify their Lord.

“Then all the hills and fields will cry out,” and this proves it: “For they will sing a hymn,” that is, they will praise God in heart and deed.

Alternatively: “You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness.” Up to this point he has said that God’s people will return from Babylon to Zion. From here onward he speaks of the reward they will receive who were not held in captivity.

O Lord, because here you will be merciful toward our iniquities, “you will bless”—you will increase—“the crown,” the multitude of the faithful surrounding you; or the victors who here proved victorious amid worldly attractions.

The crown, I say, “of the year of your goodness,” that is, prepared for you in the fullness of time, when you displayed your goodness to the human race.

“And your fields”—the Jews cultivated by the plow of your word—“will be filled with every kind of abundance,” when God will be all in all.

“The beautiful places of the desert will grow fat”: those who from the Gentile people will be made beautiful—that is, faithful—formerly without the moisture of the word of God, will be filled with every joy.

“And then the hills”—that is, the leaders among both peoples—“will be girded with rejoicing”: with great joy, carrying their sheaves.

They will rejoice because they have not labored in vain.

“The rams are clothed,” we should supply, with rejoicing, “when this mortal nature puts on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15): “the rams of the sheep,” that is, the leaders of Christ’s flocks.

“And the valleys,” that is, their subjects, “will abound in grain,” namely the bread of angels.

And when they see face to face the one whom they have long hungered for, then they will cry out. He adds what they will cry: “For they will sing a hymn,” that is, they will fulfill their vow in Jerusalem.

“Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm 83).

## Psalm 65. To the End: A Song of the Psalm of the Resurrection
“Shout for joy to God, all the earth; sing a psalm to his name, give glory to his praise. Say to God: ‘How awesome are your works, O Lord! In the abundance of your power your enemies will lie to you. All the earth shall worship you and sing to you; it shall sing a psalm to your name. Come and see the works of God, awesome in his counsels over the sons of men. He turned the sea into dry land; they crossed the river on foot; there we rejoiced in him. He rules by his power forever; his eyes watch over the nations. Let those who provoke him not exalt themselves. Bless our God, O nations, and make the voice of his praise heard. He has set my soul toward life and has not allowed my feet to be shaken. For you, O God, have tested us; you have examined us by fire, as silver is examined. You brought us into a snare; you placed tribulations upon our back; you set men over our heads. We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment. I shall enter your house with burnt offerings; I shall fulfill my vows to you, vows which my lips distinguished. And my mouth spoke in my tribulation. I shall offer you sacrifices rich in marrow, with the incense of rams; I shall offer you oxen with goats. Come and hear, all you who fear God, and I shall tell you how much he has done for my soul. I cried to him with my mouth, and I exalted him under my tongue. If I had looked upon iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have heard me. Therefore God heard me and attended to the voice of my prayer. Blessed be God, who has not removed my prayer or his mercy from me.”  

## EXPOSITION

[Col. 0471A]

“A canticle of a psalm,” that is, the exultation and joy of a good work—namely, the resurrection of our Lord. A canticle of a psalm is a spiritual hymn of knowledge acquired through works. A psalm of a canticle is the proclamation of a good work made present through the teaching of knowledge and understanding.

This psalm contains that exultation, namely, the joy of the most victorious resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, which went before in the Head and will follow in the Body—here in hope and finally in reality. The Jews claimed this hope of resurrection for themselves alone, presuming upon the righteousness of their merits and also upon the fact that they were descended from the patriarchs and prophets; and they assumed that the prophetic sayings were directed especially to them alone. In this psalm the prophet crushes their obstinacy, acting on behalf of the faith of the nations called to the same hope.

“Shout for joy to God, all the earth,” called to the glory of the resurrection. A jubilus is such great joy of heart that it cannot be expressed in words. “All the earth,” that is, the catholic Church. Whoever makes himself a part separated from the whole wishes to howl, not to shout for joy.

“Shout for joy,” that is, break forth into a voice of rejoicing—if not into words—not Judah alone, but all the earth placed in hope of the glory of the resurrection of the sons of God, already anticipated in the Head, though previously saddened by death.

“Sing a psalm to his name,” that is, do good works not for human praise but for the honor of God. To sing psalms is to make the voice correspond to the sound of a musical instrument by the striking of the hands. A psalm is a melody produced by that instrument which is called the psaltery. Shout for joy within yourselves; sing a psalm to others.

Whoever rejoices inwardly for the hearing of God should sing for the hearing of human beings—not for himself, but for his name—so that others, seeing your good works, may glorify your Father (Matthew 5).

And, while shouting for joy, “Give glory to his praise.” “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1). You nations, do not imitate the proud Jews, who, presuming upon the righteousness of their merits, begrudge the nations the grace of the Gospel—that their sins are forgiven—as though they themselves had nothing that needed to be forgiven, although it is written: “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Romans 3). They also, as righteous laborers, promise themselves the glory of the resurrection as their reward; they think themselves healthy when they are sick. And therefore they are sick in a more dangerous way: if they were sick more mildly, they would never, in their delirium, kill the physician.

But “give glory to his praise,” that is, do not give glory to us on account of righteousness, but to God. Rejoicing and glad, do not rejoice in yourselves, lest through pride you lose what you received through humility. Rather, be afraid when you see others cast down through pride. Say—not with the mouth but in the heart, to God, that is, for God’s praise: “How awesome are your works, O Lord,” that is, “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling.”

“The olive tree has been cut off, and you, a wild olive, have been grafted in. Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Romans 11); do not exalt yourself over the branches that have been cut off. For you do not bear the root, but the root bears you. If God did not spare the natural branches, he will spare you even less (ibid.), since, though sterile by nature, you have been grafted into the richness of the olive tree.

Augustine: “My brothers, just as one must not insult the old fracture, so neither the new one—that is, the heretics—but one must pray for them. For God is powerful enough to graft them in again (ibid.). Christ’s poured-out blood was given to murderers—I will not say ‘God-killers’; and the one whom they poured out in their madness, they now drink through mercy.”

Truly, your works are to be feared, “because in the abundance of your power your enemies will lie to you.” Other enemies lie about those opposed to them in order to diminish their power and glory; but your enemies lie for the purpose of making your power shine forth.

“In the abundance of your power,” that is, so that your power—your might—may be shown in abundance. “They will lie to you,” that is, for your glory. “Your enemies,” namely, the Jews. Nowhere did the power of God appear so great and so manifest as in the resurrection. To rise from death was greater than not to die.

The Lord himself first commended this power when he said: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster for three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights” (Matthew 12; John 2). Just as the sea-monster vomited Jonah out alive, so the earth did Christ.

Meanwhile, he commended the same power of the resurrection when the Jews asked, “By what authority are you doing these things?” (Matthew 21). And he replied: “Destroy this temple, and after three days I will raise it up” (John 2).

The unbelieving Jews, having seen many powers and many miracles, sought grounds for putting him to death but found none. Finally they brought forward many false witnesses, and at last they brought those who said: “I can destroy this temple and after three days rebuild it” (Matthew 26).

Augustine: “You lie, false Jewish witness. For he said, ‘Destroy it.’ He dies voluntarily, not by necessity; he lays down his soul, and no one takes it. They lied, therefore, so that you might be crucified; you were crucified so that you might die; you died so that you might rise again; you rose again so that believers might be saved.

“Again, when you died and rose from death, they lied—not to themselves but to you. Your enemies were placed as guards at the tomb. Seeing him rise, they told the truth; but the same greed that had taken captive the disciple who was Christ’s companion also took captive the soldier guarding the tomb.

“The number of liars was increased so that the number of believers might be increased. Against the liars you appeared with truthful witnesses—truthful because you made them so.”

Augustine: “Come, false witness. If you were awake, why did you not prevent it? If you were asleep, how do you know what happened? You lie against yourself and against Christ. You lie, but you make me certain of the true power. Perhaps I would have doubted; but your manifest falsehood does not permit it, and I cannot disagree with so great a falsehood.”

Therefore, in place of Judah, which has been taken away, “all the earth shall worship you,” that is, it shall venerate you as God and not despise you as a human being. Because one part of the earth adhered to falsehood, the whole world is admonished to embrace the truth. Let it humble itself before you, because shortly before you were most humble among the hands of liars, yet most high above the head of praising angels.

[Col. 0473A]

Let it worship with its mouth and sing to you through its works, not to itself, so that those who see good works may glorify you. And in worshiping you, it sings to you, because this comes from your grace; therefore let it sing a psalm to your name.

“Come” from every land by believing; leave the lying Jews; “and see,” that is, understand, the works of the Lord—namely, that he is “awesome in his counsels over the sons of men.” Do not consider the form in which he was a human being among human beings, but the awesome counsel by which he is above human beings.

The sons of men who crucified him were blinded; the one who was crucified was exalted. What they devised for the death of one, he turned into the salvation of many. What their cunning counsels contrived for destruction, he, by a just judgment, turned to salvation for some and to blindness for others, so that at last the blinded might be humbled, the humbled might confess, and those who confessed might be enlightened.

[Col. 0473B]

And in this he is awesome: “He turned the sea into dry land,” that is, he turned the world, embittered by destructive anxieties and raging with the waves of persecutions, into dry land—that is, into earth—so that it might thirst for sweet water, namely, the grace of the Holy Spirit and the teaching of the Word of God.

He advanced those who had been converted to such a degree that “they will cross the river on foot,” that is, easily. The river is the whole world, because while one thing passes away, another succeeds it. Or the order itself, the necessity governing the possession of things, is a kind of river.

In this river one crosses on foot, that is, easily, if those who are in it are turned into dry land and are not entangled in it but believe in Christ. Then there will be no need to seek a horse, because his humility will carry them: thus what is mortal and passing will finally become immortal and incorruptible.

Or “on foot,” that is, with Christ as leader. By believing in him, they will cross the river with their feet—that is, with humility—not on a horse, meaning exalted pride. He crossed this world on foot, through humility, and not on a horse, through pride. They will cross the river, that is, overcome this age.

“There,” that is, in that crossing, whether in the present or in the future, “we shall rejoice”—here in hope, there in reality—not in our merits, but in him who rules by his power through rising again, who previously served in weakness.

He rules by his own power, not by another’s, as a human being who reigns by the multitude of his soldiers. There we shall rejoice, not Jews alone but also the nations, “because his eyes watch over the nations,” that is, he calls the nations to mercy, not the Jews alone, as it is written: “The nations, however, are to glorify God for his mercy” (Romans 15).

And because all need mercy, both Jews and Gentiles, “those who provoke,” that is, those who quarrel in indignation over the calling of the nations and thereby provoke God, making him angry, “let them not exalt themselves in themselves,” that is, let them not glory in their merits. Rather, let them be humbled within themselves, confessing that they are sinners and need mercy, so that they may be exalted in God.

Therefore, because his eyes watch over the nations, “bless our God,” that is, the God common to Jews and Gentiles. Let the Jews boast of their righteousness; but you nations, bless God for the mercy bestowed upon you. “Make the voice of his praise heard,” that is, make it heard, because “all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Romans 3), not their own glory.

“Bless,” that is, humble yourselves beneath the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you (1 Peter 5).

[Col. 0474A]

He is rightly to be blessed—that is, praised—by all nations, in whom all nations receive blessing, just as in the first man they received a curse, to whom it was said: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die” (Genesis 3). “Just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Corinthians 15).

Or, “bless within yourselves; make it heard to others.”

Therefore, “bless our God,” that is, bless the one whom we Jews bless, because he has bestowed mercy not only upon you but also upon us. Bless the one whom I, David, bless:

“He has set my soul toward life,” that is, he humbled my soul and caused me to understand my sin, so that in this way it might live, according to the saying: “God imprisoned all under sin, so that he might have mercy on all” (Romans 11).

Or, he set the soul placed in death in Adam toward life in himself. Or, he humbled my soul through many afflictions by which he leads it to eternal life.

“And he did not allow my feet to be shaken,” that is, in tribulations he made me persevere in such a way that my affections were in no way shaken. For no one who puts his hand to the plough ought to look back (Luke 9).

“He did not allow them to be shaken,” but rather to be tested, for “you have tested us, O God.” Or the passage may be connected in this way: As though he were saying, “Why were the feet to be shaken?” Because one enters the kingdom of God through many tribulations.

“You have tested us, O God,” that is, you led us into examination, so that we might test our heart, something unknown to us before the labor. The scourges of the one who corrects must be endured, lest finally the sentence of the one who punishes be imposed.

In this way you tested us: “You examined us by fire,” the fire of tribulation—not to consume us, but to remove our filth, “as silver is examined.” You did not reduce us to ashes like straw, but made us pure like silver. In this way you examined us.

“You brought us into a snare,” of the body, not of the mind—a snare that would bind the body but loosen the soul’s bonds—not so that we might be destroyed, but so that we might experience your liberations.

“You placed tribulations upon our back,” previously held upright in the wrong way; that is, you made us your anvil. We were erect through pride; you bent us so that we might be humbled.

In this way you placed tribulations upon us: “You set men over our heads.” We saw those above us who were worse than we were; yet unharmed we passed through fire and water.
