The comparison is drawn from a pot which, if it is properly hardened by fire, is not dissolved by water. In the same way we were made solid through suffering, so that flatteries could not dissolve us.

[Col. 0474D]

And finally, after you tested us, you brought us into refreshment. He adds: “I shall enter your house.”

Or here you brought us into refreshment of mind after we had passed through fire and water—not so that we might grow cold, but so that, at rest, we might burn more ardently.

“I shall enter your house,” above, into the heavenly Jerusalem, into the fellowship of the citizens above, “with burnt offerings,” where I shall offer myself wholly consumed by divine fire, when “this corruptible body puts on incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15) and the soul is without offense.

Then “I shall fulfill my vows to you,” that is, I shall offer you myself, whom I vowed to you here. Whoever rightly considers what he should vow to God should vow himself and give himself wholly.

“Those vows which my lips distinguished,” first in tribulations—that is, they clearly separated them from things that should not be vowed.

This distinction is that you accuse yourself and praise him; that you attribute no good to yourself and no evil to him; that you acknowledge yourself needy and him sufficient; yourself sinful and him merciful; yourself lying and him truthful.

“And I shall offer you what my mouth spoke,” namely, the mouth of the heart made harmonious with the voice, “in my tribulation,” that is, the tribulation which I recognized as mine—that is, useful to me—because “tribulation produces endurance” (Romans 5). These are the things I vowed; these are the things my mouth spoke in my tribulation.

“I shall offer you sacrifices rich in marrow,” that is, sacrifices full of inward charity, not outward charity, desiring not transitory things but eternal ones. As though he were saying: The fire of tribulation prepares such a victim.

“I shall offer you oxen,” that is, those who reject the obstinacy of the Law and submit their necks to Christ’s gentle yoke, “with goats,” that is, with those who were previously foul through sins but afterward cleanse them through repentance and almsgiving and persevere in good works.

This is spoken in the person of the Church. But if it is spoken in the person of one believer: “I shall offer you sacrifices rich in marrow,” that is, fat and acceptable sacrifices, “with the incense of rams,” that is, by putting lust to death within me; “I shall offer you oxen,” by putting pride to death, “with goats,” by condemning the stench of vices.

Or we give God as a burnt offering a contrite spirit; but it is rich in marrow when we carry faith and action within us. When these two things have been carefully completed, the Christian becomes perfect.

“And I shall offer these burnt offerings with the incense of rams,” that is, with the prayer of prelates. By imitating them, “I shall offer you oxen with goats”: oxen, preachers ploughing human hearts with the plough of the Word of God; goats, shaggy with the thorns of vices. Yet the Church offers these also after they have been converted.

The thief was a goat, who confessed the Lord on the cross (Luke 21); the Lord looked upon him, and he became his ox, his preacher.

And because the Lord has bestowed such great mercy upon me, “come” with the steps of faith; “hear” with the inner ear, that is, understand carefully—not from Judah alone, but “all you who fear God.”

For no one is granted to hear—that is, to understand—the things that ought to be understood except those who fear God with chaste fear. In other words, let the fear of God open the ears of those who love, so that there may be an entrance for what I am about to narrate.

“How much he has done for my soul.” Hear for this reason: so that he may do the same for your souls. These are the good things he did for me.

Previously I cried out to another, and with another’s mouth, not my own. But he himself taught me to whom I should cry and how.

“I cried to him,” that is, not on account of something else. Such crying does not belong to the antiquity of the fathers but to gratuitous newness. “With my mouth,” not another’s, according to the saying, “as you were being led, go” (1 Corinthians 12).

Previously I went to a creature in the manner of the tradition of the fathers. Or “with my mouth,” that is, with a voice corresponding to the heart. It is therefore my mouth because I rejoiced under my tongue, that is, in my heart.

If you cry out one thing with your mouth but desire another in your heart, you are not crying out to him with your own mouth. Therefore one must cry out with the mouth in such a way that there is no exultation under the tongue—that is, in the heart—except in those things that sound rightly in the mouth. And insofar as divine grace grants it to the Christian soul, let him preach him alone and rejoice in him.

O supreme Good! For protection is above every glory. Therefore “I exalted him under my tongue.”

For “if I had looked upon iniquity in my heart,” while there was righteousness in my mouth, “the Lord would not have heard me.”

This is characteristic of the Body of Christ. Has someone perhaps been exposed? “He acted badly,” you say; “he acted perversely.” Yet perhaps you yourself desire what you condemn in another. You cry out not because he did it, but because he was caught—that is, you were preparing to do it yourself, if the law did not oppose you: “But love casts out fear” (1 John 4).

Iniquity should not be looked upon but looked down upon. It deserves to be despised so that it may be trampled underfoot, not looked upon so that it may be loved. Let every perverse thing displease you inwardly, if you wish to please the one who sees inwardly.

“Therefore,” that is, because I cried out as I ought to cry out, “God heard me.” He will likewise hear you if you cry out to him rightly.

Truly he heard, because he “attended,” that is, showed himself attentive, “to the voice of my prayer,” prayers made for sins.

Therefore “blessed be God,” that is, may he be multiplied in his own people, “who has not removed my prayer,” made for perseverance—that is, he did not delay giving what I prayed for—“and has not removed his mercy from me,” by which he calls and by which he justifies.

## PSALM 65. “TO THE END; IN HYMNS; A PSALM OF A CANTICLE OF DAVID”

“May God have mercy on us and bless us; may he enlighten his face upon us and have mercy on us. So that we may know your way on earth, your salvation among all nations. Let the peoples confess to you, O God; let all the peoples confess to you. Let the nations rejoice and exult, because you judge the peoples with equity and direct the nations on earth. Let the peoples confess to you, O God; let all the peoples confess to you: the earth has yielded its fruit. May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him.”

## EXPOSITION

This following psalm can be joined to the preceding one, because those earlier figures—David and the others—saw beforehand the future resurrection of the Lord and the incorporation of the nations into one body, and they pray that those other sheep may be brought in.

According to Augustine, this is the title. According to Jerome, it is as follows: David was one person, but this name does not always signify one person, just as in this psalm the voice is that of all the faithful.

The Lord says: “I am the true vine, you are the branches, and my Father is the cultivator” (John 15). Since, therefore, the Body of Christ is God’s vineyard, it asks the Lord of the vineyard to cultivate and bless it, so that it may bear abundant fruit. The first members also pray that many may be incorporated into the body.

This psalm is referred “to the end,” that is, to perfection, so that the Body of Christ may be perfected. It is to be understood “in hymns,” that is, in praises, because the multiplication of the faithful is great praise of God. And it is a psalm of a canticle, that is, the work of exultation, because to perform this and to desire it is great joy.

The Church, directing her supplication, hastens to the aid of the necessary name, saying:

“May God have mercy on us.” The one who does not presume upon merits rightly asks first for mercy. First it was necessary that he have mercy on those who had gone astray, and afterward that he bestow the gifts of his blessing.

Let us therefore sing these things, pray for these things, entreat these things—not with an empty voice but with a truthful heart, not with a barren voice but with a fertile heart.

“May God have mercy on us,” that is, may he justify us by his grace. “And bless us,” that is, may he multiply us in virtues, or multiply us in number. With this blessing, let him bless us.

“May he enlighten his face upon us.” The psalm asks for a certain singular blessing, which only the good desire—not the blessings belonging to the present age, which God willed to be common to the good and the wicked.

For if he gave such things only to the good, the wicked would think that God should be worshiped solely for this reason. If he gave them only to the wicked, the weak among the good would be afraid to convert, lest they should lack such things. Again, if such things were taken away from the good alone, the things with which the wicked are punished would themselves be regarded as the only punishment.

When, therefore, God gives these things to the good, he consoles those who fear him; when he gives them to the wicked, he admonishes the good to desire other things.

And because the psalm asks for this blessing, let us hear it: “May he enlighten his face upon us.” This does not mean that he enlighten himself in relation to us, for the light that enlightens all things cannot itself be enlightened. Rather, may he enlighten his face—that is, his will—upon us by giving us knowledge of his will.

Or, “You impressed your face upon us,” that is, you made us according to your image, which we have obscured. Send the ray of your wisdom; drive away our darkness, so that your image—namely, reason—may shine in us.

And after the enlightenment of his face, may he have mercy on us with this mercy: “So that we may know your way on earth,” not in one part only, but “your salvation among all nations,” that is, Christ.

What is “earth” above is “all nations” here; what is “way” there is “salvation” here. In this land of the dying, show us the way that leads to the land of the living—the way that does not deceive, namely, your Christ, who said: “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14).

He is the way because he leads to himself; the truth because by him we do not go astray; the life because he leads to himself, so that we may rest in him.

And so that they may know him, “let the peoples confess to you, O God”: let them confess their iniquity, confess your grace; let them accuse themselves and praise you; let them rebuke themselves and glorify you.

Let the Jewish peoples confess to you; let all peoples confess to you. For all have sinned (Romans 3).

Let me make this confession not in sorrow but in joy: “Let the nations rejoice and exult.” If thieves confessing before a judge weep, then faithful people confessing before God will rightly exult—and this because he is merciful.

He demands confession in order to free the humble. Let him find you as your punisher, so that he may send you his savior. He condemns the one who does not confess, because he rightly punishes the proud.

Therefore let those who confess to you and punish themselves exult, because they confess before the one who “judges the peoples with equity,” saving the humble and condemning the proud.

Someone might say: “There is no reason to rejoice because he judges the peoples with equity.” To this the psalm adds: “And you direct the nations on earth.” You direct them in the land of the dying so that they will not fear when they are judged in the land of the living.

Let them therefore be corrected in the land of the dying, so that, when judged, they may not be condemned in the land of the living.

Since, therefore, through mercy you direct them before you judge them, “let the peoples confess to you, O God,” with a praiseworthy confession—not the Jews alone, but “let all the peoples confess to you.”

Let them praise you for this reason: “The earth has yielded its fruit.” The earth, previously sterile before confession, now cultivated by your right hand—that is, Christ—has yielded the fruit of good works.

This right hand both thunders and rains. Let us fear the one who thunders; let us receive the one who pours down rain.

And because the earth has now been watered for fruitfulness, let its cultivator not abandon it in its fruit, but let him bless it—that is, let God the Father multiply us; let God the Son, our God, bless us; let God the Holy Spirit bless us.

And so may he multiply us that at last “all the ends of the earth may fear him,” so that the whole earth may worship the Creator and not the creature. Just as it belongs to good earth to produce fruit, so it belongs to good servants to fear the Lord.

It can also be understood in this way: “The earth has yielded its fruit.” The first earth—that is, the first human being—did not yield its fruit; that is, it did not show the obedience it owed.

The second human being, heavenly and from heaven, “did not regard equality with God as a thing to be seized”; he became obedient unto death and “yielded his fruit” (Philippians 2).

Or, “The earth has yielded its fruit,” because those who have been renewed do good—not from fear of punishment but from love of righteousness.

## PSALM 67. “TO THE END; A PSALM OF A CANTICLE OF DAVID”

“Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered; let those who hate him flee from his face. As smoke vanishes, so let them vanish; as wax melts before the fire, so let sinners perish before the face of God. But let the righteous feast and exult in the sight of God and delight in gladness. Sing to God; sing a psalm to his name; make a way for him who ascends over the setting sun—the Lord is his name. Exult in his sight; they will be troubled before his face, the father of orphans and judge of widows. God is in his holy place; God, who makes those of one mind dwell in a house. He leads prisoners out by his strength; likewise those who provoke him, who dwell in tombs. O God, when you went forth before your people, when you passed through the desert, the earth was shaken; indeed, the heavens dripped before the face of God, Sinai before the face of God, the God of Israel. You will set apart, O God, a rain of your generosity for your inheritance; it was weakened, but you perfected it. Your animals will dwell in it; in your sweetness you prepared it for the poor, O God. The Lord will give the word to those evangelizing with great power. The King of the powers of the beloved, of the beloved, and of the beauty of the house, to divide the spoils. If you sleep among the midst of the allotted portions, the wings of the dove are silvered, and the back parts of its back are pale with gold. When the heavenly one distinguishes kings over it, they will be whitened with snow on Selmon. The mountain of God is a rich mountain. A mountain made solid, a rich mountain. Why do you suspect mountains made solid? The mountain in which it pleased God to dwell; indeed, the Lord will dwell there forever. God’s chariots are ten thousandfold, thousands of rejoicing ones; the Lord is among them, at Sinai, in the holy place. You ascended on high; you took captivity captive; you received gifts among human beings. Indeed, even from those who do not believe, that the Lord God may dwell there. Blessed be the Lord day by day; our God will make our journey prosperous, the God of our salvation. Our God is the God who saves, and the Lord God has the exits from death. Yet God will crush the heads of his enemies, the crown of the hair of those who walk in their sins. I said: ‘The Lord: From Bashan I will turn back; I will turn back into the depth of the sea.’ So that your foot may be dipped in blood, the tongue of your dogs may have its share from the enemies by him. They saw your processions, O God, the processions of my God, my king, who is in the holy place. The princes came together with those singing psalms, in the midst of young women playing timbrels. In the assemblies bless God the Lord, from the springs of Israel. There is Benjamin, the youngest, in ecstasy; the princes of Judah are their leaders; the princes of Zebulun and the princes of Naphtali. Command, O God, your power; strengthen this, O God, which you have worked in us. From your temple in Jerusalem kings will offer gifts to you. Rebuke the beasts of the reed; the assembly of bulls among the calves of the peoples, so that they may exclude those who have been tested as silver. Scatter the nations that desire wars; envoys will come from Egypt; Ethiopia will hasten to stretch out its hands to God. Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing psalms to the Lord. Sing psalms to God, who ascends over the heaven of heaven toward the east. Behold, he will give his voice the voice of power. Give glory to God over Israel; his magnificence and his power are in the clouds. God is wonderful in his holy ones; the God of Israel himself will give power and strength to his people. Blessed be God.”

## EXPOSITION

The prophet, foreseeing in the Holy Spirit the reward that God’s friends will possess and the punishment that his enemies will possess, both in this life and in the future, sets both reward and punishment before us: so that through punishment he may deter the wicked, and through reward invite the good.

He speaks as follows:

God shall arise, and his enemies shall be scattered. As though he were saying: Let him die, be buried, rise again, ascend into heaven, send the Holy Spirit, and thus let God arise into the knowledge of human beings. “And let his enemies be scattered”—that is, let those who inwardly oppose him be blinded to themselves; or let them be scattered outwardly, like the Jews, who, after losing their kingdom, were scattered everywhere; or let them be scattered in a beneficial scattering, so that from enemies they may become friends.

“And let those who hate him flee from his face”—that is, let the heretics who hate him flee from his face, namely, from the saints in whom his face appears. Through them he acts as though he were present; from them his enemies flee in fear, though not by hiding. We have seen this in many cases: they would not dare to appear in the presence of the saints. Or let them flee from the angry one to the reconciled one, according to the saying: “What shall we do, brothers?” (Acts 1).

“As smoke disappears, so let them disappear.” Note that smoke, produced by fire, vanishes all the more quickly the farther it extends upward. These men, likewise, lifted high by the fire of their hatred, “setting their mouth against heaven,” perished in a great collapse: for they insulted the captive and mocked him while he hung; hence they swelled with pride as victors, but soon vanished as the vanquished. Or let them disappear in their inward self, that is, let them recognize that through their pride they have become ruined, just as smoke disappears; and thus, by assuming humility, let them lay aside pride.

But let sinners who remain in their pride perish from the face of God—that is, let them be removed from it—just as wax flows before the face of fire. For just as wax placed before fire cannot endure, so a sinner cannot remain before the face of God, since it is said: “Let the impious be removed, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26). And elsewhere: “You shall place them like an oven of fire at the time of your face” (Ps. 20).

“And let the righteous feast and exult in the sight of God.” Let sinners perish from the face of God, but let the righteous feast and exult; that is, let them exult with as much joy in the sight of God—in their inward self, where he alone sees—as feasters ordinarily exult with joy, even though they may suffer adversity in the sight of human beings. Thus at last they may rejoice in gladness, where inwardly and outwardly they will be filled with spiritual delight.

But in order that you may rejoice, “sing to God inwardly; sing a psalm to his name” (Ps. 67). That is, act outwardly in such a way that his name may be spread abroad through you with praise. “Make a way for him,” so that through the beautiful feet of the Jews who evangelize, the hearts of believers may become passable. Hence Isaiah says: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God” (Isa. 40).

“Make a way for him”—for him, I say, “who ascends above the setting,” that is, whose ascent is in those in whom the old age has set and newness has shone forth. For by ascending into human hearts through the knowledge of himself, he destroys the old man in them and gives life to the new. Or, “he who ascends above the setting”—that is, above the world, which he himself made into a setting by conquering death. Or, “he who ascends above the setting”—that is, above those who were utterly desperate and always in decline, because the sun of righteousness had not shone upon them.

And a way is rightly prepared for him, because “the Lord is his name,” not the name the Jews gave him: “You have a demon” (John 7); “In Beelzebul, the prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Luke 11).

Make a way for him; and in making the way, although you suffer many adversities in the sight of human beings, nevertheless do not fail or become sorrowful, but always exult in his sight—that is, in your inward self. But those who resist you will be troubled, being removed from his face—his, I say, who is “the father of orphans,” namely, of those who have been cut off by the sword of the Spirit from hope in a carnal father and have placed all their hope in God, “and the judge of widows.”

Widows are those who, through the word of God, have been cut off from hope in worldly union and desire only the embrace of the true bridegroom. The Lord is their judge, defending them from every diabolical assault.

How he is both father and judge is added: “For God himself is in his holy place,” that is, in the widows and orphans, making them his holy place. And God himself causes those in whom he dwells to inhabit a house—that is, his Church—so that they may be of one character, namely, unanimous and of one accord, according to the saying: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4).

“He brings out those who are bound in strength.” See how he makes them dwell in the house: by bringing the Jews out of the bonds of sins, by which they were hindered from walking in the ways of the commandments. He does this in his own strength, not because of their merits; or he gives them the strength they previously lacked. And he brings out not only those who have been conquered, but likewise those who provoke him—that is, those who embitter God by defending their sins. Such people dwell in tombs: they live already dead inwardly. Of them it is said: “When the sinner has come into the depths, he despises” (Prov. 18).

By “those who are bound,” note, are meant those who already have the will to turn back, but whom the bonds of sins prevent from rising; the Lord brings them out in strength and makes them dwell in his house. He also brings out those who are in tombs—that is, those who are immersed in sins and have no desire at all to rise.

These two kinds of sinners are signified by the woman whom the devil had bound for eighteen years and whom the Lord finally released (Luke 13), and by Lazarus, who had been four days in the tomb and whom the Lord raised from the tomb (John 11).

This same Lord, who performed these wonders in bodies, performs even more wonderfully in conduct every day. For it is more wonderful to give life to a dead soul than to call Lazarus from the tomb and restore him to the life of the flesh.

“O God, when you went out before your people, when you passed through the wilderness, the earth was shaken.” See how he brings out those who are bound and those who dwell in the tomb. For “the earth was shaken”—that is, earthly people will be moved—when you, O God, go out before your people; that is, when through good works you are understood to be present in the knowledge of your people. God will go out before the people when that people acts in such a way that God is glorified through it.

“When you pass through the wilderness”—that is, when you are everywhere brought into the knowledge of the nations.

And how will this happen? “The heavens distilled”: that is, the apostles will distill from the face of God of Sinai, namely, from the knowledge of God who gave the law on Sinai; and from the face of the God of Israel—not Israel according to the flesh, but true Israel, which receives grace and does not presume upon carnal observance. For it is written: “He who gave the law will give blessing” (Ps. 83). He who gave the law, which terrifies the one who presumes upon himself, will give blessing, which liberates the one who hopes in him.

“You will set apart a willing rain, O God, for your inheritance.” This is what the heavens distilled: a willing rain, that is, a shower of the word of God, bestowed freely and not according to human merits. You will set apart this rain for your inheritance—that is, you will entrust this rain only to your elect, because faith does not belong to everyone.

“And it was weakened”—the inheritance, namely, recognizing its sins and perceiving that it should attribute nothing to itself; thus, being weakened, it was weakened. But you, that is, in the truth of the matter, made it perfect. Hence the Apostle says: “I was a persecutor and a blasphemer, but I obtained mercy” (1 Tim. 1).

Or, in another sense, the inheritance was weakened by enduring tribulations in itself, but you strengthened it and thus made it perfect, for “strength is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12).

“You will set apart a willing rain, O God, for your inheritance,” in which inheritance your creatures will dwell—no longer belonging to themselves, but yours, subject to you and not free for themselves.

And how will this happen? For you, O God, prepared it—that is, the inheritance—for the poor, not for the rich; for the needy, not for the self-sufficient. And you did this in sweetness, that is, in your grace and not through anyone’s merit.

Note that by the inheritance are meant the apostles, namely, the first preachers, to whom the most health-giving rain was specially divided, so that they might shower others with the saving rain of divine speech. In them the creatures of the Lord will dwell, namely, the faithful converted through them, always finding in them what can refresh them.

This is said by analogy with someone who plans an appropriate place in his estate where he may store his grain and later place the animals to be fed. The Lord planned these things in the Church. He sent ahead the apostles, filled with wholesome food, from whom his creatures might receive nourishment.

We explain the preceding passage in another way: “He brings out those who are bound in strength,” and likewise those who provoke him, who dwell in tombs. And how does he do this? “The earth was shaken”—that is, earthly people will be moved; and this because “the heavens will distill from the face of God of Sinai, from the face of the God of Israel.”

And what will they distill? “A willing rain,” which you, O God, will set apart for your inheritance. All these things were not sudden, but had long ago been prefigured. For you, O God, prefigured all these things when you went out before your Jewish people, leading that people out of Egypt, going before it by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire (Exod. 13–14).

The pillar of cloud that went before by day signified that you would come gently in judgment to those who are in the day—that is, to those upon whom the sun of righteousness has shone. The pillar of fire that went before by night signified the dreadful coming of the Lord to those who love darkness more than light.

The people’s being led through the wilderness signified the Church dwelling in this world as in a wilderness. Then the material earth was shaken, prefiguring that the spiritual earth would be shaken because of its sin.

The outer heavens then distilled manna, food of every taste; and afterward the inner heavens distilled the divine word, making known Christ incarnate, the most wholesome food of every taste, concerning which he himself testifies: “My blood is true drink, and my flesh is truly food” (John 6).

The heavens also distilled Moses and the others, along with a willing rain, namely, the law given by your gracious will. You set this law apart for your inheritance, namely, the Jewish people. And the rain was weakened—that is, the law itself was weakened—but you perfected it. The law was weakened when people understood that no one could be saved through the law understood carnally.

The Lord perfected it by changing it from a carnal understanding to a spiritual one. Thus what carnal observance could not accomplish, grace supplied. “You perfected it”—namely, the rain—and in that perfected rain your creatures will dwell.

And rightly will they dwell in it. For you, O God, prepared—that is, perfected—the rain itself for the poor, that is, for the work of your poor one; and this in your sweetness, not through the poor one’s merit.

And this is how you prepared it: “The Lord will give a word to those who evangelize with great strength,” that is, with great steadfastness and many signs, according to the saying: “The Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark 16).

Note that the Lord promised the word to those who evangelize when he said: “When you stand before kings” (Mark 13), and so forth.

“The Lord will give a word to those who evangelize.” The Lord, I say, “the king of the powers of the Beloved, of the Beloved.” What this Beloved is was made known by the Father’s voice, which said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3). The powers of this Beloved are the apostles and the other preachers, who make others strong in faith.

The repetition of the name shows the prophet’s great faith and devotion toward the Beloved.

“The king of the powers of the Beloved—and of the chosen,” understood, “to divide the spoils,” that is, the human race liberated from the captivity of the strong armed one. And to whom did he divide them? “To the beauty of the house,” that is, for the adornment of his Church. For he made some apostles, some prophets, and others evangelists (Eph. 4), from among those in whom the strong armed one had trusted.

“If you sleep among the midst of the lots.” He turns to his hearers in order to incite them to evangelize. As though he were saying: The Lord will give the word to those who evangelize, namely, to the leaders in the Church; and not only to them, but also to you, if you sleep among the midst of the lots—that is, if you rest between the two Testaments, not departing from their authority, but confirming whatever arises by the authority of those two Testaments, so that every dispute may be brought to an end in peaceful concord.

Note that here the effect is put for the cause. The Testaments are the cause of the inheritance being given, and the inheritance is understood here through the word “lots.” For *cleronomia* in Greek means “inheritance”; hence *cleronomos*, “heir.” Since no inheritance is given except to one whom the testaments designate, the Testaments are understood by “lots”: the term denotes both what produces and what is produced. Thus he says: “If you sleep among the midst of the lots.”

You, I say, who are “the feathers of the dove”—that is, of the Church, which is a dove because it is innocent and without the gall of bitterness. The dove is “silvered,” because of the brilliance of divine eloquence, or because it is so pure that it does not crack beneath the hammers of tribulations. And the “rear parts of its back”—that is, its shoulders—are fit to bear the Lord’s burden, which is gentle for those who are willing but difficult for those who are unwilling. This is “in the pallor of gold,” that is, in charity and wisdom; or it signifies perfection through good works.

The pallor of gold is like greenness, for when something red grows pale, it appears almost green. And because all things ought to grow green in charity, charity is rightly signified by greenness.

Note the Greek construction, “among the midst of the lots.” Where we ordinarily say “between me and you,” the Greeks put “the midst of me and you.” This construction has particular force where the two extremes have some affinity with one another, as do the Old and New Testaments.

Or, in another sense: The Lord will give the word to those who evangelize if you who evangelize sleep among the midst of the lots—that is, between the two inheritances: the carnal inheritance promised by the Old Testament when taken according to the letter, and the spiritual inheritance which we already await in hope through grace.

Rest in such a way that you neither seize the carnal inheritance eagerly nor await it impatiently. This sleep is good: it means that we despise the inheritance in which we now are and hold firmly to the other, already possessing it in hope, although not yet in reality.

The one who eagerly and greedily seizes this earthly inheritance is far removed from that sound. Such a person is swept into every kind of turmoil and depravity, desiring in order to acquire and fearing in order to lose. Therefore you must rest between the two inheritances. If you sleep in this way, you will be the feathers of the dove, greatly exalting and proclaiming it on high.

And the rear parts of its back—that is, those who come later and take up the same burden of the Lord that the earlier ones bore—will be “in the pallor of gold,” that is, in perfect charity and good conduct. For while later generations are encouraged by the good reputation of those who came before, feathers are continually added to the Church, by which it may fly upward, be exalted on high, and be gloriously proclaimed.

Or thus: “The king of the powers of the Beloved, of the Beloved, and of the beauty of the house, to divide the spoils.” You will be in that house if you sleep among the midst of the lots—that is, if you consider it rest to remain between the two inheritances by restraining desires and earthly things, and persevering in hope of eternal happiness to the end, closing the final day of your life.

Thus, by “sleeping,” let us understand the death of the flesh. Those die well who hold the present inheritance in contempt, while they do not yet possess the eternal inheritance in reality but only in hope. Those who die in this way will be the feathers of the dove—that is, of the silvered Church, instructed by the brilliance of divine eloquence.

That the faithful are signified by these feathers is made clear by the Apostle, who says: “We shall be caught up together to meet Christ in the air, and thus we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4). This is what is meant by “the silvered feathers of the dove”: they swiftly carry themselves to meet Christ in the air. And the rear parts of the back of those who were here, bearing the burden of the Church, will be “in the splendor of gold,” that is, in royal power; for it belongs to kings to be adorned with gold.

“If you sleep among the midst of the lots, while the heavenly one distinguishes kings.” That is, while the heavenly man—the second man, who is heavenly because he is from heaven—orders and arranges them. He distinguishes you, I say, as kings over her, understood, “to be ruled,” restraining in yourselves and in others the law of the flesh and strengthening the law of the mind. Hence the saying: “They mortify the flesh and strengthen the spirit.”

“They shall be whitened like snow in Salmon.” Lest anyone think that these kings can be purified by themselves, he says that they will be whitened in Salmon—that is, in the shadow of Christ. For he will overshadow and protect them from the incitements of vices, making them whiter than snow or comparable to snow. He, I say, is the mountain of God.

Hence Isaiah says: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains” (Isa. 2), and so forth. This mountain is a rich mountain, possessing every abundance by which the mature may be refreshed. For every perfect person finds in it what can refresh him.

It is also a curdled mountain, suitable for nourishing little ones as with milk. And to make us understand that it is both rich and curdled, he repeats: “a rich mountain.”

And since this mountain is so wholly a rich and curdled mountain, why do you suppose that other mountains are curdled? Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets (Matt. 16)—but this is in vain. For this is the mountain in which it has pleased God to dwell—that is, in which God dwells. And to show that his dwelling there is superior to his other dwellings, he adds: “in it,” because he dwells in it in such a way that all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in it.

To him alone God gave his Spirit without measure; to the others in whom he dwells he gave it according to measure, because not all receive all things: to one are given kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of speech (1 Cor. 12), and so forth.

“For the Lord will dwell to the end.” As though he were saying: It is rightly in this mountain that God dwells in a more excellent manner. For this mountain, being the Lord, will dwell in the other mountains, bringing them back to himself as their end. Through him the Father also dwells in the other mountains in which he dwells.

These mountains are the chariots of God, because they are governed by God like a wise charioteer. This chariot is manifold in ten thousands; and it is multiplied not only in ten thousands but also through thousands upon thousands of rejoicing ones, because the Lord is in them.

And how is he in them? “In Sinai, in the holy place”—that is, in the completion of the holy commandment.

And how will this happen? “You have ascended on high”—that is, you will ascend into heaven—“and you will take captivity,” because you will recapture the human race, which had first been taken captive by the devil. “You have received gifts among human beings”—that is, you will receive human beings in your gifts.

For, by calling and justifying them, you made into your gifts even those who did not believe that the Lord God dwells in all things. Or, “you have received gifts among human beings”—that is, you made human beings such that the gift they received from the Father might also appear to have been received by you. For when they received the Holy Spirit, you received him in them, because without you they can do nothing.

Note that Christ rightly receives gifts in his own people, because in his great affection for them he suffers adversity. For he said to Peter: “I am coming to Rome to be crucified again,” thereby showing that he suffers in Peter.

“You have received gifts among human beings,” because the Lord God will also dwell in unbelievers—that is, in those who were utterly desperate and said to you: “You have a demon” (John 7).

Hence: “Blessed is the Lord on this present day and every day,” that is, on every future day; or, counting the day continually.

“He will make the way prosperous for us,” so that we may carry the one whose chariot we are; or he will make the way prosperous for us so that we may come to him, making us unconquerable in every tribulation. For “God is the God of our salvations,” that is, of our salvation; and “our God,” that is, of our nature, because he is also the God who makes us safe.

Nevertheless, that salvation will come through the death of the flesh, and human nature is not to be distressed on account of this, because it is mortal. “The exits of the Lord, the Lord”—that is, of that Lord who is called “Lord” by antonomasia—from this world will be an exit through death.

For in order to show the power of his salvation, he wished to die. But although his exit is an exit through death, God is no less powerful over his enemies.

“For he will crush the heads of his enemies,” that is, he will destroy the pride of his enemies, either by a salutary subjection or by a damnable curse. He will also crush “the crown of the hair of those who walk in their sins.”

By “the crown of the hair” he signifies an even greater pride than by “the head.” He signifies the great height of the pride of those who walk in their sins—that is, of those for whom sins are a delight.

Or, in another sense: “God will crush the heads of his enemies”—enemies, I say, who walk upon the crown of the hair, and this in their sins. Here “enemies” are understood as the aerial powers, whose heads are those who, through their persuasions, have wickedly raised their own head against God.

Such enemies are said to walk upon the crown of the hair because they cannot be grasped by any bodily sense; there is no bodily sense in the crown of the hair. For such enemies move around a human being in such a way that they are not perceived, until they draw him toward unlawful things.

“They walk in their sins,” namely, by persuading human beings to commit the sins that belong to them; and they will eventually be punished for this, when the Lord says: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25).

The Lord will crush the heads of his enemies. For the Lord said—that is, he decreed—this very thing: “I will convert some from Bashan,” that is, from those who are confounded in their dryness. For Bashan is interpreted as “confusion” or “dryness.”

“I will convert my grace even into the depth of the sea,” that is, to those who move wickedly in the depth of this world, which is tossed about and draws everything into bitterness.

“So that your foot may be dipped in blood.” As though he were saying: You will convert some, O Lord, from Bashan and from the depth of the sea to such an extent that each one converted from them, having become your foot, may be dipped in blood; that is, he will not hesitate, as a testimony to your blood poured out, to pour out his own blood.

Or, “your foot may be dipped in blood”—that is, you yourself will suffer through excessive affection in their passion. Hence the saying: “I am coming to Rome to be crucified again.”

“And the tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him.” That is, your preachers, who are dogs—not those dogs of whom it is said, “Mute dogs unable to bark” (Isa. 56), but faithful dogs, barking faithfully around the house of their Lord.

These dogs will be converts from the enemies, and this not through themselves, but from him who freely justifies all things.

And how will this happen? “They saw your processions, O God”—that is, they will recognize your processions, how you became known to the world through human nature. And they will recognize not only your processions, but also the processions—that is, the apostles—who are the steps of my God, who created me in the first creation; of my King, who regenerated me; who is “in the holy place,” that is, in each one sanctified by him.

Or, “in the holy place,” namely, in Christ, according to the saying: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5).

Or, in another sense: “Let your foot be dipped in blood,” and this according to your example. For they will see your steps by which you went out from this world, namely, your death, which you left as an example to your own, so that they would not hesitate to pour out their blood for you, being most beneficially instructed by the commandment of your word: “No one has greater love than that he lay down his life for his friends” (John 15).

“The steps of my God, my King, who is in the holy place.” In this way they will see your processions.

“The princes went before, joined with those who sing”—that is, the first preachers, joined with those who sing, namely, associated with others who act well. They will go before in order to announce your steps, and this “in the midst of the young women who beat the tambourines.”

Here the young women signify new churches adorned with new grace. In these churches the steps of the Lord are to be announced.

A tambourine is made from dry hide stretched over wood. Hence those who beat tambourines are people dried out from carnal desires and stretched out in virtues, according to the saying: “They mortify the flesh and strengthen the spirit.”

“In the churches, bless God.” Lest, because he mentioned young women and tambourine players, converts from Bashan should understand that the Lord is to be blessed in carnal pleasure, he adds where the Lord is to be blessed.

As though he were saying: You converts from Bashan, bless God in the churches, “from the fountains of Israel”—understood, having been refreshed by the fountains, or strengthened and instructed by them—so that your teaching may never differ from theirs. Hence elsewhere: “Tell it in his towers” (Ps. 47).

“There is Benjamin, the young man.” Among these fountains, from which Israel is to bless, will be Benjamin—that is, Paul, born from the tribe of Benjamin—a young man because he was elected last, “in an ecstasy of mind.”

An ecstasy of mind occurs either in astonishment or in exaltation. Paul was in an ecstasy of astonishment when, struck down, he lay for three days without sight or hearing (Acts 9). He was also in an exaltation of mind when he said: “I know a man fourteen years ago—whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows—who was caught up to the third heaven” (2 Cor. 12).

In this Church there will also be “the princes of Judah, their leaders; the princes of Zebulun and the princes of Naphtali.”

Some wish all the apostles to be understood in this verse as having been born from these tribes, but we have no basis on which to confirm this, just as we have no basis on which to disprove it. Therefore the interpretations of the names must be sought.

Judah is interpreted as “confession.” Here the martyrs are understood, who possess the foremost faith in the Church and fight most intensely for it. And because those who fight for the faith require strengthening and courage so that they do not fail in the struggle, it continues:

“The princes of Zebulun.” Zebulun is interpreted as “habitation of strength.” Here hope is understood, which most greatly strengthens the martyrs fighting for the faith, because while they hope for eternal things, it is not burdensome for them to exchange temporal things.

“The princes of Naphtali.” The interpretation of the name is “extension,” and here the expanded reward is understood, which those who fight lawfully in the faith will receive hereafter. For “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10; 24).

Or, in another sense: “There is Benjamin, the young man.” When Jacob blessed his sons, he said of Benjamin: “Let Benjamin be a ravenous wolf; in the morning he will eat the prey, and in the evening he will divide the spoils” (Gen. 49).

In this blessing Paul alone need not be signified; rather, all those who, in the morning—that is, after the darkness of unbelief has been driven away—greedily, as though eating, take in the word of God. And in the evening—that is, while they are still darkened by the night of ignorance—they divide the spoils, sending good preachers to others so that they may be converted, as Paul sent Timothy and Titus to announce the faith.

The faithful are called spoils because they have been taken from the devil, by whom they were held captive.

Note that the prey signifies the word of God, according to the saying: “The kingdom of God suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11).

“The princes of Judah, their leaders”—that is, the princes of faith will be leaders of those who are in the Church. “And the princes of Zebulun”—that is, the princes of hope. “And the princes of Naphtali”—that is, of charity, which is called “extension,” because in charity some are so extended that they pray for their enemies.

Note that Benjamin is in an ecstasy of mind—that is, in exaltation: from impious in himself to pious in himself, from animal in himself to spiritual in himself, from human in himself to divine in himself.

“Command, O God, your strength.” As though he were saying: So that converts from Bashan may bless you in the churches, command, O God the Father—that is, commend—your strength, namely, your incarnate Word, which is your strength. Hence Paul calls Christ “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1).

Or, “command the blessing of your strength,” so that through strength every blessing may come. Or, “command your strength”—that is, the charity that you have shown toward human beings, since “while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Rom. 5).

“Confirm this, O God, which you have worked in us”—that is, confirm the grace you have granted us; make it firm and alike for us and for the nations, beginning from your temple, which is in Jerusalem. For the word of God was first preached there. But because they were blinded and refused to receive it, the preachers turned to the nations.

“Confirm what you have worked in us.” For if you confirm it, your kings—that is, your apostles—will offer gifts to you. Peter will offer you converts from the circumcision; Paul, those from the uncircumcision; Thomas, the Indians; and each will offer those to whom he preached.

Or, in another sense: “Confirm what you have worked in us.” For if you confirm it, “the kings will offer you gifts,” beginning from your temple and reaching even to the heavenly Jerusalem.

And in order that they may offer you gifts, “rebuke the beasts of the reed”—that is, people living irrationally and therefore comparable to beasts. They are also reeds because they are carried about by every wind of doctrine.

Or, “rebuke the beasts that destroy the reed,” namely, sacred doctrine, which is understood through the reed, since among the ancients the reed was ordinarily used for writing. Hence elsewhere: “My tongue is the pen of a swift writer” (Ps. 44).

Or heretics are compared to a reed, because just as a reed is fixed in a muddy place, so each heretic submerges himself in a muddy understanding.

“[Rebuke] the assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples, so that they may exclude those who have been tested by silver.” As though he were saying: I say this because there will be “an assembly of bulls”—that is, of those who are stiff-necked and therefore comparable to bulls.

And he shows where this assembly will take place: “among the cows of the peoples,” namely, among those among the peoples who can be compared to cows.

Note that a cow freely follows a bull. Therefore understand as comparable to cows those easily seduced souls who are readily overthrown by the opinions of heretics. The Apostle indicates them when he says: “They enter houses and lead captive little women burdened with sins” (2 Tim. 3).

He adds what heretics will bring about: “so that they may exclude them”—that is, so that through them those who have been tested by silver may be made manifest, namely, those educated in divine eloquence. Hence the Apostle says: “There must be heresies, so that those who are tested may be made manifest” (1 Cor. 11).

Or, “so that they may exclude those who have been tested by silver”—that is, so that they may completely separate the perfect from the imperfect, withdrawing teachers from their disciples and incorporating them into themselves.

Therefore rebuke the beasts of the reed in this way: “Scatter the interior wars,” because you have scattered the exterior wars. “Scatter the nations that desire wars”—that is, the heretics who strive for contention and not correction, for destruction and not edification.

Hence the Apostle says: “In the last times some will depart from the faith, attending to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy” (1 Tim. 4). Scatter such people.

And truly you will scatter them, because “envoys will come from Egypt,” through whom the heretics will be confounded. Egypt is interpreted as “darkness” and signifies people darkened in heart. From among these, once illuminated and converted from unbelief to faith, they became the Lord’s envoys, so that through them his word might be made known to those who were still dwelling in darkness.

Hence the Apostle says: “We act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God” (2 Cor. 5).

“Ethiopia will hasten its hands to God.” By Ethiopians are understood those blackened in conduct. They will hasten their hands toward the Lord—that is, toward his vengeance—by clinging to God, confessing their sins, and suffering punishment for them here, lest the Lord punish them in the future. For those whose sins are not punished here will finally be punished by the Lord in the future. Therefore, lest we be punished by the Lord, let us anticipate his face in confession (Ps. 94).

Another translation has: “Ethiopia hastens to give its hands to God”—that is, to perform works acceptable to God.

Or, in another sense: “Ethiopia will hasten its hands to him”—that is, its works, understood, while clinging to God. “His” should be referred to Ethiopia, so that it has the same force as though he had said “its hands.” For, as Augustine testifies, the Hebrew has the word in the feminine gender.

Note how Ethiopia will hasten its hands—that is, its works. Confession will go before, so that works may follow; for if they were to perform good works first, their sins might appear to be forgiven on account of merit.

“Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God.” Having seen all the things that were to occur through Christ and his preachers, the prophet exhorts those who are to be converted to break forth in his praise.

As though he were saying: Since all these things will occur for you, therefore you, “kingdoms of the earth”—that is, you who have been made the kingdom of God from the earth, having been called freely—sing to God inwardly and sing psalms to the Lord outwardly.

“Sing to God,” I say, “who ascends above the heaven of heaven”—that is, above every heavenly rational creature, which is the heaven of this lower rational creature—and “to the east,” that is, to the equality of the Father, where he continually rises, though his rising had no beginning and will have no end.

Hence the saying: “The dawn from on high has visited us” (Luke 1). And elsewhere: “The rising and splendor of eternal light” (Wis. 7).

Or, literally, “who ascends above the heaven of heaven,” according to the saying: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is…”
is in heaven (John 3). For he alone ascended into heaven by himself; all the others who ascend have to ascend through him [Col. 0490A]. Or otherwise: “who ascended above the heaven of heaven.” Heaven was the human nature personally united to the Father’s Word, because Christ, also in his human nature, showers the other heavens—namely, the apostles—with the rain of God’s word. He thundered with threats and flashed with miracles. God the Son ascended above this heaven when he exalted that human nature with himself and placed it in the Father’s confession [acknowledgment]. This is what he says: “Sing psalms to God who ascended above the heaven of heaven,” that is, above heaven itself—namely, above his own human nature—“toward the east,” that is, toward equality with the Father. In this ascension, moreover, his disciples understood most clearly that he was true God and true man.

“He will give a voice of power to his voice; sing psalms to God.” For this is necessary, because the one who previously [Col. 0490B] gave the voice of humility when he said, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26), will give the voice of power, saying: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25). For the one who came in humility to be judged will come in power to judge.

And so that you may not fear the voice of power, “give glory to God,” presuming nothing on your own behalf because of your good works. Therefore I say that you should give glory to God, because when he gives the voice of power, “his magnificence will be over Israel,” that is, over all who see God, “and his power will be in the clouds.” Concerning these clouds the Lord said: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon that prostitute” (Isaiah 5). And likewise: “Amen, I say to you, from now on you will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven” (Matthew 26): in these clouds the Lord’s power will be present.

Concerning this power [Col. 0490C] Paul said: “The dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1 Corinthians 15). Or, in this life, “he will give power to his clouds.” Hence Paul likewise says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4), “so that the surpassing greatness may be God’s power, not from you.” Or, “his power is in the clouds” because he will come with the elders of the people in great power.

And lest you think that “in the clouds,” which he mentioned previously, meant something else, it follows: “God is wonderful in his saints,” giving, that is, eternal goods in exchange for temporal labor. “The God of Israel himself will give power,” that is, resurrection; or here he will give his own people power, so that they may be able to do all things through him. Hence Paul says: “I can do all things through him who strengthens me, Christ” (Philippians 4). He will give strength, that is, incorruptibility to the flesh. And to whom will he give it? To his people, now fragile, now [Col. 0490D] weak, now saying: “As long as I am in the body, I am a stranger from the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5). Therefore blessed be God, through whom all these things will come to pass.

# PSALM 68. FOR THE END, FOR THOSE WHO WILL BE CHANGED; A PSALM OF DAVID HIMSELF

“Save me, O God, for the waters have come in as far as my soul. I am stuck fast in the deep mire, and there is no foothold. I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me. I have grown weary crying out; my throat has become hoarse. My eyes have failed while I hope in my God. Those who hate me without cause have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head. My enemies, who persecute me unjustly, have grown strong: what I did not seize, I then paid back. O God, you know my foolishness, and my offenses are not hidden from you. Let those who await you, Lord, Lord of hosts, not be put to shame because of me. Let those who seek you, God of Israel, not be confounded because of me. For on your account I endured reproach; shame covered my face. I became a stranger to my brothers and a foreigner to the sons of my mother. For zeal for your house consumed me, and the reproaches of those reproaching you fell upon me. I covered my soul with fasting, and this became a reproach to me. I put on sackcloth as my garment, and I became a proverb to them. Those sitting at the gate spoke against me, and those drinking wine sang songs about me. But I directed my prayer to you, Lord, at the acceptable time, O God. In the abundance of your mercy, hear me, in the truth of your salvation. Rescue me from the mire, so that I may not become stuck fast; deliver me from those who hate me and from the depths of the waters. May the storm of water not overwhelm me, nor the deep swallow me, nor may the pit close its mouth over me. Hear me, Lord, for your mercy is kind; according to the abundance of your compassion, look upon me. And do not turn your face away from your servant, for I am afflicted; quickly hear me. Attend to my soul and deliver it; because of my enemies, rescue me. You know my reproach, my shame, and my dishonor. All those who afflict me are in your sight. My heart awaited reproach and misery. I looked for one who would grieve with me, and there was none; and for one who would console me, and I found none. They gave gall as my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. Let their table before them become a snare, a retribution, and a stumbling-block. Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and always bend their backs. Pour out your anger upon them, and let the fury of your wrath seize them. Let their dwelling become desolate, and let there be no one dwelling in their tents. For they persecuted the one whom you struck, and they added to the pain of my wounds. Add iniquity upon their iniquity, and let them not enter into your righteousness. Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous. I am poor and sorrowful; your salvation, O God, has received me. I will praise the name of God with a song, and I will magnify him with praise. And this will please God more than a young bull producing horns and hooves. Let the poor see and rejoice; seek God, and your soul will live. For the Lord has heard the poor and has not despised his prisoners. Let the heavens and earth praise him, the sea and all the creatures that move in them. For God will save Zion, and the cities of Judah will be built. They will dwell there and acquire it as an inheritance. The offspring of his servants will possess it, and those who love his name will dwell in it.”

## EXPOSITION

Change occurs in two ways: either from good to worse or from good to better. Of these, a person possesses one from himself and the other from grace. From himself, everyone possesses the change by which good is changed into worse. For the first ancestor left this inheritance to his descendants when, through disobedience, he withdrew from God (Gen. III). The same Prophet indicates this kind of change elsewhere, saying: “A spirit that goes and does not return” (Ps. LXXVII). Solomon likewise marks this same change in the following way: “Every person who walks in iniquity will not return” (Prov. II; Wis. XVI). “From himself” is to be understood. For each person has it from himself to fall, but from himself he does not have it to rise again. He has rising again only from grace; here the change from evil to good is indicated.

The psalm speaks about the cause of this change. For in this psalm the voice of Christ is presented as speaking about his Passion, which was the cause of the change from evil to good. The Lord himself, through his Passion, passed from temporal labor to eternal goods. We, in the same passage, have passed in hope from temporal things and have awaited eternal things; and everyone who has put off the old person and put on the new can safely await them. Thus each person ought to be changed from evil to good. We are admonished to make this change by the Lord’s voice, which commends his Passion to us for imitation.

Notice also that here our Head speaks some things that accord with his dignity and others that are necessary for our weakness. Our Head speaks as follows:

“Save me, O God, for the waters have come in as far as my soul” [Col. 0492C].

In this verse our Head prays both for his members and for himself, saying: “God the Father, save me in myself and in my members, so that you may grant me outward resurrection, but grant my members inward resurrection. And it is necessary that you save me, for the waters have come in”—that is, the seditious crowd of the raging people has surrounded me—“as far as my soul,” that is, with the implied purpose of taking it away.

Here the people are rightly designated by the name “waters,” since they never remain in the same condition but, like flowing water, are always rolling onward, falling from one vice into another. Or the Jewish people, especially at the Lord’s death, bore the likeness of water, because just as water rolls around a person until it submerges him, so the Jewish people rolled around the Lord until they handed him over to death. For they rolled around him by plotting against him, capturing him, judging him, and finally killing him. This is indicated here: “The waters have come in as far as my soul.”

And how did they come in? “I am stuck fast in the deep mire”—that is, I have been held among those who made their mire, that is, their earthly nature, deep, that is, far from the bottom. Concerning them it is said: “When the sinner comes into the depths, he despises” (Prov. XVIII).

Notice that all human beings are in mire, because all were created from mire and at some point, by the necessity of the journey, must sin. Those who despise newness and wholly consent to oldness are reckoned to be in deep mire. But those who do not consent to these things are in high mire, making something like gold from earth when they put off the old person and put on the new, and when they set aside the animal life and attend to the spiritual [Col. 0492D].

“And there is no foothold.” The reason why he is stuck in the mire is supplied when he says: “There is no foothold.” All who deviate from true being are not in substance. “Substance” means a thing remaining in its own creation. Those who wish to put on the new person but obey the old person in everything are not in substance, because they have lost true being. Such were those by whom the Lord was held during his Passion. For if they had been in substance—that is, in the formation in which God created them—they would not have held the one whom God begot.

Or otherwise: “The waters have come in as far as my soul,” and this because “I am stuck fast in the deep mire,” that is, in human nature, which is like deep mire because it is mortal and subject to suffering. “And there is no substance,” that is, I do not appear to be in my true essence, in which I am equal to the omnipotent Father. Notice that he never lost the Father’s equality, in which he always remained. But because he appeared to have assumed the form of a poor man, many supposed that he did not reign in divinity.

“I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me.” This is connected with the preceding interpretation as follows: “I am stuck fast in the deep mire,” that is, I am held in the depth of earthly things; and this is not by the power of those by whom I am held, but I came of my own will into the depths of the sea—that is, into the depths of worldly people, who fluctuate like the sea and live in bitterness. Therefore “the storm”—that is, the fury of the seditious people—“overwhelmed me,” so that I might be swallowed by the whale and vomited out alive. This had been prefigured in Jonah (Jon. II) by deed, not by speech.

Notice that this sea, although it ought to have been rational, was sunk into utter blindness. For the rational sea offered itself to the Lord’s feet to be trodden upon and, when stirred by the winds, ceased its disturbance. This irrational sea not only did not grow calm at his most salutary voice but also overwhelmed him, because it handed him over to death.

Alternatively: “I am stuck fast in the deep mire,” that is, in the mortality of the flesh; “and there is no substance,” that is, I did not appear in my riches, because “I came into the depths of the sea.” In that depth I labored, crying out—namely, “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matt. XVIII)—and the other things by which I would deter human beings so that they might cease from sins and press on toward the way of eternal salvation [Col. 0493C].

“And while I was crying out these things, my throat became hoarse,” that is, I became comparable to a person uttering a hoarse voice, and therefore pleasing to no one’s hearing. For there was almost no one to whom my voice was pleasing for imitation of me. “And finally my eyes failed,” that is, they prepared themselves for death, “while I hope in my God,” that is, while they saw that I had no other cause of death except that they had not seen me cease hoping in my God.

Alternatively: “I labored crying out; my throat became hoarse.” It is not read that the Lord labored in crying out during the Passion, because it is said: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII). Therefore what he says—“I labored crying out; my throat became hoarse”—must be understood as referring to the time before the Passion: “I was as diligent in crying out for their salvation as one who labors so earnestly in a cause undertaken for his own that he becomes hoarse.” Yet this did not help, because “my eyes”—that is, my apostles—“failed in faith,” while I nevertheless hoped in my God, that is, while they saw that my hope had in no way been diminished. They failed in faith when the Lord appeared to them as if a stranger, and they said: “We had thought that he was going to redeem Israel” (Luke XXIV).

“Those who hate me without cause have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head.” It is as though he said: “My eyes have failed, for those who hate me without any prior fault of mine have multiplied and become more numerous than the hairs of my head.” They had increased so greatly that they even took my disciple to augment their number.

Notice that the head is adorned by its hairs. Here those are understood who did not withdraw from the Lord at the time of the Passion. But because there were few who at that time clung to the Lord, he says: “They have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head,” because there were more who plucked the hairs than those who adorned the head. They hated me without cause, because I injured no one and came for the salvation of all.

And lest we understand only the extent of their hatred, he adds: “My enemies have grown strong”—that is, by bringing into effect what they had conceived in their minds—“unjustly.” For nothing is more unjust than to oppress one who came to give salvation.

“What I did not seize, I then paid back.” He became an offering for sin, although he had never committed any sin [Col. 0494C]. The angel seized what was not his when, by apostatizing from God, he said: “I will set my throne toward the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV). The first parent seized what was not his when he consented to the devil, who offered him death from the cup of pride. For he was reaching toward being like God, and he came to the point of not being good. The Lord paid this sin not with an armed hand but with a nail fixed in the cross.

“O God, you know my foolishness.” Lest you ask why he paid back what he had not seized, he added why he paid it back: so that the world might know that he had been sent for this purpose, to obey the Father. He says: “What I did not seize, I then paid back; and you, God the Father, know”—that is, approve—“my foolishness,” because they regarded it as foolishness. And because you approve it, it is proved not to be foolishness, since whatever is approved by God is not foolishness: “What is foolish of God is wiser than human beings” (I Cor. I).

The Jews regarded as foolish the God who said that he could do all things, yet suffered, was struck on the face, spat upon, and killed. But God the Father was not unaware of how foolishly all these things were being done, because he had committed no offense for which he wished to suffer. Hence the apostle Peter says: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (I Pet. II).

“And my offenses”—which, according to their opinion, were offenses—“are not hidden from you,” although every offense is hidden from you—not because you do not know it, but because you do not approve it.

Notice the offenses they imputed to the Lord. When they saw him healing a man on the Sabbath, they murmured, saying: “This man is not from God, since he does not keep the Sabbath” (John IX). The Jews regarded this and similar actions as offenses, although they were new deeds. This is what he says: “My offenses are not hidden from you.”

Therefore, “let those who await you, Lord,”—with “me not resurrected” understood—not be put to shame because of me; those who await you as their rewarder, you whom he calls “Lord of hosts,” that is, of the heavenly armies, a fact which fools scarcely imagine.

“Let those who seek you, God of Israel, not be confounded because of me”—with “me not resurrected” understood—those who seek you through good works, with me as mediator.

“For on your account I endured reproach.” I ask that mine not be confounded because I am not resurrected. And truly they will not be confounded, because I endured reproach only on your account: I endured the insults inflicted upon me not because of my own fault but solely so that I might obey you. No human being can say this of himself. For even if someone is judged for theft and is not guilty of theft, he has nevertheless committed something else for which he deserved to be judged.

“Shame covered my face.” Shame is what inwardly gnaws at the conscience. This shame covered the Lord’s face insofar as the Jews’ opinion was concerned, because they thought him guilty of every offense. This is what he says: “Shame covered my face.”

Therefore: “I became a stranger to my brothers and a foreigner to the sons of my mother.” He calls “brothers” those who were stronger in faith, such as the apostles. He became a stranger to them because they abandoned him and fled. The “sons of my mother” were those from whom he was born according to the flesh. He became a foreigner to them because, even if someone received him, he did not receive him as a brother but as a stranger, showing him little honor. This is what he says: “And a foreigner to the sons of my mother.”

And why? “For zeal for your house consumed me,” that is, indignation over your house consumed me. I did not patiently endure those who dishonored your house, making it a house of every luxury and disgrace, when they ought to have made themselves your house—a house of chastity, gentleness, and piety. Because of this zeal, that is, this indignation over your house, consumed me, that is, gnawed at me inwardly.

“And the reproaches of those reproaching you fell upon me,” because whoever honors the Son honors the Father, and whoever speaks reproachfully to the Son speaks reproachfully to the Father (John V). This is what he says: “The reproaches of those reproaching you fell upon me.”

And although they had reproached me, while thirsting for their salvation, “I covered my soul with fasting,” that is, I was afflicted with great emaciation because the people whom I hungered for handed me over to death. Or: “I covered my soul with fasting,” that is, I restrained my anger in that very fasting, because I did not rise up to open vengeance. “And this became a reproach to me,” because they said to me: “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” (John VIII.)

“But I put on sackcloth as my garment,” that is, I showed myself in the likeness of a wretched person, because I exposed to them my flesh—which had become mortal because of human sin and against which they raged—while my divinity was concealed.

Or let it be read as a likeness: just as sackcloth is the garment of troubled people, so I presented my flesh to them as useful; or I presented them themselves, who were sackcloth, since they were entirely perverse in their movements. I put on a garment for those who were converted to me, namely the thief and the centurion.

“And I became a proverb to them,” that is, a likeness of reproach. When they wanted to reproach others, they introduced me as an example, saying: “May you die as that man died.”

“Those sitting at the gate spoke against me, and those drinking wine sang songs about me.” That is, I became a stranger not only to my brothers but also to those who sat at the gate—namely the judges, whose seat was at the gate so that they might judge justly. They spoke against me, with “to oppress me” understood. “And those drinking wine sang songs about me,” that is, those who were drunk with temporal pleasure, or those who had drunk the wine of error [Col. 0496A].

“But I directed my prayer to you, Lord,” with the following understood: saying, “It is the time for your favor,” that is, the time for fulfilling the free grace to be bestowed upon the human race. Therefore hear me praying for my members, “in the abundance of your mercy.” Their misery is great; may the abundance of your mercy come to their aid. Hear me “in the truth of your salvation,” appearing truthful in giving me salvation—that is, incorruptibility of the flesh.

“Rescue me from the mire, so that I may not become stuck fast.” Until this point our Head prayed for himself; from here onward he prays for his members as follows: “Rescue me”—that is, my members—“from the mire,” that is, from those who remain in the mire, “so that I may not become stuck fast,” that is, so that they may not become stuck fast, with “by being incorporated” understood.

It is as though he said: “I do not ask you to rescue them in such a way that they do not suffer persecution from those people; rather, rescue them in such a way that they are not incorporated into them.” And so that this may happen, “deliver me”—that is, my members—“from those who hate my members and myself.”

“And from the depths of the waters,” that is, from the depth of sins, in this way: “May the storm of water not overwhelm me.” The storm of water is understood either as the threats of those openly raging or as the flatteries of those who praise. From this storm our Head asks that his own be delivered: “May the storm of water not overwhelm me,” so that I may not consent either to the flatteries of those who praise or to the threats of those openly raging.

Or if at some time I do consent, “may the deep not swallow me,” that is, may I not proceed to action with those who live in the depth of sins. Or if I do proceed to action, “may the pit not close its mouth over me,” that is, may the depth of iniquity not be closed over me. The depth of iniquity closes over one who, after committing a sin, does not make confession but prepares a defense of the sin [Col. 0496D]. Such people are not liberated in the future, because whoever is not in confession here will not be in liberation there. For the Lord will not be the liberator of one who is the defender of his sin here. To have him as liberator, therefore, let each person here be his own accuser.

This can be said concerning the Head: “May the pit not close its mouth over me,” that is, may it not be closed over me, in accordance with: “You will not allow your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. XV). For if I had remained in death, I would have been comparable to anyone over whom the pit had closed its mouth, so that he would be silent about confession and cry out in defense.

“Hear me, Lord, for your mercy is kind.” Notice that mercy is especially kind when someone has experienced his own misery, just as rain is especially welcome to the earth after the earth itself has long been in drought.

This is what he says: “Hear me, Lord, for your mercy is kind.” It is as though he said: “Let mine experience their misery; let them experience your mercy,” that is, your loving affection. And so, “according to the abundance of your compassion”—that is, according to the abundant display of mercy—“look upon me,” that is, upon my members, whom you had disregarded according to the abundance of your anger.

“And so that you may look upon them, do not turn your face away from your child,” that is, from my members, who have now become children—that is, humble, true children, whereas previously they were proud. “And quickly hear me,” that is, my members, “for I am afflicted,” that is, my members are afflicted.
