It is as though he said: “Do not delay your mercy, because my members acknowledge their misery.” And so that you may quickly hear, “attend to my soul and deliver it,” with “and secretly rescue it” understood—that is, my members—“because of my enemies,” with “who are to be converted or blinded” understood.

Notice that God liberates his faithful in two ways, openly and secretly. He secretly liberated the Maccabees, whom King Antiochus held captive; in this liberation Antiochus was blinded (II Macc. VII). While he exercised his power outwardly and thought that he was prevailing over them, God blinded him inwardly, because he did not understand that they had been liberated inwardly, against whom he raged outwardly.

The Lord also openly liberated the three young men under the power of King Nebuchadnezzar (Dan. III). This kind of liberation occurs for the confession of enemies, so that, when they see the Lord’s power openly manifested, they may be converted to faith. Thus Nebuchadnezzar, who, after being converted, announced the Lord’s power to others (Dan. IV).

“You know my reproach, my shame, and my dishonor.” It is as though he said: “It is right that you rescue me in my members, because you know how great the reproaches they suffered on your account were. You know the shames and dishonors that I suffered in my members—not with respect to you, but with respect to their opinion.”

The reproach occurred when they said: “He has blasphemed. Why do we still need witnesses?” (Matt. XXVI?) Shame occurred when, with their eyes closed, they struck him on the face, saying: “Prophesy to us: who is it that struck you?” (Ibid.) Shame occurs when conscience gnaws at a person inwardly. This is what the Jews chiefly imagined: they thought that he did not know who had struck him and that he therefore had shame in his conscience, although he had previously claimed to know all things [Col. 0497D].

Dishonor—that is, embarrassment—is what makes even an honorable face blush at the accusation of a false crime. All these things were present in Christ according to the Jews’ opinion, not according to the truth of the matter, because there could be no shame in such a holy conscience, nor blushing in so free a face.

Alternatively: “Rescue my members.” And it is necessary that you rescue them, because “you know my reproach”—that is, the reproach of my members—“and my shame”—that is, the shame of my members.

Reproach is what is inflicted by an enemy, although the person against whom it is inflicted may suffer inwardly in conscience because of the reproach itself. Thus holy men, when they were reproached because they believed in Christ crucified and in a dead thief, suffered no embarrassment in their consciences. Paul did not merely consider it sufficient not to be ashamed of Christ crucified; rather, he wished to glory in him alone when he said: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI).

The less perfect suffered shame when they were inwardly embarrassed and conscience gnawed at them over what was reproached to them, because they believed in a dead man. Human speech had greater force among them than the divine promise.

“All those who afflict me are in your sight.” It is as though he said: “You know my reproach, for those who afflict me are in your sight and are not hidden from you; they are not hidden from me either, because my heart awaited reproach and their misery,” with the following understood: “so that they might acknowledge themselves to be miserable and, being converted, repent.”

Or they afflict me as though I were ignorant of and unwilling to undergo the tribulations. But “my heart awaited reproach,” that is, I willingly accepted the Passion, because “no one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down myself,” and again I take it up (John X).

And my heart also awaited the misery of them being destroyed. “And I looked for one who would grieve,” that is, who would grieve together with me, over the same matter over which I grieved—namely their error, because they were unwilling to attend to their misery. “And there was none,” with “who wished to grieve over the destruction of the Jews” understood.

Notice that the disciples were saddened at the Lord’s death, but they were not saddened over the destruction of the Jews, over which the Lord was saddened. They were saddened only by his death. For although in some way they believed that he would rise again and would not die any more, they nevertheless grieved because the life in which they had seen him living so holily and piously was to be changed through death.

“And there was none who would console me.” It is as though he said: “I also awaited one who would console me over the salvation of the Jews if they were converted, and I found none. Instead, those whose misery I awaited would be destroyed, and whose salvation I wished to celebrate, gave gall as my food and gave me vinegar to drink in my thirst.”

For I thirsted for their newness as for savory and sweet food, but they gave me food filled with gall; I thirsted for them as for a pleasant drink, but they presented themselves to me as a sour drink. I thirsted for their newness, but they continued to offer me oldness.

Even now all who, by living perversely, contradict evangelical truth and believe that the Lord did not rise offer oldness and present food filled with gall for God to eat. Such people are to be tolerated by the faithful, not killed. The Lord himself indicated this when he tasted and did not wish to drink. For by this he taught that the impious should be borne but not incorporated, tolerated but not killed. He tasted gall but did not incorporate it into himself.

Or the words “they gave gall as my food” may be read literally. It is not written that they gave the Lord gall to eat, but it is known that before the Passion the Lord ate the most holy Passover with his disciples, namely sweet and pleasant food. The Jews mixed gall into this food when they offered him, hanging on the cross, vinegar mixed with gall to drink.

This is what he says here: “They gave gall as my food,” that is, they placed gall upon the food that I had eaten with my disciples. “And in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” [Col. 0499A].

Therefore: “Let their table before them become a snare,” that is, let the preparation they made for me become their destruction; “and a retribution,” that is, let them recognize that this is a repayment of their merits, because they deserved to be ensnared where they thought to ensnare me. “And let their table become a stumbling-block to them,” because they stumbled over me as a stone of offense and a rock of stumbling.

Or otherwise: “Let their table”—that is, Scripture, from which they thought they would be refreshed—“become a snare,” and let it be “before them,” that is, with their knowledge. For while they possessed Scripture, from which they could learn what ought to be done, a snare was prepared for them when they refused to understand Scripture. Or, if they did understand it, they pretended not to understand it. This will become for them a retribution and a stumbling-block.

And how will this happen? “Let their eyes be darkened”—with “their inward eyes” understood—“so that they may not see what ought to be seen.” And “bend their backs always,” toward earthly things, with “the burdens to be carried” understood. For it is just that those who did not wish to direct their hearts upward by looking upon me should be bent toward earthly things.

“Pour out your anger upon them, and let the fury of your wrath seize them” in this way: “Let their dwelling become desolate,” that is, let the city in which they dwell become desolate because of them. And because he said “dwelling,” lest anyone think that they should remain there, he adds: “And in their tents let there be no one who dwells,” so that he might show where they ought to migrate, since tents are huts used in military expeditions and by those who do not remain in one place.

Or thus: “Let their dwelling become desolate,” that is, let the house in which they constantly lived become desolate because of them. For it is just that they not be permitted to dwell where they had been permitted to cry out against the Lord. They lost the place of fury. Would that even now they might recognize the place of rest!

“And in their tents”—that is, in Solomon’s temple and in the Lord’s temple, in which they dwelt as though in tents—“let there be no one who dwells,” from the multitude of the Jewish people.

And why? “For they persecuted the one whom you struck,” that is, whom you made subject to being struck through mortality and suffering, insofar as it was permitted to them.

God struck the first human being with mortality and suffering when that person withdrew from him through disobedience; in him all posterity was wounded by the same wound. Christ, however, because he was born as a human being from that lineage, was not free from the wound, since he became mortal and subject to suffering. The Jews persecuted him. This is what is said here: “They persecuted the one whom you struck,” and “they added pain”—with “of mortality” understood—“to the pain of my wounds,” because they hastened his death.

Or: “They added pain to the pain of my wounds,” that is, to my death, because they bribed the guards so that they would deny that I had risen.

Or: “They added pain to the pain of my wounds,” with “my pain” understood, because it was not enough for them to kill my servants who had been sent to the vineyard unless they also killed me, the heir.

Or: “They added pain to the pain of my wounds,” because after killing me they raged against my apostles and against my other members by killing them [Col. 0499D].

“And therefore add iniquity upon their iniquity,” so that wicked sons may be generated from wicked fathers, as they fall from sin into sin.

Or: “Add iniquity upon their iniquity,” so that, after killing me, they may give money to the guards who say that I did not rise.

“And let them not enter into your righteousness,” that is, let them not be reckoned among your righteous. Rather, “let them be blotted out of the book of the living,” or from divine predestination, in which they claimed to have been written through presumptuous iniquity. “And let them not be written with the righteous,” insofar as your equity is concerned.

And this is because “I am poor and sorrowful” according to their estimation. But what does it matter? “Your salvation”—that is, your Word personally united to me—“has received me” into the glory of resurrection and the immortality of the flesh.

Or thus: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous. But let me and my members not be blotted out; rather, let us be enrolled, because I am poor and sorrowful. This is for my salvation and that of my members, because your salvation, O God, has received me.” For it receives no one unless that person acknowledges himself to be poor.

And because your salvation has received me, “I will praise the name of God with a song,” that is, with gladness of mind, “and I will magnify him with praise,” presuming nothing from myself. Hence elsewhere: “Give glory to his praise” (Ps. LXV).

And this praise will please God more than “a young bull producing horns and hooves,” that is, more than all the sacrifices of the Law. It was commanded in the Law that a young bull producing horns and hooves be offered in a certain sacrifice. By this bull all the legal sacrifices are understood here, because it pleases God more than all legal observances when his name is praised with a song [Col. 0500C].

Therefore, “let the poor see”—the first believers praising God in the Church—and let them rejoice by imitating them in praise.

“Seek God, and your soul will live.” He turns to the listeners in an apostrophe so that they may be stirred to praise, saying: “Seek the Lord,” not so that the body may live, as cattle also do, but “seek the Lord, and your soul will live,” even if the body does not die.

And he is rightly to be sought, because for a long time now the Lord himself has heard the poor and has not despised his prisoners, that is, those bound by his commands.

Therefore, “let the heavens”—that is, the greater members of the Church—“praise him, and the earth”—that is, the lesser members, who have already become earth so that they may be cultivated. Let “the sea”—that is, the waves of the nations—praise him, “and all the creatures that move in them,” that is, let all those praise him who are sustained through heaven, earth, and sea.

Or otherwise: “He has not despised his prisoners.” Every person is bound in the first parent by the bond of mortality and suffering. But the Lord has not despised all those who recognize that they are bound; rather, he helps them to lift the fetters by which they are bound.

Therefore let the heavens and earth praise him, that is, let all these things be material for praising God among those who are bound. They praise the Lord through heaven, earth, and sea when they seek from these things only as much as is necessary for them while they are bound by fetters—namely food and clothing—because these things lighten the fetters by which they are burdened, so that they do not weigh them down.

But if they seek beyond necessity, they no longer lighten their bonds; rather, they make them heavier and are greatly weighed down by them. For if someone bound in material iron wished to lift the iron so that it would not weigh him down excessively, he would not place many cloths beneath it to lift it. If he placed many beneath it, he would not merely fail to lighten it; he would make the iron heavier for himself.

Therefore let every person who is bound praise the Lord through heaven and earth, taking nothing from them by which the fetters with which he is bound would be made heavier.

And rightly the Lord is to be praised in all these things: “For the Lord himself will save Zion,” that is, he will establish the primitive Church.

“And the cities of Judah will be built”: a city—that is, the Church—will be built from those who confess. “And they will dwell there,” that is, those who are in the city of Judah, namely the nations confessing humbly, will dwell in the Church made from Zion.

“And they will acquire it as an inheritance,” because from that primitive Church other converts will be restored. “And the offspring of his servants will possess it,” that is, all the imitators of their preachers will possess it, with “as an inheritance” understood.

And lest some should claim that inheritance for themselves, saying: “We are Abraham’s offspring” (John VIII), and therefore we will possess that inheritance, he adds: “Those who love his name will dwell in it.” For only those who imitate Abraham in faith will possess that inheritance, not those who are Abraham’s sons according to the flesh.

# PSALM 69. FOR THE END; A PSALM OF DAVID, IN REMEMBRANCE, BECAUSE THE LORD SAVED HIM.

“O God, give heed to help me; Lord, hasten to help me. Let those who seek my life be confounded and put to shame. Let those who wish me evil turn back and be disgraced. Let those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done,’ turn back at once in shame. Let all who seek you exult and rejoice in you, and let those who love your salvation say always, ‘The Lord be magnified.’ But I am needy and poor; O God, help me. You are my helper and my deliverer; Lord, do not delay.”

## EXPOSITION

Remembrance occurs in two ways. It occurs when someone, fearing the Lord’s severity and judgment, remembers his sins. It also occurs when someone remembers that he was once a sinner and that, through God’s grace, he has been set free. This psalm is entitled “for remembrance” in the latter sense, because those who remember the salvation administered to them through the Lord’s grace are speaking in this psalm.

The title is constructed as follows: “For the end” introduces the words that follow; it is a psalm to be attributed to David, made for remembrance. Since “remembrance” is understood in two ways, the title specifies which remembrance is meant: “because the Lord saved me.”

Augustine begins this psalm as follows:

“Thanks to the grain of wheat, because it wished to die and multiply; thanks to the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ, who did not disdain to undergo our death in order to make us worthy of life. That single grain was one, but it contained within itself the fruitfulness of multiplication. For we rejoice in the many grains that imitate his passion when we celebrate the birthdays of the holy martyrs, whose voice is heard in this psalm.”

For this is the voice of the afflicted and of those endangered in persecution, yet presuming upon their Head. Let us hear the martyrs speaking here, and let us speak with them from the affection of our hearts, though not in the likeness of their suffering. They have already been crowned; we are still in danger.

Perhaps our times are fuller of scandals than theirs were. For although we do not openly suffer the devil raging through a lion, we do suffer him when he rages secretly through a dragon. The persecution of the pagans has ceased, but not the malice of those who think and speak blasphemously, from whom the faithful suffer persecution. Even if they do not inflict evils upon the bodies of the saints, their evil deeds nevertheless reproach the saints. Thus holy Lot did not suffer persecution in his own body, but the wicked deeds of Sodom and Gomorrah became his suffering.

The faithful suffer the wicked deeds of certain people within the Church. Such people flock to the Church on the festivals of the martyrs and other saints, not because they wish to have peace there, but to rage; not to pray, but to insult. The saints endure the harmonies and melodies of such people, because it is appointed for all the godly to suffer persecution from the ungodly. We must pray for such people, so that, after abandoning their madness, they may one day beat their breasts within the walls of the Church, saying, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke XVIII), and thus say with us:

“O God, give heed to help me”—that is, make yourself intent on helping me—“Lord, hasten to help me.” Notice that he does not ask the Lord to hasten to help because his help is ever slow, since he is always a helper in times of need. Rather, because nothing seems sufficiently swift to an eager spirit, and because weak human nature finds nothing swift enough, he says what we hear here: “Lord, hasten to help me.”

“Let them be confounded”—that is, let them recognize themselves as deserving confusion—and let them fear the future judgment, those who seek my life for oppression, not for imitation.

“Let them turn back”—that is, let those who wished to go ahead become ineffective and be placed behind; that is, let them strive to imitate us. “And let them be ashamed”: not only those who have done evil, but also those who wish evil for me.

Here he notes different periods of persecution: one, when the onslaught of the pagans raged against Christians; another, when the evil will of Christians persecutes the faithful. The latter still continues in the Church, because even though pagan kings and the other persecutors have been baptized, the devil has not been baptized—he secretly rages through secret agents, that is, through wicked Christians.

“Let those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done,’ turn back at once in shame.” Notice the two kinds of enemies: those who revile and those who flatter. Since the tongue of a flatterer often leads one astray more than the hand of a murderer, he says, “Let them turn back at once”—that is, without delay—and let those who say to me, “Well done, well done,” be ashamed of their former life. These are the people who flatteringly praise what ought not to be praised; let them turn back.

“Let all who seek you exult and rejoice in you”—not in themselves—those who seek you through good works. And let those who love your salvation say always—that is, at every time—“The Lord be magnified,” never the servant. Let the Lord be magnified in prosperity, because he comforts; let him be magnified in adversity, because he corrects. Are you a sinner? Let him be magnified, because he calls you. Do you confess? Let him be magnified, because he forgives. Do you live justly? Let him be magnified, because he governs you. Will you persevere? Let him be magnified, because he will glorify you.

Let each person say of himself, “But I am needy and poor”; and therefore, O God, help me—you who have condemned me as a rebel against you. And you ought to help me, because you are my helper in good things and my deliverer in evils. Therefore, Lord, do not delay—that is, do not allow me to think that you are delaying, and do not let what has been foreseen and reserved for me by you seem slow when it is needed.

For if what you have promised seems slow to someone, it may happen that he fails under the burden and seeks along the way what was promised only at the destination. Therefore let us fear the Lord who says, “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke XVII).

It is known that Lot lived justly among the Sodomites. For this reason the Lord warned him to leave Sodom and go to certain cities where he would be saved from the destruction threatening the Sodomites. But because the journey seemed long to his wife, and because she wished to have along the way what had been promised at the destination, she looked back and was changed into a pillar of salt (Genesis XIX). Nor did this happen without purpose, since she ought to be seasoning for us.

So that what has been divinely promised may not seem slow to us, let us observe her remaining behind and pass on; let us observe her looking back and stretch ourselves toward what lies ahead, forgetting what is behind, so that at last we may be able to say with the Apostle, “As for the rest, the crown of righteousness is laid up for me” (2 Timothy IV).

## PSALM LXX. THE PSALM OF DAVID, OF THE SONS OF JONADAB AND OF THE FIRST CAPTIVES

“In you, Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be confounded forever. In your righteousness deliver me and rescue me. Incline your ear to me and save me. Be for me a protecting God and a fortified place, so that you may save me. For you are my strength and my refuge. My God, rescue me from the hand of the sinner, and from the hand of the transgressor and the wicked. For you are my patience, Lord; Lord, my hope from my youth. In you I have been established from the womb; from my mother’s womb you are my protector. My song is always in you. I have become like a portent to many, and you are my strong helper. Let my mouth be filled with praise, so that I may sing your glory and your greatness all day long. Do not cast me away in the time of old age; when my strength fails, do not abandon me. For my enemies have spoken against me, and those who guarded my life have taken counsel together, saying, ‘God has abandoned him; pursue and seize him, because there is no one to rescue him.’ O God, do not be far from me; my God, look to my help. Let those who slander my life be confounded and fail; let those who seek evil for me be covered with confusion [Col. 0504A] and shame. But I will always hope, and I will add to all your praise. My mouth will proclaim your righteousness and your salvation all day long. For I have not learned letters; I will enter into the mighty deeds of the Lord. Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone. O God, you have taught me from my youth, and until now I will proclaim your wonders. And even into old age and decrepitude, O God, do not abandon me, until I proclaim your arm to every generation that is to come. Your power and your righteousness, O God, extend even to the highest heights; you have done mighty deeds. O God, who is like you? How many great and evil tribulations you have shown me! Yet, turning back, you have given me life, and from the abysses of the earth you have brought me back again. You have multiplied your magnificence and, turning back, you have comforted me. And I too will confess your truth to you with the instruments of the psalm; I will sing to you on the lyre, Holy One of Israel. My lips will exult when I sing to you, and my soul, which you have redeemed. Moreover, my tongue will meditate on your righteousness all day long, when those who seek evil for me have been confounded and put to shame.”

## EXPOSITION

It is a great gift of God and a great knowledge for a human being to attend to and understand that whatever exists does so by God’s grace and that nothing exists through itself. For the one who wishes to exist through himself tends toward nonexistence. But the one who strives to exist through God’s grace remains in true being.

This is the grace by which, when we did not exist, we were made; from ungodly people, godly; from incestuous people, chaste; from slaves, free; from condemned people, we were received into the kingdom. The Apostle commends this grace everywhere, and for that reason he had the Jews as enemies: they presumed upon the letter and so recoiled from grace.

The Apostle also commends this grace in himself when he says, “I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Corinthians XV); “but now I have received mercy, because I did this ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Timothy I). Shortly afterward he commends the same grace in this way: “This saying is trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first” (ibid.).

Notice that “first” does not mean first in time, but first in the magnitude of sin. “But I received mercy, so that in me, the first sinner, he might display all his patience [or: power], as an example for those who would believe in eternal life” (ibid.). It is as though he were saying: No one should despair of his sins, because my sins, though I committed so many, have been forgiven.

Therefore let everyone consider that my sins were forgiven and not despair, even if his sins are many. Instead, let him turn back, implore God’s mercy, and hope for forgiveness of his sins. For the Lord himself, commending his grace in the Gospel, says, “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners; nor do the healthy need a physician, but those who are ill” (Matthew IX).

This psalm everywhere commends that grace. Its title is: “The psalm of David, of the sons of Jonadab and of the first captives.”

Jonadab is interpreted as “the Lord’s voluntary one.” But who is voluntary except the one who worships God freely? Hence the saying, “I will sacrifice to you voluntarily” (Psalm LIII).

Jeremiah also commends this Jonadab to us in his prophecy. He says that Jonadab himself had commanded his sons not to drink wine and not to live in houses, but only in tents. Because his sons persevered in their father’s command, they deserved to be blessed by the Lord—not because it was the Lord’s command that they should not drink wine, but because they remained faithful to their father’s command (Jeremiah XXXV).

Scripture gives the command in this form: “Children, obey your parents” (Ephesians VI; Colossians III). One must always obey a father, unless he commands something contrary to the Lord’s command.

The obedience of these sons is set before us in this psalm, so that we may imitate it. This obedience is compared with the disobedience of the first captives, so that through the obedience of Jonadab’s sons the disobedience of the sons of Israel may be condemned. Jeremiah had foretold to them that they would be led captive into Babylon and that they should not resist the divine will, since it could not be otherwise than that they would be led captive. He foretold the captivity so that they might correct themselves; but because they did not wish to be corrected, they deserved to be led captive.

This psalm is colored by the disobedience of those people and the obedience of Jonadab’s sons. Their obedience is commended to us so that we may follow it; their disobedience is condemned so that we may flee from it.

The phrase “of the first captives” sends us back to the history in which we read that the sons of Israel were led into captivity in the first, second, and third deportations. But since the psalm speaks of none of these, let us understand the first captivity to be the captivity into which we were taken through the disobedience of our first parent.

The Apostle notes this captivity in the following words: “We were sold under sin” (Romans VII). Shortly afterward he says, “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person, but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin and death” (ibid.).

In this city we are all justly detained, because we abandoned the emperor and followed the deserter. God is the emperor; the devil is the deserter. The emperor gave a command; the devil suggested deceit. Where, then, was your eye between the command and the deceit? You believed what the deserter promised and found what the emperor threatened.

The voice in this psalm is that of the Prophet, recalling the sons of Jonadab and the first captives. He commends the obedience of the sons to us, and in commending their obedience he condemns the disobedience of the captives.

The sons of Jonadab may also be the same as the first captives, so that we may read the psalm in this way: as those captives, attending to their captivity, say with the Prophet:

“In you, Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be confounded forever.”

It is as though he were saying: I hoped in myself, and I was confounded; I transferred my hope to you, and therefore I shall not be confounded forever—that is, eternally—even though for a time you allow me to be confounded under the burden of mortality and suffering.

“And so that I may not be confounded, deliver me here inwardly in your righteousness,” by calling me and justifying me; “and rescue me” at last outwardly, so that, when the burden of mortality has been removed, I may be clothed with the glory of incorruptibility [Col. 0506A].

Here the sons of Jonadab are signified as persevering in obedience, seeking grace, and attending to their captivity. But if we understand the first captives to be those who still remain in captivity and do not seek to be liberated by the Lord’s grace, we understand their disobedience to be condemned here, while the obedience of Jonadab’s sons is set before us.

This psalm may also be the voice of our Head, transferring the voice of his members to himself and speaking on their behalf:

“In you, Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be confounded forever; in your righteousness deliver me.”

“And so that you may rescue and deliver me, incline your ear to me”—you who are high, to me who am low; you who are the physician, to me who am sick. And, having inclined yourself, save me in this way:

“Be for me a protecting God”—that is, God, be my protector, so that I may not be oppressed by enemies—and let me find you as a fortified place, so that from you I may have something to hurl against the weapons of my enemies. For no one who takes refuge in you can find a more fortified place than you.

We read of a certain man who had a dwelling on a most strongly fortified mountain. He saw a king passing by with a great, well-armed multitude and, trusting in his strong building, scorned the king, saying, “I am not speaking of you.” The king replied, “Nor am I speaking of you.” Notice: if this man was secure from enemies because of the fortification of an earthly place, how much more secure can one be who takes refuge in God, who made heaven and earth?

He says here, “Be for me a fortified place, so that you may save me.” And it is yours to save me, because you are my strength—that is, the one who makes me firm in my purpose—and you are my refuge, because, when you are angry, I find nowhere to flee except to you, once you have been appeased.

And because you are my refuge, you, my God, rescue me from the hand—that is, from the power—of the sinner; let him not prevail over me. He then explains whom he understands by “the sinner”: “From the hand of the transgressor,” that is, from the power of the Jewish people, which transgresses the law, rescue me; “and of the wicked,” who does not accept the equity of the law. Of him it is said, “Those who sinned without the law will also perish without the law” (Romans II).

Lest someone object, “Why do you ask to be delivered from persecution? Endure it; resist,” he adds:

“For you are my patience, Lord.”

It is as though he were saying: I must cry out to you, for I cannot do so without you, because you are my patience—that is, I am patient through you. And you, Lord, are my hope from my youth—that is, from the time of my invocation, in which invocation I became young, being reckoned fit for battle and placed in the ranks of your army, armed with faith, hope, and charity.

You are not only my hope from my youth; I have also been established in you from the womb—that is, from the time when I was initiated into the sacrament of faith.

“From my mother’s womb you are my protector”—that is, after I came forth from the womb of my mother, the Church. So that I might benefit not only myself but also others, you are my protector; and therefore my song is always in you.

And because I hope in you, “I have become like a portent to many,” appearing like a fool because I set present things aside and await future things. And so that I may not fail in hope, you are my helper in strength, because you have given the example of strength in yourself.

And because you are strong, “let my mouth be filled with praise,” so that I may sing your glory—that is, my disgrace—and sing your greatness and my smallness, “all day long,” in prosperity and adversity: in prosperity, because you comfort; in adversity, because you correct.

And so that I may sing your glory, “do not cast me away in the time of old age,” understood as the old age that must be put off—that is, in tribulation, when it is most necessary for me to lay aside old age and receive youth.

Or, for as long as we dwell in the mortality of the flesh, it is a time of old age, because we easily fall; and therefore we need to be sustained by God. Thus he asks, saying, “Do not cast me away in the time of old age, and do not abandon me when my strength fails,” at the moment when I presume upon nothing of myself.

You must not abandon me, because “my enemies have spoken against me”—understand: reproaching me—and those who guarded my life—understand: in order to oppress it—have taken counsel together, coming to the same intention, and saying, “Pursue and seize him.” And you can do so, they say, “because there is no one to rescue him,” for “God has abandoned him.” Elsewhere it is said, “There is no salvation for him in his God” (Psalm III).

They try to persecute me in this way, but you, God, do not be far from me; look to my help, because you are my God.

And how do I wish you to rescue me? “Let them be confounded”—that is, let them recognize themselves as deserving confusion—“and let them fail,” that is, let them prove without victory: those who slander my life, judging my simplicity to be madness; or those who slander my life and also the life of anyone—understand: every soul—persuading him to quarrel with the Lord by defending his sins.

The expression is also spoken by analogy with birds whose feathers are plucked so that they cannot fly. The feathers have been plucked from the person who is in the defense of sin. He lacks the reason by which he ought to be carried through the air of freedom as though on wings.

“Let those who seek evil for me be covered with confusion and shame.” Confusion occurs when conscience bites a person inwardly; shame occurs when he displays blushing outwardly. Thus, “Let them be covered with confusion and shame” means: Let those who seek evil for me be confounded inwardly and outwardly.

“But I will always hope, and I will add to all your praise”—that is, to all former praise I will add later praise.

The Lord was to be praised in the first human being, whom he created from the earth in his image and likeness and placed in paradise (Genesis II). He would have been worthy of praise even if, after the disobedience, he had condemned the entire mass that proceeded from the first parent by a just judgment. Yet praise must be added beyond all praise, because through grace we have been liberated from the sin transmitted to us.

Or we may understand it this way: “I will add to all your praise,” that is, I will recognize that you surpass all the praises of human beings.

Or, according to the Apostle, “I will add to all your praise”: “To him,” he says, “who is able to do abundantly beyond all that we ask or understand” (Ephesians III). What he says here, “I will add,” means that I will understand you to be adding beyond all the praise offered by us, because you work more in us than we are able to understand.

In the voice of the Head we shall say: “I will add to all your praise.” The Lord is to be praised in the ordering and governance of temporal things; he is to be praised in the height of heaven, in the fruitfulness of the earth, in the surrounding boundary of the sea, in the multiplication of creatures born everywhere, in the Israelite people liberated from Egyptian slavery, in the law that was given, and in the evangelical grace proclaimed everywhere.

But beyond all this praise the Lord’s human being will add his own praise, because he raised up flesh that would never again die—something no one before him could do.

“My mouth will proclaim your righteousness,” because we have been saved through faith; “and my mouth will proclaim your salvation all day long,” that is, your salvation and my destruction.

And from where does this come to me? “Because I have not learned letters”—that is, I am not one of those who presume upon the letter and recoil from grace. Or, “I have not learned letters” means that I have rejected doing anything perfunctorily.

For one who speaks but does not do God’s will is like someone who can indeed read, but who does not grasp in his heart what he reads with his mouth.

He says, “For I have not learned letters, but rather I will enter into the powers [potentias] of the Lord”—that is, I will discern them—so that I may glory only in the one who redeemed me through his power.

“Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone”: my captivity and your liberation. And this does not come from me, but from you, because you, God, have taught me from my youth—that is, from the time of my renewal—and until now, understand: you continue to teach me. Therefore I will proclaim your wonders.

For what is more wondrous than the plan of the restoration of the human race being due to your grace and not to anyone’s merit?

You taught me from my youth and until now, and you will also teach me into old age and decrepitude. Old age is when someone begins to become weighed down by age; decrepitude is when he is in extreme old age. Through these two terms he indicates a length of time.

It is as though he were saying: You will teach me to remember your righteousness at all times, in youth and in old age. Another translation has “into the presbyter and the geront,” where the meaning is the same, because among the Greeks *presbyteros* means “elder,” while *geron* means a heavily aged old man.

Or otherwise: “God, you have taught me from my youth.” Youth was in the Church at the beginning, when the holy martyrs, armed with faith, hope, and charity, fought to uphold the faith even to the shedding of blood.

The phrase “until now you have taught me” designates our own time, in which people are no longer martyred in the struggle for the faith, because, through the abundance of iniquity, the charity of many has grown cold.

The phrase “into old age and decrepitude” indicates the final time, when many will depart from the faith because of the persecution of the Antichrist.

“O God, do not abandon me.” It is as though he were saying: You who have taught me from my youth, do not abandon me until I proclaim through myself and through my successors your arm—that is, your power—not merely to the generation that is to come, but to every generation that is to come.

Notice that there were certain heretics who asserted that the Catholic faith would remain until a certain time and afterward be utterly destroyed. To refute their error, he says that the Lord’s power must be proclaimed to every generation.

“Do not abandon me until I proclaim your arm to the generation that is to come”; and until I proclaim your power and your righteousness—that is, your justifying grace—I will consider them reaching even to the highest mighty works that you have done. I mean those heavenly beings—principalities, virtues, dominions, and powers—as belonging to your grace, because the fact that they live well comes from you, not from themselves.

And since you are so great, O God, “who is like you?” No one, certainly. For when I wished, in the first parent, to be like you, you showed me many tribulations—that is, tribulations difficult and painful to endure, numerous and evil.

He wished to be like you who said, “I will set my throne toward the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah XIV), and he departed from you into the region of dissimilarity.

Wretched Adam also wished to be like you when he believed the deserter who said, “Eat, and you will be like gods” (Genesis III). He believed what the devil promised and found what the Lord threatened. The one who failed prevailed more with him than the one who made him. In this way you showed me many tribulations, and evil ones, but you did not condemn me irreparably, because, turning from anger to mercy, you gave me life—that is, you placed me in life.

And how did you do this? “From the abysses of the earth you brought me back again.”

Notice that he says “brought me back,” because no one is brought back unless he has first been led out. God led the human being out of the earth’s lowliness by creating him wondrously. The earth was advanced into something great when the human being was formed from the earth in the image and likeness of God, despite his lowliness.

The earth fell back when the human being failed God through disobedience; but the earth is brought back again to the heights when the Word assumed from the earth a human being free from sin. Thus he brought him back—that is, he led the human being again from the abysses of the earth, wondrously reforming him inwardly, because “we have been saved in hope” (Romans VIII).

Here it is clear what “you brought me back” means. Let us show again what will happen when mortal flesh rises into immortality, because in this way the human being is led down again and again by the Lord. This is what is meant by, “From the abysses of the earth you brought me back again.”

And how do I know this? “For you have multiplied your magnificence”—that is, you have multiplied your righteousness to such an extent that, although you did not spare your sons, you nevertheless, turning back, comforted me.

And I too, not only in my Head but also in myself, will confess your truth to you “with the instruments of the psalm.” “I will sing to you on the lyre, Holy One of Israel.” The instruments of the psalm are the psalterium.

Notice the distinction between the psalterium and the lyre. The psalterium produces its sound above; this signifies the soul, which is the higher part of the human being. The lyre produces its sound below; this signifies the flesh, which is the lower part of the human being. A person plays the lyre through the flesh when he supplies the lower things to those in need.

This is what is meant by, “I will sing to you on the lyre, Holy One of Israel.” And thus at last, “my lips will exult when I sing to you,” because sometimes now I sing for myself.

He then explains how the lips ought to exult: “My soul, which you have redeemed”—understand: will exult. And not only the soul, but also “my tongue,” the outward tongue, “will meditate on your righteousness all day long.”

He rightly says “will meditate,” because there will be no need there for elemental speech.

And when will this be? When, in contrast, those who here seek evil for me—judging my life to be madness—have been confounded and put to shame in their own consideration.

## PSALM LXXI. THE PSALM OF DAVID, CONCERNING SOLOMON

“Give your judgment to the king, O God, and your righteousness to the king’s son. Let him judge your people in righteousness and your poor in judgment. Let the mountains receive peace for the people and the hills righteousness. He will judge the poor of the people, and he will save the sons of the poor, and he will humble the accuser. He will remain with the sun and before the moon, from generation to generation. He will descend like rain upon fleece, and like drops falling upon the earth. In his days righteousness and an abundance of peace will arise, until the moon is taken away. And he will rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth. Before him the Ethiopians will fall, and his enemies will lick the earth. The kings of Tharsis and the islands will offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba will bring presents. And all kings will adore him; all nations will serve him. For he will deliver the poor from the powerful, and the poor person who had no helper. He will spare the poor and the needy, and he will save the lives of the poor. He will redeem their lives from usury and iniquity, and their name will be honorable before him. And he will live, and he will be given the gold of Arabia, and they will adore him continually; all day long they will bless him. He will be a foundation in the land upon the summits of the mountains; his fruit will rise above Lebanon, and they will flourish from the city like the grass of the earth. Let his name be blessed forever; his name remains before the sun. And all the tribes of the earth will be blessed in him; all nations will magnify him. Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, who alone does wondrous things. And blessed is the name of his majesty forever, and the whole earth will be filled with his majesty. Let it be so, let it be so.”

## EXPOSITION

Solomon is interpreted as “peaceful.” This interpretation of the name suits Christ, our Head, because through his death he dissolved our enmities and reconciled us to God the Father.

He also dissolved the wall erected between us and the heavenly rational creature, and soon united us with them in himself, the cornerstone. Upon the peace of reconciliation he also added the peace of immortality. The words of this psalm refer to him [Col. 0510D].

For the Prophet, foreseeing in prophetic spirit that he would come in the flesh, carefully explains the things that would happen in those days, so that when unbelievers see that the things prophesied about him have taken place, they may not doubt that he has come, but may humbly adore him.

The Prophet speaks as follows.

God, give your judgment to the king. As though he were saying: God the Father, send the one whom you are going to send, so that through him, once judged, you may at last judge the world, because it is written: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). For he rightly judges the world who lived in the world and was judged by the rulers of the world.

And your justice to the king’s son. What he said earlier is repeated. For what he previously called “judgment,” he here calls “justice.” What else is that judgment itself but justice? The one whom he previously called “king,” he here calls “son”; for he is both Father and king. These repetitions greatly commend the divine utterances, whether the same meaning is repeated in the same words or in different words; such repetitions are found especially in the Psalms and in that kind of discourse where the emotions of the hearers must be stirred.

Or otherwise: “God, give your judgment to the king, and your justice to the king’s son”: he, as Son, was to proclaim justice, both by deed and by word. Hence the saying: “What Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1). That God the Father is called “king” is attested by Paul, who says: “To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God” (1 Timothy 1), and so forth.

Alternatively, we may understand “the king’s son” as the Jewish people, whom the Lord the Father adopted as sons through the law that was given. “God, give your judgment to the king”: to judge your people, that is, for the judging of your people in justice, so that through justice he may distinguish his own people from those who are not his; and, finally, your poor, that is, those who wish to be your poor, not rich in themselves, abounding in you and needy in themselves. And where will they be judged? In the judgment, that is, the future judgment.

Paul explains who the Lord’s poor are: “If I distribute all my possessions to the poor, and if I give my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13). As though he were saying: If I give everything I possess to the poor, but am not God’s poor man, it profits me nothing. For charity is not puffed up, and there is no true charity of God in one who is ungrateful to his Holy Spirit.

The holy Job possessed this poverty; he was poor even before he lost those great riches. Let this poor man say with the other poor: “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God” (1 Corinthians 2). Those who presume upon their own merits are not the Lord’s poor, nor do they wish justice to be given them by God; rather, trusting that they possess it from themselves, “they are ignorant of God’s justice and seek to establish their own; they are not subject to the justice of God” (Romans 10). Such people are not God’s poor, but rich in themselves.

But God’s poor man cries out: “Judge me, God, and distinguish my cause” (Psalm 42).

Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills justice. As though he were saying: Give the king the task of judging your people, so that he may judge the mountains—that is, those who are more eminent in the world, flourishing in riches and exalted by honors—and let them receive peace for your Jewish people by preaching, and the hills justice.

The hills are again those who are more eminent in the world, but subject to the mountains. Or otherwise: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people.” The mountains are those who stand out in the Church through exceptional holiness and are capable of teaching others, instructing them faithfully by their speech and providing a salutary example by their lives. The hills, however, are those who, through their obedience, imitate the excellence of holiness belonging to those who are called mountains.

Notice that he says: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills justice.” Those who excel in the holy Church ought, with vigilant attention, to promote peace, lest by acting arrogantly on account of their honors they create schisms in the Church, breaking apart the bond of unity. The hills, too, must receive justice, that is, obedience, so that they imitate the mountains in the respect in which they are to be imitated, setting before them the mountain of mountains. They must not say, “I belong to Paul,” or “I to Cephas,” but all must say, “I belong to Christ” (1 Corinthians 1).

This is justice: neither to place servants beside the Lord nor to make them equal to him. Rather, let each one say: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains; from where will my help come? From the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Psalm 120).

One of the mountains shows how they are to be imitated: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 4); and elsewhere: “We act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us” (2 Corinthians 5). “We implore you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God.” Let these mountains receive peace for the people, that is, the word of reconciliation, which is to be preached to the people. And the hills justice, that is, the imitation of their excellence. In order that they may become mountains, let them receive justice, that is, their obedience, so that what is written concerning justice and peace may come to pass: “Justice and peace have kissed” (Psalm 84).

That “justice” can signify obedience is indicated by the Apostle when he says: “Just as through the disobedience of one man the many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one righteous man the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5).

He will judge the poor of the people. As though he were saying: Truly, let the mountains receive the word of reconciliation, as Paul indicates: “God,” he says, “reconciled us to himself through Christ and placed in us the mystery of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5). This is indicated here because God himself will judge my poor, the poor of the people—that is, the people who regard themselves as poor—and finally will save the sons of the poor.

But if we understand the mountains as those exalted in the world, we shall connect the passage in this way: “God, give your judgment to the king”—and truly you will give it, because he will judge, that is, distinguish, the poor of the people, namely the apostles; and he will save the sons of the poor, that is, he will judge the imitators of the apostles. The poor and the sons of the poor can be the same people, because Zion and the daughter of Zion are one and the same city.

And he will humble the slanderer. A slanderer is one who tries to turn another’s innocence into guilt through some carefully contrived deceit or artfully devised cunning. No one is therefore more rightly recognized here as the slanderer than the devil. His slander is: “Does Job worship God for nothing?” (Job 1). For he wished to turn the innocence of that most holy man into guilt, if he could accomplish this—namely, to make him serve the devil for earthly possessions. But the Lord humbled him by his grace, helping his own to worship God freely. He also humbled him among the Jews, whom that slanderer used as his vessels, working in the sons of unbelief.

For he was humbled because the one whom they had killed rose again and, by his death, destroyed the dominion of death. He also humbled him because he brought many from darkness into light: when the devil stretched out his hand toward unlawful things, wishing, that is, to seize Christ, he lost those over whom he had previously held power.

Alternatively, by the name “slanderer” the reprobate people are understood. For, while attempting for the most part to excuse their sins, they bring an accusation against the Creator. Hence the saying of Sallust: “The human race falsely complains about its nature.” The Lord humbles this reprobate people by making them filthy. Hence the saying: “Let the one who is filthy be filthy still” (Revelation 22).

And he will remain with the sun, that is, as long as time revolves. Hence the saying: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever” (Psalm 44). And lest we understand him as remaining only thereafter, and as not having existed before time, he adds: “before the moon.” As though he were saying: He preceded all time.

He explains how “before the moon” is to be understood by adding, “through generations of generations,” so that this may explain the earlier statement. Or thus: “He will remain with the sun,” that is, with the Father’s glory or equality, and he was “before the moon,” that is, before the Church in dignity, since he was conceived in human nature free from sin. Or “before the moon,” because by his eternity he preceded the Church, and he will remain through generations of generations.

Notice that the Church is not inappropriately represented by the moon, because just as the moon is illuminated by the sun, so the Church has no light unless it is illuminated by the true sun, namely the Lord.

He will descend like rain upon fleece. The Prophet has stated how the Lord will come: just as rain descends upon fleece without noise or perceptible sensation and does not damage the fleece itself, so the Father’s Word descended into the Virgin’s womb without carnal sensation and without corrupting the Virgin, because she was a mother who did not know man. And just as drops falling upon the earth do not drown it but water it, so the Lord lived among the human race, watering it rather than destroying it.

Or otherwise: “He will descend like rain upon fleece.” This sends us to the history that recounts what happened in the time of the judge Gideon. Warned by the Lord to attack the Philistines, he asked for a sign of the future victory: that the fleece placed on the threshing floor should be soaked while the threshing floor remained dry. Then, a second time, he asked that the threshing floor should be soaked while the fleece remained dry (Judges 6).

This happened in that way, but not without a mystery. The fleece, first watered, signifies the Jewish people, who were first drenched with the divine Word. There the Lord chose the mother in whom he would receive the form of a servant and appear to human beings; there he chose the disciples to whom he gave the same command, saying: “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans” (Matthew 10).

But because that people, persisting in hardness, did not receive the divine utterance, what is signified by the dry fleece and the soaked threshing floor came to pass. The divine utterance was taken away from the Jews and proclaimed among the Gentiles. Thus the threshing floor was soaked, because the dry hearts of the Gentiles were watered with the dew of the divine utterance. This is what he says: “He will descend like rain upon fleece, and like drops dripping upon the earth.”

And he says what will happen in his days: “Justice will arise in his days,” that is, faith justifying each person, “and an abundance of peace,” because in those days peace extends not only to friends but also to enemies. Hence the saying: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall love your friend, and you shall hate your enemy.’ But I say to you: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you” (Matthew 5).

This abundance of peace will last “until the moon is taken away,” that is, until the Church, having conquered death, is assumed into immortality. Or, according to another translation, until the moon is exalted through the glory of the resurrection, destined to reign forever with him who preceded it in the glory of the resurrection.

And he will rule from sea to sea—that is, from the eastern sea, understood, to the western sea—beginning, understood, from the river, namely the Jordan, and extending to the ends of the earth.

Notice that here he clearly expressed that Christ wished already to commend his power from the place where he also began to choose his disciples: from the river Jordan, namely, where, after the Lord had been baptized and the Holy Spirit descended, a voice from heaven sounded: “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3). Beginning from there, therefore, his teaching and the authority of his heavenly mastery spread to the ends of the earth, as “the gospel of the kingdom is preached in the whole world as a testimony to all the nations” (Matthew 24).

Or otherwise: “He will rule from sea”—that is, the sea of the Jews—“to sea,” that is, to the sea of the Gentiles. Notice that although the Jews had received knowledge of the law, they can nevertheless be called a sea, because, thirsting after earthly things, they were troubled by the storms of the world as by the waves of the sea. The Gentile people, because they received no knowledge of God at all, are rightly designated by the name “sea.” Thus he says: “He will rule from sea to sea,” beginning from the river and extending to the ends of the earth.

While he rules, the Ethiopians will fall before him, that is, those who were previously most blackened in their morals will be humbled, and his enemies will lick the earth, understood, in reverence for him.

Or his enemies, that is, heretics, will lick the earth, that is, they will delight in earthly things, claiming for themselves the authority of earthly matters, so that they may confirm to others what they have received by understanding the Scriptures perversely.

The kings of Tarshish and the islands. He shows how kings will fall before him: for the kings of Tarshish and the islands will offer gifts. Tarshish is interpreted as “the exploration of joy.” By this are understood those who proclaimed their joy in earthly things, who, having now been made kings—that is, ruling themselves and others well—will offer gifts, namely themselves, worthy gifts to God.

Tarshish is also interpreted as “contemplation.” By this are signified those who contemplate heavenly things and forget earthly things. To contemplate pertains to future things; to consider, to present things.

Lands are called islands because they are situated in the sea. By them are understood people who are shaken by the waves of the world as by the movement of the sea. Once made stable and endangered by nothing, such people will offer gifts to the Lord.

The kings of Arabia and Sheba will bring gifts. Notice that nothing is brought except what walks. Here it is already understood that in his days no command will be given concerning the sacrifice of victims; rather, these gifts that are to be brought seem to signify the human beings whom the authority of kings brings into fellowship with Christ and the Church.

Arabia is interpreted as “plain” or “humble.” By this are understood the Gentiles, who, having been humbled, are reckoned among the gifts of God. Sheba is interpreted as “burnt” or “kindled.” By this are understood those who are set aflame by the fire of divine love, so that they may be counted among God’s gifts. This is what he says: “The kings of Arabia and Sheba will bring gifts.”

To put it briefly: “All the kings of the earth will worship him,” that is, absolutely all kings, “and all nations will serve him.” And rightly so, because he delivered the poor, namely the one who humbly confesses his sins, from the powerful, that is, from the ruler of earthly power.

He goes on to say which poor man he will deliver: “and the poor man who had no helper,” the one who does not presume that salvation is to be given him on the basis of his merits, or of free will, or by any other helper except the Lord.

And how will he deliver him? Not according to their merits, but “he will spare the poor and needy,” that is, he will not reckon the sins of the poor and needy against them, and thus he will save the souls of the poor.

And how will he do this? By redeeming their souls from usury and iniquity, so that they may come from sin into sin. Usury occurs when, because of a preceding sin, someone is induced to sin again; or iniquity is sin, and usury is the punishment of sin. It is rightly called the punishment of sin “usury,” because more evil is found in punishments than was committed in sins.

For example, a murderer destroys only the body of a human being and can do nothing to the soul; yet in hell both his body and soul are lost. Thus he will redeem them from usury by redeeming sins that deserved greater punishments. He will redeem them from iniquity by helping them through grace and also enabling them to practice justice.

And their name will be honorable before him, and thus it becomes contemptible before human beings. Hence the saying elsewhere: “For my inheritance is splendid to me” (Psalm 15).

And he will live; and because he will live, “there will be given to him from the gold of Arabia,” that is, from the foremost wise people among the Gentiles. Gold signifies wisdom, and Arabia the nations. Hence it is written: “Receive prudence and wisdom like tested gold” (Proverbs 8 and 16). Or gold is so called as though from *aura* (“breeze” or “air”); hence “the gold of Arabia” signifies the most splendid intentions of the nations.

Notice that it is not without weight that he says, “he will live.” If this were said of the life that human beings commonly possess, there would be no great reason why the gold of Arabia should be given to him. Therefore it must be understood with emphasis: “he will live,” as though he were saying, “Rising from the dead, he will die no more.” For not all of us truly live, since outwardly we are destined to die and inwardly we die daily through sins.

It follows: “And they will worship because of him continually,” that is, at all times; “because of him,” that is, from his body being filled, so that his members may be multiplied, and thus “all day long they will bless him.” Or they will pray because of him continually, receiving what they pray for or seeking to obtain it on account of him.

And rightly so, because he will be the firmament on earth, where there had previously been no firmness. Coming, he established them in a stable doctrine that was never to be changed. Hence Paul says: “If anyone,” he says, “preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received from us, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1).

He will also be the firmament on the summits of the mountains, because in him all the words and deeds revealed through the highest mountains—that is, through the prophets and patriarchs—will be fulfilled.

His fruit will be exalted above Lebanon, namely those whom he chose for himself as fruit from the world. Hence the saying: “I chose you from the world, so that you might go and bear fruit, and that your fruit might remain” (John 15). “His fruit above Lebanon,” that is, above every worldly whiteness. Lebanon is interpreted as “whitening.”

Or “his fruit”—that is, charity—“will be exalted above Lebanon.” Hence Paul’s saying: “I show you a still more excellent way” (1 Corinthians 12). For this is placed first among the gifts of God, where he says: “The fruit of the Spirit is charity” (Galatians 5).

And they will blossom from the city like the grass of the earth. Since the phrase “from the city” is stated without qualification, let us understand it as the city of God, or Jerusalem. If we understand it as the city of God, we shall take “grass” as wheat. Hence in Genesis: “Let the earth bring forth wood and all its grass” (Genesis 1). Here “grass” should not be understood as dry grass, but as green grass, fruit-bearing like grain.

Or otherwise: “They will blossom from their city,” understood, “like the grass of the earth,” which exists today and tomorrow is thrown into the furnace (Matthew 9).

From all that has been said above, “may his name be blessed,” that is, multiplied, “through the ages,” that is, as long as time revolves. And rightly so, because his name remains “before the sun,” that is, before every temporal ordering; and in him, understood, in his name, “all the tribes of the earth will be blessed,” because all nations will magnify him.

Hence: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who alone performs wonders,” through himself and through his own. “And blessed be the name of his majesty forever,” that is, may his divinity be multiplied, not in itself but in human knowledge. This will indeed happen, because “the whole earth will be filled with his majesty.” May this multiplication take place in the former people; may it take place also in the later one.

## PSALM 72. “THE HYMNS OF DAVID, THE SON OF JESSE, HAVE FAILED”; A PSALM OF ASAPH

> How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart!  
> But my feet almost slipped; my steps nearly poured out.  
> For I was jealous of the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners.  
> For there is no regard for their death, and there is no firmness in their affliction.  
> They are not in the labor of human beings, and they will not be scourged with other people.  
> Therefore pride seized them; they are covered with their iniquity and impiety.  
> Their iniquity came forth as though from fatness; they passed over into the desire of their heart.  
> They thought and spoke wickedness; they spoke iniquity on high.  
> They set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue passed through the earth.  
> Therefore this people of mine will turn back, and full days will be found in them.  
> And they said: “How does God know, and is there knowledge in the Most High?”  
> Behold, these are sinners, and those who abound in the world have acquired riches.  
> And I said: “Then in vain I justified my heart and washed my hands among the innocent;  
> I was scourged all day long, and my chastisement came in the mornings.”  
> If I said: “Thus I will speak,” behold, I would reject the generation of your sons.  
> I considered that I might understand this; it was labor before me,  
> until I entered the sanctuary of God and understood their final destiny.  
> Nevertheless, because of their deceits you set them in slippery places;  
> you cast them down while they were being exalted.  
> How they have become desolation! Suddenly they have failed; they have perished because of their iniquity.  
> Like a dream of those who rise, Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing.  
> For my heart was inflamed, and my reins were changed;  
> and I was reduced to nothing, and I did not know.  
> I became like a beast before you, yet I am always with you.  
> You have held my right hand; in your will you have led me, and with glory you have received me.  
> For what is there for me in heaven? And besides you, what have I desired on earth?  
> My flesh and my heart have failed; God is the God of my heart,  
> and God is my portion forever.  
> For behold, those who withdraw from you will perish;  
> you have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you.  
> But for me it is good to cling to God,  
> to place my hope in the Lord God,  
> so that I may proclaim all your preachings at the gates of the daughter of Zion.

## EXPOSITION

[Col. 0517B]

It is not without reason that David, the son of Jesse, is named in this title, since the preceding psalms were entitled with the name of David but without mentioning his father. By inserting Jesse here—who was David’s father according to the flesh—the text seems to indicate certain Israelites who were wise according to the flesh and attached to earthly things.

The history is well known: by divine power the children of Israel were led through the Red Sea, while the pursuing enemies were drowned (Exodus 14). It is also known how that same people wandered through the desert for many years, with Moses as leader and Aaron. Many promises were made to this people. The land of Canaan, the subjection of their enemies, the fertility of their wives and children, and worldly honor were promised to them.

They received all these things and regarded them as of great importance; and the greater part of them understood that God was to be served for the sake of earthly things. But the Lord, who granted all these things to them not so that they might remain in them, but so that through them they might believe in other things to come, withdrew their temporal goods, so that at least in this way they might learn to cling to eternal things.

But the people, desiring earthly rather than heavenly things, visible rather than invisible things, murmured against the Lord when they saw that these goods were being taken from them and given to the nations. They complained because the nations, which did not worship God, received temporal goods and prospered in everything, while those who worshiped God were in misery and labor.

They argued inwardly with themselves over all these matters as follows: Either God knows everything, or he does not know. But since it was dangerous to confess that the Creator of all things was ignorant of anything, they said: If he knows, either he cares or he does not care. That he does not care is contradicted by Scripture, because it is written of him: “Ordering all things powerfully and gently” (Wisdom 8).

But if he does care, how can he allow those who do not worship him to flourish and be adorned, while those who worship him labor and are destroyed? From those who murmured in this way because their temporal goods had failed, the praises that ought to have been offered for the acquisition of heavenly goods also failed.

Yet because there were not lacking among that people those who understood that these promises, in their root—namely, in the one who made the promises—were like a shadow, while the true goods were future, their voice appears in this psalm. They exhort those who murmured in this way to cease murmuring and to prefer awaiting what is unseen to clinging to what is seen.

For those who cling to these visible things will ultimately perish; those who do not cling to them will be crowned. And it is a psalm of Asaph, that is, an operation to be attributed to one who gathers together. It was made because the praises of David had failed. I say “David,” not the spiritual but the carnal David; this is indicated by “son of Jesse.” The praises of the spiritual David never failed. Asaph therefore speaks as follows:

How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart! As if he were saying: How incomparably good is the God of Israel—that is, of those who see God—to the upright in heart, that is, to those who direct their will according to the will of God, even though he may appear small and perverse to the crooked of heart.[Col. 0518B] Elsewhere it is said: “With the holy man you will be holy, and with the perverse man you will be perverted” (Psalm XVII); not because God is perverse, but because he appears perverse to the perverse person. For to an eye suffering from a defect, the brightness of the sun does not shine forth, but appears dim, because the eye cannot look directly upon its brilliance.

But my feet were almost moved. Here Asaph takes upon himself the voice of those from whom praises had ceased. As if he were saying: “How good is the God of Israel!” But I did not attend to this, because my feet—that is, my affections—were almost moved, namely, toward falling; my steps were almost poured out, toward wandering, as I imitated those who did not walk along the straight way. He says “almost,” because he eventually came to his senses, as can be indicated later in the psalm.

Why his feet were moved is added: Because I was jealous—that is, I was indignant, or I felt envy—against the wicked, extending my consideration toward them, or desiring to be above them. And why was this? Because I saw the peace of sinners, who did not truly worship God. And what kind of peace? An earthly peace, a changeable peace, a peace not arising from grace but from judgment. While I desired this peace and wished to serve God for its sake, my feet were almost moved.

They were moved also because there is no regard for their death; that is, the death which they deserved does not regard them. And there is no firmness in their affliction, because if at some time they suffer afflictions and are corrected, their afflictions are not firm but transitory, since they are not in the labor of human beings—that is, they neither labor nor suffer correction as much as those labor who are human beings, namely, who use reason and worship not idols but the true God.

Or otherwise: seeing the peace of sinners. And why do they have peace? Namely, for their judgment, because there is no regard for their death; that is, the death which they deserved does not regard them, meaning that it does not turn away from them but continually watches for them, awaiting them. And there is firmness in their affliction, since the afflictions reserved for them are not transitory but firm and never to be changed.

And why is this? Because here, in this life, they are not in the labor of human beings, namely, of those who live according to human nature. As if he were saying: They will therefore finally be condemned with servants, because here they are not in labor with sons; and they will not be scourged with them, because “God scourges every son whom he receives” (Proverbs III). Therefore pride took possession of them. As if he were saying: Because the Lord grants them peace and does not correct them with his sons, pride took possession of them—that is, it reduced them to its own power, so that they would not live soberly. They were covered within themselves with iniquity—that is, so that they would not live justly in relation to their neighbor—and they were covered with impiety, so that they would not live piously in relation to God. To them Paul’s command was given in vain: “Let us live soberly, justly, and piously in this age” (Titus II). They did not heed this; therefore pride took possession of them, and they were covered with their iniquity and impiety.

This iniquity did not arise from necessity, as he says: Their iniquity came forth as though from fat. As if he were saying: Their iniquity is inexcusable, because it did not proceed from leanness but as though from fatness. Iniquity proceeds from leanness when a poor person, lacking necessities, commits iniquity by taking away his neighbor’s possessions, although every necessity ought rather to be endured than even the smallest iniquity committed.

Iniquity comes forth as though from fatness when the possessions of others are seized by the rich, to whom the abundance of worldly goods flows. Iniquity also proceeds from fatness when someone disdains to hear his own correction. Or iniquity proceeds from fatness when someone who ought to correct others, fearing that his temporal goods may be taken away, flatters even the rich in their wrongdoing.

Their iniquity came forth as though from fatness; and they passed beyond—that is, they exceeded—the bounds of the human race, because they did not recognize themselves as frail. They advanced into the desire of the heart, that is, they tended toward every affection of carnal pleasure.

And how did this happen? They thought and spoke wickedness: first they deliberated their wickedness within themselves, and afterward they spoke it, thus proceeding from sin to sin. For the person who publicizes wickedness after devising it doubles his guilt: it is a twofold sin, to devise evil and to propagate it as though it were good.

They spoke iniquity on high. As if he were saying: They spoke wickedness, and not in just any manner, but on high—that is, publicly. They gloried in their wickedness and, presiding in the chair of pestilence, gave others authority for wickedness. Hence Paul says: “Let clamor be removed from your midst” (Ephesians IV).

Thus they set their mouth against heaven, that is, they spoke evilly against God, against him whom no tongue is sufficient to praise; they did not fear to utter blasphemies. And their tongue passed through the earth—that is, beyond human possibility and the limits of the human race—even though it had been placed on the earth, namely, in a fragile and quickly changing vessel.

Observe how their tongue passed beyond its bounds. When they speak such things, they do not consider that they can suddenly die; but, as though they were always going to live, they make grand threats. Such people do not know how fragile a vessel covers them, nor do they know what is written: “The spirit will go forth and return to its earth” (Psalm CXLV).

Or thus: Their tongue passed through all those on earth, that is, those established in stability, despising them in the affection of their heart, while they attributed temporal goods to themselves and took them away from others.

Therefore my people here will turn.
