As if he were saying: Since those people flourish for a time, in order afterward to perish eternally, therefore my people here will turn—that is, the people of my nation, of which I am a part; “here,” that is, like me. And in that people which has turned, full days will be found, because in their consideration there will be only the days of eternity, which are full of an abundance of goods. Full days will be found—that is, a life of the fullness of times, in those times when the apostles preached that temporal things were to be despised and eternal things awaited.

Or otherwise: They set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue passed through the earth. As if he were saying: Therefore my people here will turn. Why is this description of the wicked given? So that my people may turn from their perverse understanding to possess my understanding, namely, so that earthly happiness may be despised.

And it is necessary that they turn, because, having turned away from him, they said: “How does God know all things, when the wicked rejoice in earthly happiness and the good labor in affliction?” And if there is knowledge on high, we may say that he does not care to govern these lower things. And here is why: the sinners themselves, namely, those who do not serve God, abound in the world; for they have obtained—that is, they have held against us—riches.

And I said: “Therefore I justified my heart without cause, confessing my sins; and I washed my hands among the innocent”—that is, “In vain did I live piously and innocently, joining myself to other innocent people? And in vain was I scourged all day long,” that is, continually; “and my chastisement came in the mornings,” that is, it was not delayed, but I was made comparable to one whose punishment stood at the door, so that he would be killed as soon as he left the house.

And all this was in vain, because the people who do not serve you have their punishment delayed, or have none at all. They are adorned with riches; those who serve you are oppressed by miseries and distress.

After I had considered all these things, I turned to myself and said: “If I recount that I was justified without cause, that I lived piously and innocently in vain, and that I was chastised and scourged in vain because I lack temporal goods, with which those who persecute the good abound—behold, I rejected the nation,” that is, the authority, “of your sons,” namely, Abraham and Isaac. I despised it because none of them agrees with me in this: that, once eternal things have been despised, temporal things should be possessed; nor that one ought to be scourged for temporal things, but for eternal ones.

And after seeing all these things, I thought it would be useful for me—understand: it would be useful for me—to learn how God disposes human affairs, how he takes temporal things away from those who worship him and permits those who do not worship him to possess them. And to learn and investigate this—understand: to learn and investigate this—is a labor before me, that is, greater than I am; as in the saying: “He who comes after me was made before me” (John I).

It is a labor, I say, before me until I enter, namely through consideration, into the sanctuary of God, into the hidden disposition of the Lord, and understand their last things—that is, consider the last things of those who here gape after earthly possessions and do not labor in hope of heavenly things.

It can also be punctuated thus: “I thought that I might understand this,” namely, how the wicked are permitted to flourish in this life; “but it is a labor before me until I enter into the sanctuary of God and understand their last things,” when they are to be punished.

Nevertheless, because of their deceitfulness you set it before them. As if he were saying: Although I said that they would be punished in their last things, nevertheless you have already condemned them in the present, because of the deceitfulness by which they customarily deceive their fellow citizens; or because of the deceit in signs and not in the things signified, in those who make the promises and not in the promises themselves, they remained—you supplied the understood object: in deceit.

And how did this happen? You cast them down while they were being lifted up, because in that very thing in which they thought they were being raised, they were depressed by a wretched fall.

How were they made desolation? Suddenly they failed and perished because of their iniquity. Asaph, who speaks in this psalm, foreseeing their future desolation—those whose consolations here are earthly—cries out as though grieving for them: How—that is, how miserably and irrecoverably—were they made desolation? For suddenly they failed, although they had promised themselves divine life; and thus they perished because of their iniquity, not because of any injustice on the part of the judging God.

And how will they perish? Like the dream of those who awake: they will be comparable to people dreaming that they possess riches, although they have nothing when they awaken. Thus these people appear happy to themselves while this night remains; but when they have been awakened from the dreams of this carnal life, they will recognize themselves to be poor, and will realize that they possessed temporal riches as though in dreams. This is what he says: “Like the dream of those who awake.”

And you, Lord, in your city will reduce their image—that is, in comparison with your faithful—to nothing, that is, you will utterly destroy it. You will especially destroy the image of those who in their own city destroyed your image by not living rationally and by imitating the image of the earthly man. Therefore you will reduce their image to nothing, but you will rebuild mine, because my heart has been inflamed—understand: with desire for you. My carnal desires have been changed into spiritual delight; and I have been reduced to nothing, so that I might magnify you in myself. And I did not know—that is, if at some point I sinned, I did so ignorantly after the change of carnal delight.

And again I became like a beast before you, namely, a gentle animal suited to carrying your light burden; and thus I shall always be with you. And this was not through my merit, but you held my right hand—that is, you aided my power so that it might be on the right hand, acquiring better things, namely, heavenly things and not earthly things. For by the right hand heavenly things are understood, and by the left earthly things. Hence the saying in the Song of Songs: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song II). Some books read “the hand of the right hand,” but the meaning is the same.

And in your will—that is, in your good pleasure, not according to my merit—you led me from virtue to virtue; and with glory you received me, who glory in the hope of the resurrection, which has gone before in you as in the head.

Alternatively: You will reduce their image to nothing. And deservedly so, because by their example my heart was inflamed with desire for earthly things; and my desires—that is, my spiritual delight—were changed and became carnal; and I was reduced to nothing, namely, remaining in the old state, and did not know the things that ought to be known.

But I became like a beast before you, namely, living irrationally and seeking only what pertained to the use of the body. And although I was thus turned away, I was nevertheless always with you, in that I did not agree with those who said that temporal goods should not be sought from you but from another. Thus I somehow earned a place for pardon.

And you held the hand of my right hand, so that I would no longer seek the things pertaining to the left but those understood by the right.

It can still be read in another way: “Suddenly they failed and perished because of their iniquity, like the dream of those who awake.” But you, Lord, destroyed their image—namely, the image of the earthly man, which they imitated—to nothing; you rebuilt it by placing them in your city, that is, within the fellowship of your faithful.

And how do I know this? Because I experienced it in myself: you destroyed in me the image of the earthly man and rebuilt your own image. This is what he says: My heart was inflamed with desire for earthly things, and my desires were changed into carnal desires, and I was reduced to nothing—that is, I was tending toward things that are nothing.

And this was because I did not know the things that ought to have been known. But I became like a beast before you, namely, living irrationally. Yet I was always with you, not believing that anyone other than you was the giver of earthly things. Therefore you held my right hand, so that it would no longer extend itself toward earthly things; you led me in your will, and with glory you received me.

And here is the glory: “What is there for me in heaven?” That is, how great is that which is prepared for me by you in heaven? For “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart” (1 Corinthians II).

And since the glory is so great, what did I, wretched as I was, desire from you upon earth? That is, how insignificant, in comparison with the future glory, was that which I sought from you on earth?

And from where did I have this desire? From the failure of the flesh and of the heart, namely. This is what he says: My flesh failed, both in me and in Adam; and my heart failed, that is, my reason was darkened, so that I did not seek the things that ought to have been sought.

But from now on God will be the rejoicing of my heart; and God will be my portion, and this forever. Others, however, take the world as their portion, and therefore their portion is transitory. And it is necessary, O God, that you be my portion; for those who do not choose this portion will themselves perish. This is what he says: “God is my portion forever.”

And here is why I shall take you, God, as my portion: because those who distance themselves from you—taking the world, namely, and not you, as their portion—will perish. For you have destroyed everyone who commits fornication away from you, namely, by departing from you.

The person who commits fornication is one who worships God for something other than God himself, like those who worship him for earthly advantage. For not every wife loves her husband chastely if she loves him more for his wealth than for himself.

But for me it is good to cling to God. As if he were saying: You destroyed those who commit fornication, but I will not commit fornication, because for me it is good—that is, it seems delightful to me—to despise the world and cling to God.

And how shall I cling to him? In hope, not in possession. “For in hope we were saved” (Romans VIII).

As if he were saying: I wish to place my hope in the Lord God; that is, I wish to cling to him in such a way that I place my hope in him alone. And in that hope and in that love I do not wish to be alone, like those who love the world and, in their incestuous love, do not wish to have companions.

For me it is thus delightful to cling to you, God, that I may proclaim all your proclamations, so that by proclaiming them I may join companions to myself in your love.

And to whom shall I proclaim them? To Zion—that is, to those who are engaged in contemplation of future things. Zion is also a daughter, because such care must be given to them so that they persevere in the chaste love of God as much care must be taken to guard daughters lest they become prostitutes before the time of lawful marriage.

This proclamation must be made at the gates, that is, in the virtues, which are gates to the heavenly life, because the preacher must take care that what he preaches in word he complete in deed. Or “at the gates” means openly: I shall proclaim your proclamations, and not secretly. Hence the saying: “Whoever is ashamed of me before human beings, I will also be ashamed of him before the angels of God. And whoever confesses me before human beings, I will also confess him before my Father” (Luke IX; Matthew X).

Or “at the gates” means in your apostles, confirming by their authority whatever I proclaim in your preaching. Hence elsewhere: “Tell it in his towers” (Psalm XLVII).

# PSALM LXXIII. THE UNDERSTANDING OF ASAPH

“Why, O God, have you rejected us forever? Is your anger enraged against the sheep of your pasture? Remember your congregation, which you possessed from the beginning. You redeemed the staff of your inheritance: Mount Zion, in which you dwelt. Lift up your hands against their prides forever: how greatly the enemy has acted wickedly in the holy place! And those who hated you gloried in the midst of your solemnity. They set up their signs as signs, and they did not understand, as at the exit, at the summit. As in a forest of trees, with axes they cut down its doors together; with axe and hatchet they felled it. They set fire to your sanctuary; on the ground they defiled the tabernacle of your name. Their kindred said together in their heart: ‘Let us cause all the feast days of God to cease from the earth.’ We have not seen our signs; there is now no prophet, and he will no longer know us. How long, O God, will the enemy reproach you? Will the adversary provoke your name forever? Why do you turn away your hand and your right hand from the midst of your bosom forever?

“But God is our king before the ages; he has worked salvation in the midst of the earth. You established the sea by your strength; you crushed the heads of dragons in the waters. You crushed the heads of the dragon; you gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia. You split open springs and torrents; you dried up the rivers of Ethan. The day is yours, and the night is yours; you fashioned the dawn and the sun. You made all the boundaries of the earth; summer and spring—you fashioned them.

“Remember this: the enemy has reproached the Lord, and a foolish people has provoked your name. Do not hand over to beasts the soul that confesses you, and do not forget forever the souls of your poor. Look upon your covenant, because the dark places of the earth are full of dwellings of iniquity. Let not the humble person, having been brought low, depart in confusion; the poor and needy will praise your name.

“Arise, O God; judge your cause. Remember the reproaches against you, those which come from the foolish all day long. Do not forget the voices of your enemies; the pride of those who hate you rises continually.”

## EXPOSITION

Asaph. The Latin interpretation of this name is “gathering” or “assembly”; in Greek, *synagōgē* (“assembly”). By “gathering” may be understood both an assembly of human beings and an assembly of animals. But since usage has established that by “Synagogue” we always understand the Jewish people, here too let us designate that same people by Asaph.

Not everyone in that people is to be understood here, but only those who are to be counted among the seed and not numbered among the chaff. They are not sons of Abraham according to the flesh, but those who imitate him according to faith.

To make us understand such people, the word “understanding,” which is joined to Asaph, gives us the indication. For this psalm is the voice of those who received the Old Testament and understood through it that the New Testament would come.

The commandments in these two Testaments are the same, because the commandments “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not steal,” and the others are the same in both Testaments.

But the promises of the two Testaments are different. The promises of the Old Testament are these: the land of Canaan, a fertile land abounding in milk and honey; an earthly kingdom; the subjection of enemies; and the fertility of wives and children. The New Testament, however, promises you a heavenly kingdom, and the subjection of enemies concerning whom it is said: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the powers of darkness” (Ephesians VI).

Thus the promises of the two Testaments are different. But observe that the promises of the Old Testament came first, because first comes the animal, and afterward that which is spiritual. “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly” (1 Corinthians XV). The Old Testament pertains to the image of the earthly man; the New Testament to the image of the heavenly man. Nevertheless, the author of both Testaments is the same.

For the one who promised an earthly kingdom through the Old Testament also promised a heavenly kingdom through the New. But the Old Testament, promising temporal things, came first, because the carnal people had to be led through temporal things so that they might learn to love heavenly things. The temporal things that came first were signs of heavenly things and of the things that promised them.

The earthly kingdom signified the heavenly kingdom; the subjection of external enemies signified the subjection of internal enemies; the variety of sacrifices signified Christ hanging upon the cross for the salvation of human beings.

Why? Because everything signified by those things has been fulfilled, the things that made the promises must cease. Christ has come, long foretold by the prophets. The signs demonstrate that he has come, because there are no prophets, no priesthood, and no anointing. The sacraments have also been changed and made more blessed and more salutary, because the sacraments of the Old Testament promised salvation, whereas the sacraments of the New Testament give salvation.

The wretched Jewish people see all these things fulfilled, and yet they still doubt that Christ has come. They first received temporal goods and considered them of great value. But God, who gave them those goods, did not consider them of great value, because he granted them even to the wicked. He would not have done so if he had considered them of great value, since only the good will receive those true goods.

But the Jewish people, after receiving temporal goods, did not trust in the one who gave them. Fearing that they might lose those goods, they plotted to kill him. For they said: “If we let him go on this way, the Romans will come and take away our place” (John XI). And they killed him, and lost both their place and their nation. They also lost the city in which they killed him, being themselves killed, at the very time when they killed the Lord, so that they might be warned in due time why they were suffering such things.

For at the paschal solemnity, when everyone had gathered to celebrate the feast, they killed the Lord. But while they were assembling for that same celebration, they were besieged by the Roman authorities; many thousands of people were killed, and their city was destroyed.

Thus God, who is just, although not through just people and not through good people, justly avenged himself upon his killers. Asaph laments this destruction in this psalm and distinguishes in this lament true goods from those that are not true, so that each of you may see what things you pass through and what things you should await, what things you should leave behind and to what things you should cling.

And why must one see to what things one should cling? Because if they could cling to earthly things with some excuse, since the divine promises had not yet been revealed to them through the New Testament, we cling to earthly things with far less excuse, since the divine promises have now been revealed to us through the New Testament.

Asaph speaks as follows:

Why, O God, have you rejected us forever? Is your anger inflamed? Note how great is the feeling of one lamenting, and how devout is the supplication of one mourning: he laments things that are still so far in the future as though they were present, thereby showing how devout his affection is toward them. It is as though he said: “God the Father, why—that is, for what reason—have you rejected us? Why—that is, for what benefit to us was that rejection? You rejected us forever,” that is, with complete rejection; or, “You rejected us by directing us toward the end”—toward you, who are the end of all goodness and righteousness. And “why is your anger inflamed,” that is, for what purpose has your anger been increased against the sheep of your pasture, whom you cherished and nourished? This is because we clung to earthly things and did not recognize you as shepherd.

“Remember your congregation.” It is as though he said: “If this had to be done with the chaff, nevertheless the grains must be preserved. And in order that you may preserve them, remember your congregation”—which you preserved, as it were, like grains among the chaff; which you possessed from the beginning, that is, from the time of the first righteous man, namely Abel, because from that time onward there never ceased to be among that people those who were to be counted among the seed. Or “from the beginning,” that is, from the time when Abraham was led out of Ur of the Chaldeans; or from the time of Moses and Aaron.

Remember your congregation. And you ought to remember it because you redeemed from Egyptian slavery “the rod of your inheritance,” that is, so that it might rightly be your inheritance, measured out as though by a rod. And what is that inheritance? Mount Zion, that is, the Jewish people, in which you possess an inheritance, so that you might be present in it, since signs were often seen among them such that you appeared to be present.

Or in this way: “You redeemed the rod of your inheritance,” that is, you redeemed the inheritance itself by the sign of your rod; or, you redeemed the inheritance itself so that through it you might perform many signs, just as he worked through Moses’ rod. For it is written (Exod. IV) that Moses asked the Lord for a sign, so that Pharaoh and the Israelite people might believe him. The Lord commanded him to throw upon the ground the rod that he held in his hand. The rod was thrown down and changed into a serpent; but Moses fled, terrified by fear. Then, at the Lord’s command, he returned, seized the serpent by its tail, and the rod recovered its former shape.

Let us consider the mystery of this event. The rod in the serpent was Christ in death. For death can properly be signified by the serpent, because the serpent was the cause of the first death: at its persuasion Adam fell into death. Moses’ flight signifies the fear and doubt that the disciples had at the Lord’s death. For those who said, “We thought that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke XXIV), in a certain sense despaired at the Lord’s death and had already withdrawn from him in mind.

Moses seized the serpent by the tail, and the rod was restored. What was intended to be understood by this? The tail of the serpent signifies Christ’s latter things, namely, his resurrection and ascension. When the disciples reached these two things in mind and believed them in their hearts, the serpent was changed back into a rod, because the one whose death had caused them despair they afterward worshiped alive. Thomas, who had previously doubted, placed his hand in his side and said: “My Lord and my God” (John XX).

The serpent’s tail can also signify the latter days of the Church. For if anyone looks to the Church’s latter days, he will not doubt that he can reach it, although previously he may have abhorred it as though it were a serpent and dead. Thus, the rod in the serpent signifies Christ in death, and the Church in peril during tribulation.

Elsewhere also Christ is signified by the serpent. It is written that the Israelite people suffered much in the desert from serpents, and many of them died from the serpents’ bites. To bring this plague to an end, the Lord commanded Moses to make a bronze serpent and set it high upon wood, so that anyone who had been wounded by the serpents might look at that serpent and thereby be healed. The command of the Lord was fulfilled, and many were healed (Num. XXI).

Three things are noted in this serpent: that it was bronze, that it bore the image of a serpent, and that it was dead. Through the bronze, because it is more durable than every metal, the divinity of Christ is signified. The image of a serpent signifies Christ in the likeness of sinful flesh, and not in sinful flesh. The dead serpent signifies Christ’s death; whoever looks upon it in faith and in action—namely, by imitating it—is healed from every bite of the serpents, that is, from every assault of demons.

“Lift up your hands against their pride forever.” It is as though he said: “Remember your congregation; and in order that you may remember it, lift up your hands”—that is, exercise your power—“against their pride,” that is, against the pride of the Romans, directing them toward you, the end; or “forever,” that is, with a final lifting, lift your hands against them.

And this is necessary because “the enemy,” that is, the Roman people, acted with great wickedness in the holy place—understand, your holy place—by destroying it. Hence he says: “How greatly the enemy has acted wickedly in the holy place!” And to such an extent “those who hate you gloried”—namely, the Gentiles, who are especially said to hate you because they never received knowledge of you.

And where did they glory? “In the midst of your solemnity,” that is, in the place where your solemnity ought to have taken place. Note that the Jews, gathered for the Paschal solemnity, perished at the hands of the Romans. They deserved to perish at that time because at the same solemnity they had killed Christ. Hence he says: “Those who hate you gloried in the midst of your solemnity.” And see how: “They set up signs”—military signs, understand—“their signs,” I say. These signs may be understood as the eagles, dragons, and other devices that the Roman armies customarily used in battle; or “their signs,” namely, the imaginary signs of their gods, from whom perhaps they had received an answer that they would obtain victory.

They placed these signs “above the summit,” that is, above the summit of the Temple, as is customarily done at the exits of roads. For it was the ancient custom, after a victory had been won, to place signs at the exits of roads, so that they might be a memorial of the victory. Such signs as were customarily placed at the exits they placed upon the Temple. And they did not understand that this had come about not by their own will but by divine ordinance: they did not understand that they were instruments of the one who was angry, rather than the kingdom of the one who was appeased.

For God often does what human beings frequently do: they gather some sort of twig and use it to correct their children; when the children have been corrected, they throw the twig into the fire but preserve the inheritance for the children. So God tests the godly through the wicked, and frequently exercises the discipline of those who are to be saved through the temporal power of those who are to be condemned.

Or in this way: “They set up signs,” I say, “their own,” that is, signs of their victory; “and they did not understand as it was at the exit above the summit,” that is, they did not understand that this had proceeded from the summit—from the Father’s disposition—and not from an answer of their gods.

The preceding passage may be read otherwise: “How greatly the enemy has acted wickedly in the holy place!” And deservedly so, because “those who hate you”—namely, the Jews—“gloried in the midst of your solemnity,” because, when they ought to have celebrated your solemnity, they were not afraid to kill you.

“How greatly the enemy has acted wickedly in the holy place,” because “they set up their signs,” signs, “and they did not understand as at the exit above the summit.” And they not only did this, but also “cut down its doors”—understand, the Temple’s doors—“with axes, as though it were a forest of trees,” that is, they cut into the Temple’s doors as irreverently as they would cut into a forest of trees.

A forest of trees is a place where useful trees for building are not found, but only wood fit to be burned in fire. Hence he says: “With axes they cut down its doors in the same place,” that is, agreeing in the same intention; “with axe and hatchet they cast it down,” namely, the city itself. By the axe and the hatchet are signified every kind of instrument that the Romans used in the city’s destruction.

“They burned your sanctuary with fire”—a sanctuary, I say, built only upon that land. “They polluted the dwelling-place of your name,” because in the dwelling-place consecrated to your name they made a stable for horses. “And they said,” that is, they determined in their hearts—and all their kindred agreed with them in saying this: “Let us cause all the feast-days of God to cease from the land,” namely, by expelling all those who keep sabbath in his name. And we suffer this deservedly because “we have not seen our signs.”

Here Asaph shows that the Jews deserved to suffer such things because they did not wish to recognize that the signs announcing what had been promised had been fulfilled. He says this as follows: “We have not seen our signs.” We have indeed seen them. For “there is now no prophet”—which is a sign to us that he has come, since it was prophesied: “When the Holy of Holies comes, anointing will cease” (Dan. IX).

“And he will no longer know us.” It is as though he said: “It must be said that he will not come again.” He will indeed come, but he will not come in the manner in which he came before. He came gentle; he will come terrifying. He came to be judged; he will come to judge. He came, and you stumbled over him lying there; beware of him coming from above.

“How long, O God, will the enemy reproach?” Asaph, understanding and seeing the Jews thus oppressed by the Roman rulers, speaks as though grieving with them: “God the Father, how long”—that is, for how long—“will the enemy reproach your people? And how long will the adversary”—that is, the Gentile people—“provoke your name, this name which is ‘God’?”

“Will this be forever? And why do you turn away your hand and your right hand”—that is, the Jewish people, which was your hand, and not just any hand but your right hand, because through it you performed many signs in great strength? “How long will you turn him away from the midst of your bosom”—that is, from the firm fellowship of your people? “Will this be forever,” that is, with complete rejection? Or, “you turn them away by directing them toward you, the end.”

Here note the story of Moses (Exod. IV), when he withdrew his hand from his bosom and it became full of leprosy. He put it back again at the Lord’s command, and it recovered a color like that of the rest of the flesh. The hand withdrawn from the bosom signifies those who have been separated from the fellowship of the faithful as lepers, that is, contaminated by the stains of sins. But when they return to the fellowship of the faithful, they are cleansed from sins; this is signified by the hand returned to the bosom.

What he says here—“Why do you turn your hand and your right hand away from the midst of your bosom forever?”—is as though he said: “Do not permit your hand to be withdrawn from your bosom, but allow it to be put back, recover the color of the flesh, and recognize the Creator.”

Or otherwise: “They burned your sanctuary with fire; they polluted your dwelling-place upon the land.” And deservedly have the Jews suffered this, because “their kindred”—that is, those who agreed with them—“said,” that is, determined in their hearts: “Let us cause all the feast-days of God to cease from the land.” As if he said: “Let there henceforth be no one among us who celebrates a feast for God and keeps the Sabbath.” And this was because “we have not seen our signs,” by which we might understand that he cares for us.

“There is now no prophet to console us in our affliction; therefore he will no longer know us, because he will not come again to deliver us. For the prophetic words that announced that he would come for our salvation are useless.”

“How long, O God, will the enemy reproach?” Asaph spoke the two preceding verses in the voice of the Jews; now he again takes up his own voice. It is as though he said: “The Jews say that Christ has not come. But you, God, how long will the enemy reproach you—that is, how long will he remain unrecognized by the enemy, namely, the Jewish people? Since it is certain that the Holy of Holies has come, how long will the adversary provoke your name—that is, how long will you permit the Jewish people to treat your name, namely the Christian name, as void and attack it as though it were worthless?”

“And why do you turn away your hand?” Behold, he again laments the persecution of the Jews. It is as though he said: “You, God, even if you reject the chaff from your people, why do you turn away your hand and your right hand—that is, why do you reject those who are to become your hand, namely, the grains preserved among the chaff—from the midst of your bosom, that is, from your protection? And will this be forever, that is, with final rejection? Or do you turn them toward yourself, directing them toward the end?”

“But God is our King from before the ages.” It is as though he said: “We doubted that Christ had come. But God is our King from before the ages”—understand, existing from before the ages—“who worked salvation, a firm faith in himself, in the midst of the earth,” that is, in the midst of the Gentiles, who until now were like cultivated earth while we were like heaven. Now, however, the Gentiles are heaven and we are earth. They are watchful because they have received salvation, believing that Christ has come; we have remained standing because we still doubt that he has come.

Or in this way: “God is our King,” that is, the one who assumed our nature; “he worked salvation before the ages,” predestined by the Father.

And how did he work salvation? Because you, God, “established the sea by your strength,” that is, in your steadfastness—the sea, namely, the bitterness of the Gentiles, who have always existed against you. “You crushed the heads of dragons in the waters,” that is, in the waters of baptism you crushed the pride of evil spirits.

This was prefigured when you caused the Red Sea to stand still, so that you might make the Israelite people cross over on dry ground and drown the rulers in that same sea (Exod. XXIII). Note that the sea stood still while the Israelite people were in motion. By the sea that stood still let us understand the Gentiles, steadfast in faith. The Jews, however, were walking, because, still doubting the faith, they cling to earthly movements.

“You crushed the heads of the dragon,” that is, the pride of the prince of dragons himself. This was prefigured in the head of the calf crushed by Moses (Exod. XXXII).

“You gave him”—that is, the dragon itself according to its body—“as food,” that is, as nourishment, “to the peoples of Ethiopia,” namely, to those of whom it was said: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. V). They were once Ethiopians, that is, blackened, but now they are most radiant. For you so established them that they became the holy apostles, to whom the members of the dragon were nourishment, because they incorporated them into themselves according to faith. Hence it was said to Peter: “Kill and eat” (Acts X).

This kind of food was prefigured when Moses reduced the calf worshiped by the Israelite people to powder and gave it to them mixed with water to drink (Exod. XXXII). That calf reduced to powder signifies unbelievers who, being kindled by the fire of divine love, burn away their pride and self-exaltation by humbly confessing; thus, sprinkled with the water of baptism, they are incorporated into the faithful.

Or otherwise: “You gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia,” because the persecutions of unbelievers were like food and nourishment to the faithful.

“You tore apart springs and torrents.” It is as though he said: “You established the sea, you crushed the heads, and you did this in the following way: you tore apart the springs”—that is, your apostles, in whom were springs of water welling up into eternal life—and led them through various channels.

You also tore apart torrents. Torrents are those who contradict God by their deeds, yet administer to others the word of preaching. This is by comparison, because a torrent is water descending violently from some mountain and quickly failing. So these men flow with the violence of their mouths, yet in their deeds they are dry; nevertheless, through them the Lord works the salvation of his own.

Hence the Gospel says: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat. Therefore, whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not act according to their works” (Matt. XXIII).

“You dried up the rivers of Ethan.” Ethan is interpreted as “strong” or “robust.” By this are understood philosophers and worldly men, puffed up and presuming upon themselves. The Lord dried up their rivers because he reduced their swollen power and empty teaching to nothing.

For the Lord dried up inflated power like Pilate’s swollen bladder when he said to him: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John XIX). Through his own servants he also destroyed many teachings of heretics and the empty exaltation of worldly people. Hence Paul says: “He chose the foolish and the ignoble to confound the wise and noble of the world” (I Cor. I).

“Yours is the day, and yours is the night.” It is as though he said: “Truly you tore apart the springs, because yours is the day,” that is, those who are perfected by you possess perfection itself from you. The day consists of those who devote themselves to higher things and preach them to others; the night consists of those who move within the historical and moral sense while instructing others.

Hence the saying: “Day pours forth the word to day, and night declares knowledge to night” (Ps. XVIII).

It may also be that the same person is both night and day, as Paul was both day and night. He was day when he said: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (I Cor. II); he was night when he said: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (I Cor. III).

“Yours is the day, and yours is the night”; and deservedly so, because “you fashioned the dawn and the sun.” The dawn consists of those beginning already to shine in virtues; the sun consists of those who illuminate others. Or the dawn may mean those who are wise according to the flesh, and the sun those who are spiritual.

“You made all the boundaries of the earth.” The boundaries of the earth are perfect preachers, who establish for others what must be pursued and what must be avoided. Or the boundaries of the earth are those who, through their particular gift of the Holy Spirit, have been bounded off and distinguished from others. Hence the saying: “Each one has his own gift from God” (I Cor. VII).

“You fashioned summer and spring.” By summer are understood those who burn with the Spirit, and by spring those who blossom with virtues. Or by summer are understood those gathering fruit, and by spring those beginning to act well. He says: “You fashioned summer and spring”—not that they fashioned themselves. Hence the saying: “It is God’s gift, not from works, so that no one may boast” (Eph. II).

“Remember this: the enemy has reproached the Lord.” Asaph, seeing that all these things had been done for the salvation of the Gentiles, and understanding that God had done many things in the wild olive grafted in, asks that he perform these same things in the natural olive, whose branches have been broken off.

It is as though he said: “You, Lord, fashioned summer and spring,” that is, you made those among the Gentiles who burn with the Spirit and are simple in faith. “Remember this”—understand, the creation you accomplished among the Gentiles—“so that you may do the same in the Jewish people,” namely, among the grains and not among the chaff.

And why do I say “not among the chaff”? Because “the enemy”—that is, the chaff from that people—“reproached the Lord,” saying: “We know that this man is a sinner” (John IX). And the foolish people provoked your name in this way: “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross” (Matt. XXVII); and: “Depart from us; we do not desire the knowledge of your ways” (Job XXI).

Remember this; and in order that you may remember it, “do not deliver to beasts the souls confessing you,” that is, do not allow the souls of those who humbly confess you to be made like beasts, namely, like those who live bestially—like those who said: “What shall we do, brothers?” (Acts II).

“And do not forget forever the souls of your poor,” namely, those desiring only eternal things. But “look upon your covenant,” that is, your promise, and no longer upon ours: upon the promises of the New Testament, not upon those of the Old.

For the New Testament makes this promise: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII); and: “I will love him and reveal myself to him” (John XIV). Look upon this covenant, so that you may preserve an inheritance for those who have received the tablets—namely, for the grains and not for the chaff.

And why not for the chaff? Because “those who are darkened, [as] houses of earth, have been filled with iniquity,” that is, those who have made their heart a house of earth, so that only earthly things may be stored there and not spiritual things. Hence elsewhere: “They will enter into the lower parts of the earth” (Ps. LXII).

“Let not the humble one be turned away,” that is, the one who humbly confesses his sins, having become confounded, if he is turned away.

“The poor and needy”—namely, those desiring only eternal things—“will praise your name.” And in order that they may praise it, “arise, O God, judge your cause,” that is, the cause of your own, so that the cause for which they despise the present and await the future may not appear to be in vain.

“Remember your reproaches”—namely, those spoken by the foolish person all day long. The foolish are those who do not know how to guard themselves for the future. From them comes the reproach against the faithful that they await future things and despise the present.

Remember this kind of reproach in this way: “Do not forget, in your judgment, the voices of your enemies,” so that the enemies themselves may receive from you what they deserve on account of it. “The pride of those who hate you always ascends,” that is, their pride is always increased against you. Their pride ascends against you; may your vengeance ascend against them.

# PSALM LXXIV. FOR THE END: “DO NOT DESTROY.” A PSALM OF SONG, OF ASAPH.

“ We will confess to you, O God; we will confess, and we will call upon your name. We will recount your wonders. When I receive the appointed time, I will judge righteous judgments. The earth melted, and all who dwell in it; I established its pillars. I said to the wicked: Do not act wickedly; and to the transgressors: Do not lift up your horn. Do not raise your horn on high; do not speak iniquity against God. For judgment comes neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains, because God is judge. He humbles one and exalts another, because there is a cup in the hand of the Lord, full of unmixed wine mixed. He has poured it from this vessel into that; nevertheless its dregs have not been emptied. All the sinners of the earth will drink. But I will proclaim forever; I will sing to the God of Jacob. And I will break all the horns of sinners, and the horns of the righteous will be exalted.”

## EXPOSITION

This psalm brings the medicine of humility to the swelling of pride. It does this so that no proud person may presume upon himself and no humble person may despair of God, because his promise is certain, ratified, firm, and entirely free from doubt; it consoles the afflicted.

And why the afflicted? Because human life upon earth is nothing but affliction. Hence Job says: “The life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job VII).

Yet one should not choose a prosperous life so greatly or avoid an adverse one, but both must be guarded against: the former, lest it break us; the latter, lest it corrupt us. Thus, whatever the condition in which a person lives, he should have no refreshment except God and no joy except in his promises.

For this life deceives everyone by overflowing with happiness. God deceives no one, because he is truthful in his promises. And we regard as the most faithful promisor the one who, by promising, made himself a debtor.

But because the riches of a person turned toward God must be changed, and his pleasures must be changed but not removed—for our pleasure is found not in possession but in hope—this psalm works to give us a certain hope, so that we may be led into what we hope for. For one whose pleasure is entirely in hope is not deceived.

Hence the saying: “Delight in the Lord” (Ps. CXXXVI). And lest we seem immediately to possess the object of our delight, it adds: “And he will give you the requests of your heart” (ibid.). How, then, do you delight if you do not possess what you ask, unless you have him as a most faithful debtor, who by promising caused himself to owe?

The title is explained: “Do not destroy.” What does “do not destroy” mean? Display what you promised—true faith and hope—straining toward the end, that is, toward Christ, in hope, and not toward the world in possession. For those who possess the world in reality and not Christ in hope will at last possess neither in reality nor in hope, when those who are now glorious in hope will be glorious in reality.

“A psalm of song, of Asaph,” that is, one to be held from song. This Asaph appears to signify Christ, because he especially gathered together others among that people and made them conformed to himself. His voice is heard in this psalm exhorting us to confess humbly to God and not proudly presume upon ourselves.

He says as follows:

“We will confess to you, O God; we will confess, and we will call upon your name.” Note that confession comes first and invocation afterward, because the one whom you invoke you call into yourself. God, however, does not come when called into you if you are proud, because he does not approach the exalted but the one who confesses humbly.

Let us therefore make confession, not so that it may delight him, but so that it may cleanse us. Let us cleanse our temple through confession, in which he will come when invoked.

To reach all high things, we raise and lift ourselves up; and if we are not sufficient, we seek machines and ladders by which to reach them. God is high, but he is not reached from a height; for he is near only to those who have crushed their heart.

The crushing of the heart is piety and humility. The one who crushes his heart is angry with himself. Therefore let each of you make yourself angry, so that you may feel him appeased; make yourself your accuser, so that you may find him your defender. By confessing, make him favorable to you; by denying, you do not make him unaware. Confess so that he may turn his face away from your sins and not from you; let him turn away from what you have done, not from the one whom he made.

He made the human being; you made the sinner. He is also powerful enough to turn your face away from the one sinning and not away from one who confesses humbly. Hence the saying: “The Lord is exalted, and he regards the humble, but he knows the exalted from afar” (Ps. CXXXVII). He regards the humble through the remission of sins; he knows the proud through just condemnation.

Why should we confess? So that we may invoke him, as it says: “We will confess to you, O God; we will confess, and we will call upon your name.”

Note that this repetition was not made for the sake of verbosity but for the sake of confirmation, so that you may not regret having confessed, since the one to whom you confessed is good. Hence another psalm says: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good” (Ps. CXXXV).

And because he is good, do not be afraid to confess. You are not confessing to one who insults or punishes, but to one who forgives sins. Be afraid to confess to a human judge, who punishes sins after confession; confess securely to God, who forgives after confession.

“And we will call upon your name,” so that we may be filled from you, having been emptied through confession. And he explains from what we are to be filled: “We will recount your wonders.”

It is as though he said: “I and those who are mine will recount your wonders,” which you wondrously perform in bodies and which you perform wondrously in conduct.

“When I receive the appointed time, I will judge righteous judgments.” It is as though he said: “Once your wonders have been made known, I will especially judge righteous judgments, not sparing the one who despises, though now I grant to the one who confesses.” Thanks be to the one who first wished to announce and preach righteousness before judging. For if he judged before preaching, who would be acquitted? Who would be set free? No one, certainly.

Let us therefore love him as preacher, so that we may await him as judge without fear. He received the time for judging righteousness; we received the time for doing it.

It was said of him: “I will sing mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. C). Therefore, so that we may not fear the punisher of sins, let us love the giver of forgiveness.

“When I receive the appointed time, I will judge righteousness.” Who received the time for judging? Not the Son of God, through whom we were made, but the Son of Man, through whom we were restored—not the one who assumed, but the one who was assumed.

For the one who was assumed was changed for the better; the one who assumed was not changed for the worse. He emptied himself (Phil. II) by assuming the lower nature, not by degenerating from one equal to himself; he assumed what he was not while remaining what he was. He did not receive that time for judging from anyone, but always possessed it.

“The earth melted, and all who dwell in it.” It is as though he said: “I will deservedly judge righteousness, because the earth”—that is, the Jewish people, which ought to have been earth for others, through whom they might be refreshed—“melted away,” flowing somewhere, that is, it departed from liquid and true commandments through desire. For the more someone delights in what is lower through desire, the farther he departs from the Creator; and the more he delights in what is higher, the nearer he is understood to be.

“And all who dwell in it,” that is, not Judaea alone melted away, but all those who ought to have dwelt in it by taking from it an example of good works.

“But I established its pillars,” that is, the apostles who accompanied me in my passion; I established them in the resurrection. The apostles are called pillars because others—Jews and the rest—were supported and upheld by them, lest they fall.

The passage may be continued in this way: “When I receive the appointed time, I will judge righteousness.” And meanwhile, what happens? “The earth melted, and all who dwell in it; but I established its pillars.” And through those pillars I said to the wicked: “Do not act wickedly.”

He did indeed say this, but we did not listen. And because we did not listen to him so that we might stand sound, let us listen to him at least so that, having fallen, we may rise again. And because we are not sound, let us listen to the physician coming to the sick.

“And to the transgressors: Do not lift up your horn.” It is as though he said: “I told those who were acting wickedly not to do so; but to those who did not withdraw from transgression I said: ‘Do not lift up your horn.’”

It is as though he said: “If you sin through desire, do not defend your sin through pride. Do not, I say, raise your horn on high,” that is, do not strengthen your opposition against God by rejecting God’s yoke. “Do not speak iniquity against God,” namely, by declaring him unjust and saying that he does not care for human affairs.

A person speaks iniquity when he sees the wicked flourishing and the good suffering and says that God does not govern human affairs. This is what is forbidden here: “Do not speak iniquity against God.”

Hence elsewhere: “Do not incline my heart toward words of wickedness” (Ps. CXL).

“For judgment comes neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains, because God is judge.” It is as though he said: “Do not speak iniquity against God, because the judge who will judge us will come neither only from the east, nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains. For it is God who judges, and therefore he is necessarily present everywhere.”

“And he humbles this one”—namely, the Jewish people, exalting themselves and presuming upon themselves—“and he exalts this one,” that is, the Gentile people, humbling themselves. This was represented by the publican and the Pharisee: the publican humbled himself and was exalted; the Pharisee exalted himself and was humbled (Luke XVIII). Hence it says: “He humbles one and exalts another.”

And why? “Because there is a cup in the hand of the Lord, full of unmixed wine mixed,” that is, he is comparable to a powerful cupbearer who pours sweet wine from a cup for his friends and sour wine for his enemies.

It says that the cup—namely, recompense—is in the hand of the Lord. The cup, I say, is full of unmixed wine, namely, just recompense, because he will judge with complete justice. But he will repay each person according to the equality of his merits. It is also full of mixture, because the good will drink sweet wine from it and the wicked sour wine. Nevertheless, with respect to the Lord himself, it is unmixed, however much it may be poured.

“And he poured it from this into that,” understand, from this vessel into that one that is to drink; or from this vessel of the good into that of the wicked.

“Nevertheless, its dregs have not been emptied,” that is, they have not been poured out from it, because there are no dregs there, but unmixed wine, however much it may be tilted.

And lest we think that sinners have nothing there to drink because it lacks dregs, he adds: “All the sinners of the earth will drink,” according to their due measure. They will drink what is sour, although it is unmixed.

“But I and those who are mine will not drink in this way, because I will proclaim forever,” building up others; “and I will sing to the God of Jacob,” namely, as he ought to be sung.

Or otherwise: “He humbles one and exalts another.” And how does he do this? Because in the hand of the Lord is the cup—the law that refreshes and gives drink. The cup, I say, is full of unmixed wine, that is, of pure commandments; it is also full of mixture, that is, of carnal sacraments, in which the New Testament lies hidden as though in dregs.

“And he poured the cup from this into that,” that is, from the knowledge of the Jewish people into the knowledge of the Gentiles. Yet “its dregs have not been emptied,” that is, they have not been poured out from it but have settled at the bottom, because the carnal sacraments remained with the Jews.

“All the sinners of the earth will drink” from this cup: some the unmixed wine, others the dregs. The Jews who remained in the carnal sacraments drink the dregs.

“But I will proclaim” the unmixed wine to be drunk, and this forever. Thus I will sing to the God of Jacob. “And I will break all the horns of sinners,” namely, the pride of those presuming upon their own righteousness.

“And the horns of the righteous will be exalted.” The horns of the righteous are piety, humility, and the other virtues. The horns of sinners are self-exaltation and pride, which will ultimately be broken by the Lord.

Let us therefore break our horns, lest they be broken by the Lord. If God has not said, “Do not act wickedly,” let us make ready pride and self-defense; but if he has said it, let us forestall confession, because then confession will be too late and defense will be of no avail.

# PSALM LXXV. FOR THE END, WITH STRINGED INSTRUMENTS. A SONG FOR THE ASSYRIANS. A PSALM OF ASAPH.

[Col. 0536A]

“God is known in Judaea; in Israel his name is great. And his place has become established in peace, and his dwelling-place in Zion. There he broke the powers of bows, shield, sword, and war. You illuminate wondrously from the everlasting mountains; all the foolish in heart were troubled. They slept their sleep, and all the men of wealth found nothing in their hands. At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, those who mounted horses fell into slumber. You are terrifying, and who will resist you? From that time onward, your anger. From heaven you caused judgment to be heard; the earth trembled and became still. When God arose for judgment, to save all the meek of the earth. For the thought of man will confess to you, and the remnant of thought will keep feast for you. Vow and repay to the Lord your God, all you who bring offerings around him, to the terrifying one, and to him who removes the breath of princes, the terrifying one among the kings of the earth.”

## EXPOSITION
The Assyrians are interpreted as “those who direct,” because among that people there were many who directed themselves according to carnal rites, understanding according to the letter and not according to the spirit. Against such people Asaph speaks in this psalm, setting his feet on the way of salvation by confessing humbly, and thus making himself a man of peace, in whom God dwells. He says as follows:

[Col. 0536C]

“God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel.”

Jews commonly boast when they hear this verse, as though the prophet were saying only of the prophet, “God is known in Judah.” But so that we may not understand this as referring only to the Jews, let us adhere to the interpretation of the name, so that we may understand of whom the psalm speaks. “Judah” is interpreted as “confession.” Yet confession belongs not only to the Jews but also to the Gentiles who belong to God. To all of them the prophet says: “God is known in Judah, and his name is great”—not a name of disgrace, namely “man,” which is derived from *humus*, “earth,” but that name which is “God,” known in Israel, that is, among those who see God. For they understand concerning the needy and the poor.

Observe that he says, “God is known in Judah.” For here he does not mean one who is a Jew openly, but one who is a Jew secretly; not one who is circumcised in the foreskin, but one who is circumcised in the heart. This is what he says: “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel.”

And thus his place, namely God’s place, has come to be in peace: in peace, that is, in those who have made peace within themselves, having concord with holy conduct and conflict with vices. For as long as a human being groans in this tabernacle, it cannot be that the tinder of sin does not trouble him. Yet he must not consent to it. If it rises up, he must make it such that it does not find in him the weapons of iniquity with which to stretch out its hand against his neighbor. Or, if other unlawful impulses arise, they must not find instruments of iniquity. Hence Paul says: “Sin is in our mortal body, but let it not reign” (Rom. VI).

[Col. 0537A]

Observe here the good order. Whoever in Judah—that is, through confession of sins—receives remission must first be such that he may deserve to see God, now through faith and afterward according to hope. And thus, after being a Jew and an Israelite, it remains that he become a Jerusalemite, so that he may have peace with God. For as long as anyone disdains to confess, he quarrels with God, as it were, through pride. As long as what pleases us displeases God, we quarrel with him. Drunkenness displeases him, but pleases us; theft displeases him, but we praise the thief; novelty pleases him, but antiquity pleases us. Thus we have driven ourselves away from the image in which we were created.

But whenever what pleases him begins to please us, we cease quarreling and make peace with him by restoring ourselves to his image. This is what he says: “And his place has come to be in peace.” Finally, his dwelling is in Zion, that is, in true contemplations—not in those who contemplate the things that are seen, but the things that are not seen.

And there, that is, in Zion and in true Judah, “he broke the powers of the bows,” that is, hidden ambushes; “the shield,” that is, the protection of empty presumption; “and the sword,” that is, open attacks; “and war,” namely the defense of sin. For no war displeases God more than the defense of sin.

“He broke the powers of the bows.” And how did he do this? Because you, O God, will be “illuminating wonderfully from the everlasting mountains,” that is, you will illuminate others through your apostles, who are called mountains because the true light first shone upon them and through them descended into the valleys. And this happened wonderfully, namely with signs and miracles following.

And all the foolish in heart were and will be troubled, because when they hear, “Do not put your confidence in the uncertainty of riches” (I Tim. VI), they will be troubled, like those who said, “Who is this preacher of new demons?” (Acts XVII). And why will they be troubled? Because “they slept their sleep,” that is, they took delight in earthly things, which nevertheless they possessed only as though in a dream, since temporal things are nothing.

If you do not believe, you are asleep. You will awaken and see that they are nothing. This is what he means by “they slept their sleep”: blinded by earthly things, they became like those sleeping on straw and dreaming that they were lying on mattresses and covered with a cloak. When they are awakened, they see that what they dreamed was nothing. So those who in this night of the flesh cling to earthly things will at last understand that earthly things are nothing, and they will grieve that they clung to them.

This is what he says: “And all the men of riches found nothing in their hands,” that is, in the end they were found to possess nothing. From all their riches they found nothing in the hand of the one who repays, except what is placed here in the hand of the poor. Therefore, since he wishes to have full hands there, let him attend here to the empty hand of the poor.

“At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, those who mounted horses fell asleep.” It is as though he said: They will find nothing at last because, when they ought to have been awakened by your rebuke—that is, by your preaching, O God of Jacob—paying attention to future things, they fell asleep. That is, they stopped their ears to earthly things. Thus the cry that usually awakens others caused them to close their ears. For the more frequently they were warned to abandon earthly things, the sweeter it was for them to cling to them.

And this happened because they mounted the horses of pride, presuming upon secular rank, the nobility of their ancestors, and the other things belonging to the world. Therefore you, Lord, who illuminate from the everlasting mountains, are terrifying—understand, “you will be terrifying”—when you come in the majesty of the Father, terrifying to the wicked but gentle to the just. And then who will resist you? No one, certainly, because from that time onward your wrath will be everlasting, whereas now there is also mercy. Therefore whoever wishes to be secure in the time of wrath should act well in the time of mercy.

And how will your wrath come? “Because you made judgment heard from heaven,” namely through the trumpet of the angels. Hence the saying: “For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible” (I Cor. XV). Thus “the earth trembled and was quiet”: earthly people will tremble and will be quiet, because afterward the unbelievers will have no place to rage, since they will be in everlasting fire.

And when will this happen? “When God rises for judgment,” that is, when he comes manifestly to judge the wicked. And he will not rise only for judgment, but will also rise for this purpose: “to save all the meek of the earth.” Of these it is said: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. V).

Or, alternatively: “All the men of riches found nothing in their hands.” And why did this happen? Because the first parents, who mounted the horses of apostasy in order to depart from the truth, fell asleep—that is, they were blinded—and this occurred at your rebuke.

O God, judge those who mounted them with a just judgment, because those who disdained to keep your obedience were justly blinded. And you, O illuminating God, are terrifying, and who can resist you? No one, certainly. The first man resisted you to his own detriment, because from that time your wrath began—understand, “your wrath began”—and it will be still greater in the future, because you will make your judgment heard from heaven, that is, you will manifest the judgment through the angelic trumpet.

Then “the earth trembled and was quiet,” when God rose for judgment in order to save all the meek of the earth. The meaning is the same as before.

Or thus: From that time your wrath existed, although it will be greater in the future. And how do we know this? Because you made the judgment—that is, the future wrath—heard, that is, manifest, from heaven, that is, from the Lord’s human being or from each heaven, that is, from your preacher.

Of this judgment Paul says: “At the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with the angels of his power, giving vengeance in flaming fire to those who did not wish to know God and who do not obey the gospel of his truth” (II Thess. I).

Once this judgment had been made manifest, “the earth trembled,” that is, earthly people trembled, “and was quiet,” that is, they ceased to act perversely. Hence the saying: “Cease to act perversely; learn to do good” (Isa. I).

And when did the earth tremble? When God rose for judgment, that is, when they heard from the preachers that the Lord had risen and would come to judgment. For he rose for this purpose: that he might come as judge. He wished to be judged in gentleness so that he might come to judge in terror. This is what he says: “When God rose for judgment.”

And it was not merely made known to them that God would rise for judgment, but also that he would rise “to save all the meek of the earth.”

And deservedly, Lord, you save the meek of the earth, because they do what pleases you. “For the thought of the human being”—namely, of one who lives rationally—“will confess to you, and the remnants of thought will keep a feast for you,” because they act well not from sadness but with gladness. That joy will be for God.

Observe that the first thought of a human being ought to be in faithful confession. Afterward come the remnants of thought, so that he may always be concerned about the past and cautious about the future. For the more concerned he is about the past, the more cautious he will be about the future. Indeed, someone who is negligent concerning the past may happen to sin again.

“Vow and repay to the Lord your God.” It is as though he said: In order that you may keep a feast, vow yourselves and repay to the Lord your God. For whoever vows must also repay, because by vowing he has made himself a debtor. It is better not to vow than, after making a vow, not to fulfill it.

Hear what ought to be vowed. Whoever considers what good thing he should vow should vow himself and repay himself. This is owed; this is demanded.

There are also certain vows common to human beings and certain special vows. A common vow is that one who used to steal should no longer steal, and that one should abstain from the other vices. This is professed by everyone who is baptized.

Special vows are made when someone vows to become a monk or to undertake something else. This is what he says: “Vow and repay to the Lord your God.”

And this will happen in this way, because “all who are around him,” that is, those who regard him as being in the midst and common to all, “will bring gifts”—namely, themselves. Elsewhere it is said: “The kings of Arabia and Saba shall bring gifts” (Ps. LXXI).

Observe that he says, “those around him will bring gifts.” Those who do not believe that he is common to all, saying, “Behold, Christ is among us,” will not bring gifts to him. Only those who are around him will bring gifts.

And to whom will they bring them? “To the Terrible One, and to him who takes away the spirit of princes,” that is, by whose power the pride of earthly princes is brought low. He is also terrifying among all the kings of the earth—among those who rule their earthly nature well—for “the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” (Ps. CX).

## Psalm LXXVI. For the end; for Idithun. A Psalm of Asaph

“My voice cried to the Lord; my voice cried to God, and he attended to me. In the day of my tribulation I sought God with my hands by night before him, and I was not deceived. My soul refused to be consoled. I remembered God, and I rejoiced and exercised myself, and my spirit failed. My eyes anticipated the watches; I was troubled, and I did not speak. I considered the ancient days, and I held the everlasting years in mind. And I meditated by night with my heart, and I was exercised, and I swept my spirit. Will God cast off forever? Or will he not add to this, so that he may be more favorably disposed still? Or will he cut off his mercy forever, from generation to generation? Or will God forget to show mercy? Or will he restrain his mercies in his wrath? And I said: ‘Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High.’ I remembered the works of the Lord, for I will remember your wonders from the beginning. And I will meditate on all your works, and I will exercise myself in your inventions. O God, your way is in the holy place; what god is great as our God? You are the God who works wonders. You have made your power known among the peoples; you redeemed your people with your arm, the sons of Jacob and Joseph. The waters saw you, O God; the waters saw you and were afraid, and the abysses were troubled. The multitude of the sound of the waters: the clouds gave forth their voice. For your arrows pass through; the voice of your thunder is in the wheel. Your flashes enlightened the world; the earth was shaken and trembled. Your way is in the sea, and your paths are in many waters, and your footprints will not be known. You led your people like sheep by the hand of Moses and Aaron.”

## Exposition

In this psalm Asaph speaks as one who leaps across, and by leaping across he urges us to leap across, so that we may reach Christ, who is the end, to which this leaping Asaph has already leapt. What must be leapt across in order that we may reach that end is taught by the very text of the psalm.

Everything that impedes us, everything that entangles us, everything that ensnares us, everything that weighs down our flight, must be leapt across until we reach that beyond which nothing exists, in whom all things are and from whom whatever exists has its being. Therefore whoever wishes to imitate the soul of this psalm—that is, to hold its meaning—must leap across carnal desires and trample the pomp and allure of the world. He must propose to himself nothing in which he may come to rest, except him from whom all things exist. In all these things this leaping one labors in order to reach that end, namely Christ, beyond whom nothing exists, beneath whom all things were made, and from whom all things that exist receive their being.

The title is explained as follows: these words refer to the end, and it is a psalm of Asaph, made for Idithun, that is, for “leaping across.” And he says:

“My voice cried to the Lord; my voice cried to God, and he attended to me.”

As though exhorting others, he says: “Let the one who thirsts come and drink” (John VII). From my own experience, therefore, I must be believed, because I cried to the Lord with my voice—with a voice that was intent, a voice harmonious with the heart—not like that people of whom it was said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX; Matt. XV; Mark VII, 6).

And because many cry very intently to God in order to acquire riches, avoid losses—that is, for the safety and well-being of their household—for temporal happiness, secular rank, and finally bodily health, which is the patrimony of the poor, scarcely anyone cries to the Lord for the sake of deserving the Lord himself, as though what he gives were sweeter than he who gives it, we must not think that this man uttered his voice for the sake of obtaining anything other than God alone. He who willingly sacrificed to God, who leapt across everything, who saw nothing beyond himself except the one by whom he was created, therefore adds:

“With my voice I cried”—understand, “only in order to deserve God”—“and he attended to me,” that is, he gave me attentive help, so that I would not cry in vain. Or, he made my cry attentive. And this happened because I, “in the day of my tribulation”—that is, in this present life, which is called temptation and therefore tribulation—sought God.

Hence the saying: “The life of a human being upon earth is warfare” (Job VII).

I sought God, that is, I sought him outside everything, because I disdained to seek all other things. And I sought him “with my hands,” that is, through my works, by doing what is good.

Observe that many, when they are in tribulations, cry to the Lord not for the sake of the Lord but so that through him they may escape their tribulations. Thus, when someone is imprisoned, he cries to the Lord so that through him he may leave the prison; if he suffers hunger, he cries so that he may have food with which to be refreshed; if he suffers fever, he cries to him so that he may be healed.

But this one who leaps across and cries here does not seek to escape tribulations except so that he may cling securely to God. The tribulations of the faithful are mortality and vulnerability. When they have been freed from these, they cling securely to God, because they see him face to face.

Desiring this, he says here: “In the day of tribulation”—and I call it the day of tribulation, though it is night—“and before him,” that is, in his presence, “I worked well,” and not for human approval.

Hence the saying: “Take care not to perform your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them. When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you, but do it in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. VI).

Observe that the life of the faithful may be called both day and night. It is called day with respect to the life of the faithful. Hence Paul says: “Let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light; let us walk honorably as in the day” (Rom. XIII).

It is called night with respect to the perfection of brightness that exists in the angelic life. Peter confirms this as follows: “We have the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the true sun rises in your hearts” (II Pet. I).

This is what is meant by: “In the day of my tribulation I sought God with my hands by night before him.” And I was not deceived in seeking God, according to what he himself says: “Seek and you will find” (Matt. VII).

And how he was not deceived in seeking God, he adds: “My soul refused to be consoled,” that is, to have consolation, “in earthly things.” Through this I know that I was not deceived in seeking God.

Or the passage may be connected in this way: “In the day of my tribulation I sought God.” And therefore I sought him alone, because “my soul refused to be consoled” in the things that are behind, rejecting human consolation altogether.

Observe that he says: “My soul refused to be consoled.” For he wished to pass beyond everything. He considered his companions flourishing in earthly things, and there he was overcome by grief on account of sinners who abandoned the law of the Lord (Ps. CXVIII). He turned himself toward the right-hand side, but even there it did not seem safe for him to loosen the reins of his joy. For if he loosened them and some adversity occurred, the greater sorrow would follow, the greater the joy that had preceded it. Therefore his soul entirely withdrew from earthly happiness.

This is what he says: “My soul refused to be consoled in the things that are behind, stretching myself toward the things that are before” (Phil. III), because I remembered God alone. And I rejoiced in the fact that I remembered him. And because I exercised myself in instructing others, my spirit failed, that is, my strength failed, when I saw that by myself I could not find anything worthy of saying.

And why did my spirit fail? Because “my eyes anticipated the watches.” That is, I became like a person who keeps watch more than others and, because of the great constancy of his vigils, has dim eyes. My inner eyes were darkened. Therefore I was troubled, finding myself insufficient, and I did not speak, because I feared saying something for which I might be accused and which would provide accusers with material for sinning. Therefore it seemed safer for me to remain silent.

In that very silence I considered the ancient days, that is, I set before myself the days of the ancient parents, to which they came through disobedience. And I kept the everlasting years in mind, that is, the days of eternity to which the first parents would have attained if they had remained obedient. I always kept them in mind, because from their disobedience I perceived that my spirit had failed.

And I meditated on those everlasting years by night, that is, with my rest interrupted; or by night, that is, in the tribulation itself. I meditated with my heart, that is, with complete attention. And this was not for an hour only: I exercised myself in the constant practice of this meditation, and I swept my spirit, that is, I dug up and reshaped my rationality, emptying it of earthly things, so that I might discover what it had begun to investigate.

Or “I swept” means “I leveled” my spirit away from earthly things.

Or I swept my spirit by saying: “Will God cast off his servants forever?” No. Or thus I swept my spirit. And what did you find? This: that the Lord will not be angry with his servants forever. Will he remove his servants, dissolve those who are fettered, and forever shut mercy out through wrath?

Hence Isaiah says: “I will not be avenging forever against you, nor will I be angry with you for all time; for a spirit has gone forth from me, and I myself made all his condition. But because of sin I grieved him for a little while, and I struck him, and I turned my face away from him; and he went away sad and walked in his own ways, and I healed him” (Isa. LVII).

This is what he says: “Will God cast off forever, and will he not add to this so that he may be more favorably disposed?” That is, so that the human being may please him more than he pleases him now. “Or will he cut off his mercy forever, from this present generation to the generation to come? Or will God forget to show mercy? Or will he restrain his mercies in his wrath,” that is, will wrath shut out mercy? No.

And after this inquiry I said: “Now I have begun,” that is, I have begun to investigate by sweeping my spirit. “And this change,” through which I have been changed from ignorance into knowledge, “is the right hand of the Most High,” that is, it must be attributed to divine power and not to my merit.
