But in order that I might attain this change, I remembered the works of the Lord: the ancient ordering, the new restoration, and eternal happiness. And I regarded the memory of this work as your wonders, namely the legal ordinances, which were given for this purpose: to signify the works of the Lord that were to come. Thus I understood the things signified through the things that signify.

And I did not merely remember; I will also meditate, that is, I will think frequently, “on all your works,” how powerful and wondrous you are, who work both the will and its fulfillment according to your good will. “And I will exercise myself in your inventions,” that is, in your commandments, which you devised for the salvation of all, laboring to put them into practice.

Hence the saying: “He found every way of knowledge and discipline and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved” (Baruch III).

“I will meditate on all your works.” And behold your wondrous work: “Your way, O God, is in the holy place,” that is, in Christ.

Hence he himself says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John XIV). And again: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (ibid.).

He is the way by which one passes from slavery into freedom, by which the unchaste becomes chaste, and by which the condemned is taken up into the kingdom.

What god, then, is great like our God? None, certainly, because you are the God who works wonders. Elijah and others worked wonders, but not by themselves, since they worked them with your help. You, however, need the help of no one. You alone work wonders, both outwardly and inwardly.

The blind see, the lame walk, the paralytics are healed, and the dead are raised. You also work wonders inwardly, because those who were drunkards have become sober, those who were unchaste have become chaste, and those who were robbers have become givers.

Alternatively, the preceding passage may be read as follows: “And I said: Now I have begun,” that is, I have begun to search out the spirit by examining it. “And this change”—that God will not cast us off forever, that he has not forgotten to show mercy, and that wrath does not shut out mercy—“is the right hand of the Most High,” that is, it must be attributed to the Son of God, because he is the one who reconciled us to God the Father.

And how do I know this? Because I remembered the works of the Lord, which were signified through the legal ordinances.

Or thus: I swept my spirit and found that God will not cast us off forever and that wrath will not shut out mercy. Having considered all these things, I said—that is, I resolved within myself—“Now,” that is, having discovered all these things, “I have begun,” that is, with respect to the perfection of true knowledge, I am only at the beginning.

Hence the saying: “When a human being has finished, then he will begin” (Eccli. XVIII).

And this change—the fact that I recognize myself as imperfect in all these things and consider myself now only beginning—is “the right hand of the Most High,” that is, the power of God, who is not powerless to avenge himself upon me, namely upon the first parent.

“I remembered the works of the Lord.” It is as though he said: Although, after considering all these things, I am only at the beginning, I will nevertheless not cease searching. I will remember the works of the Lord and your wonders, O God, made from the beginning.

And I will meditate on all your works, and I will exercise myself in your inventions. However much I meditate and however much I exercise myself, I can accomplish nothing by myself. But your way leads me to this, and I must investigate it in the Holy Spirit, through whom I have the power both to begin and to complete.

“What god is great like our God? You are the God who works wonders.”

And what wonders? “You made your power known among the peoples”—namely, Christ.

Hence Paul says: “We preach Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, but to the Gentiles foolishness; but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I).

“You redeemed with your arm,” that is, with your power or in Christ.

Hence the saying: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII).

“You redeemed with your arm the sons of Jacob and Joseph,” namely the people of the Jews and of the Gentiles, by preaching peace to those who were near and to those who were far away, creating the two peoples in one body.

“The waters saw you, O God,” that is, understand this as the Jewish people. They saw you, namely, and feared their past sins. And “the sound of the waters feared,” that is, the deep hearts of the Gentiles; or, their profound interpreters will be troubled into repentance. Thus “the multitude of the sound of the waters” was heard, namely the sound of the confessing and penitent people.

And how did this happen? Because the clouds, of which it was said, “I will command my clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isa. V), gave forth this voice, because “their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. XVIII).

“For your arrows,” that is, the words of your apostles, which attack hearts, “pass through,” because they did not remain in the ear but penetrated as far as the capacity of the heart.

“And the voice of your thunder,” that is, the voice of threatening preaching, “was heard in the wheel,” that is, in the world, which is compared to a wheel because of its roundness or its mobility.

“Your flashes enlightened the world,” that is, your signs appeared to the world.

Hence the saying: “The Lord working with them and confirming the word through the signs that followed” (Mark XVI).

Therefore the earth was shaken—namely, the earth of the Jews—and trembled at the fact that it had lived in this way. From this it happened that “your way was made in the sea,” that is, Christ became known among the Gentiles. And “your paths,” that is, the difficult commandments, “were made known in many waters.” Yet “your footprints,” that is, your signs, “will not be known” by many Jews, although they ought especially to have known them.

For “you led your people like sheep by the hand of Moses and Aaron.”

Observe that he says “like sheep,” because they are not true sheep, since they did not recognize their true shepherd.

Or, alternatively: “The earth was shaken and trembled”—namely the Jewish people, for evil—and therefore “your way was made in the sea.”

Hence the Apostle says: “Because you rejected the word of God, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII).

“And your paths were in many waters.” And how did this happen? Because you led your people, namely the Gentile people, like sheep “by the hand of the true Moses and Aaron.”

Christ is the true Moses, because he was truly taken up; and he is Aaron because he is truly the mountainous one, since he is the mountain of mountains.

Hence the saying: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared on the top of the mountains” (Isa. II).

This is what he says: “You led your people like sheep by the hand of Moses and Aaron.” Yet even now your footprints are not recognized by the Jews.

## Psalm LXXVII. The Understanding of Asaph

“Attend, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth. I will open my mouth in parables; I will speak propositions from the beginning. All the things that we have heard and known, which our fathers told us, were not hidden from their children in the later generation. They told of the praises of the Lord, his powers, and his wonders, which he performed. He raised up a testimony in Jacob and established a law in Israel. How many things he commanded our fathers to make known to their children, so that the later generation might know them: the sons who will be born, who will rise up and tell them to their children. So that they may place their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, and seek out his commandments. Let them not become like their fathers, a crooked and provoking generation; a generation that did not direct its heart, and whose spirit was not faithful with God. The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back on the day of battle. They did not keep the covenant of God, and they refused to walk in his law. They forgot his benefits and his wonders, which he showed them. Before their fathers he performed wonders in the land of Egypt, in the field of Tanis. He divided the sea and led them through it, and he made the waters stand as in a wineskin. He led them in a cloud by day and throughout the night in the illumination of fire. He split the rock in the wilderness and gave them water as though from a great abyss. He brought water out of the rock and brought out waters like rivers. Yet they continued to sin against him and provoked the Most High to wrath in the waterless place. They tempted God in their hearts, asking for food for their souls. They spoke evil against God; they said: ‘Can God prepare a table in the wilderness? For he struck the rock, and waters flowed, and torrents flooded. Can he also give bread, or prepare a table for his people?’ Therefore the Lord heard and delayed; fire was kindled in Jacob, and wrath rose up against Israel, because they did not believe in God and did not hope in his salvation. He commanded the clouds above and opened the doors of heaven. He rained manna upon them for food and gave them the bread of heaven. Human beings ate the bread of angels; he sent them food in abundance. He transferred the south wind from heaven and brought in the southwest wind by his power. He rained flesh upon them like dust and winged birds like the sand of the sea. They fell in the midst of their camp, around their tents. They ate and were exceedingly filled, and he brought them what they desired; they were not deprived of their desire. Their food was still in their mouths when the wrath of God rose against them. He killed their fat ones and hindered the chosen men of Israel. In all these things they continued to sin, and they did not believe in his wonders. Their days failed in vanity, and their years passed swiftly. When he killed them, they sought him; they returned and came to him at dawn. They remembered that God was their helper and that God Most High was their redeemer. They loved him with their mouth, and with their tongue they lied to him. Their heart was not right with him, and they were not regarded as faithful to his covenant. But he is merciful and will become propitious toward their sins, and he will not destroy them. He abounded in mercy so as to turn away his wrath, and he did not kindle all his anger. He remembered that they were flesh, a spirit that goes away and does not return. How often they provoked him in the wilderness and stirred him to wrath in the waterless place. They turned back and tempted God and provoked the Holy One of Israel. They did not remember his hand on the day when he redeemed them from the hand of the oppressor, when he placed his signs in Egypt and his wonders in the field of Tanis. He turned their rivers into blood and their rainstorms, so that they might not drink. He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them; and the frog, and it destroyed them. He gave their fruits to rust and their labors to locusts. He killed their vines with hail and their mulberry trees with frost. He handed over their cattle to hail and their possessions to fire. He sent against them the wrath of his indignation: indignation, wrath, and tribulation—visitations by evil angels. He made a path for the way of his wrath; he did not spare their souls from death, and he enclosed their cattle in death. He struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, the first fruits of all their labor, in the tents of Ham. He took away his people like sheep and led them like a flock in the wilderness. He led them in hope, and they did not fear, and the sea covered their enemies. He brought them to the mountain of his sanctification, the mountain that his right hand acquired. He cast out the nations from before them and divided the land among them by lot, by the measuring cord of distribution. He made the tribes of Israel dwell in their tents. Yet they tempted and provoked God Most High, and they did not keep his testimonies. They turned away and did not keep the covenant; like their fathers, they turned aside like a crooked bow. They provoked him to wrath on their hills and aroused him to jealousy with their carved images. God heard, and he despised them, and he utterly reduced Israel to nothing. He rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh, his tabernacle where he dwelt among human beings. He delivered their strength into captivity and their beauty into the hand of the enemy. He enclosed his people within the sword and despised his inheritance. Fire devoured their young men, and their virgins were not mourned. Their priests fell by the sword, and their widows were not wept for. Then the Lord awoke like one sleeping, like a mighty man overcome by wine. He struck his enemies on their backs and gave them everlasting disgrace. He rejected the tabernacle of Joseph and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim. But he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which he loved. He built his sanctuary like a unicorn on the earth, which he founded forever. He chose David his servant and took him from the flocks of sheep; from following the nursing ewes he took him to shepherd Jacob his servant and Israel his inheritance. He shepherded them in the innocence of his heart, and by the understanding of his hands he led them.”

## Exposition
In this psalm, the things narrated as having occurred among the former people are contained. But the more recent and later people are admonished to beware lest they prove ungrateful for God’s benefits and provoke the anger of the one whose grace they ought humbly to receive.

Although here these deeds plainly appear to be spoken of and narrated, the title of the psalm first admonishes us and makes us attentive. For it was not written without reason, “Understanding of Asaph,” unless perhaps these words seek a reader who understands something inwardly [Col. 0547A], beyond what the surface of the letter says.

Yet, although he is about to narrate things that do not seem to require an expositor but merely a hearer, he says: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will speak propositions from the beginning.” Who, then, would dare to pass cursorily over parables and propositions as though they were obvious, when their very names indicate that they ought to be investigated more deeply?

For parables present likenesses of things. And it is well known that, in parables, the likenesses of things that are spoken are compared with the matters under discussion—as in that parable: “The sower went out to sow his seed” (Matt. 13). The seed is compared with the word of God, because in that parable it bears its likeness.

But the propositions—which the Greeks call **προβλήματα** (*problēmata*)—are questions containing within themselves something great that must be resolved through discussion. [Col. 0547B] Who, then, would dare to read parables and propositions cursorily, as though they were obvious, rather than apply himself with the utmost vigilance so as to reach their fruits?

Asaph, then, says as follows:

Attend, O my people, to my law. This Asaph is understood as Christ, because he was especially laboring among that people to gather others to himself. The admonition given in this psalm also concerns us, since it was said even of us: “Save us, O God our Savior, and gather us from among the nations” (Ps. 105). For if the punishments signified by those events had to be avoided by the earlier people, much more must we avoid the punishments signified by them. We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come, and whatever happened to them as a figure was done for our correction [Col. 0547C] (1 Cor. 10). Therefore, if they had to avoid the evils that signified something, we must avoid still more the evils signified by them: just as the good things signified in us are more excellent than the good things that signified them, so in the case of evils the evils signified are more serious.

“Attend, O my people, to my law.” As though he were saying: You who attend to the law of a servant, attend to the law of the Lord—not according to the letter, but according to the spirit, because “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3). “Incline your ear to the words of my mouth,” that is, attend humbly. Note that “law” and “words” are the same thing; but he repeats himself for emphasis, saying: “Incline your ear to the words of my mouth.” What is it to incline the ear except to listen humbly? One listens humbly when charity inclines the ear, not when the old obstinacy raises the neck.

“I will open my mouth in parables; I will speak propositions from the beginning.” As though he were saying: I tell you to incline your ear because I will open my mouth in parables—that is, in discourses presenting the likeness of things. And would that the one who here deigns to open his mouth in the likeness of things would also deign to open his mouth in the exposition of those things! For even if we express something worthy of hearing, we nevertheless eat our bread in sweat.

You will find these words in Augustine, in his exposition of this verse: “I will speak propositions made from the beginning of this gathering.” The beginning was the Old Testament, and the end is the New; or the beginning of this gathering was when they were gathered through Moses and Aaron in order to be led out of the land of Egypt.

Note [Col. 0548A] that propositions are questions containing something that must be resolved through discussion; and in this the proposition differs from the parable. A parable expresses a likeness, whereas propositions can be understood without a likeness. He says: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will speak propositions from the beginning,” because all that we heard promised in the Old Testament and recognized as fulfilled in the New Testament was narrated to us by our fathers.

Note that although the Lord says in the Gospel by way of command, “Do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. 23), he does not command that this title of honor be removed from ordinary speech. It was assigned on account of age or a likeness of care. Rather, he says, “Do not call anyone your father on earth,” so that grace might not be attributed to anyone other than the one to whom it must specially be attributed—namely, the one who prepares all things [Col. 0548B].

Note that here our Head places himself among the number of that people, in order to show his loving affection toward them, when he says: “All that we heard and knew, and our fathers narrated to us.” Therefore these things were not hidden from the children of men—children, I say, existing in the succeeding kinship, namely, through the succession of offspring. Thus there was another generation of children, because the fathers were blinded according to the letter, while the children were enlightened through the spirit.

“Narrating the praises of the Lord, his powers, and the wonders that he did.” As though he were saying: Our fathers narrated these things to us—fathers, I say, who narrated the praises of the Lord. And they narrated them because they proclaimed his powers, not merely ordinary powers, but wondrous powers that he performed. These, namely:

“He raised up a testimony in Jacob,” that is, he raised up in Jacob—those who supplant and struggle against vices—a faith given without the law. “And he established a law in Israel,” that is, he firmly established it in Israel—not Israel according to the flesh, but according to the spirit. Hence the saying: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1).

Note that faith is called a testimony because it was testified to by the law and the prophets. Or “testimony” and “law” may be understood as the same thing. For the law is a testimony against those who use it wrongly, by which they are convicted and lawfully punished; but for those who use it rightly, it is a testimony showing where they should take refuge in order to be delivered.

“And he established a law in Israel.” Those who are Israel according to the flesh he burdened with the law as with a heavy load, because, when the commandment came, sin revived (Rom. 7). Nor is “he raised up” placed here without reason, for nothing is raised up unless it had first been sleeping. In them the natural law had fallen asleep, but through the written law it was resurrected. Thus he says: “He raised up a testimony in Jacob.” In that testimony he commanded many things to our fathers—namely, Moses and Aaron, and the other fathers who understood carnally. He commanded them, but did not give understanding.

And what did he command? “To make them known to their children.” For although the fathers themselves had understood, their children nevertheless received from others who understood carnally what was to be understood. The fathers themselves observed the law carnally until the children, through grace, understood what the law signified. Thus he says: “The things which he commanded our fathers, to make them known to their children, so that another generation might know”—a generation either following them or changed in the spirit [Col. 0549A].

And what is this generation? The children who will be born from those fathers and will rise up—or who will not set their heart, together with their fathers, on carnal understanding of the law, but will rise up in spirit. Let them raise their heart upward with the Lord, investigating the mystery in the law, and let them narrate it to their children—namely, this: that they should place their hope in God, laboring diligently over the Lord’s commandments. For those who do not labor diligently over his commandments do not place their hope in God.

“And let them not forget the works of God,” that is, let them not be ungrateful for God’s benefits, since he works both the willing and the accomplishment according to his good pleasure. “And let them seek out his commandments,” not merely in order to know them, but in order to fulfill them. This is so that they may not become like their fathers, a crooked generation—namely, distorted and exasperating, that is, making God bitter. This generation, he says, “did not direct its heart” [Col. 0549B].

Note: whoever does not have a directed heart does not have works either, even if the heart appears to be directed. God, however, is upright, and whoever wishes to have an upright heart must be leveled against the unchanging justice and uprightness of God. This generation was not leveled against them. The reason was that its spirit was not believed with God: that is, it did not possess the faith that obtains what the law commands. For when the human spirit cooperates with the spirit of God, which is at work, then what God commands is fulfilled. This cannot happen except by believing in the one who justifies the ungodly.

This statement is rightly made to express divine grace, which not only works the remission of sins, but also makes the human spirit work together with the spirit of God. The person whose spirit is believed with God is the one who believes that he cannot perform righteousness without God. This is to believe in God, which is greater than merely believing that God exists. One believes a human being, but no one believes in a human being. To believe in God means, by believing, to cling to him through good cooperation with God, who works what is good.

“The children of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back on the day of battle.” Note that the whole passage is openly understood of the children of Ephraim—namely, of the other Jews, and of that part from which especially the better hope ought to have been expected. For when Jacob’s eyes had grown dim, he commanded his son Joseph to bring his sons Ephraim and Manasseh, so that they might receive a blessing from him. Joseph brought them and placed Manasseh on the right, since he was older, and Ephraim on the left. But Jacob, seeing through the prophetic spirit that “the first will be last, and the last first” (Matt. 20), crossed his hands and gave the blessing, placing his right hand upon Ephraim (Gen. 48).

Thus Abel was preferred to his younger brother, Isaac to Ishmael, Jacob to Esau, and David was preferred to all his older brothers (Gen. 4, 21, and 27; 1 Sam. 16). In all these figures it is signified that the Christian people would be preferred to the Jewish people.

The literal explanation is as follows: “The children of Ephraim”—those, namely, who appeared to be better—“bending the bow,” that is, displaying their good works, and “shooting arrows,” that is, sending forth words of promise, because they said: “Whatever the Lord has spoken, we will hear and do” (Exod. 24)—nevertheless “turned back on the day of battle,” that is, on the day of temptation they failed [Col. 0550A].

Or let us read it by way of likeness: “The children of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back on the day of battle,” that is, they became comparable to those who practice with weapons on a day of peace but begin flight on the day of battle. For on the day of hearing they promised everything, but on the day of action they did nothing good. This is what is meant by “they turned back on the day of battle.” And here is how: “They did not keep the covenant of God,” that is, the promises made by the Lord in the New Testament.

“And they refused to walk in his law.” For even if they outwardly appeared to walk according to the law, inwardly they contradicted it. “And they forgot his benefits and his wonders that he showed them,” by which they were admonished by God not to depart from him. And here are the wonders:

“In the presence of their fathers,” Moses and Aaron and the other elders of Israel, “he performed wonders in the land of Egypt, in the field of Tanis. He divided the sea,” namely, the Red Sea, “and led them through it, and made the waters stand”—that is, made them stand as though enclosed in a wineskin.

These things mystically signify something in us, because they are understood as taking place in the land of Egypt itself. He performed many wonders inwardly, although he did not perform them outwardly in many people. And this happened “in the field of Tanis,” that is, among those who, keeping the Lord’s commandments, have been humbled. For Tanis is interpreted as “commandment,” while a field signifies the humble, because no one will be saved through the commandment except the humble.

The dividing of the sea signifies baptism, in which all our enemies are drowned, because original and actual sins are washed away. But it is divided afterward, because although all receive remission of sins equally in baptism, it is not salvation for everyone. For those who apostatize from God after the resurrection of baptism, it becomes destruction, since “it is better not to have known the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back” (2 Pet. 2).

“And he made the waters stand as though in a wineskin,” that is, he made our fluid carnal desires stand still, as though they were to be enclosed in a wineskin. For he brought them under our control in such a way that they no longer drown us unless we wish to consent to them.

“And he led them in a cloud by day, and throughout the night in the illumination of fire.” Historically, this happened to them so that they might travel in safety. We, however, are led in the cloud of day—that is, under the most splendid protection of Christ’s flesh, which is understood by the cloud. Hence the saying: “God will ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt, and he will shatter all its idols” (Isa. 19).

“And throughout the night”—that is, on the day of tribulation—the Lord will lead us in the cloud by day and throughout the night in the illumination of fire, that is, in the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Or he went before them in the cloud by day because he will appear gentle to the righteous, as though in a light cloud. At night he went before them in fire because he will appear terrifying to the unjust. By this fire the righteous will be enlightened, while the wicked will burn.

“He divided the rock in the wilderness and gave them water to drink as from a great abyss.” Note that earlier he made a rock out of the waters, whereas here he brought forth waters from the rock. Moses struck the flint twice with his staff, and abundant waters flowed from it (Num. 20). The rock that was struck is Christ. Hence the saying: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10).

The fact that the rock was struck twice signifies that Christ was stretched out upon the twofold wood of the cross. From him, thus stretched out, abundant waters flowed because the prophetic words became intelligible through his death: the veils of the temple were torn, and all the obscurity of prophetic speech was destroyed. From these prophetic words many rich people drank their fill. Hence the saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7). This is what is meant by: “He divided the rock in the wilderness and gave them water to drink as from a great abyss.”

And how did this happen? “Because he brought water from the rock and led waters down like rivers.” Yet although he had done all these things for them, they still added sin against him—that is, against him in this way:

“In anger they provoked him in the waterless place,” because they asked for water in a dry place, as though God were unable to give water in a dry place, although he had made the divided sea stand. They provoke the Most High to anger in a waterless place when, in the dryness of their mind, they call upon him for earthly advantage.

“And they tested God in their hearts, asking for food for their souls.” Note how they tested God: what they requested with their mouths, they doubted in their hearts that God could do. Even now there are many who ask food for their souls—that is, for their animal nature—like those who worship God not for his own sake but for earthly things, as though what he gives were sweeter than the one who gives it.

“And they spoke evil against God; they said: ‘Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?’” Here those who did not believe are signified, saying: “Can he give us his flesh and his blood, in portions to eat and drink?” (John 6). For he had already struck the rock, and waters had flowed, and streams—that is, teachings—had overflowed. “And because he has done this, can he therefore also give bread or prepare a table for his people?”

The Lord heard this murmuring and delayed leading them into the promised land. They could have reached it in a few days had they not needed to be delayed from their homeland and worn out in the wilderness. Or he delayed the punishment in order to satisfy the desire of the unbelieving people. First he did what the unbelieving people thought he could not do; afterward he imposed what they deserved to suffer. Thus it says: “The Lord heard and delayed, and fire was kindled in Jacob, and anger rose up in Israel” [Col. 0551D].

This fire signifies the incitements of vices, which inwardly ravage a person. Thus it says: “Fire was kindled in Jacob, and the anger of God rose up in Israel.” This happened because “they did not believe in God, nor did they hope in his salvation,” that is, they did not hope to be saved by God.

And the Lord heard—what? “He commanded the clouds from above and opened the doors of heaven, so that he might rain down upon them abundantly what he was going to send.” This shows why he delayed the punishment: namely, so that through what follows he might satisfy their desire.

“And he rained manna upon them for food, and gave them the bread of heaven, not cultivated on earth.” And he adds what it was: “Man ate the bread of angels.” He calls it the bread of angels because the bread they ate signified that bread—namely, the Word of the Father—from which they are nourished [Col. 0552A]. Hence the saying: “All ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink” (1 Cor. 10).

“He sent them provisions in abundance.” And how did this happen? “He transferred the south wind from heaven”—to earth, understood—because he destroyed the unhealthy disturbance of the air and gave them a wholesome temperature. “And he brought in the southwesterly wind by his power, and rained flesh upon them like dust; and winged birds like the sand of the sea.”

He does not say “winged” without reason, since all birds have wings. Rather, because he was going to say that they fell in the midst of their camps, he first mentioned “winged birds,” so that you might marvel that birds had fallen.

“And they ate and were filled exceedingly, and he brought them their desire,” because they were not deprived of what they desired. The Lord abundantly granted them the nourishment they requested [Col. 0552B]. “And while their food,” namely, the flesh, “was still in their mouths,” they nevertheless, ungrateful for all the benefits, deserved this: “the anger of God rose against them,” although they had placed their hope in God, so that he might have supplied them not only with carnal things but also with spiritual ones.

For the one who commanded the clouds from above, opened the doors of heaven, rained manna upon them for food, gave them the bread of heaven, and sent them provisions in abundance in order to feed unbelievers is neither ineffective nor powerless to give believers the true bread from heaven, which the manna signified and which is truly the food of angels: the Word of the Father, which nourishes incorruptibly. “And man ate the bread of angels.” “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1) [Col. 0552C].

This Word is rained upon the whole world through angelic clouds. When the hearts of preachers are opened like heavenly vessels, it is preached not to the murmuring and testing synagogue, but to the believing Church that places its hope in God.

The one who transferred the south wind from heaven, brought in the southwesterly wind by his power, and rained flesh upon them like dust and winged birds like the sand of the sea is powerful not only then but also now to feed the small faith of believers with the fleshly signs of words, which pass through the air like birds. Yet they do not come from the north, where cold and darkness prevail—that is, from eloquence that favors this world. Rather, by transferring the south wind from heaven to earth, he causes those who are small in faith, by hearing earthly things, to be nourished toward the reception of heavenly things.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “If I have spoken earthly things to you and you do not believe, how will you believe if I speak heavenly things to you?” (John 3). Paul was transferred from heaven, where in mind he had gone beyond himself, so that he might accommodate himself to those to whom he said: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal people. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Cor. 3).

Paul himself had heard in heaven secret things that are not permitted to be spoken on earth, sounding forth as though through flying birds. And the one who transferred the south wind brought in the southwesterly wind—that is, through southern winds that give light and through the fervent spirits of preachers, he made himself known to us so that we might be conformed to them.

“And they fell in the midst of their camps,” because, having been transferred from heaven, they came voluntarily to human beings and brought them words sent by God. Thus each person, among his own faithful and around his own tabernacles, might gather such birds, so that all the nations of the Gentiles might worship God.

Not only foreign preachers were sent; many also would have preachers from among their own citizens, including Silvester and their other fellow-citizens. Let us return to the letter: let us bring together in the exposition of the text what we have discussed piecemeal in the preceding explanations.

“And he commanded the clouds from above”: they are coming, because they do not depart from God; they are “from above” because they are superior and more worthy than others. Hence the saying: “Tell it in his towers” (Ps. 48).

“And he opened the doors of heaven,” that is, the hearts of preachers. And rightly are the apostles called the doors of heaven, because through them people entered heaven; their tongues became the keys of heaven, and through those apostles he rained manna for food [Col. 0553B].

This manna is not eaten with the teeth but received with the soul’s eagerness. Nor did he place “for food” without reason, because the word is preached to many who are not nourished by it. Hence the saying: “The birds of heaven ate it” (Matt. 13). And: “He gave them the bread of heaven” (John 6).

Of this bread it was said: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matt. 6). And the Lord himself said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6).

“Man ate the bread of angels.” In order that man might eat this bread, the king of angels became man. Each person is nourished by the Lord’s incarnation and death.

“He sent them provisions in abundance.” What are these provisions? In the mystery of the cross, to possess the resurrection. For he did not wish to be stretched out in this way without reason, except to admonish us to have charity stretched out and to remain unmoved by desire [Col. 0553C].

And how all these things are so is added: “He transferred the south wind from heaven,” that is, the warm wind—namely, the apostles, fervent with the warmth of faith and driving others toward faith. He transferred them from heaven, that is, from the lofty contemplation of heavenly things, so that they might blow upon the earth and stoop to human capacity.

“And he brought in the southwesterly wind by his power,” that is, he made known to us the spirits of preachers by giving us life. “By his power,” and not through the merit of the preachers, this was done, according to the saying: “So that the surpassing power may be God’s and not ours” (2 Cor. 4).

“And he rained flesh upon them like dust.” Flesh is pleasant food, which adults eat. Here we understand a subtle and solid preaching by which the perfect are to be nourished, such as: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John 1). Paul spoke of such preaching: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. 2). This is what is meant by: “He rained flesh upon them like dust” [Col. 0553D].

And how does he signify this here through “winged birds”? They are, namely, the signs of words flying through the air, winged. “Like the sand of the sea”: this signifies the abundance of the divine word, which was previously signified by dust.

Or in this way: “He rained flesh upon them like dust,” because just as dust is seized by the wind and carried through the air, so by the wind of exaltation the divine word is carried away by certain people. Hence the saying: “The thorns sprang up and choked it” (Matt. 13).

“And like the sand of the sea, winged birds.” Just as no fruit arises in the sand of the sea, so in the hearts of unbelievers the divine word produces no progress [Col. 0554A].

“And they fell in the midst of their camps,” because each person heard the preachers of the faith in his own place. “And they ate,” that is, they were refreshed. Some of them were filled exceedingly—namely, the heretics, by interpreting the Scriptures through a left-handed interpretation. “And he brought them their desire,” because he permitted them to be blinded in their perverse understanding. Thus they were not deprived of their desire, because they “bent their bow to shoot at the blameless in secret.”

“And while their food was still in their mouths,” that is, their carnal understanding was always in their mouths. For even if they understood correctly, they did not display this in their speech.

“And the anger of God rose against them.” Above he showed why he delayed, namely, the anger that rose against them.

“And he killed their fat ones,” that is, the proud and those who think lofty thoughts. “And he hindered the chosen of Israel,” so that they might not benefit those whom they desired to benefit with paternal affection. For there were some in that people who might have corrected others, but they were hindered because there was no one there who wished to be corrected.

Hence the prophet says: “I will make your tongue cling to your palate, because it is an exasperating house” (Ezek. 3).

Or he hindered the chosen of Israel because they grieved over those who were perishing. Hence: “The confusion of my face covered me” (Ps. 44).

Or the chosen of Israel are the priests, who are sometimes hindered by the Lord because of the sins of their subjects—sins that ought rightly to be corrected. But because of excessive compassion for human nature, they spare sinners too much, not considering that compassion is owed to nature, while uprightness is owed to guilt.

Judgment ought to be made concerning each sinner. But if afterward the prelate sees that someone is humbly doing penance, he is left to his own judgment, so that he may have mercy on him.

In all these matters, they sinned still more—understand, despite correction by admonition—and this because they did not believe in his wonders. “And their days failed in vanity,” although they could have advanced in truth, “and their years in haste,” because they were always tending toward death, falling from vice to vice and, through despair, falling into sins. This showed that they desired interior death.

“When he killed them, they sought him; they returned, and at dawn”—that is, watchfully and diligently—“they came to him.” Then at last they remembered that God was their helper in good things and that the Most High God was their redeemer in evils.

“And they loved him with their mouth,” that is, with their mouth they showed that they loved the Lord, “and with their tongue they lied to him.” Their heart was not upright with him, nor were they considered faithful to his covenant [Col. 0554D].

For his covenant urges us to love him not for earthly things but for his own sake alone. They were not faithful to this covenant because, by failing to do what he taught, they did not have faith in him. Therefore their heart was not upright with him, because to have an upright heart with the Lord is to seek God for God’s sake.

These things happened historically among them, but they also happen mystically among us. When he kills—that is, when he punishes someone by just judgment, or scourges us ourselves—we seek him by invoking his mercy so that he may spare us. We return to him under the appearance of humility, because we departed from him through the sin of pride [Col. 0555A].

And they do not return to him with just any kind of return; rather, “at dawn,” that is, with great diligence, we come to him. We call to mind that he alone is our helper in good things and our redeemer in evils. Thus we show with our mouth that we love him, and yet we lie, because our heart is not upright with him, nor are we faithful to his covenant.

For we love him only to avoid temporal evils or acquire temporal goods, whereas he should be loved solely for his own sake.

“But he is merciful and propitious toward their sins among their descendants, though not among their fathers.” “And he will not destroy them, because a remnant of Israel will be saved” (Rom. 9).

Many customarily use this passage to support impunity for sin, even if such people persevere to the end in the condition in which those others were. But they believe this in vain, because the statement “he will be propitious toward their sins” must be referred to their descendants, who are to be converted in the last times.

Thus it says: “He will be propitious toward their sins, and he will not destroy them; and his mercy abounded, so that he might turn away his anger.” It was necessary for abundant mercy to come to the aid of their descendants, because previously a manifold anger had gone before among their fathers. He will not kindle against their descendants all the anger that they deserved, because “he did not reject his people whom he foreknew” (Rom. 11).

“And he remembered that they were flesh,” that is, he considered that they were weighed down by the burden of the flesh and needed restoration through the Mediator.

“For they are a spirit that goes and does not return,” because each person, from himself, has the power to depart from God, but cannot return unless the grace of God recalls him. Hence in the Book of Wisdom: “Everyone who has walked along the way of iniquity will not return.” This is to be understood as meaning: by his own power he will not return.

“How often they provoked him in the wilderness.” He repeats what he had said above, to show that they deservedly provoked God’s anger, since they were ungrateful both for the benefits God had bestowed on them and for the plagues inflicted upon the Egyptians on their account.

Thus he says: “How often they provoked him,” that is, how many times, beyond counting, they made him bitter toward themselves in the wilderness, “provoking him to anger in the waterless place”—understand, the place where they asked for water. They provoke the Lord to anger in a waterless place when they remain in the dryness of the mind.

“And they turned to appease God, and again they tested him, and provoked the Holy One of Israel,” because “they did not remember his hand,” that is, the power he had displayed—namely, on the day when he redeemed them from the hand of the one afflicting them, that is, from the power of Pharaoh and the Egyptian rulers.

Nor did they remember “how”—that is, in what manner—“he placed his signs and his wonders in Egypt, in the field of Tanis” [Col. 0555D].

There is also a mystery here. Many, in the dryness of their minds, make God, who is naturally sweet, bitter to themselves, because they do not remember the Lord’s power or the day on which he wondrously redeemed them by his blood from the hand of the one afflicting them—that is, from the power of the prince of darkness, under whose yoke they were held.

Nor do they remember how many signs and wonders—both lesser and greater miracles—he performed in Egypt, that is, in this world, where there are nothing but darkness and affliction [Col. 0556A]. And this took place “in the field of Tanis,” that is, among those who were humbled by his commandment.

“And he turned their rivers and their rains into blood, so that they could not drink.” The rains are waters collected in cisterns, into which blood was mixed so that they became undrinkable for the Egyptians.

Mystically, the rivers are turned into blood in those who think carnally about the causes of things. Or the rivers are teachings that are turned into blood when they are made undrinkable by a perverse understanding. The rains are one’s own preachers, whom the Lord turns into blood when a person, blinded, abhors hearing them as though he were drinking blood.

That preachers are signified by the rains that are placed here in cisterns is shown by the authority that says: “Drink water from your own cisterns” (Prov. 5).

“He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them; and the frog, and it destroyed them.” Dog-flies are canine flies, by which the Egyptians were afflicted. They signify people having the ways of dogs, showing no reverence to their fathers, although it is written: “Obey your fathers only in the Lord” (Eph. 6).

Or the canine flies may signify carnal desires, because they harass a person, since the law of the body is always in conflict with the law of the mind (Col. 1).

The frog signifies empty loquacity, by which those who delight in it are destroyed.

“And he gave their fruits to rust, and their labors to locusts.” Rust is a hidden breath or a little worm harmful to fruits. It signifies hidden pride, which is greatly opposed to fruits and good works. The locust, because it injures with its mouth, signifies unfaithful testimony; those who rely upon it lose all the labor of good works.

Or the locust signifies those who are unstable in faith, because the locust is also an unstable creature [Col. 0556C].

“And he killed their vineyards with hail, and their mulberry trees with frost.” It is well known that the vineyard signifies the people, as in the saying: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5).

A people is struck by hail when, because of iniquity, it strives to take away what belongs to another. “The trees were moved”—trees producing fruit in great abundance, bearing mature fruit, fruit about to produce seed, and fruit beginning to ripen. Here charity is signified, in which all good works have their roots.

Thus through the frost that destroys the trees, the coldness of charity is signified, because “when iniquity abounds, charity will grow cold” (Matt. 24).

“And he delivered their cattle to hail, and their possessions to fire.” Cattle struck by hail signify damage to chastity, because from the moment concupiscence arises, its fruit is something we share with animals. If concupiscence is restrained so that it acts in a royal manner, it is the virtue of chastity.

Note that here wives can be understood by “cattle,” because they are cattle—that is, aids, as it were, for preserving chastity. They are killed by hail when someone, handed over to a reprobate mind, practices shamefulness with males. Hence Paul says: “God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what was unfitting, working shamefulness in themselves and in others” (Rom. 1).

“And their possessions to fire.” Exodus does not say that any of their possessions were delivered to fire. But the prophet inserted this here in order to admonish the reader to seek the mystery and not remain merely on the surface of the letter [Col. 0557A].

Here “possession” signifies patience, for it was said of it: “In your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21), because patience makes people possessors. Hence the saying: “Patience is necessary for us, so that we may receive the promises” (Heb. 10).

This patience is burned by fire when anger is expelled by harmony.

“And he sent among them the anger of his indignation,” that is, an anger appropriate to his indignation. Thus he says both “indignation” and “anger.” This anger was the tribulation sent through evil angels—not because God does not also inflict whatever he wills through good angels, but because he uses evil angels as well as good ones to avenge the reprobate.

He used good angels in the punishment of Sodom, since Abraham is read to have received them as guests, and through them the Lord announced his vengeance (Gen. 18). But that he inflicts temporal correction through good angels is not found in the authorities. Rather, he uses evil angels in the correction of the good, as is read concerning Job (Job 1).

This sending through evil angels is the hardening of the heart. It occurs through evil angels alone, so that those who persist in sin may deserve heavier punishments, the more serious and further sins they commit.

“He made a way for the path of his anger.” The path of God’s anger is when he permits someone to be dragged by the cords of sins, so that he commits capital offenses for which he is blinded inwardly and eventually punished outwardly.

“And he did not spare their souls from death, and he enclosed their cattle in death.” Cattle enclosed in death signify those who, through the concupiscence of the flesh—which human beings share with animals—abandoning chastity, fall headlong into death [Col. 0557C].

“And he struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, the firstfruits of all their labor in the tents of Ham.” The slain firstborn signify justice, through which the human race is capable of fellowship, since no one exists who does not possess at least some small measure of justice. But justice perishes when a person ceases to live justly.

Or the struck firstborn may signify the loss of faith, which is first among believers, because outside the Catholic Church there is no place of true sacrifice.

By “the firstfruits of every labor” good works are signified. They perish “in the tents,” that is, among those who perform good works with a certain cunning, as though under the appearance of religion. For Ham is interpreted as “cunning.”

“And he took away his people like sheep and led them like a flock in the wilderness.” Having displayed the plagues that the Lord inflicted upon the Egyptians ...

They were unwilling to release the people; therefore he showed how the Lord delivered his people from their power, saying: “And he took away his people like sheep.” This is also now accomplished inwardly among us, when we are made, in accordance with spiritual pastures, God’s sheep, walking in this world as in a desert.

“And he led them out in the hope of the land,” namely, the promised land. And they did not fear being led forth, because he covered their enemies with the sea. We too are led forth: “in hope we were saved”; and our enemies—that is, our vices—the sea covered, namely, the wave of baptism.

“And he brought them among his descendants, to the mountain of his sanctification, the mountain which his right hand acquired” [Col. 0558A]. The mountain of sanctification is the Church, which Christ acquired by the right hand of God.

“And he cast out the nations before them, and by lot divided the land among them, by the measuring cord of distribution.” Here it is signified that the evil spirits of pagan errors must be cast out from before his faithful, so that the one and the same Spirit may dwell in them, distributing to each as he wills, as though the matter were arranged by a measuring cord. The land is divided by lot among the elect because their election does not arise from merits but from grace, which comes to them, as it were, by lot.

“And he made the tribes of Israel dwell in their tents.” These tents signify the heavenly Jerusalem, where the apostate angels were, as it were, in tents for a time. They were expelled from there so that, eventually, the tribe of Israel—that is, the assembly of those who see God—might be taken into their place.

“And they tempted and embittered the Most High God, and did not keep his testimonies.” It is as though he said: Although the Lord had done all these things for the sake of that people, they nevertheless were ungrateful for everything, because by tempting him they made him bitter, not keeping his testimonies—that is, his promises. His promises were heavenly things, which were signified by earthly ones; but they did not seek the heavenly things and clung only to the earthly, just as we also embitter him by tempting him when we ask of him what ought not to be asked.

For his promises are: “Ask, and you will receive” (John XIV, XVI). We do not keep these promises because we ask for nothing in his name.

“And they turned away and did not keep the covenant, just as their fathers turned aside like a crooked bow” [Col. 0558C]. Here he shows how they did not keep his testimonies: by turning away from God, they did not keep the covenant which they had made with the Lord, namely: “Everything that the Lord has spoken, we will do” (Exod. XXIV), clinging instead to earthly things. We too enter into a kind of covenant with God, because in baptism we renounce the world and all its pomp. Since we do not keep this renunciation, we break the covenant.

“Just as their fathers turned aside like a crooked bow”—that is, they became comparable to a crooked bow. For just as a weak bow quickly relaxes, so they, having turned toward an evil intention, became lax with regard to God’s commandments. Or a crooked bow is one which, when it is drawn forward, strikes backward. Thus, when the wicked intend to harm others and, as it were, to strike them with arrows of iniquity, the arrow returns upon them, because no one sins against another without first sinning against himself.

Or the bow is crooked because it fails after one shot. These are those “who believe for a time, but in the time of temptation fall away” (Luke VIII).

“They provoked him to anger on their hills,” because each person chose for himself an elevated place from which to offend God; and this he demonstrates: “With their carved images they provoked him to jealousy.” That is, by sacrificing to empty idols, they provoked God to indignation and jealousy.

We too provoke him to anger on our hills whenever we offend him through mental arrogance; and we provoke him to jealousy with carved images whenever we satisfy the idols of the mind. There are many who worship the idol of greed and the idol of lust, rushing into sexual desire like stiff-necked bulls [Col. 0559A].

“God heard and despised them”—that is, he considered all these things; and therefore he despised them, because he reduced Israel to utter nothingness when they were defeated by the Philistines and others. Even now he despises them when he permits each person, because of his deserving sins, to be conquered by the inner enemy.

“And he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh, his tabernacle where he dwelt among human beings”—that is, among human beings, not because God dwells in things made by human hands, in accordance with the saying: “Do not trust in lying words, saying, ‘The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is this.’” For it is not a temple except insofar as it concerns you, with whom and in whom I will dwell in this place, if you bless your ways (Jer. VII). Yet he was said to dwell among all those people because he worked manifest signs through them [Col. 0559B].

Shiloh is interpreted as “plucked away” or “broken off.” By it are signified those who have been broken off from the Lord’s commandments and torn away, whose tabernacle he did not choose for his dwelling.

“And he handed over their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hand of the enemy.” Their strength and beauty were the ark of the Lord, which the Philistines captured and placed with their idols in their temple. But when, on the following day, their god was found lying in the middle of the temple with his hands cut off, and the people had been afflicted by a great plague, they eventually sent the ark back to Israel, not without gifts (1 Sam. IV–V).

Observe the mystery in these events. The ark of God signifies ecclesiastical institutions. A person places these institutions together with idols when, having received them, he still clings excessively to earthly things. But because it is said, “All things will pass away, but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. XL), the idol was rightly found with its hands cut off. For even if earthly things seem to possess some degree of splendor, in the end they will be seen to be nothing, because “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field” (Isa. XL).

Our strength and beauty are baptism and the other things that are handed over into the enemy’s hands when someone thinks he will be saved by faith alone, like the many who, neglecting good works, say: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark XVI), without paying attention to the fact that “faith without works is dead” (James II).

“And he shut up his people in the sword, and despised his inheritance.” This also happens in the Church, because many fall by the sword when they are openly attacked and defeated by their enemies. “Their young men”—that is, those who ought to be vigorous in resisting their enemies, armed with faith, hope, and charity so that they may be able to withstand the snares of the devil—the fire of tribulation, or the fire of incitements, “devoured,” that is, consumed.

Or, alternatively: “The fire devoured their young men,” so that by “young men” we may understand the rash, those prepared for every evil; such people the fire of sins will finally consume. Here again we are warned to persist in the allegorical sense, because the historical account does not say that fire consumed any young men there [Col. 0559D].

“And their virgins were not lamented”—that is, there was no one to lament the virgins who had been left desolate and corrupted. By “virgins,” understand the Church’s sterility in good works, although someone may lament it. Or by “virgins,” understand those who ought to persevere in the chastity of good works, so that at last they might be joined in the bond of a second marriage to the most chaste Bridegroom. But by living unchastely, they fornicated against him and departed from him; scarcely anyone laments this [Col. 0560A].

“Their priests fell by the sword, and their widows were not mourned.” These priests were Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli, who died in the battle in which the ark of the Lord was captured. When the wife of one of them heard this—she was already in labor—she fell dead from grief while miscarrying (1 Sam. IV).

The priests are bishops and the other prelates in the Church, who fall by the sword when through fear they cease from proclaiming the divine word. Their widows are the desolate Churches, deprived of their pastors, whose consolation few people grieve.

“And the Lord awoke as one sleeping.” Having shown the evils with which the Lord’s people were afflicted, the text proceeds to the vengeance taken upon their enemies. It says that “the Lord awoke as one sleeping.” The Lord seems to sleep when he delays coming to the aid of his people; but he awoke “as a mighty man reeling from wine”—understand: he shakes himself, since such people sleep soundly and are scarcely awakened. This indicates that the Lord long delayed coming to the aid of his own.

But at last he awoke and “struck his enemies in the rear; he gave them everlasting disgrace.” Or, alternatively: “He awoke as one sleeping, as a mighty man overcome with wine,” because although he had slept soundly and for a long time, once awakened he was powerful enough to inflict vengeance upon his enemies.

What follows, “And he struck their enemies in the rear,” is read historically. While the Philistines had the ark in captivity in their own dwellings [Col. 0560C], they suffered great plagues. To be freed from the plague, they made golden tumors and placed them in the ark, so that they might return it in this way to the children of Israel (1 Sam. V).

This also now takes place in the Church among those who extend themselves toward what is behind and abandon what is before. The “rear” of the wicked will consist only in plagues and miseries. And it will be an everlasting disgrace to them, because those who prosper here through temporal things will be tormented by eternal punishment.

“And he rejected the tabernacle of Joseph, and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim.” Joseph and Ephraim—who seemed to possess greater merit among that people, one having been exalted to high rank in Egypt and the other having been placed before his brother in receiving the blessing—signify those who ask earthly things from the Lord as though they were of great value, and are therefore rejected by the Lord [Col. 0560D].

“But he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which he loved”—that is, those who confess humbly. The tribe of Judah was chosen because of David—that is, because of Christ, since Christ was born according to the flesh from his lineage. Thus he says: “But he chose the tribe of Judah,” namely, the tribe of those who confess humbly, “Mount Zion, which he loved”—that is, those who are eminent in contemplation of future things.

“And he built his sanctuary on earth”—that is, in the Church—“his sanctification.” I say “sanctuary” as existing like that of unicorns, namely, of those who raise themselves toward heavenly things with one horn, that is, with a singular hope. Hence the saying: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek” (Ps. XXVI).

“He founded this land forever.” It will always remain, although some depart and others succeed them.

Or in this way: “He built his sanctuary,” that is, his people, “upon the land which he founded forever,” that is, by placing them in the likeness of land, insofar as land does not move [Col. 0561A].

“And he chose David his servant and took him from the sheepfolds,” because he was taken from the pastoral office of tending animals and appointed to the kingship. “From behind those giving birth he took him”—that is, he was taken from the one who was behind the pregnant sheep and placed in the foremost position among human beings.

This David signifies Christ, who was taken away from the kingdom of the Jews and transferred to the kingdom of the Gentiles. Yet he was not taken away from the Jews in such a way that he would have no fruits there; rather, he was taken away from them after some of them had been found “nursing,” that is, fruitful in faith and good works. For the apostles and the other faithful, full of faith and empty of unbelief, came from that people [Col. 0561B].

“To feed Jacob his servant, and Israel his inheritance.” Here is why he chose David: namely, so that he might feed Jacob his servant—that is, those who attend to future things and set present things aside—and Israel his inheritance, that is, those who contemplate not the things that are seen but those that are not seen. Or, by Jacob the peoples of the Gentiles are signified, and by Israel the Jewish people (1 Cor. IV).

“And he fed them in the innocence of his heart.” It is as though he said: David was chosen to feed Jacob and Israel; and this happened because he fed them—that is, refreshed them—in the innocence of his heart, namely, so that by imitating the innocence of his heart they might be refreshed.

“And he led them by the understanding of his hands”—that is, he surpassed them not only in the innocence of his heart, but also led them by the understanding of the works of his hands [Col. 0561C], so that just as he himself first did and taught, they too might afterward do.

Or, “he led them by the understanding of his hands” means that he led them by such an understanding as his hands had worked in them, because he made them in his own image and likeness: “For God is such that he is human” [reading and sense uncertain].

**Note:** It might seem more fitting if he had said: “He fed them in the innocence of his hands, and led them in the understanding of his heart.” But since there are many who have innocent hands without having an innocent heart, he did not wish to speak in that way, so that he might commend the innocence of the heart.

# PSALM 78. A PSALM OF ASAPH

> “O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have made Jerusalem a place for guarding apples. They have given the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of the sky, the flesh of your holy ones to the beasts of the earth. They have poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them. We have become a reproach to our neighbors, mockery and derision to those who are around us. How long, Lord, will you be angry to the end? Will your jealousy burn like fire? Pour out your wrath upon the nations that do not know you, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name. For they have devoured Jacob and laid his place waste. Do not remember our former iniquities; may your mercies quickly anticipate us, for we have become exceedingly poor. Help us, O God our Savior, and for the glory of your name, Lord, deliver us and be favorable to our sins for the sake of your name. Lest they perhaps say among the nations, ‘Where is their God?’ Let the vengeance for the blood of your servants that has been shed enter into your sight, and the groaning of the imprisoned. According to the greatness of your arm, possess the sons of those who have been put to death. And repay our neighbors sevenfold in their bosom the reproach with which they reproached you, Lord. But we, your people and the sheep of your pasture, will give thanks to you forever. From generation to generation we shall announce your praise.”

## EXPOSITION

We know clearly that the prophecy which we see promised here has been fulfilled. Nevertheless, when David said this, we do not read that anything of this kind had happened to that city, Jerusalem, through the hostility of the nations, such as is described here; nor had the temple of the Lord yet been built. For after David’s death, his son Solomon built the temple. David therefore speaks, as though of the past, what he saw in the spirit. He saw what was future.

Nor is it surprising that this is said: it is not spoken to one who is ignorant, by whose revelation they suffer. Rather, the faithful soul loves to speak to God, out of the affection of its heart, of what it has learned from God, and to say to him what it knows—as a disciple speaks to a teacher who is not ignorant, but who reveals things, and thereby either proves what he has taught or reproves what he has not taught.

For in prayers people customarily say to God what he has done while taking vengeance, and they add a pious petition that he may have mercy and pardon. In this manner these things are said to God by those to whom such events occurred, as though they themselves were speaking. This is lamentation and supplication, and also prophecy, because the Prophet foresaw in the spirit that persecution which the Jews suffered from Titus and Vespasian after the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, and therefore laments it in this psalm.

But someone may have it occur to his mind that that people was not Christ’s inheritance at the time when these things happened, because it handed him over to death, did not believe in him after he rose again, and killed other holy martyrs of his. Yet since there were not lacking among that people those who ought to be reckoned among the seed, the people may, with respect to them, be called the Lord’s inheritance. For from that people came Joseph, the Lord’s foster-father; from it came the most blessed Virgin Mary; from it came the Lord himself; from it came the righteous Simeon and the widow Anna; from it came another Joseph, since he too awaited the redemption of Israel; from it came blessed John and his parents; from it came the crowd of those who preceded and followed the Lord; from it came the children who cried out in the Lord’s praise, “Hosanna, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (John 12); from it came the three thousand people who believed in one day (Acts 2); from it came the five thousand who believed on another day (Acts 4); and from it came many other believers. With respect to these, that people is not improperly called God’s inheritance.

This prophecy may also concern that persecution which the Israelite people suffered under King Antiochus, when the seven Maccabean brothers suffered most cruelly but were crowned most gloriously (2 Maccabees 7). Or this prophecy may concern the persecution which the holy Church, gathered from the uncircumcision and the circumcision and joined in our Savior Jesus Christ, the cornerstone, suffered after the Lord’s resurrection. In him the two peoples, like two walls coming from opposite directions, were united into one new man; in whose body we cry, “Abba, Father” (Romans 8): “Abba” with respect to them, and “Father” with respect to us.

This inheritance belongs not only to the Father but also to the Son—not because the Father, by dying, left it to himself, but because the Son, by dying, redeemed it, and by rising again possessed it in majesty. He gathered it from both peoples. For although he had said, “I was not sent except to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel” (Matthew 15), he nevertheless said elsewhere, “I have other sheep that are not from this fold” (John 10), where he designated the nations.

Paul also confirms the same thing: “I say that Christ became a minister of the circumcision, but that the nations glorify God for his mercy” (Romans 15). Joining both peoples together, he said: “Rejoice, nations, with his people.”

Asaph therefore speaks as follows:

> “O God, the nations have come into your inheritance”—that is, against the Jewish people, because it is called your inheritance. “They have defiled your holy temple,” because they placed their idols where your name ought to be worshiped. “They have made Jerusalem a place for guarding apples”—that is, they made Jerusalem comparable to a hut for guarding apples, because, just as a shelter made for guarding apples is abandoned once the apples have been gathered, so Jerusalem, after some of its inhabitants had been killed, became desolate and deserted.

> “They have given the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of the sky.” Here he signifies a great slaughter, because it was so extensive that the birds flying through the air, corrupted and attracted by the stench, fed upon the bodies. “The flesh of your holy ones to the beasts of the earth”—that is, they not only gave the bodies of your holy ones as food to the birds of the sky, but also handed them over to the beasts of the earth, namely, unclean swine, to be devoured.

> And see how this happened: “They poured out their blood like water”—that is, abundantly or continually, and without regard for sin, because in pouring out the blood of the holy ones they cared no more than if water were being poured out, where there would be no fear of sin. And this occurred not only in Jerusalem but around Jerusalem. “And there was no one to bury them,” because so many were being killed that they could not be buried; or, there was no one who cared to bury them. This indicates their great savagery and cruelty, because piety is signified in burial, while savagery and cruelty are signified in the refusal of burial.

> “We have become a reproach to our neighbors,” namely, to the nations that were our neighbors. And to show that the reproach was great, he adds: “Mockery and derision to those who are around us.”

These words can be read in this way if the psalm is understood as referring to the persecution of the Jews. But if it is read as referring to the persecution of the Church, the psalm speaks as follows:

> “O God, the nations have come into your inheritance”—that is, into the Church, to destroy it, not to imitate it. “They have defiled your holy temple.” The Lord’s temple is defiled when someone who has been initiated into the sacrament of faith is compelled to deny Christ.

> “They have made Jerusalem a place for guarding apples”—that is, they made their Church deserted, just as, after the apples have been gathered, the hut in which the apples were previously guarded becomes deserted. For when the nations persecuted it, the gathered Church became deserted, its holy martyrs’ spirits being carried from the Lord’s garden, like exceedingly sweet apples, to the heavenly table.

> “They have given the corpses of your servants”—because, after the spirits of the holy ones had been received by the husbandman, their bodies were handed over to the birds of the sky to be devoured, as we read concerning Stephen, who after his killing was cast outside the city.

> Or it may be understood in this way: “They have given the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of the sky”—that is, the bodies of your holy ones became food, namely refreshment, for the birds of the sky, that is, for those who are mobile and uplifted in you, who delighted in the killing of the saints as though in food. Such was the torturer of Laurence, to whom it was said, “Now turn him over and eat.” For although this could be understood otherwise, it can nevertheless be understood in this way: that the tormenting of the blessed martyr was itself refreshment for him.

> “The flesh of your holy ones to the beasts of the earth”—that is, the flesh of the holy ones was given for refreshment to those who live like beasts and cling to earthly things.

> “They have poured out their blood like water”—whether on the shore, or abundantly, or to their downfall, since a fall commonly occurs when water is poured out; or, “like water,” that is, for washing for some, because there were some who were refreshed by imitating their steadfastness.

> Yet although there were some who were washed by the killing of my own people, still, in comparison with the persecutors, “there was no one to bury them”—that is, no one who took their killing into himself by imitating them.

Note the intensification in the words “around Jerusalem”: the killing did not take place in only one place, but the killing by the nations went all around the Church. Thus “we have become a reproach to our neighbors,” namely, to those who were near us, from whom reproach is all the more grievous because it occurs more frequently to those who suffer.

And we became not only a reproach to those who were near us, but also “mockery and derision to those who are around us,” because inwardly they ridicule us and mock us through bodily gestures. Mockery occurs when, in contempt of someone, the nose and forehead are drawn together into a wrinkle.

> “How long, Lord, will you be angry to the end? Will your jealousy burn like fire?”

These words and those that follow are spoken indifferently with respect to either interpretation. It is as though he said: You, Lord, in whose presence all these things take place, how long—that is, how long will your anger last to the end? And how long will your jealousy—that is, your indignation—burn like fire?

It is as though he said: “Will it burn like a fire that incinerates and does not purify? Let it rather burn so as to purify than to incinerate.” Thus there is no disturbance of the divine mind, but vengeance upon iniquity. For it is written: “You, Lord Sabaoth, judge all things with tranquillity and dispose them with great reverence” (Wisdom 12).

The jealousy of the Lord is indignation, or the exacting of chastity, because the faithful soul is restrained from departing from the Lord through fornication. This is understood by comparison with a man who virilely keeps his wife under his authority, lest, if she become her own mistress, she do something disgraceful against her husband.

> “Pour out your wrath upon the nations that do not know you, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name.”

It is as though he said: Against your own people your jealousy will burn like a purifying fire and will not incinerate them. But upon the nations that do not know you pour out your wrath—that is, fully show them that you are angry with them. And upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name fully pour out your wrath.

You will rightly pour out your wrath, because “they have devoured Jacob”—that is, they incorporated some of the faithful into themselves inwardly, compelling them to pass over to their opinion; “and they have laid his place waste”—that is, each of the places of your holy ones. Or, “his place” means the ecclesiastical institutions in which the faithful ought firmly to stand and be established: they made these desolate, because, after the saints had been killed, the ecclesiastical institutions were left desolate.

Note the intensification of the wrath in the words “the nations that do not know you.” For the servant who knows his master and does things deserving of blows will be beaten with few (Luke 12), because in some way he acknowledges that he belongs to his master’s household when he does not disdain to know him, and thus he deserves to be punished less for his offenses. But the servant who disdains to know his master’s will shall be beaten with many blows (ibid.). Thus it is said here concerning the nations:
