> “Pour out your wrath upon the nations that do not know you, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name, because they have devoured Jacob and laid his place waste.”

> “Do not remember our former iniquities.”

It is as though he said: Appear angry toward them, but favorable toward us, not bringing the iniquities of our ancient fathers back to memory, so that you may not punish but forgive those offenses for which we ought rather to be condemned than corrected. And may your mercies quickly anticipate us—that is, may they take hold of us before we come to ruin.

And this is necessary, because “we have become exceedingly poor”—that is, we ourselves are not sufficient for our salvation, because we are weak and exceedingly feeble. May your mercy therefore help our weakness and feebleness, and may we understand your commandments lest we come to judgment to be condemned.

> “Help us, O God our Savior.”

Note that he is neither ungrateful toward grace nor opposed to free choice. For the one who asks to be helped retains in himself some spark of free choice, by which he has the capacity to begin. But because “it is not man’s [power] to direct his own way” (Proverbs 16; Jeremiah 10), he asks to be helped by grace.

He says: “Help us, O God our Savior, and for the glory of your name”—that is, so that your name may be glorified—“deliver us from evils and be favorable to our sins for the sake of your name,” granting that the tribulations which we suffer may be an atonement for our sins, so that, as our sins demand punishment, we may not yield to idolaters.

> “Lest they perhaps say among the nations, ‘Where is their God?’”

They may deny altogether that there is a God, or they may reproach us, saying: “Where is the one whom you promised would come?” It is as though they said: “Behold, it is evident that he takes no care of you.”

And lest they say this, “let the vengeance for the blood of your servants that has been shed become known among the nations before our eyes”—that is, let the vengeance for the blood of your servants become manifest, carried out among the nations before our eyes, even if it escapes the notice of those nations, since they do not recognize that they have been inwardly blinded.

> “And let the groaning of the imprisoned enter into your sight”—namely, of those who have been shackled and weighed down by the mortality of the flesh.

For those lament being shackled to whom mortal life is a sorrow and death an honor, in accordance with the saying: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Philippians 1). Or it may be understood thus: “Let the groaning of the imprisoned enter into your sight,” that is, of those bound by the commandments of wisdom.

Here a question arises. Since the Lord says, “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matthew 5), how can the saints desire vengeance upon their enemies, as in the Apocalypse: “Avenge our blood, O our God” (Revelation 6)? And likewise: “The righteous man will rejoice when he sees vengeance” (Psalm 57).

The answer must be that although the good seek vengeance upon their enemies, they do not seek it in order to rejoice in the enemy’s punishment. Rather, they seek it because they want the enemy to be corrected for the correction of others, as in the saying: “The righteous man will rejoice when he sees vengeance; he will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner” (ibid.).

Even if vengeance is reserved until the end, the good person does not rejoice in the enemy’s punishment, but in the Lord’s justice: those who in this life chose to share in evil will not there share in the reward of the good. The wicked, on the other hand, desire to be avenged upon their enemies because they seek this not in order to rejoice in God’s justice, but in the punishment of their enemies.

> “According to the greatness of your arm, possess the sons of those who have been put to death.”

It is as though he said: Let the groaning of the imprisoned enter your sight in such a way that the greatness of your arm may possess the sons of those who have been put to death. For they can accomplish things in you, not in themselves, as the Apostle says: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Philippians 4).

The sons of those who have been put to death are imitators of the martyrs, because the martyrs put themselves to death inwardly together with their vices and desires, while outwardly they are put to death by persecutors.

> “And repay our neighbors sevenfold in their bosom.”

It is as though he said: Let the greatness of your power possess the sons of those who have been put to death, but repay our neighbors sevenfold—that is, with full retribution—so that through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit they may recognize themselves as confounded and seek grace in your bosom.

And thus “repay them their reproach with which they reproached you, Lord,” so that what they reproached others with may, for your sake, be reproached to them.

Or otherwise: “Repay our neighbors sevenfold”—that is, full vengeance in body and soul, understood through the parts of the number seven, namely, four and three. The body, which consists of four elements, is understood through the number four; the soul through the number three, because of its three powers, namely reason, anger, and desire.

When he says, “Repay our neighbors sevenfold in their bosom,” he means firmly, so that it does not fall away from them. “And repay them their reproach with which they reproached you, Lord,” so that they may be destroyed in the very thing by which they think to destroy us.

> “But we, your people and the sheep of your pasture, will give thanks to you forever; and finally we shall announce your praise from generation to generation”—there, namely, where all the nations that succeed one another here will be like one generation.

# PSALM 79. FOR THE END, FOR THOSE WHO WILL BE CHANGED; A PSALM FOR THE ASSYRIANS; A TESTIMONY OF ASAPH

> “You who rule Israel, attend; you who lead Joseph like a sheep. You who sit upon the cherubim, manifest yourself before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. Stir up your power and come, that you may save us. O God, turn us back and show your face, and we shall be saved. Lord God of hosts, how long will you be angry against the prayer of your servant? You will feed us with the bread of tears, and give us drink in tears by measure. You have made us a contradiction to our neighbors, and our enemies have mocked us. O God of hosts, turn us back and show your face, and we shall be saved. You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it. You were the guide of its journey before it; you planted its roots, and it filled the land. Its shadow covered the mountains, and its branches the cedars of God. It stretched out its branches to the sea, and its shoots to the river. Why have you destroyed its hedge, so that all who pass along the way gather its grapes? The boar from the forest has ravaged it, and the solitary wild beast has devoured it. O God of hosts, turn back; look down from heaven, see, and visit this vine. And perfect it, the vine which your right hand planted, and the son of man whom you confirmed for yourself. Burned with fire and dug up, they will perish at the rebuke of your face. Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand and upon the son of man whom you confirmed for yourself. And we shall not depart from you; you will bring us to life, and we shall call upon your name. Lord God of hosts, turn us back and show your face, and we shall be saved.”

## EXPOSITION

This psalm speaks of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and of his vine. Asaph, corrected and enlightened, filled with the Holy Spirit, sings it. It is a psalm for those who will be changed.

Change may be for the worse or for the better. This psalm, however, does not speak of the change that is for the worse, since it speaks of the Lord’s coming, which was the cause of change for the better. For, “just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15).

It is a testimony because it testifies concerning the king and the people, the shepherd, the priest, and the flock; concerning Christ and his vine—in short, the whole mystery of the divine Scriptures, namely Christ and the Church, because every Scripture concerns either Christ or the Church.

And it is “for the Assyrians,” that is, for those who direct, so that those who were formerly a crooked and provoking generation might thereafter direct themselves according to the Lord’s will.

He speaks as follows:

> “You who rule Israel, attend”—that is, devote yourself attentively to this rule, ruling Israel, namely, the Jewish people.

> “And you who lead Joseph like a sheep”—namely, the people of the nations, who are understood through Joseph, because they were increased within the former people, so that from both there might be one.

Or someone may ask how Joseph was sold by his brothers and exalted in Egypt. Let us therefore recall under whom and with whom we are: namely, with Israel, that is, with the Jewish people who first believed, because “salvation is from the Jews” (John 4). Therefore, wild olive tree, do not be proud, but fear; for you do not carry the root, but the root carries you (Romans 11).

> “You who sit upon the cherubim, manifest yourself.”

The cherubim is the Church of God, and the word is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” Yet human weakness need not despair, because every believer is the seat of God, as it is written: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.”

Let each person also have charity, and he has the fullness of knowledge, because “the fullness of the law is charity” (Romans 13), and “whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4).

Thus he says: “You who sit upon the cherubim, manifest yourself”—that is, appear manifest before Ephraim, namely, before those who bear fruit in good works; before Benjamin, namely, before those who are sons of the right hand, not seeking earthly things that belong to the left, but heavenly things that belong to the right.

Or, “before Benjamin” means before those who do good works not for approval, which belongs to the left; and before Manasseh. Manasseh is interpreted as “forgetfulness,” and those are understood who forget what lies behind and reach forward to what lies ahead.

In all these figures are understood those who ought to be reckoned among the seed. It is as though he said: “Manifest yourself to those who are to be counted among the grains, even if you do not manifest yourself to those who are to be left among the chaff.”

> “Stir up your power and come, that you may save us.”

It is as though he said: Your power was asleep when the persecutor prevailed against you—not because the persecutor accomplished what he wished, but because you consented. You also prefigured this when Jacob wrestled with the angel.

Jacob prevailed, not because he accomplished what he himself wished, but because the angel consented. Jacob then asked a blessing from the angel he had defeated, and the angel blessed him; touching the breadth of his thigh, he sent him away lame (Genesis 32).

In the same way, the Lord blessed that same Jewish people and made it lame: he blessed it with respect to the apostles and the other faithful, and made it lame with respect to the unbelievers.

When he says, “Stir up your power,” it is as though he said: “Though dead through weakness, rise again in majesty” (2 Corinthians 13), and come into our knowledge, you whom previously we did not know.

For we saw you performing miracles, and yet we saw you dying, and therefore we did not think you to be what you were. Hence the saying: “We saw him having neither appearance nor beauty” (Isaiah 53). But now let us see you rising, ascending, and sitting at the right hand of God.

> “And come, that you may save us.”

> “O God, turn us back.”

It is as though he said: Your enemies seek to turn us away from you, but turn them back from the error of idolatry. “Show your face, and we shall be saved.”

Previously you concealed your power under the cloud of flesh and the veil of weakness, and we became sick. But now show your face, so that we may understand what concerns the needy and the poor, and we shall be saved, in accordance with the saying: “Afterward he was seen on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3).

And because you will do what I have prayed—namely, send your Son to turn us back—you, Lord God, not only of human beings but also of the heavenly powers, how long will you be angry? That is, how long will your anger remain against the prayer of your servant—that is, against what your servant prays?

Or, “you are angry against the prayer of your servant from above,” because what your servant prays he does not have from himself, but from you.

It is as though he said: “Behold, your enemies no longer pray, but your servants, who have been led out of prison, and still you are angry.” Yet you are not angry as an avenger raging, but as a Father correcting, since it is written: “My son, when you approach the service of the Lord, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Sirach 2); and also: “God scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12).

Therefore, if you refuse to be scourged, why do you desire to be received?

When he says, “Lord God of hosts, how long will you be angry against the prayer of your servant?” he asks, “How long, namely, shall we be fed?” The following words explain this:

> “You will feed us with the bread of tears.”

It is as though he said: Although you are angry with us, in that very anger you will feed us with the bread of tears—that is, you will refresh us with our tears as with bread.

> “And give us drink in tears by measure.”

Although you permit us to suffer tribulation, you do not do so without measure. Hence the saying: “Grace has been given to each of us according to the measure” (Ephesians 4), and: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able” (1 Corinthians 10).

> “You have made us a contradiction to our neighbors.”

Here is how you fed us with the bread of tears: you made us a contradiction to our neighbors.

We plainly know that what has been prophesied here was fulfilled, because many from that heavenly people became preachers. They preached Christ incarnate, dead, and restored to life—a matter incredible to them—yet they established faith in an incredible reality through signs.

They were contradicted, but the one who contradicted them was overcome: the one who had previously been a persecutor afterward became a humble imitator.

But because the flame of anger and the flame of persecution came first, although this was itself refreshment to those preachers, he says:

> “You will feed us with the bread of tears, and give us drink in tears by measure. You have made us a contradiction to our neighbors, and to such an extent that our enemies mocked us. But you, God of hosts, turn us back to yourself, those whom the enemy seeks to turn away; and show your face, namely your Son, and we shall be saved.”

And you ought to save us because you have already begun to do so, when:

> “You brought a vine out of Egypt, drove out the nations, and planted it,”

namely, in the promised land.

This may also be referred to the Church, because it is the vine brought out of Egypt—that is, taken from the power of darkness into the kingdom of light. “You drove out the nations”—that is, the errors of the nations—and planted it in the Catholic faith.

> “You were the guide of its journey before it.”

For by day you went before it in a cloud, and by night in fire, signifying your incarnate Son, who would go before the Church through the cloud of flesh and in the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

> “You planted its roots, and it filled the land.”

It did so to such an extent that:

> “Its shadow covered the mountains.”

To signify the great multitude of the people, he compared that people to a planted vine so greatly extended that its shadow covered the mountains.

Or it may be understood thus: “You planted its roots”—namely, the patriarchs, in whom the Church was prefigured, as fruit is prefigured in the root. “And its shadow covered the mountains.” The mountains are the prophets, whom the shadow of the Church covered, because they preached the Church figuratively and under the veil of symbols.

> “And its branches the cedars of God.”

The branches are the shoots proceeding from the true vine, namely, the lesser members of the Church. They cover the cedars of God—that is, they surround those who excel in virtues—when those who are eminent, descending to those who are branches, set aside the lofty contemplation of the mind and preach to them what they can grasp, instructing them through carnal things because they cannot yet grasp spiritual things.

Or, “the branches covered the cedars of God,” because the many who are branches are supported by each one who is a cedar. The statement is made by comparison: just as one trunk supports many shoots of a vine, so many are supported by one preacher—circumcision by Peter and uncircumcision by Paul.

> “It stretched out its branches”—that is, the generations of the people—“to the sea, and its shoots to the river,” namely, the Jordan, since the Jews are not read to have lived beyond the Jordan.

Or it may be understood thus: “It stretched out its branches”—that is, the generations of the Church—“to the sea of the nations, and its shoots to the river,” namely, the river of the Jews.

> “Why have you destroyed its hedge, so that all who pass along the way gather its grapes?”

Asaph, seeing that the Lord had done so much to exalt the Jewish people, wonders and asks, as though in astonishment: Why—that is, for what benefit to them—did God destroy its hedge, namely, its defense, the kingdom and priesthood by which they thought themselves protected? And why do all who pass along the way gather it—that is, destroy and deceive it?

The way is Christ, who is the true way.

He shows how the vine was destroyed:

> “The boar from the forest has ravaged it”—that is, Vespasian, sent from the forest, namely, from the gentile people, which was compared to a forest because it received no cultivation from divine preaching.

Note the word “ravaged,” because they were placed outside their boundary: they were expelled from the city and scattered everywhere.

> “And the solitary wild beast has devoured it”—namely, Titus, raging with singular ferocity.

Note the word “devoured,” because he exercised even greater savagery against them than his father Vespasian.

The words “Why have you destroyed its hedge?” can also be referred to the Church, so that we understand the hedge as the holy martyrs by whom the Church is fortified. All who do not walk along the way—that is, who do not imitate Christ—gather and destroy them.

The boar from the forest ravages them: every unclean person, uncultivated by the plow of preaching. The reference to the boar from the forest is apt because the pig is an unclean animal, and the forest is uncultivated land.

> “O God of hosts, turn back.”

It is as though he said: The hedge of the vine has been destroyed, and the vine itself has been ravaged. But you, God of hosts—namely, of the heavenly powers—turn from anger to mercy.

> “Look down from heaven”—that is, from your Son—“and visit this vine.”

Visit it, I say, by perfecting it, not by taking up another. Hence:

> “Perfect it, the vine which your right hand planted”—that is, your power—and perfect it, founded upon the Son of man, namely Christ, who is truly the foundation.

Hence the saying: “No one can lay a foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Corinthians 3).

> “And the son of man whom you confirmed for yourself”—that is, whom you made free from sin.

> “Burned with fire and dug up, they will perish at the rebuke of your face.”

It is as though he said: I have asked you to perfect the vine, and you will perfect it, so that neither height nor depth may separate the vine itself from you.

For at the rebuke of your face they will perish: “burned with fire”—that is, sins committed through evil love, because evil love inflames evil works; and “dug up”—that is, sins committed through evil fear, because evil fear is humbled by good things.

The comparison is with a wall: just as a wall, when it is dug into, threatens collapse, so anyone struck by evil fear is inclined to fall. For just as everything good proceeds from good fear and love, so every evil proceeds from evil fear and love.

Those who want to corrupt others commonly approach those whom they wish to corrupt with flatteries and promises, and many who have been blinded by evil love are corrupted. But happy is the soul that sets before itself the medicine of salvation against those promises.

> “For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matthew 16.)

That soul is also happy which is not corrupted by threats, setting before itself this divine commandment:

> “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10).

It also carefully considers that the world promises no unjust person as much as God promises the just. For what promise is greater than this one?

> “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matthew 25).

Nor can the world threaten the just with anything as great as God threatens the unjust, to whom he will say:

> “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (ibid.).

> “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand and upon the son of man whom you confirmed for yourself.”

It is as though he said: Give him authority over all flesh, because he is the Son of man. You confirmed him for yourself when your paternal voice was heard: “In whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3).

> “And we shall not depart from you.”

For you will bring us to life by making us worship you freely. We were dead when we bore the image of the first man and worshiped God for the sake of earthly things.

> “And we shall call upon your name.”

And in order that we may call upon it:

> “Lord God of hosts, turn us back and show your face, and we shall be saved.”

# PSALM 80. FOR THE END, FOR THE WINEPRESSES; A PSALM OF ASAPH HIMSELF; THE FIFTH DAY OF THE SABBATH

> “Rejoice in God our helper; shout for joy to the God of Jacob. Take up a psalm and give the tambourine, the pleasant psaltery with the lyre. Sound the trumpet at the new moon, on the notable day of your solemnity. For it is a commandment in Israel and a judgment for the God of Jacob. He established it as a testimony in Joseph when he went out from the land of Egypt; he heard a tongue that he did not know. He turned his back away from burdens; his hands served in the basket. You called upon me in tribulation, and I delivered you; I heard you in the hidden place of the storm; I tested you at the water of contradiction. Hear, my people, and I will testify against you: Israel, if you hear me, there shall be no new god among you, and you shall not worship a foreign god. For I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it. But my people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not attend to me. So I let them go according to the desires of their heart; they will walk in their own inventions. If my people had heard me, if Israel had walked in my ways, I would perhaps have humbled their enemies with no difficulty and laid my hand upon those who afflicted them. The enemies of the Lord lied to him, and their time will be forever. And he fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock.”

## EXPOSITION
Psalm 80 is sung by Asaph to the others who are Asaph, [Col. 0572C] and it treats the things signified by the things made on the fifth day of the week. For it is read that on the fifth day the Lord said: “Let the waters bring forth every creeping creature” (Gen. I); by these are signified those who have been regenerated through the font of baptism. And it is “for the winepresses”: in the winepress there are pressing and treading, and there two things are separated—the wine that is strained into the cellar, and the grape-skins that are thrown out to be trampled in the street. Oil too is separated from dregs: oil is stored in the storerooms, while the dregs are thrown into the street to be trampled. The exposition of the title is therefore as follows: “For the end” refers to these words, “spoken for the winepresses,” that is, for the pressing—pressing, I say, which distinguishes the things signified by the things created on the fifth day. And it is a Psalm of Asaph, speaking thus: “Let us enter, let us look, let us fear, let us rejoice, let us desire, let us flee,” because we shall be able to find all these things in the psalm.

## Rejoice in God our helper.

As though he were saying: You who until now have rejoiced in the world, your deceiver, and in the devil, your deserter, and in your belly, your seducer, henceforth rejoice in God our helper. And if voices are not enough for you, nevertheless let rejoicing not cease; but “shout joyfully to the God of Jacob.” As though he were saying: Rejoice in what you can express; shout for joy over what you cannot express. For a jubilus is such great joy of the mind that it cannot be expressed in the sound of the voice.

“Take up the psalm and give the tambourine.” Here “psalm” is used for “psaltery,” the effect being named for the cause. The psaltery, which sounds above, signifies spiritual things; but the tambourine, [Col. 0573A] which produces a lower sound, signifies bodily works. Here the Prophet urges us to answer divine words with bodily works. The Apostle likewise exhorts us, expressing his concern and reproach, when he says that no one shared with him “in the matter of giving and receiving” (Phil. IV). Elsewhere he says the same thing more plainly: “If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great matter if we reap your bodily things?” (I Cor. IX). As though he were saying: If you are eager to receive spiritual things, be devoted to distributing bodily things; and if you desire to receive spiritual things, do not be sluggish in distributing bodily things. Take up our voices and offer your hands. This is what he says: “Take up the psaltery,” that is, spiritual things from the mouth of the preacher, “and give the tambourine,” by offering bodily things. And why this? Because “the psaltery with the lyre is pleasing to God.” For whoever receives spiritual things and supplies bodily things renders a sweet melody to God.

“Blow the trumpet at the new moon.” Above he dealt with the love of God; here he urges that love of God be followed by love of neighbor, so that whoever loves God may also love his neighbor. As though he were saying: “Take up the psalm; blow at the new moon,” that is, openly and confidently preach the new life.

Note that “new moon” signifies the new life. *Neon* means “new,” and *mene* means “moon”; from this comes the word “month,” and thus, taken together, “new moon” signifies the new life. The trumpet, because it has a loud voice, signifies open confidence: for the new life ought to be preached openly and confidently. This is to be done “on the notable day of your solemnity,” namely, the solemnity of new restoration, of the ancient dispensation, and of eternal blessedness.

At this solemnity every believer must blow the trumpet, because “it is a statute in Israel and a judgment for the God of Jacob.” Note that judgment follows the necessary command, because the giver of the command himself said: “I have come into this world for judgment, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John IX). And what is this except that the proud may be humbled and the humble exalted?

“He placed it as a testimony in Joseph,” that is, the command given to Israel is the testimony of Joseph, namely, of the enlarged people—that is, of the Gentiles. It is a testimony, I say, of salvation fulfilled and of condemnation neglected.

Alternatively, our mind may recall how Joseph, sold by his brothers, was exalted, so that we may understand Christ, despised by his own people and exalted among the Gentiles after the sufferings of the holy martyrs, “when he went out from the land of Egypt.” What he says also suits the multiplied people: “when he went out from the land of Egypt.” Mystically he did not add “land,” because they too belong to the fifth day of the week. They also went out from Egypt when they were freed from the power of the devil and of darkness, since the passage of the Israelite people through the Red Sea prefigured nothing other than the passage of the faithful through baptism.

The Apostle bears witness to this: “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud and passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses” (I Cor. X). What else, then, did the passage through the Red Sea signify except the sacrament of those baptized? What else did the pursuing Egyptians signify except the abundance of sins? The Egyptians press and drive them as far as the sea; so sins press and drive us as far as baptism. But if, because of a bad conscience, you despair that your sins will be forgiven, beware lest something of the sins remain—as though some Egyptian had survived.

“He heard a language that he did not know.” What did the baptized people hear except that they must despise the world and lift their hearts upward? For it was said to them: “The world is passing away, and its desire” (I John II).

“He turned his back away from burdens.” Who turns his back away from burdens except the one who said: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI)? These burdens are the load of sins. Hence elsewhere: “And like a heavy burden they have become heavy upon me” (Ps. XXXVII).

What he says is, “He turned his back away from burdens”; and as though you were to ask, “From what burdens?”—“His hands served in the basket.” The basket signifies servile works. Cleaning, removing manure, and carrying earth are done with a basket; those who are weighed down in their heart by the burden of sins carry earth, as it were, in a basket. For “everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII).

“He turned his back away from burdens,” saying: “In tribulation you called upon me.” What tribulation is greater than the burden of sins? What was the affliction of the Egyptians among them, the burden of sins produces in us. He says: “In tribulation you called upon me, and I delivered you.”

Let every Christian conscience recognize whether it has devoutly crossed the Red Sea; whether, with the faith required for believing and observing, it has heard the language it did not know; and let it recognize that it has been heard in tribulation. For it was a great tribulation to be pressed down by burdens of sins, but the conscience has been relieved from it and rejoices, because the conscience that was oppressed yesterday rejoices today.

“In tribulation you called upon me, and I delivered you.” And how did this happen? “Because I answered you in the hidden place of the storm”—not in a great storm, but in the distress of the heart, where the storm of sins was crushing you.

But because, after someone has been heard and baptized, he may permit many enemies to rise up against him, he adds: “I tested you at the waters of contradiction.” The waters of contradiction are those who insult, slander, discourage, and even threaten wherever they can, so that they may draw a believer away from the faith. A person is tested among these when he is not ashamed to preach what he can defend and, amid the blasphemies of sinners, declares with his mouth what he has believed in his heart.

For if he is heard “in the hidden place of the storm,” he believes with the heart for righteousness; but when he is tested at the waters of contradiction, confession is made with the mouth for salvation (Rom. X).

How great the contradiction was at those waters, our ancestors experienced when the Gentiles fiercely resisted the word of God and the ministry of Christ, because then “the nations raged, and the peoples devised vain things” (Ps. II). Then that lion went roaring to meet the strong man Samson, who was coming to bring himself a bride from the Philistines; that is, Christ, descending to obtain the Church from the Gentiles. But what did he do? He seized and held that lion, broke and scattered it, and it became in his hands “like a young goat” (Judg. XIV).

For what else would that people become except a weakened sinner? Once that savagery had been killed, royal power no longer roars in this way, nor does the people of the Gentiles roar in this way; the lion does not go out to meet him. Instead, what is fitting is now found in its mouth: a honeycomb. For laws have even been established by rulers of the nations for the defense of the Christian religion, and thus the waters of contradiction have dried up.

“In tribulation you called upon me, and I delivered you,” saying:

## Hear, my people, and I will testify against you.

What we have heard from the beginning of the psalm up to this verse concerned the oil; what follows concerns the dregs of the winepress. It is more grievous and must be guarded against, but it must nevertheless be heard, so that the one who recognizes himself as oil may rejoice, and the one who is still in danger may fear lest he fall among the dregs.

What he says—“Hear, my people, and I will testify against you”—means: I have you yourself as a witness, and I speak to you. For I am not speaking to a foreign people, nor to a people that does not belong to the winepress.

“Judge,” he says, “between me and my vineyard” (Isa. V). What he says is: “Hear, my people, and I will testify against you”—namely, “Israel, if you hear me, there will be no new god among you.”

What is newer than that god who has recently been brought from the workshop into the temple, recently cast, and therefore confounded? The pagans make gods of this kind for themselves. Others—namely, many heretics—also make new gods, asserting that the Son is unequal to the Father, agreeing with the pagans in their vanity.

The Manichaeans too make a new god for themselves in another way, saying that God fights against the race of darkness, fearing that he may be invaded and striving lest he be corrupted. In this way they confuse themselves with a god fabricated by themselves. Although they have not placed idols in temples, they have placed them—what is worse—in their hearts, and have themselves become temples of false and laughable images.

These idols are within. It is a great work to cleanse a place for God who comes and does not depart. All who make gods of this kind for themselves, differing according to their various images and varying their faith through falsehood, nevertheless finally agree in one thing: they do not withdraw from earthly thoughts. Their opinions are diverse, but their vanity is one, because they extend themselves toward what lies behind, forgetting what lies ahead. Therefore Samson tied together the tails of foxes and fastened fire to them, so that he might burn the Philistines’ crops (Judg. XV).

These foxes signify heretics and deceitful people who, agreeing in what lies behind, draw fire behind them, tied together as if by their tails, and burn the crops of the Philistines—that is, of foreigners, not of sons—because “the Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II), and he does not permit the crops, that is, the good works of his own people, to be burned by heretics.

These foxes are also signified in the Song of Songs, where it says: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards, hiding in crooked caves” (Song II). A person catches a fox when he convicts a heretical and deceitful person of falsehood.

Foxes usually have burrows, entering from one side and exiting from the other. Therefore, whoever desires to catch a fox must set nets at both openings. The same must be done with deceitful people, who dwell in a double meaning as if in caves—like those who approached the Lord deceitfully, saying: “By what authority do you do these things?”

But because he knew that they were foxes asking deceitfully, he stretched a net before both openings, as it were, saying: “You also answer me one question: The baptism of John—where was it from, from heaven or from human beings?” But they, sensing that he had stretched out something by which he could catch them from either side, said within themselves: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why then did you not believe?’” For John bore witness to Christ. “If we say, ‘From earth,’ the people will stone us, because they regard him as a prophet.” Sensing, therefore, that there was a way to catch them on either side, they answered: “We do not know.” And the Lord said: “Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things” (Matt. XXI).

As though he were saying: Because you claim not to know what you do know, neither will I tell you what you ask, because you have dared to escape from neither side and have remained in your darkness.

Let us therefore obey, if we can, the word of God that says: “Catch for us those foxes that destroy the vineyards.” Let us see whether we can catch some little foxes. Let us set a net at both openings, so that whichever way the fox wishes to escape, it may be caught.

For example, to the Manichaean who makes a new Lord for himself, let us say and ask: Is the substance of God corruptible or incorruptible? Choose whichever you wish, O Manichaean, and escape whichever way you wish—but you will not escape. If you answer “corruptible,” you are rightly stoned not only by the Apostle but by yourself. If, however, you say “incorruptible,” how then did he fear the race of darkness? What will a race of corruption do to one who is incorruptible? What remains, then, except to say: “We do not know”?

Yet if this is said not deceitfully but out of ignorance, he does not remain in darkness; from a fox he becomes a sheep.

“Hear, my people, and I will testify against you,” that is, I will make you yourself a witness in this: if you hear me, there will be no new god among you. That is, in your heart, in the image of your fantasy, in the deception of your error, there will not be a new god, but the eternal God according to his divinity—new according to his humanity, needing no good and fearing no evil.

This ancient God makes the new human being; the new God makes the old. “You shall not worship a foreign god,” because if you do not conceive a false god in your mind, you will not worship a fabricated god.

And why will you not worship a foreign god? Because I alone am the Lord your God. Hence the words: “I am who I am.” And: “He who is has sent me to you” (Exod. III).

“I brought you out of the land of Egypt: open your mouth, and I will fill it.” As though he were saying: You suffer distress in your heart because of the new god. Break the vain image; cast the fabricated idol out of your conscience; open your mouth by confessing and loving, and I will fill it with the light of truth and with love of the true God, not the fabricated one; with love of the eternal God, not the new one. This is what I, the Lord, said to my people.

“And my people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not attend to me,” that is, it did not make itself attentive to me when I cried out to them to open their mouths so that I might fill them. Therefore I let them go according to the desires of their hearts, that is, according to earthly and bodily things, not according to spiritual things. Thus, abandoned by me, “they will walk in their own inventions,” that is, according to the inclination of their hearts.

Behold the winepress: its openings have been opened, and the dregs too are flowing out. Hence it was said: “They will walk in their own inventions.” And why will they walk in this way? Because they did not want to hear me.

For “if my people had heard me, if Israel had walked in my ways,” that is, if it had not strayed from my commands, “I would perhaps have humbled their enemies,” implicitly, as being worth nothing. “And I would have laid my hand upon those who afflicted them,” that is, I would have exercised my power against their afflictions.

“Perhaps” is placed here as a rebuke, not as an expression of doubt. Note that although the Lord says, “I would have laid my hand upon those who afflicted them,” nevertheless nothing can happen except what he permits, both among the good and among the wicked.

But because the enemy devil works more freely in the children of disobedience than among the good—for he plows in them as though in his own ox—yet in no one does he work except by permission, the text therefore says: “If my people had heard me, and if they had walked in my ways, perhaps I would have humbled their enemies, and I would have laid my hand upon those who afflicted them.” But my people did not hear me.

For they became “enemies of the Lord” and “lied to him,” that is, to his honor. “And their time will be,” that is, the day of their domination will be in this present age, not in the future: here they rule, but there they will be tormented. Or “their time” means the time of retribution—the punishment [the source reading is uncertain]—which will be forever; for it will begin here and never end there. Here they are blinded inwardly, so that finally there they may be tormented outwardly.

This is what he says: “The enemies of the Lord lied to him.” Yet although they were enemies, “he fed them with the fat of wheat,” that is, with the sacraments of faith, [Col. 0577C] “and he satisfied them with honey from the rock.”

The honey with which they were satisfied was the wisdom of Christ, in which many take delight: namely, in contemplating the sacraments and in interpreting his parables. And they cry out: “Nothing better, nothing sweeter could be understood or said.” This honey flowed not from just any human being, but from the rock; “and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X).

# PSALM 81. A PSALM OF ASAPH.

> “God stood in the assembly of gods; but in the midst he judges gods.  
> How long will you judge unjustly and take the faces of sinners?  
> Judge for the needy and the orphan; justify the humble and the poor.  
> Rescue the poor and deliver the needy from the hand of the sinner.  
> They did not know, nor did they understand; they walk in darkness.  
> All the foundations of the earth will be shaken.  
> I said: You are gods, and all of you are children of the Most High.  
> But you will die like human beings, and like one of the princes you will fall.  
> Arise, O God, judge the earth, for you shall inherit among all the nations.”

## Exposition

In this psalm the Prophet speaks against the Jews, both the lesser and the greater: exhorting the greater that, if they had unjustly judged in killing the servants sent to the vineyard, and the lesser had unjustly consented, then at least, when the heir was sent, the greater should not judge unjustly, nor should the lesser unjustly consent to them. And Asaph speaks as follows:

## God stood in the assembly of gods, but in the midst he judges gods.

As though he were saying: You are laboring to kill the heir sent to the vineyard. But God—that is, the Word made flesh—will stand in the assembly of gods, not of idols or false gods, but of those about whom he says below: “I said: You are gods.” For all who, by imitating him, have become participants in his divinity are gods, just as he himself became a participant in our humanity.

Note that he says “God stood,” not because standing, reclining, or being in a place belongs to God, but because one who stands appears to be upright. Therefore he is always unchangeable uprightness, and for this reason God is described as though standing.

“But in the midst he distinguishes gods,” making some apostles and others prophets; or, he distinguishes gods, first making some vessels for honor and others for dishonor.

Note that he says “in the midst,” because one who is in the middle appears equally to those standing around him. And because God is common to all, he is rightly said to be placed in the midst. Hence the words: “In your midst stood one whom you do not know” (John I).

## How long will you judge unjustly?

As though he were saying: If you judge unjustly by killing the servants sent to the vineyard, nevertheless do not judge unjustly when the heir is sent. The prophets were sent beforehand to cultivate the vineyard; you either treated them with insults or killed them altogether.

But when the heir has been sent, beware at last of judging unjustly, you greater ones.

You lesser ones: “How long will you take the faces of sinners?” That is, how long will you conform yourselves to your fathers by consenting unjustly to them?

## Judge for the needy and the orphan.

An orphan is one who lacks a father, even if he has a mother. This applies to the Lord, because just as he eternally willed to be without a mother, so temporally he willed to be without a father.

What he says—“Judge for the needy and the orphan”—means: judge for the honor of the needy and the orphan; and “justify the humble and the poor,” who was made humble in this judgment and became poor, although he was rich, for our sake. That is, proclaim him just to others.

## Rescue the poor and deliver the needy from the hand of the sinner.

This was said to the lesser ones. Since so many of the lesser people were present that the rulers feared them, they ought not to have consented to the rulers’ unjustly handing Christ over to be killed. For whenever anyone is unjustly condemned by rulers, the people ought to rescue him if the people see that this can be done without strife.

## They did not know, nor did they understand.

As though he were saying: I addressed the greater ones so that they would not judge unjustly, and the lesser ones so that they would not consent unjustly. Yet the greater ones did not know, nor did the lesser ones understand. For if the greater ones had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (I Cor. II); or if the lesser ones had understood, they would never have asked for Barabbas to be released and Jesus to be crucified. This is what he says: “They did not know, nor did they understand.”

And why? Because “they walk in darkness,” driving away from themselves the true light that illuminates every human being. Hence the words: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John I).

## All the foundations of the earth will be shaken.

All the leaders of the earth were shaken either toward faith or toward disturbance. Or “the foundations of the earth” means the hope of earthly things, in which earthly rulers trusted. Hence the words: “The world is passing away, and its desire” (I John II).

Or, literally, let us say: “All the foundations of the earth will be shaken,” because while the Lord hung upon the cross, a great earthquake occurred.

## I said: You are gods, and all of you are children of the Most High.

The preceding words can be connected in this way: “God stood,” saying: “I said: You are gods, and all of you are children of the Most High.”

As though he were saying: If you had imitated me, I proposed to make you all gods by taking you to myself, so that you might be my co-heirs. I called you all children of the Most High—not children begotten from his substance, but adopted through grace.

## But you will die like human beings.

That is, remaining in your sins and imitating your first parents, who apostatized from God through disobedience.

“And like one of the princes you will fall.” One of the princes said: “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV). But because he wished to exalt himself too greatly, he deserved to fall. By his example all who exalt themselves through pride fall.

## Arise, O God, judge the earth, for you shall inherit among all the nations.

They die by imitating their first parents. But you, arise, so that you may judge the earth—that is, allow yourself to be judged according to your humanity and rise again according to your divinity. And thus judge the earth, that is, the Jewish nation, which determined to lower its eyes toward the earth.

You will do this because, rising again, you will inherit among all the nations, since God the Father will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession.

# PSALM 82. A SONG, A PSALM OF ASAPH.

> “O God, who will be like you? Do not be silent, nor be restrained, O God,  
> for behold, your enemies have sounded forth, and those who hate you have lifted up their head.  
> They have plotted wickedly against your people and taken counsel against your holy ones.  
> They said: Come, let us destroy them from the nation, and let the name of Israel be remembered no more.  
> For they have conspired with one accord; together they have made a covenant against you:  
> the tents of the Edomites and the Ishmaelites; Moab and the Hagrites; Gebal, Ammon, and Amalek;  
> foreigners with the inhabitants of Tyre.  
> Assyria too has come with them; they have become a support for the sons of Lot.  
> Do to them as to Midian and Sisera, as to Jabin at the torrent of Kishon.  
> They perished at Endor; they became like dung for the earth.  
> Set their princes like Oreb and Zeeb, and Zebah and Zalmunna;  
> all their princes who said: Let us take possession of the sanctuary of God as an inheritance.  
> My God, make them like a wheel, and like stubble before the face of the wind.  
> As fire that burns the forest and as a flame that burns the mountains,  
> so you will pursue them in your storm and disturb them in your wrath.  
> Fill their faces with disgrace, and they will seek your name, O Lord.  
> Let them be ashamed and disturbed forever and ever; let them be confounded and perish.  
> And let them know that you alone are called Lord, the Most High in all the earth.”

## Exposition

The Prophet, foreseeing the tribulations that Christ would suffer in his body from the ungodly, and especially in the last times, when Antichrist will rage against the faithful, foretells them so that when the faithful see tribulations approaching they may not be frightened by astonishment, since it has been foretold to them for so long that they would have to suffer tribulation. For arrows foreseen do less harm. And so he says:

## O God, who will be like you? Do not be silent, nor be restrained, O God.

As though he were saying: O God, who wished to be counted among the ungodly and crucified with thieves—yet who among the former ones will be like you when you appear in glory? Certainly, no one.

Or otherwise: The wretched human race strives to make itself like you when it chooses to be governed by its own arrangement, whereas what happens is determined by your predestination and will. Yet who is like you? Certainly, no one. And nevertheless you allow the ungodly to be made like you, rather than subjected to you.

Or this psalm may be connected as follows: You will inherit among all the nations, but first you will be counted among the ungodly in weakness and crucified among thieves. But when you appear in glory, who among the former ones will be like you?

“Do not be silent, nor be restrained, O God.” You were silent earlier, when you were led like a sheep to slaughter and did not open your mouth (Isa. LIII); you were silent from judgment, although not from command. But when you come a second time, do not be silent from judgment, although you may be silent from command; do not be restrained, O God.

You restrained yourself when you said that you could have from the Father twelve legions of angels to defend you; nevertheless you permitted yourself to be seized, spat upon, scourged, and crucified.

## For behold, your enemies have sounded forth.

Behold why I say, “Do not be silent”: because your enemies, suppressing all fear, have sounded forth against your own. And therefore I say, “Do not be restrained,” because those who hate you have lifted up their head—that is, they have exercised their power against your people.

And because they have lifted it up, he adds:

## They have plotted wickedly against your people.

That is, with deliberate counsel they wished to exalt themselves over your people, namely, the lesser ones. And not only have they plotted wickedly against your people, but they have also taken counsel against your holy ones, each saying to the other:

“Come, let us destroy them from the nation, and let the name of Israel be remembered no more.”

And why this? “For they have conspired with one accord; together they have made a covenant against you,” that is, they have entered into a pact against your own:

“The tents of the Edomites,” that is, of earthly people; “and the Ishmaelites,” that is, those who obey themselves and not God; “Moab and the Hagrites, Gebal, Ammon, and Amalek, foreigners with the inhabitants of Tyre.”

“For Assyria too has come with them; they have become a support for the sons of Lot.”

By the Hebrew names all the enemies of Christ are understood, those by whom his people are afflicted. To see who they are, let us seek the interpretations of these names.

Moab means “one who abuses the law.” The Hagrites mean “foreigners.” Gebal means “a vain valley,” that is, deceptively humble. Here hypocrites are understood: they display humility outwardly, while inwardly the pride of their mind exalts them.

Ammon means “a turbulent people.” Amalek means “licking the earth.” The foreigners are the Philistines, namely, those who fall through drink, whom worldly prosperity has intoxicated. All these will come with the inhabitants of Tyre.

Tyre means “distress,” by which earthly people are indicated, constrained either by the love of acquiring or by the fear of losing.

Why did all these enter into such a pact? “For Assyria has come with them; they have become a support for the sons of Lot.”

Assyria means “the exalted one.” Who is this exalted one except the devil, who works in his vessels so that they may attack the people of God? And these assist the sons of Lot.

Lot means “one who turns aside.” Through him apostate angels are understood, those who turned aside from non-being [sic] into wretched weakness. The sons of Lot are those who, turning aside from true discernment, have placed themselves in the service of that apostate angel. For evil people are the devil’s instruments, by which he attacks the saints.

## Do to them as to Midian and Sisera, as to Jabin at the torrent of Kishon. They perished at Endor; they became like dung for the earth. Set their princes like Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah, and Zalmunna.

This is not a curse, but a confession and rejoicing in divine justice. All those whose names we have heard here were scattered and defeated by the Israelite people.

This scattering can also happen today if we return to the interpretation of the names. Midian means “turning aside from judgment,” and those are understood who wish to establish their own righteousness so as not to be subject to the righteousness of God.

Sisera means “exclusion of joy,” because in the end all joy will be excluded from the ungodly.

Jabin means “wise in his generation”; here those are designated who devote themselves to worldly wisdom, although the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.

Kishon means “their hardness”; here those are indicated who remain in the aridity of mind. Hence the words: “They tempted God in a waterless place” (Ps. LXXVII).

This is what he says: “Do to them as to Midian and Sisera, as to Jabin at the torrent of Kishon.” And because he asks and prophesies that what happened to Midian and the others should happen to Moab and the others who plotted wickedly against the Lord, he adds what they suffered: “They perished at Endor; they became like dung for the earth.” Hence the words: “The cattle rotted in their dung” (Joel I).

Endor means “the fountain of carnal generation.”

“Set their princes like Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah, and Zalmunna.” Oreb means “dryness”; Zeeb, “wolf”; Zebah, “the wolf’s victim”; Zalmunna, “the shadow of disturbance.” All these were defeated by the sons of Israel. In their likeness the Prophet here foretells that the persecutors of the faithful will perish.

And to summarize them briefly, he adds:

“All their princes who said: Let us take possession of the sanctuary of God as an inheritance—you, my God, make them like a wheel,” so that they may go around in circles. A wheel is lowered in its front part and rises in its rear part. Here those are understood who, forgetting what lies ahead, exalt themselves in what lies behind.

Or, “make them like a wheel,” that is, make them unstable, casting them down in the very thing in which they think they are being raised up. And make them “like stubble before the face of the wind,” so that they become comparable to stubble, which readily yields to the wind, just as they readily yield to temptation. Hence the words: “And like dust the wind will cast from the face of the earth” (Ps. I).

## As fire that burns the forest and as a flame that burns the mountains, so you will pursue them in your storm and disturb them in your wrath.

As though he were saying: I say that you should make them like a wheel; and this will happen because it will be easy for you to pursue them in your storm, in your terrible judgment, and to disturb them in your wrath, saying: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV).

It is easy for fire to burn a forest because of its dryness, and it is easy for a flame to burn a mountain, that is, the dry grass situated on the mountains.

And how will this happen? Because you will fill their faces with disgrace—those who here neglected your beautiful and glorious face. Then they will seek your name, O Lord, but too late, because their repentance there will be useless.

“Let them be ashamed” of their evil conscience, “and let them be disturbed” because they will be separated from the fellowship of the good. This will take place in the age that follows this present age. “Let them be confounded and perish,” and thus at last let them know that you are called Lord, when they say: “We fools thought that their life was madness,” and so forth (Wis. III).

“And let them know that you alone are the Most High in all the earth,” because both the good and the evil are subject to you, and you use even the evil for the salvation of your own, as in the words: “Assyria is the rod of my wrath, but he himself did not know it” (Isa. X).

Or otherwise: “Fill their faces with disgrace”; yet some of them will seek your name, because they will be ashamed of their evil conscience, disturbed toward repentance, and will perish in what they were, because from ungodly they will become godly. Thus they will know that you are called Lord; but only those know this who willingly make themselves servants. And they will know that you alone are the Most High in all the earth, both the fruitful and the unfruitful.

# PSALM 83. FOR THE END, FOR THE WINEPRESSES; A PSALM OF THE SONS OF KORAH.

[Col. 0582C]

> “How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts!  
> My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord.  
> My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God.  
> For the sparrow has found a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest for itself,  
> where it may place its young.  
> Your altars, O Lord of hosts, my king and my God.  
> Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord;  
> forever and ever they will praise you.  
> Blessed is the man whose help is from you;  
> he has set ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears, in the place that he established.  
> For the lawgiver will give blessing; they will go from strength to strength;  
> the God of gods will be seen in Zion.  
> Lord God of hosts, hear my prayer;  
> give ear, O God of Jacob.  
> Our protector, look upon us, O God, and look upon the face of your Christ, [Col. 0582D]  
> for one day in your courts is better than thousands.  
> I have chosen to be abject in the house of my God  
> rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners.  
> For God loves mercy and truth;  
> the Lord will give grace and glory.  
> He will not deprive those who walk in innocence.  
> O Lord of hosts, blessed is the man who hopes in you.”

## Exposition
This psalm, whose title reads “For the end, for the winepresses,” appears to say nothing about a press, baskets, a vat, or the other instruments belonging to visible winepresses. Rather, the Holy Spirit admonishes us to understand in this psalm those things that are mystically signified by these visible winepresses. Therefore, let us recall what takes place in these visible winepresses, and through this let us see how those mystical realities are brought about in the Church. [Col. 0583A]

The grape certainly hangs on the vine, and the olive on the trees, and, while hanging thus, they enjoy the open air. Winepresses are ordinarily prepared for these two fruits, because a grape is not wine, nor an olive oil, before they are pressed in the winepress. So also human beings, whom God predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (Rom. 8), who was expressed as a great cluster in his Passion, enjoy a delightful freedom before they enter servitude. But since it is written, “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Sir. 2), everyone who approaches the service of God should recognize that he has approached the winepresses, because there he will be troubled, there he will be compressed and afflicted—not so that he may perish in this world, but so that he may flow into God’s storehouses. And since this occurs only through pressure, the Church of the present age is rightly compared with winepresses. [Col. 0583B]

It follows: “For the sons of Korah.” *Korah* is interpreted as “nail.” This nail is Christ, crucified at the place of Calvary and prefigured by a certain bald man, namely the prophet Elisha. This psalm exhorts us to be sons of that bald man, so that we may not mock him, as foolish, chattering boys mocked that bald man who bore the type of this one; they were devoured by beasts (2 Kings 2). We must therefore beware lest, by mocking, we be devoured by beasts—namely, by the rulers of darkness. Let us therefore be his sons, that is, imitators, and not lovers of the world. [Col. 0583C]

For it is not without reason that money, which is loved in this world, is made round: namely, to show itself mobile and unstable, and thus to deter its lovers.

Asaph says the following:

“How beloved are your tabernacles, Lord”—not only those of human beings, but also those of the heavenly powers, that is, your camps in which you will receive your beloved ones—how incomparably beloved they are! And because they are beloved, “my soul longs for the courts of the Lord,” namely, for the heavenly Jerusalem, which is compared with courts because it is found to be full of every delight, just as courts are planted with sweet herbs and beautiful flowers so that people may delight there. [Col. 0583D]

“My soul longs and, in longing, fails”—namely, with respect to earthly things, just as elsewhere it says, “my spirit failed” (Ps. 76). It failed in itself, and therefore it advances in you, because no one advances in you unless he considers his own failure.

Note that although “tabernacles” are elsewhere understood as military dwellings, here they are nevertheless appropriately understood as the heavenly habitation, because there each person will be safe as though fortified by a strong castle. There will be no anxiety; there they will neither marry nor be given in marriage (Mark 12).

Or it may be understood thus: “How beloved are your tabernacles, Lord of hosts”—that is, your military dwellings, in which you afflict your own people as though in tabernacles, namely, the Church of this present age—how beloved they are to your people! For we are not only troubled, but also glory in our troubles. [Col. 0584A]

“My soul longs and fails for the courts of the Lord.” It is as though he said: Your tabernacles, in which we are now afflicted, are therefore beloved because my soul, placed in them, longs to ascend into the courts of the Lord. For from these tabernacles we sigh for those courts: here we sow, there we shall reap, because where there is weeping, there the sowing takes place. Hence the saying: “Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds” (Ps. 125). But what they sow in weeping they will reap in exultation; hence the saying: “Coming, they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” (ibid.). [Col. 0584B]

“My heart and my flesh have exulted in the living God.” It is as though he said: Because your tabernacles are beloved, my heart—that is, my inward mind—and my flesh—that is, my outward mind—have exulted in the living God, through whom one truly lives, through whom everything that exists exists.

And rightly have my flesh and my heart exulted: “For the sparrow has found a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest where it may place its young.”

The sparrow is a plaintive bird, signifying faithful souls. In this pilgrimage they perceive that everything is fleeting and transitory; therefore they complain that their exile is prolonged and that they are kept away from their homeland. Since they groan in this longing, they have, as it were, found a house for themselves, where they already dwell in hope and to which they will eventually arrive. [Col. 0584C]

The turtledove is a mourning bird, signifying people who perform good works—feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, visiting the sick. Since many do these things fruitlessly because they lack faith, he therefore says that it has found “a nest,” that is, faith and ecclesiastical institutions, where it may place its young, that is, its good works, because the place of true sacrifice is not outside the Catholic Church.

Note that he rightly says that the sparrow has found a house for itself and the turtledove a nest. The faithful soul that is now here in love of the heavenly habitation, in which it already dwells through hope, will one day possess a greater dwelling when it arrives there. Therefore it is said to have found, as it were, a house, because its love will never fail. Since beauty is insatiable, charity will be unfailing; since there are three things—faith, hope, and charity (1 Cor. 13)—faith and hope will pass away, while charity alone will remain. And since faith will endure only for a time, it is compared with a nest. [Col. 0584D]

Note that the flesh is compared with the turtledove because of the many pains by which it is afflicted. This is what he says: “and the turtledove a nest where it may place its young.”

He then explains what he calls the nest: “Your altars, Lord of hosts, my king”—that is, my renewer—“my God”—that is, my creator. By the altars, faith and ecclesiastical institutions are signified, because just as offerings are made on an altar, so confirmations of good works are made in faith, since it is impossible for anyone to be saved without faith.

“Blessed are those who dwell in your house; throughout the ages of ages they will praise you.” [Col. 0585A]

Note that every blessed person is blessed either by possessing or by acting. But the one who dwells in the house of the Lord is blessed both by possessing and by acting: by possessing, because he possesses God, who is everything to him in all things; and by acting, because he will praise God eternally.

This praise does not arise from necessity, but from free will and supreme delight. Every ordering of human acts is carried out under necessity; in the house of the Lord, however, there is no necessity, but an insatiable beauty accompanied by unfailing love, and therefore unfailing praise.

This verse can be connected with what precedes in the following way: “How beloved are your tabernacles, Lord!” Therefore blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord—not only those who have arrived there, but also those who are on the journey. Hence it says: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you,” that is, the one who, in this pilgrimage, receives help from you so that he may be taken from pilgrimage to his homeland. [Col. 0585B]

It then adds where his blessedness lies: “He has arranged ascents in the valley of tears,” where it is difficult to ascend. But if you wish to ascend, it is necessary to love in this tearful valley.

The valley of tears is this miserable life, into which we fell through the fall of our first parent. We were in him on the mountain of joy, but our first parent apostatized and was cast from the summit of the virtues into the depths of vices and into the valley of tears. Once placed in this valley, if someone does not wish to be submerged, he must arrange ascents, going toward the place that God appointed for the first human being to inhabit.

Or it may be understood thus: “He has arranged ascents in the valley of tears,” having been placed in the condition that the human being himself created for himself, and to which his guilt compelled him to descend.

And how does a person arrange ascents in his heart? The one who gave the law that presses down will also give the grace that lifts up. Hence it says: “For the lawgiver will give blessing,” that is, grace that lifts up and multiplies every good thing. The law could not accomplish this, because the law justified no one but enclosed everything under sin. “The commandment came, and sin revived” (Rom. 7). Concupiscence was not known to be sin until the law said, “You shall not covet.” [Col. 0585C]

Hence the Apostle says: “The law entered so that the trespass might increase; but where the trespass increased, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. 5). For those who were cast down and weakened through the law were raised up and healed through grace, as is confirmed by the authority of the Gospel.

“There was in Jerusalem a pool called Probatica, having five porticoes, in which lay a multitude of sick people,” and so forth (John 5). That water having five porticoes signifies the Jewish people, enclosed by the five books of Moses. The sick lay there because all who understood the law carnally, administered through the five books of Moses, lay sick. [Col. 0585D]

But when the angel came, the water was stirred, and one person was healed. This angel is Christ, namely, the angel of the great counsel (Isa. 9). When he came, the water was stirred—that is, the Jewish crowd was stirred toward his death. Whoever approached that death in faith was healed, namely, cleansed from sins.

Only one was healed because he rejected multiplicity and chose unity. For all the elect ought to be one in Christ, because there is one Christ, one faith, one baptism (Eph. 4).

Behold how grace lifted up those whom the law had pressed down. This is what is meant here by “the lawgiver will give blessing”—not a new God, but the God of former times, who will give blessing, that is, grace that lifts up. Thus “they will go from strength to strength,” namely, from the strength of action to the strength of contemplation. [Col. 0586A]

The virtues of action are fortitude, temperance, prudence, and justice. These will cease when “the God of gods is seen in Zion,” that is, in contemplation. There will be no hostile assault there against which fortitude is necessary; no impulses will arise there that temperance must restrain; there will be no needy person to whom anything must be distributed through justice because of his poverty; and there will be no evil that must be distinguished from the good through prudence. For there “the God of gods will be seen in Zion”—the God of Christians, who have been taken up by grace so that they may be gods. [Col. 0586B]

“Lord God of hosts, hear my prayer.”

Asaph, who speaks here, sees that he still rejoices in hope and not yet in possession. He therefore asks for perseverance in good works, so that he may not fall away from that hope. It is as though he said: In order that I may see the God of gods, you, Lord God of hosts, hear my prayer, made for the increase of the virtues.

“And listen with your ears, God of Jacob,” so that, just as you made Israel from Jacob, you may likewise make me one who sees God.

And you, our protector, look upon us through grace—you who looked away through anger—and “look upon the face of your anointed,” that is, make your Christ known to us, so that through him we may go from strength to strength.

Or: “Look upon the face of your anointed,” that is, upon those in whom the face and will of your Christ appear.

I therefore ask you to hear and look upon us because “one day in your courts,” that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem, is better than a thousand. It is a continuous day interrupted by no night; yesterday’s day does not precede it, nor does tomorrow’s day press upon it, because it is a day that will remain without end. This day is better than thousands of our days, arranged according to temporal periods, because there are insatiable beauty and unfailing light. [Col. 0586C]

In these present things everything is unstable and quickly passes away. Therefore “I chose to be despised in the house of my God,” where no one is nevertheless despised—for if it were possible for someone there to be considered lowly and despised, I would still prefer to be lowly and despised there than to dwell with the Lord in the tabernacles of sinners.

Or it may be understood thus: Since one day is better, “I chose to be despised in the house of God,” that is, in this Church where the faithful are despised, rather than to associate with the dominion of sinners in their tabernacles by consenting to their evil works. [Col. 0586D]

This is because I know that the Lord will not reject those who humble themselves: here he helps them, there he rewards them. For he loves mercy, by which he calls people to faith and justifies the ungodly. He also loves truth, because he rewards the worker through love.

Or he loves truth because he is truthful in his promises. “He will give grace,” that is, perseverance in good works, “and glory,” that is, the immortality of the flesh.

And truly he will give grace and glory, because he will not deprive those who walk in innocence of good things—that is, those who live innocently.

And since those who walk in innocence are not to be deprived of good things, “Lord of hosts, blessed is the person who hopes in you.”

# Psalm 84. For the End: A Psalm for the Sons of Korah

[Col. 0587A]

“Lord, you have blessed your land; you have turned away the captivity of Jacob. You have forgiven the iniquity of your people; you have covered all their sins. You have softened all your anger; you have turned away from the anger of your indignation. Turn us, God our Savior, and turn your anger away from us. Will you be angry with us forever? Or will you prolong your anger from generation to generation? God, you turn; you will revive us, and your people will rejoice in you. Show us, Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation. I will hear what the Lord God will speak within me, for he will speak peace to his people, to his holy ones, and to those who turn to the heart. Yet his salvation is near those who fear him, so that glory may dwell in our land. Mercy and truth have met one another; righteousness and peace have kissed. Truth has arisen from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven: for the Lord will give goodness, and our land will give its fruit. Righteousness will walk before him, and he will set his footsteps on the way.”

## Exposition

In this psalm, one of the sons of Korah speaks to the other sons of Korah, prophesying to them the coming of our Savior Jesus Christ. He exhorts them not merely to rejoice together over his coming, but also to imitate his Passion. He says the following: [Col. 0587B]

“You have blessed your land, Lord; you have turned away the captivity of Jacob.”

The Prophet speaks in the past tense of what he foresees in the spirit as future. It is as though he said: Lord, you have blessed your Word—that is, while blessing your land, namely human nature, by personally uniting it to yourself.

Note that this land is blessed because it has been multiplied in every virtue, since in it “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily and substantially.”

“You have turned away the captivity of Jacob.”

This captivity is not external but internal. He did not free us from barbarian nations, which we have not yet encountered, but from dead works. Paul speaks of this captivity: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin and death” (Rom. 7). [Col. 0587D]

Paul himself shows who the liberator of this captivity is, crying out under that captivity: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid.).

Or it may be understood thus: “You have blessed your land, Lord,” that is, human nature created by you, which was cursed in our first parent, to whom it was said, “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Gen. 3).

“You have turned away the captivity of Jacob.” And how has this happened? Because “you have forgiven the iniquity of your people,” which was intense in our first parent because it involved everyone, and is forgiven to no one except the one who gives concentrated attention to it.

Confess, therefore, that you are in captivity, so that you may be worthy to be freed from captivity. For if someone does not understand his enemy, how can he call upon a liberator? [Col. 0588A]

“You have covered all their sins”—you have covered them, I say, so that you would not see them, that is, so that you would not punish them in your people.

And behold how you covered their sins: “you softened all your anger,” both with respect to original sin and with respect to actual sin.

Note that the Lord’s anger has been softened, not entirely removed. For although sins have been forgiven, the punishment of sins nevertheless remains in us. Although anger has ceased with respect to condemnation, it has not yet ceased with respect to testing.

“You have turned away from the anger of your indignation.”

It is as though he said: Now you have softened your anger, and one day you will turn away from the anger of your indignation by removing it entirely and crowning your people with the glory of incorruptibility.

“Turn us, God our Savior, and turn your anger away from us.” [Col. 0588B]

Since these things are spoken of the future, although the verbs sound as though they refer to the past, he continues and says: “Turn us, God, who have turned away from you”—you, I say, who are our Savior—“and turn your anger away from us.”

It is clear that what he said had been accomplished had not yet been accomplished, because he prays that it may come to pass. For when he first said, “You have turned away the captivity” and “you have covered the sins,” he showed that he was speaking of the future, and then turned to prayer as follows: “Turn us, God our Savior, and turn your anger away from us.”

Because of God’s anger we are mortal. Through God’s anger, in this land, amid poverty and the labor of our faces, we have eaten bread. Adam heard this when we were all in him, because “in Adam all die” (1 Cor. 15). What he heard has reached us. [Col. 0588C]

We did not yet exist, but we were in Adam. Therefore whatever was established in him by the divine judgment has reached us, so that we might die.
