The sins of parents do not pertain to children when the parents commit them after their children have already been born. Once children have been born, the children belong to themselves and the parents to themselves.

Thus, if those who have been born hold to the evil ways of their parents, they must bear their parents’ merits as well. But if they change themselves and do not imitate their evil parents, they begin to possess their own merit, not their parents’ merit.

Indeed, your father’s sin does not harm you if you change yourself; nor does it harm your father if he changes himself.

“Will you be angry with us forever, or will you prolong your anger from generation to generation?” [Col. 0588D]

It is as though he said: I say that you should turn us, who have turned away from you, and turn your anger away from us, conforming us to the one whom you will send (Exod. 4). You will indeed do this, because your anger will not remain forever. This is what is meant by, “Will you be angry with us forever?” Or will you extend your anger from the carnal generation to the spiritual generation, so that just as your anger remained against the ancient people, it may remain against the people of grace?

The first generation was mortal, arising from your anger; the second generation will be immortal, arising from your mercy.

“God, you will revive us.” [Col. 0589A]

Since he had promised that the Lord’s anger would be softened and would not remain forever, lest anyone suppose that this would happen through his own merit, he adds: “God, you turn”—that is, you call us to conversion—“you will revive us,” so that we may understand that not only our revival but also our justification and conversion come from you. Thus we will be revived, and your people, no longer belonging to themselves, will rejoice in you and not in themselves.

They rejoice in themselves to their own harm, but in their good they will rejoice in you. For when they wished to find joys in themselves, they found grief in themselves. But now, since God is our entire joy, let the one who wishes rejoice safely in him who cannot perish.

All earthly things in which a person places his joy are destined to perish, and they drag the person with them into destruction. Rejoice, therefore, in that light which yesterday’s day does not precede and tomorrow’s day does not follow.

He himself shows what that light is: “I am,” he says, “the light of the world” (John 8). By saying, “I am the light of the world,” he calls you to himself. When he calls you, he turns you; when he turns you, he heals you; when he has healed you, you will see the one who turns you, to whom it is said, “and your people will rejoice in you.” [Col. 0589B]

And so that it may rejoice in you: “Show us, Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation.” That is, show the human being to human beings, and grant us your salvation, namely, that we may contemplate God in his majesty, having been made gods through him.

Behold the great mercy: so that human beings might eat the bread of angels, the redeemer of angels became human.

Behold the maternal affection: when we were unworthy to eat in the solidity of his majesty, he offered and poured out milk for us from himself when he appeared to us, invisible as he was, in human nature. He made himself such a one as could be grasped by human beings.

No human being could grasp Christ as God, but he became human for human beings. He preserved himself as God for the gods, concerning whom it is said: “But you are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81). [Col. 0589C]

These gods will see him as he is if they remain in the one in whom they now believe as Lord God. For the one who now rejoices in hope will one day rejoice in possession, because he will see him as he is. He himself promised this: “I will manifest myself to him” (John 14).

Why, then, do we not yet see our Father? Because it has not yet appeared what we shall be. And what shall we be? John makes this clear in his Epistle: “We know,” he says, “that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

“I will hear what the Lord God will speak within me.” [Col. 0589D]

It is as though he said: I prayed to the Lord that he might show us his mercy. He will indeed do this, because inwardly I hear what the Lord God speaks within me.

And what do I hear? “For he will speak peace to his people.” Hence the Apostle says: “The Lord came and preached peace to those who were near” (Eph. 2)—the peace of which it is said, “In me you will have peace; in the world you will have tribulation” (John 16).

Or it is that peace in which “God will be all in all” (1 Cor. 15).

Or it may be understood another way: “Show us, Lord, your mercy.” And in order that you may show it, I will make myself fit for it insofar as I can, because I will restrain myself from all the world’s tumult. Closing my ear against the turmoil of this restless life, I will turn toward my inward self, so that I may hear—not with the outer ear but with the inner ear, the ear capable of hearing—what the Lord God speaks within me.

And rightly will I hear, because he will speak peace to his future people. [Col. 0590A]

Peace exists where there is no war, no contradiction, no one resisting, and no adversity. Such peace is not to be sought here, because there is no saint who does not have a conflict with the devil, and who does not struggle against vices and desires by restraining unlawful impulses.

Since true peace cannot exist in this world, let us love the peace that is to come and refresh ourselves through hope in that world. When it comes, it will be the end of every battle, without which no one is now a saint.

For no righteous person is free from the punishments of sin: hunger, thirst, and weariness, against which we must struggle, because they attack us. We struggle and seek to be refreshed by food; yet the very lack of food will again become a refreshment for us. If we take food to excess, we become weary; we seek to sit, and again we grow tired if we remain seated for too long. [Col. 0590B]

Since there is no true refreshment in these things, let us despise what attacks us and love what the Lord speaks as he comes to his people.

And lest the Jewish people, applauding themselves, should say, “We are his people; that peace will be announced to us alone,” he determines over whom that peace will come, saying: “And upon his holy ones, and upon those who turn their hearts.”

Not Judea alone will be his people, but his people will be gathered from all nations, because from every nation some will be holy, and from every nation some will turn to the heart.

Those turn to the heart who consider that they were created in the image of God, and who carve their hearts away from the unlawful and varied thoughts of earthly things, by which they are hindered from contemplating heavenly things alone. They are often told: “Return, transgressors, to the heart” (Isa. 46). [Col. 0590C]

“Yet his salvation is near those who fear him.”

It is as though he said: Although that peace will be future for all who turn their hearts, nevertheless his salvation will be near those who fear him—that is, those who serve him out of fear, not out of love—namely, near the Jews, because “salvation is from the Jews” (John 4).

He explains how salvation is near him: “so that glory may dwell”—that is, the Word made flesh (John 1)—“in our land,” namely, in the land of the Jews. For there he dwelt bodily; from there he began to preach; from there the apostles came, and they were first sent there; there was the temple; there sacrifices were offered; from there came the Virgin Mary who gave birth to Christ; there he performed miracles.

Finally, he bestowed such honor upon that people that when a certain Canaanite woman appealed to him, seeking healing for her daughter, he said to her: “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 15). [Col. 0590D]

Thus, foreseeing this in the spirit, the Prophet says: “Yet his salvation is near those who fear him.”

He was feared by the Jews alone, because they sought carnal things from him. They feared that he would send them into captivity, take their land from them, strike their vines with hail, or make their wives barren. They held fast to these carnal promises of God, and therefore they feared him.

The nations likewise sought earthly things, but not from God, because they believed that all things were given to them by their idols.

“So that glory may dwell in our land,” in which all transgressions are forgiven.

“Mercy and truth,” by which promises are fulfilled, “have met one another,” because these two converge in Christ. [Col. 0591A]

Truth was in him with respect to the Jews, because he had been promised to them and the divine utterances were there.

Where was mercy? Among those who had abandoned their God and turned to demons. But did he despise them as well? No, because he called them through mercy.

It is as though he said: Call even these who have fled far away and have withdrawn greatly from me. Call them, and they will find me seeking them, although they wished to seek me.

Behold how mercy and truth met one another in Christ.

It follows: “Righteousness and peace have kissed.”

This pertains to us, because when Christ came, righteousness and peace converged in human beings through his grace.

Note that if you do not love peace, you will not have it. These two—righteousness and peace—love each other and kiss each other, so that whoever does righteousness may find peace. [Col. 0591B]

Righteousness must therefore go before, and peace follow. Righteousness says: “You shall not steal; you shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20); “Do not do to another what you do not wish to suffer” (Tob. 4; Matt. 7).

Perhaps you despise these things, and peace says to you: “Why do you seek me? I am the friend of righteousness; whoever I find to be an enemy of my friend, I do not approach.”

Do you wish to come to peace? Do righteousness. Hence another psalm says: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36). Doing this is righteousness. Then seek peace and pursue it, and righteousness and peace will kiss one another in this way.

But in order that this may happen, “truth has arisen from the earth,” that is, Christ, who says of himself: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14).

He will be born from the Virgin Mary, and thus “righteousness”—that is, the faith that justifies—“looked down from heaven,” namely, from the Lord’s humanity, through which he will look upon us. [Col. 0591C]

And how will this happen? “For the Lord will give goodness,” that is, abundant grace. Thus our land, which previously produced thorns and thistles, will give its fruit, namely, the fruit of good works. This does not arise from merit but from God’s grace.

For “righteousness,” namely Christ, from whom all righteousness proceeds, “will walk before him.” He acts in the place of an ambassador, making reconciliation between what is above and what is below, and he will set his footsteps—that is, his affections—“on the way,” that is, in human beings who have already been made his way.

Some of the foregoing may be read differently, as follows:

“And upon his holy ones”—that is, the grains among the Jewish people—“and upon those who turn to the heart.” This was said about the nations, which had turned away from the heart because they had lost the power of reason, did not know God, worshiped idols, and preferred creatures to the Creator. [Col. 0591D]

They were turned toward the heart—that is, toward the exercise of reason—when they understood themselves to be unclean and, as it were, swine, recognized their sins, and considered that they needed a physician.

“Yet his salvation is near those who fear him.”

It is as though he said: Although the Lord’s peace—whether the future peace, namely eternal life, or reconciliation itself, presented to the human race through the wisdom of God the Father—will be upon those who turn to the heart, nevertheless it remains that “the one who stands should take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10). That is, those who have turned toward their heart should fear lest they again withdraw from the heart through their transgression.

For his salvation is near those who fear in this manner, so that glory—namely Christ—may dwell in our land, that is, in our body conformed to him. [Col. 0592A]

Hence Paul says: “Let each one know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire, like the nations that do not know God” (1 Thess. 4).

Or it may be understood thus: So that the glory of immortality may dwell, it remains that, through the disobedience we render to the Lord’s humanity, the glory of incorruptibility may return to our land.

“Mercy and truth have met one another.”

It is as though he said: The Lord will speak peace in this way to his holy ones and to those who turn their hearts, because mercy and truth will converge in him. “Righteousness and peace have kissed” in us, because, having been justified through him, we will have peace with God through him (Rom. 5).

And how does this happen? Because “truth has arisen from the earth,” that is, a true confession will arise from human beings, since nothing is truer than for a human being to confess that he is a sinner. [Col. 0592B]

The tax collector understood this and was striking his breast, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18). Behold, truth arose from the earth, because confession of sins was made by a human being.

But what follows? “Amen, I say to you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other” (ibid.).

And so that we may recognize that “truth” signifies confession, let us hear John saying: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1).

Since, after confession has been made, justifying faith looks upon us from heaven—that is, from the divinity—this same John adds: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity” (ibid.). [Col. 0592C]

It is as though divine knowledge said: Let us spare this person, because he does not spare himself; let us forgive him, because he acknowledges himself. He has turned toward punishing himself; I will turn toward freeing him.

Behold how “righteousness looked down from heaven.” This does not arise from merit but from grace.

“For the Lord will give goodness,” that is, abundant grace, so that righteousness will begin to delight the one whom iniquity previously delighted; the one who previously rejoiced in drunkenness will now rejoice in sobriety; the one whom previously it delighted to seize what belonged to another will now delight to give away what belongs to himself.

Thus our land will give its fruit. And this will happen because “righteousness”—that is, our confession, which justifies a person—will walk before him. Hence the saying: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness” (Rom. 10). [Col. 0592D]

It will be pleasing to the Lord, because he will thus set his footsteps on the way, that is, his affections in human beings.

# Psalm 85. A Prayer of David

[Col. 0593A]

“Incline your ear, Lord, and hear me, for I am needy and poor. Guard my soul, for I am holy; save your servant, my God, who hopes in you. Have mercy on me, Lord, for I have cried to you all day; gladden the soul of your servant, for to you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul. For you, Lord, are kind and gentle, and rich in mercy to all who call upon you. Listen with your ears, Lord, to my prayer, and attend to the voice of my supplication. In the day of my tribulation I cried to you, because you heard me. There is none like you among the gods, Lord, and there are no works like yours. All the nations that you have made will come and worship before you, Lord, and they will glorify your name. For you are great and do wondrous things; you alone are God. Lead me, Lord, in your way, and I will walk in your truth; let my heart rejoice, so that it may fear your name. I will confess to you, Lord my God, with all my heart, and I will glorify your name forever. For your mercy is great toward me, and you have rescued my soul from the lowest underworld. God, the wicked have risen against me, and the assembly of the powerful has sought my soul, and they have not set you before their eyes. But you, Lord God, are compassionate and merciful, patient and rich in mercy, and truthful. Look upon me and have mercy on me; give your authority to your servant, and save the son of your maidservant. Establish with me a sign for good, so that those who hate me may see and be confounded, because you, Lord, have helped me and consoled me.” [Col. 0593B]

## Exposition

God the Father could not bestow upon human beings any greater gift than to make his Word, through whom he created all things, their head, and to join human beings to him as members, so that he would be God with the Father and human with human beings. He both prays for us and prays in us, and he is worshiped by us.

He prays for us because he is priest and victim, daily interceding for us with God the Father. [Col. 0593C]

He prays in us because he is our head. Nor is it surprising that Christ and his Church are in one voice, because they are in one body.

He is prayed to by us as our God; he is prayed to in the form of God and prays in the form of a servant. Here he is the Creator; there, the creature. This psalm is entitled by his prayer.

For he prays in this psalm not out of necessity, but to teach us to pray and to establish for us a form of prayer.

He says the following.

Incline your ear, O Lord, and hear me. Our Head, speaking from the form of a servant, says this: “Lord, Word, incline your ear and hear me”; and you, servant, speak thus in the form of your Lord: “Incline, O Lord, your ear, and hear me.” He truly inclines his ear, but you do not raise your neck; for he draws near to the humbled, and withdraws from the haughty.

Notice that he speaks in human fashion when he says: “[Col. 0593D] Incline, O Lord, your ear, and hear me.” For when people are asked by their friends, they ordinarily show some affection beforehand, and thus hear their friends favorably. Hence he says: “Incline, O Lord, your ear, and hear me.” As if he were saying: “I am sick and cannot raise myself up to you, because it is not man’s task to direct his own way” (Jer. X). But you, like a faithful physician, incline your ear to me and hear me.

And you ought to hear me, because I am needy—that is, without help, having no assistance except in you—and I am poor, that is, insufficient in every respect. Notice that the needy and the poor—that is, the humble and confessing—are the ones who are heard; for God’s ear is not inclined toward the satiated person who boasts as though he lacked nothing. The rich Pharisee boasted of many things, while the needy publican confessed: the latter was heard, the former condemned (Luke XVIII).

Yet it must not be said that God in no way hears the rich. If they were born rich—that is, into an ample inheritance and a great family—or if they rose to that station among human affairs in which they became wealthy, they can be heard, provided only that they do not presume upon their riches, but cast away from themselves everything that overflows toward presumption, heeding Paul’s words: “Command the rich of this age not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches” (I Tim. VI).

Abraham observed this. Scripture announces that he possessed a great amount of gold and silver and was rich on earth. He regarded riches as nothing to such an extent that, when commanded by the Lord, he did not hesitate to sacrifice his son (Gen. XXII), the one for whom he was preserving his riches. Job likewise observed this: he lived innocently amid great riches and, after losing everything, blessed God (Job I). Let the rich of this age therefore imitate these two fathers, and the Lord will incline his ears to them as to the needy and the poor. For “I know their afflicted heart,” and riches will not harm them unless they sin through presumption. In the same way, poverty does not profit toward salvation if humility is absent. Lazarus, poor and covered with sores, was not received by the angels merely because of his poverty; nor was the rich man sent to torments merely because of his riches (Luke XVI). Rather, humility was glorified in the poor man, and pride condemned in the rich man.

“Guard my soul, for I am holy.” There were some who said that the Father’s Word assumed flesh but not a soul. So that we may not imitate their error, let us hear God himself praying and saying: “Guard my soul, for I am holy.” No one can put forward this reason for being heard except one who was without sin in this world: not because no sins had been committed, but because all had been forgiven. He is holy, not sanctified by others, but sanctifying all others who have been sanctified; and therefore he may confidently say: “Guard my soul, for I am holy.”

If, however, we understand this as spoken in the voice of the members, we shall say: “Guard my soul,” that is, the soul of my members, “for I am holy,” that is, my members are holy, sanctified by grace. Hence Paul says: “And such were some of you, but you were washed, but you were sanctified” (I Cor. VI). In this way, “for I am holy” can be understood as the confession of one who is neither ungrateful nor lifted up by pride. For if you say that you are holy of yourself, you are a liar and proud. The Apostle rebukes this pride: “For what do you have that you did not receive?” (I Cor. IV.) Again, if the faithful person in Christ and member of Christ says that he is not holy, he is ungrateful. Let each person therefore say, without presuming upon himself: “Guard my soul, for I am holy.”

“Save your servant, my God, who hopes in you,” not one who presumes upon himself. Here it becomes clear that the holy person is not proud, because he says that he hopes in the Lord.

“Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I will cry to you all day.” The body of Christ cried all day, that is, at all times, because the tribulations for which each person must cry and groan in his own days will last until the end of the age. Let the person who now lives cry now; when he dies, his inheritance succeeds him. Let him cry so that his cry may last all day, that is, extend to the end of the age.

Or, “I cried all day” means: with the whole clarity of the mind, casting away all thoughts of darkness. “Gladden the soul of your servant,” whose soul you have saddened—or rather, the soul of your freedman, namely Adam, who fell from your excellent and glorious service into the lowest and most disgraceful freedom of his own. This is what he says: “Gladden the soul of your servant.”

And you ought to do so, because “to you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul.” Notice that, in order to lift your soul to the Lord, you do not need ropes or other machines by which to raise it to the Lord. Rather, good affections are your steps toward the Lord, and your will is your road. By loving, you ascend; by neglecting, you descend. Standing on earth, you are in heaven if you love God.

The heart is not lifted in the same way as the body. For the body changes its place in order to be lifted; the heart changes its will. “To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul”—and rightly to you, because in the world my soul has nothing but oppression and bitterness, and it has nothing by which it might become sweet unless it lifts itself to you.

“For you, O Lord, are sweet,” that is, gentle, “and mild,” patiently enduring us until you perfect us. How patiently God endures us is easy for anyone to observe if he is willing to descend into himself. For scarcely anyone can end that most blessed prayer in which he ought to speak familiarly and attentively with God without falling into fantasies and empty illusions. Hence elsewhere: “For my loins are filled with illusions.”

Yet in all these things God endures us until he perfects us, and until we find our heart so that we may pray to him worthily. Hence David says: “I have found, O Lord God, my heart, that I might pray to you” (II Sam. VII).

God endures in us what no judge or friend would be willing to endure. For there is no friend who would not take it badly if, while he had decided to speak with his companion, he saw that companion turn to someone else and wish to converse with another. Nor is there any judge who would not become indignant if, after appointing a time for someone to speak with him, that person suddenly turned to someone else and began speaking with him.

“For you, O Lord, are sweet and mild, and of great mercy”: because you call freely and freely justify those whom you call; or, you are of great mercy because you reward your gifts in us—you who give the will to do good and enable us to act well according to that good will; or, in contrast with our many iniquities, you are greatly merciful to all who call upon you, that is, who call you into themselves.

This does not conflict with what Scripture says elsewhere: “They will call, and I will not hear them” (Prov. I). They are not heard because they do not call God into themselves; rather, they call money and the other things they love into themselves. But those who call God into themselves are always heard. Hence in the Gospel: “Ask, and you shall receive” (Matt. VII); and: “One thing I asked of the Lord; this I will seek” (Ps. XXVI).

Ask, then, for what ought to be asked, and you will receive it. Do not ask for the death of your enemy, because in that request you are not worthy to be heard. Instead say: “I will not ask for the death of my enemy, but for the life of my son.”

“What evil, then, shall I ask?” You were asking for no evil, as you understood it. For what if he was taken away so that wickedness might not change his understanding? But he was a sinful and unjust man, and therefore I wanted him to live so that he might be corrected; you wanted him to live so that he might become better. What if God knew that he would become worse if he lived? How, then, do you know whether it would have benefited him to die or to live? Since you do not know, return to your heart; leave your counsel to God.

Call upon God as God; love him as God. Nothing is better than he. In him alone there are joy and security, because no human being has certain joy either in himself or in another. For people are either evil, and it is necessary to endure them, or good, but one must fear that they may change into wickedness. Therefore nothing gives certain joy except God. He is perfectly good and will always remain in goodness.

This is what he says: “For you, O Lord, are sweet and mild, and of great mercy to all who call upon you.” And because you, God, are sweet and mild, therefore, O Lord, “give heed with your ears,” that is, receive with gracious hearing, “my prayer,” that is, the prayer of my members, made for the increase of virtues; “and attend to the voice of my supplication,” that is, turn your attention to my members supplicating for their beloved.

And behold why you ought to hear: “For in the day of my tribulation,” that is, in the time of my pilgrimage, namely in this life—for everyone who is estranged from God is afflicted—“I cried to you,” implicitly, in order to win your favor. The result shows this, because you heard me; for the person who has truly cried to you cannot fail to be heard.

And rightly we cry to you, because “there is none like you among the gods.” Let the pagans invent whatever gods they wish, and hire silversmiths, goldsmiths, interpreters, and sculptors to make gods for themselves. Among all these there is none like you, O Lord, because they have eyes and do not see, and so forth.

Notice that he said: “There is none like you.” This may indeed be said; but in what respect God is like, it cannot be said. For what God is not can be understood—that he is not an angel or some other creature—but what God is cannot be explained, because “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart” (I Cor. II). He is ineffable and unbounded light.

“There is none like you among the gods, O Lord,” that is, among the gods whom the pagans worship; or “among the gods,” that is, among those who have become gods not by nature but by your grace. For although many among the human race are worthy of admiration—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the other patriarchs and prophets, and many exceedingly excellent holy martyrs—nevertheless there is none like you among the gods, O Lord.

And this is because there is no one who acts according to your works. What are these works? “All the nations that you have made,” that is, some from all the nations made by you, “will come and worship before you, O Lord,” that is, in their interior selves, where you see, not merely in the temple at Jerusalem; “and they will glorify your name,” no longer their own.

Or thus: “There is none like you, O Lord, among the gods of the nations.” He proves this from the greater: there is no one who acts according to your works who is like you. Therefore “all the nations that you have made will come and worship before you, O Lord.”

It must be observed that he says “Lord,” because in the same person there are both servant and Lord: Lord insofar as he is the Word, servant insofar as he is human. Christ therefore speaks to himself, because the human being speaks to the Word personally united to him.

“And they will glorify your name forever.” And rightly so, because “you are great,” so that no one great among the human race can be compared with you, according to the saying: “A great prophet has arisen among us” (Luke VII).

“You perform wonders,” even if others appear to perform them, “and you alone are God.” Therefore, O Lord, lead me, who am placed in your way, and make me persevere in your commandments, because “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John VI).

“And I will walk,” that is, my members will walk, “in your truth,” that is, in your commandments; “and my heart will rejoice,” that is, the heart of my members, “so that they may also fear your name,” because the one who stands must take care not to fall (I Cor. X).

Or thus: “Lead me, O Lord, in your way,” that is, lead my members, already placed in your way, namely by imitating Christ, who is your way. Lead me, that is, make me persevere in your commandment. Thus let them walk in your truth, desiring what you command to be desired, not what you forbid.

Or consider Adam, whom you placed in the way, that is, in your commandment, when you said to him: “You shall not eat from that tree” (Gen. II). But you did not lead him, because he did not remain in obedience. “Let my heart rejoice so that it may fear your name.”

This will indeed happen, because the future is that “I will confess to you, O Lord my God, with my whole heart,” that is, my members will confess to you, praising you with their whole heart; “and I will glorify your name forever.” And this is justly so, because “your mercy is great over me,” that is, over my members.

And how is it great? Because “you have delivered my soul,” that is, the soul of my members, “from the lower hell.” Notice that there is an upper hell and a lower hell. This life, in comparison with that dignity in which the angels exist, can be called hell; but the lower hell is the punishment that follows this life, from which the souls of the saints are delivered.

This is what he says: “You have delivered my soul from the lower hell,” that is, from infernal punishment, although he had not delivered their souls from this life, in which they suffered many tribulations and miseries.

Or: “You have delivered my soul from the lower hell,” that is, from mortal sin, although not from venial sin.

Or let us take it literally: “You have delivered my soul from the lower hell,” that is, from the place of torments, although not from the place of darkness. For it is read that all the holy dead before the Lord’s resurrection descended into hell, where they were in darkness but not in punishments—not in that place from which the rich man saw Lazarus placed in Abraham’s bosom. This is what he says: “You have delivered my soul from the lower hell.”

Deliverance was necessary because “the wicked, O God, rose up against me,” that is, against my members; and “the assembly of the powerful sought my soul in order to crush it,” not in order to imitate it; “and they did not set God before their eyes.” A person does not set God before his eyes when he does not consider how wicked it is to call a servant of God back from obedience.

It may be read as spoken in the person of the Head when he says: “You have delivered my soul from the lower hell,” namely from sin, although not from the punishments of sin; or: “You have delivered my soul from the lower hell,” that is, from the corruption of the flesh in the tomb. Hence elsewhere: “You will not permit your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. XV).

For just as he came into the world by being born, so by dying he descended into hell; but he did not remain there, because, after freeing his own from that place, he returned with power.

“O God, the wicked rose up against me.” This continues what was said above, as if he were saying: “Lead me, O Lord, in your way,” and this is necessary because the wicked have risen up against me.

Or, according to another translation: “Transgressing wicked men have risen up against me.” If we read this of the Head, we shall understand by those transgressing the law the Jews, because they received the law and transgressed by passing it by. The pagans, however, who did not receive the law, cannot be said to have transgressed it; no one passes beyond what he has not received.

If the verse is read of the body of Christ, we shall understand by those transgressing the law the wicked Christians, who rise up daily against the body of Christ, and from whom he suffers tribulation every day.

“And the assembly of the powerful sought my soul,” that is, the assembly of the rulers crying out and saying: “Crucify him, crucify him” (John XIX). “They sought my soul.” Of them it is said elsewhere: “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. LXV). They did not strike him, but they cried out; by crying out, they crucified him.

“And they did not set God before their eyes,” because they did not understand concerning the needy and the poor.

Therefore you, O Lord God, are compassionate in your outward action and merciful in your affection; patient, because you bear with us until you make us complete; of great mercy, predestining; and truthful, bringing your purposes into action.

“Look upon me and have mercy on me,” giving your authority to me, your servant. Let the time of suffering pass, and let the time of judging come. For “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V).

He who was seen as contemptible will himself be seen as terrifying. He will display in judgment the power that he showed in the cross as patience. He will appear in judgment as a human being, but in glory. For just as you saw him go, the angels said, “So will he come” (Acts I).

He will come to judgment in human form; therefore the wicked too will see him. But they will not see him in the form of God, which only the pure in heart will see.

Appearing, then, in human form, he will say: “Depart, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV), so that what Isaiah said may be fulfilled: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. XXVI). For in the form in which he is equal to the Father, they will see him.

“Give your authority to your servant, and save the son of your maidservant,” namely of the Virgin Mary, who was not ashamed to call herself a maidservant, saying: “Behold the maidservant of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke I).

Or thus: “Give your authority to your servant,” that is, to your servants, namely the apostles, to whom it was said: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX); “and save the son of your maidservant,” that is, your Church. For although they were born of pagan mothers, insofar as they have been regenerated they are sons of the Church, which is the maidservant of the Lord.

“Make a sign with me for good.” As if he were saying: “So that you may give authority to your servant, make with me a sign for future good,” namely the sign of the resurrection. It will be a sign for future good because it will bring salvation to many, since “we have been saved in hope” (Rom. VIII), so that one day we may rise outwardly.

The Lord promised this sign to the Jews who sought a sign, saying: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah” (Matt. XII). This has already been accomplished in the Head.

Let each person say: “Make with me, O Lord, a sign for good.” This will happen at the Lord’s coming, because then the trumpet will sound and the dead will rise incorruptible (I Cor. XV).

“Make with me, O Lord, a sign for good, so that those who hate me may see that you, O Lord, have helped me in the struggle and comforted me in tribulation.”

Or: “You have helped me” by bringing my soul back from hell; “and you have comforted me” by raising my body from the tomb. Therefore those who hate me will be put to shame—either now to their salvation, or at some future time to no purpose.

Salvific shame is to feel shame for past sins and to correct through money what was committed through negligence. God now offers us access to salutary shame, if we do not despise the medicine of shame.

But those who do not wish to be put to shame profitably will eventually be put to shame uselessly, when their iniquities will lead them astray, and they will say: “Those whom we once held in derision and as an object of reproach—we foolish people considered their life madness,” and so forth (Wis. V).

## PSALM LXXXVI. A PSALM OF SONG FOR THE SONS OF KORAH

“Its foundations are in the holy mountains. The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob. Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God. I will remember Rahab and Babylon among those who know me. Behold, the foreigners, Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians: these were there. Will Zion say: ‘A man and a man was born in her,’ and he himself, the Most High, founded her? The Lord will recount in the writings of the peoples and of the princes, of those who were in her. As the dwelling of all who rejoice is in you.”

## EXPOSITION

[Col. 0599D]

Since we have heard and noted sufficiently who the sons of Korah are and what a song of a psalm is, let us pass over these matters as already known and linger over the exposition of what the psalm intends.

A certain city is set forth and commended in this psalm. We are its citizens, and from it we are pilgrims as long as we are mortal. We would eventually reach it if we followed its way, which could not be found because it was entirely blocked, as it were, by thickets and thorns. The King of that city made himself the way so that we might reach it.

Therefore, as we walk in Christ and still remain pilgrims until we arrive, let us sigh with our whole desire for it, love it, long for it, and never let the tongue of the mind fall silent concerning its love. Let us hear what one of its citizens, filled with the Holy Spirit, says about it. His voice is as follows:

“Its foundations are in the holy mountains.”

Notice that nothing has been stated earlier in the text to which what is said at the beginning of the psalm could refer: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains.” But since the foundations of a city are ordinarily constructed in mountains, there is no doubt that the speaker here wishes a certain city to be understood. Captured and filled with love for it by the Holy Spirit, and turning over in his mind much concerning its peace, communion, eternal rest, and unfailing praise, he breaks forth with these words: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains,” as though he had already said something about that city, so that the words he uttered might continue what he had received inwardly.

And as though some people were saying and asking whose city he had said was founded upon the mountains, he adds: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob.” As if he were saying: “This city, whose foundations I have indicated as being situated in the mountains, is Zion, whose gates the Lord loves above all the tents of Jacob.”

Paul shows what the foundations of this city are (Eph. II): “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets.” And lest anyone suppose that the apostles and prophets, in whom the city’s foundation rests, could stand by themselves, he immediately adds: “Jesus Christ himself being the chief cornerstone.” For in him two peoples are joined: the people from circumcision and the people from uncircumcision. Like two walls coming from different directions, they are joined by the cornerstone and meet in the construction of one house.

In the construction of this city, one must not look for what is found in our buildings. There the foundation is one thing and the gate another; what is at the bottom will not be at the top, because the bodies from which our buildings are constructed cannot exist everywhere or forever.

In this city commended to us by the psalm, however, the cornerstone is both at the foundation and at the summit, because the divinity, suffering no bodily limitations, is present everywhere. Therefore likeness can be drawn toward it from every direction, and everything may be expressed through likenesses, because none of these things exists there in its proper physical form. The divinity itself is the mountain of mountains, the foundation of foundations, and the gate of gates.

The apostles and prophets are also the foundations of this city, because their authority supports our weakness. They are also its gates, because through them we enter the kingdom of God. They preach within us so that they may open the way for us. Hence the saying: “Their tongues have become the keys of heaven.”

They are also the stones from which the city is built, living stones made square by the Lord’s skillful hand. For it was not without reason that Noah’s ark was built from squared timbers, since it prefigured the Church, whose walls ought to be square people.

Why square? So that in every temptation they may be stable and firm; and if they are pushed and, as it were, turned over, they will not fall. For a square stone stands firmly whichever side it is turned upon.

“The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob,” that is, above all legal institutions, because elsewhere it is said: “And it will please God more than a young bull” (Ps. LXVIII).

Nevertheless, it must be noted that the same people who are in the tents of Jacob will be in Zion. But because the tents prefigured that future city—for the carnal city came first so that the spiritual one might follow—he therefore said: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob.”

“Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God.” He continues by commending this city, as if to say: “O city of God, how glorious—that is, how worthy of admiration—are the things spoken of you by your very founder.” For he said: “I will remember Rahab and Babylon among those who know me,” that is, I will cause Rahab and Babylon to remember and understand me: Rahab, namely, the people fornicating with the devil; and Babylon, that is, the confused one.

Let us hear how he remembers Rahab and Babylon. For he said: “I command my clouds to rain upon this prostitute” (Isa. V), namely upon the Church from the Gentiles.

Or thus: “I will remember Rahab and Babylon among those who know me,” that is, in the presence of those who know me. I will bring Rahab and Babylon to remembrance so that they themselves may be taken into the building of this city. Hence Paul says: “God has revealed to us through the Holy Spirit so that we may know the things given to us by God” (I Cor. II).

Rahab was a prostitute in Jericho who received the spies of the children of Israel and lowered them through a window when their enemies were searching for them. They commanded her that, when the city’s persecution broke out, she should hang a scarlet cord from the window, so that by this sign she and her household might be saved; and this was done (Josh. II).

As a figure of the mystery, whoever wishes to be healed from hostile persecution must hang a scarlet cord in the window, that is, on his forehead: he must bear the sign of Christ’s blood, by which he is drawn, as it were, by a cord and bound in the Lord’s charity.

“Behold, the foreigners, Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians: these were there.”

He shows what glorious things have been spoken of the city of God: those who were despised foreigners in Babylon, when they came within the building of this city, became most beautiful and radiant.

“Behold, the foreigners,” namely the Philistines, falling through drunkenness; “and Tyre,” that is, those afflicted in earthly things; “and the people of the Ethiopians,” that is, those blackest in character. “These were there,” that is, in the building of this city.

And how did this happen? So that they might be included in this city, “a man was born in her,” that is, Christ will be born, made human; “and he himself who was born in her founded her,” being the Most High.

Notice that the one who is born in the city will be the city’s founder. He will be born in it according to humanity, but he founded it according to divinity.

And will Zion say this? “A man”—that is, will the human intellect explain this? No, because “what is foolish of God is wiser than men” (I Cor. II).

Who, then, will say it? “The Lord will recount in the writings of the peoples,” that is, in writings produced for the instruction of the peoples, “and in the writings of the princes, of those who were in her,” that is, in writings that are to be announced by those princes to others.

Notice the insoluble riddle, unless the light of the heart had shone in the darkness. He said: “Will Zion say: ‘A man’?” Yet he also says: “The Lord will recount in the writings of the peoples”—not writings that the peoples themselves wrote, but writings that became widely known among peoples succeeding and following one another.

Or thus: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her.” And this, O Zion, will a man say? That is, does a man dare to say this? He certainly dares, because the Lord will recount it, and it has become known in the writings of the peoples—that is, in the writings composed by those who were more eminent in what Zion signifies, namely in the temporal Zion in which God was born insofar as he is called “man.”

“As the dwelling of all who rejoice is in you.”

As if he were saying: “Glorious things have rightly been spoken of you, city of God, because the dwelling of all who dwell in you will be a dwelling like that of those who rejoice,” that is, of those who truly rejoice.

He says “like that of those who rejoice” so that, if he had simply said “of those who rejoice,” the sort of pleasure that people ordinarily have in drinking, dining, and worldly honors might come to mind. People are exalted and become almost insane with a certain joy. But in that dwelling there is a kind of joy that “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart” (I Cor. II).

## PSALM LXXXVII. A SONG OF THE PSALM, FOR THE SONS OF KORAH, TO THE END, FOR MAELETH, TO BE ANSWERED; THE UNDERSTANDING OF HEMAN THE EZRAHITE

“O Lord, God of my salvation, by day I cried out, and by night before you. Let my prayer enter into your sight; incline your ear to my supplication. For my soul is filled with evils, and my life has drawn near to hell. I have been counted among those descending into the pit; I have become like a man without help, free among the dead. Like the wounded sleeping in the tombs, whom you remember no more, and they have been rejected from your hand. They placed me in the lower pit, in darkness and in the shadow of death. Your anger has been confirmed over me, and you have brought all your waves upon me. You have put those who know me far from me; they have made me an abomination to themselves. I have been handed over, and I could not escape; my eyes grew weak from poverty. I cried out to you, O Lord; all day I stretched out my hands to you. Will you work wonders for the dead, or will physicians raise them up and confess to you? Will anyone in the tomb recount your mercy, and your truth in destruction? Will your wonders be known in darkness, and your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness? But I cried out to you, O Lord, and in the morning my prayer will come before you. Why, O Lord, do you reject my prayer and turn your face away from me? I am poor and in labors from my youth; but, having been exalted, I have been humbled and troubled. Your angers have passed over me, and your terrors have troubled me. They surrounded me like water all day; they surrounded me together. You have put friend and neighbor far from me, and those who know me because of misery.”

## EXPOSITION

Since we have heard and know sufficiently from the preceding psalms what a song of a psalm is and who the sons of Korah are, let us dwell on the remaining matters: “For Maeleth, to be answered, of the Jezrahelite.”

In the Hebrew language, *Maeleth* signifies a choir. What takes place in a choir must be considered. There one must be especially careful that the singers who follow the precentor in the choir answer the precentor’s singing harmoniously.

The choir signified here is the Church, in which Christ is the precentor, while the choir of martyrs are the singers who follow and answer the precentor in harmony.

Peter shows what Christ himself sings first, saying: “Christ suffered for us” (I Pet. II). Behold, we have the precentor. He also indicates those who follow: “Leaving you an example, so that you may follow in his footsteps” (ibid.). For in this they answer him.

Hence John says: “As Christ laid down his life for us, so we also ought to lay down our lives for the brothers” (I John III). This is to answer him.

Each person must also take care that, if he wishes to be an imitator of the Lord’s passion, he possess charity, because without charity he does not answer him harmoniously. Hence Paul says: “And if I deliver my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (I Cor. XIII).

“The understanding of Heman.” Heman is interpreted as “his brother.” Christ has deigned to make those his brothers who understand the mystery of the cross. They are not merely unashamed of it; they even faithfully glory in it, so that it may be said to each one: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John I).

Or, “the understanding of the Ezraite.” Ezraite is interpreted as “eastern sojourner.” Each Heman must consider that he was driven from the East—that most splendid region—through the first parent and sent into the West, where things are fleeting and transitory. Therefore each person should strive to answer harmoniously, so that by harmony he may return there from which he fell through disobedience.

The construction of the title is as follows: “A song of the psalm appointed for the sons of Korah who persevere to the end, to answer for Maeleth,” that is, for the choir. For this is what each person who answers must guard: that he return harmony and charity, so that whoever loves God may also love his neighbor; so that those who answer may accordingly follow their good examples, according to the saying: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (I Cor. IV, XI).

And this is “the understanding of Heman,” that is, of the brother; and of the Ezraite, that is, of the one who truly sees God.

Or “Heman the Jezrahelite,” that is, one who recognizes himself to be an eastern sojourner.

In this psalm there is the voice of the Lord’s human being, commending his passion to us and exhorting his brothers to hope in no one except God, in whom alone salvation exists, and to whom alone one must cry out without ceasing.

It may be asked why, since this psalm has the same subject as the preceding psalms, it is titled “For Maeleth, to be answered,” when it alone does not exhort people to answer harmoniously. Several other psalms also deal with the Lord’s passion, and perhaps a different title was assigned to this psalm so that, if all the psalms dealing with the same subject were given the same titles, the reader would not become weary.

Christ speaks as follows:

[Col. 0604A] Lord God, author of my salvation, I cried out to you by day—that is, in the time of prosperity—and by night—that is, in the very time of the Passion—and this before you, that is, in accordance with your good pleasure and not for the favor of human beings. Therefore, let my prayer enter—that is, not be rejected—into your presence. The entering of prayer means its acceptance; and this is said by comparison, since powerful men customarily admit into their presence the envoys of friends whom they love. Incline your ear to my prayer—that is, to the prayer of my people. And it is necessary that my prayer enter your presence, because my soul is filled with evils.

To say that Christ’s soul was filled with vices is not only wrong, but impious even to imagine. With what evils, then, was it filled? Unless perhaps we take “evil” to mean the pains of the flesh, in which the soul suffered together with the body joined to it. Hence the saying: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. XXVI). The Lord did not assume these emotions of human weakness from the condition of necessity, but by the will of compassion, so that he might transform himself into his body, which is the Church, of which he deigned to be the head—that is, into his members in his saints and faithful people—so that if any one of them should happen to be saddened and grieved amid human temptations, he would not therefore think himself separated from his grace, and would recognize that these things are not sins but signs of human weakness.

Or otherwise: “My soul is filled with evils,” namely, with the evils of the Jews, for whom during the Passion I said: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke XXIII). Elsewhere it is said concerning these same evils: “I looked for one that would grieve together with me, and there was none” (Ps. LXVIII).

We read and have heard the apostle Paul, a principal member in the body of Christ, confessing that his soul was filled with such evils, when he said that he had great sorrow and continual pain in his heart for his brothers according to the flesh, who are Israelites; for them he said: “I wished myself to be anathema for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Rom. IX).

“And my life has drawn near to hell”—that is, it was near destruction—or my life was considered similar to the life of those who are worthy of hell; or my life was regarded as nothing by those who are hell itself.

Or let us speak in this way concerning the members: “Incline to my prayers,” that is, to the prayers of my people. And this is necessary because the soul of my people is filled with evils, namely, with carnal vices. “And my life has drawn near to hell.” And I myself was reckoned by them among those descending into the pit; that is, they thought me similar to other human beings descending into the pit, into the misery of this life. “And I became, insofar as they considered me, like a man without help,” because they said: “Arrest him, for there is none to deliver him” (Ps. LXX). Yet I alone, reckoned among the dead—that is, among the company of the dead—was free, that is, without sin; and this is the highest freedom, because “everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John VIII).

The Lord is called free among mortals because he appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh, but was not a sinner. He also underwent death not under compulsion but voluntarily. Hence the saying: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John X). Thus he says: “I became like a man without help, free among the dead.” And yet I was reckoned by them as one of the wounded, that is, as one of the others who were wounded by the arrows of the Lord, namely by mortality and susceptibility to suffering. Hence the saying: “Your arrows are fastened in me” (Ps. XXXVII).

And I was reckoned by them as those who sleep in the tombs, of whom God remembers no more with regard to this life, and whom, once placed in the tomb, one must await until the common resurrection. “And they are rejected from your hand,” that is, you rejected those who regarded me as such, so that you no longer recalled them by laying upon them the hand of mercy, because, existing in the depth of iniquity, they despise you.

Or “from your hand,” that is, from your power, they appear to have been rejected, because they lawfully do what they wish, as though you had no power over them. Or those “sleeping in the tombs” are understood as those who in tombs—that is, in that body and in bodily desires, which are like a tomb of the soul—take as much pleasure as they would in sleep. God no longer remembers them so as to recall them, because he has already handed them over to a reprobate mind. Or he no longer remembers them in the opinion of others, because they sin so freely as though the Lord had forgotten all their sins and would no longer punish them.

In their estimation they also placed me in the lower pit, that is, among those who have fallen into the depth of iniquity; “and in darkness,” that is, they not only placed me in the lower pit, but also compared me with the dark ones, that is, with those who are dead in the inner person; “and in the shadow of death,” that is, in ignorance of the truth, which brings death. And this was not because I deserved it, but because you willed it; nor by their will, but by your permission. “Your wrath has been confirmed over me,” that is, your anger was not only stirred up but also confirmed against me, because you caused certain people firmly to believe that I had been abandoned by you. “And all your waves,” that is, all the dangers that ordinarily arise externally, you brought over me. Elsewhere it is said: “All your heights and your waves have passed over me” (Ps. XLI).

He shows how the Lord brought in the waves, saying: “You have put my acquaintances far from me,” that is, my relatives, from whom I was born; they were far from me in affection, although not in body. “They made me an abomination to themselves,” because, abhorring me, they said to the blind man whom I had enlightened: “You are his disciple” (John IX). And at last I was handed over by my disciple. “And I did not go out,” that is, I did not reveal my divinity, but patiently endured them raging against me in my flesh. Elsewhere it is said: “I clothed myself with sackcloth” (Ps. XXXIV).

“My outward eyes languished,” that is, they were closed in death; and this was “because of want,” that is, because of the human weakness that is in me. Or “my eyes,” that is, my apostles, who were principal members in my body, languished, that is, became weak—because of want, understood as want of hope—for they failed in hope when they saw me dying on the cross.

Notice that outward eyes ordinarily languish when food is withdrawn. So also the apostles languished because of want when the Lord was withdrawn from their sight, from whom they were continually refreshed spiritually. For he himself said of himself: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John VI).

“My eyes languished because of want.” Yet I did not cease in obedience, but always cried out to you, God, in order to win your favor: “All day long I stretched out my hands to you.” If we understand the stretching out of the hands as referring to the cross, it cannot be said that he stretched them out all day, since he was crucified at the sixth hour and buried in the evening. Therefore it seems more fitting to understand by “hands” the good works that he always extended, because he never ceased from doing good, but continually joined one good work to another. This is what he says: “I stretched out my hands to you.”

Yet this does not benefit everyone, because it does not benefit those who are dead in soul. Thus he says: “Will you work wonders for the dead”—namely, will you make them well?—“or will physicians raise them up,” that is, my teachers or preachers, by whose teaching the wounds of the mind are healed, “and will they confess to you?” No, because “confession perishes from the dead, as from one who does not exist” (Ecclus. XVII).

“Will anyone tell in the tomb”—that is, to those whom the depth of sins has already enclosed within them—“of your mercy,” which was displayed to the world through me? “And will anyone tell of your truth in perdition,” that is, to those who have already gone into the perdition of sins?

And because the wonders of the Lord can be recounted among sinners, but uselessly for them, since they do not hear with an ear capable of hearing, he adds: “Will your wonders be known in darkness,” that is, among darkened people deprived of the light of wisdom—your wonders that have been performed through me? “And will your justice be known in the land of oblivion,” that is, among those who are already earth and have forgotten that they were rational creatures? No.

And because I see that your wonders do not benefit such people, I therefore turned away from them and turned toward you, Lord, for the salvation of the remnant. And this is not without reason, because “my prayer will forestall you,” and will obtain from you the power of being heard. This will appear “in the morning,” that is, in the salvation of the remnant, or in the universal salvation, the resurrection of all, when every darkness of night will depart and the true morning will arise. Thus he said: “And in the morning my prayer will forestall you.”

And since my prayer will come before you, why, Lord, do you reject—or seem to reject—my prayer, that is, the prayer of my people, and why do you turn your face away from me, that is, from my people, as though you were angry with them? You do not turn it away for their condemnation, but for their salvation. For through this “I am poor,” that is, my people are made poor and humbled, “and in labors from my youth,” that is, my people labor from the time of their renewal. “But when exalted,” that is, when my people have been exalted in prosperity, so that they do not fail in labor, “I am again humbled,” that is, my people are humbled through adversity, so that they do not become proud in prosperity. And thus I am troubled in my members, namely so that your wrath might pass over me—that is, my people—the wrath that remains upon unbelievers and upon those who do not wish to be incorporated into me. “And your terrors,” that is, the terrors of the future judgment, “have troubled me,” that is, my people.

“They have surrounded me like water all day long.” This is connected with what he said: “When exalted, I have been humbled and troubled.” And how? Because unbelievers have surrounded me—that is, my people—like water, which envelops one from every side, and this “all day long,” that is, continually. They surrounded me together, both inward and outward enemies. And you have put far from me “a friend,” that is, anyone who ought to be their friend; “and a neighbor,” anyone according to the flesh; and “my acquaintances,” that is, those who ought to be acquainted with my people and to share the same faith with them—you permitted them to be put far from my people, and this “because of misery,” that is, because of the misery which they suffered from the enemies of the Church.

[Col. 0607A] These same words are also read above as spoken in the person of the head, in this manner: “I cried to you, Lord, all day long; I stretched out my hands to you.” In return for this crying and stretching out of the hands, you will raise me from death, because, since it is certain that you will perform wonders through me, either you will perform wonders through me, dead, for the dead, or through me, living, for the living. But through me, dead, you will not perform wonders for the dead. Thus he says: “Will you perform wonders for the dead”—understood as the dead in body—that is, the restoration of the human race? “Or will physicians,” that is, my preachers, “raise them up,” if this means that I should not rise again, “and will they confess to you?”

“Will anyone of them tell of your mercy,” that is, the restoration of the human race, “to those who are shut up in the tomb,” and of your truth “in perdition,” that is, to those who, because their sins demanded it, have come to the place of perdition?

Or thus: “Will anyone tell of your mercy in the tomb,” that is, in considering me buried and not raised? “And who will tell of your truth in perdition,” that is, your true commandments or your recompense, if I perish? “And will your wonders be known while I remain in darkness, and your justice”—that is, the faith that justifies—“will it be known in the land of oblivion,” that is, in my body delivered over to oblivion, if I am not raised?

Or thus: “Will your wonders be known in darkness,” that is, among those who are already in the place of darkness, “and your justice in the land of oblivion,” that is, among those who are already in that place where they deservedly ought to be delivered over to oblivion?

“And I cried to you, Lord.” As if he were saying: Since I saw that no wonders would be forthcoming through me, dead, I therefore cried to you, Lord, so that you might raise me up. “And my prayer will forestall you,” that is, it will precede you, so that your hearing will follow. This will appear “in the morning,” that is, in my resurrection, which took place in the morning. Or: “My prayer in the morning,” that is, made in continual devotion, “will forestall you,” that is, will be pleasing to you.

And since my prayer will forestall you, why do you reject—or seem to reject—my prayer, with which I shall cry out to you on the cross, saying: “Lord my God, look upon me”? And why do you turn your face away from me? Because, namely, I alone seem suitable to you for the restoration of the human race. Thus he says: “I am poor,” that is, I appear humble, so that through me, the humble one, human pride may receive healing. “And I am in labors from my youth,” that is, from the time when each person is more inclined to fall.

“I have been exalted with you, but humbled among human beings, and troubled by their persecution.” Why he was troubled he adds: “In me your wrath has passed over,” that is, your wrath, which had been incurred against the human race by consent because of the sin of the first human being, according to what the prophet says: “Because of the sins of my people I struck him” (Isa. LIII). This wrath, placed upon me, passed over, because through me it was appeased. “And your terrors”—not made by you, but permitted by you—“have troubled me.”

And how? Because they surrounded me like water, which envelops one from every side, “all day long,” that is, continually. They surrounded me together, the lesser and the greater: the lesser by giving evil consent, the greater by judging wrongly. Therefore you have put far from me “a friend,” that is, anyone who ought to be my friend; “and a neighbor” according to the flesh; and “my acquaintances” according to the faith. And this “because of misery,” that is, because of the misery inflicted upon me by the Jews.

## PSALM LXXXVIII. THE UNDERSTANDING OF ETHAN THE EZRAHITE

> “I will sing the mercies of the Lord forever. From generation to generation I will proclaim your truth with my mouth. For you said: ‘Mercy will be built up in heaven forever; your truth will be prepared in them.’ I have established a covenant with my chosen ones; I have sworn to David my servant: ‘Forever I will prepare your offspring. And I will build your throne from generation to generation.’
>
> “The heavens will confess your wonders, Lord, and indeed your truth in the assembly of the saints. For who among the clouds will be equal to the Lord? Who will be like the Lord among the sons of God? God, who is glorified in the council of the saints, great and terrible above all who surround him. Lord God of hosts, who is like you? You are powerful, Lord, and your truth is around you.
>
> “You rule the power of the sea; but you calm the motion of its waves. You humbled the proud as one wounded; by the arm of your power you scattered your enemies. The heavens are yours, and the earth is yours; you founded the world and its fullness; you created the north and the sea. Tabor and Hermon will rejoice in your name. Your arm is with power.
>
> “Let your hand be strengthened, and let your right hand be exalted. Justice and judgment are the preparation of your throne. Mercy and truth will go before your face. Blessed is the people that knows jubilation, Lord: they will walk in the light of your countenance, and in your name they will rejoice all day long, and in your justice they will be exalted.
>
> “For you are the glory of their power, and by your good pleasure our horn will be exalted. For our exaltation belongs to the Lord, and the Holy One of Israel is our king.
>
> “Then you spoke in a vision to your saints, and you said: ‘I have placed help in one who is powerful, and I have exalted the chosen one from among my people. I found David my servant; with my holy oil I anointed him. For my hand will help him, and my arm will strengthen him.
>
> “‘The enemy will gain nothing against him, and the son of iniquity will not add to harming him. I will cut down his enemies before his face, and I will put those who hate him to flight. My truth and my mercy will be with him, and in my name his horn will be exalted.
>
> “‘I will place his hand upon the sea, and his right hand upon the rivers. He will call upon me: “You are my Father, my God, and the protector of my salvation.” And I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth.
>
> “‘Forever I will preserve my mercy for him, and my faithful covenant for him. I will establish his offspring forever and ever, and his throne as the days of heaven.
>
> “‘But if his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges.
>
> “‘But I will not scatter my mercy from him, nor harm him in my truth. I will not profane my covenant, and I will not make void the things that proceed from my lips. Once I have sworn by my holiness: I will not lie to David. His offspring will remain forever.
>
> “‘And his throne will be as the sun in my sight, and as the full moon forever, and as a faithful witness in heaven.’
>
> “But you have rejected and despised; you have delayed your Christ. You have overturned the covenant of your servant; you have profaned his sanctuary on earth. You have destroyed all his hedges; you have made his stronghold a terror. All who pass along the way have plundered him; he has become a reproach to his neighbors.
>
> “You have exalted the right hand of those who oppressed him; you have gladdened all his enemies. You have turned away the help of his sword, and you have not assisted him in battle. You have destroyed him from purification, and you have struck his throne to the ground. You have shortened the days of his time; you have covered him with confusion.
>
> “How long, Lord, will you turn away forever? Will your wrath burn like fire? Remember what my substance is: have you indeed created all the sons of human beings in vain? What person is there who will live and not see death? Will he rescue his soul from the hand of hell?
>
> “Where are your former mercies, Lord, as you swore to David in your truth? Remember, Lord, the reproach of your servants—which I have held in my bosom—of the reproach brought by many nations. For your enemies, Lord, have reproached it; they have reproached the exchange of your Christ.
>
> “Blessed be the Lord forever. Let it be, let it be.”

## EXPOSITION

Ethan is interpreted as “strong.” “Jezreelite” means “an eastern foreigner.” Whoever wishes to be strong must necessarily attribute his strength and power not to himself but to God. For whoever attributes to himself the fact that he is strong becomes weak when his strength is taken away. This is what the man who said, “I will keep my strength for you” (Ps. LVIII), was considering.

This strong man speaks in this manner in the present psalm, commending to us the mercy of the Lord God, which will remain forever in his faithful people. He speaks as follows:

I will sing the mercies of the Lord forever.

As though he were saying: Hear, attend, wait patiently, because I will sing of the mercies of the Lord, which will lead you onward forever, or which will remain forever. As though he were saying: Thus mercy in Adam was temporal, but the mercy of the Lord, which will hold back wrath, will be eternal. Note that he says “mercies” in the plural, because since our iniquities precede in great number, it is necessary that his many mercies follow. What he says, “the mercies of the Lord,” that is, the restoration of the human race, “I will sing forever.” And I will not merely sing of the mercies; I will also proclaim your truth, that is, the fulfillment of the promised mercy, destined to endure from generation to generation. And I will proclaim this with my mouth, that is, with a mouth in harmony with my heart, because I will not conceal with my mouth what I conceive in my heart.

Note that he says, “I will proclaim your truth with my mouth.” As though he were saying: There are two things: one is yours, the other is mine. The truth is yours; the mouth is mine. Therefore I will proclaim your truth, because unless I proclaim it, I will not be a servant; but if I proclaim it as coming from myself, I will be a liar, since every good thing proceeds from you. This is what he says: “I will proclaim your truth with my mouth.” And I will do this confidently, because you said: “Mercy,” that is, the restoration of the human race, “will be built to remain forever.”

And this will happen because “your truth will be prepared in the heavens in them,” that is, the truth of my commandments will be prepared in the heavens, that is, in your apostles, in whom your promise will be fulfilled, so that it may be in them. For they will not be ashamed to preach your truth, which they will be able to defend by signs and arguments.

“I have established a covenant with my chosen ones; I have sworn to David my servant. I will prepare your seed forever.”

Not only will mercy be built forever, but you also said: “I have established a covenant,” namely the new covenant, given through grace to my chosen ones, that is, to my sons, for whom I established the old covenant as servants. Hence the saying: “Those whom he predestined, these he also called” (Rom. VIII). This is what he says: “I have established a covenant with my chosen ones.” And you also said: “I have sworn to David.” David was certain when he spoke, and even more certain when he swore, because an oath of the Godhead is the confirmation of a promise.

“I will build your throne from generation to generation,” that is, forever.

Note that David’s seed is prepared forever, because the imitators of Christ, who was to be born from David’s seed, will remain forever. His throne has been built from generation to generation. Thus what was promised to the carnal David has been fulfilled in the spiritual David, who came from his seed.

“The heavens will confess your wonders, O Lord.”

As though he were saying: Your truth will be prepared in the heavens, and therefore the heavens themselves will confess your wonders, that is, they will praise your wonders. What is more wonderful than that the one who yesterday was drunk is sober today; the one who yesterday was unchaste is now chaste; the one who yesterday was condemned has now been received into the kingdom? In these wonders, let each person praise God; praise him because the dead have been raised; praise him still more because the lost have been redeemed. This is what he says: “The heavens will confess your wonders, O Lord.”

As though he were saying: What is more wonderful than that God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son? (John III.) He promised this, and he did not lie. Nothing is more wonderful than the effect of this deed.

“And your truth in the assembly of the saints.”

As though he were saying: Truly the heavens will confess your wonders, because they will proclaim your truth in the assembly of the saints, that is, in the congregation of the faithful. And rightly they proclaim your truth, and not their own, because none among all those whom you have made holy can be compared with you. This is what he says: “For who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord?”

Note that God calls those “clouds” who were previously called “heavens.” They are called heavens because, by the radiance of their holiness, they shed light upon us; they are called clouds because their holiness is covered by the flesh as by a cloud, so that we do not see their inner realities. What descends from a cloud we see; but what takes place within the cloud we do not see. Thus we see the rain of holy preaching flowing from the apostles; but what is contained within them, unless they reveal it to us, we cannot know, because it is not for a human being to know the secrets of another’s heart.

“And who shall be like the Lord among the sons of men?”

No one, certainly, because he alone was born by nature, while the others are adopted. He is Son by nature; the others are sons by grace. He is God, who is glorified in the council of the saints.

The council of the saints is not to seek what belongs to oneself, but what belongs to God; not to yearn for earthly things, but to desire heavenly things. In this council he alone is rightly glorified, because he alone is great, while the others are small. He alone is “terrible above all who surround him.”

Here it is asked: Since God is unbounded light and cannot be contained in any place, how can he have anything around him? But because he had a mother from the Jewish race from whom he would assume flesh, he wished to dwell there bodily, and he also wished to preach there. Therefore, with respect to that people, it is not inappropriate to say that he has something around him. For the Jewish people were surrounded by the nations and oppressed by their persecution. The Lord was terrible to the nations because, in his name, many of their idols in which they trusted were shattered; and the nations themselves were compelled by fear of him to abandon their sect.

Or otherwise: “Terrible above all who surround him,” that is, above those who go around seeking to become his imitators.

And since you alone are great, you alone terrible, O Lord God, not only among human beings but also among the heavenly powers, who is like you? No one, certainly, because you are powerful, O Lord, and your truth is around you, that is, it always surrounds you, because you have truth from yourself, while the others have it not from themselves but from you. Hence the saying: “My prayer will return into my bosom” (Ps. XXXIV).
