Or “truth,” that is, those who fulfill your truth, are around you, that is, in your following; they surround you so that they may exist as your imitators.

“You rule the power of the sea.”

As though he were saying: Truly no one among the clouds will be equal to you; no one is like you, because you rule the power of the sea, that is, the bitterness of the nations. “But you calm the movement of its waves,” that is, the threats of rulers who rage with a certain force like waves. You will calm them, but you will not wholly disperse them, because even if the lion does not rage openly, the dragon nevertheless rages secretly.

You are powerful, O Lord, and your truth, that is, your true commandments, will be around you. For although you wished to be born among the Jewish people, you did not refuse to be made known among the nations that surround you. And then, namely when your truth is proclaimed throughout the surrounding regions, what was said will come to pass: “The lion came to meet Samson as he went to take a wife for himself from the Philistines” (Judg. XIV).

Then the lion will roar, that is, the sea, the bitterness of the nations. But what concern is that to you? “You rule the power of the sea; you calm the movement of its waves.” And you, humbled, will humble the proud “as one wounded,” that is, as anyone who, because of a serious wound, would yield to an enemy. For who, given so great an example of humility, would not lay aside pride? No one, certainly.

“You will raise the hand of your arm of strength,” that is, in your powerful might you will scatter your enemies, so that those who cease to worship the creature and adore the true Creator may become your friends.

“The heavens are yours, and the earth is yours.”

As though he were saying: Rightly do I say that they will be scattered by the arm of your strength, because the heavens through which the scattering will occur are yours, and the earth that they inhabit is yours. That is, those who will be scattered through the heavens will be yours, because you founded the circle of the earth, that is, the rounded earth, namely those less perfect in virtue, and its fullness, that is, those still more perfect than those who are the circle.

You created the north and the sea, that is, you established the most desperate people, in whom charity has grown cold and who are understood by the north, and the sea, that is, those who make themselves and others bitter, so that they might become the circle of the earth and its fullness.

And what of them? “Tabor and Hermon will rejoice in your name,” that is, those who were once darkness but are now light in the Lord, renouncing ungodliness and worldly desires, will rejoice by glorifying your name.

Tabor and Hermon are two mountains signifying Judea and the Gentile world. Tabor, because it is interpreted as “coming light,” appropriately designates the Jews, from whom Christ proceeded, the true light illuminating every person coming into this world (John I). Hermon is interpreted as “anathema,” and by it the Gentiles are understood, anathematizing themselves, withdrawing from the worship of idols, and imitating Christ.

This is what he says: “Tabor and Hermon,” that is, Jews and Gentiles, “will rejoice in your name.”

And rightly so, because “your arm,” that is, your strength, “will be with power,” that is, your power will be powerful power, because it will remain forever. The power of others, however, is weak, because it remains only for a time.

“Let your hand be strengthened, and let your right hand be exalted.”

As though he were saying: Tabor and Hermon will rejoice in your name. In order that this may happen, let your hand be strengthened, that is, consolidated in them—your hand, that is, your power—which will make them rejoice here in your name. And finally let your right hand be exalted, namely when the lambs are to be separated from the goats.

Note that here the hand is strengthened so that there the right hand may be exalted. For here the faithful live innocently together with the wicked, and therefore the hand is rightly said simply to be strengthened. But there, because the good are to be separated from the evil, the right hand will rightly be exalted, because now he comes in gentleness, but then he will come in terror.

“Justice and judgment are the preparation of your throne.”

As though he were saying: Truly your right hand will be exalted, because just judgment will prepare a throne for you. Meanwhile, what happens? “Mercy,” that is, the remission of sins, and “truth,” that is, the fulfillment of the promise, “will go before your face,” because you are to come in the majesty of the Father.

And since you are so great, blessed therefore is the people who knows jubilation, that is, who recognizes that one should rejoice in you with an ineffable affection of heart, through which the jubilus may rightly arise. For to jubilate is to possess such great joy of mind that no one can express it in words.

Another continuation: Mercy and truth will go before you; and because they will go before you, blessed therefore is the one who, attending to that mercy and truth, knows how to jubilate, as above.

“O Lord, they will walk in the light of your countenance.”

As though he were saying: Truly those who know how to jubilate are blessed, because they will walk, that is, they will delight, in the light of your countenance, illuminated by your knowledge. “And in your name they will exult all day,” that is, continually. “And in your justice they will be exalted,” not seeking to establish their own justice but yours. And rightly yours, because you are their strength. Therefore they recognize that they are virtuous not from themselves but from you; and therefore they will glory not in themselves but in you.

“And in your good pleasure,” that is, in your good will, not in our merits, “our horn will be exalted,” that is, our sublimity or our defense.

“For our exaltation is from the Lord.”

As though he were saying: Truly our horn will be exalted in your good pleasure, because our exaltation, by which we have been taken up from the mass of the lost, is from the Lord. For he took us up, and we did not take ourselves up. And this exaltation is that of our king, that is, of the Lord’s man, who rules us in every goodness.

“Then he spoke in a vision to his saints.”

As though he were saying: Truly our exaltation will be from the Lord, because it is the assumption of the man assumed by the Word of the Father. For you, God the Father, spoke in a vision, that is, manifestly or through manifold revelation, to your saints—namely when you said, “Mercy will be built forever.” You spoke, I say, and you spoke through the deeds of the patriarchs and the words of the prophets.

And what did you say?

“I have placed help”—for those who are to be saved—“in one who is powerful,” that is, in my Son, who will act powerfully in all things, stripping principalities and powers and confidently leading them forth in triumph in himself.

“And I have exalted the chosen one,” that is, my Son, beloved above all, who was to be born “from my people,” that is, from the Jewish race, because salvation is from the Jews.

“I have found David my servant.”

As though he were saying: You said, “I have placed help in one who is powerful,” and you also said, “I have found David my servant,” namely the spiritual David, not the carnal one. Hence elsewhere: “I have found David, a man after my own heart, and I have anointed him with my holy oil” (1 Kings XV; Acts XIII), namely with spiritual joy. Hence elsewhere: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV).

This too is what he says here: “With my holy oil I have anointed him.” The evidence is that my hand, that is, my power, will help him in his own affairs, and my arm, that is, my strength, will confirm him to such an extent that he will be equal to me.

“And the enemy will have no success against him,” that is, he will achieve no effect against him, even if he begins to act. The enemy, that is, the persecutor, and the son of iniquity, that is, the evil serpent, will not add to harming him.

He harmed the first man, but he will not add to harming this one. He will tempt him, but he will not thereby harm him, because by tempting him he will not overcome him.

“And I will cut down,” that is, I will cause to be cut down, “his enemies from before his face,” that is, from his thought. For those who were previously his enemies will be cut away by holy preachers from the body of unbelievers and fitted onto the body of the faithful. And all this will come from his face, that is, from his foreknowledge.

This was prefigured when Moses reduced the head of the calf to dust and gave it to the Jews to drink (Exod. XXXIII). The head of the calf signified unbelievers, who, crushed in humility through knowledge of the Lord, were to be incorporated into the faithful.

This is what he says: “I will cut down his enemies from before his face, and I will put those who hate him to flight.” For those who are now enemies will become friends by taking refuge with him.

“And my truth,” that is, the fulfillment of the promise, will be with him. Hence the Apostle says: “Through him is the Amen to God” (2 Cor. I).

“And my mercy,” that is, the restoration of the human race, will be with him. “And in my name,” with the understood addition, “being glorified,” his horn, that is, his sublimity, will be exalted.

“And I will place his hand upon the sea,” that is, his power will be among the nations. “And I will place his right hand upon the rivers,” because rulers ought to be subjected to God with greater power than subjects are, since the Lord’s power appeared more greatly in the conversion of kings than in the conversion of the poor.

This is what he says: “I will place his hand upon the sea, and his right hand upon the rivers.”

And rightly so, because he and no other will call upon me, saying: “You are my Father” according to divinity, “my God” according to humanity, “the protector of my salvation,” because your Word received me, a human being, in the human being, away from sin.

“And I will make him the firstborn, exalted above the kings of the earth.”

As though he were saying: He will call upon me, and not in vain, because I will make him firstborn, that is, more worthy than every creature. Hence Paul says: “So that he himself might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. VIII).

In ancient times firstborn sons used to possess greater dignity in their fathers’ households than the other sons. Accordingly, the Lord’s man is rightly called firstborn, because he has been exalted above every creature, and through him everyone who has been exalted has been raised up.

“Exalted above the kings of the earth,” as in the saying: “All kings will adore him” (Ps. LXXI).

“I will keep my mercy for him forever, in his people.”

As it says elsewhere: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XVIII).

“And my covenant,” that is, my pact, which I promised, namely that my inheritance would be given to the faithful, “will be faithful,” that is, trustworthy, to him, namely in his people, because no one will believe my promises unless he is joined to this head as a member.

“And I will establish his seed forever,” that is, I will firmly establish his imitators, with the understood addition, “as those who will endure.”

“And I will establish his throne,” namely those who are his seat, “like the days of heaven,” that is, I will make them remain in brightness, every darkness of night having been wiped away; or, “I will establish them like the days of heaven,” that is, as those who will remain eternally.

Note that they are understood as “days” both by the word “seat” and by the word “throne,” because those who imitate him are his seed, and they are his throne because his seat is in them.

But because the same word repeated twice would produce weariness, he expresses the same thing with different words. Or by “throne” the more perfect may be understood, and by “seat” those who are less perfect.

“But if his sons abandon my law…”

As though he were saying: I promised that I would establish his seed forever. But if his sons abandon my law in this way, that they do not walk in my judgments—that is, if they do not delight in my judgment, in my true discernment, as happens with many monks, whom the service of the Lord burdens at first, although they are destined to be perfect sons—of these it is said here: “If they do not walk in my judgments.”

“And if they profane my statutes,” that is, if they make them far from the sanctuary, from holiness; “and do not keep my commandments,” that is, if they do not possess love of God and neighbor:

“I will visit their iniquities with the rod of correction, and their sins with paternal blows,” not with the blows of a master.

Let no one disdain to be scourged with these blows, because it is better to be corrected by the rod of a father than to perish through the flatteries of a robber. Hence Paul says: “If you are without discipline, of which all have become participants, then you are not sons but adulterers” (Heb. XII).

“But I will not scatter my mercy from him.”

As though he were saying: Although I will visit the sons of David with the rod if they sin, nevertheless I will not scatter my mercy, that is, my promises, from him, that is, I will not take them away from David; nor will I harm him. And this I say in my truth. Or: I will not harm him in my truth, that is, in my true judgment, by which I visit their iniquities with the rod of correction.

Hence elsewhere: “Whatever he does will prosper” (Ps. I).

Let him therefore exercise the discipline of the Lord, but not remove mercy; let him strike the stubborn, provided that he preserves the inheritance for the son.

“Nor will I harm him in my truth, nor will I profane my covenant,” that is, my pact; “and the things that proceed from my lips,” that is, the things promised through the lips of my heralds, “I will not make void.”

Note that he would profane the covenant if he did not fulfill the promise.

“Once I have sworn by my holiness…”

As though he were saying: Therefore I will not make void the things that proceed from my lips, because I have sworn once by my holiness, with the understood addition, “when establishing it”—namely by the Holy of Holies. Or “by my holiness,” that is, by my sanctity, according to which it is impossible for an oath to lie. Hence the saying: “By myself I have sworn, says the Lord” (Gen. XXII).

And what did he swear?

“His seed will remain forever, and his throne like the sun in my sight,” that is, his seat will be in my sight, that is, in his interior, in his soul, where I alone see. There it will be like the sun, shining, namely, in virtues. This concerns the soul, which will rise here in the first resurrection, so that finally it may shine in the sight of God.

As for the body, “his throne will be like the moon,” not like the moon that undergoes increase and decrease, but like the moon that is perfect forever, that is, that will possess its perfection eternally.

Hence Paul says: “This corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality” (1 Cor. XV).

Note that he says, “Like the moon perfect forever,” because although it is true that the moon will not last forever, this does not diminish the value of the comparison, since a likeness is often drawn from the impossible. Such is the saying: “You strain out a gnat and swallow a camel” (Matt. XXIII).

He says, “Like the moon perfect forever,” and the faithful witness to this matter is in heaven, namely Christ, because he can neither deceive nor be deceived. For the Apostle says: “He raised us by his power” (1 Cor. VI).

“This I have sworn to David by my holiness.”

But if I lie to David, shall I speak truth to anyone, with respect to my Word, with whom I have ordered all things? For there is no need for him to swear a second time, because by swearing once he established everything, and he has never deceived anyone.

“But you have rejected and despised…”

Up to this point the words were the Lord’s, promising David the wonders noted above. Here the Prophet returns to his own words, as though saying:

You, Lord God, promised me that you would not take your mercy away from me, nor profane my covenant, and many other things. Yet you do not display what you promised me—that you would not take your mercy away from me—because you truly, that is, in reality, have rejected me. He uses the past tense for the future, as though saying: You will appear to reject, and you will appear to despise, that is, to abandon, your people over whom I preside.

The carnal David was rejected when he suffered many tribulations through his son Absalom. The people over whom he presided were also despised when they were held in captivity.

It follows:

“You have delayed your Christ,” that is, you will delay me, your anointed one, from your promises, because what you appear to have promised me you will fulfill in David your son, whose type I bear.

Observe that when David says, “You have rejected and despised,” he is the same David as the other David, so that in him we may see fulfilled what here appears to have been promised. But this must also be done in others, so that the prophecy may be true.

It was prophesied concerning the two brothers, the sons of Rebecca: “The elder will serve the younger” (Gen. XXV). Yet it is never read that the elder brother Esau served Jacob. Rather, it is read that Jacob, returning with his wives from Mesopotamia and sending gifts ahead, fell on his face before Esau to adore him (Gen. XXXIII).

But because these two brothers signified the earlier and later peoples, we must turn to those peoples, in whom what was prophesied about the two brothers was fulfilled. For the elder people, namely the Jewish people, serves the younger, namely the Gentile people, because the Jew bears what convicts the pagan.

Or otherwise: “You have delayed your Christ,” that is, me, your anointed one, because after I had suffered so many persecutions, you finally established me as king over the entire people. This delay signified that Christ in his body was to be delayed from the promises and was to suffer much before his body was fulfilled.

“You have overturned the covenant of your servant,” that is, you will overturn the pact that you made with your servant; “and you have profaned his sanctuary on earth,” that is, you will profane your temple, which alone was on the Jewish earth, by permitting it to be polluted by those who act against it.

“You have destroyed all his fences,” that is, the kingdom and priesthood by which the Jews were fortified. “You have made his stronghold a terror,” that is, you have made the leaders who ought to be a stronghold for others, that is, to defend them, into a terror, permitting them to be thrown into confusion by fear. For none of the leaders existed who dared to rise in defense of the lesser.

“And so all who pass along the way have plundered him,” namely the pagans who pass along the true way, Christ, without believing; or those who pass along the temporal way, that is, who attend only to transient things.

“And he has become a reproach to his neighbors,” that is, to the nations. “And you have exalted the right hand of those who oppressed him, and you have gladdened,” that is, you will gladden, all his enemies in their victory. “And you have turned away the help of his sword,” that is, they had no hope of defense in the sword. And this is because you did not help him in battle.

“And you have destroyed him from purification,” that is, from the true faith that cleanses hearts inwardly. “And you have struck his judicial seat down upon the earth,” with the understood addition, “cast down”; “and you have shortened the days of his time,” because you have taken away the kingdom and priesthood, which they were thought to possess eternally; “and you have drenched him with confusion,” that is, you will confuse him on every side.

Or we may explain it otherwise.

“You have rejected and despised; you have delayed your Christ”: not merely concerning the Jews, in what follows, but generally concerning the body of Christ, to whom the promises were made.

As though the Prophet were saying: You, Father, said, “Mercy will be built forever”; you swore to David your servant, namely to Christ, “I will prepare your seed forever, and I will build your throne from generation to generation.” You promised your Christ that you would do these things and many others, and yet you have rejected him, that is, you will appear to reject him in his members; and you will despise his members, that is, you will permit them to become contemptible; and you have delayed, that is, you will delay, your Christ, that is, the fulfillment of Christ’s body, because you will not immediately cause everyone to believe in him.

For the whole Christ is body and head, Savior and Church. The fulfillment of Christ was delayed because faith grew through great labor, by which worthy members were fitted to him.

This is what he says: “You have delayed your Christ, and you have overturned your covenant,” that is, the pact of your servant. “And you have profaned,” that is, you will permit to be polluted, “his sanctuary,” that is, his saints cast down upon the earth, that is, established upon earthly things.

The sanctuary is profaned when those who have received the faith, compelled by fear, yield to those who are of the earth and sacrifice to all idols. Hence elsewhere: “They have polluted your holy temple” (Ps. LXXIII).

Or: “You have profaned his sanctuary on earth,” that is, you will cause the life of his saints to be considered madness by those who are earthly.

“You have destroyed all his fences,” that is, you will take away from them the protection of his people.

And how will this happen? Because “you will make his stronghold a terror,” that is, those who will excel in holiness, whose example ought to strengthen the lesser, you will make a terror, because they will fear strengthening the lesser.

Or: “You will make those who are the stronghold a terror,” that is, [the wording is corrupt: perhaps] they will fear to strengthen the lesser. Or: “You will make those who are the stronghold a terror,” that is, a cause of fear, because the greater are killed and the lesser are delivered over to fear.

“And so all who pass along the way will plunder him in his members,” namely the Gentiles who do not make Christ their way. “And he has become a reproach to his neighbors, and you have exalted the right hand,” that is, the power, “of those who oppressed him, and you will gladden all his enemies in victory,” which they will have over his saints, when they are permitted to rage against the bodies of the saints.

“And you have turned away the help of his sword,” that is, you will make him in his members like a man for whom his sword is of no help in battle.

Or the sword of the saints may be the word of preaching, with which they ought to be girded and protected. But the help of this sword is turned away from them when they suffer persecution on account of that very preaching.

This is what he says: “You have turned away the help of his sword, and you have not helped him in battle,” that is, you will not appear to help his members in the battle of persecution and tribulation.

“And you have destroyed,” that is, you will permit his members to be destroyed, “from purification,” that is, to be distanced from every purity in the estimation of the wicked. Hence Paul says: “We have become the refuse of all” (1 Cor. IV).

“And you have struck his seat down upon the earth,” that is, you have struck down his saints, in whom his seat ought to be, casting them down upon the earth, that is, allowing them to be fashioned according to earthly things.

Or: “You have struck his seat down upon the earth,” that is, you have permitted his saints to be afflicted in the body.

“You have shortened the days of his time,” that is, you have shortened the life of his sons, not with respect to you, but with respect to those who desired a long life, so that they might be sustained by the comfort and authority of those men. Thus it is read concerning blessed Martin: “Why do you abandon us, Father? Or to whom do you leave us desolate?”

“You have drenched him with confusion,” that is, you will permit his members to be confused everywhere, both inwardly and outwardly.

But you, Lord, how long will you turn your face away from them? Will you turn away from them forever, that is, in a final rejection?

As though he were saying: If you have wished to deal so with the chaff, establish that you deal more gently with the grain, so that, once the chaff has been separated, the grain may be stored in the barns.

“Will your wrath burn like fire,” like fire that reduces to ashes and does not purify?

By no means, Lord. Rather:

“Remember what my substance is,” that is, how holy and how great in dignity is the substance—namely Christ—who is to be born from my flesh, and to whom human beings are to be joined as his members are joined to the head.

Let it be not like the fire of destruction, but rather like the fire of completion.

Note that Christ is properly called “substance,” because everyone who works faithfully in faith is sustained by him.

This is what he says: “Remember what my substance is.” And truly you will do so, because you did not establish the sons of men in vain. They would have been established in vain if they were not joined as members to the head.

This he says by way of a question: “Have you established all the sons of men in vain?”

No. Rather, remember among them “who the human being is,” that is, how great and how holy the human being is, who will live and therefore will not see inward death, “and will rescue his soul from the hand of hell,” that is, from the power of darkness, because he will die in the flesh but will rise in majesty.

“Where are your ancient mercies, O Lord?”

That is, in him your mercies will be fulfilled, the mercies established by you before the foundation of the world, “as you swore to David in your truth.” For you firmly promised that through him you would redeem the human race.

“Remember, O Lord, the reproach of your servants,” a reproach, I say, “of many nations,” which “I have held in my bosom,” because through the spirit of prophecy I secretly foresaw that reproach as destined to occur in your servants.

Or thus: “Remember, O Lord, the reproach of your servants,” that is, of those who suffer the reproach “which I have held in my bosom,” that is, I see that reproach destined to occur in those who are in my bosom, that is, in those who are still to be born from my flesh.

Or thus: “Remember, O Lord, the reproach of your servants,” a reproach, I say, “of many nations,” that is, the reproach which many nations utter. Remember that reproach, so that those nations themselves may suffer that reproach on your account.

“I have held that reproach in my bosom,” that is, in the secrecy of my heart, where I see nations still to be incorporated into the faithful, so that the body of Christ may be fulfilled.

Or thus: “Remember your servants,” that is, those who suffer reproach; “which reproach I have held in my bosom,” that is, I see those suffering reproach signified by the hand being brought back into the bosom.

Or: “I have held it in my bosom,” that is, I have stored it inwardly with pleasure before me, because I see in the spirit that it will not be reckoned as reproach to those who will suffer that reproach for your sake, but as great glory.

“Remember the reproach with which your enemies have reproached,” namely the Jews, “with which they have reproached the exchange of your Christ.”

Death is called an exchange because through death he was exchanged from death into life, from corruption into incorruption. From this exchange, may the Lord be blessed forever.

Let blessing be given to him in the earlier people; let it also be given in the later people.

# Psalm LXXXIX. The Prayer of Moses, the Man of God

> O Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation.  
> Before the mountains were made, or the earth and the world were formed, from eternity and to eternity, you are God.  
> Do not turn the human being toward abasement; and you said: “Return, sons of men.”  
> For a thousand years in your sight are like yesterday, which has passed.  
> And their years will be like a watch in the night, which is counted as nothing.  
> In the morning let it pass away like grass; in the morning let it flower and pass away; in the evening let it fall, grow hard, and wither.  
> For we have failed in your anger, and in your fury we have been troubled.  
> You have placed our iniquities before your sight, our age in the illumination of your countenance.  
> For all our days have failed, and in your anger we have failed.  
> Our years will be considered like a spider; the days of our years are, in themselves, seventy years.  
> But if they are in strength, eighty years; and more than this is labor and sorrow.  
> For gentleness has come upon us, and we shall be chastised.  
> Who knows the power of your anger, and who can count your wrath according to your fear?  
> Make your right hand known in this way, and make those instructed in heart wise.  
> Turn, O Lord—how long?—and be entreated on behalf of your servants.  
> We have been filled in the morning with your mercy; we have exulted and rejoiced throughout all our days.  
> We have rejoiced for the days in which you humbled us, for the years in which we saw evil.  
> Look upon your servants and upon your works, and direct their sons.  
> And let the splendor of the Lord our God be upon us; direct the works of our hands upon us, and direct the work of our hands.

## Exposition
This psalm distinguishes for us the life of the old man and of the new, the life that is mortal and the life that is truly alive, namely, the punishment of the old man and the glory of the new man. It is headed with the name of Moses—not because Moses composed it, but because he, being a minister of the Old Testament and a prophet of the New, distinguished for us within that ministry the old life and the new life. For he intimated the new life through his mystery, if he is understood spiritually; but he pertains to the old life if he is understood literally. It is called “the prayer of Moses” because that man of God loved to pray to God and frequently to converse familiarly with him. It is also called “the prayer of the man of God,” not “of the servant of God,” because those whom the Lord calls to eternal life he no longer calls harshly as servants, but admonishes as sons and friends. Hence the saying: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends of God” (John XI). Let us therefore hear what is distinguished in this psalm. Let us flee and desire: let us flee the punishment of the old man and desire the glory of the new man. The Prophet says:

**Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation.**

As though he were saying: Lord Word, maker of all things, you have become our refuge, because, by assuming humanity, you have given us a sure refuge in you—and this from the carnal generation into the spiritual generation—for you are our eternal refuge and a support for those who flee to you.

**Before the mountains were made, or the earth and the world were formed, from age to age you are God.**

As though he were saying: I rightly say that refuge must be sought in you, not in man, because you are God before every creature. He does not say, “You were,” but “You are God,” because it is not fitting to say that he was for whom all things are present. Hence he himself says: “I am who I am” (Exodus III).

Or in this way: I said, “You have become our refuge”; and yet, although I have called you “made,” you are God before the mountains were made—that is, before the rational, heavenly creature was made by you—and before the earth was formed, that is, man; and before the world was formed, that is, before the earth itself was made round; that is, before man was established in an abundance of virtues. For from age and unto age, that is, from eternity unto eternity, you are God.

Note that, since no matter preceded the creation of the angels, he rightly said, “before the mountains were made.” But in the creation of man, since earth preceded as matter, he rightly said, “the earth was formed,” because at that time the earth received its form, when it was brought into existence as man.

**Do not turn man toward humiliation.**

You have become our refuge; therefore do not turn—that is, do not permit to be turned—the man who is understood to have been placed in this condition. You turned him away when you permitted him to usurp for himself a name, as though he were going to be God. Do not turn him, in the necessity of his downfall, toward humiliation, because he made himself humble before you. For he ceased from guilt, and therefore you cease from anger.

You turned away the proud man; do not turn away the humbled man.

Or in this way: Do not turn man—that is, do not permit him to be turned—from your sublimity toward humiliation, that is, toward these lowest things, so that, abandoning heavenly things, he may desire earthly things. And therefore I say, “Do not turn,” since you said: “Turn back to me, sons of men.” They must turn back to you, because however long a life they may have led, and however far their work may have extended, nothing is found when it is compared with your eternity. Hence he says:

**For a thousand years in your sight are like yesterday, which has passed away.**

As though he were saying: I therefore say that the sons of men must turn back to you because these temporal years—even a thousand of them—before your eyes, that is, when compared with those years that are before your eyes, which is to say, those that please you, are like yesterday that has passed away, that is, which now no longer exists; for all temporal things are as though they were not.

**And their years will be like a watch in the night, which is counted as nothing.**

As though he were saying: I compared the years of this life with yesterday; but to show that they will pass away even more quickly, I say that these years are like a watch in the night, that is, like a fourth part of the night. And I will say something still less: these years will be counted among those things that are regarded as nothing.

Behold how great a downfall he displays, when he shows that we pass our days toward an end and that our years are reckoned as nothing.

**In the morning let him pass away like grass; in the morning let him flower and pass away; in the evening let him fall, grow hard, and wither.**

Here the Prophet already rejoices at the divine justice that justly takes vengeance upon man. As though he were saying: Let man pay the penalty for what he committed. He who was destined to attain eternity through complete obedience will experience corruption, because he fell through ignorance. Let the morning pass away—that is, the infancy of each person, which is like grass: today it is green, and tomorrow it will wither. Let the morning flower: let infancy come into adolescence or youth; and let it pass away, when one considers that the days of this life are nothing. Let it fall in the evening, that is, let it fall into old age; let it grow hard in old age and wither in extreme age, because incessant coughing exhausts him.

Or in this way: “In the morning let it flower and pass away; in the evening let it fall,” that is, let it fall into old age through dying; let it grow hard in the corpse, where the limbs of each person become rigid; and let it wither into dust.

Or in this way: “In the morning let him pass away like grass,” that is, let each person’s good will pass away like grass and fail to reach a good action. The will cooperates in the morning, because in the will the light of righteousness first shines forth. “In the morning let it flower,” that is, let good will be brought into action; “and let it pass away,” because it does not persevere in a good work. “But in the evening let it fall,” that is, let it fall into sins, when the sun of righteousness no longer shines upon it. For each person falls as though it were evening when he turns away from good things and falls into evil.

Let him grow hard in his sins, having already been handed over to a reprobate mind; and let him wither, that is, become useless, like dust which the wind, because of its excessive dryness, casts from the face of the earth.

**For we have failed in your anger.**

As though he were saying: Why does he say that it should pass away in the morning like grass? Because we have failed in your anger—that is, your anger demanded such a failure. We deserved it, because we have all these things as the punishment of sin. On account of sin we have failed in your anger and become weak; and in your fury we have been troubled, to such an extent that we tremble to end our weakness in death.

And the fact that we have failed is evident from this:

**You have set our iniquities before your sight,**

that is, you have not forgotten our sins, which we committed in our first parent;

**and our age you have set in the light of your countenance,**

that is, in the brightness of your presence, where you would always observe us and correct us, as it were, for that reason.

The effect demonstrates this, for:

**All the days of the nations have failed;**

and therefore it is apparent that we have failed in your anger, that is, that through your anger we have come to failure.

**Our years will meditate like a spider; the days of our years are seventy years in themselves.**

Note that, just as a spider labors uselessly to complete its web, in which it is finally killed, so our years are compared with it. In them we uselessly meditate on how to acquire earthly things; once acquired, we become entangled in them and are dragged toward death. Hence the saying: “Why are earth and ashes proud? For in his lifetime he casts away his inmost parts” (Ecclesiasticus X).

**The days of our years—**

as though he were saying: Not only will our years, that is, our prolonged labor, be useless, but our days also, that is, each of our labors, will be useless. It is brief and is compared with the spider and with something useless.

**In themselves, seventy years.**

As though he were saying: Since our days and years are like a spider—that is, they meditate like a spider—our life has therefore been shortened. In those days, during which strength increases, only seventy years are found, although in the lifetime of our predecessors there were more years. Methuselah, for example, lived nine hundred and sixty-five years (Genesis V).

Note that, although our predecessors deserved the same punishment for sin in our first parent that we have deserved, it did not dominate them as it does us, because they were not as devoted to earthly things as we are.

**But if they are reckoned among the mighty, eighty years;**

It is said that human strength increases up to seventy years, remains at that level until eighty, and then declines. He says that if the years are considered in terms of strength—that is, in such a way that strength does not decline—they will be eighty years. Whatever is beyond that, that is, what remains after eighty years, is the labor and pain of those who live through these transitory years. And from what did this arise?

**Because gentleness has come upon us, and we shall be corrected.**

That is, an evident correction has come upon us; and thus we shall be corrected gently, lest we ultimately be corrected severely.

Or otherwise:

**In themselves, seventy years.**

The seventy, which is constituted by the second unit—namely, ten multiplied by seven—pertains to the old life, which turns in the circle of the number seven. Thus by seventy we can understand the pursuit of earthly things. He says that, because our years meditate like a spider, they are seventy in themselves—that is, they are the desire for temporal things, which are marked by the cycle of seven days.

Note that the same thing is understood by seventy and by seven, because seven multiplied by ten makes seventy; and they also agree in this respect: just as the number seven contains the first seven units, so seventy contains seven units.

Alternatively, by seven may be understood the pursuit of those who observe a bad sabbath. This is because the Jews, adhering to the letter, celebrated the seventh day, namely, the Sabbath.

Seventy may also be understood as the mourning and sorrow of those living in captivity, because the Jews were held in the city for seven decades, that is, for seventy years. There our mourning and sorrow were prefigured—the mourning and sorrow we endure for as long as we lead our life within this septenary age. And this is what he says: “In themselves, seventy years.”

**But if we live out our years among the mighty, they will be eighty years.**

We live out our years among the mighty—that is, we force our way into the kingdom of heaven—when we resist carnal desires and cling to heavenly things. Hence the saying: “From the time of John the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew XI).

Note that by eighty may be understood the pursuit of eternal things, which are to come on the eighth day, at the end of the world, when the number seven will come to an end. Or, because the Lord rose on the eighth day—which eighth day we celebrate as a sign of the celebration that is to come after the universal resurrection—the pursuit of those who truly observe the Sabbath may be understood by eighty.

Note that the same thing is understood by eighty as by eight, because eighty is constituted by multiplying eight by ten. And just as eight contains within itself eight first units, so eighty contains within itself eight second units.

By eighty may also be understood the happiness of those returning to their homeland. For the Jews who were held in captivity remained there for seven decades—that is, for seventy years—and in the eighth decade they returned to their homeland. There our return was prefigured, when, clothed in the garment of immortality, we shall return to our homeland.

This is what he says:

**If we live out our years among the mighty, our years will be eighty,**

that is, our years will then be spent in the pursuit of eternal things, or in the pursuit of those who truly observe the Sabbath, or in the happiness of those returning to their homeland. For whoever forces his way into the kingdom of God attends to this.

**And what is beyond them is labor and pain.**

That is, whatever is considered beyond those years is, for the saints, labor and pain. What is beyond these years is considered by the saints when they are anxious about the things necessary for food and clothing, from which no saint can be free. It is labor for them to be anxious about such matters, and they grieve because they must be concerned with them.

Or otherwise: “What is beyond their years” means whatever each person attends to in these years beyond the fact that the temporal things belonging to the number seven are transitory while the things to come are eternal. And whatever more each person attends to in these earthly things than the fact that they were given so that future things might be understood through them—that is labor here and pain in the future.

For whoever here clings to earthly goods as though they were genuine goods labors to acquire them; and when he departs from this life, there will be perpetual pain for him.

And how does this happen?

**Because we shall be corrected with a severe correction, when gentleness has come upon us,**

that is, when he who is now gentle toward all will appear in majesty as the Terrible One.

**Who knows the power of your anger?**

As though he were saying: Since your anger by which you correct us is so great, O Lord, who is there who knows worthily your powerful anger, by which you spare while punishing and punish while sparing?

The Lord spares by sparing, because those whom he enriches outwardly he blinds inwardly. He spares by scourging, because those whom he permits to be troubled outwardly he preserves invincible inwardly.

Hence he says:

**Who knows the power of your anger, and who can number your anger according to your fear,**

that is, so that he may fear you?

Or, “to number your anger according to your fear” means: Who can worthily number the abundance of prosperity that you grant to certain people in your anger, according to your fear—that is, so as to compare the abundance of prosperity with the number of punishments? For God exalts some in order to cast them down, and prospers others in order that they may be ensnared.

**Make your right hand known in this way, and those instructed in heart in wisdom.**

As though he were saying: So that we may recognize your anger, make your right hand known to us—that is, your Son—in such a way that, by imitating him, we may number your anger according to your fear. And make known to us those instructed in heart in wisdom, that is, those whom you have instructed outwardly with your wisdom, so that by their example we may number what must be numbered between the abundance of prosperity and the number of punishments.

For this to happen:

**Turn back, Lord—how long?—and be entreated on behalf of your servants,**

you who were once entreated on behalf of your free people.

And indeed you will do this, because:

**We have been filled in the morning with your mercy;**

that is, we shall be filled with your mercy after the night of this life has passed. And:

**We have exulted outwardly and been delighted,**

that is, we shall be delighted inwardly in all our days, namely, in the everlasting days, when we shall see you face to face (1 Corinthians XIII).

And from what will this come to us?

**Because we have rejoiced for the days in which you humbled us, and for the years in which we saw evil.**

That is, we shall rejoice for the days in which you permitted us to be troubled, and for the years in which we saw evil. For no one rejoices there unless he has been troubled here; no homeland is sweet to anyone unless his pilgrimage has been burdensome.

**Look upon your servants and upon your works, and direct their children.**

As though he were saying: So that we may rejoice there, in the meantime look here upon your servants. Look, I say, upon your works, because the fact that your servants have been made your servants is your work, not theirs. And therefore direct their children—that is, their good works—or their children, meaning their imitators in good works.

And so that this may happen:

**Let the splendor of the Lord our God be upon us,**

that is, let the image of the Lord our God—namely, our reason, through which we ought to imagine him—be upon us; let it rule us and not be oppressed by sensuality.

**And direct the works of our hands over us,**

so that they may strive toward heavenly things and not be performed for the reward of earthly things.

And because all good works ought to be one in the root of charity, he therefore says in the singular:

**And direct the work of our hands.**

As though he were saying: Direct our works in such a way that they may be one work, that is, that they may strive toward one end, charity.

# PSALM XC. A SONG OF PRAISE, BY DAVID HIMSELF

> **He who dwells in the help of the Most High will abide in the protection of the God of heaven. He will say to the Lord: You are my protector and my refuge; my God, I will hope in him. For he himself will deliver me from the snare of the hunters and from the harsh word. He will overshadow you with his shoulders, and beneath his wings you will hope. His truth will surround you with a shield; you will not fear the terror of the night, the arrow flying by day, the activity that passes through the darkness, the assault and the demon of noonday. A thousand will fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand, but it will not approach you. Nevertheless, with your eyes you will look on and see the retribution of sinners. For you, Lord, are my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge. Evil will not approach you, and scourging will not come near your dwelling. For he has commanded his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways. They will carry you in their hands, lest you perhaps strike your foot against a stone. You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon. Because he hoped in me, I will deliver him; I will protect him, because he has known my name. He cried out to me, and I will hear him; I am with him in tribulation. I will rescue him and glorify him. I will fill him with length of days, and I will show him my salvation.**

# EXPOSITION

A song is placed here as an expression of exultation. But since no one would wish in this psalm to exult over human weakness, the title “a song of praise” has been added, so that you may understand it as a praiseworthy song—a song, namely, that pertains to divine power and not to human weakness.

For the Prophet, foreseeing the Lord’s incarnation, death, and resurrection, spoke for the instruction of all; and, likewise foreseeing his temptation, he disclosed it for our benefit, so that, instructed by his temptation, we might not yield to the tempter, while nevertheless presuming nothing about ourselves and attributing everything to his grace.

For he left us this example of humility. Although he was a man free from sin, and although the Word of the Father was personally united to him, he nevertheless did not rise up in vengeance against his tempters. Rather, when it was said to him, “You have a demon,” he answered humbly: “I do not have a demon” (John VIII).

He himself was also tempted, and this so that the Christian might not be overcome by the tempter. The temptation was not necessary for him; it was instruction for us.

Let us therefore walk in him who made himself the way for us, because, if we walk in him, he will lead us to himself as life along the way.

The Prophet says as follows:

Whoever dwells in the help of the Most High will abide under the protection [Col. 0626A] of the God of heaven. It is as though he said: Someone preceded in the human race, placed in an abundance of virtues; but, trusting in himself, he did not remain. The second man, however, who is to come, will dwell—that is, he will persevere in obedience—not trusting in his own help, as Adam did, but in the help of the Most High. Therefore he will dwell in the protection of God—not in just any protection, but in that of heaven; that is, he will dwell there both inwardly and outwardly, since he will not apostatize from the Lord his God even in thought. Such a man will say to the Lord: “You are my supporter”—that is, my defender—“and my refuge, my God.” He will not say, “I am my own god,” as Adam did when he wished to be a god to himself. He will say this to the Lord, and he will say it for the encouragement of his neighbor: “I will hope in him.” And this because he himself has delivered me from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word [Col. 0626B].

These hunters are the devil and his angels, who always pursue a human being as though hunting him, so that they may seize him. They also set snares in which he may be caught. For the devil suggests to him love and desire for temporal things, but the Lord frees his own from these snares by granting them the strength to close the door of the heart against the suggestion of desire.

Note that snares and nets are usually set not on the road but beside the road. Thus the devil does not set a snare for those who are on the road—that is, for those who adhere perfectly to Christ—because Christ leads them by himself, who is the way, to himself, who is the life. For those who are beside the road—that is, those who are less perfect in faith—a net is set so that they may be caught. Nevertheless, the Lord frees them by leading them toward perfection. This is what he says: “He himself has delivered me from the snare of hunters” [Col. 0626C].

The harsh word is every word of detraction or insult spoken by those who live wickedly, even if they speak flatteringly to someone, provided that they do so in order to seduce him. It is called a harsh word because God frees his own from such a word by giving them strength, so that they yield neither to flatteries nor to threats.

Note also that, just as when snares or nets have been set, stones are sometimes thrown into hedges in order to frighten birds and drive them toward the snare, so a harsh word is commonly directed at the faithful through threats and flatteries: either they are terrified by fear and fall into the snares, or, attracted by the things presented to them in flattering words, they entangle their feet in the snares.

“He has overshadowed you with his shoulders, and under his wings you will hope.” It is as though he said: He will say to the Lord; he will say it to his neighbor; and he will also say it to himself in rejoicing with gratitude: You will rightly hope in him, because he will overshadow you—that is, protect you inwardly—with his shoulders, guarding you in his presence. This is said by way of comparison, because one who holds someone between his shoulders, joined to his breast, has him as though present. Thus the Lord has, as it were, overshadowed with his shoulders the one whom he makes present to himself. This is what is meant by “He will overshadow you with his shoulders,” and “under his wings you will hope,” protected both in yourself and in those who belong to you.

These things are said by comparison, not literally, because birds, especially hens, customarily protect and warm their young under their wings. A hen, too, because of the excessive affection she has for her chicks, makes herself ruffled and weak for their sake. Thus the Lord, as though under his wings, warms his own, whom he guards with such great affection that they do not become prey to the devil [Col. 0627A].

Or otherwise: “He will overshadow you with his shoulders.” Certain birds, such as the eagle, carry their young on their shoulders and transport them in this way until they learn to fly, lest, when they first begin to fly, they suffer a fall. So the Lord, while we are weak, carries us until he perfects us, lest, if he should abandon us, we suffer a fall because of our imperfection. This is what is meant by “He will overshadow you with his shoulders”: he will defend you in those who belong to you. “And under his wings”—that is, under the love of God and neighbor—being overshadowed, you will hope in those who belong to you.

Or otherwise: “He will overshadow you with his shoulders.” Strength is commonly signified by the shoulders. The Lord’s strength is signified in those miracles by which he overshadows and sustains his own. When signs support the truth of their words, the preachers themselves are sustained, as it were, by a certain strength, because they become more fervent in faith when true preachers are confirmed by miracles [Col. 0627B]. “And under his wings you will hope”—that is, in the precepts of your commandments, by which the faithful are carried, as though on wings, into the open air of freedom.

“His truth will surround you with a shield, and therefore they will not fear who will be safe from fear: from the arrow flying by day, from the business moving about in darkness, from assault and from the noonday demon.”

Here he sets forth two things and doubles them, so that there are four things by which the faithful are attacked, while the Lord’s truth surrounds them. They are attacked by a light persecution and by a severe one. Those who are still like night yield to these, not knowing how to give an account of their Christianity. They are also attacked by a light and a severe persecution; again, some who are like day yield to them, although they know [Col. 0627C] how to give an account of their Christianity.

But because they are surrounded by truth as by a shield, all who are tested here remain unharmed. This is what is meant by “You will not fear inwardly from the terror of night”: from the light persecution that occurs among those who are ignorant, who are still like night because of their ignorance of the account they ought to give for their faith. Fear signifies a light persecution, since fear ordinarily precedes an event.

“You will not fear the arrow flying by day.” The arrow signifies a light persecution, because an arrow wounds less severely than a sword. The phrase “flying by day” signifies that it occurs among those who are like day, knowing how to give an account of their faith. Thus, “your people will not fear the arrow flying by day” means that they will not fear the light persecution that occurs among those who have understanding.

“You will not fear among your own the business moving about in darkness”—that is, the violent persecution which, because of its magnitude, is called a business, as though it denied leisure. It moves about in darkness among those who do not know that temporal things must be despised and eternal things alone hoped for.

“You will not fear the assault and the noonday demon”—that is, the persistence of a violent persecution which occurs among those who know that they have been called to eternal things, yet nevertheless yield to excessive troubles. The demon signifies tribulation; the assault signifies the persistence of tribulation. “Noonday” signifies two things: the heat of tribulation and those among whom the tribulation occurs, since they too seemed in a certain way to burn because they knew how to give an account of their Christianity.

“A thousand will fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand” [Col. 0628A]. It is as though the Prophet said: You rightly say to yourself, rejoicing with gratitude, “I will not fear the noonday demon,” because many have been overcome by the noonday demon. For even those who, according to their own opinion, were going to sit with you on the judgment seat in order to judge others lost, when the heat of tribulation came, what they presumptuously promised themselves.

Note that when Peter asked and said, “Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what, then, will there be for us?” the Lord replied: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the seat of his majesty, you also will sit, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19). Attending to this, many left what they possessed and hoped that they would sit with the Lord to judge. But because, in the good they were doing, they trusted not in God but in themselves, they fell from the Lord’s side—from the judgment seat—not because they had been there, but because they had presumptuously promised it to themselves. This is what is meant by “A thousand will fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.”

There are also many who, attending to God’s command, “Sell everything you have and give to the poor” (ibid.), sell all that they possess and give very generous alms. But because they do this not in God’s sight but for human approval, they will fall from the Lord’s right hand—not because they had been there, but because they thought they would come there.

Note that there are more who will be judged at the right hand than there are those who will sit at the side as judges. Therefore he said: “A thousand will fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.” But to you—that is, to those who belong to you—that fall will not draw near, because, although torment approaches the flesh, it does not harm the place of faith.

“Nevertheless, with your eyes you will consider, and you will see the retribution of sinners.” They will fall from your side because of the injustice of those persecuting you. Yet those persecutors, although they flourish, have not persecuted them with impunity. For with your eyes—that is, with your discernment—you will consider that this has not happened with impunity, and you will see—that is, you will make others see—that it serves as a tribulation for the sinners that they are permitted to persecute others.

Or in this way: They appear to fall from your side and your right hand. Nevertheless, with your eyes you will consider—that is, your discernment will recognize—that they were neither at your right hand nor at your side. And you will see—that is, you will make others see—that their falling is the retribution for their sins, because they gloried not in you but in themselves and in their good works [Col. 0628D].

Or otherwise: “A thousand will fall at your side.” It is as though the Prophet said: You rightly say to yourself, rejoicing with gratitude, “I will not fear among those who belong to me,” because a thousand will fall at your side—that is, from among those who truly belong at your side—namely, a thousand dangers or a thousand temptations. And ten thousand temptations or dangers will fall at your right hand, because however greatly the dangers or temptations are multiplied, they will not harm your own. This is because no danger will approach you—that is, those who belong to you. For although persecutors inflict torment on the flesh, they do not harm the place of faith.

Are they therefore afflicted in vain? No. Although they themselves are not overcome by tribulation, you will nevertheless consider with your eyes that they are not afflicted in vain, since their tribulation serves as a test. You will see that it is the retribution of sins for those who inflict tribulation on others. It is as though he said: Your discernment recognizes that tribulation is not inflicted in vain, because it is inflicted for the testing of those who endure it and for the condemnation of those who inflict it.

“For you, Lord, are my hope; you have made your refuge most high.” Here the voice is again that of the Head. It is as though he said: I rightly rejoice with gratitude in those who belong to me, and rightly do not fear among them, because you, Lord, have become my hope—that is, the hope of my people—by giving them through me what they ought to hope for. For the resurrection that preceded in me, the Head, will also follow in the members; thus you have become the hope of my people.

The human race knew that it could die, but did not know that it could rise again. Thus it had something to fear, but nothing to hope for. In order that hope might be added to them, the one who had given the fear of death for the sake of discipline gave the hope of resurrection for the sake of reward. This is what is meant by “You are my hope, Lord,” and “You have made me your refuge,” because the certain refuge that the human race has when it comes to me is from you, since you have made me most high.

What is higher than making mortal flesh immortal and corruptible flesh incorruptible? Or in this way: “You have made your refuge most high,” because through me the sins of human beings have been destroyed, according to Paul’s statement: “Whom he set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, so that he himself might be true, justifying the one who is of the faith of Jesus” (Romans 5). Or in this way: “You have made your refuge most high,” according to the saying: “He gave him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2) [Col. 0629C].

“Evil will not approach you, and the scourge will not come near your tabernacle.” The voice of the Prophet is as though he were saying: Truly, Lord, you have become hope among those who belong to you, because evil will not approach you—that is, those who belong to you. For although the persecutor rages outwardly, inwardly God has become their helper. “The scourge will not come near your tabernacle.”

This tabernacle is the body of Christ, in which he himself waged war according to the flesh and in which he suffered many scourges, because he was seized, scourged, spat upon, and finally hung on the cross. But because he rose again and took on an incorruptible body, scourges will no longer approach this tabernacle. This is what is meant by “The scourge will not come near your tabernacle.”

“For God the Father has commanded his angels concerning you”—that is, on your account—that they should minister to you in the service of servitude. Hence the saying: “And an angel appeared, strengthening him” (Luke 22). This strengthening was not required by necessity but was an exhibition of service. It was also for our instruction, because every one of the faithful has an angel strengthening him in good works. Hence the saying: “Their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matthew 18).

This is what is meant by: “Because he has commanded his angels concerning you”—namely, that they guard you in all your ways. And therefore, because he has commanded them, “they will carry you in their hands”—that is, they will offer you the service of their ministry—“lest you perhaps strike your foot against a stone.” Your feet—that is, the apostles and the others through whom you will enter, as through feet, into the knowledge of the nations—must not strike against a stone, that is, against the hardness of the Law [Col. 0630A], so that what they ought to do out of love they do out of fear, like the Jews, who served God out of fear rather than love. Therefore they received the Law written on tablets of stone, because they did not raise their hard hearts toward love but pressed them down into fear.

But in order that the love of God might be poured into the hearts of the faithful, the Lord was carried into heaven by the hands of angels, so that the Holy Spirit might be sent to the disciples. He would remove fear and provide the fullness of love, so that what had previously been difficult for those who feared would become easy for those who loved. Hence the Apostle says: “You have not received,” he says, “the spirit of servitude again in fear, but the spirit of freedom in love” (Romans 8). This is what is meant by: “They will carry you in their hands from the sight of human beings into heaven.”

And what fruit results from this? “Lest you perhaps strike your foot against a stone”—that is, lest your preachers become like those who strike against the stone of stumbling, like the Jews who stumbled over the Law written on tablets of stone, doing the good things they did not from love but from fear.

Note that the Lord was not carried by angels because he needed to be carried back by them; rather, the carrying itself was an exhibition of service.

“You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk.” Basilisk is interpreted as “royal”; hence the basilisk is called the king of serpents. Thus the basilisk signifies the devil, who is the head of all serpentine wickedness. The asp signifies all heretics and other poisonous people who kill the souls of the faithful with their venom. Nevertheless, the Lord will walk upon them in those who belong to him. “And you will trample the lion and the dragon”—that is, your people will trample those who rage openly and those who plot secretly [Col. 0630C].

“Because he will hope in me, I will deliver him.” It is as though he said: God the Father commanded his angels concerning you, saying: “I will deliver him”—that is, he has fixed the anchor of his hope in me. “I will protect him among his own from the heat of vices.” And this because he has known my name—namely, that it is “Lord.” Those know this who, through good works, profess themselves to be servants of the Lord.

“He will cry out to me, and I will hear him,” both in himself and in those who belong to him. “I am with him in the tribulation of his own [people].” Hence the saying: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28).

“I will rescue him from temporal persecution, and I will glorify him with eternal glory. I will rescue him—not so that he may hear harsh words, but so that, being ashamed by them, he may not fall into the devil’s trap [Col. 0630D]—and finally I will glorify him, because I will fill him with the length of eternal days, and I will show him my salvation,” as in the saying, “I will show him myself” (John 14).

# PSALM XCI. A PSALM, A SONG FOR THE DAY OF THE SABBATH

“It is good to confess to the Lord and to sing praises to your name, O Most High; to proclaim your mercy in the morning and your truth throughout the night; on the ten-stringed instrument, on the psaltery, with a song, on the lyre. For you have gladdened me, Lord, by your work, and in the works of your hands I will rejoice. How greatly your works have been magnified, Lord! Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep. The foolish man will not know, and the stupid will not understand these things. When sinners have sprung up like grass and all who work iniquity have appeared, so that they may perish forever and ever: but you, Most High, are forever, Lord. For behold, your enemies, Lord—behold, your enemies will perish, and all who work iniquity will be scattered. And my horn will be exalted like that of the unicorn, and my old age will be in abundant mercy. My eye has looked down upon my enemies, and my ear will hear of those who rise up against me, the malicious. The just man will flourish like the palm tree; he will multiply like the cedar of Lebanon. Planted in the house of the Lord, they will flourish in the courts of the house of our God. They will still multiply in abundant old age, and they will be patient in goodness, so that they may proclaim: For the Lord our God is upright, and there is no iniquity in him.”

## EXPOSITION

The Prophet, seeing that the Jews attended to the letter and not the spirit, and celebrated a coarse Sabbath rather than a refined one, urges us in this psalm to celebrate a refined Sabbath. This refined Sabbath is serenity of conscience, tranquility of mind, rest of heart, and cessation from evil works. For it does no good to abstain from work with the hands unless the mind also ceases from crime, since it is better to plow than to dance, and to dig than to drink to drunkenness.

The Jews, however, celebrating a coarse Sabbath, did not attend to this. Their hands rested from work, but their minds were more ready to commit wickedness. They did not understand that that Sabbath was a sign of the future rest, to which no one will attain unless conscience defends him as free.

That the Sabbath imposed on the Jews for celebration was a sign of the future rest is indicated by the book of Genesis. While it determines the preceding days by morning and evening, it does not determine that seventh day—the Sabbath on which the Lord rested from his work—by evening. For the rest that is signified as future through this Sabbath is darkened by no shadows but is experienced eternally in the purest brightness.

When it is said that the Lord rested from his works, this does not mean that he suffered any labor in working. Rather, it prefigured what was to happen—namely, in the congregation of the faithful. For no believer reaches the true rest signified as future by the Sabbath without labor. To signify this, he is said to have rested from his work on the seventh day [Col. 0631D].

The title is explained as follows: “A psalm”—that is, this is an activity—“of a song,” that is, of exultation; a song, I say, to be possessed “on the day of the Sabbath,” that is, in contemplation of the true rest, which consists in serenity of conscience. And because serenity of conscience proceeds from confession, the psalm begins with confession.

Confession is of two kinds: either when we praise the Lord for our good deeds, or when we accuse ourselves by confessing what we have done badly. He says as follows:

“It is good to confess to the Lord.” Therefore confess to the Lord by accusing yourself for your evil deeds and praising him for his good deeds. This is what is meant by “It is good to confess to the Lord and to sing praises to your name”—that is, glorifying it.

“O Most High”: your name must be praised in this way, so that each person may proclaim that it is due to your mercy that you console your own in prosperity, and that it is due to your justice that you correct them in adversity. This is what is meant by “It is good to sing praises to your name, proclaiming your mercy in the morning”—that is, in prosperity, so that your people may not fail—and “your truth”—that is, your justice—“throughout the night,” that is, in adversity, so that your people may not sin with impunity.

“On the ten-stringed psaltery.” It is as though he said: It is good to sing praises to your name. But one must sing praises on the ten-stringed psaltery, so that in our soul—which in our higher part gives a sound like that of a psaltery—we observe the ten commandments of the Law [Col. 0632B]. And this must be done not with sadness but “with a song,” that is, with cheerfulness of mind, because forced service is not pleasing to God. Hence the saying: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9).

One must also sing praises “on the lyre,” that is, in the mortification of the flesh, because everyone who wishes to sing praises well must crucify the flesh with its vices and desires. Or “on the lyre,” that is, in the service of the body, namely, in the performance of almsgiving and the other virtues administered through the body.

“For you have gladdened me, Lord, by your work.” It is as though he said: I ought rightly to sing praises to you, because when I was saddened by my creation, you gladdened me, Lord, by your work, since through you I shall reign. Hence the Apostle says: “We are his work, created in good works” (Ephesians 2).

And because you have gladdened me by your work, therefore “in the works of your hands I will exercise myself”—that is, I will attribute to you whatever good I do, because it is not I who work, but your hands—that is, your powers—work in me, if I do anything good.

“How greatly your works have been magnified, Lord!” You have gladdened me, Lord, by your work, and this work of yours—your making me rejoice in your work—how greatly has it been magnified, that is, how greatly must it be esteemed. “And your thoughts have become exceedingly deep”: it is beyond the investigation of the human mind that by exalting one person you cast down another, and by humbling one you exalt another.

Or in this way: One must sing praises to your name on the lyre. But the fact that you permit those who sing praises on the lyre to labor, while those who do not sing praises flourish—“your works, Lord, are great, and your thoughts have become exceedingly deep”—shows that in these matters you arrange everything within yourself. For the foolish man—that is, the one who does not know how to guard himself for the future, considering only temporal life—will not know this, and the stupid will not understand it.

The stupid person is one who, although in the greatest misery, thinks himself to be in the greatest happiness, like many who are exalted for the purpose of being cast down. This is what is meant by “the stupid will not understand these things.” And he says: What things?

“When sinners have sprung up”—that is, having sprung forth apart from the others—“like grass,” which is green today and tomorrow is thrown into the furnace (Matthew 6), “and he will not understand how all who work iniquity will perish forever and ever,” that is, eternally.

This will happen because you, Lord, will come as the Most High, destined to reign forever, so that you may dry up the grass—that is, dry them up like the sun which, coming from on high, dries grass with its heat.

Or, more simply: They will perish eternally, but you, Lord, whom they despise here in humility, will be Most High, and this forever.

“For behold, your enemies, Lord—for behold, your enemies will perish.” It is as though he said: They do not pay attention, and so they will perish, although in truth they will perish. “For behold, your enemies will perish.” And behold, it is destined to happen, because the time is short. To confirm that they will perish, he repeats: “Behold, they will perish.” And this because they are your enemies.

“And all who work iniquity will be scattered,” because the sheep will be separated from the goats. When they have been scattered, “my horn will be exalted”—that is, my sublimity—“like that of the unicorn.”

Unicorns are those who raise themselves toward heavenly things with one hope, as though with one horn. Hence the saying: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek” (Psalm 26).

“And my old age will be in abundant mercy.” Old age signifies the final state of the faithful, which will be in abundant mercy—that is, in overflowing mercy—because although mercy is now present in calling and justification, it will then be abundant, when eternal rest is given in place of temporal labor.

The final state of the faithful is rightly called old age, because just as in old age the hair that was previously black becomes white, so there those who previously labored in temporal struggle will rejoice in eternal rest, where there will be no blackness of perverse conduct.

“And my eye has looked down upon my enemies.” It is as though he said: Because my old age will be in abundant mercy, therefore my eye—namely, the inward eye—looks down upon my enemies.

“And my ear will hear of those who rise up against me, the malicious.” That is, when the malicious rise up so that their likeness may appear in me, so that they may conform me to themselves, my ear will hear from the truth presiding within me that it is not the faithful person who flourishes for a time. Rather, “the just man will flourish like the palm tree”—late, indeed, because everyone must enter into rest after many tribulations (Acts 14). This is also signified by the palm, because below, near its root, it is rough, while above it is adorned with flowers.

“And he will multiply like the cedar of Lebanon,” because, “planted in the house of the Lord”—that is, in the Church, founded in love (Ephesians 3)—“they will flourish in the courts of the house of our God,” that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem, where all delightful things are stored [Col. 0633D].

This is still to be awaited. Thus they will multiply in abundant old age, and meanwhile they will be patient in goodness here, because patience is necessary if we are to receive the promises (Hebrews 10).

This is what is meant by: “They will be patient in goodness, so that they may proclaim that the Lord our God is upright” in correcting his children, “and that there is no iniquity in him when he spares fugitive servants.”

# PSALM XCII. A SONG OF PRAISE OF DAVID, FOR THE DAY BEFORE THE SABBATH, WHEN THE EARTH WAS FOUNDED

“The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty. The Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself. For he has established the world, which will not be moved. Your throne is prepared from that time; you are from eternity. The rivers have lifted up, Lord; the rivers have lifted up their voice. The rivers have lifted up their waves, from the voices of many waters. The upheavals of the sea are wonderful; the Lord on high is wonderful. Your testimonies have become exceedingly trustworthy; holiness befits your house, Lord, throughout the length of days.”

## EXPOSITION

The earth said to have been founded signifies the human race, which on the day before the Sabbath—that is, in the sixth age of the world—was established and founded by the Lord in faith.

The day before the Sabbath is called Friday (the sixth day), on which he created the human being. In the sixth age of the world he also regenerated through faith the one who had flowed away from him through disobedience, and in the sixth hour of the day redeemed him by his blood [Col. 0634B].
