To understand which age is signified here by the day before the Sabbath through faith, let us distinguish the ages of the world from the beginning. The first age, like the first day, extends from Adam to Noah. The second age, like the second day, extends from Noah to Abraham. The third age, like the third day, extends from Abraham to David. The fourth age, like the fourth day, extends from David to the Babylonian captivity. The fifth extends from the Babylonian captivity to the preaching of John. The sixth extends from the preaching of John to the end of the world. The seventh will belong to those who sleep; the eighth to those who rise again.

In the sixth age the earth was founded, because the human race—which had flowed away through the disobedience of its first parents—was founded in faith through the preaching of John and the others. The Prophet speaks of this foundation in this psalm, exhorting both his contemporaries and those who came before them not to refuse to be founded by the Lord and by those who belong to him in faith. The Prophet says:

“The Lord has reigned.” It is as though he said: He who reigned before the ages in divinity now reigns in the humility of the flesh. And how has he reigned? “He has clothed himself with beauty”—that is, he has put on sobriety and comeliness. “He has clothed himself with strength and girded himself” to establish the world.

Note that “he has clothed himself with beauty and strength” is referred to different people. He clothed himself with beauty with regard to those who said, “He is good” (John 7). With regard to those who said, “No, but he deceives the crowds” (ibid.), “he clothed himself with strength,” because he endured them patiently [Col. 0634D].

Let us also put on beauty and strength. If there is someone who is pleased by our good works, let us put on beauty, giving thanks to God that an example of good action can be taken from us. If there is someone displeased by our good works, let us put on strength against him, enduring him patiently.

Or in this way: “The Lord has reigned”—that is, he has obtained the kingdom for himself. Therefore, in the manner of kings, he has adorned himself, because he has put on beauty and strength—that is, he has made his own people beautiful and strong. Thus, in those who belong to him, he girded himself so that he might be ready for action. Hence the other passage: “He girded himself with strength for war” (Psalm 17). Or, he put on sobriety and patience.

“For he has established the world.” It is as though he said: The Lord clothed himself with strength and girded himself, and the result indicates this, because through those virtuous people he established the world—that is, he made it firm in faith—making certain people into rounded spheres, as it were, through the virtues. This world will not be moved—that is, it will no longer suffer instability and departure from God—because in that world your throne is prepared, O God, from that time, namely, from the time of John the Baptist, when human beings began to be founded in faith.

Yet I will never say that your throne was prepared only from that time. You are God from eternity—from eternity into eternity.

“The rivers have lifted up, Lord.” He shows how the Lord’s throne has been prepared: the rivers—that is, the preachers of the world—of whom it was said, “Whoever drinks the water that I will give him, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 4 and 7). These rivers lifted themselves up in sublimity of mind.

The same rivers lifted up their voice: they raised it for the encouragement of others. Those rivers also lifted up their waves—that is, their threats—saying, “Unless you repent, you will perish” (Luke 13). These waves proceeded from the voices of many waters, because many other preachers harmonized with the apostles who had preached earlier.

Thus wonderful upheavals of the sea came to be, because those who were exalted among the nations swelled up against the preaching of the Lord’s throne and against the waves of the preachers. This was nevertheless not to be feared, because the Lord was wonderful in suppressing the lofty waves of the sea.

In this way, through the upheavals of the sea, “your testimonies have become exceedingly trustworthy,” because your preachers experienced in themselves what you testified: “In the world you will have distress, but in me you will have peace” (John 16). Let no one be troubled by this, because such holiness—that is, holiness made such through tribulation—befits your house, namely, the Church extending “throughout the length of days,” that is, into eternity.

Or otherwise: “Your throne is prepared from that time; you are from eternity.” And at the time when your throne, O God, was being prepared, “the rivers lifted themselves up”: the worldly philosophers were exalted in pride of mind. They also lifted up their voice so that through empty disputations they might oppose your preachers.

“The rivers also lifted up”—that is, the rulers of the nations—“their waves,” that is, threatening words. This proceeded from the voices of many waters—that is, from the agreement of many peoples. Wonderful upheavals of the sea came to be. Conversely, the Lord became wonderful in suppressing those upheavals. And thus, when those upheavals had been suppressed, “your testimonies”—that is, your miracles, which bore witness to those who belonged to you—“became exceedingly trustworthy.”

“Exceedingly,” because signs confirmed their words. Hence the saying: “The Lord working with them and confirming the word through the accompanying signs” (Mark 16). Such holiness also befits your house—that is, your Church, which extends throughout the length of days.

# PSALM XCIII. A PSALM OF DAVID, FOR THE FOURTH DAY OF THE WEEK

“God of vengeance, Lord, God of vengeance has acted freely. Rise up, you who judge the earth; repay the proud. How long will sinners, Lord, how long will sinners boast? They will utter and speak iniquity; all who work injustice will speak. They have humbled your people, Lord, and afflicted your inheritance. They have killed the widow and the stranger, and murdered orphans. And they said: ‘The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand.’ Understand, foolish among the people, and, you stupid ones, finally become wise. Does he who planted the ear not hear? Or does he who fashioned the eye not consider? Will he who corrects the nations not reprove—the one who teaches human beings knowledge? The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, for they are vain. Blessed is the person whom you instruct, Lord, and whom you teach from your law, so that you may give him relief from evil days until a pit is dug for the sinner. For the Lord will not reject his people, and he will not abandon his inheritance. Until justice is turned into judgment, and all who are upright in heart follow it. Who will rise up for me against the malicious? Or who will stand with me against those who work iniquity? Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell. If I said, ‘My foot has been moved,’ your mercy, Lord, would help me. According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul. Can the seat of iniquity cling to you, who fashion labor into a commandment? They will lie in wait for the soul of the just and condemn innocent blood. And the Lord became my refuge, and my God the help of my hope. And he will repay them for their iniquity, and in their malice he will destroy them; the Lord our God will destroy them.”

## EXPOSITION
The less learned—that is, those less perfect in the body of Christ, which is the Church—are accustomed to think perversely, to grieve silently, and sometimes even to break out into murmuring aloud when they see the prosperity of the wicked and the labor of the good: the former reigning, the latter serving; the former exalted, the latter brought low; the former abounding, the latter in need. They say that they have believed in vain, and so are stirred to imitate the wickedness of the former. Or, if they do not dare to do so because of their weakness—for they fear human judgment—although they keep their hands innocent, they nevertheless defile their minds; and among their other wicked thoughts they harbor this chief wicked thought: that God has turned his eyes away from the faithful. They say that God does not care to govern these lower things; or they say that he loves good and wicked people equally; or, what is worse, that he persecutes the good and favors the wicked. When they murmur in this way, they harm no one, but inflict the greatest evil upon themselves, because they do not possess true innocence. For true innocence is that which harms neither oneself nor another. They observed this innocence of whom it was said: “Who was able to transgress and did not transgress, and to do evil and did not do it” (Ecclesiasticus 31). [Col. 0636D]

The psalm addresses these sorrows and wicked thoughts, exhorting those who murmur not to be envious of the prosperity of the wicked, and to have patience in the labor of the good. For everyone who is truly a Christian, when he sees people murmuring in this way, grieves and laughs at them, and says: “It is not for a human being to investigate why God allows the good to labor and the wicked to prosper. It is enough for me to know that the labor of the good is temporary, and the prosperity of the wicked is temporary.” Saying this, he proposes patience to himself in the face of the prosperity of the wicked and the misery of the good. [Col. 0637A]

This is the patience taught by the present psalm, whose title is as follows: “A Psalm of David, for the Fourth Day of the Week.” On the Fourth Day of the Week, we read that God made the luminaries in the firmament (Genesis 1): the sun to rule the day, and the moon and stars to rule the night (Psalm 135). However much people may lie about these luminaries, however many hailstorms may fall, and however many dangers may occur, they are not moved from their position; rather, they complete the course appointed for them by God. [Col. 0637B]

By such luminaries are signified those of whom the Apostle says: “Do everything without disputing and murmuring, so that you may be blameless and sincere, immaculate children of God, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like fixed luminaries in the firmament, holding fast the word of life” (Philippians 2).

They shine like a luminary in the firmament who attend to the Lord’s promises in the sacred Scriptures. For those who attend to them complete their course, as it were, in the firmament, possessing patience in every respect, including in this matter: that they see the wicked prosper and the good labor. Those, however, who endure this impatiently fall, as it were, from the firmament, failing to complete the proper course of their appointed state. And since this psalm proposes patience, it is rightly entitled “for the Fourth Day of the Week”—not because the psalm concerns the things created on the Fourth Day of the Week, but because it concerns the things signified by the things created on the Fourth Day of the Week. For the voice in this psalm is that of those signified by the luminaries placed in the firmament on the Fourth Day of the Week, and they say: [Col. 0637C]

**“God of vengeance, Lord; God of vengeance has acted freely.”**

As though he were saying: Let no one envy the wicked in their prosperity, and let no one grieve if the good are suffering; rather, let him always keep his heart above, because God is the Lord of vengeance—that is, of the vengeance to be carried out—and no evil will go unpunished by him. I say that God is the God of vengeance because he acted freely in the Word, and therefore he will act freely in judgment. He acted freely in the Word, as it is written: “He was speaking as one having authority, and not as their scribes and Pharisees” (Matthew 7). [Col. 0637D]

He acted freely while destined to suffer, and therefore he will fear no one when he comes to judge. But in order that you may act freely in judgment, be born, die, and rise again; and thus be exalted, you who judge the earth—that is, who judge those who are earthly—and repay the proud according to their deserts. The proud are those who do not wish to confess their sins; to them the Lord will repay according to their works.

Or it may be connected in this way: He acted freely in the Word, and therefore he acts freely in judgment. But the wicked people did not understand when he acted freely in the Word. In order that the people may understand that you will act freely in judgment, be exalted, you who judge the earth; repay the proud who did not wish to recognize you here in humility. Or he acts freely in judgment because with him there will be no partiality, but he will repay each person according to his works. [Col. 0638A]

**“How long, sinners, O Lord, how long will sinners exult?”**

The psalm proceeds skillfully against the less learned and those who murmur against the Lord. The speaker, wishing to lead them more effectively with him toward joy and patience, first transfers their voice into his own voice, and, as though grieving with them, presents their words to them, so that afterward they themselves may take up his voice. One who consoles a friend cannot do so more effectively than by showing that he grieves with his friend, since in this way he can more easily lead the one who grieves with him toward joy.

He says this:

“How long, sinners, O Lord, will you exult?” That is: How long will you allow sinners to do what they wish, and how long will they exult in their prosperity? And now it becomes clear in what they exult: [Col. 0638B]

**“They will utter and speak iniquity.”**

The order is inverted: first they will speak inwardly to themselves, and afterward they will speak outwardly to others. What will they say? They think within themselves that their wicked life does not displease God. For if it displeased him, either he would remove them altogether from life, or he would not permit them to prosper in this way. Thinking this, they rise up against others in defense of their sins.

When it says, “They will utter and speak iniquity,” it means: They will speak—all who practice injustice—for by their actions they will speak. And now follows the iniquity that they speak:

**“For they have humbled your people, O Lord.”**

They have humbled them in faith; by conforming them to themselves, they have made those who should be humbled into people like themselves. “And they have afflicted your inheritance,” namely, the perfect, because they have been cultivated by you all the way to perfection. Those whom they could not humble, they harassed—that is, they afflicted them with many tribulations. [Col. 0638C]

The psalm then adds what the inheritance is that they have afflicted:

**“They have slain the widow and the stranger, and they have murdered the orphans.”**

Widows are all those who separate themselves from union with the devil, to whom each person is joined when he falls into sin. Strangers are those who understand that they have no lasting city here, but seek one that is to come (Hebrews 13). Orphans are those who leave the parents of the earthly city. Such people have often been harassed by the wicked, and amid that harassment they murmured against the Lord, saying: “The Lord will not see his people so beaten by the wicked. For if he sees it, why does he allow it? And if he allows it, he is not just.” In this way they could even arrive at the conclusion that God does not exist, because whoever removes justice also removes divinity. [Col. 0638D]

This is what is meant by:

**“The Lord will not see,”**

and even more strongly:

**“Nor will the God of Jacob understand.”**

The latter is greater still.

**“Understand, you senseless among the people; and you fools, acquire wisdom at last.”**

The prophet, foreseeing that they would murmur so unjustly against the Lord, reproves them for their murmuring, as though saying: You who are the senseless among the people, attending to the temporary prosperity of the wicked but not to their eternal punishment, and to the temporary labor of the good but not to their everlasting glory—understand, you senseless people; that is, act with understanding. Raise your eyes, then, toward the future, and you will understand that the Lord sees and understands.

When he says, “Understand, you senseless among the people, and you fools, acquire wisdom at last,” he means: You who prosper here and think that things are going well for you, acquire wisdom at last when things are going badly; that is, recognize finally that your prosperity is temporal, so that you may seek the future goods that are eternal. [Col. 0639A]

**“He who planted the ear, will he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, will he not see?”**

As though he were saying: Understand this, you senseless people: He who planted the ear in others—will he not himself hear? Or he who formed the eye—will he not see everything? He who rebukes the nations through prophets, through apostles, and also through martyrs who possess zeal for God—will he not himself rebuke them in the future? Or he who rebukes the nations in part—will he not rebuke them in their entirety? And he who teaches human beings knowledge—that is, he who makes a person knowing—does he not know all things? Indeed, he does.

For the Lord knows not only the works but also the thoughts of human beings. I say that he knows them not in order to approve them, but in order to regard them as vain. This is what is meant by “for they are vain”; and if he knows them, it follows that he also takes them into account, for otherwise he would not be just.

**“Blessed is the person whom you instruct, O Lord, and whom you teach from your law.”**

As though he were saying: The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, but human beings do not know the thoughts of God. Therefore let a person abandon his own vain thoughts and examine God’s true thoughts. For the person whom you, O Lord, instruct to attend to what you wish him to attend to is blessed, and whom you teach from your law. [Col. 0639B]

The law of the Lord teaches each person to endure tribulations and pressures in this world, so that he may find true peace within himself and possess his kingdom as something purchased, for which he has been commanded to labor. One would have to labor eternally for that kingdom; but if the labor were eternal, there would be no glory for those who labored. Therefore he commanded those to whom he promised eternal glory to labor for a time. Nor did he command them to labor for a long time even for great and eternal glory. He did not say, “Labor for a thousand years,” or “for a hundred,” but, “Labor as long as you live.” Yet it may happen that you will not live for three days, so that afterward you may receive eternal glory. [Col. 0639C]

Or it may be understood in this way: The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, and yet he permits the good to labor and the wicked to prosper. But what labor, O Lord, do you permit the person whom you instruct and teach from your law to endure? Why do you teach him?

**“In order to give him relief from evil days, until a pit is dug for the sinner.”**

That is, until you provide him relief by granting him repentance, until the wickedness of sinners is brought to completion. That wickedness will be a pit for the sinner himself, because the sinner who does not wish to attend to God calling him to repentance stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath, when God’s judgment is just (Romans 2).

**“For the Lord will not reject his people.”**

As though he were saying: Truly the Lord will give relief from evil days to the one who believes in him, because the Lord will not reject his people. What does this appear to be to the wicked while they rage against it? And because the Lord chastises every son whom he receives (Hebrews 12), he will not abandon his inheritance, preserving it from those who attack it, until justice—that is, each just and perfect person—turns toward this end: to come to judgment with the Lord, either to be judged or to judge. [Col. 0639D]

To judge, according to the saying: “You will sit upon thrones judging” (Luke 22), and so forth.

Or in this way: “Until justice”—namely, Christ, who is now hidden—“turns into judgment,” that is, comes openly to judge others. And who are those who are beside it—that is, who are those who will sit at his judgment on Christ’s side, since here he is our justice? All those, namely, who are upright in heart: all whose hearts here are made level with the unchanging rule of his justice. [Col. 0640A]

Or in this way: Since justice will turn into judgment, who are those who are here beside it—that is, who are those who live justly? All who are upright in heart.

**“Who will rise up for me against the malicious? Or who will stand with me against those who practice iniquity?”**

Here the one who speaks in this psalm, after earlier placing himself in the voice of those who murmured, now takes the murmurers themselves into his voice with him, so that they may now rejoice with him, to whom he previously showed compassion.

Each one speaks as follows: “I understand that this must be done, that the wicked must be tolerated; but I cannot do this by myself. Who will help me in the meantime?”

When it says, “Who will rise up for me?” it means: Who will make me rise up against those who are malicious? Or, “Who will stand with me?”—who will make me immovable, so that I do not fall among all who practice iniquity? [Col. 0640B]

**“The Lord, who helped me.”**

And how did he help me? My soul dwelt in hell, consenting to those whom God permitted to possess temporary prosperity; and it came very near to dwelling there—that is, it was very little short of remaining there—not because the Lord helped me. And how did he help me?

I said, “My foot has slipped”—that is, my affliction was moved away from the desire for the prosperity of the wicked—and he heard me. He did not merely hear me after my confession; even when I said, “My foot has slipped,” that is, as soon as I recognized the instability of my weakness, your mercy, O Lord, helped me, because your mercy corresponded to my confession.

Here you have the proof that if you acknowledge that God forgives, he forgives to the extent that you acknowledge it. The following verse will demonstrate this. [Col. 0640C]

**“According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul.”**

As though he were saying: Your mercy helped me, and not a little, because my sorrows were many, and many of your mercies or consolations followed. My bitterest wounds came first; your sweetest medicines followed. Thus they gladdened my soul, namely, because I understand that no wicked person will be your dwelling.

This he expresses by asking:

**“Can a throne of iniquity be joined to you?”**

That is: Will you finally choose as your dwelling those who practice iniquity? You, I say, who fashion labor into a commandment—that is, who cause those who remain in your commandment to labor. [Col. 0640D]

Hence Peter says: “It is time for judgment to begin from the house of God. And if it begins with you, what will be the end of those who do not obey the Gospel? If the righteous person will scarcely be saved, where will the impious appear?” (1 Peter 4).

Or otherwise: “You who fashion labor into a commandment”—that is, you make the very labor they endure to be your commandment, because your commandment is understood in their labor.

And here is how you fashion labor into a commandment:

**“For they lay in wait for the soul of the righteous.”**

That is, they acted treacherously against the soul of the righteous one, namely Christ. Therefore they lay in wait for the soul of each righteous member, who is likewise Christ; and they condemned innocent blood—that is, they condemned the blood of Christ, insofar as it lay within their power. Therefore they condemned the blood of each righteous person belonging to Christ’s body.

But this is not a matter for concern, because the Lord became for me a refuge at last, and meanwhile, until I flee to him after being overcome by my enemies, my God is the help of my hope. He helps me not to fail in my hope. And when I flee to him, he will repay them for their iniquity—not according to what their wickedness accomplished for me, but according to what they intended. For although great grace was provided for us through the iniquity of Judas, he nevertheless received the price of his wickedness, because he did not intend to contribute to our salvation but to the destruction of his Lord. Therefore the Lord will repay him and his accomplices for their iniquity. [Col. 0641A]

And how will he repay them?

**“He will destroy them in their wickedness; the Lord our God will destroy them.”**

# Psalm 94. A Song of Praise Belonging to David

> Come, let us exult in the Lord; let us jubilate to God our savior.  
> Let us anticipate his face in confession, and let us jubilate to him in psalms.  
> For God is a great Lord, and a great king above all gods.  
> For in his hand are all the ends of the earth, and the heights of the mountains belong to him.  
> For the sea is his, and he made it, and his hands formed the dry land.  
> Come, let us worship and fall prostrate, and let us weep before the Lord who made us, for he is the Lord our God.  
> And we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand.  
> Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation, according to the day of temptation in the desert.  
> There your fathers tempted me; they tested me and saw my works. [Col. 0641C]  
> For forty years I was offended by that generation, and I said: “They are always straying in heart.”  
> And they did not know my ways; therefore I swore in my anger: “They shall not enter into my rest.”

## Exposition

As you know, a song is used for exultation. But so that no one might wish to exult in this psalm because of human strength, the words “a song of praise” have been added, so that by these two expressions we may understand that in this psalm we are to exult in divine strength. [Col. 0641B]

In this psalm there is the voice of our head, calling back scattered Israel—namely, that son who, after receiving his portion of his substance, went away into a region of unlikeness, where by living dissolutely he squandered his goods, and finally was compelled by such great necessity that he fed pigs (Luke 15). [Col. 0641D]

This son, who after receiving his portion departed from his father, signifies the human race. Having received its portion—that is, reason, in which God formed it according to his image—it departed from God into a region of unlikeness, that is, into a life unlike God’s. It could not depart from him bodily, since by his divinity he is present everywhere; but it departed from him in affection and strove to live unlike God. Compelled by necessity, it fed pigs and worshiped demons, who are signified by the pigs, since no animal is found more unclean than a pig.

The Lordly Man called back the human race, apostate in this way, in the present psalm, as follows:

**“Come, let us exult in the Lord.”**

As though he were saying: You who until now have exulted in the devil, your deceiver, and in the world, henceforth exult in God, who wished the world to be reconciled to himself through me (2 Corinthians 5) and to be admonished by me, so that those who belong to God might be joined to me. And come—not by the movement of your feet, but by the affections of your hearts. [Col. 0642A]

“Let us exult in God our savior,” namely, mine and yours: mine by nature, yours by grace. “And let us anticipate”—that is, let us go before—“his face,” namely, the face of the one who is to come to judgment; and let us do this “in confession,” that is, in his praise.

Confession is twofold: it is either the confession of one who is mourning or of one who is praising. Both pertain to the praise of the Lord. There is no doubt that laudatory confession pertains to the praise of the Lord. The confession of one who mourns also pertains to the praise of the Lord, because the greater the sinner’s acknowledgment of his sin, the greater is the praise of the one who forgives. [Col. 0642B]

When it says, “Let us anticipate his face in confession, and let us jubilate in psalms,” it means: in good works. The person who jubilates in psalms is one who has a greater will toward good works than he is able to show through action.

**“For the Lord is a great God.”**

As though he were saying: We should jubilate to him because, although others are falsely called great, he himself is the great Lord God, and a great king above all gods. This does not refer to the gods of the nations, above whom there is nothing difficult for him to be placed, but to those who have been made gods by his grace, above whom it is a great thing for him to be exalted.

And truly he is a great king above all gods, because in his hand—that is, in his power—are all the ends of the earth. These are the Jews, who have put an end to their earthly condition. And the heights of the sea are his: namely, all those who are eminent in that people through their virtues, because whatever good they do they have from him. [Col. 0642C]

Hence the Apostle says: “God works in you both to will and to accomplish” (Philippians 2).

One wall in the house of the Lord has already been built: namely, the people from the circumcision. The other wall, the people from the uncircumcision, is also indicated as follows:

**“For the sea is his, and he made it.”**

As though he were saying: He is truly a great king, because the sea is his—that is, the gentile people, full of the salt of bitterness—and he made it, not so that it would remain a sea, but so that it would become cultivable land. “And his hands formed the dry land”: that is, by his power it happened that this sea became dry land, always thirsting for the rain of salvation that comes upon it. [Col. 0642D]

Now the two walls have been gathered together. Therefore let the cornerstone be joined to them, and let one building be made from them.

**“Come, let us worship.”**

As though he were saying: Since the Lord is great, come by the steps of faith; let us worship him—that is, let us honor him—and let us fall prostrate, humbling ourselves so that we may worship him worthily. If a guilty conscience weighs upon anyone, let him weep before the Lord for the sin committed.

When it says, “Let us fall prostrate and weep before the Lord who made us,” it means: he made me, namely, the human nature personally united to the Word; he is the head, and you are the members.

Or, “who made us” means: who recreated us in good works. Hence the Apostle says: “We are his workmanship, created in good works” (Ephesians 2). [Col. 0643A]

And rightly do we weep before him, because he is the Lord our God, and we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand. It would seem more appropriate to have said, “his people and the sheep of his pasture.” But to show that the people are fed by him like sheep, he said: “We are the people of his pasture, and sheep”—not sheep whom he bought or acquired by theft, but sheep of his hand, whom he himself made.

And because you are the people and the sheep, if you hear his voice through me, the sent heir, or through my apostles, do not harden your hearts. And I say this “today,” that is, for as long as this present time lasts, I exhort you not to harden your hearts.

Hence the Apostle says: “See to it, brothers, that there not be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, leading you to depart from the living and true God. But exhort one another every day, while it is called ‘today,’ so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Hebrews 3). [Col. 0643B]

Do not harden your hearts, as happened in the provocation—that is, in the provocation made against God—not only on that day itself, but according to the day of the temptation made in the desert. “According to the day” means: after the day on which your fathers tempted me, namely, the Word who in the beginning was with God (John 1). They tested me, and yet they saw my works, through which they could understand that I was not to be tested.

**“For forty years I was offended by that generation.”**

The forty years signify the entire course of our life, in which we wander in this world as in a desert and often offend God. And I said: “They are always straying in heart, and they have not known my ways”—that is, my commandments, by which they ought to walk innocently. To them I swore in my anger: “They shall not enter into my rest.”

Then, of course, none will enter. Or “if they enter” means: they will not enter. Or: They did not know my ways, and therefore they will not enter into my rest, as I swore in my anger. [Col. 0643C]

# Psalm 95. A Psalm of David, When the House Was Being Built after the Captivity

[Col. 0643D]

> Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth.  
> Sing to the Lord, and bless his name; announce his salvation from day to day.  
> Announce his glory among the nations, his wonders among all peoples.  
> For the Lord is great and exceedingly worthy of praise; he is terrible above all gods.  
> For all the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens.  
> Confession and beauty are before him; holiness and magnificence are in his sanctification.  
> Bring to the Lord, countries of the nations, bring to the Lord glory and honor; bring to the Lord glory for his name.  
> Take up sacrifices and enter his courts; worship the Lord in his holy court.  
> Let the whole earth be moved before his face; say among the nations: “The Lord has reigned.”  
> For he has corrected the inhabited world, which shall not be moved; he will judge the peoples in equity.  
> Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth exult; let the sea and its fullness be moved.  
> The fields and everything in them will rejoice.  
> Then all the trees of the forests will exult before the face of the Lord, because he comes—because he comes to judge the earth.  
> He will judge the inhabited world in equity and the peoples in his truth.

## Exposition

It is written that the temple of the Lord, built by Solomon, was destroyed by the Chaldeans and rebuilt again by Jesus the high priest (2 Kings 25; 1 Esdras 5). This house signifies human nature, which was built by the true Solomon in the first parent—that is, placed in an abundance of virtues—but afterward was destroyed and also taken captive by the Chaldeans, when the first human being yielded to the serpent’s evil persuasion. For when he ate what was forbidden, he lost the abundance of virtues, experienced what the Lord had threatened, and did not find what the devil had promised. [Col. 0644A]

The Lord threatened death if he ate; the devil promised divinity. But the human being, yielding to the serpent, ate; and not only did he fail to become God, he also became wretched and captive. [Col. 0644B]

This house—that is, human nature—was restored because the Word who in the beginning was with God (John 1) assumed human form in order to restore humanity to glory. The Prophet exhorts us in this psalm to be part of this building by praising the one who made us the building of this house, and he says:

You who until now have howled an old song by imitating the old human being, henceforth sing to the Lord the Father a new song: new grace, new humility. Sing to the Lord the Son, all the earth—not only Judea, not only Africa, but all the earth. [Col. 0644C]

Sing to the Lord the Holy Spirit, and bless—not your own name, but his name, glorifying it. Note that the three persons of the Godhead are one in essence; therefore, after saying that all three persons should be sung to equally, he added: “Bless his name.”

**“Announce his salvation from day to day.”**

As though he were saying: Sing to the Lord, all the earth. But you who are from the Jews, announce his salvation from day to day—that is, at all times—namely, Christ, through whom the captivity of humanity was restored.

Or in this way: Announce his salvation from day to day—that is, preach his salvation from virtue to virtue.

Or in this way: Go on announcing from the day of the Son to the day of the Father, so that through the works of the Son you may make known the works of the Father, since the Father and the Son are one and the same. Hence the saying: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14). [Col. 0644D]

Or announce the Father from the day into the day of the Son. Hence the saying: “Believe in God, and believe in me” (John 14).

**“Announce his works among the nations.”**

He said: “Announce his salvation from day to day.” And, as though someone might ask, “Where do you wish us to announce it?” he determines where they should announce it. He is like the builder of some building who, after assembling the craftsmen, assigns each one his work and says: “Let your task be to work in that corner, and yours in that one.”

When he says, “Announce his works among the nations,” he means the resurrection and ascension. And “announce his wonders among all peoples” means this: the Lord, who wished to be born little, lived little among human beings, preached as one little, and died as one little, became great by rising again and exceedingly worthy of praise by ascending. He will come in terror above all gods whom he deified by his grace—that is, those who, by participating in the divinity of the true God, can be called gods. [Col. 0645A]

For there are some who are called gods but are not true gods, such as the gods of the nations, who are not gods but demons.

When he says, “For all the gods of the nations are demons,” it is as though he were saying: When I spoke of gods, I was not referring to the gods of the nations, for they are demons; and it would therefore be little for the Lord to be placed above them. But the Lord made those whom I previously called gods into heavens, and it is a great thing for him to be placed above them.

**“Confession and beauty are before him.”**

As though he were saying: In this way he became terrible and worthy of praise, because confession and beauty are before him—that is, in the inner person, where his gaze is directed. [Col. 0645B]

Would you be beautiful? Confess your ugliness, and the Lord will give you graciousness (Psalm 84).

**“Holiness and magnificence are in his sanctification.”**

That is, holiness and magnificence are in those whom he sanctifies. Note that he placed holiness before magnificence, because he justifies before he magnifies. For there is no reason to expect anything great from yourself if you do not love justice.

**“Bring to the Lord, countries of the nations, bring to the Lord glory and honor; bring to the Lord glory for his name.”**

As though he were saying: Since the Lord has been announced among the Jews as great and worthy of praise, and this has occurred among you, O nations, therefore, countries of the nations—not one region alone, but all the countries of the nations—bring glory to the Lord. Bring glory to the Lord the Son, and by doing these things so that the Lord may be glorified through you, bring glory to the Lord the Holy Spirit, for his name. [Col. 0645C]

Let whoever glories glory in the Lord.

**“Take up sacrifices.”**

That is, take up good works, which are sacrifices of praise, and bring them with you, because a servant ought not to appear empty before the Lord.

**“And enter his courts.”**

That is, live well in his Church, because sacrifices are of no benefit without faith; for outside the catholic Church there is no place for the true sacrifice.

**“Worship the Lord in his holy court.”**

That is, believe him to be common to all. And thus, while you preach, let another also be moved by repentance before his face—that is, by the thought of him, which through you grows throughout the nations. [Col. 0645D]

And say among the nations: “The Lord will reign at his second coming,” because he has already reigned at his first coming.

The effect demonstrates this: he has corrected the inhabited world, which will not be moved from its faith, and finally he will judge the peoples in equity, repaying each person according to his works.

Then let the heavens rejoice—that is, all the faithful, who are called heavens because of the splendor of truth—and let the earth exult, well cultivated by the plow of preaching. Then let the sea and its fullness be moved—that is, let the gentile people and their accomplices rage. Yet the fields will rejoice: the humble, who bear good fruit; and everything in them—that is, all their works—will rejoice, meaning that they will make them rejoice, because none of their good works will remain without reward. [Col. 0646A]

Then, in that joy, all the trees of the forests, taken up into the building of the house of the Lord, will exult. The trees of the forests are the gentiles, who previously were like a forest, cultivated by no one. But they were cut from the wild olive and grafted into the good olive tree.

Therefore they will finally exult before the face of the Lord, because he came in his first coming, granting mercy. And they will exult when he comes in his second coming to judge the earth.

Then he will judge the inhabited world—that is, the more perfect, whom he took from the earth—receiving them in his equity, that is, joining them to his righteous ones. And he will judge the peoples, namely, the unbelievers, in his truth, condemning them by a just judgment.

# Psalm 96. A Psalm Belonging to David, When the Land Was Restored to Him

[Col. 0646B]

> The Lord has reigned; let the earth exult; let the many islands rejoice.  
> Cloud and darkness are around him; justice and judgment are the correction of his throne.  
> Fire will go before him and burn up his enemies round about.  
> His lightning flashes have appeared to the inhabited world; the earth saw and was moved.  
> The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord, before the face of the Lord of all the earth.  
> The heavens announced his justice, and all peoples saw his glory.  
> Let all who worship carved images, and those who glory in their idols, be confounded.  
> Worship him, all his angels.  
> Zion heard and rejoiced.  
> And the daughters of Judah exulted because of your judgments, O Lord.  
> For you, Lord Most High, are exalted above all the earth; you are exceedingly exalted above all gods.  
> You who love the Lord, hate evil. [Col. 0646C] The Lord preserves the souls of his holy ones; he will deliver them from the hand of the sinner.  
> Light has arisen for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart.  
> Rejoice, you righteous, in the Lord, and give thanks in remembrance of his sanctification.

## Exposition

The earth fell away when the human race withdrew from God through disobedience. It was restored in part when the law was given to the Jewish people. But because that people became a transgressor of the law, the earth fell away again.

It also fell away when the Apostle Peter, who had previously promised steadfastness, denied the Lord at the voice of a servant girl. But the earth was restored in him when, after the Lord asked, “Peter, do you love me?” he replied, “I do, Lord.” When the Lord asked him this a third time, Peter, saddened, said: “You know, Lord, that I love you” (John 21). Thus guilt was erased through the threefold confession that had arisen from the threefold denial. [Col. 0646D]

The earth was restored when many converts from Peter’s preaching said among themselves: “What shall we do, men and brothers?” And Peter replied: “Let each one be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”; and many were baptized (Acts 2).

The earth was fully restored when, after the Holy Spirit had been sent, the Word of life was preached by the apostles among the nations.

The explanation of the title is as follows: This psalm is to be attributed to David—that is, to the true David—and was made when the earth was restored.

Note that although the voice in this psalm is that of the Prophet, the work of which the psalm treats must nevertheless be attributed to Christ, because the restoration of the earth occurred through him. [Col. 0647A]

What it says—“the earth was restored”—may also be understood of the Lord’s resurrection, because then the flesh of Christ, which he assumed from the Virgin, was restored when it was clothed with the glory of immortality. That earth—that is, Christ’s flesh—had fallen away, as it were, when it was covered with mortality and passibility.

The Prophet says as follows:

*[The supplied source ends here, after “The Prophet says as follows.”]*
The Lord has reigned; let the earth rejoice; let the many islands be glad. As though he were saying: The Lord, the Word, assumed flesh, in which he suffered very much, died and rose again, ascended, and sent the Holy Spirit among the disciples; and thus he reigned—that is, he obtained a kingdom for himself throughout the whole world—because, while the apostles preached, faith grew everywhere. Thus the Lord reigned. Therefore let the earth rejoice, now well cultivated by the ploughshare of preaching; and let not only those who dwell on solid ground rejoice, but let the many islands also, called to the faith, be glad.

Or, “Let the many islands be glad,” that is, the many churches already established, which can be compared with islands: just as islands are surrounded by the sea and battered by the waves of the sea, so the Church is surrounded by the waves of this age and driven about by them. But what does it do? It breaks those very waves and is not broken by them. It is like the cliffs of the sea: when the waves drive against the shore, they do not break the shore if it is firm, but are rather broken by the shore itself.

Cloud and darkness are around him. As though he were saying: The Lord reigned in this manner, because cloud and darkness are around him. The clouds are the apostles, the darkness the prophets, since the very things that the apostles expressed openly, the prophets foretold beforehand, secretly and as though covered by a kind of darkness. These prophets and apostles are around him, namely, announcing beforehand the glory of the Lord, so that his kingdom might grow in faith.

Righteousness and judgment are the correction of his throne. The order has been reversed, because judgment—namely, the discernment between good and evil—must come first, so that righteousness may follow; for no one is justified except the one who attends to this judgment. These two are the correction of his throne, because through these two those who are destined to be his thrones are corrected.

And how? Because fire—that is, good love, which sets one aflame—will go before him, and this fire will inflame his enemies, burning away what is harmful in them and placing them around him, so that they may surround him through the imitation of good works. Concerning this fire it was said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke 12).

What he says—“and it will inflame his enemies round about”—and in what order was this done? Because his lightning flashes shone forth: that is, the splendors of his miracles shone upon the world, namely, upon those who, by receiving good cultivation, were to become the world of the age to come, perfected in virtues. The earth saw these flashes and was moved with the movement of repentance; and not just any earth was moved, but the mountains melted like wax—that is, those exalted in the world, having received the fire of charity, laid aside their hardness and were dissolved through tears of repentance.

What he says—“The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord”—means that, because of knowledge of the Lord, the whole earth was moved, since not only the Jews received the faith.

Or let us explain the earlier passage differently: “The Lord has reigned; let the earth rejoice; let the many islands be glad.” Yet although he himself reigned, cloud and darkness were around him, because to some he was overshadowed so that they might not see him. And although cloud and darkness were around him with regard to certain people, righteousness and judgment were the correction of his throne—that is, the correction of those who were destined to be his thrones.

“Fire will go before him.” He gives the reason why cloud and darkness were around him: because the fire of envy would go before him—not that this fire came from him, but because they themselves placed that fire between themselves and God. Therefore the Lord was overshadowed for them, so that they might not see him. And this fire will inflame his enemies with unlawful desires, and this “round about” means everywhere.

“His lightning flashes shone upon the world.” He shows how righteousness and judgment are the correction of his throne: because his lightning flashes shine upon the world. What flashes? Namely, the earth moved to repentance. For the mountains also melted like wax—that is, the hardness of the proud was changed into softness, like wax placed against fire. And the fact that the mountains melted was from the face of the Lord, by which the whole earth was moved. And how did this happen? Because the heavens—that is, the apostles—announced his righteousness, and thus all peoples saw, that is, understood, not the Jews alone.

And because all peoples saw his glory, let all who worship carved images and glory in their idols therefore be confounded in their own estimation. For images are not to be worshiped, nor is an angel to be worshiped, because we read in the Apocalypse that when someone wished to worship an angel because of the miracles he had performed, the angel himself forbade him to be worshiped, saying: “See that you do not do this, for I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers” (Revelation 19 and 22).

“Worship the Lord, all his angels.” As though he were saying: All peoples have seen his glory; therefore worship him, all his angels.

Zion heard that the peoples had seen his glory, and she rejoiced. As it is said elsewhere: “Those who were in Judea heard that the Gentiles had received the word of God, and they glorified God” (Acts 11). And the daughters of Judah rejoiced—that is, the Church formed from the Jews—because of your judgments, Lord, since they recognized that the Gentiles were worthy to be incorporated with the Jews. Hence Peter: “In truth I have discovered that God is not a respecter of persons” (Acts 10).

For Peter himself, doubting whether Cornelius ought to be baptized, was assured when he saw that Cornelius had received the Holy Spirit; for no one among the Jews had received the Holy Spirit before baptism.

The daughters of Judah rejoiced rightly, because you, Lord, are the Most High over all the earth, since you are God not only of the Jews but also of the Gentiles. And you are exalted above all the gods made previously; you are exceedingly exalted, ascending even to equality with the Father.

And lest anyone despair when he calls him the Most High, as though he could not reach him because of his height, he gives the command that he is to be reached, saying: “You who love the Lord, hate evil.” As though he were saying: The Lord is Most High; but you who wish to reach his height, hate evil. And if persecution by the ungodly should come upon you, do not fear, because although they may rage against the flesh, they cannot impede the resurrection.

For the Lord guards the souls of his saints, and in the end he will deliver them from the hand of sinners. And so that he may finally deliver them, light has arisen for the righteous—that is, inner light will shine for every righteous person—and for the upright in heart there will be joy, so that they may rejoice not only in hope but also in tribulation.

Therefore rejoice, righteous ones, in the Lord; joy belongs to you alone, because the ungodly have no joy. And confess the memory of his holiness—that is, praise him because he remembered you in order to sanctify you, when you were forgetful in your condemnation.

## PSALM 97. A PSALM OF DAVID

“Sing to the Lord a new song, because he has done marvelous things. His right hand and his holy arm have saved for him. The Lord has made his salvation known; in the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness. He has remembered his mercy and his truth toward the house of Israel. All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God. Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; sing, rejoice, and sing psalms. Sing psalms to the Lord on the lyre, on the lyre and with the voice of a psalm, with beaten trumpets and the voice of a horn. Shout joyfully before the Lord the King; let the sea and its fullness be moved, the world and those who dwell in it. The rivers shall clap their hands together; the mountains shall rejoice before the Lord, because he has come to judge the earth. He shall judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in equity.”

### EXPOSITION

The voice in this psalm is that of the Prophet exhorting us not to receive the grace of God in vain (2 Corinthians 6), not to trample underfoot the blood of the righteous (Hebrews 10), but to recognize with great devotion the time of visitation (Luke 1), to set aside the old song by imitating Christ, and to sing a new song with him. Thus he says:

“Sing to the Lord a new song.” The new song is new charity and new humility, which the old man does not know how to sing.

“Because he has done marvelous things,” namely, when he raised the widow’s son (Luke 7); but he did something more marvelous when he redeemed those who were lost from death.

“His right hand and his holy arm have saved for him.” He shows how he did marvelous things. For his right hand and his arm—namely, Christ—by their power and strength saved, that is, brought salvation to, the human race; and he did this for himself from the Lord, namely, from the Father, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for the Lord (2 Corinthians 5). Those are saved for him who are saved inwardly and do not return again to their vomit.

And how did he save? “The Lord made his salvation known,” that is, his Christ. “In the sight of the nations he revealed his righteousness,” that is, he made known to the nations the faith that justifies.

And why did he do this? Because he remembered his mercy—that is, the restoration to be made for the human race. He remembered his truth promised to the house of Israel, because the promise concerning the restoration of the human race was made there to them.

And thus all the ends of the earth—that is, all those who have set a limit to their earthliness—saw the salvation of our God. Therefore shout joyfully to the Lord, all the earth: conceive within yourselves as much freedom as you are unable to express with your voice. Sing also inwardly, rejoice outwardly, and thus sing psalms—that is, perform good works with gladness of mind, for God loves a cheerful worker.

“Sing psalms to the Lord,” I say, “on the lyre,” that is, in the mortification of the flesh. Hence the Apostle: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth” (Colossians 3).

“Sing psalms also with beaten trumpets.” Beaten trumpets are bronze trumpets which, when struck with hammers, increase in length and breadth. Our hammers are the devils and their instruments; their striking is the tribulation and persecution by which, whoever is struck, should grow in perseverance in good works and also grow in breadth—that is, in the extension of charity. This charity cannot be extended farther than for each person to have charity even toward enemies, like the one who said: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7), because “they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23).

“Sing psalms also with the voice of a horn,” that is, so conduct yourselves that, while existing in the flesh, you may surpass all carnal affections. This is according to the likeness of a horn, which, while adhering to flesh, hardens into another nature. Hence Paul: “Although we still wage war in the flesh, we nevertheless no longer live according to the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10).

“Shout joyfully before the Lord the King.” As though he were saying: Singing psalms in all these ways, shout joyfully in your interior, where your King sees; and while you shout joyfully, let the sea be moved—that is, the Gentile world, either with the movement of repentance or with the movement of anger. Let the sea not be moved in only one part, but let its fullness be moved everywhere.

Let the world also be moved—that is, let the perfect, in a certain sense still be moved toward an increase of virtues—and let all who dwell in that world, that is, all who imitate the perfect, shout joyfully before the Lord the King.

Shout joyfully, because the rivers—that is, the holy preachers, from whose belly living waters will flow (John 7)—will clap their hands together, that is, will join you in good works.

And the mountains also will clap—that is, those who are exalted in the world will rejoice before the Lord, because the Lord has come to judge the earth: now with a hidden judgment, and finally he will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in equity.

## PSALM 98. A PSALM OF DAVID

“The Lord has reigned; let the peoples be angry; he who sits above the cherubim—let the earth be moved. The Lord is great in Zion and exalted above all peoples. Let them confess your great name, for it is fearful and holy; and the honor of the king loves judgment. You have prepared uprightnesses; you have executed judgment and righteousness in Jacob. Exalt the Lord our God and worship the footstool of his feet, for it is holy. Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name. They called upon the Lord, and he answered them; he spoke to them in a pillar of cloud. They kept his testimonies and the commandment that he gave them. Lord our God, you answered them; you were propitious toward them, yet avenging all their inventions. Exalt the Lord our God and worship at his holy mountain, for the Lord our God is holy.”

### EXPOSITION

A psalm of David. All the holy patriarchs, prophets, and preachers gave us counsel in their writings, like a son of the Church, not so that we might lack anything, but so that from them we might have material by which we could be built up. The holy prophet David also attended to this in this psalm, setting before us that we should seek the Lord everywhere: let us seek him here as merciful, lest in the end we experience him as a most savage judge. For he does not abandon the one who desires him, he who redeemed the one who neglected him. Thus he says:

“The Lord has reigned; let the peoples be angry; he who sits above the cherubim—let the earth be moved.” As though he were saying: Seek the Lord who has reigned—that is, who has obtained a kingdom for himself among the Gentiles—and has cast out the prince of the world. While he reigns, let the peoples be angry.

This is a prophecy of the Spirit speaking beforehand, not a command giving orders. The Prophet foretells what he saw in the Spirit as future: because after the Lord ascended, the Holy Spirit was sent among the disciples, so that, instructed through him, they would not fear the death which they knew had been destroyed by the One who rose again.

When the Lord began to be preached by them, many peoples became angry. They became angry when the one who made them began to be preached, while they worshiped what they had made. They became angry with their Lord on behalf of their idol, when they ought to have been angry with the servant, since their servant is more worthy than their idol. The Lord made their servant, but their craftsman made their idol.

“He who sits above the cherubim”—that is, he who chose for himself a seat among those filled with love. For *cherubim* is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” Since charity is the fullness of the commandments, it is not inappropriate that the one who is perfect in charity should be called a cherub.

When he says, “You who sit above the cherubim, reign”: but why, “Let the earth be moved”? That is, [the one] having his heart set on earth [is to be moved]; yet the Lord is great in Zion—that is, among those who contemplate the things that are not seen, not the things that are seen. The Lord appears great, although to those who are on earth he may seem small; and he is exalted above all peoples, not only above the Jews but also above the Gentiles.

And since you, Lord, are great in Zion, therefore let all confess your great name by glorifying it, those who refused to confess your small name. And rightly your name must be confessed, because it is fearful to those who do not love, and holy to those who love; to them it is said: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus 11, 19). Or it will be fearful in the future, although now it is holy.

“And the honor of the king loves judgment.” The king who is honorable loves judgment, so that each person may have discernment between good and evil, turning away from evil and doing good. Or, whoever wishes to be the honor of the king—that is, to be such that the king is honored through him—should love judgment. Let him attend to the fact that his judge will leave no sin unpunished; and by attending to this, let him become his own judge, which he cannot do unless he ceases to sin.

“You have prepared uprightnesses; you have executed judgment and righteousness in Jacob.” As though he were saying: Let them confess your name, and they can do so rightly, because you have prepared uprightnesses for them—that is, certain guides by whose example they might be directed toward confession. Thus you prepared judgment, that is, discernment, and afterward righteousness; and this in Jacob, that is, in those who exchange present things for future things.

“Exalt the Lord our God.” As though he were saying: Since upright guides have been prepared for you so that you may confess, exalt the Lord our God by doing good, so that, when people see your good works, and so forth.

“And worship the footstool of his feet, for it is holy.” Notice what ought to be called the footstool. For the Lord himself said: “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isaiah 66). What, then, shall we do? Shall we worship the earth? I fear worshiping the earth, lest I be condemned by the one who made heaven and earth. For he himself said to his tempter: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matthew 4).

But since the Spirit said, “Worship the footstool of his feet,” we must see in what manner the earth is to be worshiped, which he himself said was the footstool of his feet. For he took earth from earth, namely, flesh from the Virgin Mary. No one sins by worshiping this earth.

Thus the meaning is: “Worship the footstool of his feet,” that is, revere his lower nature, because he is holy.

“Moses and Aaron among his priests.” As though he were saying: Exalt our Lord—and you ought to, because Moses and Aaron, whom you hold in such high regard, and whose sons you are, were counted among his priests.

“And Samuel among those who call upon his name.” They called upon the Lord as servants, and he answered them as Lord. In a pillar of cloud—that is, in a mystery, speaking as though covered by a cloud—he spoke to them. And they kept his testimonies; from this he is shown to be greater than they, because they received testimonies from him as from the Lord.

“And they kept the commandment that he gave them.” And you, Lord our God, answered them as Lord. You were propitious toward them in what required propitiation; and you avenged all their inventions, because, if they ever sinned, your discipline corrected them as sons.

In Moses and Aaron we can see their inventions that required correction. When Moses saw an Egyptian fighting with a Hebrew, he was moved by anger, killed the Egyptian, and covered him with sand, lest, if he had left him uncovered, he should be found guilty of murder. Again, when he saw two Hebrews fighting with each other on the following day, he rebuked them for their quarrelsome conduct. One of them answered him indignantly, saying: “Do you intend to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?” Fearing that his guilt would be revealed, Moses fled and abandoned his brothers, to whom he could have been useful if he had remained (Exodus 2).

Behold, because of these two inventions—because of the anger by which he was moved to commit murder, and because of the fear by which he was terrified and abandoned his brothers in danger—he deserved that the Lord should take vengeance upon him.

Aaron also required correction in his inventions, because, overcome by weakness of the flesh, he allowed the people over whom he presided to make a cast-metal calf for worship (Exodus 32). The Lord avenged these inventions of Moses and Aaron, because he did not lead them into the promised land (Numbers 20).

But since this happened figuratively, let us more appropriately understand the many tribulations and contradictions that they endured among that people as the Lord’s acts of vengeance, because the iniquity of unbelievers is exceedingly grievous to the saints.

In Samuel, as far as human eyes could see, there was nothing that required vengeance, because, instructed in the temple from childhood, he truly remained in the Lord’s temple (1 Samuel 3). But since, for every craftsman, something in his own construction that appears well made to others may appear defective, we can say that the Lord, before whose eyes all things are present, saw something in Samuel also that required correction, because no one is so holy as to be entirely without sin.

“Exalt the Lord our God.” As though he were saying: Since the Lord is propitious toward all, therefore exalt the Lord our God and worship him at his holy mountain—namely, in Christ, who is the mountain cut from the mountain without the hands of those who cut. Hence in Daniel: “I saw a stone cut from the mountain without hands, and it grew into a great mountain, so that it filled the face of the earth” (Daniel 2). The Lord is to be worshiped on this mountain, because he is the Lord our God.

## PSALM 99. A PSALM OF CONFESSION

“Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; serve the Lord with gladness. Enter into his presence with rejoicing. Know that the Lord himself is God; he himself made us, and not we ourselves. We are his people and the sheep of his pasture. Enter his gates with confession; enter his courts with hymns; confess to him. Praise his name, because the Lord is sweet: his mercy is everlasting, and his truth endures from generation to generation.”

### EXPOSITION

A psalm of confession. In this psalm the voice of the Prophet exhorts us to render praise to God for the former benefits bestowed upon the human race, and he says:

“Shout joyfully to God, all the earth.” This can be connected with the preceding passage, where it was said: “The Lord our God is holy.” Why, then, “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth”? As though he were saying: Words are not enough for the praise of God; rather, a shout of joy is necessary, so that you may rejoice in the Lord as much as you cannot express in words.

Notice that he says, “all the earth,” because the one who sowed blessing everywhere seeks rejoicing from everywhere. And it was necessary for him to sow blessing everywhere, because Adam had sown confusion everywhere.

For he sowed confusion in the four parts of the world, as is indicated in his name, taken from the initial letters of four names denoting the four principal regions of the world. The first letter of his name, A, is taken from ἀνατολή (*anatolē*), which in Greek means “east.” The letter D, which is found second in the name itself, is taken from δύσις (*dysis*), which in Greek denotes “west.” The third letter, A, is taken from ἄρκτος (*arktos*), which means “the northern region.” The fourth letter, M, is taken from μεσημβρία (*mesēmbria*), which means “the southern region.”

“Serve the Lord,” not in sadness but in gladness—that is, with cheerfulness of mind. And rightly he is to be served with gladness, because the service of God is free: it is served not by necessity, but by charity.

“Enter into his presence with rejoicing.” This was said by comparison with princes, because princes customarily bring before their presence those who serve them according to their will.

Or understand it thus: “Enter into his presence,” that is, cleanse your conscience, where he himself sees, so that you may empty it of defilements and adorn it with virtuous habits.

“And know that he himself is the Lord our God,” making you serve in gladness, that is, making you shout joyfully to him.

“And he himself made us, and not we ourselves.” Whatever we ourselves have made in ourselves is to be condemned; but what he himself has made is truly of salvation. Therefore, as his people and the sheep of his pasture, “enter his gates with confession” accompanied by lamentation, because whoever wishes to enter to him must lament his sins in confession. This must be the beginning of the one who enters to him.

Thus he says: “Enter his gates with confession”; and, having entered his courts—that is, his Church—“confess to him in hymns,” that is, confess to him in laudable confession. And finally, in the future, “praise his name,” because the Lord is sweet: that is, the restoration of the ancient fall, accomplished through mercy, endures forever; and truth—that is, the fulfillment of the promised mercy—endures from generation to generation.

## PSALM 100. A PSALM OF DAVID

“I will sing mercy and judgment to you, Lord. I will sing psalms and understand in the immaculate way, when you come to me. I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house. I did not set an unjust thing before my eyes; I hated those who commit transgressions. A crooked heart did not cling to me; I did not acknowledge the malicious person who turned away from me. I pursued the one who secretly slandered his neighbor. The one with a proud eye and an insatiable heart—I did not eat with him. My eyes were upon the faithful of the earth, that they might sit with me; the one who walked in the immaculate way ministered to me. The one who practices pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house; the one who speaks unjustly did not walk uprightly in the sight of my eyes. In the morning I was killing all the sinners of the earth, so that I might destroy from the city of the Lord all who practice iniquity.”

### EXPOSITION

A psalm of David. In this psalm it is the voice of our Head, teaching that no one should presume upon the impunity of sins because of mercy, since judgment follows; nor should anyone, having been changed for the better, fear judgment, since mercy comes first.

These two things—mercy and judgment—are usually changeable in human beings, because many, overcome by mercy, lose the severity of judgment; and when they sometimes wish to maintain a rigorous judgment, they lose mercy. But Christ neither lost the severity of judgment because of the goodness of mercy, nor postponed the goodness of mercy because of the need to judge severely; rather, he preserves both without alteration. For now is the time of mercy; at some point the time for exercising judgment will come. And he says:

“I will sing mercy and judgment to you, Lord. I will sing psalms and understand in the immaculate way, when you come to me.” As though he were saying: Lord Father, I will sing—that is, I will make known to my people—the mercy that you have shown to the world through me and the judgment that you will someday carry out through me. And I will attribute this to you—that is, to your grace—and not to merits.

“I will sing psalms and understand,” that is, I will act intelligently, “in the immaculate way,” that is, while placed in it; and this not through myself, but because you will come to me—that is, by personally uniting your Word to me, a human being.

“I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house.” As though he were saying: You truly came to me, because, from the fact that you came to me, I walked in the innocence of my heart—that is, in an innocent heart—and this “in the midst,” that is, in the firmness of my conscience, which is called a house, namely, a firm receptacle.

If someone is ill in this house, he will be well nowhere. But if someone has a cleansed conscience, even if he is badly off outwardly in every respect, nevertheless, if he enters into his conscience, he finds rest there.

Notice that he says, “I walked.” He walked in the innocence of his heart because he extended the breadth of charity both to enemies and to friends. For innocence is not true unless it is such that it harms neither oneself nor another. It harms oneself if one is inflamed with hatred against an enemy, even if one inflicts no injury upon the enemy.

What he says, “I walked,” means “I walked everywhere”; and this in the innocence not only of my hands but also of my heart, and this in the midst of my house—that is, in my conscience—even if it appeared otherwise to human beings.

It can also be understood of the members: “I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house,” that is, among those who are called the middle and stronger members of my house—that is, of my Church.

Or the preceding verse can also be referred to the members in this way: “Mercy and judgment”—that is, the devout affection that you had toward the human race, and true judgment, so that the creature might serve its Creator—“I will sing,” that is, my people will sing to you, O Lord, attributing this to your grace and not to their merits.

Or they will sing to you because they will place their hope in your mercy, while nevertheless taking care concerning your judgment, so that they may be prepared and await it. “And I will sing psalms,” that is, my people will sing psalms and understand, because they will sing not only with their lips but also through their purpose and life, possessing the spirit of wisdom and understanding, placed in the immaculate way. And this will be when you come to me—that is, when you make yourself known to the world through me.

They will sing, sing psalms, and understand, and this from my people. For I first walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house. I did not set before my eyes—that is, I did not take pleasure in—an unjust thing, that is, any unjust deed. “I hated those who commit transgression,” that is, I hated transgressors both of the written law and of the natural law, insofar as they were to be hated.

“A crooked heart did not cling to me,” that is, a heart distorted from the straight path did not please me, although I may at some time have associated with people acting perversely.

“I did not acknowledge the one who turned away from me,” that is, from my commandments, with favor, although I knew him with the attentiveness of anger.

“I pursued the one who secretly slandered his neighbor,” pursuing him in the manner in which he ought to be pursued, so that the one who had previously been a slanderer might become a lover, according to this: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between you and him alone” (Matthew 18).

“The one with a proud eye and an insatiable heart—I did not eat with him.” Two types are noted here: the proud and the avaricious. The avaricious person always has an insatiable heart, just as the proud person has an elevated eye, not humbly inclined. The food of both the proud and the avaricious is impiety and injustice.

Those who have a devout heart in the Lord do not feed on this food, because their food is righteousness. Hence: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matthew 5).

Or we may read the words literally, if we wish to refer them to the members: “The one with a proud eye and an insatiable heart”—that is, my people did not eat with him. Hence Paul: “If anyone does not obey our words, mark him through a letter, and do not associate with him—not so that you should regard him as an enemy, but so that you may correct him as a brother” (2 Thessalonians 3). And elsewhere: “With such a one, do not even eat” (1 Corinthians 5).

Or understand it thus: “With him I ate food in intention, although not in action.” The Lord received sinners and ate with them, but he did not consent in his will; for he ate with them only for their correction. In this he showed himself to be their teacher, since he ate with them for their correction.

“My eyes were upon the faithful of the earth.” As though he were saying: I despised the proud and the avaricious; but my eyes—that is, the regard of my mercy—are upon the faithful of the earth, that is, upon those who faithfully cultivate their earthliness.

And what does this bring them? That at last they may sit with me in my kingdom.

“The one who walked in the immaculate way ministered to me.” But the one who practices pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house—that is, he shall not please my heart, or he shall not dwell in my Church.

“The one who speaks unjustly did not walk uprightly in the sight of my eyes.”

And what finally will happen to them? “In the morning I was killing all the sinners of the earth.” Night lasts as long as we live this transitory life, in which the ungodly are permitted to live together with the ungodly. But when morning comes—that is, the resurrection of all, in which all the darkness of night will come to an end—all sinners will be killed.

He then adds in what manner they are to be killed: “So that I might destroy from the city of the Lord all who practice iniquity.” For the killing of sinners will be their separation from the congregation of the faithful. This will happen when the lambs are separated from the goats.

Or otherwise: “In the morning I was killing all the sinners of the earth.” Morning is the beginning of the day. At the beginning, all the sinners of the earth are to be killed, because when an unlawful movement arises from the devil’s suggestion, the sinners of the earth—that is, the devil and his angels—are to be removed from us, lest they bring us as far as the act of iniquity, from whose suggestion unlawful movements have arisen in us.

What he says, “In the morning I was killing,” means “I judged all the sinners of the earth to be destined for killing,” so that in this way I might destroy—that is, so that my people might destroy—from the city of the Lord, that is, from their righteous soul, all who practice iniquity.

Hence it is said to the serpent: “The woman will crush your head” (Genesis 3). The serpent’s head is crushed when unlawful movements are killed before they reach the act.

Hence also: “Blessed is the one who will seize your little ones and dash them against the rock” (Psalm 136).

## PSALM 101. THE PRAYER OF THE POOR WHEN HE IS ANXIOUS AND POURS OUT HIS PRAYER BEFORE THE LORD
«Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you. Do not turn your face away from me; on whatever day I am troubled, incline your ear to me. On whatever day I call upon you, answer me quickly. For my days have vanished like smoke, and my bones have dried like kindling. I have been struck like grass, and my heart has dried up, because I forgot to eat my bread. Because of the sound of my groaning, my mouth has clung to my flesh. I have become like a pelican of the wilderness; I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling.
