I kept vigil, and I became like a solitary sparrow on the roof. All day long my enemies reproached me, and those who praised me swore against me. For I ate ashes like bread, and I mixed my drink with weeping. Because of the face of your anger and indignation, for you lifted me up and dashed me down. My days have declined like a shadow, and I have withered like grass. But you, Lord, remain forever, and your memorial from generation to generation. You will arise and have mercy on Zion, for it is the time to have mercy on her, for the appointed time has come. For your servants have taken pleasure in her stones, and they will have pity on her land. And the nations will fear your name, Lord, and all the kings of the earth your glory. For the Lord has built Zion, and he will be seen in his glory. He has regarded the prayer of the humble, and has not despised their supplication. Let these things be written for the generation to come, and the people who will be created will praise the Lord. For he looked down from his holy height; the Lord looked from heaven upon the earth, to hear the groaning of the prisoners, to release the children of those put to death, so that they may proclaim the name of the Lord in Zion and his praise in Jerusalem, when peoples and kings gather together as one, to serve the Lord. He answered him in the way of his strength: Make known to me the shortness of my days. Do not take me away in the midst of my days; your years endure through generation after generation. In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain, and they will all grow old like a garment. And like a covering you will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail. The children of your servants will dwell there, and their offspring will be established forever.»

## Exposition

A prayer of the poor man when he was distressed and poured out his prayers and supplications before the Lord.

This poor man, whose prayer is recorded in this psalm, is the one of whom it is said: “Though he was rich, for our sake he became poor” (2 Cor. 8:9). He was rich, reigning in equality with the Father; but he became poor when the Word, which “in the beginning was with God” (John 1:1), assumed “the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:7), in which he redeemed us from sins. From this poor man come all our riches, both inward and outward. From him we have gold, silver, and other possessions. From him also we have inward riches—chastity and the other virtues by which the faithful become rich.

That this poor man was distressed did not arise from himself, but from us, for whom he assumed flesh and willed to be crucified; for whom also in this psalm he prays that they may be led by grace to the place from which we fell through the disobedience of our first parent. Let each person contemplate this man distressed for us, and let him become distressed when he considers in what great glory he had been created in Adam and into what great misery he fell through him. Considering this, let him display his prayer before the Lord, not before human beings.

“Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you.” In this prayer of our Head, some things are attributed to his person, while others pertain to our weakness. He says as follows: “Lord Father, hear my prayer”—that is, the prayer of my members, made for perseverance in the virtues—“and let my cry”—that is, the unremitting activity of my members—“come to you.”

“Cry” can be understood in both a good and a bad sense. In the good sense, as was said to Moses: “Why do you cry out?” (Exod. 14:15). In the bad sense, as in: “The cry of Sodom has come to me” (Gen. 18:20). And Paul says: “Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and shouting be removed from you” (Eph. 4:31). It is as though he said: “I see that it is impossible for iniquity to be entirely removed from you; but beware, lest there be a cry among you”—that is, lest you become examples to others of sinning. Hence another says: “Even if not chastely, nevertheless cautiously.”

“Do not turn your face away from me,” who have been humbled, because you turned it away from Adam when he was exalted. “On whatever day I am troubled in my members, incline your ear to me.”

Behold, our Head is already above, and he says that he is troubled. Where, then, is he troubled, except in the body? That he is troubled in the body he himself clearly demonstrates when he says: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). And he says to Peter: “I am coming to Rome again to be crucified.”

When he says, “On whatever day I am troubled, incline your ear to me,” this means: “Let my prayer have power with you to be heard.” When I humble myself, it is as though I exalt myself; do not be far from me. If I humble myself, incline your ear to me.

“On whatever day I call upon you in my members, answer me quickly”—that is, without delay. Quickly, because I desire what you desire: for I, who am no longer earthly, desiring earthly things, have been freed from the first captivity and desire heavenly things. Concerning this desire you yourself said: “Behold, I am present when you speak” [cf. Isa. 65:1].

Therefore you, poor man, who lie before the door of the rich God, say: “With what poverty do you beg? With what need do you knock?” Speak, so that the door may be opened to you.

“For my days have vanished like smoke.” It is as though he said: “You must answer me quickly in my members, because my days”—that is, the days of my members—“have failed,” that is, have come to an end, “like smoke” rising upward and quickly vanishing. Thus proud people rise—that is, swell with pride—and therefore “my bones have dried like kindling.”

The stronger members of the Church are called “bones,” because just as soft flesh is supported by the bones to which it clings, so the weaker in the Church cling to the more perfect and are supported by them. And because the heart of the multitude of believers ought to be one and their soul one (Acts 4:32), it often happens that the stronger in the Church, grieving for the imperfect when they see them falling into scandal, appear to be dried up, like kindling that remains dry in a frying pan after the fat has been pressed out. For great is the sorrow of the perfect in the Church when they see the less instructed falling into scandal.

Alternatively, when he says, “My bones have dried like kindling,” [he explains] from what cause this happened: “I was struck in my first parent, and my heart dried up”—that is, the strength of the reason of my members dried up—“like grass, which today is and tomorrow is thrown into the oven” (Matt. 6:30). And why was I struck in my first parent? “Because I forgot to eat my bread”—that is, I refused to nourish myself with the divine commands by which a human being ought to be refreshed.

That the divine commandments ought to be nourishment for a human being, the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “A human being does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4:4). The first human being forgot to eat this bread. At the devil’s suggestion, with the woman transgressing and persuading him, he touched the forbidden food and forgot the commandment (Gen. 3:1–6). But after forgetfulness comes remembrance.

Let us eat that bread which said of itself: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51). Let us eat that bread so that we may live. Let us not eat as our fathers ate manna, and died (John 6:49).

“Because of the sound of my groaning, my mouth has clung to my flesh.” There are some who, by not groaning over what they ought to groan over, or by groaning over what they ought not to groan over, make themselves objects of lamentation. They grieve over lost money, but do not grieve over lost righteousness; they grieve over a lost coin, but not over the heavenly kingdom taken from them; they commit fraud and rejoice.

But because those more perfect in faith cannot refrain from grieving for them out of charity, “my mouth has clung”—that is, the stronger members among my members have clung—“to my flesh,” namely, to the less instructed. The strong have clung to the weak, the vigorous to the infirm. And this is “because of the sound of my groaning”—that is, of my members groaning over those who make themselves objects of lamentation, because they cling to them in sympathy. Therefore it is necessary that you answer them quickly.

Alternatively: “I forgot to eat,” because “because of the sound of my groaning”—namely, the voice of the serpent, over which my members must always groan: “Eat, and you will be like gods” (Gen. 3:5)—“my mouth has clung,” that is, my inner human being consented to my flesh. For my Adam consented to Eve, because the strength of my rationality was weighed down by my sensuality.

“And because of this sound of groaning, I have become in my members like a pelican of the wilderness; I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling.” The pelican is a bird born on the banks of the Nile and fond of solitude. Here are understood the holy preachers who wish to seek profit for the Lord from the talent entrusted to them, mindful of the Lord’s sentence: “Wicked servant, why did you not put my money with the bankers, so that when I came I might have received it with interest?” (Matt. 25:26–27; Luke 19:22–23).

Mindful of this, he keeps himself in solitude—that is, among the nations—in order there to seek profit for the Lord. He dwells among them as in a wilderness, because he finds no one there belonging to his own way of life.

“And I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling.” The night-raven is a bird also called an owl. It sings at night and loves to be in a dwelling—that is, in deserted houses. A dwelling is a deserted and ruined house where, after the roof has been removed, only the walls remain.

Here are indicated the same preachers who were represented by the pelican, or others who again seek profit for the Lord in a dwelling—that is, in those who had already become almost a constructed house through receiving the faith, but who, because they later departed from the faith through the fault of unbelief, became like a dwelling without the roof of faith. Another translation has: “among ruined walls and in demolished places.”

“I kept vigil, and I became like a solitary sparrow on the roof.” It is as though he said: “In some of my members I became like a pelican, and in others of the same members I kept vigil”—that is, I persevered in unrest—“and I became like a sparrow,” a plaintive bird, “and I was solitary on the roof.”

Those who still have faith but live too much according to the flesh are indicated here. Among them each preacher is a sparrow, seeking those who consent too much to their flesh. He is solitary on the roof because, while the others live under their flesh as though under a roof, he is not subject to the roof: by subduing his flesh in order to strengthen the spirit, he is already on the roof, overcoming the law of the flesh by the law of the mind.

Alternatively, what he says, “I have become like a pelican of the wilderness,” can be understood of the members of the Lord. By the pelican, which loves solitude, those are indicated who set aside every burden of the world and withdraw into solitude so that they may devote themselves solely to contemplation of God.

There are others who likewise set aside the pomp of the world, but in some way depend on those who live in the world, seeking food and clothing from them. Such people are indicated where it says: “I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling.”

There are also others who keep vigil among human beings—that is, labor in unrest—in order to build others up in faith. Such people are indicated by the words: “I kept vigil, and I became like a solitary sparrow on the roof.”

These three kinds of birds and places can also be understood of our Head, so that the Head himself may speak as follows: “Because of the sound of my groaning, my mouth has clung to my flesh.” Because of this groaning, in sorrow I became like a solitary pelican.

It is said that the pelican immediately kills its young, newly hatched from the warm egg, with its beak. After killing them, it torments itself in great grief for three successive days; on the third day, tearing itself apart from extreme pain, it pours out its blood. Sprinkled with this blood, the young come back to life. Here Christ is understood, who killed the human race in that which had to be killed. For he recalled idolaters to the worship of God. He poured out his own blood in order to restore us to life. Hence the saying: “I kill, and I make alive; I strike, and I heal” (Deut. 32:39).

Christ was also a solitary pelican, for he was born in a solitary birth. No one except him was ever born without sin.

Or: “I have become like a pelican of the wilderness,” according to the saying: “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9:58).

“I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling.” He dwelt in a dwelling when he willed to live among the ruined—that is, among transgressors of the Law. He loved their darkness, not so that they would remain in darkness, but so that they might still be converted. For he said of them: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24). There he preached, there he performed miracles, and there at last he willed to die.

“I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling. Finally, I kept vigil”—that is, I rose from the dead—“and I became like a solitary sparrow on the roof,” because I alone ascended into heaven. Hence the saying: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13).

Or thus: “I kept vigil,” that is, I was given over to unrest; or, “I kept vigil,” that is, I acted watchfully. Hence the saying: “The righteous person gives his heart to keeping watch early for the Lord who made him” (Sir. 39:1).

“And I became like a solitary sparrow on the roof”—that is, I was regarded by them as comparable to that bird which is driven out of the house and dwells alone on the roof.

Because I became like a sparrow, “all day long my enemies reproached me.” Or thus: Although I was born for the purpose of taking away the voice of the groaning of my members, nevertheless “all day long”—that is, continually—“my enemies reproached me,” saying: “You have a demon” (John 8:48), and things of that sort.

“And those who praised me with their mouth swore against me in their heart.” With their mouth they said: “Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God in truth” (Matt. 22:16). Yet afterward it became clear that in their hearts they were opposed to me, as though they had conspired against me.

And why did this happen? “Because I ate ashes like bread.” That is, I drew sinners, comparable to ashes because of their uselessness, into my body as bread—that is, as the righteous are called bread because of the solidity of their good works.

“And I mixed my drink”—that is, the strong members in my body—“with weeping,” that is, with those who are called weeping because of the multitude of their sins and who compel others to weep for them. Therefore the Jews swore against me, because I chose both the impious and the pious for the perfection of my body. Hence the saying: “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” (Matt. 9:11).

Even now the pagans reproach the preachers in the Church, saying that they corrupt human morals and disciplines, because they say that preachers give permission to sin when they promise a place for repentance and hope of pardon. They do not consider that the Lord, lest people live worse through despair, promised the harbor of forgiveness; and lest they live worse again through hope of forgiveness, he made the day of death uncertain. In the greatest wisdom he established both: a place where those who return may be received, and delay by which they may be frightened.

“Because of the face of your anger and indignation, for you lifted me up and dashed me down.” It is as though he said: “That I ate ashes was because of the face of your indignation”—that is, because I came to know your anger—“for you lifted me up and permitted me and my members, when lifted up, to be dashed down.”

Humanity was lifted up because it excelled all animals through the vitality of reason. It was placed in free choice and created in such a way that it would not die if it ceased to sin. But because it fell from obedience and turned its free choice toward evil, as though it no longer possessed the power of discernment, it was dashed down.

Nor would the Lord justly have demanded more obedience from it than from the other animals if it had not surpassed the other animals in vitality.

“My days have declined like a shadow.” It is as though he said: “Because you lifted me up and dashed me down, therefore my days”—that is, the days of my members—“have declined like a shadow, and I in my members have withered like grass.”

Note that those whose days decline rightly act in this way, because they did not wish to remain in stability and eternity.

“But you, Lord, who are eternal and whose name will live forever, remain forever, and your memorial”—that is, your mercy, which is worthy of remembrance—“remains from generation to generation.”

And how does this happen? Because you, “arising through me, will have mercy on Zion”—that is, on the Jewish people. And truly you will have mercy, because it is the time to have mercy on her, according to the saying: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born under the Law, to redeem those who were under the Law” (Gal. 4:4–5).

And truly you will have mercy, because the time has come, according to the saying: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (1 Cor. 6).

“For your servants have taken pleasure in her stones.” It is as though he said: “In this way you will have mercy on Zion, because her stones”—that is, the prophets who are her foundation—“were pleasing to your servants,” that is, your apostles understood the prophets. And by explaining the sayings of the prophets, those apostles will have mercy on the earth—that is, they will make those who are still earthly worthy of your mercy, so that from earth they may become living stones in the building of Zion. For God is powerful enough to make stones from the dust that he formed from nothing.

“And the nations will fear your name, Lord, and all the kings of the earth your glory.” Behold, one wall of the city of Zion has already been constructed—the wall from the circumcision—so that another wall may come from the uncircumcision, and the two walls, joined into one in the cornerstone, may build the city.

“And they will fear”—as though he said: “You will not merely have mercy on Zion, but the nations will fear your name, Lord, with filial fear, not servile fear,” according to the saying: “I say that Christ became a servant of the circumcision, but that the nations glorify God for his mercy” (Rom. 15:8–9).

And it will not be just any nation that fears your name, Lord, but all the kings of the earth will fear your glory—that is, your exceedingly glorious resurrection.

And truly, when the wall from the circumcision has been summoned, the wall from the uncircumcision will come. For when those two have been joined, the Lord has built a spiritual Zion, not a carnal one. At last he will be seen in his glory, not in his weakness, in which he was seen by those who crucified him, but in the majesty of the Father and in the multitude of angels.

“And so that at last he may be seen in his glory, he has regarded”—that is, he will regard—“the prayer of the humble, and has not despised their supplication made for sins.”

“Let these things be written for the generation to come, and the people who will be created will praise the Lord.” It is as though he said: “The Lord will not regard only those who were in the primitive Church, but also those who will exist afterward. For these things, which were fulfilled in the primitive Church, will be written”—that is, recorded—as things that are to be future “for the generation to come,” that is, for a later generation. Thus the people who will be created will praise the Lord, not being ashamed to confess the Lord before human beings.

Or thus: Because the nations will fear your name, Lord, let this which the Lord sees and will build—namely, what was promised in the first generation—be written, that is, made known, as having been fulfilled in the generation to come. For what appeared to have been promised to the Jews was fulfilled among the nations, and the people who will be created in good works will praise the Lord.

“For, in order that it might praise him, he looked down from his holy height”—that is, from me, the assumed human being. “The Lord looked from heaven upon the earth,” in order to make heaven from earth.

Why did he look down? “To hear the groaning”—that is, the pain of mortality and suffering—“of the prisoners,” that is, of those bound by the chains of his discipline. Hence it is said: “Put your foot into his fetters and your neck into his collar” (Sir. 6:24). Therefore let no one evade discipline.

Here he speaks gently to those who must be corrected, lest they later experience the judgment of the raging Judge. Let us endure the fetters, because in the end the fetters will be removed and turned into a crown.

When he says, “To hear the groaning of the prisoners and to release the children of those put to death,” he means the imitators of the martyrs, who were put to death outwardly by their enemies and who themselves mortified their own selves inwardly.

“So that they may proclaim the name of the Lord in Zion and his praise in Jerusalem.” He will release the children of those put to death from the bonds of sins, so that, having been released, they may proclaim the name of the Lord in Zion—that is, in the Church—and his praise in Jerusalem.

What greater praise of him could there be than that a faithful shepherd should give his life for his sheep?

“They may proclaim the name of the Lord in Zion and his praise in Jerusalem, when peoples gather together as one”—that is, so that peoples may gather together as one; that is, in one charity and one faith, so that there may be no schism among them. For those who wish to be saved must gather together as one.

“The water was stirred, and one person was healed” (John 5:4). Hence also the saying: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). This is what he means by “when peoples gather together as one.”

And not only will various peoples gather together as one, but kings will gather for this purpose: to serve the Lord.

“He answered him in the way of his strength.” It is as though he said: “They will proclaim his praise in Jerusalem, and that praise itself answers those who have been called.”

Those who have been called answer the Lord; they answer him in their life, not with their tongue. Those who live perversely after being called, who produce thorns and thistles after the seed has been sown, do not answer the Lord. Rather, they answer the Lord who respond to their calling with good works, giving thanks to God.

When it says, “He answered him,” it means that each person who has been called gives thanks in the way of his power, namely in him who said of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

Note that it says, “in the way of his virtues.” The virtue of the Lord is the glory of his resurrection. He did not appear to the peoples before the resurrection, but was largely hidden because of the weakness of the crucifixion. Afterward he was preached everywhere through the power of the resurrection. For after the resurrection, the ascension, and the sending of the Holy Spirit, the word of the Lord was heard everywhere.

Thus those who have been called respond by doing good in the way of his strength—that is, in the glory of his resurrection. For the Church’s praise is not merely to believe in Christ crucified and dead; its praise is to believe in Christ crucified, dead, and risen again.

Or thus: Jerusalem answered him—not the Jerusalem that is in slavery with her children, not that one of which it was said: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling!” (Matt. 23:37).

That Jerusalem, when called, did not answer in praise. But the Jerusalem to which it was said, “Rejoice, barren woman who does not give birth; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54:1; Gal. 4:27)—that Jerusalem, when called, answers the Lord in the way of his strength, not in his weakness.

For she finds nothing in herself about which she could speak of herself except the voice of weakness, namely: “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40:5). Therefore she answered in the way of his strength, by believing in the resurrection. Hence the saying: “If you believe in your heart that God the Father raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Rom. 10:9).

She answered, saying: “Make known to me the shortness of my days.” That is, cause my members to attend to the shortness of my days—the few days during which the Church will persevere until the consummation of the age—so that they may not consent to those who will say that the Church is not universal and will soon come to an end.

The prophet, or Christ who speaks here, foresaw that some would arise who, after receiving the faith, would attack the Church, saying that it was not universal but existed only among the partisans of Donatus and would soon end there. Against them he says: “Make known to me the shortness of my days.”

It is certain that the multitude of days will endure eternally; but “make known to me the shortness of my days”—that is, set them before me with a limit—so that I may recognize that the Church will persevere to the end. Hence the saying: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28).

And lest this be understood as applying only to the partisans of Donatus, he therefore continues: “This gospel will be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come” (Matt. 24:14).

“Make known to me the shortness of my days,” namely so that “you do not take me away in the midst of my days”—that is, so that you do not permit me to be taken away in the midst of my days, in the imperfection of temporal days.

Note that he would permit him to be taken away in the midst of his days if he were led to favor the judgment of the hostile heretics who said that the Church would not endure until the consummation of the age.

This is what he says: “Do not take me away in the midst of my days, through generation after generation of your years.” It is as though he said: “For this reason I ask you to make known the shortness of my days, and not their multitude, because your years”—that is, the multitude of your days, when you will be all in all—“will endure through generation after generation,” that is, eternally.

Then, when all the generations that succeed and pass away here will be before you as one generation, in that generation will be your years—that is, your eternity.

And your eternity will not exist only then; it existed before all things. For you, Lord, “in the beginning”—that is, in your eternity, or in your Son—“founded the earth”—that is, the Church—“and the heavens are the works of your hands.” If there are any heavens—that is, seats of God—this is not from themselves, but from the works of your hands, because you have worked in them whatever good they possess.

And yet, although they are heavens and the work of your hands, “they will perish, but you will remain.”

Note that it says, “They will perish.” For if they are going to perish, they will perish according to the body; and if according to the body, where is the resurrection, which it is impious to deny? It is therefore clear that they will not perish in such a way as not to rise again.

They will perish in the resurrection itself, because when corruption has assumed incorruption, the corruption that preceded will perish in them. What was animal will perish in them, and what was spiritual will remain.

This is what he says: “They will perish, but you will remain.” And truly they will perish, because they will all grow old. This is because they are a garment: the body is, as it were, a garment for the soul, and therefore it must grow old.

“And like a covering that will be changed because of old age, you will change them.” And truly you will change them, because they will be changed from corruption into incorruption.

“But you”—who existed from the beginning—“are the same and will remain the same,” namely immutable. “And your eternal years will not fail,” in which years “the children of your servants will dwell.”

Note that it says that the children will dwell there, not the servants. For if the apostles, who were servants, will not dwell there, how will their children—that is, their imitators—dwell there? This should not be understood as though servants will not dwell there. Rather, by saying “the children of your servants,” he indicates that no one who remains in the old condition will arrive there. Those who wish to arrive there must put on newness.

This was signified in the children of Israel, when none of those who crossed the Red Sea entered the promised land except Caleb and Joshua (Num. 14:30). In these two were signified the two who would enter the true land: the Head and the body, that is, Christ and the Church.

When he says, “The children of your servants will dwell,” this means that the good works of your servants will dwell there—that is, they will be the reason why your servants dwell in those years. For we will find there such children as we send ahead of us here. Our children—that is, our works—are sent ahead for this purpose: to prepare what we need there.

This was signified through Joseph, who was sent ahead for the purpose of providing what his father needed.

“The children of your servants will dwell, and their offspring will be established forever.”

The preceding passage can also be read differently, where it says, “He answered him in the way of his strength.” It is as though he said: “The people who will be created will praise the Lord in this way, because they answer him in the way of his strength, by imitating him.” Just as he gave his life for his sheep, so this people likewise did not hesitate to give its life for its brothers; and thus it answered him, saying:

“Make known to me the shortness of my days”—that is, cause me to attend to how few my days are.

“Do not take me away”—that is, do not permit me to be taken away—“in the midst,” that is, in the imperfection, “of my days,” so that I may recognize these days as imperfect and not eternal.

Or thus: “Do not take me away in the midst of my days”—that is, from the course of this life—“until I strive to attain eternal things.”

And why this? Because “your years are to come through generations of generations.”

The rest remains unchanged.

# PSALM 102. A PSALM OF DAVID HIMSELF

«Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his benefits. He forgives all your iniquities; he heals all your infirmities. He redeems your life from destruction; he crowns you with mercy and compassion. He fills your desire with good things; your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s. The Lord performs mercies and judgment for all who suffer wrong. He made his ways known to Moses, his will to the children of Israel. The Lord is compassionate and merciful, long-suffering and exceedingly merciful. He will not be angry forever, nor will he threaten forever. He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities. For as high as heaven is above the earth, so has he strengthened his mercy over those who fear him. As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our iniquities from us. As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him, for he himself knows our formation. He has remembered that we are dust: a human being—his days are like grass—will blossom like the flower of the field. For the spirit will pass through him, and he will not remain, and he will no longer know his place. But the mercy of the Lord is from eternity and unto eternity upon those who fear him, and his righteousness is upon children’s children, for those who keep his covenant and remember his commandments to do them. The Lord has prepared his throne in heaven, and his kingdom will rule over all. Bless the Lord, all his angels, mighty in strength, doing his word, to hear the voice of his words. Bless the Lord, all his powers, his ministers who do his will. Bless the Lord, all his works, in every place of his dominion. Bless the Lord, O my soul.»

## Exposition

The voice in this psalm is that of the perfect in the body of Christ, exhorting their souls—that is, their animal faculties—so that they may agree with their prayers and bless the Lord.

Or it may be the voice of the more perfect addressing the less perfect, because the latter, on account of the weakness of the flesh to which they expose themselves, are designated as animal. In this psalm the more perfect draw such people along with themselves to bless the Lord.

It is as though each person says: “In every gift of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, in every consolation, in every correction, in that grace by which he forgave sins and did not repay according to merits…”

Bless the Lord, my soul: bless him, I say, not only with the tongue but also with your life. For he does not seek our blessing in order to profit by it himself, but so that we may profit in him. He does not seek something which, once received, would turn him away from us; rather, he seeks what will bring us to him. And all that is within me, bless his holy name. He is not speaking here to the intestines—namely, the liver and the other organs—as though they should bless the Lord; rather, what he first understood by “soul” he expresses again in other words, because of the excessive fervor that he has in this exhortation. [Col. 0667C] Or we may understand by “all that is within me” the powers of the soul—reason, understanding, and the other faculties that are within the soul. Although the voice of the mouth is silent, the inner faculties ought not to be silent in blessing the Lord.

Let the sound of voices vary according to the time, but let the inner voice be perpetual. When you come to church, sing a hymn: your voice resounds with the praises of God. Have you loved as much as you could? Have you departed? Your soul resounds with the praises of God. Are you conducting business? Let your soul bless the Lord. Are you taking food? See what the Apostle says: “Whether you eat or drink, do everything for the glory of God” (1 Cor. 10). I dare to say that, when you sleep, your soul should bless the Lord. Let no thought of wrongdoing awaken you. If the prospect of theft awakens you, your innocence, [Col. 0667D] even while you sleep, is the voice of your soul.

“Bless the Lord, my soul.” This repetition serves as an exhortation. But in order that you may always bless the Lord, do not forget all his recompenses; for if you forget them, you will be silent. You cannot keep his recompenses before your eyes unless you keep all your sins before your eyes. Let not the love of your former sin be before your eyes, but its condemnation; for if condemnation comes from you, remission will come from God.

Observe that he says “recompenses,” not “impositions,” because one thing was owed to us and another was given back to us. He first bestowed on you that you might live; he fashioned you in his image and likeness so that you might rule over all animals by the power of reason (Gen. 1). But what did you give back in return for such great benefits? Transgression, blasphemies, contradictions, and many injuries [Col. 0668A], for which you deserved judgment, not mercy. Yet the Lord himself repaid good for evil, because he said: “Confess, and I forgive.”

For all the evils you have committed, the Lord seeks that image of himself in which he created you—the image to which you return through confession of sins. He seeks no more than his own coin (Matt. 22), that is, his own soul, in which he impressed the power of reason by means of his coinage. He does not ask you to give what is yours, but what is his. Of your own you possess nothing but sin, which he does not wish to have attributed to him. Give him back, therefore, what is his: praise him in truth; for if you wish to give what is yours, you are lying. “Whoever speaks falsehood speaks from what is his own.” But whoever speaks the truth speaks from God, because whatever good we say or do, we have from him.

Therefore, do not forget [Col. 0668B] all his recompenses, namely these: that he is propitiated for all your iniquities, forgiving you your sins. And because, after the resurrection of sinners, you still bear mortal flesh in which you suffer many provocations, he therefore goes on to say: “Who heals all your infirmities,” that is, he heals the weak thoughts of the flesh through a kind of medicinal pain.

Let us endure medicinal pain, looking toward the health that is to come. It is as though we should endure a physician cutting and burning severely, although we are not yet certain of future health. How much more, then, must the medicinal hand of the Lord be endured, since it is never deceived. He gave you a command about what you should touch and what you should not touch in order to preserve health, but you refused to listen to him. At least now, listen to him in order to recover it.

What he says is: “Who heals all your infirmities.” [Col. 0668C] He also finally redeems your life from destruction, when this mortal nature will put on immortality (1 Cor. 15). He crowns you—he who grants you here to contend lawfully, so that afterward you may be crowned. Or he crowns you in the future with mercy, that is, with his promise, and with compassions, that is, with the fulfillment of his promises.

Observe that he says “with mercy.” For he crowns us in mercy, since he rewards his own gifts in us. “Who satisfies your desire with good things”: who grants you to accomplish what you rightly desire. Or, in the future, he will satisfy your desire with good things, when you see him face to face.

And lest anyone should expect this satisfaction of desire here, he adds: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s.” Here the resurrection is indicated, in which all old things will be renewed like [Col. 0668D] the youth of an eagle.

It is said that when an eagle has been weighed down by old age, it is unable to take food because its beak has grown excessively. The upper part of the beak projects over the lower part; and, curving around the lower part, the upper part does not allow the eagle to open its mouth, so that there may be some interval between the lower and upper parts. Since the hooked upper part prevents it from opening its mouth, the eagle is burdened by the weakness of old age and by the inability to eat.

After suffering this for a long time, it finally approaches a rock. There it rubs and strikes the upper part of its beak, whose growth had closed the passage for eating. By doing this for a long time, it is freed from the burden of the beak that had prevented it from taking food. It approaches food, and everything is restored. After old age, the vigor of all its limbs and the brightness of its feathers return, as though it had become young again. It flies to the heights like an eagle: [Col. 0669A] in it there comes to be a kind of resurrection.

Let us therefore examine ourselves, to see whether there is anything that prevents us from eating our bread, and let us strike our old age against the rock. The rock is Christ (1 Cor. 10), in whom our youth will finally be renewed like the eagle’s.

Meanwhile, until we reach that renewal, he comforts us in this desert, until we arrive at our homeland.

What he says is: “The Lord performs acts of mercy.” The Gospel declares toward whom he shows mercy, saying: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5). The Gospel again declares what the measure of mercy is, saying: “Love your enemies, do good [Col. 0669B] to those who hate you” (ibid.). And Paul says: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink” (Rom. 12). And again: “Give to everyone who asks” (Luke 6).

Let everyone who desires mercy therefore take heed and be merciless toward no one. Let him give himself to everyone who asks, so that at last he may fully receive from the Lord.

This command seems to conflict with what is said elsewhere: “Let your alms sweat in your hand until you find a righteous person to whom you may give it.” What, then, shall we say? It is said: “Do not receive a sinner” (Ecclus. 12); and yet it is also said: “Give to everyone who asks you.”

Give to the sinner, not as a sinner, but as a righteous person. A sinful man comes before you? When I say, “A sinful man comes before you,” I am placing two names together, neither of them superfluous. One name, “man,” signifies the work of God; “sinner,” however, signifies the work [Col. 0669C] of man.

Do not therefore give to the work of man, but to the work of God. You give to the work of man when you are pleased to give to someone precisely in what he is a sinner. For whoever gives to a hunter or a jester because of the very art that he practices does not give to the work of God but to the work of man. For if he were merely a man and were not a hunter, you would not give to him. Therefore, in him you honor not nature but an art or a vice.

Again, if you give something to a righteous person, to a disciple of Christ who needs it, but do not consider that he is a disciple of Christ, a minister of God, or a steward of God, and instead consider some temporal advantage—perhaps that he is necessary for your case—or give to him so that he may be more favorably disposed toward you, then you are not giving to a righteous person. This is just as the person who gave to the hunter did not give to the man.

But so that no one, when giving to a righteous person, should afterward look for some temporal [Col. 0669D] advantage for himself from that gift, let everyone hear the Lord saying in the Gospel: “Whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person shall receive the reward of a righteous person” (Matt. 10). It is not enough to receive a righteous person unless he is received in the name of a righteous person. He receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person who, in receiving him, considers only that in which he is righteous and does not consider gaining any advantage from it.

To those who show mercy in this way, he shows mercy in other matters. And lest anyone should say, “If I show mercy to everyone, if I love enemies as well as friends, behold, I shall suffer everything with impunity; behold, the correction imposed by moral discipline will perish,” the passage adds: “and judgment for all who suffer injury.”

It is as though he were saying: No one who suffers injury [Col. 0670A] need fear that what he endures will remain unpunished, even though, in order to preserve mercy, the one who suffers does not avenge the injury inflicted. The Lord will execute judgment here, in his name, for all who suffer injury, against those who inflict injury upon them, in accordance with the saying: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay,” says the Lord (Deut. 32).

The Lord does not forbid correction by superiors of their subjects; only this must be guarded against: that the correction be made not with a spirit of revenge but with a spirit of love. Each person ought to correct his wicked servant and his dissolute son, but everyone must beware lest he leave uncorrected in himself what he corrects in another.

Nor was the adulterous woman brought before the Lord not to be stoned. Rather, he wished to suppress the pride of those who want to avenge the sins of another while failing to notice that there are more sins in [Col. 0670B] themselves that ought to be avenged. For he said: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John 8).

It is as though he were saying: The law is holy and commands nothing unjustly; therefore, the ministers of the law must be holy. Those who wish to correct the crimes of another must first condemn their own crimes in themselves. Let the person who wishes to stone an adulterous woman stone his own adulterous conscience.

Or let us explain it this way: “The Lord performs acts of mercy,” justifying each of his own; “and judgment for all who suffer injury,” namely, that “the righteous person may still be justified” (Rev. 22).

“He made his ways known to Moses.” It is as though he were saying: The Lord performs acts of mercy and judgment, and he made these ways of his known to Moses. By “Moses” every chosen person is to be understood. For this reason he prefers to mention [Col. 0670C] Moses rather than another chosen person: Moses himself was the minister of the law, and the Lord made his ways known to him—namely, that he would show mercy to those who are merciful toward others, and judgment to all who suffer injury.

He also made this known to Moses so that no one might judge another’s sins arrogantly before making satisfaction to God for his own. When it says, “He made his ways known to Moses,” it means that through Moses he made his will known to the children of Israel, because through Moses the law was given, which encloses everyone under sin. For when the commandment came, sin revived. It was not known that desire was sin unless the law said: “You shall not covet” (Rom. 7).

The Lord is merciful in his promises and compassionate in their fulfillment, long-suffering because he bears with us until he brings us to perfection, and greatly merciful because, although sin is committed, [Col. 0670D] life nevertheless continues. Sins increase, and life is prolonged. He calls us by threats; he calls us by kindnesses. Yet the Lord, doing these things, will not be angry forever with us, nor will he threaten us eternally.

We have already experienced this: when we were sinners, we were justified; when we deserved evil, he repaid us with good.

What he says is: “He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities.” For “as high as heaven is above the earth, he has strengthened his mercy over those who fear him.” Just as the earth is protected on every side by heaven, receives light from it, and is watered by its dew and drenched by its rain, so those whom the mercy of God protects are protected by it on every side; they are illuminated by it and [Col. 0671A] drenched with the wisdom of truth.

“As far as the east is from the west, he has removed our iniquities from us.” Here is another comparison showing how the Lord performs mercy: as far as the rising of the sun is from its setting, so far is the rising of grace from the fall into guilt; for just as the fall into guilt is eternal, so also is the rising into glory.

By yet another comparison he shows how the Lord’s mercy has been strengthened over those who fear him: just as a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear him. This is because he himself knows our formation, that is, our frailty. He remembers that we are dust; and that man, like grass, withers; that his days blossom like the flower of grass, because although it blooms today, tomorrow it will wither.

And why is this? Because [Col. 0671B] “the spirit will pass through him.” To pass over is to go from good to good; to pass beyond is to go beyond the boundaries, abandoning the good and clinging to evil. Hence the saying: “A spirit departing and not returning” (Ps. 77). The passage says: “For the spirit will pass through him,” and will not remain in the vitality of reason in which the human spirit was created by God; and it will no longer recognize its place, because by itself it cannot return to its former state.

But the mercy of the Lord is from eternity and unto eternity—that is, it will endure over those who fear him, restoring their spirit whenever it wishes to pass over, or even if it passes beyond. And his justice exists in the children of children, that is, it rules over all generations. His justice is given to those who keep his covenant, that is, his pact, and who remember his commandments [Col. 0671C] in order to do them, not merely to know them.

It is necessary for everyone to do the Lord’s commandments. He has prepared his judicial seat in heaven, in which he will judge those who do not do his commandments; and his kingdom will rule over all, both the godly and the ungodly.

Or let us explain it this way: “They remember his commandments in order to do them.” As though you were asking, “Who can do the commandments?” The answer is: The Lord has prepared his seat in heaven—that is, in those who through observance of the commandments have been made heavenly—and he himself enables them to observe his commandments. “And his kingdom will rule over all.”

Therefore:

“Bless God the Father, all his angels,” that is, all who perform his embassy, “mighty in strength,” in working miracles, “doing his word,” fulfilling by their deeds what they proclaim by their word [Col. 0671D], so that others may hear through them the sound of his words. For the one who preaches by word and deed persuades.

“Bless the Lord,” namely the Son, “all his powers; bless him, his ministers who do his will. Bless the Lord, the Spirit, all his works, in every place of his dominion.”

“Bless the Lord, my soul.” A blessing at the beginning, a blessing at the end. We begin in blessing; we finish in blessing; in blessing may we reign.

## Psalm 103. A Psalm of David himself

“Bless the Lord, my soul; Lord my God, you have been greatly magnified. You have put on confession and beauty, clothed in light as with a garment. [Col. 0672A] Stretching out heaven like a skin, you who cover its upper parts with waters. You who make the cloud your ascent, who walk upon the wings of the winds. You who make your angels spirits and your ministers burning fire. You who founded the earth upon its firmness: it shall not be moved for ever and ever. The abyss, like a garment, is his covering; upon the mountains the waters shall stand. At your rebuke they will flee; at the voice of your thunder they will fear. The mountains rise up and the plains descend to the place that you founded for them. You set a boundary that they shall not cross, nor shall they return to cover the earth. You send forth springs in the valleys; the waters will pass through the midst of the mountains. All the beasts of the field will drink; the wild asses will await them in their thirst. Above them the birds of heaven will dwell; from the midst of the rocks they will give forth their voices. Watering the mountains from your upper chambers, the earth will be satisfied with the fruit of your works. Bringing forth grass for cattle and plants for the service of human beings, so that you may bring bread from the earth and wine that gladdens the human heart. So that oil may cheer the face, and bread strengthen the human heart. The trees of the field will be filled, and the cedars of Lebanon that he planted. There the sparrows will make their nests; the heron’s house is their leader. The high mountains are for the deer; the rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs. He made the moon for appointed times; the sun knows its setting. You placed darkness, and night came to be; in it all the beasts of the forest will pass through. The young lions roar as they seize prey and seek their food from God. The sun has risen, and they have gathered together; they will be placed in their dens. Human beings will go out to their work and to their labor until evening. How greatly your works have been magnified, O Lord! You made all things in wisdom; the earth is filled with your possession. This sea is great and spacious in its breadth; there are reptiles there without number, small animals with great ones. There ships will pass through, and that dragon which you formed to play with it. All things await you, that you may give them food in due season. When you give it to them, they gather it; when you open your hand, all things will be filled with goodness. But when you turn your face away, they will be troubled; you will take away their spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust. You will send forth your spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth. May the glory of the Lord endure forever; the Lord will rejoice in his works. He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble; he touches the mountains, and they smoke. I will sing to the Lord throughout my life; I will sing psalms to my God as long as I exist. May my speech be pleasing to him; as for me, I will rejoice in the Lord. May sinners disappear from the earth, and the wicked, so that they may no longer exist. Bless the Lord, my soul.”

## Exposition

“A Psalm of David himself.” Because all Christians, on account of the unity of the body of Christ, are one body, and all souls, on account of the unity of faith, are one soul, therefore, in return for the Lord’s many gifts and for all his great benefits of grace, let each person say:

[Col. 0673A]

Bless, O my soul, the Lord. And rightly bless the Lord, O soul, because you, Lord my God, have been greatly magnified. The Lord is not magnified in himself, nor diminished; but he is magnified in us when his works appear in us.

You have put on confession and beauty. As though he were saying: Truly you have been greatly magnified, because you have clothed yourself with those who have confessed and thereby been made beautiful—that is, you have made them your garment. Observe: if you wish to be beautiful, confess; and you will begin to be adorned through confession. For the Lord, so that you might pass from ugliness into beauty, though beautiful himself, became ugly. He was beautiful in this respect: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John 1). He was ugly in this respect: that “he took the form of a servant” (Philippians 2), so that, by sharing our ugliness, he might adorn us with his own beauty.

When he says, “You have put on confession and beauty,” [Col. 0673B] he adds, “clothed with light”—that is, surrounded by those who were formerly dark, as though by a garment. Hence the saying: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5).

“Stretching out the heavens like a skin.” As though he were saying: In this way you clothe those who have confessed and become beautiful, because you will stretch out the heavens—that is, Holy Scripture, which is compared with heaven because it conceals divine mysteries—like a skin, that is, like the reputation of mortal saints. That mortality is understood by “skin” is indicated in Genesis: after the first parents transgressed, the Lord made them tunics of skin (Genesis 3), signifying by this that they had become mortal. Mortality is understood by skin because skin is stripped from a dead animal.

Observe that Scripture is stretched out like a skin because the death of the saints [Col. 0673C], publicized everywhere, made their writings authoritative. The death of the saints has been more widely publicized, just as other preachers also became known to more people through their deaths; and thus, when their deaths were publicized, their writings became authoritative.

When he says, “Stretching out the heavens like a skin, who cover its upper parts with waters,” know that divine Scripture has higher and lower commandments, which have often been indicated above by “psalm” and “timbrel.” The lower commandments of Scripture are, for example, extending a hand to the poor and the other acts performed through the body. The higher commandments are observing the Sabbath and the other commands that urge us to devote ourselves to divine contemplation.

These higher commandments, when compared with charity, are covered [Col. 0673D]—that is, they are regarded as inferior—not because they are in themselves inferior, but because charity is more excellent than all the commandments, since the law and the prophets depend upon charity (Matthew 22). For “the fullness of the law is charity” (Romans 13). Concerning it Paul says: “I show you an even more excellent way” (1 Corinthians 12), and so forth.

Charity is compared with waters because, just as water makes everything hard soft, so charity softens and waters the hard hearts of human beings, so that they may produce the fruit of good works. This is what he means by “who cover its upper parts with waters”: you make its higher commandments appear as though they were inferior when compared with waters—that is, with charity.

Or as follows: “Stretching out the heavens like a skin.” After skin has been removed from the animal bearing it, it is stretched so that it will not decay; and, once stretched, it becomes durable. In the same way, Scripture is stretched out [Col. 0674A] when, so that it may not be handed over to oblivion, it is publicized everywhere. “Who cover its upper parts with waters.” The higher things of Scripture may be understood as love of God and neighbor. They are covered with waters because they are united and confirmed by spiritual gifts, so that they may endure. Spiritual gifts are signified by waters because they cleanse the soul from inward impurities.

By these spiritual gifts charity and every virtue are confirmed, since whatever charity and the other virtues a person possesses, he possesses from the gift of God: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1).

Or as follows: “Stretching out the heavens like a skin.” By “heavens” preachers may be signified, according to the saying: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 18). These preachers [Col. 0674B] are stretched out like a skin because, just as a stretched skin protects anyone from the heat of the sun, so preachers, through their imitation, protect people from the heat of sinful impulses. In ancient times tents were made from skins so that the heat of the sun would not harm those dwelling in them. By this analogy preachers are said to be stretched out, because no heat of sinful impulses reaches those over whom they are stretched.

When he says, “Stretching out the heavens like a skin, who cover its upper parts with waters,” he means: you confirm the greater commandments, which those very preachers proclaim, with spiritual gifts, because the discernment of good that those preachers possess from Scripture is a gift of the Holy Spirit.

Observe that preachers have higher and lower commandments in their discernment of the commandments. [Col. 0674C]

They proclaim the lower ones when they expound the literal sense and teach morality; they engage in the higher commandments when they open the mystical meaning of Scripture. These higher things are covered with waters because whatever the holy preachers proclaim, they possess from the gift of the Holy Spirit. This is what he means by “who cover its upper parts with waters.”

“Who make the clouds your ascent.” That is, your holy preachers, because the way by which one ascends to you is through the ministry of preachers. Or “cloud” may be understood as Scripture, which, when expounded, provides the reason why someone ascends to the Lord.

“Who walk upon the wings of the winds.” By “wind” the souls of the saints are understood, because just as a thing that is incorporeal moves a body, so the soul, being incorporeal, gives life to and moves the body. By “wings” [Col. 0674D] the love of the saints is understood, because through love of God and neighbor they are carried into the air of freedom.

Yet the Lord walks upon all the wings of the winds, because his love walks above every love, since he first loved us. Hence the saying: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15); and: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3).

Or as follows: “Who walk upon the wings of the winds,” because you loved those who did not love you first. Hence the Apostle says: “Not because we loved God, but because he first loved us” (1 John 4).

The statement “who walk upon the wings of the winds” may also be understood literally. [Col. 0675A] Nothing is swifter than wind; yet the Lord walks upon its wings because he surpasses all swiftness, since he is present everywhere.

“Who make your angels spirits and your ministers a burning fire.” As though he were saying: In this also you will be greatly magnified, because you make your angels—that is, your ministers or messengers—spirits, that is, spiritual beings, because they do not serve the body but burn in spirit for the Lord. And you make your ministers a burning fire because inwardly they burn with the flame of charity and kindle in others the desires of sinful impulses.

In this also you have been greatly magnified, because you founded the earth—that is, the Church—upon its own stability. The stability of the Church is Christ, because the Church has been founded upon him. Hence the Apostle says: “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3). The Church, founded upon him, [Col. 0675B] will not be shaken for ever and ever. Hence the saying: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever” (Psalm 44).

“The abyss, like a garment, is its covering.” Although the Church, founded upon Christ, will not be shaken for ever and ever, nevertheless the immensity of persecutions will surround the Church like a garment.

“Upon the mountains the waters will stand.” We read that this happened at the time of the Flood, when the water covered the entire height of the mountains (Genesis 7). By those mountains being covered it was prefigured that the mountains—that is, those who were prominent in the Church—would be covered by the severe persecution of the peoples. We read that this happened in the primitive Church, because everyone then cried, “Press, press, and press them down”; and they pressed them down, saying, “[Col. 0675C] Destroy them, lest they appear.” At that time even the holy apostles, who were stronger, hid themselves.

But what concern is this? “At your rebuke they will flee”—those whose immense persecutions covered the preachers—because, rebuked by a most salutary rebuke, they ceased from persecution. Hence the saying: “Reprove, exhort, rebuke” (2 Timothy 4).

When he says, “At your rebuke they will flee,” he adds: “At the voice of your thunder they will fear,” that is, they will fear the threat of the future judgment. And they themselves “go up into the mountains,” that is, those exalted in worldly honor rise up to obtain the Church; “and the plains descend,” because, recognizing that they had climbed wrongly through their pride, they descend through humility, imitating those whom, while climbing, they despised. “They descend into the place that you founded for them.” Hence the saying: “To each person his own gift has been given by God” (1 Corinthians 7; Ephesians 4). [Col. 0675D]

Or otherwise: “The mountains rise up and the plains descend.” As though he were saying: The persecutors will fear at the voice of your thunder, and then “the mountains rise up and the plains descend,” that is, the greater and the lesser in the holy Church will be made manifest. This was said by analogy with the statement, “The mountains rise up and the plains descend.” At the time of the Flood, the water towered over the mountains; but as the water receded, the mountains appeared to rise because those who had previously been covered by the water became visible.

So, during the time of persecution, the immensity of persecution covered the lesser and the greater in the Church. But once persecution ceased, they appeared to rise because they preached the word of life without fear.

“You have set a boundary that they will not cross.” [Col. 0676A]

No persecutor has power to inflict persecution except as far as you permit him to go. For you know how far persecution is useful to your people.

When he says, “You have set a boundary that they will not cross, nor will they turn back to cover the earth,” he means: although one may hear the sound of the trumpets, the Flood is not to be feared. Even if the faithful suffer temptations secretly, there is no fear that they will be delivered over to the persecutors.

“You send forth springs in the valleys.” As though he were saying: You have set a boundary that they will not cross by sending forth springs—that is, preachers—from whom the water of a most salutary drink flows. You send these springs into the valleys, that is, everywhere into the hearts of the faithful and humble, who have made themselves valleys, that is, humble.

“Among the midst of the mountains the waters will pass.” [Col. 0676B]

The waters signify the teachings of the preachers, which will pass among the midst of the mountains because the same teaching will be common to later preachers as it was to the earlier ones. There will be no schisms among them, because the last preachers will think the same as the apostles, who were the first preachers: “One God, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4).

“All the beasts of the field will drink.” As though he were saying: You send forth springs in the valleys, from which all the beasts of the field will drink—that is, the Jews. Although they lived in a beastlike manner, they are nevertheless compared with a field because, through knowledge of the law, they had in a certain way become cultivated soil.

“The wild asses will await them in their thirst.” The wild ass is the animal of the wilderness and signifies the Gentile people. They will await the waters proceeding from the springs in their thirst [Col. 0676C], because the more irrationally they recognize that they have lived compared with others, the more ardently they will desire to drink those waters.

“And above them”—that is, beyond them—“the birds,” that is, the unstable and wandering, who hold to no limit of their flight, now made birds of heaven, knowing where they ought to fly, “will dwell,” filled by the springs sent into the valleys. “And they will give voice from the midst of the rocks,” because [Col. 0676D] their teaching does not disagree with the teaching of the apostles, whose teaching was founded upon the rock, that is, upon Christ.

Or “from the midst of the rocks,” that is, from the testimonies of Scripture, they will give voice as though from rocks.

Or as follows: “Above them,” that is, above the springs—namely, the prophets and apostles, whose authority must be maintained—the birds of heaven dwell, because spiritual men are founded upon the sayings of the apostles. “From the midst of the rocks they will give voice.”

[Col. 0676D]

“Watering the mountains from his upper chambers.” As though he were saying: You, Lord, send forth springs in the valleys, watering the mountains from their upper chambers—that is, you imbue your apostles with the sayings of the prophets. Hence the saying: “For your servants have cherished its stones” (Psalm 101).

Or “watering the mountains from his upper chambers,” that is, from spiritual gifts, which are the higher things of the preachers, because whatever they preach well is a gift of the Holy Spirit.

“From the fruit of your works the earth will be satisfied,” because from the teaching of the mountains—which is the fruit of your works—those subject to them will be filled.

“And so that they may be satisfied, producing grass for cattle.” The cattle are the preachers, as the Lord’s assistance, so that his body [Col. 0677A] may be perfected. For them he produces grass, because he commands that the necessities of food and clothing be provided for them by those subject to them. Hence the Apostle says: “The Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel” (1 Corinthians 9). Hence also the saying: “Let the one who is instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs him” (Galatians 6).

The same thing is understood by “grass” as by “hay,” and by “service” as by “cattle.”

“So that you may bring bread out of the earth.” As though he were saying: For this reason you produce grass for the cattle, so that in this way you may bring true bread out of the higher earth into the lower earth—that is, heavenly preaching—by which the faithful may be strengthened in faith and refreshed. For this reason the necessities of food and clothing are supplied to the preachers, so that they may not fail while refreshing those subject to them.

This is what he means by “so that you may bring bread out of the earth,” [Col. 0677B] and “wine may gladden the heart of man”—not the wine that makes the heart of man foolish, but the wine that gladdens the heart of man: namely, the joyfulness of the teaching of God and imitation of the Lord’s Passion, by which the faithful are intoxicated, according to the saying: “And my cup, which intoxicates, how splendid it is!” (Psalm 22).

“So that he may brighten the face with oil.” As though he were saying: For this reason you bring bread out of the earth, so that he may brighten the face with oil—that is, so that the lower earth may be gladdened by spiritual grace—and so that bread, namely, the word of God, may strengthen the heart of man. And this occurs in the following order:

“The trees of the field will be satisfied,” namely, the humble peoples. “And the cedars of Lebanon will be satisfied,” that is, the powerful in the world, whom the Lord planted—that is, firmly established—in faith, according to the saying: “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted” (Matthew 15).

“And there the sparrows will make their nests,” because those powerful in the world [Col. 0677C], loving the Church of God, will, loving their estates, bestow them upon monasteries. In these the sparrows—that is, the faithful seeking to prolong their homeland for themselves—will make their nests; they will be sustained by the resources of those with which the churches have been enriched. Thus they will nest in those very churches, lest they become prey to the devil.

“The house of the heron is their leader.” The heron is a bird that nests upon the rock it finds most secure; and, for greater safety, it also desires to make its nest on sea cliffs. This rock in which the heron’s house is found is Christ, in whom every faithful person ought to nest.

“There the sparrows will make their nests”—that is, in the cedars of Lebanon—yet in such a way that “the house of the heron,” namely Christ, is principally their leader. Although they are sustained by the cedars of Lebanon [Col. 0677D], Christ is nevertheless principally their leader.

“And the high mountains,” that is, those eminent in virtues, “will be a refuge for the deer,” namely, for those who are capable of ascending the thorny and slippery paths into the mountains. Yet the rock—that is, Christ—will be the principal refuge for the deer, and will be a refuge for the hedgehogs, that is, for those bristling and sharp with sin.

This is the way in which bread is brought out of the earth, the trees of the field are satisfied, and the cedars of Lebanon are planted, in which the sparrows will make their nests.

“God made the tree,” that is, the Church, “for enduring ages.” In order to build it, “the sun knew his setting”—not this sun that we see, but Christ, whose rays eternally illumine his own. He knew his setting because he foresaw his death, [Col. 0678A], and approved it because he did not die from necessity but by his own will.

“The sun knew his setting.” As that setting was already approaching, “you placed darkness, and night came.” Darkness was placed in the hearts of the disciples, who doubted that the Lord would rise again. Night came—that is, blindness of mind came upon those who cried, “Take him away, take him away, crucify him!” (John 19).

“In this night all the beasts of the forest will pass through,” that is, the entire Jewish people who did not turn to the faith will pass through this blindness of mind, because they fall from one sin into another: from the crucifixion to guarding the tomb, from guarding the tomb to lying when they said that the disciples had stolen him. “And then the lion’s cubs will come forth roaring to seize.”

[Col. 0678B]

The cubs are apostate angels, having as their head that lion of whom it was said: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5). The cubs of this lion lie in wait everywhere in order to seize; and because they do not possess power equal to their evil will, they seek food for themselves from God.

Their food is to turn a creature away from its Creator. They seek this food from God because they cannot do more than he permits them.

“The sun has risen, and they have gathered together.” As though he were saying: The lion’s cubs seize their prey everywhere. But what concern is this? Because the sun has risen—that is, the Lord will rise—and the devil and his members will be gathered within the boundaries that have been established.

This was said by analogy with wild animals that wander about in the darkness of night and, when day comes, withdraw into hidden caves. So the angels who, before the Lord’s coming, dominated almost everyone [Col. 0678C] and wandered widely have been gathered together after knowledge of him was spread everywhere, because they do not wander so widely as before; “and they will be placed in their lairs.”

The lairs of demons are the hearts of the impious, in which they have been placed, because they no longer attack the Church through the impious as openly as in the earliest times.

And once they have been placed there, “the human being will go out to his work,” because the preachers will go out securely to cultivate the vineyard of God. Hence the saying: “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Matthew 9).

And everyone who wishes to be a human being will go out from that city to work without interruption until evening—that is, until the end of the age. At that time, as the Apostle says, “God will send them a worker of error, so that they may believe the lie, and all may be judged who do not believe the truth but consented to wickedness” (2 Thessalonians 2).

[Col. 0678D]

Or as follows: “The sun knew his setting, and so you placed darkness and night came,” because blindness occurred in Israel, “so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter” (Romans 11). “In that night,” that is, in that blindness of mind, “all the beasts of the forest will pass through,” namely, the people of the Jews, who passed from secret detraction to conspiracy, from conspiracy to betrayal, from betrayal to crucifixion, and then to guarding the tomb, from guarding the tomb to lying, and from lying to forbidding anyone to speak in his name.

Or as follows: “In it all the beasts of the forest will pass through,” that is, the devil and his angels will pass through among the blinded Jews.

“Lion’s cubs roaring to seize their prey.” The cubs were the lesser among the Jewish people who, consenting to the leaders, cried out while roaring, “Crucify him!” (John 19).

[Col. 0679A]

But if the beasts of the forest signify the devil and his angels, passing through among those blinded Jews, then this will be the reason for what was said: “Lion’s cubs roaring to seize their prey.” Blindness occurred in the hearts of the Jews because those Jews, being lion’s cubs, roared to seize the Lord, crying: “Take this man away and release Barabbas to us” (John 18).

“And they seek their food from God,” that is, in the Lord’s body they satisfied their carnal will. This food was granted to them by God because he did not die according to their will but according to the Father’s ordering.

“They seek their food from God.” But what concern is this? Because “the Sun of righteousness has risen”—that is, Christ, who is the true sun, will rise from the dead, and death will no longer rule over him (Romans 6).

When he rose, the Jews were gathered together [Col. 0679B], because those adhering to the Lord would also be placed in their lairs: for they had secretly conspired in hidden places to forbid anyone to speak in his name (Acts 4).

“The sun has risen.” When this sun rises, “the human being will go out to his work and to his labor until evening.” This verse is not changed.

How greatly your works have been magnified, O Lord!

Seeing that the Lord had been magnified both in himself and in his own, the Prophet, rejoicing with them, bursts forth into this voice of congratulation, saying: O Lord, how greatly your works have been magnified—those works by which you arrange all these things! That is, how great they have become in my contemplation!

And it is no wonder that your works are great, [Col. 0679C], because everything has been made through your Magnificent One. For “in wisdom you made” them—that is, you arranged them ineffably in your Son.

Through this Wisdom “the earth has been filled with your possession,” because “you have subjected all things beneath his feet” (Psalm 8).

And not only the earth—that is, the Jewish people—has been filled with your possession, but also “this sea, great and spacious in extent,” has been filled with your possession, that is, with your creature.

As we have often heard, the sea signifies the Gentile people. This sea is great in the Lord and spacious in extent—that is, in the works of the saints—because there the saints have room to exercise their works in many people.

“And there,” that is, in the Lord’s possession, “are creeping things,” namely, sudden suggestions fighting against the saints so that they may not perform their good work among those subject to them. There is no number to these creeping things, because apostate angels everywhere and innumerably sow suggestions.

This is what he means by “there are creeping things without number.” [Col. 0679D] “And there are small animals with great ones.” There are heretics erring in great and small matters: they err in great matters when they do not believe in the Trinity; in small matters, when they do not consent to ecclesiastical institutions.

When he says, “small animals with great ones,” he nevertheless adds: “And there,” that is, among the animals and creeping things, “ships”—that is, gathered churches—“will pass through” under the direction of the good pilot, our Lord Jesus Christ.

The Church is compared with ships because, amid the waves of the world, lest it suffer shipwreck as upon the sea, it is governed by Christ.

“This dragon whom you formed to mock him,” that is, the devil, the prince of the creeping things and animals, will resist so that this great sea may not become your possession. You formed him [Col. 0680A] to mock him because you made him so that he might be mocked by your saints. For those whom he thinks he has swallowed and wholly incorporated into himself, you draw out through your saints so that they may be incorporated into you, because you pierced his jaw with your bracelet.
