A bracelet is a round object having neither beginning nor end. Through it the grace of the Lord is signified. Although we receive it, we do not possess it through our own merit; rather, it descends from him who has neither beginning nor end.

Through the grace of the Lord the dragon’s jaw has been pierced, because his grace frees and draws out those whom the dragon desires to devour. This was said by analogy with a whale, which loses through its pierced jaw what it thinks it has swallowed.

When he says, “This dragon whom you formed to mock him,” he means: [Col. 0680B]: all the creeping things and animals, and the dragon himself as their head, await food from you, so that you may give them food in due season—but at the season foreseen by you.

“And when you give it to them,” that is, when you permit it, “they will gather” what will refresh them. They gather nothing except what you permit.

“And when you open your hand,” that is, when you reveal your Christ, “all things will be filled with goodness,” that is, with your grace. I say “all things” that are to be filled in you. When you open your hand, they will be filled.

But when you turn away your face—that is, the regard of your grace—they will be troubled by unlawful disturbances. And when they have been troubled, “you will take away their spirit,” namely, a spirit inclined toward failure, going away and not returning, because it is not for a human being to direct his own way.

Thus they will fail in themselves so that they may advance in you, and they will return to their own dust, recognizing that they are dust and can do nothing by themselves.

[Col. 0680C]

Or as follows: “You will take away their spirit,” according to the saying: “Do not consider how or what you are to speak” (Matthew 10); and thus “they will fail and return to their own dust.”

“And so you will send forth your spirit,” namely, the spirit of humility by which they humble themselves; “and they will be created” in good works. Thus “you will renew the face of the earth,” that is, the conscience of earthly people, which had grown old when they were troubled with their face turned away.

The conscience is called the face because, just as a person recognizes and distinguishes someone from another by seeing his outward face, so, when questioned, the conscience recognizes itself.

“May the glory of the Lord be for ever.” The Prophet, concerning all that has been ineffably arranged above by the Lord, urges us to glorify the Lord, according to the saying: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1).

And he says: May the glory of the Lord be not only in the future [Col. 0680D] but also in this present age. “And thus the Lord will rejoice in his works,” that is, he will be pleased with the perfection of his work.

May the glory of the Lord be—the Lord, I say, “who looks upon the earth,” that is, earthly human beings, “and makes it tremble” at the future judgment. Hence Paul says: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling” (Philippians 2). So also the saying: “Upon whom does my spirit rest, if not upon the humble and gentle, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66).

May there also be the glory of the Lord, who touches the mountains with an inward touch—that is, those exalted by an excess of temporal goods—“and they smoke,” that is, they pour forth tearful supplication.

Therefore not only will those who are in the flesh sing for these bodily matters [Col. 0681A], but I too, rejoicing so long beforehand, will sing to the Lord in my life; I will sing with my voice and play the psalm to my God through my works, not for a moment but “as long as I exist.”

Or as follows: I will sing in my present life, and at last I will play the psalm to my God in the future, as long as I exist—that is, as long as I remain in him, in unchanging being. This will be eternal, because all times will pass away.

“And I will play the psalm.” “May my speech be pleasing to him,” that is, may my confession please him, which, speaking outwardly in the written word, declares all the things I have unjustly done.

Or as follows: “May my speech be pleasing to him,” that is, may those things please him which I have spoken about him through the Holy Spirit.

“But I will rejoice in the Lord,” whatever others may do; and so greatly that, provoked by my example, “sinners may fail from the earth,” that is, from their earthly work, “and the wicked may fail,” so that they are no longer what they previously were.

In order that this may happen, bless the Lord, O my soul.

## Psalm 104. Alleluia

[Col. 0681B]

“Give thanks to the Lord, and call upon his name; proclaim his works among the nations. Sing to him and play the psalm to him; recount all his wonders. Glory in his holy name; let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice. Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face continually. Remember his wonders that he has done, his marvels and the judgments of his mouth. You offspring of Abraham, his servant, sons of Jacob, his chosen ones. He himself is the Lord our God; his judgments are throughout all the earth. He remembered his covenant for ever, the word that he commanded for a thousand generations, the covenant that he made with Abraham and his oath to Isaac. And he established it for Jacob as a commandment and for Israel as an everlasting covenant, saying: ‘To you I will give the land of Canaan, the allotted portion of your inheritance.’

“When they were few in number, very few, and foreigners in it, they passed from nation to nation, from one kingdom and people to another. He did not permit anyone to harm them, and he reproved kings on their behalf: ‘Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not harm my prophets.’

“And he summoned famine upon the land, and crushed every support of bread. He sent a man before them; Joseph was sold into slavery. They humbled his feet in fetters; iron passed through his soul, until his word came. The word of the Lord set him aflame. The king sent and released him; the ruler of the peoples freed him. He appointed him lord of his house and ruler of all his possession, to instruct his princes as himself [Col. 0681D] and to teach his elders wisdom.

“And Israel [Col. 0681C] entered Egypt, and Jacob became a sojourner in the land of Ham. And he greatly increased his people and made them strong against their enemies. He turned their heart so that they hated his people and dealt deceitfully with his servants. He sent Moses his servant, Aaron whom he had chosen. He placed in them the words of his signs and wonders in the land of Ham.

“He sent darkness and made it dark, and did not embitter his words. He turned their waters into blood and killed their fish. Their land brought forth frogs in the inner chambers of their kings. He spoke, and the gadfly came, and gnats throughout all their territories. [Col. 0682A]

He made their rains hail, and consuming fire in their land. He struck their vines and their fig trees and crushed the trees of their territories.

“He spoke, and the locust and the young locust came, whose number there was not. And it consumed every blade of grass in their land and consumed all the fruit of their land. And he struck every firstborn in their land, the firstfruits of all their labor. And he brought them out with gold and silver, and there was not a weak person among their tribes. Egypt rejoiced at their departure, because the fear of them had fallen upon them.

“He spread out a cloud as their protection, and fire to give them light by night. They asked, and the quail came, and he satisfied them with the bread of heaven. He split the rock, and waters flowed; [Col. 0682B]; rivers went through the dry land. For he remembered his holy word, which he had spoken to Abraham his servant. And he brought out his people with rejoicing and his chosen ones with gladness. And he gave them the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labors of the peoples, so that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law.”

## Exposition

This psalm is the first of the alleluiatic psalms. For “Alleluia” is interpreted as “Praise the Lord.” In this psalm the Prophet commends to us those from the former people who did not embitter God and did not murmur against him—namely, the offspring of Abraham, the children of promise, belonging to the inheritance of the everlasting covenant.

The Prophet admonishes these people [Col. 0682C] to serve God, not for the sake of temporal good, which is common to the good and the wicked, but to worship God freely, seeking no advantage of reward for God’s sake; and to do these things by praising, calling upon him, and acting well through faith, not for their own glory but for the Lord’s.

The psalm further sets before us the eternal promises made to the holy patriarchs and prophets, our fathers. Through these promises it exhorts us to be their children by imitating them and hoping in them. It also says that they were not abandoned with respect to temporal goods, in which he set an example of faith for those who were descended from their flesh and for those who wish to imitate their faith.

And it says as follows:

Confess to the Lord and call upon his name. Since the title of the psalm is “Alleluia,” which is interpreted as “Praise the Lord,” we ought to understand as praises the confession that the Prophet here promises us; and, while praising him, let us call upon his name. He hears the one who calls upon him, but the one whom he sees praising him, whom he approves as loving him. What he says—“Confess to the Lord and call upon his name”—and since whoever loves God ought to love his neighbor, he therefore adds: “Declare his works among the nations,” as though he were saying: “Love the Lord in such a way that you also love your neighbor.” For by this the Lord wished to test with what affection he was loved by his servant: when Peter said, “You know, Lord, that I love you,” he replied, “Feed my sheep” (John 21). The Prophet also teaches this here when he says: “Declare his works among the nations.”

Sing to him with your mouth, and sing psalms to him through your works; recount all his wonders—those that ought to be recounted—but with such moderation that you do not cast pearls before swine. “Be praised,” that is, order your life in a praiseworthy manner, and do so by glorifying his holy name, not your own. “Let the one who boasts boast in this,” says the Lord, “that he understands and knows me” (Jer. 9). “Be praised in his holy name,” so that the heart of those who seek the Lord may rejoice because of your people. Seek the Lord in simplicity of heart, and be strengthened—that is, by seeking him, stand firm.

Let us therefore seek him, so that by seeking we may draw near, by drawing near be enlightened, and, once enlightened, be strengthened. Let us be enlightened so that, through blindness, we do not fail to see what ought to be seen. Let us be strengthened for this purpose, lest through weakness we fail to do what we have seen ought to be done. “Seek his face always.” His face is knowledge of him. If it is always sought, when will it be found? Let us therefore seek him always in this present time, so that we may find him in the future. This is the time for seeking; this is the time for finding. Indeed, this is truly the time for seeking: even when he is found, he is still sought, because although he has been found through faith, he is nevertheless sought through hope.

For charity finds him through faith and seeks him through hope. When we have attained to hope, there will be nothing further for us to seek. That the Lord is found through faith, Scripture testifies when it says: “Seek the Lord, and when you have found him, let the impious man abandon his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts” (Isa. 55). Unless he were found through faith, he would still be sought through hope; Paul would not say: “What we do not see, we await through patience” (Rom. 8). John likewise observes this when he says: “When he appears in his glory, we shall be like him, and we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3), that is, face to face.

Or perhaps what he says, “Seek his face always,” may be understood of the future, because there the heart of those who seek will always be engaged in seeking—and always seeking because they love perfectly. Why is this so? Because the Lord will always be sought by those who contemplate him face to face, and who seek him in this manner. For what else is it to seek the Lord always than never to grow weary of seeking? We always seek, as it were, the one whose presence never becomes wearisome to us.

“Remember his wonders.” Up to this point the Prophet has exhorted us to praise the Lord, call upon him, and declare his works. Now there follow the eternal promises made to our fathers, whose children we ought to be by imitation and hope.

“Seek his face always.” If it is too much for you to seek and see him as he is, at least attend to his works, and through his works recognize him as far as you can. For when he had said, “I am who I am” (Exod. 3), knowing that this could be grasped by no understanding, he adapted his words to our capacity and said: “I am the God of Abraham” (ibid.), so that through his creatures he might make himself intelligible, whereas his essence itself was revealed to no one.

“Remember his wonders, which he performed, his prodigies, and the judgments of his mouth.” His wonders are his lesser miracles; his prodigies are the greater ones. “The judgments of his mouth” are his commandments, which he set before his own people for wholesome living.

“The offspring of Abraham, his servant, the sons of Jacob, his chosen ones.” “Remember his wonders.” And lest anyone, because he had mentioned Abraham, wish to understand only those descended from Abraham according to the flesh, he adds: “He himself, the Lord our God; his judgments are throughout all the earth.”

“He remembered his covenant,” that is, his pact, which was to extend throughout eternity. He also remembered the word that he commanded to be extended through a thousand generations. Notice that he does not here speak of a commandment of carnal observance, nor of the Jews alone, since among that people there were not a thousand generations. The thousand generations signify those who, as one generation departs and another succeeds, live according to the commandment of faith, until one generation is completed from all generations. Since the number one thousand is perfect, that generation is not inappropriately signified by a thousand generations—namely, the generation that lacks nothing for perfection.

The word that he commanded was the commandment of faith, by which the righteous must live until we arrive at the hope of which he speaks. “The word that he commanded”—the word, I say, that he appointed for Abraham when he said: “In your offspring all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 28). He remembered also his covenant made with Isaac, concerning which it was said: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (Gen. 21). And he established that word of his for Jacob as a commandment of faith, so that through the commandment of faith he might come to the eternal covenant, that is, to the eternal promise.

Here too it is indicated that the Lord’s promises made to the Jews are not to be understood as referring to a temporal kingdom and priesthood, because they did not possess a temporal kingdom and priesthood eternally. Or it may be understood in this way: “He established it as an eternal covenant,” because from that word and commandment, once fulfilled, he was going to give them a covenant that would endure forever.

Saying: “To you I shall give the land of Canaan, the measuring-cord of your inheritance,” that is, to distribute it to you as an inheritance. He promised this to them when they were still few in number and had earned nothing from the Lord. They were indeed very few before the first fathers multiplied in Egypt through their descendants. They were inhabitants of that land, because Abraham, coming from Ur of the Chaldeans, was a resident in the land of Canaan.

“And they passed from nation to nation.” This may be understood as referring to Abraham’s moving into the land of other nations because of the instability of the land of Canaan. “And from one kingdom to another people,” because they moved from the land of Canaan into Egypt.

Above, he himself showed the eternal promises; now he shows that they were not abandoned in temporal necessity. When he speaks of a kingdom, a kingdom had not yet been established in the land of Canaan; rather, their offspring, having multiplied in Egypt, was destined to reign there.

“They passed from nation to nation.” And this is not surprising, because “the Lord did not allow anyone to harm them, and he rebuked kings for their sake.” The king of Gerar and the king of Egypt, inflamed by the beauty of Abraham’s wife, wished to seize her, but they were divinely warned not to do so (Gen. 12, 20). It is not recorded in these words that the Lord rebuked them, but it may be that they were corrected by the Lord inwardly, without words.

Notice that the passage of that people from nation to nation and from kingdom to kingdom signifies that the Lord’s faithful are to be led from a changeable kingdom to an unchangeable one.

“He rebuked kings for their sake, saying: Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets.” Observe that he says “anointed ones,” although at that time there was no anointed one—that is, no *Christos*. But because the Prophet foresaw what was to come, he proclaimed it as though it were already present.

Or it may be that at that time there were *christs* who were secretly Christians. For no one, either before Christ or after Christ, has been reconciled to God except through the faith that the whole earth now holds.

“And he called down famine upon the land.” In the preceding passage he made known the temporal goods by which our fathers were consoled; in what follows, evils are set before us. Their enemies were afflicted on their account. This is what is meant by: “He called down famine upon the land.”

Notice that he says “called.” Things that are animate are ordinarily called—spirits, namely, and perceptible bodies. But famine, since it is a destruction produced by hunger, cannot itself be called. Therefore let us understand “he called down famine” as meaning “the prince of famine,” that is, an evil angel through whom famine is brought upon the earth. Or understand it this way: “He called down famine,” that is, “he commanded famine to exist upon the earth.”

“And he crushed every support of bread,” because he destroyed both the grain that had been sown and that which had not been sown. To free that people from this famine, “he sent a man before them: Joseph was sold into slavery.”

That he himself was sold was part of the Lord’s disposition, not of the brothers’ power, although they thought that by their hatred they were satisfying their desire.

“They humbled his feet in fetters.” Although history is silent about this, it is no less to be believed, since the Holy Spirit announces through the mouth of the Prophet that it happened. “Iron”—that is, the difficulty and severe tribulation of human misery—“passed through his soul.” Tribulation is also signified by iron elsewhere, when it is said to the most blessed Virgin: “And a sword shall pass through your own soul” (Luke 2). For no greater tribulation could there be than for a mother to see her son hanging upon the cross. This is what is meant by: “Iron passed through his soul until his word came.”

The word, namely, by which he interpreted Pharaoh’s dream. Yet he did not possess it from himself, because the utterance of the Lord kindled him, in accordance with the saying: “Or are you seeking proof of the one who speaks in me, Christ?” (2 Cor. 13).

“The king sent and released him; the ruler of peoples set him free. And he appointed him lord of his house and ruler of all his possession, so that he might instruct his princes as himself,” that is, as one who knew himself to have been instructed, “and teach his elders wisdom.”

History is silent about this, just as it is silent about what was previously said concerning the fetters. It is therefore to be believed, because it could have happened that he not only provided for the Egyptians during the famine but also instructed them inwardly in wisdom.

“And Israel entered Egypt, and Jacob was a resident in the land of Ham.” Here is confirmed what was said above: “They passed from nation to nation.” The land of Ham is the same as Egypt. It is called Ham from the son of Noah, Ham namely, whose land Canaan originally was; from him the Egyptian nation was descended. Noah cursed Ham, prophesying that he would become the servant of his brothers (Gen. 9). What else was intended by this than that Ham would be expelled, through his descendants, from the land of Canaan, which his brothers were to possess?

“And he greatly increased his people and made them strong against their enemies.” “He turned their heart so that they hated his people”—not because he was the author of their hatred, but because, while he exalted his own people, the Egyptians, growing envious, were turned toward hatred of them.

“He sent Moses, his servant, and Aaron, whom he chose.” “He placed in them the words of his signs”—not so that signs might come about through speaking, but just as words signify the things of which they speak, so their deeds were signs of other deeds. This is what is meant by: “He placed in them the words of his signs and prodigies in the land of Ham.”

And here are the prodigies and signs: “He sent darkness and made it dark,” and “he did not embitter his words,” that is, he did not make his commands bitter or render void the denial entrusted to his servants. This would have happened had they not been received by those to whom they were sent. But because the children of Israel were obedient to Moses and Aaron, the Lord did not embitter his words.

“He turned their waters into blood and killed their fish. And he gave their land to frogs,” because nothing appeared in the land except frogs. Or, “their land brought forth frogs,” because there was such an abundance of frogs everywhere that they seemed to have been produced everywhere from the earth itself. Frogs were produced in their inner chambers, that is, in the sleeping quarters of their kings.

“He spoke”—that is, he commanded—“and the dog-fly came, and gnats throughout all their borders.” The dog-fly is a biting fly; gnats are smaller flies.

“He placed their rains as hail, and consuming fire in their land. And he struck their vines and their fig trees, and crushed the trees of their borders. He spoke, and the locust came, and the young locust, whose number there was none.”

The young locust and the locust constitute the same plague, because the locust is the parent and the young locust its offspring.

“And it devoured every blade of grass in their land, and devoured all the fruit of their land. And he struck every firstborn in their land, the firstfruits of all their labor,” that is, all the firstborn whose rearing had been their labor.

“And he led them out with silver and gold.” Each person borrowed silver and gold vessels from his neighbor, as though they were going into the desert to sacrifice to God and would return to give the vessels back. They received the gold and silver from unjust people, since it ought to have been their payment for their labor: by working they had served the Egyptians more than they had taken from them.

Nevertheless, because they deceived the Egyptians by asking to borrow their silver and gold, God should not be thought to have either commanded or approved such deceit for those who have their hearts raised above. Rather, indeed, through the very words of God, the Lord who saw their hearts and examined their desires [the text is incomplete or uncertain].

What he says—“And he led them out with silver and gold, and there was not one infirm among their tribes”—after recalling above the plagues that he inflicted upon his enemies, he now recalls the benefits that he conferred upon his friends. Yet the plagues are not recounted here in the same order in which they were related in the history, because praise is free from the law governing narration and the weaving together of history.

“Egypt rejoiced at their departure.” This does not refer to their first departure, when they were led out of Egypt, but to the departure they made after crossing the Red Sea. And why did Egypt then rejoice? Because fear of them had fallen upon the Egyptians. For after those who pursued them had been drowned, the Egyptians feared that they might return to kill the Egyptians, since only a few Egyptians had remained alive at home.

“He spread out a cloud for their protection, and fire to give them light by night. They asked, and quail came, and he filled them with the bread of heaven.”

He calls it “the bread of heaven” because the manna eaten by the Jews signified that true bread which came down from heaven, from which all are refreshed and without which no one can exist (John 6). Concerning this bread it is said: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Luke 11).

“He split the rock, and waters flowed; rivers went forth in a dry place.” And this was so “because he remembered his holy word, which he had spoken to Abraham, his servant, to whom he said: In your offspring all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22).

“And he led out his people with rejoicing, and his chosen ones with gladness. And he gave them the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labors of peoples.”

The Lord attributed all these things to his own people—not so that they might serve him for the sake of these temporal benefits, or grow sluggish in an ill-founded security, but so that, removed from worldly cares, they might serve God more willingly and attentively, in accordance with the saying: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. 6).

This is what he means by: “So that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law.”

## Psalm 105. Alleluia

> “Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever. Who shall speak of the powers of the Lord? Who shall make all his praises heard? Blessed are those who keep judgment and practice righteousness at all times. Remember us, Lord, in the favor shown to your people; visit us with your salvation, so that we may live in the goodness of your chosen ones, rejoice in the joy of your nation, and be praised together with your inheritance.
>
> “We have sinned with our fathers; we have acted unjustly; we have committed iniquity. Our fathers in Egypt did not understand your wonders; they did not remember the multitude of your mercies. They provoked you as they went up to the Red Sea, but he saved them for his name’s sake, to make his power known. He rebuked the Red Sea, and it was dried up, and he led them through the depths as through a desert. He saved them from the hand of those who hated them and redeemed them from the hand of the enemy. The water covered those who were afflicting them; not one of them remained. They believed his words and sang his praise.
>
> “They acted quickly: they forgot his works and did not endure his counsel. They desired a desire in the desert and tested God in the waterless place. He gave them their request and sent fullness into their souls. They provoked Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord. The earth opened and swallowed Dathan and covered the congregation of Abiron. Fire burned in their assembly; flame consumed the sinners.
>
> “They made a calf at Horeb and worshiped a carved image. They exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats grass. They forgot God, who saved them, who had done great things in Egypt, wonders in the land of Ham, and terrible deeds at the Red Sea. He said that he would destroy them, if Moses, his chosen one, had not stood in the breach before him to turn away his anger, lest he destroy them.
>
> “They thought nothing of the desirable land; they did not believe his word. They murmured in their tents and did not heed the voice of the Lord. He raised his hand against them, to overthrow them in the desert; to cast down their offspring among the nations and scatter them throughout the lands.
>
> “They were initiated into Beelphegor and ate the sacrifices of the dead. They provoked him by their inventions, and destruction multiplied among them. Phinehas stood up and made atonement, and the devastation ceased. It was reckoned to him as righteousness, from generation to generation, forever.
>
> “They provoked him at the water of contradiction, and Moses was troubled because of them, because they embittered his spirit. He distinguished with his lips, and they did not destroy the nations that the Lord had commanded them to destroy. They mingled with the nations and learned their works. They served their carved images, and these became a stumbling block to them. They sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons.
>
> “They poured out innocent blood—the blood of their sons and daughters, whom they sacrificed to the carved images of Canaan. The land was polluted with blood; it was defiled by their works, and they prostituted themselves through their inventions.
>
> “The Lord grew angry with his people and abhorred his inheritance. He handed them over to the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them. Their enemies afflicted them, and they were humbled under their hands. He often delivered them, but they provoked him by their counsel and were humbled by their iniquities.
>
> “He saw when they were afflicted and heard their prayer. He remembered his covenant, and he relented according to the multitude of his mercies. He made them objects of mercy before all those who had taken them captive.
>
> “Save us, Lord our God, and gather us from among the nations, so that we may confess your holy name and glory in your praise. Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, from age to age and forever. And all the people say: Amen, amen.”

## Exposition
“Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever.” This confession, because of what follows—“We have sinned with our fathers”—is that of one groaning. But since “alleluia” precedes it, [Col. 0689A] the same confession ought to be understood as praise of God, because no confession is devout and beneficial unless God is praised in it. Praise, however, proceeds from the mouth and speech, or from the affection of the heart alone.

This psalm contains praise of God in this respect: the one who speaks here confesses him to be good and merciful, or believes him to be such. He says, “Give thanks to the Lord,” and for this reason: because he is good, that is, gracious to all who taste him worthily. Therefore give thanks also because his mercy endures forever—that is, it will endure over us, namely, eternally.

“Who will speak of the powers of the Lord? Or who will make all his praises heard?” [Col. 0689B] Filled with divine contemplation, the one who here urges that the Lord’s mercy be sought says: “Who will speak of the powers of the Lord? Or who will make all his praises heard”—that is, who will cause them to be heard, showing that they must be spoken in such a way that they are proclaimed to their hearers?

Or perhaps, because what follows is, “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do justice,” the one who speaks here, filled with consideration of the divine commandments—whose works are the praises of the one who works this in his own people—says: “Who will speak of the powers of the Lord?” He says “powers” because the Lord works this ineffably in his own. And “who will make all his praises heard”—that is, who, having heard them, will perform all the works of his commandments, which are his praises? For even if everything that has been heard is done, nevertheless, insofar as it is done, the one through whom it is done must be praised: he who works in us both the will and the good accomplishment according to his good will.

Therefore, although he could have said [Col. 0689C] “all his commandments” or “all the works of his commandments,” he preferred to say “all his praises,” because, as has been said, insofar as these things are done, he through whom they are done is to be praised. Thus he says: “Who will speak of the powers of the Lord, and who will make all his praises heard?”

And because scarcely anyone can fulfill this, therefore: “Blessed are those who keep judgment”—namely, the discernment of good and evil—and blessed are those who keep justice, so that they bring into action the good which they understand by faith to be required.

For the time will come when the judgment that is now kept in faith will also be exercised in action: when justice will be turned into judgment—that is, when the righteous will receive the power to judge rightly those by whom they were judged here unjustly. Thus he says: “Blessed are those who keep judgment, [Col. 0689D] and do justice at all times”—that is, from the time they begin to exist and live in time.

“Remember us, O Lord.” Behold the prayer of those who, converted from murmuring, ask for forgiveness. It is as though they were saying: “Remember us in the good pleasure of your people”—that is, in your Son, of whom it was said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

Or thus: “Remember us, O Lord, by placing us in the good pleasure of your people”—that is, among those in whom you are well pleased, because the Lord did not take pleasure in all people. “Visit us with your salvation”—that is, in Christ. For he is the Savior in whom sins are forgiven and souls are healed, so that they may keep judgment and do justice.

“Visit us with your salvation, [Col. 0690A] to see the goodness of your chosen.” It is as though he said: We therefore ask in your salvation that we may see you in the goodness of your chosen—that is, in that graciousness in which only your chosen will see you; not those of whom it was said: “Let the wicked be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of the Lord” (Isaiah 26).

Thus he says: “To see the goodness of your chosen, to rejoice in the joy of your nation”—that is, we desire to see you in graciousness for this purpose, so that we may rejoice with your nation. For the wicked cannot rejoice in praising you together with your inheritance. God is praised when his inheritance is praised, since that inheritance itself is praised through him.

“We have sinned with our fathers.” It is as though he said: It is necessary that you remember us, because we have sinned with our fathers, [Col. 0690B] who sinned in Egypt. This does not mean that we already existed at that time, but that we were in their loins.

Note that, just as Levi was tithed with Abraham because he was in his loins when Abraham gave tithes to the priest Melchizedek (Genesis 14; Hebrews 7), so these people also sinned with their fathers, in whose loins they were when their fathers sinned in Egypt.

When he says, “We have sinned with our fathers,” he means: “We have acted unjustly” with respect to our neighbor; “we have committed iniquity” with respect to God.

Alternatively: “We have sinned with our fathers” by committing sins similar to theirs.

“Our fathers in Egypt did not understand your wonders.” It is as though he said: We have sinned with our fathers. And here is how our fathers sinned: when they were in Egypt, they did not understand [Col. 0690C] your wonders—that is, they did not consider what you intended to provide for them through those wonders, namely eternal life rather than temporal life, the unchangeable good that is awaited through perseverance. Therefore they murmured impatiently and became embittered, and sought to make themselves blessed through present, deceptive, and fleeting goods.

“They did not remember the multitude of your mercy.” He reproves both understanding and memory, for both were necessary. Understanding was necessary so that they might understand that God was preparing eternal things for them through temporal things; memory was necessary so that they would at least not forget the miracles accomplished temporally. They should have trusted faithfully that, by the same power which they had experienced in Egypt, God would free them from the persecution of their enemies.

“They forgot what the Lord had done for them in Egypt, to crush their enemies by such great wonders.” [Col. 0690D] And because they had forgotten, they doubted whether they would be delivered when they were surrounded by dangers on four sides: enemies pursued them from behind; on one side were mountains which they could not cross; on the other side was the desert, which they feared; and before them they saw the Red Sea, which they also dreaded.

And therefore, as they went up from Egypt toward the land of Canaan, they provoked him when they were at the sea—I mean the sea that they feared, the Red Sea. Yet he saved them for his name’s sake, to make his power known.

When he says “as they went up,” this is said with reference to the situation of the place, because Egypt is lower than the land of Canaan.

“And he rebuked the Red Sea, and it was dried up, [Col. 0691A] and he led them through the depths as through a desert.” By this rebuke he does not mean some voice made from heaven, but the divine power by which this was done; that power he calls a rebuke. “And he saved them from the hand of those who hated them”—that is, from the hand of those who pursued them—and “redeemed them from the hand of the enemy.”

“And the water covered those who afflicted them; not one of them remained.” And in all these things they believed his words and sang his praise. For after they had crossed the Red Sea, they sang a hymn to the Lord, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified.”

“And they quickly acted”—that is, they quickly fell away from that praise—and forgot his works. For they did not consider that the Lord’s great works toward them were not meaningless, but were calling them toward a happiness without end, which must be endured through perseverance. Instead, they hastened to be made blessed by temporal things, which [Col. 0691B] provide eternal happiness to no one because they do not extinguish insatiable desire.

Thus he says: “They did not endure his counsel.”

“And they desired desire in the desert”—that is, they desired the desirable thing—and “they tempted God in the waterless place,” by asking for water. “And he gave them their request, and sent abundance into their souls,” satisfying their animal appetite.

“And they provoked Moses in the camp, Aaron, the holy one of the Lord.” As a result of this provocation: “The earth opened and swallowed Dathan, and covered the assembly of Abiron; and fire burned in their assembly; flame consumed the sinners.”

[Col. 0691C] Dathan and Abiron were two men who, when Aaron had been appointed to the priesthood by the Lord’s command, went before him, against the Lord’s command, to offer incense, with many others consenting to them. The earth swallowed them, and fire consumed the rest who consented to them (Numbers 16).

“And they made a calf in Horeb and worshiped a cast image.” “And they exchanged their glory”—that is, God, who makes all his people glorious—for the likeness of a calf that eats grass.

“They forgot God, who saved them, who did great things in Egypt, wonders in the land of Ham, and fearful things in the Red Sea. And he said that he would destroy them.”

And indeed they would have been destroyed if Moses, his chosen one, had not stood in the breach—that is, in humility of mind—in his presence, offering himself to that same blow, because they themselves were to be struck, saying: “Lord, forgive this people this offense; but if not, erase me from the book that you have written” (Exodus 32).

By this it was shown how powerful the intercession of the saints is with God on behalf of others. [Col. 0691D] Moses was confident concerning his own justice; for, since he could not be erased, he obtained mercy so that the Lord would not erase those whom he could justly destroy. Thus Moses stood in the breach in his presence.

“He said”—but this is not placed because God had actually said it. For if he had said it, he would truly have done it. Rather, it was said because of their iniquity, which seemed so great that they deserved to be destroyed from the earth, as though God had said it.

“to turn away his anger, lest he destroy them.” “And they regarded the desirable land as nothing.” They would not in any way be blamed for treating the desirable land as nothing, since we too ought to regard a temporal kingdom as nothing, so that we may love as truly desirable Jerusalem, our free mother, which is in heaven. [Col. 0692A]

But they are instead reproved here as deserving condemnation for unbelief, because, in treating the land as nothing, they did not believe the words of the Lord, who promised eternal things through these temporal ones.

“They did not believe his word,” namely, the word given through Moses; “and they murmured in their tents, and did not heed the voice of the Lord,” who strongly prohibited them from murmuring.

“And he raised his hand over them, to overthrow them in the desert.” That is, by raising his hand he delayed the blow, and they committed a more serious sin.

“And to cast down their seed among the nations and scatter them throughout the lands.”

Yet, although he had raised his hand for this purpose, they “were initiated into Beelphegor”—that is, they sacrificed to the idols of the nations. Phegor was a place; Beel was a god of the nations, made in honor of [Col. 0692B] a certain king named Beel. “And they ate the sacrifices of the dead,” because they ate what had been sacrificed in honor of that king.

“And they provoked him by their inventions”—not because these inventions were their own, but because they made the inventions of the nations their own—and “ruin was multiplied among them.”

It would have been multiplied still further if Phinees, the priest, son of the son of Aaron, had not stood while the others were falling. He appeased the Lord because he seized and killed together the Hebrew man and the Midianite girl whom they had embraced in adultery (Numbers 25). Thus the shaking ceased.

But if he had done this out of hatred rather than love, it would not have been counted to him as righteousness. Since it was done not out of hatred but out of love, “it was counted to him as righteousness, from generation to generation forever.” [Col. 0692C]

“And they provoked him at the waters of contradiction, and Moses was afflicted because of them, because they embittered his spirit. And he distinguished with his lips.” To distinguish with one’s lips means to speak doubtfully. Moses did this in that miracle when he said: “Can we bring water out of this rock?” (Numbers 20), not considering that the Lord would perform many wonders through him.

“They did not destroy the nations whom the Lord had told them to destroy.” For when they had been brought into the promised land, they did not expel the nations as they had been commanded. “And they mingled with the nations, and learned their works, and served their cast images, and it became a stumbling-block for them.”

“And they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons; and they poured out innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters whom they sacrificed to the cast images of Canaan.” [Col. 0692D]

This is not found in the historical account; but we must believe that it happened in this way because of the Prophet who speaks here through the Holy Spirit.

“The land was slain in bloodshed”—that is, the inhabitants of the land died through the shedding of blood. And this happened because “the Lord was angry with his people in fury, and abhorred his inheritance. And he delivered them into the hands of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them. And their enemies afflicted them, and they were humbled under their hands. He often delivered them; but they, once delivered, again provoked him by their counsel, seeking what was theirs rather than what was God’s, and they were humbled by their iniquities.”

“And the Lord saw when they were afflicted, and he heard their prayer, and he remembered his covenant”—[Col. 0693A] not the old covenant, but the new one which he established with Abraham—and “he repented,” that is, he appeared to have repented, according to the multitude of his mercy. For after the punishment of iniquity, the grace of salvation was so great that it was as though the Lord regretted having exacted such punishment.

“And he gave them into mercies”—that is, he caused them to appear worthy of the Lord’s mercy to those who had afflicted them—and this “in the sight of all those who had taken them captive,” so that from then on they would not dare to harm them.

He says “mercies” in the plural because each person has his own gift from God. A person is given into mercies when he is freed by the Lord from captivity to the devil.

Hence the Lord himself says to Herod: “Behold, I cast out demons and perform healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am perfected” (Luke 13).

The Lord casts out demons [Col. 0693B] “today”: first he erases sins through confession; afterward he perfects healings when he strengthens in good works the person whose sins he has forgiven.

We too will all be perfected into a mature man, “according to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4).

And because, after the demons by whom we were held captive have been cast out, the Lord perfects healings, therefore, after it had said, “And he gave them into mercies in the sight of all those who had taken them captive,” a prayer follows, as though the demons had been cast out, that the Lord might perfect the healings.

“Save us, O Lord our God, and gather us from among the nations, so that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise,” saying: “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, from age to age”—that is, from eternity and unto eternity. [Col. 0693C]

“And all the people shall say: Let blessing be given to him in the former people; let it also be given in the latter.”

## PSALM 106. ALLELUIA

> “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever. Let those redeemed by the Lord say so, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy and gathered from the lands: from the rising of the sun and from its setting, from the north and from the sea. They wandered in the desert, in a waterless place; they found no way to a city of habitation. Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them. And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their distresses. And he led them by a straight way, so that they might go to a [Col. 0693D] city of habitation.
>
> “Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies and for his wonders to the children of men, because he satisfied the empty soul and filled the hungry soul with good things.
>
> “Those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, bound in poverty and iron, because they embittered the words of God and provoked the counsel of the Most High. And their heart was humbled by labors; they were weakened, and there was no one to help. And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their distresses. And he led them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and broke their bonds.
>
> “Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies and for his wonders to the children of men, because he shattered bronze gates and broke iron bars.
>
> “He took them up from the way of their iniquity, for they were humbled because of their injustices. [Col. 0694A] Their soul abhorred every kind of food, and they drew near to the gates of death. And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their distresses. He sent his word and healed them, and rescued them from their destructions.
>
> “Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies and for his wonders to the children of men. And let them sacrifice a sacrifice of praise, and proclaim his works with rejoicing, those who go down to the sea in ships, doing their work upon many waters. They saw the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep.
>
> “He spoke, and a storm wind arose, and its waves were lifted up. They rise to the heavens and descend to the abysses; their soul melted away amid evils. They were troubled and [Col. 0694B] shaken like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up. And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he brought them out of their distresses. And he changed his storm into a breeze, and its waves were silent. And they rejoiced because they were quiet, and he led them into the harbor of their desire.
>
> “Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies and for his wonders to the children of men. And let them exalt him in the assembly of the people, and praise him in the seat of the elders.
>
> “He made rivers into a desert and springs of water into thirst, a fruitful land into salt because of the wickedness of its inhabitants. He made a desert into pools of water and a waterless land into springs of water. And he settled the hungry there, and they established a city of habitation. And they sowed fields and planted [Col. 0694C] vineyards, and produced the fruit of their harvest. And he blessed them, and they multiplied greatly, and he did not diminish their animals.
>
> “Then they became few and were afflicted by the trouble of evils and by sorrow. Strife was poured out upon princes, and he caused them to wander in a trackless place and not on a road. And he helped the poor in their poverty, and made families like sheep.
>
> “The upright will see and rejoice, and all iniquity will shut its mouth. Who is wise and will keep these things, and will understand the mercies of the Lord?”

## EXPOSITION

Alleluia, alleluia.

This psalm commends to us the mercies of God prophesied concerning us, and therefore it is gracious to those who have experienced them. It is remarkable if it is gracious to anyone except [Col. 0694D] the one who has learned in himself what he hears in the psalm.

It is sung concerning the universal Church of the Lord, spread throughout the whole world: from the wall that comes from the circumcision and from the wall that comes from the uncircumcision, joined into one through the one cornerstone, namely Christ, who is our peace and who made both one, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” (Romans 8; Ephesians 4). “Abba” with reference to the Hebrews; “Father” with reference to us.

And because it speaks of two walls, it has “alleluia” twice. We sing this doubled alleluia at the appointed time, but we contemplate it always. For since “alleluia” means “Praise the Lord,” even if the mouth of the flesh sometimes ceases, the mouth of the heart must never cease.

Let us therefore see what the psalm urges us to do: where we should rejoice, where we should groan, where we should ask for help; where we should desire help [Col. 0695A] and from where it should come to us; what we are through ourselves and what we are through the grace of God; how our pride is crushed so that his grace may be glorified; so that each person may encounter in himself what he hears in the psalm.

This psalm sets before us four temptations, four invocations, four deliverances corresponding to them, and four confessions of the Lord’s mercies.

The first temptation is error and lack of the word of God. The second is the difficulty of overcoming the desires of an old way of life. The third is weariness of and distaste for the word of God. The fourth is the storm and dangers involved in governing churches.

To help us distinguish these four temptations, examples must be given.

Let us therefore first imagine a person living according to his former life in a deceptive security, thinking that after this life—which will eventually come to an end—there is nothing to be punished. [Col. 0695B] His heart is buried beneath the old habit of sins and lulled to sleep by the enticements and deadly pleasures of the world.

To awaken this person to seek grace, the hand of the Lord rouses him. Once awakened, he understands that he is in error. But not yet knowing the way of truth, he knocks wherever he can, and suffers hunger for that truth. After crying out to the Lord repeatedly, he is finally heard and brought to the way of faith, namely to Christ, who says of himself: “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14). Thus he is placed in the way of truth, knowing what he ought to observe.

But since many who have been freed from this temptation, relying too much on themselves, wish to resist their desires and the old habit of sin, [Col. 0695C] they find themselves surrounded by the difficulty of vices, as though a wall of impossibility had been raised around them. This happens because they trusted not in God but in their own strength.

After being wearied for a long time by this temptation, they cry out to the Lord. And the Lord, who earlier placed them in the way of truth, breaks the bonds of difficulty by establishing them in the practice of righteousness, so that what was previously difficult becomes easy for them: namely, to abstain from evil, not to commit adultery, and not to covet what belongs to another. Thus what had previously been difficult is accomplished.

The Lord could grant all these things without difficulty. But if we possessed them without difficulty, we would not recognize the Lord as the giver of so great a good. For if, from the beginning, each person could do whatever he wished without feeling any obstacle opposed to him, he would attribute to his own strength what [Col. 0695D] he recognized himself to be capable of doing and would not give thanks to the Lord for his mercies.

But whoever has been delivered from these three temptations—from error and lack of the word of God, from the difficulty of overcoming former habits, and from weariness of and distaste for the word of God—is now worthy for the Lord’s people to be entrusted to him for governance.

There he suffers the fourth temptation: shipwreck and rebellious storms, which commonly arise from the hearts of those under authority. From these rebellions, rulers are especially endangered, because they and their subjects are like people in a ship: some are carried along, others work, and all are endangered together and are saved in the harbor.

This psalm treats of these temptations and of deliverance from these temptations. Its beginning is as follows:

Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever. Let those who have been redeemed by the Lord say so, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy and gathered from the regions. As if he were saying: Those who have been redeemed from the hand of the enemy, that is, from the power of the devil. And lest they understand that only Jews were redeemed, he says: “from the regions he gathered them.” Let all those people say this now—that is, let each tell it immediately to the other: “Confess to the Lord,” that is, “give him praise”; and this because he is good, that is, sweet to all who worthily taste him. Therefore, whoever wishes to confess should taste, because no one can confess who has refused to taste. Hence one is about to call him sweet without knowing him. But if all of you have tasted how sweet he is to all, confess to the Lord that he is sweet: taste with eagerness, and with confession belch it forth.

When it says, “Confess to the Lord, for he is good,” it also commands confession because his mercy will lead us into eternity: for here grace is bestowed so that we may live forever. And let all who have been redeemed by the Lord, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy and gathered from the regions, tell this to one another.

And lest we understand this as referring only to the Jewish people, and not to the whole Church gathered from the entire world, as though delivered from a vast Egypt and gathered from many regions, what follows says: “From the rising and the setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea.” As if he were saying: He truly gathered them from the regions, because he gathered his own from the rising of the sun—that is, from the Jewish people, for whom the sun of justice rose through the legal ordinances and prophetic utterances—and from the setting, that is, from the gentile people, among whom there was always a setting. [Col. 0696C]

He shows whom he understands by “the setting”: “From the north and from the sea.” By “the north” the nations are understood, because in them the cold of sin, rather than the warmth of divine love, will rule. They are also called “the sea” because of the bitterness of their mind. The Lord redeemed such people, and gathered them from the regions; and it was necessary that they be gathered and redeemed, because they wandered in the desert, in a waterless place, and did not find the way to the city of habitation.

Here the first temptation is already indicated—namely, error and hunger for the word of God—when he says that they wandered in the desert. What he calls here “the desert” was earlier called the desert of Idumea. Everyone who has his heart lulled to sleep by the allurements and pleasures of the world wanders in that desert. He is also in a waterless place, because there he finds no refreshment with which to extinguish the thirst of his error.

When it says, “They wandered in the desert, in a waterless place; they did not find the way to the city,” many people in this desert showed a way, such as the many philosophers—Aristotle and many others. Yet none of them gave a way to the city of habitation, because however many there were, they were citizens of Babylon, not of Jerusalem, and led their imitators to the city of confusion.

The statement “They wandered in the desert, in a waterless place” may also be read figuratively. All who walk according to this wicked age, in which people so often stray from the roads, have become like those placed in a desert, where no path appears; like those who labor with thirst and never have water available; like those who are uncertain by what route they might reach any habitation.

“Hunger and thirst consumed their soul within them.” Here is shown on whose behalf they were tempted in error: recognizing themselves, they grieve that they are in error; yet, still ignorant of the way of truth and unaware by whom they have been aroused, they hunger and thirst for righteousness, seeking everywhere where they might be refreshed. Thus we read of Cornelius, who, before he learned the way of truth through Peter, recognized that he was in error. To be delivered from that error, he labored in every way by praying, giving alms, and performing every other good work. At last he was told: “Cornelius, send and summon Simon who is called Peter; he will tell you what you must do” (Acts X).

What else may be indicated here, when it says, “They wandered in the desert,” and afterward, “hunger and thirst”? These two things indicate the greatest desire they possessed: that the city of habitation might be shown to them. [Col. 0697B]

Why did they hunger? He adds: “Their soul failed within them,” because, living according to their own desires, they found nothing in themselves except failure. Recognizing this, they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted by the tribulation mentioned above; and he delivered them from their necessities, that is, from the darkness of ignorance, which they made necessary for themselves by abandoning the light. For whoever abandons the light necessarily falls into darkness, since there is no middle state between darkness and light.

“And he led them by a straight way,” that is, to the knowledge of truth, so that they might go to the city of habitation—not to the city of confusion, toward which they had previously been going when they were in error.

We have heard the cry arising from the first temptation; we have heard the deliverance. The confession of the Lord’s mercies follows in this way:

“Let them confess to the Lord his mercies.” As if he were saying: Since the Lord led them by a straight way, let them confess to the Lord his mercy, not our merits or our strength; and let them also confess to him his wonders shown to the children of men.

Why should they do this? “Because he satisfied the empty soul; he filled the hungry soul with good things.” The soul was empty as long as it was in error; but, recognizing that it was in error, it hungered; and, crying to the Lord, it was filled with good things—namely, with the word of preaching.

“Those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death.” We have now heard the deliverance from the first temptation, namely, error and lack of the word of God. The person who has been delivered, placed on the way of truth and now knowing what he ought to do, hears these commands: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal” (Exod. XX; Matt. XIX), and other such commands.

When he wishes to fulfill all these things, relying on himself rather than on God’s help, he encounters the temptations involved in overcoming old habits. Thus, although he has been delivered from the first temptation, he sits in darkness—that is, in the obscurity of vices—which is the shadow of death because it leads to death.

“And he was bound in beggary and iron.” Why were they bound? Because “they embittered the words of God,” that is, they made the Lord’s commandments bitter to themselves, “and provoked the counsel of the Most High.” They did this because, while fighting against their own desire, they did not call upon him as their helper. Thus they labored but could not overcome. At last their heart was humbled by their labors—that is, by the difficulty of resisting their old habit—and they became weak: they recognized themselves as weak against their former customs. [Col. 0698A]

“And there was no one to help.” That is, they understood that there was no helper except God. So they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities.

How did he do this? “He led them out of darkness,” that is, out of the temptation that had been the shadow of death; and at last “he broke their bonds,” that is, the difficulty of overcoming carnal desires.

Hence: “Let them confess to the Lord his mercies and his wonders to the children of men.” Why do I say that they should confess? Because “he shattered bronze gates,” by which they were enclosed so that they could not go out to do what they understood ought to be done; “and he broke iron bars,” so that it became easy for them to resist their old habit, which had previously been difficult when they relied on themselves.

How did he break them? Because “he received them from the way of their iniquity,” with “having been delivered” understood. And it was necessary that they be received, because they were humbled on account of their iniquities—that is, their recognized iniquities.

“Their soul abhorred every kind of food.” Having now been delivered from two temptations, they fall into the temptation of weariness and distaste for the word of God. By “every kind of food” he means every refreshment of the word of God, whether through reading or prayer. Their soul abhorred this, and so “they drew near to the gates of death.”

He says this so that no one might think they were secure because of satiety, and fail to see that they were instead dying from distaste. Thus they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities.

For “he sent his word,” that is, the sweetness of his word, “and healed them.” They had been very ill while they found it burdensome to do good works; and, by healing them, he delivered them from their destructions—not from fear, not from hunger, not from the difficulty of overcoming sins, but from their corruption. For it is a kind of corruption of the mind to find distasteful what is sweet.

Therefore, for this benefit also, as for the earlier ones, “let them confess to the Lord his mercies and his wonders to the children of men.” Let them offer the sacrifice of praise—those for whom previously everything good was difficult to perform. “The sacrifice of praise is a troubled spirit, a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. L). Hence: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me” (Ps. XLIX). Let them proclaim his works with rejoicing, not with weariness and grief.

“Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing their work upon great waters.” They saw the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep.

Here the fourth temptation is indicated: the danger involved in governing the people of God. Whoever has been delivered from the three temptations is worthy to be entrusted with the people of God for governance; yet there he encounters the temptation of the gravest danger—shipwreck and the storm of sedition, which commonly arise in the hearts of subjects.

When it says, “They go down to the sea,” understand: entering ships that must be governed, “doing their work upon great waters,” that is, among many peoples. That peoples are signified by waters is testified by John in the Apocalypse: when he asked what those waters were, he received the answer that they were peoples (Apoc. XVII).

By “the sea” the world is understood. A preacher descends into this world whenever, by sharing the sufferings of his subjects, he is placed in danger.

If you ask how they descend into the sea, the answer is: in ships that must be governed—that is, in Churches being built—“doing their work upon great waters.” They saw that the works of the Lord and his wonders were necessary to be given in the deep, namely, in the human heart. What is deeper than human hearts? From there winds and storms of sedition frequently burst forth and disturb the ship through dissensions. Thus it happens that both those who govern and those who are carried—that is, prelates and subjects—are endangered together.

“He spoke, and the spirit of the storm arose or endured, and its waves were lifted up.” They saw that the Lord’s works and wonders were necessary because the Lord spoke—that is, permitted it—and the spirit of the storm stood still: the opposition of resisting subjects bristled up or continued.

He shows what he understands by “the spirit of the storm” in what follows: “and its waves were lifted up.” The spirit of the storm is said to stand in the Church when opposition is aroused in the hearts of subjects.

Again: “They rise up to the heavens,” hoping for great things from their subjects; or they rise by listening and descend to the depths by fear. Why do they descend? Because “their soul was wasting away,” that is, they experienced shame over the evils committed by their subjects. Thus they were troubled inwardly, and “they were shaken like a drunken man,” losing the counsel by which they might calm the opposition of a rebellious people.

“So all their wisdom was swallowed up,” because those rulers did not know by what means they might escape. Then they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he rescued them from their necessities.

He did this in the following way: “He turned the storm into a breeze,” that is, he turned the disturbance caused by resisting subjects into the tranquility of obedience. Thus “its waves were silent,” that is, the opposition of the rebellious people ceased.

Let us hear here the voice of a certain governor who was endangered, humbled, and delivered:

“I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of the affliction that occurred in Asia, because we were burdened beyond our strength and beyond measure” (2 Cor. I). “Indeed, we had within ourselves the sentence of death, so that we would not trust in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead.”

“Its waves were silent.” And the prelates rejoiced because they had become silent. He led them into the harbor of their desire, so that thereafter they would not be endangered at sea; and, once the sea had been calmed, they were saved in the harbor amid the opposition of the people.

Prelates are endangered at sea when they are wearied by the opposition of a subject people; but they are saved in the harbor when the hearts of their subjects are prepared for obedience.

“He led them into the harbor of their desire.” Therefore: “Let them confess to the Lord his mercies and his wonders shown to the children of men. Let them exalt him in the assembly of the people, those who are subject, and let the prelates sitting in the seat of the elders praise him.”

And rightly so, because “he made rivers into a desert and springs of water into thirst.”

In the preceding passages four temptations, four deliverances, and confessions of the Lord’s mercies on account of them were shown to us. In what follows in the psalm, we are shown what the Lord commonly accomplishes in the Church: how he gives grace to the humble and resists the proud, so that he may demonstrate that the Lord’s mercy is present in all things. [Col. 0700A]

When it says, “He made rivers into a desert,” the Jewish people are signified: to them flowed the knowledge of the Law and the prophetic utterances, but he made them a desert. And “springs of water into thirst” again signifies the Jewish people, from whom divine commandments went forth like water. He has now made that water into thirst—not because it was itself thirsty, but because it ought naturally to have been thirsty.

“He made fruitful land into saltiness,” that is, into bitterness, so that because of the bitterness it would not produce fruit. This happened not through the Lord’s justice, but through the wickedness of those who inhabited the land. The Jewish people deserved this because they relied on the letter of the Law, and so it was made a desert.

We have heard how God resists the proud; let us hear how he gives grace to the humble.

For “he made a desert into pools of water.” By the desert the gentile people are signified, deprived of all heavenly irrigation. This desert was changed into pools of water because those who had previously been dry, now receiving water—that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit—produced the fruit of good works.

“And he settled the hungry there,” because those to whom the word of God had previously been unknown he made hungry for that bread of which it is said: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Luke XI).

“And they established a city of habitation,” because they made themselves citizens of Jerusalem, not of Babylon. Babylon is a city of confusion, not of habitation.

With the city now established, “they sowed fields and planted vineyards,” because those who were first converted from the nations preached to others and made those to whom they preached into fields, so that they might be worthy to be cultivated by the plow of God’s preaching. And they were not merely made into fields; vineyards were also planted among them, so that wine might be expected from them—that is, the divine word by which human hearts are made drunk.

When it says, “They sowed fields, planted vineyards, and produced the fruit of birth,” this means native or natural fruit, because they imitated those who caused them to be born in faith. Hence: “In place of your fathers, sons were born to you” (Ps. XLIV); and elsewhere: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. IV and XI).

“They produced the fruit of birth, and he blessed them, and they multiplied greatly”—that is, beyond measure—so that they no longer sought the things that belong to God, but their own things, interpreting Holy Scripture in a distorted way.

Hence: “They bent their bow, they prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart” (Ps. X).

When it says, “They multiplied greatly,” this means that through their multiplication the number of the faithful was diminished.

“And he did not diminish their cattle,” that is, he did not permit the simple in faith to diminish, but made them increase. For “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. II).

Or it may be understood this way: “He did not diminish their cattle,” that is, he did not allow the holy preachers to be lacking, so that those who had multiplied—namely, the heretics—might seek from those holy preachers what ought to be held, if they wished.

“And they became few,” that is, those who were thought to have multiplied became few, because all who separate themselves from unity become few. There are many indeed, but they are many in unity, so long as they do not separate from unity. When the multitude of unity begins to belong to them, they become few in heresy and schism.

We heard the Apostle say of them: “In the last times difficult times will come; for people will be lovers of themselves and wholly pleasing to themselves.” Would that they displeased themselves and loved God! Would that, in their difficulties, they cried out and were delivered from their necessities—those who, relying on themselves, became few and were afflicted by the tribulation of evil angels, with apostates understood, and by the future grief that they will have when their iniquities lead them away in the opposite direction, while they say: “We fools considered their life madness” (Wis. V), and so forth.

Or otherwise: “They multiplied greatly. Through their multiplication they became few.” The number of the faithful was counted in relation to the heretics, who were in the Church only in name. Those few were afflicted by the tribulation of the wicked—that is, of the heretics—and by the grief they would feel that those people had departed from the Church.

“Contempt was poured out upon princes,” that is, the heretics were held in contempt because they wished to be princes. What greater contempt is there than excommunication? Paul said of such people: “If anyone should preach anything besides what you received, let him be anathema.” This is what he meant when he said: “Contempt was poured out upon princes,” because they became salt that had lost its savor, thrown outside.

“And he caused them to wander in a trackless place, and not on a road,” with “to be guided” understood. Earlier they were guided on the road and arrived at the city of habitation. These people, handed over to a reprobate mind and to their desires, always wander in a trackless place.

When it says, “He caused them to wander in a trackless place and not on a road,” this was not without benefit to his own people. Through their error the Lord helped the poor person—that is, his humble one—out of the poverty and imperfection of those who departed from the Church. Through them the Lord arouses his humble people to the pursuit of inquiry and to the example of error.

The heretics are the reason the faithful diligently investigate the sacred Scriptures and seek in them suitable statements by which they may defend themselves, lest they be overcome by heretical disputation. Hence: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become evident” (1 Cor. XI).

Heretics are also an example of fear to those who remain in the Church. When they see that heretics have been separated from the Church because of the empty presumption by which they presumed upon themselves, they fear presuming, lest, if they presume, they too be separated from the unity of the Church. For it is necessary that “whoever stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. X).

When it says, “He helped the poor from poverty,” this means that because the heretics were poor in truth, the poor person was helped. And because he used the singular, “the poor person,” lest we understand only one person, he adds: “and he set families like sheep,” that is, he made Churches exist under their prelates, just as sheep are under shepherds.

All these things the upright will see to have been wrought ineffably by divine power—that is, those whose hearts have been made level with God’s uprightness. They will rejoice at seeing them, and “all iniquity will shut its mouth,” that is, it will destroy the mouth of the heretics when they are judged by those whom they now judge wrongly; or, taken intransitively, “every wicked person,” namely, every heretic, will shut his mouth.

“And who is wise?” That is, who knows how to guard himself for the future? “And he will keep these things,” that is, he will store within himself what has been said above, so that whenever he is wearied by temptation, he may cry out to the Lord and be delivered, and may understand the mercies of the Lord.

Let him pay attention neither to any merit of his own, nor to his strength, nor to his power, but to the Lord’s mercies. The Lord led the person who was wandering and lacking the word of God back to the way and fed him; he released the person fighting against the difficulty of sins and bound by the chains of old habit; he freed the person who found the word of God distasteful and, almost dying of weariness, restored him by sending the medicine of his word; and he led the person endangered amid shipwreck and stormy perils into the harbor of salvation after calming the sea.

He established him among his people—not where he resists the proud, but where he gives grace to the humble—so that, remaining within, he might increase, rather than diminishing by going outside.

Let the upright see all these things and rejoice; but let the mouth of the heretics be stopped because of their iniquity.

# PSALM CVII. ALLELUIA. A PSALM-SONG OF DAVID HIMSELF

“My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody in my glory. Awake, psaltery and harp; I will rise at dawn. I will confess to you among the peoples, O Lord, and I will make melody to you among the nations. For your mercy is great above the heavens, and your truth reaches to the clouds. Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory above all the earth, so that your beloved may be delivered. Save with your right hand and hear me. God has spoken in his holy place. I will rejoice and divide Shechem, and I will measure out the valley of tents. Gilead is mine and Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is the support of my head. Judah is my king; Moab is the cauldron of my hope. Upon Idumea I will extend my sandal; foreigners have become my friends. Who will lead me into the fortified city? Who will lead me as far as Idumea? Is it not you, O God, who rejected us? And will you not go forth, O God, with our armies? Give us help in tribulation, for human salvation is worthless. In God we shall act valiantly, and he himself will bring our enemies to nothing.”

## EXPOSITION

A psalm-song of David. In this psalm it is the voice of Christ, commending his obedience to us, so that we may imitate it here and be glorified with him in the future. He says as follows:

“My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready.” As if he were saying: God the Father, my persecutors think that they are bringing about my death by their own power, and not that it proceeds from my will. But this is not so, because my heart is ready—ready, I say, to fulfill your obedience. For no one will take my life from me; I lay it down myself. This is what he says: “My heart is ready,” and also the heart of my people.

Therefore, for so great a benefit given by you to me and to mine, “I will sing in myself, and I will make melody in mine in my glory,” that is, in my resurrection, for those who were sorrowful at my death.

And so that I may sing and make melody, you, my body, which is called the psaltery and the harp, die and rise again. This will truly happen, because “I will rise at dawn.” The flesh of Christ is called the psaltery because of the miracles he performed divinely, and the harp because of his experience of death.
