“I will rise at dawn.” For what benefit? “That I may confess to you, O Lord, among the peoples”—among the Jewish peoples—and “make melody to you among the nations,” among the peoples of the gentiles.

And rightly will I confess to you, because “your mercy is great above the heavens,” that is, your mercy abounded so greatly toward all that through this mercy it made them reach the heavenly realm above, namely, the angelic creature.

“And your truth reaches to the clouds,” that is, your true promises are fulfilled in such a way that the preachers themselves become clouds, raining words, flashing miracles, and thundering threats.

So that all these things may happen: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God,” with “me, a human being, exalted” understood; “and your glory above all the earth,” that is, may your glorious resurrection be manifested, so that your beloved may be delivered, though not the chaff.

And so that they may be delivered: “Save with your right hand and hear me.” Truly you will hear me in mine, because “God has spoken in his holy place,” that is, in me, his holy one, he determined that he would hear the human race. In accordance with this: “In many parts and in many ways, God formerly spoke to the fathers in the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us in his Son” (Heb. I).

This is what he means by “He has spoken to us in his holy place.” Hence: “I will rejoice and divide Shechem,” by taking it to myself, because “one will be taken and another will be left” (Matt. XXIV). Shechem is interpreted as “shoulder.” Those are understood who find the Lord’s yoke light to carry upon their shoulders.

“And I will measure out the valley of tents,” that is, I will take to myself those who wish to serve in the tent.

“Gilead is mine,” that is, the holy martyrs, who heap up many testimonies in themselves, not hesitating to become witnesses even unto the shedding of blood.

“Manasseh is mine,” that is, all who forget what lies behind and reach forward to what lies ahead.

“And Ephraim is the support of my head,” that is, all who bear fruit for God and not for themselves will be received by my head, namely, by God personally united to me.

Or, “Ephraim is the support of my head,” that is, the resting place where I may rest as though laying down my head, in accordance with this: “Foxes have holes, and the birds of the air nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. VIII).

“Judah is my king,” that is, those who confess will be my kings and priests.

“Moab,” that is, everyone living without the Law, “will be a cauldron,” that is, the refreshment of my hope, because the greater the tribulation they inflict upon me, the greater the strengthening or certainty of my hope I possess.

And how will all these things happen? Because “I will extend my sandal over Idumea,” that is, over outsiders; I will cause my incarnation to be made known.

Or, “I will extend my sandal,” that is, feet wearing sandals—namely, preachers—in the preparation of the gospel of peace.

Thus “foreigners have become my friends,” that is, they will become so, or through preaching they have already become so.

“And who will lead me into the fortified city? Who will lead me as far as Idumea? Is it not you, O God, who rejected us?” That is, who appear to repel us by not granting that we conquer bodily.

“And will you not go forth, O God, with our armies?”

And because you do these things, “Give us help in tribulation,” so that tribulation itself may strengthen us, lest we be overcome inwardly.

Why do I ask for help in tribulation, with respect to the inner person? Because the salvation of the outward person is worthless.

And because outward salvation is worthless, therefore, abandoning that salvation, “in God we shall act valiantly, and he himself will bring to nothing” those who afflict us—that is, he will make us regard the persecutions of our enemies as nothing.

# PSALM CVIII. FOR THE ENDING. A PSALM OF DAVID

“God, do not be silent about my praise, for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful person has been opened against me. They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue, and surrounded me with words of hatred, and attacked me without cause. Instead of loving me, they slandered me; but I prayed. They repaid me evil for good and hatred for my love. Appoint a sinner over him, and let the devil stand at his right hand. When he is judged, let him go out condemned, and let his prayer become sin. Let his days be few, and let another receive his office. Let his sons become orphans, and his wife a widow. Let his sons be removed, trembling, and beg; let them be cast out of their dwellings. Let the creditor search out all his substance, and let strangers plunder his labors. Let there be no helper for him, nor anyone who has mercy on his orphans. Let his descendants be brought to destruction; in one generation let his name be blotted out. Let the iniquity of his fathers return to remembrance in the sight of the Lord, and let the sin of his mother not be erased. Let them be continually opposed to the Lord, and let their memory perish from the earth, because he did not remember to show mercy. He pursued the poor and needy person, and sought to kill the brokenhearted. He loved cursing, and it will come to him; he refused blessing, and it will be far from him.

“And he put on cursing like a garment, and it entered his inward parts like water and his bones like oil. Let it be to him like a garment with which he is covered, and like a belt with which he is always girded. This is the work of those who slander me before the Lord and speak evil against my soul.

“And you, Lord, Lord, act with me for your name’s sake, because your mercy is sweet. Deliver me, because I am needy and poor, and my heart is troubled within me. Like a shadow when it declines, I have been taken away, and I have been shaken off like locusts. My knees have become weak through fasting, and my flesh has been changed because of oil. I also became a reproach to them; they saw me and shook their heads.

“Help me, Lord my God; save me according to your mercy. And let them know that this is your hand, and that you, Lord, have done it. They will curse, but you will bless; let those who rise up against me be confounded, but your servant will rejoice. Let those who slander me be clothed with shame, and let them be covered with their confusion as with a double cloak. I will confess to the Lord greatly with my mouth, and in the midst of many I will praise him, because he stood at the right hand of the poor person, to save his soul from those who persecuted it.”

## EXPOSITION

A psalm of David for the ending. In this psalm it is principally the voice of the Head speaking about his betrayer Judas, and through him about all the other persecutors. For just as the things said to Peter—namely, “Whatever you bind” (Matt. XVI), and so forth—apply to all rulers, so the things said about Judas are adapted to the other persecutors.

The beginning of the psalm is as follows:

“God, do not be silent about my praise, for the mouth of the sinner and the deceitful man has been opened against me.”

As though our Head were saying: My persecutors did not keep silent about my reproach, saying, “You have a demon” (John 7 and 8), and many things of that kind. “But you, God the Father, do not be silent about my praise.” What greater praise is there than for it to be made known that the man is true God from true God? This now lies hidden in weakness, but afterward it will be revealed. What he says—“Do not be silent about my praise”—is also necessary, because the mouth of the sinner, that is, of the transgressor of the Law, and of the deceitful man, has been opened against me in reproaching me. But see: it is clear that the reproach is false, since the sinner and the deceitful man do not keep silent about it. It is also clear that the praise is true, since God does not keep silent about it. For God is truthful, while every human being is a liar (Romans 3), because no one is truthful except the one in whom God speaks.

The greatest praise, moreover, belongs to the only-begotten Son of God, because this very thing is praise: that he is proclaimed to be the only-begotten Son of God.

“They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue; they surrounded me with words of hatred and fought against me without cause.” They spoke against him with a deceitful tongue when, as though he were a good teacher, they praised him with cunning flattery (Matthew 22). Hence elsewhere: “Those who praised me swore against me” (Psalm 101). They surrounded me with words of hatred when they openly shouted, “Crucify him, crucify him” (John 19). And they fought against me without cause, that is, without reason, because just as the pious love without cause, so the impious hate without cause. [Col. 0705C]

“Instead of loving me, they slandered me.” He continues by explaining how they fought against him. For in the very matter by which he deserved to be loved, they slandered me; but I prayed: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23).

“And they repaid me evil for good, and hatred for my love.” There are six different forms in this category, which can very easily be observed when they are mentioned:

- to repay good for evil;
- not to repay evil for good;
- to repay good for good;
- to repay evil for evil;
- not to repay good for good;
- to repay evil for good.

The first two forms of repayment concern only the good, because those who are perfectly good repay good for evil and do not repay evil for good. The last two—not repaying good for good and repaying evil for evil—concern only the wicked. The two remaining forms—repaying good for good and repaying evil for evil—are shared by those who are moderately good and those who are moderately wicked. For the moderately good repay evil for evil, and the moderately wicked repay good for good. Of the form of repayment in which evil is repaid for good, the text here says: “And they set evils against me for goods.” [Col. 0706A]

“Appoint a sinner over him, and let the devil stand at his right hand.” Behold, he foretells what will happen to the people because of his persecution, not from ill will but in assent to the divine judgment, as though he were saying: Since that people did not wish to have me as its Head, “appoint a sinner over it”—that is, let them have Antichrist as their head—“and let the devil stand at his right hand,” that is, let them give precedence to the works of the devil.

Those who did not wish to imitate me or have me as their Head will receive another who comes in his own name, rather than the one who comes in your name.

“When he is judged,” let this people be judged inwardly, so that “the one who is filthy may become filthy still” (Revelation 22). “Let him go forth condemned,” that is, let him end his life in condemnation, so that at some point he may be condemned with a double condemnation.

“And let his prayer become sin,” because every prayer that is not made through our mediator Jesus does not blot out sin but rather increases it, since it is made in transgression.

“Let his days be few,” that is, let Judas live for only a short time. “And let another receive his episcopate,” that is, let another receive the apostleship of Judas the apostle, so that the number twelve might be completed.

Or: “Let his days be few,” that is, let the days which the Jews think they will prolong by retaining their place and nation (John 11) be shortened; “and let another receive his episcopate,” that is, let the people of the Gentiles receive me, made bishop of that people.

“Let his sons be orphans,” having lost their king, or God the Father, or their fathers. “Let his sons be continually shaken,” that is, uncertain and unstable everywhere, “and let them beg; let them be cast out of their dwellings.”

“Let the creditor search out”—that is, the devil—“all his substance,” that is, all the sin of that people, so that no sins may be forgiven them, since there is no reconciliation except through Christ.

The creditor is the devil because, when someone kills another outwardly, the devil kills him inwardly; and this killing is more serious than the outward one, because the one who is killed inwardly will finally be punished with eternal fire unless he repents. The substance of this creditor is sins, because he delights in sins and, through sins, so to speak, possesses being. [Col. 0706D]

“And let strangers plunder his labors.” Historically, this happened when the Gentile people took possession of the kingdom of the Jews. Or: let strangers seize his labors, that is, let the Gentiles receive the promise made to the Jews, according to the saying: “Others have labored, and you have entered into their labors” (John 4).

“Let him have no helper, and let there be no one to pity his orphans,” that is, the remnants of the people, now that its end has come.

“Let his descendants be destined for destruction,” that is, let them be born for this alone: that they may perish. “In one generation let his name be blotted out,” that is, let that people not be reborn so that its sins may be forgiven, but “in one generation let his name be blotted out.” [Col. 0707A]

“In one generation” the one who is not reborn remains, and without this rebirth no one can be saved, as the Lord testifies: “Unless someone is born again, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3).

“Let the iniquity of his fathers be remembered in the sight of the Lord,” so that that people may be punished not only for its own sin but also for the sins of its fathers who sinned in Egypt, according to the saying: “I will avenge unto the third and fourth generation” (Exodus 20).

“And let the sin of his mother not be blotted out,” but “let the iniquity of his fathers and the sin of his mother stand continually against the Lord, and let their memory perish from the earth,” that is, let the Lord no longer remember them, so as to call them back to repentance. [Col. 0707B]

And this for the reason that that people of the Jews did not remember to show mercy, so that, once the Head had been killed, the persecution of the members might cease.

“And he pursued the needy and the beggar, and sought to kill the brokenhearted,” that is, that people pursued Christ, brokenhearted in his own people. Those who said, “What shall we do, brothers?” (Acts 2) were brokenhearted, as was also the one who said, “What do you want me to do?” (Acts 9). In such persons that people persecuted the Lord.

“And Judas loved the curse”—or that people, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27).

“And it came upon him, and he did not wish the blessing, and it shall be far from him. And he put on the curse like a garment, and it entered like water into his inmost parts.” Judas—or that people—was cursed inwardly and outwardly: outwardly, because he became hateful to everyone; inwardly, because he was blinded. “And as oil into his bones,” that is, just as oil penetrates the bones, so the curse penetrated them. [Col. 0707C]

“Let it be to him like a garment with which he is covered, and like a belt with which he is always girded.” Those who use loose clothing customarily gird themselves so that they may be ready to carry out whatever they wish to do. In the same way that people works the curse. “And let him be girded,” that is, let him be ready to perpetrate every evil, so that he may do evil not suddenly but deliberately.

“This is the work of those who slander me before the Lord and speak evil against my life.” As though he were saying: The fact that they are clothed in the curse has not happened to them unjustly, because this is their work: they worked this curse for themselves before the Lord by slandering me and speaking evil against my life.

Or: “This is their work before the Lord,” that is, he foreknew that they would act in this way—before the Lord, I say, before whom it is established that “the one who is filthy may become filthy still” (Revelation 22). [Col. 0707D]

“And you, Lord, act with me for your name’s sake.” As though he were saying: Let this happen to them. But you, Lord, “act with me,” that is, work together with me for the glorification of your name, so that people may understand that my works and yours are the same.

Or: “Work with me,” as though he were saying: I work by persevering in obedience, while you work with me by turning to the common benefit of all what they do for the condemnation of one person.

I ask you to work with me, because your mercy is sweet—that is, the reconciliation of the human race which is to come through my death. [Col. 0708A]

“Deliver me, because I am needy and poor, and my heart is troubled within me,” because, although I appear sorrowful, my sorrow does not arise from the power of those inflicting it upon me; rather, I appear sorrowful by my own will.

“Like a shadow, when it declines, I have been taken away,” because, just as night comes when the shadow declines, so death follows from the flesh. “And I have been shaken like locusts,” because, when I was left, everyone fled (Matthew 26). Or: “I have been shaken,” that is, my people were shaken like locusts, because they were scattered everywhere by their persecutors.

“My knees have grown weak through fasting,” that is, those who were stronger among my members—the apostles—grew weak through fasting, that is, by withdrawing from my presence, from which they were always refreshed. [Col. 0708B]

And yet, although they grew weak, they were afterward changed because of the oil, that is, because of the gift of the Holy Spirit which they received. And not only were the stronger ones made weak, but “my flesh,” that is, those who were weaker among my members, were strengthened because of the oil, that is, through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Or in this way: “My flesh was changed because of the oil,” that is, the carnal understanding of my people, having been weakened, was changed through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Or: “My flesh was changed because of the oil,” that is, because of the sweetness of the resurrection.

“And I became a reproach to them,” because just as they persecuted me, so also they persecuted my people: “They saw me and shook their heads.” But you, “Lord my God, help me; save me according to your mercy.”

“And let them know,” that is, let them understand, “that this is your hand,” that is, that your power has done all these things, so that they may understand that they would have had no power unless it had been given to them by you (John 19). [Col. 0708C]

He says: “And let them know that this is your hand, and that you, Lord, have done it. They will curse, but you will bless. Let those who rise up against me be put to shame, but your servant”—I do not say “will rejoice,” but—“will rejoice.”

“Let those who slander me be clothed with shame,” that is, let them be wholly confounded inwardly and outwardly, or before God and before human beings, “and let them be covered with their own confusion as with a double cloak.” A *diplois* is a double garment with no inside-out side; here complete confusion is signified.

“I will make confession to the Lord very greatly with my mouth,” that is, I will make very great confession with my mouth. As though he were saying: Let them have what has been said of them. But I will make confession to the Lord very greatly with my mouth, that is, with a harmonious heart. [Col. 0708D]

“And in the midst of many,” that is, in the hearts of the faithful, “I will praise him.” For he stood at the right hand of the poor, that is, he who was always at my right hand and at the right hand of my poor ones—in the higher place—causing them to love the right hand, that is, higher things.

He stood at the right hand of the poor “in order to save my life from those who persecuted me,” that is, the life of me and of my people—not so that they would not suffer tribulation, but so that they would not be conformed to them, according to the saying: “Father, I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you preserve them from evil” (John 17).

## Psalm 109. A Psalm of David

“The Lord said to my Lord: ‘Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet. The Lord will send forth the rod of your power from Zion; rule in the midst of your enemies. With you is the principle on the day of your power, in the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you. The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. The Lord is at your right hand; he has shattered kings on the day of his wrath. He will judge among the nations, he will fill the ruins, he will crush the heads in the land of many. He will drink from the brook on the way; therefore he will lift up his head.’” [Col. 0709A]

God the Father established a time for his promises, and he also established a time for fulfilling what he promised. The time of the promises lasted from the time of the prophets until the time of John the Baptist. From the time of John the Baptist onward, until the end of the world, it is the time for fulfilling what he promised. [Col. 0709B]

For he promised human beings divinity, mortals immortality, sinners justification, and the rejected glorification. Whatever he promised, he promised to the unworthy, so that a reward might not be given as though it were payment for works, but grace might be given to his name.

For the fulfillment of these promises he promised as mediator not just any ruler, angel, or archangel, but his only Son, so that through his Son he might show and prove the way by which he would lead us to what he had promised.

Therefore the only-begotten Son of God, coming to human beings, was to assume a human being and, through what he had promised, become human, die, rise again, ascend into heaven, sit at the right hand of the Father, and fulfill among the Gentiles what he had promised. After the fulfillment of the promises, he was to come to fulfill the remaining work, claim what he had granted in advance, distinguish the vessels of wrath from the vessels of mercy (Romans 9), and repay the wicked what he had threatened and the righteous what he had promised. [Col. 0709C]

All this, then, had to be prophesied, announced, and commended, so that when he came suddenly he would not be feared, but would be awaited in faith. The Prophet announces and commends all these things to us in this psalm, saying:

“The Lord said to my Lord: ‘Sit at my right hand.’” That this verse must be understood of the Lord the Son, our Lord and Savior himself, the Son of God, demonstrates in the Gospel. When he asked the Jews whose son they said the Christ was, and they answered, “David,” he immediately replied: “How then does David call him Lord, saying: ‘The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand’?” (Matthew 22). [Col. 0709D]

The Lord did not ask this question because he wished to learn from the Jews, but to teach them, if they did not know, so that they might say, “You tell us.” But because they were wretched and ruined, they preferred to burst with swollen silence rather than be instructed through humble confession.

Let our teacher speak, then, and teach us what answer we should give. Let us answer that he is the Son of David, as the Jews did, because if he were not the Son of David, the Gospel would certainly not say: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the Son of David” (Matthew 1).

“How then does David, in the Spirit, call him Lord, saying: ‘The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand’?”

He is truly David’s Lord, because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). But because, on account of our weakness, we lay despised in the flesh, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” Behold the Son of David and the Lord of David.

The Jews would have answered correctly if they had believed him to be David’s Lord, of whom David himself says: “The Lord the Father said to my Lord, according to his humanity to my son, and according to his divinity to my Lord.”

And what he says—on account of tested wickedness and completed obedience—“Sit at my right hand,” means: Receive me at my right hand, that is, in my higher place, never to be moved from there and not to be revealed to anyone according to the flesh, “until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet,” that is, until I subject all his enemies to his power. [Col. 0710A]

This will happen on the last day, when each person will recognize himself as bound to the Lord’s power, because everyone will be beneath his feet, either conquered or adopted, and will have there either a place of punishment or a place of grace.

Note that he says, “Sit.” In this the human nature assumed by the Word of the Lord is indicated. Divinity is said neither to sit nor to stand.

Wonderful is the mystery of Christ sitting at the right hand of the Father. He is hidden so that he may be believed; he is withdrawn so that he may be hoped for. This is justice: that through faith we should hope in the one whom we do not see, so that, cleansed by faith, we may afterward see the one in whom we now believe without seeing him.

Concerning this justice the Lord, as he was about to ascend into heaven, said: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you, he will convict the world concerning sin, and concerning justice, and concerning judgment” (John 16). [Col. 0710C] And he explained what he meant by justice: “Concerning justice,” he said, “because I go to the Father.”

This, then, is true justice: that we believe he went to the Father and sits there at his right hand until he comes to judge both the pious and the impious.

“The Lord will send forth the rod of your power from Zion; rule in the midst of your enemies.” As though he were saying: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.” This will happen in the following order: the Lord himself, the Father, is “the rod of your power,” that is, the scepter of your dominion, namely, the powerful kingdom; and this was to begin in Zion, because “salvation is from the Jews” (John 4). [Col. 0710D]

The Lord the Father also said to you, O Lord Son: “Rule in the midst of your enemies,” that is, exercise your power in the midst of the pagans and heretics who surround your people on every side.

Or: “Rule in the midst of your enemies,” that is, in the hearts of those who will become your friends from being your enemies.

And rightly will you rule, because “I am a principle with you, and you are my principle”—not as though there were two principles, but because I am in you and you are in me (John 17). This will appear not on the day of your weakness but on the day of your power, that is, in the brightness of eternity, a brightness ineffable, an ineffable light, an inexhaustible fountain, truth without defect.

“And I shall be a principle with you in the splendors,” that is, when the holy ones are in splendor, that is, in immense brightness, no longer bearing earthly flesh or groaning in a mortal body, but shining in the glory of incorruption and immortality, according to the saying: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13). [Col. 0711A]

Or otherwise: “With you I shall be a principle on the day of your power,” and I shall be a principle “in the splendors of the holy ones,” that is, in the Holy Spirit, through whom the holy ones possess whatever splendor they have. He speaks in the plural because of the various gifts of the Holy Spirit.

“From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you,” as though he were saying: Truly I am a principle with you, because I begot you from the womb, that is, from my innermost substance and hidden being, before the morning star, that is, before all works.

The morning star is the more distinguished of the other stars. Therefore, just as it is certain that the Lord the Son existed before the morning star, so it is certain that he existed before all the others, and therefore before all times, because all things were made through him.

“The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” As though he were saying: This is what the Lord the Father said concerning your kingdom, O Lord Son. What did he say concerning your priesthood? “The Lord has sworn.” [Col. 0711B]

Behold, the Lord swears, although he forbids human beings to swear lest they fall into perjury. God, on the other hand, cannot fall into perjury; the human being, who through the habit of sinning can fall into perjury, is forbidden to swear. The farther he is from swearing, the farther he will be from perjury.

Why, then, should the Lord not swear, since the Lord’s oath is the confirmation of his promise (Hebrews 6)? A human being swears and calls upon God as witness in his oath. For this is what it means to swear: to make the Lord a witness. Therefore one must beware of making God a witness to any falsehood.

If, then, a human being bears witness to God by swearing, why should God not bear witness to himself by swearing?

When it says, “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent,” repentance signifies a change of circumstances. Just as you, a human being, when something causes you regret, grieve over what you have done, so when God changes something into something else contrary to human expectation—that is, contrary to what human beings expect—he is said to repent, even to the point that he regrets our punishment if we regret our evil life. [Col. 0711C]

Therefore the Lord has sworn, that is, he has confirmed it, and he will not repent, because he will not change. What has he sworn? “You are a priest forever.” For this reason he is a priest forever: because he will not repent.

But according to what order is he a priest? Not according to the order of Aaron, who commanded that offerings and sacrifices of the Old Testament be presented. Those things have been removed: the Temple has already been overthrown, that priesthood has been taken away, and both sacrifice and priesthood have perished. [Col. 0711D]

He is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek. Melchizedek is interpreted as “high priest” or “king of righteousness.” He himself was both king and priest, the first to offer bread and wine as a figure of our sacrifice and of that holy Eucharist which is daily made in the Church in the body and blood of the Lord.

Therefore the sacrifice of Melchizedek is also more excellent than the sacrifice of Aaron, because the former came first and the latter afterward.

“The Lord is at your right hand; being so, he has shattered kings on the day of his wrath.” As though he were saying: You, Father, swore concerning your Son and said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” [Col. 0712A] And rightly so, because the Son himself, being at your right hand, shattered kings on the day of his wrath—that is, he shattered the kings, the eminent ones of this world, in consideration of his future wrath.

And how did he do this? He will judge, that is, he will exercise just judgments, among the nations, that is, among the Gentiles. In judging, he will fill the ruins, that is, he will cause some to be humbled so that they may be exalted in themselves. Finally, he will crush the heads, that is, the stiff-neckedness and pride, of many living on earth, or even of those who are dying.

And in what order will this happen? “He will drink from the brook on the way.” The brook here signifies the flow of mortality. The Lord drank from this brook on the way because he also tasted death in a human body.

“Therefore he will lift up his head,” because he will be given “the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2).

This psalm can also be read in inverted order, as follows: “The Lord the Father said to my Lord,” the Son, this namely: “I am a principle with you,” that is, being equal to you. This will appear “on the day of your power,” that is, in the brightness of your eternity, when you will appear equal to me, that is, in that glory of which it is said: “Let the wicked be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of God” (Isaiah 26), because both the wicked and the pious will see the human form.

The form of his glory, however, has been granted only to the vision of the pious. [Col. 0712B]

When he says, “With you is a principle on the day of your power,” and not only is a principle with you, O Son, but also a principle “in the splendors of the holy ones,” that is, with the Holy Spirit, he means that I, the Father, am a principle in you, the Son, and in the Holy Spirit. For you, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are from me, not I from you; yet together with the Son I, the Father, am a principle, and together with the Holy Spirit.

The Father is a principle, the Son is a principle, and the Holy Spirit is a principle.

And I, the Father, O Son, begot you from the womb before the morning star.

Therefore, on account of tested wickedness and completed obedience, “sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet.”

And as though you were asking how, or in what order, this would happen, the text continues:

“The Lord will send forth the rod of your power from Zion; rule in the midst of your enemies. With you is the principle on the day of your power, in the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.”

This concerns his divinity. But with regard to his assumption of flesh, what is said?

“The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. The Lord is at your right hand.” [Col. 0712D]

As though he were saying: The Lord the Father swore this concerning you, O Lord Son; and the Lord himself, being at your right hand, is in accordance with the saying: “He stood at the right hand of the poor” (Psalm 108).

“He will shatter kings on the day of his wrath,” that is, he will humble the powerful of this world on the day of his wrath, namely, at the time when those kings will be permitted to rage most fiercely.

Or: “On the day of his wrath” means on the last day, when the Lord’s anger will appear to everyone.

And in the meantime he will judge among the nations, that is, among the Gentiles, and “fill the ruins and crush the heads in the land of many.”

And how will this happen? Because the Lord the Son “will drink from the brook on the way; therefore he will lift up his head.”

## Psalm 110. Alleluia

[Col. 0713A]

“I will make confession to you, Lord, with my whole heart, in the council of the righteous and in the assembly. Great are the works of the Lord, sought out in all his wills. Confession and magnificence are his work, and his righteousness endures forever and ever. The merciful and compassionate Lord has made a memorial of his wonders; he has given food to those who fear him. He will remember his covenant forever; he will announce the power of his works to his people, so as to give them the inheritance of the nations. The works of his hands are truth and judgment. All his commandments are faithful, confirmed forever and ever, made in truth and equity. The Lord sent redemption to his people; he commanded his covenant forever. Holy and terrible is his name; the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. Good understanding belongs to all who do it; his praise endures forever and ever.” [Col. 0713B]

## Exposition

“Alleluia, alleluia, alleluia,” as was said above, is interpreted as “Praise the Lord.”

We sing the doubled Alleluia at the appointed time, namely from the Saturday of Easter Week until the Saturday that falls within the days of Pentecost, so that the fifty days may be completed. All of this is for our instruction and as a figure.

For just as the forty or seventy days that precede the day of the Lord’s bodily resurrection signify the sorrow of this present age, so the fifty days that follow solemnly in unearned gladness signify the year of jubilee, in which everyone is released from debt and a slave is made free (Leviticus 25). [Col. 0713C]

The Jews always observed this jubilee year after fifty years. It was a figure of those days in which those who labor here as servants will be received as sons, and, while they labor in this life, the reward will be paid which the householder gave equally to the first and the last (Matthew 20).

The reason he gave an equal reward is that each—the first and the last—will receive a single denarius.

Already existing in consideration of this eternity, and exhorting others not to be idle in the vineyard, so that at last they might receive the denarius in the evening, the Prophet says:

“I will make confession to you, Lord, with my whole heart, in the council of the righteous and in the assembly.” [Col. 0713D]

Confession is not always confession of sins; sometimes it is praise of God, expressed through the devotion of confession. The former mourns; the latter rejoices. The former shows a wound to the physician; the latter gives thanks to the physician for health.

This confession not only freed someone from every evil but also separated him from wicked people. Therefore let us hear where he makes confession to the Lord.

For he says: “I will make confession to you, Lord, with my whole heart.” And in order that I may make confession, I shall be here in the council of the righteous, so that at last I may be in their assembly.

The council of the righteous consists not in following one’s own desires but the Lord’s desires. Whoever is found here in this council will eventually be received into the assembly of the righteous.

Or in this way: “I will make confession to you, Lord, with my whole heart,” being placed—understand: in the council of the righteous—and not in secret, but in the assembly, that is, before human beings, attentive to your saying: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I also will confess before my Father” (Matthew 10). [Col. 0714A]

This psalm may also be the voice of the Head, speaking as follows: The Father exalted me as the Prophet foretold; and, having been exalted, I will make confession—that is, my people will make confession—“with my whole heart, in the council of the righteous and in the assembly.”

And rightly will I make confession to the Lord, because the works of the Lord are great for those who seek them, and they are searched out as they proceed—understand: into all his wills.

What are the works of the Lord if not the justification of the sinner, or the condemnation of the sinner if he refuses to be converted? Nothing happens contrary to the Lord’s will. [Col. 0714B]

For just as his mercy does not abandon the one who trusts in him, so his justice permits no one’s iniquity to go unpunished, when he chastises even the son whom he receives (Hebrews 12). Thus, whatever you choose, the Almighty will not lack the means by which to fulfill his will concerning you. Therefore let a person choose for himself either to be saved through mercy or to be condemned through justice.

These are “the works of the Lord, searched out into all his wills.” The works of the Lord were not established in such a way that the creature, placed under free choice, could overcome the will of the Creator, even if it acted contrary to his will.

God does not will that you sin, for he forbids it. Yet if you sin, do not suppose that the human being has done what he wished while something happened to God that he did not wish. [Col. 0714C]

For just as he wills that a human being not sin, so he wills to spare the sinner, so that the sinner may return and live. Finally, he wills to punish the one who persists in sin, so that the stubborn person may not escape the power of justice. Thus, whatever a human being chooses, the Almighty will not lack the means by which to fulfill his will.

“Confession and magnificence are his work, and his righteousness endures forever and ever.”

Since he said that the works of the Lord are great, he explains what they are. His work is confession, which he produces in his own people, making them magnificent through confession. And his righteousness endures forever and ever, because he gives perseverance to his own, so that they may remain in righteousness and not look back toward the meat-pots of Egypt (Exodus 16), because “the gifts and calling of God are without repentance” (Romans 11). [Col. 0714D]

Or in this way: His righteousness, by which he will repay the pious what he promised and the impious what he threatened, “endures forever and ever.”

“The merciful and compassionate Lord has made a memorial of his wonders; he has given food to those who fear him.”

Because he said that confession is his work, he adds, so that we may know from where confession proceeds: the Lord is merciful in his promises and compassionate in displaying what he promised. He will make a memorial of his wonders, that is, he causes his people to remember what once occurred in figure and to recognize in those events what was to be fulfilled spiritually at the end of time.

And how will this happen? “He has given food to those who fear him,” namely, food that does not perish: the bread that came down from heaven, by which the faithful are daily refreshed, and, having been refreshed, understand the wonders of the Lord. [Col. 0715A]

“He will remember his covenant forever.” As though he were saying: For this reason he gave food to those who fear him, because he remembered his covenant forever, that is, the covenant which was to extend forever—the covenant namely that all nations would be blessed in the seed of Abraham (Genesis 22).

“He will announce the power of his works to his people.” The people of the Lord are those who are Jews inwardly. The power of the Lord was announced to them because they received spiritual understanding in those things that were formerly done in figure (1 Corinthians 10). For through the Red Sea which they crossed, they understood baptism.

They came out of Egypt through the Red Sea; we came out of the world through baptism. They were circumcised in the flesh; we are circumcised with a circumcision not made by human hands. They celebrated an austere Sabbath; we celebrate a gracious Sabbath. [Col. 0715B]

All these things are the adornment of the works of the Lord—or the power of his works—which he works in his own people: to will and to persevere according to his good will (Philippians 2).

He announces this when he says: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10 and 24).

“He will announce the power of his works to his people,” namely, in order to give them the inheritance of the nations: he will cause the nations themselves to imitate his people, and thus bring in other sheep that are not from this fold (John 10).

That he might give them the inheritance of the nations—those, I mean, in whom are the works of his hands, namely, truth and judgment. [Col. 0715C] For by working truth and judgment in them, he makes them fit to possess the nations as an inheritance, because “everyone who does the truth comes to the light” (John 3), and is worthy of imitation; and likewise the one who practices judgment. Hence Paul says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. 11). “The works of his hands: truth and judgment.” These two, truth and judgment, will not go unrewarded, because all his commandments are faithful—that is, they deceive no one—and, having been rewarded, they are confirmed as destined to be rewarded throughout the age of the age that follows: “made in truth and equity.” It is true and equitable that one should labor here and rest there.

Or, they were made in truth and equity. True equity is not that which the law administers—[Col. 0715D] giving “an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth” (Exod. 21)—but that true equity which the Lord both enacted and taught (Acts 1), namely, to return good for evil. Hence the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “You have heard,” he says, “that it was written, ‘You shall love your friend and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you, do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5). “Made in truth and equity.” And what will come about through all these things? “The Lord sent redemption to his people”: that is, he permitted his Son to become incarnate, through whom the redemption of the human race was accomplished, and through whom “he commanded his covenant forever. Holy and awesome is his name.”

The Lord’s name is holy insofar as he is God, and awesome insofar as he will be the future judge. [Col. 0716A] Or, it is holy to the devout and awesome to the impious. “The beginning of wisdom is fear of the Lord.” Since he said, “The mercy of the Lord is for those who fear him,” we understood this as referring to the New Testament, not the Old, which was imposed upon our fathers only for a time. Lest anyone therefore think that the law was given uselessly, he shows what value the law possesses. It is as though he said: Although the New Testament has been confirmed forever, nevertheless no one should judge the law superfluous, because the fear of the Lord has been made known through the law.

The beginning of wisdom—that is, of a good life—is the fear of the Lord, because each person ought to begin doing good out of fear of punishment, so that at last he may act more perfectly out of love, and not out of fear, because “perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4). And this “understanding” is “good for all who practice it,” that is, for those who act according to this understanding; [Col. 0716B] and “his praise,” namely, the praise of the one who acts in this way, “endures forever,” not merely for a time. Let no one therefore think himself praiseworthy if he is praised only for a time.

## PSALM 111. ALLELUIA. OF THE RETURN OF HAGGAI AND ZECHARIAH

> “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he will greatly desire his commandments.  
> His offspring will be powerful in the land; the generation of the upright will be blessed.  
> Glory and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever.  
> Light has risen in the darkness for the upright: merciful, compassionate, and righteous.  
> The man who is gracious and lends is good; he will order his words in judgment, because he will not be shaken forever.  
> [Col. 0716C] The righteous man will be in everlasting memory; he will not fear evil report.  
> His heart is ready to hope in the Lord; his heart is strengthened, and he will not be shaken until he looks down upon his enemies.  
> He has scattered and given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever; his horn will be exalted in glory.  
> The sinner will see and be angry; he will gnash his teeth and waste away; the desire of sinners will perish.”

## EXPOSITION

“Alleluia: of the return of Haggai and Zechariah.” These two men, Haggai and Zechariah, lived under Darius, king of Babylon, and were filled with the Holy Spirit so that they might begin to prophesy about matters pertaining to the rebuilding of the temple. But since the things that were done there bodily [Col. 0716D] were later fulfilled in the faithful, the faithful are not unsuitably understood as the temple of the Lord. Hence the statement: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3). And since no one is taken up into the building of this temple except the blessed, the Prophet shows us how blessedness is to be attained, exhorting us to pursue blessedness and to be joined together as living stones in the temple of the living Lord. He says as follows:

> “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he will greatly desire his commandments.”

It is as though he said: Everyone desires to become blessed. Behold, they have at hand what they desire: let each person fear the Lord, and let him be blessed. “He will greatly desire his commandments.” To desire greatly to be in his commandments is to hasten with the greatest longing to become fit for the building together of his temple.

[Col. 0717A] “His offspring will be powerful in the land.” It is as though he said: Truly blessed is the one who fears the Lord—that is, every imitator of the Lord will be powerful in the land of the living. What is more powerful than possessing the kingdom of heaven, which is possessed not only by Zacchaeus through half of his goods, but also by the widow through two small coins (Luke 19 and 21), so that each possesses as much there as the other? What is more powerful than for the same kingdom to be worth the treasure of the rich man and a cup of cold water given to the poor (Matt. 10)?

He says, “His offspring will be powerful in the land,” because “the generation of the upright”—that is, of those who have an upright heart—“will be blessed,” that is, multiplied. To have an upright heart means not to resist the Father when he disciplines and to believe him when he promises. The generation that possesses such a heart will be blessed, because “glory and riches”—that is, glorious riches—“are in his house,” namely, in the upright heart. [Col. 0717B] Glorious riches are the testimony of a good conscience. Hence Paul says: “Our glory is the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1). This glory is in his house, that is, in the heart of the upright generation.

Or, “in his house,” namely, in the house of the Lord—that is, in those who make themselves the house of God. “And his righteousness endures forever,” that is, the righteous works of the upright generation remain forever.

And from where do they have this? Because “light has risen in the darkness for the upright,” that is, light of uprightness will rise for those who were in darkness. Hence the statement: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5). That light which has risen in the darkness is the Lord: merciful in his promises, compassionate in their fulfillment, and righteous both in saving the devout and in condemning the impious.

[Col. 0717C] And lest anyone be frightened because he called the Lord righteous, after previously calling him merciful, he adds: “The man who is gracious and lends is good.” It is as though he said: Do not fear the Lord’s justice, blessed man; be good, show mercy, and lend, so that you will not fear the Lord’s justice. “Have mercy on your soul, and you will be pleasing to God” (Sir. 30), and lend yourself to others as a good example. The good man is one who shows mercy both to himself and to others, in accordance with the statement: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6); and he lends himself to others as a good example.

Or, “he lends,” that is, he supplies his neighbors with what they need, attending to the Scripture that says: “Give, and it will be given to you” (ibid.). Such a man “will order his words in judgment,” that is, he will rationally conduct his good works in view of the future judgment, so that when the judgment arrives he will not fear the Lord’s justice, which examines everything justly.

[Col. 0717D] This is said by way of comparison when it says, “He will order his words in judgment.” Just as a good advocate arranges his words beforehand, considering how he should address each person so as to defend himself in court, so the good deeds arranged here by the faithful will defend them at the future judgment. This is what is meant by, “He will order his words in judgment.”

The result proves it, because “he will not be shaken forever.” And finally, “the righteous man will be in everlasting memory; he will not fear evil report,” which those who will be placed on the left will hear when it is said to them: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25). Or, “he will not fear evil report,” that is, the voices of those who persuade him to evil.

[Col. 0718A] And rightly so, because “his heart is ready to hope in the Lord; his heart is strengthened, and it will not be shaken” from this hope “until he looks down upon his enemies,” that is, until they become inferior to him in the land of the living—those who had tried to be superior in the land of the dying.

And in order that he may look down upon them, “he has scattered and given to the poor,” that is, he will scatter worldly goods by giving them to the poor. He will not do this merely for a time, but “his righteousness endures forever,” that is, he will persevere in this disposition.

Hence “his horn,” that is, the exaltation of the one who was despised here by the impious, “will be exalted in glory.” The sinner will see this exalted horn and be angry, when his iniquities lead him in the opposite direction. “He will gnash his teeth,” because then there will be “weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 24); “and he will waste away,” that is, he will repent—but it will be a late repentance, because “the desire of sinners will perish.”

[Col. 0718B] Or, alternatively: The righteous man “has scattered and given to the poor,” but the sinner “will see” this “and be angry,” that is, he will envy his good deeds. “He will gnash his teeth and waste away,” that is, he will seek to undo them, but in vain, because “the desire of sinners will perish.”

## PSALM 112. ALLELUIA

> “Praise the Lord, children; praise the name of the Lord.  
> May the name of the Lord be blessed from this time forth and forever.  
> From the rising of the sun to its setting, the name of the Lord is worthy of praise.  
> The Lord is exalted above all nations, and his glory is above the heavens.  
> Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high and regards the lowly in heaven and on earth?  
> [Col. 0718C] Raising the needy from the earth and lifting the poor from the dung heap,  
> to place him with princes, with the princes of his people,  
> who makes the barren woman dwell in a house as a joyful mother of children.”

## EXPOSITION

“Alleluia. Praise the Lord, children.” In sacred Scripture humility is often commended to us through the age of childhood. Hence the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Let the little children come to me, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Matt. 18). Often, too, the pride of antiquity is expressed through the age of childhood, as in the statement: “Do not become children in understanding; but in wickedness be infants” (1 Cor. 14). [Col. 0718D] And because this psalm seems to incite children to the praise of God, no adult should say that this exhortation is not addressed to him, since the adult who lays aside the wickedness of pride and assumes humility is designated by the name “child.” He says as follows:

“Praise the Lord, children; praise,” I say, “the name of the Lord.” Let the one who voluntarily makes himself a servant praise the Lord’s name. Praise, saying: “May the name of the Lord be blessed from this time forth,” that is, rejoice and persevere forever.

And let this blessing be not only in Judea, but “from the rising of the sun to its setting,” let “the name of the Lord be worthy of praise.” By the rising of the sun the Jews are signified, because through knowledge of the law the light of the true sun shone upon them; by its setting the nations are signified, because the true sun was hidden from them before the time of Christ.

[Col. 0719A] “From the rising of the sun to its setting, the name of the Lord is worthy of praise.” And rightly so, because “the Lord is exalted above all nations, and his glory is above the heavens,” that is, he appears especially glorious above his saints.

And rightly does he appear glorious above them, because “who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high,” and from his dwelling others become exalted and glorious? “And he regards the lowly,” that is, he seeks humility “in heaven and on earth,” that is, among the exalted and among the lowly.

“Raising the needy from the earth and lifting the poor from the dung heap.” “From the earth” he raised “the needy”: he brought the Jews, who were in a certain sense like cultivable earth, to knowledge of the true faith. And he lifted the poor from the dung heap, because he brought the Gentile people, lying as though in dung because they served their desires and various pleasures, to the height of his glory.

[Col. 0719B] He did this in order “to place him with princes,” that is, he will make the Gentile people, previously lying in the dung heap, worthy of a judicial seat, and will make them sit with the princes of his people, that is, with the Jews who were previously his people.

“Who is like the Lord our God, who makes the barren woman dwell in a house,” that is, the Gentile people who produced nothing good, “as a joyful mother,” because she became the mother of children? Hence the statement: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54).

## PSALM 113. ALLELUIA

[Col. 0719C]

> “When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people,  
> Judea became his sanctuary, Israel his dominion.  
> The sea saw and fled; the Jordan turned back.  
> The mountains leapt like rams, and the hills like lambs of the sheep.  
> What ails you, sea, that you fled, and you, Jordan, that you turned back?  
> Mountains, why did you leap like rams, and hills like lambs of the sheep?  
> At the presence of the Lord the earth was moved, at the presence of the God of Jacob,  
> who turns the rock into pools of water and the cliff into springs of water.  
> Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory,  
> because of your mercy and your truth.  
> Let the nations never say: ‘Where is their God?’  
> But our God is in heaven; he has done whatever he willed.  
> The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands.  
> [Col. 0719D] They have mouths, but they will not speak; they have eyes, but they will not see.  
> They have ears, but they will not hear; they have noses, but they will not smell.  
> They have hands, but they will not touch; they have feet, but they will not walk;  
> they will not cry out with their throat.  
> Let those who make them, and all who trust in them, become like them.  
> The house of Israel hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and protector.  
> The house of Aaron hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and protector.  
> Those who fear the Lord hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and protector.  
> The Lord remembered us and blessed us.  
> He blessed the house of Israel; he blessed the house of Aaron.  
> He blessed all who fear the Lord, the small with the great.  
> [Col. 0720A] May the Lord add to you—to you and to your children.  
> You are blessed by the Lord, who made heaven and earth.  
> Heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord, but he gave the earth to the children of men.  
> The dead will not praise you, Lord, nor all who descend into the underworld.  
> But we who live bless the Lord, from this time forth and forever.”

## EXPOSITION

Alleluia, alleluia. The history is well known: the Israelite people were delivered from the unjust domination of the Egyptians and crossed through the various waves of the sea (Exod. 14). It is also known how this same people crossed the river Jordan on dry ground when they entered the promised land (Josh. 3).

[Col. 0720B] These same events are recounted in this psalm, but here some things are said differently from what is found in Exodus, and some things are touched upon here that are not narrated there. Nowhere there, for example, is it read that the Jordan turned back, nor that the mountains or hills leapt. Only this is read about the Jordan: when it was touched by the feet of the priests carrying the ark of the Lord, one part of it flowed down into the sea, while the other part rose up in a heap (ibid.). Therefore, in this psalm the Spirit seems not so much to recount past events as to prophesy.

Those events were our figures, and these words exhort us to recognize ourselves, because if we retain with steadfast heart the grace of God that has been given to us, we are Israel, the seed of Abraham (John 8). “For we,” says the Apostle, “are the circumcision, who serve God in the spirit” (Phil. 3); and elsewhere: “Therefore you are the seed of Abraham” (Gal. 3). And elsewhere: “Abraham’s faith was counted for righteousness not in circumcision but in uncircumcision” (Rom. 4).

[Col. 0720C] He was not made the father only of a nation circumcised in the flesh, since it was said: “I have appointed you the father of many nations” (Gen. 17). This is shown more clearly when it is said to him: “In your seed all nations will be blessed” (Gen. 22). Therefore, let no Christian consider himself a stranger to the name of Israel.

For we are joined to those who believed from the Jews—in whose number we find the apostles principally—through the cornerstone. Hence the Lord says: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10).

Why, then, is the faithful people more truly Israel, and more properly seen as the house of Jacob, than that crowd of Jews? For since that crowd, rejected on account of its deserved faithlessness, sold its birthright, it belongs not to Jacob but to Esau.

[Col. 0720D] “When Israel went out of Egypt.” This is the voice of the Prophet exhorting us to leave Egypt and to be sanctified in Judea. What he says is: “When Israel goes out of Egypt, and the house of Jacob from a barbarous people, Judea became”—that is, will become—“his sanctuary.”

Egypt is interpreted as “affliction,” and is used as an image of this world, from which we must withdraw spiritually, lest we become yoked together with unbelievers (2 Cor. 6). For just as that people could not enter the promised land unless it first left Egypt, so no one becomes a fit citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem unless he has first renounced this wicked world.

[Col. 0721A] And just as that people could not leave without divine assistance, so no one turns his heart away from this wicked world unless he is aided by the gift of divine mercy. What was prefigured there once is fulfilled at this end of the age through the daily tears of the Church in each believer. Israel leaves Egypt every day when the faithful person spiritually leaves this world.

Hence Paul says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud and all passed through the sea” (1 Cor. 10), and so forth.

“The house of Jacob from a barbarous people.” A barbarous people is one that does not know how to praise God but clings to carnal works.

[Col. 0721B] “Judea became his sanctuary.” Behold, he shows where the one who leaves Egypt must arrive: namely, in Judea, where he is now sanctified. What does Judea signify except confession? Through this confession everyone who leaves Egypt is sanctified, in accordance with the statement: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10).

“Israel his dominion.” Hence the statement: “He gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1). Let each person therefore question his own heart: whether faith has circumcised it, whether confession has cleansed it. Then Judea has become his sanctuary, and Israel his dominion.

“The sea saw and fled.” What is signified by the sea except this wicked world, which is an impediment to every believer, preventing the heart from being cleansed through confession?

[Col. 0721C] Each person can see this in himself when he wishes to attach his heart to the Lord and, withdrawing from the desires of his former ignorance, submit his devoted spirit to the Lord’s gentle yoke. When he abandons the carnal deeds of this world, in which he labored without fruit as though lying hidden in Egypt under the harsh domination of the devil, he sees how worldly obstacles arise as the voices of those who discourage him.

But when a person strives not to be drawn back from a good purpose by worldly impediments, then, once those impediments have ceased, the sea flees, so that the way to spiritual freedom may open without opposition.

This is what is meant by: “The sea saw and fled.” The prophet Micah says the same thing in other words: “According to the day of their departure from Egypt,” he says, “I will show them wonders. The nations will see and will be confounded at all their strength; they will place their hands over their mouths, and their ears will become deaf” (Mic. 7), and so forth.

[Col. 0721D] “The Jordan turned back.” Here the Spirit rebukes certain people who have turned their back toward the Lord and not their face. For whoever abandons his beginning and turns away from his Creator slips, like a river into the sea, into the bittering wickedness of this world.

But when he recognizes that he has gone astray and cleanses his heart through confession, then “the Jordan has turned back,” because, having been humbled, he sets God before the face of the one returning to him—God whom, when departing, he had placed behind his back. Thus the sea of this world becomes behind him, whereas previously, when he was flowing into it, he had made it before him.

In this way he forgets what lies behind and stretches forward to what lies ahead (Phil. 3), which is beneficial to one who has been converted.

[Col. 0722A] “The Jordan turned back,” that is, those who received the grace of baptism but wandered in this wicked world have been humbled and turned back to God. Hence “the mountains,” that is, the leaders in the Church, rejoiced in God their helper and not in the world their deceiver. They rejoiced, I say, “like rams,” that is, as leaders of the flocks; and “the hills,” that is, the imitators of the mountains, rejoiced “like lambs of the sheep.”

“What ails you, sea, that you fled, and you, Jordan, that you turned back?” Seeing God work so wondrously in his own people, the Prophet asks these questions not out of ignorance but in fellowship with their joy:

“What ails you, sea, that you fled, and you, Jordan, that you turned back? And what of you, mountains, that you leapt like rams, and hills like lambs of the sheep?”

[Col. 0722B] Behold why: because “at the presence of the Lord the earth was moved,” that is, at the knowledge of the Lord the hearts of earthly people will be moved. “At the presence of the God of Jacob”—of God, I say, not of a recent deity—the earth was moved.

And how did this happen? Because “he turned the rock into pools of water and the cliff into springs of water.” Christ was the rock. He seems hard to those who do not understand, but he was turned into pools of water because at last he melted his hardness when he made himself intelligible for the watering of his faithful, so that he might become in them a spring of water welling up into eternal life (John 4).

[Col. 0722C] Christ was hard to those who, troubled and unwilling to wait until he might flow into them and flood them through the sacred Scriptures, said: “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?” (John 6). But the hardness was turned into pools of water when, rising from the dead, he opened the Scriptures to his faithful, beginning with Moses and proceeding through all the prophets, because “it was necessary that Christ should suffer” (Luke 24), and when he sent the Holy Spirit (John 7), of whom he said: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (Acts 2).

By the cliffs are understood the holy preachers—Paul and the others—who were turned into springs of water.

Hence: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory.” Give glory because of your mercy, that is, because of the restoration of the human race given from above, and because of your truth. The Lord’s truth is that by which his promises are fulfilled.

[Col. 0722D] “Let the nations never say: ‘Where is their God?’” It is as though he said: Give glory to your name because of mercy and truth; grant also that the nations—who display their gods as visible to bodily eyes—may not at some time say reproachfully to your people, “Where is their God?” Although they say this now, since they cannot see you, God, with bodily eyes, a time will come when the nations will no longer say this: at the very end, when he will no longer be preached to them as one to be believed, but will already be revealed as one to be feared.

Or, may they not at some time say, “Where is their God?” but instead believe in the one whom they do not see when they see the blind being given sight and lepers being cleansed (Luke 7).

“But our God is in heaven; he has done whatever he willed.” It is as though he said: They say, “Where is their God?” because they do not see him in his substance. But our God, besides whom there is no other, although he cannot be seen in his substance, has done whatever he willed in heaven—that is, in those whom he made heavens, namely, the saints.

[Col. 0723A] Note that he does not say that God works only in heaven, as though anything could happen anywhere apart from his will, namely, among those who act well; rather, he says this because his will appears most clearly in heaven.

Or, he works whatever he wills in heaven, that is, in the Lordly man assumed by the Word; in him he did whatever he willed.

But the gods of the nations do nothing, because they are not gods—not even human beings. For “the idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands.” Hence Augustine says: “Do not add human hands, so that from that metal which the true God made you may make a false god—or rather, a false man, whom you would not venerate as a god. Whoever received him into friendship as a real man would be completely insane.”

[Col. 0723B] And because “they have mouths, but they will not speak; they have eyes, but they will not see; they have ears, but they will not hear; they have noses, but they will not smell; they have hands, but they will not touch; they have feet, but they will not walk; they will not cry out with their throat,” by saying that they do not cry out with their throat he takes away from them even the possibility of being beasts.

Therefore, let those who make them become like them—and not only those who make them, but also all who trust in them become like them—having inward eyes and yet not seeing; having hands and not touching, that is, doing nothing good.

But “the house of Israel,” that is, the lesser members of the Church, “hoped in the Lord,” and therefore he is their helper in good things and their protector in evil things.

The house of Aaron also, that is, the greater members from the Synagogue, are understood through Aaron because Aaron held the preeminence of the priesthood in the Synagogue. All these hoped in the Lord, and the Lord is their helper and protector.

[Col. 0723C] And not only should the house of Israel and Aaron hope in the Lord, but also all who fear the Lord should hope in the Lord, and he is their helper and protector. This comes not from our works but from the grace of the one who calls (Rom. 9), because “the Lord remembered us and blessed us. He blessed the house of Israel; he blessed the house of Aaron”—the wall and the circumcision.

He also blessed all who fear the Lord, that is, the wall from the foreskin, “the small with the great.” And so that the blessing may be complete, the Lord will add to you the number of the faithful—to you and to your children—so that when your own have departed he may substitute others for you, and when those too have departed, others may be substituted for them.

[Col. 0723D] This has indeed happened, because the faith of all the nations has been added, and the number has grown not only of wise bishops but also of obedient peoples. This is what is meant by: “May the Lord add to you, to you and to your children.”

And may you be “blessed by the Lord, who made heaven and earth,” that is, the greater and the lesser. “Heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord”—understand, for worship. He made the minds of certain saints so exalted and elevated that they became teachable not by any human being but by God himself, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “I make known to you,” he says, “that the Gospel preached by me was not received from a human being, nor did I learn it from one, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (Gal. 1).

[Col. 0724A] This same Apostle was a heaven of heaven, because he introduced some people, such as Timothy, in such a way that they became heavens for others. This is what is meant by: “Heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord; but the earth”—that is, those who were still imperfect—“he gave to the children of men,” understand, for worship, because many were called to the faith through Timothy.

Or, we may understand “heaven of heaven” as the Lordly man, because he was worshiped by no teacher but only by the Lord himself.

Therefore, we who live by the inner life bless the Lord, both now—that is, without delay—and forever. And truly you are to be blessed by the living, Lord, because “the dead,” that is, those who are like their idols, “will not praise you, Lord, nor all who descend into the underworld,” that is, into the depths of sins. “But we who live bless the Lord, from this time forth and forever.”

## PSALM 114. ALLELUIA

[Col. 0724B]

> “I have loved, because the Lord will hear the voice of my prayer.  
> Because he has inclined his ear to me, and in my days I will call upon him.  
> The pains of death surrounded me, and the dangers of the underworld found me.  
> I found tribulation and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord.  
> O Lord, deliver my soul. The Lord is merciful and just, and our God has mercy.  
> The Lord preserves the little ones; I was humbled, and he delivered me.  
> Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt well with you.  
> For he has rescued my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling.  
> I shall please the Lord in the land of the living.”

## EXPOSITION

[Col. 0724C] Alleluia. In this psalm the Alleluia is sung by the one who is a pilgrim away from God (2 Cor. 5), the sheep that had been lost (Luke 15), the son who had been dead and came to life, who had been lost and was found (ibid.).

Recognizing that hope and belief are to be placed in the Lord alone, this son instructs us here to love God, to hope and believe in him now, so that at last we may please him in the land of the living. Let us therefore sing, brothers, and be instructed; and, so that we may remain with the saints, let us sing these things.

“I have loved, because the Lord will hear the voice of my prayer, because he has inclined his ear to me.” [Col. 0724D] Three things are set before us here: faith, hope, and charity. But since charity is the greatest (1 Cor. 13), he begins with charity in this way: “I have loved.” And this is because he hoped, as the result shows: “Because the Lord will hear the voice of my prayer.” Since he hoped, he deserved that the Lord should hear “the voice of his prayer.”

“Because he has inclined his ear to me.” How can we know that the Lord’s ear has been inclined to us except by the fact that we believe in him through faith? Thus three things are noted here: faith, hope, and charity, each of the three proceeding from another. Faith kindles hope, and hope kindles love.

“Because he has inclined his ear to me, and therefore in my days”—“in my days,” that is, in the days of mortality and suffering which he made my days in the first man by withdrawing from God through private presumption—“in those days I will call upon the Lord.” And this is necessary, because “the pains of death surrounded me,” that is, the fetters of mortality, “and the dangers of the underworld found me,” that is, the darkness of ignorance found me when I departed from the region of light in which I had been placed. For if I had remained there, neither the pains of death nor the darkness of ignorance would have found me.

[Col. 0725A] And so at last “I found tribulation” that was useful to me, and I also found sorrow that was useful to me. I did not find a tribulation that I did not have, but one that I had without knowing it—the tribulation of which it is said: “Give us help in tribulation” (Ps. 59).

I also found useful sorrow, because when I thought that earthly things would make me blessed and heard the Lord say, “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matt. 5), I understood that mourning was more beneficial to me than rejoicing.

[Col. 0725B] Yet we are not moved to seek misery when we do not have it, but to discover the misery that we have without knowing it. Nor are we required to deprive ourselves entirely of earthly things, but to mourn because, having lost heavenly things, we need earthly things here.

Let people therefore recognize this misery, mourn, and allow those who always wish to be miserable here to make them blessed through their mourning.

“I found tribulation and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord,” saying: “O Lord, deliver my soul.” “The Lord is merciful” in his affections; “just,” because he chastises even the son whom he receives (Heb. 12).

I called upon him, “and our God has mercy,” because “the Lord” himself is “preserving the little ones,” that is, the humble. As one who has experienced this, I must therefore believe: “I was humbled, and he delivered me.”

[Col. 0725C] And because I have been delivered: “Return, my soul, to your rest,” that is, to your Lord, who alone is rest. And the fact that you return is not something you possess from yourself, but through the grace of God.

“For the Lord has dealt well with you,” namely, because he has rescued your soul from death, that is, from original sin or from a carnal crime; and my eyes from tears, so that I no longer weep over my misery, from which I have been delivered through hope.

He also rescued my feet—that is, my afflictions—from falling, that is, from evil consent, which was the cause of my tears. And, rescued from all these things, I shall at last please the Lord in the land of the living, not in the land of the dying.

## PSALM 115. ALLELUIA

[Col. 0725D]

> “I believed; therefore I spoke, but I was humbled exceedingly.  
> I said in my alarm: ‘Every man is a liar.’  
> What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me?  
> I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord.  
> I will fulfill my vows to the Lord before all his people.  
> Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.  
> O Lord, for I am your servant; I am your servant and the son of your handmaid.  
> You have broken my bonds; I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise and call upon the name of the Lord.  
> I will fulfill my vows to the Lord in the sight of all his people,  
> in the courts of the house of the Lord, in your midst, Jerusalem.”

## EXPOSITION

[Col. 0726A] Alleluia. “I believed; therefore I spoke.” In this psalm it is the voice of the holy martyrs instructing and teaching us that what we believe in our heart we should not be silent about with our mouth (Rom. 10), and that we should not speak before we believe, but once we have believed we should not hesitate to speak. For those who are unwilling to speak what they believe do not believe perfectly.

To faith itself belongs the statement: “Whoever confesses me before men, I will also confess him before the angels of God” (Luke 12). For this reason that faithful servant was called a servant, to whom it was said: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy” (Matt. 25), because he not only received but also expended what he had received, and gained profit.

[Col. 0726B] But the servant who did not distribute to his neighbors what he had received was sent into the outer darkness (ibid.). Let us therefore believe and speak; let us hope for a reward by speaking, and fear punishment by remaining silent. He says as follows:
