I believed, and therefore, because I believed, I spoke; for one who does not speak, when need arises, is not to be reckoned a believer. But I, by speaking, was humbled exceedingly—that is, I was so afflicted by persecutions and insults that I was reduced to astonishment.

It should be noted that he says, “I was humbled.” By this he wishes to show that he himself was humbled, not his faith, nor his preaching, which he preached, as having been humbled. Hence Paul, speaking of his chain, says: “The word of God is not bound” (II Tim. II).

“I was humbled exceedingly, and I said in my alarm”—that is, in the fear of my mind I recognized that no one ought to presume upon himself, because every person who presumes upon himself is a liar. I perceived this when, by speaking the word of God, I was humbled: in contrition I considered my weakness and saw that I ought not to presume upon myself, because whoever presumes upon himself is a liar.

Peter discovered this when, through fear, he denied God. Having first presumed upon himself, he had resolved that he would never deny him; and therefore he had to be instructed that, in fear, one must not presume upon a human being, but upon him who is truthful (Rom. III), who says: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. LXXXI). Insofar as we are not liars, we are not human beings but gods.

Or otherwise: “Every person is a liar,” that is, a person of every condition is a liar, because in every condition there are some who devote themselves to falsehood rather than to truth.

“What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” As though he were saying: Since every person, insofar as he is human and presumes upon himself, is a liar, and insofar as he is truthful possesses this not from himself but from the Lord, what, then, “shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?”

God renders good for evil to those to whom human beings have rendered evil for good. Human beings offered falsehood; he offered truth.

“I will receive the cup of salvation.” Considering what he could render to the Lord, and finding nothing more worthy to render than what the Lord himself had first given, he continued: “I will receive the cup of salvation”—that is, I will imitate the saving passion of the Lord; and in this I will not presume upon myself, but “I will invoke the name of the Lord. I will fulfill my vows to the Lord”—namely, I will offer myself, and this not in secret but “before all his people,” so that they may have in me an example of imitating the Lord’s passion.

And I will fulfill these vows because “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints,” even if it is contemptible in the sight of human beings. Or, it is precious because it was bought at a great price—namely, with his own blood, which he first poured out for us—and this so that servants would not hesitate to pour out their blood for him.

“O Lord, because I am your servant, and the son of your handmaid.” As though he were saying: Because, in your sight, the death of the saints is precious, therefore, O Lord, “I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise,” namely, I will bring my life to an end for you.

And rightly do I call God, because I am your servant, bought, that is, with your precious blood; and not only bought, but also by nature, because I am the son of your handmaid—of a handmaid who is nevertheless free from sin, but a handmaid of righteousness, whose son—in the uncertain phrase *adhuc praegnantibus* (“while still pregnant”)—is said: “You were called to freedom” (Gal. V). And elsewhere the same people are told: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness. But now, freed from sin and made slaves of God, you have your fruit for sanctification, and the end is eternal life” (Rom. VI).

Let no one be ashamed to confess himself the son of the Lord’s handmaid, because everyone is the son of a handmaid insofar as every creature is subject to the Creator and owes the true God true service. When he offers this service, he is free, receiving from God the grace by which he serves him not out of necessity but willingly.

“I am the son of your handmaid.” And rightly so, because you have broken my bonds, lest my enemies bind me; or, you have broken my bonds, that is, the difficulty of resisting the practices of the old man.

For the breaking of this difficulty, “I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise, and in sacrificing I will invoke the name of the Lord. I will fulfill my vows to the Lord in the sight of all his people.”

And what it means to fulfill vows in the sight of the people, he adds: “In the courts of the house of the Lord”—that is, in the churches, which are called the courts of the Lord’s house—I will fulfill my vows, placed “in the midst of you, Jerusalem.” In fulfilling my vows I will regard nothing except reaching the vision of peace, because what is rendered is pleasing when it is rendered from peace and in peace.

But lest anyone suppose that “the courts of the house of the Lord” and all his people signify the Jews, since this psalm concluded by saying, “in the midst of you, Jerusalem,” a name in which the carnal Israelites glory, let us hear the following psalm, which says:

## PSALM CXVI. ALLELUIA

[Col. 0727D]

“Praise the Lord, all nations; praise him, all peoples. For his mercy toward us has been confirmed, and the truth of the Lord remains forever.”

## EXPOSITION

“Praise the Lord, all nations; praise him, all peoples.” Since both the nations and the Jews have been called to the house of God, let those who did not wish to be sons of Jerusalem hear these words, since they cut themselves off from all fellowship with the nations.

“Praise him, all peoples, because” in our restoration “his mercy toward us has been confirmed”—that is, his promise—“and the truth of the Lord”—that is, the fulfillment of his promise—“remains forever,” because although “the world and its desire pass away” (I John II), nevertheless “the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. LX).

## PSALM CXVII. ALLELUIA

“Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever. Let the house of Israel now say: for he is good, for his mercy is forever. Let the house of Aaron now say: for he is good, for his mercy is forever. Let all who fear the Lord now say: for he is good, for his mercy is forever.

“From tribulation I called upon the Lord, and the Lord answered me in a broad place. The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me. The Lord is my helper, and I will despise my enemies.

“It is good to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in man. It is good to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in princes.

“All nations surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord—for I took vengeance on them. They surrounded me, yes, they surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord—for I took vengeance on them. They surrounded me like bees, and they burned like fire among thorns, and in the name of the Lord—for I took vengeance on them.

“I was pushed and overturned so that I might fall, and the Lord received me. The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation.

“The voice of rejoicing and salvation is in the tents of the righteous. The right hand of the Lord has done mighty deeds; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me; the right hand of the Lord has done mighty deeds.

“I shall not die, but live, and I shall recount the works of the Lord. The Lord chastising has chastised me, but he has not handed me over to death.

“Open for me the gates of righteousness; entering through them, I will give thanks to the Lord. This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it.

“I will give thanks to you, because you answered me and became my salvation. The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This has been done by the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes.

“This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it. O Lord, save me; O Lord, prosper me. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.

“We have blessed you from the house of the Lord. God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us. Establish the solemn day amid the dense crowds, up to the horns of the altar.

“You are my God, and I will give thanks to you; you are my God, and I will exalt you. I will give thanks to you, because you answered me and became my salvation. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever.”

## EXPOSITION

The preceding psalm, which contained the words “May the Lord add to you” (Ps. CXIII), indicated to us those with whom we have been joined in the grace that is theirs, and whose mercy is forever. For we have been joined to the Israelites who believe in Christ—among their number are the apostles, our fathers—in the one cornerstone, so that with those earlier people we may be one flock under one shepherd.

[Col. 0729A]

Their voice instructs us in this psalm to praise God, saying:

“Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever,” understood as enduring. God’s praise could not be expressed more briefly than by confessing that he is good; for it belongs properly to him alone to be good.

When he heard, “Good Teacher,” from the one who, looking with bodily eyes and not understanding the fullness of divinity, supposed him to be merely a human being, he himself replied: “Why do you ask me about the good? No one is good except God alone” (Matt. XIX; Mark X; Luke XVIII). As though he were saying: If you wish to call me good, understand that I am also God.

“Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever. Let the house of Israel now say”—that is, without delay, let the lesser members of the Church exhort others, saying: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever.” “Let the house of Aaron now say”—that is, let the greater also say: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever.”

Let those who have been converted not only from the Jews but also “all who fear the Lord” say: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever.”

And rightly must thanks be given to him, because “from tribulation”—that is, on account of the tribulation of mortality and suffering, so that it might be removed—“I called upon the Lord, and the Lord answered me in a broad place,” namely, in the breadth of love, so that our heart might be extended in charity toward all.

“For narrow is the way that leads to life” (Matt. VII), yet no one runs along it except with an enlarged heart.

Rightly did I call upon the Lord, because the Lord is my helper; therefore I will not fear what man can do to me. And because the Church has not only human enemies but also evil angels, from whom it is necessary that she be delivered, he adds: “The Lord is my helper, and I will despise my enemies.” Whatever kind of enemy may arise—whether from the number of evil angels or from the number of evil human beings—they will be despised through God’s help.

Once the enemies have been despised, let no human being offer himself to me any longer so as to command me to place my hope in him, because “it is good to trust in the Lord,” and not merely good, but better “than to trust in man.”

“It is good to hope in the Lord,” and better “than to hope in princes”—that is, in angels—because even if a human being and an angel help, the one who works these things through them is he who, according to their capacity and our need, makes them good.

“It is good to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in princes.” And I must believe this from experience, because “all nations surrounded me,” and this happened “in the name of the Lord,” understood as for his glorification, “for I took vengeance on them,” incorporating some of them into myself.

Here the labors suffered by our fathers in the primitive Church are noted when he says: “All nations surrounded me.” When the apostles each undertook the conversion of particular provinces, it was not unknown or unfamiliar to the faithful how great a persecution by the nations surrounded them; but there is reason for rejoicing, because they obtained victory. This is indicated where he says, “for I took vengeance on them.”

“They surrounded me, yes, they surrounded me”—that is, they surrounded me with excessive encirclement—and “in the name of the Lord,” understood as for his glorification, “for I took vengeance on them.”

“They surrounded me like bees.” It should be noted that when bees surround a honeycomb, they make it honey-filled; so persecutors, by surrounding the saints with their persecution, make them as though honey-filled, because they make them sweeter and more delightful to imitate. For the more the saints are afflicted, the more others strive to imitate their steadfastness.

“And they burned like fire among thorns.” When shepherds place fire among thorns, it does not damage the trunk but burns whatever dry material it finds clinging to the trunk. So persecutors, when they apply torments, do not injure the soul but the body, which is as though the soul’s garment. Hence the words: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. X).

“And in the name of the Lord, for I took vengeance on them.”

Or it may be understood in this way: “They surrounded me like bees.” When bees harm others, they place their own life in the wound; so persecutors, when they think they are harming others, kill themselves with inward death, because no one sins first against another rather than against himself.

“I was pushed and overturned so that I might fall, and the Lord received me”—that is, he sustained me lest I fall—in accordance with the words: “The righteous falls seven times a day and rises again” (Prov. XXIV).

And because I was sustained by the Lord, not by myself, let the Lord be my strength. Hence Paul says: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me, and the Lord is my praise” (Phil. IV). That is, the Lord himself is to be praised, not I; and this because he has become my salvation—not that he became something he was not previously.

Therefore let the Lord be my strength, and not I myself, because those who trust in their own strength fall when they are pushed. No one falls in the contest except the one whose strength and praise fall.

Let the Lord, then, be our strength and our praise, so that we may stand with him who never falls. “And he has become my salvation.” Hence there should be “a voice of rejoicing and salvation in the tents of the righteous”—that is, in the hearts of the faithful, where persecutors think there is a voice of grief and sadness. Let there instead be a voice of exultation and joy.

Hence Paul says: “We glory not only in hope, but also in tribulations” (Rom. V). And all these things are from God, because “the right hand of the Lord has done mighty deeds”; this “mighty deed the right hand of the Lord has exalted me.” And lest, once exalted, we should presume upon ourselves, he adds again: “The right hand of the Lord has done mighty deeds.”

What greater mighty deed is there than to exalt the humble, give life to the mortal, provide perfection from weakness, glory from subjection, victory from suffering, and help from tribulation, so that the true salvation of God might be revealed to the afflicted and the vain salvation of man remain with those who afflict?

“The right hand of the Lord has exalted me.” Therefore I will not die the death of the inner person by consenting to my persecutors, but I will live in the Lord, whose right hand has exalted me.

Hence Paul says: “I live, yet no longer I; rather, Christ lives in me” (Gal. II), “and I shall recount the works of the Lord,” because “neither death nor life shall separate me from the love of Christ” (Rom. VIII). Instead, I shall always make his works known to others.

And rightly so, because “the Lord chastising has chastised me,” renewing me inwardly in spirit, although the outer person is corrupted. Therefore the raging of the wicked in the persecution of the faithful must not suppose that it has accomplished anything by its own strength, because the master of a household often corrects his sons through very wicked servants, while nevertheless preparing fetters for the servants and preserving an inheritance for the sons.

“The Lord chastising has chastised me, and he has not handed me over to death.”

And because in this chastisement I will not be handed over to death, you, my persecutors, “open for me through your persecution the gates of righteousness,” and entering through them I will give thanks to the Lord—that is, I will glory in the Lord, not in myself.

The gate of righteousness is that the righteous person may live by faith (Rom. I) and patiently await in hope the promises reserved for him in the future. This hope is kindled more intensely in each faithful person when he endures persecution from an unbeliever.

“This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it.” As though he were saying: I ask that the gates of righteousness be opened to me so that, entering, I may give thanks to the Lord, because this kind of gate belongs to the Lord. He himself first entered through this gate, because he first suffered and left us an example of suffering. Through this gate only the righteous will enter.

“I will give thanks to you, because you answered me and became my salvation.” As though he were saying: I said that the gates of righteousness should be opened to me; this will happen, because, now entering, “I will give thanks to you,” O Lord, “because you answered me.” Even in that answering, “you became my salvation.”

This thanksgiving does not expose a wound to a physician; it gives thanks for health.

“You became my salvation,” and in this way: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.”

This stone was Christ, “whom the builders rejected”—namely, the Jews, who, presuming upon the letter, wished to establish their own righteousness and therefore refused to submit to the righteousness of God (Rom. X).

But, rejected by them, he “became the cornerstone,” so that in himself he might unite the new person from two peoples—namely, the people of the uncircumcision and the people of the circumcision.

And that this stone “became the cornerstone” was “done by the Lord.” For although this could not have happened unless he had suffered, nevertheless the cornerstone did not proceed from those by whom it was made, but from the Lord. “And it is marvelous in our eyes”—namely, our inward eyes—even though to the Jews it is a stumbling block and to the nations foolishness (I Cor. I).

“This is the day that the Lord has made”—the day that Abraham desired to see: “He saw it and rejoiced” (John VIII). Therefore let us also rejoice and be glad in it, because this is the day of our redemption, not the day of misery that we ourselves made for ourselves.

Hence it was said above: “And in my days I will call upon you” (Ps. CXIV). This is the Lord’s day of which it was said: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI).

“Let us rejoice and be glad in it,” saying: “O Lord, save me; O Lord, prosper me”—that is, prepare a prosperous path for us. And it is necessary that your people prosper, because you are blessed, who are coming in the name of the Lord, seeking that suitable members may be added to you, the head.

“We have blessed you from the house of the Lord.” Behold the voice of those from the primitive Church who bless the later people, saying: “Blessed is he who is coming in the name of the Lord.”

And we, “from the house of the Lord”—that is, reaching God with the mind—bless you, that is, we announce to you, that the Lord Christ is God, equal to God the Father. He himself has shone upon us, so that we might understand what we believe and proclaim it to you, who do not yet understand but do believe.

But so that you also may understand, “establish the solemn day,” separating yourselves from carnal desires and from dead works, so that you may devote yourselves to divine contemplation (I Pet. II).

And do not do this sluggishly, but, advancing “amid the dense crowds,” proceed “up to the horns of the altar”—that is, up to the higher parts of the veil (Heb. VI)—so that you may understand the inner divinity of him who deigned to provide us with his outward humanity as milk for those who must be nourished (Heb. V).

Note that it says, “up to the horns of the altar.” It was the custom of the Jews to assemble at Jerusalem for the feast of Passover in order to celebrate the solemn day. And because the crowd was great when they gathered in the temple, they pressed forward as far as the horns of the altar, so that they might stand there.

Therefore whoever establishes the solemn day should proceed to the horns of the altar, understanding divinity in humanity, where the altar is exalted and upon which altar the sacrifice of praise is offered.

“Establish the solemn day amid the dense crowds, up to the horns of the altar,” saying: “You are my God,” and I, a creature, “will give thanks to you; you are my God, and I will exalt you. I will give thanks to you, because you answered me and became my salvation,” saying also to those nearby: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever.”

## PSALM CXVIII. ALLELUIA

“**ALEPH.**—Blessed are the blameless in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are those who search his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart. For those who work iniquity have not walked in his ways. You commanded that your commandments be kept exceedingly. Would that my ways were directed toward keeping your ordinances. Then I shall not be put to shame when I have looked upon all your commandments. I will give thanks to you with an upright heart, in learning the judgments of your righteousness. I will keep your ordinances; do not utterly forsake me.”

## EXPOSITION

From its beginning this psalm exhorts us to blessedness, which no one fails to desire. For there is no one who does not wish to be blessed. What need, then, is there for exhortation toward something that the human mind desires of its own accord?

Indeed, the one who exhorts aims to rouse the will of the person with whom he is dealing toward that for which the exhortation is offered. Why, then, are we urged to desire what we cannot fail to desire?

Because all desire blessedness, but many do not know by what order they may reach it, this psalm teaches the matter, saying:

“Blessed are the blameless in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.” As though it were saying: I know what you want; you seek blessedness. Therefore, if you wish to be blessed, be blameless.

Everyone wants the former, but few want the latter, although without it one cannot reach what everyone wants. Where must you be blameless? “In the way.” And what it means to be blameless in the way, he adds: “Those who walk in the law of the Lord.”

Those are blameless in the way who delight in the law of the Lord; through delight in the law one reaches blessedness.

This is not said to us pointlessly; rather, necessary exhortation is applied to our minds. The goodness of that toward which many are sluggish—that is, walking blamelessly in the way, which is the law of the Lord—is shown when he declares that those who do this are blessed, so that, for the sake of what everyone wants, what most people do not want may also be done.

To be blessed is indeed so great a good that good and evil alike desire it. It is not surprising that the good are good for the sake of being blessed; but it is surprising that the wicked are wicked in order to be blessed.

For whoever burns with the fires of greed and pours himself out in lust strives toward this end: to reach blessedness by whatever means, although he instead arrives at the highest misery.

The way by which such people must reach blessedness is shown to them, as though they were being told: Where are you going? Where do you desire to arrive by these ways? Abandon wickedness, since you cannot abandon the desire for blessedness. You exhaust yourselves by striving in vain toward the place where, by arriving, you are defiled.

Therefore be blameless, you who wish to be blessed.

“Blessed are those who search his testimonies”—that is, the sacred Scriptures, which are called his testimonies because they bear witness to him.

And because many investigate the Scriptures only in order to know, not in order to have something that they may do, he shows who are blessed when they search the Lord’s testimonies: namely, those who seek him with their whole heart in those Scriptures, not merely by understanding the Scriptures but by doing good according to the command of the Scriptures.

“For those who work iniquity have not walked in his ways.” Those who are blameless walk in the law of the Lord. But those who work iniquity, and are therefore defiled, do not walk—that is, they do not delight—in his ways.

Here a question arises. Since every sin is iniquity, and no one is without sin, how can anyone walk in the law of the Lord, when those who work iniquity do not walk?

No one is without sin. Hence John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth of God is not in us” (I John I).

What, then, shall we say? Does no one walk in the law of the Lord? Did Paul not walk in it, when he said: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness on that day”? (II Tim. IV.)

Was this man without sin? Was he deceiving himself? Let us hear him speaking and confessing that he was not without sin. For he said: “I do not do what I want, but sin that dwells in me” (Rom. IV).

He did what he did not want because, when tempted by unlawful desires, he did not give consent to them and did not carry them into action. The weakness of the flesh working in him produced the unlawful desires by which he was tempted; this weakness is called sin because it is contracted as the punishment of sin.

After every guilt of crime had been erased in the sacrament of baptism, only weakness remained, from which unlawful impulses arise. When these arise, if no consent is given to them and no action is allowed to follow, no iniquity is committed.

Thus the weakness of the flesh does not harm, provided that through it no work of iniquity is committed—by “iniquity” I mean either an act or consent. It is of this iniquity that it is said here: those who work iniquity in consent or deed have not walked in his ways.

“You commanded that your commandments be kept exceedingly.” Truly those who search your testimonies, O Lord, are blessed, because you have never commanded anything except what pertains to blessedness. You commanded that your commandments be kept exceedingly—that is, very greatly—not merely in knowledge but in action.

For it is useless to hold something in knowledge if it is not held in one’s life.

“Would that my ways were directed toward keeping your ordinances.” Hearing the voice of one who desires this, put aside the pride of one who presumes upon himself. No one desires what is so completely within his power that he can accomplish what he wishes through free choice.

This faithful soul, therefore, seeing that it is not sufficient by itself to keep the Lord’s commandments, expresses its desire in this way and asks help from God, as though saying:

“Since you commanded that your commandments be kept, would that my ways”—that is, my works—“were directed toward keeping your ordinances,” which you established and thus taught.

And therefore I ask that my ways be directed, because then—that is, when my ways have been directed—I shall not be put to shame like the one of whom it may be said: “This man began to build and was not able to finish” (Luke XIV).

“I shall not be put to shame,” I say, “when I have looked upon all your commandments”—that is, when your commandments themselves make me a mirror to myself. For in the Lord’s commandments each person can see what he is, in accordance with the apostle James, who says:

“If anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is compared to a man looking at the face of his birth in a mirror. For he looked at himself and went away, and immediately forgot what he was like” (James I).

But whoever has looked into the law of perfect freedom and has remained in it—not a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work—will be blessed in his deed.

This man also wishes to be such that he may look upon God’s commandments as in a mirror, so that he may not be put to shame, because he does not wish to be merely their hearer but their doer. Hence he says: “Then I shall not be put to shame when I have looked upon all your commandments.”

Therefore “I will give thanks to you”—that is, I will praise you—“with an upright heart,” that is, with a heart that is straight and never turned away from your will.

And I will praise you not only in the action itself but also in its beginning, namely, in having learned the judgments of your righteousness—that is, in having understood the discernment that proceeded from your righteousness, namely, discerning what a servant owes the Lord and what a creature owes the Creator.

“I will keep your ordinances; do not utterly forsake me.” Because, when your ordinances are kept, I shall not be put to shame, therefore I will keep your ordinances. And in order that I may keep them, do not utterly forsake me.

If you have forsaken me so that I might be in need, do not forsake me so that I might perish. Or, do not forsake me in any respect in which I could be called forsaken—namely, so that I might glory in myself.

For the one who glories in himself in his good works is forsaken by God.

“**BETH.**—How does a younger person correct his way? By keeping your words. With my whole heart I have sought you; do not reject me from your commandments. In my heart I have hidden your sayings, so that I may not sin against you. Blessed are you, O Lord; teach me your ordinances. With my lips I have proclaimed all the judgments of your mouth. I have delighted in the way of your testimonies as in all riches. I will exercise myself in your commandments, and I will consider your ways. I will meditate on your ordinances; I will not forget your words.”

## EXPOSITION

“How does he correct his way?” “I will keep your ordinances.” For “by keeping your words”—that is, your commandments—the younger person corrects his way, that is, his life.

The “younger person” is the younger people, namely, the people of grace, bearing the image of the new person and working through love the word of faith preached to them.

This younger person is not Cain but Abel; not Ishmael but Isaac; not Manasseh but Ephraim; not Esau but Israel; not Saul but David. Each of these corrected his way by keeping the Lord’s words—indeed, in what other way could he do so? The others, imitating the old person, distorted their ways by not keeping the words.

And because those who keep your words keep their ways, “with my whole heart I have sought you,” and therefore “do not reject me from your commandments.”

The one who is not helped by grace is rejected from the Lord’s commandments. Therefore do not reject me from your commandments, because although others hide silver and gold in a chest, I have hidden in my whole heart—that is, I have stored up—your sayings, that is, your commandments, so that I may not sin against you by keeping your commandments in memory.

One sins against God; one sins against one’s neighbor. But one first sins against God, because when anyone considers committing a sin against his neighbor, he already sins against God, even if he has committed no sin against his neighbor, since no one sins first against another rather than against himself.

Or it may be understood thus: “In my heart I have hidden your sayings,” so that I would not give what is holy to dogs or cast pearls before swine. Therefore, “teach me your ordinances,” so that I may learn by doing what I have already learned by retaining it in memory.

Or: It belongs to you to teach, because you are blessed, O Lord—that is, naturally multiplied—and everyone is taught by you toward what is good.

“Teach me your ordinances,” because I have hidden your sayings not only for myself but also for the benefit of my neighbors:

“With my lips I have proclaimed all the judgments of your mouth”—that is, the commandments that I learned through your mouth, namely, through your words.

“All,” I say, both hidden and manifest, which had to be proclaimed. And I did this not in sadness or under compulsion, but “I delighted in the way of your testimonies”—that is, your commandments. I delighted in them as in all riches.

And “in your commandments,” namely, in proclaiming them, “I will exercise myself”—that is, I will persevere—and I will consider your ways, so that I may fulfill in deed what I say with my mouth.

And in this I do not presume upon myself but upon you, because I will meditate—that is, remain constantly occupied—in your ordinances, by which I have been justified through you, not through myself; and I will not forget your words, as the first man did, who forgot the word of God when God said to him: “You shall not eat” (Gen. II).

## GIMEL

“Render to your servant; give me life, and I will keep your words. Reveal my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law. I am a sojourner on the earth; do not hide your commandments from me. My soul has desired to desire your ordinances at all times. You rebuked the proud; cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments. Take away from me reproach and contempt, because I have sought your testimonies. Indeed, princes sat and spoke against me; but your servant was occupied with your ordinances. For your testimonies are also my meditation, and your ordinances are my counsel.”

## EXPOSITION
[Col. 0736C] **“Repay your servant.”** As though he said: So that I may not forget your words, you, Lord, repay your servant—namely, by this: give me life. There are four kinds of repayment. Two belong to justice: namely, returning good for good and evil for evil. For God will return evil for evil to the ungodly when, by a just judgment and in accordance with the merit of their sins, he sends them to be eternally punished in everlasting fire.

The third repayment is that of grace, which God exercises here, returning good for evil. This repayment of grace must naturally come first, because unless God here returned good for evil, there would be no one to whom, at the final judgment, he could return good for good. It is this repayment that the speaker seeks. He asks to be given inner life by God, so that, made alive by him, he may be able to guard his words; for one who is inwardly dead is not worthy to guard the words of the Lord.

Note that the one who asks here to be given life had not been wholly dead. For he had received the beginning of good desire while still asking to be given life, so that he might be able to keep the commandment of obedience. And since God’s commands are not kept through obedience unless they are perceived through understanding, he continues, asking that he may have understanding:

**“Reveal my inner eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders proceeding from your law,”** but once it has been observed. What is more wondrous than that, through keeping the Lord’s law, earth should become heaven, a servant free, and he should at last be crowned forever?

**“Reveal my eyes,”** and this for the following reason: **“For I am a sojourner on earth,”** that is, I am one of those who say: **“We have no lasting city here, but we seek the one that is to come”** (Hebrews 13). Therefore, **“do not hide your commandments from me,”** so that I may not fail to fulfill them—namely, by putting them into practice.

It is remarkable that he asks here that the Lord’s commandments not be hidden from him, since God wishes to be proclaimed everywhere. Would that they were as precious to many as they are clear! Those two commandments on which the whole law and the prophets depend are manifest both to believers and to unbelievers: since God is to be loved, he must necessarily be known. But he cannot be known except through the divine utterances. Therefore, this man asks that the utterances not be hidden from him, so that, by knowing God, he may love God; and, by loving God, may bring himself to love himself, so that in this way he may finally be taught how he ought to love his neighbor. For unless each person knows how to love himself, he cannot be ardent in love of his neighbor, since it is written: **“You shall love your neighbor as yourself”** (Leviticus 19).

**“Do not hide your commandments from me,”** and rightly so, because **“my soul longed to desire”**—that is, my soul was moved by great desire to desire—**“your justifications,”** that is, your commandments that justify; and this **“at all times,”** namely, in tranquility and adversity, in accordance with: **“I will bless the Lord at all times”** (Psalm 33).

Therefore, my soul longed to desire your commandments because **“you rebuked the proud,”** that is, the first parents who grew proud against you and did not desire your commandments. You rebuked them—that is, you punished them with death—when you said: **“Cursed is the earth in your work”** (Genesis 3). And not only were they rebuked in this way: all who, imitating their pride, turn aside from your commandments are accursed.

Note that it is one thing not to fulfill the Lord’s commandments through ignorance or bodily weakness, and another to turn aside from the Lord’s commandments through negligence; the latter belongs to the proud: **“Accursed are those who turn aside from your commandments.”**

And so that I may not be subject to the curse, **“take reproach and contempt away from me,”** so that I may not commit anything deserving reproach and thereby become contemptible to you. Or: **“Take reproach away from me,”** so that the Christian name may not be reproachful to me and through it I may come to contempt. I say, take it away, because **“I have sought your testimonies.”**

It is also necessary that you take it away, because there are those who have long sought to crush me. For earthly princes **“sat and spoke against me.”** I say, they spoke by threatening and inflicting tribulations.

**“But your servant was occupied with your justifications. For your testimonies are also my meditation,”** that is, I have always meditated on those things to which you bore witness. The Lord’s testimonies are his martyrdoms, in which he provided an example so that those who were to be martyred might love those by whom they suffered. This is what he says: **“Your testimonies are my meditation.”**

For the meditation of the holy martyrs is to love those by whom they suffer, whereas the meditation of their persecutors is to hate those whom they persecute. Again, the counsel of the princes who sat was to destroy the martyrs they had found; the counsel of the suffering martyrs was to find those who had been destroyed. Thus the persecutors returned evil for good, while the martyrs returned good for evil. In this way the persecutors, by killing, failed; but the martyrs, by dying, conquered.

## DALETH [Cols. 0738B–0739A]

**“My soul clung to the pavement; give me life according to your word. I have declared my ways, and you answered me; teach me your justifications. Instruct me in the way of your justifications, and I shall be occupied with your wonders. My soul grew drowsy from weariness; strengthen me in your words. Remove from me the way of iniquity, and graciously grant me your law. I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments. I have clung to your testimonies, Lord; do not let me be put to shame. I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart.”**

### EXPOSITION

**“My soul clung to the pavement.”** As though he said: Although your testimonies are my meditation, I am still afraid, because my soul has clung to the pavement—that is, to the body, which is the lower part of the human being, just as the pavement is the lower part of a building.

And because **“the flesh always desires against the spirit”** (Galatians 5), therefore, as long as the soul clings to the body, one must fear and pray lest the desire of the flesh overcome the spirit. This is what the speaker asks, saying: **“My soul clung to the pavement, and therefore give me life,”** so that what desires against the spirit may be restrained.

**“Give me life,”** I say, as I act according to your word—that is, your commandment. Or: **“Give me life according to your word,”** that is, according to your promise. For you promised: **“In Isaac shall your offspring be called,”** that is, **“the children of the flesh are not the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring”** (Genesis 21; Romans 9).

Or: **“Give me life according to your word,”** because you said: **“Turn to me, and I shall turn to you”** (Zechariah 1).

And you ought to give me life because **“I declared my ways,”** namely, my foul ways: I confessed them to you, and you answered me by wiping away my sins. Therefore, **“teach me your justifications.”**

And since many are taught in the justifications in such a way that they know them but do not demonstrate them in their works, this faithful soul shows how it wishes to be taught, saying:

**“Instruct me in the way of your justifications,”** that is, in the works of your commandments; **“instruct”** them in me. And thus, once instructed, **“I shall be occupied with your wonders,”** that is, with your commandments, which make wondrous the person who imitates them; for they lead him from the lowest misery to the highest glory.

You must instruct me because **“my soul grew drowsy,”** that is, grew lukewarm, from weariness at hearing the word of God. Hence: **“Their soul abhorred every kind of food”** (Psalm 106).

Or: **“My soul grew drowsy from weariness,”** because it is wearisome for me to dwell among sinners. Therefore, you, Lord, strengthen me in your words, so that I may act forcefully and advance.

And so that you may strengthen me, **“remove from me the way of iniquity,”** which obstructs my progress, **“and graciously grant me your law,”** giving me not only the beginning but also the completion of your law. This comes **“not from the one who wills or the one who runs, but from you who show mercy”** (Romans 9).

You ought to have mercy because, insofar as I could, **“I chose the way of truth”** along which I might run, **“and I have not forgotten your judgments.”** So that I might run, **“I clung to your testimonies, Lord,”** while I ran. Therefore, do not let me be put to shame, so that it may not be said to me: **“This man began to build and was not able to finish”** (Luke 19). Rather, may I reach the goal toward which I run, and arrive where I am aiming. This will happen.

For **“I ran in the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart,”** that is, when you enlarged my heart in love. Hence the Apostle: **“Our heart is enlarged,”** he says; **“you also be enlarged”** (2 Corinthians 6).

## HE [Cols. 0739B–0741C]

**“Establish a law for me, Lord—the way of your justifications—and I shall seek it always. Give me understanding, and I shall examine your law, and keep it with my whole heart. Lead me in the path of your commandments, for I have desired it. Incline my heart toward your testimonies, and not toward avarice. Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity; give me life in your way. Establish your utterance for your servant in your fear. Cut away the reproach that I have suspected, because your judgments are pleasing. Behold, I have longed for your commandments; give me life in your righteousness.”**

### EXPOSITION

**“Establish a law for me, Lord—the way of your justifications—and I shall seek it always.”** As though he said: Because I have run in the way of your commandments, therefore, Lord, lest I fail while running, establish for me the way of your justifications—that is, your works that justify—as a law, not to be changed but to be continued, so that I may always advance in the law.

The Apostle says: **“The law is not laid down for the righteous but for the ungodly and sinners”** (1 Timothy 1). Why, then, might this person seem to be one who asks that a law be established for him? But since he said above that he had run in the way of God’s commandments in love, he does not belong to that stiff-necked people for whom the law was written on stone tablets (Exodus 31). Rather, he may be understood to belong to the children of the free Jerusalem above, to the children of promise and of the eternal inheritance, for whom the law is written by the Holy Spirit, as by the finger of God, not on stone tablets (2 Corinthians 3), but in their hearts.

It is not a law that they hold in memory while neglecting it in life, but one that they know through understanding and perform through love, in the breadth of love and not in the narrowness of fear. For whoever performs the work of the law out of fear of punishment and not out of love of righteousness certainly performs it unwillingly. What someone does unwillingly, he would prefer not to be commanded to do. Accordingly, he is not a friend but rather an enemy of the law whose existence he would not want; nor is he pure in deed who is impure in will.

Such a person cannot say what this speaker said in the preceding verses: **“I ran in the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart.”** And since enlargement signifies love, according to the Apostle who says: **“Love is the fullness of the law”** (Romans 13), why, then, does this man ask that a law be established for him—a law in whose absence he would not have run in love?

But because he wishes to advance in the law he has received, and understands that he cannot do this without God, he asks that a law be established for him—not one that he lacks and must receive, but that he may advance more and more in the one he possesses. It is like holding a cup full of liquid and beginning to give it to someone thirsty: he both drinks by drawing from it and asks by desiring it.

In this way, too, this man asks that a law be established for him, saying: **“Establish a law for me, Lord—the way of your justifications—and I shall seek it always,”** namely, for as long as seeking is necessary. For as long as we live here, seeking is necessary, so that we may always advance in it. Or it is always sought, both here and there: here, so that one may advance in it; there, so that the one who advances here may enjoy its reward.

Because he said, **“I shall seek it always,”** and no one can seek unless God grants this to him, this seeker of the law asks that, through the Spirit, he may do what he knew through the letter:

**“Give me understanding, and I shall examine your law.”** As though he said: Once the law has been established, understanding is necessary; and you must grant it so that he may examine your law.

The one who acts according to the higher commandments of the law examines the law. For the higher commandments of the law are those two commandments **“on which the whole law and the prophets depend”** (Matthew 22). Hence the Apostle: **“I will show you a still more excellent way. If I speak in the tongues of humans and of angels, but do not have love, I have become like a sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal”** (1 Corinthians 12–13).

**“Give me understanding, and I shall examine your law, and I shall keep it with my whole heart.”** I say, I shall keep it not only in knowledge but also in life.

And so that I may keep it in this way, lead me—that is, lead me from virtue to virtue. I mean, lead me who have been placed **“in the path of your commandments,”** that is, in your difficult commandments, in accordance with: **“The narrow way is the one that leads to life”** (Matthew 7). One can run in it only with an enlarged heart.

**“Lead me in the path of your commandments,”** and this because **“I have desired that path,”** that is, I observe it willingly, not under compulsion or through fear of punishment.

And because good will does not arise from free choice but from God’s help, who gives both the willing and the power to fulfill the good will (Philippians 2), this man asks for the affection of good will:

**“Incline my heart toward your testimonies.”** As though he said: Because I have desired that path, incline my heart—that is, perfect my will—in your testimonies, so that I may worship you freely.

For Scripture everywhere testifies that God is to be worshiped freely, not for the sake of some profit from a reward. And since avarice prevents many from worshiping God freely, he therefore adds: **“and not toward avarice.”**

But lest avarice alone seem to prevent the free worship of God, he adds further: **“Turn my eyes,”** my inner eyes, **“away, lest they see vanity,”** that is, lest in your service they seek some temporal advantage for themselves, such as human approval or something similar—all of which are vanity.

Hence Solomon: **“I considered all things that are under heaven”** (Ecclesiastes 1), and so forth.

Note that avarice is properly *philargyria*, namely, love of money. But lest love of money accuse anyone, let us hear the Lord saying in the Gospel: **“Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven”** (Matthew 6).

And lest we seek approval for our good works, the Lord’s word admonishes us: **“Beware of practicing your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them”** (ibid.).

And lest we wish to do good works for the sake of food and clothing, the Lord says: **“Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ For your Father knows what you need”** (ibid.).

This man considered all these things when he said: **“Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity; give me life in your way.”**

**“Establish your utterance for your servant.”** Establish your utterance firmly in me, so that I may not believe for an hour only but persevere always in your utterance; and let this be in your filial fear, not slavish fear.

**“And I shall cut away my reproach, which I have suspected”** concerning others. For I suspected that others whom I saw doing good works did so for temporal advantage, rather than worshiping God freely. And so that I may not henceforth suspect this, cut away my reproach.

For judging rashly is a sin. Hence the Lord: **“Do not judge, so that you may not be judged”** (Matthew 7).

Note that this suspicion concerning one’s neighbor can arise from anyone who has already labored in God’s service for temporal advantage. For whatever someone experiences in himself, he is quicker to suspect in another.

Therefore, since the one who speaks here had asked that his heart be inclined so that he might worship God freely, he asks that rash judgments be cut away from him, so that he may not judge his neighbor to possess what he had previously felt in himself.

He says: **“Cut away my reproach, which I have suspected, because your judgments are pleasing,”** while mine are bitter.

And behold how they are pleasing: **“For I have longed for your commandments,”** and therefore **“give me life in your righteousness,”** that is, in your love.

## VAU [Cols. 0741D–0743A]

**“May your mercy come upon me, Lord, your salvation according to your utterance. Then I shall answer the one who reproaches me with a word, because I have hoped in your words. And do not take the word of truth from my mouth altogether, because I have placed my hope in your judgments. And I shall keep your law always, forever and ever. And I walked in an open place, because I sought your commandments. And I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and was not put to shame. And I meditated on your commandments, which I loved. And I lifted my hands toward your commandments, which I loved, and I was occupied with your justifications.”**

### EXPOSITION

**“Give me life,”** and, so that you may give me life, **“may your mercy come upon me, Lord,”** that is, may your merciful one come—namely, Christ, through whom you have displayed manifold mercy.

May he come upon me not to crush me, in accordance with: **“The one upon whom that stone falls, it will crush him”** (Matthew 21), but to defend me, as my head.

He explains whom he calls mercy by adding: **“Your salvation,”** that is, may your Savior come according to your utterance. For you promised that through him you would free the human race.

Or: May he come upon me—I mean, upon me who act according to your utterance.

Or: According to your utterance, so that I may be counted among the offspring.

And because it is not enough to believe in the heart unless confession is made with the mouth (Romans 10), he adds:

**“And I shall answer the one who reproaches me with a word.”** As though he said: May your mercy come upon me, and when it comes I shall answer those who reproach me concerning my faith with a word of faith. For the answer will not proceed from me but from you, because **“I have hoped in your words,”** not in mine. For my words are yours, in accordance with: **“It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you”** (Matthew 10).

And since many tribulations were prepared for those who answered with the word of faith by those who resisted that word of faith, this faithful soul asks that, in the face of the impending tribulation, it not cease proclaiming the truth:

**“And do not take away,”** that is, do not permit tribulations to take away, **“the word of truth from my mouth altogether,”** that is, to such an extent that the word itself might in any way be said to have been wholly abandoned by me.

As though he said: If it should happen that at some time I am silent through fear of punishment, do not allow me to remain entirely silent, but grant me through your grace to look back, as is seen in Peter. For he was abandoned when he denied, restored when he wept, and crowned through a threefold confession.

**“Do not take it away altogether,”** because **“I have hoped in your judgments,”** that is, in your judgments coming from above. I mean those paternal scourges of yours that, by your just judgment, were inflicted upon me and became for me the reason to hope for future glory.

Or: I have hoped beyond your judgments because I hoped to have more glory than the punishment I suffered. Hence: **“I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory”** (Romans 8).

Or: **“I have hoped beyond,”** that is, beyond what we ask or understand, I have hoped to possess, in accordance with: **“To him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly beyond what we ask or understand”** (Ephesians 3).

**“I have hoped beyond your judgments,”** and therefore **“I shall keep your law,”** that is, love of God and neighbor, **“always,”** namely, forever and ever, which is in the future, when we shall love God more fully. For the one whom we now love without seeing, we shall see face to face. The neighbor, too, will be loved more fully, because there will be no place for suspicion where one will not be hidden from another.

I shall keep your law in the future, and here **“I walked,”** that is, I shall walk, **“in an open place,”** that is, in love of God and neighbor, because I sought your commandments—that is, I shall seek them. Thus the other past-tense expressions that follow may also be understood as future.

Or the statement **“I walked in an open place”** may be read as having its proper force, so that the faithful soul shows itself to have been heard concerning the future by showing that certain things have already been granted to it through which it can be certain about the future. For the granting of past things is a certainty about future things.

It is as though he said: I know that there I shall keep your law because I have already received, as it were, a pledge from there: for even now **“I walked in an open place,”** that is, in love of God and neighbor. And this was not by my own power but by yours, because **“I sought your commandments.”**

**“And I spoke of your testimonies,”** even **“before kings, and was not put to shame,”** by turning aside from your commandments through fear of kings.

And **“I meditated,”** that is, I was occupied in frequent thought, **“on your commandments,”** on your precepts, **“which,”** that is, because I loved them.

And in all these things I shall lift my hands—that is, my works—toward your commandments, **“which,”** that is, because I loved them.

The one who lifts his works toward the Lord’s commandments is he who, when he does good works, glories not in himself but in the Lord. He depresses the good work who, by doing good, seeks human approval.

He says: **“I lifted my hands toward your commandments, which I loved, and I shall be occupied,”** that is, I shall persevere, **“in your justifications.”**

Therefore, Lord, because in speaking, meditating, and acting I have not turned aside from your precepts either to this side or to that:

## ZAIN [Cols. 0743B–0744B]

**“Remember your word to your servant, in which you gave me hope. This has comforted me in my humiliation, because your utterance gave me life. The proud acted unjustly against me to the utmost; but I did not turn aside from your law. I remembered your judgments from of old, Lord, and I was comforted. Faintness seized me because of sinners who abandon your law. Your justifications were songs for me in the place of my pilgrimage. I remembered your name by night, Lord, and kept your law. This happened to me because I sought your justifications.”**

### EXPOSITION

**“Remember your word to your servant,”** namely, the word that is to be fulfilled, so that I may be counted among the blessed and the children of promise, because **“in it,”** that is, in that word, **“you gave me hope.”**

As though he said: Others place their hope in gold or similar things; I place mine only in your word, and not without fruit. For this hope held in your word **“comforted me in my humiliation,”** that is, in my abasement or affliction, which I suffer in this life.

And therefore your hope **“comforted me, because your utterance gave me life,”** because you promised that you would be a helper in tribulations, in accordance with: **“God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond what you are able”** (1 Corinthians 10).

**“This comforted me in my humiliation.”** And behold from where the humiliation arose: **“The proud acted unjustly against me to the utmost.”**

The proud are those whom the loss of immortality and glory—which they lost in the first parent—did not subdue. They acted unjustly, for what is more unjust than to hate one whom one knows to be deserving of love? And **“to the utmost,”** that is, in every possible way they acted unjustly, because they were not merely unashamed of being ungodly but strove to make the godly ungodly.

But I **“did not turn aside from your law,”** and **“I remembered your judgments from of old, Lord,”** namely, the judgments concerning the future vessels of wrath, while I was comforted concerning the vessels of mercy, which I considered destined to be saved by your grace.

And because I remembered the judgments concerning the vessels of wrath, **“faintness seized me because of sinners who abandon your law,”** that is, I was weary of dwelling among sinners.

And because I was comforted by the promised riches of the vessels of mercy, your justifications—that is, your scourges that justify—**“were songs for me,”** that is, worthy of praise, **“in the place of my pilgrimage,”** namely, in this life, where everyone is a pilgrim away from the Lord and where one should not sing but groan.

And how were your justifications songs for me? Because **“I remembered by night,”** that is, in tribulation, **“your name, Lord,”** namely, that name by which you are Lord, making me willingly your servant, **“and I kept your law.”**

And this keeping of the law did not proceed from me, but **“happened to me”** from you, **“because I sought your justifications.”**

Or the earlier statement **“This comforted me in my humiliation”** may be read otherwise, so that we understand it as follows: The hope that you gave me in your word comforted me in my humanity, that is, in my mortality, which was imposed upon me by the first parent. Therefore it comforted me because **“your utterance will give me life,”** so that I might have hope of life, though cast into death.

And from where did the humiliation arise? The proud—that is, the unjust parents—acted unjustly by withdrawing from obedience to God, and this **“to the utmost,”** that is, in every possible way, because they made themselves gods to themselves.

But I, having received the hope of your word, **“did not turn aside from your law,”** but **“remembered your judgments from of old,”** that is, those displayed to the first parents at the beginning of the world. And **“faintness seized me,”** that is, weariness held me, **“because of sinners who abandon your law.”**

And yet **“your justifications were songs for me in the place of my pilgrimage.”** For **“I remembered by night your name, Lord, and kept your law. This happened to me because I sought your justifications.”**

## HETH [Cols. 0744C–0745C]

**“You are my portion, Lord; I said that I would keep your law. I pleaded for your presence with my whole heart; have mercy on me according to your utterance. I considered my ways and turned my feet toward your testimonies. I am ready and have not been troubled, so that I may keep your commandments. The cords of sinners have entangled me, but I have not forgotten your law. At midnight I arose to confess you because of the judgments of your justifications. I am a participant with all who fear you and keep your commandments. The earth, Lord, is full of your mercy; teach me your justifications.”**

### EXPOSITION

**“You are my portion, Lord.”** Because I sought your justifications, therefore, Lord, teach me your justifications—which is what is said at the end of the psalm. Teach me, I say, so that I may always advance in them.

And you ought to teach me because you are my portion, Lord. Let others choose the world; I choose you as my portion. And how is this so? Because I said—that is, firmly determined within myself—to keep your law.

The Lord is the portion of the one who keeps his law. The law is kept when the spirit, which must be given life, helps me so that the letter may not kill.

And since it is not within human power to keep the Lord’s law by oneself, the Lord must be invoked. For faith obtains what the law commands. Attending to this, the speaker says:

**“I pleaded for your presence.”** As though he said: So that I may keep your law—for I cannot do so by myself—**“I pleaded for your presence,”** that is, I earnestly pleaded for your help and knowledge, with my whole heart, saying: **“Have mercy on me,”** namely, on me who am walking, **“according to your utterance.”**

And you ought to have mercy because **“I considered,”** that is, I resolved upon, **“my ways,”** my foul ways, so that I might turn away from them; and **“I turned my feet,”** that is, my afflictions, **“toward your testimonies,”** that is, toward your beautiful ways.

And to such an extent that **“I am ready”** for this, **“to keep your commandments, and I have not been troubled”** in those tribulations or pressures, although there was no lack of cause for me to be troubled, because **“the cords of sinners have entangled me.”**

The cords of sinners are the impediments of enemies, whether spiritual enemies, such as the devil and his angels, or carnal ones, in whom the devil works as in children of unbelief. For by increasing sin upon sin they make, as it were, cords, and drag their sin along like a long rope. From this they try to entangle the saints, and sometimes they are permitted to do so.

But if they entangle the body, they do not entangle the soul. This is evident in the speaker, who says: **“I have not forgotten your law,”** but rather:

**“At midnight I arose,”** that is, I became stronger, **“to confess you.”**

By midnight the more severe tribulation is understood. In that tribulation, affliction would not cast him down but exercise him, so that he might rise and advance more vigorously toward confession.

Peter spoke of this tribulation: **“It is time for the scourging to begin with the household of God. And if it begins with us, what will be the end of those who do not obey the Gospel? And if the righteous are scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and sinner appear?”** (1 Peter 4).

**“At midnight I arose to confess you,”** always attending **“to the judgments of your justifications,”** your scourges that justify.

It should be noted that he says **“because of the judgments,”** since the Lord’s scourges did not burden him but delighted him, because he attended to the fact that **“God scourges every son whom he receives”** (Proverbs 3).

**“I arose to confess you,”** to such an extent, that is, **“that I became a participant with all who fear you,”** fearing you in such a way as to keep your commandments.

And to show that there are many of whom he has become a participant, he adds: **“The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.”**

As though he said: You have blessed all who fear you, because the earth is full of those restored through the mercy of the Lord.

Therefore, Lord, **“teach me your justifications,”** so that I may always advance toward what is better.

## TETH [Cols. 0745D–0747B]

**“You have dealt kindly with your servant, Lord, according to your word. Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge, because I have believed in your commandments. Before I was humbled, I went astray; therefore I kept your utterance. You are good, and in your goodness teach me your justifications. The iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me, but I shall examine your commandments with my whole heart. Their heart has congealed like milk, but I have meditated on your law. It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I may learn your justifications. The law of your mouth is good for me, more than thousands of pieces of gold and silver.”**

### EXPOSITION

**“You have dealt kindly with your servant, Lord.”** As though he said: You ought to teach me your justifications. For you have already dealt kindly with me, your servant—that is, you have given me the sweetness of goodness; that is, you have made me such that goodness delights me.

When God mercifully inspires someone with delight in goodness, and when the love of the Lord is granted to someone so that through love he comes to love his neighbor, God deals kindly with him. For the one whom goodness delights possesses a great gift from God.

The person whom goodness delights does not perform the good he does from fear of punishment but from love of righteousness. But the one whom goodness does not delight performs the work of the law from fear of punishment and not from love of righteousness.

When God is feared but not loved, the service is slavish rather than free. But **“the slave will be cast out; the son remains in the house forever,”** because perfect love casts out fear (1 John 6).

It is equivalent to what he says—**“You have dealt kindly with your servant”**—to say: You have made your servant a son, and this **“according to your word,”** that is, according to your promises.

Or: You have dealt kindly with your servant while your servant acted according to your word, that is, your commandment.

**“Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge.”** Behold, the one who first confessed that the Lord had dealt kindly with him now asks to be taught in goodness. And why this, unless because he wishes to advance in the sweetness of goodness?

Note that he sets down three things: goodness, discipline, and knowledge.

When God mercifully inspires someone with delight in goodness, that person ought certainly to pray earnestly that this gift may be heard so clearly within him that, because of it, he not only despises other delights but also endures every kind of pressure and tribulation.

Thus discipline is appropriately added to sweetness, because discipline is instruction through hardships. And discipline must not be added to a slight sweetness or a slight love, but to so great a love that no tribulation can extinguish it.

Knowledge is placed third, because if knowledge precedes love in its greatness, it does not build up but puffs up. When love in the sweetness of goodness has become so great that it cannot be extinguished by the tribulations supplied by discipline, then knowledge is useful, so that through knowledge a person may consider what he was, what he deserved, and what he received from God.

Therefore it was rightly said: **“Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge.”**

As though he said: Teach goodness by inspiring love; teach discipline by inspiring patience; teach knowledge by illuminating understanding. And you ought to do all these things **“because I have believed in your commandments,”** that is, I have believed that all these things are commanded by you, although they were administered to human beings through human beings.

And why is it necessary for you to apply discipline, which will correct me and teach me the sweetness of your commandments? Because **“before I was humbled, I went astray.”** Sin came first so that humiliation might follow.

Therefore, because I was humbled and came back to myself, **“I kept your utterance,”** that is, your commandments, so that I might not be humbled again.

This humiliation is to be understood in the first parent, in whom the whole human race was corrupted as in its root. And because humanity did not wish to be subject to truth, it was subjected to vanity. It was beneficial for the vessels of mercy to experience this, so that, once pride had been cast down, obedience might be loved and misery that would not return might perish.

**“I kept your utterance.”** And you, Lord, **“teach me your justifications in your goodness,”** that is, make me attend to them so that, by acting and always advancing toward what is better, I may experience how sweet your commandments are.

And it belongs to you to teach, because you are good, that is, naturally sweet. And you must teach because **“the iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me,”** those who wish to make your commandments bitter to me.

**“But I shall examine your commandments with my whole heart.”** As though he said: However greatly their iniquity may abound, love has not grown cold in me.

**“Their heart has congealed like milk.”** Truly, the iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me, for their heart has been hardened in its wickedness, in accordance with: **“The heart of Pharaoh was hardened”** (Exodus 7, 9).

**“But I have meditated on your law,”** so that I might not consent to their wickedness.

**“It is good for me that you humbled me.”** As though he said: I was humbled because of my sin, and this is good for me—that you humbled me—so that in that very humiliation I might learn your justifications, that is, experience how good it is to keep your commandments.

For the experience of evil taught me how delightful it is to remain under your obedience.

**“The law of your mouth is good for me.”** Others consider silver, gold, and similar things to be good; for me, your law is good, **“more than thousands of pieces of gold and silver.”** For love values the law of the Lord more than greed values a thousand talents of gold and silver.

## IOTH

“Your hands made me and fashioned me; give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments. Those who fear you will see me and rejoice, because I have placed my hope exceedingly in your words. I know, O Lord, that your judgments are justice, and that in your truth you humbled me. Let your mercy come, that it may comfort me, according to your word to your servant. Let your mercies come to me, and I shall live, because your law is my meditation. Let the proud be put to shame, because they acted wickedly against me unjustly; but I shall exercise myself in your commandments. Let those who fear you turn toward me, and those who know your testimonies. Let my heart be blameless in your statutes, so that I may not be put to shame.”

### Commentary

“Your hands made me and fashioned me; give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments.” As if he were saying: Your law, proceeding from your mouth, is good to me, and you “give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments”—that is, reform me, so that I may rise in the first resurrection. Hence the words: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Ephesians 4). It belongs to you to reform me, because your hands—that is, your power—made me according to my soul and fashioned me according to my body.

For this reason you will also reform me: once I have been reformed, those who fear you with chaste fear will see me persevering in your obedience, and they will rejoice, prompted by my example to do good. This is because I placed my hope exceedingly in your word—that is, in your observed commandment—hoping beyond what we ask or understand. It is as if he said: They imitated me, not insofar as I belong to myself, but insofar as I cling to you. Hence Paul says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 4).

“I hoped in your words,” because “I know, O Lord, that your judgments are justice”—that is, that all your judgments are just—“and that in your truth you humbled me” in the first parent. Because I did not wish to be exalted by remaining in your obedience, you justly humbled me: for you punished me with death in the first parent.

And because you humbled me in your true judgment, “let your mercy be upon your servant, that it may comfort me.” That is, let me, your servant and not my own freedman, receive consolation through your mercy. By departing from you, I received desolation through your anger. This happens “according to your word,” because you said: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zechariah 1). Or, “that it may comfort the one who acts according to your word.” Or it may be understood in this way: “Let your mercy come, that it may comfort me” in the future, and let this be “according to” your word, by giving me immortality, which you promised to the first man if he had persevered in obedience—the obedience in which I now stand.

And that it may then comfort me, “let your mercies come to me” now—that is, the manifestations of your mercy—“and I shall live,” clinging to you, whereas I was dying by departing from you. You ought to do this, because your law is my meditation: that is, I meditate continually upon your law, specifically the law of faith that works through love. This meditation proceeds entirely from the commandments, so that love may not grow cold.

According to the earlier reading, the exposition will be as follows: “Let your mercies come to me” for this purpose, “that I may live, because your law is my meditation.” I shall live, but let the proud be put to shame, so that their wickedness may not extinguish love in me. Let them be put to shame, I say, because they acted wickedly against me unjustly—that is, without cause. I labored for their salvation, while they labored for my destruction. Yet however much they labored to devour me, I exercised myself in your commandments.

Why should those who fear you turn toward me—that is, be associated with me? In accordance with the words: “Let the one who belongs to God join himself to me.” And let those who know your testimonies turn toward me. He explains “those who fear you,” so that we may understand what kind of fear he means. It is as if he said: Let those who fear you in such a way that they know your testimonies not merely through knowledge but through life be associated with me. For this to happen, “let my heart be made blameless in your statutes, so that I may not be put to shame,” either here or in the future.

## CAPH

“My soul has failed in your salvation, and I have placed my hope exceedingly in your word. My eyes have failed while waiting for your word, saying: When will you comfort me? For I have become like a wineskin in frost; I have not forgotten your statutes. How many are the days of your servant? When will you execute judgment upon those who persecute me? The wicked have recounted fables to me, but not as your law. All your commandments are truth. The wicked persecuted me; help me. They almost completely destroyed me on earth, but I did not abandon your commandments. According to your mercy, revive me, and I shall keep the testimonies of your mouth.”

### Commentary

“My soul has failed in your salvation, and I have placed my hope exceedingly in your word.” As if he were saying: My heart will rightly be made blameless, because my soul—that is, my animal nature—has failed by going out from itself toward your salvation, restraining itself within your salvation, and I have placed my hope exceedingly in your word.

This failure is not one of guilt and punishment but is praiseworthy and desirable. For failure is not always used in an evil sense, just as its opposite, progress, is not always used in a good sense, but sometimes in an evil one. Hence Paul says to Timothy: “Avoid profane novelties of words and old-womanish questions, for they advance toward ungodliness” (1 Timothy 4, 6). And concerning certain women he said: “They are always learning and advancing toward worse things” (2 Timothy 3).

Thus failure is used here in a good sense, because it signifies holy desire. The saints possessed this desire before the Lord’s incarnation, as did the righteous Simeon, who said: “Do you suppose I shall see it? Do you suppose I shall endure? Oh, if that birth should find me here!” All the saints also possessed this desire after the incarnation, awaiting the revelation when the Lord will judge the living and the dead.

“My soul has failed in your salvation, and I have placed my hope exceedingly in your word”—that is, I have hoped in your promises beyond what we ask or understand. These promises cause what is not seen by believers to be awaited with patience.

“My inner eyes have failed”—that is, the reasoning faculty of my soul, not merely my animal nature—by going toward your word, saying with the affection of desire: “When will you comfort me?” by granting increase in virtues? This too is a blessed failure of the eyes, since it does not arise from weakness of spirit but from excess of desire.

“When will you comfort me?” For consolation is also necessary, “because I have become like a wineskin in frost.” A wineskin is a vessel sewn from leather, made suitable for receiving and holding wine. But when placed in frost, it hardens and becomes an unusable vessel. So too, when a human being had been a good vessel for receiving pure liquid—that is, true discernment—he became hardened against the rain of God’s grace through the merit of disobedience and became useless. This is what is meant by: “Because I have become like a wineskin in frost.” Yet, insofar as I was able, I did not forget your statutes.

Or it may be understood thus: “When will you comfort me,” so that this mortal nature may put on immortality? And you ought to do this, because, insofar as I was able, I made myself fit for it, “because I have become like a wineskin” placed “in frost.”

Alternatively, the wineskin may signify carnal desires, and the frost the dew of divine grace, by which the fluid desires of the flesh are restrained and curbed. It is as if he said: The heat of desire has grown numb in me, so that the memory of love might burn within me. Therefore “I have not forgotten your statutes.”
