“How many are the days of your servant?” Seeing that the consolation for which the faithful soul earlier prayed is delayed, and desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ, he says: “How many are the days of your servant?” That is, how long will the days of humiliation last, which your servants have made for themselves? And lest we think that these days will end before the final judgment, he adds: “When will you execute judgment upon those who persecute me?”—separating the grain from the chaff.

Some have said that the Church will come to an end before the consummation of the world. Against them the Lord said in the Gospel: “This Gospel will be preached in the whole world, and then the end will come” (Matthew 24).

“When will you execute judgment upon those who persecute me?” For it is necessary. Indeed, in order to overthrow me, “the wicked have recounted fables to me, but not like your law”—that is, a law to be heard—because in your law it is not merely words that delight me, but truth. For all your commandments are truth.

And because I consented to the truth, the wicked persecuted me; but you, Lord, help me. Help is necessary, because those sinners almost completely destroyed me on earth. “Almost completely” means very nearly, in their estimation, since they thought that I, who had not made heaven and earth, could be destroyed. Yet although this seemed so to them, I did not abandon your commandments.

And so that I may not abandon them, Lord, according to your mercy manifested to the world, revive me with an inward revival, lest I receive the grace of God in vain; and, revived by you, I shall keep the testimonies of your mouth.

## LAMED

“Forever, O Lord, your word remains in heaven. Your truth is from generation to generation. You founded the earth, and it remains. By your ordinance the days endure, for all things serve you. If your law had not been my meditation, I might perhaps have perished in my humiliation. Forever I shall not forget your statutes, because through them you revived me. I am yours; save me, because I have sought your statutes. Sinners waited for me in order to destroy me; I understood your testimonies. I have seen the end of every consummation; your commandment is exceedingly broad.”

### Commentary

“Forever, O Lord, your word remains in heaven.” As if he were saying: Revived by you, I shall keep the testimonies of your mouth, which no one can keep except through your revival. For your word—that is, your commandment—remains in heaven, that is, in the angels who are in heaven, all the way to the consummation of the world, through your revival.

And your word remains in heaven not only through your revival; your truth also remains from generation to generation: the generation belonging to the law and the generation belonging to grace. For you founded the earth—that is, you made your Church firm upon the foundation of faith—and it “remains,” because “your throne, O God, is forever and ever” (Psalm 44).

“By your ordinance the days endure”—that is, all who are days, meaning those who are enlightened, are able to persevere through your disposition; for all things—that is, all who are days—“serve you.”

“If your law had not been my meditation, I might perhaps have perished in my humiliation.” Seeing through whom the earth was liberated, in what it was founded, and through whom it remains, the faithful soul says: I might have perished—indeed, certainly—in my humiliation, that is, in my condition, when I was humbled in the first parent, if your law had not been my meditation: specifically the law of faith, not an empty faith, but faith that works through love (Galatians 5). Through it grace is obtained, and that grace acts amid temporal tribulation so that the wretched human being may not perish in mortal humiliation.

Or the passage may be connected in this way: “According to your mercy, revive me.” This is necessary, because I might perhaps have perished in my humiliation then—that is, when “they almost completely destroyed me on earth”—if your law had not been my meditation. Therefore “forever I shall not forget your statutes, because through them you revived me.”

And because you revived me, save me by granting perseverance. For I am yours: you first willed me to be yours, but I was lost; now I seek to be yours so that I may be saved, because I sought your statutes, even though many wished to hinder me. For delay and the file—that is, persistent obstruction—“waited for me in order to destroy me.” But “I understood your testimonies,” and “I saw the end of every consummation,” because I recognized that it is good to endure the greatest labor for the sake of the supreme good.

The end of consummation is to rejoice without end in the kingdom of Christ. “I have seen the end of every consummation,” not through myself but through your exceedingly broad commandment—that is, through your love, extended even to the point of loving enemies.

Or it may be understood thus: I saw your exceedingly broad commandment—that is, your love extended even to enemies—as the end of every consummation, that is, of all perfection, because the whole law and the prophets depend upon love (Matthew 22). Without it, the whole collection of good works is useless, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “If I deliver my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13).

## MEM

“How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all day long. Through your commandment you have made me wiser than my enemies, because it is mine forever. I have understood more than all who teach me, because your testimonies are my meditation. I have understood more than the elders, because I sought your commandments. I restrained my feet from every evil way, so that I might keep your words. I did not turn aside from your judgments, because you established your law for me. How sweet your words are to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth! Through your commandments I have gained understanding; therefore I hated every way of iniquity.”

### Commentary

“How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all day long.” As if he were saying: Because your commandment is exceedingly broad, therefore I loved your law in the manner in which it ought to be loved. For it is my meditation all day—that is, continually.

By such meditation desire is conquered, since desire often opposes the carrying out of the law’s commands. But because he meditates all day upon the Lord’s law, he drives every desire from himself.

“Through your commandment you have made me wiser than my enemies, because it is mine forever.” As if he were saying: For this reason I loved your law, because through that law you made me wiser than my enemies.

The enemies were those who understood the law carnally, in opposition to those who understood it spiritually. They were like the sons of Hagar, who, generating children into slavery, were enemies of the sons of Sarah (Galatians 4). They sought temporal rewards in the Lord’s commandment, while the others were striving toward eternal things.

Thus he says: “Through your commandment you have made me wiser than my enemies”—that is, through your precept—and this because your commandment is sweet to me forever. It is as if he said: I am wiser than my enemies in your commandments because they sought temporal things in them, whereas I sought eternal things.

They say: “What enters the mouth defiles a person.” I say: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but the thoughts that come out of the heart; these defile a person” (Matthew 15).

“I have understood more than all who teach me”—that is, more than those who boasted that they were teachers and doctors of the law. Of them it was said: “Woe to you who have the key of knowledge; neither do you enter yourselves, nor do you permit others to enter” (Luke 11). I understood more than these because your testimonies are my meditation.

In ancient times it was said: “You shall love your friend, and you shall hate your enemy” (Leviticus 19). But your testimonies say: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matthew 5). These testimonies were always my meditation.

And I understood more than the elders, because I sought your commandments, seeking spiritual understanding in them rather than observing them carnally. For “I restrained my feet from every evil way”—that is, my affections—from every evil way, so that I might keep your commandments.

And because it is not enough to turn away from evil unless good follows, it is added: “I did not turn aside from your judgments,” which you established and through which you taught, “because you established your law for me,” so that whoever perseveres to the end may be saved (Matthew 10, 24).

And because you established it, how sweet your words are to my throat—the throat, namely, of the heart. They are not merely sweet to me for my own edification; they are also sweeter than honey to my mouth, so that I may utter them for the edification of my neighbors. For the edification of my neighbor delights me more than any other sweetness of earthly things.

“I have understood through your commandments.” He understands God’s commandments because he demonstrates them in his works. Hence the saying: “Do you desire wisdom? Keep the commandments” (Matthew 19). One reaches the wisdom of hidden things through obedience to the commandments. And there is also the saying: “Whoever increases wisdom increases sorrow” (Ecclesiastes 1).

“I have gained understanding through your commandments; therefore I hated every way of iniquity,” because no one perfectly loves love who does not hate iniquity.

## NUN

“Your word is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths. I swore and resolved to keep the judgments of your justice. I have been humbled exceedingly, O Lord; revive me according to your word. Make the voluntary offerings of my mouth pleasing, O Lord, and teach me your judgments. My soul is always in my hands, and I have not forgotten your law. Sinners set a snare for me, but I did not go astray from your commandments. I acquired your testimonies as an inheritance forever, because they are the rejoicing of my heart. I inclined my heart to perform your statutes forever, because of the reward.”

### Commentary

“Your word is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths.” As if he were saying: For this reason I hated the way of iniquity, because your word—not the Word who is Christ, but the word of Christ given to the prophets and proclaimed through the apostles, contained in all the Scriptures—is a lamp for my feet, that is, for my affections.

A lamp does not shine through itself but through something else. Thus the apostles did not shine through themselves, but through Christ, the true light, they sparkled in the brilliance of light. Therefore the word of preaching proclaimed through the apostles was like a lamp for the feet.

But the truth that Christ preached, because it shone by itself with an excess of radiance, is called not a lamp but a light; and it is a light on the paths—that is, in the more demanding commandments. For he himself was an example to us of pressing along the narrow way: that is, of investigating through knowledge the more demanding commandments, which we ought to test in practice. What he taught with his mouth, he completed through his works.

And because the word we hear through preachers is not brought to the completion of action unless he inspires and assists, it is properly called the light on the paths of God.

“I swore and resolved to keep the judgments of your justice.” Because your word is a light on the paths, therefore I swore—that is, I confirmed by an oath—and, as if you were asking what I had sworn, he adds: “I resolved”—that is, I irrevocably purposed—“to keep the judgments of your justice.”

The mind must be so fixed in keeping the Lord’s judgments that what it resolves should be regarded entirely as an oath. The Lord’s just judgments are kept when, under God the just judge, it is believed that neither sin remains unpunished nor good work unrewarded.

And because the saints suffer many pressures and persecutions while keeping the Lord’s judgments, he says, seeing this in the prophetic spirit: “I have been humbled exceedingly, O Lord.” That is, I have been humbled by every possible humiliation, insofar as concerns those by whom I have been humbled. For they thought that I had been wholly abandoned by you.

But lest the word of faith perish because of humiliation, he asks to be revived: “Revive me according to your word,” because I died through the transgression of the first human being.

“Make the voluntary offerings of my mouth pleasing, O Lord.” That is, do not reject them but approve the voluntary sacrifices of praise, offered from the confession of love and not from fear of necessity. “And teach me your judgments”—that is, your commandments—advancing my progress still further.

And you ought to do this, because “my soul is always in my hands”—that is, in my works—so that I may offer it to you. Or: I am always concerned for the progress of my soul, and therefore I have not forgotten your law, although there are certainly those who would like me to forget it.

Because sinners set a snare for me, wishing to entangle me in their commandments, nevertheless “I did not go astray from your commandments.” Rather, “I acquired your testimonies as an inheritance”—that is, I counted it as an inheritance to keep your commandments—or I acquired your testimonies, that is, your martyrdoms, comparable to an inheritance.

Just as Christ received an inheritance from the Father, so the holy martyrs received from the Lord, as if in place of an inheritance, the opportunity to become his witnesses through martyrdom—a thing many desired but could not attain. Yet no one could attain it except by desiring it, because they could not have done so had they not desired the testimonies of God.

And because the holy martyrs do not seek human glory from those who seek empty things in the Lord’s testimonies, but eternal glory through suffering for a short time and rejoicing without end, he adds: “forever.”

It is as if he said: For this reason I acquired your testimonies, because they are forever, leading me, namely, to what is eternal. For they are the rejoicing of my heart, although they are an affection of the body. Therefore “I inclined my heart to perform your statutes forever, because of the reward.”

Here he repeats what he said above: “Incline”; here he says: “I inclined.” What else do we understand by this than that he shows the inclination of his heart to be both a divine gift and not his own doing?

But it is puzzling that he says: “to perform your statutes forever,” since the works of mercy that we perform for the needs of our neighbors are not eternal, because neither are those needs eternal. These works of mercy, if they are not performed with love, are no statutes at all; but if they are performed from love, they justify. Love, however, because it remains forever, causes the one who loves eternally to seek to possess what he loves. This is what he says: “I inclined my heart to perform your statutes forever, because of the reward.”

## SAMECH

“I hated the wicked and loved your law. You are my helper and protector, and I have placed my hope exceedingly in your word. Depart from me, evildoers, and I shall search out the commandments of my God. Receive me according to your word, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my hope. Help me, and I shall be saved; and I shall meditate forever on your statutes. You have despised all who depart from your judgments, because their thought is unjust. I have regarded all the sinners of the earth as transgressors; therefore I loved your testimonies. Nail my flesh with your fear, for I feared your judgments.”

### Commentary

This passage is both a sign and an exhortation, so that anyone hearing what is said here—“I hated the wicked, and in this the Lord is my helper, and in him I placed my hope”—may pay attention and not, by taking it superficially or passing over it, suppose that it contradicts the harmony of the Evangelists: namely, that vice must not be loved because of a person, nor a person hated because of vice.

“I hated the wicked.” I did not stray from your commandments; rather, I hated the wicked who strayed, and in this I loved your law. This is more than if he had said, “I fulfilled it,” because I hated not the wicked themselves but their errors. This is good and perfect hatred.

“You are my helper and protector.” In hating the wicked, as I did and do, you are my helper and co-worker, because I act and you cooperate. You were my helper in this hatred of enemies and in love of the law; previously you were my protector—that is, my physician and guardian—healing me from sins in baptism.

And because, in hating the wicked, I was proceeding toward your word, since you command this, I placed my hope exceedingly in it—that is, I possessed a hope more intense than can be expressed or imagined.

And because I hated the wicked, “depart from me, evildoers”—that is, desist from your persuasions, by which you strive to overthrow me. Once you have ceased, I shall search out—that is, diligently investigate—the commandments of my God, with no one hindering me.

“Receive me according to your word.” So that I may be fit to search out your commandments, receive me, Lord, according to my advancement, through your protection, making me live according to your word—that is, according to your commandment. If you receive me, I shall live: I shall be diligent in fulfilling your commandments, through which one advances toward eternal life. And “do not put me to shame in my hope”—that is, do not allow me to be put to shame, because I have long awaited and desired that you receive me.

“Help me.” Earlier he indicated grace when he said, “Receive me.” Now he also indicates free will when he says, “Help me”—that is, cooperate with me. With your help I shall be saved, and I shall always meditate upon this: that you alone justify.

“You have despised all who depart.” Therefore I pray that you receive me and help me to persevere according to your word, because you have despised—that is, condemned—all who depart from your judgments, that is, those who do not persevere in your commandments. And rightly so, because their thought is unjust.

Everyone who departs from the Lord’s commandments either thinks and supposes that he is so merciful that he will not punish his creature, or that he is powerless, or ignorant, or something of this kind. For such a thought he is rightly condemned.

“I have regarded transgressors.” As if someone were to say: I do not depart from the Lord’s commandments, because although I sin, I remain in the faith. He responds that he has regarded not only those who apostatize from the faith but all sinners as transgressors—sinners, namely, who belong to the earth, that is, who are earth and remain earth. He regarded them as transgressors, that is, as those who violate God’s commandments, and therefore depart from God’s judgments.

He calls them “sinners of the earth” because they sin criminally. Just as earth is heavier than the other elements, so capital crimes are more serious than venial ones.

And because I understood that such people are condemned by you, therefore I loved your testimonies, lest you condemn me in the same way.

“Nail me with your fear.” Just as I love you in my mind, so also nail my flesh—that is, my sensual impulses, namely, the five bodily senses, or the evil suggestions arising from the flesh—with your chaste fear. Bind them so tightly through your love that I neither wish nor am able to accomplish anything displeasing to you, like someone fastened with nails who, even if he wished, could not move his limbs in any direction.

And it is right that you should do this, because I have not trusted in my own strength but have always feared, and still fear, falling away from your judgments—that is, from your commandments.

## AIN

“I have acted with judgment and justice; do not hand me over to those who slander me. Receive your servant for good; let not the proud slander me. My eyes have failed while waiting for your salvation and for the word of your justice. Deal with your servant according to your mercy, and teach me your statutes. I am your servant; give me understanding, that I may know your testimonies. It is time to act, O Lord; they have destroyed your law. Therefore I loved your commandments above gold and topaz. Therefore I was directed toward all your commandments; I hated every way of iniquity.”

### Commentary

The one who speaks here truly possesses an eye, because, having drunk from the fountain of wisdom, he has true understanding. With a spiritual eye he sees the old law and spiritually performs what it commands. Because of this, the Jews, possessing a carnal eye, slander him. But he prays that he not be handed over to their power and will; rather, that they cease and be converted.

“I have acted with judgment.” I loved your testimonies, Lord, and because I loved them I acted with judgment—that is, I understood spiritually what is stated there according to the letter. Once I had understood it, I acted with justice—that is, I acted according to what I understood. Therefore I had the Jews as slanderers.

But because I acted with judgment and justice, “do not hand me over to those who slander me.” Slander occurs when something false is imposed upon someone, or when what is done through virtue is overturned through detraction, as the Jews said of the Lord: “He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons” (Luke 11).

“Receive your servant,” and I ask not only that you not hand me over to those who slander me—that is, that I not fall away from the state in which I am—but also that you receive me, your servant, for advancement toward good: that I may go from virtue to virtue, or that I may perform judgment and justice better and better.

“Let not the proud slander me”—that is, let them cease from their slanders and receive spiritual understanding.

“My eyes have failed.” For this reason also, Lord, receive me, because my eyes—that is, my understanding and mind—have failed with respect to every evil intention and every desire for outward things, striving toward your salvation—that is, toward your commandments, which, when observed, are salvation and life.

And toward the word of your justice, which you commanded through your mouth to be justly performed, deal with your servant. And because “my eyes have failed while waiting for your salvation,” “deal with your servant according to your mercy”—that is, cooperate with me according to the measure of your mercy, making me henceforth more diligent in doing good. “And teach me your statutes”—that is, make me recognize that my justice is yours and must not be attributed to me.

“I am your servant.” O Lord, I am your servant, obedient to you in all things. Give me understanding—that is, an increasingly spiritual eye—so that I may know your testimonies, namely, the writing of the old law, which bears witness to all the things now observed in the new law.

“It is time to act.” And now, Lord, it is the appropriate time for acting—for you to grant me understanding—because those who lack the eye and slander me have destroyed your law, neither believing nor observing what is commanded in the law.

Therefore I loved your commandments. In order that you might give me understanding, therefore I loved your commandments—that is, your new precepts—above gold and topaz, above all things regarded as most precious among temporal goods. Topaz is exceedingly precious both because of its brilliance and because of its rarity. The rarer it is, the more precious it is.

“Therefore I was directed toward all your commandments.” I did not love your commandments for this reason alone; therefore I was also directed toward all your commandments in the execution of action. And therefore I hated every way of iniquity—that is, the vices of the flesh and the carnal understanding of the law.

## PHE

“Your testimonies are wonderful; therefore my soul has searched them out. The explanation of your words gives light and grants understanding to the simple. I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit, because I desired your commandments. Look upon me and have mercy on me according to the judgment of those who love your name. Direct my steps according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me. Redeem me from the slanders of men, so that I may keep your commandments. Let your face shine upon your servant, and teach me your statutes. Streams of water poured from my eyes, because they did not keep your law.”

### Commentary

This collection of verses differs from the preceding one in this respect: there the principal reason for prayer was that he not be handed over to the slander of the Jews. Here, however, the principal intention is to show the causes of their error. Therefore this letter is interpreted as “he erred”—namely, the Jewish people.

For this is where they erred: they did not regard the testimonies of God’s mouth as wonderful, nor did they become humble and simple by searching them out.

Miraculous are your testimonies. O Lord, give me understanding [Col. 0757C], that I may know your testimonies, because they are miraculous—that is, worthy of admiration. And therefore my soul searched them out, that is, diligently investigated their meaning. For there are many precepts in the Law that, to those who do not know them, rightly seem unacceptable: for example, the command that the head rather than the tail be offered as a sacrifice, that a sparrow be killed with its neck twisted beneath its wings, that the ear of a Jewish slave be pierced with an awl, and many things of this kind (Exod. XXI; Lev. V). When understood spiritually, these provide great edification; but the Jews do not marvel at them, because they neither understand them nor strive to learn.

The explanation of your words. This is a response to the question: if someone were to say, “Since they are miraculous, how can you search them out?”—the explanation of your words, that is, the Gospel, which explains your words, namely, the Law [Col. 0757D] and the Prophets, enlightens me. And because it could not enlighten me according to literal knowledge, he specifies how it enlightens: it gives understanding to the little ones, that is, to the humble, not to the proud. In other words, it makes the humble understand these things spiritually. He says “to the little ones” in the plural to indicate that spiritual understanding is not given to just anyone who searches, but only to those who persevere in humility.

I opened my mouth. And so that I might search them out, and so that you might enlighten me through the explanation and give me understanding, I opened my mouth—that is, I enlarged my heart with great eagerness, just as someone wishing to be filled opens his mouth outwardly—and I drew in the spirit, that is, I received within me the Holy Spirit, who gives understanding. I obtained this [Col. 0758A] Holy Spirit from God because I desired your commandments, that is, the New Law; I fulfilled them with desire.

Look upon me. “I opened my mouth,” saying this within myself: “Look upon me,” that is, enlighten me according to understanding. He now says, “Look upon me,” that is, “Enlighten me inwardly,” and “Have mercy on me,” that is, do this out of mercy, according to the judgment that ought to be made concerning those who love your name, which is “Lord.” Here “judgment” is used passively. This amounts to saying: “Look upon me in mercy, not according to merit.”

Direct my steps according to your word. Do not merely give me understanding; also direct my steps, that is, give me good dispositions for observing your commandments. And let no injustice rule over me, that is, let no sin or vice [Col. 0758B] reign in me.

Redeem me. Once I have been enlightened and my steps have been directed, those who slander me will be people who neither understand nor observe the Law. But you, Lord, redeem me from the slanders of those who are merely human and think only of earthly things. And he specifies in what respect he ought to be redeemed from them. I do not ask that they refrain from slandering me, but that they not turn me away from your commandments; rather, may I persevere in keeping them.

Make your face shine. Above he said, “Look upon me,” but he did not say through whom you would do this. Therefore he repeats the request in order to add this, saying: “Make your face shine,” that is, your Son, through whom you are known, just as someone is known through his face, “upon your servant,” that is, upon my higher part, since I am your servant. And I ask to be enlightened so that you may teach me your ordinances [Col. 0758C], that is, the Old Law according to faith, understanding, and practice.

Streams of water flowed down from my eyes. People slander me, and on their account streams of water flowed down from my eyes, that is, springs of tears—not because they slandered me, but because they did not keep your Law, whether in faith, understanding, or practice.

**SADE.**—“You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right. You commanded righteousness in your testimonies, and your truth exceedingly. My zeal made me waste away, because my enemies forgot your words. Your word is exceedingly fiery, and your servant loved it. I am young and despised; I have not forgotten your ordinances. Your righteousness is righteousness forever, and your law is truth. Tribulation [Col. 0758D] and distress found me; your commandments are my meditation. The equity of your testimonies is everlasting; give me understanding, and I shall live.”

**EXPOSITION.**

This faithful man, who in the preceding section prayed for enlightenment and for the direction of his steps, and who was saddened by those who slandered him, here shows that he has been comforted because of God’s just judgment: for God both heard him and blinded his Jewish enemies. In both matters he exercised a just judgment.

You are righteous, O Lord. I, whose eyes brought forth streams of water, receive consolation from this, Lord: that you are righteous by nature, and that your judgment is right—that is, you display in your works the righteousness that is [Col. 0759A] naturally in you.

You commanded righteousness. Truly your judgment is right, because you gave me what had long before been far removed, namely, your testimonies, that is, your precepts, and righteousness, that is, the understanding that the Old Law is righteousness, which, when fulfilled spiritually, justifies; and exceedingly your truth. But you commanded—the New Law, which is truth, and truth to an even greater degree in comparison with the former, which was a shadow.

My zeal made me waste away. You therefore gave me the New Law, which is truth and righteousness, because my zeal made me waste away—that is, the love I had for my enemies made me languish and grieve exceedingly because those enemies of mine had forgotten your words, that is, your precepts.

Your word is refined by fire.

And there is greater reason to waste away and grieve for [Col. 0759B] those who forget your commandments because your word is exceedingly fiery. Fire performs three things: it consumes, enlightens, and kindles. In the Lord’s commandment it consumes vices in human beings, enlightens according to knowledge, and kindles according to charity. And because they lack all these gifts, it is right to grieve for them. And because your word is exceedingly refined by fire, I, who am your servant, love it.

I am young. Although I love it—I who am young, that is, renewed, with nothing old in me—I am nevertheless despised and held in contempt, whether I myself consider myself worthless or others have consigned me to contempt. But although I may seem so despised, I have not forgotten your ordinances [Col. 0759C], that is, I have not withdrawn from observing the Law.

Your righteousness. Even though I am despised, I rightly do not forget your ordinances, because your righteousness, that is, the Old Law, is righteousness leading into eternity, and your law, namely, the New Law, is likewise truth leading into everlasting life.

Tribulation and distress. I am not merely despised—for that alone would not be a sufficiently powerful reason to forget the Lord’s precepts—but tribulation, which belongs to the body, and distress, which belongs to the soul, found me, namely, fit to suffer. That is, God, seeing me fit and strong enough to endure tribulations and distresses for the salvation of my soul, allowed such things to happen to me. For God is said to seek, through distresses and tribulations, which are certain gifts of his, those who are worthy to be crowned in this way, and tribulation itself finds such people. [Col. 0759D] For there are very many who, if they suffered adversity, would fail. God spares them lest they fall, but nevertheless they are of lower rank than those who suffer. Although tribulation and distress found me, your commandments are still my meditation, that is, I meditate on fulfilling the precepts of your New Law.

The equity of your testimonies. And rightly I meditate on your commandments in tribulation, because your testimonies are righteousness—that is, righteous and honorable in themselves, and leading into eternity. And because this is so, I ask, Lord, that you give me understanding and make me understand them more perfectly hereafter; then I shall live forever.

**COPH.**—“I cried with my whole heart; hear me, O Lord, and I shall seek your ordinances. I cried to you; save me, [Col. 0760A] and I shall keep your commandments. I anticipated others in immaturity and cried, because I placed my hope exceedingly in your words. My eyes went before you at daybreak, that I might meditate on your words. Hear my voice according to your mercy, O Lord, and according to your judgment give me life. Those who persecute me drew near to iniquity; but they have gone far from your law. You are near, O Lord, and all your ways are truth. From the beginning I learned from your testimonies that you founded them forever.”

**EXPOSITION.**

This letter indicates that the faithful man who speaks here has been confined and surrounded by many great tribulations, and cannot be rescued from them in any way except by divine help. Therefore he urgently called upon the Lord [Col. 0760B] to give him a more perfect understanding and the carrying out of his commandments.

I cried with my whole heart. When I was in contempt, and tribulation and distress had found me, I sought no other refuge but cried out. And I did this not with an outcry of the mouth, but with my whole heart, so that your heart might be empty for the cry. But to cry with the heart is different from crying in the heart, because even those who cry aloud cry with the heart. To cry in the heart, however, is to show the intention of the heart to the Lord without a voice.

Thus I cried with my whole heart, saying: “O Lord, hear me for this alone: that I may seek your ordinances,” that is, that I may seek and continually seek your precepts with great desire, and observe them.

I cried to you. I cried, I say, not to neighbors and friends, but to you, who are willing and able [Col. 0760C], saying: “Save me,” that is, grant me this salvation, so that I may keep—that is, fulfill—your commandments. Here salvation is understood to consist in keeping the Lord’s commandments.

I anticipated others in immaturity. And rightly you ought to hear me crying out and asking for what is honorable, because I anticipated others in immaturity, that is, in youth, an age that is immature and undisciplined for keeping your commandments. For the younger people are, and the more ardent they are in age, the more prone they are to pride, anger, lust, and other vices. Although I still seemed immature in age for such things, I nevertheless cried to you and surpassed others by living well. And I placed excessive hope in your word, that is, in your utterance: I had a hope more intense than the hope I had previously [Col. 0760D]. For hope always grows with merits.

My eyes went before you. And therefore you ought to hear me, because my eyes, directed toward you, went before others at daybreak. Every morning I kept watch, directing the intention of my mind continually toward you. For this reason, that I might meditate on your words, that is, exercise myself in your commandments, like someone who hurries to his work early in the morning.

Or “at daybreak” means “in the light of virtues”: my eyes went before others toward you, that is, I attributed to you whatever virtue there was in me, so that I might meditate on your words.

Hear my voice. And because I went before others in youth, and my eyes went before them at daybreak, hear my voice, Lord—not merely according to my merits, but according to your mercy, that is, according to grace, and according to your judgment, that is, according to what you judge to be right, namely, according also to my merit. [Col. 0761A] Give me life, that is, make me keep your commandments, which are life to me.

Or: hear my voice according to your mercy here in the present, lest I fail, and in the future give me life according to your just judgment, granting me eternal life.

Those who persecute me drew near. And it is just that you give life to me as I draw near to righteousness, because “those who persecute me drew near to iniquity.” Some are in iniquity and continually draw nearer and nearer, while they become far from your law. Although these things are joined together, it is one thing to be separated from God’s law and another to draw near to iniquity. To draw near to iniquity is to love vices and do evil; to become far from God’s law is to neglect virtues and [Col. 0761B] good works.

Or it is necessary for you to give me life because “those who persecute me drew near to iniquity,” that is, wishing to make me like themselves, by persecuting me they draw nearer and nearer to deformity and darkness, and become far from your law—spoken by comparison with someone who, the nearer he draws to darkness, the farther he becomes from the light.

You are near, O Lord. And lest anyone think that those who have become far from God’s law, even if they repent, can never return to the Lord, he says: Because they draw near to iniquity, they have no excuse as though they could not have a helper if they wished to turn their gaze back, because you, Lord, are near, that is, you are merciful and ready to help. And since you are near and they do not turn back, this cannot be [Col. 0761C] charged to you, since all your ways are truth, that is, your judgments are both just and true even in the very fact that you blind them.

Or I pray in this confidence that you hear my voice because you are near to all who call upon you. And therefore also, because all your ways, that is, all your commandments, are truth, that is, just, I learned from the beginning. For this reason also I ask you to hear my voice, so that I may keep your commandments, because you founded them forever, that is, they are effective for eternity for the one to whom you firmly founded and gave them.

I learned this by contrast from your testimonies given at the beginning to the first parents, in whom they were not founded, because they were not kept by them. From this I learned that those in whom they are founded—that is, those by whom they are firmly kept—they lead to eternal life. [Col. 0761D] For if our first parents, through transgression, came down from eternal things to temporal things, we, through observing God’s commandments, shall be raised from temporal things to eternal ones.

**RES.**—“See my humility and rescue me, because I have not forgotten your law. Judge my judgment and redeem me; because of your word give me life. Salvation is far from sinners, because they have not sought your ordinances. Your mercies are many, O Lord; according to your judgment give me life. Many are those who persecute and afflict me; I have not turned away from your testimonies. I saw transgressors, and I wasted away because they did not keep your words. See that I have loved your commandments, O Lord; in your mercy give me life. [Col. 0762A] The beginning of your words is truth; all the judgments of your righteousness are everlasting.”

**EXPOSITION.**

Lest this faithful man seem to have proposed such merits out of arrogance when he says, “I cried,” “I rose before dawn,” and “my eyes went before others,” he adds humility, which is the head, origin, and end of all virtues, and confirms each of them. For just as all the senses are vigorous because of the head, and when it is removed the body remains a headless trunk without a name, so all virtues are vigorous because of humility; when humility is removed, the others should not even be called virtues.

This man, conformed to the head who went before him in humility and gave the law of humility, prays that the Lord rescue him from his persecutors lest he become like them. And so that in the future, according to [Col. 0762B] his promise, he may give him life, he puts forward that same humility, saying:

See my humility. Lord, see my humility so that, in consideration of it, you may rescue me from my persecutors, because those who draw near to iniquity wish to make me like themselves. Therefore rescue me, because I have not forgotten your law, that is, humility itself, which you both commanded in words when you said, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. XI), and demonstrated by your example when you humbled yourself unto death; I have never consigned it to oblivion.

And lest he seem to pray to be rescued in such a way that he would suffer nothing further, he explains as follows:

Judge my judgment. I do not pray to be rescued in such a way that I suffer nothing. Rather, judge here such a judgment as is mine, that is, fitting for me: make [Col. 0762C] me, who am your servant, be chastised here, lest I be judged in the future. For your servants who flourish here are to be judged in the future.

He says more by saying “judge my judgment” than if he had said “bring about judgment.” For many bring about judgment who carry out what must be judged, but do not judge.

And redeem me, namely, from future condemnation. And do not merely redeem me, but also give me life, that is, grant me eternal life according to your promise.

Salvation is far from sinners. Truly you will give me life and salvation, since you deem it right to chastise me through tribulations; but this salvation is far from sinners, whom you neglect because of their sins, because they have not sought your ordinances, that is, those same tribulations by which you justify your own people—they have not loved them.

Your mercies are many, O Lord. Lest any sinner despair because it was said, “Salvation is far from sinners,” [Col. 0762D] he adds: “O Lord, your mercies are many,” that is, manifold toward those who wish to be converted. And therefore give me life according to your judgment, that is, according to what you justly judge concerning the one who has persevered from childhood or youth in humility and in the other virtues mentioned above.

Many are those who persecute and afflict me. Give me life also for this reason: because I did not turn away from your testimonies when many persecuted me, driving me from city to city, and afflicted me by tormenting me.

I saw transgressors. And for that reason I persisted in your testimonies; even while they persecuted and afflicted me, I grieved for them out of love. This is what he says: “I saw transgressors,” [Col. 0763A] that is, I considered and understood the misery of my persecutors, who transgressed your Law, and I wasted away out of compassion—not because they persecuted me, but “because they did not keep your words.”

See that I have loved your commandments. And that I did not turn away, I have you as my witness. You, Lord, see everything: see that I not only did not turn away from your testimonies, but also loved your commandments, which is much greater.

And because my merits mentioned above are not sufficient for me to deserve that you give me life, you, Lord, in consideration of your mercy, give me life—eternal life.

The beginning of your words. I loved your commandments for this reason: you did not command them to be done for your own benefit, but because the beginning of your words, that is, the principal [Col. 0763B] and highest intention of those commandments, is truth; that is, you gave just precepts. Other people customarily impose upon their slaves precepts that concern their own benefit. God, however, imposes those that benefit the people who carry them out, not himself.

All the judgments of your righteousness are everlasting. That is, all your commandments, which you judge rightly to be done, are themselves righteous; and, likewise observed, they lead into eternity.

**SIN.**—“Princes persecuted me without cause, and my heart was afraid because of your words. I shall rejoice over your words, like one who finds abundant spoils. I hated iniquity and abhorred it, but I loved your law. Seven times a day I praised you because of the judgments of your righteousness. There is abundant peace for those who love your law, and there is no stumbling-block for them. I awaited [Col. 0763C] your salvation, O Lord, and loved your commandments. My soul kept your testimonies and loved them exceedingly. I kept your commandments and your testimonies, because all my ways are before you.”

**EXPOSITION.**

The wound of the soul is sin. Therefore this man who acts here understands that the fact that many persecute and afflict him is like a plaster for healing the wound of his soul. Although he has climbed to the citadel of the virtues, he nevertheless recognizes that he is not without sins, which are cleansed in him through his persecutors. He says that the present tribulation is such great medicine for him that, in comparison with the future punishment, he no longer fears what is immediately before him, but rather rejoices in God’s [Col. 0763D] promise, which is signified through the teeth.

Princes persecuted me. Many persecute and afflict me—not just any people, but the princes of this world themselves. This is, in addition to the wound, a medicine for me. And they did this without cause, that is, in vain, because they could not divert me.

Or “without cause” means “without fault,” because although I have a wound, that is, a fault, against God, which is healed through their persecution, nevertheless, as far as they are concerned, I am without fault.

And while I was suffering and fearing present punishments, my heart was afraid because of your words, in which it is said: “Fear rather the one who can destroy both body and soul in Gehenna” (Matt. X). And elsewhere: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man [Col. 0764A] will be ashamed of him” (Luke IX). My heart feared such words to such an extent that they completely drove out fear of the present punishment.

I shall rejoice over your words. Considering, therefore, the present tribulation light and momentary, and regarding it as almost nothing in comparison with future condemnation, I remained steadfast in every persecution. And therefore, while still mortal and fragile, I rejoice and shall rejoice over your words, that is, contemplating your promises in which you said: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. V), and “Blessed will you be when people hate you” (Luke VI), and so forth. I contemplate such promises like someone who has found a great sum of money.

Or, founded upon your words, I shall rejoice in the future, like one who has found abundant spoils, that is, [Col. 0764B] the manifold glory of the heavenly kingdom. It is aptly called spoil because it is acquired by a kind of force, according to the saying: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. XI). He says “finds” because no merit can suffice for that glory unless it is granted through divine mercy.

I hated iniquity. Now it is shown how the things mentioned above are medicine for him. Persecution benefits me in this respect: chastened through it, I now hate the iniquity for which I was chastened. He says more: I also abhorred it, because it seemed to me abominable. And I not only hated iniquity, but also loved your law, that is, fulfilled it through love.

Seven times a day. I was so healed in persecution that I hated iniquity and loved your law, and I praised you [Col. 0764C]—that is, sang a hymn to you—seven times a day. This means throughout the present life, which turns according to the number seven days; or through the seven hours that we celebrate each day.

Or thus: placed in the day, that is, in the light of virtues, I praised you seven times, that is, through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, contemplating the judgments of your righteousness, that is, understanding that by your just judgment I am chastised here.

There is abundant peace for those who love your law. It is as though someone were to say: “You say that you have loved the Lord’s law, but you do not do so with impunity, since you are disturbed by many troubles and have no peace.” He replies: “I am not without peace; rather, there is abundant peace for those who love your law.” Their souls are already in paradise here. They have indeed much peace, but not complete peace, which will exist only in the future.

But if they are sometimes sad here [Col. 0764D] in the meantime, this will not be a stumbling-block for them, that is, an occasion of the offense of sin, so that through a sadness arising within them they should at some point sin.

Or there is no stumbling-block because, on account of some tribulation, they are not ashamed to confess Christ crucified, but persevere in patience.

I awaited your salvation, O Lord. And because I loved your law, O Lord, through this I awaited your salvation, that is, the salvation you will give in the future to those who love your law. And because of that hope in the New Law, I observed out of love the precepts added to the precepts of the Old Testament.

My soul kept your testimonies. For the sake of the same hope, my soul kept your testimonies, that is, the precepts of the Old Law, which bear witness to the New Law. He says that his soul kept them because keeping them according to [Col. 0765A] the flesh is of little value; and I loved them, namely, the testimonies, exceedingly, with the fervor of my entire intention.

I kept your commandments. And that I loved your new commandments and kept your ancient testimonies, I do not attribute to myself. Rather, I kept them because all my ways, whether in thought or in action, were in your sight, that is, in accordance with your good pleasure and dependent upon your help.

**TAU.**—“Let my supplication draw near before you, O Lord; according to your word give me understanding. Let my petition enter before you; according to your word rescue me. My lips shall pour forth a hymn when you teach me your ordinances. My tongue shall proclaim your word, because all your commandments are righteousness. May your hand [Col. 0765B] be there to save me, because I have chosen your commandments. I desired your salvation, O Lord, and your law is my meditation. My soul shall live and shall praise you, and your judgments shall help me. I have gone astray like a sheep that has perished; seek your servant, because I have not forgotten your commandments.”

**EXPOSITION.**

This faithful man who speaks here, having climbed to such sublimity, considers that he went astray in Adam and, when he had descended from Jerusalem, fell among robbers. Although the true shepherd had already left the ninety-nine sheep in the desert and carried back on his shoulders the one that had perished (Luke XV), he nevertheless does not yet see himself restored to that perfection from which he fell, and therefore prays to be brought back to his former state.

Earlier [Col. 0765C] in this psalm, where it says, “My soul clung to the pavement,” the phrase “he went astray” is also found; but there the error is understood as occurring after baptism, whereas here it occurs before baptism. He therefore prays that God grant him an understanding of truth, and he gives this as the sign that his prayer has been heard: once heard, he will proclaim and pour forth a hymn to the Lord.

Let my supplication draw near. O Lord, I who have kept your commandments and your testimonies ask that my supplication, made before you—that is, concerning the things for which supplication must be made—may draw near to you. Specifically, I ask that you give me understanding according to your word, that is, according to the way in which I have kept your precepts.

Alternatively: “Let my supplication draw near,” that is, make me draw near through good living to the homeland from which I justly went astray through the disobedience of Adam and Eve.

Let my petition enter. In the present give me understanding; in the future let my petition [Col. 0765D] enter, where it is said, “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV), before you—that is, having been made or accomplished in the heart, where you alone see it. Specifically, let this petition enter: that according to your promise, which you gave to those who observe your precepts, you rescue me from this punishment of sin, that is, from mortality and the capacity to suffer, and from everlasting condemnation.

My lips shall pour forth. Give me understanding, because when you teach me your ordinances, that is, when you give me perfect knowledge of and ability to carry out your commandments, my lips shall pour forth a hymn, that is, through the abundance of benefits they shall offer you praise. This means the fullness of your law, which is in my heart. My lips also [Col. 0766A] will hymn you inwardly, but nevertheless with an audible voice.

My tongue shall proclaim. I shall not merely praise you inwardly, on the summit of my lips, out of the fullness of my mind; my tongue also shall proclaim your word by preaching to others. And I am not ashamed to announce your Gospel, because all your commandments are righteousness, that is, true and just.

May your hand be there. Since I shall proclaim your word without shame, I know that I shall suffer many adversities. Therefore may your hand, that is, your protection, be upon me to save me, lest I succumb in tribulations.

Alternatively: because a great multitude of visible and invisible enemies will attack me on account of proclaiming your word, let your hand—that is, let a multitude of the heavenly host—come to my aid for salvation against the multitude attacking me [Col. 0766B]. And therefore may your hand be there to save me, because above all else I have chosen your commandments.

I desired your salvation. Your hand must also be there to save me, Lord, because I desired your salvation, that is, the salvation you will give. And I desired it as I ought, because your law is my meditation, and through prior meditation I fulfilled your law.

My soul shall live. I desired your salvation, and it will truly come to me. This is what he says: “My soul shall live and shall praise you,” as it is said elsewhere, “They shall praise you forever and ever” (Ps. LXXXIII). And your judgments, that is, the scourges I suffer by your just judgment, shall help my soul live and help me reach the homeland, cleansing the stains of the past and making me cautious concerning the future, so that I may not offend again.

I have gone astray like a sheep. So that my soul may finally live there, as I desire and trust through your mercy, not only may a multitude of angels come to save me, but you yourself seek me after the manner of a good shepherd. This is necessary for me because I have gone astray like a sheep that had perished.

You have already sought me. And it is necessary that you continue to seek me for as long as life is lived here. Therefore you ought to seek me because I am your servant, and because I have not forgotten your commandments, that is, from the time I believed and came to know your commandments, I faithfully carried out what you commanded.

**PSALM 119. SONG OF ASCENTS.**

“To the Lord, when I was afflicted, I cried, and he heard me. O Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips [Col. 0766D] and from a deceitful tongue. What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, for a deceitful tongue? The sharp arrows of the mighty one, together with desolating coals. Alas for me, because my sojourn has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar, and my soul has been a long-time sojourner. With those who hate peace I was peaceful; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause.”

**EXPOSITION.**
First, it must be considered why the degrees designated by these psalms are said to number fifteen rather than ten or twenty. In Solomon’s Temple there were fifteen steps arranged by which the high priest ascended to the Holy of Holies, entering it once a year [Col. 0767A] (Exod. XXX; Heb. IX). That temple is the Church, in which all the faithful exist according to the mysteries of faith. Those steps are the virtues by which faithful souls ascend and advance to the true holy places, into the house not made with hands, which remains in the heavens, where the Lord Jesus has already been placed at the right hand of God the Father. He alone entered there, because he received a unique exaltation and deserved to be exalted uniquely. The multitude of the faithful also ascends there by these fifteen steps, because the more advanced and higher they are in the virtues, the nearer they are to the heavenly homeland; the more they approach the Holy of Holies—not in place, but in the likeness of their life.

Fifteen is composed of eight and seven. By seven, however, the Old Testament is understood, because of the Sabbath [Col. 0767B], concerning the observance of which a commandment was given in the Law. Alternatively, by seven this present world may be understood, since it revolves from its beginning through seven days. And because observance of the Old Testament looked toward a temporal and transitory reward—it was undertaken for safety, length of life, abundance of children, victory, and other temporal benefits—the Old Testament belonged to the number seven and to the things of this world. Therefore it is rightly understood through seven.

By eight, however, the New Testament is signified, because of the eighth day on which our Lord rose again, where the beginning and confirmation of the New Testament took place. He is therefore said to have risen on the eighth day, not the first, because he did not rise for these days that revolve through the number seven, but rather [Col. 0767C] into eternal and unfailing life: that is, into eternity and into the eighth day that will come after the passing of these seven days, and that will be nothing other than eternity. Alternatively, the New Testament may be understood through the number eight because all our labor and all our good activity—that is, observance of the New Testament—looks toward the eighth day and the future reward.

The carrying out, therefore, of the commandments of both the Old and the New Testament is designated by fifteen steps, by which faithful souls are granted ascent to the true Holy of Holies. Through seven we shall also reach eight, because through all our good works performed in this temporal life we shall finally reach the eighth day, that is, the perpetuity of the heavenly homeland.

Among us, “step” signifies both descent and ascent [Col. 0767D]. Therefore, by “step” we must not understand descent, but ascent alone. These psalms, which are called Songs of Ascents and number fifteen, were not made in imitation of the steps that existed in Solomon’s Temple, since David preceded Solomon by a long time and sang these psalms, as well as the others, in praise of God. Rather, those steps were established by Solomon in imitation of the same virtues that are signified by the number of these psalms, because the same Spirit who taught David to sing these psalms mystically concerning the angels also taught Solomon to foreshow, through a certain prefiguration of things, the same mysteries that were later to be enacted in the house of God, which is the Church.

This psalm is called [Col. 0768A] a Song of Ascents, that is, one among many steps. They are called songs because everything designated in these psalms pertains to the future reward, where joy is everlasting. By using the plural “of ascents,” he indicates the multiplicity, conjunction, and coherence of the virtues, until one reaches the Holy of Holies, the kingdom of eternal glory.

Those faithful, therefore, whose way of life is in heaven (Phil. III), who have already reached the highest step, report here to others the steps of their ascent and their advancement in the virtues, so that the others may follow them in ascending and imitate them in the advancement of virtue, until what is said above is fulfilled in them: “They will go from strength to strength; the God of gods will be seen in Zion” (Ps. LXXXIII).

It should be understood, however, that sometimes a step proceeds from one virtue to another virtue, and sometimes it is founded in the same virtue, because in each virtue we can be more or less slack or intense. The first step is prayer for the foundation of faith. It seems to be of this kind: those who are already in the temple, in the Church of God through faith, pray that knowledge of the Scriptures and the authority of the holy Fathers may be granted to them, for the confirmation of their faith against the faithlessness of blasphemers and the attacks of heretics.

## “To the Lord, when I was in distress, I cried out”

When I was troubled by the blasphemous words of unbelievers and by the attack of heretics, who were attempting to shake my true faith from me, I cried out to the Lord, who could strengthen me; and I was not disappointed, because he heard me. He says this [Col. 0768C] by way of anticipation, so as to urge his hearers more strongly to cry out, as though he were saying: “When such distress comes upon you, cry out after my example, and the Lord will hear you.”

## “Lord, deliver my soul”

Therefore I cried out, saying: “O Lord, who are powerful, deliver my soul, which exists in the uprightness of faith and already lives through the mystery of faith, from lying lips”—that is, from the blasphemous words of the faithless, who openly attack your faith—“and from a deceitful tongue,” that is, from the words of heretics, lest their hidden poison infect it. They mix many true and useful things with falsehood so that they may deceive more easily.

## “What shall be given to you?”

Before I cried out, before I prayed to the Lord for deliverance, I deliberated and meditated within myself, wondering at the magnitude of the danger and saying: “O my soul, what shall be given to you against a deceitful tongue?” [Col. 0768D] That is: what weapons can be given to you with which to overcome a deceitful tongue? Or, if you are not given anything by which you can overcome it, then at least what—what protection—can be placed upon you so that you are not killed?

He seeks protection against the heretics’ deceitful tongue because the danger and the difficulty of defense are greater where deceit is practiced than where one is attacked openly.

## “The sharp arrows of the mighty one”

When I considered that such weapons could be given to me, I thought of “the sharp arrows of the mighty one,” that is, the declarations of sacred Scripture and knowledge of the words of God. These are sharp and effective for piercing the hearts of enemies. They are sharp not only in themselves, but also because they belong to the mighty one, that is, because they have been directed by almighty God [Col. 0769A].

This was said from an analogy: if someone skilled in archery shoots arrows, they are effective for killing; but if an unskilled person shoots, then, although the arrows are good in themselves, they are ineffective.

These arrows, I say, of the mighty one can be given to me “with coals that do not go out, but devastate,” that is, coals that destroy and set ablaze. These are the life and authority of the holy Fathers—namely, the apostles and other teachers—who are not extinguished coals in the face of the attacks of heretics, but burn with the fire of the Holy Spirit and set fire to and devastate every heresy.

And if both of these cannot be given to you, O soul, then at least let the authority of the holy Fathers, which is more useful, be placed at your disposal for your defense.

## “Woe is me”

He continues to show [Col. 0769B] the magnitude of the danger. “I cried out,” I say, and it is necessary that you hear and deliver me, because “woe is me”—that is, I am in pain—because my sojourning, that is, my pilgrimage, during which I am kept away from my homeland, seems to me to have been excessively prolonged.

Yet I do not grieve merely because of my sojourning, but because “I dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar,” that is, with those who suffer the darkness of ignorance in such a way that they remain in it and almost inhabit it. And lest anyone think that he is speaking of the sojourning of the body, he adds: “My soul has been a long-time sojourner,” that is, before I cried out and prayed for deliverance, it was far removed from its homeland.

And in order that I might approach the true Holy of Holies and the homeland promised to all the faithful, it was necessary for me to cry out, to possess sharp arrows and devastating coals, so that [Col. 0769C] my soul might return to itself from such great forgetfulness of itself, and might direct its eyes, raised above the deceptions of this world, toward the true homeland and draw nearer and nearer to it.

All souls here are sojourners, that is, pilgrims; but those whose way of life is in heaven (Phil. III) do not wander as far as the others.

## “With those who hate peace”

And I do not say “woe is me” only because I dwelt with them, but because they hated me, although I was peaceable with them—a very difficult circumstance. They not only hated me, but also attacked me with words, because I had not yet ascended to the torments. And they did this “without cause,” that is, I had deserved it in no way.

Or “without cause” means “in vain,” because they were unable to overcome me.

## “When I spoke to them”

That is, when I gave them admonitions of salvation [Col. 0769D].

# PSALM 120. SONG OF ASCENTS

> “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where help will come to me. My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. May he not allow your foot to be moved, and may he who guards you not sleep. Behold, he will neither slumber nor sleep, he who guards Israel. The Lord guards you; the Lord is your protection over your right hand. By day the sun will not burn you, nor the moon by night. The Lord guards you from every evil; may the Lord guard your soul. May the Lord guard your entering and your going out, from this time forth and forever.”

## EXPOSITION

In the preceding step, placed in danger, he cried out for the sake of the faith. In this one, having already obtained certainty of faith, he says that he has been heard, both in the knowledge of sacred Scripture and in the authority of the holy Fathers [Col. 0770A].

## “I lifted up my eyes”

I am the one who cried out to the Lord in distress. Having been heard, I lifted up the eyes of my mind, previously weighed down by ignorance and lack of an example, toward the mountains—that is, toward the teaching or life of the mountains, namely, the prophets and apostles—from whom help comes and will come to me. For no one makes such progress in the divine page that he cannot always progress more and more.

## “My help is from the Lord”

Although I have said that help comes to me from these people, nevertheless my help must rather be said to be from the Lord [Col. 0770B], who made heaven and earth—that is, who made them heaven and me earth.

Or, “who made the greater and the lesser.”

## “May he not allow [your foot] to be moved”

Now, turning to his hearers or to himself, he prays that God may make him steadfast in the confirmation of faith, saying: “May the Lord not allow your foot to be moved,” that is, may he not permit your affection—or your faith—to be changed. And may he who guards you in perseverance not sleep, that is, may he not allow you to waver or to be dull in that very faith.

## “Behold, he will neither slumber”

As I prayed, so it will certainly be. He who guards Israel—that is, those who see God and believe in him—“behold,” that is, in the present and without delay, as may be proved and recognized, “will not slumber,” that is, he will not allow you to waver; “nor will he sleep,” that is, he will not permit [Col. 0770C] you to fail in tribulations.

## “The Lord guards you”

He truly guards you. This can be proved from the fact that the Lord himself is powerful in events to accomplish this, and that he himself is your protection against attacks.

He not only strengthened you in faith, but will also exist “over your right hand,” that is, over your endurance and your faith, for which you will be placed at the right hand of God. It is called yours because you will enjoy it.

Or, “existing over the hand” means existing over activity; and he defines this by adding “your right hand,” that is, over good activity, in which he will protect you in perseverance.

## “By day the sun will not burn you”

He will guard you in such a way that the sun will not burn you by day. That is, Christ, who is the true sun in respect of the illumination of his divinity, will not darken you—that is, he will not permit you to be scandalized in faith and in your understanding of his divinity, so that you do not hold a sound view of it [Col. 0770D].

Nor will the moon—that is, the same Christ, who is called the moon in respect of his humanity, which was mortal and capable of suffering—burn you by night, that is, in your faith concerning his humanity, so that you do not hold anything improper concerning either nature.

## “The Lord guards you from every evil”

The Lord will guard you not only from heresy concerning the nature of his divinity and humanity, but also from every evil of this world, or from every heresy or faithlessness, so that you may hold no perverse opinion either concerning the mysteries of the Church or concerning the resurrection of the dead and other matters.

And if you suffer anything according to the body for the observance of the faith, the Lord will guard your soul.

## “May the Lord guard your entering”

And just as I have proclaimed, so may it be. May the Lord guard your entering—that is, your faith, through which you entered the Church—and your going out from faith into death. That is, may he guard you especially at the end, because the gravest temptations usually occur especially near the end.

“May he guard” means that he begins this guardianship from this time forth, that is, from the present moment, and continues it forever, that is, until the end of the present life.

# PSALM 121. SONG OF ASCENTS

> “I rejoiced in the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord. Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem. Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose participation is in the same thing. For the tribes went up there, the tribes of the Lord, the testimony of Israel, to give praise to the name of the Lord. For there thrones were set for judgment, thrones over the house of David. Pray for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem, and abundance for those who love you. Let there be peace in your strength, and abundance in your towers. For the sake of my brothers and my neighbors, I was speaking peace concerning you. For the sake of the house of the Lord our God, I sought good things for you.”

## EXPOSITION

This person, ascending after the confirmation of faith, says that he has ascended as far as hope—not because hope is a higher step than faith, but because the person who possesses both, that is, faith and hope, is higher than one who possesses only one of them. The same should be understood of the remaining steps [Col. 0771C].

## “I rejoiced”

After I had been so fortified in faith that I not only did not fail but also attacked blasphemers and heretics, I rejoiced—that is, I had an increased hope—in the things that were said to me. That is, I rejoiced in considering the promise made to me by the prophets, apostles, and other holy men, who said: “We shall go into the house of the Lord,” that is, “We shall reach the heavenly Jerusalem.”

When he says “to me,” he indicates the unity of all the faithful. When he says “we shall go,” he understands the multitude of those who ascend.

## “Our feet were standing”

We were so certain that we would go into the house of the Lord that our feet—that is, our affections and thoughts—were standing, that is, remaining firmly, in your courts, O Jerusalem. This means in the breadth of your glory, where no one will be cramped by another’s possession, but all will possess the kingdom spaciously and abundantly.

## “Jerusalem, which is built”

Lest anyone think that he is speaking of earthly Jerusalem, he specifies which Jerusalem he means. I speak of the courts of that Jerusalem which is still being built daily “as a city,” that is, after the manner of some earthly city. For just as some city is built from inanimate stones, so that city is built from living stones, who are sent there each day.

Having made this specification, he commends the city itself. Its participation is in that reality which tends toward the same thing, that is, toward unity. All who participate in it seek the same reality, namely Christ, who will be the supreme good, and all will receive the same denarius.

## “For the tribes went up there”

I have this certainty that we shall go into the house of the Lord, that is, into the Jerusalem above the heavens, because the tribes that are of the same condition and composition as we are went up there. For they follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Apoc. XIV).

And it was not just any tribes, but “the tribes of the Lord”; the Lord was “the testimony of Israel,” that is, he testified to Jacob that human beings would ascend into heaven through the vision of the ladder, in which he saw angels ascending and descending (Gen. XXVIII).

He specifies why the tribes went up: namely, to give praise to the glory of God, whose sight and praise are for them the highest glory and rest.

## “For there thrones were set”

This also is an argument for my ascending there: there, in the heavenly Jerusalem, those who will be thrones—that is, judges at the future judgment—have already rested, namely, the apostles and the other saints [Col. 0772B]. “Over the house of David,” I say, thrones will sit; that is, those who are the thrones of God will sit judging the faithful, for the unbelieving have already been judged.

By “tribes” we understand the less perfect; by “thrones,” the perfect.

## “Pray for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem”

After these ascending persons, who here act as exhorters of their hearers, had demonstrated the certainty of their hope, namely, of reaching Jerusalem—both on account of the tribes and on account of the thrones that have already ascended—they now pray to the tribes and thrones themselves to intercede for them, so that they too may eventually reach that place. They say:

“Pray for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem,” that is, pray for things capable of bringing us to the rest that leads into Jerusalem. Obtain these things for us through prayers before God: ask that he grant us such merits that, by doing good, we may deserve to ascend into the heavenly Jerusalem.

In this way the heresy of those who said that the saints should not be entreated is destroyed. They claimed that the saints did not know what was happening here around their dust, although even demons are of such lightness and speed that they can be almost in the same moment both here and in Babylon. The efficacy of this must be believed much more strongly of the souls of the saints: the happier they are than the demons, the more perceptive they are.

## “And abundance for those who love you”

You, I say, saints of God, pray that God may grant us the things that are for peace and that are effective for attaining the blessedness that is in the homeland above the heavens.

And we also pray for ourselves and for all others in this way: “O Jerusalem, may there be an abundance of peace for all who love you.” That is, may every good thing come to those who, through true love, prefer to inhabit you.

## “Let there be peace in your strength”

Now he explains what kind of abundance he is asking for. “Let there be peace,” he says, that is, true rest, “in your strength,” that is, in Christ, who is your author and your strength. Let there be peace for us in such a way that we may be conformed to him.

And let there be abundance in your towers, that is, let there be for us such peace as existed in your towers, that is, in the apostles. This belongs to the most perfect, who pour out this reasoning for the instruction of others, so that they too may ascend through prayer.

## “For the sake of my brothers”

Here he shows the intention of his prayer. It is as though he were saying: “O Jerusalem, when I spoke concerning you, that is, when I announced the peace that exists in you, I did not do so for my own sake, but for the sake of my brothers” [Col. 0773A]—namely, the other, less perfect faithful—“and my neighbors,” that is, those more perfect persons who love me with mutual charity and imitate me in goodness, for the sake of the house of the Lord.

He shows why he sought good things for Jerusalem: namely, because it is the house of the Lord. It is as though he said: “For the sake of building the house of the Lord our God”—that is, for the sake of the faithful from whom the house of the Lord is constructed and in whom he himself dwells—“I sought good things for you, O Jerusalem,” that is, I labored to bring citizens to you. From this, joy would be increased for the honor of your magnificence, which is good.

# PSALM 122. SONG OF ASCENTS

> “To you I lifted up my eyes, who dwell in the heavens. Behold, as the eyes of servants are toward the hands of their masters, as the eyes of a maidservant are toward the hands of her mistress, so are our eyes toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us. Have mercy on us, Lord, have mercy on us, because we have been filled exceedingly with contempt. Because our soul has been filled exceedingly with reproach for the prosperous and contempt for the proud.”

## EXPOSITION

After certainty comes hope as a step, so that those who hope to reach the heavenly Jerusalem may direct the eyes of their mind—which they had previously lifted toward the mountains—toward the Lord himself and toward fulfilling the will of the king of that same city. Therefore this faithful person, speaking in the person of all the faithful, shows that he is at the same step by saying:

## “To you I lifted up my eyes, who dwell in the heavens”

O Lord, who rule and inhabit the heavenly creatures or holy human beings—your grace having made them heavens—so that I might reach peace and the dwelling above the heavens, I lifted up my eyes to you. That is, I turned the reasoning of my mind and all my affections away from the temporal fantasies of this world, directing them toward the fulfillment of your will [Col. 0773C].

## “Behold, as the eyes of servants”
