Now these ascending persons speak sometimes in the singular and sometimes in the plural: they are many and one. They are many according to the diversity of persons, but one according to faith and love.

I truly lifted up my eyes to you, because, behold—that is, in the present or openly—our inner eyes are raised toward the Lord our God until he has mercy on us. That is, until he releases us from the misery of this present age, makes us recline, and, passing by, ministers to us.

Thus, I say, our eyes are directed toward the Lord as the eyes of disciplined servants, who watch with careful attention the hands of their masters. This is said from the analogy of trained servants, who look very attentively at their masters’ hands so that, when they give signs that something is to be done, they may immediately obey.

## “As the eyes of a maidservant are toward the hands of her mistress”

He mentions maidservants because in them there is greater diligence and service toward their mistresses than in male servants.

In this way, after the manner of such servants or maidservants, all our affection is intent on carrying out the Lord’s will, until, released from the burden of our present servitude, he transfers us [Col. 0774A] into the kingdom of his freedom.

## “Have mercy on us, Lord”

And may you do this, Lord: have mercy on us, at some time leading us into freedom. He repeats “have mercy on us” because it is not enough to say once what he desires very greatly to happen.

And it is necessary that you have mercy, because we are greatly contemptible in the eyes of people who make us objects of ridicule and contempt. “Because our soul has been filled exceedingly”—not merely according to the body are we contemptible, but our soul has been filled exceedingly with contempt, because they regard us as foolish and insane.

He explains how they are objects of contempt: our soul is a reproach to the prosperous, that is, to the wealthy of this age, when they see us poor; and it is a contempt to the proud, who despise us on account of our humility.

# PSALM 123. SONG OF ASCENTS

> “If the Lord had not been among us, let Israel now say, if the Lord had not been among us, when people rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive. When their fury was enraged against us, perhaps water would have swallowed us. Our soul passed through the torrent; perhaps our soul would have passed through unbearable water. Blessed is the Lord, who did not give us as prey to their teeth. Our soul, like a sparrow, has been rescued from the snare of the hunters. The snare has been broken, and we have been set free. Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

## EXPOSITION

Here the same multitude of the faithful speaks again. It no longer offers an example as above, but simply admonishes us that, after someone has ascended to hope and has become so steadfast through the fulfillment of God’s commandments that he cannot be moved from it, even though many people may be calling him away through their malicious attacks, he should ascribe that steadfastness to the Lord, not to his own strength.

The holy confessors of Christ, remembering that, through the Lord’s mercy, they escaped dangers like the force of a torrent, confess that they have been delivered from so many hardships by God’s mercy alone, and they say:

## “If the Lord had not been among us”

Whoever is Israel—that is, whoever sees God, so that he has advanced toward the homeland through faith and the fulfillment of God’s commandments—should say, that is, should think and understand within himself now, without delay [Col. 0774D], that if the Lord were not among us, governing and strengthening us, illuminating our reason with his light and strengthening our mind, then, when people who walk according to the flesh rose up against us, they would have swallowed us alive with flattering and deceitful words.

That is, they would have incorporated us into themselves, even though we were prudent and knowledgeable. Although we knew that their sect was detestable, we would nevertheless have agreed with them. This would have happened like something that perhaps occurs—that is, recklessly and unexpectedly, as far as human beings are concerned.

For although we might have been prudent, we would not have been able to provide for ourselves when their fury was enraged against us.

And unless the Lord were among us, when they were raging inwardly and outwardly became angry against us with malicious and slanderous words, perhaps—that is, as it seems to us—water would have swallowed us. This means either that they themselves, flowing away into various desires and dissolving others, would have swallowed us, or that their slanders and harsh words, which were like violent water, would have submerged the stability of our mind and weakened our footing when they had called us into agreement with their wickedness [Col. 0775A].

## “Our soul passed through the torrent”

As far as we ourselves were concerned, we would not have been able to stand. But because the Lord was among us, our soul, whose danger was at issue, passed through the torrent. That is, it attacked those deceitful and slanderous people who were pressing upon us vehemently. I say that it passed through, and perhaps it would have passed through.

They speak doubtfully because of the magnitude of the danger, as though they were still afraid.

## “Perhaps our soul would have passed through unbearable water”

Our soul would perhaps have passed through water unbearable in relation to our strength, that is, through their attack, which was intent on drowning us and which we would not have been able to endure by our own powers.

## “Blessed is the Lord”

And since our soul passed through them, let the Lord be blessed—that is, glorified and exalted—because he did not give us as prey to their teeth. That is, he did not permit us to succumb to their malicious attacks and slanders.

## “Our soul, like a sparrow”

We not only escaped their attacks, but our soul, cautious like a sparrow that escapes both snares and the attacks of other birds, was rescued from the snare of the hunters, that is, from the tricks and flatteries of those who were hunting us.

No bird is more cunning than a sparrow in avoiding snares. In its likeness, our soul, being cunning and cautious, wisely passed beyond the snares prepared for it, always striving upward with the lofty and eternal swiftness of the mind and with spiritual reasoning. It was rescued from the crafty and deceitful words by which they attempted to ensnare and overthrow us [Col. 0775C].

And we were rescued for this reason: the snare of their deception was broken and rendered ineffective. That is, from now on they will cease to oppose us with malicious and deceitful words.

## “Our help”

And the fact that we had such help did not arise from our merits, but “in the name of the Lord,” that is, in his mercy, from which he himself is to be glorified.

The Lord, I say, who was fully able to help us, because he made heaven and earth. That is, he made both those who, already ascending to the highest step, have become heavens and those who, placed lower down in the ascent, have not yet entirely ceased to be earthly [Col. 0775D].

# PSALM 124. SONG OF ASCENTS

> “Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; whoever dwells in Jerusalem will not be moved forever. Mountains surround it, and the Lord surrounds his people, from this time forth and forever. For the Lord will not leave the scepter of sinners over the lot of the righteous, so that the righteous do not stretch out their hands toward iniquity. Do good, Lord, to those who are good and upright in heart. But those who turn aside into obligations, the Lord will lead away with those who practice iniquity. Peace be upon Israel.”

## EXPOSITION

After these ascending persons attribute to God, not to themselves, the fact that they were not swallowed and absorbed, they advance still farther—namely, to contempt for temporal things. Thus they place all their confidence, which is even more certain than hope, in the Lord, and their way of life is in Jerusalem.

By their example they instruct others in this, promising them the benefit that will come from it: that they will be fortified by God both inwardly and outwardly [Col. 0776A].

## “Those who trust in the Lord”

All those who trust in the Lord and place hope and confidence in him—not in riches and nobility, but in the Lord—possess complete confidence. None of those who dwell in Jerusalem, that is, whose way of life is in heaven (Phil. III), will ever be moved, however greatly he may be attacked.

He will not be moved forever “like Mount Zion,” that is, like Christ, who is the strength and refuge of the Church, which looks toward the future and puts aside the present.

## “Mountains surround it”

He will not be moved because mountains—that is, the apostles—are around it, fortifying it by preaching, by example, and also by intercession. This is said from the analogy of a city situated among mountains, against which an attack cannot easily be made.

And not only are mountains around it, but the Lord himself is around his people, in their defense. He will persevere in this, beginning from this very moment and continuing to the end of life, in accordance with the saying: “Behold, I am with you all days” (Matt. XXVIII).

## “For the Lord will not leave the scepter of sinners”

He will truly not be moved, because the Lord will not leave the scepter—that is, the authority and dominion—of sinners over the lot, that is, over the election, of the righteous; namely, over the righteous themselves, who are God’s elect.

That is, he will not permit them to labor beyond their strength, as the Apostle says: “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear” (1 Cor. X).

And he will not leave the scepter of sinners over the righteous to such an extent that the righteous—not, I say, that they will not sin, but that they will not stretch out their hands, that is, their affections, toward iniquity—will have no desire to sin.

## “Do good, Lord”

Now, for the instruction of the hearers, whom they invite to ascend in conformity with themselves, they pour out a prayer so that the hearers too may ascend through prayer, saying:

“O Lord, do good to those who are good,” that is, to those who do good, so that they may persevere; and to those who are upright in heart, that is, the innocent, so that they may remain so [Col. 0776D].

## “But those who turn aside into obligations”

And truly the Lord will do good to those who are good. But those who turn aside into obligations—that is, into sins by which people are bound as if by a chain—or into obligations understood as the persuasions of sinners, the Lord will lead away with those who practice iniquity.

That is, he will condemn them to the same punishment as the workers of iniquity, namely, those who call them away.

The Lord who does these things is the one who, being peace over Israel, will reward those who see him and place their hope in him with eternal rest.

# PSALM 125. SONG OF ASCENTS

> “When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are comforted. Then our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation. Then they will say among the nations: The Lord has done great things for them. The Lord has done great things for us; we became joyful. Turn back our captivity, Lord, like a torrent in the south. Those who sow in tears will reap in exultation. Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds. But coming, they will come with exultation, carrying their sheaves.”

## EXPOSITION

After contempt for temporal things, there is still a higher step: after the turning back of captivity, it becomes free and joyful for them to do good.

For many people set aside all temporal things and do good, yet doing good is not joyful or pleasurable for them. Perhaps, if punishment and reward did not follow, they would cease from doing good.

In some of these steps, however, these ascending persons set themselves forward as an example; in others, they simply exhort. In both ways they act.

When the Lord turned the captivity of Zion—that is, the bondage of us who had previously served under compulsion and necessity, like captives—into freedom and joyful willingness, we who contemplate the future became like those consoled.

The captivity of Zion existed when the wickedness of the persecutors oppressed the Church of God, which at first was confined to a few. But it was converted into freedom when, through the regard of divine mercy, even the rulers received the faith, and believers were then permitted freely to render service to Christ. The conversion of this captivity made very many so joyful and delighted that they now took pleasure in doing good as though of their own free will. Here the removal of sadness itself is called consolation. Hence it says: “We became like those consoled,” because however great the consolation may be here, it is only like a shadow and a certain likeness of the future consolation.

“Then it was filled.” And not only did we become like those receiving consolation in that conversion of captivity into freedom, but then—that is, at the same time as the conversion—our mouth, namely our inward self, was filled with joy. And our tongue, too, being outward, could not conceal it in exultation.

“Then they shall say among the nations.” But the wicked do not recognize that so great a freedom and grace has been granted to us here. But then—that is, in the future, when they will not be able to conceal it—they shall say among the nations, that is, those who lived here in a pagan manner, whether wicked Christians or unbelievers. Or even here, some among the nations, observing religion flourishing among the Christian people and various good gifts of grace abounding in the saints, shall say: “We thought them mad” (Wis. V), “but the Lord has magnified his doing with them.” The Lord does good with his own insofar as he makes them do good; but he magnifies his doing with them when he makes doing good pleasurable and spontaneous.

“The Lord has magnified.” This is what will be said among the nations. And truly the Lord has magnified his doing with us, just as they say: “We became like those who rejoice,” that is, through the joy of the Lord we fulfill the commandments.

“Convert, O Lord.” They turn themselves to prayer, exhorting each person who ascends to do the same, saying: “O Lord, convert our captivity into freedom.” Lest anyone think that this conversion of captivity had occurred in such a way that it could not be intensified and increased, he adds:

“Although we say that your doing with us, O Lord, has been magnified, nevertheless we pray: convert our captivity more and more into freedom, because as long as we remain in this life, we continually need to be converted more and more into freedom.” Freedom, I say, existing “like a torrent in the south.” When the south wind blows, ice and snow melt into a torrent, because it drives away every obstacle. In the same way, hearts breathed upon by the warmth of the Holy Spirit are released from the ice of vices into freedom, because, driving away all the impediments of this world, it rushes with the greatest force toward the homeland.

Someone might say: “You are praying for a freedom in which you will suffer very many tribulations.” Or: “What kind of freedom is that in which you endure so many tribulations?” To this you reply: “What concern is that of mine? If I sow in tears, I shall reap in joy,” because all who sow in tears—that is, who do good amid tribulations—“shall reap in exultation,” that is, they shall receive the fruit of good works in return for what they labored at here.

“They went on their way.” And so that we may sow in tears, we have an authority in those who preceded us, namely the holy martyrs who went toward death. And he specifies how they went: “They went and wept,” that is, “sowing their seeds in tears,” namely their good works.

“But coming.” Thus they went toward death, as we have said, but, coming from death into life, they shall come not in just any manner, but “with exultation,” in contrast to the tears they shed here, “carrying their sheaves,” that is, receiving the reward of their good works.

## Psalm 126. A Song of Ascents, of Solomon

> Unless the Lord builds the house,  
> those who build it labor in vain.  
> Unless the Lord guards the city,  
> the one who guards it keeps watch in vain.  
> It is vain for you to rise before dawn;  
> rise after you have sat down,  
> you who eat the bread of sorrow.  
> When he gives his beloved sleep,  
> behold, the Lord’s inheritance: sons;  
> the reward, the fruit of the womb.  
> Like arrows in the hand of the mighty,  
> so are the sons of those who shake out [spoils].  
> Blessed is the man who has fulfilled his desire through them;  
> he shall not be put to shame  
> when he speaks with his enemies at the gate.

[Col. 0778D]

### Exposition

This Song of Ascents is Solomon’s warning, that is, it recalls his downfall. Solomon was of such great eminence that the Holy Spirit spoke through his mouth, and he built the Lord’s temple in a wisdom surpassing all human beings; yet he fell, and not in just any way, but into idolatry. Through the exhortation concerning what is done here, he warns everyone that, even if after despising temporal things one ascends so far as to do good out of love (Gal. V), one should nevertheless not presume in any way to promise oneself security unless one has first passed through the sitting-down, that is, unless one has brought one’s humility to an appropriate conclusion—especially since a man of such dignity and wisdom fell so criminally. The subject here is security at the eighth degree because there is no security before one reaches the eighth.

“Unless the Lord builds the house.” The same people who spoke above address their hearers here for their instruction, as if saying:

“After you have ascended as far as we have said, do not presume upon your own guardianship, as though you could preserve the good that is in you, since you could not previously have done it unless God were working in you. For unless the Lord builds the house”—that is, unless he first establishes someone as a dwelling for himself and builds that person’s soul, which ought to be God’s house, through the beginnings of good works—“those who build it labor in vain,” that is, they would have labored in vain, both superiors who preach and subjects who obey. “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (I Cor. III).

“Unless the Lord guards the city.” Once you have been built up and have gathered a multitude of virtues as fellow citizens, do not, as was said, presume upon your own ability to guard them. For unless the Lord guards the city—that is, the soul in which the virtues are contained like citizens—the one who guards it watches in vain, that is, the person who applies himself to guarding it by his own power, whether preacher or one preached to, is anxiously and fruitlessly concerned.

“It is vain for you.” And since the city cannot be guarded except by the Lord, it is therefore vain for you to rise—that is, to promise yourselves security—“before dawn,” that is, before the clear and universally visible reward that will exist at the general resurrection. And lest anyone think that this prostration must last forever, he adds: “Rise after you have sat down,” that is, then be secure, when this sitting and prostration of yours—namely mortality and susceptibility to suffering—has come to an end.

Yet he does not say that even then they can be secure unless they are guarded by the Lord. But that guardianship will then be very different from this one, since they will then be so firmly established that they will have neither the will nor the desire to sin, just as the angels do not.

The phrase “rise after you have sat down” is spoken by comparison with the condemned, who in the midst of the judgment are ordered to sit on the ground until sentence is also passed concerning the others, so that they too may be condemned.

“Then,” I say, “rise,” that is, “be secure”—you, namely, “who eat the bread of sorrow.” As if he were saying: “Even then I do not promise security to everyone, but only to you who eat the bread of sorrow,” that is, to those for whom the present and continuous tribulation, in comparison with heavenly things, is a pleasure and refreshment, like bread, which is continual nourishment.

“When he gives his beloved sleep.” And as though they were anxious because of the long delay of their expectation and were saying, “When will it be that, after sitting down has ended, we may rise?” he says: “Then, when he gives his beloved”—that is, those predestined to life—“sleep,” that is, eternal rest.

And that rest is not delayed, but “behold”—that is, it is near and, as it were, manifest—“the Lord’s inheritance,” that is, the rest itself and its reward. For however much it may be delayed, nevertheless, in relation to the fact that afterward it will not change, it must already be called “behold,” because even if there are a hundred or a thousand years, it will still be soon in comparison with eternity.

When, therefore, the Lord gives his beloved sleep, that is, rest after the miseries of this life, behold, the Lord’s inheritance will immediately appear. And this inheritance will not be of just any kind, but “the reward of the Son,” that is, the reward will in its own manner be such as belongs to the one who is properly called the Son. In its own manner they will possess the same immortality and freedom from suffering as the Son of God, although they will possess them through that Son.

This is understood where it determines which son is meant: “sons,” I say, “the fruit of the womb,” that is, of the Son who deservedly is called “the fruit of the womb,” namely the fruitful birth from the virginal womb, from which the greatest fruit and the greatest benefit for the human race proceeded.

Hilary: “It is shown when those who were previously ordered to sit must rise—namely, at the time when the faithful are received into rest, for whom death is sleep and secure repose.”

“Behold, the Lord’s inheritance: sons,” namely of the Church, regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit. And these sons are “the reward of the fruit of the womb,” that is, of the birth from the virginal womb. The whole of his inheritance is called a reward: he rises and is sent into possession of the heavens, and he will rejoice in eternal happiness with the Lord. The reward is said to have been given to his humanity, concerning which the second Psalm also says: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.” His divinity, on the other hand, received nothing by which it might increase.

“Like arrows.” Since he had said above that those who build labor in vain and those who guard keep watch fruitlessly, lest preachers appear altogether crushed and worthless and become lukewarm through letting their hands fall, he consoles them in this way:

“Although I said, ‘It is vain for you to rise before dawn,’ nevertheless the sons of those who shake out [spoils]”—that is, those equipped to strip spoils, namely imitators of the apostles—“are like arrows placed in the hand of a mighty man,” with “archer” understood, because there they are very effective.

Those who shake out [spoils] are properly called those who keep watch around strongholds in order to free and strip spoils. In this way preachers are appointed to snatch souls from the power of the devil, by whom they have been taken captive. Or, those who shake out [grain] are threshers who beat the grain free from the chaff. This too refers to preachers.

“Blessed is the man who has fulfilled his desire through them.” Since the sons of those who shake out [spoils] are like arrows in the hand of a skilled archer, they are blessed. And not only are they themselves blessed, but every person is also blessed who fulfills in action the good will conceived through them, that is, through their examples and teaching.

He shows this blessedness in part, because such a person “shall not be put to shame” in any way “when he speaks with his enemies,” that is, heretics, persecutors, and the other people who contradict God, “at the gate,” that is, in public. This is said by comparison with a brave soldier who would come boldly to the gates of his enemies and speak with them there.

Or “at the gate,” that is, remaining in Christ himself and speaking the things that belong to Christ.

## Psalm 127. A Song of Ascents

[Col. 0781A]

> Blessed are all who fear the Lord,  
> who walk in his ways.  
> You shall eat the labors of your hands;  
> you are blessed, and it shall be well with you.  
> Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine  
> on the sides of your house.  
> Your sons shall be like olive shoots  
> around your table.  
> Behold, thus shall the man be blessed  
> who fears the Lord.  
> May the Lord bless you from Zion,  
> and may you see the good things of Jerusalem  
> all the days of your life.  
> And may you see your children’s children:  
> peace upon Israel.

### Exposition

Again the faithful, who were mentioned above, address those whom they have advanced to this degree, so that they may never promise themselves security as long as they are in this life. They exhort them to a higher degree, namely to fear—that is, to love—God. This love ought not to be idle, but they should walk in his ways. And they say how much blessedness a person attains through these things, both here and in the future.

“Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways.” All who fear the Lord with a true and chaste fear—that is, with the true love described above, in view of his benefits—and who thus walk and advance themselves in his commandments, are blessed.

“You shall eat the labors of your hands.” He proves that they are blessed because you, whoever you are, are blessed with present blessedness. And it shall be well with you in future blessedness, because you shall eat the labors of your hands, that is, the good works at which you labored here will be a delight to you; in other words, you will enjoy the reward of the good works in which you were diligent here.

And just as all those who fear the Lord are blessed, so you too, whoever you are whom I admonish, are blessed if you fear him.

“Your wife shall be like a vine.” He explains how a person is blessed in the present: namely, because your wife—that is, your sensuality, which you have properly subjected by marrying it to reason—will be like a vine abounding in the multiplicity of good works “on the sides of your house,” that is, in all the outward members of your body, just as a vine planted beside a house is more fertile and abundant than vines planted elsewhere.

“Your sons shall be like olive shoots.” You are also blessed in the present on this account: your sons, that is, your works, grow up toward perpetual peace, just as olive shoots grow into the mature olive tree, through which peace is signified.

“Your sons,” I say, “existing around your table,” that is, in relation to Christ, who is the table—that is, the refreshment—of our soul. This is said by comparison with a father who has a fertile wife and greatly rejoices in the many sons surrounding his table.

“Behold, thus shall the man be blessed.” After setting forth the blessedness that those who fear the Lord will attain, he adds: “Behold, thus shall the man who fears the Lord”—that is, who loves the Lord—“be blessed,” that is, he shall be made blessed and exalted with such a blessing and blessedness.

And this “behold” means: in the present. As if he were saying: “Blessedness has been set before you; now see whether you wish to lose so great a good, which you can possess in exchange for love.” He sets blessedness before them in order to attract them more strongly to love.

“May the Lord bless you.” After making the exhortation, they offer a prayer in this way:

“We said that the man is blessed in the manner described. And in order that this may happen, may the Lord bless you,” that is, may he exalt you by multiplying and intensifying good works in you. And may he do this because you are already Zion, that is, one who contemplates and attends to future things, and you cannot guard yourself by your own power.

May he bless you in such a way that you may “see the good things of Jerusalem,” that is, experience those good things that belong to the heavenly Jerusalem, namely good works, “all the days of your life,” that is, as long as you live.

“And may you see your children.” May he bless you in such a way that you may experience your children’s children, that is, the reward of good works, namely—“peace,” I say—“upon Israel,” that is, future peace extending over Israel, or exceeding the faithful of God, because they cannot merit it by their own strength.

## Psalm 128. A Song of Ascents

[Col. 0782B]

> Often they have attacked me from my youth,  
> let Israel now say.  
> Often they have attacked me from my youth,  
> yet they have not prevailed against me.  
> Sinners have built upon my back;  
> they have prolonged their iniquity.  
> The just Lord has cut the necks of sinners.  
> Let all who hate Zion be put to shame  
> and turned back.  
> Let them become like the grass of the roofs,  
> which withers before it is pulled up.  
> With which the reaper does not fill his hand,  
> nor the one who gathers sheaves his bosom.  
> And those who passed by did not say:  
> “The blessing of the Lord be upon you;  
> we have blessed you in the name of the Lord.”

### Exposition

After these ascending people have reached the point I described, fearing the Lord, they must so conduct themselves that, in steadfastness amid tribulation, they can say that they have not been overcome by those who attack them. Therefore they invite others, by their example, to do good and, if tribulation arises for them from it, not to fail. This degree sets forth that steadfastness.

“They often attacked me.” Whoever is Israel—that is, whoever has ascended so far that he sees God with his heart—should say now, that is, should soon dispose and prepare himself in such a way that he can say:

“They often attacked me,” that is, my adversaries often assaulted me. And this attack began “from my youth,” that is, from the time when I was renewed, or they attacked me because of my renewal.

“They often attacked me.” The repetition is made to confirm the assertion.

“They often attacked me from my youth.” And they attacked me often because they could not prevail against me. For if they had conquered me once, they would not have attacked me a second or third time.

“Sinners have built upon my back.” He explains how they attacked me. They made my back their own building by scourging it. In it they [uncertain surviving fragment: “fab”; lacuna] prolonged, that is, brought forward, their iniquity, and, by contrast, my righteousness. He says this for the consolation of his hearers, so that tribulation may not trouble them, since their righteousness grows through it.

“The just Lord has cut down.” They, I say, extended their iniquity, and in return the Lord, who is the just judge, cut down—that is, will break—the necks, namely the pride, of sinners.

[Col. 0783A]

By contrast, understand that he will reward my humility; and therefore we ought rightly to be steadfast.

After exhorting those who are ascending, he prays for the persecutors in this way:

“And lest they be altogether cut down in the future, may all who hate Zion”—that is, those who persecute the faithful out of hatred alone—“be put to shame” because they were haters, “and turned back,” that is, become followers and imitators of those whom they wished to surpass.

“Let them become like grass.” If they do not wish to turn from their perversity, I concede to divine justice that they become like the grass of roofs, that is, comparable to grass growing uselessly on a roof, so that whatever usefulness and goodness was in them may wither in them before they are lifted from this life.

“With which he does not fill.” Let them be comparable to such grass, with which “the reaper does not fill his hand,” that is, which no one takes the trouble to reap.

As for what follows, “nor his bosom, the one who gathers sheaves,” the reapers and those who gather sheaves are the same: the holy angels, who daily lead the faithful from this life into the kingdom of heaven. In the hand and the bosom, which is more capacious, a difference of greater and lesser dignity is understood.

As if he were saying: “The holy angels, who are the reapers at the end of the world, will not fill their hand or bosom with them,” that is, they will not gather them among the number of the less perfect, who will receive the thirtieth or sixtieth fruit, nor among the number of the more perfect, who will receive the hundredfold fruit (Matt. XIII).

“And those who passed by did not say.” They will not be gathered by the angels because those who pass along the way of this world and its temporal things and advance toward the homeland did not say to such grass, that is, to such people: “The blessing of the Lord be upon you,” that is, by their words and preaching they did not cause the blessing of faith and action to be exalted. In other words, their preaching did not benefit them.

Nor did they say: “We have blessed you in the name of the Lord,” that is, by their preaching they did not cause those who had been blessed and exalted by faith to live in the name of the Lord, namely to give glory to the Lord’s name by doing good.

As if they were saying: “We did indeed bless you, but not in the name of the Lord, so that you might be established with the rest.” This is to be understood of false Christians, just as the earlier part of the verse concerns unbelievers. For all sinners are either ungodly, unbelievers, or false Christians.

The apostles, however, preached to everyone, both those who would be saved and those who would not be saved. But to some they were “the fragrance of life unto life,” and to others “the fragrance of death unto death” (II Cor. II).

## Psalm 129. A Song of Ascents

> Out of the depths I cried to you, O Lord;  
> Lord, hear my voice.  
> Let your ears be attentive  
> to the voice of my supplication.  
> If you observe iniquities, O Lord,  
> Lord, who will endure?  
> For with you there is forgiveness,  
> and because of your law I have waited for you, O Lord.  
> My soul has waited for his word;  
> my soul has hoped in the Lord.  
> From the morning watch until night,  
> let Israel hope in the Lord.  
> For with the Lord there is mercy,  
> and abundant redemption with him.  
> And he himself will redeem Israel  
> from all his iniquities.

### Exposition

After beginning steadfastness amid tribulations, the faithful must recognize that they can in no way stand by their own strength. However far they may have ascended, they may fail and be unable to persevere unless their merits are entirely sustained by God. They should recognize that from the very depths of tribulations they must cry out to God, and let them cry out so that the Lord, as he commanded, may guard them in steadfastness until the night of death.

This Psalm is also regarded as penitential. But in that case it is not counted as a degree. It is not surprising that one and the same Psalm is understood in different ways, since we believe that the Prophet intended whatever can be expounded well and according to the faith in each Psalm.

“Out of the depths I cried.” When the persecutors pressed upon me with every kind of tribulation and afflicted me in every way, I, placed in an abyss of tribulations and distrustful of my own strength, cried to you, O Lord, to whom one must cry because you are the Lord powerful to help.

And you, O Lord, hear my voice, that is, the cry expressed by my voice.

“Let your ears be attentive.” Just as I was stretched out in crying, so, O Lord, let your ears—that is, the power and readiness of your hearing—be extended toward the voice of my supplication, granting what the voice of my supplicant signifies.

“If you observe iniquities.” “Hear my voice,” I say, and do not regard or observe my iniquities. For if you, O Lord, observe iniquities—that is, if you keep them in memory, intending to punish them with strict judgment, whether mine or those of others—O good Lord, who will endure, that is, who will be able to bear it?

Or “who will endure” means “who will wait?” If you observed iniquities, no one would endure.

But although I have said, “Who will endure?” nevertheless someone will endure. And this can be proved in my case. I have waited for you, O Lord, that is, I have patiently awaited a reward from you—not because I failed to understand that I am a sinner and have in no way deserved it, but because “with you,” that is, in your nature, “there is forgiveness,” that is, mercy, because you act mercifully and do not observe the iniquities through which we suffer deficiency.

And also “because of your law observed by me,” that is, because of the condition you set before us: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke VI, VII). Or, stated universally, because of your law, that is, your commandments, being observed.

He adds this so that he might not seem to despair, and therefore might attract less strongly to the cry those whom he is inviting here.

“My soul has waited.” He now turns to the hearers in this way:

“My soul waited,” not only because of his forgiveness and because of the law observed, but also “in his word,” that is, in consideration of his promise, by which he promised forgiveness to penitents who receive pardon, indulgence to those who seek it, and everlasting glory to those who merit it.

“My soul has hoped,” namely in him who rewards legitimate striving. And he rightly says that his soul has hoped. Just as certain virtues properly belong to the body, such as fasting and keeping vigil, so faith, hope, and charity are properly called virtues of the soul.

“My soul has hoped,” I say, not in just anyone, but “in the Lord,” that is, in consideration of his omnipotence.

“From the morning watch.” This hope began “from the morning watch,” that is, from the time of my illumination or assent, namely from the beginning of my holiness, and so it will persevere until night, that is, until death.

Or, as it is found in Hebrew, “from the morning watch until the morning watch,” that is, from the illumination beginning here, persevering until the true morning that will begin to dawn after this life.

And just as I hope in the Lord, so let all Israel hope in the Lord.

“For with the Lord.” And rightly all Israel—that is, every faithful person—will hope in the Lord, because with him there is mercy, that is, he is merciful by nature.

And lest anyone despair because of the multitude of sins, “with the Lord there is abundant redemption,” both from original and actual crimes, both from mortal and venial sins. Or abundant redemption means redemption both of the Gentiles and of the Jews.

“And he himself will redeem.” Redemption is abundant with him because he forgives sins daily. And in the future he himself will redeem Israel from all its iniquities, because no one at all who needs to be absolved through the offering of sacrifice and prayers will pass from this world without stain.

## Psalm 130. A Song of Ascents

> O Lord, my heart has not been exalted,  
> nor have my eyes been lifted up.  
> I have not walked in great things,  
> nor in wonders beyond me.  
> If I did not think humbly,  
> but exalted my soul:  
> as a weaned child is upon his mother,  
> so is recompense in my soul.  
> Let Israel hope in the Lord,  
> from this time forth and forever.

### Exposition

In this Psalm the faithful who have ascended to high things again admonish their followers that, when they have advanced so far that they cry out to the Lord for steadfastness amid tribulation, they should ascend still higher. Namely, when they have been heard in this matter, they should not glory in themselves by turning their eyes toward their own virtues, through which they could become proud. Rather, as they ascend the degree of humility, they should recognize that the great things in them are not theirs but God’s, saying:

“O Lord, my heart has not been exalted.” O Lord, after your benefits described above, my heart has not been exalted, that is, I have not become proud in my mind. Nor have my eyes been lifted up, that is, I have displayed no outward pride, which is especially detected in gestures and the lifting of the eyes.

“I have not walked in great things.” Not only have I not become proud, but even in those things in which there seems to be occasion for pride—namely, in great and wondrous things—I did not glory in myself, so that I might preserve my humility. That is, I advanced in virtues that were so great that they were even wondrous, but not in such a way that I attended to the virtues themselves by saying within myself, “How excellent I am; how glorious I am.” Instead, I said: “How far I differ from others who are superior to me in virtues.”

And I did this because they were “beyond me,” that is, they had been bestowed upon me from above by the Lord.

“If I did not think humbly, like a weaned child.” He now places himself under a kind of devotional imprecation:

“If I did not think humbly,” that is, if I did not always keep myself in humility after all the degrees mentioned above, “but exalted my soul” through pride, then let recompense come upon my soul, so that I may perish as a weaned child would perish, because he ought still to lie upon his mother; if removed, he would not be sustained by the help either of his mother or of anyone else.

He makes this imprecation so that, through the repentance he imposes upon himself, he may remove helpers of pride.

“Let Israel hope.” Whoever is Israel should hope in the Lord in the same way as I, thinking humbly, hoped—or as I did not become proud in great and wondrous things. Thus everyone who is Israel, while in such circumstances, should not become proud, but should hope in the Lord, beginning “from this time forth,” that is, from the present moment, and persevering forever.

## Psalm 131. A Song of Ascents

> Remember, O Lord, David  
> and all his meekness,  
> just as he swore to the Lord  
> and vowed a vow to the God of Jacob:  
> “If I enter the tent of my house,  
> if I climb upon the bed of my couch;  
> if I give sleep to my eyes  
> and slumber to my eyelids,  
> and rest to my temples,  
> until I find a place for the Lord,  
> a dwelling for the God of Jacob.”  
> Behold, we heard of it in Ephratha;  
> we found it in the fields of the Wood.  
> We shall enter his dwelling;  
> we shall worship in the place  
> where his feet stood.  
> Arise, O Lord, into your rest,  
> you and the ark of your sanctification.  
> Let your priests be clothed with righteousness,  
> and let your saints rejoice.  
> For the sake of David your servant,  
> do not turn away the face of your anointed.  
> The Lord swore truth to David,  
> and he will not frustrate it:  
> “I shall set upon your throne  
> one from the fruit of your womb.  
> If your sons keep my covenant  
> and these testimonies of mine  
> that I shall teach them,  
> their sons also shall sit forever  
> upon your throne.”  
> For the Lord chose Zion;  
> he chose her as a dwelling for himself.  
> “This is my rest forever and ever;  
> here I shall dwell,  
> because I have chosen her.  
> I shall bless her widow, blessing her;  
> I shall satisfy her poor with bread.  
> I shall clothe her priests with salvation,  
> and her saints shall rejoice with rejoicing.  
> There I shall make the horn of David flourish;  
> I have prepared a lamp for my anointed.  
> I shall clothe his enemies with shame,  
> but upon him my sanctification shall blossom.”

### Exposition

After the multitude of the faithful has ascended so far that it does not become proud in any way because of its virtues, it prays here for the apostolic life: namely, that it may live in fellowship and concord with the brothers, not under its own authority but under the power of another.

And because it does not consider itself capable of attaining this through any merits of its own, although it has ascended so far, it prays the Father, for the sake of David—that is, for the sake of Christ and his obedience—to rise, that is, to bring this about.

This degree is called desire.

“Remember, O Lord, David.” O Lord the Father, remember in us David, that is, Christ, acting courageously in all things.

“And all his meekness,” that is, his patience and obedience. Remember his meekness, I say, displayed in every respect just as the Son of God himself swore to God the Father, that is, confirmed by an oath.

“And as he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob,” that is, to the God of those who wrestle, because he too was wrestling according to his human nature.

Here “to swear” and “to vow a vow” are understood not as spoken words but as God’s firm disposition, spoken by comparison with human beings who swear to something and make a firm vow.

“If I enter.” “If I give sleep to my eyes and rest to my temples.” He swore, saying:

“If I enter the tent of my house,” that is, into the dwelling of my abode, so as to rest my body in anything for pleasure; “and if I climb upon the bed of my couch; and if I give sleep to my eyes”—which is less than climbing upon the bed—“and slumber to my eyelids, and rest to my temples,” which happens when the temples grow heavy with sleep.

I will in no way rest or cease “until I find a place for the Lord,” that is, people in whom the Lord may have his place and his rest; and until I find a dwelling, that is, those who serve the God of Jacob—“of those who wrestle” being understood—I shall not be a truthful promiser, or something of this sort that may properly be understood.

What he says, “If I enter the tabernacle of my house” [Col. 0787C], is said by comparison with some soldier so devoted to his lord that he would never wish to enter his own house until, by destroying his enemies, he had served in accordance with his lord’s will. When he says, “into the bed of my couch,” by “bed” he means the couch itself, but by “couch” what is placed on top of it, such as a mattress, pillow, and so forth.

“Behold, we have heard of it.” This was said: David, that is, the Lord Jesus, swore; and just as he promised, behold, we see it fulfilled in the present and openly, because “we have heard of it,” that is, of the seat or Church which he previously foretold, “in Ephratha,” that is, in the Jewish people, which we understand here both through the place that is in Judea, called by another name Bethlehem, and through the interpretation of the name. For Ephratha is interpreted as “mirror” [Col. 0787D]. This aptly suits the Jews, who, under the shadow of the Law, contemplated as through a mirror, in an enigma, what is now seen face to face (I Cor. XIII).

And when it is said, “we have heard of it in Ephratha,” this is attributed to that part which here speaks from among the Gentiles. What follows, “we found him in the fields of the Wood,” is ascribed to the Jews. It is as though the Jews were saying: “We found it,” that is, the Church, “also in the fields of the Wood,” that is, among those who were a wood but have now become fields, that is, fruitful. “It” is not relative to any word placed in the book, but to the significance of the place: “We shall enter into the tabernacle.”

Now they explain in what matter they pray that David may remember them, namely, because “we shall enter,” that is, we have resolved to enter into “his tabernacle” [Col. 0788A], that is, into his service, so that we may stand worshipping, that is, venerating him, “in the place,” that is, in the state where “his feet stood,” that is, the apostles. It is as though he said: “In conformity with the apostles,” so that we may be of one mind in the will in which they firmly persevered (Acts II). And for this we shall worship, that is, we have resolved to do this through prayer.

“Arise, O Lord.” We resolve to enter into the apostolic life and to worship. And in order that we may be able to enter, arise, O Lord—that is, show yourself powerful by going into your rest, making us such persons in whom you may rest and delight. And when you arise, let the ark of your sanctification also arise, that is, let us arise, who, sanctified and purified in baptism, are your ark, carrying within us the tabernacles of the covenants, that is, the commandments of the Old [Col. 0788B] and New Testaments; and the manna, that is, Christ, the food of angels and the bread of life and understanding; and the rod of Aaron, that is, our own governance, by which we rule unlawful impulses.

“Your priests.” Now he explains how they pray that the ark of sanctification may arise, namely in this way: “O Lord, let your priests be clothed with righteousness,” that is, let us, who are a royal priesthood (I Pet. II), offer ourselves as a sacrifice and be engaged in good works. “And let your holy ones exult,” that is, let us ourselves, sanctified by you, exult according to the purity of innocence.

“For David’s sake.” We do not pray for this on account of our merits, but rather for the sake of David, whom you loved, who is your servant and obedient to you in all things. After good works and innocence, do not turn away “the face of your anointed,” that is, his beauty and [Col. 0788C] loveliness, namely his conformity, from us. And this is on his account, as he said above: “Remember his meekness.”

“The Lord swore truth to David.” It is as though someone were to say: “With what confidence do you dare to pray for conformity to Christ?” With this confidence, namely, that the Lord the Father swore—that is, firmly ordained or promised—“truth” to David, that is, to the Lord Jesus Christ, his Son: namely, himself, who is the Truth. “And he will not frustrate it,” that is, he will not deceive him concerning this promise.

And what did he swear? “Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne,” that is, I will cause certain ones among those whom you beget in faith to enjoy with you, in your kingdom, the same blessedness of immortality and freedom from suffering. This was promised to David concerning Christ according to the flesh; to Christ, concerning the faithful according to the spirit.

“If your sons keep” [Col. 0788D]. Then your sons will sit upon your throne, if they keep “my covenant,” that is, the pact promised to me in baptism, “and my testimonies,” that is, my commandments—namely, those which I shall teach them, that is, which I shall enjoin upon them. And not only your sons, that is, the apostles and the other first believers, but also their sons, that is, their imitators, will sit upon the same throne forever, that is, eternally.

Alternatively: I will make some of the regenerated who will be your sons kings, that is, rulers of themselves and of others. And if they persevere in my commandments and cause their sons to persevere, they and their sons will sit upon your throne here and eternally: here, ruling themselves; in the future, reigning together.

“For the Lord chose Sion” [Col. 0789A]. Truly they will reign, because the Lord chose Sion for this purpose. Sion is called “watching”; that is, he freely took the Church, which watches for future things, from the mass of the lost, without any preceding merits. He chose it as a dwelling for himself, that is, one which he would inhabit and cultivate according to its advancement in virtues, saying:

“This is my rest,” that is, “This Sion will be my rest”; in other words, I will establish it as such that I may delight and rest in it, not only here but forever and ever. “Here,” that is, in that Sion, I will dwell, both here and in the future. For I chose it for this purpose, that I might dwell in it.

“I will bless her widow.” He proves what he said, “I will dwell here,” in this way: “Her widow,” namely, Sion’s widow, that is, those who in her have been deprived of temporal pleasure, I will bless here by exalting them in virtues, and I will bless them with future glorification [Col. 0789B]. Or, “blessing I will bless,” that is, I will greatly exalt.

“Her poor,” that is, Sion’s poor, namely, those who exist in humility, like those who attend to their poverty, I will fill with bread, that is, with the manifold understanding of the Holy Scriptures; for those who set aside all temporal things are prepared for understanding. He calls the same persons “widow” and “poor” for different reasons.

“Her priests.” Those also who are not merely humble but offer themselves as a sacrifice of righteousness, I will clothe with salvation, that is, with Christ—that is, with conformity to the Savior, namely, in good works. And “her holy ones,” namely, Sion’s holy ones, will exult with exultation; they will rejoice in perfect innocence.

We understand “the widow and the poor, the priests and the holy ones”—the very persons [Col. 0789C] who speak in this psalm—as those whom I shall lead there, exalting them in this way here, but in the future leading them there. “I will raise up the horn of David,” that is, upon these same persons I will extend the exaltation and conformity of the Lord Jesus, though not so that they should be exalted with equal rank and measure, but each in his own manner.

“For I have prepared them a lamp for my Christ,” that is, I will make them recognize that they are not themselves the light but a lamp: that is, that they bear within themselves Christ, who is the true light, and receive from him the radiance by which they themselves are illuminated and illuminate others.

“His enemies.” I will exalt them in the manner I have described, but his enemies, that is, Christ’s persecutors or heretics who were hostile to him, I will clothe with perpetual confusion, that is, condemnation. “But my sanctification,” that is, my sanctified ones [Col. 0789D], will blossom from virtue to virtue, or through the flowers of good works toward the maturity of eternal reward, being founded upon Christ himself, without whom they can be nothing.

Alternatively: “There,” that is, to the holy ones, I will raise up the horn of David. And not only to them, but also to his enemies, that is, his persecutors, I will clothe with good confusion, so that they may feel shame because they persecuted him. And they will not merely feel shame, but afterward, having become “my sanctification,” sanctified in baptism, they will blossom in the advancement of virtues, founded upon him in good works.

## PSALM CXXXII. SONG OF ASCENTS

“Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together [Col. 0790A]. It is like oil upon the head, which ran down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron. It ran down upon the edge of his garment, like the dew of Hermon, which descended upon Mount Sion. For there the Lord commanded blessing and life forever.”

## EXPOSITION

These are the same faithful who, in the preceding psalm, prayed with humility for conformity to Christ and the apostolic life. They now ascend a still more advanced step, namely, that after attaining what they sought, they may willingly strive to dwell together as one.

“Behold, how good.” We have obtained what we prayed for. Behold, we dwell together as one; that is, we have everything in common [Col. 0790B] and exist in the same will, leading the apostolic life. Therefore you also, hearers, learn how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one, that is, with a concordant will, so that they may desire the same thing. This is better and more pleasant than can be expressed in words.

Many dwell together, such as Cain and Abel, Esau and Jacob, but not as one. Many things are also good but not pleasant, such as fasting and disciplining the body. Many things are pleasant but not good, such as living indulgently. But since this dwelling together of brothers is both good and pleasant, it is rightly to be embraced.

Now he shows by comparison what it is like: “It is like oil.” Truly it is good and pleasant, like oil upon the head, as a spiritual gift with which the perfect are anointed, like kings and priests, existing in the power of Christ, who [Col. 0790C] is our head. And such a gift “ran down upon the beard,” that is, upon the strong, since strength and wisdom are signified by the beard.

He explains in detail which strong persons he means: “upon the beard of Aaron,” that is, upon the apostles, who in the first place adhered to Christ the supreme priest. Or, according to the interpretation of the name, Aaron is called “mountain” or “mountainous.” And although Christ lived in the world, he nevertheless always remained himself a mountain and continued upon a very high mountain and in an impregnable fortress.

“It ran down upon the edge.” This oil did not merely descend, that is, flow, upon the beard of Aaron, but also upon the edge of his garment, that is, upon the top of his clothing. For the spiritual anointing first flowed from Christ into the apostles, as from the head into the beard; then through the beard [Col. 0790D] into the garment, that is, from the apostles into the martyrs, who, after the apostles, were the first to surround Christ; and so into the edge, that is, the extremity of the garment, namely, into all the faithful of the Church.

Through this he greatly commends this step, namely, dwelling together as one, because he recalls that such eminent men, namely apostles and martyrs, were part of it.

The oil flowed “like the dew of Hermon,” that is, as a gratuitous gift of exalted light, namely Christ, since he conferred this gift on no one before his exaltation, as it is written: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII). Hermon is interpreted as “exalted light,” or “their anathema” [Col. 0791A].

Dew, which descends without human labor to make the earth fruitful, signifies God’s gratuitous gift, bestowed without merit. Thus the dew of Hermon descended upon Mount Sion, because the grace that was first bestowed upon the Jews, after they separated themselves from Christ by anathematizing Jesus Christ, came to the Church of the Gentiles, which contemplates God in mind.

Or, it may mean the gratuitous gift of God bestowed upon the Gentile people, which had previously been anathema, coming to Sion when Jews and Gentiles were joined in the unity of faith.

Alternatively, by Mount Hermon and Mount Sion let us understand the more eminent and perfect persons in the Church, upon whom the grace of the Holy Spirit descends more abundantly.

“For there the Lord commanded.” And therefore it is also good and pleasant to dwell together as one, because there, that is, among those existing in that common dwelling, the Lord commanded, that is, entrusted through his teachers, “blessing,” namely, increasing exaltation, more and more and increasingly day by day according to advancement in virtues; and not merely exaltation in this life, but also “life forever,” that is, life extending to eternity.

## PSALM CXXXIII. SONG OF ASCENTS

“Behold, now bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord. You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God. In the nights lift up your hands in the holy places, and bless the Lord. May the Lord bless you from Sion, he who made heaven and earth.”

## EXPOSITION

Now these same faithful invite all who have ascended so far [Col. 0791C] that they have one heart and one soul, so that they may persevere in this state; or, since they have been advanced by God, so that they may not attribute it to themselves, but may do everything they do with regard to heavenly reward, and for all these things bless God.

“Behold, now bless the Lord.” O all you servants of the Lord who have climbed so far: behold, now—that is, in the present, when nothing else remains for you—bless the Lord through perseverance, or so that you may attribute to God what you have climbed thus far.

“You who stand in the house of the Lord.” I mean you, servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord, that is, in the Church, attending to God’s commandments and in no way lying prostrate. And let there be a reason for blessing, because you stand “in the courts of the house of our God,” that is, in the breadth of love leading us [Col. 0791D] into the eternal house of our God.

“In the nights lift up.” Bless the Lord, I say, and lift up your hands, that is, your works, “in the holy places,” that is, work well with regard to heavenly things, “in the nights,” that is, throughout this entire life, where there are various deficiencies and which, when compared with the future life, must be called nothing other than night.

Human beings are understood to be in the night in two ways: either on account of sins, as in the statement, “Those who sleep, sleep at night” (I Thess. V); or because even the good are here in night in comparison with the light and glory of the future life.

“And bless the Lord,” that is, praise the Lord by the very fact that you lift up your hands in the holy places.

“May the Lord bless you.” Now those who have hitherto exhorted them generally, in order to show that they are not sufficient for this by free choice, and that all the foregoing acts of assent are from the grace of God, address them individually [Col. 0792A], saying: “May the Lord proceeding from Sion,” that is, he who is God and man, bless you both in advancement and in the preservation of advancement. The Lord, I say, who is powerful, who made heaven and earth, that is, the greater and the lesser.

## PSALM CXXXIV. ALLELUIA

“Praise the name of the Lord; praise the Lord, servants. You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God. Praise the Lord, for the Lord is good; sing praises to his name, for it is sweet. For the Lord chose Jacob for himself, Israel as his possession. For I know that the Lord is great, and our God is above all gods [Col. 0792B]. Whatever the Lord wished, he did in heaven, on earth, in the sea, and in all the abysses. Bringing clouds from the end of the earth, he made lightning into rain. He brings forth winds from his treasuries. He struck the firstborn of Egypt, from man to beast. He sent signs and wonders in your midst, O Egypt, against Pharaoh and all his servants. He struck many nations and slew mighty kings: Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan. And he gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel his people. O Lord, your name is forever; O Lord, your memorial is from generation to generation. For the Lord will judge his people, and he will be entreated on behalf of his servants. The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths, and they will not speak; they have eyes, and they will not see; they have ears, and they will not hear; for there is no spirit in their mouth. May those who make them and all who trust in them become like them. House of Israel, bless the Lord; house of Aaron, bless the Lord; house of Levi, bless the Lord; you who fear the Lord, bless the Lord. Blessed is the Lord from Sion, who dwells in Jerusalem.”

## EXPOSITION

The prophet speaks in this psalm, inviting everyone, both Jews and Gentiles, to praise God on account of his goodness: both because he has freely bestowed many good things upon them and with regard to the wonders [Col. 0792D] that he enumerates in various ways throughout his treatment of this psalm.

“Praise the name of the Lord.” O you servants of the Lord, praise with devotion of heart and mouth that name which is “Lord,” or the glory of the Lord.

“You who stand in the house,” and so forth. This verse is to be explained as above, “Praise the Lord” (Psalm CXXXIII).

Therefore also praise the Lord because he is naturally good in himself. And do not praise him with your voice alone, but also sing praises to his name, that is, work well for the glory of his name, which is “Lord,” because the name of such a Lord is not harsh or bitter like that of others, but is sweet and exceedingly delightful. Or: it is pleasant and sweet to sing praises to him.

“For the Lord chose Jacob [Col. 0793A].” Let this also be material for your praise, because the Lord chose Jacob for himself, that is, he freely took up those among you who are still less perfect and engaged in struggle. “And Israel as his possession,” that is, the more perfect among you, who already see God with the heart. By mercy alone he took all these from the mass of the lost for this purpose: that he might possess and cultivate them as someone might cultivate his inheritance.

“For I know.” And rightly you ought to praise such a Lord, because he is not only good but also great and powerful. I know this with full knowledge, revealed to me by the Holy Spirit. And he is “our God,” not a recent god, but the God of the ancient fathers, such that he is above all gods, whether those sanctified by him or those falsely adopted by human beings.

“Whatever the Lord wished.” He proves that he is great above all, because he himself did whatever he wished in heaven and on earth [Col. 0793B], that is, among rulers and subjects; and not only among the good, but also among the evil, which is the sea; and not only among any kind of evil persons, but also among those who were the abyss, that is, who were in the depths of vices—among all these he did whatever he wished.

“Bringing forth clouds.” He did in heaven what he wished, namely this: bringing forth from that extremity those who were, as it were, the lowest among human beings in nobility and poverty, he made them clouds to rain upon others. And he made lightning in them, that is, illumination of knowledge, into rain, that is, into teaching. The office is signified by the clouds, teaching by the rain. This means: He not only enjoined upon them the office of preaching, but also made them carry it out.

“He brings forth winds.” He continues to prove that the Lord is great, since he brings forth [Col. 0793C] winds, that is, the same spiritual persons whom he called clouds, but clouds on account of their office and winds on account of their spirituality, “from his treasuries,” that is, from his hidden disposition, in which they existed before the foundation of the world (I Pet. I).

And he is to be praised because he “struck the firstborn,” that is, destroyed original sins, which are born first in human beings, “of Egypt,” that is, of those who were in degradation and the darkness of ignorance, “from man to beast,” that is, both those who were wise in worldly matters, such as philosophers or Jews and Greeks, and those who in their simplicity could be compared with beasts, such as barbarians.

“And he sent signs.” In this way and order, therefore, he destroyed the firstborn of Egypt. And he sent signs and wonders, that is, public miracles. And this was not in just any part of you [Col. 0793D], O Egypt, but “in your midst,” because miracles occurred throughout the whole world: against Pharaoh, that is, against the devil who was to be destroyed, for he is truly called “dissipation”; and against all his servants, namely those who were to be destroyed, his ministers, that is, the evil spirits subject to him, who serve him in the dissipation of the human race.

“He struck many nations.” And he did not merely destroy the firstborn, that is, original sins, but also struck many nations, that is, destroyed the multitude of actual sins arising after baptism through temptations. And he slew mighty kings, that is, such vices as habitually reign and dominate powerfully in certain persons and have such force that scarcely anyone can free himself from them.

“Sihon king of the Amorites [Col. 0794A].” He explains which kings he slew: Sihon, that is, a vehement temptation, so vehement that it either already reigned by prevailing or could already have reigned. Sihon is interpreted as “a burning temptation,” “temptation of the eyes,” “growing weary,” or “useless sprout.” The Amorites are called “those who make bitter.” Og means “conclusion” or “one who heaps up.” Bashan means “fatness,” or “disgrace,” or “confusion.” Canaan means “their movement,” or “prepared for humility,” or “for degradation.”

He did not, however, destroy temptation altogether so that it would no longer attack; rather, he destroyed it in what belongs to the Amorites, that is, insofar as it is accustomed to dominate and prevail, with respect to consent, among those who are Amorites, that is, those who make God bitter by consenting. This means: He destroyed and weakened the suggestion of assaults, so that they would not reach consent; or, among those in whom it prevailed, he forgave.

According to the interpretation [Col. 0794B] by which Sihon is called “temptation of the eyes,” through the temptation of this sense we understand, by implication, the temptations of the whole sensual faculty. For we are tempted especially through the eyes, and as blessed Augustine says: “This applies to all the other senses. For one commonly says: ‘See how great a crash he made. See how good it tastes. See how good it smells. See how rough or smooth it is to the touch.’”

“And he slew Og king of Bashan.” By Og we understand an evil action leading into confusion, since each person can free himself from an action with much greater difficulty than from consent. But the Lord slew Sihon and Og, that is, he destroyed the conclusion of the act together with consent. For when one reaches action through consent, people are then enclosed and ensnared [Col. 0794C], so that they cannot easily escape.

This enclosure has the power to lead people into confusion, that is, from vice to vice so long as they are in this life, and afterward into eternal condemnation. And, not to go through each one individually, he “slew all the kingdoms of Canaan,” that is, destroyed every wicked habit by which a person is moved and departs from God into the region of unlikeness, prepared to obey humility and degradation.

“And he gave their land as an inheritance.” He not only destroyed vices according to consent and action in his own people, but also their land, namely, the land of those kings: the sensuality of the flesh, which, as a punishment for sin, is always inclined toward evil and suggests wicked things to reason. Where vices previously reigned, he gave an inheritance to his people.

He repeats [Col. 0794D] “inheritance” in order to specify to which people he gave it, namely to Israel, that is, to those who believe and see themselves, so that they might cultivate it well and completely subject it to reason, making it produce good fruit.

“O Lord, your name.” Now the prophet turns to the Lord with thanksgiving for all these things, saying: O Lord, you who forgave past evils and in the present wilderness lead us securely against enemies who arise, your name, that is, your glory, will remain forever, because through us you will be glorious eternally. And your memorial, that is, the meaning of what was historically done for the children of Israel, will endure in the present generation and in the future generation.

“For the Lord will judge.” Therefore the glory of the Lord will also be forever, because he will judge his people [Col. 0795A], that is, reward his faithful after they have departed from this life. And he will exalt them by rewarding them to such a degree that he himself will be entreated in his servants, that is, prayed to through them, so that they may be mediators and intercessors for us with him, as happens daily among the saints. This is said by comparison with that servant whom his lord exalts so greatly that he is able to intercede for his fellow servants.

“The idols of the nations.” The Lord did all the things that have been mentioned, and therefore such a Lord is rightly to be praised, not the idols of the nations, which are merely likenesses of things and are made of gold and silver or of some cheaper material. They are “the work of human hands,” that is, made bodily by human beings, not possessed according to understanding.

Although they have [Col. 0795B] the forms of human limbs, they enjoy the function of none of them. For there is no spirit in their mouths, so that they cannot even make a sound in the manner of brute animals.

This condemnation of the idols serves the praise of God. It is as though he were saying: “I disparage their gods in this way so that they may withdraw from the worship of such things.” But if they refuse, I leave it to divine justice that those who make them and those who place their trust in them may become like them in their inner selves, so that they lose the power of reason in the same way as those idols lack bodily senses.

“House of Israel, bless the Lord.” Whatever may happen concerning these things, you who are the house of Israel, that is, faithful subjects from the Jews, bless the Lord with devotion of mind, mouth, and action. And not only subjects, but also the house of Aaron, that is, rulers, bless the Lord. The house of Levi, that is, Aaron—or you who are in the ministry of the Lord’s priests—bless the Lord [Col. 0795C].

“Blessed is the Lord.” All together, bless the Lord, saying: “May the Lord coming from Sion,” that is, born from the Jewish people, who is so great that he dwells in Jerusalem, that is, reigns among heavenly creatures, be blessed,” with the implied phrase “in all things.”

## PSALM CXXXV. ALLELUIA

“Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever. Give thanks to the God of gods, for his mercy is forever. Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for his mercy is forever. To him [Col. 0795D] who alone does great wonders, for his mercy is forever. To him who made the heavens with understanding, for his mercy is forever. To him who established the earth upon the waters, for his mercy is forever. To him who made great lights, for his mercy is forever. The sun to rule the day, for his mercy is forever. The moon and stars to rule the night, for his mercy is forever. To him who struck Egypt with their firstborn, for his mercy is forever. To him who brought Israel out from among them, for his mercy is forever. With a mighty hand and an exalted arm, for his mercy is forever. To him who divided the Red Sea into divisions, for his mercy is forever. And brought Israel [Col. 0796A] through its midst, for his mercy is forever. And shook Pharaoh and his power into the Red Sea, for his mercy is forever. To him who led his people through the wilderness, for his mercy is forever. To him who struck great kings, for his mercy is forever. And slew mighty kings, for his mercy is forever. Sihon king of the Amorites, for his mercy is forever. And Og king of Bashan, for his mercy is forever. And gave their land as an inheritance, for his mercy is forever. An inheritance to Israel his servant, for his mercy is forever. For he remembered us in our humiliation, for his mercy is forever. And redeemed us [Col. 0796B] from our enemies, for his mercy is forever. To him who gives food to all flesh, for his mercy is forever. Give thanks to the God of heaven, for his mercy is forever. Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for his mercy is forever.”

## EXPOSITION

The subject matter in this psalm is the same as that contained in the preceding one, except that here the prophet adds certain things that are not found there.

“Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good.” O all you faithful, give thanks to the Lord, that is, praise the Lord with devotion, voice, and deed: both in consideration of the fact that he is naturally good, and because his mercy, which he has shown in the human race, endures forever [Col. 0796C], since it will not cease until he brings you into eternity.

“Give thanks to the God of gods.” Therefore also praise him because he is the God of gods, that is, surpassing all those made divine; and because he is the Lord surpassing all earthly powers. This is so because his mercy, which began here in you, will remain forever.

This phrase, as an intercalary refrain, is added to each verse in order to commend the greatness of God’s mercy.

“He who does wonders.” Although I have spoken of gods and lords, nevertheless he alone is God and Lord, doing wonders—not just any wonders, but great ones—and doing so alone. Give thanks to him, for his mercy is forever.

“He who made the heavens.” He explains which wonders he did and continually does: namely, these. He made the heavens, that is, the apostles and other spiritual men, exalted in the dignity of life. And he made them “with understanding,” that is, in himself, who is the wisdom of the Father, without assistance from anything external.

“He who established the earth [Col. 0796D],” that is, the Church, founded upon the waters of baptism; or made superior to persecutors, who were intent on drowning it in the waves of persecutions.

“He who makes great lights.” He also did what makes him worthy of praise, because he made great lights, that is, he illuminated certain faithful with wisdom, one more and another less: making some suns to rule the day, so that they might possess power in knowledge, and thus making them suns in perfect brightness and illumination of wisdom; making others the moon, that is, shining less brightly in knowledge; and stars [Col. 0797A], that is, those knowing still less, yet all existing as great lights, so that they might rule the night, being powerful in historical knowledge and in those matters that pertain to the end. This knowledge is called night in comparison with more perfect knowledge.

“He who struck Egypt.” Through the sun and moon he destroyed the darkness of ignorance and unbelief in those who loved the world; or actual sins, which afflict people in conscience, together with their firstborn, that is, with original sins.

“He who brought Israel out.” Once sins had been destroyed, he brought the faithful out from the midst of the sins themselves, or from the mass of the lost. This implies that he left some there. For he did not take up everyone, but some, “with a mighty hand.” He brought them out with a mighty hand, that is, with strong cooperation, and with an exalted arm [Col. 0797B], that is, with strength surpassing all others.

“He who divided the Red Sea.” To ensure that all those who left Egypt and in whom the firstborn had been destroyed would not be secure in salvation without carrying out good works, he explains how he struck Egypt: namely, by dividing the sea into divisions, that is, by granting the sacrament of baptism to some for salvation and to others for condemnation.

If he had said merely “he divided,” we would understand only two parts. But when he said, “he divided the Red Sea into divisions,” we understand that multiple divisions were made, because baptism itself is condemnation for many of those who are to be condemned: for some through heresy, for others through adultery, for others through homicide. In the same way we can see the opposite among those who are to be saved.

“And he brought Israel out.” Those who were renewed as Israel [Col. 0797C] he brought through its midst, that is, through the midst of the sea; in other words, he drew some out from the midst of baptism away from others, namely the saved away from the condemned, so that they would differ in conduct and life from those who remained in Egypt.

“And he shook Pharaoh,” that is, the yoke and dominion of the devil, “and his power,” that is, sins, which are his power and authority, he shook away from Israel in baptism.
