“He who led his people through.” He not only drowned the pursuing enemies there, but afterward led them safely through the wilderness of this world against enemies who arose.

“He who struck great kings,” that is, when vices rose up again after baptism through wicked habit, he struck the multitude of vices, which are powerful and prevailing kings [Col. 0797D]. Of these he says: “And he struck mighty kings,” that is, he destroyed those sins which had already held people bound with great force.

“Sihon king of the Amorites.” He explains which kings he struck: namely, the burning and vehement temptation that had been regenerating among those who made the Lord bitter.

“And he slew the conclusion,” that is, the evil action leading into present and future confusion. “And he gave their land as an inheritance.” That land which the aforesaid kings had possessed—namely, the carnal people themselves, that is, their senses—he gave as an inheritance to Israel his servant, that is, to his faithful, so that they might possess it by a blessed right.

“For in our humiliation.” And rightly you ought to give thanks to him, both because his mercy is forever and because he remembered us [Col. 0798A] in our humiliation: not because of any preceding merits of ours, but he had mercy upon us in our humiliation and degradation.

“And he redeemed us,” that is, he remembered us in such a way as to redeem us from our enemies, by whom we were held captive.

“He who gives food to all flesh.” Therefore also give thanks to him, because the price he gave for our redemption, namely his body, he gives to all the redeemed, so that they may be refreshed by the sacrament of his body.

“Give thanks to the God of heaven.” You ought rightly to give thanks because he is not only the God of gods, as I have said, but also the God of heaven, that is, of heavenly creatures.

“Give thanks to the Lord of lords.” After enumerating the benefits, he repeats the exhortation stated above. It is as though he were saying: Therefore, for such benefits, give thanks to the Lord, for his mercy is forever [Col. 0798B].

## PSALM CXXXVI. PSALM OF DAVID, OF JEREMIAH
«By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered Zion. On the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments. For there those who led us captive questioned us about the words of songs. And those who carried us away said to us: “Sing us a hymn from the songs of Zion.” How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land? If I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand be given over to forgetfulness. May my tongue cleave to my throat, if I do not remember you. If I do not set Jerusalem at the beginning of my joy. Remember, Lord, the sons of Edom on the day of Jerusalem, who say: “[Col. 0798C] Empty it, empty it, down to its foundations within it.” Wretched daughter of Babylon: blessed is he who will repay you with the repayment that you repaid us. Blessed is he who will seize and dash your little ones against the rock.»

## EXPOSITION

This psalm is attributed to the perfect faithful, who here act on Jeremiah’s behalf—that is, according to Jeremiah’s prophecy. They possess the same understanding of the captivity of the human race that Jeremiah had when he described, literally, the lamentations over the captivity of the children of Israel in Babylon. For just as, in the account of that captivity, we learn how the children of Israel mourned their exile and degradation in Babylonia for seventy years, sighed in remembrance of earthly Jerusalem, and, by ceasing from the praise of God, hung up their instruments, so in these words the faithful recount their misery and degradation, in which they remain throughout this life, which proceeds according to the number seven. They show the intensity of their groaning, which arises from their desire for the heavenly Jerusalem. In this way they suspend the words of life from the citizens of Babylon, whom they regard as unworthy of knowledge of the divine word. This account is given for the instruction of the less perfect, so that they too, recognizing their misery, may act in the same way.

### By the rivers of Babylon

We, dwelling beside the rivers of Babylon—that is, beside the studies and affairs of this world, and beside temporal things that lead and hurl human beings [Col. 0799A] into confusion—nevertheless were not in those rivers, but sat above them there. That is, we were in great degradation and misery, precisely in the condition in which we were because of the nearness of danger, although we were above it.

And we wept—that is, we felt great sorrow—while remembering you, Zion, because we remembered you, O Zion; that is, we kept in mind how long the glory that we shall possess in you would be delayed, namely, among the willows. We wept both because we remembered you, O Zion, and because we were among the willows, from which the word of the Lord had to be removed.

Or let the passage be connected in this way: We not only wept, but hung our instruments among the willows—that is, we withdrew the admonition that sweetly and mercifully resounded from various commandments [Col. 0799B], considering those who were sterile and unfruitful, concerning whom we had no hope, as with the fruit of the willow. They were so sterile that they were in its midst—that is, in the midst of Babylon—not at the edge, but in the depth of degradation and confusion. They were already in completed wickedness, now scorning even to sin; such wickedness leads to eternal confusion. And because they had fallen so far, it was unworthy that preaching should be offered to them, lest they treat it as a mockery.

### For there they questioned us

As though someone were to say: “Why do you say that you hung up your instruments? Were there people seeking instruments?” He answers: Truly, because there, that is, in Babylon, or among the fortunate, those who led us captive questioned us. These were the evil spirits who had taken us captive in our first parent. Through the willows—that is, through their ministers—they asked us to play the words of songs, that is, words of divine melody.

And those who carried us away—that is, caused us to depart from God—asked such words of songs from us so that we might announce eternal life and the day of judgment. These are words of delight, not with respect to them, but with respect to us, who find in them the highest delight.

Thus they asked these things of us, saying: “Sing us a hymn,” that is, one song, “from the songs of Zion,” that is, from the divine commandments belonging to the heavenly Jerusalem. They asked, as it were: “Are we to have wives, children, dogs, and other things of this sort there?”

### How shall we sing?

We gave such people this answer: How—that is, by what reason or with what benefit—shall we sing the song, that is, the commandments, of the Lord in a foreign land? That is, in consideration of you, who are a foreign land, unfit to bear fruit for the Lord. It is as though they were saying: “You are willows and cannot bear fruit; therefore we shall not sing to you.”

### If I forget you

Because they said that they had hung their instruments from the willows, lest they also be thought to have kept silent before the good, he says: Although I withdraw my admonition from such people, nevertheless, if I forget you, O Jerusalem—that is, if I do not say what must be said and preached concerning you—may my right hand, that is, my good action, be given over to forgetfulness, that is, be without reward in the future; or may I become unable to act well.

### May my tongue cleave

And not only may I be deprived of reward in the future, but here also may my tongue cleave to my throat [Col. 0800A]. That is, may my inner tongue cleave to my inner throat, so that even here I may be unable to think well, if I do not remember you—that is, if I do not announce you to those to whom you must be announced.

Or let the passage be connected in this way: “If I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand be given over to forgetfulness.” Let the ability to act well be taken from me altogether, and not only the ability to act, but also the ability to speak. This is what follows: “May my tongue cleave to my throat.” This interpretation is better than the preceding one. Here it is understood that the word of God is to be removed from the unworthy and proclaimed to the worthy.

### If I do not set you first

Then let my right hand, O Jerusalem, be given over to forgetfulness if I do not set you at the beginning of my joy—that is, so that you may be the beginning of my joy. It is as though he were saying: “I have no delight in temporal things when compared with the delight I have in you.”

### Remember

And because I will not forget you, O Jerusalem, and will make you the summit of my joy, I will suffer many anxieties from the sons of Edom—that is, from the sons of Esau, who, having received lentil stew from his brother in exchange for the birthright, was called Edom (Genesis XXVII), that is, “bloody.” Historically also, his sons greatly hindered the children of Israel from rebuilding Jerusalem; this signified the present matter.

And you, Lord, remember the sons of Edom, and repay us for the tribulations that we suffer from the bloody Babylonians, on the day of Jerusalem, when the heavenly Jerusalem will be fully built from among us.

I mean those sons of Edom who say, exhorting one another: “Empty it, empty it”—that is, empty out whatever goodness and virtue is in it—“down to its foundations within it,” so that not even faith may remain in its faithful, that is, in Jerusalem. [Col. 0800C]

### Wretched daughter of Babylon

And lest the words “Remember, Lord, the sons of Edom” appear to have been spoken out of ill will, he turns toward them under the persona of the daughter of Babylon and designates them with the feminine gender, on account of their weakness and because they fornicate away from their bridegroom and husband, Christ.

O wretched daughter of Babylon—that is, O you persecuting, bloody sons of Edom—you think yourselves strong and blessed in your persecution, but you are wretched, because you have killed your own souls in it. You act dissolutely and effeminately, and there is nothing manly in you, because you yield to every evil suggestion. But blessed is the one who will repay you with your repayment, that is, with such a repayment as you made to us. You tried to take away children from us, though we had deserved well; blessed is the one who, because you have deserved evil, will take away your children from you, lest they perish altogether. I mean the one who strives to empty you—that is, to destroy you insofar as you are evil.

### Blessed is he who will seize

He explains what repayment he means. Blessed is he who, while your little ones—that is, your children—are still inexperienced and capable of conversion, will seize them so that they do not consent to you, and will dash them against the rock—that is, unite them to Christ—because he will receive a reward for their conversion.

Alternatively: Our flesh may appropriately be understood as the daughter of Babylon, which leads those who consent to it into the greatest confusion. Whoever restrains and afflicts its desires, and dashes its little thoughts against Christ so that they do not grow strong in evil works according to their pleasures, will be proclaimed blessed, because he will be granted the reward of eternal blessedness.

# PSALM CXXXVII. PSALM OF DAVID HIMSELF

«I will confess to you, Lord, with my whole heart, because you have heard all the words of my mouth. In the sight of the angels I will sing psalms to you; I will worship toward your holy temple and confess your name. Because of your mercy and your truth, for you have magnified your holy name above every name. On whatever day I call upon you, hear me; you will multiply strength in my soul. Let all the kings of the earth confess to you, Lord, because they have heard all the words of your mouth. And let them sing in the ways of the Lord, for great is the glory of the Lord. For the Lord is exalted and regards the lowly, and knows the proud from afar. If I walk in the midst of tribulation, you will revive me; and against the anger of my enemies you have stretched out your hand, and your right hand has saved me. The Lord will repay on my behalf. Lord, your mercy is forever; do not despise the works of your hands.» [Col. 0801B]

## EXPOSITION

This psalm is to be attributed to David himself, that is, to the Lord Jesus Christ—not because he himself speaks in it, but because the perfect, who speak here, direct their words to him. They set themselves forward as an example to the less perfect, so that by their example they may confess to the Lord with their whole affection [Col. 0801C] and act well, with the intention of seeking nothing other than the Lord.

### I will confess to you, Lord

O Lord, Son of God, who are Lord equally with the Father—a statement useful for the confirmation of faith—I will confess to you with my whole heart, that is, I will praise you with the whole affection of my mind. And rightly so, because you have heard my prayer uttered aloud. This says more than if he had specified in what matter he would hear him, since it can be understood of anything he might ask.

### In the sight of the angels

I will not praise you only with devotion, but I will also sing psalms, that is, act well, for you, that is, for your glory, in the sight of the angels—that is, with the intention of the angels, who praise you through love alone and not through fear.

Or I praise you for this reason: that at last I may be placed in the angelic vision, so that I may know and see you openly, face to face, as the angels see you. Or I will act as one who always appears before the angels, through whom my deeds are daily reported to you.

I will worship—that is, I will direct my petitions exclusively toward you—striving for this: that I may be your holy temple, that is, such a temple as is worthy of you; or I will worship with reference to the man assumed by you, who is the temple and dwelling-place of divinity.

And I will not only worship, but also confess your name, which is “Lord”—that is, I will praise you in word and deed.

### Because of your mercy

He shows what the mercy is for which he confesses. Here “I will confess” contains all the things mentioned above, namely confessing, singing psalms, and worshiping. I will confess to you, he says, because you have shown mercy and truth to the human race, mercifully fulfilling what you promised.

And because you have made your holy—that is, glorious—name great in the evident manifestation of the resurrection, above every name that is named, whether gods or angels.

### On whatever day

And because you have become powerful in the resurrection, I ask: hear me on whatever day I call upon you—that is, at every time of my prayer. And you ought to hear me, because I will ask that you multiply strength, not in my body but in my soul.

It is as though he were saying: “You are powerful enough to hear me, and this is what I ask, for which I rightly ought to be heard.”

### Let all the kings of the earth confess to you

Now he shows his intention, namely, the purpose for which he had introduced what was said above: so that, following this example, all the kings of the earth—that is, the great ones in the world—may confess to you, Lord Jesus, not despising submission to him who appeared in humility. And if kings ought to confess to him, then the lesser ought to do so much more.

Or, if we speak of the things signified by kings: let kings—that is, all who rule their sensuality—provoked by my example, confess to you, that is, praise you, because you are Lord.

They will not be able to excuse themselves from this confession, because they have already heard all the words of your mouth: that is, by your own teaching they have received everything you commanded concerning faith and conduct. Therefore there is no need for me to exhort them to learn these things.

### And let them sing in the ways of the Lord

Let them not merely confess, but also advance to the point of singing—that is, of taking delight—in the ways of the Lord, that is, in the commandments by which one goes to the Lord; or in the ways in which he himself went before them. The latter belongs only to the perfect.

And rightly they ought to confess to the Lord and sing, because the glory—that is, the reward—that he will give in the future to those who confess and sing will be great.

### For the Lord is exalted

There is no need to fear or dread this arduous work, because the Lord is exalted—that is, omnipotent and powerful enough to help. And just as he is powerful, so also he regards—that is, he helps—the lowly, that is, those who do not presume upon themselves and humbly implore his help.

And he knows the high—that is, the proud who presume upon themselves—from afar. He considers them from afar, not in place but by the withdrawal of grace. It is as though he were saying: Although he himself is high and exalted, his mercy is near to the humble but far removed from those who exalt themselves.

### If I walk

Now he confirms what he has proclaimed, turning toward the Lord and saying with a certain affection: Truly you regard the lowly, as can be proved in me. For if I walk—that is, persevere—in the midst—that is, in the depths—of severe and great tribulation, you will revive me: you will renew me inwardly, however much the outward person may decay.

And the very fact that I persevere will not arise from myself, but from the regard of your mercy—that is, from your giving me life and regarding me in my humility.

And you will not merely revive me so that I may withdraw from the battle without failing, with an equal hand, but you will also extend your helping hand against the anger of my enemies, so that by your help I may conquer my enemies.

### And your right hand has saved me

That is, in return for the extension of your hand, your right hand—that is, your power—will ultimately save me. [Col. 0803A]

### The Lord will repay

Now he makes an assertion concerning the other side. Truly the Lord will know the high—that is, he will consider them in order to punish them. When he has saved me by placing me at his right hand, the Lord himself will repay those enemies and persecutors of mine on my behalf—that is, he will give them punishment because of me, repaying them in my place, since I did not wish to avenge myself but waited for him who said: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deuteronomy XXXII).

Now he turns what he said above into a prayer, saying: Lord, just as your mercy is forever—that is, because you are merciful by nature—so do not despise the works of your hands. That is, do not allow the good work that you began in me to fail [Col. 0803B], but give better outcomes to good beginnings, making me persevere in good works, which are yours and not mine.

I ask this with confidence because your mercy will remain forever.

# PSALM CXXXVIII. A PSALM OF DAVID, FOR THE END

«Lord, you have tested me and known me; you have known my sitting and my rising. You understood my thoughts from afar; you investigated my path and my course. And you foresaw all my ways, because there is no word on my tongue. Behold, Lord, you have known all things, the last and the first; you formed me and placed your hand upon me. Your knowledge has become wondrous because of me; it has been strengthened, and I cannot reach it. Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings at dawn and dwell at the farthest limits of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me. And I said: Perhaps darkness will trample me, and night will be my illumination in my delights. For darkness will not be darkened by you, and night will be illuminated like day; its darkness is like its light. For you possessed my kidneys, you received me from my mother’s womb. I will confess to you, because you have been magnified wondrously; your works are marvelous, and my soul knows this exceedingly. My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret, nor my substance in the depths of the earth. My imperfect state was seen by your eyes, and in your book all will be written; the days will be formed, and no one will be in them. But your friends, O God, have been honored exceedingly by me; their rule has been strengthened exceedingly. I will number them, and they will multiply beyond the sand; I rose up, and I am still with you. If you slay sinners, O God, men of blood, depart from me. For they say in thought: “They will take their cities in vain.” Have I not hated those who hate you, Lord, and wasted away over your enemies? I hated them with perfect hatred; they became enemies to me. Test me, God, and know my heart; question me and know my paths. And see whether there is a way of iniquity in me, and lead me in the eternal way.» [Col. 0804A]

## EXPOSITION

This treatise is attributed to our true head, David, who goes toward the end—that is, toward the completion of justice and knowledge. Nothing was lacking in him concerning the perfection of the virtues; nevertheless, he speaks here with this intention: that his hearers, provoked by his example, may strive to be conformed to him. For although previously they might in some way have been able to excuse themselves, from now on they will be entirely without excuse if they do not obey, since in him they have before them a perfect example of justice and holiness.

Lord, you have tested me. O Lord Father, you tested me, [Col. 0804B] that is, you placed me in the experience of your commandments; in other words, you made me put your commandments into practice, and you knew me, that is, you loved me, because I fulfilled your commandments. And although you had loved me and do love me, nevertheless you will know my lying down, that is, it will please you to humble me in suffering and thus bring me to the glory of resurrection. Or it is as though someone were to say: “If he knew him, why did he permit him to be killed?” He says: You knew, that is, although it may be hidden from others, you nevertheless know for what purpose you wished me to suffer and rise again; you understood my thoughts. And you did not test me only in completed commandments, but you also understood my thoughts, that is, they were such as were worthy of your understanding—and this “from afar,” that is, from the beginning of my life.

You investigated my paths, that is, my difficult and singular virtues; and you investigated the cord, [Col. 0804C] that is, the lot of my inheritance—namely, the salvation of the human race, which is my inheritance. In other words, you made me investigate it, so that I would consider nothing there except the restoration of the human race. This is said by comparison with a traveler, who seeks rest after the labor of a journey. Hence the Hebrew has: “You investigated my lying down,” that is, you made me investigate the rest of immortality and freedom from suffering.

From the beginning, I say, from the time I came into being, you made me think such thoughts as were worthy of your understanding. And you investigated in me not only the common virtues, which are found in many, but also the singular ones, which are found in few: for example, remaining a virgin, setting temporal things aside, and devoting myself solely to divine matters. Above all, you investigated in me the relinquishing of my inheritance, which consists in the salvation of human beings, that is, you considered whether I was concerned about these things. [Col. 0804D]

And you foresaw all my ways. Someone now speaks more forcefully in praise of himself. What need is there, he says, to mention my thoughts and paths individually? Rather, I shall speak generally: you foresaw all my ways, that is, you made me foresee them, and therefore I arranged my conduct through them rationally and well.

And so that no one might think these words were spoken arrogantly, as though they had no basis in reality, he says: I declare these things so freely because the word is not merely on my tongue; I speak from truth, and for the usefulness and instruction of my hearers. Behold, Lord, you have known. I said that the word in my tongue is not merely speech—that is, deception. And behold, what I say is manifest to you, that is, before you, who cannot be deceived and in whom there is no lying. For you have known all things, the last things, that is, the past; how much more the present? [Col. 0805A]

You tested me, I say, and foresaw my ways, and through this testing and foresight you formed me, that is, you made me beautiful and comely. And after granting me this beauty, which is the progress toward perfection, you placed your hand upon me, that is, your protection; in other words, you made me persevere in that beauty, namely, in the virtues mentioned above.

Your knowledge has become wondrous. Up to this point he has commended the perfection of justice that was in him. And because complete blessedness could not yet be in him unless he possessed perfect wisdom, he also says that full wisdom was in him, when he says: Your knowledge—which you inspire in the faithful, or by which you can be known—has become wondrous, [Col. 0805B] that is, worthy of admiration and desirable to others, through me. Through the first parent, who rejected it from himself as something worthless, it had become contemptible. But because I persevered in it and taught that wisdom fully—the wisdom that had previously been regarded as something worthless—it was considered wondrous, precious, and exceedingly desirable by human beings.

That knowledge, weakened in human beings through Adam’s disobedience, so that they possessed only a small knowledge of God, was strengthened, that is, made firm, through my obedience in my members; and it became ever more strongly established. And I shall not be able to reject it from myself even if I should wish to do so, that is, I do not find it possible by free choice to drive it away from me. Nor shall I misuse the powers of free choice, deeming myself capable of rejecting it, as Adam made himself capable of doing when he believed that he would become divine. [Col. 0805C]

Alternatively: Although this knowledge has become wondrous to others through me, nevertheless I shall not be able to attain it—that is, I consider myself insufficient to obtain it by myself, given the weakness of human nature—unless you preserve me. In this he prescribes the greatest humility to his members, so that they do not become vain in their thoughts if they are advanced to some knowledge, since he in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Colossians II) confesses that he is unable to obtain it.

Where shall I go from your Spirit? And since you formed me so beautifully in innocence of conduct, and since you so illumined me with the perfection of knowledge and wisdom, if I should now withdraw from you, where shall I go from your Spirit—that is, to what other place could I betake myself [Col. 0805D] where such formation and such wisdom might be given to me? And where shall I flee from your face? In what place could I hide so as to escape the punishments owed me for withdrawing, if I wished to depart from you? Nowhere shall I find such an illuminator or giver of wisdom.

But neither shall I be able to escape your hands, for I shall find no place of concealment either in heaven, or in hell, or in some intermediate hiding place. And this is what follows:

If I ascend into heaven. If it could happen that I were able to ascend into heaven without you—either because I wished to be illumined by the heavenly creatures without you, or because I could there hide from your face—you are there, illumining those who are heavenly. For whatever light they possess is from you. And therefore, if I depart from you, I shall be able neither to be illumined by them nor to hide from them. [Col. 0806A]

And if I descend locally into hell, either to hide there so that you would not punish me there, you will be present there, exercising your power.

If I take up my wings. Nor in this way can I escape your presence. For if I take up my wings, that is, the agility of virtues by which someone flies up into heaven, I say, placed at dawn—that is, in the primordial illumination of my way of life, having ceased to be a merely animal being—and dwell at the ends of the sea, that is, place my hope entirely in the farthest end of the sea, namely, in the harbor and tranquility of the future life, which is the limit of this storm-tossed worldly sea, you are there.

For your hand will lead me there, that is, the activity of your help will lead me to this end: that I take up my wings at dawn and possess this hope. And your activity will not only lead me to this, but your right hand will hold me, that is, your mercy will make me persevere there. [Col. 0806B]

On this occasion, in these words beginning with “Where shall I go from your Spirit?”, he seems to have transferred the persons of others into himself, so that he might display himself to them as the perfect example of justice, knowledge, and humility. For if the one who was born could not find another illuminator or formator, nor escape punishment if he withdrew from God, much less should others believe that they could do so.

And I said: Perhaps darkness. He speaks for the instruction of his members, so that they may not flee when they suffer persecution. Although you had made me so beautiful and wise, nevertheless I said—that is, I understood and saw—that because you had so adorned me, darkness, that is, the Jews, who are dark and, in their unbelief and sins, oppose the light, would trample me, that is, hand me over to death. And this “perhaps” means through a rash impulse, without any foresight of reason. [Col. 0806C]

This will not happen fruitlessly, because by the very fact that they hand me over to death, not only will others but also night—that is, the Jews themselves, who are darkness—become my illumination, that is, they will be illumined by me, existing among my delights, that is, among those in whom I take pleasure. In Hebrew it reads: “Night also will be light before me.”

For darkness will not be darkened. Truly they will be my illumination, that is, they will be illumined by me, because darkness—that is, the Jews—will not be darkened by you; rather, you will illumine them. And because you will illumine them, I will illumine those who once were darkness, that is, who had been blinded by your just judgment. [Col. 0806D]

As though he were saying: The illumination is mine because it is yours, since I and you are one (John X), that is understood, in substance.

He now shows how great their illumination will be, as follows: And night will be illumined like day, that is, those who previously existed as darkness will be illumined after the manner of the apostles, or in the likeness of the brightness of day. As is its darkness, that is, the darkness of night, so also is its light: in other words, great sinners will recognize themselves to be sinners. And insofar as they recognize that they have been blinded by sins, they will be illumined.

Because you possessed. Someone might say: Why will the illumination of night come through your death rather than through the death of another? To this he replies: “The ruler of this world has nothing in me” (John XIV), which will not be true of others. And this is what he says: Because you possessed my inmost parts, that is, you were the possessor and knower of all my affections and delights. Therefore I did not commit actual sins. You received me from my mother’s womb, that is, I had you as my patron and defender from the time when I was in my mother’s womb. And therefore original sin was not in me, whereas all others are received by you in baptism for the remission of original sin. [Col. 0807A]

I will confess to you. And because I am free from actual and original sin, I will confess to you, that is, I will attribute it to you and praise you. I also attribute to you the fact that you have been glorified through me, because I always glorified you in my works in a fearsome manner—that is, I carried out your service so courageously that, like a good soldier, while all the others [Col. 0807B] were fleeing, I alone on the battlefield struck fear into everyone if they did not act well, since in me they had the perfect example of justice, seeing one of the same condition and nature.

And therefore night will also be illumined through my death, because your works were wondrous through me. For I showed that the rational human creature, which through Adam’s disobedience had been regarded as something weak and feeble, was, according to creation, something glorious and worthy of admiration, while I lived innocently and proceeded with equal perfection. And it was entirely fitting that human nature should be restored through me, through whom it was shown to be exalted and wondrous.

And just as your works have hitherto been wondrous through me, so also my soul will know them exceedingly—that is, it will attend to the fact that they are wondrous. I will not conceal my knowledge of them, as Adam did; rather, in the very result, that is, in the very perseverance of my obedience, I will show that I know your works to be wondrous.

My mouth has not been hidden. In Hebrew it reads: “The works of my bones are not hidden from you.” He explains how he glorified God, namely in this way: my mouth—that is, the strength and power granted to me by you, which are reason and free choice—has not been hidden, that is, will not be hidden, from you. [Col. 0807C]

As though he were saying: The sword and weapons that you gave me for battle I shall neither cast away nor conceal, but, like a good soldier, I shall bring them forth by fighting courageously. And he specifies what strength he means: the strength that you made in secret, that is, in my interior, where reason is.

And my substance. Someone might say: We are not in a place where we can use our powers. If we were in paradise, as Adam was, we would not conceal them. He answers this objection as though saying: You will not be able to excuse yourselves on this account either, because in this also you have me as an example. My substance, which I called “my mouth,” that is, reason and free choice, through which I subsist above all, was not hidden even in the lower parts of the earth, that is, in this degradation of mortality and susceptibility to suffering. [Col. 0807D]

Indeed, while existing in the higher parts of the earth with respect to dignity, where it was easiest for him to exercise reason, he nevertheless concealed it, although he was not pressed by hardship, since neither cold nor heat drove him toward failure.

My imperfect state. Someone might say: Since you were so perfect, why then did you undergo death? He replies: This did not arise from any fault of mine. From what, then? Because your eyes saw my imperfect state, that is, it pleased you that this imperfection of mine according to outward appearance should be such that I underwent death.

And it pleased you for this reason: all those whose days are complete—that is, who are perfectly illumined, like the apostles—will be written in your book, that is, in my consideration, since I am set before them as an example of justice, so that they may suffer in the same way if necessary. And in that inscription they will be formed so as to be days, that is, a certain form and beauty will be impressed or infused into them in imitation of me, so that they themselves may be days and, in turn, many others may be formed by their example. [Col. 0808A]

This is said by comparison with a writer, who by writing makes forms after the likeness of another book.

They, [Col. 0808B] I say, will be formed in my likeness; nevertheless no one formed through them will subsist or remain in them—understood: in the days. This is to say: Although many will be formed through their ministry, no one will remain in them for the purpose of believing in them, placing the trust of hope in them, and inscribing his own form upon them; rather, he will remain in me.

But to me exceedingly. No one in them, but in me. And this is what he says: O God, your friends, that is, all who will love you through the apostles’ instruction, have been exceedingly honored, that is, exalted by virtues—and this for me, that is, for my glory, not for Paul’s, Cephas’s, or anyone else’s.

And they have not merely been exceedingly honored through the apostles’ instruction; their principalities also—that is, the apostles themselves, who rule over them—have been exceedingly strengthened for me. In other words, the fact that they have been so strengthened inwardly will redound to my honor, because they will attribute it to me. And if this was done by the leaders, much more will it be done by those under their leadership. [Col. 0808C]

I will number them. They will rightly attribute to me what they are, because I will number them, that is, I will choose them for my warfare, separating them by a definite number from the mass of the lost. This is said by comparison with a commander or emperor who chooses and enrolls suitable soldiers for an expedition.

And so that those who are to be saved may not seem few, because I said “I will number them,” they will multiply—that is, they will be more numerous than the sand, so many that they will be less capable of being counted than the sand. For sand is a thing that remains within our knowledge, whereas human beings pass from our sight and therefore are less capable of being counted. They are nevertheless countable to God. [Col. 0808D]

This multiplication will occur not only through my death, but also through my resurrection. And I shall not have this power only after the resurrection; I shall also still say, while living as a mortal: I am with you, because just as you are true God, so am I. By “with you” we understand a distinction of persons; by “I am,” the consubstantiality of the name with eternal power.

This may also be understood as the saying in the Gospel: “I was telling you these things while I was still with you” (Luke XXIV).

If you kill sinners, O God. O God the Father, if you kill some people by your just judgment because they are sinners, saying: O men of blood, depart from me—where “depart” means permitting them to be plunged into sins. [Col. 0809A]

And this is why you say, “Depart from me, because you say in your thoughts,” even if you do not say it outwardly: “Let Christians receive their cities,” that is, their gatherings and conspiracies, in vanity. For just as they are vain, so they lead others into vanity, namely, to lose what appears—that is, temporal things—and cling to things that are uncertain, that is, eternal things, which do not appear. This is the hostile mockery by which God’s faithful were oppressed; understood: and I will kill.

“Do I not hate those who hate you, Lord?” Truly I hated them, and hatred of them is nothing other than their destruction. And although I hated them insofar as they were evil, nevertheless I was wasting away, that is, I was afflicted with grief, “over your enemies,” that is, over the consideration of those who are your enemies. In other words, I nevertheless grieved over their destruction, [Col. 0809B] because I loved them in what you had done in them.

As though he were saying: I loved what you did in them; I hated what they themselves had done. “With perfect hatred I hated them.” Someone might say: You command love; why, then, did you hate them? He says: I hated them with a perfect and just hatred, hating the evil in them and yet wasting away with grief on their account. And although I was so affected on their behalf, nevertheless they became enemies to me, hostile in their attitude toward me.

“Test me, O God.” He is not praying for perseverance in the things he declared above about himself. “O Lord, test me,” that is, lead me into the experience of your will, that is, of good works. And because the words “test me” could be understood ambiguously, namely, either of affection or of action, he determines their meaning by saying: “And know my heart,” that is, test me in such a way that you may know whether my thoughts and affections are worthy of your knowledge. Or “know,” that is, love my thoughts themselves, making them such as may rightly be loved by you. [Col. 0809C]

Examine me, that is, lead me into the experience of good action; this is the same as “test me.” And “know my paths,” that is, make me act in such a way that my actions are worthy of being known by you.

And see whether there is a way of iniquity in me. Test my desires and my paths. And “see,” that is, do this with regard to mercy. And although I invoke mercy, nevertheless, if there is a way of iniquity in me, neither test nor know me. But if there is none, lead me in the eternal way, which leads to eternal life; that is, make me persevere in the way pleasing to you until I reach eternity.

## PSALM 139. A PSALM OF DAVID, “TO THE END”

[Col. 0809D]

“Deliver me, Lord, from the evil man; from the unjust man deliver me. They have plotted iniquities in their heart; all day long they were preparing battles. They sharpened their tongue like serpents; the venom of asps is under their lips. Guard me, Lord, from the hand of the sinner, and from unjust men deliver me. They plotted to trip up my steps; the proud hid a snare for me. They stretched out ropes as a snare; beside the road they placed a stumbling block for me. I said to the Lord: You are my God; hear, Lord, the voice of my supplication. Lord, Lord, strength of my salvation, you have overshadowed my head on the day of battle. Do not hand me over, Lord, to the sinner’s desire; [Col. 0810A] they have plotted against me; do not abandon me, lest they be exalted. The head of their circuit, the labor of their lips, will cover them. Coals will fall upon them; you will cast them into the fire; they will not endure in their miseries. A man of many words will not be directed in the land; evil will seize the unjust man unto destruction. I know that the Lord will execute judgment for the needy and vengeance for the poor. Nevertheless the righteous will confess your name, and the upright will dwell in your presence.”

## EXPOSITION

This psalm is David’s—that is, it belongs to the faithful who act courageously and look toward the end, that is, toward Christ, in whom the end of perfection, justice, innocence, and wisdom is found, as was shown in [Col. 0810B] the preceding psalm. In this psalm the faithful, instructed by the head himself and contemplating the perfection of faith and justice, observe that the multitude of heretics establishes battles against them everywhere through sharp questions, and that the venom of asps is under their lips. They pray, as an example for others enduring a similar danger, that the Lord may deliver them from conformity with the heretics and from their treachery. And afterward, in accordance with perseverance, they pray that he may guard them from the hand of the sinner, the devil, and from unjust men.

Deliver me, Lord. You, Lord, who are able to do so because you are Lord, deliver me by the power of your strength from the evil man, or from the devil, who, polluted by the contagion of sins, is no longer called a heavenly angel but, from *humus* (“earth”), an evil man; or from the heretics who sin against themselves. [Col. 0810C]

“And from the unjust man deliver me,” that is, from those same heretics who sin against others.

They have plotted. What he previously said in the singular, he now expresses in the plural, because they are one mass and yet are multiple according to their individual members. From these, then, Lord, I ask you to deliver me, so that I may not be conformed to them.

“They have plotted iniquities,” and such iniquities as they discovered by their own ingenuity, not from books or from any authority, but in their hearts. After discovering them, they were preparing battles all day long, that is, continually: battles of arguments with which they attacked us.

They sharpened their tongue. It is necessary that you deliver me, because they do not attack me in an ordinary way. In their very questions they sharpened their tongue, that is, they employed sharp and subtle argumentation, existing like serpents. They creep along lightly, so that they are not noticed until they strike. In the same way, they proceed by creeping through certain implications of their own, so that they cannot be deceived until they have deceived others. Nor do they advance by a straight path, any more than serpents do; instead, they bend from one opinion to another. [Col. 0810D]

And they do not merely wound like ordinary serpents, but the venom of asps—that is, a highly effective error—is under their lips, that is, under their tongue.

Guard me, Lord. He repeats what he said above, “Deliver me,” to show the greater necessity of deliverance. There he did not specify whether their attack was directed against himself or against others. Here he speaks about himself.

O Lord, he says, guard me in perseverance from the hand—that is, from the activity or power—of the sinner, namely the same one [Col. 0811A] whom he previously called the evil man, so that I may not become an imitator of such people in the perversity of life.

“From unjust men deliver me,” from those same people, so that I may not assent to their opinion.

They plotted to trip up. It is greatly necessary that you deliver me from those who plotted to trip up—that is, cast down—my steps, that is, the uprightness of the faith in which I was walking. And they not only plotted this, but also secretly prepared a snare for me: in many things that I had said well and usefully, they craftily sought a trap. For they too, being proud—as is characteristic of heretics—explained many things well, usefully, and rationally, and possessed a certain religious appearance, so that they might persuade others of falsehood all the more easily.

And they stretched out ropes. To ensnare more easily, they wove and stretched out ropes, that is, firm and extremely strong arguments, which no one could break without the assisting grace of God, so that they might become a snare for me, that is, a deception. [Col. 0811B]

And where they are especially to be feared, beside the road—that is, beside the authority of the sacred Scriptures—they placed a stumbling block for me, that is, an offense: sometimes drawing examples from the Gospels, sometimes from the Epistles, sometimes from the writings of the other Fathers, and explaining them in another sense.

As though he were saying: They are to be feared both because they stretch out ropes and because they often disturb authority. And it is rightly said, “beside the road,” because they are neither wholly in the way nor wholly removed from it. For this reason they are less easily guarded against.

I said to the Lord. He turns to his hearers, presenting himself as an example to them and saying: When they attacked me beside you, [Col. 0811C] I did not trust in my own wisdom or in my own strength, nor did I seek an external patron. Rather, I turned to the Lord and said, both with an inward voice and with an outward voice:

O Lord, my God, you are my Creator. Just as I could not subsist in the first creation except through you, so I cannot be guarded except through you. Therefore hear the voice of my supplication, that is, grant me what my supplicating voice indicates.

Lord, Lord, strength. He now explains what the supplication is: “Lord, Lord,” of which one is an adjective and the other a proper name. As though he were saying: You, Lord, who are truly Lord—you, I say, are my strength in the attack, and this strength effects my salvation in the future.

This is proved by the fact that, while I have hitherto been placed in the day of battle, that is, in the attack of the heretics, you have overshadowed me, that is, given me shade and refreshment, over my head, that is, over my mind, so that I would not fail in the heat of tribulation. [Col. 0811D]

You, I say, Lord, do not hand my desire over to the sinner, that is, to the devil or to the heretics—understood: into their power—so that I may not assent to them. For my desire is to persevere in the sincerity of faith, so that my senses may not be corrupted, as Eve’s senses were corrupted when she consented to the serpent.

And it is necessary that you not hand me over, because they have plotted against me, that is, with the intention of opposing me. He uses the past tense to indicate that they have already begun and still persist in this course.

Do not abandon me, lest they be exalted, that is, lest their teaching [Col. 0812A] and authority spread and they glory in it. In saying, “Do not hand my desire over” and “Do not abandon me,” he indicates free choice together with grace. As though he were saying: I remain in the battle according to free choice; according to grace, do not abandon me.

The head of their circuit. It is necessary that you not abandon me, because this is especially to be feared: the labyrinths of their disputations might cover their head, that is, the summit of their error, so that scarcely anyone could penetrate those circuits. This is said by comparison with a serpent, which covers its head—the place of its life—with many coils, so that it cannot easily be wounded in the head. In the same way, heretics fortify their opinions with various arguments so that they cannot be shaken, and thus their heresy may remain alive.

And he explains what he said: The labor of their lips, [Col. 0812B] that is, the words they discover with great effort, will cover them, that is, conceal them.

Coals will fall upon them. Here he shows that he did not pray from lack of confidence, but for the instruction of others. I prayed, he says, that they not be exalted. And so it will be. Upon some of them will fall burning, desolating coals, that is, the authority of the apostles and the other teachers will crush them with great weight, so that they will have nothing with which to hiss back, according to the saying: “Every iniquity will close its mouth” (Psalm 106).

And they will not merely be crushed in this way; you will also cast them down from their pride, throwing them into the fire, so that they may be kindled and illumined by the flame of the Holy Spirit. And because they will be crushed and inflamed, they will no longer “endure in their miseries,” that is, in their errors.

A man of many words. Some [Col. 0812C] of them who humble themselves will be illumined. But a man of many words, that is, one who persists in loquacity and pride, striving to defend his error, will not be directed even in the land, where there is a place of direction. Instead, he always proceeds crookedly, falling from one error into another.

“Evil will seize the unjust man unto destruction,” that is, punishment will befall him not only in the present but also in destruction, that is, when he is separated from the body. Then evil will seize him: then the eternal punishments, which here he in some manner escapes, will begin for the first time. Here he strikes fear into others, so that they may not be conformed to the heretics.

I know that the Lord will act. “Evil will seize the unjust man,” that is, I know that the heretic will be seized by evil from this: I have known that “the Lord will execute judgment for the needy,” that is, in the future he will reward his humble ones, and he will avenge the poor, punishing the persecutors who attacked them. [Col. 0812D]

This is repeated to show that they will truly suffer punishments on account of the poor.

Nevertheless the righteous. In mentioning vengeance, the attack upon the poor is understood. To this the word “nevertheless” refers, as follows: Although the righteous are attacked and punished, nevertheless they will “confess your name,” that is, they will praise you without ceasing. And therefore, in the future, they will “dwell in your presence,” that is, they will remain in your presence; or, with your Son, who is the image of your face.

Alternatively, as though someone were to say: How do you know that “evil will seize the unjust man”? He says: Because “the Lord here executes judgment for the needy,” that is, by his just judgment he [Col. 0813A] chastises here the one whom he receives. And he will make vengeance for the poor, understood: he will do so, that is, here he will avenge upon his poor whatever they have done wrong. If he does not spare his own now, much less will he spare the unjust in the future.

Nevertheless the righteous will not cease from praising you, even if you punish them by your judgment. And therefore, in the future, they will “dwell in your presence,” that is, with your Son, who is your image. Of them he himself said: “Father, I will that where I am, there my servant also may be” (John XII, 17).

## PSALM 140. A PSALM OF DAVID

[Col. 0813B]

“Lord, I cried to you; hear me. Attend to my voice when I cry to you. Let my prayer be directed like incense in your presence; let the lifting of my hands be an evening sacrifice. Set a guard, Lord, over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips. Do not incline my heart toward words of malice, to make excuses for sins, with men who work iniquity; and I will not share in their chosen ones. The righteous will correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let the oil of the sinner not fatten my head. For my prayer is still among their good pleasures; their judges have been swallowed up, joined to the rock. They will hear my words, for they have prevailed, just as when the thickness of earth is broken up upon the earth. Our bones have been scattered beside hell, because my eyes are toward you, Lord, Lord; in you I have hoped. Do not take away my soul. Guard me from the snare they set for me, and from the stumbling blocks of those who work iniquity. [Col. 0813C] Sinners will fall into his net; I alone am until I pass over.”

## EXPOSITION

This is David’s psalm, that is, the psalm of the perfected faithful. Here they pray for the whole perfection of life: first, that they may be given to pray for what ought to be prayed for, and with the intention that is fitting; then, that they may be given to act well, so that they may be worthy to be heard; and that they may become so perfected that they do not sin with the tongue—or, if they should happen to sin, do not excuse themselves. Finally, they pray that they may be strengthened in tribulations.

O Lord, I cried out to you. O Lord, who are omnipotent and therefore able to hear, I cried out—that is, I prayed with devoted intention, looking toward you, who are merciful; and because you are able, grant what I ask. And because there is never completion in this life, I cried out, and I shall continue to cry out. And when I cry out to you, looking toward you, attend to my voice—that is, make it intense in the accomplishment of this matter which my voice, whether interior or exterior, will indicate.

Let my prayer be directed. Now he explains what he cries out for: namely, this is what I ask first, that my prayer be directed—that is, that it be rightly directed. And because it could be directed with regard to human beings, he adds, “in your sight”—that is, according to your good pleasure—so that it may be pleasing to you, and so that I may ask for those things which ought to be asked. And because he could still ask for things that ought to be asked, but not with the intention with which he should, since many pray for such things out of a desire to be proud, he further specifies:

Like incense, so that the prayer itself may become the cause of heavenly things—that is, eternal things—just as the smoke of incense rises toward what is above. This is to say: Do not merely make us pray for what ought to be prayed for, but also with a good intention—that is, with regard to eternal things—so that, if we pray for health, it may be for the purpose of applying ourselves more diligently to prayers and other good works.

And not only may the prayer be directed, but also “the lifting up of my hands”—that is, of my good works—may be an evening sacrifice. This means that it may be not merely the completion of the morning sacrifice, that is, of the old law, but also of the new law, which, when observed, is a sacrifice—that is, something pleasing to God. But just as no other law follows the new law, so no other hour of the day follows evening; therefore he does not mention morning. Yet by mentioning evening he implies that the morning preceded it, by whose mere completion no one can be saved.

Set, O Lord, a guard. And advance me, O Lord, toward perfection to such a degree that you set a guard over my mouth, so that I may know when and to whom I ought to speak, and when I ought to remain silent. And lest someone think that he prays for such a guard in order never to speak, he specifies:

Set a door over my lips—that is, inspire within me that power by which my mouth is neither always opened nor always closed, just as a door in a house is made to be opened and closed in turn. And not just any door, but “a door of restraint”—that is, one which protects all the senses of the body on every side, so that I may not sin through them.

“Do not incline my heart.” In this also hear me, so that I may not sin in thought. And this is what he says: Do not merely set a guard over my mouth; but if it should happen that I sin—for that is human—do not incline, that is, do not permit my heart, meaning my mind, to be humbled to such a degree that it descends into words of wickedness. Let not only speech be absent from me, but let me also not approve, according to my understanding, the wicked speech of evil people by which they excuse their sins, attributing them either to fate or to the weakness of human nature. These words appear to justify, when in truth they are words of wickedness.

Even if it should happen at some point that I excuse myself, “do not incline my heart to excuse excuses, I who have been placed in sins”—that is, do not permit me to defend the excuse brought forward either on my own behalf or on behalf of others, nor to assert that I have spoken well.

“With men who work iniquity.” If you grant me this—that my prayer be directed and that the lifting up of my hands be an evening sacrifice—I will not share, that is, I will have no fellowship, with men who work iniquity. And I am not speaking only of the lesser among them; I will not even share with their chosen ones, which is the more serious matter. For one more readily gives consent to a rich man than to a poor man.

Alternatively, the passage may be connected in this way: Do not incline my heart so that I excuse myself in sins, as those who work iniquity are accustomed to excuse themselves. And if you do this, I will have no fellowship with their chosen ones—that is, with their prelates and principal men.

He will correct me. Even if you have not inclined my heart to words of wickedness, so that I do not sin in thought, nor excuse myself in sins, this good will follow: some righteous person will correct me through ecclesiastical discipline, namely, by fasts and sometimes by beatings. And he will correct me because I wholly accuse myself; and he will rebuke me with admonitions and teachings. He will do this in mercy, because I understand that it is done mercifully. I would not act in this way if I wished to excuse myself.

The correction, I say, of the righteous person will please me, and I will understand it to be mercy. But let the oil—that is, the flattery—of the sinner not fatten my head, that is, let it not delight my mind; in other words, may it not fatten me. He says this as a prayer or wish because many even of the good are overturned by the flattery of the wicked. And therefore, because of the difficulty and danger, he does not express it as a declarative statement, but as a prayer.

For still. In truth, I will not share with their princes, nor will “the oil of the sinner fatten my head,” because they themselves will rather share with me. “For still”—understand, “there will still be”—not only my works, but also “my prayer among the things pleasing to them.” That is, it will be among the things that please them; it will please them to pray for the same things for which I pray, namely, that they may pray rightly and act well.

And this contributes to the intention of the passage, because these faithful people here aim to persuade others to perfection in prayer. And this is what I said: it will not concern only the lesser ones, but also their judges—that is, their superiors and prelates, whose office it is to judge. “They have been absorbed,” that is, they will be absorbed in this: they will be overcome and destroyed with respect to what they are, because they have been joined to the rock, that is, to Christ, through faith.

He does not simply say, “My prayer will please him,” but adds “still,” in order to suggest the shortness of the time.

They will hear my words. He explains how they are joined to Christ: namely, through the words of my preaching, for hearing and receiving which they will be suitable. “Because they were powerful”—understand, those same words—that is, they prevailed among them and had both power and effectiveness for persuasion. In Hebrew it is rendered, “Because they are beautiful.” It is said by affinity of meaning, since beautiful words are usually powerful for persuasion.

Here he gives an example to others, so that they may be concerned for the salvation of their neighbors, and so that prelates may devote themselves to preaching.

“Like the fatness of the earth. Our bones have been scattered.” The beginning of this verse is joined to the end of the preceding one, as follows: Some will receive my words; but from those who do not receive them, our bones will be scattered beside hell—that is, the stronger among us will be scattered beside the judgment of those who are worthy of the name “hell.”

This scattering will be “like fatness cast upon the earth”—that is, just as dung cast, or spread, upon the earth makes it fertile, so our death bestows fertility upon the Church, while through the sufferings of the martyrs it is made fruitful for producing the fruit of faith, because for one person who is killed many would succeed him.

In this he prescribes a model for others, so that they may not shrink from suffering, since just as their life is useful, so also is their death.

And although we are bones, nevertheless we do not trust in our own strength; rather, in our very scattering, with a doubled utterance arising from excessive affection, we say:

“Lord, Lord, although you permit the body to be afflicted, do not permit my soul to be taken away, so that it may yield to their judgment.” This is just, because my eyes—that is, the regard of my intention—are directed toward you, not toward temporal things and not toward the protection of another.

And because I have hoped in the things that are in you, and not in things unlike you, guard me. He explains in what respect the statement “Do not take my soul away” is to be understood:

“Guard me from the snare which they have set for me”—that is, from their promises and flatteries, by which they strive to draw me away, so that they may deceive us neither by gifts nor by flattery. And guard me from scandals—that is, from the torments and open persecution of those who work iniquity, by which they attempt to take away my soul and make it like themselves.

They will fall into his net. I therefore pray that you guard me, because I see certain people falling; but only sinners will fall, those who are in his net—that is, in the net of iniquity. I do not mean those who have sinned at some time and then ceased, but those who are entangled in sins according to habit and love temporal things more than eternal things.

And it is right that you guard me, because I am “alone,” that is, in a unique hope—not in the desire for multiplicity, like sinners—but I have asked one thing from the Lord, and in it I shall persevere until I depart from this life.

## PSALM 141. THE UNDERSTANDING OF DAVID, WHEN HE WAS IN THE CAVE, A PRAYER

“With my voice I cried out to the Lord; with my voice I entreated the Lord. I pour out my prayer before him, and I declare my tribulation before him. When my spirit failed within me, you knew my paths. On the way by which I walked they hid a snare for me. I looked to the right and saw, but there was no one who knew me. Escape has perished from me, and there is no one who seeks my soul. I cried out to you, O Lord; I said: You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living. Attend to my supplication, for I have been humbled exceedingly. Deliver me from those who persecute me, for they have grown stronger than I. Bring my soul out of prison, so that I may confess your name; the righteous await me until you repay me.”

## EXPLANATION

This psalm is attributed to the Lord Jesus, who is called “understanding” because it designates his good devotion and action, which pertain to intellectuality—that is, to discernment.

I mean a psalm which was uttered when he was placed in a cave—that is, when he was concealed in a mortal and passible body. For this reason the Jews did not recognize him as God. Or it was uttered when he was concealed in this world, where neither the evil spirit nor the Jews recognized him. “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2).

He also directs us to the historical account (1 Samuel 24), where we read that, when Saul was pursuing David and David had hidden himself, Saul happened by chance to enter the same cave to relieve his bowels; and David, approaching secretly, cut off the edge of his cloak.

In the mystery, however, Christ, the true David, cut off part of Saul’s garment when, concealing himself in this world, he took from the devil a part of his divided possession—that is, certain of those whom he held under his power and by whom he was, as it were, clothed and concealed. The devil himself had entered this world in order to deposit and discharge his foul works.

Thus, in this psalm the Lord Jesus speaks, showing with what devotion and intimacy he related to God the Father when the time of his passion was approaching. He does so for the instruction of his members, so that in tribulations they may have their one hope in the Lord in the same way.

“With my voice I cried out to the Lord.” I, looking toward the Lord, cried out—that is, I was intent with my voice, my interior voice, meaning with my will and exceedingly great love. And I not only had an intense love toward him, but I also entreated him—that is, I prayed, not with the sound of my lips or with an alien voice, but with my own voice, meaning an attentive voice.

For one could pray according to outward utterance and yet not with one’s own voice in the sense of attention, because the mind might be drawn here and there.

“I pour out before him.” I prayed, I say, and not merely in any manner, but in such a way that I pour out—that is, I explain and make manifest—my prayer by praying with intention. I speak of a prayer existing “before him,” that is, in his good pleasure, because I pray concerning those things about which one ought to pray.

And beyond this, “I declare my tribulation before him”—that is, I speak with him about my tribulation, showing my merit so that my prayer may be heard. I show my merit not in order to obtain human favor, but “before him,” that is, according to his good pleasure; or I, myself, exist before him—that is, in intimacy with my Lord. And he himself speaks to him, not through an intermediary.

“When my spirit failed within me.” I declare my tribulation. And I make this declaration when my spirit fails—that is, when my soul is distressed—or in the awareness that my spirit will help me, as it is said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26).

In Hebrew it is rendered: “When my spirit is distressed.” This failure or distress will arise “from me”—that is, from my permission and will—because I have the power either to suffer or not to suffer.

Alternatively: In truth, I declare my tribulation before him because I am “failing,” that is, destroying and setting aside, “from myself” the wills that could arise from the nature of the flesh. It is as though he said: I do not declare my tribulation in such a way that I wish it to be removed from me; rather, I do so by failing in my spirit—that is, by destroying my will in this way.

For, insofar as the nature of the flesh is concerned, everything tends toward preserving its own existence for as long as it can.

And I was not only intent upon prayer and love, but I also persisted in good works. This is what he says, turning to the Lord with thanksgiving: “And you knew my paths”—that is, you approved my good works—because I performed such works as were worthy of your knowledge, on this path along which I walked.

And although I was thus devoted, praying and acting, nevertheless, on this path along which I walked—that is, in this purpose of mine, by which I was advancing more and more in proportion to the manifestation of my hidden action—they thought to conceal a snare from me, that is, the danger of death.

By saying that they concealed a snare from him, he shows his greater merit and virtue: for although he knew beforehand of the danger of death and could have escaped it, he nevertheless remained.

“I looked to the right.” To the other disadvantages there was added this: while they were preparing the snare, I looked to the right—that is, toward those who were superior to me, such as the apostles—and I saw, that is, I tested whether there was anyone who looked upon me with due regard. But there was no one who knew me—that is, no one who understood me and recognized me as God, remaining with me and giving judgment on my behalf.

“Escape has perished.” Although the Jews were preparing a snare for me and those superior to me did not recognize me, nevertheless escape perished from me—that is, I did not flee, but remained in place.

And not only was there no one who recognized me as God, but there was no one who sought my soul—that is, no one who paid attention to how holy and justly I had lived according to human nature, so that he might at least regard me as a good man and therefore stand on my behalf.

All these things contribute greatly to the formation of others.

“I cried out.” Again he prescribes a pattern for his members concerning what should be done amid the distress of this world. It is as though he said: When they were concealing a snare for me and my friends had abandoned me, O Lord, I did not seek human protection, but I cried out to you, saying:

“Attend to my supplication”—that is, make yourself intent upon granting what I ask. And this is just, because you, who are omnipotent and merciful, are my hope, since I do not trust in my own strength but in you.

And therefore, because my portion—that is, my inheritance—is in the land of the living, those who are the land of the living, namely the righteous, are my inheritance. And I pour out prayers in order to obtain that inheritance. I suffer for no other reason than that the righteous may be my inheritance.

And it is necessary that you attend, because I have been humbled exceedingly—that is, by enduring scourges, spitting, and many other things.

“Deliver me.” He first explains how he wants his supplication to receive attention, namely in this way: “Deliver me from those who persecute me,” lest, overcome by tribulation, I yield to their judgment and be made like them.

This would rightly be something for me to fear, because they have grown strong against me according to their own estimation, thinking that they prevail over me. But it is not right for you to satisfy such people concerning me.

And I pray not only that, overcome by tribulation, I may not be made like them, but also this:

“Bring my soul out of prison”—that is, bring my soul out of imprisonment; in other words, free my body, made alive, from the guarded tomb. He puts “soul” for “body,” or a part for the whole. For although they did not keep the soul in prison, he nevertheless says “soul” more appropriately than if he had said “me” or “my body,” because the body might be understood to have been taken away without the soul, as the wretched Jews still assert.

Bring me out, I say, “to confess your name”—that is, so that I may establish people who will praise you in contemplation of your name. And he explains by whom this confession ought to be made: by the righteous, who await me until you repay me—that is, until you cause me to rise again, repaying me according to my obedience.

## PSALM 142. A PSALM OF DAVID, WHEN HIS SON ABSALOM PERSECUTED HIM

“Lord, hear my prayer; listen with your ears to my supplication in your truth; hear me in your righteousness. And do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight. For the enemy has pursued my soul; he has humbled my life to the earth. He has placed me in dark places like those who have been dead for ages, and my spirit has been distressed over me; my heart within me has been troubled. I remembered the days of old; I meditated on all your works; I meditated on the works of your hands. I stretched out my hands to you; my soul is like land without water before you. Hear me quickly, O Lord; my spirit has failed. Do not turn your face from me, and I shall be like those who descend into the pit. Make me hear your mercy in the morning, for I have hoped in you. Make known to me the way in which I should walk, for I have lifted up my soul to you. Rescue me from my enemies, O Lord; I have fled to you for refuge. Teach me to do your will, for you are my God. Your good Spirit will lead me into a level land. For the sake of your name, O Lord, you will give me life in your righteousness. You will bring my soul out of tribulation, and in your mercy you will scatter all my enemies. And you will destroy all who afflict my soul, for I am your servant.”

## EXPLANATION

This psalm is attributed to David—that is, to any faithful person who is already beginning to be David, meaning “strong of hand,” resisting sin manfully, whereas previously he had succumbed to it effeminately.

I mean a psalm composed when—that is, because—his son persecuted him: namely, sin, which he himself begot, since it was not sent into him by God but arose from himself.

The first persecution by sin, by which he was driven into guilt, was the reason why he uttered this prayer, so that the foulness and dishonor generated in the soul by the sin committed might be forgiven.

The later persecution, which continued to assail him even in penance because of his evil habit, is the reason for this prayer: that he may not consent to it according to his will. He also prays that the ability to act well may be granted him.

“Lord, hear.” O Lord the Father, whom I now regard as my Lord, hear my prayer—that is, grant me what I ask. “With your ears”—that is, by the power of your hearing—“listen to my supplication,” that is, to such a prayer as is a supplication.

Prayer is the term used when we simply pray; supplication, when we pray under adjuration, saying, “by your coming,” “by your cross,” and similar expressions.

And I do not pray this in consideration of my own merit, for I have in no way deserved it, but “in your truth”—that is, in consideration of your Son, through whom you fulfilled your true promise. This is to say: Grant what we ask through his merit and intercession.

The phrase “in your truth” is a supplication; what follows afterward appears to be a simple prayer. And he explains how he says that the Son is the truth, adding a clarification in his foreknowledge:

“Hear me in your righteousness”—that is, in your Son, in whom you fulfilled this truth, so that through him you might give us life. As the Apostle says: “He was made for us righteousness and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1).

“And do not enter into judgment.” He now makes another prayer, as follows: Hear me, I say, in your righteousness. And do not enter into judgment with your servant—that is, do not deal with me according to the judgment of the guilty, so as to punish me as I deserve, but deal with me mercifully. This means: Since I am your servant, do not deal with me according to your strict judgment.

I ought to fear this because I will not be able to be justified in your sight, since I have died in sins. Even if I appeared just in my own sight or in the sight of other human beings, I would not be just in your judgment, because not even every living person—that is, every holy person truly living in the virtues—will be justified in your sight. No one is so just that something requiring correction is not found in him before you.

“For the enemy has pursued.” It is therefore necessary for you not to enter into judgment with me, because the enemy—that is, the tinder of sin, an evil suggestion, or the devil—has pursued my soul according to its impulse.

And he did not merely attack my soul, but he also humbled my life—that is, he cast it down from its dignity and weakened my soul according to consent—“to the earth,” that is, into the desire for earthly things and the filth of vices. Previously raised up by the virtues, it sought lofty things. This is said by analogy with birds: when they are captured, their wings are bound or cut off so that they cannot fly upward.

“He has placed me.” He not only humbled my life—that is, my consent and action—but also placed me, making me rest and persevere according to habit, “in dark places,” that is, in sins which blind my soul, just as virtues illuminate it.

He placed me, I say, “like those who have been dead for ages”—that is, like those who have died in the world, meaning in the desire for temporal things, and who now disdain sinning and regard it as nothing.

And therefore it is necessary for you not to enter into judgment with me. And because for this very reason God ought all the more to deal judicially with him, he sets forth his merit, saying:

Therefore also do not enter into judgment with me, because my spirit has been distressed—that is, my soul has grieved over me, understanding this as its consideration and regard for my humiliation and downfall.

And because it could be distressed without this being meritorious, as someone may be distressed over earthly things or over an inflicted punishment, he adds:

“My heart within me has been troubled”—that is, my reason has been so distressed that the distress is within me, meaning within free choice, so that just as I sinned voluntarily, I may also repent voluntarily.

“I remembered.” My spirit has been troubled within me for this reason: first, because I considered my downfall and foulness; and second, because, on the other hand, I remembered the days of old—that is, I remembered my former state, namely the innocence and holiness that were previously in me. Both causes were sources of the greatest distress. For when someone looks at the foulness in which he is and, by contrast, at the beauty in which he once was, he is distressed all the more.

Alternatively: I was distressed because I remembered the days of old—that is, the condemnation which the first human being suffered in ancient times because of disobedience, and with him the entire human race, since it was thrust into these miseries of suffering and mortality, as well as into infernal punishments. And therefore I feared for myself that I might be punished by a similar penalty.
