Fearing this—or rather striving toward merit—I meditated, that is, I devoted myself to fulfilling all your works, which you yourself command to be done. I meditated, I say, concerning the past, and I shall meditate in the future on the works of your hands—that is, on such works as you perform in me and which cannot be completed unless you perform them.

“I stretched out my hands.” For this reason also do not enter into judgment with me, because I stretched out my hands—that is, my affections—toward you, embracing you. Previously I had drawn them back when I was in the filth of vices.

And I loved you so greatly that my soul, longing for you, is like land without water: my soul desires to come to you and cling to you as dry land desires water.

“Hear me quickly, O Lord.” Up to this point he has given the reasons why he prayed that God not enter into judgment with him. Now he explains in parts what he previously prayed for more generally, as follows:

Because I meditated on all your works and stretched out my hands toward you, “hear me quickly”—that is, without delay, by wiping away the stain which I contracted through my former offense.

This “hear me” differs from the earlier one because the earlier statement was made generally concerning all the things that follow, whereas this one concerns only the remission of the sin committed before repentance.

Hear me, I say. And this is just, because my spirit has failed—that is, I have set aside my own will, while yours prevails in me more and more each day.

“Do not turn your face.” And do not merely hear me concerning the remission of sin; do not turn your face from me—that is, after remitting my sins, grant me the beauty of the virtues which is in you and which you inspire, but which you previously turned away from me when, by sinning, I departed from you.

And if you turn your face away, I shall be like those who descend into the pit—that is, into hell, or from one judgment into another. This is to say: I therefore ask you not to turn your face away, because if it is turned away, I shall perish completely.

“Make me hear.” In this also hear me: cause me to hear—or cause me to be heard for my benefit—your mercy, namely that voice by which your mercy is signified, when the righteous hear: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matthew 25).

The voice of judgment will be “in the morning,” that is, in the future resurrection, when, after the night and darkness of this age, that day first dawns.

And it is just that you hear me in this, since I hoped to attain that same mercy through you, not through my own strength.

“Make known.” And in order that this mercy may be heard by me, meanwhile make known to me the way of your commandments—not merely according to knowledge, but the way in which I should walk, that is, so that I may often practice it in action.

It is just that you do this, because I have lifted up my soul to you—that is, I have entrusted it to you so that you may direct it. This is the lifting up of the soul. The same thing is signified by “I hoped in you,” though it is expressed differently.

“Rescue me.” Do not merely make your way known to me; also, in your omnipotence, rescue me from my interior enemies—that is, from unlawful suggestions—so that they may not please me.

And this is rightly requested because I have fled for refuge to you, not to my own strength. And do not merely rescue me from my enemies so that I may not consent to them; afterward also teach me to do your will. That is, let your teaching cause me to fulfill what you command me to do, since it would not be enough merely not to consent to an evil suggestion unless good action also followed.

And I rightly seek this from you because you are my God. Just as I could not persist in the first creation except through you, so I cannot persevere in your will except through the gift of your grace.

“Your Spirit.” Now, trusting in God’s mercy, lest he appear to have prayed out of distrust, he announces with certainty for the consolation and strengthening of other penitents that what he prayed for will come to pass, saying:

O Lord, it will be as I have prayed. Your Spirit, who is good by nature and also good in effect for me, will lead me—that is, transform me—from what I was, earth producing thorns and thistles, into “level land,” that is, into what I may be: fertile earth, responding suitably to the good sower.

That earth is just which returns whatever seed is entrusted to it. And you will not do this because of my merits, but “for the sake of your name,” that is, for your glory. “You will give me life in your righteousness”—that is, in your commandments, which ought to be called righteousness, whereas previously I was dead in unrighteousness.

“You will bring me out of tribulation.” And you will not merely give me life by restoring the virtues; you will also bring my soul out of the distress of an evil conscience by forgiving my sin. And for this reason you will scatter all my interior enemies, namely the evil suggestions attacking me on every side. You will do this not because of my merit, but in your mercy.

And you will not merely scatter evil suggestions, but you will also destroy all who afflict my soul, whether interior or exterior enemies—that is, you will render them ineffective.

And this is just, because I am your servant: I set aside my own wills and carry out yours in all things.

Ambrose, in the *Hexameron*, says:

“Not to obey a command is not always evil. For if the command is good, obedience is honorable. But if the command is wicked, not to obey is useful. Therefore it is not always evil not to obey a command. But not to obey a good command is wicked. Now knowledge of the good is good and productive, whereas knowledge of evil is malign and unproductive.

“Therefore we must know whether the command is good or evil, since God says: ‘Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil’ (Genesis 3).

“The command of the law says: ‘You shall exchange the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep’ (Exodus 13). Thus, in the literal sense, he commands that the firstborn of a donkey—that is, an unclean animal—be exchanged for a sheep, which is clean and suitable for sacrifice.

“But if someone pursues more deeply the spiritual meaning of the law, he will consider that the donkey is a laboring animal, whereas the sheep is fruitful. Therefore he says that fruit is to be exchanged for labor, so that the result of one’s work may be fruit.

“Alternatively: You shall commend all your labor and all your industry with a pure and simple affection.

“But if you do not exchange it, you shall redeem it. Thus, according to the literal sense, another animal is commanded to be offered in place of an unclean animal, or a price is to be offered, so that among the tithes of the fruits neither something lesser nor something unclean may appear to be offered.

“The deeper understanding, however, teaches you to free your soul so that it may cease from those things which produce no fruit. For whoever redeems frees himself and in a certain manner removes himself from a debt.

“Works which cannot have true fruit and good progress must be abandoned, such as all these worldly things whose use cannot be lasting. In them the person himself is made naked and truly empty.”

## PSALM 143. A PSALM OF DAVID AGAINST GOLIATH

“Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war. My mercy and my refuge, my protector and my deliverer. My defender, and in him I have hoped, who subjects my people beneath me. Lord, what is man, that you have made yourself known to him? Or the son of man, that you regard him? Man has become like vanity; his days pass away like a shadow.

“Lord, bend your heavens and descend; touch the mountains, and they will smoke. Flash forth lightning, and you will scatter them; send out your arrows, and you will trouble them. Send out your hand from on high; rescue me and deliver me from many waters and from the hand of foreign sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity.

“O God, I will sing a new song to you; on a ten-stringed psaltery I will sing praise to you. You give salvation to kings; you redeemed David, your servant, from the evil sword—rescue me. And rescue me from the hand of foreign sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity.

“Their sons are like young plants in their youth. Their daughters are adorned and ornamented like the likeness of a temple. Their storehouses are full, overflowing from one thing into another. Their sheep are fruitful, abundant in their pastures; their oxen are fat. There is no breach in the wall, no passage through it, and no cry in their streets.

“They called that people blessed which possesses these things; blessed is the people whose God is the Lord.”

## EXPLANATION

This psalm is David—that is, every faithful person who is strong of hand or desirable in appearance.

I mean David fighting against Goliath (1 Samuel 17), that is, against the devil and his members: against heretics and all interior vices.

He does not mention Goliath because the interpretation of that name contributes anything here, except according to the event itself. For just as the bodily David killed Goliath, and did so on a rock, so in spiritual combat the faithful, through Christ, overcome enemies both interior and exterior.

In this psalm these faithful people give thanks to God because he makes them so skilled in battle that they do not succumb in the attack of their enemies. This is also for the instruction of the less perfect: when they are attacked, they should pray to the Lord for the skill to fight.

And when they have obtained it, they should glory not in themselves but in the Lord.

Blessed is the Lord. The Lord the Father, who is my Lord according to governance and my God according to creation, is blessed—that is, I glorify him by returning thanks and attributing to him everything good that takes place in me: both because he is Lord in relation to created things and because he is my creator, and also because of the benefit bestowed upon me, namely, that he teaches my hands for battle—that is, because he instructs me and makes me learned for fighting against a sharper and more violent attack, whether interior or exterior. For at times there is an exterior attack that is more violent, such as the attack of a philosopher or a subtle heretic; at other times there is one that is not so violent, such as that made by unlearned heretics. In the same way, one interior suggestion attacks more than another. Therefore, blessed is the Lord, who teaches my fingers for war—that is, who makes me learned for waging war against less forceful attacks, whether interior or exterior, so that they may not prevail against me. The only comparison to be noted is that he mentions hands and fingers. Since combat with a sword is conducted at close quarters and by hand, the danger is greater than when combat is conducted at a distance with arrows and other missiles, because those can be avoided more easily. Thus sword-fighting is signified by the hands, and the throwing of missiles by the fingers.

My mercy. The Lord showed mercy to David when, through Samuel, he chose him, the last of his brothers, for royal dignity (1 Kings 16). He was his refuge when he gave him the counsel by which he overthrew his enemy, whom he could not defeat with a sword (1 Kings 17). He was his supporter when he caused Saul to receive him as a son-in-law (1 Kings 18). He was his deliverer when he rescued him from the danger of the king’s anger (1 Kings 19). He was his protector when, while hiding in a cave, David took vengeance for the king’s benefit (1 Kings 24).

Alternatively: The Lord is therefore blessed because he is my mercy—that is, because he freely established and instructed me for battle. Even if he had bestowed the knowledge of fighting on the basis of merits, he would still have deserved to be glorified; but he deserves it much more when he grants this solely by grace. In that battle he also so encouraged me by the Holy Spirit that he was my refuge, because I fought with a certain security and no longer feared falling in defeat. He does not say that he was wholly secure, since it is written, “Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10); rather, he says this in relation to his former condition, in which he was intensely afraid, and in relation to another condition—as when someone recovering somewhat from a serious illness says that he is well, although he has not yet been entirely freed from it.

And let him be blessed not only for this present benefit, but also for the primordial benefit, because he was my supporter—that is, my procurer in baptism—restoring the weakness of nature to the freedom of reason and free will. I therefore also glorify him because he was my deliverer: he rescued me from enemies pursuing me from behind in baptism, that is, from actual and original sin. He was my protector; therefore let him be blessed because, when enemies rose up after the primordial deliverance, he protected me from the attacking enemies, namely, vices, so that they could not wound me. For this reason he speaks in the past tense: “In him I have hoped,” to show that he had long possessed such hope and that, because of past benefits, he hoped in him for the true and future goods that are in him.

This too is a reason for blessing him: he subjected a people under me—that is, to me—my people, namely, heretics or other enemies made my own, that is, conformed to me. Or: he subjected a people to me, that is, the vices arising from the nature of my own flesh; in other words, he made me rule over all my unlawful impulses.

Lord, what is man? I do not bless you, Lord, only for those benefits that you have bestowed upon me individually, but also for common benefits—for these, namely: What is man? That is, man is something great and excellent, and is of great dignity; and this is not from himself, but because you have made yourself known to him, that is, because you have disclosed yourself to him according to faith and knowledge.

Or rather, in what sense shall I say, “What is the son of man,” that is, the son of the first sinners and the son of perdition, he who was a son of death? What do you regard him as? That is, you remember him, justifying him and giving him other spiritual gifts. If I attend simply to the fact that you have made yourself known to man, I find him to be something great. But if I attend to the fact that you regard him—that is, remember him, that is, keep him in your memory—by placing him in good devotion and action, although previously liable to perdition, I find him to be something even greater. But if I consider both things together, I regard him as much greater still.

Alternatively:

**Lord, what is man?**

[Note: The mention of Remigius’s name, expressed three times in the exposition of this psalm, could raise some doubt concerning the author of the book itself. But no one is unaware that authors of expositions contemporary with us, when they reproduce the opinions of the ancient Fathers almost word for word, were accustomed to express their names—and even their own names when they added something of their own—as can be seen in Rabanus. They placed these notes in the margin; through the negligence of scribes, they are known to have been introduced into the text again and again, whether omitted or removed. Indeed, no one can fail to see that this mention of Remigius, as well as that of Gregory and certain others whose names are found inserted throughout the text of this book in entirely unsuitable places, was formerly written at the edge of the codex. —EDITOR.]

**Remigius:** This should be said as a question and with contempt: “What is man?”—as though he were dust possessing no firmness—because you have made known to him the immeasurable mystery of the Godhead. Or, “the son of man”? The same answer should be given, because you count him among your sheep, among the number of the predestined.

Man is like vanity. In one respect man is great, because you have made yourself known to him and have counted him among your own; but in himself he has been made like vanity. That is, by sinning in his first parent he made himself like vanity, approaching in some manner nothingness—that is, what is changeable—so that he might become nothing.

He shows in part how he “has been made like vanity”: “His days pass away like a shadow.” It is as though he said: It can be seen from this that he has approached nothingness, because his days—that is, his life, the life of man—pass like a shadow, which never remains in the same condition. In the same way, his age is vanity. He passes from infancy to boyhood, from there to adolescence, then to youth, and from there to old age. From this vanity—that is, from this decline—he will one day be withdrawn, just as in his soul he has been withdrawn from a certain vanity, namely, sin.

“Lord, bow down the heavens.”

Having given thanks for himself individually and for the common benefit, he prays for those whom the Lord has not yet shown to be exalted, to whom he has not yet made himself known, saying:

O Lord, since the faithful who serve you possess such great dignity, as has been said, so that even those who are still governed by the senses may become instructed for battle, bow down your heavens—that is, your preachers, who are exalted in contemplation of your Godhead. Make them descend from the height of understanding to the measure of the capacity of the weak. Descend in this way—that is, make yourself known to them in some degree, at least in historical knowledge—so that they may understand your birth and passion, since they have not yet risen to those higher things.

And because their preaching is ineffective without your action, touch the mountains—that is, touch inwardly, with the hand of mercy and with fear of future punishment, the proud of this world. In this way they will smoke—that is, they will send forth tearful prayers because they have persisted in unbelief.

Alternatively:

**“Lord, bow down the heavens.”**

**Remigius:** The bending down of the heavens took place when the honor of heavenly things descended to man.

“Flash forth lightning.” Since the bending down of the heavens alone would not be sufficient, he adds, “Flash forth lightning,” that is, make manifest miracles that will enlighten their minds.

“And you will scatter them,” that is, in this way you will separate them from the mass of the lost.

And after you have descended into their innocence according to faith, “send out your arrows,” that is, make your commandments and institutions for right living known to them. They are called arrows because they pierce the hearts of hearers and kill vices opposed to salvation. Or he calls the apostles arrows, because by their preaching, like feathered darts, they pierced the breasts of men.

By the sending forth of the arrows you will trouble them concerning their former life. When they hear that they must devote themselves to chastity, sobriety, and the other virtues, they will understand that their previous life was wicked.

“Send forth your hand.” Having prayed for those who still remained in their own dignity, he prays for himself in this way:

I pray not only for the other faithful, but also for myself. “Send forth your hand,” that is, make your help manifest to me—your help proceeding from your omnipotence—so that, as you are powerful, you may work powerfully in me. In this sense I say, “Send forth your hand,” so that by your power you may rescue me from many waters, that is, from diverse doctrines. For in ecclesiastical doctrine there is no multiplicity, but one faith and one baptism (Ephesians 4). Thus I pray that you rescue me in such a way as to free me—that is, make me able to act with a certain freedom against them, so that I may not fear being overthrown. And rescue me not only from the errors of heretics, but also from the hand—that is, the activity—of those who were once sons of the Church but are now alienated, having departed from the unity of the Church.

Alternatively:

**“Send forth your hand.”**

**Remigius:** He calls the Lord the Savior “the hand,” and prays that he may come to free the world, from on high—that is, from the height of power. “From the waters,” that is, from peoples turbulent and agitated as though by a storm. “From the hand of the sons of strangers,” who do not know how to spare the faithful and are begotten by the devil.

“Whose mouth has spoken.” I therefore ask to be rescued from their doctrine because their mouth has spoken vanity, that is, falsehood and not truth. Everything opposed to truth is vain.

I therefore ask to be rescued from conformity with them because their right hand—that is, their activity, which appears good—is the right hand of iniquity, directed toward iniquity. They act well for the very purpose of deceiving more easily. Or “right hand” means their prosperity, by which, once elevated, they assume permission to sin.

**God, a new song.** O God, if you rescue me from many waters, I will sing a new song to you—that is, I will praise you by observing the new law. I will also sing praise to you—that is, I will act well to your honor—on the ten-stringed psaltery, that is, in a soul resounding harmoniously through the fulfillment of the ten commandments of the old law.

He says that he will sing in the soul to show that he acts well in will and affection. For many works are performed outwardly in which the soul has no part, because there is no corresponding affection in them.

Because you give salvation to kings. He returns to his prayer to show that he cannot be saved from any other source. And to show the necessity of being rescued, he says, “Rescue me from the evil sword,” that is, from the errors of heretics, who kill the soul. Or from the devil’s sword, which is evil because it separates from the good. Christ’s sword, however, is benevolent because it separates from evil.

For just as the word of God is called a two-edged sword and is good because it cuts toward salvation from both Testaments, so the wicked doctrine of heretics is a sword because it draws from both Testaments; but it is evil because it turns everything toward condemnation.

And rightly I ask you to rescue me, because you are so great that you give salvation—understand, complete salvation: here according to virtues and good works, and finally eternal glory—to kings, that is, to those who rule themselves spiritually.

You are also so great and such that you redeemed David, your servant—that is, each faithful person devoted to you and acting courageously—redeeming him through the blood of your Son.

“Rescue me,” I said, “from the evil sword, and deliver me from the hand of the sons of strangers.” He repeats all this in order to establish the many reasons why one must pray repeatedly concerning such danger, as follows:

Therefore, Lord, it is necessary for you to rescue me from the many waters and from the hand of heretics, because their sons are like young plants: their thoughts and opinions are comparable to newly planted trees. He explains in what respect they are comparable to them: “in their youth,” that is, in the fact that new opinions are discovered daily and are joined to older opinions. In this respect they are comparable to new plantings, which, because they have been newly made, are frequently compared in number with the others.

And therefore it is necessary that you free me.

Their daughters are adorned and ornamented; that is, their words are decorated with every kind of exhortation—and not merely in part, but on every side. He calls thoughts “sons” and words “daughters,” using the feminine gender because greater care is customarily applied to daughters; and just as daughters themselves usually ensnare men more effectively, so the words of heretics do more harm than their thoughts. If they merely thought these things, they would by no means deceitfully entangle so many simple and uneducated people in their heresy.

And therefore it is necessary that you free me, because their words are “like the likeness of a temple,” that is, they are truly like the words of a temple, namely, of the faith. Just as Catholic men proclaim the triune and one God and certain other doctrines, so do they. In this way their words resemble the words of the faith. The faith is called a temple because, just as sacrifices are commanded to be offered in a temple, so in faith we are commanded to offer every good work to God; and outside the Catholic Church there is no place for a true sacrifice.

And therefore it is necessary that you free me, because their storehouses are full: in their grammar, where multiple opinions are contained like the chambers of a wealthy house in which many kinds of cups are stored. And from there—that is, from this fullness—they are “eructating,” that is, sending out, many arguments, moving, as I may say, from one thing to another: from the Old Testament to the New, or from one argument to another, or from one reasoning to another.

And therefore it is necessary that you free me, because their sheep—not the simple and uneducated people who are among them, but pregnant sheep, that is, their teachers, who give birth to others in error—are abundant, possessing many offspring, not, that is, according to the condition in which they entered the faith, but “in their departures,” that is, according to the condition in which they departed from the faith.

And therefore it is necessary that you free me, because their oxen are fat: that is, those same teachers of theirs are wealthy in riches, and what they cannot accomplish through knowledge, they accomplish by spending money. He calls their teachers “sheep” because of their extreme weakness of spirit; “pregnant,” because they give birth to others in error; and “fat oxen,” because of their excessive deceit. A fat cow deceives a bull more readily than a sheep deceives a ram.

And therefore it is necessary that you free me because “there is no breach in the wall,” that is, their arguments—their complex reasonings—cannot be demolished.

And therefore free me because there is no passage, understand, in their arguments: many are unable to resist where they are repeatedly trapped.

“Nor any outcry in their streets.” This is not a separate cause, but the sentence continues in this way: Although they are disgraceful, wealthy, and teachers of others, there is nevertheless no outcry—that is, no subtlety or intensity—in their arguments. “Outcry” signifies both subtlety and intensity. Thus the Lord is often said to have cried out in the Gospel, not with regard to the height of his voice, but with regard to the intensity and subtlety of his prayer.

There is therefore no outcry in their arguments because they are in their streets, that is, in the breadth of error and of the other vices.

And therefore it is necessary that you free me, because foolish men have called blessed the people to whom these things belong—namely, the aforesaid abundance of words, by which they can pass from one thing to another; riches; and arguments that can be restrained by no one or by only a few.

But my judgment is this: blessed is the people whose Lord is himself their God—that is, their creator.

## Psalm 144. Praise of David himself

“ I will exalt you, my God and king, and I will bless your name for ever and ever. Each day I will bless you, and I will praise your name for ever and ever. Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise, and of his greatness there is no end. Generation after generation will praise your works, and they will declare your power. They will speak of the magnificence of the glory of your holiness, and they will recount your wonders. They will proclaim the power of your awesome deeds, and they will recount your greatness. They will pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness, and they will rejoice in your righteousness. The Lord is compassionate and merciful, patient and greatly merciful. The Lord is sweet to all, and his mercies are over all his works. Let all your works confess to you, Lord, and let your saints bless you. They will speak of the glory of your kingdom, and they will proclaim your power, so that they may make your power known to the sons of men, and the glory of the magnificence of your kingdom. Your kingdom is a kingdom of all ages, and your dominion is in every generation and generation. The Lord is faithful in all his words, and holy in all his works. The Lord raises up all who fall, and lifts up all who are crushed. The eyes of all hope in you, Lord, and you give them their food in due season. You open your hand and fill every living creature with blessing. The Lord is righteous in all his ways and holy in all his works. The Lord is near to all who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth. He will do the will of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayer and save them. The Lord guards all who love him, and he will destroy all sinners. My mouth will speak the praise of the Lord, and let all flesh bless his holy name for ever and ever.”

## Exposition

This psalm contains praise that is to be attributed to David himself, that is, to Christ. In this exposition all the faithful who are perfect after the apostles exhort others in their own person to praise the Lord by considering him in himself. But they admonish those who have now been moved to this purpose—namely, to praise the Lord—to praise him at least by considering his works, so that they may eventually advance to praising him for his own sake. They speak as follows:

“I will exalt you, my God and king,” that is, Lord, who are my creator and ruler. “I will exalt you,” namely, in the active life, according to virtues and good works. “And I will bless your name,” that is, I will praise you by considering your name, with a blessing extending into the age of the age—that is, I will praise you in the contemplative life, which is lived in the present as far as possible and will be possessed more perfectly in the future.

And in doing this, “each day”—that is, through each virtue—I will bless you, that is, I will attribute each virtue present in me to you, whether in the present or in the future.

Or in this way: “I will bless you,” I say, that is, I will praise you, as I said, both in the active and in the contemplative life, and I will do this “each day,” that is, in prosperity and adversity.

And rightly I will praise you, because the Lord is great, that is, he is so powerful that there is no end to his greatness—that is, his power cannot be comprehended by the understanding of any creature. Or “there is no end” means that he is without limit with respect to spatial capacity. Or “there is no end” with respect to time means that he is eternal. And since he is so great, he is also exceedingly worthy of praise in his nature, that is, more than can be thought or said.

I will praise you, I say, by considering you in yourself, because I know that you are great and worthy of praise. But others, who are not sufficient for this, will praise you by considering your works, and they will do so for as long as one generation succeeds another. This is what he says: “Generation after generation will praise your works.” That is, they will praise you by considering your works, namely, heaven and earth, the sea, and the other visible things; and, moved by admiration of these, they will declare your power—that is, they will prove you powerful and worthy of praise.

And because of these things they will speak, among themselves and to others, of “the magnificence of the glory of your holiness,” that is, of the magnificent glory that you bestow upon your saints.

Or in this way: They will speak of you as magnificently glorious by considering your saints. And, in addition, they will recount your wonders, such as the resurrection of the dead and similar things.

Besides these, they will declare inwardly to themselves and to others “the power of your awesome deeds,” that is, your power by which you perform such acts of vengeance according to your just judgment, by which human beings are terrified—as in the case of Ananias and Sapphira, who lied to blessed Peter (Acts 5)—and in other cases.

They will also recount your greatness, that is, your power by which in the present you advance your saints toward complete holiness. Therefore they will “pour forth”—that is, proclaim fully—“the memory of the abundance of your sweetness,” that is, your abundant mercy, through which you remembered to do these things, although previously you seemed almost to have forgotten them: the holiness, miracles, and advancement of your saints in virtues and good works.

“And they will rejoice in your righteousness,” that is, they will proclaim your righteousness with rejoicing. They will say that your awesome works are just, and they will say that the things mentioned above—holiness, miracles, and the advancement of the saints in this life—are mercies of the Lord.

And rightly so, because this is the reality. The Lord is compassionate, that is, he performs all these acts of mercy, and he is merciful—not merely somewhat merciful, but greatly merciful. Once the word “compassionate” had been placed, it had been said that he is merciful; but he added this word because he wished to say that he is greatly merciful and patient.

For he patiently awaits every sinner, even the one whom he sees will never be converted and will therefore eventually be punished more severely. Yet, because he is kind and merciful, he does not wait for him to be destroyed with the intention of punishing him more harshly at the end. Rather, in his supreme and ineffable clemency he patiently sustains him, and he cannot deny himself (2 Timothy 2): what belongs to him he mercifully offers to everyone in the present. Although the sinner negligently practices what belongs to him until the end, he consequently deserves to be punished more harshly in the end by God’s just judgment.

The Lord is sweet—that is, I said that the Lord is compassionate, and so he is. Truly the Lord is sweet, that is, compassionate, to all: to free and slaves, to wise and foolish, to old and young, and to people of every condition and sex.

Or in this way: He is sweet to all, that is, greatly merciful. And his mercies are over all his works, that is, they are above such works of his as chastity and every other virtue. For he grants many people who have received chastity and other virtues from him the ability to persevere worthily in them until the end. Thus it is said that his mercies are “over” his works, as though he were saying: In addition to giving virtues, he also grants perseverance in them.

Having just said that generation after generation will praise the Lord by considering his works, holiness, and miracles, and that they will proclaim that he did these things from his abundant mercy, and having asserted this on his own authority by saying that he is compassionate and merciful, he now says in prayer the same thing that he had said in declaration:

“Let all your works confess to you, Lord.” That is, I pray, Lord, that your visible works may be material for human beings to confess you—that is, to praise you.

I said that they would speak of you as glorious by considering your saints, and so it will happen: “Let your saints bless you,” that is, let human beings praise you by considering your saints.

“They will speak of the glory of your kingdom.” From the place where he said, “and they will rejoice in your righteousness,” up to this verse there is an interpolation. The sentence continues in this way: They will rejoice, as I said, in your righteousness, and besides this they will speak of the glory of your kingdom—that is, they will proclaim the blessedness of the glory that those who will be your kingdom will possess. They will also proclaim your power, that is, the magnitude of the punishment with which the impious will be afflicted.

They will therefore proclaim that power “so that they may make your power known to the sons of men,” that is, so that they may make it known to human beings and thus terrify them away from vices.

They will therefore proclaim the glory of your kingdom so that they may make known to human beings “the glory of the magnificence of your kingdom,” that is, the magnificent glory that those in whom you will reign will possess, and so that they may be more greatly inflamed to desire it.

Therefore they will say: “Your kingdom is a kingdom of all ages.” That is, they will say that your glory is a glory given to some people from every age and from every generation, from the first righteous person to the last righteous person—now according to the soul, and eventually according to both soul and body. They will proclaim that your glory is eternal.

It is one thing to proclaim glory simply, and another to proclaim that glory to be eternal. They will proclaim this because “your dominion is in every generation and generation.” That is, the punishment inflicted upon the wicked will exist both in this generation—which can now be called universal according to the diverse conditions of human beings—and in that generation which will be one, namely, in the resurrection. Thus it will be eternal. It already begins with the first wicked person and will continue forever.

And lest anyone, irrationally relying upon God’s mercy, suppose that this punishment will not be perpetual, he confirms it in this way:

Truly both things will be eternal—the glory of the righteous and the punishment of the wicked—because “the Lord is faithful,” that is, truthful, “in all his words.” If he is truthful in all his promises, then he is truthful both in the promise of glory and in the threat of eternal punishment. This is directed against anyone who flatters himself by saying that God is merciful and therefore punishes no one eternally.

And lest it again seem to anyone that he acts unjustly if he imposed eternal vengeance for a temporal offense, and so that person might wish to remove the punishment, he says: “And holy in all his works.” That is, it is not as it seems to you; God is just and upright, not only in inflicting eternal punishment but in everything whatever that he does.

This is only a parenthetical digression. Because he is truthful in his promise of glory, therefore “the Lord raises up,” that is, raises to himself and glorifies, “all who fall,” that is, all who fall in any manner—namely, into sins. He says this with reference to the statement: “No one has ascended into heaven” by himself “except the Son of Man” (John 3).

And in order to raise them up, he first lifts up, through the remission of sins in this life, “all who are crushed,” that is, all who are broken in every manner—namely, in sins.

After they have been raised up: “Lord, the eyes of all,” namely, their interior eyes, that is, reason and free will, “hope in you,” that is, place their hope in you, awaiting you to give them food, that is, spiritual doctrine. They desire this, and you give them their food—that is, food suited and necessary for them—“in due season,” that is, in this age, in which it is fitting for the faithful to be taught spiritually.

And in giving them spiritual food, “you open your hand,” that is, you are generous. This is said by comparison with someone opening his hand to give generously. And because you are generous, “you fill every living creature with blessing,” that is, you abundantly fill every humble and gentle person with spiritual doctrine.

The Lord not only raises them up and gives them spiritual food abundantly; he also does the will of those who fear him, that is, those who love him, and he hears their prayer—that is, their petition, namely this: that he will save them.

He will give them this salvation, namely, good will and good action. This, I say, the righteous Lord will do “in all his ways.” From this it is clear that he will do their will, because he himself commands that such a will be possessed, and he is righteous in issuing these commands. That is, he will help them because he gives these commandments—both because they are just and because they themselves desire them.

From this it can be seen that he will do their will, that is, he will not deny them what they desire, because he is holy in all his works.

He will, I say, do their will and hear their prayer, and he will not delay this for long. “The Lord is near,” that is, he is ready for all who call upon him—namely, for those who call upon him in truth, that is, with true intention, asking for things that ought to be desired and in the manner in which they ought to be desired.

He will not only do their will by giving them virtues and good works; “the Lord also guards all who love him,” that is, he makes them persevere in these gifts. He will guard them, and he will destroy all sinners—that is, he will condemn sinners to punishment: here through greater blindness, and in the future through eternal vengeance.

Because the Lord will do these good things mentioned above, therefore not only my heart but also my mouth will speak the praise of the Lord. That is, I will proclaim the things that pertain to his praise. And by my example, “let all flesh bless his holy name,” that is, let every kind of carnal person praise him with a blessing that will endure “for ever,” that is, throughout this age, “and for ever and ever,” that is, throughout the age to come.

## Psalm 145. Alleluia of Haggai and Zechariah

“Praise the Lord, my soul. I will praise the Lord in my life; I will sing praise to my God as long as I live. Do not trust in princes, in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation. His spirit will go forth, and he will return to his earth; on that day all their thoughts will perish. Blessed is he whose helper is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them. He keeps truth for ever; he executes judgment for those who suffer wrong; he gives food to the hungry. The Lord releases those in chains; the Lord gives sight to the blind. The Lord raises up those who are crushed; the Lord loves the righteous. The Lord guards strangers; he will receive the orphan and the widow, and he will destroy the ways of sinners. The Lord will reign for ever; your God, O Zion, from generation to generation.”

## Exposition

In this psalm the faithful who are perfect admonish the less perfect not to trust in fleshly lords by placing their hope in them for temporal support. Such lords possess neither the will nor the power except by the grace of divine permission; and this trust has been the cause for many people of committing murder and other crimes. Rather, they should praise God and hope in him alone, from whom every salvation proceeds.

But in order that their admonition may be held in higher esteem, they first show that they themselves possess what they urge others to seek.

Praise the Lord, my soul. These are the words of every perfect believer exhorting himself and answering himself on account of the different natures—namely, rationality and sensuality—in this manner: “You, my soul, which by using your senses wrongly have departed from the Lord, praise the Lord,” that is, by using your sight, hearing, and your other senses well, “and so it shall be.” Truly, I shall praise the Lord in my life, that is, in all my senses—namely, in the proper administration of my senses. And this not merely for a time; rather, I shall sing praise to my God, that is, I shall praise my God in this way as long as I exist, namely, in this age. Here the effect is put for the cause: “praise” for “trust.” For trust is the cause that someone praises the one in whom he trusts.

I have said that I shall praise him; therefore you also praise the Lord. And in order that you may be able to praise him, do not trust in princes—that is, do not place your hope in human beings on the grounds that they are princes and powerful. “In the sons of men,” as though he were saying: Although they are princes, they have not on that account received a nobler or more honorable birth or origin than other human beings. “In whom there is no salvation,” that is, in whose power temporal salvation does not lie; they have neither the will nor the ability to benefit you in this world unless God gives it to them. Therefore one must not hope in them, but only in the Lord.

From this it is clear that they can do nothing of themselves, because “his spirit shall go forth” [Col. 0834B]—namely, the prince’s spirit departs from him—“and he shall return to his earth,” that is, he will not merely die, but, as regards his body, will also be reduced to the dust from which he was made. Then, at that departure, “all their thoughts shall perish,” that is, they will not only lose the will and ability to harm or benefit anyone, but will no longer think about such matters at all. Therefore those who trust in them are wretched.

But blessed is the one whose Lord, the God of Jacob, is his helper—that is, the one who has as helper the one whom he has as Creator, and no other god, but the one who is the God of Jacob, that is, of those who struggle. By saying this, he warns those who wish to be helped by God that they must struggle against vices and must not give themselves over to idleness or pleasure.

It is therefore evident that God will be his helper, because “his hope is in the Lord his God,” [Col. 0834C] that is, because he hopes in him and not in another. Nor does he hope in vain, because he is so powerful that he “made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them.” And because he created everything from nothing, he can easily help the one who trusts in him.

He is not only powerful, but also truthful. This is what he says: “who keeps truth forever,” that is, he is like someone possessing that power of mind by which he fulfills what he promises—and not merely for a time, but throughout this entire age. Therefore one does not hope in him in vain, because he is so powerful that for those suffering injury—that is, tribulations for his name’s sake—he “executes judgment,” namely, by protecting them here more and more, finally glorifying them, and punishing the wicked.

He also “gives food to the hungry,” that is, he supplies those who hope in him [Col. 0834D] with the necessary nourishment for bodily sustenance. Moreover, “the Lord frees those in fetters,” namely, those bound by the perverse habit of sin, so that they may serve him freely.

He does not do only this, but also “gives light to the blind,” namely, according to moral knowledge, which is necessary for all who are to be saved, and, in the case of some—namely, the more perfect—according to spiritual understanding. Furthermore, he “raises up those who are bowed down,” namely, according to the forgiveness of sins: those who are broken by sins. Afterwards he makes them just, that is, having been made just, he directs them—that is, advances them—to higher things.

Then he “protects sojourners,” that is, causes those who recognize themselves here as sojourners and pilgrims to persevere in that good state. And “the orphan,” that is, those who have departed from their true Father through grave sins because of greed. “And the widow,” that is, those who, by loving temporal things through covetousness, have departed from their true husband; “he will receive,” that is, he will also pardon their sins if they repent worthily.

He will not merely forgive, but will also “destroy the ways of sinners,” that is, the perverse consciences which are a way leading to sins; he will destroy them utterly.

Note that all the things said here—namely, that the Lord executes judgment for those suffering injury, frees and raises them up, and the other things that follow—are causes and, as it were, proofs that he truly has the power to help those who hope in him.

“The Lord shall reign forever, your God, O Zion,” that is, O Zion, the ruler and creator performs these foregoing works in his faithful ones. He will reign in them not merely for a time, but forever in this manner; that is, he will work in them for as long as these ages endure. And he will not reign in them only in the present generation: he will reign in them in the generation to come as well, rewarding them eternally.

## PSALM 146. ALLELUIA

“Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good; let praise to our God be sweet and beautiful. The Lord builds Jerusalem; he will gather the dispersed of Israel. He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by their names. Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number. The Lord receives the meek, but humbles sinners to the ground. [Col. 0835C] Sing beforehand to the Lord in confession; sing praise to our God on the cithara. He covers the heavens with clouds and prepares rain for the earth. He makes grass grow on the mountains, and plants for the service of human beings. He gives their food to the beasts and to the young ravens that call upon him. He will not take pleasure in the strength of the horse, nor will the legs of a man be pleasing to him. The Lord is pleased with those who fear him and with those who hope in his mercy.”

## EXPOSITION

In this psalm the Prophet exhorts all the faithful to praise the Lord in consideration of spiritual gifts—namely, faith, the forgiveness of sins, and perseverance in good works—adding many reasons why they ought to do so. His purpose is that they should assent to this exhortation. He therefore says:

“Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good.” There are three things in a psalm: strings, sound, and the movement of the finger. By the strings we understand the drying up of the flesh; by the sound, virtues; by the movement of the fingers, good works. In these ways the Prophet exhorts the faithful to praise God here, as follows: “Praise the Lord,” by performing a psalm for him in the manner we have explained. And it is right that you praise him in this way, “for the psalm”—namely, a psalm of this kind—is fruitful. Therefore let the psalm be offered by you to our God, because praise of this kind is “sweet,” that is, pleasing to God, and “beautiful,” that is, honorable in itself.

The whole meaning is: Perform a psalm for the Lord both because the psalm is useful and because it pleases God, since it is honorable in itself.

And therefore praise the Lord, because he will gather “the dispersed of Israel,” that is, those who have been scattered among various forms of idolatrous worship, gathering them according to the unity of faith so that they may be Israel. He will therefore make them Israel here—that is, faithful and doers of good—so that from them he may finally rebuild the heavenly Jerusalem, which was diminished through apostasy and the fall of the first human being. This is what he says: “The Lord builds Jerusalem.”

Therefore praise him, because by forgiving sins he “heals the brokenhearted,” that is, those who grieve and humbly lament over their sins. He does not do only this, but also “binds up their wounds,” that is, restores and strengthens their reason and free will, namely in baptism, and makes many of them stars.

He does not merely make them stars; he also “numbers the multitude of the stars,” that is, he guards them in the state of being stars—illuminated by the light of wisdom—so that they may persevere. He says “numbers” instead of “guards.” For a thing is numbered so that it may be guarded. In addition, “calling them all by their names,” that is, assigning them different gifts. To one, according to the Apostle, he gives the word of wisdom, to another kinds of tongues (1 Cor. XII).

Therefore praise him, because “great is our Lord,” that is, God the Father is omnipotent, and “great is his power,” that is, his Son is likewise great. Although the Father is called great and the Son great, nevertheless “there is no number of his wisdom”—namely, the Son’s wisdom—with the Father. That is, the Son does not form a number with the Father: the Father and the Son are not two with respect to essence, but they are two with respect to persons.

Therefore, in order that you may be able faithfully to believe and understand that the Father and the Son are distinct persons and entirely the same essence, be meek. For “the Lord receives the meek,” that is, he advances the humble to understanding; but he “humbles sinners to the ground,” that is, he casts down the proud and indignant because they cannot understand them, bringing them down to the ground—that is, to unbelief—so that they understand nothing about the Lord except what is earthly, even if previously they had understood something.

And in order that the Lord may receive you—that is, humble you in understanding—“sing beforehand to the Lord in confession,” that is, first confess your sins to the Lord; and then “sing praise to our God,” that is, perform good works to his honor, and do this “on the cithara,” that is, in the mortification of your flesh.

Therefore praise him, because he “covers the heavens with clouds,” that is, he conceals his mysteries in the writings of the prophets. And he prepares for the earth that same thing which is hidden there: rain, that is, doctrine for his Church, through preachers to whom he has revealed it.

Therefore praise him, because he brings forth “from the mountains”—that is, from the writings of the mountains, namely the prophets—“grass and plants,” that is, grains: the historical and spiritual meanings existing in those mountains. “Grass,” that is, spiritual understanding, he gives to the beasts, that is, to the simple and uneducated, as their food—that is, doctrine suited to them.

He gives grass and plants not only to the faithful from among the Jews, but also to “the young ravens,” that is, to the children of the nations who were blackened by sins. To them as well he gives grass and plants, that is, food of the same kind—not to everyone, but to those who call upon him, that is, only to those who are faithful and live well.

As I have said, the Lord heals those who are brokenhearted and directs the meek. But “he will not take pleasure in the strength of the horse,” that is, he does not love the proud. Nor will “the legs of a man be pleasing to him,” that is, he does not love those who act manfully in lust.

By the legs are signified the lustful, because from the loins downward the body is especially devoted to lust. Alternatively, by the legs may be understood any grave sins committed with delight, apart from pride, which is signified by the strength of the horse. The legs are a musical instrument covered with delight; these are the sort whom the Lord does not love. Rather, he loves those who love him and hope in him.

This is what he says: “The Lord is pleased with those who fear him,” that is, with those who love him, with the Lord who provides for and regards them. He is pleased in them, and also in those who hope in his mercy, that is, in those who do not trust in their own merits but in his grace. To love is one thing, to hope another; therefore, after saying “those who fear,” meaning those who love, he added “those who hope.”

## PSALM 147. ALLELUIA OF HAGGAI AND ZECHARIAH

“Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion. For he has strengthened the bars of your gates; he has blessed your children within you. He has placed peace within your borders, and he fills you with the fat of grain. He sends forth his word to the earth; his message runs swiftly. He gives snow like wool; he scatters mist like ashes. He sends his ice like morsels; who can stand before his cold? He will send forth his word and melt them; his spirit will blow and the waters will flow. He announces his word to Jacob, his statutes and judgments to Israel. He has not dealt so with every nation, and he has not made his judgments known to them.”

## EXPOSITION

In this psalm the Prophet again exhorts the same people whom he admonished in the preceding psalm to praise the Lord, but from a different consideration. In that psalm he invited them to praise because he had given them faith and the forgiveness of sins, restored reason and free will, and bestowed the other things that follow. In this psalm, however, he admonishes them to praise the Lord because he has given them excellent defenders against the heretics who attack both Testaments: the Old Testament, as the Manichaeans did; and the New, as the Marcionists and many others did, who believed that the carnal observances of the Law ought to be introduced and the institutions of the New Law abandoned.

He also praises the one who associated those same heretics with the Church and formed them in such perfection that through their preaching they converted many to the faith. The psalm begins as follows:

“Praise the Lord, Jerusalem,” that is, O Jerusalem, praise the Lord with every dignity of life because he is Lord—that is, your ruler—and praise God because he is God—that is, your Creator. Praise him in such a way that you may be Zion, that is, one who watches for the future, seeking not a temporal reward but only an eternal one.

Therefore praise him, because he “has strengthened the bars of your gates,” that is, he has made strong and unconquerable the defenders of the prophets and apostles, who are your gates, through which you entered into the faith and into every good work.

He calls Augustine, Gregory, and the other holy Fathers “bars,” by comparison: just as bars secure the things to which they are attached, so the holy Fathers rationally defend the prophecies and the other teachings of the divine Scriptures against every heresy by their judgments.

Therefore praise him, because “he has blessed your children within you,” that is, he has multiplied your children—according to the advancement and increase of virtues and good works—those who remain within you, that is, in conformity with you. Or in this way: “He has blessed,” that is, he has given you many children who remain within you.

Therefore praise him, because “he has placed peace within your borders,” that is, he has placed peace among the heretics who are related to you—those who are neither wholly within the faith nor wholly outside it. This is said antonomastically: he has made them firmly reconciled to you according to the unity of faith and truth.

Therefore praise him, because he “satisfies you with the fat of grain,” that is, with the spiritual understanding of Scripture. Grain signifies divine Scripture. In grain there are both fat and husk. By the fat the allegorical sense is signified; by the husk, merely the literal sense, which only the Jews use.

I have said that he will give you spiritual understanding. Therefore praise him, because through those whom he satisfies with the fat of grain he “sends forth his word to the earth,” that is, he sends his preaching out throughout the world against the heretics.

Therefore praise him, because “his message runs swiftly,” that is, he will make them so wise that no one can resist their preaching, and within a short time they will pass through many nations.

Therefore praise him, because he “gives snow like wool,” that is, he sanctifies those who have been chilled by vices in such a way that through them he warms others and heats them with spiritual warmth, just as wool warms something.

“He scatters mist like ashes,” that is, he makes those who are ignorant of the truth into ashes: he illuminates them so that their life and example make the Church fruitful, like ashes scattered over the earth and making it fertile.

Therefore praise him, because “he sends his ice like morsels,” that is, he will make those who have been hardened in the depths of the snow and mist of vices and ignorance so wise that they will know how to preach more subtly and perfectly than the capacity of their hearers can receive. He will thus fill them with the spirit of wisdom so fully that none of their adversaries will be able to resist their preaching.

This he presents as a question in order to make it more impressive: “Before his cold, who can stand?” That is, before the presence of those who were formerly cold but were to become his own. “Who can stand?” That is, who will be able to contradict them? No one, as it is said there: “They could not resist the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke” (Acts VI).

And that he will make snow like wool, mist like ashes, and ice like morsels—that is, those who are hardened in snow and mist—will not happen only through the preaching of those whom he satisfies with the fat of grain and through whom his message runs swiftly. Rather, he will send forth his Word, that is, his Son, whom he eternally and ineffably sends forth from himself; he will cause him to work in them, and thus “melt them,” that is, soften them, giving them virtues and good works and first destroying in them the hardness of vices and interior blindness.

Not only the Son works in this, but also the Holy Spirit. This is what he says: “His spirit will blow,” namely, in them. In this way, through the operation of the whole Trinity and through the preaching of those whom we have mentioned, the heretics who were previously snow, mist, and ice will be converted to the faith and “the waters will flow,” that is, they will become abundant in doctrine, like waters flowing in great quantity.

For through those converts the Lord will again announce to human beings his word, namely, “his statutes and judgments,” that is, his just commandments, which he judges ought to be carried out justly. He will make some of those to whom they preach Jacob and others Israel, that is, more perfect.

“He has not dealt so with every nation.” I have said that he will convert such people, but he will not do this with every nation—that is, with the various sects of heretics. “Every,” that is, with respect to all their divisions; “and he has not made his judgments known to them,” that is, he has not revealed to them why he permits some of them to be blinded in this way: he will save some of them by grace and condemn others by justice.

## PSALM 148. ALLELUIA OF HAGGAI AND ZECHARIAH

“Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights. Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his powers. Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and light. Praise him, heavens of heavens, and let all the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord. For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created. He established them forever and for the age of the age; he gave a command, and it shall not pass away.

“Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all the abysses, hail, snow, ice, and storm winds, which do his word. Mountains and all hills, fruit-bearing trees and all cedars; beasts and all cattle, creeping things and winged birds; kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth; young men and virgins, old men together with the young: let them praise the name of the Lord, because his name alone is exalted.

“His praise is above heaven and earth, and he has exalted the horn of his people. A hymn belongs to all his saints, to the children of Israel, the people drawing near to him.”

## EXPOSITION

In the preceding psalm, “Praise the Lord,” the Prophet invites all the faithful to praise the Lord in consideration of spiritual gifts—namely, faith and the other things mentioned there. In the second psalm, “Praise, Jerusalem,” he again admonishes all to praise the Lord because he firmly strengthens his Church against the assaults of heretics and afterwards also converts those same heretics to the faith.

In this psalm, however, he invites the faithful to praise the Lord in consideration of all creatures, saying:

“Praise the Lord from the heavens,” that is, let the heavens be for you the subject matter of praising the Lord. Since the heavens contain both more worthy and less worthy creatures—namely, incorporeal creatures—he invites praise by considering them individually, beginning with the more worthy, as follows:

“Praise him in the heights,” that is, let the highest and loftiest creatures be for you the subject matter of praising the Lord. He then lists those higher creatures individually:

“Praise him, all his angels,” that is, you, his messengers to the faithful dwelling on earth; and not only the angels, but also “all his powers,” that is, all the heavenly spirits, should be the subject matter of your praise.

And not only heavenly incorporeal things should be the subject matter of praising the Lord, but also heavenly corporeal things—namely, the sun, moon, and stars—both because they exist and because they emit brightness from him. This is what he means by “and light.”

“Heavens,” that is, the firmament and the ether, the visible whole composed of them; “of heavens,” that is, the seven circles in which the fixed stars and planets are situated: let these be for you the subject matter of praising the Lord.

That there are waters above the firmament is clear from Genesis, where it is said: “He divided the waters that were beneath the firmament from those that were above the firmament” (Gen. I).

Therefore praise him, because “he spoke,” that is, by speaking alone—by his mere will—they were made, namely, all things according to the raw and unformed matter. “He commanded,” that is, he willed, “and they were created,” that is, the individual things, previously confused, received their proper forms.

After they were created, “he established them forever and for the age of the age,” that is, he made them stable and enduring throughout this age and the next. In addition, he imposed a commandment—that is, a law and function governing how they should exist and what they should do—and “it shall not pass away,” that is, none of these things will depart from his commandment; rather, they will continually fulfill the purpose for which they were created.

Having thus exhorted them to praise God in consideration of heavenly things, he again invites them to do the same in consideration of earthly things:

“Praise the Lord from the earth,” that is, let all earthly things be for you the subject matter of praising the Lord—namely, “dragons,” which are the chief animals among earthly creatures, “and all the abysses.” In this passage abysses means the deepest pits where dragons lie.

“Fire, hail, snow, ice, and storm winds,” that is, winds which make storms: let all these, which do his word—that is, observe his commandment—be for you the subject matter of praising the Lord.

“Mountains and all hills, fruit-bearing trees and all cedars,” that is, both fertile and sterile trees; beasts, namely wild animals; “and all cattle,” that is, domesticated animals; “creeping things and winged birds,” both in consideration of their being birds and of their being winged.

“Kings of the earth and all peoples,” that is, their subjects; “princes and all judges of the earth,” namely, those who are princes but nevertheless have responsibility for the commonwealth.

“Young men and virgins”—here he indicates different sexes; “old men together with the young”—here he indicates different ages: let them praise the name of the Lord. That is, let all the things mentioned above be for you the subject matter of praising the Lord.

And rightly ought you to praise him in consideration of all these things: first, because “his name alone is exalted,” in accordance with the saying, “He exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name” (Phil. II); second, because “his praise is above heaven and earth,” that is, his praise is found in the higher and lower creation; and third, because he will finally “exalt the horn of his people,” that is, he will justly reward the exaltation of his people.

Praise him, I say, saying to one another: “A hymn”—that is, praise—“belongs to all his saints,” that is, let all the saints praise him with every dignity of life. These are those who, from among the Jews, have become Israel, that is, the faithful, and those who have been added to them from among the nations, the other part.

This is what he says: “To the children of Israel, the people drawing near to him,” that is, to those same children of Israel.

According to blessed Jerome, whenever “Alleluia” occurs at the beginning of a psalm, another occurs at the end.

## PSALM 149. ALLELUIA

[Col. 0841B]

“Sing to the Lord a new song; let his praise be in the assembly of the saints. Let Israel rejoice in him who made him, and let the daughters of Zion exult in their king. Let them praise his name in the choir; let them sing praise to him with the tambourine and psaltery. For the Lord is pleased with his people, and he will exalt the meek to salvation.

“The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their dwellings. The exaltations of God shall be in their throat, and two-edged swords shall be in their hands, to execute vengeance among the nations and rebukes among the peoples; to bind their kings with fetters and their nobles with iron chains; to execute upon them the judgment that is written. This glory belongs to all his saints.”

## EXPOSITION

In this psalm the Prophet invites the faithful to praise God, adding the same reasons that he gave in “Praise the Lord, for he is good,” together with some others:

“Sing to the Lord a new song,” that is, with joy perform a new song to the Lord’s honor. Let this praise of his—that is, this new song—be in you in such a way that you are “in the assembly of the saints,” that is, in the faith of the elect. “Assembly” is used for “faith,” as it is said elsewhere: “There is no place of true sacrifice outside the Church,” that is, outside the faith.

And when some Israelite—that is, some perfect person—has performed a new song in such a way that he is in the assembly of the saints, let him rejoice—not in himself, but in the one who made him such. That is, let him attribute nothing of this grace to himself, but to God.

“And the daughters of Zion.” This is expressed intransitively: the daughters who are Zion—that is, those who are more perfect and especially adorned with virtues, like daughters to whom greater care and attention are devoted. These daughters of Zion, I say, those who contemplate the future, “let them exult in their king,” that is, in consideration of so great a ruler, who preserves them in this dignity of virtues.

He now explains what he means by saying that they should sing a new song. I have said that they should sing a new song, that is, praise his name. They should praise according to what this name, “Lord,” requires—namely, that they be “in the choir,” that is, in harmony, in the love of God and neighbor.

“And with the tambourine,” that is, in separation from all grave sins. This is signified by the tambourine being wrapped in the hide of a dead animal, from which all the fleshly moisture that had been in it has been completely removed.

“And with the psaltery let them sing praise to him,” that is, let them praise him in a soul adorned with virtues.

Therefore they ought to sing this new song to the Lord—that is, praise him in the choir, with the tambourine and psaltery—“because the Lord is pleased with his people,” namely, with a song of this kind. Such a song pleases the Lord, and also because he will finally “exalt the meek to salvation,” namely, to this: “The saints shall exult in glory.”

Although all will share the same glory and the same good, nevertheless some will have more and others less, according to the different merits of each. This is what he says: “They shall rejoice in their dwellings,” that is, in their different gifts, in accordance with the saying: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John XIV).

This is said so that each person may strive to sing more perfectly, the more he hears that rewards will be rendered there to each according to his merits.

And in order that they may finally exult there, in the meantime here let “the exaltations of God be in their throat,” that is, let them exalt God so that they may not cast out the word of God.

And in order that they may know how to proclaim it competently, let “two-edged swords” be in their hands—that is, in their power. These swords are the word of God, which is two-edged: either because it confirms from both Testaments the things that are proclaimed, or because it cuts away both interior and exterior filth.

“To execute vengeance among the nations,” that is, they ought to have two-edged swords for the purpose of subjecting some from among the nations to themselves—namely, from the various sects of heretics. I mean those existing among the nations, that is, among the heretics, who devote themselves especially to this: just as they have drawn some of the faithful away, so these others, as if taking vengeance, may draw some away from unbelief.

And therefore, in order that they may know how to rebuke those “among the peoples”—I mean those existing among the peoples. Here “peoples” and “nations” have the same meaning.

There is a difference between executing vengeance and rebuking. Therefore let them first “bind their kings with fetters,” that is, the heretical teachers, with arguments that cannot be overcome; “and their nobles with iron chains,” that is, those who live among them under the appearance of holiness and are regarded as famous and distinguished.

And therefore, let them “execute upon them”—that is, upon those heretics—“the judgment that is written,” that is, established by many holy Fathers. Let them judge them in the manner prescribed in the writings of their holy predecessors.

Furthermore, they ought to be in the choir, with the tambourine and psaltery, and in the doctrine of both Testaments, because “this glory belongs to all his saints.” That is, this glory—which, so far as I am concerned, is also attested by me, a prophet of great authority—is also confirmed by the authority of all the saints.

## PSALM 150. ALLELUIA

“Praise the Lord in his saints; praise him in the firmament of his power. Praise him in his powers; praise him according to the multitude of his greatness. Praise him with the sound of the trumpet; praise him with the psaltery and cithara. Praise him with the tambourine and choir; praise him with strings and organ. Praise him with well-sounding cymbals; praise him with cymbals of jubilation. Let every spirit praise the Lord. Alleluia.”

## EXPOSITION

In this psalm the Prophet invites all the faithful to praise the Lord solely in consideration of the future blessedness of the saints:

“Praise the Lord in his saints,” that is, in consideration of his saints. He specifies according to what consideration they ought to praise the Lord:

“Praise him in the firmament of his power,” that is, in consideration of the fact that he will so establish his saints in virtue that thereafter they will be unable to sin.

Lest anyone think that they will be established in only one virtue, he adds: “Praise him in his powers,” that is, in consideration of the many virtues in which the saints will be glorified, understood as referring to the soul.

“Praise him according to the multitude of his greatness,” that is, according to the manifold glorification by which they will be magnified in the body—namely, according to the body’s extraordinary agility, beauty, and impassibility, and many other qualities.

He now explains that blessedness of the body in detail:

“Praise him with the sound of the trumpet,” that is, in consideration of that perfect victory, when death and every calamity will be at an end. Hence it is said: “Where is your victory, O death? Where, O death, is your sting?” (1 Cor. XV.) The trumpet is sounded at the beginning and at the end of battle; therefore here it signifies victory.

“Praise him with the psaltery,” that is, in consideration of the glorification of the soul, which will consist in perfect knowledge and complete knowledge of God.

“And with the cithara,” that is, in consideration of the glorification of the body.

“Praise him with the tambourine,” that is, in the separation from every corruption; “and with the choir,” that is, in the harmonious blessedness they will possess with the angels.

“Praise him with strings,” that is, in the blessedness they will attain through the immense tribulation of this world. The tambourine signifies separation from everything carnal. The strings signify the same thing in harmony, and, moreover, how it is attained.

“And praise him with the organ,” that is, in the harmony of different gifts. Although these gifts are diverse, each person will possess them unanimously and without envy. This is said by comparison with an organ, in which there are different pipes, yet they do not produce discord in the sound.

“Praise him with well-sounding cymbals,” that is, in the radiance and beauty of the bodies of the saints. Their beauty will not be moderate but exceedingly great. By the cymbal we signify radiance and beauty; by “well-sounding,” extraordinary beauty.

“And praise him with cymbals of jubilation,” that is, in the fact that from the very beauty of their holy bodies the saints will praise God perfectly.

“Let every spirit praise the Lord,” that is, do not praise him only in consideration of that glorification of the body which will consist in the tambourine, choir, and the other things mentioned above, but also in consideration of the fact that it will become spiritual—that is, agile and subtle like a spirit.

Or in this way: do not praise him only in consideration of the glorification of the body mentioned above, but also in consideration of the complete glorification of souls, which will then exist forever.

# TREATISE ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

[Note: [Col. 0845C] The Codex of Saint-Ouen of Rouen, written six hundred years ago, from which we transcribed that treatise, bears the name of no author. Yet in the same codex there immediately follows Remigius of Auxerre’s, the monk’s, *Exposition on the Celebration of the Mass*, [Col. 0846C] and its style does not seem to differ from the manner of writing found in our Treatise. Until more certain evidence becomes available as to whom it ought to be attributed, we have therefore judged, conjecturally, that it should be assigned to the same author. MARTEN.]

(From Martene, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*.)

## What the Twelve Candles Signify

[Col. 0845A]

The custom maintained by the holy Church in the solemn consecration of the Lord’s house is not the affair of just any rank of person; this is recognized by anyone who, recalling ancient history, remembers with what great solemnity the Tabernacle of the Testimony and the Temple constructed by Solomon were dedicated to the Lord at his command. For when twelve leaders, symbolizing the twelve apostles, had brought their gifts to the Tabernacle on a single day, the Lord decreed that each was to offer his offering on a separate day, so that the splendor of the festival might increase and the very truth of the historical account might fittingly correspond to its future symbolism.

In the fact that the individual leaders offered their gifts on separate days, it was already prefigured that the apostles would not remain evangelizing indiscriminately among one people, but that, through the distribution of the Holy Spirit, each would receive as his portion many nations, or even more than one nation, to evangelize. In the fact, however, that all offered the same gifts, it was prefigured that a harmonious and shared doctrine would cooperate in the apostles for the building up of the Church, and that its sanctification would be adorned not by diversity of schisms but rather by a single [or: united] confession of the truth.
