These are also the signs irrigated by the fountain of the Holy Spirit, whose fruit is for use—as is read in Ezekiel and in the Apocalypse—and whose leaves are for healing, bearing their first fruits each month. In their likeness, before the bishop enters to consecrate the basilica, twelve candles are lit around it.

For these are the ones to whom the Truth says: “You are the light of the world.” And again, exhorting them to distribute the word of preaching to his faithful, he says: “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place or under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light.” These are the ones who, in order to teach others to burn with charity [or: with eagerness of mind] and to shine by their word, first received tongues of fire, so that they might signify both burning with love and shining by their speech.

Thus the twelve shining lights around the house to be dedicated demonstrate that apostolic doctrine, luminous and ardent, is to be preached in it. The Lord’s house itself is called “church” improperly or by metonymy, not in the strict sense. It is called “church” by metonymy when what contains is signified by what is contained.

For *ecclesia* means “assembly”; but, as we have said, the house cannot properly be called a church, since it cannot be summoned into an assembly. Yet the prophet says: “Gather the elders; summon the church.” It must be understood, however, that this usage was taken from the ancient people, who indiscriminately called the synagogue, the people, and the place where they customarily gathered for prayer and reading by one and the same name.

Of the people it was said: “And Moses spoke to the whole synagogue of the children of Israel.” Of the place where they gathered to worship and read, the Gospel says that when the centurion had sent the rulers of the Jews to the Lord to ask for the healing of his servant, those same rulers came to the Lord and earnestly entreated him, saying: “He is worthy that you should grant this to him, for he loves our nation, and he himself built us our synagogue.”

Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles: “And entering the synagogue, they sat down. After the reading of the Law and the Prophets, the rulers sent to them, saying: Brothers, if there is among you a word of exhortation for the people, speak.”

Clearly, then, as with many other matters, we have received this usage from the ancients: both the people, called “church,” and likewise the house where the people gather are called by the single name “church.” Yet a great difference appears between these two names, namely, “synagogue” and “church.”

For “synagogue” means a gathering, a term that may be used both of stones and of irrational animals. “Church,” however, which means a convocation, belongs only to those who excel in understanding, so that it may be shown how far Christian dignity is removed from Jewish lowliness.

Blessed Augustine, in his book *On the Origin of the Soul*, speaks of this matter as follows:

“Just as we call the basilica which contains the people—the people who are truly called the Church—‘church,’ so that by the name ‘Church,’ that is, by the name of the people who are contained, we signify the place which contains them, so also, because souls are contained in bodies, the bodies of the children of Israel may be understood through the souls named. Strictly speaking, however, in Greek the basilica is called *basilikē*, which in Latin means ‘royal,’ so that it may be shown to be the dwelling place of the eternal King.”

## Why the Threshold Is Struck Three Times and “Peace to This House” Is Said

When the candles have been lit, it is customary for the bishops to approach the entrance of the basilica, with the clergy and people following, and to strike the threshold three times with the staff that antiquity calls a *cambuta*, while singing the antiphon: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, you everlasting doors.”

These things must certainly not be understood as they appear to children, or to those who understand in a childish manner. Rather, one must carefully examine why they were instituted in this way by the ancients. For we believe that these and other practices have come down to us through the teaching of the apostles and their disciples.

We know that holy bishops represent the person of the Lord Jesus Christ, as he himself says to them: “As the Father sent me, so I send you.” And again: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me.” Blessed Paul likewise supports this understanding when he declares that he acts in Christ’s place, saying: “We are ambassadors for Christ; we beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to the Lord.”

The priest’s staff signifies the priestly power that Christ conferred upon them when, sending the apostles to preach, he permitted them to take nothing else on the journey except a staff, as the Gospel says. For with the staff holy priests both console the humble, terrify the proud, and strike the unrepentant.

This same staff is curved, prefiguring the concern and compassionate care of the shepherd. So that none of the sheep may go astray, they use both the bridle of the commandment and the affection of charity, imitating him who once cried out through the prophet: “Return, returning children, and I will heal your apostasies.” And through the Gospel he calls them, mercifully and beneficially, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest.”

The Son received this power from the Father when he obtained dominion over heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings, as the Apostle says: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.”

Hence the realms below also opened to him when he descended, as the Psalmist says: “For he shattered the bronze gates and broke the iron bars.” And the heavens received him with new obedience as he ascended to the Father. The hard hearts of mortals, previously closed through obstinacy, were also opened afterward through humble confession.

The Savior therefore grants this same power to his bishops when he gives Peter, and the leaders in the place of the Church, the power, saying: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”

Since it is said to him that the gates of hell shall not prevail, and since the privilege of binding in heaven and loosing on earth is granted to him at the same time, it is plainly evident that he rules heaven, earth, and hell. Therefore, when the bishop strikes the threshold of the future church three times with his staff, he shows that the power of heaven, earth, and hell yields to him.

Accordingly, after the striking, the door is opened, signifying that the opposing power cannot resist one who rightly preserves his authority. For the house itself, before the bishop enters it, represents the people enclosed by the barriers of ignorant unbelief. The Lord came to lead all of them out of darkness, and the Father had said to him: “I will go before you, and I will humble the glorious ones of the earth; I will shatter the bronze gates and break the iron bars.”

Again, afterward the Father says to him: “That you may say to those who are bound: Come out; and to those who are in darkness: Be revealed.” The Lord accomplished this in person when he came in the flesh, and he does not cease to accomplish it through his representatives until the end of the world.

The bishop sings the antiphon, saying: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, you everlasting doors,” and so forth. By divine authority the bishop commands demons or various vices to lift up their gates, so that the heavenly gates may be raised and the King of glory may enter.

The gates of death are sins, concerning which the Prophet glorifies the Lord, saying: “You who raise me up from the gates of death.” The gates through which we enter into life are everlasting gates; concerning them the same Psalmist continues: “That I may declare all your praises [or: your praises] in the gates of the daughter of Zion.”

The gates that are raised in the Church are especially three: the grace of baptism, the honor of chrism, and the preaching of the sacred word. Through these the King of glory entered, when Christ makes his presence known through holy works in his Church.

The glory of our King consists in the preaching of his power, mercy, and justice in the Church, as Scripture says: “It is the glory of kings to conceal a word, and the glory of the Lord to investigate a matter.”

When the door has been opened, the bishop enters and, with the clergy and people, says three times: “Peace to this house.” For when the Lord entered the world by assuming flesh, he reconciled the human race to God and, by the mercy of his coming, restored that peace which discord had severed through sin.

This is why, when he was born, the angels cried out: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.” This is why the Prince of Priests himself, instructing the preachers whom he placed over the Church, commanded them: “When you enter a house, greet it, saying: Peace to this house.”

And when he himself entered the house of Zacchaeus, he said: “Today peace has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham.” Likewise, after the resurrection, appearing to his disciples, he said: “Peace be with you.”

Therefore, when the bishop enters the church and cries, “Peace to this house,” it is because the holy teachers strive for this: that the people who have been estranged from the Lord through sins may be reconciled to him through the practice of good works.

Paul does this throughout nearly all his Epistles when he writes to the disciples: “Grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” Peter likewise says: “May grace and peace be multiplied to you.”

The bishop cries out three times so that the equality and parity of reconciliation may belong to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, whose divinity is one. For there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism.

Through these things we have obtained reconciliation and peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, as the Apostle says: “He made peace through his blood, not only for the things in heaven but also for those on earth, in him.”

As the bishop enters the church, the clergy with the litany, and the priests and levites prostrate on the ground, cry out to the Lord for the sanctification of the house. This signifies what the Lord also did before his Passion when, praying to the Father for his disciples and for all the faithful who would follow afterward, he said: “Father, sanctify them in your name, those whom you have given me. I do not pray for these alone, but also for those who will believe in me through their word.”

The apostles also write in their Epistles to their disciples that they pray to the Lord for them without ceasing and remember them in their prayers. Moreover, through the tradition of the apostles, the custom has arisen in the Church that they seek the Lord’s mercy not only for the faithful but also for heretics and schismatics, as well as for Jews and pagans.

For blessed Paul, as though he had entered the church, exhorts everyone to prayer, saying: “I urge, first of all, that prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and for all who are in positions of authority.”

Therefore, when the bishop enters the new church to sanctify it and immediately turns to prayer, he fulfills the Apostle’s command, which asks that prayers first be made for all people—that is, both for believers and for those who do not yet believe.

Nevertheless, he still represents those who are beginning to instruct an unformed people. For this reason, when he rises from prayer, he does not yet greet the people by saying, “The Lord be with you,” but instead exhorts everyone to pray. The newly formed people have not yet attained such dignity that they seem worthy of the priest’s greeting.

They are still like the grass on the housetops, of which the mower does not fill his hand, nor the one who gathers sheaves his bosom, so that those passing by may say to them: “The blessing of the Lord be upon you; we bless you in the name of the Lord.”

In their likeness, that very strong Boaz, when he visited his reapers, said: “The Lord be with you.” For our Lord is truly strong—which is what the name *Boaz* means—and when he sees his reapers laboring within the harvest [or: in the sacred Mass], he increases them with the abundance of his blessing and fulfills his promise to both those set over others and those subject to them, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.”

But to those who have not yet merited being united with the Church in the fellowship of faith, he not only did not give a blessing, but even forbids [or: refuses] association with them, saying through the Apostle: “What fellowship has Christ with Belial? What agreement has the temple of God with idols?” And again through the prophet: “Separate yourselves, says the Lord, and do not touch what is unclean.” And again through blessed John: “If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not even say ‘Hail’ to him.”

One must therefore pray for such people, since they have not yet been initiated; but they are not to be greeted, because one must neither consent to them nor flatter them. For the Lord commands the preachers themselves, when they go out to preach, to greet no one on the way.

This is also why the true Elisha, when he sent a boy to raise the dead man, commanded him to greet no one on the way—namely, no one who seeks the fleeting joys of this life and eagerly pursues them, allowing himself to be soothed by false hope or flattery. Rather, he should hasten to carry out with complete dedication the ministry entrusted to him.

## What It Signifies That the Priest Writes the Alphabet on the Pavement

When these rites have been properly completed, the bishop begins at the left-hand eastern corner and writes the alphabet across the pavement to the right-hand western corner; then, similarly, from the right-hand eastern corner to the left-hand western corner of the basilica.

This would appear to be a childish game unless it were believed to have been instituted by great and spiritual men, such as the apostles. For that reason, the more carefully one must seek what sacred meaning is hidden in such an act, the more contemptible it may appear to those who do not understand.

It must nevertheless be understood, as has already been said above, that everything done in such rites was preceded by the example of the Lord, and that what was prefigured in him remained unaltered in his successors.

Above, the bishop merely poured out a prayer; now, however, he inscribes the order of the alphabet across the future church under the mystery of a definite symbolism. What, then, should be understood by the alphabet except the beginnings and elementary principles of sacred doctrine?

Thus Paul, reproaching the Hebrews, says: “Although by this time you ought to be teachers, you again need someone to instruct you in the elements of the world and the beginnings of the words of God.”

The bishop therefore writes the order of the alphabet when he teaches the simplicity of faith and says with the Apostle Paul: “I gave you milk to drink, not food. For you were not yet able—and indeed you are still not able.”

Just as it is suitable for the education of little children first to learn the elements of letters, then syllables, and afterward words, gradually arriving at an understanding of sentences, so there are various levels of understanding within the household of the holy Church.

The first level belongs to those who, while living simply, are nevertheless progressing toward the strength of doctrine and remain content, as it were, with the first elementary lessons. But let us observe how these same elements are to be written: not randomly, but in an ordered line from the left eastern corner to the right western corner.

First, it must be understood that the four corners of the basilica designate the four regions of the world, toward which ecclesiastical doctrine extends, signified by the letters written upon the ground. The alphabet written there signifies the simple and pure preaching of the Gospel.

There is no duplicity or falsity in the alphabet, because evangelical purity seeks nothing deceptive and nothing false, but, supported by simple truth, wholly rejects outward falsity.

The fact that the first line ends at the western corner from the eastern corner, and then returns from the eastern corner to the left western corner, accords with a twofold figure. The first is that the cross is represented in this arrangement, so that Christ’s death may always be joined to evangelical doctrine.

Letters are formed in the figure of the cross when Christ’s death is simply indicated to the simple-minded. Hence Paul says to certain such people: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.”

The fact that he begins writing from the left eastern corner and proceeds to the western corner signifies the Jewish people as the left-hand corner. The eastern corner is the one from which the Lord arose.

The bishop reaches the western corner as he writes because, although our Lord arose from the Jews, his death was received by the Gentiles. Alternatively, the eastern corner signifies his birth, and the western his ascension, where he set—that is, where afterward he was no longer visible to us.

Luke writes from the left eastern corner to the right western corner when he first speaks of all that Jesus began to do and teach until the day when, after giving commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up.

But when this same line returns from the right eastern corner to the left western corner, it appears to indicate that, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved.

These two lines therefore signify the gathering of both peoples, yet within the single framework of the cross. This is why Jacob, when blessing Joseph’s sons, crossed his hands to form the figure of the cross and placed his right hand upon the head of the younger Ephraim and his left hand upon the head of the elder Manasseh, signifying that the people who had once been on the right would be turned to the left, and the people on the left to the right.

Nor is it without reason that this same order or writing is carried out with the priest’s staff. It prefigures that the same transfer which came from the Jews to the Gentiles was accomplished through the ministry of preachers, and that the further conversion to be completed at the end of the age will likewise be brought about through priestly work—that is, through preaching.

## Why Water Is Mixed with Salt and Ash, and a Cross Is Formed over the Water from Salt and Ash

After this the priest proceeds to higher matters. Standing before the altar, he calls upon God to be his helper, as though he were then beginning the work. For the preceding rites were, as it were, preliminary.

He says: “O God, attend to my help,” and so forth, adding: “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit,” without *Alleluia*.

This verse belongs to martyrs calling upon the Lord for help as they hasten toward martyrdom. It also belongs to teachers who undertake hard and uncertain struggles against the powers of the air on behalf of the holy Church, knowing that “their struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this age, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places.”

The weaker they recognize themselves to be through their own frailty, the more earnestly they implore God’s help on account of his goodness. Yet they do not yet add “Alleluia” to God’s praises, because they recognize that they remain amid labors and sweat.

*Alleluia* is a cry of exultation belonging solely to the praises of God. But as long as the holy teachers remain in affliction—as those who cannot yet rejoice in the progress of their disciples—they do not cease to implore the Lord’s help.

They will then sing a joyful *Alleluia* when they see the life of their disciples advancing before the Lord, as Paul says: “Now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord.” And again: “I know that when I come to you, I shall come in the abundance of Christ’s blessing.”

They will resound with perfect *Alleluia* when what is written is fulfilled: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; throughout the ages of ages they will praise you.”

Hence the custom has arisen that during the days of affliction, namely, the forty days before Easter, *Alleluia* is not sung, because those are days of mourning and repentance; but after the Lord’s resurrection has been accomplished, it is sung without interruption.

The bishop, therefore, who is still struggling against the unlearned resistance and opposition of his disciples asks the Lord’s help to overcome these things, but does not yet sing *Alleluia* fully with them, because, according to Scripture, “praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner.”

Nor can those who still cling to their first elementary lessons yet undertake the office of those whose perfected minds know how to occupy themselves solely in the praise of the Almighty.

The prophet David understood this well. He placed the seven psalms that he composed in praise of the Lord, and marked with the title *Alleluia* and concluded with it, not at the beginning of the Psalter, nor in the middle, nor in any other section, but at the end. He plainly indicated that those truly sing *Alleluia* who already know how to escape vices and stand steadfastly at the summit of perfection.

Conversely, those who still weakly succumb to vices are restrained from the praise of God, as the same Psalmist says: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recite my ordinances and take my covenant upon your mouth?”

For this reason the Apostle exhorts certain people so that, together with those set over them, they may be able to sing a full *Alleluia*, saying to them: “Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch as those who will give an account for you, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning.”

After this, the water is blessed with the addition of salt and ash.

The Apocalypse of John testifies that water signifies the people, saying: “The waters are the peoples.” Salt signifies the doctrine of the Word of God. Hence the Law commands that salt be offered with every sacrifice, as the lawgiver says: “With every sacrifice you shall offer salt, and you shall not remove the salt of the covenant of the Lord your God from your sacrifice.”

This means plainly: all the works that you wish to offer to God must be seasoned with divine authority. Do not think anything pleasing to God that has not been sanctioned by his law.

Ash signifies the completion of the Lord’s Passion, which was signified by the ash of the heifer that was commanded in the Law to be slaughtered for the expiation of the people.

The ash of the red heifer is the flesh of the Savior, red through the blood of the cross and consumed by the fire of tribulation. Thus the Savior himself, when he was led, as it were, like a log to be burned, toward the fire of his Passion, says: “For if the blood of goats and bulls and the ash of a heifer, sprinkled upon the defiled, sanctifies for the cleansing of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself unblemished to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God?”

The water is therefore blessed, and, so that it may be sanctified, salt is mixed with it together with ash. This signifies that, through the ministry of the bishop, the people are instructed in the word of God so that they may be sanctified, and are sufficiently taught how they may be joined and sanctified to Christ as to their head through his Passion.

A cross is formed over the water from salt and ash when the people are taught to give thanks to the Holy Trinity for their instruction and redemption.

Wine is added to this mixture together with water. These two elements display the twofold nature of the Lord Jesus Christ in one person. Water signifies his humanity, while wine signifies his divinity.

When wine mixed with water is added to the preceding mixture, it is signified that the people must be instructed through the mouth of the preacher that our Lord and Savior is God and man. As wine is mixed with water, however, his divinity was not changed into humanity, nor his humanity into divinity. Rather, while the natures remain intact, divinity assumed humanity, forming one person without changing the properties of the natures.

The order in which the rite proceeds step by step should also be observed. First the bishop opens the door; then he prays for the people. After this he writes the alphabet. Next he blesses the water with ash and salt, and adds wine to it.

This signifies that each person first opens the door through confession; then it is the priest’s office to pray for him and, as it were, make him a catechumen; then to teach him through sacred doctrine how he may be united to the body of his Savior; then carefully to instruct him that Christ is God and man; and finally to cleanse him in the sacred font.

The Lord maintained this order and consecrated it by his example. When a deaf and mute man was brought to him to be healed, he took him aside from the crowd, put his fingers into his ears, spat, touched his tongue, looked up to heaven, groaned, and said to him: “Ephphatha,” which means “to open.”

A person is led away from the crowd when, through confession and renunciation, he abandons his former vices. Fingers are put into the ears when, after hearing the word of God, he is catechized.

The Lord looked up to heaven and groaned so that God’s priests might learn to ask the Lord’s mercy with groaning for those whom they have been appointed to govern. The tongue of the mute is touched with the Lord’s saliva so that those initiated into the sacred mysteries may be instructed by the divine word.

## What It Signifies That the Priest Makes a Cross with His Finger over the Four Horns of the Altar

After this the priest dips his finger into the water and makes a cross over the four horns of the altar.

The altar bears the figure of the Church. It has four horns because the Church extends through the four quarters of the world, as the Lord once promised to Abraham: “You shall spread out toward the east and west, north and south.”

It is fitting that a cross be made over the altar with water, over its four horns, so that it may be shown that the whole Church must be cleansed from the stains of sins through the washing of water and through the Passion of the cross.

The cross is made over the four horns to show that no one is excluded from salvation. As the Apostle says: “In Christ Jesus there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, neither male nor female, but we are all one in Christ.”

Then he comes before the altar and sprinkles it seven times. The number seven signifies the fullness of the Holy Spirit, as Isaiah testifies when he says of the Lord: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.”

Thus, to show that the Holy Spirit is bestowed upon the baptized, the altar is rightly sprinkled seven times with sanctified water.

The hyssop with which the same water is sprinkled is a lowly herb. It is said to penetrate the hardness of rocks with its roots and to remedy the inner afflictions of the sinner [or: of the heart]. Its sprinkling also removed impurities under the Law.

It signifies the humility of Christ, which breaks the hardness of our obstinacy and knows how to heal our inward sufferings and impurities. Water is therefore sprinkled with hyssop when the baptism of Christ, sanctified by his Passion, is bestowed upon the Church.

The priest goes around the altar sprinkling the same water, signifying that teachers must not give themselves over to idleness, but must always care for those whom they have initiated into the Lord and work for their cleansing, continually praying that the Lord may send his angel around them and rescue them.

He goes around the entire church and sprinkles its walls to demonstrate that he devotes his whole care to both sexes, every age, and every rank.

Then, coming again before the altar, he sprinkles it a second time, as well as the entire church, teaching that a person must be cleansed not only from the sin of action [or: by ceasing from sin], but also from the sin of thought.

The Lord demonstrates this in the Gospel, saying: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall not kill. But I say to you that whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment.”

The twofold sprinkling of water therefore signifies, as has been said, a twofold cleansing: outward and inward.

When the same church is lustrated with water a third time, it is determined that it must be cleansed from a third kind of sin, namely, that of speech. Whoever neglects this will hear the prophet’s terrible threat: “There shall be distress [or: a cry] from the Fish Gate, and wailing from the Second Gate, and great destruction from the hills.”

Meanwhile the antiphon or psalm is sung: “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered.” Although this is believed and understood to have been written concerning the Jews, nevertheless those who established this rite understood it as capable of applying both to the devil and to his ministers.

The antiphon is also sung: “He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High shall abide under the protection of the God of heaven.” This asserts that no one can be protected by God except one who dwells in his help—that is, one who has continually implored him to be his helper.

In the fact that the bishop sends ministers to sing psalms and sprinkle the water around the basilica, while he himself proceeds through the middle of the church, sprinkling and making a cross on either side, he gives a clear indication that a bishop ought to associate helpers with himself who will assist in guarding the watches of the Church.

Thus blessed Moses chose seventy elders to attend to the needs of the people. And the Lord himself, after choosing the twelve apostles, sent seventy-two others to complete the preaching.

The bishop himself, however, must in no way give himself over to security or lethargy. He must proceed conspicuously through the middle of the Church, forming everyone by his example and impressing upon all the mysteries both of the cross and of the Lord’s death, by word and deed, saying with the Apostle: “Always carrying in our bodies the dying of Christ, so that the life of Jesus may be manifested in us.”

He also sings, saying: “My house shall be called a house of prayer,” so that he may prepare such a Church of God as is not a den of thieves but a house of prayer—that is, so that demons, thieves, and robbers may not exercise dominion in the bodies of sinful people subject to them, but that they may instead prepare themselves so that, whether they eat, drink, or do anything else, they may do everything for the glory of the Lord, bless the Lord at all times, and always have the praise of God in their mouths.

In this way they may freely sing the following verse: “I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the church I will praise you,” imitating the Lord, who, when he had risen from the dead, said to the women: “Go, tell my brothers to go to Galilee.”

The bishop performs these things well when, for everything that he begins with good deliberation, he obtains through divine invocation and prayer the ability to bring it to completion.

Therefore, when these rites have been completed, the bishop turns to prayer, asking that all who come into the same house to pray may rejoice that their prayers have been heard.

The Apostle Paul did both things: as he says, he bore daily concern for all the churches; when others were weak, he was weak; when others were scandalized, he burned; and he confessed that night and day he remembered them in his prayers.

## What the Pouring of Water at the Base of the Altar Signifies
Having completed the expiation, the hymns, the prayers [Col. 0856C], and everything mentioned above, the bishop turns to the altar and begins the antiphon: “I will go in to the altar of God, to God who gives joy to my youth.” As the psalm is sung, he goes before the altar and pours at its base whatever remains of the water of purification.

What this water signifies, by which the church is purified, has already been explained above: namely, ecclesiastical teaching, which is chiefly contained in the sacred instruction of the word, signified by the salt; in preaching the Savior’s death and our redemption, signified by the ashes; and in proclaiming his twofold nature, signified by the mixture of water and wine. Thus the priest, following the footsteps of his Savior, purifies the church when, as far as possible, he instructs, disciplines, consoles, and encourages the people who hear him, and teaches them to arm themselves against all the enemy’s snares. He pours what remains of the purifying water at the base of the altar because what he himself cannot accomplish he humbly entrusts to the Lord—namely, the purification of his disciples, in which he can indeed cooperate and labor together with them as a human being. Complete cleansing, however, belongs to him alone who foreknew and predestined those whom he would make conformed to the image of his Son.

This is why, in the law of the Old Testament, the blood of sacrificial victims, as had been commanded, was either placed on the horns of the altar or sprinkled seven times with the priest’s finger, from certain victims, toward the house, while what remained was poured out at the base of the altar. It is the priests’ task to labor as much as they can for the benefit of the flock entrusted to them; whatever exceeds their strength, they must commend most devoutly to the Lord [Col. 0857A]. Our first Shepherd, the Lord and Savior himself, left them this pattern impressed upon them. When he was already approaching his Passion, he graciously commended to the Father, as an example to be handed down to pastors, the disciples whom he seemed about to leave on earth, saying:

“I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, because they are yours. And all that is mine is yours, and yours is mine, and I have been glorified in them. And now I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, preserve in your name those whom you have given me, so that they may be one, as we are. While I was with them, I kept them in your name,” and so forth.

In that same prayer he graciously deigned to pray for his disciples, like a fountain of goodness [Col. 0857B]. So too Paul, when he knew that he was about to leave his disciples and had told them that they would no longer see him, poured out, as it were, the water left over from the purification at the base of the altar when he commended the faithful to the Lord at the threshold of their present life, saying: “And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and give you an inheritance among all the sanctified.” The antiphon itself also suggests this. For he says that he will enter the altar of God—that is, the spiritual altar signified by this visible one, which the bodily eye cannot penetrate to see, which John saw in the Apocalypse, from which rose the smoke of the spices that are the prayers of the saints [Col. 0857C] before the Lord, with the angel offering them. This is signified by what follows: “to God who gives joy to my youth.” This is called youth because, in the battle line taken up against the devil, it makes itself strong when it hears John say: “I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and you have conquered the evil one.”

## What is signified by wiping the altar with linen

Afterward the altar is wiped with linen. What is meant by linen except the example of the Lord’s Passion? Flax grows from the earth and is brought to whiteness through great labor. So too the flesh of our Savior arose from the earth, since it came from the blessed Virgin Mary, but through various tribulations it reached the whiteness and glory of the resurrection. The altar is therefore wiped with linen when the tribulations of the holy Church [Col. 0857D] amid worldly pressures are smoothed away through the Savior’s example. Hence he himself says to the disciples: “A disciple is not above his teacher.” And again: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you.”

With this linen the blessed Peter took care to wipe away the sweat of the disciples when, as they labored, he placed before them the Lord’s example, saying: “Since Christ suffered in the flesh [another reading: on the cross], arm yourselves with the same disposition.” And again: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow in his footsteps.” Paul likewise says: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him.” And again: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us.”

When, therefore, the teacher sets such things and others like them before the Church entrusted to him in order to strengthen the disciples’ hearts, he wipes the altar, wet with the labor of human suffering, with the linen of imitation of the Lord. Then he offers incense. That incense signifies the virtues of prayers is attested by the Psalmist, who says: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight.” The Apocalypse of John likewise says of the angel that much incense was given to him so that he might offer it, from the prayers of the saints, upon the altar before the Lord [Col. 0858A].

Rightly, therefore, does that priest fulfill vows through prayers who guards the life of his disciples with the great love described above. He prays well and confidently both for himself and for others when no private affection and no sluggish idleness turns him back from the benefit of his neighbor. After the water has been poured at the base of the altar, the altar is wiped with linen and incense is offered [Col. 0858B], because it is necessary that the priest who commends the salvation of the people entrusted to him to the Lord accomplish this act of pious intercession both through bodily affliction and through inward intention. Thus, after the Lord had commended his disciples to the Father, he immediately, as he was about to undergo his Passion for them, poured out a prayer of pious intercession.

The blessed Paul too is read to have done the same with his fellow preachers. For it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “And when they had appointed presbyters and deacons for them in each city, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord in whom they had believed.”

## What is signified by the various anointings of the altar

Meanwhile the bishop pours oil upon the altar, making a cross with it in the middle [Col. 0858C] of the altar and upon its four corners. The order is quite fitting: after the cleansing by water and the other rites mentioned, the altar is drenched with oil, because the holy Church too is first cleansed with water in the baptismal font and then marked by anointing through the hands of the bishop, so that it may merit the coming of the Holy Spirit. For oil signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit; when oil is applied externally to bodies, the coming of the Holy Spirit is signified internally. Hence it was promised through Isaiah: “The yoke will rot before the oil.” The yoke of demonic domination rotted in the human race through the coming of the Holy Spirit.

But it must be asked why a cross is made with oil in the middle of the altar and then upon its four corners. The answer is that the foundations and beginnings of the Church first arose in Jerusalem, which we know to have been placed in the middle of the world, as Ezekiel testifies when he says: “This is Jerusalem; I have placed her in the midst of the nations, with lands around her.” The Psalmist likewise says: “But God our King before the ages worked salvation in the middle of the earth.”

Oil is therefore poured into the middle of the altar in the form of a cross and then upon its four corners because the gift of the Holy Spirit first came upon the Church established in Jerusalem and from there spread into the other parts of the world. For it is written: “From Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.” Hence, after the Savior had commanded his disciples, “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” he nevertheless commanded them to await the coming of the Holy Spirit in Jerusalem and then hasten to teach, saying: “But you must remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.”

Remembering both the ancient history and the ministry, the bishop sings: “Jacob set up the stone as a monument, pouring oil over it.” For Jacob, when he was in exile, placed a stone beneath his head at Bethel and slept. The house of God is his Church, as Paul says to Timothy: “But if I am delayed, know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is his Church.” That stone which Jacob had beneath his head expressed a type of the Savior. Therefore, he deserves to contemplate the foundations of the house of God who has the stone at his head; for he truly perceives divine things who has fixed his head—that is, his mind—in Christ.

He anointed that same stone because he foresaw the stone that was to come and be anointed: the one rejected by the Jews who were building, but anointed by God the Father with the oil of gladness above his companions. Hence Peter says: “God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power,” from this anointing Christ—that is, “the Anointed One”—is named.

The bishop anoints that stone with his own hand because it was in the power of our true Priest when he sent the Paraclete Spirit upon the Church. Hence he says to that same stone, which he first anointed with his hand: “If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you.” When, therefore, he bestowed the Holy Spirit upon the primitive Church whenever he wished [Col. 0859C], he certainly anointed the stone with his own hand, because he bestowed the oil of the Holy Spirit when and as he wished. The hand signifies his power, as it is written: “The word of the Lord came through the hand of Haggai,” or of any other prophet.

Hence Peter says: “Therefore, exalted by the right hand of God and having received the promise of the Holy Spirit, he poured him out upon us who believe.” But when another priest places incense around the altar, this corresponds to the time when the Holy Spirit was sent upon the apostles, of whom it is written that, before the coming of the Holy Spirit, “they were always in the temple, praising God and blessing the Lord.”

When, therefore, the bishop anoints the altar and another priest places incense around it, this signifies that, when the Lord and Savior was about to send the Holy Spirit upon the Church, the apostolic chorus itself—which is our second priesthood—was sending the power of prayer to the Lord. At the same time it is shown that no one is worthy of the coming of the Holy Spirit unless the power of sacred prayer commends him.

It may also be asked why the altar is anointed twice with ordinary oil but a third time with chrism. We answer that, although the gifts of the Holy Spirit are many, the holy Church nevertheless has three virtues that are absolutely necessary, without which it cannot be saved: faith, hope, and charity. Since the human race is enriched by these three virtues, the sacred altar is adorned with three anointings. The fact that it is first enriched with a cheaper oil and third with chrism—that is, with the more precious ointment—signifies that, although faith and hope are very necessary, charity is nevertheless considered more precious than they [Col. 0860A]. Hence Paul says in his Epistle: “Now these three remain: faith, hope, and charity; but the greatest of these is charity.”

Charity is greater than faith and hope because, when these fail, charity remains; or because the beginning of the charity by which we love God begins here, when we see through a mirror and in an enigma, but it will be brought to completion when we see face to face.

When the chrism has been poured upon the altar, the priest sings the antiphon: “See, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a field that the Lord has blessed.” Recalling the prophecy once spoken by Jacob, he declares that it is now fulfilled in the building [another reading: glorification] of the Church, whose Son is our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh. Jacob foresaw him then, though he was to be born only after many ages [Col. 0860B]; his field is the whole breadth of the world, through which the Church has been spread.

This field has produced various flowers of excellent fragrance: roses in the martyrs, lilies in virgins, violets in those who despise the world, green grass in beginners, flowering plants in those making progress, and full blossoms in those who are mature and perfect. The fragrance of the Son is therefore the fragrance of a full field when the meadow of the holy Church shines with various virtues and conveys a sweet fragrance to Christ. Hence that aromatic herb, speaking of itself and its kind, said: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place.”

Then, around the Church, the bishop makes a cross on the walls with his thumb, using the same chrism, beginning on the right side and continuing to the left. The entire altar is smeared with sacred anointing, but the walls are marked with the bishop’s thumb, because by the altar are signified those who are imbued with the more excellent gift of the Holy Spirit—those whose minds always burn with love of the Lord and who, therefore, are enriched with a greater measure of that gift in proportion to their greater delight in it.

The walls signify those of a lesser order, for whom it is enough that they are stones of the Church and remain united in the Church’s structure. Thus, through faith in the Passion and resurrection and through fraternal charity, they merit the gifts of the Holy Spirit. The cross is painted from right to left when someone enters the Church with upright intention and, remaining in its fellowship and remembering the sufferings of his Savior, brings this life to an end.

Meanwhile the bishop sings the antiphon: “The Lord has sanctified his Tabernacle” [Col. 0860D]. The Church is God’s tabernacle because in the present life it is, as it were, on a journey toward its homeland, or because it has undertaken warfare against the aerial powers. The Lord sanctified it in such a way that, as the Apostle says, he made it “without stain or wrinkle.”

He also sings: “All your walls are precious stones.” The walls of Jerusalem are the fortifications of the Scriptures, by which Jews, heretics, and pagans are kept at bay. These walls are built of precious stones because those who composed the sacred Scriptures under God’s authorship and left them for us to read were exceedingly precious to God. They are called stones because of their unconquerable firmness. To one of them it was said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.”

When the bishop again makes a cross of incense upon the altar [Col. 0861A], he indicates that, before we merit grace, we must also ask God for it through the persistence of our prayers. Nor, after receiving his goodness, should we become lax and negligent; rather, it is fitting to repay him with boundless thanks for the benefits bestowed, lest by accepting the gift we become ungrateful for what we have received and at the same time be deprived of it—like that negligent and undevoted servant who, after receiving his master’s talent, not only proved unfaithful but also became insolent and malicious, bringing accusations against his master.

Avoiding this, after the bishop has anointed the Lord’s altar with spiritual [another reading: special] chrism, he devoutly submits himself to prayer and thanksgiving, knowing that it is written: “The rivers return to the place from which they flow, so that they may flow again.” For no rivers can continue to flow; rather, they all dry up unless they return to the motherly abyss. Likewise, unless those who receive divine gifts humbly strive to submit themselves to the power of the one from whom they received the ability to flow, their willing and doing will wither in perpetual dryness. Rebuking certain such people, the Apostle says: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?”

The Bishop of bishops also, our Lord and Savior, who sits at the right hand of the Father’s majesty, makes a cross of incense upon the altar when, as the Apostle says, he intercedes with the Father for us. To make a cross of incense is to display his Passion to the Father and intercede for us. The Apostle Paul says: “Christ Jesus, who died, who also rose, who also ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father, who also intercedes for us.”

After the prayer the bishop begins the antiphon: “Strengthen, O God, what you have wrought in us, from your holy temple which is in Jerusalem,” with “Glory to the Father.”

When the ministry of human salvation has almost been completed, he prays either—as the Lord himself, entreating the Father—that he confirm what he has wrought, so that the whole earth may be subjected to him for whose redemption he did not hesitate to die, as he had promised him before the Incarnation: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance,” and what follows; or every bishop, acting in his place, begs that what is carried out by his gift may by his favor be brought to completion, so that, according to the Apostle, neither tribulation, nor distress, nor nakedness, nor danger, nor any creature may be able to separate us from the charity of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

He added where that work of God in us had arisen, saying: “from your holy temple which is in Jerusalem.” For what he wrought in us proceeded from his temple in Jerusalem, because from his Church proceeded those who exercised among us preaching and signs of power. The Church refers all these things to the glory of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, since it acknowledges one true God existing in Trinity and unity.

After this, the subdeacons or acolytes bring the linens, vessels, and all the church cloths to the bishop for blessing [Col. 0862A]. Who are signified by these ministers except those appointed to the service or adornment of the Church, who must contribute many things to the Church’s beauty, each according to his various ability? Just as various gifts were offered among the people of Israel when the tabernacle was built at God’s command, so various gifts are offered through the ministers of the holy Church for the adornment of the Church and presented to the Lord.

Some offer linens—that is, bodies brought to the whiteness of chastity through various exercises of virtue. Others offer red garments, that is, hearts prepared for martyrdom. Others offer hyacinth-colored garments, for they know how to say: “Our citizenship is in heaven.” Others offer scarlet garments, glowing with the heat of charity. Others offer checkered garments, inseparably joined by the bond of peace. Others offer golden and silver vessels [Col. 0862B], shining with the beauty of understanding and eloquence.

Considering all these things, the Psalmist acclaims that due honor is rendered by the Church to the true King, saying: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in gold, surrounded by variety.” Hence that same Prophet, seeing with such order that honor ought to be displayed to God, exhorts the angels or apostles, saying: “Gather to him his saints, those who established his covenant over sacrifices.” The Lord himself also graciously deigns to bestow blessing upon such people, as the same Psalmist says: “The Lord has blessed those who fear him, the small together with the great.”

## What the translation of the relics and their placement in the altar signify

When these rites have been duly completed, the bishop goes to the place where the relics had remained during the preceding night with vigils and lifts them up. What is signified by this except that, after our true Bishop has prepared for us, as the Apostle says, a city, he returns to take up also the saints who dwell in the present night and carefully guard themselves, watching as the Lord says: “Watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation,” and to bring them from their places into his Father’s house?

After the bishop has prepared the altar in which the relics are to be placed, he takes them up and carries them to the prepared place, because the Bishop of bishops himself, whose office this man represents, promised his apostles, and through them all the faithful: “I go to prepare a place for you; and if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be.”

The Holy of Holies is the place to which no iniquity or defilement can approach. It is not on earth but in heaven. The bishop prays that he may reach it when he lifts up the relics of the saints in the sanctification of souls. They are lifted with great honor and divine songs because those ministers who are guides and rulers of souls greatly rejoice in their dignity when they see them joined with themselves in the heavenly realm.

They sing: “You walk, saints of God; enter the city of the Lord,” that is, the heavenly Jerusalem. Hence the Apostle says: “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.” What follows, “A new church has been built for you,” refers to this same Church, which is also the city that the Apostle calls the primitive Church [Col. 0863A].

Various other antiphons suited to the same meaning are also sung, imitating the rejoicing and exultation of the angelic powers that accompany those departing from the body until they are received, according to their merits, into dwellings not owed to them.

As the bishop enters the church, he says a prayer, asking that the Lord mercifully enter his house and establish a perpetual dwelling in the hearts of his faithful. His house were and are the saints while they remain in the body, as he himself promises: “I will walk among them and dwell in them.” Likewise in the Gospel: “We will come and make our dwelling with him.” And again in the Apocalypse: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens to me, I will enter in to him and dine with him, and he with me.”

He establishes a perpetual dwelling in them most fully when not only no evil deed, but not even the thought of a slight defilement, drives him from the hearts of the faithful. For now he does not remain in us perpetually, since our thoughts waver among different things and, drifting now here, now there, cannot perpetually retain as a dwelling-place the one who flees all pollution.

The bishop then comes to the altar where the relics are to be deposited, stretches a veil between himself and the people, and himself places them in the altar’s location. For our Bishop, as Paul says, stands as the Bishop of future blessings and stands before the face of God for us [Col. 0863C], in order to place those freed from the prison of the present age in the dwellings of the heavenly altar. Beneath that altar the blessed John saw them in his Apocalypse, crying out and awaiting vengeance upon those who had afflicted them, or perhaps seeking the improvement of their way of life.

He stretches the veil between himself and the people because, now, both he himself and the hidden places of holy souls are separated from the sight of mortals. The blessed Apostle Paul says in his Epistle to the Hebrews that the high priest of the Old Testament, entering the Holy of Holies, held the role of a type of the true and eternal Bishop, our Lord Jesus Christ.

The veil is interpreted as heaven. Entering beyond it, the Son of God daily intercedes for us and places those who come to him in the holy altar—that is, in eternal rest—where this is truly sung: “The saints will exult in glory; they will rejoice in their resting places.”

That is the glory in which the Son will glorify them and say: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” There they rejoice in their resting places, that is, in their hearts or in their various dwellings, when, as the blessed John says in his Apocalypse, “God will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and there will be no more death or mourning, for the former things have passed away” [another reading: “because the first things have passed away”].

The bishop’s prayer harmonizes with this, saying: “Lord God, who from the whole assembly of the saints build for yourself an eternal dwelling.” In churches he builds for himself an eternal dwelling from the whole assembly of the saints, because, receiving all the saints there, he dwells eternally in them [Col. 0864A]. This dwelling that we see is earthly and transitory; nor is it built from the assembly of the saints, but from stones and wood. That dwelling, however, is eternal because it is subject to no change, and it is made from the saints, who are true stones through their participation in that cornerstone in whom the eternal temple, compacted and constructed, grows into the increase of God—now in the Holy Spirit, but then it will be perfect when the whole number of the saints has been gathered and has clung eternally to its Head.

After this the altar is clothed. If we understand the altar as the Church, whether in pilgrimage on earth or taken up into heaven, it is not unfitting to understand its garments as the bodies of the saints. The altar is naked while souls stripped of their bodies and placed in heaven await the day of resurrection [Col. 0864B]. It will be clothed when, as the Lord says, the Son of Man sends his angels with a trumpet and a great voice, and they gather his elect from the four corners of the earth. The altar is clothed when, as the Apostle says, “this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.”

The bishop blesses the altar itself when the Lord and Savior embraces each of the faithful with worthy approval because each has conducted himself worthily in the things he received as a gift from him, saying: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, enter into the joy of your Lord.” These are the gifts that are sanctified by the one Bishop and delivered to his faithful for consumption [Col. 0864C], as Scripture says: each person should eat the fruit of his labors and be satisfied with his works.

The fact that the bishop returns to the sacristy with his ministers and puts on other garments after the altar has been clothed signifies to us that, when our Bishop comes to judgment, he will not be clothed in ceremonial garments, since he will by no means display the glory of his eternity to all; rather, he will appear in the form of a servant to both the elect and the reprobate. After the resurrection has taken place, however, he will display the glory of eternity to his faithful. Of them it is written: “His eyes will see the King in his beauty.” As for the separation of the reprobate from the lot of the righteous, lest they see what is reserved for the elect alone, it is written: “Let the impious be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of God.”

Hence the Lord says of servants who are watchful and await his coming: “Amen, I say to you, he will gird himself, make them recline, and, passing by, minister to them” [Col. 0864D]. He will gird himself when he prepares to repay the elect with their reward. He makes them recline when he causes them to rest in eternal blessedness, as though upon a certain altar. He ministers while passing by because he hastens from judgment to the kingdom.

The Church is adorned and many lights are kindled when, at the resurrection, each person displays the ornaments of virtue that he bore while living in the body. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the counsels of hearts [Col. 0865A]; and then each person will receive praise from God.”

The Church shines with many lights when, as the Apostle says, “star differs from star in glory,” so also is the resurrection of the dead. The Lord likewise says in the Gospel: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.” Daniel also says: “Those who are learned among the people will shine like the splendor of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like stars for everlasting ages.”

Then the cantor begins to say: “How awesome is this place.” For what is more awesome than the day of judgment, of which the Lord speaks to Job when discussing the devil’s condemnation: “When he is lifted up, the angels will fear, and, terrified, they will be purified”? After the separation of the many, however, the elect will not endure punitive terror; they will only marvel at the power of their Creator in the condemnation of the wicked and at his mercy in the liberation of the good.

Even now there is no torturing terror in the holy angels; nevertheless, Ezekiel, seeing the heavenly hosts, says of them: “When a voice came from above the firmament, the living creatures stood, and their wings were lowered.” What mind can conceive the substance of God without great trembling of spirit, when the Apostle says: “The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding”? Since no understanding is capable of fully conceiving him, it follows that anyone who thinks about him is not entirely free from all terror.

Then the bishop proceeds solemnly, and the service is performed with joy, because, once the judgment has been completed, he will be seen face to face, not through a mirror and in an enigma, as it is said through the prophet: “Everlasting joy will be theirs.”

[Col. 0865]

# THE TWELVE HOMILIES OF REMIGIUS

(Fontani, *New Pleasures of the Learned*, vol. III, pp. 83–220.)

## HOMILY I. ON THE FOLLOWING WORDS OF MATTHEW: “For as lightning comes forth from the east and appears in the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.”

[Col. 0865B]

By the terms “east” and “west” he also wished to signify the whole world, throughout which the holy Church was destined to exist, since the Gospel began at Jerusalem. For the Lord appropriately warned his disciples—in fact, all the faithful—that whoever wished to believe in him, now that the Church had been established throughout the world and had become manifest, should not believe heretics or schismatics. Every schism and every heresy had its own place in the world and gained adherents in its own regions; or at any rate the heretics themselves, in their secret and hidden gatherings, deceived as many uninstructed people as they could.

This is what the Lord’s statement refers to: “If anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ,’ or, ‘There he is,’ do not believe it.” This signifies the various parts of the earth and its provinces. When he adds, “Look, he is in the desert; do not believe it,” he signifies the hidden and secret gatherings of the heretics. Thus, when the Lord says that his coming will extend from east to west, this is directed against those heretics who lived in particular regions of the world and claimed that Christ existed only among themselves. But when he says “as lightning,” this applies to those who gather secretly, as though in inner chambers, and to the few who meet as though in a desert place.

It must also be understood that these words show that the Lord’s second coming will not be in humility, as his first was, but will be displayed in glory, like lightning. It is as though he were saying openly: “It is foolish to seek him who is the light of the whole world in some part of the earth or in some secret and hidden place.”

And lest we remain ignorant of the place to which he himself would come, he therefore added: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered.” The meaning is this: “When I have raised the body of my assumed humanity into heaven by the power of my divinity, there the eagles will be gathered”—that is, the souls of the elect.

The souls of the elect are beautifully compared with eagles, because, just as eagles always penetrate the heights, so the souls of the elect despise what is low and earthly and desire heavenly things. Hence the Lord says of Job: “Does the eagle rise at your command?” Spiritual men are fittingly called eagles because they imitate the Lord’s humility and passion, since they are, as it were, nourished by his body. That body is also called a corpse, because it fell through death; for a corpse (*cadaver*) is so called from falling (*cadendo*).

Some, however, have understood this statement historically in the following way: “Wherever the body is”—that is, wherever my crucified body is, and wherever the sacrifices are offered—“there the eagles will be gathered,” that is, the Roman soldiers.

For what great thing is it that the Lord says, “Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light,” when such signs are also frequently recorded as having occurred before his first coming in the books of the pagans and in the sayings of philosophers? Or why does he say that the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, when the stars remain so fixed that they cannot possibly fall? How will the sun be darkened and the moon not give its light, when Isaiah, speaking of the future resurrection, says: “The light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, like the light of seven days”?

This statement can therefore be understood more appropriately of the Church. For she is the sun, and she is also the moon; in her there are also stars. That she is both moon and sun is made clear by Solomon, who says: “Beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun.”

When the wicked persecutors rage beyond measure, and, with worldly prosperity smiling upon them, say, “Peace, peace, and security,” the sun will be darkened and the moon will not give its light, because the holy Church will not appear. The stars will fall from heaven because those who seem to shine like stars through the grace of faith and the other virtues will fall away from the faith, since they will easily be deceived by Antichrist.

“And the powers of heaven will be shaken”—that is, those who are strongest in the Church will be thrown into confusion. John makes this clear in the Apocalypse when he speaks of the great dragon, saying: “And it dragged a third of the stars with its tail.” [Col. 0867B]

This is also why the Lord speaks to Job about Behemoth, saying: “He will spread gold beneath him as though it were mud.”

When he says, “Immediately after the tribulation of those days,” this should not be understood to mean that these things will occur only after the tribulation has ended, but rather when it has begun and is still impending. The tribulation will come first, so that the falling away of many may follow.

And because that tribulation will last through all the days, the Lord therefore says: “Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven.” The sign of the Son of Man may be understood as the sign of the cross, so that, in accordance with Zechariah and John, the Jews may “look upon him whom they pierced.” Or it may be understood as the banner of faith and triumphant victory. “And then all the tribes of the earth will mourn.” Those, namely, will mourn who did not possess citizenship in heaven, but whose names will be written on earth.

It follows: “And you will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven.” This sentence can be understood in two ways.

The holy Church is a bright and shining cloud, bearing fruit and growing from what she began to preach: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” The Lord will therefore come in his members as though in clouds, or in his body, which is the Church, as in a bright and shining cloud—just as he also does not cease to come spiritually every day.

But if the holy Church is to be understood as the bright and shining cloud, what does he mean when he says, “with great power and majesty”? He fittingly says “with great power and majesty,” because the greater and more severe that final tribulation will be, the greater will be the power and majesty displayed in the saints, to whom he will give strength so that they are not overcome by such great persecution.

It can also be understood in this way: the Lord will come openly to judgment in the clouds, in the very body—that is, the body he took from the Virgin, in which he died, in which he also rose again, and in which he ascended into heaven, placing it at the right hand of the Father. He will therefore come openly to judgment in the clouds, just as he ascended in the clouds.

That he ascended in a cloud is made clear in the Acts of the Apostles, where we read that, while the apostles were watching, “he was lifted up, and a cloud received him, and he was carried into heaven.” And that he will come in the clouds is testified by the angels who, while the apostles wondered, said: “Why do you marvel as you look into heaven? He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.”

The Lord will come with great power and majesty—that is, in terror and splendor. He will appear both terrible and gentle: terrible, to terrify the wicked; gentle, to console the godly. And he will send his angels “with a trumpet.”

This trumpet should not truly be understood as corporeal, but as the voice of the archangels. He fittingly added “with a loud voice,” because that voice will be so loud that, at its cry, all the dead will rise from the dust of the earth.

The Apostle mentions this trumpet when he says: “In an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet; for the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.”

He adds: “And they will gather his elect from the four winds of heaven.” By “the four winds of heaven” he means the four regions of the world: east, west, north, and south. And lest anyone suppose that the elect will be gathered only from the four quarters of the world, and not from the regions and places between them, he expressly added: “From the highest heavens to their boundaries”—that is, from every limit of the earth, wherever the circles of heaven extend far apart and the earth lies beneath them, even to their boundaries, through the central and intermediate regions, all the way to the earth’s furthest limits.

No elect person, then, will remain at that time who does not meet the Lord as he comes to judgment in the air, whether found alive in the body or raised to life from the dust of the earth.

The reprobate also will come to judgment, whether found alive in the body or raised from the dust of the earth, but there will be a great difference. The saints and elect will enter into the joy of their Lord; but the Lord’s enemies, after the resurrection has been completed, will perish and be scattered from his presence.

“But from the fig tree learn the parable.” Because the Lord had foretold in many words both the destruction of Jerusalem, the persecutions of Antichrist, and the signs of his coming, he therefore, following the custom of the Palestinians, introduced a parable, saying: “From the fig tree learn the parable.” It is as though he were saying: “To understand the force of my words more closely, observe the nature of the fig tree.”

Using the example of a tree, he taught about the coming of the consummation. The meaning is this: Just as, when the tender shoots appear on the fig tree, the bud bursts into flowers, and the bark produces leaves, you understand that spring is beginning and summer is approaching, so, when you see all these things, do not suppose that the day of judgment has already arrived. Rather, understand that these things come as forerunners, showing that “it is near, at the doors.”

It should be noted that he did not merely say, “when you see these things,” but added “all,” because not some but all the things that have been written must precede the day of consummation.

The evangelist Luke says: “When these things begin to happen, look up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.” This should not seem contradictory, because this is precisely what Matthew means by saying, “It is near, at the doors”—that is, it is near to coming forth and appearing openly to reign with his elect.

Spiritually, this tree signifies the Synagogue. For this is the fig tree to which the Lord came, found no fruit, cursed it, and at once, at his word, it withered. This tree—that is, the Synagogue—because it refused to offer any fruit of righteousness to the Lord when he came, was therefore condemned to perpetual barrenness.

But if this tree, which first withered through unbelief, should be restored so that it blossoms with renewed greenness and is adorned with flowers and fruits—that is, if, after its long blindness of unbelief has been removed, it receives the light of faith and is adorned with the fruits of good works—then the tree that had long been barren will begin to produce the fruit it previously denied, in accordance with the words of blessed Job:

“A tree has hope: if it is cut down, it grows green again, and its branches sprout. If its root has grown old in the earth, and its trunk has died in the dust, it will germinate again at the scent of water, and it will produce a crown of foliage as when it was first planted.”

This tree—that is, the Synagogue—which withered through unbelief and was cut down, will again germinate at the scent of water—that is, at the word of holy preaching. It will produce foliage as when it was first planted, because, when Elijah and Enoch preach, it will return to the former dignity that it possessed in the patriarchs and prophets.

Therefore, when we see all these things happening—that is, when the Synagogue is converted to the faith and to the former dignity it once possessed—we ought to understand that the day of consummation is near.

“Amen, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened.” Truth itself has used this form of speech so that every doubt might be driven from the hearts of readers and hearers.

By “generation” he means the multitude of the entire human race, or certainly that Jewish people. In truth, this generation itself will not pass away before all the things that have been written have been accomplished in reality.

“Heaven and earth will pass away.” The heaven said to pass away must not be understood as the ethereal or starry heaven, but as the aerial heaven, from which the birds of heaven and the clouds are named.

The Apostle Peter makes this clear when he says: “The heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God; through these the world that then existed was destroyed, being inundated with water. But the heavens and earth that now exist have been stored up by the same word, reserved for fire on the day of judgment and the destruction of ungodly people.”

Blessed Peter plainly shows in these words that the heavens destined to perish by fire are the same as those that previously perished by water. These are the empty and cloudy, windy spaces of the air, through which birds and clouds move. The fire will reach as far as the water reached: that is, the power of the fire will extend as far as the water rose above all the mountains—fifteen cubits, namely. Heaven and earth will burn only as far as our wickedness has been able to defile them.

The question now arises why the Lord says, “Heaven and earth will pass away,” when Ecclesiastes says: “One generation goes, and another generation passes away, but the earth stands forever.” If the earth stands forever, then heaven does also; and if heaven and earth stand forever, how will they pass away?

It must be understood that they will pass away through improvement and renewal, in accordance with John’s statement: “There will be a new heaven and a new earth.” But they will not pass away through annihilation. They will pass away with respect to the form and appearance they now possess, as the Apostle makes clear when he says: “The form of this world is passing away,” and the Psalmist: “You will change them, and they will be changed.” But they will not pass away with respect to the essence they now retain.

Again, the question arises why the Lord says, “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away,” when in the nature of things nothing is more enduring than heaven and earth, and nothing passes more quickly than speech.

Words are not words as long as they remain incomplete. Once they have been perfectly formed, they are no longer present, since they can be completed only by passing away. But it must be understood that by “the Lord’s words” he does not mean sounds, voices, or letters, but the things themselves and the meanings expressed by words.

The meaning is this: “My words”—that is, the things and meanings themselves—will not pass away before they are accomplished in reality. My speech, which passes away, explains them.

It follows: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven, except the Father alone.”

The evangelist Mark says not only that the angels do not know, but also the Son. For he says: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, except the Father alone.”

The question arises why he says that the Son does not know this and that the Father alone knows, when the Son himself says: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father”; and again: “All that the Father has is mine”; and: “I and the Father are one.”

For if he and the Father are one, how does the Son not know what the Father knows?

To understand this passage soberly, we must consider what it means to know and what it means not to know. For God, to know means to approve. Thus he says to Moses: “I have known you by name”—that is, “I have approved you.”

Alternatively, for God to know means to make others know. Thus Moses said to the children of Israel: “The Lord your God is testing you, so that he may know whether you love him.” This must not be understood as though there were something God did not know.
