Rather, “so that he may know” means “so that he may make you know how far you have advanced in his love,” something that could not otherwise be known unless it were demonstrated by trials.

If, then, for God to know means to approve, not to know means to reject. Hence, at the end of the world he will say to the wicked: “I do not know you”—that is, “I do not find you in my teaching and discipline; I do not approve you.”

Again, if for God to know means to make others know, not to know means to make others usefully ignorant. Accordingly, blessed Mark says that the Son does not know because he himself usefully causes others not to know the day of judgment, since knowing it would not benefit them.

For if a person knew the day of judgment, or the day of death, he would assign one time to pleasures and another to repentance. The Lord therefore wished the day of judgment to be hidden from everyone, so that it would always be feared. He wished it to remain unknown so that all might be ready and fully watchful.

Blessed Matthew, however, says that the Father alone knows because by the name “Father” he wishes the Son also to be understood, “since he himself is in the Father, and the Father is in the Son.” The Father cannot be called Father unless he has a Son, nor can the Son be called Son unless he has a Father.

Since, therefore, the Father and the Son are one substance, what the Father knows the Son certainly knows, and what the Father does not know the Son does not know.

“But as were the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.” The Lord confirmed the suddenness of the day of his coming through various testimonies. Above, he compared it to lightning flashing and quickly passing across the sky. Now he compares it with the days of Noah and Lot, as another evangelist says, explaining how destruction suddenly overtakes all mortals.

Because these words of the Lord could be understood and examined in many different ways, the Lord himself therefore explained them, saying: “As people were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, before the flood…”

When it says “eating and drinking,” it does not condemn food according to the most impious doctrine of Marcion, Manichaeus, and Tatian, nor does it condemn the good of marriage. God granted the one for the propagation of offspring and the other for the support of this life. Rather, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement, “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial,” it condemns and reproves the immoderate use and desire of things that are lawful.

They did not perish because they were doing these things, but because they wholly surrendered themselves to them, and for their sake despised God’s judgment and withdrew from him. That is why they perished by fire.

It follows: “Until the day when Noah entered the ark.”

Noah is interpreted as “rest,” and thus signifies Christ. The ark signifies the holy Church. Noah builds the ark because Christ constructs the holy Church from various believers, as though from smoothed timbers.

When the ark has been perfectly completed, Noah will enter it, because, on the day of judgment, when the number of the elect has been completed, Christ will illumine the holy Church through the presence of his vision.

As long as the ark is being built, the wicked indulge themselves and rejoice in temporal goods, in accordance with Solomon’s statement: “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things.” But when the ark has been perfectly completed, the wicked will perish.

This signifies that those who here insult the saints while they labor and struggle will there be punished with the penalty of eternal condemnation when the saints have been crowned.

“Then two will be in the field”—that is, when the day of consummation has arrived. But who are the two in the field, the two women grinding at the mill, and the two in bed, one of whom will be taken and the other left?

These words signify three orders within the holy Church: namely, preachers, the continent, and the married. The field signifies the holy Church.

The two in the field therefore beautifully represent the order of preachers, to whom the field of the holy Church has been entrusted. The two in bed represent the order of the continent, who choose leisure and rest and are not entangled either in the cares of this age or in earthly business. Their rest is therefore fittingly signified by the name “bed,” because, being separated from the cares of this age, they rest as though in a bed.

The two women grinding at the mill signify the order of the married, who, while being bent now toward one concern and now toward another by their various cares, draw a millstone round and round. And because this order is weaker within the Church, married people are fittingly represented by the feminine gender.

When he says that one will be taken and the other left, this should not be understood as though he were speaking of two individual people. Rather, these words signify two kinds of disposition. Within these orders there are good and bad, just and unjust.

There are many who labor in the field of the holy Church for the love of God and in hope of the reward of the heavenly homeland. These will certainly be taken up into the joys of eternal blessedness. Conversely, there are others who labor for earthly profit and worldly business; these will be left for the punishment of eternal condemnation.

Similarly, within the order of the continent there are those who strive to preserve purity of heart and body for the love of God. They are fittingly represented by the wise virgins; they will be taken up into the kingdom of everlasting blessedness. Conversely, there are others who preserve the integrity of heart and body for the sake of human approval. These are beautifully represented by the foolish virgins, and they will be left for the punishment of eternal condemnation.

There are also some among the married who keep God’s commandments and strive to fulfill them so that they may please God. These will certainly be taken up into the kingdom of eternal blessedness. Likewise, there are others who not only despise God’s commandments but are also defiled by various stains of vice. These will be left for the punishment of perpetual condemnation.

These three orders are also beautifully represented by the three men whom the Lord mentions through the prophet Ezekiel, saying: “As I live, says the Lord, even if these three men were in their midst—Noah, Daniel, and Job—they would not deliver their sons or daughters; they alone would deliver their own souls.”

Noah guided the ark upon the waters. He therefore fittingly signifies the order of preachers, who guide the holy Church amid the waves of this present life.

Daniel chose a celibate life—that is, he rejected earthly marriage—and remained continent continually in the king’s court. He therefore rightly represents the order of the continent.

Job had a wife, sons, and daughters. Accordingly, he clearly represents the order of the married.

What the Lord says there—that they will not deliver their sons or daughters—means here what he says: “One will be taken, and one will be left.”

## HOMILY II. ON THE FOLLOWING WORDS OF MATTHEW: “When John heard in prison about the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples and said to them…” etc.

This question of blessed John and the Lord’s answer is also mentioned by the evangelist Luke [Col. 0872D], but not in the same place as by blessed Matthew; and therefore it is uncertain which of them preserved the order of events, or which, recalling them, wrote them down. But we must ask why John the Baptist, a prophet and more than a prophet, stationed beside the waters of the Jordan, bore witness to the Lord, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” And again: “After me comes a man who was made before me”; and likewise: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom.” And elsewhere, to demonstrate his own humility and the Lord’s excellence, he says: “He who is from the earth speaks from the earth, but he who comes from heaven is above all.”

Afterward, however, when he had been placed in prison, he sent his disciples to Jesus and asked: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” [Col. 0873A] Was blessed John ignorant that he was the Son of God, to whom he had previously borne witness? Certainly not. But first we must know that there were some who, understanding this passage simply, said that he asked because he was ignorant. Yet he did not ask as one who was ignorant about the one whom he had previously confessed. For he did not fail to know that he was the Son of God, since he had heard the Father’s voice thunder from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased”; and he had recognized him while still in his mother’s womb. Rather, he wished to provide for the ignorance of his disciples. For he feared that his disciples might join themselves to the scribes and Pharisees and become their followers.

Therefore he sent them to Jesus, so that, while they themselves seemed to be asking on his behalf, they might learn; and when they saw him performing signs [Col. 0873B] and miracles, they might believe that he was the Son of God, believe in him, and understand that the one whom John himself confessed as the teacher of all was the only one to be followed and imitated.

Blessed Pope Gregory says that blessed John knew one thing and did not know another: he knew that Jesus was the Son of God and the Lamb who had come to take away the sins of the world; nevertheless, he did not know whether Jesus himself would die and descend to the prison-house of hell in order to draw out from there his chosen ones, who were being held there unjustly, or whether he would send another in his place to redeem the human race.

Therefore he sent his disciples to Jesus in order in every respect to fulfill the office of his forerunner—as though he were saying in other words: “Since you deigned to be born for human beings, indicate whether you will also deign to descend to the prison-house of hell, so that I who became the forerunner of your birth may also become the forerunner of your death, and announce in hell that you are to come, just as I announced to the world that you had come.”

Accordingly, when the Lord was questioned, he enumerated the miracles of his power—namely, “the blind see, the lame walk”—and immediately answered concerning the humility of his death, saying: “And blessed is he who is not offended because of me.” [Col. 0873C] By these words he demonstrated the humility and lowliness of his death, as though he were saying in other words: “I certainly perform wondrous deeds, but I do not disdain to endure humiliation. Therefore people must be very careful not to despise death in me while they venerate my signs.”

After seeing so many signs and such great miracles, people ought not to have been offended but rather to have marveled. Yet unbelievers took grave offense at him when, after the miracles, they saw him dying. The Apostle makes clear that the passion of the cross was a cause of offense to them when he says: “We preach Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumbling block, but to the Gentiles foolishness.” For to the Jews it was a stumbling block, and to the Gentiles it seemed utterly foolish that the Author of life could die. Thus human beings took the greatest offense against the Lord precisely from that by which they ought to have become his greatest debtors: the Son of God deserved to be honored by human beings all the more magnificently the more unworthy were the things he endured for human beings.

Blessed Jerome says that John’s disciples had been offended because the crowds were leaving John and following the Lord. Therefore they came to John and said: “Rabbi, behold, the one to whom you bore witness beyond the Jordan is baptizing, and everyone is coming to him” [Col. 0874A]—as though they were saying: “You caused this evil, and this matter must be charged to you; for unless you had borne witness to him, the crowds would never have abandoned you and followed him.”

To this John replied: “No one can receive anything unless it has been given to him from above”; and again: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” Elsewhere he says: “He who is from the earth speaks from the earth, but he who comes from heaven is above all.” It was as though he were saying: “Because I am from the earth, I speak as an earthly and fragile human being; but he who comes from heaven is above all, because he is God, and therefore he speaks as God.”

And because they were envious of the Lord, blessed John feared that they would perish through the disease of pride and envy. [Col. 0874B] Therefore he sent them to Jesus so that, when they saw him performing signs and miracles, they might believe that he was the Son of God and cling to his discipleship.

Thus the Lord, understanding blessed John’s intention as God, answered not the question of his disciples but John’s purpose, saying: “Go and report to John what you hear and see”—as though he were saying: “I have done what he wished; I have carried out what he asked. You see the signs; believe, if you wish.”

For he said two things: “You hear and see.” One refers to teaching, the other to action. They saw signs and miracles; they heard the teaching of evangelical grace.

He calls his disciples “the poor,” because they were poor in spirit—that is, humble in heart—or he calls them poor in possessions, thereby showing that in the preaching of the Gospel there is no distinction between rich and poor.

But when the Lord says: “And blessed is he who is not offended because of me,” by this statement he struck those messengers themselves—that is, John’s disciples—as though he were plainly saying: “You have been offended on account of me; but you cannot be blessed unless you lay aside your offense and believe in me.”

Spiritually, John bound signifies the Law bound and, as it were, shut up in prison darkness by the sins of the people and the evil interpretation of the scribes and Pharisees. The Lord can be understood as grace of the Gospel, just as John signifies the Law; for just as John bore witness to the Lord, so the Law bore witness to the grace of the Gospel.

John therefore sent some of his disciples to Jesus because the Law sent the doubting scribes and Pharisees concerning the coming of the Lord Savior. The Lord answered them, as it were, saying: “Go and report to John what you hear and see” [Col. 0874D]—as though he were saying: “The time has come for what the prophet Isaiah foretold long ago to be fulfilled: ‘Behold, our Lord will come, and he will save us.’” And shortly afterward: “Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped; then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will be clear.”

It follows: “As they were going away, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John: What did you go out into the wilderness to see?” These words of the Lord, by which he placed John above all praise, plainly demonstrate that they did not doubt that he was the Son of God, to whom John had previously borne witness [Col. 0875A]; rather, for the reasons stated above, John sent his disciples and asked: “Are you the one who is to come?”

But we must ask why the Lord praised John after his disciples had departed, rather than in their presence. It was so that he would not appear to be seeking human praise—that is, to be wishing to be praised by John.

And why did the Lord wish to place John above all praise before the crowds after they had departed? The crowds had heard John bearing witness to the Lord and saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” They had also seen that, after sending his disciples, he asked him: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?”

The crowds could therefore have thought that John was unstable and like a reed carried about by every wind: now bearing witness to the Lord, but then doubting about him. To prevent the crowds from thinking this, the Lord placed John above all praise before them, saying: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” [Col. 0875B]

When the Lord said: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see?” this is an inquiry; what follows—“A reed shaken by the wind?”—is a question. For the ancients distinguished between an inquiry and a question: they said that many answers could be given to an inquiry, but to a question only one, namely: “No.”

Or again, when the Lord says: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” he says this not by affirming but rather by denying, as though he were saying: “When you went out into the wilderness to John, did you go out for this purpose—to see a man like a reed carried about by every wind, so that he would now doubt about the one to whom he had previously borne witness?” Certainly John is not such a man that he would now doubt that the one to whom he had previously borne witness is the Son of God. He asked not for himself but for his disciples.

And we should know that the reed has various and diverse meanings in the divine Scriptures. It signifies the word, as in: “My tongue is the pen of a ready writer.” It signifies the teaching of holy preachers, as in: “In the dens where dragons once dwelt, greenery of reed and rush will arise.” For in those whom the malice of the ancient enemy possessed, the knowledge of teachers and the obedience of hearers were restrained. “Greenery of reed and rush will arise in it,” that is, writers and hearers will arise in the holy Church.

By the rush, however, hearers should be understood. A rush and a reed usually grow from moisture supplied by water; both arise from one and the same water. The reed is taken up for writing, whereas one cannot write with a rush.

What, then, should we understand by the rush and the reed, except that there is one teaching of truth which irrigates many hearers? Some, once irrigated, progress so far in the word of God that they even become writers, like reeds. Others hear the word of God and retain the greenness of good hope and upright works, but are nevertheless entirely unable to progress to writing.

The reed also signifies the minds of hypocrites, empty of every fruit of good works, as in: “Under the shadow it sleeps in the secret place of the reed, in wet locations” [Col. 0876A].

Moreover, it signifies the brightness of the blessedness of the elect, as in: “And like sparks they will run through the reed-bed.”

Finally, it signifies a carnal mind, as in this passage. For a reed is an empty thing, having no pith within and no fruit outside; and, because of the lightness of its nature, it is bent not only by the breath of winds but even by some slight breeze.

The carnal mind is therefore fittingly represented by a reed, because if a breeze of favor or praise blows from the mouth of a neighbor, it immediately becomes cheerful and is lifted up, bending its whole self toward approval. But if it happens that a breeze of detraction arises from the same place from which the breeze of favor had previously blown, it is stirred to violent anger and wrath.

John was not a reed shaken by the wind [Col. 0876B], because neither the favor of anyone made him indulgent nor anger made him harsh; neither prosperity knew how to lift him up nor adversity to bend him. He was not a reed shaken by the wind, because no change of circumstances deflected him from the rectitude of his position.

Let us therefore also learn not to be reeds shaken by the wind—that is, let us make our minds firm amid the breezes of human speech, and let the condition of our minds always remain unbent amid worldly changes, so that neither prosperity may exalt us nor adversity disturb us, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “Be fighters both in prosperity and in adversity.”

It follows: “But what did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing?”

John is reported to have been dressed not in soft clothing but in camel hair; the same evangelist makes this clear elsewhere, saying: “Now John himself had a garment of camel hair” [Col. 0876C].

But as far as the surface meaning of the historical account is concerned, virtue is shown in the rejection of worthless clothing. If the desire for costly garments were not sinful, the Lord would never have praised John for the harshness of his clothing. And if this were not a fault, the Apostle Peter would never have restrained women by his letter from desiring costly clothing, saying: “Not in expensive clothing.” Here we should observe how great a fault it is for men to desire what the very shepherd of the Church took care to prohibit to women.

The meaning is: “Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in the houses of kings”—that is, those who flee from enduring hard and harsh things for God serve not a heavenly kingdom but an earthly one, and seek the softness and pleasure of this age. Those, therefore, wear soft clothing who live according to the pomp and pleasures of this age and put on ambitious garments. Such people seek the courts of kings and rejoice to dwell in their houses.

We should also know that false doctrine always seeks human praise, so that through it it may accumulate earthly gain and abound in the riches of earthly things. For just as those who are splendidly adorned in silk, purple, and fine linen seek the courts of kings and rejoice to dwell in their houses, so, conversely, holy men are admonished to be content with necessary clothing and always to strive to avoid the courts of kings.

This passage can also be understood in a deeper sense, so that soft clothing signifies carnal pleasures [Col. 0877A] and desires. Those are clothed in soft garments who, through carnal desires and pleasures, are clothed in their sins as though in garments. Hence the Psalmist says: “He clothed himself with cursing as with a garment.”

Alternatively, those are clothed in soft garments who flatter evil people, cherish the lives of wicked persons as though with certain caresses, and cover their sins through various persuasions. John was not clothed in soft garments, because he did not support the life of sinners with flattery; rather, with the severity of harsh denunciation he rebuked them, saying: “Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?”

Hence Solomon says: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deeply.” The words of the wise are aptly compared to goads and nails, because they do not know how to stroke the faults of sinners but to prick them; they do not know how to indulge them but to rebuke them.

“But what did you go out to see? A prophet.”

When the Lord says: “But what did you go out to see?” he does not say this by denying, as above, but rather by affirming; hence he immediately adds: “Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.”

But we must ask why the Lord calls John more than a prophet, since elsewhere, when questioned, John denied that he was a prophet. Does Truth proclaim one thing while the herald of Truth announces another?

This should not seem contradictory, because John denied himself to be a prophet for the very reason that the Lord calls him more than a prophet. The office of a prophet is to predict what is to come, not also to point out what is present [Col. 0877C]. John was a prophet as long as he foretold the future; but he was more than a prophet because the one whom the other prophets foretold as future, he pointed out in person with his finger, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God.”

Because the Lord had said that John was neither a reed shaken by the wind nor dressed in soft clothing, and had shown that the name “prophet” was inadequate for him, he added, to demonstrate what name could rightly be given him: “This is the one about whom it is written: Behold, I send my angel.”

This testimony is taken from the prophet Malachi. There it is spoken in the person of the Son, whereas here it is spoken in the person of the Father. This should not seem contradictory, because those whose nature, power, and divinity are one also have one utterance.

“Behold, I send my angel”—that is, John—“before your face,” that is, before the mystery of your incarnation; “who will prepare your way before you,” that is, by preaching and baptizing repentance.

For the one who preaches right faith and good works prepares a way for the Lord. “Angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature; for what is called *angelos* in Greek is called *nuntius*—“messenger”—in Latin. John was therefore called an angel not because he shared the angelic nature, but because of the dignity of his office.

It is right, then, that the one who had come to announce the heavenly Judge should be called an angel, so that he might bear in his name the dignity that he fulfilled in his work. The name “angel” is indeed lofty, but John’s life was not inferior to it. He could rightly be called an earthly angel and a heavenly human being.

We should also know that John alone was not called an angel; all who are counted under the name of the priesthood are also called angels. Hence the Prophet says: “The lips of a priest will guard knowledge, and they will seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.”

And not only priests, but also all the faithful may be called angels. Whoever draws his neighbors away from wickedness, urges them to do good, and announces to them eternal punishment and the heavenly kingdom may rightly be called an angel, in accordance with what is read in the Apocalypse: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’”—that is, whoever receives some spiritual grace through hidden inspiration should strive to announce it to his neighbor, so that his neighbor may come and receive it with him.

For this reason also, in the temple of the Lord not only bowls but also cups were made.

It follows: “Amen, I say to you, [Col. 0878B] among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist.”

Because the Lord had said above that John was more than a prophet, he now used the language of truth to establish his greatness, saying: “Amen,” which is interpreted as “truly.” For if John had doubted about Christ and had not known him to be the true Son of God, the Lord would never have placed him above all praise before the crowds.

But we must ask why the Lord says: “Among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist.” For if no one born among them has arisen greater than John, then neither has Christ himself, since he too was born of a woman, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Born of a woman, born under the law.”

This should not seem contradictory, because in this passage “woman” is used to signify sexual corruption. The Lord therefore placed John above those who were born of women—that is, from the corruption of male and female—but not above the one who was born from the Holy Spirit and from a Virgin.

## HOMILY III. ON THE PASSAGE OF MATTHEW: “John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judea, saying: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near,” etc.

What the holy evangelist says, “in those days,” if it is connected only with the preceding words, where it says, “Joseph, having been warned, withdrew into the regions of Galilee,” appears highly contrary to Luke, who says that the child remained in the temple at the age of twelve, and that his parents went up to Jerusalem every year on the solemn feast of Passover, and afterward relates that John began to preach. Therefore, if matters stand as Matthew says—that is, that John began preaching immediately after Joseph returned from Egypt with the child and, coming there, settled in Nazareth—how can Luke’s account be true? For Luke relates that the child remained in the temple at the age of twelve, that his parents went up to Jerusalem every year on the solemn feast of Passover, and that the child grew, especially since John began preaching when he had reached mature age?

To remove all contradiction, what he says, “in those days,” should not be referred specifically to that time: “After Joseph returned from Egypt with the child and, coming there, settled in Nazareth,” [Col. 0879A] but generally to the whole period of the Lord’s infancy and childhood, so that the meaning is: “in those days”—that is, after these or those events had taken place, which the other evangelists relate concerning the Lord’s infancy and childhood up to his thirtieth year—“then John came.” It should also be understood that all the evangelists mention this preaching of John.

Behold, blessed Matthew, after relating that Joseph returned from Egypt with the child and came to live in Nazareth, immediately joins this statement: “John the Baptist came preaching,” and so forth. Mark, his companion, mentioned this preaching at the beginning of his Gospel, saying: “The beginning of the Gospel,” and so forth, up to the point where he says: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness.” Since he had said nothing beforehand, he therefore did not say “in those days,” [Col. 0879B] or anything similar. Luke, after relating that the child remained in the temple at the age of twelve and that his parents went up to Jerusalem every year, immediately adds: “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, the word of the Lord came to John, the son of Zechariah, in the wilderness.” John, the last and more eloquent than the other evangelists, after relating that the Word was in the beginning with the Father, that the Father created all things through him, that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, immediately adds: “There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.”

Behold, the holy evangelists mention this preaching in various ways and in different places. Why? Because it was their task to prepare the heart, whereas it was the Lord’s task to direct the pen and the intention; for each of them wrote as the Holy Spirit dictated. It should be understood that St. Matthew demonstrates through these words not only the time, place, and person, but also the office and purpose of blessed John. He identifies the person when he says, “John came”; the office when he adds, “the Baptist”; the purpose when he says, “preaching”; the place when he says, “in the wilderness of Judea”; and the general time when he says, “in those days.”

John fittingly began his preaching with repentance. He began with repentance because through repentance faults are corrected—not only natural and original faults, but also those that have been committed. Yet it must be understood that he was neither the first nor the only one to preach repentance; he had testimony from the ancients. [Col. 0879D] For many examples of repentance are found in the Old Testament. The Lord says through the prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner,” and again: “Turn back to me and do penance.” Job says: “If I have sinned unknowingly and concealed my iniquity.” And because through repentance we are made nearer to God and can draw near to the kingdom of heaven, he fittingly adds: “The kingdom of heaven has drawn near.”

The kingdom of heaven is spoken of in four ways. It is called Christ, as in: “The kingdom of God is within you.” It is called sacred Scripture, as in: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.” It is called the holy Church, according to: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king,” and again: “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins.” It is also called the heavenly throne, as in: “Many will come from east and west and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.”

All of this can be understood here, so that the meaning is: “The kingdom of heaven has drawn near”—that is, so that Christ may reign in you; or, “The kingdom of heaven has drawn near”—that is, so that you who understood Scripture carnally may understand it spiritually; or, “The kingdom of heaven has drawn near”—that is, so that you who were the Synagogue may become the Church; or, “The kingdom of heaven has drawn near”—that is, so that you may reign with Christ upon the heavenly throne.

“This is the one who was spoken of through Isaiah the prophet.” There is a question as to whose words these are: those of the Baptist or of the evangelist. [Col. 0880B] They do indeed appear to be the evangelist’s; but if we consider soberly the words of the holy evangelists, they may not unreasonably be attributed to the Baptist.

Matthew, speaking of himself, says: “As Jesus passed on, he saw a man sitting at the tax booth, named Matthew”; he did not say, “he saw me.” John says: “the disciple whom Jesus loved,” and again: “This is the disciple who bears witness to these things and wrote them”; he did not say, “I am he.” In the Old Testament we read: “Moses was the meekest of all who dwelt on the earth.” Job is also described as: “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job”; he did not say, “I was.” Thus these words may not unreasonably be John the Baptist’s, as though he himself had said: “This is the one who was spoken of through Isaiah.”

And why should it be surprising if he said this about himself, when elsewhere, asked who he was, he replied: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness”? Why was John called a voice by the prophet? Because he went before the Word of God. From our own speech we can recognize that a word cannot be heard unless a voice first precedes it. In the same way John preceded that Word of whom it is written: “In the beginning was the Word.” He was sent for this reason: so that, through the mystery of his preaching, the Father’s Word might be recognized by human beings.

Where he cried out he makes clear by adding: “in the wilderness.” Historically, he cried out in the wilderness because he was removed from the crowds of the Jews. Spiritually, however, he is said to have cried out in the wilderness because he announced the comfort of redemption to deserted and forsaken Judea, if it was willing to believe.

What he cried out he makes clear when it is added: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.” He prepares a way for the coming Lord into the hearts of his hearers who preaches right faith and good works, so that the power of grace may penetrate and the light of truth may illumine. He makes straight paths who, through the word of good preaching, forms pure thoughts in the mind.

It should be understood that Isaiah alone did not foresee the coming of this forerunner of the Lord; the Psalmist also did so when, speaking in the person of God the Father, he said: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ”—that is, John, for my Son. John is rightly called a lamp, for just as the morning star goes before the sun, a lamp before its master, and a soldier before the king, so John went before Christ.

A soldier sent by a king prepares a road for him in this way: he fills valleys, levels what is swollen, and removes every obstacle, so that the footsteps of the one walking may not stumble. Thus John prepared the way of the Lord. How the Lord’s way is to be prepared another evangelist—and indeed the prophet himself—makes clear when he says: “Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low.”

The humble are signified by valleys, and the proud by mountains and hills. At the Lord’s coming, the valleys were filled and the mountains and hills brought low, because, as he himself says: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” Hence it is written elsewhere: “He has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted the humble.”

This may also be understood of the Jewish and Gentile peoples. The Gentiles were valleys—that is, humble—because they were worshipers of idols and entangled in various crimes. The Jews, however, were mountains and hills—that is, proud—because they had received the Law and possessed knowledge of God. But at the Lord’s coming the valleys were filled and the mountains and hills humbled, because the Gentile people, humbling themselves through faith, received the gift of grace, which the Jewish people, in their pride, rejected.

This may also be understood of every humble and proud person. Morally, whoever is held by uncleanness, fornication, gluttony, and drunkenness is a “valley.” But the one who persists in pride, boasting, and empty glory is a “mountain and hill.” When people, aided by God’s grace, pass from uncleanness to purity, from fornication to continence, from gluttony to abstinence, [Col. 0881C] and from drunkenness to sobriety, the valleys are filled.

Likewise, if, aided by divine grace, they pass from pride and boasting to humility and from empty glory to contempt for their own flesh, then the mountains and hills are truly humbled. In this way each of us ought to prepare the way for the Lord. For he prepares the Lord’s way who passes from vices to virtue, since the Lord’s ways are faith and justice, while his paths are the other virtues.

The Psalmist desired that these ways be made known to him when he said: “Make your ways known to me, O Lord, and teach me your paths.” He then took care to indicate clearly what these ways are, saying: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.” The other virtues—that is, faith, justice, and the like—are his paths.

The prophet Jeremiah also urges us to seek these ways when he says: “Stand upon the ways, and ask about the ancient paths, which is the good way, and walk in it.”

It follows: “And the crooked things shall become straight.” The crooked things are the hearts of wicked people, distorted by injustice. But they are changed into straight things when the hearts of wicked people are directed according to the rule of justice.

The minds of people disturbed by rage and indignation are rough; they disdain to hear the word of the preacher. But then “the rough places are changed into level ways,” when those minds, stirred to anger, return to the grace of gentleness, and those who previously refused to hear the word of preaching, once converted to blessedness and mildness, listen with delight [Col. 0882A] in tranquility.

“Now John himself had clothing made of camel’s hair.” Up to this point the words appear to be John’s, beginning at the place where he says, “Repent.” From here onward, however, they are the words of the holy evangelist.

Since blessed Matthew had said above that John had come and begun to preach repentance in the wilderness of Judea, in order to show that he had approached the office of preaching not without reason but worthily, he began to praise him for the roughness of his clothing and the simplicity of his food, saying: “John himself had clothing made of camel’s hair.”

His clothing was God and justice; his food was the law of Christ and divine contemplation. And because he was dead to the world, and the world was crucified to him, he could not desire costly garments or seek more luxurious foods.

Yet by this roughness of clothing and simplicity of food blessed John did not condemn temporal goods, nor did he teach that earthly goods were evil, since all things were created by the good God. Rather, through the manner of his clothing and the simplicity of his food he showed that he mourned the sins of the whole human race.

For many of the holy Fathers in former times mourned the sins of the world. Moses was afflicted with excessive grief because of the people’s grave sin, and he loved the people so greatly that he wished to be erased from the Book of Life if the people’s sin were not forgiven. Joshua, his minister and successor, lay prostrate before the Lord from morning until evening because of the people’s sin. Samuel mourned Saul and the people throughout all the days of his life because they had departed from the Lord.

Elijah was afflicted by much fasting and hunger because of the people’s iniquity and sins. Jeremiah, grieving and lamenting, could not refrain from saying: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep day and night for the sins of my people?” Daniel says: “For a period of three weeks, sitting in my house, I did not eat desirable bread, and I did not drink desirable water, mourning the sins of my people.”

As these men did, so also many of the saints mourned the sins of the human race. So did John. If we consider the outward clothing of the human being, we can recognize the merit of the inner person. For the one who wore such clothing outwardly possessed great merit inwardly; and these words demonstrate that John’s life was heavenly, and that his humility and the honor of his chastity were glorious.

The holy evangelist’s words also receive confirmation elsewhere from the Lord, when he says to the crowds concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A man dressed in soft clothing?” The implied answer is, “No.” For what the Lord says here—that John was not dressed in soft clothing—is what blessed Matthew shows when he says that he was clothed in camel’s hair.

By the fact that both the Lord and the evangelist praise John for the roughness of his clothing, they show that John was not a supporter of the wicked but their reprover. He did not cherish the lives of sinners with flattering words, but rebuked them with harsh denunciations, saying: “You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?”

Morally, whoever wishes to follow John’s footsteps ought not to nurture sinners with flattery, but to rebuke them harshly, according to Solomon’s saying: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deeply.” The words of the wise are fittingly compared to goads and nails, because they do not know how to stroke the faults of sinners, but to prick them; they do not know how to indulge them, but to rebuke them.

The leather belt signifies John’s mortification; the wild honey, his sweet preaching. For it was of such great sweetness that Christ himself was thought by human beings to be John. His very reputation is fittingly compared to a locust. A locust, lifted from the earth, quickly falls; so the people’s opinion by which John was thought to be Christ quickly collapsed. The one who had been thought a prophet was soon recognized as Christ, and the one who had been thought Christ was soon recognized as a prophet.

John, whose name is interpreted as “the grace of the Lord,” signifies Christ; and he is appropriately called the grace of God who brought God’s grace to the world.

His clothing signifies the Church of the Gentiles, which is rightly called God’s clothing, according to what the Lord says through the prophet Jeremiah: “As I live, says the Lord, you shall be clothed with all these things as with a garment.” John’s clothing was woven from camel’s hair, and the holy Church was gathered from the Gentiles.

The camel is an unclean animal according to the precept of the Law, and it signifies the Gentiles. The unclean Gentiles are fittingly represented by the camel, which is an unclean animal; Isaiah makes this clear when he says: “The flood of camels shall cover you.”

The leather belt signifies the mortification of the holy Church. Hence the Apostle says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth,” and again: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires.” The Lord also says in the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning.” Those who are about to celebrate Passover are likewise commanded to have “their loins girded.”

Elijah was recognized by this belt, and by this belt—that is, by this sign of mortification—all the faithful are recognized, according to Paul’s saying: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.”

The locusts signify those who, from among the Gentile people, were unstable in mind before they came to the faith. Bending neither this way nor that, they were rebellious and opposed to the Law. Such people, overcome both by John’s preaching and by the apostolic preaching, were converted [Col. 0883D] into God’s food. Hence the Lord says: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me.” The Lord’s food, therefore, is the Father’s will, and the redemption and salvation of the human race.

That the Gentiles are signified by the locusts Solomon shows when he says: “Locusts have no king, nor leader, nor commander, yet each one proceeds in its own bands.” So the Gentiles, when they did not have Christ as king, nor a leader, nor a commander—that is, anyone who gave them a law, or any teacher or prophet—went forth in bands; that is, they ran from unbelief to the grace of Christ under the unity of faith.

The wild honey signifies those among the Gentile people who, before they came to the faith, possessed a gentle way of life, a holy manner of living, and a good reputation. One of these was Cornelius the centurion, of whom it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that he “was a just man and feared God, giving alms to the people every day and entreating God day and night.” Therefore he deserved that an angel be sent to him to say: “Cornelius, your prayers have been heard, and your alms have risen into the sight of God.”

Among these was also the powerful eunuch of Queen Candace. His devotion was so great that he not only went up to Jerusalem every year, but, sitting in his chariot, also read the prophet Isaiah. Therefore he deserved that Philip the deacon be sent to him so that he might baptize him.

When such people were wild honey in the forest of the human race, they were converted to the faith and became domestic honey in the bosom of the holy Church.

“Then Jerusalem went out to him, and all Judea.” The word “then” refers back to the preceding passage where he says: “John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness.”

Yet it must be asked why John baptized, since he could not forgive sins through his baptism. For sins are forgiven us only through the Lord’s baptism. He baptized, therefore, so that he might fulfill in every respect the office of his forerunning, so that he who had become the Lord’s forerunner by being born and by preaching might also become his forerunner by baptizing.

Alternatively, he baptized because his baptism represented the condition of catechumens. Just as children are now catechized so that they may become worthy of approaching the sacrament of baptism, so he baptized those whom he plunged beneath the water, so that afterward, by living more devoutly, they might become worthy to approach Christ’s baptism.

It must also be asked why he baptized in the Jordan. He should be thought to have done this for two reasons: namely, so that he might open there the door of the heavenly kingdom where an entrance had been granted to the children of Israel for entering the promised land; or because the Jordan arises from two springs, namely “Aior” and “Dan,” which rise at the foot of Mount Lebanon.

He therefore baptized in the Jordan to show that all who are reborn through the water of baptism must strive to fulfill the commandments of the two Testaments while confessing their sins. From this also arose the ecclesiastical custom that those who are to be baptized first renounce the devil, his works, the world, and its spectacles. [Col. 0884D]

“Seeing many of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” Pharisees is interpreted as “divided,” while Sadducees means “just” or “justified.” The Pharisees were presbyters—that is, elders—of the Jews; the Sadducees, however, were their heretics. For they denied the Holy Spirit and the angels, and that the soul lives after death; therefore they denied that there was a resurrection. What these men denied, the Pharisees confessed.

Perhaps blessed John saw that these Pharisees and Sadducees were not coming to his baptism with a sincere intention, and for that reason he rebuked them sharply, saying: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” As though he were saying: “If you wish to come to my baptism, come with a sincere intention; and if you wish to hear my counsel, produce fruits worthy of repentance.”

Those who were once called children of Abraham on account of the merit of their faith are now, because of their unbelief, called children of the serpent—that is, of the devil. The devil is rightly called a serpent, because through the serpent he deceived the first-formed human beings. Scripture makes clear that the devil is called a serpent when it says: “I will raise up Leviathan, the crooked serpent, against them.”

It should also be understood that it is customary in the holy Scriptures to impose names according to a person’s imitation of deeds, as in: “Hear, princes of Sodom, and give ear to the law of our God, people of Gomorrah”; and elsewhere: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite.” Were the Jews therefore called this because they were descended from the Sodomites or from the people of Gomorrah? No, but because they imitated their deeds; they imitated their actions.

These Pharisees and Sadducees are likewise fittingly called a brood of vipers because they imitated them. For it is said that both parents of vipers are killed at the moment of conception and at the time of birth. In the same way, these Pharisees and Sadducees are called “a brood of vipers,” because Christ was to be crucified chiefly through their counsel: their father, and the Synagogue, their mother, was extinguished through its evil interpretation. For evil children, imitating the deeds of evil parents, are rightly called “a brood of vipers,” since poisonous children are born, as it were, from poisonous parents.

It follows: “Who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” “Who” means, by implication, God. But if “who showed you” is understood with reference to the future, it means: What teacher, what preacher, will give you counsel so that you may escape the wrath of eternal vengeance?

He calls it “coming” because it is eternal damnation. Hence the Apostle Paul says: “For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved from wrath through him.” And again: “But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s just judgment.”

But we who have sinned and become entangled in the practice of evil habits—how can we escape the wrath of final vengeance? Let holy John tell us what we must do. He says: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance.”

In these words it should be noted that blessed John does not merely urge the production of fruits of repentance, but of worthy fruits of repentance. For it is one thing to produce fruits of repentance and another to produce fruits worthy of repentance. The effort required of one who has committed many offenses should not be the same as that required of one who has committed few, or of one who has committed only some unlawful act.

The person who has committed no offense may rightly be permitted to use lawful things. But the one who has committed an offense must cut away from himself lawful things to the same degree that he remembers having committed unlawful things.

By this judgment the conscience of each one of us is constrained. Each of us ought to acquire greater gains for himself through repentance in proportion to the greater losses he has inflicted upon himself through sin. For the one who, after performing repentance, commits the same or similar sins for which he repented either pretends to be doing penance or does not understand how to repent. [Col. 0886A]

**HOMILY IV. ON THE FOLLOWING PASSAGE OF MATTHEW:** “When Mary, the mother of Jesus, had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to have conceived in the womb from the Holy Spirit.”

The birth of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh, by which the Son of God graciously became human, the evangelist Matthew described in brief but fully truthful speech. For he began by recounting the generations of the fathers from Abraham and brought them down to Christ; and, to show how far the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ differed from the birth of other human beings, he added: “When the mother of Jesus, Mary, had been betrothed to Joseph.” For he showed that the others were begetting and begotten according to the customary union of male and female, but that the Just One was neither begetting nor begotten, but conceived and born of a Virgin through the Holy Spirit.

And because the Son of God was to be born in the flesh, it was fitting that he should be born from none other than one who was a virgin; and because a Virgin was to give birth, it was fitting that she should give birth to none other than one who was the Son of God.

But it should be understood that blessed Matthew does not relate the time, place, or sequence of the conception—all of which blessed Luke demonstrates most clearly when he says: “In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee whose name was Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary.” And because the Virgin was to give birth to the Son of God, it was fitting that she should first be greeted by the angel, then illumined by divine power, and only thereafter receive the Son of God within herself.

It must now be asked why our Lord Jesus Christ wished to be born not from an unmarried virgin but from one who was betrothed. It should be understood that the holy Fathers have handed down many reasonable causes; nevertheless, these are the principal ones.

The first is that through Joseph the lineage of blessed Mary might be revealed, since both belonged to one and the same tribe. The second is that she might not be stoned by the Jews as an adulteress if she had no husband yet had borne a son. The third is that, when she fled into Egypt, she might have the support of a husband by whom she could be sustained—that is, one who would take the Lord to Egypt and bring him back, provide what was necessary for female weakness, serve as a faithful guardian and protector of her perfect virginity, a most trustworthy witness, and the Lord’s most faithful foster-father. The fourth, which the martyr Ignatius added, is that her childbirth might be concealed from the devil: that is, that the devil might not suspect the birth when he saw that the child had been born from a wife. For if he had been born from an unmarried virgin, the devil would easily have recognized him as the Son of God and he would never have been crucified. Hence the Apostle says: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty.”

It follows: “before they came together.” This expression, “to come together,” signifies not sexual intercourse itself but the time of the wedding—that is, when she who had been betrothed begins to be a wife. The meaning is: “before they came together,” that is, before they properly celebrated the solemnities of the wedding. For that he later took her is made clear by the evangelist in what follows, when he says that, warned by the angel, Joseph took her; and because they did not have intercourse, he adds: “and he did not know her.”

Yet “she was found to be with child,” and certainly this was discovered by no one other than Joseph, since, by the right of marriage, he knew almost everything concerning his future wife; and therefore, with an attentive gaze, he detected that her womb was swelling.

“But Joseph her husband, being a righteous man and unwilling to expose her, resolved to dismiss her secretly.” He is rightly called righteous, because he was a guardian of righteousness. He saw that his betrothed had conceived, although he knew that she had been touched by no man; he saw her pregnant, although he truly knew her to be chaste. And because he had read in the prophet: “From the root of Jesse a shoot shall come forth, and a flower shall rise from his root,” and knew that blessed Mary traced her origin from the stock of David, who was the son of Jesse, he had also read: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and shall bear a son.” Therefore he did not disbelieve or doubt that this prophecy was to be fulfilled in her.

And since he was righteous and wished to act justly in everything, he considered it fitting to disclose this to no one, and yet not to take her as his wife, but, changing his intention concerning the wedding, to dismiss her so that she might remain betrothed as she had been. This is what the evangelist means when he says, “and was unwilling to expose her,” that is, to make her public; rather, he wished to dismiss her secretly, that is, to change the time of the wedding. If he had done this, very few would have failed to regard her as a prostitute rather than as a virgin. Therefore Joseph’s plan was suddenly changed by a divine plan, for “while he was considering these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream.”

To righteous Joseph, who was considering and arranging everything justly, a rightly directed messenger was sent, who advised him, for the preservation of the Virgin’s reputation, to take her as his wife. Hence the most blessed Ambrose says:

> The Lord preferred that some should doubt his origin rather than his mother’s modesty; he preferred that some should be ignorant of the manner of his conception rather than defame the chastity of his Mother; that is, he chose that he should be called the son of a carpenter rather than that his mother should be called an adulteress.

But by the fact that the angel appeared to Joseph in a dream, the repose of the mind is signified. And because he was resting from worldly cares, he deserved to enjoy both angelic visitation and speech.

“Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid.” The angel addresses Joseph with the affection of one who soothes him, calling him by his proper name and calling him the son of David. For he was the son of David not only by descent but also by faith and imitation.

“Do not be afraid to take Mary your wife.” He instructed him to take her as his wife in name, not for the exercise of marital relations. “For that which has been born in her is of the Holy Spirit.” And, to reveal the dignity of the birth, he says: “She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus,” that is, the Savior of the whole world and the Author of salvation for all.

He saves not the faithless or unbelieving, but his own people—that is, those who believe in him. He saves not so much from visible enemies as from invisible ones, that is, from sins. He saves not by fighting with weapons, but by forgiving sins.

That he was to be called by such a name he had foretold long before through Isaiah, when he said: “The righteous and saving Lord, there is none besides me.” And that he was to be called by such a name he himself foretold, even before he was born, through the prophet: “From my mother’s womb the Lord called me by my name.”

It follows: “Now all this took place so that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled.” It must be asked here why the holy evangelist said that all this had taken place, when above he had related only the conception.

It should nevertheless be understood that the holy evangelist said that all this had taken place in order to show by this that everything had already taken place beforehand in the foreknowledge of God, before it took place among human beings; or because he was recounting things that had already happened, and therefore everything had taken place. For it was the custom of this holy evangelist to confirm nearly everything he said by examples from the Old Testament, especially for those Jews who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ in such a way that they were afraid to depart from the carnal observance of the Law. Thus he might more easily draw them away from that fear when they already saw and recognized that the things foretold or accomplished in the Old Testament had been fulfilled for the grace of the Gospel.

“Behold, a virgin will have a child in her womb.” That a Virgin would conceive and bear the Son of God is demonstrated by many examples. Solomon says: “Wisdom built herself a house; she hewed out seven pillars.” Wisdom is Christ, of whom the Apostle says: “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God.”

This Wisdom therefore built herself a house: either the mother from whom she took flesh, or the body in the Virgin in which she appeared visibly among human beings. And the Psalmist says: “The mother of Zion will say: ‘A man,’” and so forth. The mother of Zion is blessed Mary the Virgin, and Christ “became man in her,” because the Son of God took flesh from her. “And the Most High himself founded her,” because the Most High himself, who became man, made for himself a mother from whom he would be born according to his humanity.

Hence Isaiah also says: “From the root of Jesse, he says, a shoot shall come forth, and a flower shall rise from his root.” A shoot came forth from the root of Jesse because blessed Mary traced her origin from the stock of David, who was the son of Jesse, as we have said; and she conceived and bore the flower of purity, namely the Lord Jesus Christ, without the stain of sin.

This is that rod of Aaron which blossomed and produced leaves leading to the almond. For just as that rod produced flowers and leaves ending in an almond without any moisture from the earth, so blessed Mary the Virgin conceived without any human seed and bore Christ.

And our Lord Jesus Christ is rightly compared with an almond. For just as an almond consists of a stone, a shell, and a kernel, so our Lord Jesus Christ consists of divinity and humanity—namely, flesh and soul. And because he was born of the Virgin without human seed, he speaks through the Prophet, saying: “But I am a worm and not a man.” For just as a worm is born from wood without any seed, so Christ was born from the Virgin.

Hence also, according to the Seventy Interpreters, the scarab cries out from the wood.

It must also be asked why the holy evangelist says “will have,” while the prophet says “will conceive.” It should be understood that because the prophet was proclaiming something future, he used “will conceive,” for what is not yet possessed is conceived. But the evangelist, because he was narrating a history already past, changed “will conceive” and used “will have,” since what is possessed is no longer being conceived but is held.

As for the statement, “His name will be called Emmanuel,” it should be thought that this name was interpreted in this way by some translator, not by the prophet or the evangelist, so that it would not remain obscure or confused among the Latins. For by this name the two substances of our Lord Jesus Christ—namely, divinity and humanity—are designated in one person. He who was ineffably begotten by God the Father before all ages became Emmanuel at the end of time, that is, “God with us,” from a Virgin mother.

The expression “God with us” may be understood in this way: He became with us—that is, capable of suffering, mortal, hungry, thirsty, weary, and in every respect like us except for the disposition toward sin. Or “Emmanuel” means that God became with us because he united and joined the substance of our weakness, which he assumed, to the substance of his divinity in the unity of his person, when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” Thus, in a wondrous manner, he began to be what we are, yet did not cease to be what he was.

“When Joseph awoke from sleep, he did what the angel of the Lord had commanded him.” Life returned by the same entrance through which death had entered: through a virgin woman and an obedient man. Adam was created from virgin earth; Christ was born from a virgin woman. Through Adam’s disobedience we were all lost; through Joseph’s good obedience we are all restored to our former state.

For by these words the great virtue of obedience is commended to us: “He did as the angel of the Lord commanded him.” Namely, he took Mary after the wedding had been celebrated, and he took her so that she would be called his wife, though they were not to have intercourse, since it follows: “and he did not know her.”

There were also some who said that Joseph took blessed Mary without celebrating the wedding. But Bede rightly says:

> Let the one who has learned this show where it was ever permitted among the Jews for betrothed men and women to come together without the celebration of a wedding; and if he can show this, we shall yield to the soundness of his judgment. Let him only take care not to produce anything that would disgrace the Lord’s mother. Since he cannot show this, let him believe our assertion.

“And he did not know her.” The verb “to know” is sometimes used in the sacred Scriptures for knowledge, as in: “Joseph recognized his brothers, but they were not recognized by him”; and again: “The boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it.”

It is also used for intercourse, as in: “Adam knew his wife again, and she bore him sons and daughters.” Thus it is used in this passage for intercourse: “and he did not know her,” that is, he did not have intercourse with her, “until she bore her firstborn son.”

There were also some heretics who said that Joseph and blessed Mary came together after the Lord’s birth and produced children whom the holy evangelists call the Lord’s brothers. To confirm their error, they took this testimony, saying that the holy evangelist would certainly not have said “until” unless they had come together after the Lord’s birth.

But may God drive this error far from the hearts of the faithful. It should be understood that at that time—that is, before the birth—the holy evangelist was concerned to deny that Joseph had known her, so that no suspicion might arise. After the birth, however, he believed there could be no doubt that they had not come together, and therefore did not take care to deny it.

For if that Mary of the Law, after she had been granted the privilege of enjoying divine speech, is not read to have entered into carnal intercourse; if Noah and Moses likewise, after they had been granted the privilege of enjoying divine speech, are read not to have had intercourse; who of sound faith would dare to say that this Gospel Mary and this Gospel man, Joseph, came together after the Lord’s birth—especially since, while they remained in chastity, the Son of God was born by a singular grace?

Nevertheless, it should be understood that “until” is often taken in an indefinite sense, as in: “Until you grow old, I am he.” Did he cease to be God after that person had grown old? No; rather, the meaning is: “I shall always be, even after you have grown old.”

Again: “I live, says the Lord; this sin of yours shall not be blotted out until you die.” Was their sin blotted out after they died? No; for if it was not blotted out beforehand, it certainly was not afterward.

And the Psalmist says: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.” Did the Son cease to sit at the Father’s right hand after his enemies had been made the footstool of his feet? No; rather, the meaning is: “Your enemies will indeed be subjected beneath your feet, and you will always sit at my right hand.”

And in the Gospel it is written: “Truly I say to you, you will not leave there until you repay the last penny.” The meaning is: “Because you will never repay, you will never leave.”

So also in this passage “until” is taken indefinitely: “and he did not know her until she bore her firstborn son,” that is, he never knew her.

It should further be understood that there were some heretics who said that the Son of God did not assume true flesh from the Virgin but possessed an imaginary body. Therefore the evangelist added “his,” that is, his own and proper son, not an adopted one, not from elsewhere or from nothing, but conceived and born from her substance through the Holy Spirit.

It follows: “firstborn.” There were also heretics who, to confirm the position of their error, seized upon this word, saying that the holy evangelist would certainly not have said “firstborn” unless he had brothers. This is false, for “firstborn” refers not only to one who is followed by brothers but also to the one who is born first, whether or not others follow.

For the commandment of the Law was that “every male who opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord, and all the firstborn shall be offered to God in the temple, and shall remain seven days beneath their mothers’ breasts, but on the eighth day shall be offered to the Lord.”

Were only those firstborn offered who were followed by brothers? No, but all who were born first.

It is likewise written: “God struck the firstborn in the land of Egypt.” Did he strike only those firstborn who were followed by brothers? No, but all who were born first, both among human beings and among animals.

Therefore every only-begotten child may rightly be called firstborn; nevertheless, not every firstborn is called only-begotten.

Accordingly, although the Lord Jesus Christ is only-begotten, he is rightly called firstborn, because he was born first from the Virgin. And he was born without violating the virginity of his mother, who remained a virgin forever. For it is written of her: “This gate shall remain closed, and no man shall pass through it; the Lord alone shall go through it, and it shall remain forever closed.”

And what wonder is it if the only-begotten Son of God is called firstborn because he was born first from the Virgin, when he is also called “the firstborn from the dead”? Hence the statement: “He is the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth.”

He is rightly called the firstborn from the dead because he was the first to rise from the dead and gave us access to rise from death to life.

He is also called “the firstborn among many brothers,” as the Apostle says: “Those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.”

Among which many? Among those of whom the apostle John says: “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God.”

And it should be understood that he is called firstborn not only among those who came after him but also among those who existed before his birth. They could rightly say with John: “After us comes a man who was made before us.” Although he was born after us, he preceded us by the power of his divinity.

He may also be called firstborn according to the very nature of his divinity, as in: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature.” Wisdom is speaking, and Wisdom is Christ, of whom the Apostle says: “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God.”

This Christ, the power and wisdom of God, the Virgin Mother conceived and bore at the end of time, while God the Father ineffably begot him before all ages.

Moreover, he is called firstborn because he was the first to open the womb of holy Mother Church for the begetting of children for God through the water of baptism.

“And he called his name Jesus.” It is clear that this name was well known to the holy Fathers and prophets of God, especially to the one who said: “My soul has failed for your salvation,” that is, “My soul has failed while contemplating your salvation”; and again: “My heart has rejoiced in your salvation”; and also to the one who said: “But I will rejoice in the Lord and exult in my God Jesus.”

Most excellent of all is the statement: “God, save me by your name,” that is, “Glorify in saving me the glory of your name by which you are called Savior, so that your name may be upon me.”

## HOMILY V. ON THE PASSAGE IN MATTHEW: “Jesus said to the crowds of the Jews: Behold, I am sending to you prophets, wise men, and scribes,” and so forth

As for what he says above, “Fill up the measure of your fathers,” this appears to refer to the person of Christ, since he was to be killed by them; or it may refer to the apostles, concerning whom he now says: “Therefore, behold, I am sending to you prophets, wise men, and scribes,” so that you may fill up the measure of your fathers by killing them, and may show yourselves to be sons of murderers, and may be convicted of falsely adorning the tombs of the prophets.

For not only those who foretold the future coming of the Lord’s incarnation are called prophets, but also those who announce the joys of the heavenly kingdom and interpret the Scriptures. Concerning them the Apostle says: “Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge.”

Some think that the prophets of the Old Testament should be placed before the apostles in the order of the catalogue. But it should be understood that the Lord called his apostles prophets, wise men, and scribes.

They were called prophets because they were filled with the prophetic Spirit. They were wise because they had been instructed in heavenly teaching, that is, in the grace of the Gospel. Hence he calls them prophets, that is, persons instructed in wisdom of heart. They were scribes because they brought forth new and old things from their treasures.

“And some of them you will kill,” as Paul and James; “and you will crucify,” as Peter and Andrew; “and you will scourge in your synagogues,” as all the apostles are read to have been scourged. Of them it is said in the Acts of the Apostles that they went away rejoicing because they had been scourged before the council.

“And you will persecute from city to city.” The meaning is: “You will persecute them, I say, and they will be driven from the borders of Judea, so that at the proper time a fitting migration to the Gentiles may take place for the sowing of Christ’s Gospel.”

“So that all the righteous blood that has been shed upon the earth may come upon you, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah.”

Who this Abel was is established not only by this sentence of the Lord but also by the testimony of the book of Genesis, where his offerings are said to have been acceptable to God. For it is written: “The Lord looked upon Abel and upon his offerings.” God is first said to have looked upon Abel, and then upon his offerings; therefore he is shown to have been righteous.

But it must be carefully investigated who this Zechariah was, for we read of many Zechariahs.

The last but one of the Twelve Prophets was called Zechariah. The father of John was also called Zechariah. And that son of the priest Jehoiada was likewise named Zechariah.

But that last-but-one of the Twelve Prophets is nowhere read to have been killed. Although some say that Zechariah, the father of John, was killed between the temple and the altar because he foretold the future coming of Christ, this is not found in the sacred writings. And lest freedom to err be granted through the confusion of different persons, the Lord expressly added: “whom you killed between the temple and the altar.”

Accordingly, Zechariah may appropriately be understood as the son of Jehoiada the priest, whom Joash, king of Judah, killed between the temple and the altar.

But it must be asked how the Lord here calls him the son of Barachiah, when, as we read in the Book of Kings, he was the son of Jehoiada the priest. For it is written: “Joash did not remember the kindness that Jehoiada his father had shown him.”

This question is resolved in the following way: either he certainly had two names, according to the custom of his people, or the matter is resolved through the interpretation of the names. For Barachiah means “blessed of the Lord,” while Joiada means “the righteousness of God.” Therefore it makes no difference whether he is said to have been the son of Barachiah, that is, of the blessed one of the Lord, or of Joiada, that is, of the righteous one of the Lord, since the meaning is one and the same.

Accordingly, because of his greatness and in his praise, the Lord called him the son of Barachiah, that is, “of the blessed one of the Lord.”

Again, it must be asked how the Lord says that all the blood of the righteous is to be required from the generation of the Jews, from righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, when the Jews themselves killed neither of them—neither Abel nor Zechariah.

Will one generation discharge the deserts of all generations, including those that follow? It is not just that one person should be punished for another’s sins.

It should therefore be understood that it is customary for the sacred Scriptures to speak of two generations: one good and the other evil, one of the righteous and the other of the impious.

Christ is the head of all the elect, and all the elect are his members; accordingly, all the elect from Abel to the end of the world will constitute, as it were, one generation.

The devil, however, is the head of all the wicked, and all the wicked are his members. Therefore all the impious, from Cain to the end of the world, will constitute one generation.

Of the good generation it is written: “The generation of the upright shall be blessed,” and again: “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord.”

Of the evil generation he says: “An evil and perverse generation, this you repaid to the Lord,” and again: “A generation whose eyes are lofty and whose eyelids are lifted high.”

These are the two cities: one belonging to Christ and the other to the devil—that is, one is Jerusalem, the vision of peace, and the other Babylon, the city of confusion.

Therefore it is beautifully said that all the blood of the righteous that has been shed, from righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, will be required from the generation of the wicked.

Again, it must be asked how he says that all the blood of the righteous is to be required from Abel alone up to Zechariah son of Barachiah. Why from Abel is not difficult to understand; but it is very difficult to understand why up to the blood of Zechariah, since the blood of many holy and innocent people was shed afterward, including that of Christ himself and of the apostles, as well as that of countless martyrs, and will continue to be shed until the end of the world.

The matter is resolved as follows. Abel was a shepherd of sheep and was killed in the field; Zechariah was a priest and was killed in the court of the Lord’s temple. The Lord therefore mentioned these two because all holy martyrs are represented through them: those of the lay order and those of the priestly order.

Moreover, Zechariah means “the memory of the Lord.” Thus through him all the elect are beautifully represented, including the one who will be born at the end of the world and who will be mindful of the Lord.

It follows: “Truly I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation,” that is, the retribution and vengeance for the righteous whose blood was shed upon the earth. It will be required not only of the Jews but also of all the wicked, so that those who were equal in the guilt of impiety may be equal in enduring the punishments of just judgment.

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you.” By “Jerusalem” the Lord calls not the stones or buildings but the inhabitants of that city. He mourns over it with a father’s affection. Hence, as another evangelist reports, Jesus, “seeing the city, wept over it, saying: ‘If you too had known.’”

For the Lord foresaw the wound and ruin that were to come upon that faithless city—not only the temporal destruction that was to come from the Romans, but also that which it was to undergo in eternal damnation.
