Therefore, lamenting and grieving over it with fatherly affection, he addresses it and says: “Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to you,” and he adds: “How often I wanted to gather your children.”

By this he shows that all the prophets of earlier times had been sent by him. Thus the heretics are refuted who said that the Lord began to exist from the Virgin, and that the God of the Old Testament was one and the God of the New Testament another, since it was the same Lord who sent the prophets before the Virgin.

He adds: “As a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings.” He appropriately adopts this comparison, for this animal has great affection for its young. Other birds, even if they have young, cannot easily be recognized as mothers unless perhaps they are seen sitting in their nests.

A hen, however, even if the chicks do not follow her and one does not see her young, can easily be recognized as a mother. She lowers her wings, becomes rough with ruffled feathers, grows hoarse in voice, and appears weakened and abject in all her limbs. Because she is affected by the weakness of her young, she herself becomes weak. Moreover, she protects her young with her wings and enters into battle against the kite.

Therefore the Wisdom of God the Father, who is the mother of us all—namely, the Lord Jesus Christ—likened himself to a hen because of the weakness of the flesh he assumed. Hence the Apostle says: “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings.” He wished to become weak in order to protect us by his power, so that the devil might not snatch away those whom he defends. For what the hen does by the natural affection of her kind, entering into battle against the kite, the Lord does by his own power against the devil.

And to show the affection he had for the salvation of the human race, and especially of that Jewish people to whom he was speaking, the Lord likened himself to a hen.

But it must be asked what the Lord’s statement means: “How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks, and you were unwilling.” For the words seem to sound as though God’s will had been overcome by the will of wicked people, and as though the Almighty, hindered by the unwillingness of the weakest, had been unable to do what he wished.

Where, then, is that omnipotence of which it is written: “All that he willed, he did”? It does not say that he did some of the things he willed, but all of them.

It must therefore be understood in this way: “How often I wanted to gather your children, and you were unwilling”—that is, while you were unwilling, I gathered from your children those whom I wished.

It follows: “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate.” It should be noted that he does not say “my house” but “your house,” and therefore it is desolate, as if he were saying: “You are not worthy of my protection.” Hence the voices of the angels resounded, saying: “Let us pass away from these dwelling places.”

This too had long before been foretold by the prophet Jeremiah, who said: “I have forsaken my house; I have abandoned my inheritance.”

Jerusalem, which according to another Gospel the Lord calls a nest, he here calls a house. Deprived of divine aid on account of its own desert, it has been abandoned to its own power, because it not only disdained being protected by the wings of that most powerful bird whom he calls a hen, but that bird himself—that is, Christ—was handed over to two foxes, namely Herod and Pilate.

Therefore the Romans, like people who envied an empty house and nest, plundered everything: the place, the nation, and the kingdom.

“For I say to you, you will not see me from now on.” The Lord continued to speak to Jerusalem and to the Jewish people, as if he were saying: “Unless you repent and confess that I am the one of whom the prophets sang, the Son of the Almighty God, you will not see me”—that is, you will not possess knowledge of me.

Some understand this concerning the Lord’s second coming, when he will come in glory. The meaning would then be: “You will not see me from now on,” namely, “you will not see me coming in glory.” For even now the Jews have been granted a time for repentance.

Let them therefore confess that Christ is the Son of God and say: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” and they will see his face—that is, they will be able to possess knowledge of him—who lives and reigns, and so forth.

## HOMILY VI. ON THE PASSAGE IN MATTHEW: “When Herod had died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying: Arise, take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel.”

First of all, it must be asked why Matthew says that Herod had died, when Luke says that John began to preach under Herod. This question is resolved by the fact that two men bore the same name: for there were two Herods, namely father and son. When Joseph was in Egypt, Herod the father was reigning; but when he returned, Archelaus, his son, held the kingdom. When John began to preach, Herod the son was governing Galilee; hence Matthew calls the former a king, while Luke calls the latter a tetrarch.

It must likewise be asked why Matthew says that Joseph, out of fear of Archelaus, withdrew into Galilee, when Luke says that Herod governed Galilee—and why he ought to have feared Archelaus more than Herod, since they were brothers and sons of the same father. This question is resolved by the change of times: Archelaus ruled Judaea at one time, and Herod governed Galilee at another. For when Herod returned from Egypt, Archelaus was ruling over Judaea, while Herod did not yet govern Galilee; consequently, the Lord’s parents could safely live in Galilee.

It may also be asked why Matthew says that Joseph, out of fear of Archelaus, withdrew into Galilee and settled in Nazareth, whereas Luke seems to say that, because of his native city, he went down into Galilee and lived in Nazareth. The matter is resolved as follows: when Joseph was warned by the angel in Egypt to return to the land of Israel, he understood “the land of Israel” to mean the land of Judaea. But after he had returned, he heard that Archelaus was reigning there. He then understood that the land of Israel meant not Judaea alone, but Galilee as well, because Israelites inhabited it. [Col. 0896B]

Was this brought about by an error on the part of the angel? No, but by Joseph’s. For when the angel warned him to return to the land of Israel, he did not specify to which place he should turn. Perhaps Joseph believed that a child of such authority ought to be brought up nowhere except in the distinguished city where the king, the chief priests, and the teachers of the Law were present, and therefore wished to go up to Jerusalem; but after he heard that Archelaus was reigning there, he began to be distressed, and for that reason the angel warned him a second time to return to Galilee.

It must likewise be asked why Luke says that the Lord’s parents went up to Jerusalem every year, when Matthew says that Joseph, out of fear of Archelaus, withdrew into Galilee. How, then, did they go up every year if, because of their fear of Archelaus, they did not dare to live there? The matter may nevertheless be resolved in this way: perhaps Archelaus reigned only for a short time, and therefore the Lord’s parents were able to go up safely to Jerusalem every year. For, as the historian Josephus relates, after scarcely ten years of possessing the kingdom, Archelaus was accused by the Jews before Caesar on account of his excessive insolence and ferocity of spirit, and was banished into exile at the city of Vienna.

But perhaps someone will say that Archelaus reigned for a long time. To this one should reply as follows: people often visit places for a time in which they do not dare to live permanently. Our Savior’s parents feared Archelaus in such a way that they would not be contemptuous of the Law; therefore they were able to go up to Jerusalem every year, although they did not always dare to live there. Alternatively, they could go up amid the very large crowds of people, so that they would not be recognized. [Col. 0896D]

It may also be asked why the evangelist Luke says that the Lord was presented in the Temple on the fortieth day and that offerings were made for him, whereas Matthew says that Herod was troubled when the magi came and announced that the King of the Jews had been born. If Herod was troubled because of what the magi reported, how did Jesus’ parents dare to go up to the Temple?

Anyone who has even a little experience of human affairs knows that the hearts of kings are preoccupied by various cares and anxieties, especially the hearts of those who are subject to another’s authority. For who can know how much this man had heard either from Caesar’s side, or from the side of his enemies, or because of some greater concern that had preoccupied him? Thus, for a time, he consigned the magi to oblivion, and the Lord’s parents were able to go up to the Temple safely. Or perhaps Herod believed that the magi had not found the child and, consequently, would have been ashamed to return to him; for that reason he did not trouble himself to seek the child.

But after word reached his ears that the child had been brought to the Temple, that offerings had been made for him, and that Simeon and Anna had prophesied many things about him, he realized that he had been deceived by the magi and became exceedingly angry.

In the fact that the Lord fled, he left us an example of fleeing. It would have seemed blameworthy among his saints if they fled while he himself had not first fled; for what he first demonstrated by example, he later taught by his words, when he said: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another.”

By the fact that the little children were killed while the child Jesus, whom they sought, escaped alive, it was signified that the bodies of the holy martyrs could be killed, but that the faith which was in them could in no way be extinguished. They could truly say with Paul: “Whether we live, we live for the Lord; whether we die, we die for the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s.”

By the fact that Joseph fled into Egypt because of Herod’s persecution and, after Herod’s death, returned to the land of Israel, it was signified that many of the saints would be driven from their own homes, and some would even be sent into exile; but when their persecutors had been destroyed and peace had once again been restored to the Church, they would return to their own places.

That the child Jesus would be sought by Herod and not found had already been foretold. Solomon predicted this in the person of the Church when he said: “Who will give you to me as my brother, nursing at the breasts of his mother?” By these words he showed the impossibility of finding Christ. The Psalmist says: “From the womb, from my mother’s belly, you have been my protector.” And the Lord says through Solomon: “They will seek me and will not find me”—with “the wicked” understood. Moses also foretold this very thing in mystical words when he said: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk.” By these words he showed that Christ would be crucified not in infancy or childhood, but in mature age.

Sinners are understood by the kid; and therefore the Lord is called a kid, either because he assumed the likeness of sinful flesh, or because he offered himself to God as a sacrifice for us upon the altar of the cross.

“Those who sought the child’s life have died.” It must be asked why he says “have died” in the plural, when above he narrated that only Herod had sought the child’s life. This question may nevertheless be resolved in two ways: either the holy evangelist spoke by a figure of speech in which many are mentioned for one, or it is meant that not only Herod but also many Jews consented to the Savior’s death.

But if there were many of them, it must be asked how they were destroyed within so short a time. The ecclesiastical history relates how they were destroyed. It says that Herod was tormented by various sufferings because of the slaughter of the children: he was continually afflicted by fever, severe pain in the intestines, and swelling of the feet; among other things, his private parts began to swarm with worms. While he still had hope of living, he was taken to Jericho. After receiving the advice of physicians, he used hot baths and entered hot oil. All his limbs were so weakened that even his eyes seemed likely to be forced from their sockets. He had such an enormous appetite for food that nearly all his cooks could scarcely prepare as much as he himself could eat.

When he had already been given up as hopeless with regard to the health of his body, he ordered all the nobles and leading men from the villages, fortresses, and cities of the whole of Judaea to be gathered before him. He commanded that they be shut up in the place called the hippodrome. When he saw that the day of his death was approaching, he summoned his sister Salome and her husband Alexander and said to them:

“I know that the Jews will rejoice at my death, but I can have many mourners and a noble funeral if you are willing to obey my commands. When you hear that I am dead, prepare soldiers and kill all those whom I have confined in custody, so that the whole household—and the whole of Judaea, even against its will—may mourn my death.”

He also had the custom of peeling an apple for himself and eating it after every meal. One day, after he had done this, he looked around in every direction to see whether anyone was there who might restrain him. When he saw no one, he brandished a knife, struck his own chest, and fell dead.

After this had happened, all those who were being held in custody were killed. Thus it came about that all those who had sought the child’s life were suddenly destroyed. [Col. 0898C]

In the fact that the holy evangelist says “the child’s life,” the heretics are refuted who claimed that Christ had not assumed a soul, but had divinity in place of a soul. But since the whole human being had perished, the Son of God assumed the whole in order to redeem both parts, namely soul and flesh. That he possessed a true soul, he himself makes clear when he says: “I have authority to lay down my soul, and I have authority to take it up again.” And again: “No one takes my soul from me.” And again: “My soul is sorrowful unto death.” The evangelist says: “Bowing his head, Jesus gave up his spirit.”

It follows: “When he had risen, he took the child.” By the fact that Joseph returned to the land of Israel after Herod had died, it was signified that, when the envy in the hearts of the Jews has been destroyed at the end of the age, the Lord will visit Judaea through his preachers, with Elijah and Enoch preaching.

It follows: “But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning in Judaea.” Archelaus is interpreted as “recognizing lion,” and signifies that lion of whom Peter says: “Be vigilant and watchful, because your adversary, like a roaring lion, prowls about.”

By that part of the people in which Joseph did not dare to live are designated those who, near the end of the age, will receive Antichrist; in them Archelaus—that is, the devil—will dwell. By that part in which Joseph lived securely are designated those who, near the end of the age, when Elijah and Enoch are preaching, will receive Christ; in them Joseph—the order of preachers—will dwell securely. Hence Galilee is appropriately interpreted as “migration” or “revelation brought about.”

Nazareth is called “flower” or “pure.” For the more the holy Church passes from visible things to invisible, and from earthly things to heavenly, the more it abounds in the flowers of virtues.

It follows: “So that what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled.” Blessed Jerome says that if the evangelist had set down a fixed testimony from the Scriptures, he would not have said here “through the prophets” in the plural, but “through the prophet” in the singular. Since he did not find a fixed testimony, he therefore said “through the prophets.” For all the prophets foretold that Christ, the Nazarene—that is, the holy, righteous, and pure one—would come.

Something similar to this is found in the words of the prophet Isaiah according to the Hebrew truth. For he says: “A branch will go out from the root of Jesse, and a Nazirite will rise from his root.” [Col. 0899B]

Jesus was called “the Nazarene” from the place—that is, from the small city in which he was conceived and brought up. He is also called “the Nazirite” on account of his office. For all those who made vows to the Lord, kept themselves chaste, and over whose heads no razor passed until the appointed time were called Nazirites.

He was beautifully called a Nazirite because it is written of him: “He vowed a vow to the God of Jacob.” He vowed a vow to God the Father that he would come and redeem the human race; he came and redeemed it.

He also says of himself: “My head is full of dew, and my locks with drops of the night.” By the very appearance of his head he shows himself to be a true Nazirite.

It should also be known that all those Nazirites in the Old Testament bore the figure of this true Nazirite, who is the Nazirite of Nazirites—that is, the Holy of holies. Above all, that exceptionally strong man Samson bore his figure in nearly all his deeds.

For just as Samson had seven locks, so Christ had the sevenfold Spirit. And just as Samson killed the lion, drew honey from its mouth, and ate it, so Christ killed the devil and snatched the holy Church from his mouth, whose sweetness delights the good.

And just as Samson, shut inside Gaza, rose at midnight, carried away the gates of the city, and climbed to the summit of the mountain, so the Lord, shut within the tomb, destroyed the dominion of death, rose on the third day, and ascended into heaven.

And just as Samson killed more people in his death than while alive, so Christ killed more after his Passion than before it—that is, he caused more people to be converted to the faith, so that they began to be what they had not been and ceased to be what they had been.

## HOMILY VII. ON THE PASSAGE IN MATTHEW: “When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judaea, in the days of King Herod, behold, magi came from the East to Jerusalem,” etc.

Sacred Scripture customarily places three things at the beginning of an account: the person, the place, and the time. In accordance with this usage and custom, the holy evangelist placed these three things at the beginning of this Gospel reading.

He indicated the person when he said: “When Jesus had been born”; the place when he said: “in Bethlehem of Judaea”; and he showed the time when he added: [Col. 0900A] “in the days of King Herod.” These three things are included for the confirmation of the event being narrated.

Bethlehem was formerly called Ephrathah. But after the patriarch Jacob had pastured his flocks there, seeing through the Holy Spirit that the Lord would be born there, he changed its name and called it Bethlehem, that is, “house of bread.” It was appropriately called “house of bread,” because there he was to be born who said of himself: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.”

Blessed Jerome says that one should read “of Judah,” not “of Judaea,” since there is no other Bethlehem belonging to another nation for the distinction of which the holy evangelist would have said “of Judaea.” Nevertheless, there is another Bethlehem in Galilee; to distinguish it from that one, he said “of Judah,” showing that the Lord was born in that Bethlehem which is in the tribe of Judah.

“In the days of Herod.” The holy evangelist Matthew mentioned this foreign king, namely Herod, in order to show that Jacob’s prophecy had been fulfilled, in which it is said: “The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah.”

This Herod was a foreigner, with an Idumaean father and a Philistine mother. Hyrcanus, who was the last prince of the Jews, raised him. Since Hyrcanus frequently sent him to Rome to Caesar, Herod, after taking counsel with Caesar and his advisers, cunningly killed Hyrcanus and assumed the kingdom.

Christ was therefore born in the thirty-first year of Herod’s reign. But perhaps someone will ask how it can be said, “until he comes,” when he did not come immediately after the scepter was removed. It should be understood that when “until” is used on several occasions, an interval is implied. There is therefore no contradiction, because the one who was to be sent was already on the point of coming.

Thus, in order that the prophecy might be fulfilled, it was divinely arranged that Hyrcanus should die and that Herod, a foreigner, should succeed him.

It follows: “Behold, magi came from the East.” We must now ask who these magi were and from where they came. It should be understood that the doctors hold differing opinions about the magi.

Some say that they were Chaldaeans, for the Chaldaeans worshiped a star as a god; therefore, they say, their titular god showed them that the true God had been born.

Others say that they were Persians, on account of this verse by Metrocarius:

> “Then he commands the Persians also to hasten their steps.”

Some say that they were from the remotest ends of the earth. But it must be asked: if they were Chaldaeans, Persians, or people from the ends of the earth, how could they have reached Jerusalem in so short a [Col. 0900D] time, when many seas, many mountains, and many regions lie between? It should be understood, however, that those who say this usually object that a child was then born such as had never been born before and would never be born afterward; and for that reason he could easily have brought them to himself in so short a time, even from the ends of the earth. For we read of a short journey being lengthened and a long journey shortened.

A short journey is from Egypt to the Promised Land—namely, forty days—yet it was lengthened to forty years. A long journey is from Judaea to Babylon, but it was shortened; for we read that the prophet Habakkuk was carried by an angel from Judaea to that place in the space of one hour.

Others say that they were descendants of Balaam, which [Col. 0901A] is more credible. Balaam prophesied many things about Christ, and among other things said: “A star shall arise out of Jacob.” When they, possessing this prophecy, immediately saw a new star, they understood that a king had been born, and they came. And because their region is not far from the Promised Land of the children of Israel, they were able to come to Jerusalem in so short a time. For we read that, after the children of Israel came to the borders of the Ammonites, they entered the Promised Land not long afterward.

But if they were descendants of Balaam, it must be asked why the holy evangelist says that they came from the East. It should be understood that anyone who comes from that region which lies in the eastern part may properly be said to come from the East. For this reason it is more credible [Col. 0901B] that they were descendants of Balaam, since the region of the Ammonites was near the land of the Jews.

Spiritually, it is fitting that these Magi are said to have come from the East, because all who come to God come from him and through him. For he himself is the East, as in the words: “Behold, the man whose name is the East”; and: “For you who fear God the Sun of justice shall rise.” Therefore no one can reach this East unless he comes from the East, because, as he himself says: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him”; and again: “No one comes to the Father except through me.”

It follows: “They came to Jerusalem.” The Hebrews relate that this city was first founded in Assyria after the flood by Shem, the firstborn of Noah, who was also called Salem by another name; he called it Salem after his own name. [Col. 0901C] He is also Melchizedek. Later the Jebusites lived there and, after themselves, called it Jebus. Thus, when the names Jebus and Salem were joined, and the *b* was changed into *r*, it was called Jerusalem.

Afterward Solomon built in it the most famous temple and adorned it with many ornaments, and after his name it was called Hierosolyma, as though “the city of Solomon.” After this it was destroyed by the Chaldaeans and rebuilt by Ezra the priest and Zerubbabel. Then it was destroyed by Vespasian and Titus, rulers of the Romans, and rebuilt by the emperor Hadrian, who was also called Aelius; for this reason it was called Aelia. Hence, in the Canons as well, we read of the bishops of the city of Aelia.

Moreover, it must be asked why the Magi came to Jerusalem when the Lord [Col. 0901D] was not born there. It is clear that this happened for many reasons. They recognized the time of his birth but did not know the place. Jerusalem was the royal city and the metropolis of that province. The king and the chief priests were there; the scribes and Pharisees were there; the ark of the Lord and the most famous temple were there. Therefore they came to Jerusalem because they believed that such a child ought to have been born nowhere other than in a distinguished city.

Or they came so that they might learn the place of his birth more quickly; or so that what is written might be fulfilled: “From Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.” The word of the Lord went forth from Jerusalem because it was there that Christ’s birth was first announced.

Or they came so that the Jews might not remain without excuse. [Col. 0902A] They could have said: “We knew the place of his birth, but we did not know the time, and therefore we do not believe.” Or they came so that the diligence of the Magi might condemn the Jews’ sluggishness: the Magi believed one person, while the Jews refused to believe many; the Magi came from far away, while the Jews remained nearby; the Magi sought what belonged to another, while the Jews abandoned what was their own. Hence they are aptly compared to milestones, because they showed the way but themselves remained behind.

In the evangelist’s statement that they came from the East, it is mystically signified that no one comes to the East except from the East—that is, no one comes to the Lord except from him and through him.

It follows: “Where is he who has been born?” They fittingly say, “Where is he who has been born?” because it is written: “A child has been born for us.” When they say, “King of the Jews,” [Col. 0902B] this is understood as “King of those who confess,” that is, of the saints, because *Judas* is interpreted as “confessor.”

And as though someone had asked them, “How do you know that the King of the Jews has been born?” they answered: “We saw his star in the East.” The opinion about the star is groundless, as is that about the Magi. Some say that it was the Holy Spirit, so that he who afterward descended upon the baptized Lord in the form of a dove had now also appeared to the Magi in the form of a star. Others say that it was an angel, so that he who appeared to the shepherds also appeared to the Magi. Others say that it was a new star, which is more credible, because a child had then been born such as had never been born before and would never be born afterward; therefore a star ought to have appeared such as had never appeared before and would never appear afterward.

It should also be observed that they do not say “our star” or “the star of heaven,” but “his”—[Col. 0902C] that is, a new star.

But it may be asked why, when the Lord was born, an angel appeared to the Jews, namely, to the shepherds, while to the Gentile Magi not an angel but a star appeared. It was fitting that to the Jews, who used reason, a rational creature—that is, an angel—should appear and proclaim the Lord’s birth. To the Gentile Magi, however, as though they were irrational, an irrational creature—that is, a star—ought to appear, announcing that God had appeared in the flesh.

It should further be understood that the mathematicians believed each person to be born under fate, and they took as support for their error the fact that, when the Lord was born, a new star appeared. But far be it from the hearts of the faithful to say that there is any fate. For when not the child ran toward the star, but the star toward the child, it is plainly demonstrated that the star was not the child’s fate. Rather, if one may speak in this way, the child who appeared was the star’s [Col. 0902D] fate: the star did not rule over him by command, but served him in obedience.

What is said—“in the East”—may be understood in two ways: either, “We were positioned in the eastern region, saw the star above Judaea, and understood that a king had been born there”; or, “We were positioned in whatever region is ours, saw the star in the eastern part of the sky, and understood that a king had been born in Judaea.”

It follows: “We have come to adore him.” In these words the Magi confessed a true man, a true king, and a true God. They confessed a true man when they said, “Where is he who has been born?”; a true king when they said, “King of the Jews”; and a true God when they added, “We have come to adore him,” because the Law commanded that no one be adored except God.

Herod [Col. 0903A] is interpreted as “leather-worker,” or “skin of glory,” and signifies the devil. He is rightly called a leather-worker because he stripped the first-formed human beings of the robe of immortality and made them put on leather tunics. And because he gloried in having conquered them, he received the name “skin of glory” from that victory.

Therefore, while Herod was reigning—that is, while the devil was reigning in the world—Christ was born in Bethlehem, which is interpreted as “house of bread” and signifies the holy Church, in which the knowledge of Christ is found every day.

Morally, Bethlehem signifies each faithful soul, which is the house of the bread—that is, of God—according to what is written: “The soul of the just is the seat [Col. 0903B] of wisdom.” Christ is the wisdom of God the Father. Therefore, if the soul of the just is the seat of wisdom, it is the seat of Christ and the dwelling place of God, according to what Paul says: “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are.”

For if someone passes from vices to virtues and from unbelief to faith, Christ is born in Bethlehem: that is, Christ is formed every day in the faithful soul; he is born every day through good thoughts and actions, and every day he is stoned and extinguished through evil thoughts and actions. For as many evil thoughts as a person receives within himself, so many stones, as it were, does he cast at Jesus. And if he carries those evil thoughts through to deliberation or effect, then he extinguishes Christ within himself—that is, the grace of Christ.

The apostle Paul, speaking plainly to the Galatians, says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.” He had previously brought [Col. 0903C] them to birth through preaching and had formed Christ in their hearts through faith. But Christ had been extinguished in them through the preaching of the false apostles; and therefore the excellent preacher labored to bring them to birth again and to form Christ in their hearts.

Jerusalem is also interpreted as “vision of peace” and signifies the primitive Church. The Magi signify the firstfruits of the Gentiles. For just as the Magi learned the place of the Lord’s birth from the Jews, so the firstfruits of the Gentiles learned the faith from the primitive Church—that is, from the apostles.

It follows: “But when King Herod heard this, he was troubled.” Blessed Gregory says: “When the King of heaven was born, the king of earth was troubled, because earthly height is confounded when heavenly exaltation is revealed.” For human power [Col. 0903D] and earthly pride are suppressed all the more as the power of true dignity is recognized and understood.

Why was Herod troubled? For two reasons. He was troubled because he feared being deprived of his earthly kingdom; or he was troubled—that is, angered and indignant—because someone had dared to be called king without Caesar’s command.

It may be asked why he says that all Jerusalem was troubled. Were Simeon and Anna, or the other faithful who were there, troubled? No. This question is resolved through synecdoche, a figure of grammatical usage in which the whole is understood from a part or the part from the whole. Since the greater part was troubled, the evangelist therefore said that the whole city was troubled. Or he says that all Jerusalem was troubled because the disturbance of the king is ordinarily the disturbance of the whole people; in accordance with this usage he said that all Jerusalem was troubled. Some were genuinely troubled, while others were troubled only outwardly.

It follows: [Col. 0904A] “And gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where Christ was to be born.” These words show that Herod was a foreigner. For if he had been a Jew, he would have known the prophecy and would not have been ignorant of the place of the birth.

The scribes were called so not merely from the office of writing, but rather from their interpretation of the Scriptures; for they were teachers of the Law.

It should further be observed that he did not say, “Where has Christ been born?” but “Where would he be born?” For he questioned them craftily, so that he might discover whether they rejoiced at the birth of their king or not. They, however, pointed out the place and confirmed it by the testimony [Col. 0904B] of the prophet, saying: “For thus it is written: And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah.”

Here the Jews are reproved for their ignorance, because the prophet said: “You, Bethlehem Ephrata,” whereas they said only, “You, Bethlehem, land of Judah,” omitting “Ephrata.”

As for the statement, “You are by no means least among the rulers of Judah,” its meaning is this: although you may appear small among the cities that hold the chief rank, you are nevertheless not the least, “because from you shall go forth a ruler who will govern my people Israel.”

This ruler may [Col. 0904C] be understood as David or as Christ. If David is understood, he indeed ruled the Israelite people nobly, with the Lord’s command and assistance, although only temporally. But because the prophet was proclaiming future things, this ruler is more properly understood as Christ, because together with the Father and the Holy Spirit he rules and governs eternally his faithful people who believe in him and leads them into the vision of the everlasting homeland.

It follows: “Then Herod, secretly calling the Magi.” The word “then” refers back to what preceded, that is, to the time after he had learned the place of the birth from the scribes and Pharisees.

At this point the historical account is incomplete, because the holy evangelist does not state how much time had passed from the appearance of the star until the Magi came. Consequently, there are various opinions about their arrival. Some say that they came on the thirteenth day after Christ’s birth; others on the thirteenth day after one year; and still others say that they came after two years, and that the child was born not in Bethlehem but in Egypt.

It is more credible, however, that these were the descendants of Balaam, as we said above; that they came to him on the thirteenth day; and that they found him not in Egypt but [Col. 0904D] in Bethlehem: “He learned carefully from them the time of the star.”

Why “carefully”? Because Herod was crafty. He feared that they might not return to him, and therefore he carefully learned the time of the star, so that, if they did not return, he would know what to do—that is, kill all the boys who were in Bethlehem and throughout its territory.

“And sending them to Bethlehem, he said: Go and inquire carefully about the child; and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and adore him.”

Herod craftily said that he was seeking the Lord and pretending that he wished to adore him; [Col. 0905A] for this reason he never deserved to find him. Herod here signifies hypocrites, who, because they seek the Lord deceitfully, never deserve to find him.

Of such people it is written: “No hypocrite shall appear in the sight of God.” And again: “Let the impious be taken away, lest he see the majesty of the Lord.” Job also said: “The crafty and the hypocritical provoke God’s anger.”

It should be understood that those who provoke God’s anger are worse than those who deserve it. Those deserve it who do openly evil; but those provoke it who practice evil under the appearance of holiness.

“When they had heard the king, they departed.” They heard Herod in order to seek the Lord, but they did not hear him in order to return to him.

Herod here signifies evil preachers, who preach good things but practice evil. The Magi signify good hearers, who do the good things they hear from evil preachers but do not imitate their conduct. Of such people it is written: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat; [Col. 0905B] therefore, whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not act according to their works, for they say and do not do.”

It follows: “And behold, the star that they had seen in the East went before them until it came and stood above where the child was.”

It should be understood that the Magi lost the star as soon as they entered to Herod, but when they came out they deserved to find the star again. Herod here signifies the devil, while the star signifies the grace of God. Therefore, whoever enters to Herod—that is, to the devil—and submits to him through some sin immediately loses the star, that is, the grace of God. But if someone, helped by divine grace, departs from Herod—that is, from the devil—through repentance, he immediately finds the star again, namely, the grace of God.

The holy evangelist fittingly says, “until it came and stood above where the child [Col. 0905C] was,” because the star did not abandon the Magi until it had led them to the child’s house. This signifies that the grace of God does not abandon those whom it once receives, until it leads them to the child’s house—that is, to the holy Church—in order to unite them to its unity.

“When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy.” It should be understood that it was not enough for the evangelist to say, “They rejoiced.” He added “with joy”; and not merely “with joy,” but “with great joy.” And as though even that were insufficient, he added “exceedingly.”

What else did the holy evangelist wish to demonstrate through this accumulation of words, [Col. 0905D] except that people have greater joy over things that were lost and then found again than over things always possessed?

For example, a person possesses the good of chastity, but, deceived by the devil’s fraud, falls into fornication and becomes so entangled in that sin that he despairs of ever being able to preserve chastity again. But if, helped by the grace of God, he rises through repentance and begins to preserve the good of chastity, he will have greater joy than if he had always been chaste.

Again, a person possesses the spirit of prophecy, but, deceived by the devil’s fraud, loses that same spirit. If, however, helped by the grace of God, he rises through repentance and receives that same spirit again, he will have greater joy than if he had always possessed it.

For this reason David [Col. 0906A] ardently prayed, saying: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation.” He calls “the joy of salvation” the spirit of prophecy, by which he had seen that Christ would be born from his offspring. He had possessed the spirit of prophecy, but, deceived by the devil’s fraud, fell into adultery and lost that same spirit of prophecy. But after he rose through repentance and received the same spirit again, he had greater joy than if he had always possessed it.

It follows: “And entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother.” The child is rightly placed before the mother, because he existed as a child before she was a mother.

“And opening their treasures.” It was the tradition of the ancients that no one should enter before the Lord or before a king empty-handed. Since these men regarded him as the true king and the true Lord, they did not come empty-handed.

The works of God are wondrous and astonishing. [Col. 0906B] Behold, an angel addresses Zechariah and announces that Elizabeth will give birth, yet the priest, not believing, becomes mute. An angel addresses the shepherds; a star brings the Magi from distant regions to the Lord. The Magi see a little child and believe him to be great; they see a man and adore God. He was placed in a manger whom the world could not contain; he was carried in hands who sustains the whole world.

And why is this so? Because he was the one of whom it is written: “A child has been born for us, a son has been given to us, and dominion has been made upon his shoulder.” His dominion was made upon his shoulder because he carried upon his shoulders the cross by which he redeemed the Church, in which he now rules through grace.

It should be understood that these Magi were three kings, and that the Psalmist had long before foretold that they would come to the Lord and offer gifts, when he said: “The kings of Tharsis and the islands shall offer gifts.” The Psalmist himself foretold that they would offer gold when he said: “To him shall be given of the gold of Arabia.” Isaiah foretold that they would bring gold and frankincense when he said: “All those from Saba shall come, bringing gold and frankincense.”

The Psalmist also says concerning them: [Col. 0906C] “Ambassadors shall come from Egypt.” It should be understood that these Magi were the firstfruits of the Gentiles and were sent, as it were, from the breadth of the whole Gentile world to obtain peace. For the Gentiles had departed from their Creator through the worship of idols, and therefore they sent these three ambassadors to obtain peace.

It should be understood that they did not offer one gift apiece, but each offered three—that is, each of them offered gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Through these sacred gifts, which they offered, they proclaimed him to be the true king, true God, and true man: king through the gold, God through the frankincense, and mortal through the myrrh.

Gold is ordinarily [Col. 0906D] the more precious element in royal gifts; frankincense was placed in the sacrifice of God; and myrrh was used to embalm the bodies of the dead, so that they might be preserved unharmed for a longer time. The holy Church offers these three things to him every day because it confesses him to be the true king, true God, and true man.

There were, however, heretics who offered him frankincense but not gold, because they believed him to be God but did not believe that he had always reigned with the Father. There were others who offered him gold but not frankincense, because they believed him to be king but not God. There were also others who offered him myrrh but neither gold nor frankincense, because they believed him to be merely a man.

Let us therefore [Col. 0907A] offer gold to our king Christ—that is, let us believe him to be the true king. Let us offer him frankincense—that is, let us adore him as the true God. Let us offer him myrrh—that is, let us venerate him as the true man.

Alternatively, gold signifies heavenly wisdom, as Solomon says: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise.” Frankincense signifies pure prayer, as in the words: “Let my prayer, O Lord, be directed like incense in your sight.” Myrrh signifies the mortification of the flesh. Hence, in the Song of Songs, the Church says of her faithful who contend for God even unto death: “My hands dripped with myrrh”; and again: “I gathered my myrrh with the spices”; and elsewhere: “Who is she that comes up through the desert like a column of smoke from the spices of myrrh and frankincense, and from every powder of the perfumer?”

We offer him gold, then, when we shine before him with the light of heavenly wisdom. We offer him frankincense when we direct pure prayer to him. Finally, we offer him myrrh when, through abstinence, we mortify our flesh with respect to vices.

It follows: [Col. 0907B] “And having been warned in a dream.” The prophet Isaiah comprehended in a single statement that these men would come to God, offer gifts, and not return again to Herod, saying: “Before the child knows how to call his father or his mother, he shall receive the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians.”

He calls these three kings “the strength of Damascus,” and the gifts they offered “the spoils of Samaria”; he calls Herod “the king of the Assyrians.” Before this child, according to his humanity, knew how to call his father or mother, he received the strength [Col. 0907C] of Damascus, because he caused these three kings to come to him from distant regions. He received the spoils of Samaria because he received the gifts they offered against the king of the Assyrians, since, contrary to Herod’s will, they did not return to him.

It follows: “They returned to their own country by another way.” Spiritually, we ought to imitate these Magi and return to our own country by another way.

Our country is paradise, from which we departed through the sin of the first man. We departed from that country through pride and by eating the forbidden food. Therefore, we must return to it by another way—that is, by humbling ourselves, obeying God’s commandments, and despising visible things.

[Col. 0907D]

# HOMILY VIII ON THE PASSAGE IN MATTHEW: “When Jesus had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him; and behold, a leper came and adored him, saying: Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me.”

This mountain from which the holy Evangelist relates that the Lord descended—what mountain it was, or where it was located, as certain holy teachers maintain, is already known. Spiritually, this mountain signifies heaven; the Lord’s descent from the mountain signifies his Incarnation, because “he emptied himself, becoming obedient unto death.” The Lord descended from the mountain when he assumed the flesh of our mortality.

And beautifully, after relating that the Lord descended from the mountain, the holy Evangelist adds: “Great crowds followed him,” because he who previously had been known only in Judea, and whose name alone was held great in Israel, after “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” became wondrous throughout the whole world. Great crowds followed him because all nations, all languages, every sex, and every age, believing in him, imitated his footsteps.

“And behold, a leper came and worshiped him.” This leper certainly could not climb the mountain; for one full of leprosy could not hear the Lord’s lengthy sermon. It should be known that this man was the first after the Magi to worship the Lord, and that after the Lord descended from the mountain he is the first recorded as healed; next came the centurion’s servant, and third Peter’s mother-in-law.

This leper was undoubtedly a man of great faith, humility, and steadfastness. For by command of the Law he had been excluded from the camp, and he understood that he could not be saved by the Law. But he judged that God’s grace was not under the Law but above the Law, and therefore believed that he could be saved by the Lord’s grace; for this reason he approached in order to be healed. Just as the power to heal is believed to belong to the Lord, so the steadfastness of faith must also be observed in this man.

The other Evangelists describe how he worshiped: they say that he fell down and worshiped him, or that he knelt. In worshiping him, he showed that he believed him to be the true God, since the Law commanded that no one be worshiped except God. Falling down, or kneeling, is therefore a sign of humility and reverence. Yet reverence itself did not suppress the goodness of his confession: he approached humbly, displayed his wound, and requested a remedy.

His confession was itself full of faith, devotion, and great propriety, for he said: “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me.” He attributed the power to the Lord’s will. He who asked according to the Lord’s will did not doubt his power; and in regard to the Lord’s will he did not doubt God’s compassion like an unbeliever, but, mindful of his own weakness and conscious of his uncleanness, he did not presume. The meaning is: “The power is present; only let the will be present.”

“And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying: ‘I will; be cleansed.’” It must be asked why the Lord stretched out his hand and touched him. Could he not heal without touching? Certainly he could, by a word alone. Yet according to the command of the Law, whoever touched a leper became unclean. Therefore, in order to show that he was not subject to the Law but above the Law, the Lord stretched out his hand and touched him. He who could not be defiled by contact with leprosy wished, by his own touch, to heal others.

O wondrous humility and gentleness of the Lord! He bestowed healing in the same manner and order in which he had been entreated. The leper said, “If you will,” and the Lord replied, “I will.” The leper then added, “You can cleanse me,” and he himself added, commanding, “Be cleansed.”

As blessed Jerome says, these two words are not to be uttered together, as certain Latins maintain, but separately: first, “I will,” and then, by way of command, “Be cleansed.” He said “I will” because of Photinus, who denied that Christ had assumed a true soul and said that he had Divinity in place of a soul. The Lord therefore said “I will” to show that he had assumed a true soul, since will proceeds from the soul. He commanded because of Arius, who said that he was lesser than the Father; and for this reason he stretched out his hand, to show that he was equal to God the Father. He stretched out his hand and touched the leper because of Manichaeus, who denied that he had assumed true flesh; therefore he touched him in order to demonstrate that he possessed true flesh.

And beautifully, after the Lord said, “Be cleansed,” the holy Evangelist added: “And immediately his leprosy was cleansed.” By these words he showed that the healing was neither accidental nor restored, as with physicians, over intervals of time, but was bestowed immediately by God’s power, without any delay.

It should be understood that when the Lord said, “Be cleansed,” the leprosy was immediately cleansed. The holy Evangelist, who added these words from his own account, showed that nothing intervenes between God’s will and his work, since it is written: “He spoke, and all things came to be; he commanded, and they were created.” Thus will remains in works, and works in will; will remains in power, and power in will.

“And Jesus said to him: ‘See that you tell no one.’” Why did the Lord command him to tell no one? What need was there to conceal in words what he made manifest in the body? He commanded him to tell no one in order to leave us an example, so that we should not wish to publish or display our good works and benefits, but rather restrain and conceal them; and so that we should abstain not only from the reward of money and gifts, but also from the reward of human favor and praise.

It follows: “But go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses commanded as a testimony to them.”

It should be noted that although the Lord is read to have healed many, he sent none to the priests except lepers. He sent them to the priests for various reasons. First, he paid the priests their due honor, leaving us an example of humility, so that we might always strive to render priests their due honor. Or he sent the leper so that, when they saw him cleansed, they might understand that the Lord was not under the Law but above the Law, and might believe that he had not been healed by the Law but by the grace of God, which is above the Law. Alternatively, he sent him so that, when they saw him cleansed, they might be saved if they wished to believe; otherwise they would remain without excuse. Again, it was because the Law commanded that people be presented to the priests for examination, to determine whether they were clean or unclean. Or he sent him so that he would not appear to be a transgressor of the Law, a charge they frequently brought against him.

Perhaps someone will say: Why does holy Church no longer retain that Mosaic sacrifice, which the Lord appears to have approved? It must nevertheless be understood that those sacrifices bore the figure of this true sacrifice, which is the Holy of Holies. For this true sacrifice had not yet been revealed—that is, the sacrament of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ—because he had not yet offered his body to God the Father on the altar of the cross for the salvation of the human race. Therefore it was not fitting that those meaningful sacrifices should be removed before this true sacrifice was revealed; nor was it fitting that the type and shadow should depart before the truth and light appeared.

As for what he says, “as a testimony to them,” the meaning is this: “If they believe in the Lord, if the leprosy of impiety departs from them.” Or: “Let this be a testimony to them, that I am almighty and able to save them if they believe in me, just as they see you healed.”

Spiritually, this mountain signifies heaven, as we said above. The Lord descended from the mountain because the Son of God, although invisible and immortal, became visible and mortal for the salvation of the human race. Hence the Psalmist says: “His going forth is from the end of heaven.”

After the Lord descended from the mountain, “great crowds followed him, and behold, a leper came and worshiped him.” This man typologically signifies the whole human race, weakened by sins. Thus he is rightly called not merely a leper but, according to Luke’s Gospel, is described as being full of leprosy. For the whole human race had been corrupted and disfigured by the leprosy of unbelief and the stains of every vice. Hence the Apostle says: “For all have sinned and lack the grace of God.”

What grace? The extension of Jesus’ hand. For all needed the Son of God to become the Son of man, so that, when the Word of God had become incarnate, they themselves might be cleansed from the leprosy of unbelief and the stains of every vice.

In the fact that he fell down and worshiped him, adding, “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me,” the faith of the ecclesiastical people is signified. They believed the Son of God to be almighty and placed the whole abundance of their salvation in his will. For to say, “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me,” means nothing other than to believe him almighty.

“And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him.” The extension of Jesus’ hand signifies his Incarnation. The Lord stretched out his hand and touched the leper when, in mercy, he assumed our nature and powerfully cleansed the leprosy of unbelief and the stains of every vice.

This is also what his saying “I will” points toward, since “of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth.” What he says in relation to “be cleansed” refers to what he says elsewhere: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature.”

When the Evangelist adds, “and immediately his leprosy was cleansed,” this refers to what is added there: “He who believes and is baptized will be saved.”

And when Jesus says to him, “Tell no one,” these words teach the ecclesiastical people not to entrust the mysteries of their salvation and the sacraments of their faith indiscriminately to the detractors and opponents of holy Church. Elsewhere the Lord teaches this openly, saying: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine.”

It follows: “But go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses commanded as a testimony to them.”

The priest to whom the leper is commanded to offer the gift is to be understood as the one of whom the Psalmist says: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” By these words the ecclesiastical people are admonished to recall daily and continually offer to God the Father that legal sacrifice which was offered figuratively for the cleansing of the leper and was afterward truly offered for the salvation of the whole human race.

For the Law commanded that a leper offer two sparrows to the priest for his cleansing. The priest, taking them, was to offer both to the Lord: he was to sacrifice one with cedar wood, scarlet, and a bundle of hyssop in an earthen vessel over living water; the other he was to dip in the blood of the slaughtered sparrow and release alive to fly away into the field. The leper was to be sprinkled seven times with the bundle of hyssop dipped in the blood of the slaughtered sparrow. On the seventh day he was to shave all the hair of his head, his beard, and his entire body, so that on the eighth day he might be restored clean to the camp.

Some understand this sacrifice as signifying the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the whole human race has been rescued from the leprosy of unbelief and the stains of its vices.

By the two sparrows they understand the Lord’s two substances, namely, soul and flesh, which he assumed from the holy Virgin. By the cedar wood the wood of the holy cross is signified; by the scarlet, which is red in color, the shedding of the Lord’s blood; by the one sparrow that was slaughtered, the fact that our Lord Jesus Christ offered only his body to God the Father on the altar of the cross for the salvation of the whole human race.

By the other sparrow, which was dipped in the blood of the slaughtered sparrow, it is signified that the pain of the Passion belongs to the soul, and that through his soul he experienced the pain of the Passion.

By the fact that it was released alive to fly away into the field, it is signified that, once the mystery of the Lord’s Passion had been accomplished, our Lord Jesus Christ rose from the dead on the third day and ascended from the field—that is, from this world—to heaven on the fortieth day. Hence the Psalmist says: “And its circuit reaches to the end of it,” and again: “He mounted the cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds.”

The holy apostles are signified by the bundle of hyssop; by the water, the water of holy Baptism; and by the fact that the leper was sprinkled seven times with the bundle of hyssop dipped in the blood of the slaughtered sparrow, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Mystically, it was signified that the whole human race, redeemed by Christ’s blood through the preaching of the holy apostles, through the water of holy Baptism, and through the seven gifts of the Spirit, obtained the remission of all sins. Hence the Psalmist says: “You will sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed.”

By the number seven the whole condition of the present life is signified, since it revolves through seven days. By the eighth day, the day of the Resurrection is signified. And by the fact that on the seventh day the leper shaved all the hair of his head, his beard, and his entire body, so that on the eighth day he might be restored clean to the camp, it was signified that in this present life vices must be cut away and sins cleansed, so that on the eighth day of the Resurrection those who had previously been lepers and unclean, cleansed and purified from the leprosy of unbelief and the stains of their vices, might deserve to be gathered among the assemblies of the saints.

Morally, this leper not incongruously signifies the sinner. For what are sins other than leprosy? If leprosy makes the skin unclean, discolored, and spotted, so sins make the soul unclean, disordered, and wretched.

This leper cannot climb the mountain, because the sinner cannot contemplate heavenly things. What, then, is he to do? Is he to despair? By no means. Since he cannot climb the mountain, he must see Jesus descending from the mountain.

The leper sees Jesus descending from the mountain as often as the sinner remembers that the Lord descended from heaven to earth for the salvation of sinners. The leper then falls down and worships Jesus when the sinner is ashamed of his former deeds. He falls on his face when, in remembering his crimes, the sinner blushes. Hence blessed Paul the Apostle said to certain sinners who had already been converted but still lay on their faces: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?”

Nevertheless, that shame must not suppress the remedy of repentance. The leper displayed his wound and requested a remedy. Similarly, the sinner must confess his crimes and ask for the remedy of repentance, saying: “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me,” as though saying in other words: “My sins are many, Lord, but much greater is the mercy of your compassion. It is mine to ask that you be willing; it is yours to erase my sins like a cloud.”

“And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying: ‘I will.’” The extension of Jesus’ hand signifies the assistance of divine mercy. Jesus stretches out his hand when he grants the sinner the help of divine mercy; the leper is touched by Jesus’ hand when, through hidden mercy, the sinner is restored to life.

In his saying “I will,” the affection of divine compassion is shown, which he has toward the salvation of sinners. He seems to say: “O sinner, you are anxious whether I wish to forgive your sins or not, but know that I do wish it.” This is what he says through the prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.”

By the fact that the Lord commands, “Be cleansed,” and the holy Evangelist adds, “and immediately his leprosy was cleansed,” it is shown that, as soon as the Lord mercifully deigns to look upon the sinner, just as he looked upon Peter when he was weeping.

“And Jesus said to him: ‘See that you tell no one, but go, show yourself to the priest.’” By these words the converted sinner is admonished not to entrust the mysteries of his salvation and any divine sacraments indiscriminately to just anyone.

Because the Law was so sacred that the Lord himself directed lepers to the priests, it is signified that when someone wishes to return from pagan error, Judaism, or heretical depravity to fellowship with holy Church, he must not be received before presenting himself to the priest, so that his faith may be approved by the priest’s judgment.

Similarly, when someone is expelled from the Church for a sin, he must not be reconciled except by the judgment of the priest. This is to be understood of capital and criminal sins, for which people are expelled from fellowship with holy Church. Lesser faults, however—that is, small and light daily sins—are cleansed through the confession of the brethren, according to the saying of the Apostle James: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved.”

As we said above, this priest is the Lord Jesus Christ. For man—that is, the soul—is a temple; hence the Apostle says: “For you are a holy temple.”

But where should the sinner seek this sacrifice to offer to the priest? Within himself, according to the Psalmist’s words: “Your vows are upon me, O God; I will repay them with praises to you.” And again: “A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit.” Elsewhere: “I will offer you burnt offerings rich in marrow.” And the Apostle says: “I beseech you, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your rational service.”

The sinner ought daily to offer that legal sacrifice to the priest, namely, two sparrows. Some understand the two sparrows as the two substances of the human being, that is, body and soul. The leper must offer both of these sparrows to the priest, because the sinner must pour out his whole self to God.

One sparrow is slaughtered when the body is afflicted and the vices of the flesh are put to death. For the more one sparrow is slaughtered, the more the other is released to fly into the field: the more the body is afflicted and the vices of the flesh are put to death, the freer the soul becomes to contemplate heavenly things.

This is done with cedar wood, because the sinner ought to offer himself to God in imitation of the Lord’s Passion, and with a bundle of hyssop. Hyssop is a humble herb that cleanses the breast, and its root splits rocks. Thus hyssop rightly signifies the virtue of humility, which splits and cleanses the stony breast.

The earthen vessel can be understood as the body, because the sinner must perform these things in the very body in which he dwells. By living waters the Scriptures are signified, and the sinner ought to do all these things according to the example of the sacred Scriptures.

## HOMILY IX. ON THE FOLLOWING WORDS OF MATTHEW: “When Jesus had entered the boat, his disciples followed him, and a great storm arose on the sea.”

[Col. 0913D]

In this voyage, too, the two substances of one and the same person, our Lord Jesus Christ, are demonstrated—namely, his divinity and his humanity. In the fact that he slept, the substance of his humanity is shown. In the fact that he rose, commanded the winds and the sea, and restored calm, the substance of his divinity is demonstrated.

There are works that belong only to the substance of his humanity, and there are others that refer solely to the substance of his divinity. Sleeping belongs only to humanity, not to divinity; but rising, commanding the winds, and calming the sea belong to divinity alone. In this passage the errors of those who said that our Lord Jesus Christ had one substance, just as he had one person, are destroyed.

[Col. 0914A]

But it is greatly wondrous that he deigned to enter a small boat who by his power contains, rules, and governs all things that exist. He entered the boat because he created everything from nothing. Yet he slept in the boat, of whom it is written: “He neither slumbers nor sleeps, who keeps Israel.”

By these words it is plainly shown that created things experience the command of their Creator. Nevertheless, when the elements are said to experience the command of their Creator, this is not to be understood according to the opinion of the heretics who said that everything possesses life. Rather, it must be understood that things which are insensible to us are sensible to God, the Creator of all things.

And because it was to happen that the Lord Jesus Christ would sleep and his disciples would awaken him, David, prophesying long beforehand in the person of the apostles, foretold it, saying: “Awake; why do you sleep, O Lord?”

And because he was likewise to command the sea—that is, “The abysses were troubled, the multitude of the sound of the waters; the clouds gave voice to the Most High”—the clouds in this passage are to be understood as the holy apostles. The clouds gave voice to the Most High when the holy apostles cried out in a loud voice, saying: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.”

And because he was to command the winds, the same prophet David previously showed this, saying: “He spoke, and the spirit of the storm stood still.”

And because the Lord Jesus Christ himself was to make such great calm that people would marvel, saying, “What sort of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?” the Prophet likewise says: “Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing their works upon the many waters—these have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep.”

It follows: “Then the men marveled, saying: ‘What sort of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?’”

The men who marveled, as blessed Jerome prefers, are not to be understood as the holy apostles, but as the sailors or others who were with him in the boat. They are rightly said to have marveled because they were men, that is, carnal.

But if someone stubbornly wishes to say that the holy Evangelist calls the apostles “men,” the response must be that they too were rightly called men because they did not yet possess that perfect faith which is compared with a mustard seed. Hence another Evangelist says: “Their faith was not yet perfected.” If they had possessed perfect faith, they would have understood that no one could perish while the Lord was present.

Allegorically, this sea which the Lord wished to cross with his disciples rightly signifies the bitter and dark turmoil of this world. The Psalmist makes clear that the sea signifies the present age when he says: “This sea, great and broad, in which are creeping things without number, animals small and great.”

The Evangelist reveals how the Lord crossed this sea when he says: “When he had entered the boat, his disciples followed him.” This boat can be understood as nothing better than the most sacred tree of the Passion. Supported and assisted by it, each of the faithful crosses and despises this dark and bitter sea in spirit and strives toward the security of the firm shore—that is, toward blessed rest.

The Lord entered the boat to sleep when he was lifted up on the cross to die. He slept in the boat when, placed upon the cross, he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.

What follows—“his disciples followed him”—is mystically signified by the fact that the holy apostles followed the footsteps of his Passion. For what is it to follow the Lord except to imitate the footsteps of his Passion? Hence he himself explains this when, proclaiming the mysteries of his Passion and Resurrection, he adds in summary: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.”

Many appear to take up their cross, but it does not profit them because they do not follow Christ—that is, they do not imitate the footsteps of his Passion. Therefore, whoever wishes to cross this bitter and dark sea must take up his cross and follow Christ, that is, imitate the footsteps of his Passion.

While the disciples were sailing, Jesus fell asleep. For the holy apostles and each of the faithful, as they tread upon and despise the present age in spirit and strive toward the shore of perpetual happiness, carried along either by the favorable breath of the Holy Spirit or by their own rowing, hastening in hope, the time of the Lord’s Passion soon approaches.

Hence blessed Mark beautifully relates that this happened in the evening, that is, after sunset, so that not only the sleep itself but also the setting of the declining light might signify the setting of the true Sun, that is, the death of the Lord and Savior.

[Col. 0915C]

While the Lord slept in the boat, a great storm arose on the sea, because when he had fallen into the sleep of death upon the stern of the holy cross, as the winds blew—that is, as unclean spirits incited and demons suggested things—the waves of the blaspheming Jews began to rise, and their hearts were stirred to persecute the holy apostles.

The Lord’s patience was not disturbed by these storms, but the weakness of the apostles was shaken, frightened, and endangered. So great a storm arose on the sea that the boat was covered by the waves, because the hearts of the Jews were so stirred to persecute the apostles that their faith was almost endangered. One of them denied the Lord three times; the others abandoned him and fled.

But what did the holy apostles do? They approached—not bodily, but in mind and devotion—because, although they had seen his death, with every desire and affection of their minds they sought his Resurrection, saying with the Psalmist: “Awake; why do you sleep, O Lord? Awake, and do not reject us forever.” For if the Lord had remained asleep in the sleep of death any longer, the minds of the apostles would have been condemned to eternal death.

When the disciples awakened him, Jesus rose, and standing, rebuked the wind and the sea. He rebuked the wind when, by rising again, he overthrew the pride of the devil and, by dying, destroyed him who held the power of death.

He commanded the winds because he restrained and suppressed the power of the demons. He also commanded the sea because he destroyed the mad faithlessness and fury of the blaspheming Jews who shook their heads and said: “If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him.” For it was greater to rise from the tomb than to come down from the cross.

What follows—“Why are you afraid, you of little faith?”—signifies that, when he rose from the dead and appeared to them, he “rebuked their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they did not believe those who had seen him risen from the dead.”

It follows: “And a great calm came about.” A great calm came about because, when the Lord rose and appeared after his Resurrection, saying to his disciples, “Peace be with you; it is I; do not be afraid,” faith was firmly established in the apostles. It was so firmly established in them that those who had previously remained inside with the doors shut because of fear of the Jews afterward, strengthened, confessed him boldly and with a free voice before rulers and authorities.

Alternatively, the boat signifies holy Church, whose helmsman is our Lord Jesus Christ, while the rowers are the holy apostles. The Lord entered this boat when he began, by grace, to dwell in holy Church.

That the boat signifies holy Church is shown by Solomon, who speaks under the figure of a woman, saying: “She has become like a merchant’s ship, bringing her bread from afar,” or her price. The merchant—that is, the trader—is our Lord Jesus Christ. Holy Church has become like the ship of the merchant, namely, of the Lord and Savior.

The bread signifies the sacrament of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. Holy Church carries her bread from afar because, coming even from the ends of the earth, she carries—that is, celebrates—the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood.

This is the great price by which the human race was redeemed. The same Solomon says: “The track of a ship in the sea is not found,” because the way of life of holy Church is not earthly but heavenly. For this reason one of her rowers said: “But our citizenship is in heaven.” Although holy Church may appear to perform earthly duties, nevertheless her intention is spiritual and heavenly.

While the disciples were sailing, Christ fell asleep. For it frequently happens to the faithful who are striving in hope toward their heavenly homeland that Jesus sleeps in this boat—that is, that he withdraws the consolation of his mercy from holy Church.

The Lord slept in this boat when he permits the rulers of this age, heresiarchs, or certain wicked people to persecute his holy Church, so that those who are approved may become manifest among us. Hence the Lord himself says: “It is necessary that scandals come,” and the Apostle Paul says: “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest.”

Often the rulers of this age have threatened to devastate holy Church and destroy her children. For while the Lord slept in the boat, a great storm arose on the sea: when he withdrew the help of his mercy from his faithful, he permitted the wicked to persecute holy Church to such an extent that she seemed almost annihilated.

But what did the faithful do? They approached in mind and devotion and implored his help, saying with the Psalmist: “From the ends of the earth I have cried to you when my heart was in anguish”; and again: “Arise, Lord; help us and deliver us for the sake of your name.” For the cry of the apostles is the devotion of faithful peoples.

When the disciples awakened him, Jesus rose, because he grants the consolation of divine mercy to his faithful. Hence it says: “And rising, he commanded the winds and the sea.” He came and commanded because he causes the bold adversaries of holy Church to vanish and troubled the desires of wicked people so that they could not obtain their intended effect.

He commanded the sea because, through the syllogisms of his preachers, he exposed the craftiness of the heretics, so that they would not be accepted by the faithful.

“And a great calm came about.” God brought about a great calm so that people marveled at how holy Church, after such great persecution and tribulation, immediately returned to her long-desired former peace.

Morally, the boat signifies every faithful soul. Solomon bears witness to this when he says: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.” If the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom, it is the seat of Christ; and therefore it is the Lord’s boat.

The Lord boards this boat when he begins to dwell in it by grace. As any faithful person sails—that is, as he journeys in hope toward the heavenly homeland—it frequently happens that Jesus sleeps in this boat.

Jesus sleeps when he permits temptations of unclean spirits, assaults of evil thoughts, the pleasures of one’s own flesh, or persecutions by wicked people to rise against the faithful soul. These storms commonly shake those virtues on which the salvation of the human race especially depends: faith, hope, and charity.

The Lord permits these storms to rise against the boat to such an extent that it is almost covered by the waves. For he permits the faithful soul to be tempted so severely that it seems almost to sink: the splendor of faith grows dark, the height of hope withers, and the flame of charity grows cold.

But what is the soul to do? Is it to despair? No. Following the example of the apostles, it must approach and cry out to God with all its strength.

When we cry out, he who neither slumbers nor sleeps, who keeps Israel, will rise like an army, calm the storm, restore tranquility, and grant the harbor of salvation—he who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God forever and ever.

## HOMILY X. ON THE FOLLOWING WORDS OF MATTHEW: “Jesus answered and said: ‘I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones.’”

The blessed Luke also makes mention of this confession, saying: “At that very hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said: I confess to you, Father.” But this should not seem contradictory, because blessed Matthew says “at that time.” He placed this expression beforehand for the purpose of giving the evangelist Luke room to insert the events that took place between the reproach of the cities and this confession; these events are so few that, if blessed Matthew had said “at that very hour,” there would have appeared to be no contradiction.

Thus, taking occasion from the unbelief of the cities, which were unwilling to receive the Lord’s word or believe in him, the Lord gave his response, recounting the cause—namely, praise and thanksgiving to God the Father for those to whom he had revealed the mystery of his Incarnation. The order of the words must also be carefully examined, because he did not say merely, “I confess to you, Father,” but added, “Lord of heaven and earth.” By these words the Lord Jesus showed that the one who is Lord of heaven and earth is his Father.

In this passage the heretics who said that the Lord Jesus was a creature [Col. 0918B], and not the Creator, are refuted.
