For if he were a creature, and a creature could also call its own lord “father,” he would not say specifically, “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth”; rather, he would say either, “I confess to you, Father of heaven and earth,” or, “I confess to you, Lord of heaven and earth.” For it must be known that confession does not always signify penitence and accusation of sins, but also praise and thanksgiving. Thus we read: “I will confess to you, Lord, with all my heart”; and again: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good.” Likewise, in the book of Ecclesiasticus it is written: “You shall say this to the Lord your God in confession, for all his works are exceedingly good.” Here it should be noted that confession does not signify penitence or confession of sins [Col. 0918C], but praise, as it does in this passage.

The blessed evangelist Luke also clearly demonstrates this when he says that “at that very hour” Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit. For if we examine the Lord’s words carefully, we shall certainly understand that the Son of God confesses to God the Father and renders him thanksgiving and praise, as though he had already suffered and been glorified—not for his own sake, but for ours. In this confession the gift of his mercy and the grace of our reconciliation are also revealed.

Why the Son of God confesses to God the Father and renders him praise, he makes clear when he adds: “Because you have hidden these things from the wise.” What, then, are the things he has hidden? Those, clearly, of which the Apostle says: “The mystery was revealed to me, which in other generations was not made known to the sons of men [Col. 0918D], as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets: that the Gentiles are fellow heirs and fellow members of the promise in Christ.” This is the mystery of the Incarnation: namely, that he who was ineffably begotten by God the Father before all ages assumed flesh from a virgin mother at the end of the ages. This, indeed, he hid.

From whom he hid it he makes clear when he adds: “From the wise and prudent.” Yet they were not truly wise; they were wise through presumption in their own folly, not through the keenness of true wisdom; wise through rashness, not truth; wise through arrogance, not understanding. Of them the prophet says: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight.” And again: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise [Col. 0919A], and I will reject the prudence of the prudent.”

The blessed apostle Paul explains the meaning of these testimonies when he says: “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the one who weighs the words of the law? Has not God made the wisdom of this world foolish?” And because the world could not know God through wisdom, it pleased him through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. Concerning this worldly wisdom the same Apostle says elsewhere: “The wisdom of this world is an enemy of God and is not subject to the law of God”; indeed, it cannot be.

Who, then, were these wise people? Certainly, on the one hand, the teachers of the law of that time—namely, the scribes and Pharisees—who, although they were foolish, boasted that they were wise; or, in the present age, heretics or philosophers, who, because of their inflated wisdom, are unable to receive the Lord’s humble teaching and [Col. 0919B] preaching.

But to whom did he reveal these things? He immediately makes this clear by saying: “To little ones,” that is, to the humble in heart. The Lord calls “little ones” those who recognize themselves as little and humble. He revealed the secrets and powers of the heavenly mysteries to little ones—that is, to the holy apostles, who were truly little, not in understanding but in malice. Of them the Psalmist says: “From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise.” And again: “The testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to little ones.” And once more: “The declaration of your words gives me light and grants understanding to little ones.”

The Lord confirmed the reasons and justice of this act by the judgment of the Father’s will, so that those who disdain to become little ones might become fools before God in their own wisdom. And to show that he had condemned not intellectual ability or the understanding of wisdom but the swelling of pride, the Lord fittingly added: “Yes, Father, for thus it was pleasing before you.”

With loving affection the Son addresses the Father, so that the benefit already begun and the grace might be confirmed and brought to completion in the little ones, that is, in the holy apostles. Fittingly he says: “Thus it was pleasing before you,” as though he were openly saying in other words: “To you, who are just, nothing unjust can be pleasing; therefore it was rightly pleasing before you in this way, and you have arranged everything justly, that you hid these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones.”

By these words, therefore, those who are accustomed to complain and murmur—asking why some are chosen, others rejected, some saved and others destroyed—are reproved, since the Son of God himself extols the Father’s will and his just ordering in praises [Col. 0919D]. Considering this sentence concerning the divine ordering, accomplished by God’s hidden yet just judgment, the blessed apostle Paul, unable to comprehend it, burst into wonder, saying: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!”

It follows: “Everything has been handed over to me by my Father.” These words concerning divinity must be understood spiritually, not carnally. We must likewise understand spiritually both the Father who hands over and the Son who receives. For if they were understood according to human custom, as soon as the one who receives began to possess something, the one who handed it over would cease to have it. But God the Father did not hand everything over to his Son [Col. 0920A] in such a way that he ceased to possess what he handed over, because he possesses all things timelessly together with the Son.

Therefore, insofar as his divinity is concerned, the Son of God received nothing from the Father in time, because, as the evangelist says, everything the Father has also belongs to him, since “the Son and the Father are one.” But in that he became human, he received everything from the Father in time. Hence the Father says to him: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.” And likewise the Son says in the Gospel: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.”

Therefore, when he says, “Everything has been handed over to me by my Father,” we should not understand that heaven and earth, the sea, and the other elements were handed over to him—things which he created and brought into being together with the Father—but that holy and elect men, and little ones from all nations, were handed over to him, for whom he himself gave thanks while supplicating God the Father.

“And no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son.” These words seem to mean that no one can know the Father except the Son, and conversely that no one can know the Son except the Father. But this should not be understood in that way. Rather, it should be taken to mean that the Father and the Son are revealed through him.

The meaning is this: no one knows what is in the Son except the Father, and no one knows what is in the Father except the Son, and the one to whom he himself wishes to reveal it. For it is one thing to know what he knows through equality of nature, and another to know what he knows through the gracious condescension of the one who reveals. He himself is the light of our minds.

God, therefore, in his power reveals himself through the Word, that is, through his Son. The Word—that is, the Son—reveals both himself and the Father; and while he reveals himself, the Father also reveals him, because he and the Father are one. Therefore what follows, “and to whomever the Son wills to reveal him,” must be referred to both the Father and the Son.

The Apostle makes clear that the Father reveals him when he says: “When it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me by his grace to reveal his Son in me, so that I might proclaim him among the Gentiles, I immediately did not consult flesh and blood.”

It follows: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.” In these words the Lord addresses the human race and calls to himself those who labored under the difficulties of the law or were burdened by idolatry and the sins of the world, but especially those who were found worthy to hear and follow the Lord’s voice.

For he says: “Come”—not with your feet but by your conduct, not in body but by faith. This is the spiritual approach by which each person is able to appear before God. Concerning it the Psalmist says: “Draw near to him and be enlightened.”

“To me”—that is, not to a human being, not to a stranger, not to a deceiver, but to the Savior. Fittingly he added: “All,” because, as the Apostle says: “He himself desires all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” Therefore with him there is no distinction between nation and nation, sex and sex, language and language, age and condition.

“You who labor”: in worldly business, or laboring under the heavy burdens of the law. “And are burdened”: with various crimes and sins. From the deception of the first man the human race labored under the dominion of the devil, except for those who were found worthy to be freed by the grace of God alone. Hence the Psalmist said: “My iniquities have risen above my head, and like a heavy burden they have weighed upon me” [Col. 0921A].

Fittingly the Lord added: “I will refresh you,” because he is the bread of angels and the highest refreshment and satisfaction of blessed spirits. Hence the prophet, contemplating this in his mind, said: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.”

He then shows the manner of this refreshment when he says: “Take my yoke upon you,” as though he were saying: “Lay aside the yoke of the law and take mine”—that is, not the yoke of the Destroyer but of the Redeemer. For there is a great difference between the yoke of the devil and that of Christ, and between the yoke of the law and that of the Gospel.

The yoke of the devil weighs sinners down [Col. 0921B], but Christ’s yoke raises them up. The yoke of the law burdens sinners with the weight of its severity; the yoke of evangelical grace lifts them up by promising the hope of pardon.

The prophet Zephaniah foretold long beforehand that the human race would take up Christ’s yoke when he said: “And all shall call upon the name of the Lord and serve him with one shoulder beyond the rivers of Ethiopia; from there my suppliants, the children of my dispersed ones, shall bring me an offering.” They shall serve him with one shoulder—that is, with one devotion of faith, as though under a single yoke.

“And learn from me.” He makes clear what is to be learned when he adds: “For I am gentle and humble in heart.” It is as though he were saying: “You were once harsh and proud; learn humility and gentleness from me and in me.”

“And you will find rest for your souls” [Col. 0921C]. It is as though he were saying: “You are already weary, because you sought rest and could not find it. For life is not found in the province of death, nor joy in the homeland of sorrow, nor rest in the region of labor. Come, therefore, to me, because I am everything that you seek.”

And lest people who heard the word “yoke” become frightened, he therefore added: “For my yoke is pleasant and my burden is light”—that is, “Do not be afraid when you hear the word ‘yoke,’ because it is pleasant and light.”

But it must be asked why the Lord calls his yoke pleasant and his burden light, when the Psalmist says: “I kept difficult ways,” and he himself says in the Gospel: “How narrow the gate is, and the way is constricted.” These statements should nevertheless not seem contradictory.

His yoke is light for those who are willing, but heavy for those who are unwilling; heavy for beginners, but light for those who progress and reach the end of perfection. It is hard and rough because it is sought by many but found by few.

Alternatively, he calls his yoke light in order to show that the yoke of the law was heavy. The yoke of the law was heavy because, by the weight of its severity, it put people to death; Christ’s yoke, however, is light because it gives sinners life through the hope of pardon and the promises of heavenly things.

That the yoke of the law is heavy the apostle Peter makes clear when he says: “Why do you now wish to place the yoke of the law upon them again?”

What is sweeter than Christ’s yoke, or what is lighter than the burden of evangelical grace? Truly it is light not to consent to crimes, to become worthy of approval before enemies for the Lord’s sake, to love friends in the Lord, to love everyone, to hate no one, to desire what is good, to reject what is evil, and not to inflict on others what one does not wish to be done to oneself [Col. 0922A].

## HOMILY XI. ON THE FOLLOWING PASSAGE OF MATTHEW: “As Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took his twelve disciples aside and said to them: ‘Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that has been written through the prophets concerning the Son of Man will be accomplished,’” etc.

Foreseeing that the minds of the disciples would be disturbed by his passion, the Lord therefore foretold both the punishment of that passion and the glory of his resurrection, so that when they saw him dying, just as he had predicted, they would not doubt that he would rise again, as he had promised. When he foretold the evils he was going to suffer, he armed them, since evils foreseen are borne more lightly than those that occur suddenly.

These words destroy the error of unbelievers and the madness of those who are accustomed to mock the Lord and say that he was compelled to be led to his passion. For, as this passage makes clear, he both foresaw the time of his passion and went fearlessly to the place of that passion.

This event also admonishes holy preachers that they should foretell to their hearers the snares of the ancient enemy and whatever evils may occur, so that they may be able to overcome the snares of the ancient enemy courageously and bear more lightly the adversities that befall them.

It follows: “Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee approached him with her sons, worshiping and asking something of him.” The word “then” refers back to what precedes: that is, to the time when he foretold to the disciples the punishment of his passion and the glory of his resurrection.

But it must be asked where this mother of the sons of Zebedee found the occasion to approach the Lord and ask something of him. The Lord had foretold sadness to the disciples; that is, he had predicted the disgrace of his passion. From where, then, did she take the opportunity to approach the Lord and ask him for the glory of reigning?

She remembered that the Lord had earlier promised his disciples, saying: “You who have followed me in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” And because the Lord had said afterward, “and on the third day he will rise again,” she thought that immediately after his resurrection he would come to reign, and that what was to be fulfilled at the second coming would be fulfilled at the first.

Therefore, in feminine eagerness and forgetful of the future, she desired only present things.

“He said to her: ‘What do you want?’” The Lord did not question her as though he were ignorant and wished to hear what she wanted. Rather, once she had explained it, he wanted to show that her request and that of her sons was irrational and blameworthy. They were asking as though they were religious people and lovers of the heavenly homeland, but not as people possessing sound judgment concerning useful and harmless petitions.

The Lord often allowed his disciples to think, say, or even do something incorrectly, so that he might take occasion from their fault to teach and explain the rule of piety. He knew that their error would do them no harm while the Teacher was present, and that his instruction would edify everyone, not only in the present but also in the future.

But she said: “Let these two sons of mine sit, one at your right and one at your left, in your kingdom.” This mother made her request through womanly error and out of affection, not knowing what she was saying. And what wonder if she is reproved for ignorance and lack of understanding, when it was earlier said of Peter, when he wanted to make three tents, that he did not know what he was saying?

But it must be asked why blessed Matthew says that this woman approached the Lord, whereas Mark says that her sons approached him. It must be understood that the mother approached the Lord at the prompting of her sons. They knew that their mother was beloved by the Lord, and therefore wanted to make their own desire and intention known to the Lord through her.

For this reason blessed Mark, in order to make their desire and plan known to his readers, omitted mention of the intervening mother and narrates that they alone approached—the sons at whose prompting the mother approached.

Accordingly, the Lord, in agreement with both evangelists, answered not the mother but the sons, saying: “You do not know what you are asking.” They did not know what they were asking because they were requesting a seat of glory that they had not deserved. Or they did not know what they were asking because they thought that someone could sit on the left in that kingdom, whereas on the day of the final judgment all the faithful will be placed at the right hand of the supreme King and Judge, since his kingdom has nothing on the left and that blessedness contains nothing rejected.

Although these men ought not to have received what they were seeking, their simplicity nevertheless did not deserve to be put to shame, because it had arisen from love of the Lord. And because they made their request simply, the Lord did not rebuke their affection or simplicity; he blamed their ignorance and lack of understanding, saying: “You do not know what you are asking.”

It was as though he were saying in other words: “Your desire is indeed good, but your request is inconsiderate. You ask for an honorable thing, because you wish to be joined to me in the kingdom. You delight in the height of honor, but first it is necessary for the way of labor to exercise you.”

It follows: “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?” He calls the cup his most bitter passion. By the name of “cup” he wishes the passion of martyrdom to be understood, through which it was necessary that he and they should be brought to completion.

Hence, as the passion approached, the Lord said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” And the Psalmist says: “I will take the cup of salvation.”

But it must be asked why the Lord questioned these men: “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?” Did he not know whether they would be able to imitate him through suffering? He did know. But he wished to ask them so that, when he questioned them and they answered, “We can,” we might hear and understand that no one is able to reign with Christ in heaven unless he strives to imitate him through suffering. No one can reign sublimely with Christ unless he has first humbly striven to suffer for him.

Hence the Apostle says: “If we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be united with him in his resurrection.” And again: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him; and if we become companions in his passion, we shall also be companions in his consolation.”

Nevertheless, these men answered, “We can,” not so much from confidence of heart and trust in their own strength as from ignorance. Those who know it find warfare desirable, but to those who do not know it, it is extremely frightening. Likewise, to the inexperienced, the trial of suffering and death seems easy.

For if the Lord, as his passion approached, prayed, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” [Col. 0924B], these men would have answered “We can” much less readily if they had known what the pain of present suffering and the fear of death were like. Suffering contains great pain, and death great fear.

It follows: “You will indeed drink my cup, but to sit at my right or left is not mine to give you, but is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.”

Fittingly he says “mine”—that is, whether by imitating me or for confessing my name.

But it must be asked why the Lord says, “You will drink my cup,” when one of them, namely James, ended his life by the shedding of blood, while the other, namely John, rested in the peace of the Church.

Luke makes James’s passion perfectly clear in the Acts of the Apostles when he says: “King Herod sent his hands to afflict some of those belonging to the Church; and he killed James, the brother of John, with the sword” [Col. 0924C].

As for John, as we read in the writings of the Fathers and as faithful histories relate, when he had grown old and, knowing that the day of his death was approaching, had summoned the faithful after the celebration of the Mass and given them his final farewell together with words of exhortation, he then descended into the excavated place of his burial. After praying, he was laid among his fathers, and thus remained free from the pain of death, just as he had been free from the corruption of the flesh.

How, then, did John drink the Lord’s cup, since he departed from the world without the pain of death? It must be understood that the Lord’s cup is drunk in two ways [Col. 0924D]. In one way, when death inflicted by a persecutor is patiently endured; in the other, when the spirit is ready to endure death and a life worthy of martyrdom is lived.

John therefore drank the Lord’s cup because he was ready to endure death, and his life was worthy of martyrdom. For there are two kinds of martyrdom: one in open persecution, the other in the hidden mortification of the flesh.

John therefore drank the Lord’s cup. Although he did not drink it in open persecution, he drank it in the hidden mortification of the flesh.

Nevertheless, John also drank the Lord’s cup through suffering. For, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, he endured imprisonment and scourging with the other apostles: “They went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus.”

Moreover, because of his unconquerable preaching of the Gospel, he was sent by the most impious emperor Domitian into a vessel of boiling oil. From it he emerged unharmed by the pain of suffering, just as he had remained free from the corruption of the flesh, and he was exiled to the island of Patmos.

John therefore drank the Lord’s cup together with his brother, because one who endured such and so many things plainly showed that he was ready to endure death as well, if the persecutor had inflicted it upon him.

But it must be asked how the true Teacher can say, “To sit at my right or left is not mine to give,” when elsewhere he says: “Everything has been handed over to me by my Father”; and again: “Everything that the Father does, the Son also does in the same way.”

For if the Son does everything that the Father does in the same way, what is the meaning of his saying, “To sit at my right or left is not mine to give”?

This can be understood in three ways.

First, by saying, “It is not mine to give,” he means that the kingdom of heaven is not a matter of the giver but of the recipient. With the Lord there is no partiality, and therefore the kingdom of heaven is not granted according to respect for persons but according to the quality of one’s merits. That kingdom has been prepared not for a person but for a way of life.

Whoever, therefore, presents himself as worthy to receive it will immediately obtain it. Thus, if you prove yourselves worthy to attain it, you will immediately receive the kingdom that my Father has not prepared for the sluggish but for the victorious and triumphant.

Alternatively, “It is not mine to give you” means: “It is not mine to give it to such proud people as you are, who desire to be exalted, but to the humble in heart, for whom it has been prepared by my Father.” Therefore, if you wish to receive it, do not remain what you are; it has been prepared for others, so become others, and it will also be prepared for you.

What does “become others” mean? Humble yourselves first, you who desire to be exalted.

Alternatively, as Bede says: when the Lord’s left is understood in a good sense, it signifies the present life of the holy Church, while his right signifies the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom.

Hence Solomon says: “Length of days is in his right hand; glory and riches are in his left.” Why is length of days in his right hand? Because in that blessed life unfailing light is granted to the saints. In his left are glory and riches, because in the pilgrimage of this life we are refreshed by the glory of faith and the riches of virtues.

A person receives a seat at the right when he rejoices in the kingdom of heavenly blessedness at the present vision of his Creator. He also receives a seat at the left when, during the pilgrimage of this life, he undertakes to preside over others through the governance of the priesthood.

It is therefore clear and well known that these two sons of Zebedee did not receive one a seat at the Lord’s right and the other at his left. Rather, for a time both were at the left, because they presided over others through the office of the apostleship; now both sit at the right, because they rejoice in the present vision of their Creator.

As for Christ’s saying, “To sit at my right or left is not mine to give you,” it must be known that the Lord sometimes speaks from the substance of his humanity and sometimes from that of his divinity. Because this mother of the sons of Zebedee referred the honor to the substance of his humanity and placed the glory of reigning in his bodily presence, the Lord answered them according to that same substance, as though he were saying:

“According to this substance, by which I shall drink the cup with you, it is not mine to give you. Yet according to the substance of my divinity it is mine to grant it, because in all things I am equal to God the Father.”

It follows: “When the ten heard this, they were indignant at the two brothers.” The other ten apostles were indignant, therefore, not at the mother of the sons of Zebedee but at the two brothers. They attributed the audacity of the request not to the mother but to the sons, at whose prompting the mother had approached [Col. 0926B], since, ignorant of their own measure, they had been inflamed by immoderate desire.

It must also be understood that just as the two had made a carnal request to be above everyone else, so these ten were carnally indignant. If they had understood spiritually, they would never have asked to be above everyone else; and if these others had understood spiritually, they would never have been indignant at the desire of the two.

For just as it is blameworthy to wish to be above everyone else, so it is exceedingly glorious to endure patiently that others should be placed above oneself.

But that compassionate and gentle Teacher neither rebuked the two for their immoderate desire nor reproved the ten for their indignation and envy. Rather, he recalled them all to the way of humility and showed them an example by which he taught that the one who is greater than all is the lesser, and that the one who is Lord is the servant of all.

He said: “Do you not know that the rulers of the nations lord it over them?” It is as though he were saying: “Those who are rulers among the nations command their subjects, and those who are greater exercise authority over those who are lesser. But it will not be so among you. Whoever wishes to be greater among you will be your servant, and whoever wishes to be first will be your slave.”

By these words the Lord showed that one reaches the kingdom through humility, while heaven is entered through simplicity. Whoever desires to hold to the footsteps of divinity must follow the example of humanity.

Whoever wishes to precede his brother in reigning must first precede him in serving. And since they might perhaps despise an earthly likeness, he set himself before them as an example, so that if they disregarded his words, they might be ashamed in the face of his deeds.

Thus he says: “Just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life for many.”

He says “for many,” meaning for those who wished to believe in him. And when he says “life,” the error of those who claimed that the Lord had not assumed a true soul is destroyed.

## HOMILY XII. ON THE FOLLOWING PASSAGE OF MATTHEW: “The scribes and Pharisees approached Jesus, saying: ‘Why do your disciples transgress the traditions of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread?’”

Remarkable indeed was the folly of the scribes and Pharisees, who reproached the Lord because he did not observe the precepts [Col. 0927A] and traditions of men! “Why,” they say, “do your disciples transgress the precepts of the elders?” These words clearly reveal the intention of the scribes and Pharisees in coming: namely, that they came not to learn but to criticize. They criticized the Lord’s disciples not for the ordinary washing customarily practiced, but for that excessive washing which had been adopted through the elders’ superstitious tradition.

What this was is made clear by Mark when he says: “For the Pharisees and all the Jews, unless they wash their hands frequently, do not eat bread, keeping the tradition of the elders; and when they return from the marketplace, unless they have washed themselves, they do not eat. And there are many other things which they have received to observe: the washings of cups and pitchers, of bronze vessels, and of beds.” [Col. 0927B] Therefore hands must be washed not so much as parts of the body as the whole heart; that is, deeds must be cleansed, so that God’s word may be fulfilled in them.

[Col. 0927D] The Lord refuted the scribes’ and Pharisees’ accusation with a true answer, and rebuked them, saying: “Why do you also transgress God’s commandment because of your tradition?” The meaning is: Since you neglect God’s commandments in order to observe the traditions and precepts of men, why do you judge my disciples deserving of rebuke because they disregard the traditions and precepts of men in order to keep God’s commands?

In this deed it is shown that what Isaiah had prophesied has already been fulfilled, when he said: “He rebuked iniquity on behalf of the meek of the earth.” And as though they themselves were asking, “Where do we transgress God’s commandments?” he replied: “For God said: [Col. 0927C] ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘Whoever curses father or mother must die.’ But you say: ‘Whatever gift is from me will benefit you, father or mother.’”

In the sacred Scriptures, “honor” does not always signify subjection, or the bowing of the head in greetings, or the performance of certain services; it also signifies the generosity of alms and the offering of gifts. That this is so the Apostle makes clear when he says: “Honor widows who are truly widows.” Here “honor” means a gift: that is, provide widows with what they need.

Elsewhere he instructs that presbyters are to be held worthy of double honor; above all, he urges that those who labor in word and teaching should be rewarded. Hence the command in the Law that the mouth of the ox treading out the grain should not be muzzled; hence also the Lord says in the Gospel: “For the laborer is worthy of his wages.”

The Lord, therefore, taking thought for the weakness, age, and poverty of parents, commanded in the Law that children honor their parents—that is, support their parents’ poverty. For this reason, the scribes and Pharisees, wishing craftily to overturn and violate God’s most provident law, taught children to consecrate and vow to God what ought to have been supplied to their parents, and to say: “Whatever gift is from me will benefit you.” It was as though they were saying: “O father and mother, whatever I ought to have supplied for you I have consecrated to God; and therefore the gift that is from me will benefit not only me but also you.” Thus, when the parents heard this, they would choose rather to endure hunger and suffer want than to demand what they heard had been consecrated to God.

[Col. 0928A] This passage can also be understood in another way: “Whatever gift is from me will benefit you,” that is, “Whatever I am able to possess, O father and mother, I spend on your needs and food; and for this reason I have nothing to offer to God.” Thus, when the parents heard this, they would likewise prefer to endure want and suffer poverty rather than take away what their children wished to offer to God.

The scribes and Pharisees acted cunningly, so that what ought to have been given to parents might be diverted to the priests’ uses, enabling them under this pretext to accumulate earthly profits for themselves. In doing this they violated the meaning of the Law; hence they are rightly rebuked by the Lord, who says: “And you have made God’s commandment void because of your tradition.”

[Col. 0928B] “Hypocrites, Isaiah rightly prophesied about you, saying: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.’” A hypocrite is called a pretender, one who simulates one thing in his actions while harboring another in his heart. These men are therefore rightly called hypocrites, because under the honor of God they desired to accumulate earthly profits for themselves.

The Jewish people appeared to draw near to God and honor him with lips and mouth, because they boasted that they possessed the worship of the one God; but in heart they had withdrawn far from him, because, although they saw his signs and miracles, they were unwilling either to recognize his divinity or to receive him.

[Col. 0928C] This saying may also be understood not only of the Jewish people but of certain people in the Church. We draw near to the Lord not bodily but mentally. For there are many in the Church who fortify their foreheads with the sign of the cross, yet withdraw far from him because by their wicked deeds they contradict him.

“For they worship me in vain, teaching my doctrine.” “In vain” means without the fruit of salvation, without any advantage, and without any reward.

It follows: “And he called the crowds to himself and said.” By “the crowds” he means the crowds of disciples and believers: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person.”

The Jews thought that their highest and greatest religious observance consisted in the regulation of foods, but all their superstitious observance is destroyed by these words, in which the Lord says: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what proceeds from the mouth.” By these words the Lord shows that, through those kinds of animals which were forbidden to be eaten in the Law, God’s creature is not condemned, nor is it declared unclean; rather, the vices of human beings are censured.

[Col. 0928D] For the command was given in the Law that those animals which neither chew the cud nor divide the hoof were not to be eaten; nor those which chew the cud but do not divide the hoof; nor those which divide the hoof but do not chew the cud.

By those animals which neither chew the cud nor divide the hoof may be understood unbelievers, who do not know how to separate good from evil and who do not ruminate on God’s commandments by meditating on them and committing them to memory.

By those which chew the cud but do not divide the hoof may be understood the Jews, who appear to ruminate by meditating on God’s commandments and committing them to memory, yet do not divide the hoof, because they do not separate good from evil.

By those which divide the hoof but do not chew the cud may be understood bad Catholics, who know how to separate good from evil but do not ruminate on God’s commandments by meditating on them and committing them to memory.

[Col. 0929A] The raven may also signify those who rejoice in shedding human blood; swans designate the arrogant; hawks and kites those who seize what belongs to others; and fish which have neither scales nor fins and which chiefly live in mud designate unclean and impure people who wallow in the filth of sins.

Alternatively, such fish may be understood as bad Catholics who possess neither the scales of good works nor the feathers of virtues, and therefore cannot leap above the waters—that is, they are unable to penetrate heavenly things.

But perhaps someone will ask: Since the Lord says, “It is not what enters the mouth [Col. 0929B] that defiles a person,” why is it not lawful to eat food sacrificed to idols? Or why does the Apostle say: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons”?

It must be understood that every creature of God is in itself good and clean, but the invocation of demons makes such things unclean; therefore it is not lawful to eat food sacrificed to idols. Whoever has such great faith as to understand that God’s creature cannot in any way be defiled may sanctify it through the word of God and prayer, and eat whatever he wishes.

For this reason the Apostle commanded that whatever is sold in the market should be eaten, with no questions asked. But if someone says, “This has been sacrificed to idols,” he commanded that it should not be eaten because of another person’s conscience—namely, the conscience of the one who is scandalized.

[Col. 0929C] “Then his disciples came to him, saying: ‘Do you know that the Pharisees were scandalized when they heard this saying?’”

The Pharisees were scandalized when they heard the Lord say, “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person,” because they thought that the regulation of foods constituted the highest and greatest religious observance.

But concerning this word, “scandal,” although it is extremely common, we must nevertheless see what it signifies. Scandal is a stumbling block, or a fall, or a striking of the feet. Thus what the Lord says—“Whoever scandalizes one of these little ones”—is to be understood as meaning: Whoever by word or deed gives one of these least of all an occasion for falling.

“And he answered them: ‘Every planting that my Father did not plant will be uprooted.’” [Col. 0929D]

The meaning is: Every false doctrine and superstitious observance, together with its authors, cannot endure; and because it is not from God the Father, it will be uprooted along with them. Therefore only that planting which is from God the Father will remain.

We must therefore ask whether the planting which the Apostle planted is to be uprooted or not. For he says: “I planted, Apollos watered.” This apostolic planting will remain because it is from God the Father; hence he immediately adds: “But God gave the growth.”

It follows: “Leave them; they are blind, and leaders of the blind.” This is what the Apostle says: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted and self-condemned.”

In accordance with this meaning, the Lord commands here [Col. 0930A] that all heretics and every kind of wicked teacher be left to their own judgment, since they can with difficulty be led to knowledge of the truth. And because they were blind, they led blind peoples into error.

The scribes and Pharisees were blind because they were scandalized; they were leaders of the blind because they led those whom they taught into error. Hence what follows is beautifully added: “But if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit.”

This may be understood not only of the scribes and Pharisees but also of heretics and all who teach perversely; for if a heretic gives guidance to a heretic, or a sinner to a sinner, both are hurled into the pit of eternal condemnation.

[Col. 0930B] It follows: “But Peter answered and said: ‘Explain this parable to us.’” The Lord was accustomed to speak in parables. Therefore, when Peter heard him say, “It is not what enters through the mouth that defiles a person,” he thought that the Lord had spoken figuratively, and so he questioned him.

And because he said this on behalf of the others and with their mouth, he was corrected and rebuked together with them by the Lord, who said: “Are you also still without understanding?”

These words clearly show that an auditor is faulty and deserving of rebuke when he wishes to understand a straightforward statement figuratively, or a figurative statement straightforwardly.

It follows: “Do you not understand that whatever enters the mouth goes into the stomach and is expelled into the latrine?”

There were heretics who said that the Lord was ignorant of physical science because he said: “Whatever enters the mouth goes into the stomach and is expelled into the latrine.” [Col. 0930C] Physicists say that as soon as foods and nourishment are taken, their power and liquid moisture are diffused through the limbs, veins, and nerves. Hence some people, even when they vomit after lunch or dinner what they have consumed because of a stomach disorder, nevertheless tend to appear more ruddy and more corpulent.

Those men, while wishing to display the Lord’s ignorance, demonstrated that they themselves were ignorant and foolish. For although the power of foods and their most subtle moisture are diffused through the limbs, veins, and nerves, nevertheless they descend through hidden passages—which the Greeks call *poroi*, “pores”—to the lower parts and are expelled into the latrine, so that people may again take new food.

[Col. 0930D] It follows: “For evil thoughts come out of the heart.” These words destroy the Platonic error, which said that the ruling faculty of a person—that is, sensation and understanding—is in the brain. According to Plato, therefore, the ruling faculty of a person is in the brain; according to the Lord, it is in the heart.

Those who say that all evil thoughts are injected by the devil and do not arise from one’s own will are also rebuked in this passage. The devil can be the helper and inciter of evil thoughts, but he can in no way be their author.

When the devil kindles and inflames some slight spark of evil thoughts with the fuel of his own malice, we must not understand this to mean that he is able to investigate the inner recesses of our hearts or understand our thoughts. Rather, he sometimes recognizes what is within from the behavior and movement of the outward person.

[Col. 0931A] For example, if he sees us gazing intently at a woman’s face, he understands that our mind has been wounded by the dart of love, and he strives to kindle it with the flame of carnal pleasure.

Regarding the vices he has named, which are forbidden in the divine Law, the Lord fittingly adds: “These are the things that defile a person”—that is, they make a person unclean and impure.

[Col. 0932A] When he adds, “Eating with unwashed hands does not defile a person,” he clearly shows that he prefers and most greatly approves not bodily washing but spiritual washing. Concerning this washing the Lord says through the Prophet: “Wash yourselves; be clean.” And lest we should think that this washing is bodily, he adds: “Take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes.”

For this reason he says here that evil thoughts come out of the heart, while there he commands that they be taken away. The fruits of evil thoughts are the vices which follow from them.

[Col. 0931]

# REMIGIUS’S MUSIC

*(In D. Gerbert, Scriptores de Musica, vol. I.)*

## NOTICE

I did everything I could to make the following collection of glosses by Remigius of Auxerre on Book IX of Martianus Capella’s *On the Marriage of Philology and Mercury* more accurate by collating four Parisian manuscripts—one from the Royal Library, and then one from the Victorine Library—but all in vain, as is clear from the following words, which Father Stephen Clement, a Benedictine of the Congregation of Saint Maur, whose copy I possess, sent to me on 29 August 1774:

> “I would equally like to be in a position to satisfy you concerning the two manuscripts of Remigius of Auxerre’s commentary on Martianus Capella. But I have the honor of repeating to you what I have already written: there is no antiquarian here capable of deciphering them. If they were entirely alike, they could serve mutually to explain one another. But they differ so greatly from each other that one would take them for two different works. The man who had made the rough copy which I sent you at the time no longer exists, and I know no one who can guess what escaped his penetration. One would need someone who had made a special study of the abbreviations of music—but where could such a person be found?”

It was therefore possible only to compare these glosses with Martianus’s own text, which we have printed in cursive type.

# [REMIGIUS’S MUSIC]

[Col. 0931B] Every musical art consists of proportions, that is, consonances. I say that whatever sounds correctly is either a tone, or a semitone, or a quarter of a tone, which is called a *diesis*.

A *diesis* is a division of the tone, made either into two, three, or four parts. A tone, however, is a space—Greek *systema*, Latin *spatium*—between one string and another, with a proper quantity, that is, according to the ratio of the *epogdous*, or “super-eighth,” a proper quantity, namely an eighth part. For in music the tone is *epogdous* in arithmetic, and a tone in music is as eight to nine in arithmetic.

The proper quantity is the ratio of the *epogdous*, which measures the whole of music. This tone consists of two sounds—that is, of two strings different from each other—so that one is lower and the other higher. [Col. 0931C] For example: “Then he commanded them.”

A semitone is so called because it occupies half a tone, that is, half the tone, although it can never be divided into two equal parts.

There are three *dieseis*, the Greek genitive of distance, that is, difference. *Tetrartemoria* means a fourth part: *tetarte* means “fourth,” *moros* means “part.” Hence *enarmonios*, “one part,” that is, “not joined,” because it is divided into both the greatest and the smallest intervals. It is divided into the greatest intervals because two tones are often found in one interval, and often only a fourth part [Col. 0931D] is found—namely that *diesis* which is called *tetrartemoria*. For this reason the *enarmonic* type of melody is a harmony, that is, a consonance and joining together of voices; by this fourth part we measure especially.

The second distance of the *diesis* from that one—that is, the first, which is also the fourth—is greater than the *diesis*. For *tritemoria*, that is, the third part of a tone, is so called because it has a third part of a tone. It is also called *enchromatice* [Note: [Col. 0931] In Martianus it is read: “and it is likewise called chromatic, because the chromatic type of melody is divided through it.”], namely the *tritemoria* itself. *Chromatice* means “colorable”: just as some color lies between white and black, so the chromatic occupies a middle position between the diatonic and the enharmonic. *Chroma* is Greek for “color”; it is divided and measured.

The third distance has a third part of a tone and half of a third, that is, a sixth; half of a third is a sixth, while a sixth and a third make a half.

For the number twelve places its third part in four and its sixth part in two. The sixth part, that is, two, added to the third part, namely four, makes half of twelve, that is, the number six, in the half—namely the *diapente* or sesquialter ratio.

*Hemiolion* is composed of *hemis* and *holon*, that is, “half” and “whole.” It is the ratio in which the larger number contains the smaller number and the whole of the smaller plus half of it, as three is to two and half of two, namely one. For two and one make three; this ratio is called sesquialter.

And the division of harmony—that is, consonance—completes, contains, or embraces.

A tone is therefore often also called a sound. [Col. 0933A] The difference between a sound and a tone is that a tone is the striking of two strings, or two voices sounding differently from each other; a sound is produced on one string and is a voice proceeding uniformly and evenly. Sometimes, however, a tone is also called a sound.

There are eighteen sounds—that is, strings—which occur throughout every mode; the modes themselves are fifteen in number. The first of these sounds is called by the Greeks προσλαμβανόμενος (*proslambanomenos*), but by the Romans it is called *acquisitus*, “acquired.” Then, by way of parenthesis, because we use the same word, namely the Roman one, Jupiter himself has ordained that we should do so. The work is speaking of music, which was Greek and wished to explain the arts in Greek.

*Proslambanomenos* is the lowest of all the strings and is placed outside the others.

The second sound is ὑπάτη ὑπάτων (*hypatē hypatōn*), that is, “principal of the principals.” *Hypatos* is Greek for “consul” in Latin; but he translates not word for word, but sense for sense.

The third is παρυπάτη ὑπάτων (*parhypatē hypatōn*), that is, “subprincipal of the principals.” *Par* (παρὰ) is expressed as “beside” and “adjacent,” although he, not attending to the force of the word, has used *par* for “sub,” and elsewhere also for another meaning, as will be seen below.

The fourth is ὑπάτων διάτονος (*diatonos hypatōn*), that is, “the extended [string] of the principals.”

The fifth is ὑπάτη μέσων (*hypatē mesōn*), that is, “principal of the middle [strings].”

The sixth is παρυπάτη μέσων (*parhypatē mesōn*), namely, “subprincipal of the middle [strings].”

The seventh is μέσων διάτονος (*diatonos mesōn*), that is, “the extended [string] of the middle [strings].”

The eighth is μέση (*mesē*), that is, “middle.”

The ninth is τρίτη συνημμένων (*tritē synēmmenōn*), that is, “third of the conjunct [strings].”

The tenth is συνημμένων διάτονος (*diatonos synēmmenōn*), that is, “the extended [string] of the conjunct [strings].”

The eleventh is νήτη σηνημμένων (*nētē synēmmenōn*), that is, “the last of the conjunct [strings].”

The twelfth is παραμέση (*paramesē*), that is, “near the middle.” [Col. 0933C]

The thirteenth is τρίτη διεζευγμένων (*tritē diezeugmenōn*), “third of the disjunct [strings].”

The fourteenth is διεζευγμένων διάτονος (*diatonos diezeugmenōn*), that is, “the extended [string] of the disjunct [strings].”

The fifteenth is νήτη διεζευγμένων (*nētē diezeugmenōn*), that is, “the last of the disjunct [strings].”

The sixteenth is τρίτη ὑπερβολάιων (*tritē hyperbolaiōn*), that is, “third of the higher,” namely the acute [strings].

The seventeenth is ὑπερβολάιων διάτονος (*diatonos hyperbolaiōn*), that is, “the extended [string] of the higher,” namely the acute [strings].

The eighteenth is νήτη ὑπερβολάιων (*nētē hyperbolaiōn*), that is, “the last of the higher,” namely the acute [strings].

These, then, are the sounds which compose melody suitably and rationally; for without reason the voice is confused.

Every melody consists either of the gravity of sound—that is, of unequal sounds—or of acuteness. Every melody consists of unequal elements; for if it were otherwise, it would no longer be melody.

“Gravity” is that by which the mode—that is, the sound—is softened, sweetened, and relaxed through a certain emission, that is, descent, relaxation, or prolongation.

“Acuteness” means height: the voice is drawn sharply upward into its edge, that is, into the sharpness of the voice, made thin and slender, in a graceful and elevated melody—that is, one extended rather than relaxed.

From the sounds mentioned above—that is, the eighteen sounds, which properly belong both to each individual mode and to all the modes, that is, fifteen in each and in all modes—for all modes are composed of the sounds mentioned above, and they are found in each mode—there are three symphonies.

The first is the *diatessaron*, as in “My heart has said to you.” In Latin it is called “from four,” because it is made on four strings and receives four sounds, that is, strings or voices, and three intervals, which lie between the strings. Thus there are four strings, two prolongations—that is, two tones—and a half, that is, a semitone.

But [Note: [Col. 0933D] I judge that *mirum* should be read instead of *verum*.] it is said that the *diatessaron* has tones and a semitone, that is, five semitones, although one tone has only two semitones. To this it must be answered that the fifth semitone which arises there is produced incomprehensibly, growing between those four. For I have called a sound—that is, a tone—a prolongation.

The *diatessaron*, then, consists of five semitones, which are equivalent to full and complete prolongations—that is, tones—up to the middle; and of ten *dieseis*, the Greek genitive, that is, ten fourth-parts of a tone. (*Diesis* means, as I said above, a fourth part of a tone.)

This *diatessaron* is therefore a symphony, that is, a consonance of the voice, as in “God, come to my assistance.” It is made on four strings, in the epitrite ratio, that is, the sesquitertian ratio.

An *epitritus* is one which contains the number three and a third of three, namely one; thus four is to three.

The other symphony is fivefold, that is, it is made on five strings. It is called the *diapente*, that is, “from five.” It consists of five sounds, namely five strings, divided from one another by four intervals [Note: [Col. 0933D] Martianus: “It has three prolongations and cuts through the middle one.”].

Thus the five [strings] have three prolongations, that is, tones, and cut through the middle one, namely the prolongation of the semitone. It therefore has three and a half tones, in the hemiolic or sesquialter ratio, that is, the ratio of the *diapente*, as in “my eyes.” It is made on five strings, as there are four [intervals] [Note: [Col. 0933D] In Martianus this is expressed as follows: “Three tones and a half; seven semitones and fourteen *dieseis*, and it possesses the hemiolic ratio. This form also retains the same number in the comparison, and its middle, as three is to two.”].

The third symphony is the *diapason*, that is, “from all.” It is made from eight strings, διὰ πάσων (*dia pasōn*), “through all,” and is called “from all” because the ancients used only eight sounds—or certainly because it consists of two simple symphonies, namely the *diatessaron* and the *diapente*.

For example: tone, tone, semitone—this is the *diatessaron*; tone, tone, semitone, tone—this is the *diapente* [Note: [Col. 0934D] Martianus adds: “It receives eight sounds, seven intervals, six prolongations, twelve semitones, and twenty-four *dieseis*, and it consists of,” and so forth.].

It is in the double ratio, that is, the twofold ratio; for its highest sound exceeds its lowest by twofold, as μέση (*mesē*) is to ὑπάτη ὑπάτων (*hypatē hypatōn*).

There are fifteen modes, but five of them are principal. It should be noted that the Greeks established the number of modes according to the number of divisions of the languages they use; to each principal mode two modes are attached.

The first is the Lydian: it is called Lydian because the Lydians use it. Attached to it are the ὑπολύδιος (*hypolydius*) and ὑπερλύδιος (*hyperlydius*), that is, “above the Lydian,” namely sharper than the Lydian; and *hypolydius*, that is, “below the Lydian,” namely lower than the Lydian.

The second mode is the Iastian. Ἰάστιος (*Iastios*) is so called [Note: [Col. 0935D] These words do not cohere, but some material has been omitted in the copy. Martianus has: “The second is the Iastian, to which the ὑποιάστιος (*hypoiastius*) and ὑπεριάστιος (*hyperiastius*) are joined.”] because the Ionians use it.

The third is the Aeolian. Aeolian is so called because the Aeolians use it, together with ὑποαιολίῳ (*hypoaeolius*) and ὑπεραιολίῳ (*hyperaeolius*).

The fourth is the Phrygian. It is called Phrygian because it was discovered and used in Phrygia, together with the two modes ὑποφρυγίῳ (*hypophrygius*) and ὑπερφρυγίῳ (*hyperphrygius*).

The fifth is the Dorian. It is called Dorian because the Dorians use it and it was discovered by them, together with ὑποδωρίῳ (*hypodorius*) and ὑπερδωρίῳ (*hyperdorius*).

Among these fifteen modes there is a certain friendly concord by which they are related to one another, that is, harmonious. Five are low, five high, and five intermediate. Thus there is concord between ὑποδώριον (*hypodorius*) and ὑποφρύγιον (*hypophrygius*), and likewise between ὑποιάστιον (*hypoiastius*) and ὑπολύδιον (*hypolydius*); and there is also a suitable and fitting correspondence [Col. 0935B] between ὑποφρύγιον (*hypophrygius*) and ὑποαιόλιον (*hypoaeolius*), which are joined in pairs.

For the sharper exceeds the lower twofold; a tone sounds in relation to a semitone, and a tone is twice a semitone.

The middle modes, which are concordant with the lower modes, become *proslambanomenoi* in relation to those which are sharper—that is, they take the place of the *proslambanomenos* string.

The *proslambanomenoi* are not found only among the lowest modes; they are also low in the acute modes, although they are not as low in the acute modes as in the lowest.

For example, if someone asks me how the last string should sound in relation to the first in a tetrachord, the answer will be: according to the epitrite ratio.

Each of the fifteen modes also makes five tetrachords, and the tetrachord is the element of the whole of music.

A tetrachord is a certain disposition [Col. 0935C]—that is, a joining and concord—of four sounds composed in order, namely natural voices, which surpass one another by an eighth part. The two outermost sounds ought to agree with one another. [But this will be discussed later. Now let us return to] the established order of beginnings—that is, of origins and discoveries—in which harmony was discovered.

The things stated above were stated first by me for this reason: so that they might be held at a higher level, that is, fixed more deeply in the memory.

Before he disclosed these matters—the genera of harmony—to mortals, Lasus of Hermione [Note: [Col. 0935D] Meibomius rightly notes that all the manuscripts are extremely corrupt here. He himself has: “For at first, when Lasus from Surse disclosed the power of harmony to mortals, only three were attributed to him,” and so forth. But he considers this the best emendation: “Lasus from the city of Hermione disclosed the power of harmony,” and so forth. Lasus, certainly from the city of Hermione in Achaea, is remembered as the first among the Greeks to write about music.]—Lasus of Surse, namely of a town and region—was thought to have had only three genera of *mei*, that is, of harmony; *mei* is the genitive of the primitive form.

The first genus is *Ydikon* [Note: [Col. 0935D] Some manuscripts read this way, others ἰδικὸν (*idikon*); but from what follows it seems entirely necessary to read ἐιδικὸν (*eidikon*).], that is, the genus in which forms are found.

There are three kinds of forms: the first in sounds, the second in numbers, and the third in words.

The first, namely that which is found in sounds, belongs to harmony; for in it we seek not words signifying something, but only sounds joined to one another according to some proportion.

The second, which belongs to numbers, requires nothing other than a suitable number of sounds, whether signifying nothing or signifying something, without any limit.

The third, which is called metrical, seeks not only sounds bounded by definite durations but also requires that they signify something and not exceed a definite number and limit. Examples of these are verse and meter, in both of which a definite limit and number of feet is established: in verse, six; in meter, eight.

It should be noted, however, that these three forms can be found in human voices, whereas in harmony—in voices that lack meaning—there is only one, namely the first. In it sound alone is found, though not without numerical proportion.

In the human voice, on the other hand, sound is sometimes found without meaning, though not without number, if it is joined according to some proportion; and sometimes sound is found together with meaning and number, which has deserved to be called “words.”

Εἰδικὸν (*eidikon*) means “formal”; ἐῖδος (*eidos*) means “form” or “species.”

Ἀπεργαστικὸν (*aperga­stikon*) means “active” or “operative,” that is, the exercise of an art.

Ἐξαγγελτικὸν (*exangel­tikon*), or ἑρμηνευτικὸν (*hermēneutikon*), is called “interpretative,” for it gives an account of everything.

Ἐιδικὸν (*eidikon*) is that which, from enduring—that is, unchanging—and similar sounds, sounded consonantly, that is, sounded together, in sound, numbers, and words. For as long as there is sound, number and words endure.

But those elements among these three which pertain to *melos*, that is, to sound, are called harmonic; those pertaining to numbers, namely durations, are called rhythmic; and those pertaining to words are called metrical.

The difference between rhythm and meter is that rhythm is merely the consonance of words, without any definite number or ending; it pours forth indefinitely, constrained by no law and composed in no definite feet. Meter, however, is arranged according to its proper feet and definite limits.

The smallest meter is one that consists of a foot and a half-foot, and the progression continues in order up to eight feet; it does not go beyond the number eight.

Ἀπεργαστικὸν (*aperga­stikon*) [Note: [Col. 0936D] Some manuscripts in Meibomius read πρακτικὸν (*praktikon*), a reading which fits Remigius’s interpretation above just as well as ours.] is a certain treatment of matter—that is, of the voice—a prolongation. For the voice is the matter or beginning of music, and in music the voice has the force that a point has in geometry, a unit in arithmetic, and a letter in grammar. It effects the exercise of this matter.

It likewise has three parts: Μελοποιΐα (*melopoiia*), that is, the making of melody, which pertains to sounds; λέξις (*lexis*), that is, diction [Note: [Col. 0936D] We think it should be pointed out that Meibomius was mistaken here and there in his notes on Martianus. This is clear partly from the context and partly from the exposition of our Remigius supplied here. Thus, in this very passage, he says that λέξις (*lexis*) has been improperly placed instead of λήψις (*lēpsis*), although the accompanying interpretation, “diction,” supports the former reading. Likewise, immediately above he advises that *tractus* should improperly be read as *tractatus*, and so elsewhere in other passages.], which pertains to rhythm; [Col. 0937A] πλοκή (*plokē*), “doubling,” when one foot is used repeatedly in several ways.

Ἐξαγγελτικὸν (*exangel­tikon*) appears to pertain to exposition—that is, to a model—and to interpretation, when we explain and interpret each item. It has three parts: ὀργανικὸν (*organikon*), which comes from *organon*; ᾠδικὸν (*ōdikon*), that is, “singable,” from ᾠδὴ (*ōdē*), “song”; and ὑποκριτικὸν (*hypokritikon*), “simulative” or “representational.” The order of the subject matter will arrange all these genera below, that is, in what precedes or follows.

Now we shall speak of the first voice, that is, of voice itself, which is first, as the parent of all sound.

Every voice is divided into two genera, continuous and divided. The continuous is like uninterrupted conversation—that is, frequent narration—which takes place between two persons and is not arranged by cola, that is, clauses. The divided genus is that which is divided by cola and clauses and observes definite feet in modulation, that is, in song. [Note: Meibomius reads: “The divided, which we preserve in modulation.”] There is also a middle kind, namely poetry, which is neither continuous nor divided but mixed between the two. It does not preserve the manner of either species—the continuous—but is not cut up or broken by the frequent division of the other species, namely divided voice. Thus, in the manner of pronunciation, that is, by a similarity of delivery, all poems are recited and read. (That form which we lead into divided parts and definite intervals is called *diastematic*.) Diastematic things are said to be spacious, because they are divided by spaces; for *diastema* (διάστημα) means “space” and “interval.” *Systema* (σύστημα), however, is a voice sounding uniformly, and the part that is called harmonic—that is, the part which must be adapted to modes. The harmonic part has seven divisions of its exposition, which are called “virgules.” [Note: I think one should read throughout: “which Virgil calls.”]

It addresses the seven distinctions of voices by numbers.

The first part concerns sounds; the second concerns spaces, that is, diastemata; the third concerns systems—here Greek uses the genitive where Latin uses the ablative. The fourth part concerns genus, which is threefold: chromatic, diatonic, and enharmonic. The fifth concerns tones, that is, *phthongi*; the sixth, changes, that is, metabolae; the seventh concerns modulation, which we call *melopoeia*, that is, the making of melody. Let us first speak of sounds, where the element of the art—that is, the material of the art—is found.

A sound has for us, musicians, as much importance as a sign, that is, a point, has in geometry, and a single unit has in arithmetic. We call sounds *phthongi*; hence *diphthong* means a dual sound. (A phthong, properly speaking, is a part of modulated voice produced with one tension, that is, with a similar tenor, whether grave or acute.) Tension is the production which we call *tasis*, in which the voice consists and remains, namely, equally sustained. A phthong is called either specifically—that is, of individual voices—or generally. The general term, namely “sound,” has specific terms, which are called *idiotita* (ἰδιότητα), “specific properties,” that is, things possessing their own position, and are designated by Greek terms.

If we consider how something ought to be written for us—that is, with what accent—just as each syllable has its own accent, so every sound has its own notation. This property of the phthong shows what degree of raising and lowering it has: we extend it, draw it upward, and make it higher, or we lower it more gently and make it grave. But among these phthongs some act and others undergo an action. Tension and relaxation act: tension, when the string is tightened, and relaxation, when the string is loosened. Acuteness and gravity undergo the action. In the string, the action occurs through tension and relaxation; the effect occurs in the voice, which undergoes—that is, endures—the tension and relaxation of the string and the arteries.

Production is *epitasis*, that is, super-tension: the movement of the voice from a lower place to a higher one. *Anesis* is the opposite, when it moves from a high place to a low one (for it descends from the summit of sharpness to something grave and solemn). *Paracterica* is the striking back of the voice, a slow and grave reverberation. (A grave sound is produced when) some breath is drawn from within, that is, from the depth of the chest; sharpness, however, is sent out from the surface of the mouth, that is, from the lips.

There are therefore innumerable sounds, but only fifteen and twenty-eight can come together specifically in the individual modes. All these things can be detected in song. If you wish to mention only the diatonic genus, you will have eighteen. But if you introduce the chromatic and enharmonic genera, you will have ten more, making twenty-eight; under one name, however, five chromatic and five enharmonic sounds are added, that is, in place of the monochord. But these matters are expressed subtly and obscurely. In Boethius’ *Music*, however, the Dorian mode can be recognized here. I have named the names of these sounds above. [Note: Since the copy here is very mutilated and corrupt, we have restored Martianus’ text within brackets from Meibomius; the same should be understood of the preceding and following passages.]

(The first of these is the *Adquisitus*, “Acquired,” which is therefore) called by this name, “acquired,” because it agrees with none of those things called tetrachords, but approaches from outside like something acquired, on account of its association—that is, its conjunction—with the middle string, namely the *mese*, with which it is accustomed to sound together; the Acquired is separated from the principal of the principals by one tone, that is, from the *hypate hypaton*.

(The) principal of the principals—because it is placed first in the tetrachord and has thus received, as it were, the name of a ruler—is called *hypate hypaton*. For *hypatos* means consul or ruler of the following tetrachord. (The subprincipal) is called *parypate hypaton*, not “from equality of the hypaton,” as the corrupt text has it; it is subject and joined to the principal.

The principals are three: *diatonos*, *enarmonios*, and *chromatike*. We, musicians, perhaps scarcely correctly call the chromatic species “colorable,” and it received this name because whatever is found between the principal colors, white and black, is called “colorable” in the Greek sense. White and black are called colors; whatever appears between white and black is called colorable. (Thus *enarmonios*, *chromatike*, and *diatonos*, which we call “extended,” are indications of the genera of modulation.) The manifold structure of the tetrachords is therefore established in this way, by the addition of the enharmonic and chromatic genera.

The principal of the middles, namely the *hypate meson*, received this name because it is the first of the middle tetrachord: “principal of the middles.” The element of all music is the diatessaron, since the musical proportion is not made smaller than in four strings; this we call the diatessaron. (Joined beneath it) is said to be the subprincipal of the middles, namely the *parypate meson*. Finally, the remaining three strings—*diatonos*, *enarmonios*, and *chromatikos*—obey in their corresponding use, that is, according to a similar use of themselves. [Note: Meibomius reads: “Finally, the remaining three, similar to one another, obey.”]

This tetrachord of the middles is so called because it is placed in the middle between the tetrachord of the principals, namely the *hypaton*, and the tetrachord of the joined strings, namely the *synemmenon*. After the aforementioned principals of the middles, the one that follows is called the middle: it is the *mese*. (It is called “middle” because it is both) the end of the grave mode, namely the diapason, (and, in all the modes, the beginning of the future) acuteness. The two are connected by a kind of bond in the *mese*, so that both grave and acute modulation are joined together. This is the case in the Lydian mode, that is, in the mode where the upright iota is the *mese*, where the upright iota is used as a sign, namely in Boethius’ book on music.

After the middle, that is, the *mese*, comes the third of the joined strings, which extends and sharpens the semitone: the *trite synemmenon*. It is the third from the end of the joined strings, and the interval of a semitone lies between the third of the joined strings and the *mese*. (In the same middle, that is, Lydian,) the inverted lambda will have the form of a V as its sign.

After this, the *trite synemmenon*, the three strings previously mentioned follow: *enarmonios*, *chromatike*, and *diatonos*. The latter is also called *paranete*, which we render in Latin as “next-to-last.” After the *paranete* comes the last, the *nete*, which is joined. It is called the last of the joined strings, the *nete synemmenon*, because it holds the end in this tetrachord.

The entire tetrachord of the joined strings, the *synemmenon*, is so called because it is joined to the middle itself, the *mese*, which first completed the perfect consonance, the diapason. As the middle produces the following tone, the *mese* produces the tone that lies between the *mese* and the *paramese*. The following sound, that is, the string *paramesos*, meaning “beside the *mese*,” is so called because this sound, the *paramese*, encounters the tone of the adjoining modulation very near to itself.

Next follows the third of the divided strings, the *trite diezeugmenon*, the third from the last. It completes the full system, that is, the space of the diapason; hence it is called the third from the end of the disjoined strings. After this third, the remaining sounds follow: *enarmonios*, *chromatikos*, and *diatonos*.

The sound of the divided strings received this name because it is separated from the *mese* by one and a half tones, that is, by three strings, as in “All that you have done for us, O Lord,” where three strings are found, just as there are three from the end of the *mese*. The *mese* is called the end because it terminates the graver sounds and begins the sharper ones.

After this the tetrachord of the highest strings is placed, namely the *trite hyperbolaeon*. It received the name “highest” because in every mode—fifteen in all—it rises to the greatest acuteness and is raised to the summit in every modulation, that is, it is elevated and sharpened.

Among these sounds—that is, *phthongi*, the plural form of *phthong*, meaning sounds—some must remain and persevere in their own place; others are wandering and variable, being often sharpened and often lowered. They are therefore called *lichanoi*, from the finger after the thumb, because that finger strikes and moves those strings.

Some are called *barypyknoi*, “heavily fixed”; others *mesopyknoi*, “moderately fixed,” because they are changeable; others *oxypyknoi*, “sharply fixed.” The dense genus is a certain quality formed from three sounds, namely when three tones are joined together. The *barypyknoi* are those which, like regions—that is, strings—retain or occupy the first places of the dense tones. The *mesopyknoi* possess the middle places; the *oxypyknoi* hold the last. The *apyknoi*, “not fixed,” are those which, in the arrangement of the three sounds that are dense, are joined in no genus or rule.

(The standing and persevering sounds are called either *apyknoi* or *barypyknoi*, since they will claim, possess, or retain for themselves something like a species and form of the principals.) Some are therefore called “stationary,” namely the first kind, because they cannot receive differing extensions, whether grave or acute. They are called stationary because they remain uniform: they are neither extended upward into acuteness nor lowered into gravity.

Others are regarded as wandering and errant because at times they receive longer and graver intervals, and at times smaller—that is, sharper—ones. Among these wandering sounds some are *parypatoeideis*, “like the principals,” and others *lichanoeideis*, “like the digitals,” from the finger that strikes those sounds or those strings.

The first, the *parypatoi*, are so called because they are immediately joined beneath the preceding strings, namely the *hypatai*, or principals. The *lichanoeideis* are called “digital” from the finger, which is the servant of the art and moves each sound in song. It is the first finger after the thumb, namely the index finger, by which the string is moved.

Some of these sounds agree with one another, meet, and harmonize; others differ, are discordant, and clash—that is, they are dissonant, disagreeing and opposing one another. Those that are joined to one another are called *homophōnoi*, “like-sounding”; these are the consonant sounds. The *aphōnoi* are dissonant. The *diaphōnoi*, that is, discordant sounds, are those which, when struck, differ from one another.

The *homophōnoi* carry another meaning and quality of voice, but preserve the same impulse, that is, the same striking. One and the same sound is compared with many sounds in different qualities: for example, with one it forms a tone, with another a semitone, and with a third a diesis.

There are also other differences among sounds. The first difference is through tension, that is, through the extension of the string, so that one differs from another in sharpness or gravity. The second difference is through the perception of intervals, that is, tones or semitones, when one interval or several are joined together—when one tone is gathered from two intervals and a semitone from two intervals.

The third difference in sounds occurs through the conjunction of a system, that is, through the quantity or magnitude of voices. The distinction between a *diastema*, that is, an interval, and a *systema*, that is, the magnitude of a voice, is that an interval is found between two, three, or four sounds, and beyond these; whereas a system is not smaller than the diapason. It may contain one interval, as a tone does, or several, as the diapason does, which contains seven intervals or eight strings.

What is called “according to custom,” that is, *kata ēthos* (κατὰ ἦθος), also produces difference. Modes have been discovered according to the customs of individual nations: some peoples prefer a grave sound, others an acute sound, and others a middle sound. Acute sounds signify one custom of peoples, grave sounds another, since some nations take pleasure in the sharpest sounds and others in grave ones.

Now we must discuss intervals, in Greek *diastemata*—here Greek uses the genitive where Latin uses the ablative, since Greek has no ablative and uses the genitive in its place. A *diastema* (διάστημα) is the space of a voice within which the acute voice, insofar as it is acute, and the grave voice, insofar as it is grave, are contained.

But among intervals—again using the Greek genitive in place of the ablative—some are smaller (Meibomius reads “shorter”), namely those found in the diesis of the enharmonic genus, that is, in the quarter-tone. Others are larger: these intervals, taken through the individual modes, make twice all things, or twice the diapason, beyond which nothing greater can be found among the modes.

Among intervals, some are composite, others disjoined and asyntheta. Composite intervals are those which proceed in order, that is, in the same sequence, through equal intervals of tones and semitones. Incomposite intervals are those which are joined together from different voices. Again, some are logical, that is, rational, and others alogical, that is, irrational.

The rational intervals are those whose agreement—that is, whose concord and correspondence—we can express as a proportion, so that we can state what proportion they have to one another. The irrational intervals have no underlying ratio and are joined together by no proportion. Some are consonant, that is, agreeing and harmonious with one another; others are discordant.
