Some are enharmonic, agreeing with one another; others chromatic, “colorable”; others diatonic, that is, extended; others *archia*. [Note: Thus the manuscript reads; in Greek this would be *archeia*. Meibomius has *arthia*, which is not a Greek word. Perhaps *artia* (ἄρτια), “equal,” “even-numbered,” is preferable, opposed to the following *perissa*, “uneven-numbered.”] Others are *perissa*, that is, exceeding or uneven.

I shall first speak of *archia*, the equal, as it is called in Latin; then I shall mention and explain *perissa*, the exceeding or uneven. (The equal intervals are those which can be divided into equal parts, as a tone can be divided into two semitones.) The *perissa* are those which are divided into three semitones.

Next, some intervals are dense and others more open. (The dense are those) formed by dieses, that is, by quarter-tones; the more open are formed by tones. (Among these) some agree with one another through proportion, that is, correspond; others differ, that is, are discordant.

But there is a very great multitude of discordant sounds. The consonant intervals in each mode, however, are six: the *diatessaron*, which means “through four”; the *diapente*, which means “through five”; and then the *diapason*, which sounds through all, that is, is consonant.

There is also a fourth interval, composed of the whole, that is, the diapason, and the four, that is, the diatessaron. There is a fifth, composed of the whole, that is, the diapason, and the five, that is, the diapente. There is a sixth, called the twice-whole, that is, the bisdiapason.

The interval called the diatessaron, “through four,” contains four sounds, that is, four strings; three spaces or intervals; two and a half tones; five semitones; and ten dieses. It is in the epitritic proportion, that is, the sesquitertian proportion, like four to three.

The diapente, “through five,” contains five sounds, that is, five strings; four intervals; three and a half tones; seven semitones; and fourteen dieses. It is in the hemiolic proportion, that is, the sesquialteral proportion, namely three to two.

The diapason contains eight sounds, that is, eight strings; seven intervals; six tones; twice the semitones, that is, twelve semitones; and four times the dieses, that is, twenty-four dieses. It is governed by the diplasic, that is, duple, proportion, which is one to two.

The interval composed of the whole, namely eight—the diapason—and the four, namely the diatessaron, is said to contain eleven sounds, that is, strings. Although it is said to be composed of eight and four, it does not contain twelve, but eleven, because the diapason ends on the eighth string and the diatessaron begins on that same string. It contains ten intervals and eight and a half tones; it doubles the semitones, that is, has seventeen; and it multiplies the dieses according to the aforementioned reckoning fourfold, giving thirty-six. It follows the rule of the duple and the diameter, as eight is to three. For the number eight contains twice three and two-thirds of three, which it calls the diameter.

The rule of the diameter can be understood as follows: wherever there is a binary division, it is called a diameter, because every diameter divides through two, that is, divides the middle.

The interval composed of the whole, namely the diapason, and the five, namely the diapente, contains twelve sounds; eleven intervals; nine and a half tones; nineteen semitones, doubled; and thirty-six dieses, the dieses being multiplied fourfold. It is in the triplasic proportion, as four is to twelve.

The interval called the bisdiapason contains fifteen sounds; twice seven intervals, that is, fourteen; twelve tones; twenty-four semitones, namely twelve doubled; and forty-eight dieses, four times twelve. It is in the tetraplasic, that is, quadruple, proportion, as twelve is to six.

A tone is in the epogdoic, or sesquioctave, proportion. *Epogdous* (ἐπόγδοος) is said as though it were *epiogdous* (ἐπιόγδοος), “over the eighth,” because it has one over eight. Everywhere we must understand the diesis in the enharmonic genus; this diesis is in the fourth division, that is, in the division of the tone. A fourth division is one part.

(Now what the system is) must be stated and explained. A system is the magnitude of a voice, that is, a large interval, consisting of many modes, that is, sounds, whether of five and three, or of more. (Although it admits many kinds of divisions, nevertheless, since I have) mentioned the same kinds in the smaller intervals, I shall pass them over.

There are eight complete, integral, and perfect systems.

The first is that which extends from the Acquired, which we call the *proslambanomenos*, to the middle, which we called the *mese*. This entire system is called the diapason.

The second kind of system extends from the principal of the principals, that is, from the *hypate hypaton*, all the way to the *paramese*.

The third extends from the subprincipal of the principals, that is, from the *parypate hypaton*, to the third of the divided strings, that is, the *trite diezeugmenon*.

The fourth extends from the extended string of the principals, that is, the *lichanos hypaton*, to the diatonic string of the divided strings, that is, to the *paranete diezeugmenon diatonos*.

The fifth extends from the principal of the middles, that is, from the *hypate meson*, to the *nete* of the divided strings, that is, to the *nete diezeugmenon*.

The sixth extends from the subprincipal of the middles, that is, from the *parypate meson*, to the third of the highest strings, that is, to the *trite hyperbolaeon*.

The seventh rises and extends from the extended string of the middles, that is, from the *lichanos meson diatonos*, to the diatonic string of the highest strings, that is, to the *paranete hyperbolaeon diatonos*.

The eighth extends from the middle, that is, from the *mese*, to the last of the highest strings, that is, to the *nete hyperbolaeon*.

Having gone through these systems, I shall discuss the genera of the tetrachords and of modulation, that is, briefly explain them. *Tetrachordon* is a Greek nominative; it is a division of strings with a definite quality, that is, proportion.

There are three genera of modulation: *Enarmonion*, *Chroma*, and *Diatonon*. *Enarmonion* is interpreted as “not joined together”; *chroma* as “colored”; *diatonon* as “extended.”

The enharmonic genus is so called because it is separated and distinguished by larger intervals and narrower proportions, namely dieses. The diatonic genus is rich in tones, that is, abundant in tones. The diatonic genus consists of two tones and a semitone. It is the clearest and smallest genus, although it suits different peoples, such as the Goths, who sing in very small intervals; the Theodisci, who sing at a high pitch; and the Wends and Hebrews, who sing with a murmur. [Note: This may perhaps be read: “Theodisci sing in a high voice,” or “at the highest pitch.”]

The chromatic genus is composed of semitones. Just as what lies between white and black is called a color, so this third genus is called chromatic because it lies between the other two, namely between the enharmonic and the diatonic.

The enharmonic genus, when it is enclosed—that is, surrounded—by the immutable, that is, graver, sounds, (thus rises: a tone, a tone, and a diesis upward through division; it rises in the diatonic and enharmonic [genera], that is, through two incomposite tones; since two tones in one region are three semitones. All this is plainly evident in the pages of Boethius’ *Music*; toward the grave melody it proceeds differently, that is, in the opposite order, changed.) [Note: We give the whole parenthesis as it stands, corrupt, in the copy. Since no sense can be elicited from it, we give here at least Martianus’ text restored from Meibomius: “when it is enclosed, it will obey modulation upward into acuteness through diesis and diesis and an incomposite ditone; downward, however, the whole modulation is lowered into a grave sound in the opposite direction. But chroma receives melody in this way: through a semitone and a semitone and three semitones, which arise incompositely; in the grave direction, however, it returns by the reverse course. But …”]

The diatonic genus, however, being composed of these sounds, takes its modulation upward in such a way that through a semitone, a tone, and a tone it completes the full mode; but in the graver direction—that is, in the joined direction—it proceeds in the reverse order, through a tone, a tone, and a semitone.

At present we use the diatonic genus most of all—that is, we have it in common use—because it is more beautiful than the others. This is said for the reason that this man was an African; for the diatonic genus is especially prevalent in Africa.

Of these genera we modulate some by *agogē* (ἀγωγή), that is, by leading upward or ascending into acuteness; others by *plokē* (πλοκή), that is, by doubling or joining. *Agogē* is modulation in which the sound follows itself in order. *Plokē* is said to occur when we join different things, that is, different strings—joining the fourth string to the first. *Plokē* means conjunction or doubling; whatever is doubled or gathered together from different places is called *plokē*.

From this point, in modulation, one kind is called *euthia* (εὐθεῖα), meaning straight—modulation upward into acuteness. Another is *anakamptos* (ἀνάκαμπτος), meaning returning, that is, descending into gravity. Another is *peripherēs* (περιφερής), meaning surrounding or revolving, a reflexive form which singers call *vinola*.

*Euthia* is modulation that rises from grave to acute. *Anakamptos* is modulation that, conversely, falls from acute to grave. *Peripherēs* is a circular or revolving modulation, adapted to both directions—that is, either when it is raised upward toward acuteness or when it bends downward toward gravity.

Since the divisions of the tetrachords—which we call fourfold tetrachords, because they contain four strings—are innumerable, there are seven known divisions. [Note: Meibomius has a different reckoning, reading: “There are six notes: one of the enharmonic genus …” This reading agrees with Aristides, Book I, *On Music*.] Two are known divisions of the enharmonic genus; three are known divisions of the chromatic genus. Of these, the first is the soft and relaxed one, which is called soft or wanton because it has three semitones in one region and is separated from the other regions, that is, is broad. When three semitones of one interval are compared with two semitones, the hemiolic proportion results; therefore the second division is called hemiolic.

The second division is the hemiolic, because in it the sesquitertian division predominates.

The third is called *tonia* [Note: In this place Meibomius restores the reading *toniaea*. I would prefer *tonaia* (τοναῖα), as Hesychius uses the word for a voice under tension, although Aristides in the cited passage calls the chromatic genus *teniaeum*.] because one tone is divided there into two semitones.

There are two divisions of the diatonic genus: one is soft, on account of the complete tone; the other is strong, that is, acute, on account of the hemiolic proportion.

The enharmonic genus receives its modes from the tetartemorian diesis, that is, from the quarter of a tone, for *moria* means “part.” What we called softer, namely the chromatic genus, is joined through the tritemorian diesis, that is, in the chromatic genus called soft, the tone is divided into three parts, and for this reason it is called tritemorian.

The chromatic hemiolic—that is, diatonic—genus is produced from the hemiolic diesis, that is, from the semitone in which the sesquialteral proportion appears. Its diesis is formed from the enharmonic genus: two quarter-tones separated in the enharmonic genus are joined together into one in the hemiolic, that is, in the diatonic genus, and produce the semitone from which the diatonic genus begins. It is called hemiolic diatonic because in this genus the diapente predominates, and at its extreme sounds it is joined by a sesquialteral proportion.

But now let us speak of tones. A tone is the magnitude of a space, that is, of the interval between one string and another, or one voice and another. It is called a tone because through this space the first voice of all—the first among voices and divisions of voices or strings—is extended: that is, from any note to another note, or from one string to another. For each string has its own little notation, as is found in Boethius.

Thus from the middle string, that is, from the *mese*, to the *paramese*, the string near the middle, as in the Lydian sound, the signs may correspond: from the upright iota, that is, from the *mese*, to the signs lying in the *paramese*. The semitones and dieses—that is, the quarter-tone and the third-tone, when it is called tritemorian—I have explained: what they are, how large they are, and of what kind. I have also shown the names of the modes, that is, how they are called, and their number, namely that there are fifteen.

Now let us speak of tetrachords. (For each and every mode preserves five tetrachords, as I noted above as well.) The extreme sounds of these tetrachords—the first, the *hypaton*, and the last, the *nete hyperbolaeon*—are joined to one another by a sesquitertian proportion. It is therefore beyond doubt that the extreme sounds of all the tetrachords are suited to one another.

A tetrachord is a congruent and faithful—that is, exact—concord of four sounds, or strings, placed in order. The tetrachords are those of the principals, namely the *hypaton*; of the middles, namely the *meson*; of the joined strings, namely the *synemmenon*; of the separated strings, namely the *diezeugmenon*; and of the highest strings, namely the *hyperbolaeon*.

The first tetrachord, which is the graver, begins with the principal of the principals, namely the *hypate hypaton*, and ends at the principal of the middles, namely the *hypate meson*.

The tetrachord of the principals and middles, namely the *hypaton* and *meson*, is connected, that is, joined. The tetrachord called the *synemmenon*, the joined tetrachord, is that which is joined to the tetrachord of the middles; it extends from the middle, that is, from the *mese*, to the last of the joined strings, namely the *nete synemmenon*.

Another tetrachord, divided from and far removed from these two aforementioned tetrachords, is the fourth of the divided strings. It extends from the submiddle, that is, from the *paramese*, to the *nete*, the last of the separated strings, namely the *nete diezeugmenon*. The tetrachord of the separated strings is so called because it is entirely separated from the *mese*, with which it has no consonance.

The tetrachord formed from different, that is, separated, strings begins in an acuter sound and extends into the fifth tetrachord, namely that of the highest strings, the *hyperbolaeon*.

(Enough has been said about tetrachords. Let us now examine pentachords.)

Likewise, there are evidently five pentachords. The first pentachord, the graver one, belongs to the principals, namely the *hypaton*. It begins with the Acquired, that is, the *proslambanomenon*, and ends at the principal of the middles, namely the *hypate meson*.

The following, the second pentachord, rises in acuteness and extends from the extended string of the principals, namely the *lichanos hypaton diatonos*, to that string of the middles which, in the Lydian mode, has the upright iota.

The third pentachord belongs to the joined strings, namely the *synemmenon*. It extends from the extended string of the middles, the *lichanos meson diatonos*, to the last of the joined strings, namely the *nete synemmenon*.

The fourth pentachord is formed by division. The tetrachord of the joined strings is inserted between it, whereas the remaining strings are joined together. It normally extends from the middle, that is, from the *mese*, to the third of the divided strings, namely the *trite diezeugmenon*.

The fifth pentachord rises into acuteness and is extended among the acute strings and the *hyperbolaeoi*. Alternatively, it rises into acuteness by beginning with the extended string of the divided strings, namely the *paranete diezeugmenon diatonos*, and ending at the *nete* of the highest strings, namely the last of the *hyperbolaeon*.

These matters, which I have stated, are approved—that is, praised—by the most learned philosophers of our art. I am not unaware of *litotes*, but I know that some people assert that certain tetrachords can take their beginnings from semitones, that is, from acute sounds. This belongs to diatonic modulation, about which I have said much above.

I wish it to be known and understood that the Acquired, namely the *proslambanomenon*, is placed in all pentachords that begin from a tone. But in those tetrachords in which the *proslambanomenos* does not sound in consonance, and which begin from semitones, it cannot be placed. It is added, however, to all pentachords that begin from complete tones. Those structures which are made not through sounds, that is, not through tones, but through semitones, cannot be made in tetrachords; for in these, the principles—that is, the beginnings—are always derived from a semitone.

(In the others, however, which are called pentachords, although they are not subject to the modulation made through semitones, they appear to consist of sounds, that is, of two tones; the *proslambanomenos* is added.) For in these pentachords we can place the semitone after the second string, the *hypate hypaton*.

Now the subject of transition—that is, the alteration of melodic modes—must be discussed. He calls “transition” a change, [Col. 0947C] when a transition is made from one genus to another, and from one sound to another. Transition is the alteration—that is, the transformation—of a voice into another form of sound. Transition occurs in four ways: by genus, when a transition is made from the enharmonic genus into the chromatic genus or into the diatonic genus; or by system, that is, by magnitude, when a transition is made from the principal of the principals, namely hypate hypaton, perhaps into the subprincipal, namely parhypate hypaton, or into some other system; or when we pass from the conjunct notes, that is, the synemmena, to the disjunct notes, that is, the diezeugmena; or by tone, when a song is transferred from the Lydian mode into the Phrygian or another mode. [Col. 0947D] Here “tone” is used for “mode,” since modes are constituted by sounds; or by modulation, when we leap or descend from one kind of melodic movement into another—for example, from the low register into the high—or when a transition is made from a manly song, that is, a robust or trumpet-like one, into feminine, that is, delicate, modes.

I shall next explain the genus of melodic composition, that is, [Col. 0948A] expound it. Melopoeia, that is, the production of melodies, is a disposition—that is, an arrangement by which an affected [Note: Meibomius reads “produced.”] or adapted modulation is obtained. A melos, however, is the activity of a high or low sound—that is, the song itself when it is being performed, together with its high or low sound. Modulation is the expression of a manifold, that is, varied, sound; this does not occur with a single voice, but through many different voices, namely low and high ones.

There are three species of melopoeia: hypatoid, that is, the principal species, which is low—for this reason it is called a species; mesoid, that is, middle, which is neither excessively low nor excessively high; and netoid, that is, last and high, which is produced on the smaller strings.

The hypatoid is called tragic; it is constituted by lower sounds. It is called tragic because of its low sounds, for tragic song is always grave. The mesoid, which is also [Col. 0948B] called lipara iambic [Note: Meibomius rightly ridicules this reading, since his reading, “dithyrambic,” is confirmed by Aristides.], is called lipara, that is, rich or full, because its sounds are neither low like those of the hypatoid nor high like those of the netoid. It is called iambic because of the iambic foot, which is composed neither entirely of a long syllable nor entirely of a short one. (It is called dithyrambic.) It preserves equal, that is, complete, tones—middle tones, that is, moderated and situated midway between low and high.

The netoid, that is, the last, is also accustomed to be called nomic, that is, lawful, because of the law of sharpness, or high pitch, which it observes. It receives many sounds, that is, all high sounds, from the uppermost notes.

There are also, besides these three, other intervals, which are called tropical melodies, that is, melodies suited to the modes—fifteen in number. Others are comiological, that is, appropriate to comedies. Just as comedy is intermediate between tragic and satyric poetry, so a comiological melody is said to be [Col. 0948C] appropriate to the middle. And there is also homological [Note: We cannot agree here with Meibomius, who reads “homological,” or “having a similar relation,” according to the nature of the thing. Aristides plainly also called comic modes species of melopoeia, which can be reduced to the preceding general categories; and this very exposition by Remigius supports our reading. In truth, however, this gloss too has been inserted here. We can therefore easily persuade ourselves that the glosses of two authors were appended together, or rather confused, both here and in the other passages of this author.], that is, having a similar relation according to the nature of the thing.

(But these are more suitably) substituted—that is, changed—according to the things themselves; nor will the strings themselves be able to produce or indicate their own divisions more than the material permits. These species, mentioned above, are also called modes, that is, divisions of sounds.

The melopoeiae themselves differ—that is, disagree—with one another in several ways: by genus, so that one is enharmonic, another chromatic, and another diatonic. The genus is of three kinds: enharmonic, chromatic, and diatonic; all sounds are found within these. The species, however, are found in the individual sounds, that is, in all the strings. They also differ by species: one is hypatoid, that is, [Col. 0948D] low; another mesoid, that is, middle; another netoid, that is, high. They differ also by modes, such as the Dorian, Lydian, and the others, namely the five modes.

Nevertheless, every singer—or every person—who begins a melos must first attend to the system, that is, the greater intervals of sound, which are the diatessaron, diapente, and diapason. Then he must mingle, that is, join and combine, the sounds.

[Col. 0949A] Let what has been said above about the seven parts of our art suffice. Now let us touch briefly upon rhythms, that is, numbers, since there is no doubt that this portion, this part—that is, rhythm—also belongs to our subject.

Rhythm, then, is a certain composition made from perceptible things. There are intelligible and incorporeal numbers, which are discerned by no bodily sense; and there are perceptible numbers, when they relate to sight, hearing, and touch, brought together with times—that is, suitably adapted or joined to some disposition and order, connected with the time that is present, past, or future.

Although all music is constituted by number, only the human voice is called rhythm because of the dignity of its rationality. Hence Virgil says:

> I remember the rhythms, if only I retained the words.

[Col. 0949B] Rhythm is defined again in this way: it is the ordered connection and joining of different kinds, tones, times, and feet, serving and conforming to time according to the principle of modulation, according as the voice is to be raised and lifted toward the high register, or pressed down toward the low register. Number restrains us from the license of ordinary, that is, disorderly and ruleless, modulation, directing us toward art—that is, toward something definite—and toward disciplined practice, lest the voice wander and flow away freely.

There is nevertheless a difference between rhythm and the rhythmized element. [Col. 0949C] The rhythmized element, that which can be numbered or reduced to number and art, is the material of numbers—namely, the feet, which furnish the material for numbers, since scanning is performed through feet. Number, however, like an artisan or a form of modulation, is applied—that is, added—to the material because of the material of the number itself.

Every number is therefore distinguished in three ways, namely by sight, hearing, and touch. By sight, as in things apprehended through bodily movement, that is, bodily gestures and dances; by hearing, when we attend to the judgment of modulation [Note: The manuscript copy has: “when we attend to assistance.”], whether in instrumental or human voices; and by touch, a category belonging to physicians, when we examine through the fingers the signs of the veins in human bodies, namely the pulse, for the pulses themselves occur according to rhythms, and their signs are examined. For us, that is, [Col. 0949D] for musicians, number belongs chiefly to hearing and sight.

Rhythmics, however, is the art—that is, the numerical arrangement—of everything in numbers, receiving certain patterns of its own movement, that is, its own returns, so that the voice returns to the point from which it came and acquires legitimate, that is, rational, inflections and circuits.

(There is also a considerable difference between rhythm and meter, as I shall mention later. But since sight and hearing were said by me to occur through number,) these two also, namely sight and hearing, are likewise divided into three kinds: bodily movement, that is, gesture; the method of sounds and of melodic performance; [Col. 0950A] and words, which a suitable arrangement has joined together with modes, that is, with melodies. These three elements, joined together, produce a complete song.

Number in speech is divided through syllables, which belongs to words; in modulation, through arsis and thesis, which belongs to sound, when the voice is raised or lowered; and in gesture, it is completed through determined—that is, distributed—figures and movements of the limbs, and through schemata. “Figures” and “schemata” mean the same thing.

There are seven kinds of number. The first concerns times, namely long and short times. The second concerns the counting of words, when we consider which meters or rhythms admit four parts—those which cannot fall within number because they exceed [Col. 0950B] the legitimate feet, which are four in number. Such words are judged rhythm-like, that is, similar to numbers, and are scanned in this way because a part terminates for itself where the foot ends.

Rhythm-like forms, that is, every form or species of number, are distinguished by three terms: enrhythmon, arhythmon, and rhythm-like. Enrhythmon means “numerable” and “having the form of number”; arhythmon means “innumerable,” lacking number, and falling within no fixed number; rhythm-like means “having the appearance of number,” partly resembling numbers and partly differing from them.

The third kind concerns feet. The fourth concerns the genus of those feet. The fifth is what we call rhythmic agoge, that is, ascending or conducted counting: by what kind of meter—dactylic or iambic—the number and modes of modulation are led. The sixth concerns transformations, that is, how one kind of meter is transformed into another. The last, that is, the seventh, is rhythmopoeia, that is, the production of number, namely how the generation of number can be shaped in a meter or verse.

The first kind, then, is time—the present time, when a song begins. It admits no cutting, that is, no division into parts or moments, after the manner of an atom, that is, something indivisible. In geometry this is the point; in arithmetic, the monad: a certain singular nature contained in itself, that is, self-sufficient.

Number is found in words through the syllable; in modulation, through the sound, that is, the tone itself, or through an interval, that is, a division of the tone, when it is singular—that is, indivisible and one. The greater interval is called a system, the smaller a diastema.

In gesture, time occurs through the initial movement of the body, which we called a schema, that is, a figure, as in the arrangement of the limbs. This is the briefest time, namely the present time which I said was indivisible.

Compound time, however, is artificial time, which can be divided into species and which, beginning from the first—that is, the present and indivisible—time, is either double, triple, or quadruple. Thus far [Col. 0951A]—that is, up to the quadruple number of legitimate feet—every time of number is produced. Here “time” has been used for number, or number for time.

Legitimate feet are either double, consisting of two syllables; triple, consisting of three; or quadruple, consisting of four. The matter can also be understood in another way: take two times of one long syllable as one time. In this way the number of syllables, and also the number of times, does not exceed the number four, and four is its limit. So, among created things, the number four itself is the limit, since every creature was formed according to its pattern, and it is the limit of complete reason.

For just as the number three is the first of all numbers, so the number four is the last of all numbers and the limit of complete reason. This follows from the nature of the number itself, since the number ten is formed from four and its parts: one, two, three, and four make ten—that is, monad, dyad, triad, and tetrad.

In this respect the number is found to resemble the tone, which is divided into four dieses. For just as the tone is divided into four species, namely dieses, so here the foot is enclosed within a fourfold arrangement of times: double, triple, and quadruple.

Of those times which are joined to numbers, some are called enrhythmic [Col. 0951C], that is, numerable, and others arhythmic, that is, without number and innumerable; still others are described as rhythm-like, that is, similar to numbers.

Enrhythmic times are those which preserve their order according to a definite rule, as in the double or hemiolic ratio—that is, the sesquialter or three-to-two ratio—or in the other ratios, namely the epitrites, which are joined according to another principle, namely the triple and quadruple. Arhythmic times are those which agree with one another under no law whatever and are gathered together without a definite principle. Some feet are of this kind, so that they do not agree with one another in any way, such as the amphibrach, which metricians judge to be formless and unknown [Note: Perhaps “unformed” is preferable.].

Rhythm-like times preserve number in some respects but disregard it in others. Some of these times are called strongyla, that is, round. A strongylus—στρογγύλος, “round”—is a verse in which no integral part of the speech occupies the position of a foot, as in:

> Nothing immortal is held within the structure of the world;

for in this verse no foot terminates a part of the sentence.

Others are called periples [Note: In Aristides the term is περίπλεω, or περίπλεα, or also περιπλεής; these forms amount to the same thing.], that is, superabundant.

Round times proceed more rapidly and easily than certain steps, as occurs in verses in which vowels collide, for example:

> And while these things are being carried out in a wholly different part.

Or this occurs when a part ends in every foot, as in:

> Look upon me, Father, so that you may not grant me the good things I ask for;

[Col. 0952A] and the legitimate order demands that they be rushed—that is, sung and scanned rapidly.

Periples, however, attach or impose more delays than the composed modulation requires, as in verses where a multitude of consonants comes together, for example:

> Each, having placed his hope in himself, and himself in himself,

they suspend and retard the pronunciation through slower delivery because of the frequent consonants they contain.

(Among times, some are simple, which are also called podic.) Podic—ποδικά—means “pedal” or “suited to feet,” for πούς, pous, is the Greek word for “foot.” A foot is the first progression, arrangement, or element of number—that is, of rhythm, whose form I described above—joined together by legitimate, that is, proportional and necessary, sounds.

[Col. 0952B] Those feet which are arranged proportionally are called legitimate. A foot has two parts: arsis, that is, elevation, and thesis, that is, lowering and relaxation of the voice.

(There are seven differences among feet.) The first is by magnitude, that is, quantity, when we place some simple feet and others multiple feet, one foot being greater than another.

(Simple feet include the pyrrhic; compound feet include the paeons and their equals, namely the epitrites. Simple feet are so called because they are divided only by times, that is, only according to times. Compound feet, however, are those which are also resolved into feet, that is, divided not only into times but into other feet as well.)

We call other feet alogoi, that is, irrational [Col. 0952C], because no account can be supplied for them and no principle of their division can be given. Instead, an unformed, that is, uncombined, composition is produced without any composition according to division.

There is then another difference, namely the fourth division, which is sought through division. This division is sought in the simple proportions of feet. The question is ποία, poia, that is, “of what kind?” It concerns what kind of legitimate foot is meant, that is, what kind of proportion it has, when connected elements are divided in various ways and according to several patterns: through arsis and thesis, or into an equal, double, or sixfold division (and this is the distinction by which simple feet are multiple) [Note: Meibomius’s text is better here; we have reproduced it as it appears in our Remigius.].

[Col. 0952D] There is another division, namely the fifth: the distinction by which multiple feet are different from simple feet. For simple feet can be multiple, since they are divided into two feet, and thus simple feet can be multiple. They are called multiple when they are restored into syzygies.

The sixth division is that which is customarily made through division, especially in syzygies, when a compound foot is resolved into two.

The seventh division is made through addition, that is, through comparison between two feet, when two feet are taken, compared, and considered, and one foot has the longer time, which comes first in order, as in the trochee, in which [Col. 0953A] the first syllable has a long time and the last a short one. The following time is narrower, that is, shorter. Or the preceding times are reversed in the opposite order, as in the iamb, where the short time comes first and the long time afterward; this is the reverse of what occurs in the trochee.

The kinds of rhythmics, that is, of numerical order, are three. They are sometimes called dactylic, which is an equal division; iambic, which is a double division; and paeonic, which is a sesquialter division, namely hemiolic and sesquialter. At other times they are called equal, that is, dactylic; hemiolic, that is, paeonic; and double, that is, iambic. Finally, the epitrite is also associated with them in the sesquitertian ratio.

A foot is always fitted to itself, as it were, so that it agrees as an equal—for example, [Col. 0953B] the pyrrhic, which is divided according to an equal proportion. Three in relation to two is the sesquialter, sescuple, or hemiolic number, as in the prone. A double ratio is the ratio or relation in which something stands to a single unit, preserving a twofold ratio both of syllables and of times.

The iamb and trochee have a double proportion in times, but not in syllables. The tribrach and molossus possess a double proportion not only in times but also in syllables. Four in relation to three produces the epitrite, that is, the sesquialter measure.

What we called equal we shall also call dactylic, because this division occurs in the dactyl. In the dactylic genus, therefore, the signs of times [Col. 0953C]—that is, the strokes by which short and long units are represented—are joined to one another with equal value, according to the proportion of the signs. Thus one is related to another, that is, one to one, as in the pyrrhic, which is said, according to Boethius, to be an alternative or doubled number. There the proportion is equal, one to one.

This means that all feet divided according to an equal proportion are included in the dactylic genus, since they receive their rule of division from the dactyl. When the rule proceeds from the dactyl, the other feet are considered according to the same rule.

This is what is meant by the statement: “But numerical equality will proceed either in relation to the other, or two to the doubled number, perhaps.” After the dactylic genus, numerical equality proceeds as far as sixteen feet; but that equality is in relation to the other, that is, one to one, as in the pyrrhic, or two to the doubled number, that is, two to two, as in the proceleusmatic, if one considers only the times in dactyls, anapaests, and similar feet. He said “perhaps” as though he had said: if you take feet of the same form from syzygies, the numerical quantity will be greater. For under this rule of equality there are only ten simple feet, while six are added from syzygies; or, as two are to the doubled number, two to two in the proceleusmatic, the two times are, as it were, numerous and abundant.

(The iambic genus follows; I previously described it as diplasion, that is, double, in which) [Col. 0954A] the signs of the feet, that is, the strokes, preserve a double ratio among themselves just as above: one to two, or one in relation to two, as in the iamb, (or to four) doubled, that is, two by two, as in the iamb, (or whatever proceeds according to the double ratio).

The hemiolic, or semitone, that is, sesquialter, ratio—which has been called paeonic—occurs when the signs of the feet, that is, those strokes, follow the hemiolic ratio throughout, so that there are three in relation to two. It also often occurs according to the epitrite ratio, when a foot is taken under that rule which stands as four to three. Martianus calls this the superquartile ratio. But let us now return to the order of our discussion.

The equal genus, then, is the genus of equal division. It proceeds [Col. 0954B] from the diseme, that is, the foot of two short times, such as the pyrrhic, up to sixteen feet, namely those that rejoice in an equal proportion.

The diseme is called the foot which is said first to consist of arsis and thesis, such as the lion. The double genus, that is, double division, begins with the triseme, the foot of three short times, such as the tribrach. It extends to eighteen syllables—or rather, “feet,” for syllables have been put in place of feet—until it completes eighteen feet. Of these, six are found among the simple feet, while twelve are added from syzygies.

The hemiolic, that is, sescuple, begins with the pentaseme, the foot of five times. It is completed at the number fifteen, that is, at fifteen feet. Of these, seven are simple: the amphimacer, bacchius, antibacchius, and the four paeons; eight are added from syzygies.

The epitrite begins with the heptaseme, the foot of seven times [Col. 0954C], and sets fourteen similar units—that is, units preserving its proportion. There are four epitrites among the simple feet, and ten are added in syzygies.

It should be noted that simple feet are added from syzygies not for the sake of legitimate meters but for the sake of rhythms composed of feet having similar proportions. The epitrite is difficult—that is, its use is rare—because it is seldom employed.

(We have recalled all these orders of number so that) they may be preserved throughout all the divisions for each of the individual feet.

Of numbers—that is, of these numerical forms—some are compound, some uncompounded, and some mixed. Compound forms are joined from two genera, as from the dactyl and iamb, or from several, as from the dactyl, iamb, prone, and epitrite. Uncompounded forms consist of one kind of foot, such as the dactyl, and the tetrasemes, namely the dactyl and similar feet, which consist of four times.

[Col. 0954D] Mixed forms are sometimes resolved into different feet—for example, the iamb into two iambs and the distrochee into two trochees—and sometimes into similar numbers, as the dactyl into two pairs of times.

Thus, in the hexaseme number we must understand that a foot is resolved into times: the molossus, for example, is resolved into two feet and into numerical times. It has three times twice over, and into feet it is resolved into two iambs. The molossus is therefore resolved into numerical times. Alternatively, someone might say that it can be divided into a spondee and one long syllable, which is taken in place of a pyrrhic.

[Col. 0955A] (Among those which are called compound,) some are joined by copulas, that is, by connections of feet, namely syzygies, as when we speak of composition and addition; others are joined through a period, that is, connected with one another.

The difference between a syzygy and a period is as follows: a syzygy consists only of two feet [Note: We could make no sense of what follows, since everything in the manuscript copy is so corrupt. Aristides summarizes the matter briefly: “A syzygy is a copula, a composition of two simple and dissimilar feet; a period, however, is a composition of several.”]. (A syzygy, that is, a copula, is the connected joining of two feet into one; these appear to be placed in dissimilar relation to each other. A period, however, is the composition of several feet, and) a period is produced from the copula of many feet, which are dissimilar—that is, very dissimilar—such as dispondees. They are joined together despite differing in genus and being unequal to one another according to some proportion.

[Col. 0955B] There are three differences of dissimilarity: by magnitude, by genus, and by opposition. By magnitude, when a number is composed from a diseme, such as a pyrrhic, or from a tetraseme, such as a proceleusmatic. (By genus, when) we join a diplasion, that is, double division, to a hemiolic, that is, sesquialter division, or when something is joined from several divisions in equal proportion, that is, in a syzygy. (By opposition, that is,) by antithesis, or contrary arrangement, when we place the initial disemes before much stronger succeeding units, or conversely place the tetrasemes first and attach the disemes afterward.

It should also be understood that one foot can be sufficient [Col. 0955C]. This is called a monocolon, that is, “of one member,” to complete a period, if that single foot is inserted among the others—that is, if it is unequal and dissimilar to them because it belongs to another genus.

As for those divisions which fall into a foot, that is, which come under the rules of feet, such as the simple and the remaining forms, the dactylic genus, that is, equality, is first and principal. (In this genus the feet) are called uncompounded because they are similar to one another. They are six in number: the proceleusmatic, anapaest, (simple spondee,) and the greater spondee, that is, the dispondee.

The proceleusmatic is itself a pyrrhic, which retains both a short position, thesis, and a short elevation, arsis. This same proceleusmatic most often uses the tetraseme, that is, the foot of four times. For its diseme, namely the pyrrhic, is also formed; it is a proceleusmatic but is called the shorter one because it is filled by two times. The greater one is formed from four short syllables.

The shorter one, that is, the diseme, is called syneches [Col. 0955D], “continuous” or “continued.” Hence the disease synecha is called a continuous fever, because the very persistence and frequency of the syllables following one another does not extend to any magnitude, that is, length, or to any measured division of its power into two distinct syllables. Since all the syllables are short, it should therefore be used rarely in meter [Col. 0956A], lest the constant succession of short syllables intrude upon, diminish, and wear down the poem itself, which ought to be delivered with a certain dignity.

In the mixture of other feet, which are placed as longer, the greater pyrrhic, that is, the proceleusmatic, is suitably adapted, so that by its speed it may compensate and moderate the extended delay of feet composed of long syllables.

Therefore the proceleusmatic, which is adapted to numbers—that is, to rhythmic forms—ought to begin with the quadriseme, the foot of four short times.

(The anapaest, which is called the lesser, takes an elevation of one time and makes its position two times.) [Col. 0956B] He calls the iamb the lesser anapaest because of the similarity of their syllables: the anapaest consists of two short syllables and a long, while the iamb consists of a short and a long.

A time is called monochronon, that is, “of one time,” in the anapaest—that is, in the iamb—even when a long syllable is placed there, for a long syllable normally receives two times. Likewise, when three short times are placed together, it is called monochronon, as in the iamb and trochee, in which three times are counted; or when there are four in number, as in the spondee, in which four short syllables and two long syllables are counted. All these short syllables are counted in comparison with the long syllable.

The greater anapaest, then: either the anapaest itself or the dactyl, which has the same number of times, is called greater; or he calls the anapaest greater by comparison with the iamb, which is called the greater [read: lesser] anapaest. [Col. 0956C] It will receive an elevation—that is, the elevation of a syllable, namely the arsis—which is said to be monochronon, while its position, that is, its thesis, is shown to have two times.

Therefore, when the two times in the position are placed in equal relation, the elevation ought to receive a double time, that is, one syllable must contain as many times in elevation as are contained in deposition. The arrangement must nevertheless be such that in the following time one part appears to correspond to the preceding part, namely the elevation: whatever is in the position must be equal to everything in the elevation.

For this reason, that is, according to this arrangement, we call the anapaest apomizonos [Col. 0956D], “joined upward,” and dactylic, because it resembles the dactyl. The anapaest called apelassonos, “less sonorous,” however, is composed of two short syllables in the elevation and one in the position.

The simple spondee is formed from a long syllable in both arsis and thesis. The greater spondee, that is, the dispondee, appears to admit a fourfold elevation and likewise a fourfold position—that is, eight times in all.

[Col. 0957A] Through the copula, that is, the doubling of two feet, double numbers—that is, different feet—are added. (One is from the greater ionic, the other from the lesser. The one that proceeds from the greater consists) of the simple spondee, since it has two long syllables at the beginning, (or of the proceleusmatic, which) is a diseme, that is, a pyrrhic of two short times. The one that is from the lesser—that is, the lesser ionic, which consists of a pyrrhic and a spondee—does the opposite: what the former has first, the latter has last.

(These forms) are placed in the dactylic genus, that is, in equal division, because they have an equal proportion. The uncompounded rhythms, that is, feet derived from feet, are those which precede according to numerical order. Uncompounded numbers consist of identical feet; compound numbers are joined from different feet. (The compound numbers) will all be seven in number.

[Col. 0957B] The dactyl is so called because it forms an arrangement of syllables resembling a human finger. The anapaest is so called because it returns upward in its order: anapaest comes from the verb ἀναπάιω, “I return upward,” for ἀνά means “upward” in Greek.

The pyrrhic, or lesser proceleusmatic, is so called because it was used (whether continually, in a contest, or) in a certain children’s game called the Pyrrhica, Πυρρίχη.

The spondee is sacrificial, from the verb σπένδω, spendo, “I sacrifice,” and is generally employed in sacrifices.

[Col. 0957C] The ionic is unequal because of the unequal sound of its numbers: it has two long syllables and two shortened ones. Because of the poetic form of this foot, many were often censured. For in ancient theaters they censured what was reprehensible through this foot, that is, the ionic.

Concerning the dactyls—that is, those which have a dactylic division—we have said enough. Let us now recall the iambic, that is, the double, rhythm. In the iambic kind, four uncomposed numbers, that is, simple ones, wander, or run about, vary, and range; two are composite through a coupling, that is, a syzygy; but through a period, that is, through the conjunction of many feet, there are twelve.

Those, therefore, which wander, that is, run about, uncomposed, are these. The iamb consists of half an elevation, that is, of a short time, which is brief, and of a position, that is, an arsis, which is double. (The trochee consists of a double elevation and a position that is brief.)

The orthius is the foot which consists of a spondee and a dispondee. It is called orthius, ὄρθιος, either as though “straight,” since ὄρθον in Greek means “straight,” or as though *orcitus*, that is, “honest”; for *orcita* is likewise said in Greek to mean “honesty.”

[Note: It is uncertain where this is taken from, for this is not a Greek word. Herodotus, Book I, supports the earlier explanation; according to him, an ὄρθιον song is one sung in a very high voice. In any case, all this is taken from Book I of Aristides’ *On Music*.]

It consists of a tetraseme—that is, as is the spondee—of elevation, that is, arsis, and of an octaseme, that is, of eight times, as are the proceleusmatic and the dispondee. ὀκτώ means “eight” in Greek. (It will consist of a position, so that this foot appears to have received twelve times.)

And this orthius itself has some affinity with the iambic foot, for in its first four times it agrees with the iamb, with the remaining eight times added. For just as in the iamb one is joined to two in a double proportion, so in the orthius four is joined to eight in the same proportion.

Next is the Croesus, Χροῖσος, which consists of a trochee and a ditrochee. It is called Croesus because it pleased Croesus, king of the Lydians. But if it is read “trochee,” as many manuscripts have it, then it will be so called from the trochee, which is called semanticus, that is, “slower,” because it is compressed and constricted through a coupling, that is, a syzygy.

(The trochee which is called semanticus—that is, which, conversely, consists of eight initial positions and is constricted by four brief elevations in the remaining part. The composite feet are those which are joined through a coupling. These are:)

The bacchius derives its beginning, its starting point, from the trochee, but ends with the iambic ending . . . as a complete form. Among the Greeks ἀρχή and τέλος mean “beginning” and “end”; thus, among the Latins, *finis* signifies not only an end but also a beginning. The bacchius therefore begins with two long syllables, in the manner of the trochee, but ends with one short syllable, in the likeness of the ending—that is, the beginning—of the iambic foot.

The antibacchius, which is the antispastus, takes its beginnings from the iamb and is adapted in opposition to these feet, namely the bacchius and the iamb, which we have mentioned.

Through a period there is, namely, a syzygy, because it reaches a fixed course as though by itself, that is, it runs forward. An order is that which advances along a fixed course as though by itself.

In this kind, that is, through a period, although there are twelve feet in number, it is taught by the art itself that four feet are to be taken in each period: one iamb and three trochees.

(And of these same four, the first, which is shown to contain an iamb,) is called a trochee from the iamb: that is, the trochees begin from the iamb. That rhythm which receives the iamb second, that is, in the second place, will be called a trochee from the bacchius. That which receives the iamb third, that is, in the third place, may be called a bacchius from the trochee. But that which admits the iamb fourth, that is, in the fourth place, is called an epitrite iamb.

Among those in which the trochee revolves among the iambs, those which are made from a single trochee are named as follows. The first iamb is called an iamb from the trochee. (The second iamb is called from the bacchius; or it may certainly be called the middle bacchius.) That which receives the third trochee is called a bacchius from the iamb. That which receives the fourth trochee, that is, in the fourth place, is called an epitrite trochee: that is, a trochee after three iambs.

We have, however, spoken of eight.

[Note: These things do not cohere, and no greater connection or clearer meaning can be obtained from Meibomius. We therefore judge that it should be read according to Aristides: “But four, which have two trochees and an equal number of iambs,” and so forth; thus the words “eight, however” in Martianus are superfluous.]

(Four of those twelve which we have mentioned are said to exist through a period: those which preserve two trochees and iambs in a period. And) that which receives the first trochees, namely before the two iambs, is called a double bacchius from the trochee; but that which has the second trochees is called a double bacchius from the iamb. When the middle trochees are placed in the middle, it is rightly called the middle trochee. When the iambs are placed in the middle, namely between two trochees, it is called the middle iamb.

(All those rhythms, whether uncomposed through a period or) joined through a coupling, that is, a syzygy, (have been counted as eighteen.)

The iamb is so called because the Greeks said *iambizein*, ἰαμβίζειν, “to reproach” or “to disparage.” In this kind of song the ancients used to reproach people. The name *iamb* is also derived from the fact that it pours in the poisons of a curse, that is, of malediction, or of bitterness, that is, envy. It therefore has two etymologies: either from the verb ἰαμβίζειν, “to reproach,” or from the noun ἰός, which means “poison.”

(The trochee, however, is so called because it makes a swift return, like a wheel.) Τρόχος means “wheel” in Greek; hence τροχαῖος, “rolling” or “rotating.”

The orthius consists of a spondee and a dispondee. In Greek, *orcita* means “honesty”; (it was named on account of the honesty of its position.) Semanticus means “delaying” and “holding back.” Semanticus consists of a dispondee and a spondee, (because it is slower in time,) and forms the signification, that is, the name, of prolonged stopping and remaining. Since its elevation is of such length that it is thought to include not only elevation but also deposition—that is, cessation—it is therefore called semanticus, “delaying” or “remaining.” It depicts and represents cessation and slowness.

(The bacchius is so called because it is especially suited to Bacchic sounds; and the bacchius is the dance or song which is fitted to those verses.) Bacchic means “belonging to the priests of Bacchus,” during whose rites the priests raged in frenzy.

In the kind, that is, in the division, (which is called paeonic,) two uncomposed rhythms are said to exist. Of the four paeons he makes two feet, which he also calls paeons. He joins the first and second paeon into one foot, and likewise the third and fourth into another; but the former is in a sesquialterate proportion, four to six, while the latter is six to four. They call it a double position because in it the times are doubled in one syllable; the arsis is longer, having six times, while the thesis has four.

One of these paeons is called the diagyios, διάγυιος,

[Note: Thus it is correctly found in Aristides, for whom διαγυιος means “two-membered.” Our copy has *Lydios*, to which name the interpretation also alludes. A little farther below, however, another form is given, namely λύσιος, from λύω, “to loosen.” This comes from the later Greeks in Martianus below, who also called διάγυιον λύσιυμ (perhaps λύσιον).]

from a long position, that is, thesis, consisting of two times, and a long elevation, that is, arsis, likewise consisting of two times. It is called Lydian from Lydia, because the paeon foot is abundant in the Lydian mode.

The other paeon is the epibatus, ἐπιβατός, that is, “placed upon” or “in the thesis”; epibatus means “heavy.” (It is joined by a prolonged double position and a longer arsis.) These are the numbers, that is, the feet, of the paeonic kind, which we said were uncomposed.

Nor will a rhythm arise in this kind through conjunction, that is, through a syzygy, because they are not joined from different kinds, (nor through a period). That is, in this paeonic kind, it will not advance or arrive through a period.

Hence διάγυιος, Lydios, is as though *lysios*, λύσιος, “loosened into double members.” Double members are so called either because two feet are made from four, or because in those two feet the members—that is, the feet—are doubled. (It is indeed said as though it) distinguishes double members, that is, twin feet.

Epibatus, however, is so called because it uses members, that is, feet, as though there were four: namely, because it has four syllables, or four members, four paeons, from which two differences are produced—that is, two uncomposed feet—and because it is joined by two differences, namely, that two and two are joined.

[Col. 0960B] But when all these kinds, namely all those mentioned above, have been mixed, that is, when syzygies have been made from them, the first species among the kinds of numbers will be those called dochmiac, δοχμιακά, or docimenae, that is, “approved.”

[Note: Aristides has δοχμιακά; others have δοχμαϊκόν. Remigius, in his copy, read δοκίμεναι, which he also interprets.]

The docimenae are so called from the verb δοκῶ, “I approve”; hence docimenae species, that is, “approving species.”

(The first of these is composed according to the following rule: it consists of an iamb and the paeon called διάγυιος, which later Greeks called λύσιυμ.)

The second is a species of period or syzygy, which is shown to consist of a dactylic iamb and a paeon. Those numbers which are called *deducti*, that is, extended, drawn out, or prolonged, appear to be so named because of their continuous and composite sound.

Numbers, that is, feet, are also formed which are called prosodiac, because they are pronounced under a single accent.

[Col. 0960C] Some are formed from three feet, namely from the pyrrhichius, (the iamb,) and the trochee; others from four, namely from the probacchius, (so that the first iamb is fitted to these three feet).

The bacchius is counted among the syzygies because it is resolved into two feet. Its first syllable occupies the place of the pyrrhichius; the rest is a trochee. The greater ionic consists of a spondee and a pyrrhichius. (Others, however, are accustomed to consist of two syzygies, that is, couplings, a bacchius and) the greater ionic, called *apomizonos*, that is, “greater.”

There are also feet which are said to be irrational. They are joined from similar feet, in which no profound rule is sought; we call them *alogoi*, and we are also accustomed to call them *chorii*. A chorius is called a tribrach and a trochee.

There are two such feet, namely irrational ones. One of them resembles the form of the diiambus and consists of an elevation, which is long, and two positions. The first iamb is taken as one syllable, just as in the trochee the first syllable occupies the arsis. The second iamb is divided into one short and one long in a double proportion.

If anyone asks why he has made one long elevation from one short and one long, the answer is that this foot is irrational. In number, that is, in its division, it is like the dactyl, which has one long syllable in the arsis and two in the thesis, and likewise in its syllables. But in its parts, that is, in its syllables, it is related to the number of the ionic; it is said to derive from the lesser ionic and is joined into the double, the iambic double.

(The other is the number called *trochoides*, that is, one which appears to have a certain form and appearance of the trochee, consisting of twin elevations and a long position.) It is produced in opposition to the preceding foot. It is called “in opposition” because what the former has at its beginning, this one has at its end.

There are five mixed kinds, namely numbers: the dactyl through the iamb, that is, together with the iamb; the dactyl in the bacchius, that is, the number which proceeds from and ends in the bacchius; the number which comes from the trochee that begins with a long syllable, namely the antibacchius; the dactyl through the

[Col. 0961B] bacchius, that is, the antibacchius, which has proceeded from the iamb; the dactyl through the chorius, that is, through the tribrach, in which number the chorius precedes the dactyl. Therefore it borrows its beginning from the likeness of the iamb, since the iamb and the chorius are divided in the same proportion, and it borrows and receives the likeness of the iamb. (The dactyl through the chorius appears to be expressed and formed in the likeness of the trochee.)

The cretic, or amphimacrus, is consonant with the position of the trochee—that is, with its constitution—and with the indication or sign of the number to be composed, and it provides a full apprehension and understanding of all the figures.

This is divided into the parts which are also called parts of melopoeia. They are these: λῆψις, *epilepsis*, ἐπίληψις, that is, “apprehension.” We, however, say that *epilepsis* in Greek means “suspension,” for a person is suspended, that is, alienated, by the force of the illness called “falling sickness.” *Epilepsis* is indeed the name of that illness (through which we know how much, or for how long, a number is to be used); χρῆσις means “use,” whence *catachresis*, that is, “abuse,” through which we appropriately fit positions or elevations; μῖξις means “mixture,” through which we mix together from the art whatever is suitable, namely the feet.

(The tropes, both in melopoeia and in rhythmopoeia, are three. We) call them *systaltic*, that is, “standing,” because each of them always stands uniformly, and in the harmonic and musical works these tropes, which I mentioned above, are found.

Let us understand the number, that is, the rhythm, to be masculine, and the melody to be feminine. *Melos* in Greek means “song.” (For) melody, that is, the voice, has no form by itself until the number is added. Its operation, through elevation and

[Col. 0961D] deposition, gives it form and various effects. (It is matter which, without) its proper figure, is reckoned without the dactylic and the other kinds.

Rhythm, however, calls a determinate number, and through a certain masculine operation provides both the form of the sound—whether it is raised or lowered—and various effects.

(When this harmony) proceeded with august, ample, and noble (sweetness), while the peoples of the heroes—that is, the demigods—listened attentively,

[Note: Meibomius reads: “with the demigods and the peoples of the heroes,” and so forth.]

it briefly explained these matters, and then, returning appropriately to the sweetness of songs and verses, fell silent—or held itself back.

If *continuit* is read, as this text has it, it means that it wished to persevere, so that it might prove by examples of song what it had taught through the rules of the art. But if we read *conticuit*, it means “it fell silent,” and “from the matters understood” must be supplied.

(Then, when Jupiter rose and the gods) who went before him—that is, who preceded that Jupiter—had come, the harmony itself modulated a *symesis*,

[Note: The same author has *cymesis*, but notes that it should be read *caemesis*, or κοίμησις, as though an epithalamium or a song for putting someone to sleep. Our author appears to have read σύνεσις.]

that is, a Greek word for a mixed and varied kind of song, and it reached even the maiden’s bridal chamber with great pleasure and delight for all.

[Note: Meibomius presents what follows from Martianus rhythmically. This was not possible here because of the glosses attached to it, especially since the manuscript likewise does not do so.]

You have, old Martianus—that is, my son—your old tale, now completed: the iambic senarius, a trimeter. This is the epilogue of Martianus the father to his son Martianus.

*Senilem* means “old,” “ancient,” or “aged and foolish”; for old women are delirious because of old age. *Miscillo* means “varied” or “mixed”; *famen* means a speakable or poetic tale. *Miscillum famen* is a mixed story made from truth and falsehood, which tale he composed playfully as a satire, by lamplight, or with lamps and for the lamps, because he had labored over it at night.

The Pelasgians are the Greeks. While it strives to teach them the arts—that is, the seven liberal arts—the satire calls them *creagri*, either “rustic,” “wild,” or “ingenious.” *Creager* is understood in two ways: either from *creos*, κριός, and *agros*, ἀγρός, that is, “a rustic ram”; or from *creagra*, κρέαγρα, that is, “a small fork” or “grappling hook.”

*Creagris* may mean “Attic,” “rustic,” or “sharp,” so that the sense is: while the satire strives, that is, attempts, to teach the Greeks the arts, the arts are scarcely accepted by rustic Attics; or, alternatively, they are scarcely approved by sharp Attics.

It fell into nine volumes—that is, nine books—and was completed. Seven books concern the liberal disciplines, and two were written fictionally about the marriage of Philology and Mercury. It is therefore called *Miscillum famen*, partly because it expounds the truth of the arts and partly because it invents fables.

This satire or tale is loquacious, wordy, learned, true because of the arts, and unlearned and fabulous because of the fables. Learned for the unlearned, it heaps together the arts and the fables; being at once true and false, it stuffs, fills, and intermixes things to be kept silent—false fables—among things to be spoken, namely true arts. I have narrated the mixture.

(The Muses and the gods,) the cyclical disciplines, are winding or circular; for a circle has neither beginning nor end. Thus the arts are also called cyclical because of their difficulty: they are scarcely ever grasped as perfect and complete, for no one attains perfect knowledge of them, which in Greek is called κατόρθωμα. Hence Cicero says of someone: “He had attained the *catorthoma* of the arts,” that is, perfect understanding of the arts.

The cyclical disciplines are otherwise so called because, in the likeness of virtue, they return into themselves. Therefore every art and discipline is called by the name of virtue.

*Garrire* means “to speak dishonorably”; *agresti* means “rustic”; *plasmate* means “fabrication” or “fiction.” The satire herself formed it, that is, pretended it, as she says: “Raw,” that is, new or unlearned, this very satire, *nauci*, worthless, torn, with her conscience angered, and swelling—that is, puffed up, indignant, and angry—with gall, namely the bitterness of pride, and bile, that is, poison.

With a great cloak, namely when the satire said this, she came forth; the cloak stands for every ornament. To proceed, to approach, to be approved—that is, to be praised—by learned adornments and arts: I too could have done so, with the idle phrase *comis*, “adorned,” and as though

[Col. 0963B] from the court of Mars, from the Areopagus, where the philosophers’ court was, because they were always disputing there.

(“Of blessed Capella,” he says,) with inspiration or spirit, because through you I am brought forth. I appear unlearned; rabid, insane, or most eloquent—or a babbler, as though always telling fables. Hence *rabulatio*, “babbling,” is used. The ages may see him—that is, Felix Capella—with scornful, wicked, gluttonous banqueters, with gaping mouths, and with canine, powerful barking . . . that is, growling or howling. *Pendere* here means “to be owed” or “to be rendered,” instead of “to be expended.”

The proconsular [office], however, is a part of the expression, that is, an honorable proconsular eminence, or “in the proconsular eminence.” It indicates that he was proconsul of Carthage when he wrote this book: giving or writing his fables, and with himself,

[Col. 0963C] once a “bomber”—that is, one who speaks pompously, since *bombus* means a sound and hence *bombus* denotes a noise—he is a mere flower of speech, or a superfluity of fables, or the beauty of expression.

*Decertum* (Meibomius reads *decerptum*) stands for *decertatum*, that is, “a contestant,” with the sickle, namely, when he used the expression “with the sickle,” speaking of time, because Saturn carries a sickle, and when the wheel of his age was already growing gray—that is, growing old. Saturn, the god of time, is depicted as an old man. Thus this man too was old when he wrote these books, and for that reason he says, “with the wheel of his age already growing gray.”

The blessed city of Elisa—that is, Carthage, of Dido—saw Martianus as her nursling, that is, as a youth and one brought up there. Martianus was born in the province of Lugaria in Africa.

[Note: Meibomius has *Ingariorum*. Neither *Inguria* nor *Lugaria* appears as an African province in Strabo, the Peutinger Table, or Cellarius’ account of the ancient world. Cassiodorus calls him a man of Madaura.]

He inhabited a withered—here for *marcida*, “withered” or “aged”—neighboring region, that is, a neighborhood or proximity, as a poor man, divided, and scarcely sprinkled,

[Note: Meibomius reads *obsidentem*, “occupying” or “besieging.”]

enduring and covered, sprinkled with that thing, that is, with a covering;

[Note: Meibomius reads *lucro*, “gain.”]

winking, namely at night, that is, keeping watch, because of care and study, sleepy during the daylight hours—that is, sleeping all day and keeping watch at night. Therefore, on this account, so that he might draw from the Pegasian stream, that is, the fountain of the arts, he drank suitably . . . whenever he could draw it in a cup.

He therefore gives as a witness our testament, namely Martianus, whom old age, adorned, brought forth—that is, the satire made him manifest. Thus far the satire has spoken.

You, Martianus, having followed—that is, while you follow—speak to your son: “Forgive the trifles, my son, while you read them often.”

In this final verse it appears that it is not the younger Martianus addressing his father, as occurs in some books of Martianus, but the elder Martianus addressing the younger, that is, his son, when he says: “Having followed, forgive the trifles, my son, while you read.”

The Glosses on Martianus end here.

# APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF REMIGIUS

## TWO LETTERS OF R. TO D., BISHOP OF VERDUN

(From Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, volume I.)

## FIRST LETTER

He excuses himself for being unable to go to him because he is old. He urges patience in adversity. He explains what is to be understood by Gog and Magog in Ezekiel and relates various matters concerning the origin of the Hungarians.

To the most blessed lord, truly apostolic, lover of true and eternal wisdom, D., hierarch of the holy Church of Verdun, most worthy of veneration by all, R.,

[Note: The inscription designates the writer of this letter only by the first letter of his name, R.; the person to whom it is written is designated by the first element of his name, D., and by his episcopal dignity, namely that of the Church of Verdun. Among the bishops of Verdun we find only one to whom these details apply: Dado, who began to occupy that see in the year 880 and held it until 829. At that time Remigius of Auxerre, a monk of Saint Germanus, flourished in virtue and learning and is designated by the first letter of his name. I have no doubt that he was the author of this letter; this is sufficiently and abundantly indicated near its end by these words: “All the congregation of Saint Germanus, your most faithful and devoted brothers, lords, and petitioners, begs eternal rewards for you.”]

his faithful servant and the least little servant of his servants, sends the most faithful and devoted prayers in Christ and perpetual service.

I give thanks to almighty God, and with all the strength of my heart I praise his mercy, for he has deigned to inspire your sacred mind with such great compassion that you have deigned to recognize me, insignificant as I am, and to honor me with your sacred writings, sweeter than every kind of nectar.

I say nothing of the fact that you have adorned me, undeserving as I am, with the bestowal of many gifts, although I am not even worthy to be compared with the least of your little servants. You certainly do this because you believe that I possess some usefulness, whereas I am conscious of no merit or knowledge in myself. But if there is anything of the kind in me, it is all due to the grace of him who holds the condition of man in his hand, who is the giver and governor of our life, and who very often gives his gifts even to the unworthy and undeserving.

It is entirely certain that you love this grace in all things and in each particular, because you yourself are full of it, being one who, according to the Apostle, has drawn more abundantly from the first fruits of the Spirit.

But concerning what you said—that you wished me to be with you—I am miserable, because you did not happen to wish this while my blood was still warm and nourished my marrow, and while my strength stood firm in its own blood. Now, after long old age, my decaying body and limbs weakened by diseases following one another deprive me of this desirable good.

I would certainly be with you; I would stand beside you, cling to you, be instructed by your conversation, strengthened by your example, and consecrated by your blessings. But since this is not permitted, I do what I can: I hold you in memory and longing by night and by day, and continually contemplate you in spiritual vision.

I know, most holy Father, that what you have declared—that you cannot help grieving over the miseries of Christ’s people, which we endure because our merits demand them—is entirely true. For, if I may say so with everyone’s peace, it is evident that you are either the principal person, or the only one, who groans over the calamities of the holy Church of God, whose children you see crushed by the gravest disasters and struck by the sword of divine vengeance, now drawn, now hanging over their necks.

What increases the burden of your grief is that you see some people abusing God’s power for their pride. They not only fail to repent of their sins, but even amid the scourges become worse, while they despise the riches of God’s goodness and store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s just judgment.

The prophet says of such people: “When the wicked comes into the depth of sins, he despises” (Prov. 18:3). And the Apostle says: “They are always filling up their sins.” It is therefore just that God’s wrath is brought upon such people, so that they deserve no mercy but perish forever.

For scourges are inflicted upon the elect not by an angry God but by a gracious one. Through them they are purified as through fire, and every rust of vice is melted away in them. Thus some are corrected by God’s scourges, some are trained, and others are punished. In a wondrous and ineffable manner it happens that sometimes the wicked are tolerated by an angry God, while the righteous are scourged by a gracious one.

The former are permitted to flourish for a time so that they may perish forever; the latter are afflicted temporarily so that they may rejoice eternally.

Since these things are so, thrice-blessed Father, you ought to venerate and admire the judgments of God, which are sometimes hidden but always just, and not grieve excessively over what is clearly done either for the correction of the good or for the most just condemnation of the wicked.

For has anything new happened? These things are most customary and are the lamentable complaint of the human race in general. And, not to ramble on at greater length about many matters, blessed Gregory, in the final part of the prophet Ezekiel, laments these very things, saying: “Our tribulations have increased; we are surrounded everywhere by swords; everywhere we fear the danger of death hanging over us.” And shortly afterward: “What therefore remains, except that amid the scourges which we suffer because of our iniquities, we should give thanks with tears?”—and the other things which that eminent teacher pursues in mournful lamentation.

The author of our salvation himself promised us not prosperity but adversity, saying: “In the world you will have distress” (John 16:33). But immediately afterward he deigned to console those who were terrified and fearful, saying: “Take courage; I have overcome the world” (ibid.).

Blessed Father Augustine, writing to a certain bishop who was grieving more than was proper over the ruin of his city, said among other things: “He is not great who considers it a great matter that stones collapse and mortals die.”

Blessed Gregory likewise, urging us to despise this life, says: “Far be it that those who believe another life exists and strive toward it by merit should grieve over the disturbances of the world.”

To grieve over the end of the world belongs to those who have planted the roots of their hearts in love of it and either do not know that another life exists or do not love it. And since the Apostle says, “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this age is made an enemy of God” (James 4:4), anyone who is shaken by grief over the persecutions of the world is shown to be an enemy of God.

What reason is there, then, for a wise man to grieve over the persecutions of the world, when he knows that the world will be brought to an end by those very blows?

I know that I may perhaps be presumptuous, since I speak so boldly, or perhaps irreverently, with my lord, without any modesty restraining me, as though I wished to console one in whom, by God’s authorship, the fullness of consolation and wisdom resides. But I hope that you will pardon the obedience which makes me attempt what I cannot do, and that you will not charge me with arrogance for presuming to undertake impossible things, but rather with devotion.

Amid these matters you especially ordered me to turn the attention of my mind to the last part of the prophet Ezekiel and to investigate more carefully what the prophetic discourse means when it describes Gog and Magog and the other nations gathered together with them.
