First, it must be said that the opinion which has spread among innumerable people both in your region and in ours is frivolous and contains nothing true: namely, the opinion that the God-hating nation of the Hungarians is Gog and Magog, along with the other nations assigned to them. This is especially contradicted by the words: “You shall come from the sides of the north, and after many days you shall be visited; in the last of the years you shall come to a land that has been laid waste by the sword” (Ezek. 38:8).

For they say that the present is the final age of the world and that the end of the world is near, and therefore that Gog and Magog are the Hungarians, who were never heard of before but have appeared only now, at the end of time.

But we must consider more attentively which nations are said to come with them. “Son of man, set your face against Gog and Magog, the prince of the head of Mosoch and Tubal” (ibid.). And shortly afterward: “Persians and Libyans with them, all shield-bearing and helmeted; Gomer, and so forth; the house of Thogorma, and so forth” (ibid. 5).

If, then, the Hungarians are Gog and Magog, where are the nations which are said to come with them? For, according to Josephus, Mosoch means the Cappadocians; Tubal means the Iberians or Spaniards, or, according to the Hebrews, the Italians. The Persians and Libyans are the well-known peoples of Persia and Ethiopia; Gomer means the Galatians, whom we call Gallo-Greeks; Thogorma means the Phrygians; Sabaeans are mentioned among them; and later he names the Arabs, the Vedan, the Carthaginians, and Tarsis, the Cilicians or maritime traders.

Where, then, are these nations with the Hungarians, whose names or regions they do not even know?

Moreover, when they are said to take up arrows and bows and later to possess spears, do only the Hungarians use this kind of weaponry? Almost all the eastern and southern peoples, and many other nations as well, rely upon this kind of armament. The Philistines too are read to have been especially skilled with arrows. We read that Saul was wounded by archers, and concerning David we read that, after becoming king, he ordered the sons of Judah to be taught the bow, so that they might learn to fight the Philistines with the same kind of warfare.

The Jews, and some among our own people who Judaize, reckon that Gog and Magog are Scythian peoples, savage and innumerable, extending beyond Mount Caucasus and the Maeotian swamp, beside the Caspian Sea, all the way to India. They think that after a period of a thousand years these peoples will be stirred up by the devil, so that they may come into the land of Israel and reign against the saints, gathering many nations with them.

Concerning them it is also said in the Apocalypse of John: “When the thousand years have been completed, Satan will be released from his prison, and he will go out to deceive the nations at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog,” and so forth (Rev. 20:7).

Since this book is marked beforehand by the title *Apocalypse*, that is, “Revelation,” who could doubt that the whole of it is mystical and requires revelation, that is, interpretation?

Accordingly, Gog and Magog are not to be understood as any bodily nations. Rather, by these names the most savage persecution of heretics is signified. At the devil’s instigation they rose up against the city of God, that is, the holy Church, from the corners and caves of error.

These are the corners beside which the harlot sits. She hastens to deceive young men—that is, every kind of fool—as they pass through the streets, that is, along the broad and spacious way which leads to death.

In the Gospel the Pharisees are likewise reproved because they pray at the corners of the streets in order to be seen by human beings, and they have received their reward.

Gog is interpreted as “roof,” while Magog means “from the roof.” By Gog we understand the heresiarchs, that is, the leaders of heresies; by Magog, a name derived from Gog, we understand their followers and helpers.

Gog, therefore, that is, “roof,” and Magog, that is, “from the roof,” are heretical teachers standing with their followers upon the lofty roof of pride and glorying in knowledge falsely so called. Concerning them Isaiah says in rebuke: “What is the matter with you also, that you too have climbed upon the roofs, city full of noise, exultant city?” (Isa. 22:2).

Because these matters have been expounded by Blessed Jerome, and because the brevity of the letter does not permit us to say more about them, let us come to the Gog and Magog of our own time—that is, to the Hungarians—and investigate what this people may be and what land it inhabits.

For in no histories do we read the name of this monstrous nation. And certainly there is no inland region in the world, no middle passage, no central island to which Roman power has not penetrated. Those who have pursued the name with the greatest curiosity even established, at the cost of immense labor and danger to their lives, that the outermost of all islands is [Fileta?], located beneath the very scorched [region]; [variant: “of the islands, Thule, and also the island of Taprobane, located beneath the scorched … region”], and that the Hyperboreans themselves live happily beyond our pole. Their diligence proved that the ocean is navigable in every part of the world.

Since, therefore, they came to know all regions and transmitted their knowledge to succeeding ages in writing, why did they alone omit this people of the Hungarians and, condemning it to eternal silence, choose not to know of it?

Someone may say that this people once had another name, which was changed by the passage of time, just as the names of cities, rivers, or places commonly change. For the Tiber was once called the Albula, whence Virgil wrote:

> “The ancient Albula lost its name.”

And Italy was formerly called Saturnia, as the same poet says:

> “And the Saturnian land gave it its name.”

So perhaps this nation too is recorded in the histories under another name, and, because its name changed, the people cannot be recognized.

I shall relate what I first heard from my elders. When the name of this accursed people was heard among us—whether the account is history or fable—a most terrible famine once invaded all Pannonia, as well as Histria, Illyria, and the neighboring peoples. When the slaughter of the common people was already occurring in companies, the rulers of those regions decided after deliberation that the individual households should be counted, and that from each household its masters should retain as many people as they thought they could save from the danger of famine. But the rest of the innumerable multitude, of different sexes and ages, was disowned and cast out into deserted and unknown regions. Those who led them threatened that they would put to death anyone among them who wished to return.

Thus cruelly abandoned by their own people, they wandered for a long time through vast wildernesses. At last they entered the Maeotian marshes. There, after the greater part of that multitude had been consumed by hunger, the few who were stronger and more resourceful began to devote themselves to hunting, since that region is extraordinarily rich in wild animals, birds, and fish. They lived on the flesh of the animals they captured and clothed themselves in their skins.

In this way their innumerable army grew, and from the hunger they had suffered they were called Hungarians. Relying, therefore, on their countless numbers, they left those uncultivated and savage regions and first invaded the lands of neighboring peoples. They devoted the full strength of their military training to archery, an art they had learned from necessity while living a wretched life in the wilderness.

Now, by the just judgment of God, they rage against our necks, and everywhere unbearable fear runs ahead of them. Through such monsters of humanity God is taking vengeance upon us, because, although we knew his grace, we did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but chose to serve greed—which the Apostle defines as the service of idols—and allowed ourselves finally to be taken captive from the freedom with which Christ liberated us, and to be bound patiently by the harshest chains of sins and evils.

Nevertheless, the Lord will not be angry forever, nor will he threaten for all eternity. He will remember his mercy and will not permit the triumph of the passion he endured for us to be made void. He will have mercy on those who repent; he will open the bosom of his clemency to those who flee to him; he will save his people for himself and will give glory to his name. Amen.

These are the things, O thrice-blessed lord, brighter even than light, which at your command we have been able to write. We ask that you deign kindly to receive them and, with the piety innate in you, to correct and protect them.

My brothers and lords, your most faithful and devoted petitioners—namely, the entire congregation of the most blessed Germanus—pray eternal rewards for you and render every kind of thanks for the benefits you have conferred upon them. How faithful they are to you is shown by the prayers they pour out for you privately and publicly, by night and by day.

I commend to your gentleness, my lord, as far as I dare, your personal servant E. [variant: “and”], our most beloved brother. For I know that he is greatly devoted to you and, if necessary, is prepared to lay down his life for you.

May the grace of almighty God always and everywhere guard you; may his mercy surround you; may he advance you in prosperity, protect you in adversity, and, after the long course of your life, join you with the highest priests in heavenly glory, most blessed lord bishop.

## LETTER II. Why no churches are dedicated in honor of the saints of the Old Testament

It has pleased your blessedness, most holy Father, to ask our unworthiness why, in the Christian world today, churches are not built or dedicated in memory or in the name of the patriarchs, prophets, and other saints who preceded the coming of our Lord and Savior, as is customarily done in the case of the blessed apostles, martyrs, and other saints.

The following explanation may be given. Very few of the ancient Fathers have natal days—that is, anniversaries of their deaths—handed down to memory. For the Jews, envious of every good thing, refused to commend the days of their passing or martyrdom to memory, lest the glory of those who suffered should become a greater punishment for the crime of those who killed them, and lest the revered remembrance of the former should become an eternal disgrace to their enemies.

But they gained nothing by doing this. Although the particular days were taken away from them through forgetfulness, all time is granted to them through honor. For even if we do not know when the martyrs suffered, we nevertheless know that they were martyrs.

Meanwhile, it is either impossible or difficult to find their relics, and without relics it is not customary to build or consecrate temples. Since, therefore, the natal days of innumerable holy Fathers are unknown, and nothing is found of their relics, while the death or passion of only very few is known, it follows that memorials are not celebrated for them and temples are not built. Their small number is hidden within the multitude of the others.

In this connection it should be known that in the Old Testament, after the tabernacle had been completed by Moses in the wilderness according to the model divinely shown to him, there was one temple constructed by Solomon, and nowhere else was it lawful to offer sacrifices.

All these things were then figures, since the time had not yet come for the altar to be built on which the unique Lamb would be sacrificed, bringing an end to the figurative sacrifices and demonstrating that everything which had at that time been foreshadowed in ineffable mysteries had been fulfilled in himself.

Therefore, when the sacraments of the old law had been abolished, the public veneration of the saints who lived at that time and who, both by their words and by their deeds, had set forth the symbols of future things, rightly declined, insofar as solemn worship is concerned. Thus prayers are not offered in the Church under their names, nor are chapels built.

Now, however, the veil of the figures has been removed and the light of truth revealed. Throughout the whole world, among all peoples, churches are everywhere built and dedicated in the names of the saints, to the praise and glory of the name of him who is wonderful in his saints. This will continue until we reach that one and unique temple—namely, entrance into the heavenly kingdom. After that there will not be many temples, but one temple, and it will be said:

> “Bless God in the churches.”

For there will be one Church gathered from the ten holy orders of angels and from human beings, and then God will be all in all.

This is that temple; this is that altar. Between the two, Zachariah is read to have been killed. For he says:

> “From the blood of righteous Abel,” and so forth. (Matthew 23:35.)

Abel, whose name is interpreted as “mourning” or “vapor,” signifies the saints who preceded the Lord’s Passion. Zachariah, whose name is said to mean “in the memory of the Lord” or “remembering the Lord,” signifies those who suffered, or who patiently endure suffering for the Lord from the Passion of the Lord until the end of the world.

And he is rightly said to have been killed between the temple and the altar, because between the altar of the Lord’s Passion and the entrance to the heavenly kingdom the multitude of all the saints will suffer for Christ, until the kingdom of God is revealed.

## IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 911. POPE SERGIUS III

## LIFE OF POPE SERGIUS III

*(In Mansi, Amplissima Collectio of the Councils, vol. XVIII, p. 249.)*

That infamous Sergius, relying on the very powerful arms of Adalbert, margrave of Tuscany—a man enslaved to every vice and the most criminal of all men—who together with Stephen VI had treated Pope Formosus with extraordinary cruelty, seized the seat of Christopher, not that of Formosus, as Liutprand mistakenly asserted. He was consequently regarded by everyone not as a legitimate pontiff but as an invader of the Apostolic See.

That he became pope from the presbyterate, not from the diaconate or episcopate, as Liutprand and Sigebert state, is indicated by the Acts of the Roman Council held under John IX.

Sigebert says that, driven by ambition for the Apostolic See, he went to the Franks. With their assistance he captured Christopher, the usurper, and thrust him into prison; then, having secretly entered Rome, he seized the papacy and compelled the Romans by threats and terrors to regard all the ordinations of Formosus as invalid.

Auxilius, in Sigebert, also testifies that Sergius degraded those whom Pope Formosus had ordained and imposed new ordinations upon them. At this time Auxilius wrote a dialogue against the internal discord of the Roman Church concerning the ordinations and degradations of Roman pontiffs and of others ordained by them.

Let no faint-hearted person, however, take scandal from this event. Let him remember that these things were perpetrated by usurpers and intruders, who appropriated the name of pontiff and illegitimately invaded the Apostolic Throne. By the Church’s judgment they ought to have been called not so much apostolic as apostate. Those who were legitimately created Roman pontiffs, such as John IX, vehemently detested these actions.

It is therefore not surprising that Sergius, together with Stephen, the most powerful invader of the Apostolic See, attempted and usurped things forbidden by the sacred laws. An invader of what belongs to others is a plunderer; who, then, could demand from such a man anything just or legitimate?

And although, astonishingly, Sergius was such a man, and added the most shameful unchastity to his detestable sacrilege, and fathered a son named John by Marozia, daughter of that most noble harlot Theodora, whom Liutprand discusses in Book II, chapter 13, nevertheless all the faithful—especially the northern peoples living far away—showed such honor and reverence toward the Roman Church that, whenever they heard whoever sat in it called pontiff, they venerated him, amazingly, as Peter, without investigating his accession.

Crantzius testifies in Book III, chapter 1, of his Ecclesiastical History that Sergius granted pallia to the churches of Cologne and Hamburg. Adam writes in Book I, chapter 42, that the Church of Bremen was completely exempted from the authority and jurisdiction of Cologne, contrary to what had been established by the authority of Pope Formosus at the Council of Tribur.

Thus everyone understands with what providence the good and almighty God rules and governs the universal Church. Although it was set ablaze by the will of harlots, and all evils and scandals were increasing, and there was fear that it would be torn apart by a great schism, he nevertheless defended it from every heresy and schism in such a way that the faithful everywhere among all peoples continued firmly united to it by the bond of faith and the covenant of obedience and adhered to it steadfastly.

After he had occupied the usurped see for three years, he died in the year of our Lord 910. [Note: More correctly, in the year 911, says Pagius under the year 910.] This will become clear below from the beginning of the pontificate of John X.

# LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF POPE SERGIUS III

## I. BULL OF SERGIUS III FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT GALL  
*(Year 904, 8 March)*

*[In Neugart, Codex Diplomaticus, vol. I, p. 533.]*

Sergius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of the holy Church of God.

Let your beloved religious devotion know that a certain venerable man from the regions of Germany, named Solomon, bishop of the Church of Constance and venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall, came to Rome for the sake of prayer and humbly implored the intercession of the holy apostles for his sins.

When he was received kindly and humanely by the Apostolic See, and had been admitted to the familiar friendship of our apostolate by the authority granted to him, he reported to us among other things how that same monastery had possessed from ancient times until King Arnulf—who granted this to it [Note: Moreover, Pope Sergius bestows such praise on King Arnulf because he held the memory of Pope Formosus in hatred; Formosus had crowned Arnulf.]—a power and privilege from kings or emperors, namely, that the brothers should elect an abbot from among themselves and should be subject to no human being except kings, apart from their own bishop in matters pertaining to ecclesiastical discipline.

But because this had been interrupted on his account, [Note: Through the intervention of royal authority, Solomon was succeeded by Abbot Bernard.] it became known to our apostolate that, for the love of God and affection for those brothers, he had obtained through submissive prayers from King Arnulf and from his son, King Louis, that they should once again restore and strengthen by their authoritative commands the privilege and power anciently granted by kings to those brothers, and should leave what had been strengthened to their successors forever.

This was to be done in such a way that the aforesaid brothers, if that same bishop, while still alive, wished to leave the monastery—or, if not, immediately after his death—should have the firmest authority, as stated above, to elect and appoint an abbot for themselves, and also to dispose, as they wished, of all the possessions assigned to that monastery.

The religious bishop therefore asked us, in our clemency, to confirm most firmly by a written privilege of our apostolic authority the privileges and statutes granted by kings or emperors to the aforesaid monastery.

Graciously granting his petition, we decree by the authority of our apostolate that all the matters written above shall possess inviolable stability for all time.

If anyone, which we do not wish, should presume to act against this privilege of our authority and attempt to oppose it, let him know that, unless he repents, he is to be bound by the chains of anathema and alienated from the kingdom of God. But may he who proves to be its true guardian and observer deserve to obtain blessing and grace from the Lord God.

Written by the hand of Leo, notary of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of March, in the seventh indiction. + Farewell in goodness. +

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of March [Note: I believe this is a scribal error for the eighth day before the Ides of March. Since this papal letter was written in March, it could not have been issued earlier.] by the hand of Nicholas, bishop of the holy Church of Sutri and librarian of the Holy Apostolic See, while the most pious and perpetual lord Louis, crowned by God, august emperor, was reigning, in the fourth year, and in the fourth year after the consulship [Note: The year of the consulship proceeded at an equal pace with the year of the empire, and this was almost the standard formula in papal bulls: “after the consulship,” that is, after the consulship inaugurated by the emperor. D. de Vaines, a monk of the Congregation of Saint Maur, argues in the *Dictionnaire raisonné de diplomatique*, p. 346, that this formula ceased at the end of the ninth century and that later bulls which contain it are therefore suspect of fraud. I do not, however, think that this rule should be restricted precisely to the final year of the ninth century.], in the seventh indiction.

## II. LETTER OF POPE SERGIUS III TO AMELIUS, BISHOP OF UZÈS  
*(Year 904)*

He informs Amelius that he has condemned Pope Formosus.

Sergius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy Amelius, bishop of the holy Church of Uzès.

Since the whole world bears witness that Formosus was condemned as an invader of the Holy Apostolic See, we were astonished by your letters, in which you named him among the priests.

Therefore, if this is hidden from you and has not been reported to you, learn from these apostolic letters of ours that the aforesaid Formosus has been condemned.

Nevertheless, consult the sacred canons, which we believe your holiness understands well, and you will find that a bishop may not leave his own see and invade another’s. It is evident that Formosus did this; therefore he has been condemned forever.

Furthermore, if the monastery of Saint Peter in Gothia was granted to you by our predecessors, the pontiffs Marinus, Hadrian, and Stephen, you ought long ago to have sent us a pension from it, so that the rights of the Holy Apostolic See might remain more secure for you. If it was offered by you, we have committed no offense in this matter.

Therefore, if you wish to retain that monastery, send us its pension and show in writing how you received it from the Apostolic See; then we shall again confirm the monastery to you in writing.

Nevertheless, if you can receive that monastery without scandal and with the rights of the Apostolic See preserved, receive it and pray for us.

## III. PRIVILEGE OF POPE SERGIUS III FOR THE CHURCH OF SILVA CANDIDA  
*(Year 904)*

*[In Ughelli, Italia Sacra, I, 91.]*

Sergius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our beloved and most holy Hildebrand, brother and fellow bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida, and through you to that venerable bishopric and to your successors forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid, with pious religion and benevolent compassion, of those endowed with devotion, and to grant with eager dedication the assent requested by their hearts. For the chief reward of gain is stored up with God, the creator of all, when venerable places, suitably ordered, have without doubt been brought to a better condition.

Therefore, considering the desolation of the Church of Saints Rufina and Secunda, which is called Silva Candida, suffered at the hands of the most wicked race of the Saracens—as the ruin of the place itself bears witness—and considering the population and farmsteads which are known to be almost without cultivators and inhabitants, for the restoration and repair of that holy place and for the remedy of our soul, we grant to you, brother Hildebrand, venerable bishop, and through you to that holy Church forever, the estate called Caesarea in its entirety, together with its estates called Furculae, Tondilianum, and Martinianum.

Likewise, we grant the colony of Solarium, the colony of Cortina, the colony of Gradolfus, the colony of Micinnus, the colony of Valle, or the colony of Fontana, the colony of Sanctus, the colony of Corilianus, as well as the colony of Castanea Cupa, the colony of Cabelli, and that of Caesarius, or by whatever other names they may now be called, together with houses, vineyards, farmsteads and appurtenances, and with all their boundaries, termini, and limits; lands, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, willow groves, fruit-bearing and non-fruit-bearing trees of various kinds, wells, springs, streams, perennial waters, buildings, ruined walls, sandpits, and their attached and adjoining properties.

This includes the church called Saint Andrew the Apostle, built within that estate, together with the tenant farmers and agricultural workers, taxpayers and laborers, male and female, their sons and daughters, and their grandchildren residing there or belonging to it, wherever they may be found, with every rent, payment, and due, as well as labor services, or whatever from the estate called Caesarea ought customarily to be paid in full to our Holy Roman Church.

It includes everything generally and wholly belonging to the said estate called Caesarea, situated in the territory of Nepi, twenty miles from the city of Rome, from the body of the Tuscan patrimony belonging to the Holy Roman Church, which, by God’s authority, we serve.

Its boundaries are as follows: on one side, the land of the monastery of Saint Stephen, called Major, belonging to Saint Peter; on the second side, the woodland and the land of John the Grammarian; on the third side, part of the estate of Torricius Donicus; and on the fourth side, the estate of Elodianus.

From the present eighth indiction, we give, grant, concede, and perpetually establish all this to you and to your successors in that venerable bishopric, for the use and benefit of that venerable bishopric and of the bishops who shall serve there in due course.

It is provided, however, that every day the priests and clerics of that church shall cry out in the same church, for the remedy of our soul, one hundred times “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”) and one hundred times “Christe eleison” (“Christ, have mercy”); and that the priests shall offer sacred oblations during the solemn celebrations of Mass three times each week for the absolution of our soul and those of our pontifical successors.

By apostolic censure, under the testimony of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we decree that no successor of ours, no person who has performed public functions, and no person, great or small, shall ever presume to act against this our pontifical privilege, alienate, or take away any of the aforesaid estates, together with all their places, households, tenant farmers, agricultural workers, and taxpayers, with all their appurtenances and dependencies, as set out above.

Rather, we decree that they shall remain firm, stable, perpetual, and for all time, just as we have established them.

If anyone, which we do not desire, should prove contemptuous toward this our apostolic privilege, choose to transgress it in any respect, presume to break it, or refuse in everything to be obedient and observant, let him know that, by the authority of almighty God, of our Lord and of the apostle-prince Saint Peter, whose place, though unworthy, we hold by God’s arrangement, he is bound by the chain of anathema and excluded from the kingdom of God.

But may those who, with pious intention, prove to be true guardians and observers of this our apostolic privilege deserve, through the merits and prayers of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and of the holy martyrs Rufina and Secunda, to obtain rewards in the heavenly courts, the grace of blessing, mercy from the Lord our just judge, and eternal life.

Written by the hand of Melchisedech, chief notary of the Holy Apostolic See, in the month of May, in the aforesaid eighth indiction; dated on the Kalends of June, by the hand of Theophylact, chancellor of the Holy Apostolic See.

In the year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of Sergius, lord, supreme pontiff and universal pope, the third, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter, in the third month, and in the aforesaid eighth indiction.

## IV. LETTER OF SERGIUS III TO ADALGAR, BISHOP OF HAMBURG  
*(Year 905)*

He vindicates the rights of the Church of Bremen.

*[In Mansi, vol. XVIII, p. 251.]*

Sergius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends apostolic blessing and paternal consolation to the most reverend and holy Adalgar, bishop of the Church of Hamburg.

Having received the letters of your brotherhood and learned of the injury inflicted upon your Church and upon you—not only concerning that injury, but also concerning the wicked consent of Pope Formosus and the unjust circumvention by Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, the archbishop of Mainz, and other bishops, and …—we were deeply grieved.

For what is more injurious than to deprive Churches of honors justly granted to them? What is more unjust than to violate and break the many privileges of the apostles granted by the charters of emperors and kings? Nothing further shall be established by us or by our successors in the Church as ratified, firm, or stable.

But since, according to the Lord’s words, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church,” and according to the Apostle’s words, “You have been built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone,” it is clear that the holy and universal Church has been founded upon the rock and upon the foundation of the prophets and apostles, and has been joined together in Christ Jesus himself, the firmest cornerstone.

It is therefore necessary that, just as that rocky and apostolic foundation and that holy joining in the cornerstone are firm, eternal, and immovable, so every ecclesiastical superstructure should be valid and stable and inviolable against every human presumption.

We therefore act according to the Lord’s and the Apostle’s voice and according to this judgment of blessed Gregory: “Whatever privileges have once been granted to a Church ought thereafter to remain valid and stable.”

Accordingly, whatever was rashly perpetrated against you and the Church of Hamburg by the wicked consent of Pope Formosus and King Arnulf, and by the machinations of Archbishop Hermann, we oppose and utterly destroy by our authority, by the judgment of many of our fellow bishops, and under anathema.

Whatever was granted to the Church of Hamburg by Pope Nicholas and our other predecessors—namely, that it should possess archiepiscopal authority over the kingdoms of the Danes, Norwegians, Swedes, and all the northern nations, and that the Church of Bremen and the Church of Hamburg should be not two Churches but one Church and one diocese—we decree and confirm.

Therefore, by apostolic authority and censure, under the invocation of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we establish that no person, whatever his order or dignity, shall alter what was granted by our predecessors to your Church and to you, whether concerning archiepiscopal dignity or concerning the union of the Churches of Bremen and Hamburg, and which has been restored by us.

Whoever changes or presumes in any way to violate these provisions shall, by the authority of God, of blessed Peter the Apostle, and of us, who exercise his vicarious office, be bound by the chain of perpetual anathema.

As for Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, and Haddon [Hatto], archbishop of Mainz, we have suspended them from divine office as a penitential satisfaction until the time fixed by us, because at Tribur the privileges granted by the Apostolic See to your Church and to you were unjustly annulled by them, and the charters of the glorious emperors were invalidated.

We have also, as you requested, admonished by apostolic letters Wigbert and Biso, your most reverend neighboring bishops, to assist you, to come to you, and to ordain bishops in those places where you find them canonically necessary and where suitable reason indicates.

Therefore, most holy brother, let your holiness pray for us and for the universal holy Roman Church, and report to us how and where you have ordained bishops.

Given by the hand of Peter, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Nones of February, in the third indiction.

## V. PRIVILEGE OF SERGIUS III FOR THE CHAPTER OF ASTI  
*(Year 907)*

At the request of Bishop Audax, he confirms the possessions of the chapter of Asti.

*[In Ughelli, Italia Sacra, vol. IV.]*

Sergius, venerable pope, servant of the servants of God, to all the priests, deacons, clerics, and canons serving according to the established number in the canonical institution of the bishopric of Saint Asti, constructed by the reverend and most holy Audax, bishop of the Church of Asti, for the remedy of his soul and for the praise and honor of almighty God, and to them and their successors forever.

Since by divine institution we have been placed at the head of all the Churches of God, we ought humbly to incline our hearts to those who ask, to grant them assistance from our own resources, and also to extend the arm of apostolic gentleness toward the confirmation of what they have built, so that what they have established in holy and inviolable statutes may remain perpetual.

Those who seek apostolic help—without which nothing in ecclesiastical affairs appears complete—we ought to strengthen with the great power of our authority, according to the power granted to us by blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

Therefore, at the request of Audax, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Asti, we confirm by privilege all the priests, deacons, clerics, and canons serving according to the established number in the canonical institution founded by him, together with its cloister, constructed beside the basilica of our Lady, the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, in his Asti bishopric.

We confirm to them all the possessions which the same reverend and most holy Audax appears to have conferred upon this canonical institution for those serving there for the remedy of his soul.

These are: one estate called Quartum, and another small estate called Azanis, situated beyond the river Tanaro, which his predecessor Ehilulf had conferred upon the Church of Saint Mary, together with all the property and households belonging to the aforesaid estates.

Also, all the tithes payable from them, so that the canons of the aforesaid canonical institution and their ministers who serve there in due course may possess and administer them in their entirety for their own and common uses, according to what ecclesiastical and canonical rule prescribes, without any contradiction from us or from our successors.

Likewise, one parish dedicated in honor of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of God, situated in the village called Pisentiana, with its titles and all their tithes, together with all the property and households belonging to that parish; also the tithes of the city of Asti and the tithes of the villages which are paid to its Church in due course; likewise the vineyard which lies near the wall of Saint Mary, together with its cloister and all that belongs to it.

We establish and confirm by our apostolic authority all the aforesaid places, with their appurtenances and tithes, in the same way in which they were granted by the same most holy Bishop Audax to the aforesaid canonical institution and to those serving there. We decree that they shall possess them in their entirety forever, in a quiet and peaceful manner.

By apostolic sanction we forbid any person of any office or dignity to disturb the canons who are established from time to time in the aforesaid canonical institution concerning the matters written above and granted to that institution, without daring to do so in any way.

Rather, we admonish everyone who has the power to do so to provide assistance to the canons of the aforesaid canonical institution for the love of the apostles named above, so that they may serve almighty God at all times without any disturbance.

We also decree by this our apostolic authority that the privilege which the aforesaid Audax, venerable bishop, established forever in the aforesaid canonical institution and for its canons concerning the aforesaid property, possessions, tithes, parishes, and estates, with all their appurtenances, shall remain unshaken.

If anyone should presume to act against our apostolic censure, attempt to diminish the property of the aforesaid canonical institution, or in any way try to break the privilege confirmed concerning these matters, let him be excluded from the thresholds of the Holy Church of God until he repents and comes to full satisfaction before the priests.

Written by the hand of Melchisedech, chief notary of our see, in the month of May, in the tenth indiction.

+ Farewell in goodness. +

On the Nones of May, by the hand of Theodore, archchancellor of the Apostolic See, in the year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of Sergius, lord, supreme pontiff and pope of the universal world, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter, in the eleventh indiction.

## VI. LETTER OF SERGIUS III TO LEOPARD, ABBOT OF NONANTOLA  
*(Year 907)*

He confirms the privileges of the monastery.

*[In Ughelli, cited above, vol. II.]*

Sergius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Leopard, religious abbot of the monastery of Nonantola.

Having read the letters of your humility, we were deeply grieved concerning the monastery of Nonantola entrusted to you, and concerning the flock committed to your care, which is suffering various hardships.

For we hear that your monastery was ravaged by the sword of the barbarians and burned by those same men, and that you yourself, together with your people, have been disturbed by the attacks of evil men.

But trust in the mercy of almighty God and, aided by the intercession of the blessed apostles, take courage because you have prevailed to this extent: after so many scourges and through the struggle of your labor, you have raised the church of your monastery to its summit.

We decree that it, together with your entire monastery, shall remain under the protection of our Apostolic See, just as it was under the time of our predecessors, for love of blessed Silvester, pontiff of the Roman See, which by God’s authority we serve.

We ought to assist and protect you wherever you may be, and we shall gladly extend the right hand of our pontificate to you, confirming whatever privileges were granted to your religious and holy monastery of Nonantola in ancient times.

Furthermore, if you are seeking a bishop to consecrate the church of your monastery, we do not wish you at this time to ask anyone to consecrate that church except John, venerable bishop of Pavia, or Guido of Piacenza, or Elbungus of Parma, most reverend bishops. Choose whichever of these three you wish and bring him to consecrate your church.

## VII. PRIVILEGE OF SERGIUS III FOR THE CHURCH OF VIENNE (908)

He confirms the privileges and possessions of the Church of Vienne and specifically assigns to it the churches of Maurienne and Susa.

[Bosco, *Bibliotheca Floriacensis*, left-hand section, shelfmark 57.]

[Col. 0978C] SERGIUS, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brother ALEXANDER, archbishop of the holy Church of Vienne, and through you to your Church forever.

Since great concern persistently urges us to watch over all the Churches of God and pious places, lest they suffer any loss through necessity, but rather obtain the resources of their proper benefit, it is therefore fitting that, with complete pastoral integrity of mind, we should especially provide for the full stability of these venerable places and diligently confer support upon their interests. Thus what we are known to have bestowed upon venerable places for the honor, praise, and glory of the divine majesty of our almighty Lord and God may be acceptable to him, and, through his richest mercy, a worthy reward for such a pious work may be granted to us in the heavenly courts, with everlasting recompense.

Therefore, since your Holiness has requested that we confirm a privilege for the holy Church of Vienne, over which, by God’s authority, you appear to preside, moved by your prayers, through the page of this privilege we ratify and establish with perpetual stability for you and for the aforesaid Church of Vienne whatever pertains to the dignity of your priesthood, and whatever possessions and properties your Church appears to possess or to have possessed, both in parishes and among suffragan bishops. Together with all the clergy, we grant you complete authority, under the confirmed right of the privilege which the most blessed Pope Sylvester established for the seven provinces of your Church.

Accordingly, together with everything that our predecessors conferred upon your predecessors, we decree that this same privilege shall remain forever unshaken and inviolable for your Church. We order and, by apostolic censure, command that the customary payments owed annually to your Church, both by the suffragans and by all the churches established within your diocese, be rendered without delay or excuse.

Whatever the Church of Vienne appears to possess or to have possessed, including households—that is, ecclesiastical servants—and slaves of either sex, in whatever territories and places they may be, whether granted to it by kings or by pious persons, we confirm to you and to your successors for perpetual possession under eternal right.

And [lacuna] King Guntram, with the consent of the Apostolic See, made the Church of Maurienne, with all its districts, subject in perpetuity to the holy Church of Vienne; thus, together with the Church of Susa, the churches belonging to it in the same valley, and all the districts, we confirm it to be wholly subject to that Church.

We prohibit anyone, whatever his dignity or order, from ever presuming to diminish in any respect you, your successors, or your Church in their rights and dignity. Rather, we command all the faithful to observe this apostolic admonition, so that, while preserving the reverence due to honor, they may receive the blessing of our apostles and of us; and henceforth may the ordinances of the holy canons and the established institutions remain unimpaired, so that the Creator of all things, God, may confer upon us above all the reward of profit.

But if anyone—which we do not wish—should presume, with criminal audacity, to oppose or in any way transgress what we have established for the praise of God and the protection of your holy Church, let him know that he is bound by the bond of anathema and appointed to be burned with the devil, his most dreadful pomp, and Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the punishment of eternal fire.

But whoever, with pious regard, observes and guards in every respect this apostolic constitution, looking toward the worship of God, may obtain the grace of blessing in abundance from our most merciful Lord God and deserve to become a participant in eternal life.

Written by the hand of Sergius, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, indiction 11. Farewell.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, by the hand of Stephen, chief of the defenders of the holy Apostolic See. In the fifth year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of Lord Sergius III, pontiff and universal pope, in the most sacred seat of the blessed apostle Peter.

## VIII.

[Note: In this forgery of the bull, the forger of the Hamburg archives has entangled posterity in almost inexplicable complications. For although the copy that appears to present the form of the archetype ends with these words: “Written by the hand of Stephen, notary of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of May and indiction 6,” in the old copies one reads not only, more correctly, “indiction 14,” but also the following addition: “Given on the Kalends of June (III), by the hand of Theophylact, treasurer of the Holy Apostolic See, in the eighth year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of Lord Sergius, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the most sacred seat of the blessed apostle Peter, indiction 14.” Since these words could have been drawn only from the genuine document, how did it happen that in the very closing clause, where the reliability of the archives is chiefly understood, the text departed from it? JAFEL.]

## LETTER OF SERGIUS III TO HOGER, BISHOP OF HAMBURG (911)

He sends the pallium to Hoger.

[In Lappenberg, *Hamburg Documents*, vol. I, p. 37.]

[Col. 0980A] SERGIUS, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy HOGER, bishop of the holy Church of Hamburg: apostolic blessing, and, through the grace of God, the attainment of rest worthy of eternal life.

If shepherds of sheep are content to endure sun and frost day and night in the protection of their flock, and so that no [lacuna], we are judged.

But the pallium, for your Holiness, on [lacuna] Mary, likewise on the day of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, on the feast-day of your church, and on the day of your birth, as [lacuna] may be assumed. Since, on account of this garment, [lacuna], let the impartial find favor; let the good recognize you as kind, the wicked as strict; let an evil accusation not make an innocent man guilty before you [lacuna].

Behold, dearest one, these among many other things are the duties of the priesthood; these are the duties of the pallium. If you diligently observe them, what you show that you have received outwardly, you will possess inwardly.

May the Holy Trinity surround your Holiness with the protection of its grace, direct us in the way of its fear, and grant that, after the bitterness of this life, we may together deserve to reach eternal sweetness.

Written by the hand of Stephen, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May and indiction 6.

## IX. PRIVILEGE OF POPE SERGIUS III FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MARTIN OF TOURS (904 [or 911])

After the devastation inflicted upon Tours by the Normans, he confirms the monastery’s privileges.

[Works of Launoy, vol. III, part II, p. 36.]

[Col. 0980C] SERGIUS, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to all priests, canons, and clerics, present and future, and to those serving in the monastery of the most blessed confessor of Christ, Martin, which is called the monastery of Tours, and in the basilica of that same Saint Martin: greetings.

The mystery of the divine dispensation has mercifully provided that the solicitude of pontiffs should diligently attend to this matter, since the same Shepherd of shepherds determined to entrust the care of faithful peoples to shepherds appointed by him, saying to Peter, the prince of the apostles: “If you love me, feed my sheep.” And again: “Behold,” he says, “Satan has demanded you, to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers.”

Therefore, as is fitting, lest the Lord’s flock be torn apart by the savage bites of wolves, or be wrecked without protection amid the turbulent storm of tempests, let it be defended by a pastoral sword, supported by a staff, and raised up by assistance.

Accordingly, the holy Roman Church, carefully consulting the interests of holy fraternity, through Sergius, pontiff of that Apostolic See, determined to bring to the knowledge of many of the faithful how, through the envoys of Erbernus, archbishop of the holy metropolitan Church of Tours, and through Robert, abbot, and Rainald and Tetolo, it had learned of the monastery of the most blessed confessor Martin’s grievous ruin and desolation. Namely, how that place had suffered the sad evil of destruction at the hands of the faithless Norman people, and how it had endured the dangerous losses caused by the destructive movements of that fleet’s army.

But for the restoration of that place and for the support of the clergy established there, Charles, prince of that kingdom, after consulting his faithful, sought, as an act of his piety, to renew and issue a command of his authority from the property specially belonging to that place and to the brothers of that congregation, and from the privileges of our apostolic predecessors and the commands of orthodox kings, assigned under their proper names. His purpose was that, removed from secular cares and separated from worldly snares, and devoted to heavenly service, they might freely apply themselves to their daily ministry.

Accordingly, under pastoral consideration, the aforesaid prince, together with a college of priests and many faithful, sent the said command to the gentleness of our fatherhood and, by humble petition, determined that a privilege of confirmation from this holy Roman See, which by the Lord’s authority we serve, should be sought for the sake of greater and more abundant firmness. Thus, with the sheep entrusted alike to the priest and to the king fortified by protection, they might attend to the divine commands without stumbling.

In assent to the decree of generosity, and likewise to the wishes and prayers of so many faithful, we establish and confirm by the decree of this holy Apostolic See that, as the text of the same command contains, and as the ordinances of our holy apostolic predecessors—namely Gregory, Leo, Adeodatus, Adrian, and Nicholas—and, in addition, the commands of emperors and kings, namely Charles Augustus, Louis Augustus, and the other illustrious Augustus Charles, clearly demonstrate, whatever special privileges remained to the clergy of Saint Martin after the fires of the Normans shall be preserved.

Specifically, no administrator of public affairs, whether of higher or lower rank, shall presume to enter their churches, villages, dwellings, or territories, wherever they may be located in provinces or districts, to hear lawsuits; nor shall anyone presume to constrain their free or servile dependents or take sureties from them. No one shall exact tolls or transport dues. The tithes and ninths from all their possessions shall be rendered in full, without any opposition from bishops or princes, for the use of their household and of their noble and poor members.

Moreover, whatever other benefit their other apostolic privileges, the commands of bishops, and the decrees of emperors and kings preserve for them, as well as the prebends granted, with the permission and consent of the aforesaid lord Robert, their own abbot, by the present king Charles through a written command, and those to be granted in the future, together with all their appurtenances, they shall possess perpetually and in full, just as we have stated above. No person holding any power shall presume to take anything from their dominion or possession.

In this way the dignity of the kings, in their mercy, determined to bestow benefits upon the brothers dwelling in the same monastery of blessed Martin.

But whoever attempts to violate the institution of this constitution, or tries to overthrow it by any presumption or pretext, or attacks the tithes lawfully subject to their authority, shall know that he will suffer the burden of perpetual damnation with the transgressors of holy law, unless he corrects by worthy satisfaction what he has attempted through rash greed.

Since, therefore, the Lord has granted us through blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the power of binding and loosing, saying: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven,” relying upon the confidence of this power, we close the entrance of heaven with the barrier of anathema against the malice of greed for anyone who consents to or cooperates in the subtraction of the goods and honors granted through this most necessary benefit, unless, as we have stated, trusting in divine aid, he repents through the act of correction, restores what he has seized, and makes satisfaction for what he has neglected.

We ask all the faithful to observe inviolably the judgment of this definition and apostolic determination. So that it may be believed with greater certainty and observed without dispute, we have taken care to record it with our own subscription and decree that it remain forever.

Written by the hand of Leo, chief notary of the holy [Col. 0982D] Roman Church, in the month of May, indiction 11. Farewell.

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 911. BLESSED NOTKER THE STAMMERER, MONK OF SAINT GALL.

[Col. 0983]

## HISTORICAL EULOGY OF BLESSED NOTKER BY MABILLON

(*Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. VII, p. 11.)

[Col. 0983A] 1. Among the illustrious monks of the celebrated monastery of Saint Gall in Helvetia, NOTKER, surnamed the Stammerer, is by no means to be counted least. Ekkehard wrote his Acts in the thirteenth century; he must be distinguished from four other monks of the same place and name: the first was dean under Otto I; the second was chaplain and teacher of Otto II; the third was likewise dean in the eleventh century; the fourth, called Junior in relation to this one, composed around the year 1040 a book on the misfortunes of the monastery of Saint Gall, in which certain deeds of Notker are reported; while the fourth mentioned above was the author of the Life during the pontificate of Innocent III.

I am reluctant to reprint here this life, full of errors, especially since it may be found in Canisius, volume VI of the *Ancient Readings*, in Goldast, and among the Bollandists under 6 April. I have therefore thought it preferable to compose Notker’s eulogy, insofar as possible, from Ekkehard and other authorities.

But lest confusion arise here from the shared name, as it does in Ekkehard, the author of the Life, it should be noted that three Notkers succeeded one another in the same place within a short interval: the Stammerer, whom we are undertaking to discuss; Notger of Liège, who became bishop after having been a monk; and Notker the abbot, nephew of another Notker, “whom,” says Ekkehard Junior in chapter 9, “they surnamed Pepper-grain because of the severity of his discipline.” He was a teacher, painter, physician, and poet.

These men flourished in the tenth century; in the eleventh century there was Notker Labeo, honored with the name “Blessed,” and in the thirteenth century Notker, most learned and most kind. We must first discuss the Stammerer.

2. Ekkehard, the author of the Life, gives an etymology of the name Notker, as though it meant “one who necessarily desires,” where Papebrochius notes that *Noth-ghere* signifies “desire,” or “one desiring necessary things.”

“Blessed Notker was therefore born in the district called Thurgau, in a village called in Latin *Sacer-pagus* and in the vernacular Heiligowe, of most noble parents,” as it is said; and, if this author is to be trusted, his parents’ lineage was of the family of the Carolings and of the blood of the ancient Saxons. He is wrongly called by the same writer a grandson of Charlemagne, Charles the Bald, or Charles the Fat.

Ekkehard Junior says nothing about his family except that he was born of distinguished and illustrious parents at the beginning of chapter 1, and that in chapter 9 he is said to have had a niece named Kerhilda. This is the Kerhilt who, according to Hepidannus, “in the year 952, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, on the sacred day of the Lord’s Ascension, was clothed in the holy veil and enclosed on the Nativity of Saint Mary.”

He received the surname Stammerer because of an impediment of the tongue. Hence, in his hymn on Saint Stephen, in Canisius, volume V, p. 776:

> Sick and stammering, full of faults,  
> With polluted mouth I sang the triumphs  
> Of Stephen, unworthy Notker, at the command  
> Of the holy bishop.

[Col. 0984A] As a boy he was offered to Saint Gall around the year 840. He had Marcellus and Iso as teachers, as he himself testifies in the letter to Liutward reproduced below; his principal fellow students were Tutilo and Ratpert.

“Iso the teacher,” says Hepidannus, “died in the year 851, on the day before the Ides of May.” Ekkehard Junior describes his deeds, especially in chapter 2, where he is called the son of holy parents. It is reported that, at the request of Rudolf, king of the Burgundians, he taught letters among the monks of Grandval in Alsace, where he also shone through miracles and died. His body, buried in the church of Saint Germanus, is believed to have been transferred to Burgundy.

Marcellus was discussed at length in part II of the fourth century of the Benedictine era. According to Ekkehard Junior, chapter 3, he led Notker, Ratpert, and Tutilo “through the seven liberal arts, but especially through music.”

From this it is possible to determine the age of Notker the Stammerer, especially from the time of Iso, his first teacher, whom, as we have just said, he died in the year 871. Therefore Notker was living among the monks of Saint Gall long before that year, undoubtedly during the reign of Charles the Bald, not Charlemagne, as many recount from the fabulous Ekkehard.

Some do not properly understand these words of Ekkehard Junior in chapter 1:

> “After a time, the cloister school was entrusted to Marcellus, with Notker, later surnamed the Stammerer, and the other boys in monastic dress; the outsiders, that is, the canonical students, were entrusted to Iso, with Solomon and his companions.”

The former words signify that the cloistered, or inner, schools were entrusted to Marcellus, whose pupils were Notker and the other younger monks. This occurred under Abbot Grimald after the year 841.

3. It is worthwhile to explain what discipline was like at Saint Gall during that period. Solomon the canon, educated in the outer schools, although he held a benefice and had been admitted among the enrolled brothers, could not obtain admission to the cloister unless he made a vow that he would one day become a monk, wearing a monastic cloak which he would remove upon going out to the threshold of the cloister.

Ekkehard Junior gives an amusing account of the matter in chapter 1:

> “At that time,” he says, “the senate of our commonwealth was exceedingly holy. Hartmannus, great in counsel—the man who composed *With Humble Prayer*—was consulted, as were Notker, who composed the Sequences; Ratpert, who composed *The Lofty Hope of the World*; and Tutilo, who had composed *Today He Must Be Sung* and many other works. They had learned his character when they were fellow students.
>
> “Hartmannus said: ‘He is seeking not the likeness of a monk but the monk himself.’
>
> “Notker said: ‘If he desires this outer garment which I have put over myself, I would not object if he were to offer a robe.’”

It was granted that he might enter the cloister wearing the cloak, provided that he would at some time become a monk. He agreed.

> “In return for this favor he prepared a notable cross for Saint Gall. For twelve days each year, that is, on the Kalends, our man in the outer garment used joyfully to provide banquets for the brothers, as long as he lived in the world.
>
> “Some other enrolled brothers had previously been accustomed to offer the same sign of charity to our people. Above all, King Charles, surnamed the Fat, who himself, during Saint Othmar’s week, served as host and cupbearer for three days from the village of Stainhem and made us eat poultry.
>
> “Adalbero of Augsburg, too, a bishop for a long time, having heard from many people about the place and the miracles of Saint Gall, came to the site on Saint Gall’s day to pray. Seeing many things there in person, he said: ‘The grace of this place is greater than the report I heard.’
>
> “When he returned there a second time, he said: ‘I do not know what the others think; I will declare what is in my own mind. I sought one holy man, and that man dead, but I found living brothers who, if I speak truly, are most holy. Their learning and discipline can be seen in their works of virtue.’”

What was later done by the Emperor Otto to investigate the discipline of that place will be explained below.

4. I return to Notker, who was so closely joined with Ratpert and Tutilo that “they were one heart and one soul,” as Ekkehard Junior says in chapter 3:

> “They were united in their desires. Notker was slender in body, though not in spirit; stammering in voice, though not in courage; upright in divine matters, patient in adversity, gentle toward all, but strict in exacting discipline from our people. He was somewhat timid in sudden and unexpected situations, except when confronted by attacking demons, whom he was accustomed to oppose boldly.
>
> “He was most assiduous in praying, reading, and composing; and, to sum up briefly all the qualities of his holiness, he was a vessel of the Holy Spirit, of which there was none more abundant in his time.
>
> “Tutilo was a good and useful man, a musician, cheerful in seriousness and in jest.
>
> “Ratpert had been master of the schools from adolescence, benevolent but stricter in discipline, rarely advancing his foot beyond the cloister except for the brothers. He called excursions death and often warned Tutilo, as a traveler, to beware. He called impunity the greatest stain of the cloister.
>
> “Since these three were senators of our commonwealth, as is always the case with learned and useful men, they endured continual slanders and backbiting from those who were idle and walked in frivolity. This happened especially because holy Lord Notker, to speak truthfully, was less accustomed to refute them.”

Ekkehard then adds the story of a certain monk named Sindolf, who, because he was especially hostile to Notker, was put in charge of the workmen by Solomon, bishop of Constance and abbot.

> “It was the custom of those three inseparable men, with the prior’s permission, to meet during the interval of the night office in the scriptorium and to hold conversations about Scripture especially suited to that hour.
>
> “Sindolf, knowing the hour and their discussions, secretly approached one night from outside the glass window beside which Tutilo was sitting. Pressing his ear against the glass, he listened to see whether he could seize upon anything that he might distort and report to the bishop.
>
> “Tutilo, a stubborn man who relied upon his strength and addressed his companions in Latin so that the man who understood nothing would not perceive it, sensed him.”

Then, because Notker was timid, he was ordered to withdraw into the church, while the other two received the man splendidly, having seized the brothers’ whip that hung from the *pyralis* [object uncertain]. Ratpert carried this out; he was a man exceedingly sharp in matters of discipline.

5. “At that time,” Ekkehard Junior continues in the same chapter 3,

> “there were at Saint Gall other holy monks whose righteousness before God is not forgotten. We have heard many distinguished things about their deeds. Among them were Hartmannus, himself the most learned abbot of the monastery after Solomon; Waltramnus, whose melodies, too, do not conceal what he was; Rueggerus, whom we mentioned above; and many others, holy among the holy and chosen among the chosen.
>
> “Since it would be too long to recount everything we have heard about them, let us believe that the three whom we have selected as examples will suffice for posterity.”

6. “But Notker was always the same and always new, day and night; what Ratpert did in the schools, he himself did in the cloister, exercising every discipline of charity except the use of blows.”

From this we understand that Notker was placed in charge of the cloistered, or inner, schools.

> “With the prior’s permission, and even more at his urging, the younger boys who were still capable, day and night whenever they rested from prayers, were as though lying in ambush”—that is, under observation, and specifically under Notker’s observation.
>
> “For no hour was called unsuitable”—Saint Benedict calls those unsuitable hours in chapter 48 when the brothers are not permitted to converse or meet together—“if someone was speaking with Lord Notker while holding a book.
>
> “But because, in accordance with the rule, he sometimes drove them away with hisses and noise, the abbots imposed upon him by obedience what he had refused to do.”

How honey-sweet he was in his answers is testified by the tears of those who saw the man.

7. “Indeed, through the Spirit of God, he foretold many fortunes or misfortunes to good and bad alike, as, for example, in the case I shall recall above concerning a certain proud-spirited chaplain of Charles.

> “When that king came to the monastery, as he was accustomed, to perform acts of charity for the brothers, and stayed there for the entire three days out of reverence for those living there, and, as Ratpert also writes, having been generous to our holy men, was preparing to depart after the abbot had already *musato* [reading/meaning uncertain], that proud-spirited chaplain saw the man of God sitting with his psalter, as usual.
>
> “Recognizing that this was the man who had solved the questions Charles had put to him the previous day, he said to his companions:
>
> “‘Behold, this is the man whom they say is more learned than anyone in Charles’s kingdom. But, if you wish, I will test that exceedingly learned man for your amusement and ask him something that a man of such great reputation certainly does not know.’
>
> “When they eagerly urged him to do this, they all approached and greeted him. The humble man rose and asked what they wanted.
>
> “Then the wretched man we have mentioned said: ‘We know, most learned man, that you know everything. But if you know, we wish to hear from you what God is doing in heaven now.’
>
> “‘I know,’ he replied, ‘and I know very well. For he is now doing what he has always done, and certainly what he will soon do to you: he exalts the humble and humbles the proud.’
>
> “The tempter and mocker departed, mocked by his own companions, paying little attention to what he had said would happen to him.
>
> “Immediately the signal was sounded for the gathering and the praises of the emperor who was about to depart. The wretched man, destined for misfortune, seized the standard by which he was to precede the lord of his order that day. Riding proudly on horseback, he encountered an obstacle before the city gate, fell, and, striking his face miserably, broke his leg.
>
> “He was entrusted to Berinhard, who was to care for him under the new abbot, Hartmuot, who had been appointed as his successor. When Berinhard himself disclosed to him the prophecy of Notker and the entire matter, he desired the man of God, if he would deign to visit him, to grant him absolution and a blessing for his present condition.
>
> “But since he had heard Notker spoken of contemptuously and maintained that nothing bad had happened to him through the latter’s prophecy, the fracture could be neither knitted nor joined by any remedies or bandages.
>
> “At last, in the middle of one night, those who pitied his cries pleaded with Notker. When he arrived and touched the leg, the injured man immediately felt it begin to seethe, and thereafter learned sternly to think humble thoughts.”

Thus far Ekkehard Junior in chapter 3. I pass over what he adds immediately concerning the evil arts practiced against Notker and Ratpert by that illiterate monk, mentioned above, whose name was Sindolf. The same author continues the rest as follows.

8. “But Notker, spiritually strong, as we have said, was as powerful against demons as Tutilo was against men.

> “It happened that one night he arrived early at the church and, as he was accustomed, went around the altars, shouting. When he came to the crypt of the Twelve Apostles and Saint Columbanus, and his eyes, shedding tears, peered more keenly behind the altar, he heard something like a dog muttering.”

It was a demon. Notker ordered him to stand still as he approached the place.

> “Hastening to the altar of Saint Gall, he seized his staff and that of his master Columbanus, which was effective in producing many virtues, together with the famous sphere of the holy cross. Having placed the sphere on the right side at the entrance of the crypt, he attacked that canine devil with the staff in his left hand.”

Then he beat the demon so forcefully that he broke the holy staff. The demon cried out horribly.

When the sacristan heard this, he asked Notker who had broken the holy staff and who had uttered the cries. Out of reverence for the silence of the night, Notker remained silent.

But when the sacristan, who did not understand the mystery, found no one in the church, he stood astonished, pondering what had happened.

> “Finally, he did not dare presume further to address the religious man, who had already once kept silence toward him.
>
> “But Notker, humble and prudent as he was, drew the sacristan aside outside the church and, after giving a blessing, said:
>
> “‘How, my son, did I break the staff? Unless you help, my secrets are bound to be disclosed. But since it is not mine to walk among great and wondrous things beyond me, I entrust what happened to the silence of your faith.’
>
> “And he explained the matter to him exactly as it had happened.”

The sacristan secretly had the staff repaired by a craftsman and concealed the matter for a time; but as time passed, the truth became known.

9. “That basilica of Saint Gall has small chapels, in one of which, near the angular doorway, Notker was accustomed to sing.

> “It happened that one day he did not come to the office of None, nor sing it himself. But when, after Compline, he was still praying in that seat, while it was still broad daylight, he saw a demon sitting above him on the beams of the broken ceiling, writing with a stylus on a board.
>
> “When he asked him what crime he was writing, the demon replied: ‘I am writing the None which you criminally omitted today.’
>
> “Then Notker, immediately reciting ‘O God, come to my assistance’—you see that no prayers are prefaced—saw him erase with the greatest speed what he had written.
>
> “When Notker prostrated himself on the ground for the prayers of the office, the demon threw the board from the broken ceiling down upon him. But when he saw it, Notker quickly leapt up to avoid the blow.
>
> “The demon finally laughed and said: ‘I made you rise for me.’
>
> “But Notker replied: ‘Indeed; and if you are like the dog you were recently, I have work to do with you again.’”

At last the demon vanished.

Some brothers praying at the far end of the church heard the sound of the board and the voices and, wondering what they were, quickly came over. Seeing Notker prostrate as usual, they did not wish to disturb him, since the hour was also unsuitable.

At last, however, Tutilo, one of them, gave a signal and, drawing him out in a friendly manner, whispered quietly in his ear:

> “You and your demons are accustomed to cause great disturbances for the brothers.”

When Notker asked what he meant, he denied it, but the event was not concealed by the others who had witnessed it.

In this story observe the observance of silence among the senior monks of Saint Gall, especially in the church: if anyone needed to say something, he first withdrew outside the church with the person with whom he wished to converse. Then, after a blessing had been requested or given—as may be gathered from the preceding section—he whispered briefly in the other’s ear whatever was relevant.

Also note that after Compline had been completed, the regular office of special prayers was held. This perhaps refers to the prayer that was customarily made after the psalmody had been completed in the time of Saint Benedict, as Gregory the Great testifies in book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 4.

10. Hepidannus briefly records, in the year 876, an event that requires fuller explanation: “Wolo fell.” Ekkehard the Younger explains the matter in the same chapter 3:

> “At that time there was in the monastery a certain young monk, exceedingly learned, the son of a count, named Wolo, restless and wandering. Because of his obstinacy, neither the dean himself, nor Lord Notker, nor the other brothers could command him; although he was frequently corrected with words and blows, nothing was accomplished, and everyone grieved for a man of such disposition. For although Saint Gall had never had a monk except a free man—that is, one born free—the nobler men nevertheless more often went astray.
>
> “His parents had come, anxious on his account, and when their admonitions achieved little, he was again there after their departure. But one day at dawn the devil appeared to Lord Notker: ‘I shall bring about a bad night for you and your brothers,’ he said. ‘An evil bird,’ replied Notker, ‘usually announces evil news.’ Then he disclosed beforehand to the brothers what he had heard, so that they might be on their guard that day.
>
> “When Wolo himself heard this from those who reported it, he said: ‘Old men are always dreaming vain dreams.’ It was, moreover, the very day on which everyone knew that the dean had forbidden him, as usual, to go out into the cloister. As he sat writing, his final written words were, ‘For he was beginning to die’ (John 4). Immediately he sprang up, while the others called out to him, ‘Where are you going now, Wolo? Where are you going now?’ He began to climb by the steps into the bell tower of Saint Gall—steps indeed prepared for this purpose for us—in order that, since he was not permitted to walk about, he might at least satisfy his wandering spirit by looking out with his eyes upon the surrounding mountains and fields.
>
> “As he climbed and reached the chapel above the altar of the Virgins, he fell through the ceiling, driven—as is believed—by Satan, and broke his neck. When many who had seen or heard what happened came running and hurriedly brought him the viaticum, he received Communion after making his confession. But when they wished to carry him out and take him to the infirmary, he said: ‘Let me first call upon the holy virgins. For they know that, although I have been utterly wicked in other respects, I have never known a woman.’
>
> “Meanwhile, after he had lamented loudly, Notker came running, and Wolo stretched out his hands to him: ‘To you, my lord, and to the holy virgins whom you have always loved, I commend my sinful soul.’ But Notker, throwing himself down beside him, said: ‘Holy virgins, trusting in you, I take upon myself the sins of this brother and commit both of us to you.’ As he said this, he wept and lamented.
>
> “When Wolo was being carried out before the church doors, after asking for quiet, he clasped Notker’s hand most tightly. While everyone was pouring out prayers, he gave up his spirit. During the funeral rites Notker washed him, placed him in the bier, performed the service, and himself arranged the whole burial. For as long as he lived, he himself always saw to the performance of the services of two monks.
>
> “On the day of the man’s death, while Compline was being concluded, one of the simpler brothers recited the prayer containing the petition that, just as we have passed the day joyfully, so we might also spend the night joyfully. The man of God sprang up and said: ‘What are you asking, remarkable brother? What are you asking? The day’s own evil would have been enough—and more than enough—and yet you are asking the same for the night as well?’
>
> “On the seventh day after the man’s death, when Notker had remained through the night in the church, he rested for a little while upon his knees near the hour of the night office. He then saw what seemed to be his own Ratpertus awakening him and saying: ‘Many sins have been forgiven him, because he loved much’ (Luke 7). When Notker awoke, he said: ‘How do you know this, my soul? How do you know it?’ He added that Ratpert had departed with measured steps.
>
> “Thinking that Ratpert had left the church so that he might speak there more freely, Notker followed him beyond the curtain”—for at that time too there was a curtain before the doors of Saint Gall’s church—“but he could perceive no sound either from Ratpert himself or from his footsteps. After lighting a candle, he looked for him in bed. He found him rising so that he too, as was his custom, might be among the first to awaken the others and call out to them. When the candle had been extinguished, he returned to the church and, weeping silently for joy, sang the *Te Deum laudamus*—that is, recited it in a subdued voice. When daylight came, Ratpert asked whether he had come at night to awaken him. Notker disclosed to his beloved what he had seen, and at last the great event was no longer hidden from the other brothers.”

Here it is worth observing that Ratpert, although appointed to teach the young, nevertheless did not abstain from the night praises; neither did Notker. Indeed, Notker anticipated the appointed hour. As for Wolo, the fabulous Ekkehard calls him the son of Count Kiburg and the nephew, through his sister, of Notker the Stammerer.

11. Concerning Ratpert’s death, Ekkehard the Younger continues:

> “Ratpert, himself also a holy man, went about the cloister of Saint Gall in weakness, yet did not cease teaching. Forty of his former disciples in the canonical life, then priests, had come to the place for a feast. To each of them he entrusted his soul, and each had promised him thirty Masses after his death. Thus, in the greatest joy, asking God to prolong his illness and refine him through it, he became like shining bread and passed, as we believe, into paradise among the hands of his disciples. For him Notker and Tutilo, grieving more than the other brothers who remained after him, did many things.”

He wrote the litanies published by Canisius, volume V, p. 742, and a book *On the Fortunes of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, from the time of Blessed Columbanus to Abbot Solomon, published by Goldast.

12.

> “When Tutilo was laboring at engraving near the city of Metz, two pilgrims stood beside him as he engraved an image of Saint Mary and asked for alms. When he secretly gave them coins, they turned away from him and said to a cleric who was standing nearby: ‘Blessed in the Lord is this man, who has comforted us well today!’
>
> “‘But is that splendid lady his sister,’ they asked, ‘who so conveniently hands him the rays and teaches him what to do?’ The cleric, astonished at what they were saying—for, having only just left Tutilo, he had seen nothing of the kind—returned and, as though in an instant and in the blink of an eye, saw what they had described.
>
> “The cleric and the pilgrims said to him: ‘Blessed are you, Father, in the Lord, that you employ such a teacher for your work!’ When Tutilo declared that he did not know what they were talking about, he inveighed vehemently against them and threatened them never to say such a thing to anyone.
