On the following day, when he heard many people repeating such praise of him, he withdrew from their midst and no longer wished to work in that city.
>
> “After he had left the flat surface of the circle in that golden plate blank, letters were later engraved upon it by I know not whose art”—Mary herself had engraved this pious whole design—“and the image itself, seated as though alive, is still to be venerated by all who look upon it. . . .
>
> “Concerning his death”—that is, Tutilo’s—“since we have learned nothing certain, we confidently assert only this: that he departed to joys. His death occurred on the fifth day before the Kalends of April.”

13.

> “The remaining matters concerning Notker we shall narrate boldly, since we have no doubt that he was a chosen vessel of the Holy Spirit. That most holy man remained bereft and orphaned in spirit, and eventually an evil befell him which struck him with inward anguish of heart.
>
> “He had copied, with much toil, the canonical Greek Epistles requested from Liutward, bishop of Vercelli. And behold, Sindolf”—that scoundrel mentioned above—“already great and powerful in the monastery, happened upon that finely written book, stole it, tore apart and damaged each gathering after cutting it with a knife, as can be seen today, and then, folding it up again, put it back where he had stolen it.”

These are the matters that Ekkehard the Younger records concerning Notker, Tutilo, and Ratpert in chapter 3. He then adds which odes, or Sequences, each of them composed and arranged for choral performance. He says no more about Notker’s death. Hepidannus writes:

> “In the year 912 Notker the teacher died.”

Keroldus, his most devout disciple, was, according to the same Ekkehard, chapter 14, “buried not far from Notker the Stammerer, formerly his teacher and his very dear friend.”

In the Necrology, Notker’s death is recorded as follows:

> “The eighth day before the Ides of April: the death of Notker, who composed the Sequences. On his anniversary a smaller *stoupus* [cup] is given from the Bath-house behind the walls, and from the other two houses adjacent to it, with the gardens above them, which belong to the church of Saint Peter.”

Wion and others must therefore be corrected, since they place the day of his death on the sixth day before the Ides. His epitaph, as given by the Bollandists, reads:

> Behold Notker, the glory of his fatherland and doctrine of wisdom;  
> this tomb contains him as a mortal man.  
> On the eighth Ides of April, freed from the flesh,  
> he is borne to heaven and received in song.

He is numbered among the long-lived by those who, together with the fabulous Ekkehard, think that he lived from the time of Charlemagne. Nor do those who attribute blindness to Notker the Stammerer, following the same Ekkehard, judge more accurately, since that blindness must be attributed to Notker the physician.

14. Notker the Stammerer composed various Sequences, that is, rhythmic prayers of the kind customarily sung at Mass before the Gospel on the more solemn feasts. Ekkehard, the author of the later *Life*, attributes to him the Sequence beginning with the words, “May the grace of the Holy Spirit be with us,” and says that Notker sent it to the emperor Charles, who sent back to him the hymn *Veni, Creator*, composed by Charles himself. It is clear, however, that what is said about Charles is false. More probably, the same author adds, that pious Sequence concerning the Holy Spirit, *Veni, sancte Spiritus*, was composed by Pope Innocent III, during whose time he lived.

Of all Notker’s writings, the most important is his *Martyrology*, published by Canisius in volume VI. Notker himself assigns the date of the work to the seventh day before the Kalends of May, in these words:

> “I have thought that this should be mentioned for this reason: so that our patriarch Hatto of Mainz, who in this same year from the Incarnation of the Lord . . . carried its head”—that is, the head of Saint George—“and another member, together with many of the greatest relics of the saints, into Alamannia for his new monastery, after obtaining them from the apostolic Formosus.”

The year is not stated in the manuscript used by Canisius, but it can be understood approximately from the pontificate of Formosus, who occupied the Roman see for five years beginning in 891. More about Hatto below. See the entry for the tenth day before the Kalends of June, where there is discussion of the relics of Saint Desiderius, bishop of Vienne, sent by Ado in the year 870 through the priest Beroldus, who was still alive.

15. Furthermore, Notker the Stammerer explained to a certain friend who asked him about the letters of the alphabet formerly used to indicate musical notation, according to Ekkehard the Younger, chapter 4. The friend’s name was Lantbertus; the material is published by Canisius in volume V, p. 739, and by Goldast.

The same Notker translated the Psalter into the Alamannic language for Emperor Arnulf. Joachim Vadianus, in Goldast’s *Book II on the Monasteries of Germany*, says that he did so with such difficulty of expression that it can be understood only by an attentive reader. The same Vadianus, p. 47, gives a specimen of that language in the Lord’s Prayer and the Apostles’ Creed written after the Psalter.

Canisius reports various hymns by Notker in volume V, beginning on p. 769, and on p. 790 gives a fragment of a metrical *Life of Saint Gall* written by the same Notker in three books. Notker himself mentions this work in a letter to Liutward, bishop of Vercelli and abbot of Saint Gall, which our Stephanotius extracted from a manuscript at Cluny. See below, at the beginning of the book of Sequences.

Liutward was the bishop of Vercelli and chancellor of the emperor Charles the Fat, to whom Notker, as stated above, had sent the Greek Epistles of the Apostle Paul. He dedicated the Sequences to him; they are published by Canisius in volume V, p. 758.

The monastery of Gimedia is Gemeticum, or Jumièges, in Neustria on the Seine below Rouen. According to William of Jumièges, it was devastated by the Northmen in the year 851, at which time Notker was a young man. From this alone it is evident that he did not belong to the time of Charlemagne and did not live to the great age that many invent for him.

This letter was written before the year 887, when Charles the Fat departed from both imperial power and life, while Solomon had not yet become abbot of Saint Gall. After the foregoing letter there follow hymns under this title: “Here begins the book of hymns of Notker the Stammerer, of the little monastery of Saint Gall,” namely, for the Nativity of the Lord, “The day is sanctified”; for Saint Columbanus, “From the setting of the sun”; and for Saint Gall, “Christ, the sole hope of the saints.”

16. Finally, Goldast, without offering any reason, believes that Notker the Stammerer was the author of two books *On the Wars of Charlemagne*, published under the name of a monk of Saint Gall and dedicated to the emperor Charles the Fat. Certainly the date agrees, and these words in book II, chapter 26, support the attribution:

> “With these matters, then, I, stammering and toothless, have attempted to deal . . .”

Nevertheless, Notker’s character seems more grave and severe in his *Martyrology* than to allow those two books to be attributed to him. The passage should nevertheless carry considerable weight. In a similar way Notker called himself stammering above, in number 2, in the hymn concerning Saint Stephen.

Whatever the truth may be, the passage in book II of *On the Deeds of Charlemagne*, chapter 8, must be corrected: “And with him my lord Gallus,” where it should read “Grimaldus.” In the manuscript this was unmistakably indicated only by the initial letter. Grimaldus was abbot of Saint Gall during Notker’s early years.

17. It remains to discuss the cult of our Notker, whose letters were published by Canisius and Goldast, and from them by Papebrochius.

Formerly Ulrich, abbot of Saint Gall, had gone to Rome, sent there by Frederick II to Pope Innocent III. After the Masses had been completed, at which the pope had been present with the abbot, the pontiff asked about Notker, the author of the Sequences—perhaps he had actually read them—and asked how his anniversary was celebrated and whether, finally, they observed his feast.

The abbot replied that Notker had been a simple monk, born of parents from the noblest families of the land, highly learned and holy; but that “only a private commemoration was made for him, as for any other deceased person.”

Moved by these words, the pope said: “O most wicked men! To your own misfortune, you do not celebrate the feast of so great and holy a man, who was completely filled with the Holy Spirit. You will be miserable.”

Thus it is reported in the later *Life of Notker* and in the *Deeds of Abbot Ulrich*. The matter, however, remained unresolved until the pontificate of Julius II. He ordered Hugh, bishop of Constance, to investigate the institution of a feast and office for Notker and to decide according to his judgment, but with the provision that, on the basis of anything he might do, decide, or order, “the aforesaid Notker should not thereby be considered canonized or approved.”

Hugh entrusted this task to John Zwicho, a canon of Constance, and, when John failed to carry it out, to Leonard Altweger, a notary, in the year 613 [the date is as printed and appears corrupt]. Finally, after completing the investigation, Hugh permitted the abbot and convent,

> “and any other persons, on one day of whatever year they may choose, or on the day on which blessed Notker departed from this world, solemnly and lawfully to celebrate, and cause to be celebrated, in the said chapel of Saints Peter and Paul and of the same monastery, as well as in other churches and chapels subject to that monastery, without requiring anyone’s permission, the feast of a lesser confessor, together with the Mass and office of the same blessed Notker, from First Vespers through Second Vespers of that day,”

but with the further provision that,

> “as Pope Julius II desired in his letters, the same blessed Notker should not thereby be considered canonized or otherwise approved.”

This was done after Julius’s death, namely in the year 1514 under Leo X.

18. Before we leave Notker, it is useful to say a few things here about two other Notkers: Notker the abbot and Notker, bishop of Liège.

Notker the Stammerer ended his life while Solomon was abbot; Solomon himself died in the year 919. In 921 Hartmann succeeded him, and after two years Engilbert succeeded Hartmann. In 933 Thieto became abbot, and in 942 he resigned the abbacy to his uterine brother Cralo. During Cralo’s time Anno, otherwise a respectable man, was intruded into the abbacy and remained there for a year and a half.

After Cralo’s death in 959, Burchard, Notker’s predecessor, was appointed in his place. During his time, when suspicion arose that the discipline of Saint Gall was unsound, an inspection of the place was carried out at the command of Otto Augustus. Hepidannus briefly reports the event as follows:

> “In the year 968, the arrival and installation of eight bishops and an equal number of abbots in the monastery of Saint Gall to examine our life and observance of the Rule. By God’s gift they promised to give the best testimony, became brothers with us, and departed in charity.”

Ekkehard the Younger gives a fuller account of the whole event in chapters 10 and 11. It is worth reading, especially for monks, and is neither unprofitable nor inappropriate; from it we learn the names of the bishops.

The first was Henry, archbishop of Trier, to whom supreme authority was entrusted; then Arnulf of Toul, Dietrich of Metz, Hiltebald of Chur, Poppo of Würzburg, Palzo of Speyer, and Erpho of Worms. The abbots named are Kebo of Lorsch, Kerho of Würzburg, and Milo of Ellwangen; the names of the others are unknown.

The occasion for this visitation was provided by the abbot of Reichenau, who was himself present at the visitation: Ruodmannus, who had denounced and accused the monks of Saint Gall before Hadwig, the daughter of Duke Henry and, after her husband Burchard, duchess of the Swabians, as though they were insufficiently observant.

She reported the matter to the two Ottos, father and son, in whose court Ekkehard was then serving as chaplain, while the other Ekkehard held the office of dean at Saint Gall. Otto the Younger said to the chosen bishops and abbots:

> “Go, you named bishops with the abbots, and correct the monks of the monastery of Saint Gall, who have been defamed.”

Arnulf of Toul replied that the matter was difficult and had arisen from envy; that he had recently visited the place as a pilgrim; and that he had scarcely found similar charity anywhere else. Heaven is not reached by one path or by one rule.

Then Hiltebald of Chur said:

> “Everything known to be practiced there, pious king, is worthy of praise, except that they have certain possessions of their own, and some of them eat meat. They have always done these things with the permission of their abbots, so that they would not perish.”

To this the king replied:

> “Indeed, if, as you say, they live from what is their own, we command you all to act with the greatest possible care so that they do this according to the Rule of Benedict. Since we too recognize some of them as venerable, we do not wish to attack them as enemies. Rather, we are sending so many counselors, all close friends, that you may support my weak brother the abbot—for my father calls him his son—so that the many good things they do may henceforth be directed according to the Rule of Benedict.”

They departed under the law given by Otto the Elder: they were to spare Abbot Burchard, who was his nephew, and not depose him.

They went to the place where most of them had been educated—Dietrich and Palzo among the others. The abbot was summoned before them and ordered Dean Ekkehard and Notker the physician to rise and state the discipline of their institution.

After hearing them, Kebo, abbot of Lorsch, and the other abbots said to the bishops:

> “Indeed, everything we have heard belongs to the Rule of Benedict, except for this one matter: they labor according to the Rule, but according to it they are not nourished. Yet this very fact compels them to seek from every source whatever will sustain their life. Since what they obtain is obtained with the abbot’s permission, and they put it away when he orders them to do so, and use whatever they have according to his nod and judgment, we shall be able truthfully to affirm that they are not acting against the Rule.”

At last everyone agreed that whatever each man privately possessed should be brought faithfully to the common workshops; that all should abstain from meat except those to whom the Rule granted an exemption; and that they should eat together at common tables, even if those tables were poor.

Archbishop Henry promised that he would see to it that the Ottos provided for the monastery’s poverty, and this was done.

> “Because of this, everyone went joyfully into the church; each man, received by the hand, was written into the book of life.”

When the visitors were about to depart,

> “the brothers went into the church to pray for a prosperous journey for those leaving and to receive blessings from so many bishops, after first making confession and receiving absolution from the vested clergy.”

After the envoys had reported everything to the Ottos, Kebo of Lorsch was sent to repair what was lacking at Saint Gall and to bring from the royal treasuries “sixty pounds of silver at the fixed weight.”

19. Not long afterward, Abbot Burchard voluntarily resigned the government of the monastery and shut himself up in the chapel of Saint Gall. “With Ekkehard’s support, he asked that Notker, his nephew through Notker the physician’s sister, be elected in his place, and sent him to the kings to be enthroned on his behalf.”

Letters concerning this matter were sent to Otto. When Otto the Younger presented them to his father, “and, having been ordered by his father to break the seal, he placed it in his hand—for it bore the half-face of Saint Gall.” The younger Otto, after reading the letter, “faithfully interpreting it to his father and mother, Adalheid, explained it and asked them to grant what was requested.”

Ekkehard the chaplain, “highly skilled in note-taking,” recorded on tablets the words spoken back and forth.

Otto the Elder, whom Otto the Younger called “the Lion,” admitted the envoys the following day and said in Romance, “Have a good man.” Finally, after receiving the pastoral staff that Burchard had sent, “he gave it to Notker with this agreement: while his abbot was alive, Notker was to care for it as the abbot himself wished, and he was to undertake nothing of capital importance without the abbot’s consent and the advice of Ekkehard and Notker.”

“‘You shall be mine,’ he said, and kissed him after taking his hands. Soon afterward, when the Gospel had been brought, Notker swore his oath of loyalty. After dismissing him to the church for the *Te Deum laudamus*, he summoned the soldiers of Gallus—that is, of Saint Gall—who were present and ordered them to swear before him when Notker returned.”

Notker was “gladly received by everyone at Saint Gall, placed in the seat of power by the hand of Burchard, and, after leaving the basilica to hold a meeting in the chapter house, was elected by everyone in place of Saint Benedict.” He subsequently conducted himself extremely well and “carefully revived the teaching of Kebo, abbot of Lorsch, which had for a time fallen asleep.”

All this comes from chapters 12 and 16 of Ekkehard the Younger.

As for the remaining discipline of the place, “at Saint Gall the offices used to be changed annually according to Roman custom,” chapter 15. The cloister, however, “had been held in such great veneration from the ancient memory of the Fathers that no one, not even the most powerful canons or laymen of the world, was permitted to enter it or even to look inside,” chapter 16.

Ekkehard says:

> “I myself saw, before the schism of the monks that we suffer from the Gauls, counts and other powerful men, as well as the soldiers of the place, who, out of affection, followed the cross with us through the cloister on feast days. Some young and old men, bearded to the belt and dressed in monastic *roccae*”—that is, cloaks; see above, no. 3—“entered with us wherever we went.”

What Ekkehard says about the Gauls is to be understood of Sandrad, a monk of Trier and a man especially dear to Otto the Elder, who had caused the people of Saint Gall no little trouble under the pretext of restoring discipline there.

I have pursued these matters at greater length because many things occur in them that illuminate monastic affairs.

Ekkehard the Younger ends his account with Notker the abbot, who was appointed abbot in the year 973 and died in the year 981, according to Hepidannus.

20. Finally I come to Notker, bishop of Liège. His acts are reported at length in the *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège*, but no mention is made of his monastic profession. Nor is there any such mention in Sigebert, who dates the beginning of his pontificate to the year 971, the year in which the Magdeburg Chronicle places the death of Everacius, while placing Notker’s succession in the following year.

The same Chronicle declares, under the year 1008, that Notker had been provost of Saint Gall, in these words:

> “Notker, bishop of Liège, and formerly provost of the monastery of Saint Gall, departed to Christ.”

Balderic calls him a bishop “of good memory” in book I, chapter 110, of his *Chronicle of Cambrai*. In the *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège* he is called Notgerus, but in the charters he is consistently called Notkerus.

21. I had almost omitted what Goldast observes in volume II of *Alamannic Affairs*, p. 195, concerning Notker the Stammerer: namely, that he himself wrote a “History of Saint Gall and of the following times down to his own age, in the Ciceronian manner, that is, in dialogues.” Goldast says that this history “exists in the Palatinate, in the possession of the widow of Wolfgang Wecter of Saint Gall.”

The same Goldast attributes certain charters to Notker, p. 6, which he is said to have written in the place of Winidhard, monk and chancellor. But enough of this.

[Col. 0993]

## B. A BOOK OF NOTKER THE STAMMERER, MONK OF SAINT GALL, ON THE INTERPRETERS OF THE DIVINE SCRIPTURES

*(In Pez, Thesaurus Anecdotorum, vol. I, part I.)*

## NOTKER’S NOTE ON ILLUSTRIOUS MEN WHO EXPLAINED THE SACRED SCRIPTURES INTENTIONALLY OR, ON OCCASION, EXPLAINED CERTAIN STATEMENTS OF DIVINE AUTHORITY; WRITTEN TO SOLOMON, HIS DISCIPLE, LATER BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF CONSTANCE

[Col. 0993C]

Since you are prudent and have inherited the name of a prudent man, I am astonished that you keep returning to foolish matters. Because I cannot dissuade you from what you urge, I shall undertake it, first admonishing you by way of reproach: if you had listened to me, you would possess all our most renowned authors.

In this matter I thought I should take account both of my own foolishness and of your modesty: since I am able to write useful things and you deserve to receive the best, the reputation of both of us should be suppressed beneath the seal of silence in such foolish matters. Take care that you do not wish to disgrace us in the vilest manner.

### CHAPTER I — On those who wrote on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, and so forth

If you desire to know what the Hebrews think about the historical interpretation of Genesis, examine Jerome’s book entitled *Hebrew Questions*, based solely on the translation of the Seventy Interpreters. If, however, you seek moral interpretation, attend to Origen. If you do not grow weary of traversing Augustine’s twelve books of disputation, then, if you seek a defense of the Creator and of the ancient Fathers against the blasphemies of their slanderers, read Augustine’s two books *Against the Manichaeans*, his other two books *Against Faustus*, and books eleven, twelve, thirteen, and fourteen of his *City of God*, written by the prophetic Spirit.

If you delight in the beauty of created things, make a habit of rereading Ambrose’s *Hexameron* as a game, since you are playful. If you wish to be nourished by the sweetest marrow of that same book and desire to rejoice in its reasoning concerning truth, strive to retain Bede in your most tenacious memory.

If you should ever be able to find the excerpt of Paterius, which he compiled by gathering, in order, selections from the individual books of blessed Gregory, it will suffice for you as complete wisdom.

For Exodus and Leviticus, labor to learn Origen’s wonderfully argued homilies. For the whole Heptateuch, read Augustine’s seven books of *Questions* and his other six books of *Expressions*, concerning the diversity of interpreters.

Above all, I think it useful for you to acquire Eugippius, who collected from all the books of that most profound and penetrating Augustine a most useful and highly necessary volume concerning every authority of Scripture. In it you will find many mysteries disclosed from Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, and the prophets.

Although Jerome, who labored and toiled most intensively over all the prophets, is sufficient for the diligent reader, if you wish to be his disciple you must keep silent about the weariness that has grown in you from the tedium of books, so that the most ardent reading may suit an ardent disciple.

This is what concerns the Law and the Prophets.

### CHAPTER II — On those who interpreted the Psalter, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs

You will be instructed about the hagiographical books in what follows. The first of them is the Psalter, according to the circumcision. Among us, however, because Christ was born from it, David is the head of all the prophets.

Many have expressed many things concerning his book. Of these the first and chief among the Greeks is Origen, and among us Augustine. From Augustine’s books, as we have learned, Prosper, bishop of Aquitaine, excerpted a most useful volume for students, weaving into it much from the little works of others. Thus, at the very beginning, he placed a preface from a homily of Saint Basil.

Arnobius the rhetorician also left us in this same book a monument of his talent. Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, wrote on it as well.

In his explanation, Cassiodorus the senator discussed many matters, but he seems useful to us chiefly because he demonstrates that all secular wisdom—that is, the most delightful variety of figures and tropes—lies hidden in it.

Above all, for understanding this prophecy it is helpful if someone wishes to commit to memory the Psalter that blessed Jerome translated from Hebrew into Latin.

In the Proverbs of Solomon, Jerome left brief sayings, which were like a very few seeds from which Bede, our own writer, reaped and gathered the greatest harvests.

The same Jerome wrote on Ecclesiastes according to the tradition of the translators of the Seventy, that is, according to the Vulgate interpretation. For the Hebrews say that they translated no more than the five books of Moses.

You must therefore attend most carefully to this exposition, so that you can apply it to an understanding of the modern reading, since you will find nothing else concerning the same book among any Latin author, except for a few testimonies placed with an exposition in the books of blessed Gregory.

In the *Song of Songs*, Saint Jerome interprets two homilies of Adamantius. In the preface to them he first said:

> “Although Origen surpassed others in all other matters, in the Song of Songs he surpassed himself.”

Because Jerome himself was overtaken by death and could not translate this interpretation for us, I impose upon you this exchange for our labor and manifold service: if you should ever have abundant means and enjoy the friendship of a man learned in Latin and Greek, prevail upon him not to consider it burdensome to translate the explanations into Latin, and into the barbarian languages, as a very great gift or most celebrated prize.

Meanwhile, read the little book of Justus, bishop of Lyon, on the bridal song: brief in words, but full of spiritual meanings.

If Roman eloquence has despised the writings of barbarian peoples, then Bede’s exposition of the same book must suffice for us barbarians. God, the disposer of the natures of things, who on the fourth day of the world’s creation brought forth the sun from the east, directed a new sun from the west in the sixth age of the world for the illumination of the whole globe.

But if you also delight in feasting at the sumptuous banquet of Roman delicacies, whatever sweetness Pope Gregory left scattered most abundantly on this subject, Bede arranged in a very small dish for the hungry to swallow.

### CHAPTER III — On the interpreters of the Book of Wisdom, Jesus son of Sirach, Job, Tobit, Ezra, Judith, Esther, Chronicles, and Maccabees

Concerning the book entitled *The Wisdom of Solomon*, I have learned of no author’s exposition, except for a few testimonies explained incidentally in other books. For this book is utterly rejected by the Hebrews and is regarded among our people as uncertain. Nevertheless, because our predecessors customarily read it for the usefulness of its teaching, and because the Jews do not possess it, it is also called *Ecclesiasticus* among us.

You should think the same concerning the book of Jesus son of Sirach, except that this book is both possessed and read by the Hebrews.

The apostolic father Gregory explained the exceedingly difficult book of blessed Job the prophet, which all earlier teachers had left untouched, in such a way that he built an edifice of moral interpretation upon the foundation of the historical sense and placed an outstanding summit of anagogical interpretation upon it.

He wove into and disentangled from this book so many testimonies from all the writings of divine authority that, on this occasion, he seems to have explained both the Old and the New Testament.

If, because of poverty of household means, occupation with worldly affairs, the constant demands of the palace, or the labor of military service, you do not have the opportunity or leisure to devote yourself to it, seek out the excerpt of Ladkenus the Irishman. After the exposition of the testimonies brought forward there, you will find that nothing is lacking for complete understanding.

In various places, too, you can find various collections and excerpts from this and other writings, if you search for them; these will be discussed later.

On the books of Tobit and Ezra, Bede the priest wrote some things more entertaining than necessary, since he attempted to turn the straightforward history into an allegory.

What shall I say about the books of Judith, Esther, and Chronicles—by whom or in what manner they are explained—when even the literal text in them is regarded not as authoritative but only as a matter of memory and admiration? You may suspect the same concerning the Books of the Maccabees.

### CHAPTER IV — Who expressly interpreted the books of the New Testament
Regarding the New Testament, you should know that, although once the more opaque coverings of the letter have been removed it appears lucid and intelligible to everyone, nowhere is error more dangerous unless it is learned with the most reverent humility. Thus, for Matthew Jerome should suffice for you; for Mark, Matthew’s attendant, Bede, the attendant of Jerome; for Luke, Bede, who strides broadly where Luke walks alone, to such a degree that he compiled into one volume everything he found in the Gospel itself. Augustine, the cloud-roaming climber of heaven, pursued John with equal wings. Besides these there is Augustine’s book *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount according to Matthew*. Another consists entirely of Questions on the Gospel. In addition, there is Eugippius’s *Collectary*. Moreover, there are homilies by John Chrysostom, Origen, Augustine, Gregory, Maximus, Leo, and Bede, and Jerome’s responses to the questions of Algasia and Denobia—if, that is, as a priest soon to be, you deign to read books addressed to the instruction of women. But you, young man, should not disdain to read what Jerome, an old man, deigned to write.

Origen wrote much that is remarkable on the Epistle to the Romans; his opponents inserted certain perverse passages into it, one of which—as I recently whispered in your ear—he himself condemns most sharply in the same volume. Ambrose, bishop of Milan, left brief commentaries on the Gospel according to Luke and on all the Epistles of Paul; but many maintain that he did not write the explanation of the Epistle to the Hebrews inserted in his volume, and the truth confirms this. Pelagius likewise wrote brief observations on the same Epistles. Jerome left extensive treatises on Galatians, Titus, and Philemon. That same Jerome, together with Augustine the bishop, wrote highly useful letters on various questions concerning the Apostle, according as they had been asked.

On the Acts of the Apostles, read the priest Bede. On the Epistle of John, read Augustine; through his explanation you will recognize who is a Christian. Inquire into the interpretation by the priest Bede of the seven Epistles called canonical, and also his elucidation of the most obscure vision—or rather revelation—of blessed John. Know, however, that Augustine, Jerome, and Gregory were the seedbeds of this exposition, although Bede himself very often says that he inserted into his volume the explanation of Tychonius the Donatist. In it he also included many statements of Primasius, a disciple of Saint Augustine, so that anyone who takes care to read these same commentators can readily perceive the fact. If you want brief glosses on the whole of divine Scripture, Archbishop Rabanus of Mainz is sufficient.

## CHAPTER V — On those who, on the occasion of their own discussions, explained certain passages of divine authority

Enough has now been said about those writers who deliberately attempted to elucidate the sacred Scriptures. You will now be instructed about those who, in the course of their own discussions, explained certain passages of divine authority.

Augustine, in the innumerable books he composed, whenever the occasion of places and matters presented itself, expounded almost—or rather truly—the whole of Holy Scripture. Proofs of this are his thirteen books of the *Confessions*; the excellent book *On the Good of Nature*; *On the Usefulness of Believing*; *Questions on the Proverbs of Solomon and the Other Scriptures*; likewise the works *On Grace*, *On Free Will*, and the *Enchiridion*, that is, *On Faith, Hope, and Charity*. In these above all the understanding of Scripture shines forth, as it does in his thousand other books, as was said before us: if Augustine is present, he himself is sufficient for you. Seek out his *Mirror*.

What shall I say about Cassian—if at some point you cease to be weary of monks? In the twenty-four books of the *Conferences*, which he compares in number with the twenty-four elders of John’s Apocalypse, he discusses the Law and the Prophets so fully in connection with the eight principal vices that you will not doubt that he undertook to treat everything. But no one will be able to believe how he discussed the Gospels and the writings of the Apostles unless he has devoted himself diligently to reading those same *Conferences*. Remembering the character of his profession, however, he attributes this teaching to the holiness of the Fathers, not to his own industry.

The books of Isidore, the Spanish bishop, entitled *Etymologies*, perfect you in every kind of knowledge. His extremely useful book of *Sentences* is also available. So too another book on the Fathers of the Old and New Testaments, and another on ecclesiastical offices and orders. These will be especially necessary for you, who by God’s grace are soon to be a priest. In them you will find the entire rationale and the names of the individual festivals and fasts, so that you may announce beforehand to the peoples, as God’s herald, the future appointed observances; for if you do not announce it to the people—you who desire the office of watchman—and the sword comes and takes him away, he will die in his iniquity, but his blood will be required at your hand (Ezekiel 33).

## CHAPTER VI — On books necessary for adorning the priesthood, on letter-writers, and so forth

Since the opportunity has arisen to instruct you more attentively in this place concerning the ministry which you are about to undertake—and since I acknowledge myself unequal to so great a matter, being unable either to guard my own life or adequately to express what I understand to some degree—I send you to the book of blessed Pope Gregory called the *Pastoral Rule*. In my judgment—or rather, as I believe, in his and that of all wise men—it could more properly and truthfully have been called a *Mirror*. In it every person will find himself portrayed, especially bishops and priests, so that every person’s words and deeds, and even the thoughts and affections which each has conceived either previously or while in the priesthood, are displayed as though alive and moving.

In this book he set down and explained so much from the New and Old Testaments that, if you commit it to memory, you will seem to be filled with the knowledge of all books. From this book, therefore, you must weigh and examine whether, for the salvation of your soul, you ought to decline the priesthood and flee the danger of those whom you will be unable to correct; or whether, for your own protection—for the ministry itself prevents you from submitting to vices—and for the gain of those whom you will be able to convert, you ought to undertake it, or even seek it ambitiously, although this is an exceedingly dangerous and disgraceful word, and one that should not even come into effect among Christians, especially priests.

You have Eucherius—I do not know whether he is the same man whom blessed Augustine, in the twenty-second book of *The City of God*, describes as a priest from Old Spain suffering from the chronic disease of stone and cured through Saint Stephen, or another bishop or teacher—who set forth and resolved many highly useful interpretations, tropologies, and anagogies of the sacred Scriptures.

What shall I say about Albinus, the teacher of Emperor Charles? He, as you yourself are accustomed to admit, wished to be second to no one, but strove to surpass everyone in pagan and sacred letters. He founded such a grammar that Donatus, Nicomachus, Domisitheus, and our Priscian seem to be nothing in comparison with him. But for you, foolish man, he also discussed much concerning dialectic, faith, hope, and charity, to such a degree that he even presumed to lay a hand upon the Gospel of John. He wrote very extensively to his friends, especially to Witon. I do not dare recommend his letters to you, because to you, as a boy, they seem to have been written with arrogance. I do not think so, however, since he spoke, lived, and wrote in accordance with the authority by which he surpassed everyone after the most powerful of kings.

I recommend the letters of Jerome—not that pagan Greek idolater, but our ecclesiastical worshipper of the true God. In them you will find every kind of seriousness, marvelous wit, explanations of the sacred Scriptures, exhortations to virginity and widowhood, encouragement for the fallen, and attacks upon clerics, monks, and virgins, indeed even upon contemporary prostitutes, so vehement that, if you remember that you yourself are a cleric, you will have nothing to reproach monks and nuns for.

But I recommend especially that one letter most suited to your age, ancestry, relatives, character, and ministry: the letter to Nepotian, the relative of Bishop Heliodorus, who was expected to become bishop after his uncle but was taken away by sudden death. Strive to live according to the instruction by which Jerome trained him, and do not pant after the episcopate after your mother’s cousin; rather, strive to fear and prepare yourself for the sight of God, since, as for everyone, the hour of your departure is uncertain.

## CHAPTER VII — On the composers of meters, hymns, and epigrams

If you also seek meters, the fables of the pagans are not necessary for you. In Christianity you have the very wise Prudentius, who sings most sweetly of the world’s beginning, of the martyrs, of the praises of God, and of the Fathers of the New and Old Testaments; who presents the conflict between virtues and vices with the sweetest tropological charm; and who fights most fiercely against heretics and pagans.

Alcuin—named Avitus [so the manuscript; elsewhere *Alcimus*]—although he took up the history of Genesis as though it were his sole subject, nevertheless sang all our themes in the sweetest verse. He also wrote a very beautiful book on virginity for his sister, and another on the formation of mortals, in place of which you read Cato’s book; but make his book yours as quickly as possible.

I know that you have already committed Juvencus and Sedulius the orator, as well as the Ambrosian hymns, to memory. If you desire to know ecclesiastical writers, you are wasting away in fruitless labor, since even today, and until the end of the age, there is no lack of those who can write useful works. If, nevertheless, you wish to know the ancient authors, read blessed Jerome’s book *On Illustrious Men*, from Saint Peter up to Jerome himself, and that of Gennadius, bishop of Toledo, from Ambrose up to Gennadius himself.

Farewell, and let what has been exhausted be sufficient for you. But why do I blame your eagerness, when I myself reproach my own sluggishness? Just now God, who prospers everything for you, brought Prosper to my mind, whose epigrams, though unwillingly, you have inscribed in your heart. You do not yet know his books *On the Active Life* and *On the Contemplative Life*. If you learn and observe them—as I shall at last reveal what I continually mean by the name “priesthood”—you will be most worthy of the episcopate. Alas! Yet how gently my bones will then rest! Farewell again and again.

## CHAPTER VIII — On the book *The Harmony of the Evangelists*, and on Augustine’s *On Faith to Peter*

I might compare you to the Lernaean swamp, to the Hydra’s head, or certainly to a blazing pyre: when the first is stopped, the thing that erupts most frequently bursts forth again; when one head of the second is cut off, a thousand heads sprout; and the third, the more wood it has devoured, the more wood it desires to devour. So you, whenever I have satisfied one request, do not shrink, fear, or tremble before imposing upon your very weak neck further new and impossible burdens; nor do you, moved at least by pity, cease to impose them.

I therefore fit weak shoulders to a heavy load. It is the duty of my pious overseer to relieve me from this burden whenever he can. Yet know that I say this before God: if you wish to lay anything upon me as a brotherly request and not as an imperial command, I desire to be most ready to fulfill your will as long as I live.

By God’s ordinance, as I believe, and not by human choice, it happened that I left unmentioned the books of Saint Augustine which he himself called *Harmony*, or which his opponents chatter about as the *Anaphony of the Evangelists*, so that I might now have an opportunity to instruct you more fully about them.

The first of these did not receive its name from its subject matter but from what follows; indeed, whatever title you give it, it surpasses them all. If you wish to call it the helmet or breastplate of the Old and New Testaments, you will find that name inadequate, once you have learned that against heretics, all idolaters, and also false brothers it is a bronze shield fastened with golden nails and clothed in the purest silver; or, excessively heated against dry wood, hay, and straw (1 Corinthians 3), an arsenal of every kind of weapon against the gathering of human and spiritual wickedness (Ephesians 6), as you will prove with your own eyes and by experience.

What shall I say about the books that follow? They are so firmly supported by the reasoning of truth itself that, if you commit them to memory, you will already be able to oppose every contradictor of the Gospel, always and everywhere, as a son of the Gospel. In them you will also find many statements set forth with extremely clear explanations.

There is another book by the same Augustine, *On Faith to Peter the Deacon*, arranged in such a way that, if you grasp it firmly, it will make you invincible and establish you as victor against all the heresies that have arisen up to now or will arise hereafter.

## CHAPTER IX — On the books of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine

Devote yourself to Prosper’s most beautiful work *On the Promises and Predictions of God*. Know that it is a rule for all the divine Scriptures: what in them happened only historically; what happened historically but also morally or according to anagogy; what is merely future; what belongs to the present time; what belongs under Antichrist or after his destruction; what is foretold jointly for the wicked and the elect in the age to come; and what is specially promised to the elect alone.

In this volume you will also find many useful passages drawn even from the books of pagans concerning the consummation of the age and the transference of mutable things. Give equally close attention to his books *On Grace and Free Will*. From the innumerable books of Saint Augustine and the other Fathers, Prosper painted in them, as it were, upon a very small tablet—or rather, a true cosmography—for man, contrary to the philosophers, is not a lesser world but a greater one, since the world was made for man, not man for the world.

## CHAPTER X — On those who wrote the lives and passions of the Apostles and martyrs

Moreover, you must diligently seek out the struggles and victories of the holy martyrs, so that by their example, through the grace of God and the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, you may become accustomed not only to reject the allurements of the world but also to lay down your life for Christ and regard bodily torments as nothing.

First among these are the accounts of the chief Apostles Peter and Paul, Andrew, James the brother of John, and also James the brother of the Lord. The Church, however, detracts from the authority of the histories concerning Andrew and John, and also from the passions of the remaining Apostles. Nevertheless, you should know that the passion of Bartholomew is highly credible, or certainly the most truthful.

The history of Peter and Paul and of their disciples Processus and Martinianus, the jailers; of Nicomedes the priest; of Nereus and Achilleus; of Maro, Victorinus, Eutychus, Marcellus, Petronilla, Felicula, Domitilla, Potentia, and Euphrosyna, is read for the edification of all. There is also the book of Hermas entitled *The Shepherd*, although the book circulated under the name of Clement is rejected.

After the Apostles comes the passion of Saint Clement. Then follows the remarkable book concerning Saint Alexander, Eventius and Theodulus, Hermes, Quirinus, and the others.

## CHAPTER XI — On ecclesiastical chronographers and librarians

There is also the history called *Ecclesiastical History*, by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, and by our Jerome, beginning with the birth of the Lord. It contains not only every kind of passion of the saints throughout the world but also whatever else seemed worthy of remembrance up to Jerome himself. Jerome, in accordance with what you imposed upon me, wrote a book *On Illustrious Men*, from his own time back to Saint Peter, recording what each one left in writing.

After him, Gennadius, bishop of Toledo, composed another work of similar kind, extending up to himself. There is also another history called *Tripartite*, because Cassiodorus the Roman senator brought together in one volume what seemed most important from three writers, namely Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret.

If you can find the passion of Saint Lawrence complete and not in fragments, you will find there how many battles and how many victories of the martyrs there were: namely, those of Polychronius, bishop of Babylon in Persia, together with the priests and deacons; and of the little kings Abdon and Sennen, at the time when, not by persecution but by the devastation carried out under Decius Caesar, the Christian religion was destroyed in those regions. When he returned to Rome, he put to death by various tortures all the Christians he could find.

Yet by such slaughter he could not accomplish what he attempted—to eradicate the Christian name. Indeed, in Persia, though much later, the practice of Christianity was recovered through Cyriacus, a Roman deacon, in the time of the Emperor Diocletian and his sons, namely Maximinus in the East and Maximianus in the West, who were the greatest persecutors of our faith.

But although they could shake the Church founded upon the firmness of the rock, they could not overthrow it, which was what they chiefly desired; nor could the detestable apostate Julian after them. When he was slain from heaven, as though after the harshest winter the flowers of spring had begun to appear in our land, those who had previously been held shut up as though in a case or shell began to emerge: Basil, bishop of Cappadocia, and his remarkable brothers; Gregory; Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria; and John, bishop of Constantinople.

Even deserted places produced new fruits: Pauls and Antonys, Macarii and Serapions, and the twenty-four elders, together with an innumerable multitude germinating under their shelter.

## CHAPTER XII — He teaches that the Western Church is in no way inferior to the Eastern in its multitude of saints. He commends the reading of Priscian, Josephus, and Hegesippus

The West too, although late, eventually burst into flower: Martin, born among the Pannonians, who not only illumined Germany, Italy, and Gaul by his presence, but also, according to the testimony of the Easterners themselves, surpassed all of them in the brilliance of his light. His teacher Hilary also went to illumine them bodily. Thanks be to God.

I believe that our tardiness made up for their precedence when I contemplate Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine—our living one and our departed one—so that sterile Africa may not dare boast of such fecundity; and Maximus, Clarus, Simplicianus, Eusebius, Aurelius, Severus, Severinus, Brictius, Paulinus of Trier and of Nola, proceeding together like stars; and, toward the end of the night, many others whose names also presage their virtues: namely, the Congelli, who are interpreted as “Fausti”; Columbas, Columbans, Gauls; Gregory the Fifth, who takes the name Chrysostom away from the Greeks; Benedicts, Honorates, Libertines, our Othmars, and the Belgian Othmar.

Moreover, if you wish to know pagan authors, read Priscian. Read also the histories of Josephus the Jew and the legends of our Hegesippus.

And I bring this little book to an end. Amen. Explicit.

---

# B. NOTKER BALBULUS, MONK OF SAINT GALL, BOOK OF SEQUENCES

*(In Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum Novus*, vol. I, part I.)*

## NOTKER’S PREFACE TO LIUTWARD, BISHOP OF VERCELLI

While I was still a young man, and my unstable little heart often let the very long melodies that had been committed to memory escape, I began silently to ponder how I might join them together. Meanwhile it happened that a certain priest from Gemidia, recently devastated by the Northmen, came to us, bringing his antiphoner with him. In it some verses had been set to melodies for sequences, but even then they were excessively corrupt. As I was delighted by their appearance, so I was embittered by their taste.

Nevertheless, in imitation of them I began to write: “Let the whole world sing praises to God, by whom it has been freely liberated.” And below: “The serpent, evil counselor of Adam.” When I presented these to my teacher Yso, he rejoiced in my effort and, taking pity on my inexperience, praised what pleased him; but what pleased him less he took care to correct, saying: “Each movement of a melody ought to have its own syllable.” On hearing this, I corrected completely those passages that came under *ia*; but those under *le* or *lu* I neglected to adjust, as though they were impossible—although afterward I discovered that even this was very easy, as the following testify: “The Lord on Sinai,” and “Mother.” Instructed in this way, I soon dictated in a second voice: “Let the Church sing, the undefiled mother.”

When I presented these little verses to my teacher Marcellus, he was filled with joy at my happiness, gathered them into little rolls, and taught different ones to different boys to sing. When he told me to have them collected into a little book and offer them as a gift to one of the leading men, I drew back in embarrassment and could never be compelled to do so.

Recently, however, my brother Otharius asked me to undertake to write something in praise of your eminence. Although I rightly judged myself unequal to the task, I was at last, and only with difficulty, encouraged to venture to dedicate this very small and worthless little book to your highness. If I discover that it pleases your piety, so that you may be a support for my brother with the lord emperor, I shall hasten to send you for examination—and to be kept and explained by you—the meter on the *Life of Saint Gall* which I persist stubbornly in working on, although I had previously promised it to Brother Solomon.

## HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF SEQUENCES

## CHAPTER I — At cockcrow

Come, let us recall  
with devout praises  
the songs worthy of this day,  
on which the most welcome light rises for us.

Amid the misty darkness of night  
the shadows of our sin perish.

Today the Star of the sea  
has borne forth the joys of new salvation.

The abyss trembles before him;  
cruel Death itself is afraid,  
for through him it will perish, dead.

The ancient plague groans, captured;  
the livid serpent loses its spoils.

The fallen man, the abducted sheep,  
is recalled to everlasting joys.

On this day the heavenly  
ranks of angels rejoice,  
because the tenth drachma,  
which had been lost, has been found.

O Virgin, exceedingly blessed,  
through whom nature has been redeemed.

God, who created all things,  
is born from a woman:  
a wondrous nature, wondrously clothed,  
assuming what it was not,  
remaining what it was!

Divinity is clothed  
in human nature:  
who, I ask, has heard  
of such things being done?

The merciful shepherd  
had come to seek what had been lost.  
He put on a helmet and fights  
like a soldier in armor.

The enemy falls headlong  
upon his own weapons.

The weapons in which he trusted  
are taken away;  
his spoils are divided,  
his prey is captured.

Christ’s most mighty battle  
is our true salvation.

After victory he led us  
to his homeland,  
where eternal praise belongs to him.

## CHAPTER II — At first light

Now let us all  
give thanks to the Lord God,  
who by his birth  
liberated us  
from the devil’s power.

To him we ought always  
to sing with the angels:  
“Glory in the highest.”

## CHAPTER III — On the Nativity of the Lord

The Son of God, born before the ages,  
invisible, without end,  
through whom the structure of heaven and earth,  
the sea and all that dwell in them, comes to be;  
through whom days and hours glide  
and turn back again in their cycles;  
whom the angels in the citadel of heaven  
always sing with harmonious voice—  
he assumed a fragile body,  
without the stain of original sin,  
from the flesh of the Virgin Mary,  
to cleanse the guilt of our first parent  
and Eve’s wantonness.

This little present day speaks of it,  
shining brightly, increased in length,  
because the true sun, by the ray of its light,  
has driven away the world’s old darkness,  
having been born.

Nor is the night deprived  
of the light of the new star,  
which terrified the knowing eyes  
of the Magi.

Nor was light lacking for the shepherds,  
whom the brightness of God’s host  
struck with wonder.

Rejoice, Mother of God,  
whom the singing angels surround,  
in place of midwives,  
singing glory to God.

Christ, only-begotten of the Father,  
who for our sake assumed human form,  
refresh your suppliants.

And since you deigned  
to become a participant in their condition,  
Jesus, graciously receive  
their prayers,  
so that you may deign,  
only-begotten God,  
to make them participants  
in your divinity.

## CHAPTER IV — On the Nativity of Saint Stephen the Martyr

Let us honor this solemnity  
with united service,  
taught by the example  
of that kindly Author,  
who prayed for the deceit  
of his persecutors.

O Stephen, standard-bearer  
of the supremely good King,  
hear us profitably,  
you who were heard  
for your enemies.

Paul, once your persecutor,  
through your prayers, Stephen,  
believes in Christ  
and dances with you  
in the kingdom  
to which no persecutor draws near.

Therefore may your most holy prayer,  
as we cry to you  
and knock at you with prayers,  
always commend us  
to our God.

Peter appointed you  
a minister of Christ;  
you establish for Peter  
the rule of belief,  
showing at the right hand  
of the supreme Father  
the one whom the raging crowd crucified.

Christ chose you for himself, Stephen,  
through whom he might strengthen  
his faithful,  
revealing himself to you  
as consolation amid  
the whirling stones.

Now you shine among  
the glorious purple robes  
of the martyrs, crowned.

## CHAPTER V — On the Nativity of Saint John the Evangelist

John, virgin,  
much beloved by Jesus Christ!

For love of him  
you left your earthly father  
in the ship.

You rejected the easy affection  
of a wife and followed the Messiah,  
so that you might deserve  
to drink the sacred streams  
of his heart.

While placed on earth,  
you beheld the glory  
of the Son of God,  
which is believed to be reserved  
for the saints alone  
to contemplate in everlasting life.

Christ, triumphing on the cross,  
gave you to his mother  
as her guardian,  
so that you might preserve  
the Virgin for the Virgin  
and provide her care.

You yourself, broken by prison  
and scourges,  
rejoiced in your testimony  
for Christ.

You also raise the dead  
and, in Jesus’ name,  
boldly overcome poison.

To you the supreme Father  
reveals his Word,  
kept silent from the others.

You, dear John of Christ,  
commend us all  
unceasingly to God  
with diligent prayers.

## CHAPTER VI — On the Nativity of the Holy Innocents

Praise to you, Christ,  
Son of the best Father,  
God of omnipotence,  
whom the harmony  
of the people who remain  
joyfully celebrates in heaven  
above the stars.

The hosts of infants  
praise you with ringing hymns  
in the heavenly citadel—  
those whom the impious man,  
because of hatred for your name,  
struck down with a pitiful wound,  
and whom you now piously reward  
in heaven, Christ,  
where they shine in their punishments,  
you who, using your accustomed grace,  
splendidly adorn your own  
with crowns.

By their sacred prayers,  
we beg you, mercifully wipe away  
the sins of our life,  
and graciously grant us here  
the favor of those  
whom you had joined  
to your praises.

Grant them the light  
of eternal glory;  
grant us victory  
over earthly things,  
so that by peaceful deeds  
we may fully attain  
the gifts of your grace.

May no one who hastens  
to exercise himself  
in praise of these children  
become a companion of Herod,  
but may he be with them forever  
in their ranks, Lord, with you.

## CHAPTER VII — On the Epiphany of the Lord

Let all Christendom  
celebrate the feasts of Christ,  
which are adorned  
in wondrous ways  
and worthy of reverence  
among all peoples,  
through the coming  
of the All-Sustaining One  
and the calling of the nations.

When Christ was born,  
a bright star appeared  
to the Magi.

They, not thinking  
the glory of so great a sign  
empty, bring gifts with them  
to offer to the little one  
as to a king,  
whom the star of heaven proclaims.

Passing by the golden couch  
of the proud ruler,  
they seek the manger of Christ.

Hence the fierce anger  
of Herod, envious  
of the ruler newly born:  
he commands the infants  
of Bethlehem to be destroyed  
by the cruel sword.

O Christ, how great an army  
while still a young man, instructed  
for the greatest battles,  
you gather for the Father  
by preaching to the peoples,  
while sucking at such wretched breasts.

In the thirtieth year of human life,  
God had bowed beneath  
the hands of his glorious servant,  
consecrating baptism for us  
for the remission of sins.

Behold, the Spirit,  
in the form of an innocent bird,  
visits him above all others,  
to anoint him as holy,  
always content  
to dwell in his breast.

The Father’s gracious voice  
also sounded,  
forgetful of his former saying:

“It repents me that I made man.”

“Truly you are my Son,  
my beloved,  
in whom I am well pleased.  
Today I have begotten you,  
my Son.”

Listen to him, all you peoples,  
your teacher.

## CHAPTER VIII — On the Purification of Holy Mary

With equal song,  
the people here honor you,  
Mary,  
and worship you  
with devout hearts.

You are the daughter  
of noble Abraham,  
venerable queen,  
born from David’s line.

Rejoice, noble Mother and Virgin,  
who, trusting in the archangel Gabriel’s  
oracle,  
gave birth to a son  
while remaining closed.

In his most sacred blood  
the whole of the most wretched race  
is cleansed,  
as God promised Abraham.

The dry branch of Aaron,  
beautiful with flowers,  
figures you, Mary:  
you flowered,  
giving birth without a man’s seed.

You are the ever-closed gate  
to which Ezekiel’s voice bears witness,  
believed to be accessible  
to God alone.

Yet you, wishing to commend  
to us an example  
of the mother of virtues,  
underwent the remedy  
prescribed for polluted mothers.

You brought yourself  
to the Temple for purification,  
together with him who, born  
God and man,  
increased the glory  
of your integrity,  
unviolated Mother.

Rejoice, you whom  
the Searcher of hearts and kidneys  
proved worthy in a singular way  
by his own dwelling,  
holy Mary. Rejoice: the little child then smiled upon you,  
he who grants everyone  
the power to rejoice  
and to stand firm by his nod.

Therefore, all of us  
who celebrate the feasts  
of little Christ,  
who was made for our sake,  
and of his pious mother Mary,  
if we cannot fulfill  
such a great work of God,  
let his Mother  
be for us a model  
of humility.

Praise to the Father of glory,  
who, revealing his Son  
to the nations and to the people,  
joins us to Israel.

Praise to his Son,  
who, reconciling us to the Father  
by his blood,  
has joined us  
to the citizens above.

Praise also to the Holy Spirit  
forever.

## CHAPTER IX — On the holy day of Easter

Let us sing the praises  
of the Savior with a suppliant voice,  
and with devoted melodies  
let us rejoice for the heavenly Lord,  
the Messiah,  
who emptied himself  
in order to free us,  
lost human beings.

Concealing the glory  
of his divinity in flesh,  
he is wrapped in swaddling clothes  
in the manger,  
taking pity on the transgressor  
of the commandment,  
cast out naked  
from his homeland, paradise.

He is made subject  
to Joseph, Mary, and Simeon;  
he is circumcised  
and cleansed with a legal offering,  
as though a sinner,  
he who is accustomed  
to release our sins.

He submitted to the hands of servants  
when he was baptized,  
endured the deceits of the tempter,  
and fled the stones  
of his persecutors.

He suffers hunger,  
sleeps, and is sorrowful,  
and washes the feet  
of his disciples—  
God and man,  
the Most High made humble.

Yet amid these bodily humiliations  
his divinity could by no means  
remain hidden,  
revealed by various signs  
and teachings:

He gives water  
the flavor of wine  
at the wedding;

he clothes blind eyes  
with bright light;

by a gentle touch  
he drives away  
yellow leprosy;

he raises decaying corpses  
and heals weakened limbs;

he stopped the flow of blood  
and satisfied five thousand  
with five loaves;

he traverses the fluctuating lake  
as though it were dry land  
and calms the winds;

he opens a bound tongue;

he opens ears deprived  
of sound;

he drives away fevers.

After such wonders  
and miracles,  
he is willingly seized  
and condemned,  
and did not disdain  
to be crucified.

But the sun did not behold  
his death.

The day dawned  
which the Lord made,  
destroying death  
and appearing victorious,  
alive to his beloved,  
first to Mary,  
then to the Apostles,  
teaching the Scriptures  
and opening their hearts,  
so that they might unlock  
what had been closed  
concerning him.

All things therefore favor  
the risen Christ with joys:

flowers and crops bloom  
with renewed fruit,  
and the birds,  
once the bitter frost is removed,  
sing sweetly.

The sun and moon shine more brightly,  
which had been troubled  
by Christ’s death.

The grassy earth applauds  
the risen Christ,  
although trembling  
it had threatened to fall  
at his death.

Therefore let us rejoice  
on this day,  
on which Jesus,  
rising again,  
opened the way of life for us.

Let the stars, the earth,  
and the sea be glad,  
and let all the spiritual choirs  
in heaven rejoice with the Trinity.

## CHAPTER X — Monday

Let us celebrate  
the glory of the Creator  
and Redeemer,  
who by his grace restored  
those whom he had created well  
but whom the cunning serpent  
had deceived;

who foretold that in the future  
a holy woman would bring forth  
a shoot  
which would overcome  
the harmful heads  
of the ancient enemy;

which, lost at first,  
our later ages behold,  
when Mary shines as a splendid branch  
with a new little flower;  
the one wondrously brought forth  
performed wondrous deeds.

Not only as a young man,  
but immediately from  
the beginnings of his birth,  
by the light of the star  
and by Simeon’s words,  
he drew to himself  
the Jewish hearts  
and the gentile gifts  
by his will.

The Father glorifies him by his voice  
and the Holy Spirit by his appearance,  
while they show forth the teacher—  
or chief physician—  
by their authority.

After he had bestowed  
many gifts of salvation  
and proclaimed from his mouth  
many most health-giving words  
of teaching,  
he came to insults,  
spitting, blows, and scourges,  
to the garment sought  
for sport,  
and to the crown of thorns,  
to the arms of the cross.

Today, rising from the dead  
in triumphal victory,  
he despised death,  
leading with him  
to heaven the first members  
and recalling the sheepfolds  
recently scattered.

He also promises us,  
though we are the final members,  
gifts to be hoped for  
at the end.

## CHAPTER XI — Tuesday

Let all Christian souls  
make themselves worthy  
by sincere conduct  
of eating and drinking  
the Paschal Lamb,  
for whom the supreme Pontiff  
offered himself to God  
as a sacrifice.

Let their foreheads be upon the doorposts  
[so in the manuscript],  
smeared with his most sacred blood,  
and let them be safe  
from the Canopic disaster.

Let their cruel enemies  
be drowned in the Red Sea.

Let them gird their loins  
for chastity,  
guard their feet  
against vipers,  
and continually carry  
spiritual staffs in their hands  
against the dogs,  
so that they may deserve  
to follow the Passover of Jesus,  
from which he returned victorious  
from the abyss.

Behold the world,  
renewed in ornament,  
rising again with Christ,  
admonishes the faithful  
that after death  
they will live better with him.

## CHAPTER XII — Wednesday

Let all inhabitants  
give thanks to the Savior  
and King, Christ God,  
whom they have long awaited  
and now behold,  
and let them receive his laws  
with ready minds—  
those whom he chose,  
having abandoned  
the Jewish people,  
born from Abraham’s flesh.

[The supplied source ends here, mid-sentence.]

And through faith, those whom [You] made Abraham’s offspring and kinsmen, holy through [Your] blood.

O Christ, kinsman of our nature, cherish us and, by divine power, guard us from every attack and ambush of the enemy, whom by the bait of flesh You deceived with the hook of Your majesty, Son of God. Rising again, You rule, never again to die; rising, You made our mortal and earthly nature incorruptible and carried it into heaven.

### CHAPTER XIII.—On the Ascension of the Lord

Let us pursue with praise the triumph of the supreme King, who rules the scepters of heaven and earth, having lawfully subdued hell, who for our redemption gave Himself as a very great price.

A fitting name is found for Him: Idithun, for He vigorously leapt over all the mountains and hills of Bethel. He made a leap from heaven into the virginal womb, and from there into the sea of the world. After He had calmed it by His power, He sprang into the grim darkness of Phlegethon. Having shattered the power of that prince and rescued from it many companies, He illumines the world with His radiance and, victorious, led away with Him the captivity held there.

[Col. 1012C] And now risen again, He presented Himself to His servants and friends. Finally, today He made the greatest leap, crossing the clouds and the heavens in swift flight.

Therefore let the believing people celebrate this day, on which the Son of God carried the sickly bodies of His Idithun into the lofty seats of heaven in His own person; and let them tremblingly await the Judge who is to come, as the two brother angels taught:

“He who has been taken up from you, this Jesus, into heaven, will come again as you have seen Him go.”

For let us all beseech our Idithun with constant voices, that he may send us the Holy Spirit from the right hand of the Father, who is seated there. May He Himself also always be with us until the end of the world.

### CHAPTER XIV.—On the holy day of Pentecost

May the grace of the Holy Spirit be present with us, making our hearts its dwelling after expelling from them every spiritual vice.

Nourishing Spirit, enlightener of humanity, cleanse the dreadful darkness of our mind. Lover of holy thoughts, mercifully pour Your anointing into our senses. Spirit, purifier of all crimes, purify the eye of our inner person, so that the supreme Father may be seen by us, whom only the eyes of a pure heart can behold.

You inspired the prophets, so that they might foretell the glorious proclamations of Christ. You strengthened the apostles, so that they might carry Christ’s trophy throughout the whole world. When God made the structure of heaven, earth, and sea through His Word, You, Spirit, brooded over the waters and spread Your divine power over them.

You make the waters fruitful for the giving of life to souls; by breathing upon them, grant that human beings may be spiritual. You, Spirit, united the world divided by languages and customs. You recall idolaters to the worship of God, excellent Teacher.

Therefore, hear us who implore You, merciful Holy Spirit, without whom all prayers are believed to be empty and unworthy of God’s ears. You who, by the prompting of Your divinity, taught the saints of all ages to embrace spirits, by granting the apostles of Christ today a gift unusual and unheard-of through all generations, You made this day glorious.

### CHAPTER XV.—On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist

As we celebrate the solemnities of the holy Baptist, the herald of Christ, let us follow him in conduct, so that he may lead his followers to the way he foretold.

Most holy of men, friend of Jesus Christ, we devotedly beseech You to let us receive the joys that Gabriel, appearing to Zachariah, promised to those who celebrated Your birth with acts of service. Through these festivities may we attain eternal joys, in which the saints of God rejoice happily together amid sacred delights.

You prepare the hearts of the faithful, so that God may find nothing crooked or slippery in them; we ask You to strive by continual prayer to absolve our crimes and misdeeds, so that, appeased, He Himself may always deign to visit His faithful and make His dwelling in them. May He will to clothe us in the fleece of the Lamb whom You had shown with Your finger as taking away the sins of the world, so that we may deserve to follow Him with the angels through the radiant gate in white garments, friend of Christ, John.

### CHAPTER XVI.—On the Nativity of the Apostles Peter and Paul

Peter, supreme shepherd of Christ, and Paul, teacher of the nations, may your prayer help the Church, illumined by your teachings, throughout the circuit of the earth.

For the Lord, Peter, gave you the keys of heaven as a gift. Christ knows you, Benjamin, as His armed warrior and chosen vessel. Christ granted your foot, Peter, to trample the sea underfoot; He made the shadow of your body a remedy for the sick and the weak.

Christ grants you, Paul, power by His word to overcome the *spermologoi* philosophers. You, Paul, won many victories for Christ among the peoples. Finally, after all the barbarians had been conquered, you proceed to the citadel of the highest summit, now about to force the divided Germans, pacified under Christ’s yoke, into unity.

[Col. 1014C] There the ferocity of Nero had subjected you, Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles and victors in many battles, to different punishments of death: the cross joins you, Peter, while the bloody sword sends you, Paul, to Christ.

### CHAPTER XVII.—On the Nativity of Saint Benedict the Abbot

Let our instruments resound, as far as ability and knowledge permit, with the celebrated merits of holy Benedict, of revered sanctity and leader of monks.

His blessed mother, Nursia, bore him; Rome, mistress of the world, nourished him as foster-mother. Thus, anticipated by the best gift of the Holy Spirit, he despised human wisdom and obtained angelic wisdom.

Supported by complete faith, he restored what was broken. He subdued the fires of the flesh; by the cross he drove away poison. He restores the monk of wandering mind and turns a spring into a stream. At his command iron rises from the hidden depth of the lake. A disciple runs over the waters with dry feet; a raven carries out an order. He makes a huge rock smooth. He restores the sight of brothers already deceived by fires. By his prayer he returned to life a fallen monk whose body had been crushed limb by limb.

He exposed the guilt of presumed food and condemned a guest for a similar offense. He shrewdly stripped bare the schemes of a treacherous king. After ten years, through the Spirit, he announced the end of his life.

He freed a cleric possessed by an enemy and entrusted him with a precaution. He rebuked the secret mind of a proud man and relieved hunger. By a word he binds souls released from the flesh, yet he absolves them with mystical bread.

Glass vessels preserve embers without danger. He himself mourns a crushed rival. By a mere look he untangled a rustic; but by prayer he raised again the rustic’s son, already dead.

May he himself reconcile us in devotion to Christ, asking pardon for our sins and a share in the seats of rest, where He triumphs gloriously.

### CHAPTER XVIII.—On the Nativity of Saint Lawrence the Martyr

Lawrence, martyr and mighty soldier of great David, you despised the emperor’s tribunal and the bloody hands of torturers, following the desirable and strong-handed One who alone was able to overcome the kingdoms of the cruel tyrant. The love of whose holy blood makes His soldiers lavish of their own, provided only that they may be permitted to behold Him at the cost of their present life.

You despise Caesar’s fasces and laugh at the judge’s threats; the executioner’s claws and the torturer’s gridiron are consumed in vain.

[Col. 1015D] The impious prefect of the City grieves, defeated by a roasted fish, Christ’s food. The Lord’s guest rejoices over the honeycomb, filled with the hope of rising again with Him.

O Lawrence, most unconquerable of the soldiers of David, the eternal King, always pray to Him for pardon for His little servants, martyr and mighty soldier.

### CHAPTER XIX.—On the Assumption of Saint Mary

The choirs of angels rejoice with the glorious Virgin, who without intercourse with a man bore the Son who heals the world with His own blood.

For she herself rejoices as she now beholds the Prince of heaven, for whom, once on earth, she, a virgin, offered her breasts to suckle.

How greatly Mary, the mother of Jesus, is honored by the angels, who acknowledge themselves the appointed servants of her Son!

With what glory this Virgin is honored in heaven, who offered the Lord of heaven the lodging of her most holy body! How splendidly in the heavens shines the Star of the Sea, who bore the light of all stars, of human beings, and of spirits!

[Col. 1016B] This humble people celebrates you, Queen of heaven, with devout minds. With harmonious song it raises you above the ether together with the angels.

The books of the prophets sing of you, Virgin; the choir of priests rejoices; the apostles and martyrs of Christ proclaim you. The people of both sexes follows you, loving the virginal life and imitating the inhabitants of heaven in chastity.

Therefore the whole Church, celebrating you in its hearts and in its songs, manifests its devotion to you and implores you with humble prayer, Mary, that you may deign to be its help beside Christ the Lord forever.

### CHAPTER XX.—On the Nativity of Saint Mary

Born from royal stock, Mary, bearing Jesus the king worthy of the praise of the holy angels, look kindly also upon us sinners devoted to you.

You display in yourself the pious ways of the Fathers, yet you surpass them. In you shines the wisdom of your father Solomon, and the upright heart of Hezekiah before God, never to be corrupted in you. The religious devotion of your father Josiah was fulfilled in you; likewise, the faith of the supreme patriarch, your father, wholly possessed you.

But why should we enumerate these heroes, when your Son surpasses all of them and all peoples throughout the world?

On this day, Virgin, preserve us gathered to you, on which you came forth to the light of the world, about to give birth to the light of heaven.

### CHAPTER XXI.—On Saint Emmeram

Let the Church rejoice and celebrate this little day by venerating it, and let it sing in loud voices, on which blessed Emmeram deserved to ascend by his breath to the shining kingdoms of the King above.

His mother, Pictavis, the happiest of all the cities of Aquitania, bore him as a sweet son, pregnant with him in the flesh. From the very years of childhood he rejected the affairs and joys of passing things, already meditating on heavenly joys.

Then his beautiful neck was covered with the robe of glory, and spiritual anointing soon filled his head and heart. The Shepherd had appointed him shepherd in succession over His sheep, lest the cunning rage of the wolf should prowl around the gentle fold.

Then, having equipped the flock entrusted to him, the man eagerly girded himself for the task of spreading the seeds of faith in barren soil. Thus traveling through many regions and leaving everywhere a sweet memory, he came to Radaspona, the royal seat of Noricum.

O how fortunate the people who at that time served such a pilgrim in earthly matters, one who would feed you with spiritual abundance!

He strengthened you by shedding his blood and adorned you with a tomb; now he embraces you by diligently helping you. At his resting place the blind see with clear sight; the deaf hear a distinct voice; the weak rejoice when their bodies are restored; the lame leap like a stag; the possessed shout in freedom.

Therefore let praise resound from the harmonious mouths of princes and peoples for the great joy of this healing. And let us all together beseech the Lord to grant that we may obtain rest with Emmeram, now placed in the seat of heaven.

### CHAPTER XXII.—On the Dedication of a Church

Let the immaculate Church, mother and virgin without wrinkle, sing the honor of this church.

This house is shown to share in the palace of heaven, rivaling, in the praise of the King of heaven, in ceremonies, and in perpetual light, the city without darkness, and cherishing in its bosom the bodies of souls that live in heaven.

May the right hand of God protect it for a long time to His praise.

Here, made fruitful by the Holy Spirit, may grace give birth to a new offspring. Here the angelic citizens visit their own. Here the body of Jesus is received. Everything harmful to the body flees; the sins of the sinful soul perish. Here the voice of joy resounds; here peace and joys overflow.

In this house, praise and glory forever resound to the Trinity.

### CHAPTER XXIII.—On the Feast of Saint Michael the Archangel

Because we regard you, Michael, as the great pledge of our fellow citizens—provided that we strive to be servants of God—we ask that through your prayers we may deserve to become companions of their ineffable blessedness, which we trust they possess in God’s presence, since He is the true blessedness everlasting for the saints.
