Because we know that this cannot happen unless one strives for good merits, we ask that you always beseech God to instruct us in holy conduct, so that we may be able to enter the palace that admits no stain.

You who retain the love of God, Michael, have remained immortal; pray to Him for rest for us after death.

### CHAPTER XXIV.—Another

Let every melodious choir now join in harmonious songs and let our assembly offer odes to you in celebrated praises, O heavenly King, now that the glorious feasts of Michael are renewed, through which the whole structure of the world is joyfully adorned.

The ranks of spirits are divided into nine groups, made by you. Yet, whenever you will, you make these fiery beings through the angelic workshops.

For these were created among the first of your works, whereas we are the last work; but your theological image classifies these threefold symbols for us according to their separate offices:

The angelic people; the phalanx of Archangels; the princely host of Principalities; the heavenly Virtue and beneficent Power; the ruling Dominions; the divine Thrones; the ethereal Cherubim; and the fiery Seraphim.

You, O Michael, governor of heaven, and Gabriel, who truly give the messages of the Word, and Raphael, servant of life, transfer us among the inhabitants of paradise.

Through you all the commands of the Father which He gives are fulfilled. His Wisdom’s equal also, the Spirit, remaining one in essence—you who administer sacred service to God, thousands of thousands—

Your companies stand in the palace in ranks of ten times two, twice over, and five hundred; hundreds and thousands attend in the hall to which the King, the Word-begotten One, led the hundredth sheep and the tenth drachma to your images.

You through the ether, we through the earthly fields, let us, the chosen portion of harmony, offer our vows. From this place we offer them with lyrical lyres, so that after Michael’s glorious battles our golden incense may be acceptable to God upon the altar, and so that in coeternal glory we may sing the alleluia together.

### CHAPTER XXV.—On Saint Gall

Beloved by God, Gall, and by human beings and the companies of angels, obedient to Jesus Christ’s difficult summons, you despised your father’s estates, your mother’s embrace, your wife’s care, and the childish pleasures of your offspring; following the poor Lord as a poor man, you preferred the cross to slippery joys.

But Christ compensates for these things with a hundredfold reward, as this day testifies, while in sweet affection He subjects us all to you as sons and has given you, Gall, Suevia, your pleasant homeland; moreover, He has made you sit in heaven as a judge joined to the choir of the apostles.

Now we humbly pray you, Gall, to ask Jesus Christ to grant us and to fill His bodily dwelling with peace, and to lift up your suppliants by frequent prayer, so that we may always deserve joyfully to pay you the honor due to you, O Gall, beloved of God.

### CHAPTER XXVI.—On the Feast of All Saints

All you holy Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones; Dominions, Principalities, Powers, and Virtues; Archangels and Angels: praise and honors are fitting for you.

Nine orders of blessed spirits, love has established you in the praises of God; establish us fragile human beings by your prayers, so that, strongly overcoming spiritual wickedness with your help, now and forever we may be worthy to take part in your solemn sacred rites.

You whom God’s grace made victorious over earthly things and companions of the angels in heaven; patriarchs, prophets, apostles, confessors, martyrs, monks, virgins, and all the peoples of holy widows and of all who please the supreme Lord: may your help cherish and protect us now and forever, as we ask on the day of your joys.

### CHAPTER XXVII.—On the Nativity of Saint Martin the Bishop

Let the whole Church of Catholic peace sing throughout the world of Christ’s priest Martin, and let every heretic flee his name in pallid fear.

Let Pannonia, his mother, rejoice in such a son; let Italy, his foster-mother, exult in so great a youth; and let the threefold division of Gaul contend in sacred dispute over which of them should possess him as bishop.

But let all rejoice equally that the people of Tours alone have him as father and cherish his body.

Let all the people of the Franks and of Germany applaud him, for whom he brought the Lord to be seen in His own garment.

He is renowned among the Fathers of Egypt and also among all the wise men of Greece, who recognize themselves unequal to Martin’s merits and to his healing power. For he calms fevers, drives away demons, joins together paralyzed limbs, and by his prayer restores the bodies of three dead people to their former life.

He destroys sacrilegious rites and gives idols to the flames for the glory of Christ. Here he performs mysteries with bare arms and is endowed with heavenly light. With eyes and hands raised toward heaven and with all his strength fixed upon it, he rejects all earthly things.

Christ was never absent from his mouth, whether justice or whatever pertains to true life.

Therefore we all ask you, O Martin, that you who displayed many wonders here may also, through your supplication, always pour Christ’s grace upon us from heaven.

### CHAPTER XXVIII.—On the Nativity of Saint Otmar the Abbot

Let Suevia, his mother, sing the holy Otmar, worthy of praise, always rejoicing in the progress of such a son.

Here, like an outstanding star pleasing to God, he shines among the darkness of his brothers. Here he promptly obeyed the commands of Jesus Christ. Here he was generous in assisting His least members.

Now he presents himself as a witness of his perfected life, healing the weak and cherishing suppliants.

Now joined to the companies of the saints, let us all pray to him, that he may always reconcile us, fragile as we are, to the Lord God, who reigns as the Holy Trinity.

### CHAPTER XXIX.—On the Nativity of Saint Columban the Abbot

From the setting of the sun to its rising, Your name, God, is worthy of praise among all. From there You send forth a new sun by wondrous law, which illuminates the world with its rays and gives life to the earth by its warmth.

This man, Columban by name, lived a dove-like life and was worthy in this life to possess the pledge of the Holy Spirit.

He left his land and relatives with Abraham for God’s sake. With John, he did not fear to rebuke the king’s incest. With Moses, God gave him food in the desert. With Joshua, heaven was ready to obey him. He tamed wild beasts and ravens, like Elijah and Daniel. With the apostles of Christ, he endured persecution.

To him the enemy of truth himself, by God’s command, bore witness that he was a worshiper of the truth.

Therefore we ask you, blessed one, that you commend us to the Lord.

### CHAPTER XXX.—On the Nativity of the Apostle Saint Andrew

God, Saint Andrew rejoices and exults in Your power, following it.

He himself was first made a fisherman of peoples through the fishing of Your Son; he properly caught the long-wandering, wave-tossed Myrmidons, idolaters, for the faith.

By Your laws, God, He subdued Achaia, victorious over it, and fixed there the trophy of Your Christ, showing himself a good soldier. Whatever spoils were sought through miracles, powers, and teachings, he brought to You, O King, and inscribed the titles of Your triumphs among kings with his own blood, O Lord.

We believe this companion of the cross and of the kingdom to be a little brother of Christ Your Son.

Therefore, weighed down by our sins, we ask You, God, to protect us through the intercession of him who, always following Your commands, pleases You forever.

### CHAPTER XXXI.—On the Apostles

Illustrious senate of the holy apostles, princes and rulers of the world and of kingdoms, govern the customs and life of the Churches, which everywhere are faithful through your teaching.

Antiochus and Remus grant you, Peter, the throne of the kingdom. You, Paul, invaded Alexandrian tyranny and Greece.

Matthew, you clothed the dreadful Ethiopians in the white fleece of the Lamb that knows no stains.

Thomas, Bartholomew, John, Philip, Simon, and James, alike in dignity; Andrew and Thaddeus, glorious warriors of God: behold, the West and the East, indeed the whole round circle of the world, rejoice and await having you as fathers and judges.

And therefore the whole world humbly offers you praise and the honor due to the saints.

### CHAPTER XXXII.—On the Martyrs

This day of the triumphant contest of the soldiers of the supreme King is celebrated among peoples who believe in Christ the King.

They rejected the delights of worldly things and then daily carried the shameful cross.

No ferocity separates them from Christ, so that by thousands of deaths they may hasten to Him. Neither prison nor chain softens the strong hearts of those who are in Christ. Nor do the savage bites of beasts hollow out the steadfast mind of the martyrs.

No sword hanging over their heads terrifies the bravest soldiers of the excellent Lord.

Now, clasping the hand of God, they mock the furies of their persecutors, once so cruel; and they supply consolation to Christ’s people in all the labors of the slippery world.

You, martyrs of Christ, take care continually to commend us, exceedingly fragile as we are, to the just Judge by your sincere prayers.

### CHAPTER XXXIII.—On One Martyr

Why do you weep, mother virgin, beautiful Rachel, whose face delights Jacob? Like an old sister’s bleary-eyed appearance, it pleases him. Wipe your flowing eyes, mother. How becoming to you are the little furrows of your cheeks!

Alas, alas, alas! Why do you accuse me of having poured out tears in vain, when I am bereft of my son, who alone would care for my poverty? He would not yield to enemies within the narrow boundaries that Jacob acquired for me, and he would have been useful to his foolish brothers, whom—alas!—I raised with so much care.

Should this man be mourned, who possessed the heavenly kingdom and who by frequent prayer helps his wretched brothers before God?

### CHAPTER XXXIV.—On One Confessor

King of kings, our God worthy of veneration, You govern the Christian army, assigning men skilled in warfare to dreadful battle. You give wise magistrates to the state and teachers to Your peoples.

For You, wise in choosing, are not deceived about whom You should appoint to each ministry, O God. Among these is this holy priest, who, living in peace, considered how he might fortify the holy Church against the assault of the enemy that is accustomed to ravage the unwary.

Hated by heretics and pagans, and also by every author of evil [thus the manuscript], he rejoices to hold a share in the Lord, enduring His enemies together with Him.

O excellent dispenser, continually impart to us the wheat of the Lord’s teaching, so that we may return to our heavenly homeland with abundant nourishment, O exalted soldier of God.

### CHAPTER XXXV.—On Virgins

Let us companions celebrate the feast of the venerable virgin, from the number of the wise: daughters of the Mother of the supreme King, the most holy Mary, whom the Son adopted for Himself as a sister of God.

She subdued her body with the bridle of fasting and cut down lust with the sword of spiritual combat. She fought against every assault of death and, trusting in Christ’s right hand, struck down the bloody enemy.

Joyfully, with a glad heart, she followed the Bridegroom visiting her from the palace of heaven and entered His bridal chamber.

Now, filled with sweet delights, present our wretchedness to Christ and pray Him to grant us consolation.

### CHAPTER XXXVI.—On the Holy Trinity

Blessed forever be the Holy Trinity, that is, the one Godhead, equal in glory: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. These are three names, but all have the same substance.

God the begetter, God the begotten; in both, the Holy Spirit, sharing their divinity. Yet there are not three gods. God is truly one: thus the Father is Lord, and the Son and Holy Spirit likewise.

There is distinction in the persons and unity in the essence. Equal majesty, power, dignity, and honor in all things.

The stars, seas, surrounding fields, and all created things alike [proclaim] His equal majesty, power, dignity, and honor. The impious underworld trembles at Him, and the lowest abyss also worships Him.

Now every voice and tongue must confess Him with the praise due to Him. The sun praises Him, the moon; angelic dignity adores Him.

And now let us all jubilate with exalted voice to the Lord enthroned on high, offering praises in the heavens. Come, come, let us all together fashion harmonious songs with instrumental music and sweet melody.

O venerable Trinity! O adorable Unity! Through You we were created, true Eternity; through You we were redeemed, supreme Love.

Protect, save, free, rescue, and cleanse the whole people. We adore You, Almighty; we sing to You; to You belong praise and glory.

### CHAPTER XXXVII.—Another

Let the nourishing choir of the Lord join together the names of the supreme One: Messiah, Savior, Emmanuel, Sabaoth, Adonai.

The Only-Begotten is the way, the life, the hand, the one of the same substance (*homousion*). Beginning, firstborn, Wisdom, Power.

Alpha, called both beginning and end, that is, omega (ω). Fountain and source of good, Paraclete, and mediator.

Lamb, sheep, calf, serpent, ram, lion, worm; mouth, Word, splendor, sun, glory, light, and image.

Bread, flower, vine, mountain, gate, rock, and stone. Angel, bridegroom, and shepherd; prophet and priest.

Immortal (*athanatos*), strong (*ischyros*), O God (*ho Theos*), almighty (*Pantocrator*), equal (*isos*).

May He save us, to whom be glory (*doxa*, δόξα) throughout all ages.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.—On the Nativity of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite and Bishop, and of His Companions

Let us rejoice in this solemnity, brothers; let the whole Church likewise rejoice, honoring the annual day.

On this day Dionysius, the magnificent bishop, together with Rusticus and Eleutherius, his companions, splendid with the crown of martyrdom, sought heaven.

Once a philosopher at Athens and called an Areopagite, he was first among his people. But he despised the summit of this primacy and all the glory of the world at the exhortation of Saint Paul. Instructed by him and washed clean by the grace of baptism, he was appointed bishop and teacher over the Athenian people, whom, like a radiant Lucifer, he stripped of the darkness of error.

He announced the light of sacred doctrine to his homeland and also to neighboring peoples.

Afterward, inspired by divine love and sent by the apostolic bishop, he visited peoples living far away and the savage kingdoms of Gaul. There he preached continually and converted very many people to the Lord. Finally he was seized by the impious and punished with his companions for Christ’s name.

O how fortunate the city of Paris, in which the buried bones of the body of so great a martyr are known to rest! But no less blessed is Radaspona, which, by heavenly command, now holds those same bones after their translation.

Therefore, venerable martyr Dionysius, commend both peoples, and all who rightly seek your help, to the supreme King by your constant prayers.

**THE END.** Another hand, not later than the twelfth century, added the following in the margin:

The invincible king of kings, Arnulf, had transferred to this monastery the most holy treasure of the body of Dionysius.

---

## B. The Poems of Blessed Notker

(See *Patrologia*, vol. LXXXVII, cols. 40 ff., in the Appendix to the writings of Saint Gall.)

## The Martyrology of Blessed Notker Balbulus, Monk of Saint Gall

(From Canisius, *Lectiones antiquae*, vol. II, from the library of Saint Gall.)

### Canisius to the Reader

In the codex from which we publish this Martyrology, the Reverend Father Jodocus Metzlerus, professed member of the monastery of [Col. 1026C] Saint Gall, made the following note:

“The author of this Martyrology was a monk of Saint Gall is manifest from the feast of Saint Desiderius on the tenth day before the Kalends of June; from the feast of Saint Columba the Confessor on the fifth day before the Ides of June; from the Nativity of Saint Gall; and from the feast of the basilica dedicated in honor of Saint Gall. It is also clear from the Catalogue of Our Father Iso, which you have in the oldest red codex, on a small parchment leaf.

“That the author of this Martyrology was Notker is equally clear from another very ancient parchment sheet prefixed to the Martyrology or Calendar of Ado in the large codex of the *Historia Scholastica*. There, histories of Saint Desiderius, Verena, and others are written in the hand of an ancient Father; and, as the copyist himself testifies, they were taken from Notker’s Martyrology. This is none other than our own, since those histories agree word for word with our copy.

“Since there were two men among us renowned for the writings of Notker—the one, namely, Balbulus, who died in the year of the Lord 912; the other, the Physicus, who died in the year of salvation 1033—it becomes clear that the former was the author of this work from the fact that he was still alive when Ado, bishop of Vienne, sent the relics of Saint Desiderius the Martyr to the monastery of Saint Gall. This happened in the year of our Redeemer 870.

“Moreover, this Martyrology lacks the months of November and December, and in some places also several days; I do not know through what misfortune.”

This is Metzlerus.

## Jacob Basnage’s Observation on Notker

### I. On Notker, Bishop of Liège

There were very many Notkers at nearly the same time. Let us begin with Notker the bishop of Liège, although he was somewhat later in age, for he was superior in rank.

The Benedictines make him a monk on the authority of the Magdeburg Chronicle, in which he is called provost of the monastery of Saint Gall. They ought to have noticed that the author of the Chronicle was seriously mistaken in asserting that Notker was provost of the monastery in the year 1008 (Chapeaville, *Gesta pontificum Leodiensium*, vol. I, p. 214), since he had already been bishop in 971. Indeed, many charters of Otto II are recorded by which he granted the county of Huy and various other possessions to Notker, already bishop of Liège.

Therefore he could not have been a monk in 1008, nor was he ever one. He is called the founder of the city of Liège, since he surrounded it with walls, adorned it with buildings, brought the Meuse into the city, and introduced the study of letters. He was so severe toward wrongdoers that they suffered from him not only canonical but also secular punishment. For every sinner:

He went into exile unless he hastened to repent,

Or broke his neck, or lost his beloved limbs.

Such was he toward the reprobate, so fearsome to every

Perjurer, and so forth.

(Anselm, ibid., chapter 58, p. 220.)

Who would not have feared a bishop made dreadful by such deeds?

### II. On Two Other Notkers

Another was Notker, abbot of Saint Gall. When Burchard voluntarily resigned the office, Notker was appointed abbot by Otto, on the condition that he undertake nothing of capital importance without the approval of Burchard, who was still alive. At nearly the same time he assumed the office, while another Notker was promoted to the episcopal see. For the abbot was appointed in 973 and died in 981.

This abbot was the nephew of another Notker, a teacher, painter, physician, and poet, whom they called “Peppercorn” because of his sharpness or excessive severity of character; this man died blind.

In the following century, the eleventh, there lived another Notker, called Labeo, later honored with the title of blessed. Finally, in the thirteenth century there was a fifth, or rather sixth, Notker, often described as most learned and kindly. All these were different from the Notker now under discussion.

### III. On Notker Balbulus

He is distinguished from the others by the title *Balbulus* (“the Stammerer”), and was older than all of them. As a boy he was offered to Saint Gall in the year 840 and received holy orders. He devoted himself to study under the teacher Iso, who died in 871.

Eckerhardus, and many writers after him, made him a contemporary of Charlemagne. One should marvel not so much at their credulity as at Eckerhardus’s, since, when he set out to write Notker’s Life, he did not know Notker’s age.

If you believe this panegyrist, Notker was a prophet, often played with demons and grappled with them. You will learn scarcely anything else from him.

He died on the eighth day before the Ides of April in the year 912. It is disputed whether this epitaph was engraved on his tomb; nevertheless it is reported by the Bollandists:

Behold the glory of his homeland, Notker, the doctrine of wisdom,

Who, as a mortal man, is enclosed in this tomb.

On the eighth Ides of April, released from the flesh,

He is carried into heaven and received in song.

### IV. On Notker’s Sequences

Eckerhardus says the following about Notker’s writings in his *Life*, chapter 33:

“Holy Father wrote little besides Sequences and a few other things.”

But Eckerhardus seems to have erred about Notker’s writings, as in other matters. For who could call his Martyrology a small work? Yet who would forgive an author who was unaware of that book?

Many works are attributed to Notker Balbulus. First, it is beyond doubt that he composed Sequences—that is, rhythmic prayers customarily sung before the Gospel on the more solemn feasts. Eckerhardus identified this as his principal work.

It should nevertheless be observed that here too he fell into error. For he says that Notker sent to Charlemagne the Sequence he had composed, “May the grace of the Holy Spirit be with us,” and that, in thanksgiving, Charlemagne returned the hymn *Veni, Creator*, dictated by his own mouth.

“Such wings,” he says (Eckerhardus, *Life of Notker*, ch. 18), “are customary among winged animals when they strike one another; that is, perfect and learned men, instructed in spiritual knowledge, customarily exercise one another through different exhortations. Thus Saint Augustine [did so] with Blessed Jerome,” and so forth.

How foolish! For he cannot escape the charge of falsehood, and from what has been said above it is evident that such an exchange of hymns between Notker and Charlemagne could not have taken place, since Charlemagne had long before departed from this world.

### V. On His Various Works

Notker composed various other small works. First, for the benefit of his friend Landbert, he elucidated the letters of the alphabet which formerly served to indicate melody; second (the same author, in the same work, chapter 20), “That same holy man translated the Psalter from the Latin language into the barbarian language, [Col. 1028D] as it is today in the library”—that is, toward the end of the twelfth century or the beginning of the thirteenth; for Eckerhardus, whose words we have quoted, was writing at that time. Third, he composed various hymns and songs. Fourth, among these there occurs a fragment of the Life of Saint Gall, written in verse. But Goldastus further asserts (Rerum Alamannicarum, vol. II, p. 195) that in the Palatinate, in the possession of the widow of Wolfgang Wecterius, there exists a History of Saint Gall and of the following periods down to his own age, composed in the Ciceronian manner—that is, in dialogues. Fifth, Goldastus attributes to the same Notker certain documents written in place of Weinhard, the chancellor. Sixth, two books on the Deeds of Charlemagne, written under the name of a monk of Saint Gall, are claimed for Notker Balbulus.

### VI. On the Martyrology

As for the Martyrology, there is no doubt that it was composed by Notker, and it rightly holds the first place among his writings. I do not see why Pinus, in the *New Bibliotheca*, doubted whether it was written at the end of the ninth century or the beginning of the tenth; for he himself indicates the time when he undertook this work: the eighth day before the Kalends of May. He wrote, namely, while Formosus occupied the Roman see—not indeed in the first year of his pontificate, but in one of the following years. Formosus was seated in 891; therefore we have assigned this Martyrology to the year 894. Many observations could be made about it, and [Col. 1030A] it deserves to be read by scholars. It was in use among the Germans. Concerning Anacletus, it reports, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, that he was ordained priest by Peter, was compelled by force to sacrifice to idols, and afterward, moved to repentance, was crowned with martyrdom under Domitian. I do not know where it obtained what it reports about Anacletus’s apostasy; Platina, Bale, and many others assert that he either died or suffered martyrdom under Trajan.

## IN THE NAME OF THE LORD BEGINS THE MARTYROLOGY THROUGHOUT THE YEAR OF OUR HOLY FATHER NOTKER, CALLED BALBULUS, MONK OF SAINT GALL

[Col. 1029]

## JANUARY

The month of January has thirty-one days, while the moon has twenty-nine.

[Col. 1029B]

### Kalends of January.—The octave of the Lord’s Nativity

On this day the same Lord was circumcised in the flesh according to the law of Moses and received the name Jesus, which had been given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb (Luke 2).

At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Almachius the martyr, who, at the command of Alipius, prefect of the City, said: “Today is the octave of the Lord’s day; cease from the superstitions of idols and from polluted sacrifices.” For this reason he was killed by gladiators.

Likewise at Rome, Saint Martina, virgin and martyr, who under the emperor Alexander was tortured for the faith of Christ by many kinds of torment and finally struck with the sword. She also subdued the ferocity of a lion by the power of the Holy Spirit dwelling within her, and by her prayer destroyed idols and converted many to the faith of Christ. In vengeance for this, the emperor ended his impious life by tearing himself apart.

On the same day at Spoleto, a city of Tuscia, the passion of Saint Concordius, a Roman presbyter of the title of Pastor, in the time of the emperor Antoninus. Because he refused to sacrifice to idols, he received a capital sentence from the count Torquatus. Likewise at Rome, on the Appian Way, Corona and thirty soldiers, who under the emperor Diocletian were found worthy to be crowned with martyrdom for confessing the Christian faith.

[Col. 1029D] In Caesarea, the metropolis of Cappadocia, the death of Saint Basil, bishop, who wrote the Rule for the brothers and many other useful works. In addition to the many miracles he performed, by prayer he was found worthy to recover the written acknowledgment of a lost man, which the man had made to the devil; and, for the conversion of the Jew Joseph, he postponed the day of his own death. Even after death he annulled the written record of a certain abominable crime.

In Africa, the commemoration of Saint Fulgentius, bishop and confessor of the Church of Ruspe. During the Vandal persecution, on account of the Catholic faith and his outstanding learning, he suffered much from the Arians and was long banished in exile to Sardinia. At last he was permitted to return to his church, and, illustrious in life and word, he rested in a holy death, in the twenty-fifth year of his episcopate and the sixty-fifth year of his entire life.

At Alexandria, Saint Euphrosyne, virgin, who was born after her father Paphnutius had prayed for her to a barren mother. While still a child, she secretly had herself tonsured and sought the monastic life, taking for herself the name Smaragdus. Afterward she remained for twenty-eight years in complete holiness within seclusion. When afflicted by illness and recognizing that death was approaching, she revealed herself to a religious man—her father, who by then had repeatedly and tearfully sought her. Her name and manner of life are celebrated among the Romans under the interpretation “most chaste.”

### Fourth day before the Nones of January.—The octave of Saint Stephen

At Rome, Pope Telesphorus. He established that a fast should be observed for seven weeks before Easter, that Mass should be celebrated on the night of the Lord’s Nativity, and that the angelic hymn—namely, “Glory to God in the highest”—should be sung. During all the remaining time, no one was to presume to celebrate Mass before the third hour, at which the Lord is said to have been crucified. He too was crowned with martyrdom and buried beside the body of Saint Peter in the Vatican.

At Antioch, Macarius the abbot. And in Pontus, in the city of Tomis, the three brothers Argeus, Narcissus, and Marcellinus, boys. Likewise at Tomis, Philip, bishop. Under Caesar Licinius, he was seized among the recruits. When he refused military service, he was beaten nearly to death, long tormented in prison, placed in the stocks, and then drowned in the sea; thus he completed his martyrdom. His body was cast upon the shore and buried by religious men, and it shines with great miracles.

At Vienne, the death of Blessed Florentius, bishop.

In the territory of Lyons, in the monastery of the Jura, Saint Eugendus the abbot, whose life shone forth, full of virtues and miracles.

[Col. 1031B]

### Third day before the Nones of January.—The octave of Saint John the Apostle

At Rome, Antherus, pope and martyr, who was the twentieth after Blessed Peter, governed the Church for twelve years, and diligently investigated the deeds of the martyrs. He suffered under Maximian and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way.

At Paris, Saint Genevieve, virgin, who was dedicated to Christ by Blessed Germanus, bishop of Auxerre. She became widely renowned for wondrous virtues and miracles and grew old in Christ’s service until the age of eighty.

### Second day before the Nones of January.—The octave of the Innocents

At Crete, the commemoration of Saint Titus, a disciple of the apostles.

In Africa, Saints Aquilinus, Geminus, Eugentius [Eugenius], Martianus, Quintus, Theodotus, and Trypho, most illustrious martyrs.

On the same day at the city of Rome, Saints Priscus, presbyter, and Priscillianus, cleric, together with Benedicta, a religious woman. In the time of Julian, the most impious emperor, they completed their martyrdom by the sword.

Likewise at Rome, Blessed Daphrosa, wife of Fabian the martyr. After the condemnation of her blessed husband, she was first banished into exile and afterward, by order of the impious Julian, put to death by beheading.

On the same day, the commemoration of Theogenes the martyr, who under Caesar Licinius completed his passion through the tribune Licentius. In the Hellespont he was first stretched between four pillars and beaten with clubs; afterward he was thrown into prison to die there of hunger. But through the invisible mercy of the Lord, he was fed there for forty days with heavenly food. He continually remained in the praises of God. Finally he was thrown into the sea and became a martyr. Eutychus, Eustochius, and Zoticus took him from the seashore and buried him in the forum of the Hellespont.

On the same day, the passion of Peter, surnamed Balsam, who under the emperor Maximian, while Severus was governor, was suspended and torn with hooks; finally he was struck with the sword and buried in the city of Aulona.

On the same day, the passion of Lucian, presbyter and martyr. Sent from Rome to preach the word of God in Gaul, after converting many to Christ in those regions, he was beheaded under the emperor Julian. [Col. 1032A] At his tomb many miracles are displayed and very many healings occur.

### Nones of January.—The vigil of the Epiphany

At Jerusalem, the death of Saint Simeon the prophet, who, having recognized the Lord Jesus Christ through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, received him from the hands of his parents into his arms. Not only concerning him but also concerning his mother, he foretold the future in mystical speech (Luke 2).

At Antioch, the death of Saint Simeon the monk, a man of admirable virtue. At the age of thirteen, renouncing this world, he sought the enclosure of a monastery. There, with astonishing abstinence—allowing himself food scarcely on the seventh day—he learned the Psalter within four months. Then, through an excessive determination to discipline his body, he bound his loins tightly with a cord of vine branches and was severely lacerated. He next shut himself in a certain well, but the brothers forcibly brought him back to the monastery. Fleeing secretly, he sought the desert. After remaining there for a long time, burning with holiness, he enclosed himself upon a higher column. He allowed himself to be seen neither by an unrelated woman nor even by his own mother. To this day no woman enters the basilica of that column. For a certain woman, dressed in men’s clothing, tried to enter; but as soon as she touched the threshold, she fell backward dead.

In Africa, Felix, Secundus, Honorius, Lucianus, Candidus, Januarius, Telesphorus, Jocundus, and Anastasia.

### Eighth day before the Ides of January.—The Epiphany of the Lord

This is interpreted as “manifestation.” Among the Romans the same feast is called Theophany, so that from the composition of the name it may be understood that it is the manifestation of God. On this day the Magi, according to the prophecy of Balaam, whose successors they were—“A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a rod shall spring up from Israel; it shall strike the leaders of Moab and lay waste all the sons of Seth, and Edom shall be its possession” (Numbers 24); and again, “From Jacob there shall arise one who rules and destroys the remnants of the city” (ibid.), namely Ar, which is now called Areopolis—having seen in the East, at the hour of the Lord’s birth, the previously unknown star, that is, at home, and having observed it toward Jerusalem, were more certainly instructed in that royal city by Micah’s prophecy concerning the place of Christ’s birth. Guided by that same star, they found the child Jesus in Bethlehem with Mary his mother, and, worshiping him, honored him with mystical gifts.

Although this is believed to have been brought about by divine inspiration, so that the nations living nearby might already then become participants in the Lord’s birth and in prophetic teaching, it is nevertheless not without historical rationale and a temporal aspect of Christ’s dispensation: the leaders of the Moabites, having once offered gifts to the parents of the king whom they suspected, might obtain favor, and the same gifts might be useful for the journey into Egypt. For these Magi were not Chaldaeans, Indians, or finally Persians, as some maintain, nor did they come to worship him in the second or third year of the Lord’s birth. Rather, they were Moabites, Ammonites, or Midianites—Saint Jerome himself supporting this view—and on the thirteenth day of his birth they were found worthy, through the zeal of devotion, to find him not in lofty Jerusalem, as they had supposed, but in humble Bethlehem, and to receive a spiritual reward.

On the same day, the passion of Saint Macra, virgin. When the governor Rictiovarus ordered her to be tortured and thrown into the fire, she remained unharmed. Then, after her breasts had been cut off and she had been afflicted by the squalor of prison, she was rolled over extremely sharp potsherds and glowing coals, and, while praying, departed to the Lord.

In Africa, Florus, Jocundus, Peter, Marcus, Acutius, and Januaria.

In Syria, Saint Anastasia.

At Rennes [Rhedonis], the feast, episcopal ordination, and death of Saint Melanius [Melanii], bishop and confessor. A cloak placed over his body amid the flames was found unharmed.

[Col. 1033B]

### Seventh day before the Ides of January.—The return of the child Jesus from Egypt

And the commemoration of Saint Lucian, presbyter and martyr of the Church of Antioch, a most learned and eloquent man. He suffered at Nicomedia for confessing Christ and was cut into four pieces. The pieces, each tied to a stone and sunk into the sea, were later found at Helenopolis in Bithynia, with the body intact, and were honorably buried. When that city had previously been called Drepana, the emperor Constantine restored it in honor of the same martyr and named it Helenopolis after his mother.

Likewise at Antioch, Blessed Clerius, deacon, who, because of his confession of Christ, was tortured seven times and long tormented in prison; finally he was beheaded and completed his martyrdom.

The passion of Saint Fausta, virgin, under the emperor Maximian. By the power of her endurance she first converted Evilasius, the palace official and her torturer, to the faith, as well as the prefect who had ordered her to be tortured. First she was suspended and torn with iron instruments; afterward she was handed over to beasts, but was defiled by none of them. Then nails were driven into her head. Later she was thrown into a frying pan of boiling pitch, but was not harmed. Thus, together with Evilasius and the prefect, she underwent torments and gave up her spirit. When the Christian people heard this, they buried the bodies of the saints.

### Sixth day before the Ides of January.—In Greece, Polyeuctus and Palladius

At Naples in Campania, the commemoration of Saint Severinus, bishop and confessor, brother of the most blessed Victorinus, a man renowned for miracles. He too was an imitator [possibly: “emperor,” but the contextual reading is uncertain] of his brother and, after performing many virtues, rested full of holiness. He was buried in the place where, before being called to the episcopate, he had lived with the greatest abstinence.

In Greece, Rusticus, Timothy, and Jocundus.

At Bellovaci, Saint Lucian, companion of Blessed Dionysius. Likewise Messianus.

At Metz, Saint Patiens, bishop.

### Fifth day before the Ides of January.—In Mauritania, in the city of Caesarea, the passion of Saint Martiana, virgin and martyr

On the same day at Antioch, Saint Julian the martyr and Basilissa the virgin. Because they were their only children, their very wealthy parents, concerned for them, resisted and unwillingly joined them outwardly in marriage. Yet, by a most holy vow, they remained together in virginity for several years and established monasteries from their own property in the districts of Antioch, so many and so populous that Julian became the father of ten thousand monks, while Basilissa became the mother of many virgins. Sending them before her to the kingdom of heaven, she herself followed them.

Later Julian was sought by the governor Martianus. At that time the most savage rage, inflamed under Diocletian and Maximian to persecute the saints of God, forced a multitude of priests and ministers of Christ’s Church to flee to him because of the ferocity of the persecution. He was therefore seized with this great multitude and reserved for the governor’s hearing; the other servants of God, at the command of the most cruel ruler, were consumed by the fire that had been kindled and applied to the place where they stood. It is said that, to honor the precious death of the saints, choirs singing to God were heard at the third, sixth, and ninth hours, and also in the evening.

Blessed Julian, however, was first beaten with the most rigid clubs in the presence of the governor. While he was being beaten, one of the officials, indispensable to the governor, lost an eye. At the prayer of Blessed Julian he immediately recovered it; and, believing in Christ, he was at once beheaded by the insane judge.

Then Blessed Julian was led to a temple of demons, where five hundred idols were smashed together and reduced to dust. For this he was shut in the deepest and darkest prison with the boy Celsus, the governor’s son. They were granted a most pleasant fragrance and a wondrous light. Seven brothers and twenty soldiers who came to visit them were handed over to the fire first, while the latter were killed by the sword.

Finally Julian and the boy Celsus, together with the presbyter Antonius and Anastasius, were afflicted with various punishments and, along with the matron Marcionilla, were killed by the soldiers.

### Fourth day before the Ides of January.—The commemoration of Blessed Nicanor

Nicanor was one of the first seven deacons. He was gloriously crowned at Cyprus and was honorably buried there.

In the Thebaid, the commemoration of Saint Paul, the first hermit, who from the age of sixteen until his ninety-third year remained alone in the desert. Antony saw his soul carried by angels into heaven among the choirs of the apostles and prophets.

[Col. 1034D] At Rome, Melchiades, bishop, who established that the faithful should in no way fast on Sundays in the Church. Pope Hyginus, who organized the clergy and distributed the ecclesiastical ranks.

### Third day before the Ides of January.—The Lord’s departure from Egypt

According to some, this is celebrated on the seventh day before the Ides of January; according to others, on the Nones of January, because of the journey, which lasted many days.

At Alexandria, Saints Peter, Severus, and Leucius, confessors.

In Africa, the commemoration of Saint Salvius the martyr, on whose feast Saint Augustine preached a sermon to the people of Carthage.

### The day before the Ides of January

In Achaia, Cyriacus.

In Egypt, Philoromus.

In Arabia, Saturus. Passing before a certain idol’s temple, he blew upon it and signed his forehead; it immediately collapsed. For this reason he was beheaded by the judge of the place.

On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Arcadius the martyr, illustrious by birth and miracles.

### Ides of January.—The octave of the Theophany

At Rome, on the Lavican Way, Secundina, Corona, and forty soldiers under the emperor Gallienus.

At Poitiers, the death of Saint Hilary, bishop and confessor, who under Constantius Augustus, the heretic, was banished into exile in Phrygia for four years because of the Catholic faith. Among his other virtues, it is reported of him that he raised a dead man by prayer.

### Nineteenth day before the Kalends of February

At Antioch, Glycerius, a deacon, one of the ancients, who suffered many torments and was drowned in the sea.

[Col. 1035B] At Nola in Campania, Felix, presbyter. When his bishop Maximus, terrified by the persecution, had fled into the desert, Blessed Felix was captured, bound in chains, brought before the governor, and beaten with clubs. Then he was tortured on the rack, bound in prison, and covered with snails and potsherds. At night an angel of the Lord broke his chains and split the beam that bound his feet, commanding him to seek his priest.

When he had finally found him, weighed down by age, consumed by hunger, stiffened by frost, with eyes closed and teeth clenched, half alive and scarcely breathing—and when he had nothing to offer the feeble old man—he suddenly saw, with amazement, a bunch of grapes hanging from the thorns. He pressed it into the confessor’s mouth, and, after restoring his strength, placed him on his shoulders and carried him to the city. There he secretly fed him under the shelter of a widow’s hut.

Later he was captured and driven into exile. After converting many there by the display of signs, he returned. When he was again sought for torture, he was hidden by divine providence and, at Nola, shone forth with so many virtues that the entire people demanded him as their bishop. He did not consent; instead, after another had been ordained in his place, he nevertheless devoted himself to God’s service for twelve years and, after celebrating the mysteries on the Lord’s Day, departed to Christ. He was buried not far from the city of Nola, in a place called Pincis.

In the city of Spoleto, the commemoration of Pontianus the martyr, who suffered in the time of the emperor Antoninus under the judge Fabianus. Because he refused to sacrifice to idols, the judge ordered him to be cruelly beaten with rods. Then he ordered him to walk barefoot over burning coals, afterward to have two lions released upon him. When they did not harm him, molten lead was poured over him; and when he was not injured even by this, he was beheaded.

### Eighteenth day before the Kalends of February

In Palestine, the death of Habakkuk the prophet, whose relics, together with the bones of the prophet Micah, were found by divine revelation in the time of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius.

Likewise, Macarius the abbot, a disciple of Saint Antony.

Likewise, Blessed Isidore, renowned for the holiness of his life, faith, and miracles.

### Seventeenth day before the Kalends of February

At Rome, on the Salarian Way, in the cemetery of Priscilla, the commemoration of Saint Marcellus, pope. He established cemeteries on the Salarian Way and twenty-five titular churches in the city of Rome for the baptism and penance of the many who were converted from paganism, and for the burial of martyrs.

By order of the emperor Maximian, he was first beaten with clubs and expelled from the presence of the man whom he had rebuked. Later, when the emperor heard that Marcellus had made the house of Saint Lucina—which he himself had condemned to confiscation because she had given her property to Christians—into a church and celebrated Masses there, he ordered boards to be laid in the middle of the city, in the church, for the animals of the public stable, and assigned the same bishop to serve the animals under public guard. After serving there for many years, dressed in a cilicium cloak, he died; John the presbyter and Blessed Lucina embalmed him with spices and buried him in the cemetery of Priscilla.

At Arles, Saint Honoratus, bishop and confessor. Among his other miracles, it is said that by prayer he drove a dragon from the island of Hilarina and founded a monastery there.

In the district of Mandes, in the monastery of Péronne, Saint Fursa, an Irishman. Rapt from this world, he saw many wondrous things, and, after returning, related things worthy of wonder to mortal people; afterward he departed this life in austere discipline.

### Sixteenth day before the Kalends of February

In Egypt, in the Thebaid, the death of Blessed Antony the monk. Although he had no knowledge of letters, it is universally proclaimed that by hearing he retained the divine Scriptures in memory, understood them through wise reflection, and led from childhood to decrepit old age an incomparable life made illustrious by miracles, leaving throughout the Christian world many disciples of his holiness.

He died in peace under the emperor Constantine, in the one hundred and fifth year of his life, and was buried in the desert by his disciples, as he himself had commanded while living, so that the place would remain hidden. His body, found by divine revelation under the emperor Justinian, was brought to Alexandria and buried in the church of Blessed John the Baptist.

At Langres, the commemoration of the holy twins Speusippus, Elasippus, and Melasippus [Eleusippus and Meleusippus]. When they were twenty-five years old, they were crowned with martyrdom together with their grandmother Leonilla, and with Jonilla and Neon, in the time of the emperor Aurelian.

The twins were hung from a single tree, their hands bound upward and their feet downward, stretched so far that they seemed almost to be torn apart from the very structure of their limbs. Then they were thrown into the fire, but were not harmed by the flames; amid their prayers they departed together to the Lord.

Seeing this, Jonilla confessed that she too was a Christian. Seized by the crowd, she was hung by her hair and afflicted with many punishments. Since she refused to deny Christ, she was killed by the sword together with Leonilla. Neon, the recorder of the deeds, also confessed the name of Christ and was crowned with martyrdom.

Benignus the presbyter taught and baptized these twins. Blessed Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna and a hearer of the apostle John, sent him from the East to Gaul with Andochius, his fellow presbyter, and Thyrsus, a deacon. The twins were buried two miles from the city of Langres. Turbon, who wrote of the victories of those confessing the Lord, suffered martyrdom not long afterward.

### Fifteenth day before the Kalends of February.—The Chair of Saint Peter the Apostle

This was the chair on which he first sat at Rome. For when that same prince of the apostles had first preached the Gospel in Jerusalem, Caesarea, and the other cities of the Jews, he was afterward sent to preach to the Gentiles. He came to Antioch, founded the Church there, and governed it for . . . years [according to Baronius, seven years]. From there he proceeded to Rome in the second year of Caesar Claudius. Preaching the Gospel there with the greatest zeal, he governed the episcopate of that city for twenty-five years.

Likewise at Rome, the commemoration of Saint Prisca, virgin and martyr.

In Pontus, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Moses and Ammonius. Since they were soldiers, they were first assigned to the mines and finally consigned to the fire.

### Fourteenth day before the Kalends of February

At Jerusalem, the commemoration of the holy sisters Martha and Mary, the sisters of Lazarus.

At Smyrna, Saint Germanicus the martyr, condemned to the beasts.

In Africa, Paul, Quintus, and many other martyrs. At Carthage, Picaria, Pia, and thirty-eight others.

### Thirteenth day before the Kalends of February

At Rome, Fabian, pope. After presiding over the Church for twenty-five years, he suffered in the time of Decius and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus. He divided the regions among the deacons and arranged for seven deacons to supervise an equal number of notaries, so that they might collect the deeds of the martyrs in full. He also ordered many buildings to be constructed throughout the cemeteries. At his election, it is said that the Holy Spirit appeared to many in the form of a dove.

Likewise at Rome, on the same day, the commemoration of Saint Sebastian the martyr. He was so dear to the emperors Diocletian and Maximian that they entrusted him with the command of the first cohort. When Diocletian learned that he was a Christian and could not be recalled from the faith, he ordered him to be tied in the middle of the field like a target for arrows and shot by the soldiers. When he stood full of arrows, like a hedgehog, they thought him dead and departed.

At night a woman named Irene came to take away the body and found him alive. She brought him into her house and cared for him. When he recovered, he strengthened many in the faith. Before long he appeared before the emperors themselves and rebuked them as they deserved.

Then Diocletian ordered him to be led into the palace hippodrome and beaten until he died. They threw his supposedly dead body into the great sewer. But he appeared in a dream to the holy matron Lucina and said: “Near the circus you will find my body hanging from a hook. When you have taken it down, carry it to the Catacombs and bury me in a crypt beside the remains of the apostles.” That same night she came with servants and fulfilled everything as he had said.

On the same day at Rome, the holy martyrs Marinus [Marius] and Martha, with their sons Audifax and Ambacuc [Abachum], noble Persians who had come to Rome to pray in the time of the emperor Claudius. After enduring beatings, the rack, fires, hooks, and the cutting off of their hands, Martha was killed in a pool, while the others were beheaded.

### Twelfth day before the Kalends of February

At Athens, Publius, bishop. When Paul the apostle had been cast by shipwreck onto an island, Publius showed him considerable kindness after his father had been cured of fevers and dysentery. Converted to Christ through Paul’s preaching, he advanced so greatly by God’s grace that he was ordained bishop of the Athenians by the Apostle himself and crowned with martyrdom.

At Rome, Saint Agnes. Under the prefect of the City, Symphronius, because for love of Christ and of virginity she refused to take his son as her husband, she was taken naked to a brothel as a means of mockery. At first she was covered by her own hair, then clothed with a heavenly garment. When the prefect’s son pursued her with excessive shamelessness and was consequently strangled by the devil, she restored him to life by the power of prayer. After this she was thrown into the fire, but the flames were extinguished through the merit of her holiness, and she was struck with the sword.

Later she appeared to her parents amid a multitude of virgins clothed in gold-woven garments and openly proclaimed on earth the glory of God, which she enjoyed in heaven.

In Spain, in the city of Tarragona, the commemoration of Saints Fructuosus, bishop, and Augurius and Eulogius, deacons. In the time of the emperor Gallienus, under the governor Aemilianus, they were first thrust into prison and afterward thrown into the flames. With their bonds burned away, praying with hands outstretched in the form of a cross, they obtained that they should be burned. Immediately afterward, some of the brothers and the governor’s daughter, who was standing there, saw the souls of the saints ascend to heaven crowned.

### Eleventh day before the Kalends of February

At Troyes, the passion of Saint Patroclus the martyr.

In Spain, the commemoration of Saint Vincent, deacon and martyr. Together with his bishop Saint Valerius, he was brought from the city of Caesarea Augusta to Valencia in heavy chains, by order of Datianus. There he was long tormented by hunger and the filth of prison, afflicted by the tortures of the rack and the horrible tearing of hooks, and for a very long time roasted upon an iron bed. He was sprinkled with drops of fat and crackling salt.

After this he was thrust into a dreadful prison, his legs spread apart in a stock, and thrown upon extremely sharp fragments of pottery. There a great light appeared at night, and the martyr, freed by God’s power, sang a hymn among the angels, by whom he was found worthy to be visited, so that the prison guard himself believed in Christ.

When morning came, Datianus sent for him and ordered him to be laid upon a very soft bed, so that, after being somewhat restored, he might be tortured more harshly again. But he gave his tireless spirit back to Christ.

Then Datianus ordered his body to be thrown into a field and exposed to beasts and birds. But a raven, divinely assigned to guard it, not only drove away the other birds but also repelled a huge wolf from the holy body. When this was reported to Datianus, he ordered Vincent to be sewn into a leather sack and sunk into the depths of the sea with a very heavy stone. But before the rowers could touch the harbor, by God’s power he floated upon the waves, was carried to the shore, and buried in the sand.

Afterward the holy martyr revealed himself to a certain faithful old woman. When the fury of the persecution had ceased, Christians reverently took up his body and buried it in a church.

The commemoration of Saint Anastasius, monk and martyr, from Persia. After suffering many torments of prison, beatings, and chains in Caesarea of Palestine at the hands of the Persians, he was finally afflicted with many punishments in Persia and at last beheaded by their king Chosroes, together with seventy others. His bodily relics were first brought to the monastery at Jerusalem and afterward to Rome; they are venerated in the monastery of Blessed Paul the Apostle, called at the Salvian Waters.

On the same day in Gaul, in the city of Embrun, Saints Vincent, Orontius, and Victor, martyrs.

### Tenth day before the Kalends of February

The commemoration of Saint Parmenas, one of the first seven deacons. Delivered by the brothers to the grace of God, he completed with full faith the office of preaching entrusted to him, obtained the palm of martyrdom, and rested at Philippi.

At Rome, Emerentiana, virgin of Christ and martyr, who was the foster-sister of Saint Agnes. While she was praying at Agnes’s tomb and defending those praying with her from the violence of the pagans, she was stoned by them.

In Mauritania, in the city of Neocaesarea, the commemoration of Saint Severianus and his wife Aquila, who were burned by fire.

### Ninth day before the Kalends of February

The commemoration of Saint Timothy, disciple of Blessed Paul the Apostle. Ordained bishop at Ephesus by the blessed Apostle, he slept after many struggles for Christ. In the twentieth year, his body was transferred to Constantinople together with the relics of Blessed Andrew and Luke.

At Antioch, Saint Babylas, bishop, with three children. Under . . . [according to Baronius, under Decius], after he had frequently glorified the Lord by his sufferings and tortures, he obtained a glorious end to his life in chains. Buried not far from the Castalian spring, he condemned Apollo to silence in the very place most famous for its oracles.

In the city of Neocaesarea, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Mardonius, Musonius, Eugenius, and Marcellus, all of whom were delivered to the fire, while their relics were scattered into the Axus River.

### Eighth day before the Kalends of February

At Rome, the translation of Saint Paul the Apostle and his conversion near Damascus; and there also, the commemoration of Saint Ananias, who baptized Paul.

Elsewhere, the commemoration of Saint Projectus the martyr. At Constantinople, Gregory the Theologian.

[Col. 1040A] At the city of Gabala, Saint Severianus, bishop, a man of admirable holiness and learning.

### Seventh day before the Kalends of February

The commemoration of Saint Polycarp, who, as a disciple of Blessed John the Apostle and ordained by him bishop of Smyrna, was foremost throughout all Asia.

Later, during the reign of Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus, in the fourth persecution after Nero, while the proconsul was seated at Smyrna and the entire people were shouting against him in the amphitheater, he was delivered to the fire. But the flame bent into the shape of a vaulted chamber, appearing like a sail swollen by the wind, and stood above the martyr’s body. The body placed within it was not like burning flesh, but as though gold or silver were glowing in a furnace.

Moreover, those standing around inhaled a fragrance through their nostrils, as though incense were burning or the most precious ointment were giving off its scent. Finally, when the agents of the crime saw that the body could not be consumed by fire, they ordered the executioners to come closer and pierce with a sword the body from which the fire had recoiled. When this was done, such a great quantity of blood poured out that it extinguished the pyre.

Together with him, twelve others who had come from Philadelphia completed their martyrdom in the aforementioned city. At that time also Germanicus, an illustrious athlete of Christ, was condemned to the beasts. Voluntarily provoking them to devour him, he received the crown of eternal life through a swift death.

On the same day, the holy martyr Theogenes with thirty-six others.

Likewise at Bourges, Blessed Sulpitius, bishop and confessor.

### Sixth day before the Kalends of February

In Africa, the commemoration of Saint Julian, Vincentia, and thirty-two others.

The commemoration of Saint John, bishop of Constantinople, who, on account of his remarkable and most precious doctrine, is called Chrysostom—interpreted in Latin as “golden-mouthed” or “having a golden mouth.” Through many struggles he earned eternal life.

Likewise, Marius, abbot of the monastery of Bodocae, renowned for his life and virtues.

In Bethlehem of Judaea, the death of Paula, mother of Eustochium [Eustochius], a virgin of Christ. Although she was of the most noble senatorial family at Rome, she renounced the world and, distributing her wealth among the poor, attained the poverty of Christ. At the aforesaid town, glorified by the Lord’s Nativity, she became the mother of a monastery of virgins. Saint Jerome, writing her Life, admirable for its virtues, testifies that she was crowned with martyrdom in a far higher sense. At her request he also composed many little works.

**V Kal. Febr.** — The octave of Saint Agnes, or, according to some, her true [double] birthday.

In the city of Apollonia, the martyrs Leucius, Thyrsus, and Callinicus. In the time of the Emperor Decius, under the governors Cymbricius, Silvanus, and Baudius, they were tortured with various kinds of torments. The first and the last completed their martyrdom by beheading; the one in the middle, summoned by a heavenly voice, gave up his spirit. This occurred in Greece.

On the same day, at Alexandria, blessed Cyril, bishop, who proved a most distinguished defender of the Catholic faith.

In the monastery of Reomans [Rheims], Hicanus [John], a priest and man of God.

**IV Kal. Febr.** — At Rome, the feast of Papias and Maurus, soldiers, in the time of Diocletian. Seeing the steadfastness of the martyrs Saturninus and Sisinnius, they were converted to the faith. Immediately Laodicius, prefect of the City, ordered that their mouths—the mouths with which they confessed Christ—be crushed with stones, and that they be thrust back [pushed back] into the prison where they had been baptized by Pope Marcellus. Twelve days later he ordered them brought out, laid in the street, and beaten with clubs; then, after being raised from the ground, they were beaten with leaded scourges until they expired. The priest John gathered their bodies by night and buried them on the Nomentan Way, at the Springs of blessed Peter, where he baptized. This is written in the Acts of blessed Pope Marcellus.

On the same day at Trier, the burial of blessed Valerius, bishop and disciple of Saint Peter the Apostle.

**III Kal. Febr.** — At Antioch, the passion of Saint Hippolytus, who, having been somewhat deceived when the schism of Novatus arose, was corrected through the working of Christ’s grace and returned to the charity of the Church. For it, and within it, he later completed a glorious martyrdom.

At Jerusalem, the burial of the most blessed Matthias, bishop, concerning whom marvelous and faith-filled deeds are related. He ruled the Church as its eighth bishop after James and, having suffered much for Christ, finally ended his life in peace.

Also blessed Alexander. During the Decian persecution he was brought before tribunals for confessing the faith and handed over to prison bonds. When he shone with the venerable gray hair of an advanced age, and after he had often glorified the Lord through his sufferings and tortures, he was taken from his bonds to the tribunals and recalled from the tribunals to his bonds. Amid the successive torments that followed one another in turn, he rested with a good end.

Also in the monastery of Malbodium, the feast of Adelgund, a virgin. Born of noble family in the time of Dagobert, king of the Franks, she chose the purpose of virginity and persevered in it. An angelic vision was often revealed to her, exhorting her to remain faithful to her purpose. Finally, with great brightness of heavenly light, she departed to eternal life.

**Pridie Kal. Febr.** — At Alexandria, the feast of Saint Metranus, martyr. The pagans seized him and ordered him to utter impious words. When he refused, they battered his whole body with clubs. Piercing his face and eyes with sharp reeds, they drove him outside the city amid tortures. There they stoned away whatever spirit still remained in him.

Also at Alexandria, Tarsitius, Zoticus, and Ammonius.

In Africa, Victor, Publius, Saturninus, and Polycarp. Also Thyrsus, Gelasius, and Callinicus.

On the same day, at the city of Tridentum [Trent], blessed Vigilius, bishop and martyr.

# February

February has twenty-eight days, twenty-nine according to the lunar calendar, and thirty in a leap year.

**Kal. Febr.** — At Antioch, Saint Ignatius, bishop and martyr.

In Greece, Polycarp, bishop.

At Ravenna, Saint Severus, bishop.

At Smyrna, the feast of Saint Pionius, martyr. During the persecution of Antoninus Verus, after his unshakable constancy in answering and the squalor of the prison—where he strengthened many of the brethren for martyrdom by his exhortations—he was at last afflicted with many tortures, fastened with nails, and placed upon a blazing pyre; thus he received a blessed end for Christ. Fifteen others suffered with him.

On the same day, blessed Ephrem, deacon of the Church of Edessa.

In Ireland, the feast of Saint Brigit, virgin, who is said to have possessed great merits and holiness. When she touched the altar wood as a testimony to her virginity, it became green.

On the same day, Saint Paul, bishop of the city of Troyes. His life shone with virtues, and his precious death is commended by miracles.

**IV Non. Febr.** — The Hypapante of the Lord, or the Purification of blessed Mary, when she presented the Lord Jesus with the offerings prescribed by the Law in the Temple, and Simeon and Anna recognized through the Holy Spirit that he was the Christ and proclaimed him to those awaiting the redemption of Jerusalem (Luke 1).

At Caesarea, the feast of the most blessed Cornelius the centurion. When an angel announced to him that his prayers and almsgiving were acceptable to God, he immediately, at the angel’s instruction, sent messengers to the holy Apostle Peter, asking him to deign to bring salvation. Taught by a heavenly vision not to shrink from the uncleanness of the Gentiles, Peter hastened to him, spoke in the hearing of the Gentiles concerning faith in Jesus Christ, and, recognizing without doubt that they had received the Holy Spirit through the gift of tongues, ordered them to be baptized. After the conversion of many thousands of Jews, he consecrated these firstfruits from the Gentiles to God. Cornelius, having abandoned military service, was elevated to the dignity of bishop at the aforesaid city and rested there.

At Rome, Saint Apronianus, registrar, who was baptized by Sisinnius, deacon of Pope Marcellus, and beheaded by Laodicius, prefect of the City, in the time of the Emperor Maximian Augustus.

Also at Rome, at the Forum of Symphronius, on the Flaminian Way, at the 163rd milestone from the City, Laurentius and Hippolytus, and the feast of Saint Fortunatus.

In Africa, Victor, Maurinus, Honoratus, Urbanus, Hilary, Perpetuus, Julian, Privatula, and seventy-four others.

At Orléans, the burial of blessed Flosculus, bishop and confessor, and of Sicharia, virgin.

**III Non. Febr.** — At Sebaste, a city of Cappadocia, the passion of Saint Blaise, bishop and martyr of Christ, who was beheaded under the governor Agricolaus, together with two little boys, the sons of one woman, among those seven women who, strengthened by his preaching, suffered martyrdom under the same governor.

In Africa, blessed Celerinus, deacon and confessor, and the holy martyrs Celerina, his grandmother, Laurentinus, his paternal uncle, and Ignatius, his maternal uncle.

At Lyons, the burial of Saint Lupicinus, bishop.

**Pridie Non. Febr.** — At the Forum of Symphronius, the feast of the holy Gemini, Gelasius, Mannius [Magnus], Aquilinus [Aquilius], and Donatus.

In the Egyptian city called Thynius [Thmuis], the passion of blessed Phileas, bishop of that city, and of Philoromus, a tribune of the Roman soldiers. Philoromus admired the bishop’s steadfastness and praised it; he was beheaded together with him. With them also an innumerable multitude of believers from the same city, following the footsteps of their shepherd, were crowned with martyrdom in the persecution.

**Non. Febr.** — At Patras, the episcopal ordination of Saint Andrew the Apostle.

In Sicily, at the city of Catana, the passion of Saint Agatha, virgin, under the Emperor Decius and the proconsul Quintianus. After blows and imprisonment, after the rack and tortures, after the cutting off of her breasts—but also their healing by the Lord—and after being rolled over potsherds and coals, she finally completed her course in prison.

At Vienne, blessed Avitus, bishop. Through his faith, diligence, and admirable teaching, Gaul was defended from the assault of the Arian heresy in the time of King Gundobad.

**VIII Id. Febr.** — At Rome, on the Appian Way, in its cemetery, the passion of Saint Soteris, virgin and martyr.

At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the feast of Saint Dorothea, virgin. Together with two sisters, Christe and Callista, who had recently apostatized from the faith, she was entrusted to the pains of life so that they might turn her away from Christ; instead, she converted them again to Christ. Thus, when they were thrown by the governor into a vessel of boiling liquid, they attained the palm of martyrdom. Afterwards she herself, under Sapricius, governor of that province, was first tortured by stretching on the rack, then beaten for a very long time with palms, and finally punished by sentence of death.

As she was being led from the governor’s residence to execution, a certain schoolmaster named Theophilus said to her: “Come now, bride of Christ, send me apples from the paradise of your Christ.” She immediately promised that she would send them. When they reached the place where she was to be slain, she prayed briefly, brought out her handkerchief, called to her a certain six-year-old boy, and sent him to Theophilus, saying: “Tell him: Dorothea, the handmaid of God, sends you apples from the paradise of her Christ.”

He received them and gave thanks because she had fulfilled his request. He began wiping his face with them. Suddenly he was filled with such sweetness that, entirely changed in mind, he repeatedly exclaimed with great rejoicing and a clear voice: “Blessed is the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.” Because of this confession he too was immediately seized and hung upon the rack, and tortured with such cruelty that all who stood around were horrified. Finally, after being beheaded, he completed his martyrdom.

On the same day, the feast of Antholianus, who was crowned with martyrdom near the city of Clermont.

In Gaul, at the city of Arras [Aderatum], the burial of Saint Vedastus, bishop and confessor.

In the monastery of Hellone, the burial of Saint Amandus, bishop and confessor.

**VII Id. Febr.** — In Britain, the venerable Saint Moses [Moyses], bishop. At first he led a solitary life in the desert and became widely renowned through his merits, virtues, and the signs that the Lord performed through him. Later, at the request of Mavia, queen of the Saracens, he was made bishop of that people. He kept the fellowship of the Catholic faith undefiled and converted a large part of the people over whom he had been appointed bishop to faith in Christ. Thus, perfected in virtues, he rested in peace.

**VI Id. Febr.** — In Lesser Armenia, the feast of the holy Dionysius, Aemilianus, and Sebastian.

On the same day at Alexandria, the feast of Saint Cointha, martyr. The pagans seized her, led her to the idols, and forced her to worship. When she cursed and refused this, they fastened fetters to her feet, dragged her through the streets of the entire city, and tore her apart in a dreadful punishment.

At Rome, the burial of Saint Paul, bishop, and of Pope Julius.

**V Id. Febr.** — At Suevo [Soli], in Cyprus, the feast of Alexander and Ammonius. Also Ammonius and thirty-seven others.

At Alexandria, Apollonia, virgin. Her persecutors knocked out all her teeth; then they built and set alight a pyre and threatened to burn her alive unless she uttered impious words with them. She deliberated briefly within herself, then suddenly tore herself from the hands of the wicked and leapt voluntarily into the fire they had threatened.

**IV Id. Febr.** — At Rome, the feast of the holy martyrs Zoticus, Hyrenaeus, Hyacinthus, and Amantius.

Also at Rome, on the Lavican Way, ten soldiers.

On the same day in the East, Saint Soteris, virgin. After being beaten severely and for a very long time with blows, and after overcoming the other kinds of punishment as well, she completed her martyrdom by the sword.

In Campania, Saint Silvanus, bishop and confessor.

In Bethlehem of Judaea, under King Herod, the passion of the holy Andrew and Aporius.

At the city of Saintes, the burial of Saint Trojanus, bishop and confessor, and of Baldegund, abbess.

On the same day, the burial of Saint Scholastica, virgin. Her brother, Saint Benedict the abbot, saw her soul ascending to heaven in the form of a dove. After the morning hymns had been completed, he announced this to the brethren and gave thanks to God for it.

**III Id. Febr.** — At Rome, Calocerus and Parthenius.

At Apamea, Paeon and Eupraxius.

At Lyons, Desiderius, bishop and martyr. This blessed man suffered at the village of Prisciniacum, in the territory of Lyons, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June. He was afterwards transferred to Vienne, the city of his bishopric.

At Alexandria, the burial of Saint Euphrosyne, who shone in the monastery through her remarkable virtue of abstinence and also through miracles.

**Pridie Id. Febr.** — In Spain, at the city of Barcelona, the feast of Saint Eulalia, virgin and martyr. She suffered in the time of the Emperor Diocletian, under Datianus, prefect of Spain. At the same time, under the same prefect, Saint Cucufas at Barcelona and Saint Felix at Gerunda are known to have received glorious crowns of martyrdom.

In Africa, the passion of Saint Damianus, soldier.

At Alexandria, Modestus and Ammonius, children.

At Rome, Pope Gregory II, who ruled the Church for sixteen years, in the time of the Emperors Leo and Constantine. A chaste man and learned in the divine Scriptures, he preached the word of salvation in Germany through Bishop Boniface. He also instituted the practice that, during Lent, fasting and the celebration of Mass should take place on Thursday, which had not previously been done.

**Id. Febr.** — At Antioch, the feast of Saint Agabus the prophet. In the Acts of the Apostles it is reported of him (Acts 11 and 21) that he foretold both a great famine and the passion of the Apostle Paul.

At Melitene in Armenia, the feast of Saint Polyeuctus, martyr, whose name is interpreted in Latin as “praying much.”

At Lyons, the burial of Saint Stephen, bishop.

**XVI Kal. Mart.** — At Rome, the feast of Saint Valentinus, priest, who, after many notable acts of healing and teaching, was beaten with clubs and then beheaded under Caesar Claudius.

On the same day at Rome, the passion of Saint Valentinus, bishop of Terni. He was seized by pagans and beaten with rods; after a long beating he was committed to custody. When he could not be overcome, he was taken from the prison in the silence of midnight and beheaded at the command of Placidus, the furious prefect of the City. His disciples Proculus, Ephebus, and Apollonius brought him back to their city. When this was reported to the consul Leontius, he ordered them to be beheaded. They were buried not far from the body of Saint Valentinus.

Also at Rome, on the Ardeatine Way, Felicula, Vitalis, and Zeno.

At Aegea, Saint Julian.

At Alexandria, the feast of the holy martyrs Bassus, Antonius, and Protolichus, who were drowned in the sea. Also Cyrion, priest, Moses, Bassianus, lector, and Agatho, exorcist, all of whom were burned in the fire.

Also Dionysius and Ammonius, who were beheaded.

**XV Kal. Mart.** — At Rome, Craton, martyr. He had a son named Chaeremon who fell into a very serious illness. Craton summoned blessed Valentinus, bishop of Terni, to heal him and offered himself to him on the condition that, if the boy were healed, he and his entire household would become Christians. When the boy was healed, Craton fulfilled what he had promised. He was baptized with his wife and his whole household and, not many days later, completed his martyrdom.

At Terni, Saint Agape [Agapis], virgin.

At Brescia, Faustinus, martyr.

At Antioch, Josephus, deacon.

At Sebaste, the passion of Saint Blaise, bishop. A performer of many miracles, under the governor Agricolaus he endured a prolonged beating, imprisonment, and then suspension on a wooden frame, where his flesh was torn with iron combs. Afterwards he endured again a dreadful imprisonment and immersion in a lake, from which he emerged floating, safe and sound. Finally, at the command of the most wicked judge, he was beheaded together with two boys and entered the blessed kingdom with them.

While he was still struggling, seven most blessed women, who had gathered the drops of his blood flowing from the most blessed wounds of his body, were discovered to be Christians. After the furnace of fire, into which molten lead was poured over them; after the iron combs with which their flesh was torn; and after glowing bronze tunics, they were finally condemned and struck with the sword. Having paid the price of their blood, they merited eternal life.

**XIV Kal. Mart.** — The feast of Saint Onesimus, for whom the blessed Apostle Paul sends a personal letter to Philemon. The same blessed apostle ordained him bishop, entrusted him with the word of preaching, and left him at the city of Ephesus. He himself presided there as bishop after blessed Timothy. Brought to Rome and stoned there for the faith of Christ, he was buried there as the first martyr of Christ. From there his body was carried to the place where he had been ordained bishop.

At Cumae, the feast of Saint Juliana, virgin. In the time of the Emperor Maximian, she was first beaten and severely tortured by her father Africanus; then by the prefect Eleusius, whom she had been betrothed to, she was beaten naked with rods, suspended by her hair, and drenched from head to foot with molten lead. She was then returned to prison, where she openly struggled with the devil. Summoned out again, she overcame tortures involving wheels, flames, and a boiling cauldron, and completed her martyrdom by beheading. She suffered at Nicomedia, but after a short time, by God’s arrangement, was transferred to Campania.

On the same day in Egypt, Julian and five thousand others.

In Spain, at the city of Barcelona, Saint Cucufas, martyr.

In Africa, Saint Maximus.

Also Secunda and Saul [Seleucus].

**XIII Kal. Mart.** — In Persia, the feast of blessed Polychronius, martyr, bishop of Babylon and Ctesiphon. In the presence of the Emperor Decius, his mouth was beaten with stones; with his hands extended and his eyes raised to heaven, he gave up his spirit. This is written in the Passion of Saint Laurence.

In Africa, the holy Donatus and Secundianus.

At Aquileia, Chrysanthus, Eutychius, Concordia, Justus, Romulus, Salonius, Silvanus, and eighty-four others, whose names God knows.

Elsewhere, Januarius and a very great number of others.

**XII Kal. Mart.** — At Jerusalem, blessed Simeon, bishop and martyr, who is said to have been related to the Savior according to the flesh. It is nevertheless established that, since he was the son of Cleopas, he was the brother of Joseph.

On the same day, the feast of the holy martyrs Claudius and his wife Praepedigna, their sons Alexander and Curia, and Claudius’s brother, blessed Maximus. Since they were of distinguished family, they were baptized by blessed Gaius, Roman pontiff, through the agency of their brother Gabinius, a priest. Afterwards they were seized by order of Diocletian by the judge Julius. Claudius, together with his wife and sons, was deported into exile; then they were burned in a fire and offered God the fragrant sacrifice of martyrdom. Afterwards they were thrown into the sea at Ostia. Christians searched for their relics and buried them near the city.
