In Africa, Rutulus, Silvanus, Classicus, Secundinus, Fluctulus [Fructulus], and Damasus.

At Terni, Paul and many others.

**XI Kal. Mart.** — At Rome, the feast of Saint Gabinius, priest and father of the most blessed Susanna. Diocletian afflicted him for a long time in custody and chains; by a precious death he merited the joys of heaven.

In Africa, the feast of blessed Publius, Julian, and Marubius [Marcellus].

Also Julian, Barachus, Paul, Marcellus, Tullius, Lampasius, Majulus, and Julius.

**X Kal. Mart.** — At Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Callistus, the burial of Gaius, bishop.

In Cyprus, the feast of Potamius, Nemesius, and Didymus.

Elsewhere, Victor and Corona, and twenty others.

At Tyre, the very large and celebrated city of Phoenicia, the blessed martyrs whose number is known only to God. By order of Diocletian, Veturius, master of the soldiers, killed them with various kinds of tortures following one another. First the martyrs of God were torn throughout their bodies with scourges. Afterwards they were handed over to beasts: lions, bears, leopards, every kind of wild animal, and also horses and bulls; iron and fire were added to the beasts’ ferocity.

When none of the animals harmed them, the beasts’ fury passed into men. With swords they carried out what the beasts had been unable to do, and they even cast the bodies of those killed into the waves of the sea. The first and foremost among them were Tyrannio and Silvanus, bishops, who completed their martyrdom shortly afterwards through the teeth of beasts; and Peleus and Linus, bishops, who were burned with very many clerics. Zenobius, a venerable priest, was also beheaded.

**IX Kal. Mart.** — In Sicily, seventy-four martyrs. Under Diocletian, through various tortures, they merited receiving from Christ the crown of their confession prepared for them.

In Africa, the holy Verulus, Secundinus, Servulus, Syricius, Felix, Jucundus, Saturninus, Fortunatus, and seventeen others.

Elsewhere, Victorinus, Mappalicus, and very many other martyrs.

Also the burial of Eucherius, bishop.

**VIII Kal. Mart.** — At Antioch in Syria, the chair of Saint Peter the Apostle.

At Alexandria, Abilius, bishop, who after blessed Mark was the second bishop and administered the priesthood for thirteen years.

At Hierapolis, Saint Papias, bishop and hearer of Saint John the Apostle.

Also blessed Aristion, who was one of Christ’s seventy-two disciples.

At Nicomedia, the feast of Saint Tecla [Thecla], virgin, disciple of Saint Paul the Apostle. Under the Emperor Nero, she was handed over to the fire for the name of Christ, but was not burned. Afterwards she was assigned and thrown to beasts and serpents, but was harmed by none of them. Finally, at Seleucia, she departed to the Lord in the sleep of peace, together with the martyrdom of her virginity and the honor of her virtues.

At Rome, on the Tiburtine Way, at Saint Laurence, the feast of Saint Concordia, who was slain in the Decian persecution.

**VII Kal. Mart.** — At Smyrna [Sirmium], Saint Synerius [Sirenus], a monk. In the time of the Emperor Maximian, when the wife of one of the emperor’s household had been walking at an unsuitable hour in the garden that Synerius cultivated for himself, Synerius rebuked her sharply and drove her away. At Maximian’s command he was seized, confessed that he was a Christian, and was beheaded.

Also seventy-two others who suffered there.

At Rome, Saint Polycarp, priest, who with blessed Sebastian converted many to the faith of Christ and led them to the glory of martyrdom.

At Smyrna, the feast of the holy Erotes and Carpophorus.

In Pannonia, the holy Senerotus, Antigonus, Rutulus, and Libius.

In Africa, Grysonius, Zeno, and many others.

**VI Kal. Mart.** — In Palestine, the feast of Saint Matthias the Apostle, who was chosen from among the seventy disciples for the apostolate in place of Judas the traitor. He preached the Gospel in Judaea.

Also the discovery of the head of the Lord’s Forerunner in the time of the Emperor Marcian, when the same Forerunner first revealed to two monks where his head lay hidden. It is established that he was beheaded as the Paschal feast approached, as is clear from the Gospel, and that in the following year, when the Paschal season returned, the mystery of the Lord’s Passion was completed.

Therefore, because his feast is recorded in the Book of Sacraments on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, and in the Martyrology marked with the names of Eusebius and Jerome it is read that on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, at Emissa [Edessa], a city of the province of Phoenicia, the feast of Saint John the Baptist is celebrated on the day on which he was beheaded, this does not designate specifically the day of his beheading, but rather the day on which his head was found in that city and placed in the church.

Two monks from the East had come to worship at Jerusalem and to see the holy places. The same Forerunner of the Lord appeared to them in a revelation and instructed them to go to the former dwelling of King Herod, search there for his head, and, once found, bury it again with due honor.

For this reason wicked women had carefully preserved it, cut off from the body, in their chamber, lest, if attached to the body, it should again convict them of impiety. The head was found and taken up by the aforesaid brothers through divine grace, but it was stolen by their traveling companions and carried from place to place and from person to person to Emissa, as though it were something else. It was dishonorably hidden for a considerable time in an urn beneath the ground in a certain cave, until the head again revealed itself to a certain devout priest named Marcellus while he lived in that cave.

From that time the beheading of the blessed Forerunner began to be celebrated in that city on the very day on which the head had been found or raised. Finally, among some people its discovery is celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, the day on which he is said to have been conceived; among others it is celebrated on the fourth day before the Kalends of September.

He was beheaded in a certain fortress of Arabia called Macherus. His body was buried in the city of Samaria, now called Sebaste, while his head was buried at Jerusalem. In time his bones were transferred to Jerusalem and soon sent to Alexandria; they are now preserved there in the church consecrated in honor of his name.

His head was also carried from Edessa to Constantinople by the Emperor Theodosius and is honored outside the city in a church furnished with imperial magnificence. This is clearly arranged by divine providence so that, when the relics of the blessed martyr were carried to several places, many signs of his virtues might occur, and more people might be drawn through the memory of his teaching and life to the faith and love that he preached; and that more might be converted through the memory of his teaching and life to the faith that justifies and saves.

Also at Rome, Absalon.

At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Herolus, Lucius, and Sergius, martyrs.

In Africa, Julian, Julia, and many others.

At Nicomedia, Lucian, priest.

**V Kal. Mart.** — In Egypt, the feast of the holy Victor, Victorinus, Nicephorus, Claudianus, Dioscorus, Serapion, and Papias, under the Emperor Numerian, while Sabinus was commander.

The first was placed in a hollow ball of oak, pierced through on every side, and for a very long time stabbed through each of its openings. When an excessive quantity of blood flowed, he was taken out of the ball and beheaded.

The second, after his hands and feet had been cut off, was placed in the same ball, endured the tortures of the first, and was finally struck with the sword.

The third voluntarily entered the ball. The indignant judge ordered him brought out, partly roasted and turned over a grate laid upon burning coals. When he persisted in his confession, he was taken away, cut into pieces with a sword, and gave up his spirit.

Of the remaining four, Claudianus and Dioscorus were burned in flames, while Serapion and Papias were killed with the sword.

In Africa, the holy Donatus, Justus, Rutulus, Hyrenaeus, and Pision.

In Pamphylia, Nestor and Casta.

**IV Kal. Mart.** — At Perge, a city of Pamphylia, the feast of blessed Nestor, bishop. During the persecution of Decius, while he devoted himself day and night to prayer that Christ’s flock might be preserved, he was arrested by a certain Irenarchus, chief magistrate of the city, and offered to the governor Pollio like a spotless ram.

When he confessed the name of Christ with remarkable freedom and eagerness, and called the gods of the Gentiles the worst demons, the governor ordered him suspended on the rack and tortured with extreme cruelty. He sang joyfully, saying: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Psalm 33).

The governor, astonished at such endurance and wishing to turn him from the faith with flattering words, said to him: “Do you wish to be with us or with your Christ?” Saint Nestor answered with great joy: “With my Christ I was, and am, and shall be.”

Then the governor, enraged, pronounced sentence against him: since he confessed that Jesus had been crucified under Pontius Pilate, he should, as one devoted to his God, undergo his sentence and be fastened to the wooden gallows. Affixed to it, he taught the people standing by, who were Christians, to persevere in the faith and charity of Christ and to suffer willingly, so that they might also be glorified together.

After this he asked the entire crowd of believers standing there to bend their knees and pray with him. When he had completed the prayer and all had said, “Amen,” he gave up his spirit. He completed his martyrdom on Thursday, at the third hour.

On the same day, blessed Alexander, bishop of the city of Alexandria, a glorious old man. After blessed Peter, he expelled Arius, his own priest, because of his heretical impiety and separation from divine truth; later, among the three hundred and eighteen Fathers at the Council of Nicaea, he condemned him.

Also at Alexandria, Felix with his companions.

**III Kal. Mart.** — In Spain, at the city of Seville, the feast of Saint Leander, bishop, to whom blessed Gregory wrote the books of the *Moralia*. Through Leander’s preaching and diligence, the entire Gothic people were converted from Arian impiety by King Reccared. He also corrected his brother, King Hermenegild, while their heretical father was still alive, leading him from the same Arian heresy to the Catholic faith and, through his exhortations, all the way to the glorious suffering of martyrdom.

On the same day at Alexandria, the feast of Saint Julian, martyr. He was so crippled by gout that he could neither walk nor stand, yet he was brought before the judge together with those who carried him in a small chair. One of them immediately denied the faith; the other, named Eunus [Eum], persevered with the aged Julian in confessing the Lord. Both were ordered to be placed upon camels, led around the entire city, and torn by scourges while the people pressed in on every side, until they met their end beneath the blows.

At Lyons, Saint Baldomerus [Baldomerius], a man of God, whose tomb is made illustrious by frequent miracles.

**Pridie Kal. Mart.** — At Alexandria, the holy Celerus and Pupillus [variant readings: Caerealis and Pupulus], Gaius, and Serapion.

In the territory of Lyons, in green places, blessed Romanus, abbot. He was the first there to lead an eremitical life and, renowned for many miracles and virtues, later became the father of very many monks.

# March

March has thirty-one days and thirty according to the lunar calendar. In this month will occur the first fast of the Four Ember Seasons.

**Kal. Mart.** — At Rome, two hundred and sixty holy martyrs in the time of Claudius. They had been condemned for the name of Christ while digging sand on the Salarian Way. Claudius ordered that they be taken to a pottery outside the walls at the Salarian Gate, enclosed there, and killed by the arrows of soldiers in the city amphitheater.

Also at Rome, Pope Simplicius, who sat for fifteen years. He condemned Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, and Peter, bishop of Alexandria, as Eutychians.

At Angers, Albinus, bishop.

**VI Non. Mart.** — At Rome, on the Latin Way, the holy Jovinus and Basileus, who suffered under the Emperors Gallienus and Valerian.

On the same day, very many martyrs who suffered under the Emperor Alexander. After torturing them for a long time, the impious Alexander condemned them to death.

**V Non. Mart.** — In Spain, at the city of Calahorra, the feast of the holy martyrs Emeterius [Hemiterius] and Chelidonius. At first they were soldiers at the Galician city of León. When the storm of persecution arose, they were afflicted with many tortures for confessing the name of Christ, brought as far as Calahorra, and there subjected to martyrdom and crowned.

When the executioner was cutting off their heads, a great miracle appeared to the people. For one man’s ring and the other’s handkerchief were received by a cloud and carried up into the heavens. All who were present saw this, and as far as the range of their eyes could follow, they watched in astonishment the gleam of the gold and the brightness of the linen. Aureolus writes this in the book of the *Crown-Bearers*.

At Caesarea in Palestine, the holy martyrs Marinus, a soldier, and Asterius, a senator, under the persecution of Valerian. When the former was accused by his fellow soldiers of being a Christian and, questioned by the judge, openly declared in a loud voice that he was a Christian, three hours were granted him for deliberation.

After leaving the tribunals, he was greatly strengthened in the faith by blessed Theotecnus, bishop of the same city. Returning immediately to the judge’s tribunal, he answered with the utmost confidence: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5). At once he received the crown of martyrdom by beheading.

When the aforesaid Asterius received the beheaded body of the martyr upon his shoulders and on the garment he had spread beneath it, he himself immediately received the honor of martyrdom. This is written in the seventh book of the *Ecclesiastical History*.

**IV Non. Mart.** — The feast of Saint Lucius, pope and martyr. He ordered that in every place two priests and two deacons should not leave the bishop, as a testimony of the Church. Banished into exile for the faith of Christ during the persecution of Valerian and Gallienus, and afterwards permitted by divine will to return to his church, he completed his martyrdom by beheading. He was later placed on the Appian Way at Saint Xystus. He sat in the episcopate for three years, three months, and three days.

Also at Rome, on the Appian Way, nine hundred holy martyrs who were placed in the cemetery at Saint Cecilia.

On the same day, Saint Gaius and Palatinus, drowned in the sea.

**III Non. Mart.** — At Antioch, Saint Phocas, martyr. Through the many insults that he endured for the name of Christ the Redeemer, it is shown even today to the people how he triumphed over that ancient serpent. Indeed, if a serpent in that region fastens its bite upon anyone and spreads its venom, the person who has been bitten is immediately saved when, believing, he touches the door of the martyr’s basilica: the power of the poison is emptied.

Also on the same day, Eusebius, Palatinus, and eight other martyrs.

Also at Antioch: Saturninus, Castus, and Syria.

Also Saturninus, Martinus, Peter, and many others.

## 2 March

At Nicomedia, the natal day of the holy martyrs Victor and Victorinus. For three years they were afflicted with tortures together with Claudianus and his wife Bassa, and then confined in prison, where they completed the course of their lives.

At Nicopolis in Paphlagonia, the martyrs Alexander and Diodorus.

In Italy, at the estate of Fagonia, Victorinus and Silvanus.

## 7 March

In Mauretania, in the city of the Tiburbitans, the passion of the holy martyrs Perpetua and Felicity, together with Revocatus, Saturninus, and Secundulus. The last of these died in prison. All the others were handed over to the beasts under the emperor Severus, on his birthday. While they were still being kept in prison and Felicity was in labor, the prayers of all the holy fellow soldiers obtained that she should give birth in her eighth month. It was also granted to Perpetua, among other things, that her mind should somehow be turned away from her body, in which she endured the attack of a cow, so that she still awaited as future what she did not know had already happened to her.

At Antioch, Leucius, Saturus, and Nestor.

[Col. 1053A] In Thrace, Danda, Eunica, Secundus, Sergius, and Optatus.

## 8 March

At Carthage, the holy deacon Pontius, of the blessed bishop Cyprian. He endured exile with him until the day of his passion and left behind an excellent volume on his life and passion. Always glorifying the Lord in his sufferings, he earned the crown of life.

At Nicomedia, Quintilis the bishop and Capitulinus.

In Africa, Rogatus and Felix; also the natal day of the bishop Cyril, together with Silvanus and Manilius.

## 9 March

At the city of Nyssa [Mysena], the holy bishop Gregory, brother of the blessed Basil of Caesarea, a man most learned and renowned for eloquence.

[Col. 1053B] At Barcelona, the bishop Pacianus, distinguished both in life and in speech. He died at a very advanced age in the time of the emperor Theodosius.

In Africa, Felix and Philip, Marianus, Rogatus and Concessus, Gorgonius and Hesychius.

## 10 March

The natal day of the holy martyrs Alexander and Gaius of Eumenia, who were crowned with martyrdom at Apamea during the persecution of Antoninus Verus. Apollinaris, bishop of Hierapolis, writes about them in his book against the Cataphrygians.

In Persia, forty-two holy martyrs.

At Antioch, Agape [Agapes], a virgin, and Marina.

At Nicomedia, the martyrs Palatinus, Firmanus, and Rusticus.

[Col. 1053C] At Alexandria, Heraclius, Zosimus, Alexander, and Gaius.

In Italy, at the monastery of Bobbio, the holy abbot Atala, a man of admirable holiness and a disciple of the blessed Columbanus.

## 11 March

At Sebaste in Lesser Armenia, the natal day of forty martyrs who, in the time of the emperor Licinius, the governor Agricolaus, and the commander Lysias, were crowned with martyrdom for the name of Christ. When the governor Agricolaus could not convert them to the worship of idols, he ordered them to be overwhelmed with stones. But their torturers, striking one another with the stones, could not harm the martyrs. The commander Lysias, burning with anger, picked up a stone to strike one of the saints. But by the wondrous will of God the stone itself reached the face of the governor. Enraged, he ordered the saints of God to be thrown into a pool bound by ice.

But by divine will the ice dissolved and the extremely cold water was changed to the warmth of a bath, so that, strengthened by the Holy Spirit, they emerged in praise of God. One of their number, however, having become fainthearted, fled to the bath that had been prepared nearby; as soon as he touched its warmth, he dissolved and died. Meanwhile, while all those who had been assigned to guard them were overcome by sleep, only the jailer remained awake. Hearing them praying and seeing an immense light and the ice melting, he looked to discover where the light itself came from and saw crowns descending over the saints, thirty-nine in number. He began to think:

[Col. 1054A] “There are forty,” he said; “where is the crown of the one?” And, having first confessed Christ, he leapt into the pool and completed the appointed number.

When morning came, they found them unharmed, broke their legs with clubs, burned their bodies in a fire, and threw them into the river. But by divine providence their relics were revealed in the depths of the water to devout men and were buried with due honor.

At Nicomedia, Eunicus and Gorgonius, Firmus and Agapitus.

## 12 March

At Rome, the blessed pontiff Gregory, teacher and apostle of the English, whom he converted to the faith of Christ through the most faithful evangelists Augustine, Mellitus, and John. He sat in the episcopate for thirteen years, six months, and ten days.

[Col. 1054B] Also Innocent, who governed the Church for fifteen years, two months, and twenty-one days. He issued a decree concerning the Church of God, condemned the heretics Pelagius and Celestine, and established that anyone born of Christian parents should be regenerated through baptism, which Pelagius condemned. This was done by Innocent. Gregory, however, enlarged it, adding [f. *addens*, “adding”] to the prayer of the Canon: “and order our days in your peace.”

At Nicomedia, the blessed martyr Peter, who was one of the companions of the martyrs Dorotheus and Gorgonius, who were in the king’s chamber. By order of Diocletian, because he had spoken too freely about the punishments inflicted on the martyrs, he was suspended on the rack, his entire body torn by scourges, and, when his entrails were already exposed after the skin had been stripped away, he was drenched with vinegar and salt. When he had steadfastly and courageously endured this kind of torture, a grate was ordered to be placed in the middle with burning coals beneath it; what remained of his body, exhausted by the beatings, was laid upon it and burned not suddenly but slowly and gradually, so that the punishment might be prolonged. Crowned by this martyrdom, Peter truly proved himself both heir to Peter’s faith and heir to his name.

Also at Nicomedia, the natal day of the holy presbyter Egdunus and seven others, who were strangled one by one on successive days so that fear might be instilled in the others.

On the same day, the passion of the martyr Maximilian and many others.

## 13 March

At Nicomedia, the natal day of the holy presbyter Macedonius, his wife Patricia, and their daughter Modesta.

At the city of Nicaea, the natal day of the holy Theusea [Theuseta] and her son Horis [Horrisa], Theodora, Nymphodora, Marcus, and Arabia, all of whom were handed over to the fire.

Also Julius the bishop and Alexander.

Also at Nicomedia, many martyrs.

## 14 March

At Rome, forty-seven martyrs who were baptized by the blessed apostle Peter while he was being held in the Mamertine prison with his fellow apostle Paul, where they were detained in chains for nine months.

Also Pope Zacharias, who sat at Rome for ten years. In the patriarchium of the blessed martyr Gregory [George; Baron], he found the martyr’s head enclosed in a box; in it he also found a small written document, bearing this very text in Greek letters. He was buried in the church of the blessed apostle Peter.

At Carthage, Donatus, Euphrosius, and Fronimus.

At Nicomedia, Felicissimus, Dativus, and Frontina.

In Africa, the martyrs Diona, Alexander, Peter, Mammarius, and Nabotus.

## 15 March

In Cappadocia, the holy martyr Longinus. When he had pierced the Lord’s side with a lance during the Passion, he believed in Christ after seeing the earthquake and the signs that occurred. Repenting of his former deeds, he served Christ for thirty-eight years and converted many to the faith of God. At last he completed his course in Cappadocia under the governor Octavius. After his martyrdom he was granted sight, having been struck with bodily blindness because of the unbelief of his mind.

[Col. 1055B] At Thessalonica, the holy Matrona. She was the maidservant of a certain widow named Plautilla and secretly worshiped Christ, attending the church daily for private prayers. Discovered by her mistress, she was stretched out and bound upon a bench and scourged almost to death. Then she was left bound to the bench overnight, with the doors carefully sealed. On the following day she was divinely released and found praying with great grace upon her lips. Again she was bound to the same bench with raw cords and beaten with leather thongs until she became speechless, and there she was left for three days with the doors sealed. When the third day came, she was again divinely released [Col. 1055C] and found praying. Then she was beaten with stout clubs until death. In confessing Christ, she gave back her incorrupt spirit.

At Nicomedia, Lucius the bishop and martyr.

At Carthage, Paul and Salutaris.

Also Alexander and Theophilus.

## 16 March

At Rome, the martyr Cyriacus. The blessed Pope Marcellus ordained him deacon. Together with Sisinnius he performed many wonders under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian and drove demons from possessed bodies. After enduring many and excessive tortures, he was finally beheaded by the vicar Carpasius on the order of Maximian.

At Aquileia, Hilary.

[Col. 1055D] At Nicomedia, Castor, Dionysius, and Nonnus.

In Greece, Cyriaca, Florentius, and Jovian.

## 17 March

At Aquileia, Largus, Tatianus, Cato, and Dativus.

At Rome, Alexander the bishop and Theodulus the deacon.

In Scotland, the natal day of the holy bishop Patrick, a Briton by birth. In the island of Ireland he first preached the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to the Scots and converted them to the true faith through the display of miracles.

On the same day, the passion of the holy martyr Maria. She was the maidservant of a distinguished man named Tertullus and refused, on the birthday of his son, to participate in her master’s banquets, preferring instead to devote herself to fasting in the Christian manner. Her master tore her with savage scourges. But when this could not recall her from her steadfast service to Christ to the worship of idols, she was handed over to the public judge for punishment.

There, when the executioners wished to consign her to the fire, the people’s prayers obtained a reprieve of three days for her. When the three days had passed and they again unanimously pressed for her punishment, she was wonderfully rescued by God’s mercy. For when she had poured out a prayer to God, a huge rock that stood before her split down the middle, received her within itself, and, enclosing her on every side, resisted the fury of her enemies. When the people rushed toward it and wished, in accordance with the ruler’s command, to destroy the stone itself, lightning and thunder were sent down from heaven, and many of them perished. Thus 2,700 of them were extinguished by divine judgment; [Col. 1056B] the few who remained, however, turned to the Lord and continued in the Christian religion.

On the same day, the natal day of the holy virgin Gertrude. Among her miracles this most celebrated event is reported: on her birthday, an old woman who had recently entered the monastery could not be compelled to break her fast because the feast of Easter was approaching. Her daughter was sent to draw water from the monastery well, but she herself fell into it and was brought out dead. Through the merits of the holy virgin she was restored to life, and by her recovery tripled the joy not only of her mother but also of the entire community, at the height of the solemnity of Saint Patrick and of Gertrude herself.

## 18 March

The natal day of the holy bishop Alexander. [Col. 1056C] Coming from his city in Cappadocia, he was traveling to Jerusalem out of a desire to visit the holy places. Narcissus, bishop of that city, was already advanced in age and governing the Church. To Narcissus himself and to many of his clergy it was revealed that on the following morning a bishop would enter who was to be an assistant to the episcopal chair. Thus, when the matter was fulfilled just as it had been foretold, and all in Palestine had assembled together, chiefly through the efforts of Narcissus, Alexander assumed with him the governance of the Church of Jerusalem.

When he was already distinguished by the venerable gray hair of a very advanced age during the persecution of Decius, he was taken to Caesarea, confined in prison, and crowned with martyrdom for confessing Christ.

In Alexandria, the deacons Collegius and Colytus.

[Col. 1056D] At Nicomedia, Aprilis and Servulus.

In Campania, Quintus, Rogatus, and Ingenua.

In Mauretania, Timothy and Salda.

## 19 March

At the city of Pinarus [Pinna], the blessed John, a man of great holiness. Born in Syria, he came to Italy. When an angel of God showed him a place not far from that city where he could settle, he was found there by hunters in winter beneath a tree covered with leaves. Through this report he became known to the people and founded a monastery. For forty-four years he was the father of many servants of God there, and, resting in peace, shone forth, renowned for daily miracles.

On the same day at Sorrento [Surrentum], Quintus, Quintilis, Quartilla, Marcus, and nine others.

[Col. 1057A] At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the holy and devout presbyter Theodore.

In Africa, Bassa, Lucilla, Fuscianus, and many others.

## 20 March

At Colossae, the bishop Archippus, fellow soldier of the blessed apostle Paul.

At Antioch, the holy Joseph.

In Syria, Paul, Cyril, Eugenius, Serapion, Victoricus, and others.

In Britain, the holy Cuthbert. From being a hermit he became bishop of the Church of Lindisfarne and led a life renowned for signs and miracles from childhood to old age. After his body had remained buried for eleven years, it was found incorrupt, as though he had died at that very hour, together with the clothing in which it had been covered. [Col. 1057B] The holy presbyter Bede writes this in his little book on his life.

## 21 March

At Alexandria, the holy monk Serapion.

Also Joseph, Volutianus, and Philocalus.

At the fortress of Cassinum in the territory of Beneventum, the holy abbot Benedict. The blessed Pope Gregory writes of his life, glorious for virtues and miracles, in the books of the *Dialogues*. He also praises him for having written a rule for monks with great discernment and in polished language.

In the territory of Lyons, the holy abbot Lupicinus of the monks of Condat. Together with his brother Romanus, after an anchoritic life that they had led with the greatest austerity from adolescence, he became a founder of monasteries and a director of souls, and both were workers of miracles.

When, after many struggles that they had visibly endured against the devil and his angels, and after the service that they had faithfully rendered to Christ for many years, they recognized that the end of their labors and the receiving of their rewards was approaching, Lupicinus decided that they should be buried together in one tomb at a more remote monastery in the wilderness. Romanus, who was of a gentler disposition, declined this out of compassion, but, preserving charity, obtained from him permission that Lupicinus himself should be buried in the monastery for the protection of the brothers, while he should allow Romanus to be placed in an oratory at the entrance, for the relief of the poor and especially of women suffering from infirmity.

Although this was initially done in that way, the body of the blessed Lupicinus is now, for an uncertain reason, visited with great devotion in the region of Besançon at the monastery of Lacon.

## 22 March

At the city of Narbonne, from which Gallia Narbonensis took its name, the natal day of Saint Paul, whom the blessed apostles ordained bishop and sent to that city. It is said that he was the same Sergius Paulus, the prudent proconsul from whom the apostle Paul received his name because he had brought him under the faith of Christ. After diligently fulfilling the office of preaching in that region, he was crowned by his confession of Christ, renowned for miracles, and buried.

In Africa, Saturninus and nine others.

## 23 March

The natal day of the holy martyrs Victorianus, Frumentius, another Prumentius, and two brothers. During the Vandal persecution, under the Arian king Hunneric, all of them were tortured with the most savage punishments for their steadfast Catholic confession and were gloriously crowned in the regions of Africa.

Also in Africa, Fidelis and twenty others.

At Antioch, the presbyter Theodore.

At Caesarea, Achatius and Alexander.

## 24 March

In Africa, Agapitus and Romulus.

In Mauretania, Secundulus, Verulus, Felix, Saturninus, and many others.

At Rome, Saint Pigmenius the presbyter. He had nourished the apostate and impious Julian from childhood and also instructed him in the sacred writings. When Julian became emperor and abandoned the worship of piety, he heard that Pigmenius was burying the bodies of the holy martyrs whom Julian had killed and sent him this command: “Go wherever you wish; for here your life will not be purchased. Nevertheless, I repay this service to your services, not to you.”

Saint Pigmenius then went to Persia. After returning four months later, he was climbing the slope of the Sacred Way with a boy, begging for alms, when he happened to encounter the emperor Julian seated in a golden chariot. Seeing Pigmenius from a distance, Julian ordered him to be summoned and said to him: “Glory to my gods and goddesses, because I see you.”

The man of God Pigmenius immediately replied: “Glory to my God Jesus Christ the Nazarene, crucified, because I see you.”

At these words Julian became angry and ordered him to be thrown from a bridge into the Tiber. His body was found, gathered up, and buried in the cemetery of Pontianus, not far from Saints Abdon and Sennen.

## 25 March

At the city of Nazareth in Galilee, the Annunciation of the Lord.

Outside the gate of Jerusalem, our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified and revealed, for the most part, the greatest of the prophets’ hidden predictions.

On the mountain of the vision, the sacrifice of Isaac.

Also at Jerusalem, the passion of Saint James, the brother of the Lord. During the solemnity of Passover, he bore witness to Christ before the Jews, was thrown down from the pinnacle of the Temple, and struck with a fuller’s club.

At Rome, Quirinus, who was killed by Claudius and thrown into the Tiber, was found on the island of Lycaonia, and buried in the cemetery of Pontianus. This is written in the passion of Saint Valentine.

[Col. 1058D] At Smyrna [Sirmium], the natal day of Saint Irenaeus the bishop. In the time of the emperor Maximian, he was first tormented with extremely severe tortures under the governor Probus, then worn down for many days in prison, and finally completed his course by beheading.

## 26 March

At Rome, on the Via Labicana, in its cemetery, the natal day of Saint Castulus. He was a notary [*zetarius*] of the palace and a host of the saints, as is read in the Acts of the blessed Sebastian. Seized by the persecutors, he was hung up three times and interrogated three times. Persevering in confession of the Lord, he was thrown into a pit, and a mass of sand was poured over him. Thus, bearing the palm of martyrdom, he departed to Christ.

[Col. 1059A] On the same day at Pentapolis in Libya, Theodore the bishop, Irenaeus the deacon, and Serapion and Ammonius the lectors.

Also at Smyrna [Sirmium], the natal day of Saint Montanus the presbyter. He was seized together with his wife Maxima and thrown into the river. Their bodies were found nine miles from the city.

## 27 March

At Jerusalem, the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ.

In Africa, Romulus, Acutius, Pinarius, Missia, Matutina, and others.

Also Donatus, Saturninus, and Martianus.

In Egypt, the blessed John the hermit, a man of admirable holiness. Besides the many miracles he performed, he was also filled with a prophetic spirit and foretold to the most Christian emperor Theodosius victories over the savagery of tyrants.

## 28 March

At Caesarea in Palestine, the natal day of the holy martyrs Priscus, Malchus, and Alexander. During the persecution of Valerian, while they lived on a farm in the suburbs of that city and heavenly crowns of martyrdom were being offered there, they were inflamed by divine zeal for the faith. They voluntarily approached the judge and rebuked him for raging so fiercely against the blood of the righteous. He immediately handed them over to the beasts to be devoured.

Also . . . at Rome, Pope Sixtus, who sat for eight years. He took his accuser Bassus, who had died by divine will, and, handling him with his own hands together with linen cloths and spices, buried him near the blessed Peter.

[Col. 1059C] At the city of the people of Chalon, King Gunthramnus of the Franks, a religious man. He devoted himself so entirely to spiritual works that, having abandoned the splendors of the world, he distributed his treasures to churches and the poor.

## 29 March

At Nicomedia, Pastor, Victorinus, Saturninus, and Julian.

In Africa, the holy confessors Armogastes, Archimimus, and Satyrus. During the Vandal persecution under the Arian king Geiseric, they were most shining members of the Church of Christ and frequently reproved the depravity of the Arians with Catholic freedom. After enduring many severe punishments and insults for confessing the truth, they completed the course of their glorious struggle.

[Col. 1059D] In Burgundy, the burial of the blessed abbot Eustasius, a disciple of Saint Columbanus. He was father to nearly six hundred monks and, conspicuous for the holiness of his life, also shone forth through miracles.

In the city of Pisa, the holy martyr Torpes.

## 30 March

At Rome, Quirinus, tribune and martyr, under the emperor Trajan. On Trajan’s command he had cast the blessed Pope Alexander and the prefect Hermes into chains. Quirinus had a daughter whose neck was encircled by a tumor. After the prayers of the blessed Hermes had been heard, and after he had seen the signs that the Lord performed through His martyrs Alexander and Hermes, he offered this daughter to them for healing.

[Col. 1060A] The blessed Alexander said to him: “Take the collar from my neck and put it on her.” When her father obediently carried this out, she was suddenly healed by divine will. Her name was Balbina. Thus her father Quirinus, she herself, all those who were being held in custody, and his entire household were baptized.

When the clerk reported this to the judge Aurelian, the latter became angry and ordered Quirinus to be brought before him. He said to him: “I loved you as a son. But you mock me, deceived by Alexander.”

Quirinus said to him: “I have become a Christian. Do you wish to kill me? Do you wish to beat me? Do you wish to burn me? I will be nothing else. For I have made all who were in the prison become Christians, and they did not wish to go anywhere.”

Aurelianus became angry and ordered his tongue to be cut out, then ordered him to be suspended on the rack. When Quirinus did not yield to Aurelianus’s outrages, he ordered his hands and feet to be cut off, then ordered him to be beheaded and thrown to the dogs. But Christians seized his body and buried it on the Via Appia in the cemetery of Praetextatus.

In the city of Thessalonica, Domninus, Philopulus, Achaicus, and Palatinus.

Elsewhere, Victor and the virgin Aquilina.

At Orléans, the burial of Saint Pastor.

## 31 March

At Rome, the holy virgin Balbina, daughter of the martyr Quirinus. Since she frequently kissed the collar [Note: [Col. 1059D] That is, chains. Scriverius, manuscript note in CAN.] of the blessed Alexander by which she had been healed, he warned her to stop kissing it and instead seek out the chains of the blessed Peter and honor them with kisses. With the greatest devotion and intense desire she reached those chains and handed them over to the most religious Saint Theodora, sister of the prefect and martyr Saint Hermes.

Balbina herself, instructed by the blessed Alexander, remained a virgin, full of good works. After overcoming the world, she was buried beside her father, the martyr Quirinus.

In Africa, the holy Anesius, Felix, Diodulus, Protus, Cornelius, and Valeria, together with their companions.

## April

The month of April has thirty days; the lunar cycle has twenty-nine.

## 1 April

At Rome, the natal day of the most blessed Theodora, sister of the illustrious martyr Hermes. The blessed Pope and martyr Alexander instructed her, baptized her, and taught her in the faith of Christ. She suffered martyrdom under the emperor Aurelian and was buried beside her brother the martyr on the Via Salaria, not far from the city of Rome.

In Armenia, Parthenius, Quintianus, Victor, and Secundus.

On the same day, Saint Venantius the bishop and martyr.

In the district of Jumno, Saint Wiolaricus [Walericus] the confessor, whose tomb is illuminated by frequent miracles.

## 2 April

At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the passion of the holy virgin Theodosia. At the age of eighteen, during the time of Diocletian, she voluntarily joined the holy confessors in prison. Seized by the prefect Urbanus, she was tortured on the rack, then loaded with chains and thrust into prison, where by God’s power all her bonds were broken.

After this she was tied to a stone and thrown into the sea. But soon she was returned unharmed to the shore and thrown to the beasts in the amphitheater. They did not touch her, and she completed her martyrdom by beheading.

In Africa, the natal day of the holy Amphianus, Victor, and fourteen others.

At Lyons in Gaul, the burial of Saint Nicetius the bishop and confessor. His life was renowned for miracles, and his precious death was likewise commended by miracles.

## 3 April

At Thessalonica, the natal day of the holy virgins Agape, Irene [Hirene], and Chionia under Diocletian. At first they were worn down in prison and afterward thrown into the fire. But, unharmed by the flames after pouring out a prayer to God, they gave back their souls.

In Scythia, at the city of Tomis, the natal day of the holy Evagrius and Benignus.

At Tauromenium in Sicily, Saint Pancratius.

At Nicomedia, Donatus and Amplianus.

## 4 April

At Thessalonica, the natal day of the holy deacon Agatho and Theodulus.

Elsewhere, Paul, Matutinus, Urbanus, Saturninus, Quintilianus, Publius, Victor, Successus, and Julian.

At Milan, the burial of the blessed bishop and confessor Ambrose. Through his zeal, among the other marks of doctrine and miracles, all Italy was converted to the Catholic faith during the time of the Arian treachery. He had been sent to that place because of his prefecture and was still a catechumen. At the deposition of the white robes, a suckling child pointed him out as bishop. Through angelic prompting, his address to his hearers, the expulsion of demons, the granting of healings, the raising of the dead, and the endurance of every kind of outrage, he deserved truly to be proved and named an imitator of the ancient martyrs and apostles.

## 5 April

At Thessalonica, the natal day of the holy Irene, who, after enduring imprisonment, was struck by an arrow by the count Sisinnius, under whom her sisters Agape and Chionia also suffered martyrdom.

When Dulcitius, his predecessor, had shut all three of them in a very dark cell filled with vessels for cooking, he became inflamed with an ardent desire for them. He secretly entered the cell and spent the entire night rolling among the pots, cauldrons, and kettles. Thus he was cheated of his attempt against the holy virgins. At first he was considered abominable by his household or servants because of this disgrace. Seeking the imperial palace so that there too he might obtain vengeance for his injuries, he was expelled because of the intolerable foulness that he did not recognize even with his eyes closed, and thereafter was deprived of all honor.

In Egypt, the natal day of Martianus, Nicanor, and Apollonius.

At Caesarea in Lycia, the natal day of Saint Amphianus.

In Cilicia, the natal day of the holy Taracus, Andronicus, and Probus. They were tortured with many torments, so that after the third interrogation, because of the excessive laceration of their bodies, they could not walk. On the soldiers’ orders they were carried into the amphitheater to be consumed by beasts.

When no beast could be provoked by anyone, or even by the martyrs themselves, to injure the saints, the governor Maximus ordered gladiators to be brought in so that they might kill the holy martyrs of God with the sword. When this had been done, Maximus withdrew from the amphitheater, leaving ten soldiers there to mix the bodies of the martyrs with the bodies of the gladiators.

Soon afterward there was an earthquake, with thunder, lightning, flashes, and an extremely violent storm of falling rain. The guards, driven away by great terror, fled. Some devout brothers who had been hiding nearby approached and, guided by a star going before them, found the bodies of the saints and hid them in a cave in a neighboring mountain.

Because only a very small part has been recorded of their very long history, it is fitting, as a supplement, to recall both the presentation and the cessation of gladiatorial games on the occasion of those holy men who were killed by gladiators.

Among the many foolish and sacrilegious practices by which the ancients were bound before the knowledge of the one true God, this custom also deceived mortals: the more eminent men seemed all the more spectacular if, through lavish expenditure, they sent into the arena men fattened for a long time, who, after various criminals—or even holy martyrs—had first been killed, would then perish cruelly by mutual wounds.

Although this folly could not be abolished even when the Christian religion prevailed, because of its antiquity, it happened that a certain monk came to Rome from the East for the sake of prayer and unexpectedly encountered gladiators striking one another. Taking pity on them, he tried to prevent them from killing one another, but was killed by a shower of stones from those who organized the spectacles. Moved by zeal for God because of this shameful death, the religious emperor forbade those ill-fated games to be held thereafter.

At Alexandria, Saint Didymus the presbyter.

## 6 April

At Rome, the pope and martyr Sixtus, who governed the Church for ten years, two months, and one day and suffered in the time of the emperor Hadrian. He established that the sacred mysteries should be administered only by sacred ministers. He also decreed that any bishop summoned to the apostolic see and returning to his parish should not be received unless he had brought the people a letter of greeting, that is, a formal letter, from the apostolic see. He likewise established that during the celebration of Mass the words “Holy, holy, holy” should be sung.

At Sirmium, Saint Irenaeus, bishop of that place.

In Africa, the holy bishop Epiphanius, Donatus, Sixtus, Rufinus, Modestus, and eleven others.

At Nicomedia, Timothy and Theogenes.

At Upper Pentapolis in Libya, the passion of Saint Theodore the bishop and many martyrs.

## 7 April

The burial of Hegesippus, a most holy man. He lived near the apostolic age and, weaving together histories of ecclesiastical events from the Passion of the Lord up to his own time and gathering from various places many matters useful to readers, composed five books in simple language, so that he might express in the character of his writing the lives of those whom he followed.

[Col. 1063A] In Alexandria, the holy presbyter Pelusius.

At Nicomedia, the natal day of Saint Cyriacus and ten others.

In Scotland, Finian the confessor.

## 8 April

At Rome, the burial of Pope Celestine, who governed the Church for eight years. He established that the 150 psalms of David should be sung antiphonally before the sacrifice. Previously, only the apostolic Epistles and the holy Gospel were read.

[Col. 1063B] At Tours, the holy bishop Perpetuus, a man of admirable holiness. Through his work, a church was completed over the revered bones of the blessed bishop Martin, and his sacred body was transferred by angelic direction from the place where it had first been buried to the place where it is now venerated with due honor.

In Africa, the holy Januarius, Macharius, Maxima, and Concessa, and many others.

## 9 April

The natal day of the blessed deacon Prochorus, one of the first seven, a man distinguished for faith and miracles. He completed his martyrdom at Antioch and rests there.

At Sirmium, the natal day of seven virgins, who deserved to be crowned together.

[Col. 1063C] Also the natal day of five virgins.

Elsewhere, Demetrius the deacon, Hilary, and Concessus.

## 10 April

The natal day of the blessed prophet Ezekiel.

Near Rome, many blessed martyrs whom the blessed Pope and martyr Alexander baptized while he was being held in prison and they had likewise been confined with him. The emperor Aurelian had all of them placed on an old ship, taken out to the open sea, and sunk into the depths with stones tied around their necks.

In Alexandria, Apollonius the presbyter.

At Antioch, Saint Theodore the presbyter.

In Thrace, the natal day of Saint Gaianus.

In Africa, sixteen martyrs whose names God knows.

## 11 April

In Crete, at the city of Cortyna, the natal day of the blessed bishop Philip, who was renowned for his life and teaching in the time of the emperors Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus.

In Mauretania, Salona, Maximus, and Concessus, together with the other saints.

At Salona in Dalmatia, Domnio the bishop and eight thousand others.

In Africa, Fortunatus, Donatus, and 240 others.

At Rome, Pope Leo, who was the forty-seventh after the blessed apostle Peter and sat in the episcopate for twenty-one years. He exposed two heresies. After sending a delegation to the Catholic emperor Marcianus, he had a synod of 256 bishops assembled at Chalcedon in the martyr-church of Saint Euphemia. There they set forth, in accordance with the Catholic faith, two natures in the one Christ the Lord, namely, a human and a divine nature, and condemned the heretics Eutyches and Nestorius.

## 12 April

At Pergamum in Asia, the natal day of the holy Polycarp the bishop, Paul, Isaac, and Agatho.

At Rome, on the Via Aurelia at the third milestone, in the cemetery of Calepodius, the natal day of the holy Pope Julius, confessor. Under Constantius the Arian, son of Constantine, he endured tribulations and exiles for ten months. After Constantius’s death he returned to his see with great glory.

He established that no cleric should conduct any legal case except in the church; that a record of the faith should be collected by notaries; and that securities, documents, donations, exchanges, transfers, wills, allegations, and manumissions involving clerics should be executed in the church.

In the city of Verona, the holy martyr Zeno. Concerning his miracles, the holy Pope Gregory reports that when the river Adige overflowed, it rose as high as the upper windows of the church where Zeno’s body lay buried, but could not enter the church, where a crowd of the faithful had gathered.

## 13 April

At Pergamum, a city of Asia, the commemoration of the holy bishop Carpus, the deacon Papylus, Agathonica, an excellent woman, and many others, who were crowned with martyrdom for the blessed confessors. With them also suffered the remarkable man Justin the philosopher, who, even while continuing to wear the philosopher’s garb, labored greatly for the Christian religion. Thus he presented to Antoninus Pius, his sons, and the senate a book written against the pagans, and was not ashamed of the disgrace of the cross. After he had already presented a second book to the successors of the aforesaid emperor—namely Antoninus Verus and Aurelius Commodus—in defense of our religion, he received the reward of martyrdom for his faithful tongue.

At Chalcedon, Saint Euphemia, and Eucarpia, who came to rest after many torments.

In Spain, the commemoration of the blessed Hermenegild, whom his father Leovigild, the Arian king of the Goths, cast into prison and chains because of his unshakable confession of the Catholic faith. There, on the night of the Lord’s Resurrection, by order of his treacherous father, he was struck on the head with a sword and entered the heavenly kingdom in place of an earthly one, a king and martyr. The blessed Pope Gregory writes of him in his *Dialogues*.

## 14 April

At Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Praetextatus, the commemoration of the holy Tiburtius, Valerian, and Maximus, under Almachius, prefect of the city. The first two were beaten with clubs and struck with the sword; the last was beaten for so long with leaded rods that he gave up his spirit.

At Interamna, Saint Proculus the martyr.

Likewise, Saint Domna the virgin, crowned with her fellow virgins.

At Alexandria, the blessed Fronto, a monk of Nitria. He led seventy monks with him into the desert so that, separated from human beings, they might devote themselves to divine contemplation. But when they lacked food, the Lord admonished a certain wealthy householder to arrange for provisions to be sent to his servants who were suffering from hunger. Since he did not know where their dwelling was, he was instructed, through the advice of prudent friends, to send seventy camels loaded with provisions into the desert without any human guide, so that almighty God might lead them by his providence wherever he wished.

Through byways and pathless places, the camels nevertheless reached the cell of the saints by a straight route. When the exceptionally discerning Fronto saw them, he gave thanks to God and, taking care to avoid greed, took half of everything for himself and his companions; the other half he placed upon the camels and sent back by them to their master. Astonished by both the miracle and the benefit, the man supplied the saints with provisions in the same way every year. Refreshed by these gifts and sustained also by the assistance of other religious people, they persevered devotedly in the service of God.

## 15 April

In Persia, in the city of Cordula, the commemoration of Olympias and Maximus, noble persons. By order of Caesar Decius they were beaten with clubs, then with leaded rods; finally their heads were battered with axes until they gave up their spirits.

In Tuscany, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Maro, Eutyches, and Victorinus. While they were undergoing a long exile with the blessed Flavia Domitilla on the island of Pontia, and were supporting her with pious consolation in her confession of Christ, they were later, through the jealousy and persecution of Aurelian—the husband and persecutor whom she had rejected for Christ—handed over by the emperor Nerva to that same Aurelian as slaves.

He first divided them up individually among his estates as though they were slaves, ordering them to dig the earth by day and, in the evening, to eat *cantabrum* [as written in the manuscript]. Then, when they converted very many people to the faith of Christ and increased the community of believers, he was filled with anger by the devil and sent men to kill them by various kinds of punishment.

He ordered Eutyches [Eutychetes] to be beaten in the middle of the road until he breathed out his spirit. The Christian people seized his body. Victorinus he ordered to be tortured at a place called Cotilias, where foul waters issue forth with sulfur, suspended head downward for three hours. After enduring this for three days for the name of Christ, he departed to the Lord.

When his body had lain unburied for one day by order of Aurelian, Christian people from Amiternum came, seized it, and carried it into their own territory. As for Maro, Aurelian sent his friend named Turgius and ordered him to be led away and crushed beneath an enormous stone. But because the Lord protected him, they were unable to harm him in any way. The governor, having received an order from Aurelian, killed him. The Christian people seized his body and buried it with fitting honor near the Picene city, on Mount Aureus.

In Spain, in the city of Caesaraugusta, the commemoration of eighteen holy martyrs: Optatus, Lupercus, Successus, Martialis, Urbanus, Julia, Quintilianus, Publius, Fronto, Felix, Caecilianus, Evotius, Primitivus, Apodemius, and the remaining four, all of whom are reported to have been called Saturninus.

## 16 April

In Achaea, in the city of Corinth, the commemoration of the holy Callixtus, Charisius, Leonidas, Christiana, Galla, and Theodore, all of whom were drowned in the sea.

In Mauretania, Saint Basilia.

At Rome, Anicetus, pope, who sat in the episcopate for eleven years and, in the time of Severus and Marcus, was crowned with martyrdom and buried in the cemetery of Callixtus. He decreed that the clergy should not grow their hair long, according to the apostolic precept.

## 17 April

At Antioch, the commemoration of the holy Peter the deacon and Hermogenes, and of Peter, Fortunatus, and Martianus.

In Africa, Saint Mappalicus, who was crowned together with many others. The blessed Cyprian writes of them, among other things, in his letter to the martyrs and confessors as follows:

> I both desire and exhort you to follow this now most blessed martyr, and the other leaders and companions of the same congregation—steadfast in faith, patient in suffering, victorious in the trial—so that those whom the bond of confession and the fellowship of prison joined together may also be joined by the completion of virtue and the heavenly crown.

## 18 April

At Messana [Mesenna], a city of Apulia, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Eleutherius, bishop, and Anthia, his mother. Ordained bishop at Aquileia, he first converted Felix and Correnus [Corebus], his companions, to the faith of Christ.

Brought to Rome under the emperor Hadrian, and renowned both for the holiness of his life and for the power of his miracles, he overcame, in his confession of Christ, an iron bed heated in the fire, a grating placed over fire, and a frying pan boiling with oil, pitch, and resin. He was also thrown to lions, but when they were pacified he was not harmed. Finally, together with his mother, he was beheaded with the sword.

At Rome, Parthenius and Calocerus [Calocer].

Likewise at Rome, Apollonius the senator. Betrayed by a slave under the emperor Commodus because he was a Christian, he composed a distinguished volume in order to give an account of his faith before the emperor, and read it in the senate. Nevertheless, by sentence of the senate he was beheaded for Christ, since an ancient law prevailed among them that Christians who had once been brought before their tribunal were not to be released unless they denied their faith.

In the city of Thessalonica, the commemoration of Saint Septimus the deacon.

In Africa, Victor and his companions.

## 19 April

At Corinth, the commemoration of the blessed Timo, one of the first seven deacons.

In Armenia, in the city of Melitene [Militana], the commemoration of the holy Hermogenes, Gaius, Expeditus, Aristonics, Rufus, and Galata, crowned on the same day.

At Caucoliberi in Spain, the commemoration of Saint Vincent the martyr.

## 20 April

At Rome, Saint Victor, bishop, who governed the Church as the thirteenth after the blessed Peter for ten years and was crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Severus. He decreed that holy Easter should be celebrated on Sunday and observed from the fifteenth moon of the first month through the twenty-first. Until then it had been celebrated on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, without regard to any distinction of day or observation of the moon. He also decreed that, when necessity compelled it, people coming from the Gentiles could be baptized in a river, in the sea, or in springs, with a Christian confession.

Likewise at Rome, the holy martyrs Sulpitius and Servilianus. Converted to the faith of Christ through the preaching and miracles of the blessed Flavia Domitilla—who had also won their brides, Theodora and Euphrosyna, to the hope of eternal life and perseverance in holy virginity—they refused to sacrifice to idols during the persecution of Trajan and were beheaded by Anianus, prefect of the city. Christians seized their bodies and placed them on their estate beside the Latin Way, at the second milestone.

On the same day in Gaul, in the city of Ebrequensis, the commemoration of Saint Marcellus, the first bishop and confessor of that city. Coming from Africa by divine command with his holy companions Vincent and Domnius, he converted the greater part of the Maritime Alps to the faith of Christ by his preaching and wondrous signs, by which he still shines to this day.

Thus the baptistery that he founded near the aforesaid city was, during the sacred vigils of the Paschal feast, flooded each year by waters suddenly rising through divine power, and remained filled for the seven days of that solemnity through an overflowing of grace. His venerable companions, buried at the city of Dimensium, are likewise commended by glorious miracles.

## 21 April

In Asia, the commemoration of Saint Maximinus the martyr, who in the time of the emperor Decius was brought before the proconsul named Optimus. When the proconsul tried by tortures to force him to sacrifice to idols and he refused, he was tortured for a long time on the rack and finally crushed with stones.

At Alexandria, the commemoration of the holy Fortunatus, Arator the priest, Felix, Silvius, and Vitalis, who came to rest in prison.

At Rome, Saint Soter, pope, who sat in the episcopate for nine years and was buried in the cemetery of the blessed Callixtus. He decreed that no nun should touch the consecrated pallium in church or place incense.

In Persia, the commemoration of Saint Simeon, bishop of Seleucia and Ctesiphon, royal cities. During the persecution of Sapor, king of the Persians, he was arrested by order of the same tyrant and loaded with iron. Brought before him amid cruel tribulations, he testified in a free and most steadfast voice concerning the Lord Jesus Christ.

First, he was worn down for a long time in a prison workhouse together with a hundred others, some of whom were bishops, others presbyters, and others clerics of various orders. Then, after all those before him had been slaughtered, he too was finally struck by the executioner’s blow and attained the palm of martyrdom.

It was Good Friday, on which, before the feast of the Resurrection, the yearly remembrance of Christ’s passion is celebrated. With him also suffered Ustazades, the king’s tutor and chief officer of the royal household; Abdella and Ananias, venerable old men; and Pusicius, chief of the royal craftsmen. Pusicius had seen the aforementioned old man Ananias trembling beneath the sword and had confidently cried out:

> For a little while, old man, close your eyes and be of good courage; soon you will see the face of Christ.

The daughter of that same Pusicius, a consecrated virgin, was also killed.

## 22 April

At Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Callixtus, the commemoration of Saint Gaius, pope. After governing the Church for eleven years, four months, and twelve days, he was crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Diocletian.

His brother, the blessed presbyter Gabinius, already renowned for many sufferings, had completed the triumph of his victory under the same impious ruler on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March. Gaius decreed that anyone who was found worthy to become a bishop should first ascend through all the grades: namely, that he should be doorkeeper, lector, exorcist, subdeacon, deacon, and presbyter. He also wrote a very useful book on the Incarnation of the Lord.

Likewise, Agapitus the pontiff, who sat at Rome for eleven months. When he entered Constantinople to visit the emperor Justinian, he deposed Anthimus, bishop of Constantinople, who denied the two natures in Christ, and consecrated the Catholic Mena in his place.

In Persia, in the city of Cordula, the commemoration of the holy presbyters Parmenias, Helina [Helimena], and Chrysotelus, and the deacons Luke and Mark of Babylonia. The first of these continued to speak even after his tongue had been cut out. All were hung upon the rack and stretched by cords. Then they were burned with glowing plates placed against their sides and torn with claws; finally, in the presence of the persecutor Decius, they were slaughtered with the sword. This is written in the passion of Saint Lawrence.

Likewise in Persia, the commemoration of very many holy martyrs who, by order of Sapor, king of the Persians, were seized throughout the entire region of Persia on the annual day when the remembrance of the Lord’s Passion is celebrated, and were beheaded with the sword for the name of Christ.

In this struggle of faith Saint Milesius [Milles] the bishop also suffered, distinguished for holiness and the glory of his miracles. Acepsimas, bishop, together with his presbyter James, and Mareas and Bicor, likewise bishops, with nearly two hundred clerics and fifty monks, as well as very many consecrated virgins, also suffered. Among them were the sister of Saint Simeon, bishop and martyr, named Tarbua [Tarbula], and her attendant. They bound them to stakes and, splitting them with a saw, killed them with the utmost cruelty.

At Lyons in Gaul, Saint Epipodius. During the persecution of Antoninus Verus, after the glorious sufferings of forty-eight martyrs who suffered in the same city, he was arrested with Alexander, his beloved companion. Alexander was meanwhile thrown into prison; Epipodius was first beaten in the mouth with hard blows of the fists, then tormented by being stretched on the rack, and finally completed his martyrdom by the cutting off of his head.

## 23 April

[Note: See Rabanus’s *Martyrology*.]

In Persia, in the city of Diospolis, the passion of Saint George the martyr, who under Datianus, a most powerful king ruling over seventy kings, became renowned for many miracles and converted very many people to the faith of Christ. He also strengthened Alexandra, Datianus’s wife, even unto martyrdom.

After many unheard-of tortures, he was finally beheaded and completed his martyrdom by the shedding of his blood. Although the account of his passion is counted among the apocryphal writings, the Church of God nevertheless venerates his most illustrious martyrdom among the crowns of the martyrs.

At Rome, Saint Nabor. At Alexandria, the martyr Corona.

In Gaul, in the city of Valence, Felix the presbyter and Fortunatus and Achilleus the deacons. Sent by the blessed Irenaeus, bishop and martyr of Lyons, to preach the word of God, they converted the greater part of the aforesaid city to the faith of Christ. They were then thrust into prison by the commander Cornelius and beaten for a very long time with the harshest scourging of sinews.

Afterward, their hands were bound behind their backs, their kidneys and legs were broken, and they were fastened around the turning of wheels. Bitter smoke was placed beneath them continuously day and night; they were suspended on the rack and finally killed with the sword.

At the monastery of Fontenelle, Saint Wolfram, bishop, a man distinguished for miracles and learning.

## 24 April

In Babylon, the metropolis of the Chaldeans, Ananias, Azariah, and Misael—who, with their names changed, are called Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego—were delivered from the furnace of blazing fire.

At Alexandria, Victor and Zoticus with many others.

In Africa, Faustinus, Victorinus, and very many other martyrs.

At Lugdunum Clavatum, the commemoration of Saint Alexander the physician, a citizen of Pergamum. On the third day after the passion of Epipodius, he was brought out of prison and first so savagely mangled by those beating him that, with the flesh torn from his ribs and his entrails exposed, his innermost organs were completely laid bare. Then, fastened to the cross, he breathed out his blessed spirit in death. Thirty-four others suffered with him.

In Britain, the deposition of Mellitus, bishop, who governed the Church of Canterbury as the third after Augustine, the first bishop of the English.

## 25 April

At Alexandria, the commemoration of Saint Mark the evangelist. A disciple and interpreter of the apostle Peter, he wrote the Gospel at Rome when the brethren requested it. Taking it with him, he went to Egypt and was the first to announce Christ at Alexandria.

Peter also mentions this Mark in his first Epistle, figuratively signifying Rome under the name Babylon: “The Church that is in Babylon greets you, and Mark, my son.” After establishing and confirming churches throughout Libya, Marmarica, Ammoniaca, the Pentapolis, Alexandria, and all Egypt, he was finally seized by the pagans who remained at Alexandria.

When they saw him celebrating Mass on the holy day of the eighth day before the Kalends of May, they put a rope around his neck and dragged him to the places of Bucolia, which were beside the sea beneath cliffs where a church had been built. As they dragged him, they mocked him, saying: “Let us drag the ox to the places of the calf.” They said this because he was tall in stature.

From the excessive torment, his flesh fell onto the ground, and the rocks were stained with blood. When evening came, they put him in prison. There, around midnight, he was first strengthened by an angelic visitation; then the Lord himself appeared to him and called him to the heavenly kingdoms.

At dawn, while he was being dragged to the places of Bucolia, he gave thanks and said, “Lord, into your hands I commend my spirit,” and died. Religious men buried him with glory in a place of quarried stone.

He had appointed Anianus bishop at Alexandria in his place. He had also appointed many other bishops, presbyters, and deacons for churches far and wide. He suffered in the eighth year of Nero.

In the city of Syracuse in Sicily, the commemoration of the holy Evodius, Hermogenes, and Callista.

In Persia, Saint George the martyr, according to the *Calendar* of the most discerning Jerome. His passion is celebrated among the Romans and almost all other peoples on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, as noted above.

I thought this ought to be mentioned so that our patriarch Hatto of Mainz may act cautiously when announcing his solemnity, since this year he carried his head and another part of his body, together with many and very great relics of the saints, into Alemannia to his new monastery, having obtained them from the apostolic pope Formosus.

[Note: Here the number of the year seems to have fallen out.]

The feast of Saint Mark the evangelist was designated by the aforesaid holy Jerome, on the preceding day, namely the eighth day before the Kalends of May, on the authority of Eusebius of Caesarea.

At Rome, the Greater Litany. Since we, being barbarians and situated at the farthest edge of the world, are ignorant of the reason for it, or of the reason for the one that seems to have been instituted for religious purposes before the Lord’s Ascension, we have thought it useful to disclose here, according to the tradition of our ancestors, the explanation: if anything contracted during the days of indulgence appears to have stained us with guilt, it may be washed away by this three-day fast.

Saint Avitus, bishop of Vienne, reports in a homily that he wrote about the Rogations that these very Rogations, which we celebrate before the triumph of the Lord’s Ascension, were instituted by Mamertus, bishop of that same city of Vienne, which he then governed, while the city was being terrified by many prodigies.

For it was frequently shaken by earthquakes, while the fierceness of deer and wolves entered through the gates and, as he wrote, roamed throughout the city without fear of anything. When these events continued throughout the year, as the feasts of Easter approached the entire people devoutly awaited God’s mercy, hoping that at least the days of that great solemnity would bring an end to this terror.

But during the vigil of that glorious night, while the solemnities of the Mass were being celebrated, the royal palace within the walls was suddenly set on fire by divine flame. Everyone was terrified and left the church, fearing either that the whole city would be consumed by the fire or that the earth, splitting open, would swallow it. The holy priest prostrated himself before the altar and, with groans and tears, implored the Lord’s mercy.

What more need be said? The prayer of the illustrious bishop penetrated the heights of heaven, and a flood of flowing tears extinguished the burning of the house. As these things were happening, and the Ascension of the Lord’s majesty was approaching, as we have said, he imposed a fast upon the people, established an order of prayer, regulated the manner of eating, and arranged a generous distribution of alms.

When the terrors also ceased, the fame of what had happened spread through all the provinces and urged all priests to imitate what the priest had done in faith. This Litany is celebrated to this day in all churches in the name of God, with compunction of heart and contrition of spirit.

## 26 April

At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Anacletus, pope, who governed the Church for twelve years [Bede: nine years], as the fourth after the blessed Peter [Bede: “the fourth after blessed Peter”], and was crowned with martyrdom during the persecution of Domitian.

He built a memorial for the blessed Peter and arranged the places where bishops were to be buried. He had been ordained presbyter by the blessed Peter. Once he was led away to sacrifice to idols, he sacrificed; afterward, moved to repentance, he was beheaded for confessing the true faith.

On the same day, the commemoration of Saint Marcellinus, pope. After governing the Church for nine years and four months, during the reigns of Diocletian and Maximian he was beheaded by Diocletian himself, together with Claudius, Cyrinus, and Antonius, for the faith of Christ. Thirty-five days later he was buried on the Salarian Way, in a chamber, by the presbyter Marcellus and the deacons with hymns.

At that time there was a great persecution, so that within one month seventeen thousand were crowned with martyrdom.

In Gaul, Richarius, bishop and confessor.

## 27 April

At Rome, the commemoration of Saint Anastasius, pope, who was the forty-first after the blessed Peter and sat in the episcopate for three years and ten days. Finding Manichaeans in the city of Rome, he condemned them. He also decreed that no foreigner from overseas should be received into the clergy unless he presented a written attestation from five bishops.

At Nicomedia, Saint Anthimus, bishop and martyr, who during the persecution of Diocletian received the glory of martyrdom by beheading for his confession of Christ.

Almost the entire multitude of his flock followed him, as a good shepherd leading the way along the path of martyrdom. The aforementioned tyrant, who was then residing in that city, ordered some of them to be beheaded with the sword, others to be burned in fire, and others to be placed in small boats and submerged in the sea.

The crowds of the faithful were so inflamed by the grace of God with faith that they would not even allow themselves to be interrogated, but rushed voluntarily into the flames or offered their necks to the swords of those striking them. This is written in the seventh book of the *Ecclesiastical History*.

At Tarsus in Cilicia, the commemoration of Saint Castor. In Lydia, the commemoration of Genesius, Sodalis, Zoticus, Elpidius, and Eutychius.

## 28 April

At Ravenna, the commemoration of Saint Vitalis the martyr, father of the holy Gervasius and Protasius. A soldier, he entered Ravenna with Paulinus the judge. When he saw in the presence of his judge a Christian named Ursicinus, a physician by profession and a Ligurian by birth, receive a capital sentence after immense tortures—the place where Christians were beheaded being called “the Palm,” because ancient palm trees stood there—Ursicinus, as we have said, was on his way to the Palm to be beheaded.

He became afraid, and, while wishing to escape disgracefully, cried out loudly. Vitalis said:

> Do not, do not, Ursicinus the physician—you who are accustomed to heal others—wound yourself with the dart of eternal death. You who have come to the Palm through such great sufferings, do not lose the crown prepared for you by the Lord.

Hearing this, Ursicinus knelt and urged the executioner to strike, repenting that he had been afraid. Thus he made himself a martyr of Christ.

Immediately the blessed Vitalis seized his body, buried it within the city of Ravenna, and refused to go voluntarily before the judge. Therefore he was arrested by Paulinus the governor. After being tortured on the rack, he was ordered to be taken to the Palm. A deep pit was dug until water was reached; he was laid there on his back and covered with earth and stones.

His blessed wife Valeria, traveling to Milan after her husband’s death, came upon people sacrificing to Silvanus. When they took her down from her pack animal and urged her to eat sacrificial food, she declared that this was entirely forbidden to her because she was a Christian. They beat her so severely that her people could scarcely bring her half-dead to the city of Milan, and within two days she departed to the Lord.

At Alexandria, Saint Theodora the virgin. Refusing to sacrifice, she was handed over to a brothel but was rescued by God’s wondrous favor.

When a crowd of shameless young men was already standing at the door of her cell, one of the brethren, named Didymus, a man full of faith and divinely inspired, suddenly took military clothing, rushed first into the brothel, and explained to the holy virgin why he had come. He put military clothing upon her and himself put on the virgin’s garment.

Thus the virgin left and escaped toward the city without being recognized by anyone. Didymus was brought before the governor. He steadfastly explained everything, confessed that he was a Christian, and was beheaded and handed over to the fire.

The blessed virgin, who had fled from the brothel to preserve her virginity, immediately returned to the arena out of love for the crown. She was struck and crowned together with Didymus.

In Pannonia, Eusebius the bishop, Tiballus, and Pollio.

In Africa, in the province of Numidia, the commemoration of Manilius, Donatus, Maurilius, Lucianus, Victorinus, Narcissa the virgin, and seventy-two others.

Likewise, Lucianus with two hundred and seventy others.

At Tarsus in Cilicia, Malina with one hundred and seventy others and many more.

## 29 April

On the island of Paphos, the commemoration of Saint Tychicus, a disciple of the apostles.

At Alexandria, the commemoration of the holy Germanus the presbyter and Prosdocus the deacon.

At Perusia in Tuscany, Valentinus and Martianus.

At Bologna, Vitalis and Agricola.

In Numidia, at the colony of Cirta, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Agapius and Secundinus, bishops. During the persecution of Valerian, after a long exile at the aforesaid city, where at that time the blind fury of the pagans and the military authorities was especially intent on testing the faith of the righteous, and the rage of the devil’s persecution was fiercely active, they were made glorious martyrs from their distinguished priesthood.

Their companions in suffering were Aemilianus the soldier, Tertulla and Antonia, consecrated virgins, and a certain woman with her twin children.

## 30 April

In the city of Saintes, the commemoration of Saint Eutropius the martyr. Consecrated bishop by the blessed Clement, successor of the apostles, and sent into Gaul to preach, he fulfilled this office. When the pagans rose against him—whom the author of envy did not allow to believe—he died victorious when his head was split by the blow of an axe.
