At Alexandria, the commemoration of Saint Aphrodisius the presbyter and thirty others.

At Rome, the deposition of Quirinus, bishop.

The passion of the holy Marianus and James. The first was a lector, the second a deacon. Having already long before overcome the assaults of the Decian persecution in the confession of Christ, they were again arrested with their beloved companion at the colony of Cirta.

After dreadful and elaborate tortures—Marianus being suspended by the tips of his thumbs with a heavy weight fastened to his feet, and cruelly tortured—the others were worn down in prison but wonderfully strengthened by divine revelations.

Then they were sent to the city of Lambesa before the governor and again confined for a long time in a prison workhouse, but once more relieved by divine revelations. Finally, together with many others, they were brought to completion by the sword.

## May

The month of May has thirty-one days; the moon, thirty.

## 1 May

The repose of the prophet Jeremiah.

The beginning of the preaching of our Lord Jesus Christ.

The feast of the apostles Philip and James.

Philip converted almost the whole of Scythia to the faith of Christ, established deacons, presbyters, and bishops there, and returned to Asia. There, devoting himself to continual preaching for several years, he won multitudes of peoples for Christ, always serving him through devoted labors.

[Note: Here Philip the apostle is confused with Philip the deacon. See Baronius.] He fell asleep with his fathers at the city of Hierapolis in Asia, after the Ebionite heresy had been extinguished. The Ebionites denied that Christ Jesus had existed before the time of his incarnation, and Philip was buried in peace.

James, who is also called the brother of the Lord because he is said to have been the son of his maternal aunt Mary, and who was surnamed the Just, was immediately ordained bishop of Jerusalem by the apostles after the Lord’s Passion.

He was holy from his mother’s womb. He drank no wine or strong drink, ate no meat, was never shorn, never anointed with oil, and never used a bath. He alone was permitted to enter the Holy of Holies. Indeed, he did not wear woolen garments but linen ones.

When he was publicly compelled in the council to deny that the Lord Jesus Christ was the Christ and the Son of God, he protested in a very loud voice to the people:

> Why do you question me about the Son of Man? Behold, he sits at the right hand of power and will come in the clouds of heaven.

He was thrown down from the pinnacle of the Temple. With his legs broken, while still half-alive, he lifted his hands toward heaven and said:

> Lord, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.

Then he was struck on the head with a fuller’s club and died.

He is the one about whom the apostle Paul also writes to the Galatians: “I saw none of the other apostles except James, the brother of the Lord” (Gal. 1). The Acts of the Apostles also repeatedly testify to this.

The Gospel called “according to the Hebrews,” translated by the blessed Jerome into Greek and Latin, likewise reports the following about him after the Savior’s Resurrection:

> The Lord came to James the Just and appeared to him. James had sworn that he would not eat bread from the hour when he had drunk the Lord’s cup until he saw him risen from the dead.

A little later it says again:

> “Bring,” said the Lord, “a table and bread.”

Immediately it adds:

> He took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to James the Just, saying to him: “My brother, eat your bread, for the Son of Man has risen from among the sleepers.”

Some therefore think that this is why Paul’s Epistle to the Corinthians specifically says that he appeared to James:

> Then he was seen by James (1 Cor. 15).

Thus he governed the Church of Jerusalem for thirty years, that is, until the seventh year of Nero, and was buried beside the Temple where he had been thrown down. He wrote only one Epistle, which is among the seven canonical Epistles.

In Gaul, in the territory of Viviers, Saint Andeolus the subdeacon. The holy Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna and disciple of the blessed apostle John, sent him from the East, together with the blessed presbyters Benignus and Andochius and the deacon Thyrsus, to preach the word of God in Gaul.

When Caesar Severus learned of his preaching, he ordered him to be scourged most cruelly with thorny clubs and handed over to prison. The next day, when he saw that Andeolus could not be overcome, he ordered a sword-shaped blade to be made from extremely hard wood and Andeolus’s head to be split in the form of a cross. When this had been done, his brain dashed upon the ground, he was transferred by a glorious death to eternal life.

Likewise at Jerusalem, the passion of Saint Judas, or Quiriacus, bishop, to whom the wood of the Lord’s cross was revealed, and of Anna, his mother, tortured by every kind of suffering.

Likewise in Gaul, in the territory of Sidon, at the place called Agaunum, the passion of Sigmund [Sigismund], king, son of Gundewald, king of the Burgundians. When he realized that he could not resist the Franks, he fled alone, cut off his hair, and took up the religious habit. Devoting himself day and night to fasts, vigils, and prayers, he was captured by the Franks and died when he was thrown into a well together with his wife and children.

Afterward he was revealed to a certain abbot and buried reverently by him. He still shines through miracles, so much so that those suffering from fever are accustomed to seek from him, as though from a special source, the remedy they desire; those who faithfully seek it are never deprived of it.

## 2 May

The commemoration of our holy father Athanasius, bishop and confessor of the city of Alexandria. He endured many plots by the Arians, especially those of the emperor Constantius, so that he hid for six continuous years in a waterless cistern, never seeing the sun, while the entire power of the kingdom conspired for his death.

Even there he was betrayed by a certain maidservant of the householder who had arranged to provide him a hiding place; yet, protected by divine grace, he was saved and restored to his see when Constans, ruler of Gaul, obtained this from his brother Constantius.

Again, after Constans’s death, he was driven into exile because of his steadfastness in the Catholic faith and remained hidden until the reign of Jovian. Jovian summoned him by honorable and most respectful letters, restored him to his see, and granted him authority to order the churches.

In the fortieth and later years of his priesthood, after many struggles and many crowns of patience, he came to rest in peace during the reigns of the emperors Valentinian and Valens. He left for future generations a written Life of the anchorite Saint Antony, composed in elegant language and filled with abundant wisdom.

Likewise at Alexandria, Saturninus and Neopolis, who came to rest in prison.

At Auxerre, Optatus the bishop and Sanctianus the presbyter.

## 5 May (V Non. Maii)

In Jerusalem: the finding of the holy cross of our Lord Jesus Christ by Queen Helena, 233 years after the Lord’s Passion, during the reign of the emperor Constantine, the son of Helena herself. After it had been found, following so long a time, through divine revelation and confirmed by the raising of a dead man, and after it had been divided through the middle, she arranged for it to be displayed as a healing gift to the whole world: one part was left in Jerusalem, at the place of the Lord’s Passion, so that it would not be distant from the peoples of the East and the South; the other part was carried to Constantinople to her son, so that it might seem somewhat nearer for the peoples of the North and the West to visit.

This cross of the Lord, retaining in insensible matter a perceptible and without doubt living power, accommodates its wood almost daily to the innumerable requests of human beings, so that it does not suffer loss and remains, as it were, untouched—continually divided among those who receive portions, yet always wholly venerated. It is believed that it received this imperishable power and indestructible solidity from the blood of the one who, having suffered death, did not see corruption, but rather provided immortality and incorruption for all who believe in him.

[Col. 1075D–1076A]

On the same day, at Rome, on the Nomentan Way, at the seventh milestone: the nativity of Saint Alexander, pope. He governed the episcopate of the Roman Church, fifth after blessed Peter, for ten years, two months, and ten days; incomparable in holiness and illustrious in faith, he converted the greater part of the city’s senators to the Lord.

He established that water for sprinkling, mixed with salt, should be blessed in the dwellings of the faithful, and he joined the Lord’s Passion to the preaching of the priest when Masses are celebrated. By order of Caesar Trajan, he was committed to prison by Aurelian, commander of both armies. From there, through a heavenly messenger, he was led to the house of the tribune Quirinus, where blessed Hermes the prefect was being held in custody. After he had healed Quirinus’s daughter, named Balbina, of a swelling of the neck in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, given sight to her nurse, strengthened Quirinus himself in the faith of Christ, and baptized and freed those whom the prison had confined—including the two most holy priests Eventius and Theodulus, whom Quirinus, still a pagan, held in chains—he was, after all these things and many others accomplished in apostolic fashion, brought before Aurelian together with the two priests mentioned above.

[Col. 1076B–C]

He was raised onto the rack, tortured with claws, and most severely tormented with lamps. When he uttered no cries, Aurelian said to him: “Why are you silent?” Saint Alexander replied: “Because at the time of prayer a Christian speaks with God.”

Then, after he had been taken down, Aurelian ordered Eventius and Theodulus to be brought forward and asked him: “Who are these men?” Saint Alexander said: “Both are holy men; both are priests.”

When he found them equally steadfast in confessing Christ, he ordered a furnace to be fiercely heated and commanded that blessed Alexander and Eventius, bound, be thrown into its midst. The unconquered Theodulus then voluntarily leapt into the flames to join them. When the fire did not injure them, Aurelian ordered blessed Alexander to be pierced with countless punctures throughout all his limbs until he died, while the two holy priests were brought to completion by the sword.

Severina, a devout woman, gathered their bodies and carefully placed blessed Alexander and Eventius in one tomb, but Saint Theodulus in another.

On the same day: the nativity of Saint Juvenal, bishop.

In Asia: Saint Hermogenes, “of the ancients.”

At Auxerre: the burial of Saints Eusebius the priest and Avitus the deacon.

On the same day: the martyr Heraclius.

## 4 May (IV Non. Maii)

In Palestine, in the city of Gaza: the nativity of Saint Silvanus, bishop of that city, who was crowned with martyrdom during the persecution of Diocletian, together with many of his clergy.

Likewise, at the Phennensian [Fanensian] Mine: the forty holy martyrs who were beheaded together.

In Jerusalem: Quiriacus, bishop, surnamed Judas. After he had found the Lord’s cross and advanced in the faith of Christ, he was ordained bishop of Jerusalem by blessed Eusebius, bishop of Rome.

When Julian the Apostate learned of his reputation, as he was setting out for the Persian war, where he was also killed by divine judgment, he ordered Quiriacus to be brought before him. Since he could not move him from confessing Christ by any threats or promises, he ordered his right hand to be cut off, saying: “Writing many letters with this hand, he has turned many away from sacrifices to the gods.”

[Col. 1077A–B]

But when he saw him unmoved and steadfast in continuing in Christ, he ordered boiling lead to be poured into his mouth, so that his inner organs might also be melted. When even this could not weaken his constancy, he ordered a bronze bed to be brought, the holy man to be stretched upon it, burning coals to be placed beneath it, salt and fat to be scattered over him, and for him to be beaten from above with rods.

His mother, who watched all these things with perseverance and remained not only fearless but also utterly steadfast, encouraging her son with maternal affection, the most impious tyrant ordered to be suspended by her hair and clawed for nearly three hours; large lamps, burning with flame, were also applied to her sides. Persevering in thanksgiving amid such savage tortures, she surrendered her spotless spirit to God.

[Col. 1077C]

Then the wicked Julian ordered a deep pit to be dug and summoned many snake-charmers. He commanded them to bring the most poisonous serpents, place them in the pit, and throw Saint Quiriacus into their midst. When the serpents had been killed by divine command and Ammon the snake-charmer had believed because of so great a miracle, he was beheaded.

Then Julian, in his customary manner, urged blessed Quiriacus to deny the Crucified One. After being checked by him with a fitting rebuke, he ordered a large cauldron filled with oil to be heated and Saint Quiriacus to be thrown into it. But when the cauldron had become so hot that those standing nearby could not endure the heat, the saint said: “Go far away, little children, so that none of you may be burned.” Making the sign of the cross on his forehead, he entered the cauldron as though entering a bath.

When even then he was not harmed, the tyrant ordered him to be struck in the chest with a *macrocontus* [a reading preserved in the text; perhaps a large club]. Struck, he breathed out his spirit with a confession on his lips and reached Christ in the triumph of martyrdom.

According to some, the day of his Passion is celebrated on this day; according to the Martyrology of Saint Jerome, it is celebrated on the Kalends of May.

Likewise, on the day written above, at Nicomedia: Saint Antonina. After being tortured excessively and afflicted with various torments, suspended by the arm for three days and confined in prison for two years, she was finally burned in the flames by the governor Priscillian.

On the same day, in Noricum Ripense, at the place of Lauriacum: the nativity of Saint Florian. During the reign of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, while the most wicked governor Aquilinus was raging, Florian was ordered, after many beatings and lacerations, to be thrown into the river Anisus with a stone tied to his neck.

When the executioners, seized with divine fear, shuddered at and recoiled from the impious deed, a certain young man, bolder and more unfortunate than the others, threw him from the bridge into the river, and immediately his eyes burst. But the obedient current placed the body of the holy martyr in a more secluded spot, upon a prominent rock. There an eagle guarded it for a long time, until he revealed it to a devout woman and commanded her to transfer his body.

## 3 May (III Non. Maii)

From Bethany, situated on the Mount of Olives near Jerusalem: the ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ into heaven.

Although a church constructed and roofed with royal magnificence is seen there, that particular place where he last stood and from which he lifted his incorruptible body toward the heavens is believed to have been so consecrated by the impression of divine majesty, and is even perceived by unbelievers, that it does not permit a roof to rest above it, nor marble or any other pavement to be laid below. Rather, in the middle of the basilica, the final footprints of God and man are seen impressed in sand at all times, so that those who approach the place may rightly burst into the words of prophetic praise: “We worshiped in the place where his feet stood” (Psalm 131).

At Alexandria: the nativity of Saint Euthymius the deacon, who rests in prison.

At Thessalonica: Irenaeus, Peregrinus, and Irene, burned by fire.

[Col. 1078C]

In Gaul, in the region called Provence, at the city of Arles: Saint Hilary, bishop, a great, learned, and most distinguished man. A lover of poverty and attentive to the provision of the needy, he was concerned for them not only through the piety of his mind but also through the labor of his body. For the restoration of the poor, he even practiced farming, contrary to his strength and accustomed way of life, although he was noble by birth and had been brought up in a very different manner.

Nor was he negligent in spiritual matters: he possessed grace in teaching and imposed correction upon everyone without respect of persons. He also detected the Pelagian heresy especially in the *Collator* and strove to correct it. Among his works, for the benefit of many, he composed with immortal talent the Life of Saint Honoratus, his predecessor, a work of necessary usefulness.

He died during the reigns of the emperors Valentinian and Marcian.

[Col. 1078D]

At Vienne: Nectarius and Nicetius, bishops.

At Auxerre: the passion of Saint Jovian the confessor.

## 2 May (II Non. Maii)

At Rome, before the Latin Gate: the passion of Saint John the apostle.

From Ephesus, where he was accustomed to remain, he was brought to Rome by order of Domitian, the brother of Titus, during the second persecution of Christians that Domitian himself carried out after Nero. In the presence of the senate, before the Latin Gate, he was thrown into a cauldron of boiling oil. The impious ruler, the fiercest persecutor of Christians, did this so that, once so powerful a head had been cut off, the weaker members of the Church might yield.

But the blessed apostle emerged from that savage punishment as unharmed as he remained free from the corruption of the flesh. Then, exiled to the island of Patmos, he saw and wrote the Apocalypse.

To honor his worthy memory and his apostolic steadfastness in faith and confession of our Lord Jesus Christ, Christians built a basilica of splendid workmanship in his name and memory at the aforesaid place before the Latin Gate. There, annually, they do not cease to hold a festive gathering on the day before the Nones of May, as is also piously customary in many places of the Catholic Church.

After Domitian’s death, when all his enactments had been annulled by judgment of the senate, blessed John, among others condemned by him for various reasons and driven into exile, was released through the clemency of the emperor Nerva and permitted to return to Ephesus. By his arrival he gladdened the Church, which had been deprived of and saddened by his absence for a time, and he strengthened it forever through examples and instruction in word and writing.

Moreover, because of the excessive cruelty and crimes of his most impious persecutor Domitian, the imperial household and the name of the Caesars, as historians report, came to an end under him. But afterward, the ancient custom prevailed—especially among barbarian nations—that the kings of the Romans should also be called Caesars.

[Col. 1079A–B]

On the same day: the nativity of blessed Evodius, bishop of the Church of Antioch, who was the first bishop ordained there by the apostles. Concerning him Paul himself, writing to the Philippians, says: “I ask Evodius, and I appeal to Syntyche, to be of the same mind in the Lord Jesus Christ” (Philippians 4).

Likewise: the nativity of blessed Lucius of Cyrene, who was established by the holy apostles as the first bishop of Cyrene. Saint Luke the evangelist also mentions him in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 13), in the list of men of the highest perfection.

Likewise: Marianus and Jacobus, according to some, and many others.

At Auxerre: the burial of Saint Valerius, bishop.

## 1 May (Non. Maii)

The nativity of Saint Juvenal the martyr and of the most blessed and illustrious servant of God, Flavia Domitilla.

She was the niece through his sister of Flavius Clemens the consul, and Saint Clement had entrusted her to the sacred veil for perseverance in purity. During the persecution of Domitian, in the fifteenth year of his reign, because of the testimony she bore to Christ, she was deported with many others into exile on the island of Pontia. There she endured a long martyrdom.

Finally, when she had been transferred to Terracina, a city of Campania, by Aurelian her betrothed—whom she had rejected for Christ and through whose accusation she had been sent into exile—she converted first Euphrosyna and Theodora, her foster-sisters and fellow virgins, and then others to faith in the Lord through her teaching and miracles.

Among these great deeds, the aforesaid Aurelian, her most hostile persecutor, was destroyed by divine power. Then Luxurius, his brother, set fire to the room in which she was confined together with the aforementioned virgins. Thus she completed the course of her glorious martyrdom under the persecution of Trajan.

[Col. 1079D–1080A]

On the following day, the holy deacon named Caesarius found the bodies of the holy women unharmed. They had fallen forward upon their faces and departed while praying to the Lord. The same holy deacon and renowned martyr placed their bodies together in a new sarcophagus, buried it deep in the earth, and buried them.

As Luxurius was hurrying to a banquet, a serpent entered through the collar of his garment from a tree branch and reached his heart; it left him dead and swollen as a spectacle and example to unbelievers.

Likewise, at Rome: the burial of Benedict, bishop, who occupied the see for ten months during the reign of Constantine. From his earliest age he served in the Church and was always a lover of poverty. He was buried near blessed Peter.

At Nicomedia: the passion of the holy martyrs Flavius and Augustinus, and of the three brothers Marcellinus, Macrobius, and Eutychius.

In Africa: Celerinus, Maximus, Victorinus, Potentilla, Faustina, and countless others.

At Autun: the burial of blessed Placitus, bishop.

## 8 May (VIII Id. Maii)

At Milan: the natal day of Saint Victor.

A Moor by nationality and a Christian from his earliest age, he was a soldier in the imperial camp and was already distinguished by his gray hair when the emperor Maximian compelled him to sacrifice to idols. Remaining most steadfast in confessing the Lord, he spent six days in prison without food or drink. First he was severely beaten with clubs and whips; then he was covered with molten lead, but was not harmed at all. Finally he completed the course of his glorious martyrdom by the cutting off of his head.

His body was thrown to beasts and birds in the wood called ad Ulmos, but none of them touched it for an entire week. Saint Maternus, bishop, gathered it and buried it honorably.

He was a fellow citizen of the saints Narbor and Felix, who, after being beheaded in Africa, were transferred to Milan together with Januarius and Marinus.

At Constantinople: Agatho the soldier and very many others.

In Egypt: Victor and Stephana.

At Saintes: the burial of Saint Martin the priest.

At Auxerre: Helladius, bishop.

## 7 May (VII Id. Maii)

At Axiopolis: Quirillus, Quindeus, and Zeno.

[Col. 1080D]

At Tarsus in Cilicia: Aphrodisius.

At Constantinople: the translation of Saint Timothy.

In Persia: three hundred and ten holy martyrs.

At Nazianzus: the burial of blessed Gregory, bishop, called the Theologian, a nobleman educated at Athens and colleague of blessed Basil, later bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia.

When Gregory had devoted himself entirely to the service of God, he presumed so much upon his colleague’s affection that he removed Basil, who was seated in the teacher’s chair, and led him away with his own hand to the monastery. There they devoted themselves for thirteen years, excluding all secular books of the Greeks and applying themselves solely to the volumes of Sacred Scripture.

Later ordained bishop at Nazianzus, he dispersed the storm of the heretics through the serenity of faith. Then, when he was summoned to Constantinople for its correction, he did not refuse to go and assume its care. After he had strengthened it in the Catholic faith, lest he be considered an invader motivated by a desire for a richer see, he returned to his very poor see and spent the rest of his life there.

Since he was now worn out by age and weak in body, he appointed a successor, so that while the successor governed the Church, Gregory might enjoy the leisure of weakness and old age.

## 6 May (VI Id. Maii)

The burial of blessed Job the prophet.

At Rome: Faltonis, Piniana, and Anitia, and Lucina, his wife, with many other martyrs.

Likewise at Rome: Calepodius, an elderly priest, under the emperor Alexander. Alexander had him killed by Laodicius, dragged through the city, and thrown into the Tiber on the day of the Kalends of May. Fishermen found the body, lifted it out, and reported it to Bishop Callistus. He took it, prepared it with aromatics, wrapped it in linen cloths, and buried it in the cemetery bearing his name, on the Aurelian Way, three miles from the city, in a crypt, on the sixth day before the Ides of May.

Then Palmatius the consul was beheaded by Alexander, together with his wife and children, and forty-two others of both sexes. Among them was the senator Simplicius, who had recently been baptized through the teaching of Pope Callistus and the priest Calepodius. This is written in the Passion of blessed Callistus, pope.

On the same day: the natal day of blessed Gordian, martyr, who suffered under the most impious emperor Julian.

When the aforesaid tyrant had ordered Gordian, still a pagan and his vicar, to examine the priest Januarius carefully to see whether he could somehow turn him away from the faith of Christ, the holy Januarius instead won him more fully for Christ, together with his wife Marina and their household, of both sexes, numbering fifty-three and more, and consecrated them all through the waters of baptism.

When the most impious Julian heard this, filled with anger he condemned Saint Januarius the priest by proscription, but placed Saint Gordian in public custody and entrusted him to a certain Clementianus, whom he had appointed as Gordian’s replacement. He also had Gordian’s wife Marina oppressed at the Waters of Salvias in the service of farm laborers.

When Clementianus saw that he could in no way turn Saint Gordian from the position of his faith, he ordered him first to be beaten with leaded scourges, then beheaded, and his body thrown before the temple of Apollo into a marsh [the text reads *intellude*, with *palude*—“marsh”—supplied as a correction].

When Christians learned what had happened, they secretly seized his body during the night and placed it roughly one mile from the city of Rome, in a crypt in the cemetery of Praetextatus, where the body of blessed Epimachus the martyr had long before been buried.

He is said to have been one of the seventy disciples of the Lord Jesus Christ.

## 11 May (V Id. Maii)

The passion of Saint Evellius the martyr.

He had previously been a counselor of the emperor Nero. But when he saw the steadfastness of the Christians in how they suffered martyrdom, and especially the patience of Saint Torpes, as well as the miracles performed through him, he believed in Christ, so that he too suffered for him.

At Rome, on the Salarian Way, at the twenty-second milestone: Saint Anthim—

In Africa: Majolus, Victorinus, Fortunatus, and many others.

In Asia: the nativity of Saints Demetrius and Thaddaeus.

At Vienne: blessed bishops Martin and Maternus. We have related that Maternus instituted solemn litanies before the Lord’s Ascension because of impending disasters.

Likewise: the burial of Nepotianus the priest, nephew through his sister of Bishop Heliodorus. In the consolation of his epitaph, Saint Jerome turned the whole world into mourning and lamentation because of the evils occurring in it and the calamities that befall it.

## 12 May (IV Id. Maii)

At Rome, in the cemetery of Praetextatus: the nativity of the holy brothers Nereus and Achilleus.

They were eunuchs of blessed Flavia Domitilla, and with her they endured a long exile on the island of Pontia for Christ. Later, Aurelian, Domitilla’s betrothed, whom she had rejected for love of Christ, first subjected them to severe beatings and then handed them over to the consular official Moninius Rufus [Memmius Rufus].

When he attempted to compel them with the rack and flames to sacrifice, they said that they had been baptized by the blessed apostle Peter and would in no way sacrifice to idols. They were beheaded.

Auspicius, their disciple and the foster-father of the holy virgin Domitilla, took away their bodies and buried them in a sandy crypt on the Ardeatine Way, one and a half miles from the wall of the city.

[Col. 1082B–C]

Likewise, on the Aurelian Way, at the second milestone: Saint Pancratius the martyr. At fourteen years of age, he completed his martyrdom under Diocletian by decapitation. Octavilla, a most illustrious woman, secretly removed his venerable body during the night, embalmed it with aromatics, and buried it.

On the same day: blessed Dionysius, the uncle of Saint Pancratius. Through Dionysius’s efforts Pancratius had been baptized, strengthened in the fear of God, and encouraged to martyrdom. Dionysius himself, dear to God and worthy of heavenly rewards, peacefully brought the final day of this life to its close.

Likewise: the passion of the most sacred virgin Soteris, noble by birth, under the emperor Diocletian.

Likewise: the passion of Saints John, Achilleus, Moses, and Aphroditus, with five hundred and four others.

In Cyprus: Saint Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis, our holy Father.

## 13 May (III Id. Maii)

The nativity of Saint Mary *ad Martyres*. The reason for this feast is as follows: under the emperor Phocas, blessed Pope Boniface, after removing the filth of idolatry from the ancient temple called the Pantheon, dedicated it as a church of blessed Mary, ever-virgin, and of all the martyrs.

The most sacred day of that dedication is observed at Rome on the third day before the Ides of May. The feast of All Saints, however, is celebrated throughout the world with the greatest devotion on the Kalends of November.

[Col. 1083A]

On the same day: Saint Servatius, bishop of the Church of Tongeren. When the Huns were ravaging Germany, he was warned by divine revelation and, so that he would not see the destruction of his city and Church, crossed over to the settlement of the people of Maastricht. There he died and was buried in the middle of the public causeway.

To demonstrate his merit to the people, although winter filled everything around with snow, his tomb was never covered until, through the diligence of the citizens and also at the urging of his successor Munolfus, a basilica was built over it.

At Auxerre: the burial of Saint Marcellianus, bishop.

At Alexandria: Aphrodisius, Agrippa, and many martyrs.

At Pollentia: the passion of Saints Victor and Saturninus.

## 14 May (Pridie Id. Maii)

In Egypt: the burial of Saint Pachomius, our holy Father. Distinguished by deeds of apostolic grace and founder of the Egyptian monasteries, he wrote the Rules of the monks, which he had learned at an angel’s dictation, as well as a work concerning the time of Easter.

In Syria: the nativity of Saints Victor and Corona under the emperor Antoninus, with Sebastian as governor of Alexandria.

Victor was a soldier from Cilicia. Sebastian ordered the fingers of his hands to be crushed and torn from the skin in his confession of faith; then he ordered him to be thrown into a furnace, where he remained for three days without being harmed. Next he was ordered to drink poison, but he did not die; rather, he converted the poisoner to the faith.

Then Victor’s bodily sinews were ordered to be removed; afterward boiling oil was poured onto his private parts. Next burning lamps were applied to his sides while he was suspended. Then vinegar and lime were mixed together and poured into his mouth. His eyes were then torn out. Afterward he was suspended upside down for three days.

While he was still breathing, the unjust judge ordered him to be flayed. Then Corona, who was the wife of a certain soldier, began to bless Saint Victor for the glory of his martyrdom. As she did this, she saw two crowns fall from heaven, one sent for Victor and the other for herself.

When she testified to this before all who were listening, she was seized by the governor. It was ordered that two palm trees be bent toward each other and tied together with hempen ropes, with Corona bound by her hands and feet to each of them, and that the trees then be released. When this was done, Corona was torn into two parts. She was sixteen years old.

Then Victor too was beheaded and, victorious in all things, received together with Corona the crown of eternal life and the palm of martyrdom.

In Asia: blessed Maximinus.

At Milan: Victor, Nabor, Felix, and Rusticus.

Likewise: four hundred saints who suffered with Saint Quiriacus.

In Africa: Secundianus and many martyrs.

## 15 May (Id. Maii)

In Spain: the nativity of the blessed confessors Torquatus, Ctesiphon, Secundus, Indaletius [Indaletius], Caecilius, Hesychius, and Euphrasius. They were ordained bishops at Rome by the holy apostles and sent to Spain, then still entangled in pagan error, to preach the word of God.

When they had come to the city of Acci and, resting a little because of the exertion of their journey, had sent disciples into the city to buy provisions, a multitude of pagans, who happened then to be celebrating festivals for their gods, immediately pursued them as far as the river. A bridge of remarkable size and strength had been built there; when the saints crossed it, it collapsed utterly by God’s will with the whole multitude of their pursuers.

Terrified by this miracle, the rest followed the example of a certain great senatorial lady, Luparia, who, divinely inspired, received them kindly and believed; abandoning their idols, they believed in Christ the Lord. Thereafter they evangelized different cities and subjected countless multitudes to the faith of Christ. Torquatus rested at Acci, Ctesiphon at Vergi, Secundus at Abula, Indaletius at Urci, Caecilius at Heliberri [Iliberi], Hesychius at Carcesa [Caertesa], and Euphrasius at Heliturgis [Illiturgis].

To this day there remains a notable miracle in commendation of their precious death: at the same feast, by the tomb of Saint Torquatus at the aforesaid city of Acci, an olive tree divinely blossoms and is laden with ripe fruit.

On the island of Chios: the nativity of Saint Isidore, martyr, in whose basilica is the well into which he too is said to have been thrown. Those often given its water to drink—persons possessed, sufferers from fever, and other sick people—are healed.

At Lampsacus: the passion of Saints Peter and Andrew, Paul and Dionysia. In Sardinia: Simplicius.

## 16 May (XVII Kal. Jun.)

In Isauria: the nativity of Saints Aquilinus and Victorianus.

At Auxerre: the passion of Saint Peregrinus, first bishop of that city.

In the city of Picenum: Florentius and Diocletian. At Ephesus: Miogenes, Gaianus, and Jovinus.

In the city of Cortina: Vincentius and others.

At the fortress of Troyes: the burial of Fidulius [Fidolus], priest.

In the district of Fréjus, at the village called Calidianus: Saint Maxima, virgin, renowned for many virtues, who rested in peace.

## 17 May (XVI Kal. Jun.)

In Tuscany, in the city of Pisa: the nativity of Saint Torpes, martyr, under the emperor Nero. He had previously held an important office under Nero Caesar, but was baptized by the blessed priest Antoninus and instructed in the faith of Christ. When Nero learned that he was a Christian, he handed him over to a certain relative of his, Satellicus, to compel him to sacrifice.

But strengthened by the Spirit of God and immovably founded in the faith, the blessed man remained steadfast. Satellicus had him struck with slaps and, bound to a column, beaten with scourges until blood dripped from his body. But suddenly, while the martyr was being beaten, the falling column crushed the judge and fifty men with him.

Then, seized by the attendants, he was put upon the wheel. Then he was exposed to beasts by Satellicus’s son, but was not injured by them. Observing his constancy and power, a counselor of Nero named Evellius believed in Christ and, shortly afterward baptized, was beheaded in the city of Rome and crowned with the honor of martyrdom.

But Saint Torpes too, by order of Sylvius, was led outside the city of Pisa and completed his martyrdom by decapitation on the third day before the Kalends of May. His feast and the assembly of the citizens are held on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June. It is also reported of him that an enormous machine which Nero, God’s adversary, devised and built in imitation of heaven, was cast into the river Auxar by his merits and prayers, so that it was never seen anywhere.

At Alexandria: Victorias and Basil.

At Rome: blessed Parthenius.

At Levidunum: Heraclius [at Noviodunum, Heradius], Paul, and others.

Likewise: the burial of blessed Praeandinus [perhaps Brandanus], confessor.

## 18 May (XV Kal. Jun.)

At Alexandria: Potamon, Hortasius, and Serapion, priests.

Likewise in Egypt: Dioscorus, lector, upon whom the governor inflicted many and varied tortures, tearing out his nails and burning his sides with lamps. But the attendants, terrified by the brilliance of heavenly light, fell down. Finally, burned with red-hot plates, he completed his martyrdom.

At Constantinople: Hesychius and Eustachius.

## 19 May (XIV Kal. Jun.)

At Rome: the nativity of Saint Pudentiana, virgin, daughter of Pudens, a man of most illustrious family and disciple of Saint Paul the apostle. Her mother was Sabinella, sister of Praxedes. Their most devout father Pudens instructed them in every observance of Christ’s religion and left them as virgins to Christ.

After their father’s death, they advanced so far in every exercise of piety that day and night, without ceasing, they served the Lord with their household in hymns and prayers. The most blessed Pius, bishop of the city of Rome, consecrated that whole household with the water of baptism and strengthened it with chrismal anointing and daily exhortation.

After innumerable struggles for Christ, after reverently providing burials for many martyrs, and after depositing all their possessions in the bosoms of the poor and faithfully entrusting them to Christ, the blessed virgins of Christ at last passed from earth to the heavenly kingdoms. Pudentiana was laid in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June; Praxedes, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August. They kept unstained to the end of life the white baptismal garment received in Christ from the apostles.

Likewise at Rome: the nativity of Saints Calocerius and Parthenius, eunuchs of the wife of the emperor Decius. One was chamberlain and the other chief officer; refusing to sacrifice to idols, they were killed by Decius and buried by Christians near the Appian Way.

At Alexandria: Saint Irenaeus, deacon.

In Africa: Saints Quintus, Primulus, Salustius, and many martyrs.

## 20 May (XIII Kal. Jun.)

At Rome, on the Salarian Way: the nativity of Saint Basilia, virgin and martyr of Christ. Though she was of royal stock and had a most illustrious fiancé named Pompeius, she was converted to the faith of Christ through blessed Eugenia and the holy men of God Protus and Hyacinthus. Her aforesaid fiancé accused her before the emperor Gallienus of being a Christian.

Gallienus, at that time the most savage persecutor of the Church, decreed that Basilla should either seek her fiancé again or perish by the sword. When questioned about this, she replied that she had as her fiancé the King of kings, Christ, namely the Son of the true God. Having said this, she was run through with a sword.

In Gaul, at the city of Nîmes: the passion of Saint Baudelius [Baldelius]. Seized by pagans while they were celebrating sacrifices to their gods, he refused to sacrifice and remained immovable in the faith of Christ amid beatings and torments. He received the palm of martyrdom through a precious death and shone forth renowned for very many signs.

At Bourges: the burial of Austregisilus, bishop and table-companion.

## 21 May (XII Kal. Jun.)

In Mauretania, at the city of Caesarea: the nativity of Saints Timothy, Pollius, and Eutychius, deacons. As they spread the word of the Lord in that region, they deserved to be crowned together.

At Caesarea in Cappadocia: Saints Polyeuctus, Victorius, and Donatus.

In Britain: Timothy, deacon.

At Auxerre: the burial of blessed Valis, priest, from whom, I think, our people have borrowed the name Valens.

## 22 May (XI Kal. Jun.)

At Rome: the nativity of Saints Faustinus, Timothy, Venustus, and their companions.

In Corsica: Saint Julia, who was crowned by the punishment of the cross.

In Africa: Castus and Aemilius, who completed martyrdom through the fire of their suffering. Blessed Cyprian writes of them in the book *On the Lapsed*.

In the city of Auxerre: the burial of blessed Helena, virgin.

## 23 May (X Kal. Jun.)

At Langres: the passion of Saint Desiderius, bishop. When he saw his people being ravaged by the army of the Vandals, he went out to entreat their king on its behalf. The king immediately ordered him to be put to the sword; for the sheep entrusted to him, he willingly offered his neck, and, struck by the sword, passed to Christ. His slayer was at once seized by madness and died.

The blessed martyr was buried in a basilica within the city walls. The body of the faithful people entrusted to him by Christ arranged this out of special love and devout devotion toward him, for the protection of the citizens, against the very bad custom of certain persons who refused to bury even the holiest within cities, saying that a city belongs to living citizens, not to the corpses of the dead. Many others from the number of his flock also suffered with him and were buried at the same city.

On the same day, at Vienne, the nativity of Saint Desiderius, bishop of that same city. He suffered in the territory of Lyon, in the village of Prisciniacum, on the river Calaron; but now, buried in the church at Vienne, he is honorably venerated. Since the venerable Father Ado, bishop of that same Church in our own time, was present there and therefore [Col. 1087A] was known to his people in everything, he considered it superfluous to say anything particular about him. We, however, following the written account which that apostolic man sent to us in the year 870 from the Lord’s incarnation, in the third indiction, through the very holy priest Berold, a native of those same regions but now devoted to Christ’s service in the castle of Zurich, together with relics of that holy martyr Desiderius and the relics and conflicts of other saints, while we were staying in the monastery of blessed Gall, have thought it worthwhile to communicate a brief summary of it to those ignorant of these matters.

Accordingly, the most incestuous queen Brunhild, proud of Spanish wealth and infected with the poisons of the Arians, and therefore corrupted by every vice, after expelling from the Frankish territories the chosen foreigners—indeed, strangers to the world but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household—namely Columbanus [Col. 1087B] and his disciples, among whom our Gallus was a principal member, because they could not endure her crimes, received this response from Saint Desiderius, who, deprived of such support, was now striving to correct not a wandering sheep but an untamable beast: she sent him into exile as a reward for his services.

There he was worn down by various hardships for four years, yet, aided and refreshed by the grace of God, which accompanied his own people everywhere, he was so sustained that he not only lacked none of the necessities of life himself, but also supplied useful things to all who sought him with devoted gentleness. For a certain man, covered and tormented by leprosy, was restored to health by the touch of the holy man in the sight of the people. Moreover, a small lamp which he himself had lit with his own hand when he first entered the island to which he had been carried into exile remained burning throughout that entire period without being extinguished. It showed the inhabitants both the holiness of God’s servant and, through its oil, restored complete health to many who were ill.

He also found a small vessel of wine, which his minister had carefully preserved in order to refresh a poor man of Christ but had feared would be emptied when, at his command, it was distributed to the many who arrived, joyfully filled again by divine generosity. But when, long desired by his fellow priests, he had returned to his see, and had not allowed the spring flowing with iniquity to run freely, but had endeavored to restrain it within its lawful bounds, then Brunhild, exceeding all the limits of justice like a most rapacious—or rather raging—river, ordered the defender of truth to be handed over to workers of iniquity [Col. 1087D] and taken to the city of Lyon, supposedly to a council but in reality to punishment.

While some of them concealed their part in killing the man of God, others, who were even more savage, first struck him praying with a stone and grievously wounded him in the head, then pierced his neck with a very sharp stake, and with excessive cruelty drove him from this life of misery. Saint Desiderius suffered without being accused of any crime, but hated by criminals, on the day mentioned above, in the village of Prisciniacum, in the time of the emperor Maurice and Theodoric, king of the Burgundians, through the conspiracy of Brunhild—who was not a queen but a prostitute—with the counts Bettō, Ephanus, and Gasifred assisting.

In the days of Etherius, his successor, he was transferred to Vienne with great honor and buried outside the city, in the church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, among his predecessors, martyrs and confessors, on the third day before the Ides of February. Each day he appears, living, marvelous through signs and miracles.

On the same day, in Spain, of Epictius [Epitacius] and Saint Basil [Basileus].

In Africa, of Quintus and Lucius and many others.

## Ninth day before the Kalends of June

The nativity of Saint Manahe, foster-brother of Herod the tetrarch, a teacher and prophet, resting in Christ under the grace of the New Testament at Antioch.

Likewise, of blessed Joanna, wife of Chuza, Herod’s steward [Col. 1088B], who is mentioned in the Gospel (Luke 8:24).

At Porto Romano, of Saint Vincent the martyr.

In Gaul, in the city of Nantes, the passion of the holy brothers Donatian and Rogatian. After the impious governor had placed them in fetters, they were committed to the prison-workhouse. When they were brought out from there and could not in any way be restrained from confessing the name of Christ, they were ordered to be suspended on the rack and tortured for a long time. Since even then they could not be softened into consenting to idols, they were pierced through the necks with a military lance and finally completed their martyrdom, their heads being cut off with a sword.

But because, through an unexpected popular accusation, the holy men of God had been summoned before the governor’s tribunal, so that Rogatian might not be cleansed by the water of baptism, I have judged it not merely useful but highly necessary to set forth the statements of the most careful teacher of the Church, Augustine, concerning what he thought about this matter:

“Those who are to be initiated into the sacraments of baptism,” he says, “customarily renounce the devil and all his works and pomps first; then, after confessing the one true God—namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—they are immersed in or sprinkled with water. Martyrs, too, having despised and renounced idols, for the sake of that same confession are plunged into fire or certainly into water, or are bathed in the shedding of their own blood.

“It is also customary for the baptized to be anointed with sacred chrism and confirmed by the invocation of the Holy Spirit. Unless martyrs were strengthened by the anointing of that same Spirit, they would never approach the contest or endure with the utmost steadfastness every kind of torture. Those already baptized and faithful ordinarily become incorporated into him through participation in the Lord’s body and blood; and martyrs, when they suffer for the Lord, become his body.

“Therefore martyrs receive all the Church’s sacraments more perfectly, inasmuch as, after receiving them, they are immediately taken from this wretched life without any contamination.”

On the same day, in Istria, the nativity of the saints Zoellus, Servulus [Servilius], Felix, Sylvanus, and Diocles.

## Eighth day before the Kalends of June

At Rome, on the Nomentan Way, in the cemetery of Praetextatus, the nativity of Saint Urban, pope and martyr, whose teaching, during the persecution under Alexander [Col. 1089A], led many to be crowned with martyrdom. He decreed that Christians should reject no food that was reasonable and human.

At Milan, of Saint Dionysius, bishop and confessor. Condemned to exile in Cappadocia for the Catholic faith by the Arian emperor Constantius, he died there. After the relics of his body had been received by Saint Basil, bishop of the aforesaid city, blessed Ambrose buried them with fitting honor. Others, however, maintain that he was exiled to Armenia, to the city of Reditium, and died there; that he was transferred to Milan by Saint Aurelius, bishop of that same city; and that Aurelius himself, having fallen ill and died there, was buried in the same tomb with Saint Dionysius, as they had agreed during their lifetime.

[Col. 1089B] Likewise at Rome, of Pope Eleutherius, who occupied the episcopate for fifteen years and received letters from Lucius, king of the Britons, asking that he be made a Christian through Eleutherius’s command. This is also reported by Timothy, a holy man: Lucius, rejecting all worldly possessions, undertook a pilgrimage naked and unencumbered, and is believed to have converted by miracles and preaching part of Bavaria and all of Raetia situated among the Alps to the faith of Christ. His tomb—that is, the tomb of the man resting in Raetia, whether he was once that king or any other servant of God—is glorified by very frequent miracles.

On the same day, in Moesia, in the city of Durostorum, the nativity of the holy martyrs Pasicrates, Valention [Col. 1089C], and two others crowned together.

## Seventh day before the Kalends of June

The nativity of Saint Quadratus, a disciple of the Apostles. Appointed bishop of Athens in place of blessed Publius, he gathered by his faith and diligence the Church, which had been scattered in great terror. When Hadrian had spent the winter at Athens, visiting Eleusis, and had given nearly all those initiated into the sacred rites of Greece an opportunity—namely, to those who hated Christians—to harass believers without the emperor’s command, Quadratus presented him with a book composed in defense of our religion, very useful and full of reason and faith, worthy of apostolic teaching. In it, showing also the antiquity of his own age, he said that he had seen alive many who, after being afflicted by various calamities in Judea under the Lord, had been healed. He was exceedingly renowned in prophetic grace, together with Philip’s daughters.

Likewise in Africa, of Saint Quadratus the martyr, on whose feast sermons of Saint Augustine are found to have been delivered.

At Rome, of Symmitrius the priest and twenty-two others, whom the emperor Antoninus ordered to be punished with the sword for Christ. Blessed Praxedis gathered their bodies at night and buried them in the cemetery of Priscilla.

At Todi in Tuscany, of Felicissimus, Heraclius, and Paulinus.

In the territory of Auxerre, the passion of Saint Priscus the martyr with a great multitude.

In Britain, the burial of Saint Augustine, bishop [Col. 1090A] and confessor. Sent by blessed Pope Gregory, he first preached Christ’s Gospel to the English people and, glorious in virtues and miracles, rested there in peace.

## Sixth day before the Kalends of June

In Alexandria, the nativity of the holy priests Aquila and Evangelus and twelve others.

At Tomi, of Elias, Lucian, Zoticus, Martial, Victor, and Maurinus.

In Sardinia, of Salustian.

In Moesia, in the city of Durostorum, the nativity of Saint Julius. A veteran who had completed his military service, he was arrested by officials and brought before the governor Maximus. Refusing to sacrifice to idols and steadfastly confessing the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, he was condemned to death [Col. 1090B].

As he was being led to the place where the execution was to be carried out, a certain soldier named Hesychius, who had himself been arrested and detained for the faith of Christ, asked him, saying: “Remember me, for I too am following you. Greet also Pasicrates and Valention, servants of God, who through their good confession have already gone before us to the Lord.”

Julius kissed Hesychius and said: “Brother, hasten to come; those whom you greeted have already heard your greetings.” Then, taking a cloth, he bound it over his eyes and received the martyr’s palm as the sword struck.

In Gaul, in the city of Orange, of Saint Eutropius, bishop, whose illustrious life, rich in virtues and miracles, Bishop Verus described in eloquent speech.

## Fifth day before the Kalends of June

In Sardinia, the passion of the saints Aemilius, Felix, Priam, and Lucian.

At Rome, the nativity of Saint John, pope. Because he was orthodox and had been received with honor by Justin, the orthodox emperor, when he came to Constantinople, Theodoric, the Arian king, detained him in custody on his return at Ravenna and brought him to death along with other equally Catholic men. Saint Gregory mentions him in the Book of Dialogues. His body was transferred from Ravenna and buried in the basilica of the holy apostle Peter, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, during the consulship of Olibrius. At that time King Theodoric killed two eminent senators and former consuls, Symmachus and Boethius. On the ninety-eighth day after Pope John died, Theodoric suddenly perished and, thrown into Vulcan’s cauldron [Col. 1090D], was seen no more.

Likewise near the city of Paris, the burial of Germanus, bishop and confessor. He was born of noble parents, but, subjected in every way to the plots of malicious people, was protected by divine grace. He not only escaped alive and unharmed but also grew into manly strength, adorned with virtues and wisdom, to such an extent that, ordained priest by Saint Nectarius, he was unwillingly placed in charge as abbot of the monastery of Saint Symphorian. In its governance he pleased both divine judgment and human opinion so greatly that he received the keys of the gate of Paris, first through the Lord in a vision and later, at his episcopal election, through the acquiescence [Note: [Col. 1089D] Perhaps “connivance.” CAN. Concerning this word, see Goldast, [Col. 1090D] on the edicts concerning images. SCRIVER. Manuscript note in [Col. 1091D] CAN. There Charlemagne indeed asserts that this work was undertaken with the acquiescence of the bishops, that is, with their agreement or consent. This word should therefore be retained, although Canisius thought it should be emended, since the prefect was elected through the consent of the bishops. BASN.] of the people.

He administered this dignity with such authority that, following the example of blessed Martin, he nevertheless did not abandon the monastic way of life or its virtue. Therefore, both while living in the flesh and while seeking heaven in spirit, he appeared in every respect like Martin in the manifestation of miracles, and at the same age—namely, eighty years—he departed to Christ, full of holiness, when Christ himself called him.

## Fourth day before the Kalends of June

At Rome, on the Aurelian Way, the nativity of Saint Restitutus.

On the Tiburtine Way, of the Seven Brothers.

At Iconium in the province of Isauria, the passion of Saint Conon and his son, under the emperor Aurelian and the judge Domitian. Conon, distinguished in faith, was brought before the judge with his twelve-year-old son. By a true confession they manifested that the Holy Spirit dwelt within them. First they were placed upon heated iron; then upon a grating with burning coals beneath it and oil poured over them; afterward they were thrown into a falling frying-pan. They overcame everything in the name of Christ. Then they were suspended, with a strong fire applied beneath them, and finally, with their hands crushed by a heated hammer, they gave up their spirits in praise of almighty God.

On the same day, in the region of Anagnia, near the city of Trent, the passion of the saints Sisinnius the deacon, Martyrius the lector, and Alexander the doorkeeper. Sent by blessed Vigilius, bishop of Trent, to neighboring places for the sake of preaching, they converted many to the faith of Christ. Those who preferred to persist in the error of paganism slaughtered them in various ways.

Blessed Sisinnius, after being subjected with the others to prolonged slaughter, was struck on the head with a bronze trumpet and pierced with axes; he lay dying near the threshold of his own church. Saint Martyrius, wounded in the head with axes and pierced through with stakes, also gave up his spirit. Then the pagans carried the bodies of Saints Sisinnius and Martyrius, together with Saint Alexander, who was still half alive, to the altar of Saturn, where a great fire had been lit for burning them. They beat Saint Alexander with whips, and when they could not compel him to sacrifice to the idols, they threw him alive into the fire. Thus completing the course of his martyrdom, he received the palm of glorious suffering.

Immediately after their death, a certain shadow close to the earth covered the whole region while very frequent lightning flashed everywhere, so that the impious themselves, struck with terror, confessed that this happened because of the saints. Later, when the people of Milan received their relics with the greatest devotion, a certain blind man from the Dalmatian coast, coming by divine prompting, touched the tomb and received his sight, as blessed Paulinus writes in the Life of blessed Ambrose.

At Trier, the burial of Saint Maximin, bishop. His priestly garments, preserved in a bronze urn, were seen incorrupt even into our own times—or rather, until the time of the Northmen—as a testimony [Col. 1092A] to his holiness. Saint Athanasius, fleeing the persecution of Constantius, was honorably received by him.

But because I have learned that some fearful—or certainly blasphemous—people misuse Saint Athanasius’s flight to argue the contrary, I have thought it necessary to set forth the words of Augustine, that most faithful steward of the Church, concerning his judgment on the matter. In a letter written to Bishop Honoratus, when consulted whether bishops should flee from their sees during persecution, he says among other things:

“What, then, is the meaning of what you wrote in your letter? For you say: ‘If we must remain in the churches, I do not see what benefit we can provide either to ourselves or to the people, except that men may fall before our eyes, women be violated, churches burned, and we ourselves perish under tortures, when what is sought from us is something we do not possess.’”

Augustine replied:

“God is indeed powerful enough to hear the prayers of his household and avert these things that are feared. Nevertheless, because of such uncertain events, there ought not to be a certain abandonment of our duty, without which certain destruction threatens the people—not concerning the affairs of this life, but of the next, which must be cared for incomparably more diligently and anxiously.

“For if these evils that are feared were certain to occur in the places where we are, all those for whose sake we must remain would first flee from there and release us from the obligation of remaining. No one can say that ministers ought to remain where there are no longer people whom they must serve.

“Thus certain holy bishops fled from Spain, after their congregations had partly escaped with them, partly been killed, partly consumed by siege, and partly scattered in captivity. But many more remained, because those for whose sake they were to remain stayed there amid the same dense dangers. If some abandoned their congregations, this is precisely what we say ought not to happen. They were not led by divine authority, but were deceived by human error or overcome by fear.

“Why do they think they must obey indiscriminately the command in which they read that one should flee from city to city, and yet do not shrink from the hireling who sees the wolf coming and flees because he has no concern for the sheep? Why do they not strive to understand these two dominical and true statements—one in which flight is permitted or commanded, the other in which it is condemned and reproved—in such a way that they are not found to contradict each other, just as they do not?

“And how can this be understood unless attention is paid to what I argued above: that Christ’s ministers should flee from the places where they are under the pressure of persecution when Christ’s people are no longer there to be served, or when they are there but the necessary ministry can be fulfilled by others who do not have the same reason for fleeing? Thus the Apostle fled by being lowered in a basket when he himself was specifically sought by the persecutor, while others who had no similar necessity remained, so that the Church’s ministry there would not be abandoned [Col. 1093A]. In the same way Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, fled when the emperor Constantius specifically desired to seize him; yet the Catholic people who remained in Alexandria were by no means abandoned by the other ministers.

“But when the people remain and the ministers flee, and the ministry is withdrawn, what is that flight except the condemnable flight of a hireling, since he has no concern for the sheep? For the wolf will come—not a human being but the devil—who has often persuaded the faithful to become apostates because the daily ministry of the Lord’s body was lacking; and the weak brother, for whom Christ died, will perish through your ignorance—not through knowledge.

“As for those who are not deceived by error in this matter but are overcome by fear, why do they not rather fight bravely against their fear, with the Lord showing mercy and helping them, lest evils incomparably worse—which are far more to be dreaded—occur? Let this be done where the love of God burns, not where worldly desire smokes.

“For love says: ‘Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not inflamed?’ (1 Cor. 11). But love is from God. Let us therefore pray that it be given by him who commands it; and through it let us fear more that the sheep of Christ be slaughtered in the heart by the sword of spiritual wickedness than by iron in the body, wherever, whenever, and by whatever kind of death they are destined to die.

“Let us fear more that the chastity of faith perish through the corruption of the inner sense than that women be violently violated in the flesh. For violence does not violate modesty if it is preserved in the mind; indeed, it does not violate it even in the flesh when the will of the victim does not shamefully use her body but, without consent, endures what another does.

“Let us fear more that the living stones be extinguished because we carry them away than that the stones and timbers of earthly buildings be burned while we are present. Let us fear more that the members of Christ’s body, deprived of spiritual nourishment, be killed than that the members of our own bodies be tortured under the attack of an enemy.

“Not because these things should not be avoided when they can be avoided, but because they must rather be endured when they cannot be avoided without impiety. Unless perhaps someone would argue that a minister is not impious when he withdraws the ministry necessary for godliness precisely when it is most necessary.

“Do we not consider that, when the extreme point of these dangers is reached and there is no power to flee, people of both sexes and every age customarily flock together in the Church? Some demand baptism, others reconciliation, others even the performance of penance; all seek consolation and the preparation and distribution of the sacraments. If ministers are absent, what destruction follows for those who leave this world either unregenerated or bound by sins? What grief the faithful suffer over the loss of their children, whom they will not have with them in the rest of eternal life! Finally, what groaning there is among all, and what blasphemy among some, because of the absence of the ministries and ministers!

“Consider what the fear of temporal evils produces, and how great an acquisition of eternal evils it contains. But if the ministers are present, then, according to the strength God supplies them, everyone is helped: some are baptized, others reconciled, and no one is deprived of communion in the Lord’s body. All are consoled, built up, and exhorted to pray to God, who is powerful enough to avert everything that is feared. They are ready for either outcome, so that if this cup cannot pass from them, the will of him who cannot will anything evil may be done.

“Now surely you see what you wrote that you did not see: how much good the Christian peoples gain if, amid present evils, the presence of Christ’s ministers is not lacking [Col. 1094B]. You also see how greatly their absence harms them when the ministers seek their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ. They do not possess the love of which it is said, ‘It does not seek its own’ (1 Cor. 12), nor do they imitate the one who said, ‘Not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, so that they may be saved’ (1 Cor. 10).

“He would not have fled from the plots of that persecuting ruler unless he had wished to preserve himself for those to whom he was necessary. Therefore he says: ‘I am constrained between the two: I desire to depart and be with Christ, for that is much better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake’ (Phil. 1).

“Here, however, someone may perhaps say that God’s ministers ought to flee when such evils threaten, so that they may preserve themselves for the Church’s benefit in calmer times [Col. 1094C]. This is rightly done by some when there are others through whom the ecclesiastical ministry can be supplied, so that it is not abandoned by everyone—as we said above that Athanasius did. For how necessary that man’s bodily presence was to the Church, and how greatly it profited her, the Catholic faith knows; it was defended against the Arian heretics by his mouth and his love.”

This brief account of the holy Father, inserted here by us on Athanasius’s behalf, will, I believe, bring great benefit to readers and, through its sweetness, encourage them to seek out the entire little work.

## Third day before the Kalends of June

At Rome, on the Aurelian Way, in the cemetery, of Saint Felix, pope. After governing the Church for five years under the emperor Claudius, he was crowned with martyrdom. He decreed that Masses be celebrated at the memorials of the martyrs.

At Antioch, of Saints Isychius [Sycius] and Palatinus, who, as Saint Jerome writes, suffered many torments for the name of Christ.

At Turris in Sardinia, of the holy martyrs Gabinus and Crispulus.

At Nicomedia, of many martyrs.

## The day before the Kalends of June

At Rome, the nativity of Saint Petronilla, virgin, daughter of blessed Peter the apostle. At the request of the faithful, he cured her of paralysis; but as soon as he had displayed the miracle of health in Christ’s name, he ordered her to return to her bed, for the sake of the salvation of her soul. [Col. 1095A] When she had become perfect in the fear of God, she was not only herself saved but also restored health to many through her prayers.

Because she was exceedingly beautiful, the count Flaccus wished to marry her. But the holy virgin asked him for a three-day delay and, together with Felicula, her foster-sister and an equally holy virgin, spent that entire period in fasting and prayer. When Saint Nicomedes the priest came and celebrated Christ’s mysteries, as soon as she received the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood, she departed to eternal joys.

On the same day at Aquileia, the passion of the holy siblings Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantianilla, who completed the course of their martyrdom under the emperor Diocletian.

At Turris in Sardinia, of Saint Crescentianus.

[Col. 1095B] In Spain, in the city of Girona, of Germanus, Victurus, Sylvanus, Telesphorus, Victorinus, and many others.

## June

The month of June has thirty days. In this month, in the second week, the celebration of the Fasts will take place.

## Kalends of June

At Rome, the dedication of Saint Nicomedes, priest and martyr, whose martyrdom is celebrated on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October.

Likewise at Rome, the nativity of Luceia [Lycia], virgin, and Auceia, a barbarian king, and of Rogatus, Germanus, Sylvanus, with more than three hundred others.

At Thessalonica, the nativity of Saint Octavius.

[Col. 1095C] At Antioch, of Zosimus and Thecla.

At Caesarea in Palestine, the passion of Saint Pamphilus the priest, a man of admirable faith and holiness. He was crowned with martyrdom during the persecution of Maximinus. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, encompassed his life in three books. Blessed Jerome also writes that he found several volumes written in Pamphilus’s own hand: “I embrace and preserve them,” he says, “with such joy that I believe I possess the riches of Croesus. If it is a cause for joy to possess a single letter of a martyr, how much more to possess so many thousands of verses, which seem to me to have been marked by the traces of his blood.”

On the same day, the burial of Saint Caprasius, abbot of the monastery of Lérins.

At Vienne, of the bishops Claudius and Helladius.

## Fourth day before the Nones of June

At Rome, the nativity of Saints Marcellinus the priest and Peter the exorcist. While converting many in prison to the faith of Christ, they were beheaded after terrible chains and numerous tortures, during the persecution of Diocletian under the judge Severus. But the man who beheaded them saw their souls, splendidly adorned, being carried by angels to heaven. He repented and, under Pope Julius, was baptized in his old age, receiving the name Dorotheus.

Among the many who were baptized through their teaching and believed in Christ—three hundred men and an even greater number of women—Artemius was beheaded together with his wife Candida and his daughter Paulina, who had been freed from a demon through blessed Peter the exorcist.

[Col. 1096A] Likewise at Rome, of one hundred eighty martyrs and many more, whose names God alone knows.

At Lyon in Gaul, the nativity of forty-eight martyrs, in the time of Marcus Aurelius Verus and his sons Antoninus and Lucius. At that time, through the shouting and sedition of the populace, persecutions against Christians were stirred up with extreme violence in many provinces of the Roman world, so that many thousands of martyrs were made in each place.

At that time, in the cities of Gaul, Lyon and Vienne, a measure of punishments and tortures was inflicted upon God’s servants beyond all power of narration. First they were forbidden to live in their homes; then they were denied the use of wine and baths; afterward they were prohibited from appearing in public; finally, they were not to be seen anywhere at all, whether at home or abroad, in public or private.

At length, on a certain occasion, while the tribune and the leading citizens stood by, Christians were seized merely because of the people’s shouts and thrust into prison until the governor’s arrival. As each was brought before him, he treated them with such cruelty that no one could describe the separate forms of his savagery.

Among these martyrs, although all were found faithful and exceedingly brave in Christ, the following appeared especially distinguished before God and humanity: Photinus the bishop, weighed down by ninety years of age, who, while being carried from the church to the tribunal and from the tribunal to prison, after excessive beatings and insults, soon gave up his undefiled spirit; Zacharias the priest, who, in defending his brothers and following Christ’s example, laid down his life [Col. 1096C]; and Epagathus, who, following his example, was of the highest nobility and learning and was killed on behalf of all, as though he were the Christians’ advocate.

Also Saint Sanctus, a deacon in name and in deed, endured unheard-of tortures. The torturers repeatedly applied red-hot plates of bronze and iron to the most delicate parts around his groin, and placed him on an iron chair with fire beneath it; yet they could not turn him from the faith of Christ. Together with Attalus and Maturus, his neck cut through by the sword, he gained the palm of martyrdom.

There was also a woman named Blandina, whose frailty everyone feared for. From first light until evening, the torturers continually renewed her torments; at last they confessed themselves defeated. Although tortured a second time, she was not overcome. On the third day she was tied to a stake, stretched out in the form of a cross, and prepared as food for the beasts. Since none of them dared touch her, she was taken back to prison. On the fourth day, driven through beatings, burned on grates, and subjected to many other sufferings, she was finally killed with the sword.

Then the boy Ponticus, fifteen years old, was tortured with her through every kind of torment. Strengthened by her maternal encouragement, he completed his martyrdom before her. How Alexander the physician, a Phrygian by birth, overcame every kind of torture and went victorious to Christ may be found more suitably in the fifth book of the Ecclesiastical History [Col. 1097A], from which we have excerpted this account.

The names of these martyrs are: Photinus the bishop, Zacharias the priest, Sanctus the deacon, Vetius, also called Epagathus, Macarius, Asclepiades, also called Alcibiades, Silvius, Primus, Ulpius, Vitalis, Comminus, October, Philominus, Geminus, Vilia, Albina, Grata, Rogata, Aemilia, Potamia, Pompeia, Rhodana, Biblis, Quarta, Matema, Elpis, also called Ammas.

These were killed by very diverse deaths. The following were handed over to the beasts: the aforementioned Sanctus, Maturus, Attalus, Alexander, Ponticus, Blandina, Aristeus, Cornelius, Zosimus, Titus, Julius, Zoticus, Apollonius, Geminianus, Julia, Ausonia, Aemilia, Jannica, Pompeia, Domna, Justa, Throphima, [Col. 1097B] and Antonia.

The remains of all of them were consigned to fire and scattered in the river Rhône. But when the martyrs themselves revealed the matter, the relics were collected and buried in the church of the Apostles. By their very frequent miracles they are shown to live before God.

The citizens of Lyon celebrate their feast by proceeding joyfully from every direction down the river, with hymns and songs of thanksgiving, and by solemnly offering the rites of Mass to the Lord in that same church. Following the tradition of the ancients, they call that day the Day of Miracles. The place where they suffered is called Athenacum; for this reason they are called the Athenacene martyrs.

## Third day before the Nones of June

At Rome, the nativity of the holy martyrs Marcellus, Avidus, Gaius, and Donatus, with more than one hundred fifty others.

[Col. 1097C] In Africa, of Quirinus, Abidianus, Neophorus, Pambo, Januaria, Demetria, Zincus, and one hundred forty-nine others.

At Arezzo, a city of Tuscany, of the holy brothers and martyrs Pergentinus and Laurentinus. During the persecution of Decius, under the judge Tertius, although still boys, they endured terrible punishments, displayed many miracles, and were struck down with the sword. They were buried near that same city; and there are four hundred other martyrs.

In Campania, of blessed Erasmus, bishop and martyr of Antioch. He lived the eremitical life for seven years on Mount Lebanon and performed many miracles there. Later, arrested by the emperor Diocletian, he was first cruelly beaten with leaden clubs at the emperor’s command, then tormented at length with rods. Afterward, when resin, sulfur, lead, pitch, wax, and oil had been melted together, he was drenched with them and, by an immense miracle, appeared unharmed. Many who witnessed this rejected their idols and embraced the faith of Christ.

Then bound with an enormous weight of iron, he was shut in prison under terrible guard. He was released and rescued from it by an angelic visitation. But when the fame of his miracles was reported to the emperor Maximian, his tortures were renewed. He suffered so greatly that he was dressed in a heated bronze tunic and placed in a cauldron in which lead, pitch, wax, resin, and oil had been brought to a boil. Yet by the Lord’s power he overcame everything and emerged unharmed. Preserved by the Lord and strengthened to confirm the others, he reached Campania, warned and protected by angelic consolation.

There, after strengthening many in the faith or converting them to the faith of Christ, he rested in a holy death, glorified by martyrdom, when the Lord called him.

At Orléans, the burial of Saint Leifard, priest.

## Second day before the Nones of June

At Nevers, of Zoticus, Attalus, Eutychius, and many others.

In Sicily, of the holy martyrs Expergentius and Crista.

In Pannonia, in the city of Savaria, of Rutulus and two others.

In Illyria, in the city of Fiscia, the nativity of Saint Quirinus, bishop. During the persecution of Maximian, for the faith of Christ, he was thrown into a river with a millstone bound to his hand. After speaking at great length with those standing around, so that they would not be terrified by his example, he at last obtained, only with difficulty and through prayers, that he be submerged. His relics were transferred to Rome and placed at the Catacombs.

**NONES OF JUNE.**—In Egypt, the nativity of the holy martyrs Marcian, Nicander, and Apollonius.

At Rome, at the seventh milestone, Felicula and Felicitas, with many others.

In Istria, Zoelus, Satyrus, Thyminus, Saturninus, Servulus, Felix, Silvanus, and Fortunatus.

Likewise at Rome, Saint Boniface the martyr, who suffered under Diocletian and Maximian at Tarsus in Cilicia, but was buried at Rome on the Via Latina. He was the steward of the affairs of a certain noble matron named Aglaes, and was involved with her in sexual immorality. At last, however, both of them, moved by divine prompting, formed the plan that Boniface should be sent to seek the bodies of the martyrs, so that, by serving and attending upon them, they might perhaps deserve to be saved through their merits.

After reaching Tarsus several days later, he hurried to the place where the holy martyrs were contending in the struggle.
