He saw one suspended by the feet with a fire placed beneath him; another stretched out upon four pieces of wood and tortured for a very long time; another raked with claws; another with his hands cut off; and another with a stake fixed in his neck, raised up from the ground. When he saw from a distance these various torments arranged by the wicked executioner, he too, inflamed with love for Christ, began to cry out: “Great is the God of the holy martyrs!” He ran up and sat at their feet, kissing their bonds and saying: “Strive, martyrs of Christ; trample down the devil; persevere for a little while. The labor is small, but the rest is great, and afterward there is an ineffable satisfaction.”

When the judge Simplicius saw this, he ordered him to be brought before the tribunal and said to him: “Who are you?” Saint Boniface said: “I am a Christian, and I am called Boniface.” Then the angry judge ordered him to be suspended and his body scraped with claws until his bones appeared. Next he ordered sharp reeds to be driven beneath the nails of his hands.

While the holy martyr, looking toward heaven, endured his pains cheerfully, the impious judge, seeing this, ordered his mouth to be opened and boiling lead to be poured in. But the holy martyr said: “I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God.”

Then the judge ordered a cauldron to be brought and filled with pitch, and the holy martyr to be put headfirst into the boiling pitch. But when he remained completely unharmed, the wicked judge ordered that his head be cut off with a sword. When this had been done, there was a great earthquake, so that many unbelievers, seeing Christ’s power in the martyr, believed.

His companions took up his body, embalmed it with spices, and brought it to the city of Rome. An angel of the Lord appeared to his former mistress and informed her of what had happened to the blessed martyr. She immediately went out with every mark of reverence to meet the holy body, built for him a worthy memorial, and laid it to rest five stadia from the city of Rome.

Blessed Aglaes renounced the world and its pomp, distributed all that she possessed among the poor and monasteries, and released her entire household from the yoke of slavery. She obtained such grace from the Lord that she became renowned for signs of power performed in his name. She lived for thirteen years afterward in the habit of a holy woman and was buried beside the same martyr, having completed her life in pious works.

Blessed Boniface was martyred on the fourteenth day of the month of May at Tarsus, the metropolis of Cilicia, but was buried at Rome on the Nones of June.

On the same day, in Frisia, the passion of Saint Boniface, bishop. Coming from Britain and preaching the faith of Christ, after he had brought a very great multitude in Frisia under the Christian religion, he was finally killed by the sword by the pagans who remained and completed his martyrdom together with Bishop Eobanus and the other servants of God whose names are these: Wintrug, Walthere, Skirwald, Bosan, Hamund and Hethere, Wacchar, Gundachar, Willehere, and Hadovolf. It is also reported that Willibald, a priest renowned for his virtues and learning, and his sister Waldburg, distinguished for holiness, belonged to their company.

**EIGHT DAYS BEFORE THE IDES OF JUNE.**—The nativity of Saint Philip, who was one of the first seven deacons whom the apostles ordained immediately after Christ’s Passion. Concerning him it is related in the Acts of the Apostles (chapters VI and VIII) that, by performing signs and wonders, he converted the Samaritans to the faith of Christ through his preaching, and baptized the eunuch of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was well versed in the Scriptures, in the spring near the village of Bethzur, in the tribe of Judah, on the road from Aelia to Hebron, at the twentieth milestone.

He afterward rested at Caesarea. Near him his three daughters, virgins and prophetesses, lie buried; for his fourth daughter, filled with the Holy Spirit, died at Ephesus. Some, however, think that they were buried at Hierapolis, where Philip the apostle, one of the Twelve, rests. Some writers have thought that these were his daughters. The authority of blessed Luke refutes their opinion, for he writes: “We entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven; he had four virgin daughters who prophesied” (Acts XXI).

At Tarsus in Cilicia, twenty martyrs who, under the judge Simplicius, in the time of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, glorified God in their bodies through various torments, as was stated above in the passion of blessed Boniface.

[Col. 1100A] At Rome, the holy Artemius, with his wife Candida and his daughter Paulina. Artemius was keeper of the prisons and held blessed Peter the exorcist in custody. When his only daughter Paulina was freed from a demon, he believed in Christ, and was baptized by the blessed priest Marcellinus together with his entire household and many others. When the judge Serenus—turbulent in mind—heard of this, he ordered Artemius, Candida, and their daughter Paulina, who had been brought before him, to be buried beneath an immense mass of rubble. Thus the holy servants of God were led to the place of their passion: blessed Artemius was struck with the sword, while holy Paulina and Candida were thrown down through the entrance of a crypt and buried beneath stones.

At Novidunum, Amantius, Lucius, and blessed Alexander.

[Col. 1100B] At Alexandria, Donatus and Peregrinus.

**SEVEN DAYS BEFORE THE IDES OF JUNE.**—At Caesarea in Cappadocia, blessed Lucian the martyr.

At Byzantium, the nativity of Saints Primus, Fortunatus, Macrius, and Macarius, monks.

At Constantinople, formerly called Byzantium, the nativity of Saint Paul, bishop of that city. During the time of the Arian perfidy, he was expelled into exile by the emperor Constantius to a certain small town of Cappadocia called Cucusus because of the Catholic faith. He was strangled through the schemes of the Arians and departed to the heavenly kingdoms.

In Africa, Victurius, Evasus, Privata, Januaria, Donata, Spisma, and Quirillus.

**SIX DAYS BEFORE THE IDES OF JUNE.**—In Egypt, the nativity of Saint Martian.

[Col. 1100C] At Caesarea in Palestine, Cristus.

In the city of Doroscoro, the nativity of Saint Mark.

At Nicomedia, Eutychius, Nestorius, and Marina.

In Sardinia, the nativity of Saint Salustian.

In Gaul, in the city of Soissons, the feast of Saint Medard, bishop and confessor, whose life, full of virtues, was nobly written in prose and verse by Fortunatus, bishop of Paris. He was generous in almsgiving, distinguished in virtues, and outstanding in the spirit of prophecy. For fifteen years he governed the bishopric of the city of the Veromandui; indeed, by his example and teaching he governed the whole of the West. His soul was led into heaven by angels, while his body was carried to Soissons and honorably buried there; it is commended as glorious through the manifestation of miracles.

[Col. 1100D] At Angers, Saint Licinius, bishop.

Likewise on the same day, Carlenius the confessor.

**FIVE DAYS BEFORE THE IDES OF JUNE.**—At Rome, on Mount Caelius, the nativity of the holy martyrs Primus and Felician, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. These most glorious martyrs, ever living in the Lord, were accused by the priests of the temples before the emperors of being Christians. They were investigated—for they were Roman citizens—and brought into the presence of the emperors, who ordered them bound with iron and thrown into prison. There an angel of the Lord came to them and consoled them.

After several days the emperors ordered them to be brought before them again, and instructed the soldiers to lead them to the shrine of Hercules and, if they refused to sacrifice, to afflict them severely with punishments. But when they could not move them by any means, and the martyrs preferred to die for the name of Christ, the soldiers stretched them out and beat them violently with rods.

When they had reported to the emperors what had been done, the emperors became extremely angry and ordered them handed over to Promotus, governor of the city of Nomentum, so that he might kill them with various punishments. The soldiers took them, bound with iron, along the road called the Nomentan Way, at the thirteenth milestone, and put them in prison near the city forum. There they were again strengthened by an angelic visitation.

After a long time, Promotus ordered the holy men of God, Primus and Felician, to be brought before his tribunal. Having separated them from each other for the first public interrogation, he ordered blessed Felician to be beaten with leaded scourges. When he saw that he was unconquerable under this form of punishment, he ordered him bound to a stake, with spikes driven into his hands and feet, and tortured for a very long time; for three days he was given neither water nor any kind of food.

When he had remained continuously for three days in the praises of God, the governor ordered him beaten with whips, then taken down from the stake and confined in custody. Afterward, in the presence of blessed Felician himself, he had Saint Primus brought forward. After he had been beaten with very powerful clubs, taken down from the rack, and laid on his back upon a bed, the governor ordered boiling-hot lead to be poured into his mouth.

But when the invincible holy martyrs remained steadfast, the distressed governor ordered them led to the amphitheater and two lions released against them. When the lions fell at the feet of the saints, the fiercest bears were released as well, but they too lost their ferocity through the martyrs’ power. Seeing this, those who had come to the spectacle—nearly fifteen hundred men—were struck by the miracles and believed in the Lord.

When the governor saw that they could not be conquered, he ordered them executed with the sword. Their bodies were secretly taken by Christians at night and buried at the Nomentan arches within the sand-pit, on the fifth day before the Ides of June, at the thirteenth milestone from the city of Rome.

In Gaul, in the city of Agen, at the place called Pompeiaca, the passion of Saint Vincent, levite and martyr, concerning whom it is related in the Book of Miracles by Gregory of Tours.

Likewise at Rome, fifteen soldiers.

In Scotland, the island of Ireland, the burial of Saint Columba, called Columbkilli among his own people because he was the institutor, founder, and ruler of many cells—that is, monasteries or churches. Thus, although he was abbot of the monastery over which he last presided and where he rests, contrary to ecclesiastical custom he is regarded as the chief of all the bishops of the Irish. Not without reason, since this same holy man, through the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, appears to have been second to no one after the apostles and the wonderful Martin in prophecy, teaching, the manifestation of miracles, and angelic visitations.

This may be perceived from the following few examples. While he was sitting on one island writing, and on another a very high house was being built, a man began to fall from the summit of that huge structure toward the ground. In the very danger of his sudden fall, he said to the angel of God standing beside him: “Help, help!” And immediately, in that very instant, the falling man was helped by the angel, as though the angel had always been present not with a writer but with a craftsman.

When a serious illness—indeed, an intolerable plague and pestilence—was devastating nearly the entire population, he blessed a stone from the shore and ordered it to be put into water wherever he commanded, and the sick to drink or be sprinkled with that water. Once placed in the water, the stone floated contrary to its nature like foam, thereby testifying that it had received divine blessing, and it cured every disease. It was more precious than gold and every jewel, and more beneficial than all medicines.

To increase the miracle, although it was guarded and sought with the greatest care, it could ever be found by no one who was to die during that time.

Having mentioned this one example of manifold healing, let us recall another concerning abundant assistance in time of want, so that the prudent reader may learn from these two examples, even in silence, to judge the rest. To a certain poor man, lacking everything, the saint sharpened a spit and ordered him to drive it into the woods and waters. When he did so, he became so wealthy that his house could not contain the abundance, and his wife, disdaining earthly delicacies together with those of the sea, had the same spit cut up by her husband for her own destruction.

In teaching, blessed Columba equaled all those who came before him; yet he is rightly considered to have surpassed them in this respect: during the final three days of his dwelling on earth, all the mysteries of sacred Scripture were revealed to him. These had either been entirely hidden from all mortals before him or, as the Apostle says, had been known “through a mirror and in an enigma” (1 Cor. XIII), indeed presented as matters to be sought and elucidated.

Because Battheneus, his most intimate disciple, was absent—or rather, because of the unworthiness of the human race—these revelations were not committed to writing.

Moreover, in the gift of prophecy he so far surpassed all mortals that, at a single glance of his unfailing eye, he perceived both present things hidden from others and absent things—not only nearby but also far away—as well as past and future things.

A vessel full of milk was brought before him as a customary blessing. When he had blessed it and the vessel immediately cracked, he reproved the servant for not having first, through the sign of the holy cross, forbidden the ancient enemy to remain in it before the milk was poured in.

Likewise, by blessing from a distance, he changed into its proper nature—that is, blood—the likeness of milk expressed from the testicles of a bull.

He both foresaw the wars of neighboring kings and sometimes restrained them; at other times he favored those who had the more just causes, while, joined to divine justice, he disregarded the more unjust by refusing to help them.

He also saw the destruction of the city now called Nova in Italy: it was overthrown in sudden terror by a cleft in the earth, or rather through the visitation of heavenly wrath. While others marveled at his ecstasy, he announced the same event to them. He also foretold that Gallic sailors, as indeed happened, would report the same event in Scotland that very year.

On the final day of his mortal life, that is, on Saturday, after he had written the thirty-third psalm as far as the verse: “But those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing” (Ps. XXXIII), he said to those standing by: “Let Baitheneus write what remains.” The one who was to succeed him in the governance of the brothers was thus to call the disciples to himself not only by teaching but also by writing: “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (ibid.).

He added: “This day is called the Sabbath in sacred Scripture, that is, rest; on it eternal rest is being prepared for me. For behold, this night I am going to the Lord Jesus Christ, the author of the great resurrection. And know this: for successive days the sea will be held closed by a violent storm, so that my funeral rites may be celebrated not superstitiously by common crowds but religiously by my holy brothers.”

Although he had many disciples or companions equal to him in holiness, he nevertheless left one man, namely Comgellus—renowned in Latin by the name Faustus, teacher of the most blessed Columbanus, the master, lord, and father of our Gallus—as his unique heir of virtues and merits, like Isaac.

**FOUR DAYS BEFORE THE IDES OF JUNE.**—At Rome, on the Via Aurelia, at the thirteenth milestone, the nativity of Saint Basilides the martyr, of Tripodis and Mandalis, under the emperor Aurelian and the governor Plato, and of twenty other martyrs. In some books, however, instead of Tripodis and Mandalis, “Tripoli Magdaletis” is found written.

[Col. 1103C] On the same day, blessed Getulius the martyr, in the time of the emperor Hadrian, under the judge Licinius. He was extremely learned in every divine law, and through his teaching many were instructed in the faith of Christ. When the emperor Hadrian heard of his reputation, he sent Cerealis, the deputy governor, to seize him. But after hearing his word of truth, Cerealis believed in Christ and was baptized by blessed Sixtus, the pope; through the instruction of Saint Getulius, he was strengthened in the faith of Christ.

When Hadrian learned this, he sent Licinius, the consul-governor, to seize Cerealis. Blessed Getulius, his brother Amantius, and their most holy friend Primitivus were found with him and seized together. At the order of Licinius they were stripped and beaten and then thrust into prison for twenty-seven days.

Then, coming to Rome and informing Hadrian of what had happened, Licinius received orders from him to burn them all in the fire. But when Saint Getulius survived the fire, he completed his martyrdom with his head shattered by clubs.

The blessed martyrs were brought to completion at the estate of Capreoli, on the Salarian Way, somewhat more than thirteen miles from Rome, above the Tiber River, in the region of the Sabines. Blessed Symphorosa, the wife of the martyr Getulius—who not long afterward suffered martyrdom with her seven sons, namely on the twenty-seventh day of the month of June—gathered their bodies and buried them on her estate in a sand-pit, at the place and settlement mentioned above.

At Nicomedia, Saint Zachariah.

[Col. 1104A] At Auxerre, the burial of Saint Censor, bishop.

**THREE DAYS BEFORE THE IDES OF JUNE.**—In Cyprus, the nativity of Saint Barnabas the apostle. Although he had been named Joseph by his parents, the apostles called him Barnabas, or “son of consolation,” because, having owned a field and sold it, he laid its price at the apostles’ feet for the consolation of the poor.

Although he was a Jew by race, indeed a Levite, but a Cypriot by nationality, he took care not only to bring the other Jews under the faith of Christ but also to associate with the company of the apostles Paul himself, who had been called by Christ from heaven but was viewed with suspicion by Christians because of the enormity of his former persecution.

Ordained with him by the apostles as the apostle to the Gentiles, and suffering many injuries from unbelievers, he nevertheless fulfilled the task of evangelical preaching entrusted to him. He was separated from Paul in body because of Mark, their common disciple—or rather, by divine dispensation—but remained united with him in mind.

One testimony of blessed Luke concerning his holiness ought to be sufficient for the faithful, namely, that “he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith” (Acts XI).

His body was found in the time of the emperor Zeno, when he himself revealed its location. He is said to have written one epistle for the edification of the Church, but it is reckoned among the apocryphal writings.

On the same day, at Corinth, Sosthenes, a disciple of blessed Paul the apostle. When he was being mistreated by the Gentiles in Judaism, while Gallio the proconsul paid no attention, he converted to Christianity and was honorably commended by blessed Paul himself in the apostolic letters (1 Cor. I).

Likewise at Aquileia, the nativity of the holy martyrs Felix and Fortunatus, under the persecution of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, with Euphemius as governor. They were brothers by birth, fervent in the faith of Christ. When Apamius, one of the governor’s officials, informed against them, they were bound with iron and brought to Aquileia before the judge Euphemius.

There, when they most steadfastly confessed Christ, the angry judge first had them suspended upon the rack, with burning lamps placed at their sides. But soon, while the martyrs were singing psalms, the lamps were extinguished. Then they were drenched over the belly with burning oil. Finally, while they persisted in confessing Christ, they were led outside the city and beheaded beside the river nearest the city.

That night, religious men of the city took them away, wrapped them in linen cloths with spices, and secretly buried them. But citizens arriving from Vicetia tried to carry their bodies to their own city, Vicetia. When the people of Aquileia refused and resisted, the pious dispute was at last settled by divine will: the people of Vicetia were to have Felix, and the people of Aquileia Fortunatus, provided that the people of Aquileia received the head of blessed Felix, while Vicetia received the head of Saint Fortunatus. This arrangement remains to this day in praise of our Lord Jesus Christ.

At Rome, Anacletus, pope, who first built and arranged a memorial for blessed Peter the apostle. He had been ordained a priest by Peter and was buried beside his body.

**TWO DAYS BEFORE THE IDES OF JUNE.**—At Rome, the nativity of Saint Cyrinus. By order of the emperor Claudius II, after all his possessions had been confiscated and after prolonged imprisonment and torture, he was beheaded at night, and his body was thrown into the Tiber. It was found on the island of Lycaonia and honorably buried by the faithful. When or how it was transferred to Rome is unknown to us, but we believe that it was not unknown to blessed Gregory.

Likewise at Rome, Nabor and Nazarius. Together with the martyr Gorgonius—whom I think is the one designated in Ecclesiastical History—the bishop Ruodgang of Metz transferred them from Rome to Gaul, or, more truthfully, to ancient France, with the permission of Paul, pope of Rome, in the year 765 from the Lord’s Incarnation.

He placed Saint Gorgonius in the monastery called Gorze, Saint Nabor in another monastery called Nova Cella, and Saint Nazarius in the monastery called Lorsch, where signs and miracles are frequently displayed in the restoration of health to the sick and weak.

On the same day, at Milan, the nativity of the holy martyrs Nazarius and Celsus the boy. Blessed Nazarius’s father was Africanus, and his mother Perpetua; they had been baptized by blessed Peter the apostle. Saint Nazarius himself was instructed and baptized by Saint Clement.

Anulinus, during the fury of the persecution stirred up by Nero, ordered him, after he had been long tortured and afflicted in prison together with the most blessed boy Celsus, whom Nazarius himself had raised, to be struck with the sword.

Christians secretly took their bodies and buried them outside the gate called the Roman Gate, in their own gardens, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August. The blessed martyrs revealed themselves to a certain man named Caeratius, whose wife was Fortunata, and in a vision directed that they be concealed because of the fury of the persecution that the impious Nero had stirred up.

They remained hidden until the time of the emperors Honorius and Arcadius. Blessed Ambrose found them when the Lord revealed their location. When the tomb in which the body of blessed Nazarius lay was opened—for until that time it was unknown when he had suffered, as Saint Paulinus writes—those present saw the martyr’s blood as fresh as though it had been shed that very day.

His head too, which had been cut off by the impious, was so whole and incorrupt, with the hair of his head and beard, that it appeared to have been washed and arranged in the tomb at the very moment when it was lifted out. They were also filled with such a fragrance that it surpassed the sweetness of every spice.

After the body had been lifted and placed on a bier, the holy bishop immediately went in prayer to Saint Celsus the martyr, who had been laid to rest in the same garden, and transferred both of them to the Basilica of the Apostles, which is on the Roman Way.

They were found and transferred on the day before the Ides of June. Their feast commemorating their martyrdom, however, is celebrated on the fifth day before the Kalends of August. Their public and most celebrated commemoration is nevertheless held on the day of the holy martyrs Protasius and Gervasius, as though they were companions of the same time.

*(Here several pages are missing from the manuscript.)*

At Antioch, Saint Marina the virgin, who suffered many torments for the name of Christ under the prefect Olibrius: chains, prison, scourges, and the rack. The devil attacked her in the form of a dragon and an Ethiopian and tried to overthrow her, but, driven away and overcome by her through the sign of the holy cross, he departed. Finally, she was beheaded by the same prefect, ending her mortal life and receiving from Christ the true and eternal life.

At Ravenna, Macarius, Felix, Aemilius, and Crispinus.

**THIRTEEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY.**—At Milan, the nativity of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. These most blessed men, instructed by the holy apostle Paul, had spent ten years shut up in one upper room, devoting themselves to readings, prayers, and fasts. In the tenth year they were betrayed by the priests of the temples to the count Astasius, seized and interrogated by him, and reached the palm of martyrdom in the following manner.

When he could compel them neither by threats nor by flatteries to deny that they were Christians, he ordered Gervasius to be beaten with leaded scourges until he breathed out his spirit, while Protasius, after being beaten with clubs, was beheaded.

Their bodies were secretly taken away by Philip, a religious man, together with his son, and buried inside his house in a marble sarcophagus. Many years later, under the emperor Theodosius, blessed Ambrose found their tombs when the Lord revealed them. Their bodies were so incorrupt as though they had been killed that very day. When they were being brought into the city, a man who had long been blind received his sight through touching the bier.

Likewise there, according to the Martyrology of Saint Jerome, the nativity of Saint Nazarius and Celsus the boy.

At Ravenna, Saint Ursicinus the martyr, who, under the judge Paulinus, after excessive torments remained unmoved in confessing the Lord, completed his martyrdom by the cutting off of his head and was buried in the same city by blessed Vitalis, the father of Saints Gervasius and Protasius.

At Rome, Sylvester, pope, who occupied the see for one year. With the consent of the emperor Justinian, he was deposed by the patrician Belisarius and made a monk; he died in exile as a confessor.

**TWELVE DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY.**—At Rome, the burial of blessed Novatus, brother of Timothy the priest, both of whom had been instructed by the blessed apostles. Concerning Novatus, Pastor writes in the Acts of the virgins Pudentiana and Praxedis that after the death of blessed Pudentiana, when blessed Bishop Pius and Saint Praxedis visited him, with a large company of martyrs also present, he departed to Christ.

At Tomi, the city, Paul, Cyriacus, Paula, Feliciana, Felix, Aemilius, Vitalis, Crispina, and Martyria.

Likewise, the translation of Saint Zeno the martyr.

**ELEVEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY.**—In Sicily, in the city of Syracuse, the nativity of the holy martyrs Rufinus and Martia.

At Rome, Saint Demetria the virgin, who was the daughter of blessed Faustus. When she was brought before the impious Julian for the faith of Christ, she surrendered her spirit while confessing him. She was buried by blessed John the priest beside her mother Dafrosa and her sister Bibiana, near the Licinian Palace.

At the city of Mainz, the nativity of Saint Alban the martyr. Coming from the island of Namsia in the time of the emperor Theodosius, he came to Milan with Saint Theonestus and Ursus. Departing from there, with the Lord’s help he reached Gaul. Persevering in the Lord’s service and ready for martyrdom in the name of the Savior, after blessed Ursus had completed the course of martyrdom in the city of Augsburg, Saint Alban reached Mainz with Theonestus.

While preaching the word of God there, he completed his martyrdom and was buried there near the city mentioned above.

At Caesarea, the burial of Saint Eusebius, bishop.

**TEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY.**—At Antioch, the nativity of the holy martyrs Agathalica, Julian, Graphius, and eight hundred fourteen others, whose names God has in the book of the living.

In Britain, Saint Alban the martyr, who in the time of Diocletian was beheaded in the city of Verulamium after lashes and bitter torments. When he fell to the ground, the eyes of the man who struck him fell out at the same time.

One of the soldiers also suffered with him because, although ordered to strike him, he refused, having been terrified by a divine miracle: he had seen the blessed martyr, as he hurried toward the crown of martyrdom, make the channel of the intervening river passable by prayer.

At that time, the most savage persecution crossed the rim of the Ocean into Britain and condemned Aaron and Julius, together with eight hundred eighty-nine others, to a blessed death.

In the city of Nola in Campania, Saint Paulinus, bishop. In the time of the Vandals, when all others had already been exhausted, he handed himself over to the barbarians as a slave in place of the son of a certain widow. After being recognized by their king through a terrifying vision, he had the entire population of his city restored to him and, with ships loaded with grain, returned from Africa to his own see in great glory.

He was distinguished not only by learning and abundant holiness of life but also by power against demons.

On the same day, the burial of blessed Nicetius, bishop of the city of Rome.

**NINE DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY.**—At Nicomedia, the passion of the holy virgins Pistis, Elpis, and Agapis—called in Latin Faith, Hope, and Charity—and of their mother Sophia, which is interpreted as Wisdom, together with many others.

At Rome, Saint John the priest, whom the impious Julian ordered to be beheaded, without a hearing, on the old Salarian Way before an image of the Sun. His body was gathered and buried by blessed Concordius the priest near the martyrs’ council.

In Britain, the burial of Saint Edeldruda, virgin and queen. Although her body had been buried for ten years, it was found incorrupt.

Likewise, the vigil of Saint John the Baptist.

**EIGHT DAYS BEFORE THE IDES OF JULY.**—In the province of Palestine, in the city of Sebaste, formerly Samaria and, many centuries earlier, called Shechem, the celebration of the nativity of Saint John the Baptist. His body had been decapitated in the fortress of Macherus in Arabia but was buried there by his disciples.

According to the authority of the holy Gospel of Luke and the Book of Joshua, he is believed to have been born and brought up in the city of Hebron in Judah, which had been assigned to the priests, indeed to the sons of Aaron, as a refuge for fugitives. The holiness of his life, the austerity of his conduct, the quality of his preaching, and the bitterness of his passion in defense of the truth are commended not only by the writings of the Evangelists but also by the testimonies of the Lord himself, the inward judge.

At Ephesus, the falling-asleep of blessed John the apostle and evangelist. Although his praises may more appropriately appear on the sixth day before the Kalends of January, when the solemnity of his feast is celebrated throughout the whole Church, some of them may nevertheless be recalled here for the benefit of readers.

When he knew that the day of his departure was approaching, in the sixty-eighth year after the Lord’s Passion, he summoned his disciples and, during the sacred celebrations of God’s Mass, did not cease to admonish them repeatedly and frequently concerning contempt for the world and its desires and concerning the observance of mutual charity.

They became weary of his repetition of the same teaching and begged him to say something else, since this was sufficient for them and more than sufficient. He replied: “Because the preservation of holy and undefiled love would either scarcely be preached worthily by any mortal or be kept unblemished to the end amid the scandals of the world.”

After saying this, he gave peace to everyone and communicated both himself and them with the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. Then he reclined in the tomb as though in a bed, believed to be as free from the pain of death as he was untouched by the contagion of corruption.

At Autun, the burial of Saint Simplicius, bishop; Festus and Lucerius.

**SEVEN DAYS BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JULY.**—At Beroea of Pyrrhus, the nativity of Saint Sosipater, disciple of blessed Paul the apostle.

Alexandria: Saint Gallicanus, martyr. He was commander of the Roman army. When he had been besieged by the Scythian people inside the Thracian city of Philippopolis [Philoppolis/Philippopolis], and, at the urging of the saints John and Paul, had renounced the worship of idols and entrusted himself to the protection of the Lord Jesus [Col. 1108D] Christ, both he and all Thrace were freed from the enemy’s attack. Returning to Rome and becoming a Christian, he made five thousand of his slaves free Roman citizens, and also gave them estates and houses. He caused all his possessions to be sold and distributed to the poor, except the legal inheritance of his daughters, Attica and Artemia, whom the most holy virgin Augusta Constantina had won for Christ. He joined himself, while remaining in the city of Ostia, to a holy man named Hilarinus. He enlarged Hilarinus’s dwelling to receive travelers, a service that he himself provided for very many. With the assistance of the servants whom he had already freed—and whom, for that reason, he bound more closely to himself—he did not cease to offer the services of holy servitude to all the needy who came to him and to all the sick, until Julian the Apostate, having become Caesar, promulgated a law that Christians were to possess nothing in this world.

Even then, in the very few huts that Gallicanus had kept reserved for the service of the poor, he was deemed worthy to find Christ as his defender: whoever presumptuously entered them maliciously, or to place there the legal notices of the treasury, was immediately either filled by the devil or covered with the spots of leprosy. When this was reported to Julian, he ordered Gallicanus either to sacrifice to the gods or to leave the borders of Italy. Blessed Gallicanus therefore soon abandoned everything and went to Alexandria, where for a full year he joined the confessors of Christ. Afterward [Col. 1109B] he withdrew into the wilderness. There he was forcibly compelled by Raucianus, commander of the temples, to sacrifice to the gods; but when he refused, he was struck in the body with a sword, became Christ’s martyr, and thus went to the Lord, rejoicing in triumph. They immediately built a basilica bearing his name, in which the martyr’s benefits abound, from that time and now and forever.

At Rome, Saint Luceia, virgin, and Auceia, king, who were crowned with martyrdom together with twenty-two others.

### VI Kalends of July

At Rome, the feast of Saints John and Paul, brothers. The former was superintendent; the latter was chief secretary of Constantia the virgin, daughter of the Emperor Constantine. Every day they refreshed the bands of Christians from the resources that the most holy virgin Constantia, Christ’s servant, had left behind. This came to the attention of Julian, the most impious Caesar. Since he could neither by threats nor persuasion draw them away from the love of Christ or entice them to the worship of idols, he granted them a reprieve of ten days, so that they might bow to the veneration of his gods.

Then the saints of God, inviting Christians to themselves, arranged everything that they were able to give away. Throughout all ten days, by night and day, they devoted themselves without interruption to almsgiving. At the end of the tenth day, at the hour of dinner, they were seized inside their house while praying by Terentianus, commander of the camp. Since no argument or threat could make them deviate even slightly from the love of Christ, they were beheaded by that same Terentianus. A pit was dug inside their house, and they were placed there; a report was spread that, by order of the Caesar, they had been sent into exile.

Demons were expelled from possessed bodies inside the house of John and Paul, confessing their holy passion. Thus the only son of Terentianus, who had beheaded them, came into the house of the saints, and the demon cried out through his mouth that Paul and John were burning him. Terentianus, then pierced by divine grace and reborn in Christ, continued in prayer over the bodies of the saints until he obtained cleansing for his son.

In Alexandria, Agathon, Diogenes, and Bigatus.

In Africa, Gaudentius, Felix, Agapitus, and Emerita.

### V Kalends of July

In Galatia, the feast of blessed Crescent, disciple of blessed Paul the apostle. He also crossed into Gaul and converted many to faith in Christ by the word of his preaching. Returning to the people over whom he had been specially appointed bishop, he strengthened the Galatians in the work of the Lord until the blessed end of his life.

At Tibur, a city of Italy, the feast of Saint Symphorosa, wife of blessed Getulius the martyr, with her seven sons—Crescent, Julian, Nemesius, Primitivus, Justinus, Stacteus, and Eugenius—with whom she suffered under the Emperor Hadrian. He ordered Symphorosa herself to be beaten with palms and then suspended by her hair. When he could not overcome her in any way, he ordered her to be thrown into the river with a stone tied to her. Her brother Eugenius, a leading member of the council of Tibur, gathered her body and buried it.

The next morning the emperor ordered seven stakes to be fixed in place. Her sons were stretched upon racks there: Crescent was pierced through the throat, Julian through the chest, Nemesius through the heart, Primitivus through the navel; Justinus, stretched limb by limb, was torn apart at each joint and articulation; Stacteus was fixed to the ground with countless lances until he died; and Eugenius was split open from the chest down to the lower parts. The priests of the sacred rites named that place “At the Seven Victims” (*ad Septem Bithanatos*). Their bodies rest on the Tiburtine Way, at the ninth milestone.

On the same day in Spain, in the city of Córdoba, the feast of Saints Zoellus and nineteen others.

At Ephesus, the feast of the Seven Dormant Brothers: Maximianus, Malchus, Martinianus [Martinia/Martiniani], Dionysius, John, Serapion, and Constantine. Fleeing the persecution of Decius after enduring exceedingly many and severe tortures, they hid themselves in a large cave on Mount Caelius and remained there in continual prayer. When the Emperor Decius heard this, he ordered the mouth of the cave to be blocked so that they would die there.

After 372 years—that is, in the thirtieth year of the reign of Theodosius, son of the Emperor Arcadius—when heresy had begun to spread and sought to empty faith of its hope and deny the resurrection of the dead, the seven brothers, who had been resting in that cave until then, were raised from their very long sleep by divine providence. Some people seized them because they had brought to the market money from their own time, now exceedingly ancient, in order to purchase their daily food. They were brought before the people of that age and, as though discoverers of ancient treasures, were compelled to hand over what they were thought to possess.

After much dispute and the saints’ great distress—for they supposed that they had left the city in the evening and returned in the morning, although everything before their eyes had changed—Marinus, bishop of Ephesus, finally arrived. Once the truth of the matter had with difficulty been uncovered, they were freed from the hands of the violent. The Emperor Theodosius was summoned from the distant parts of the world; they were presented to him as witnesses of the future resurrection, and afterward returned to their former place of rest.

In the city of Amiens, the discovery of the bodies of Saints Fuscianus, Victoricus, and Gentianus.

### IV Kalends of July

At Lyon in Gaul, the feast of Saint Irenaeus, bishop. When blessed Photinus, nearly ninety years old, had been crowned with martyrdom for Christ, Irenaeus succeeded him. It is also established that he had been a disciple of the most blessed Polycarp, disciple of Saint John the apostle, priest and martyr. During the persecution of Severus, he was gloriously crowned with martyrdom together with almost the entire population of his city. He was buried by the priest Zacharias in the crypt of the basilica of blessed John the Baptist, beneath the altar. On one side of him Epipodius was buried, and on the other the martyr Alexander.

On the same day at Alexandria, the passion of the holy martyrs Plutarch, Serenus, Heraclides, and Heron. Also Serenus, Potamiena, Marcella, and a catechumen named Hera, who attained baptism through martyrdom. Among them Potamiena the virgin was especially distinguished. First she endured immense and innumerable struggles for her virginity; afterward she suffered extraordinary and unheard-of tortures for Christ’s martyrdom; finally, together with her venerable mother Marcella, she was consumed by the punishments of fire and departed from earth for heaven.

On the same day, the burial of Saint Leo, pope. After the apostle blessed Peter, he was the forty-seventh to sit in the city of Rome. He held the see for twenty-one years, one month, and thirteen days. Abounding in extensive learning and explaining the Catholic faith together with many bishops, he condemned the Eutychian and Nestorian heresies and, through his efforts, caused the most holy Council of Chalcedon to be convened. He established that the words “the holy sacrifice” should be said within the liturgical action, and that a nun should not receive from a bishop a blessed veil for her head unless her virginity had first been tested.

In Africa, Fabianus and Felix with many other martyrs.

The vigil of the most holy apostles Peter and Paul.

### III Kalends of July

At Rome, the feast of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, who suffered under the Emperor Nero, when Bassus and Tuscus were consuls.

After the conversion to the Lord Jesus Christ of many thousands of Jews, after the calling of Cornelius and very many Gentiles, after his episcopate of the Church of Antioch and his preaching to the dispersion of those from the circumcision who had believed in Christ in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, Peter was sent by God in the second year of Claudius to defeat Simon Magus—or rather, to enlighten the peoples of the West and provide medicine for those sick in soul and body—and he reached Rome.

There he held the priestly chair for twenty-five years, until the final year of Nero. Nero had him fastened to a cross, and he was crowned with martyrdom, with his head turned toward the earth at his own request and his feet raised upward, because he considered himself unworthy to be crucified in the same manner as his Lord. He was buried near that city in the Vatican, beside the Triumphal Way. He is celebrated by the veneration of the whole world and assists in many indescribable ways all who seek him in faith.

He wrote two letters called Catholic Epistles. The second is denied by many because of its difference in style from the first, but all sound-minded people approve that it truly belongs to him. He appointed two bishops, namely Linus and Cletus, to provide all priestly ministry in the city of Rome to the people and to those arriving. He himself devoted himself to prayer and preaching, just as at Jerusalem, when deacons had been appointed to serve widows and orphans, he continually persisted with the other apostles in prayer and the word.

Paul likewise, in the twenty-fifth year after the Lord’s passion—that is, the second year of Nero—after he had filled the region from Jerusalem to Illyricum with the Gospel of Christ, was sent to Rome in chains. But he was miraculously freed by God and entered under open custody. As he himself writes in the Second Epistle to Timothy (chapter 4), he was delivered from the mouth of the lion, namely from Nero, that most savage persecutor. He also preached the Gospel of Christ in the regions of the West. In the fourteenth year of Nero, on the same day as Peter, he was beheaded at Rome for Christ and buried on the Ostian Way, in the thirty-seventh year after the Lord’s passion.

He wrote nine—or rather ten, corresponding to the Decalogue of the Law—letters to seven churches: one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, and one to the Hebrews. Although some once doubted the letter to the Hebrews because of the difference in its statements and arguments, and because his name is not found in the title, it is now unquestionably held both among the canonical Scriptures and as belonging to blessed Paul the apostle.

In addition, there are four others to his disciples: two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon. Some also read a letter to the Laodiceans, but among the wise it is considered worthless.

Having recalled what seemed to concern his apostleship or martyrdom, let us, although in an inverted order, bring a few things concerning his genealogy, upbringing, and calling to the memory of diligent readers.

Saul—or certainly Saul, to speak according to the Hebrew idiom, since that name was especially distinguished in the tribe of Benjamin from which he came, because of King Saul—was born in the town of Giscalis. When it was captured by the Romans, he migrated with his parents to Tarsus in Cilicia. They sent him to Jerusalem because of his devotion to learning. He was so thoroughly instructed by Gamaliel, most learned in the ancient Law and afterward called to the Gospel of Christ, that he deserved with good reason to be called by the giver of spiritual gifts a chosen vessel.

When he consented to the killing of blessed Stephen, Christ’s protomartyr, together with the Jews who persecuted Christians, and afterward fiercely attacked throughout that entire province all who were marked by that name—and, as he himself confesses, persecuted the worshipers of Jesus the Nazarene even among foreign nations—he was on his way to Damascus, the metropolis of Syria, when by a sudden revelation, or rather by a punishment fully deserved, he was compelled to faith and transferred from persecutor into teacher of the Gentiles. When Sergius Paulus, proconsul of Cyprus, first believed through his preaching, because Paul had brought him under the faith of Christ, he received the proconsul’s name.

Since we have offered a few remarks on blessed Paul’s origin and calling, let something also be narrated about the other apostles, without prejudice to the learned, for the instruction of the ignorant.

First, it must be known that although the Lord is reported to have chosen twelve apostles, the homeland, tribe, or even calling of some of them does not appear to be expressly stated. Yet when the pages of divine Scripture are examined more carefully, these matters are not denied to those who piously seek them.

Concerning Peter, Andrew, and Philip, no one who has read the Gospel is unaware that they came from Bethsaida, whose proper name prefigured our hunters. Luke also indicates that this should be understood of James and John, when he commends them as companions of Simon, who on account of the firmness of his faith deserved to be called Peter by the Lord.

James the Younger, who is commonly called the brother of the Lord not only by the faithful but also by Josephus, the Jewish historian, and his brothers Simon and Judas, or Thaddeus: no Christian is permitted to doubt that they belonged to the tribe of Judah.

Matthew’s calling is reported most clearly by the agreement of the three Evangelists, but his tribe or homeland seems to be left unmentioned. Yet while Mark and Luke call him Levi, suppressing the familiar name, some indicate that he was Dionymus [Dionymon], while more careful writers indicate that he belonged to the tribe of Levi.

Of Bartholomew and Thomas, some apostolic writings seem to signify nothing more than that they were chosen from the multitude of disciples for the apostolic rank. But if anyone examines them more keenly, searching out the deepest treasures of the sacred Scriptures, he will rejoice and marvel that he has found the riches of Jerusalem [Israel].

Thus it is sung in the psalm composed concerning the Lord’s resurrection and ascension, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the apostles’ preaching, and also the faith of the Gentiles and the cruelty of the persecutors (Psalm 67):

> “In the churches bless God the Lord, from the fountains of Jerusalem [Israel].”

There Benjamin is the youth—namely Paul—as Luke also recalled concerning him, “at the feet of the young man” (Acts 7); and, in an ecstasy of mind, as he himself declares:

> “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are self-controlled, it is for you” (2 Corinthians 5).

“The princes of Judah, their leaders”: namely James, Simon, and Judas.

“The princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali”: unquestionably all the rest, apart from Judas Scarioth, whose name is interpreted as “meditation of death.” [Note: Col. 1113D: Something appears to be missing.] His designation may not inappropriately be understood, even by a transposition of letters, since the Gospel interpreters state both that he sprang from the tribe of Issachar—which in Latin means “reward”—and that, by destroying himself, he became heir to his own name.

Having briefly recalled these matters by way of digression, let us return to our subject.

On the same day, that is, the third day before the Kalends of July, which is one day before those Kalends, at Rome, the passion of 976 martyrs.

In Persia, the feast of Saints Simon and Jude, apostles.

### II Kalends of July

At Rome—or rather throughout the whole world of Christ—the feast of Saint Paul the apostle.

Also the feast of the most blessed Lucina, who was baptized and instructed by the apostles. Sharing from her resources with the needs of the saints, she always strove to relieve bonds and prisons and to serve reverently at their burials. Associated herself with them through their merits, she obtained a precious death by confessing Christ and deserved, by fulfilling her vows to the Lord, to enter the courts of the heavenly Jerusalem. At Rome she was honorably buried in a praiseworthy crypt that she herself had built for burying the bodies of martyrs.

In Africa, Timothy and Zoticus.

At Agrippina, Asclepius and Pamphilus.

At Limoges, the burial of Saint Martial, bishop and confessor.

## JULY

The month of July has thirty-one days.

### Kalends of July

On Mount Hor, the burial of Aaron, the first priest under the Law.

At Rome, the feast of Saint Gaius, pope, and many other martyrs.

In Mesopotamia, Zoellus with very many others. At Tours [Uronis/Turonis], the most holy woman Monegunda [Monegundia], enclosed near blessed Martin, but renowned through the display of miracles.

In the territory of Lyon, at the place called the Vebrona Valley, the burial of the most blessed man of God, Domitianus the abbot. He was the first to practice the eremitical life there; gathering very many people to himself in God’s service, he established a monastery. Famous for great virtues and glorious miracles, he was gathered to his fathers in a good old age.

On the same day, the burial of Areleffus the confessor. Dedicated to God from childhood, he desired the monastic life. Saint Maximinus, bishop of Orléans, ordained him priest together with his companion Avitus. Although he desired a solitary life, he could not remain hidden because his merits advanced—for this happened by God’s will—and he built monasteries in various places. He became famous for many virtues both while remaining in the flesh and after his death.

Since the name of virtues sometimes signifies holiness of life and sometimes the efficacy of miracles, it is enough to recall in this brief compendium of ecclesiastical histories one of the miracles displayed through his holiness, to restrain the boldness of presumptuous women.

A woman named Gunda heard that Saint Areleffus had forbidden women—through whom masculine strength is usually softened—access to his monastery. She therefore assumed a man’s clothing, as though intending to mock God’s saint, and, believing that she had already achieved her wish, made her way to the monastery among a crowd of men. Suddenly she was turned to madness: she began baring her thighs, spreading her legs, and exposing her private parts, which she began to name after her own name; and, shameful to say, she attempted to kiss them. Like Lot’s wife—although she was not changed into a pillar of salt, but became through her punishment a seasoning for fools—she inspired fear of curiosity in those present, absent, and even future.

### VI Nones of July

At Rome, the feast of Saints Processus and Martinianus. When they saw the miracles that the Lord Jesus Christ performed through his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, they began to wonder. At that time the most blessed apostles had been handed over to the illustrious Paulinus and were under the custody of Mamertinus on the Tarpeian Hill. There, by their prayers, they caused water to flow from the mountain.

Then Processus [Col. 1115B] and Martinianus, together with forty-seven people of both sexes, were baptized by blessed Peter the apostle. When this was reported to Paulinus, he sent soldiers, seized them, and ordered them to be thrown into custody. On the following day they were brought out, and when they steadfastly . . .

Here several pages are again missing from the manuscript codex.

Rusticus, on the contrary, replied: “Now we have recognized that you are an irreligious man, an enchanter, and a magician, since you eat in the morning, milk deer, and hang a garment from a ray of the sun—unless you make an infant speak in the name of God.”

At last, after a very long dispute, the holy man was compelled to put aside his humility for a little while and reveal his power. Turning to the infant, he said:

> “I adjure [Col. 1115C] you by Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, to confess before everyone who begot you or who gave birth to you.”

The infant, having received from the Author of all things the ability to speak, answered in perfectly clear speech:

> “My father is this Rusticus, the bishop, and my mother is that religious woman.”

Thus that obstinate bishop was exposed in his crime. He received from God’s truthful servant the counsel of repentance, and the holy priest Goar, glorified by Christ, returned to his place. Advancing from day to day in the increase of his virtues, he rested in peace.

### Nones of July

At Alexandria in Egypt, the feast of Saint Pantaenus, an apostolic man adorned with every kind of wisdom. He possessed such zeal and love for the word of God that, moved by the warmth of faith and devotion, he proceeded even to preach the Gospel of Christ to all the nations hidden in the farthest retreats of the East, and reached Nearer India by preaching.

There he found Bartholomew, one of the twelve apostles, who had preached the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ according to the Gospel of Matthew. Pantaenus brought this Gospel, written in Hebrew letters, back with him to Alexandria, and there completed his distinguished and noble life with a blessed end.

In the same place, Heraclius, Helius, Apollonius, Publius, and twenty others.

At Rome, the passion of the blessed martyrs Nicostratus, first keeper of the archives, Claudius, registrar, Castorius or Castulus, Victorinus, and Symphorianus—or, as it is contained in the Book of Sacraments, Sempronianus. We had believed that we had celebrated their feast on the sixth day before the Ides of November, until the venerable Father Ado indicated that other and different saints were to be honored in their place. Their lives will be discussed more suitably in their proper place.

Blessed Sebastian taught these men to believe in Christ, and the priest Saint Polycarp baptized them. While they were searching for the bodies of the saints along the mouths of the Tiber, they were captured and brought before Fabianus, prefect of the City. For ten days he tried by threats and flatteries to induce them to sacrifice to idols, but could not move any one of them from the firmness of faith. He therefore reported them to the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, who ordered them to be tortured. Since they yielded under no compulsion, the emperors ordered them to be thrown headlong into the sea. Bound with enormous weights, they were given to the waves of the sea, so that in a pure place amid the waters they might be deemed worthy to receive the crown of martyrdom.

### VIII Ides of July

In Asia Minor, the feast of Saint Aquila and his wife Priscilla. In the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 18) we read that blessed Paul the apostle stayed and worked with them because they shared the same trade, after they had come from the city of Rome to Achaia.

In Palestine, Saint Procopius the martyr. He was led from Scythopolis to Caesarea and, at his first confident answer, was beheaded by the enraged judge Fabianus.

At Nicaea, Sostratus the senator, Severus, and Honoratus, with many others.

At Tauromenium, Speratus and Cornelianus with sixty others.

In the district of Austria—that is, in the castle, or rather city, of New Francia, as its German name reveals, Würzburg, situated beside the river Main—the passion of Saint Kilian, the first bishop of that city, and his two disciples, namely Colonatus [Colomannus], a priest, and Totnanus, a deacon.

They came from Ireland, the island of the Scots, and, having received authority from the pontiff of the apostolic see, preached the name of Christ in that place and throughout the surrounding region. When this apostolic man was winning a great multitude for the Lord through signs and preaching, he was killed by the local duke, named Cozpertus, because he was trying to separate him from his marriage to his brother’s wife. This was done through the plotting of that exceedingly incestuous woman, Geila, together with companions inflamed by the same zeal.

Since many miracles continually occur at their memorials, their precious death was first commended to mortals by these signs. The man who killed them while they were praying in silence at night ran about here and there in madness, proclaiming himself guilty of the saints’ murder and tearing himself with his teeth, because he seemed to himself to be burned by an invisible fire from Saint Kilian. Thus he himself made his crime known.

A malignant spirit also attacked Geila, whose name itself signifies wantonness, and ended her unworthy life with a death fully deserving of it. Gozbert, however, was killed by his own servants with a sword, while his son was driven from the kingdom by the people.

To increase and manifest the holiness of the martyrs, when they were uncovered many years later for the purpose of translation, their books and all their clothing, buried together with them, were found—against the nature of that region, which is exceedingly damp—so untouched that they seemed to have been enclosed in a chest placed above ground.

### VII Ides of July

At Rome, at the ever-flowing spring called Gutta, the feast of Saint Zeno and 10,203 others.

Also Florianus and Faustus.

In the city of Tyro [Thora], not far from the city of Rome, Anatolia and Audax under the Emperor Decius. When Anatolia had healed many sick, epileptics, and demoniacs in Picenum, she was led, by order of Faustinianus, to the city of Tyri [Thorae]. She was tormented with various kinds of blows and then enclosed for an entire night with a serpent, but suffered no harm.

Indeed, she rescued from being devoured the very Marsus who had released the serpent, a man named Audax, and converted him to Christ’s martyrdom. After this, he too was placed in custody for confessing the truth and, without delay, was crowned by a capital sentence.

The virgin of Christ herself was pierced through with a sword while standing in prayer with her hands outstretched, so that the sword entered through her right side and came out through her left. She suffered on the seventh day before the Ides of July and was buried in the morning by the citizens of Tyre [Thorenses].

At Milan, the feast of Saint Mochimus [perhaps Saint Mona].

In Egypt, Cyril, bishop. Lycius the commander threw him into the flames, but he escaped unharmed. Astonished by so great a miracle, the judge released him. When Cyril again preached the word of God eagerly and converted very many more effectively to faith in Christ, the judge, filled with impiety, ordered him to be beheaded, and he completed the desired end of martyrdom.

Also in Egypt, Saint Serapion, bishop and confessor.

In the city of Martulana, Saint Brictius [Bricius], bishop and confessor. After his mouth had been crushed with a stone and he had been cruelly tortured on the rack, he remained steadfast in confessing the Lord and was thrown into prison. During the night the city was struck by a great earthquake, which, among many others, also killed Martianus. The confessor of Christ was visited by a holy angel and by blessed Peter the apostle and was strengthened to preach the Gospel. Winning great multitudes of believing peoples for almighty God, he rested in peace. Those standing by saw his soul received into heaven in the form of a snow-white dove.

### VI Ides of July

At Rome, the feast of the seven sons of Saint Felicitas: Januarius, Felix, Philip, Silvanus, Alexander, Vitalis, and Martialis. They were first brought before the prefect of the city, Publius, in the time of the Emperor Antoninus, and then sent before different judges to be torn apart by various punishments.

Januarius, after being beaten with rods and imprisoned, was killed with weighted scourges (*plumbatae*). Felix and Philip were slaughtered with cudgels. Silvanus was killed by being thrown from a height. Alexander, Vitalis, and Martialis were punished by a capital sentence. In death they were not divided from the love of Christ or from the unity of faith.

Also at Rome, at the tenth milestone, on the estate of Plautilla called Buxus, the holy sisters Rufina and Secunda, born to the distinguished father Asterius and the mother Aurelia. During the persecution of Valerian and Gallienus, under the judges Junius the prefect and Archisilaus the commander, they were beheaded at the place mentioned because they refused to accept their betrothed, who had apostatized from Christ.

In Africa, Saints Januarius, Marinus, Nabor, and Felix, beheaded for the steadfastness of the Christian faith. Their bodies were afterward transferred to Milan.

### V Ides of July

At Rome, the passion of Saints Stephen, Leontius, Mauritius, and many others.

In Africa, Marinus [Marianus] and Januarius.

In Lesser Armenia, in the city of Nicopolis, the holy martyrs Januarius and Pelagia. They were tortured on the rack, with hooks and fragments of pottery, for four days, and became martyrs.

The translation of Saint Benedict the abbot from the castle of Cassino, or Cassianus, to Gaul or Aquitaine. After, as he had foretold while alive, his monastery was devastated by the heathen, with only the persons spared, according to his saying, “I scarcely obtained from almighty God that souls should be yielded to me from this place,” they being saved through his intercession, his body was found by certain religious men through a revelation from the Lord and transferred to Gaul. It was honorably buried in the territory of Orléans, in the monastery called Fleury, and has continually been honored still more worthily by the frequent visits of the devout.

The bones of blessed Scholastica, his virgin sister, were also transferred at the same time and buried through the devotion of religious people in the region of Le Mans. The man of God had seen her soul leave the body and enter the secrets of heaven in the form of a dove. He ordered her body to be placed with his in a single tomb, so that those whose minds had always been one in God would not be separated even by burial.

But woe to the merits of the wretched, through whom those who had deserved to be joined by the arrangement of the Holy Spirit suffered separation. Yet that place, made honorable by the saints’ relics, did not long remain empty of the gathering of the faithful. The brothers who were able to escape the hands of the enemy gathered together again, were increased by others brought in to replace those who had been scattered, and, now acting with greater caution, cared for the sacred ashes with sufficient reverence, until recently they were scattered in every direction by the invasion of the Saracens.

### IV Ides of July

At Aquileia, the feast of Saint Hermagoras, or, as it is found in ancient books, Hermechoras, the first bishop of that city and disciple of Saint Mark the evangelist.

Also Fortunatus, concerning whom Bishop Fortunatus wrote:

> “And Aquileia bears her own Fortunatus.”

In Cyprus, blessed Naso [Jason], an ancient disciple of Christ.

At Rome, in the Vatican, the burial of Saint Pius, pope, who sat in the episcopate for eighteen years. During his time Hermes wrote the book called *The Shepherd*, because an angel appeared to him in the form of a shepherd.

At Milan, the translation of the holy martyrs Nabor and Felix. Beheaded in Africa with Januarius and Marinus on the sixth day before the Ides of July, they were brought to Milan on this day. Concerning them, I believe blessed Victor prayed in his passion:

> “Do not separate me, Lord, from my fellow citizens, your martyrs Nabor and Felix.”

At Lyon in Gaul, the burial of Viventiolus, bishop.

### III Ides of July

The passing of Ezra, restorer of the divine Law.

In Alexandria, Serapion, Evangelus, Zeno, and others, and Trophima the virgin.

At Rome, Saint Cletus, pope, who sat in the episcopate for twelve years. When he was chorepiscopus of blessed Peter the apostle, he ordained twenty-five priests in the city of Rome at Peter’s command. He was buried beside Peter’s body.

In Africa, the feast of the holy confessors—or rather, most victorious martyrs—Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, glorious in faith, virtues, and miracles, and the entire clergy of that Church. Nearly five hundred or more of them, worn down by slaughter and starvation, among whom were very many readers and little children, were driven out into cruel exile far away, rejoicing in the Lord.

Among them were the most distinguished archdeacons, one named Salutaris, and Mauritta, second in the office of ministers. After enduring very many punishments for the Catholic confession and becoming confessors a third time, they were illumined by the title of glorious perseverance in Christ.

At Antioch, the passion of Margaret the virgin. The consul Olibrius desired to seduce her from faith in Christ and violate her. When she refused to consent, he afflicted her with many tortures: he ordered her to be suspended on the rack and torn with exceedingly harsh hooks, and afterward thrown into a dark prison. There she overcame, in the name of the Lord Jesus, the manifold seductions of the devil, which he attempted to impose upon her in the form of a dragon and an Ethiopian. Finally beheaded, she departed to eternal rest.

### II Ides of July

In Alexandria, the feast of the holy martyrs Mammarius, Peter, and others.

In Africa, Donata.

In Pontus, Saint Phocas, or Phocatis, bishop of the city of Sinope. Under the Emperor Trajan and the prefect Africanus, he overcame prison, chains, iron, and even fire for Christ. His relics are kept in the basilica of the Apostles in Gaul, in the city of Vienne.

In Lyon of Gaul, Saint Justus, bishop and confessor, who died in the fervor of divine contemplation while living as a hermit, and was gloriously transferred to his own city, leaving behind distinguished monuments of his intellect in the *Song of Songs*.

Likewise Saint Amicus, bishop.

[Col. 1120A]

**ID. JUL.**—In the city of Nisibis, the feast of Saint James, bishop, a man of great virtue, so that through his prayers the city was often delivered from danger. He was one of the confessors under the persecution of Maximinus, and one of those who at the Council of Nicaea condemned the perversity of Arius by setting the *homoousios*—“of the same substance”—in opposition to it. At the emperor Constantine’s command, he was buried within the walls of his city as its protection and defense; later, through the zeal of Julian the Apostate, he was removed and buried outside the city. But soon that same city, deprived of the relics of so great a patron, succumbed to Persian rule. Even while still alive he performed many signs, and he alone was granted the privilege of seeing Noah’s ark on Mount Taurus in Armenia—a sight that no one else among those who had gone there with him was permitted to see.

[Col. 1120B]

At the Roman Port, Eutropius, Zosima, and Bonosa, sisters.

At Alexandria, Saints Philip, Zeno, Narseus, and ten children.

At Carthage, Saints Catulinus the deacon, Januarius, Florentius, Julia, and Justa, who are buried in the basilica of Faustus.

At Sirmium, Agrippinus, Secundus, Maximus, Fortunatus, and Martialis.

**XVII KAL. AUG.**—At Ostia, the feast of Saint Hilarinus, the most cheerful of the saints’ hosts and providers. When, during the persecution of Julian, he could not be compelled to sacrifice to idols, he was beaten with clubs and completed his martyrdom.

At Antioch of Syria, Saint Eustachius [Eustathius], [Col. 1120C] bishop and confessor, who under the emperor Constantius was driven into exile within the city of Janopolis [Trajanopolis] in Thrace on account of the Catholic faith, and there first entered his rest.

Likewise Theodosius, Dionysius, and Theodotus.

At Caesarea in Cappadocia, Saint Paul, whose deeds, as Saint Jerome himself admits, were known to him but are unknown to our slowness.

Near the same city, the passion of Saint Mammes. By divine calling he reached Mount Sinai and received a staff—not his own, but one that had fallen from heaven—for the performance of miracles. When he touched the earth with it, the Gospel immediately sprang forth. As he began to read it, every kind of wild beast became gentler than domesticated animals, so much so that nursing females willingly offered themselves to be milked. When he had pressed the milk curds into cheese, he proceeded to Caesarea of Palestine and ministered to widows, the weak, and the other poor.

When the Jews of Jerusalem saw this—envious of every good thing—they reported him to the governor of Cappadocia as a man instructed in magical arts. Alexander the tyrant had been sent to administer those regions. When he dispatched a military unit to bring Mammes before him, the holy Mammes, out of charity, fed the very men who had been sent to arrest him and afterward read the Gospel to them. Then such a great gathering of wild beasts and animals took place that the soldiers thought they would have no means of escape. The most kindly man comforted them gently, sent them ahead of him, and ordered the fiercest lion to follow him to the theater. The soldiers followed immediately after him.

[Col. 1121A]

They handed him over to the governor. The governor cruelly interrogated him, and even more cruelly tore him with claws while he was stretched upon the rack; then he sent him to prison. There Mammes found forty others endangered by hunger and thirst. He restored them with honey and milk brought to him from heaven by a dove, and invisibly released them through the keys of his merits, while he alone remained in the prison. He was again brought before the governor.

The governor sent him into a furnace of fire. After five days he was found unharmed among choirs of angels. He was then exposed to a bear of extraordinary ferocity. It rushed forward with great force to tear him apart, but by divine command it suddenly fell back and crouched down, as though accusing itself of its own audacity. A leopard was also brought against him, but it obeyed him rather than injuring him.

Then the governor, filled with anger, ordered a most savage lion to be brought for his devouring. And behold, that Arabian lion, enraged and rushing into the theater at such speed, had been tamed by the constant reading of the Gospel. It addressed blessed Mammes in these words:

“Greetings, tested worshiper of God, in whom the Holy Spirit has built for himself a delightful dwelling. Behold, by angelic command I have received a voice for a time. Your faith has surpassed the laws of nature; for your sake, a human voice is granted to mute animals. I return service to the shepherd; I remember whom we obeyed on the mountain.”

As it spoke, the angels shut the doors of the theater. Immediately, roaring with dreadful jaws, it raged indiscriminately through all the crowd. Some the lion [f. *leo*] deliberately tore; others it seized in its mouth; some it crushed in its embrace; others it shattered with its claws; and some it consumed by terror alone.

[Col. 1121C]

After all the pagans and Jews had been killed, Mammes ordered that the governor and his officers be spared. But the governor, repaying a kindness with injury, ordered the lion to be released, in which he believed all hope of victory lay. When the beast came nearer, however, it licked the saint’s footprints, begged pardon, and rolled at his knees.

Then the entire crowd tried to overwhelm it with stones, but in vain, for the blows flew about from every direction and did not injure the martyr. Thus he departed unharmed, paying his vows to God.

And behold, a voice fell from heaven, saying:

“Ascend, Mammes; heaven is open to you, and all the gates of paradise have been unlocked. Now the Lord rejoices over you, rewarding you with prizes [Col. 1121D] for your triumphs. Now Christ awaits you with a crown. Hurry, with the Holy Spirit who guides you.”

Having heard these words, the most victorious martyr joyfully prayed and then rested in peace.

**XVI KAL. AUG.**—At Carthage, the feast of the holy martyrs of Scilla, namely Speratus, Martialis or Narthalis, Aquilinus, Cythinus, Beturius, Felix, Lactantius [Letarius] or Lactatius, Januaria, Generosa, Bessia, Donata, and Secunda. They were brought from their city of Scilla to Carthage under the governor Saturninus. After their first confession of Christ, they were sent to prison and fastened to a wooden stake; in the morning they were beheaded with the sword. Their relics, together with the bones of blessed Cyprian and the head of Saint Pantaleon, were transferred from Africa to Gaul and are venerated at Lyon in the basilica of Saint John the Baptist.

At Milan, Saint Marcellus.

At Auxerre, the burial of blessed Theodosius, bishop.

**XV KAL. AUG.**—At Rome, on the Tiburtine Way, at the eighth milestone, the feast of Saint Symphorosa the martyr and her seven sons, who is buried with them. The names of the sons are Peter, Marcellian, Januarius, Dionysius, Symphronius, Clement, and Hireneus.

[Note: [Col. 1121] Their names are given differently in the Roman martyrology.]

At Carthage, the feast of Saint Gudena [Gundenis]. Under the consulship of Plutius [Plancianus] and Rhetus [Geta], by order of the proconsul Rufinus, she was tortured at four different times by being stretched upon the rack and by the dreadful tearing of claws; she was also afflicted for a very long time by the filth of prison, and finally was struck down with the sword.

At the city of Metz, the burial of Saint Arnulf, bishop, illustrious for holiness and the grace of miracles. Even as a bishop he cherished the eremitical life, and he rested in a blessed death.

**XIV KAL. AUG.**—In Spain, the feast of Saint Justus. And in the city of Seville, Saints Justa and Rufina, who were arrested by the governor Diogenianus, tortured by stretching on the rack and by the tearing of claws, and then thrust into prison, where they were afflicted by hunger and pain. After this the governor ordered them to follow him barefoot wherever he went. At last Justa breathed out her spirit in prison.

[Col. 1122C]

Her body was thrown into a well and lifted out by Bishop Sabinus; it was buried in the cemetery at Seville. Rufina’s neck was broken, and her body was given to the fire; the faithful cared for her relics.

In Egypt, our father Arsenius. Concerning him it is reported in the *Sayings of the Elders* that, because of the abundance of his tears, he always kept a handkerchief in his bosom or in his hand for wiping them.

At Alexandria, Saint Sisinnius.

At Antioch, Lucian and his companions.

At Constantinople, Daria.

In Spain, Justus.

At Lyon in Gaul, the burial of Saint Rusticus, priest and confessor.

[Col. 1122D]

In Italy, in the city of Tyre, according to some accounts, the feast of Saint Christina, virgin.

**XIII KAL. AUG.**—The feast of blessed Joseph, who was surnamed Justus and who was appointed by the apostles, together with blessed Matthias, to complete the number twelve. But when Matthias filled the place of Judas the traitor, blessed Joseph nevertheless continued to serve in preaching and holiness, enduring many persecutions from the Jews on account of the faith of Christ, and he rested in Judaea with a most victorious end. It is reported of him that he drank poison and suffered no harm from it because of his faith in Christ.

At Damascus, the feast of Saints Sabinus, Maximus, [Col. 1123A] Julian, Macrobius, Cassius [Cassia], and Paula, with ten others.

At Corinth, Cyriacus with many others.

At Rome, Saints Passeria, Macrinus, Saturus, and Aemilius.

**XII KAL. AUG.**—The burial of Saint Daniel the prophet.

At Rome, Saint Praxedes, virgin. She and her sister, blessed Potentiana or Pudentiana, were instructed in all chastity and divine law by their most holy father Pudens, who had been taught the faith by blessed Paul the apostle. After their father’s death, she devoted herself continually to vigils, prayers, and fasts, and together with her blessed sister distributed all their patrimony for the support of the poor and the saints of Christ.

At the church [Col. 1123B] that their father Pudens had dedicated in the name of blessed Pastor, the sisters also undertook, with the counsel of blessed Pius, bishop of the holy and apostolic see, to construct a baptismal font, so that their household might be baptized on the holy day of Easter. Blessed Pius washed ninety-six freed persons in the saving waters. After countless works of mercy and the burial of many martyrs, that most blessed virgin departed to the Lord, destined to receive the crown of righteousness from the just Judge. She was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way, beside her sister and their father Pudens.

In Gaul, in the city of Marseille, the feast of Saint Victor. He was a soldier under the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian. Because he was unwilling either to serve as a soldier or to sacrifice to idols, he was first thrust into prison by his tribune, Austerius; but every night an angel led him out to visit and console the sick.
