Then, by order of the prefect Eutychius, his arms were twisted backward and bound with thin straps, his feet were tied with a rope, and he was dragged through the middle of the city. After this he was beaten most cruelly with clubs and suspended, and tortured with leather thongs. When they brought out an altar on which he was to sacrifice, he could not even bear to look at it and kicked it from the priest’s hand. Therefore the governor ordered that his foot be cut off.

Finally, because he remained steadfast in confessing Christ, he was sent into a mill used for grinding grain, in which scattered grain is ordinarily ground by the turning of an animal; thus mangled, he completed his martyrdom. Three soldiers suffered with him: Alexander, Felicianus, and Longinus. The boy Deuterius also breathed out his spirit while praying at his tomb.

In the city of Cesena, the feast of Saints Adrian, Helius, Victor, Patroclus, and others.

At Verona, the translation of Saint Zeno the martyr. Blessed Pope Gregory recalls his holiness, saying that when the river Adige rose as far as the upper windows of the church in which his venerable body rested, although the doors stood open, the water did not enter that church, yet it did not deny its draught to those within.

**XI KAL. AUG.**—The feast of Saint Mary Magdalene, concerning whom, as the evangelists report (Mark XVI, Luke XVIII), the Lord cast out seven demons. She also, among other distinguished gifts, was worthy to be the first to see Christ risen from the dead and to preach him to the apostles.

The burial of Saint Syntyche, who lies buried at Philippi. Concerning her the blessed Apostle writes to the Philippians: “I urge Euodia, and I entreat Syntyche, to be of the same mind in the Lord” (Philippians IV).

At Antioch, Cyril the bishop, Andrew, and Actebellus.

At Ancyra in Galatia, Saint Plato.

**X KAL. AUG.**—At Ravenna, the feast of Saint Apollinaris, bishop and martyr. Ordained at Rome by blessed Peter the apostle, he was sent there. In Aemilia, in the regions of Corinth, in Mysia, on the banks of the Danube, and in the regions of Thrace—places to which he was banished into exile—he boldly proclaimed the Gospel [Col. 1124B] of Christ. Wherever he went, he displayed countless wonders and endured many sufferings.

He was frequently and for a long time subjected to extreme slaughter, placed barefoot upon burning coals, suspended upon the rack, and tortured most cruelly. His mouth was crushed with a stone; he was confined in a dreadful prison with a very heavy weight of iron and stretched upon a wooden frame. There he was neglected by human beings but publicly fed by an angel. Then he was chained and thrust into exile; there again he was beaten and wounded with clubs, and once more sent to prison and beaten. Thus he completed his martyrdom under Caesar Vespasian and the patrician Demosthenes. He governed the Church for twenty-eight years, one month, and four days.

[Col. 1124C]

At Rome, on the Tiburtine Way, at the eighteenth milestone, the feast of Saint Vincent.

On the Acula Way, Saint Primitive.

At Laodicea in Phrygia, Miniseus and Isicius.

**IX KAL. AUG.**—At Rome, the feast of Saint Victorinus.

In the city of Amiternum, eighty-three soldiers.

In Tuscia, near the city of Tyre, which lies beside Lake Bolsena, the passion of Saint Christina, virgin. While still a very young girl, strengthened by the faith and grace of Christ, she smashed the golden gods of her father Urbanus, the prefect, and distributed them to the poor. For this reason, at her father’s command, she was struck in the face, torn by scourging, loaded with iron, and thrown into prison.

After this, when she had been torn most cruelly for a very long time, she threw pieces of her own flesh into her father’s face. When she was bound to a wheel with fire placed beneath it and oil poured over it, the bursting flame killed a thousand pagans. She was again handed over to prison, where an angel visited, healed, and restored her.

Then, when she was thrown into the sea with a great weight of stone, she was delivered by angelic protection. Dion, her father’s successor, afflicted her again with many tortures; but when she prayed, the statue of Apollo, whom she had been ordered to worship, was suddenly reduced to ashes. Through this miracle three thousand people were converted to the faith of Christ.

Finally, after the successor of Dion, Julian, had subjected her to a glowing furnace in which she remained unharmed for five days, and after serpents sent by a sorcerer had been overcome by her faith in Christ, and after her tongue had been cut out, he ordered her to be pierced with arrows. Thus the blessed virgin completed the course of her martyrdom in the tenth year of her age.

At Emerita, a city of Spain, Saint Victor the soldier, who completed his martyrdom after being subjected to various tortures together with his two brothers, Stercatius and Antinogenes.

On the same day, the feast of Saints Nicea [Niceta] and Aquilina. Converted to Christ through the preaching of blessed Christopher the martyr, they received the palm of martyrdom by beheading.

**VIII KAL. AUG.**—The feast of blessed James the apostle, son of Zebedee and brother of John the evangelist. By order of King Herod he was beheaded at Jerusalem, as the book of the Acts of the Apostles teaches (chapter XII). The most sacred bones of this blessed [Col. 1125B] apostle were transferred to Spain and buried at its farthest limits, namely opposite the British Sea; they are honored with the most celebrated veneration of those peoples. Not without reason, for those peoples are said to have been converted to the faith of Christ through his bodily presence, teaching, and miraculous power. For the confirmation of their faith, the most blessed apostle Paul also promises that he will go to them.

In the province of Lycia, in the city of Samone, the feast of Saint Christopher. He was crushed with iron rods and saved by the power of Christ from raging flames; finally, pierced by blows of arrows, he completed his martyrdom by decapitation.

In the Spanish city of Barcelona, Saint Cucufas [Col. 1125C] the martyr, who was originally from the city of Scilla but suffered at Barcelona under the proconsul Galerius and under Maximian and Rufinus. First he was tortured and beaten most severely; then, bound with chains, he was stretched upon a grating, covered with vinegar and mustard, and ordered to be roasted.

When he appeared unharmed by the fire and the balls of flame, he was led outside the city by order of the impious judge and thrown again into a great fire. When it was extinguished by divine command, he was again bound with iron and thrust back into custody. There, consoled by divine radiance, he was again beaten most cruelly with iron thorns and leather thongs, and finally completed his martyrdom by the sword.

His body was buried there by Christians at that time, but afterward transferred from there and buried not far from the city of Paris, in the church of the blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius. It has been honored there with every mark of respect down to these times of the Normans.

At Rome, Pope Eutychianus and martyr. He decreed that produce placed upon the altar—namely, only beans and grapes—should be blessed. During his lifetime he personally buried 341 martyrs in various places. He also decreed that no member of the faithful should bury a martyr without a dalmatic or purple colobium, until the matter had been made known to him.

**VII KAL. AUG.**—The feast of blessed Erastus, whom blessed Paul left as bishop at Philippi; he was crowned there with martyrdom and entered his rest.

[Col. 1126A]

At the Roman Port, Hyacinthus, under the consul Leontius, when Luxurius, the first citizen of Terracina, handed him over. He was sent into the fire but could not be harmed in any way. From there he was thrown into a very powerful torrent and cast out unharmed upon the bank. When this was reported to Leontius, he sent an executioner with soldiers to strike him with the sword. Then a matron named Julia gathered his body and buried it honorably on her estate.

At Laodicea in Phrygia, Jovianus, Julian, Aemilius, Felix, Martian, Maxima, Saturninus, and Gloriosa.

**VI KAL. AUG.**—At Nicomedia, the feast of blessed Hermolaus the presbyter, whose teaching converted blessed Pantaleon to the faith of Christ. This most holy presbyter was arrested by Maximian and punished with a capital sentence for confessing Christ.

[Col. 1126B]

Likewise there, the passion of Saints Julia, Jocunda, and Januarius.

In Sicily, Simeon the monk.

In the city of Nola, Saint Felix, concerning the episcopal ordination, where many wonders take place.

At Auxerre, the burial of Saint Aetherius, bishop.

**V KAL. AUG.**—At Laodicea in Phrygia, the feast of Saints Auxentius, Prudentius, Theophilus, Philip, Alexander, Zoticus, Byssia, Secunda, and Macarius.

At Nicomedia, Saint Pantaleon, a boy. While learning the medical art at the command of Maximian, he was converted to the faith of Christ by the presbyter Hermolaus. He performed many miracles and brought his father Eustorgius, a senator, under the faith of Christ. For this reason Maximian subjected him to the torture of the rack and the burning of lamps; but in the midst of these torments the Lord appeared to him and gave him relief. At last, by a stroke of the sword, he completed the course of his martyrdom.

At Milan, the feast of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, and Nazarius and Celsus the boy.

At Lyon, Peregrinus, whose blessedness is attested by the glory of his miracles.

At Rome, Pope Victor and martyr. He decreed that whenever necessity arose in the Catholic Church, anyone from paganism hastening to the faith of Christ, after first making confession of the true faith, might be lawfully baptized either in a font, a river, or the sea.

Likewise Pope Innocent. He issued decrees concerning the whole Church, the rules of monasteries, Jews, and pagans. He found many Cataphrygians, whom he relegated into exile in monasteries; he also discovered the heretics Pelagius and Coelestinus and condemned them. He decreed that those born of a Christian should be born again through baptism, which Pelagius condemned.

At Milan, the commemoration of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, Nazarius and Celsus the boy.

**IV KAL. AUG.**—At Rome, on the Aurelian Way, the feast of Saint Felix, pope, under Constantius, son of Constantine. The emperor Constantius, approving the council of the heretics and of the Arians Valens and Ursacius—for he himself was also an Arian and had been rebaptized by Eusebius of Nicomedia—expelled Saint Felix, the bishop of the city, from his episcopal see. A great persecution then arose against the clergy, so that many priests and clerics were killed and crowned with martyrdom.

After blessed Pope Felix had been deposed, he lived on his small estate, which was on the Portuensian Way. Later, through the actions of the heretics, he was brought into the city and crowned with martyrdom by beheading.

On the same day, the feast of the holy martyrs Simplicius, Faustinus, and Beatrice, during the time of Diocletian and Maximian. After many and various tortures, they were ordered to undergo a capital sentence. A stone was tied around their necks, and they were thrown from the bridge commonly called the Stone Bridge, but called the Lepidian Bridge by more discerning people, into the currents of the Tiber.

Their bodies, found by God’s command, were lifted by their blessed sister Beatrice and the most blessed presbyters Crispus and John, and buried in a place called the Sixth of Philippus, on the Portuensian Way. When Lucretius, a neighboring landowner, learned this, he had Saint Beatrice suffocated at night and, as though no one now remained to hinder him, seized the saints’ properties.

While a certain woman was nursing her little son, the infant, as Lucretius was feasting with his accomplices, uttered these words:

“Hear, Lucretius: you have killed and seized, and behold, you have been given over into the possession of the enemy.”

At these words Lucretius was attacked by an evil spirit there at the banquet and tormented for three hours. He breathed out his spirit and gained everlasting death.

The burial of blessed Lupus, bishop of Troyes. He came to Britain with blessed Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, and after exercising the priesthood there for fifty years, he ascended to Christ, whom he had always loved, victorious over the world and the devil. Among his other miracles, during the time of King Attila, who was devastating Gaul most cruelly, it is sung in his hymn:

“While all wars were destroying everything, by prayer he fortified Troyes.”

At Orléans, Prosper, bishop, a most holy and learned man. He wrote much for the benefit of the Church and took particular care to defend the grace of God against the arrogance of heretics.

**III KAL. AUG.**—At Rome, in the cemetery of Pontianus, at the Bear with the Cap, the feast of Saints Abdon and Sennen. Decius captured them in the Persian city of Cordula, bound them with chains, and had them brought to Rome. Adorned with gold and precious stones, they were presented to Decius and the senate in the temple of Intelludis [probably Tellus], and became a spectacle to the entire Roman people, because they were nobles and subordinate kings and, moreover, divinely enlightened by the Lord Jesus Christ.

Then Decius, moved by anger, ordered the prefect Valerian that, if they would not worship the god Sun, they should perish by the bites of wild beasts. Valerian seized them and led them before the statue of the Sun near the amphitheater, so that they might sacrifice. But when they despised it and spat upon the statue of the Sun, Valerian ordered them to be beaten with leaded clubs.

Then, after they had been brought into the amphitheater, two lions and four bears were let loose against them. Roaring, the animals came to the feet of the saints and did not injure them in any way; rather, they guarded them. Valerian, however, filled with fury, ordered gladiators to enter, kill the blessed subordinate kings, bind their feet, and throw them before the statue of the Sun.

[Col. 1128A]

Their bodies lay there for three days. After three days a subdeacon named Quirinus came, gathered their bodies by night, and hid them in a leaden coffin in his own house on the third day before the Kalends of August. They remained hidden there until the time of Constantine. Then the blessed martyrs revealed themselves, were lifted up, and transferred to the cemetery of blessed Pontianus.

In Africa, in the city of Tyburbolucernaria, the feast of the holy virgins Maxima, Donatilla, and Secunda. They suffered during the persecution of Gallienus under the judge Anulinus. He tried to compel them to deny Christ through prolonged hunger and thirst; but when he found them contemptuous and scornful, he ordered them to drink vinegar and gall.

[Col. 1128B]

Then, when they were beaten most cruelly in his presence, he ordered lime to be scattered over their wounds and rubbed in. Afterward he ordered them to be stretched and tortured on the rack, and a *stativa*—thus in the manuscript—to be offered to them for drinking; then to be laid upon a grating over glowing coals, and burning embers to be brought over the hair of their heads. Later they were placed in the theater for mockery and trampled by everyone.

When he saw that they were invincible in every respect, he condemned them to the beasts. Bound with iron, he again ordered them to be brought into the theater for the people’s spectacle. As they were being led into the middle of the arena, they kissed one another so that they might complete their martyrdom in peace.

A most savage and ferocious bear was brought against them, but it was changed into gentleness and began to lick their feet. Then Anulinus, filled with fury, ordered the holy [Col. 1128C] martyrs of God to be put to death by the sword.

Likewise in Africa, Rufus, Priscus, Paterna, Septima, Optio, Ammonius, Justus, Julia, Potamia, and also Maxima.

At Auxerre, the burial of blessed Ursus, bishop.

**II KAL. AUG.**—At Caesarea, the passion of Saint Fabius the martyr. When he refused to carry the governor’s standards, he was first thrust into prison for several days. Then he was brought out and made to stand before the tribunal. Questioned once and again, he persisted in confessing Christ; immediately the frenzied judge condemned him to death.

Even burial was denied to his beheaded corpse for three days while it was kept under guard. Later, his body was enclosed in a net and submerged separately in the depths of the sea, with his head likewise submerged separately. But by the Lord’s power the net was torn apart, the limbs were brought back to the head, and the neck was joined to the shoulders, bearing the marks of the passion. Thus restored to its wholeness, the body was carried by a gentler wave to the shore of Cartenna and buried by the faithful in a basilica with fitting honor.

In Africa, in the city of Sinnada, the feast of the holy martyrs Democritus, Secunda, Dionysius, and Thyrsus.

At Auxerre, the burial of Saint Germanus, bishop and confessor, distinguished by many virtues, learning, and continence. He defended the faith of the Britons against the Pelagian heresy on two occasions. His feast, however, is celebrated more solemnly among the Gallican Churches on the Kalends of October.

**AUGUST.** August has thirty-one days; the lunar month has twenty-nine.

[Col. 1129A]

**KAL. AUG.**—At Antioch of Syria, the feast of the seven Maccabean brothers with their mother. As blessed Augustine says, “Before the time of revealed grace, tested by manifold suffering, they were found faithful. Their most savage persecutor, Antiochus, the forerunner of the Antichrist, expelled them from their homeland and, envious and ignorant, made the Gentile land holy through the shedding of their sacred blood.”

At Rome, a station at Saint Peter in Chains. He himself first built and consecrated this church, the first in Europe. The chains with which he was bound at Jerusalem and from which he was freed by an angelic visitation were later placed there through the care of the faithful; they are sought out and venerated by the devotion of the four quarters of the world, as an ancient distich also bears witness concerning them.

In Arabia, in the city of Philadelphia, a gathering of martyrs is celebrated.

There also, the feast of the holy martyrs Cyril, Aquila, Peter, Domitian, Rufus, and Menander, crowned together on one day.

In Italy, in the city of Vercelli, Saint Eusebius, bishop and confessor. Because of his confession of the Catholic faith, he was banished by the emperor Constantius to Scythopolis in Arabia and then to Cappadocia. Under the emperor Julian he returned to his Church. Finally, when the Arians were persecuting him, he suffered martyrdom by being dragged down a staircase, but was saved by Jesus Christ the Savior. He completed his confession in the peace of the Church, after a vision had first revealed to him that on the Kalends of August he would fly from mountain to mountain.

The Fathers interpret this to mean that, having confessed on earth the humanity of Christ—who for our sake was made man, true God—he would reach in heaven the vision of God the Father, lifted up by the grace of the Holy Spirit, on those same Kalends.

In Spain, in the city of Girona, Saint Felix the martyr. Originally from the city of Scilla, when he learned that persecutions were being carried out against Christians in Spain, he boarded a merchant ship and hurried there out of love for martyrdom.

After preaching the word of God for some time at Barcelona, Emporiae, and Girona, and strengthening many in the faith of Christ, his fame spread far and wide. At the command of Datianus, he was suddenly arrested by the official Rufinus. When he most steadfastly confessed the name of Christ, he was first beaten with clubs and thrust into the deepest part of the prison; then, with hands and feet bound and food and drink denied him, he was thrown into a filthy place.

After this he was bound with heavier chains, dragged through all the streets by untamed mules, and almost torn to pieces. Then he was sent to prison, where an angel visited him by night, released him, and healed him. When day came, he was summoned again to the contests.

His skin was then torn with claws, and he was suspended upside down from the third hour until evening, yet he felt no pain at all. Afterward Rufinus ordered him returned to prison. There, throughout the entire night, a great radiance shone, and the voices of angels singing psalms were heard.

When the guards reported this to Rufinus, he ordered Felix to be submerged in the depths of the sea with his hands bound behind his back. Immediately his bonds broke, and, with angels holding his hand, he walked over the waves and came to shore.

Then Rufinus ordered his skin to be stripped away again with claws and afterward his flesh to be torn down to the bones, and the wounds to be renewed with further wounds until he gave his unconquered spirit back to Christ. His body was buried at Girona in the tomb that he had prepared for himself, on the Nones of August.

In Gaul, in the city of Bourges, the burial of blessed Arcadius, bishop.

**IV NON. AUG.**—At Rome, in the cemetery of Callixtus, [Col. 1130B] the feast of Saint Stephen, pope and martyr, under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus. He decreed that priests and deacons should not use sacred vestments in daily life, but only in the church.

When a savage persecution was raging, he gathered all his clergy and exhorted them to receive the crown of martyrdom for Christ with eagerness. He had ordained three priests, seven deacons, and sixteen clerics, with whom he continually taught concerning the kingdom of God.

By divine grace, many pagans also came to him, including honorable men seeking baptism. Among them were the tribune Nemesius with his entire household and his daughter Lucilla, who was blind but had been given sight through blessed Stephen; and another tribune, Olympius, with his wife Exuperia, his son Theodulus, and many others. These later obtained the palm of martyrdom through a glorious confession.

Blessed Stephen celebrated Masses and councils in the crypts of the martyrs. Valerian and Gallienus, having sought him with the greatest determination, had him seized by soldiers together with a crowd of clerics, priests, and deacons.

When he came before Valerian’s tribunal, he entered alone. Condemned to death, he was led by the soldiers outside the walls, through the Appian Gate, to the temple of Mars, so that he might either worship the statue of Mars or perish.

While blessed Stephen prayed to his God, a crash of thunder accompanied by terrifying flashes of lightning occurred, and most of the sacrilegious temple collapsed. The soldiers, struck with fear, fled. Stephen himself went with all the Christians to the cemetery of Saint Lucina [Col. 1130D], consoled them with many words, and offered sacrifice to almighty God on their behalf.

When Valerian heard what had happened, he sent many soldiers to punish blessed Stephen. They arrived and found him offering sacrifice to God. While he remained fearless and steadfast before the altar and was completing the rites he had begun, they beheaded him in that same place, in his own seat.

At Antioch, the feast of the relics of Saint Stephen, the protomartyr of Christ and the first deacon in the Church. It is said that one of the stones with which he was struck during his passion is kept there, and that many healings are performed through it.

On the same day, the passion of Saint Theodota with her three sons, in the province of Bithynia, in the city of Nicaea, during the time of Diocletian and under the count Leucadius. He bound her with iron and sent her, together with her sons, to Nicetius, the governor of Bithynia.

Nicetius ordered her firstborn son, Evodius, who was boldly confessing Christ, to be beaten with clubs in his mother’s presence. When the devout mother did not cease strengthening her son with holy exhortations, Nicetius ordered a certain Hirtacus first to violate her and then to place her among public prostitutes. Hirtacus tried to seize her, but an angel of God struck him on the nose with his fist; endangered by a great flow of blood, he withdrew from her.

Then the governor Nicetius, inflamed with overwhelming fury, ordered a great fire to be kindled and blessed Theodota with her three sons to be thrown into it. Thus, having completed her confession of Christ, she departed to heaven.

In Italy, in the city of Verona, the feast of Saints Felix and Nicetius.

### 3 August

**III Non. Aug.** — At Jerusalem, the discovery—or rather, the seizure—of the body of Saint Stephen, Christ’s protomartyr. When he had been stoned by the Jews and for some time kept under guard lest Christians bury him, he was finally removed through the compassion of the blessed Gamaliel, and was buried and mourned in Gamaliel’s estate, as Gamaliel himself explained when he appeared in a divine vision, in the seventh year of the reign of Honorius, to a certain presbyter named Lucian. Saint Luke also briefly indicated this, saying (Acts 8): “Devout men took care of Stephen and made great mourning over him.” We shall, with God’s permission, explain the sequence of this vision more suitably at its proper time—that is, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, when his sacred body was revealed and transferred to Jerusalem, with his life as our guide. Some people, reading this revelation less carefully, think that it occurred at this time, although it is proved to have begun around the beginning of December and, without doubt, to have been completed near the end of that same month, so that the celebration of Christ’s protomartyr might be placed immediately before the nativity of Jesus Christ.

At Rome, the nativity of the holy martyrs Diogenes and Stephen.

At Constantinople, Saint Achillas.

At Augustodunum, the burial of Saint Euphronius, bishop.

**II Non. Aug.** — The feast of Saint Aristarchus, about whom the apostle Paul writes to the Colossians: “Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you” (Colossians 4). Since I have learned that interpreters of the divine Scriptures have gone so far astray concerning this imprisonment that some have thought souls to have been taken captive from heaven and condemned to bodies, while others, with a pious meaning indeed but one quite out of keeping with the historical account, have understood the matter in this way—that the blessed Apostle called Aristarchus his fellow prisoner because he alone almost shared with him, and grieved in sharing, the captivity that we all endure—I shall pass on to those who come after me without envy what I freely received from those before me:

When the Jews had undertaken a rebellion against the Romans, the Romans, as was their usual practice, pretending to disregard the offense and meanwhile sparing Judea, devastated Basanitis and Galilee, or Galaaditis, and, invading Giscala, the homeland of the blessed Paul and Aristarchus, transported the boys themselves with their parents into Cilicia. Thus the same Apostle, recognizing himself truly and in many ways as an exile, continually sighed with the holy Fathers for the Jerusalem above, but also frequently visited the earthly Jerusalem for the sake of learning, as we indicated above.

At Rome, in the sand quarry, the blessed martyr Tertullinus, whom the blessed Pope Stephen baptized and ordained presbyter while he was still wearing the white baptismal garment. Two days after his ordination, he was arrested by the prefect Marcus and brought before the emperor Valerian, who ordered him stretched out and beaten with clubs. While he gave thanks to Christ amid the blows, Valerian ordered fire to be placed against his sides. When he continued joyfully and steadfastly, he ordered him lifted up and handed over to the prefect Sapricius. Sapricius first ordered his mouth to be smashed with stones; then, stretched out on the rack, to be tortured for a long time with sinews; and afterward to be roasted in fire. When he continued steadfastly, strengthened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, confessing Christ the Lord, Sapricius reported this deed to the tyrant Valerian. Valerian replied that his head should be cut off. Then Sapricius ordered him removed from the rack and taken along the Lavican Way, at the second milestone, where he was beheaded. The holy Pope Stephen gathered his body with the clergy, and, after hymns had been offered to God, buried it in the same place, in the sand quarry.

Likewise at Rome, on the Tiburtine Way, Crescentianus and Justus.

Likewise Justin the presbyter, of whom it is related in the Passion of Saint Lawrence that he converted many to the faith of Christ and buried the bodies of many martyrs.

At Lyon in Gaul, the arrival of the body of Saint Justus, bishop, from the desert.

**Non. Aug.** — In Gaul, in the city of Châlons, the burial of Saint Memmius, bishop and confessor. It is said of him that, ordained bishop by the blessed apostle Peter, he was sent into Gaul together with Saint Dionysius and Eucherius to preach the word of God. After completing an admirable life and displaying many miracles, he passed into eternal life.

At Rome, Pope Hormisdas, who sat for seventeen years, organized the clergy, and instructed them in the psalms; he was buried in the church of Saint Peter.

In Augusta Euphratensis, the nativity of Saint Afrus, martyr. Because of the similarity of the names—namely, Augusta and Afrus—our countrymen, misled by this, have thought that on this day the passion of Saint Afra was completed at Augusta Raetia, or Vindelica. We shall speak of her later, God willing.

At Augustodunum, the burial of Saint Cassianus, bishop.

Elsewhere, the nativity of Saints Florianus and Caelestinus.

**VIII Id. Aug.** — At Rome, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Callistus, the nativity of Saint Sixtus, bishop and martyr.

Likewise, in the cemetery of Praetextatus, Felicissimus and Agapitus, deacons, under the emperor Decius and the prefect Valerianus. Valerianus seized the most blessed old man, Saint Sixtus, bishop of Rome, with all his clergy, shut him in public custody, and kept them there for many days. Later Decius ordered the blessed Sixtus, with the two deacons Felicissimus and Agapitus, to be brought before him in the temple of Intelludus [Note: [Col. 1133] Above also, on the third day before the Kalends of August, he used this word.], and, because they refused to sacrifice to idols, to be confined in private custody. When they were brought before Decius and Valerianus again, at Valerianus’s suggestion Decius ordered them taken to the temple of Mars; if they refused to sacrifice, they were to be beheaded in that same place.

When they had been brought there, the blessed Sixtus said to the temple of Mars: “May Christ, the Son of the living God, destroy you.” When all the Christians had answered, “Amen,” part of the temple suddenly collapsed and was shattered. Then the blessed Lawrence began to cry out, saying: “Do not abandon me, holy Father, for I have already spent the treasures that you entrusted to me.” The soldiers who had brought them, hearing about treasures, seized the blessed Lawrence, the archdeacon, while they took Saint Sixtus, Felicissimus, and Agapitus to the slope of Mars and beheaded them there.

During the night the clergy and a very large part of the Christians came, gathered the bodies of the saints, and buried them honorably in the places named above. Four others were beheaded with them—Januarius, Magnus, Vincentius, and Stephen, subdeacons—as is read in the Pontifical Acts. Saint Quartus also suffered with them, as the great teacher Cyprian writes.

The blessed Sixtus was born and educated at Athens. He was first a philosopher, but afterward became a disciple of Christ. He occupied the episcopal see for one year, ten months, and thirty-three days.

Likewise at Rome, one hundred and sixty-five soldiers, and the passion of Saint Afra, virgin.

On the same day, in Spain, in the city of Complutum, Justus and Pastor, brothers. While they were still being instructed in letters, they threw down their writing tablets at school and voluntarily ran to martyrdom. They were immediately ordered to be seized by the count Datianus. While they strengthened one another with the greatest steadfastness through mutual exhortation, they were led outside the city and slaughtered by the executioners in the Field of Laudable.

**VII Id. Aug.** — At Rome, the passion of twenty-five holy martyrs.

Likewise, the holy martyrs Peter and Juliana [Julianus], with eighteen others.

In Tuscany, in the city of Arezzo, the nativity of Saint Donatus, bishop and martyr. He was brought up by the priest Saint Pigmentus at the title of Saint Pastor and was very thoroughly instructed not only in divine learning but also in secular literature. Julianus grew up with him and was ordained subdeacon; afterward, rejecting his rank, he became a worthless apostate and aspired to imperial power. At that time he committed the blessed Pigmentus to custody at Rome and killed Donatus’s holy father and mother with the sword.

Donatus, who was a lector, fled to the city of Arelium and lived with Hilarinus, a most devout monk, serving the Lord continually with prayers and fasts. It happened that a woman named Suranna, a gentile and pagan, whose eyes were diseased and who was truly blind, came with her only son, named Herculius, seeking the cell of the blessed Hilarinus, with whom the holy man lived. Hilarinus and Donatus instructed her in the faith of Christ and brought her to the blessed Bishop Satyrus. He accepted her faith, gave thanks to God, imposed a fast upon her, and ordered her to humble herself in haircloth and ashes. Then he catechized and baptized her, as well as her son. Immediately Suranna’s eyes were opened.

When Apronianus heard what had happened, he also brought his demoniac son to the blessed Donatus. As Donatus prayed together with the blessed Bishop Satyrus and the blessed Hilarinus, the demon was expelled, and he left the boy sound.

Not long afterward, a certain man named Eustasius, governor of Tuscany and collector of the treasury, was detained somewhere on business when enemies suddenly arrived. His wife, Euphrosyna, hid the treasury money, and after a few days, while her husband was still absent, she died. When her husband returned and was summoned to account for the treasury money, he came to the blessed Satyrus and Donatus and told them of his distress.

Donatus then stood over her grave and cried out in a loud voice: “Euphrosyna, by Christ crucified I adjure you to tell us what became of the treasury money, because your husband is being greatly afflicted by the collectors on account of it.” She immediately replied from the grave: “The money you seek lies buried at the entrance of the house.” The money was recovered, and Eustasius was freed from the charge brought against him.

After the blessed Satyrus had been received among his fathers, the blessed Donatus assumed the priesthood in his place. One day, after he had celebrated Mass for the people, while the people were being reverently refreshed by the body and blood of Christ, a deacon named Anthimus was distributing the sacred blood of Christ. Suddenly, pushed by pagans, he fell and shattered the holy chalice. Both he and Christ’s people became very sorrowful.

The Lord immediately relieved this sorrow through the blessed Donatus. The fragments of the Lord’s chalice were gathered and brought to the holy man. Weeping, he received them, and after praying, restored the vessel to its original form. Struck by this sign, the pagans confessed Christ’s divinity together with the Christians, and about seventy-eight souls who believed in Christ were saved through baptism.

Thus, after glorifying his saint through many signs, the Lord led him forward to the crown of martyrdom. Finally, in the time of the emperor Julian, he was seized by Quadratianus the Augustal, and the man of God Hilarinus was ordered to sacrifice to idols together with him. When Donatus faithfully resisted, Quadratianus ordered his mouth to be crushed with stones; but Hilarinus the monk he ordered to be beaten with clubs in Donatus’s presence until he gave up his spirit. Then he ordered the blessed Donatus shut in custody.

While he was there and the Lord performed innumerable miracles through his servant, Quadratianus sent for him and struck him with the sword on the seventh day before the Ides of August. Christians buried his body reverently near the city, while the bones of the martyr Hilarinus are preserved, buried in the city of Ostia.

At Milan, Saint Faustinus, martyred in the time of Aurelius Commodus.

In the province of Raetia, in the city of Augusta, the nativity of Saint Afra. Although she had been a pagan and a prostitute, through the teaching of Saint Narcissus, bishop of Gerunda, who had been directed there by God’s grace, she was converted to Christ and baptized with her entire household. For confessing the Lord, she was handed over to the fire together with her mother Hilaria and the girls Digna, Eumenia [Eunomia], and Euprepia.

**VI Id. Aug.** — At Rome, the nativity of Saint Cyriacus. After the long imprisonment and affliction he endured under Maximian together with his fellow deacon Sisinnius, and with Largus and Smaragdus, and after performing many miracles—including healing and baptizing, at her own request, Artemia, the daughter of Diocletian, who was possessed by a demon; and, sent there by Diocletian for this purpose, likewise freeing from a demon and baptizing Jobia, the daughter of Sapor, king of the Persians, together with the king himself and three hundred and thirty others—he returned to Rome after Diocletian’s death.

There he was seized among other Christians by Diocletian’s son Maximian [Note: [Col. 1135D] Colleague. See Baronius in the Annals.], and sent into custody because he had made his sister a Christian. Then Maximian ordered that, on the day of his procession, Cyriacus should be stripped, bound with chains, and dragged before his chariot. After this he was brought out of prison with his companions Largus, Smaragdus, and Crescentianus. By the vicar Carpasianus, his head was drenched with melted pitch.

Four days later he was brought out of prison again, stretched on a frame, pulled with cords, and beaten with clubs. Several days afterward, at Maximian’s command, he was beheaded with Largus, Smaragdus, and twenty others. The priest John gathered their bodies by night and buried them on the Salarian Way, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of April.

Eight days later, the blessed Bishop Marcellus came with the most Christian matron Lucina and embalmed the bodies of the saints with spices and linen cloths. He then took them and transferred them to his estate on the Ostian Way, seven miles from the city of Rome, and with his own hands placed them in stone sarcophagi, on the eighth day of August.

The vicar Carpasianus then requested the house of Cyriacus, which the emperor Diocletian had given him, and Maximian immediately granted it. When Carpasianus entered, he found the place where Saint Cyriacus the deacon had built a font, which the blessed Bishop Marcellus had consecrated and where the blessed Cyriacus baptized those coming to the faith. In that place Carpasianus established a bath for himself. While he and his companions were bathing and being served a meal, Carpasianus and nineteen others with him mocked the Christian faith; suddenly they fell and died.

At Nicomedia, the nativity of the holy Nazarius, Julianus and Agape, virgin, Eutychianus, Philadelphia, and Leonidas.

At Vienne, a city of Gaul, the nativity of Saint Severus, presbyter and confessor. As his deeds testify, he was an Indian by nationality and fervent in Christ’s faith. Having undertaken a very arduous journey for the purpose of preaching the Gospel, he reached the city named above and converted a great multitude of pagans to the faith of Christ by his word and miracles. When he had peacefully died, he was buried in the basilica of Saint Stephen. Renowned for signs and miracles, he is honored with wondrous devotion by the faithful.

**V Id. Aug.** — The vigil of Saint Lawrence.

On the same day at Rome, the nativity of Saint Romanus, martyr. Struck with remorse by the confession of the blessed Lawrence, he asked him to baptize him. Immediately, by Decius’s order, he was brought forward, beaten with clubs, and beheaded.

In the city of Verona, Firmus and Rusticus, who suffered in the time of the emperor Maximian and his counselor Anulinus.

In the East, the passion of many martyrs.

In Cologne, Faustinus, Marcellinus, Secundianus, and Verianus, according to the Martyrology of the blessed Jerome. Our countrymen, following the ravings of apocryphal writings, say that they were baptized by the blessed Sixtus because of the continuity of the times and were killed by Decius.

**IV Id. Aug.** — At Rome, on the Tiburtine Way, the nativity of Saint Lawrence, archdeacon and martyr, under the emperor Decius. As the blessed Sixtus proceeded to the crown of martyrdom, he left him all the resources and treasures of the Church. Lawrence took care to distribute them with generous liberality to the weak and other poor, to widows, and to those in need.

When Decius Caesar heard this, he had him brought before him and handed him over to Valerianus, prefect of the city. Valerianus in turn committed him to a certain Hippolytus, and Hippolytus shut him up with many others. There the blessed Lawrence healed the widow Cyriaca and restored sight to the blind Lucillus in the name of Jesus Christ. When many blind people heard of this, they came to the blessed Lawrence and were given sight. Seeing this, Hippolytus believed; after being catechized, he was baptized.

When the three days had been completed during which, with Hippolytus’s permission—Hippolytus now being a Christian—the blessed Lawrence distributed all the Church’s resources to the poor, he presented himself at the Sallustian Palace. Decius, enraged, ordered him stripped and beaten with scorpions. Then the blessed Lawrence, bound with chains, was taken to the Palace of Tiberius to be interrogated there. Decius, filled with anger, ordered him beaten naked.

As he was being beaten, he cried out to Caesar: “See, wretch, recognize even now that I do not feel your tortures.” Then Decius ordered the clubs to be increased and red-hot iron plates to be placed against his sides.

The blessed Lawrence said: “Lord Jesus Christ, God from God, have mercy on me, your servant, because when accused I did not deny you; when questioned, I confessed you as Lord Jesus Christ.” When he had been beaten for a very long time with leaded rods, he said: “Lord Jesus Christ, who for our salvation deigned to take the form of a servant so that you might free us from slavery to demons, receive my spirit.”

A voice was heard: “Many more contests are still owed to you.”

Then, stretched on the frame and beaten most grievously with scorpions, he smiled and gave thanks, saying: “Blessed are you, Lord God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who have granted us the mercy we do not deserve. But you, Lord, because of your goodness, give us grace, so that all who stand around may know that you console your servants.”

Then one of the soldiers, named Romanus, believed in the Lord Jesus Christ and said to the blessed Lawrence: “I see before you a most beautiful man standing with a linen cloth and wiping your wounds. I adjure you by Christ, who sent you his angel, do not abandon me.”

The blessed martyr was therefore lifted from the frame, released, and returned to Hippolytus, who was still in the palace. Romanus came with a vessel, threw himself at the feet of the blessed Lawrence to be baptized, and was immediately baptized. After publicly professing himself a Christian, he was led outside the walls at the Salarian Gate and beheaded.

Caesar Decius then went by night to the baths near the Palace of Sallustius. When Saint Lawrence was brought before him, every kind of instrument of torture was brought out: leaded rods, clubs, plates, claws, beds, and staffs.

Decius said to the blessed martyr: “Now abandon the deception of magical art and tell us your lineage.”

The blessed Lawrence replied: “As to my lineage, I am a Spaniard, educated or brought up as a Roman, and a Christian from the cradle, instructed in every holy and divine law.”

Decius said: “Sacrifice to the gods, for unless you sacrifice, this night will be spent upon you in punishments.”

“My night,” he replied, “has no darkness; it all shines in the light.”

When his mouth was beaten with stones, he laughed, was strengthened, and said: “I give you thanks, Lord, because you are the Lord of all things.”

A bed with three ribs was brought in. The blessed Lawrence was stripped of his clothing, stretched upon an iron grating, and flayed from above with iron forks. He said to Decius: “I have offered myself as a sacrifice to God for a pleasing fragrance, because a broken spirit is a sacrifice to God.”

The executioners, however, diligently fed the coals, placing them beneath the grating and pressing him from above with iron forks.

Saint Lawrence said: “Learn, wretch, how great is the power of the Lord Jesus Christ, my God: your coals provide me refreshment, but eternal punishment for you. For the Lord himself knows that when accused I did not deny him; when questioned, I confessed Christ. Roasted, I give thanks.”

With an exceedingly beautiful expression he said: “I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, because you have deigned to strengthen me.”

Then, raising his eyes toward Decius, he said: “See, wretch, you have roasted one side; turn over the other and eat it.”

Giving thanks and glorifying God, he said: “I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, because I have deserved to enter your gates,” and he gave up his spirit.

Early in the morning, while it was still twilight, Hippolytus carried away his body, embalmed it with linen and spices, and reported what had happened to the presbyter Justinus.

Then the blessed Justinus and Hippolytus, weeping and deeply sorrowful, carried the body of the blessed martyr Lawrence and came along the Tiburtine Way to the estate of a widowed matron named Cyriaca, in the Veran field. The blessed martyr had visited her there by night and had given her the linen cloth with which he had wiped the feet of the saints. There, in the evening, they buried him on the fourth day before the Ides of August.

For three days they fasted and kept night vigils with a multitude of Christians. The blessed presbyter Justinus offered the sacrifice of praise, and all partook.

Then Claudius, Severus, Crescentius, and Romanus suffered, on the same day as the blessed Lawrence, three days after the martyrdom of Saint Sixtus.

On the same day at Rome, one hundred and forty-five soldiers.

**III Id. Aug.** — At Rome, between the Two Laurels, the nativity of Saint Tiburtius, son of Chromatius, prefect of the city. Since he was highly educated, the blessed Sebastian, Saint Tranquillinus, and the glorious presbyter Polycarpus instructed him in the faith. Polycarpus renewed him in the sacred font of baptism and baptized with him his household, of both sexes, numbering one thousand four hundred.

When the persecution became extraordinarily fierce, Tiburtius’s father, together with a great multitude of Christians, went with him into Campania on the advice of Pope Gaius. But Tiburtius, burning with love of martyrdom, remained in the city of Rome. While he was occupied there with the blessed Pope Gaius in fasts and prayers, one day as he was passing by he encountered a man who had fallen from a height and had so injured his head and all his limbs that those to whom he appeared to belong were already considering only his burial.

Tiburtius approached him and began slowly to recite the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed over his wounds. The man’s limbs were thereby restored, and he became whole and unharmed, as though nothing had happened to him.

Tiburtius then took hold of his parents, separated them from the crowds, and explained to them Christ’s power. Seeing that their minds were firmly fixed in the fear of the Lord, he brought them to Pope Gaius, who baptized the healed young man, giving thanks to God, together with his parents.

Meanwhile, as the storm of persecution grew increasingly severe, a certain man named Torquatus, pretending to have faith, joined the true servants of Christ and contrived by deceit to have the pagans seize the holy Tiburtius while he was praying.

After Tiburtius had been seized and brought before Fabianus, prefect of the city, and had most steadfastly confessed Christ, Fabianus ordered burning coals to be poured before his feet. He said to him: “Choose one of two things: either offer incense to the gods on these coals, or walk barefoot over them.”

Making the sign of the cross, Tiburtius steadfastly stepped onto them with his bare feet and began to say: “Put away your unbelief and learn that the God whom we confess alone rules over all creatures. For, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, it seems to me that I am walking over rose-colored flowers, because creation itself serves the authority of its Creator.”

Fabianus said to him: “Who does not know that you taught Christ magic?”

Then the blessed Tiburtius cried out: “Be silent, wretched man, and do not inflict this insult upon my ears, so that I should hear you barking with a rabid mouth against that sweet and holy name.”

Fabianus became angry and pronounced the capital sentence, that he should be killed with the sword. The glorious martyr Tiburtius was led along the Lavican Way, three miles from the city, struck once with the sword, and departed this life. A Christian relative buried him in the same place on the third day before the Ides of August.

On the same day at Rome, Saint Susanna, virgin and martyr, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, with Macedonius as judge. She was the daughter of the glorious presbyter and martyr Gabinus, brother of Pope Gaius and himself a martyr, and was born of noble lineage. Her father had brought her up with the greatest care and instructed her in the divine writings.

When Diocletian heard that the girl surpassed others in beauty and wisdom, he sent to Gabinus one of his cousins, named Claudius, and asked that she be given in marriage to his son, the Augustus Maximianus. When the daughter, her father, and especially her uncle rejected this request, Claudius himself was instructed by the blessed Gaius and baptized with his wife Euprepia and his sons Alexander and Cutia. He grew so strong in the faith that he sold all his possessions and distributed them to poor Christians.

When Diocletian heard this, he sent Claudius’s brother, named Maximus, to deal with the girl Susanna. Maximus too was carefully instructed by the blessed Gaius and Gabinus and baptized in Christ. He began selling his possessions and, through a certain friend named Thrason, a most Christian man, distributing them through the streets and prisons.

When Diocletian learned of these things, he sent Julius to punish Claudius, Maximus, Euprepia—who is also called Praepedigna, a name compounded or interpreted from Greek and Latin—and Alexander and Cutia. He ordered his son Maximianus to abuse Susanna in his house as he pleased.

When Maximianus entered the house where the holy virgin was praying, he saw an immense brightness over her and, terrified, returned to the palace. When Diocletian heard this, he sent Macedonius to confine her within her father’s house. Macedonius stripped her and began beating her with clubs. When the blessed virgin persevered in confessing Christ, she was struck with the sword and gave her undefiled spirit back to the Lord.

The Augusta Serena, secretly a Christian, gathered her body by night, embalmed it with her own hands with spices, wrapped it in linen cloths, and placed it beside Saint Alexander on the third day before the Ides of August. She wiped away the blood with a sea-cloth and placed it in a silver chest in her palace, where day and night she poured herself out to the Lord in secret prayers.

At Nicopolis, the passion of many martyrs.

**II Id. Aug.** — In Sicily, in the city of Catina [Catana], the nativity of Saint Euplus, deacon, under the Augusti Diocletian and Maximian. When he had confessed himself a Christian outside the curtain of the tribunal chamber, he was brought inside, at the command of the consular Calvisianus, into the courtroom. While he most steadfastly confessed his faith there, Calvisianus, moved by anger, ordered him to be tortured more harshly. Finally he pronounced sentence, saying: “We order Euplus to be killed by a just judgment.”

The blessed Euplus gave thanks to God, bent his knees, prayed, and prepared his neck. He was beheaded on the third day before the Ides of August. His body, embalmed with spices, was buried in a venerable place in the city of Catina [Catana] on the day before the Ides of August.

On the same day, the passion of Hilaria, mother of the blessed martyr Afra. While she kept vigil at Afra’s tomb, she was handed over to the fire there by the persecutors for the faith of Christ, together with Digna, Emenia [Eunomia], and Euprepia, who had been the holy Afra’s maidens.

In Historia [possibly Istria], Saint Julianus with his companions.

In Syria, in the village of Magaritus, the nativity of Saints Macarius and Julianus, where a great religious community of monks is gathered.

**Id. Aug.** — At Rome, the nativity of Saint Hippolytus. In the time of the emperor Decius, his feet were tied to the necks of untamed horses, and he was dragged through thistles and thorns, over precipitous and rugged ground, until he gave up his spirit. Also Concordia, his nurse, who was beaten with leaded rods and martyred before him. And nine others from his household, who were beheaded at the same time.

At Dorosyllae [at the Forum of Sulla], Saint Cassianus. When he refused to adore idols, the persecutor asked him what trade he practiced. He replied that he taught children their letters. Immediately stripped of his clothes and with his hands bound behind his back, he was placed in the midst of the assembly. The children whom he had offended by teaching were summoned, and they were given permission to kill him.

They hated learning as much as they rejoiced in taking revenge. Some beat him with writing tablets and boxwood tablets; others wounded him with styluses. The weaker their hands were, the more severe a punishment of martyrdom their prolonged killing inflicted. The poet Prudentius wrote this.

At Poitiers, the burial of Radegund, queen. Previously, in the palace, she had striven to please God through fasts, prayers, and generous almsgiving. Later, consecrated as a nun by Saint Medardus, bishop of Soissons, she took care to present herself to Christ as a living offering, so that among the thousand crosses she endured for his love she even had her most holy arms bound with bronze rings, after the custom of sacrilegious people.

But the Rewarder of the faithful also deigned to repay these tribulations in the present life, granting her everything she asked in his name.

**XVIII Kal. Sept.** — The vigil of the Assumption of Saint Mary.

At Rome, the burial of Saint Eusebius, bishop and confessor. In the presence of the emperor Constantius, an Arian, he most steadfastly defended the Catholic faith and grieved that Pope Liberius had consented to Arian impiety. By that same Constantius’s command, he was confined in a small room of his own house, four feet wide. There he persevered steadfastly in prayer for many days and, after seven months, while still confined, received his death on the tenth day before the Kalends of September.

The presbyters Gregorius and Orosius gathered his body and buried it in a crypt beside the body of the blessed Sixtus, bishop and martyr, on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Callistus. There they also wrote his epitaph and placed it thus: “To Eusebius, a man of God.”

When Constantius heard that Gregorius and Orosius had buried the blessed Eusebius’s body in the same crypt where it had been placed, he ordered Gregorius to be confined alive. The presbyter Orosius rescued him from there by night, scarcely alive, and when he died shortly afterward, buried him beside the body of Saint Eusebius the presbyter.

A most severe persecution was then carried out against the Catholic Church by the Arians, while Liberius held the apostolic see.

At Mendara in Syria, the nativity of Saint Fortunatus.

In Africa, Demetrius.

Elsewhere, Eutychius, Paulus, Heraclius [Eraclius], Possessor, Parmus, Disseus, Herma, Prospolinus, and Prosalamus.

Likewise Heraclius with three companions.

At Aquileia, the nativity of Saints Felix, Fortunata, and Vincentia.

Likewise elsewhere, Eusebius, founder of the title.

**XVII Kal. Sept.** — The Assumption of blessed Mary, Mother of God.

Since, in the passing of other saints, the terms burial, falling asleep, or indeed nativity are ordinarily used for this event, it is worthwhile, for the benefit of readers, to report what the venerable Father Gregory, bishop of Tours, thought about this Assumption in his Book of Miracles:

“After the wonderful glory of the Lord’s ascension, which, crushing the head of the devil’s wickedness, inspired the minds of the faithful to contemplate heavenly things, the holy apostles of the Lord and our Savior, together with blessed Mary his mother, gathered in one house, placed everything in common, and no one said that anything was his own; rather, each possessed everything in charity, as the sacred style of the apostolic account relates.

“After this they were dispersed through various regions to preach the word of God. Finally, when blessed Mary had completed the course of this life and was now being called from the world, all the apostles were gathered from their separate regions to her house. When they heard that she was to be taken from the world, they kept vigil with her.

“And behold, the Lord Jesus came with his angels, and, taking her soul, entrusted it to the archangel Michael and departed. At daybreak the apostles lifted her body, placed it in a tomb, and guarded it while awaiting the Lord’s arrival.

“And behold, the Lord appeared to them again, and ordered the holy body, which he had taken up into a cloud, to be carried into paradise. There, now reunited with her soul, she rejoices with his elect and enjoys the good of eternity, which will never pass away.”

Thus far Gregory.

If anyone is troubled about how Gregory, situated in the sunset regions, could have learned what happened in the East, let him learn from Gregory’s other writings that people came from the whole world to Saint Martin as to philosophers, and that the holy places in Judea were frequented by people from the western regions of the world. This continued to be practiced even down to the times of the Normans.

But lest this same Catholic and venerable Father appear to have thought contrary to the Apostle, where he says: “Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep. For since death came through a man, resurrection of the dead also came through a man. And just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ, but each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to Christ at his coming” (1 Corinthians 15), it must be understood that either this special assumption of the body of the venerable Mother of God, Mary, or that of those who are said to have risen with the Lord and are believed to have ascended into heaven, supports apostolic authority more than it opposes it.

For it is unquestionably fitting that the body into which God deigned to become incarnate should be raised more quickly into heaven, and that those who were true witnesses of our resurrection and ascension should go before us.

Since the most learned interpreters appear to disagree among themselves about these matters, it is not my task to settle them in so brief a work. Yet this we certainly believe and confess with the universal Church: if that most revered body from which God became incarnate is still hidden somewhere on earth, its revelation is reserved for the destruction of Antichrist.

On the same day at Nicomedia, the nativity of Saints Strato, Philip, and Eutychianus, with their companions.

At Rome, Saint Tharsicius the martyr. When pagans found him carrying the sacrament of Christ’s Body, they began questioning what he was doing and what he was carrying. [Col. 1142C] But he judged it unworthy to hand pearls over to swine, and so he was beaten with clubs and stones until he breathed out his spirit. When the sacrilegious interrogators searched his body, they could find none of Christ’s sacraments in his hands or clothing. The Christians, however, gathered his body and buried it in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way.

**Seventeenth day before the Kalends of September.**—At Nicaea in Bithynia, the birth into eternal life of Saint Ursatius the confessor, under the persecutor Licinius. He later abandoned military service and lived an eremitical life in a tower of the aforesaid city. He became so renowned for his virtues that he is said to have expelled demons and killed an enormous dragon by prayer. Written in the fifth book of the *Tripartite Ecclesiastical History*.

At Rome, Saint Serena, once the wife of Diocletian [Col. 1142D] Augustus.

At Alexandria, the birth into eternal life of Saints Orion, Aemilius, and Agnatus.

In Persia, Thyrsus with his companions.

**Sixteenth day before the Kalends of September.**—At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the birth into eternal life of Saint Mamas, or Mammetis. In the time of the tyrant Aurelian, when the persecution of Christians was at its height, he was ten years old. Abandoning everything, he fled to a mountain with his animals, which he grazed there and whose milk he drank. There divine visitation came upon him and showed him beforehand how he would suffer for the name of Christ. Thus, when wild beasts came to him while he sat reading the Gospel each day, they behaved most gently [Col. 1143A] around him; and by their milk the servant of God supported both himself and other poor people. When the governor Alexander heard that he lived communally among wild beasts, he attributed this to magic. He summoned him and afflicted him with many tortures: he stretched and twisted him on the rack and threw him into a blazing furnace, but the fire could not harm him at all. Afterwards he ordered him to be stoned, until almost his entire body was covered with stones. Believing him dead, the persecutor withdrew. But the Lord preserved his martyr unharmed and later summoned him by his own calling to the heavenly kingdoms; thus, giving up his soul in peace, he passed into eternal rest.

In Africa, Saints Liberatus the abbot, Boniface the deacon, Servius [Servus] and Rusticus the subdeacons, [Col. 1143B] Rogatus and Septiminus [Septimus], monks, and Maximus, a boy, martyrs. During the Vandal persecution, by order of the most cruel and impious king Henry [Hunneric], they were dragged from the territory of the city of Capsa, from their monastery dwelling, and brought to Carthage. There, for confessing the Catholic faith and defending the one baptism, they were first committed to prison, tightly bound with cruel iron weights, and confined in dark places. There, by day and night, they strengthened the most Christian people in steadfastness of faith. The tyrant, inflamed with rage, ordered a ship to be filled with bundles of wood and all of them to be bound together in it and burned by fire set beneath it in the open sea. When, at the command of the wicked king or his cruel ministers, their hands [Col. 1143C] and feet had been stretched out and raised, and fire had been applied to the wood, it was immediately extinguished by divine command before everyone’s eyes. Whenever it was rekindled, the balls of flame were extinguished again and again. Therefore the tyrant, filled still more with rage and shame, ordered them to be killed with the shafts of oars, and so one by one they were destroyed, their brains shattered like those of dogs. Thus, with the Lord crowning them, they completed the glorious course of their contest. Their bodies were thrown into the sea, but at that same hour were returned unharmed to the shores. The Christian people reverently lifted them up, and, with the clergy leading the way with solemn hymns, buried them in the monastery adjoining [for *contiguous to*] the basilica called Celerina’s. Blessed Victor the African bishop writes in his history of that same Vandal persecution—which he himself endured with the others and set down in a faithful and distinguished style.

In Alexandria, Orion.

**Fourteenth day before the Kalends of September.**—At the city of Praeneste, thirty-three miles from Rome, the birthday of Saint Agapitus the martyr, under the emperor Aurelian and the governor Antiochus. He was fifteen years old and burning with love of Christ and the desire for martyrdom. By order of the emperor he was arrested, first beaten for a long time with raw sinews, and then handed over to the governor to be compelled to sacrifice. The governor shut him in a very harsh and gloomy prison and denied him all food for four days. Then, when he had been brought from prison before the governor, the latter ordered burning coals to be placed on his head. [Col. 1144A] But while the martyr gave thanks to God, he was beaten with whips and suspended naked with his head downward, while a sharp smoke was made beneath him. When he said to the governor, “Let your wisdom and your vanity labor in smoke,” he was beaten again by four men relieving one another. Then the ministers of the devil poured boiling water over his belly. Meanwhile the judge fell from his tribunal, was gathered up by his attendants, and laid back on a bed. Sensing God’s power in the martyr, he soon afterward lost his life in sorrow.

Concerning blessed Agapitus, word was brought to the emperor, who ordered that the holy man be thrown to lions. But the beasts, tamed, bent down at the martyr’s feet to lick them. When the agents of the crime saw this, they removed the holy martyr and came toward the city [Col. 1144B] of Praeneste. There are two columns there, and they struck him with a sword on the day . . . [lacuna].

*(Here several leaves are again missing from the manuscript codex.)*

“His head is like a mountain before me; therefore I tremble all over.” He is then handed over to others, and, filled with joy, he washed his hands in water, bent his knees, lowered his neck to the ground, poured out his prayer upon the ground, and accepted martyrdom.

At Capua, the birthday of Saint Rufus the martyr, taught and baptized by blessed Apollinaris.

At Tomis, Saints Marcellinus the tribune, his wife Mannea, his son John, Serapion the cleric, and Peter the soldier, martyrs.

In Gaul, at the city of Arles, Saint Caesarius the bishop [Col. 1144C] and confessor.

At Augustodunum, Saint Syagrius the bishop and confessor.

**Fifth day before the Kalends of September.**—The most blessed Hermes the martyr. While he was prefect, he was baptized by Alexander the pontiff and martyr, together with his sons and household. Later, after being thrown into prison by the emperor Aurelian, he converted the tribune Quirinus and his entire household to the faith. When Aurelian heard this, he ordered blessed Hermes [Hermes] to be beheaded.

On the same day, in Africa, the deposition of Saint Augustine the bishop, a man remarkable in every branch of learning. He was converted from the heresy of the Manichaeans to the grace of Christ by the teaching of Bishop Ambrose and was appointed the most worthy bishop of the Church of Hippo. His venerable body, [Col. 1144D] first transferred from his own city to Sardinia because of the barbarians, was recently brought back to Pavia by Luitprand, king of the Lombards, and honorably buried there.

On the same day, at Emona, a city in the province of Carniola, the passion of Saint Pelagius the martyr. In the time of the emperor Numerian, under the judge Velasius [Evilasius], he was first burdened with an iron weight around his neck and hands for the faith of Christ and thrust into prison. Brought out, he was beaten with rods, then struck with clubs. Afterwards he was suspended on the rack and torn with hooks; boiling oil was poured into his belly; he was dragged over fragments of pottery with his hands and feet bound; finally he was beheaded.

[Col. 1145A] On the same day, at the town of Brillia, the birthday of Saint Julian, who was killed by his persecutors for confessing Christ, his throat having been cut.

At Constantinople, Saint Alexander the bishop and confessor, by whose power of prayer Arius burst open in the middle and all his entrails were poured out upon the ground.

On the same day, at Saintes, Saint Vivianus the bishop.

**Fourth day before the Kalends of September.**—At Rome, Saint Sabina the martyr, who suffered under the emperor Hadrian and the city prefect Elpidius; all her property is marked as belonging to the Lord or assigned to public purposes. She was buried in the tomb in which she herself had placed blessed Seraphia the martyr, her teacher in the faith, at the Arch of Faustinus, beside the Vinditian estate, in the town of Vindinum.

[Col. 1145B] On the same day, the beheading of Saint John the Baptist, who was first buried in Samaria and is now in Alexandria. His head, moreover, was carried from Jerusalem to the Phoenician city of Edessa.

**Third day before the Kalends of September.**—At Rome, on the Ostian Way, Saints Felix and Adauctus, martyrs. When Felix was being taken to the images of various gods and forced to sacrifice, he blew upon and threw down the statues of Serapis, Mercury, and Diana. For this he was suspended on the rack, then taken alive from the gallows and ordered to be beheaded. As he was being led away, a certain Christian met him and, suddenly moved by divine inspiration, cried out: “I too worship the one whom this holy presbyter confesses, the Lord Jesus Christ.” He too was immediately arrested and beheaded with blessed Felix. Later the Christians called him Adauctus, because, although his name was unknown, he had been added to the martyr Felix for the crown, and the crown of martyrdom had been increased for him through his confession of the faith.

**Second day before the Kalends of September.**—At Trier, Saint Paulinus the bishop and confessor. During the Arian persecution, he was exiled by the emperor Constantius because of the Catholic faith and worn down there until death; in Africa he received the crown of a blessed passion.

On the same day, at Athens, blessed Aristus [Aristides], renowned for faith and wisdom. He presented books concerning the Christian religion to the emperor Hadrian and, in his presence, argued most eloquently that Jesus Christ was the true God.

**September.** September has thirty days, while the lunar month has twenty-nine.

[Col. 1145D]

**Kalends of September.**—Joshua son of Nun and Gideon.

On the same day, the birthday of the most holy virgin Verena, of Theban origin. Her parents entrusted her to a certain bishop, Chaeremon, who was later crowned with martyrdom, to be instructed. Afterwards she went with other faithful people to Lower Egypt and joined the blessed legion—that is, Maurice and his companions—who at that time were staying there, as though preparing to serve under Diocletian and Maximian. The virgin of Christ, wishing to come to Italy, joined herself to them. Reaching Milan, she sought out the places where the holy martyrs were kept [Col. 1146A] and supplied them with works of mercy, while also desiring to offer herself for martyrdom. She remained there, detained by a certain holy man named Maximus.

At length, hearing that the holy Theban legion and Victor, whom she loved above all, had completed their martyrdom, she went over the Alpine passes to Agaunum [Acaunum] to learn the truth. From there she settled near the river Aar, not far from the fortress of Solothurn, continuing day and night under an extraordinary discipline of fasts, vigils, and prayers. She shut herself in a very narrow cave for a time, to mortify her flesh somewhat. An old Christian woman lived not far away. Whatever the holy virgin was able to make, this woman sold, and from the proceeds provided food for the saint of God. For the sacrilegious worship of the pagans [Col. 1146B] still held the Alamanni. But as the Lord worked many signs through his handmaid, the Alamanni began to be moved toward the faith of Christ.

The virgin’s reputation grew so greatly through the miracles made known that, having become a mother of virgins, she was revered by all the people for her discerning charity. The devil, jealous of her admirable life, inflamed a certain tyrant under the authority of the Roman name. He subjected the virgin of God, after many afflictions, to public custody. In that prison a young man of extraordinary splendor appeared to her, and she asked who he was. When he replied that he was Maurice, he was immediately removed from the virgin’s sight, surrounded by a multitude of purple-clad persons, while she implored prayer. That same night the tyrant was seized by a very severe fever. He summoned the virgin to [Col. 1146C] him and was immediately healed through her prayer; thus, with everyone praising her, he was sent back to the place of the virgins.

One day the bread ran out there, and a complaint arose about it. She reminded the sisters to trust in divine generosity and prostrated herself in prayer because of the pressing need. Suddenly, forty sacks filled with the purest flour were found at the door of the cell. From these the community was sustained for several years.

When the end of her life was already approaching, she became physically ill but did not abandon the rigor of her purpose, and lay down on a little bed. As she awaited the moment of her death, the virgin Mary, Mother of God, appeared, preceding innumerable choirs of virgins. Verena gazed upon her with complete devotion and asked by what merit she had obtained this. [Col. 1146D] The Mother of God answered her: “I have come so that you may be rewarded by him whom you have faithfully served.” Having said this, that blessed soul left the body. The blessed virgin was buried in the place called Zurzach.

At Capua, the birthday of Priscus the martyr, who was one of the ancient disciples of Christ.

On the same day, at Sens, Saint Lupus the bishop, illustrious for holiness and miracles.

Likewise, at Caesarea in Cappadocia, Longinus the soldier and martyr, who is said to have opened the Lord’s side with a lance. Afterward, when he was baptized by the apostles, he was arrested by the governor Octavius. His tongue was cut out, his teeth were knocked out, and he was beheaded for Christ. With [Col. 1147A] him Aphrodisius the records clerk was crowned; even after his tongue had been cut out, he spoke of Christ fluently.

**Fourth day before the Nones of September.**—The birthday of Saint Justus, bishop of Lyons. He secretly abandoned his bishopric and migrated to Egypt, accompanied by a certain lector named Viator. There, associating with monks for several years, he ended his life in holy conduct. His body was brought to Lyons by devout citizens, together with the bones of Saint Viator, his servant, and placed in the basilica of the Seven Maccabean Brothers.

On the same day, in the aforesaid city, Elpidius, bishop of that same city.

At Apamea, blessed Antonius the martyr.

[Col. 1147B] **Third day before the Nones of September.**—At Rome, Saint Seraphia the virgin, who suffered under the emperor Hadrian and the judge Berillus. By birth an Antiochene, she was staying with Saint Sabina when she was seized and brought before the governor. When she rebuked him with words of faith, the angry governor ordered her to be handed over to two young men so that the virgin might be violated by their lust. When they attempted to touch her, they suddenly fell to the ground dead. The virgin was brought again, and the young men were carried before the governor. Approaching them with prayer, the virgin restored them to their former state. After this, by order of the governor, she was beaten with clubs; a splinter knocked loose from them flew into the tyrant’s eye and immediately blinded him in one eye. He then pronounced sentence and ordered her to be struck with a sword. She was buried beside her companion Sabina.

[Col. 1147C] **Second day before the Nones of September.**—Moses the prophet. And at Ancyra in Galatia, Saints Rufinus, Silvanus, and Vitalicus, martyrs.

At Chalon, the birthday of Saint Marcellus the martyr. In the time of Antoninus, he was one of fifty martyrs thrown into prison at Lyons. When the prison doors were miraculously opened, he escaped and converted to the Lord the man who had received him as a guest, together with his entire household. Later, coming to Chalon, he was subjected to many tortures by the governor Priscus, then stood upright and was buried in the earth up to his waist; thus, on the third day, he gave his soul back to God.

**Nones of September.**—At the suburb of Rome, Victorinus the martyr. [Col. 1147D] With his brother Severinus, under a mutual service of charity by which for a long time they served one another, he grew so greatly in virtue that, after distributing their possessions to the poor and after the long period of service in which each served the other, naked and alone, he entered the solitude of the wilderness for God.

While he was exercising himself in every kind of virtue there, behold, the devil in the form of a woman threw himself before the man’s door, uttering laments of this sort: “Alas,” she said, “for me, miserable woman, wandering in the forests, roaming in darkness, destined to be devoured by beasts! Whoever you are, inhabitant of this place, rescue me; for if I live, it will be yours; if I die, it will be yours.” As she cried out these and still more pitiable words, Victorinus opened the door.

Shortly afterward, amid other bodily movements, the apparition stretched out its foot, touched the man of God, inflicted a harmful heat, wounded him, [Col. 1148A] and struck him down. The devil, victorious, exclaimed that Victorinus had now been defeated: “What are you doing,” he said, “most perfect man? Why are you joining yourself to another, when you have withdrawn from your brother?” After many insults of boastfulness and mockery, the devil disappeared from the eyes of the deceived man. Since he had fallen, Victorinus became as though lifeless.

At last, returning to consciousness, he went back to his brother Severinus. At first he remained silent out of shame; then he disclosed the matter and imposed a punishment upon himself. For, splitting open a tree, he inserted his hands into the clefts and shut the tree’s wound by driving in wedges. Even when the bishop, to whom his brother had made the matter known, wished to release him, he did not consent, but remained in that punishment for three full years. Only on the Lord’s Day did he receive a little bread and water, compelled by his brother, who likewise mortified himself with a similar fast for his brother.
