[Col. 1148B] Only afterward was he withdrawn from the punishment by the bishop. He led a life wholly devoted to holy discipline and was later chosen bishop of the city of Amiternum. As time passed, during the reign of Nerva, he was examined by Judge Aurelian with prolonged tortures. At a place called Cotialis, he was ordered to be suspended head downward for three hours in foul, sulphurous waters. When this had continued for three days, he was crowned with martyrdom and departed to the Lord.

Likewise at Rome, Saint Herculanus.

At Capua, Quinctus, Acontius, Donatus, Eutyches, and Maro.

**Eighth day before the Ides of September.**—The birthday of Saint Magnus the confessor, disciple and companion of blessed Gallus, a wondrous and most holy man.

[Col. 1148C] Likewise, Zachariah the prophet, and the birthday of Onesiphorus, a disciple of the apostles.

In Africa, the birthday of Saints Donatianus, Praesidius, Mansuetus, Germanus, and Fusculus, confessors and bishops. During the Vandal persecution, by order of the Arian king Hunneric, they were cruelly beaten with clubs and condemned to exile. Among them, a bishop named Laetus was also consumed by fire. Then, on one day, that same tyrant closed all the churches of Africa and gave all the bishops’ property to his own bishops.

**Seventh day before the Ides of September.**—At Nicomedia, the birthday of Saint John, distinguished by nobility, honor, and worldly rank. Under Maximian and Diocletian, inflamed by the fervor of faith, he tore the book of their impious law into pieces before the watching crowd. When the tyrants learned this, they ordered him to be tortured by every kind of cruelty. But although the executioners raged against the holy martyr until his entrails were exhausted, they could not make him sorrowful even through his sufferings.

**Sixth day before the Ides of September.**—The birthday of Mary, holy Mother of God.

On the same day, at Nicomedia, Saint Adrian the martyr with twenty-three others. Although their passion is read about everywhere, I think that, for the sake of brevity, something should nevertheless be recalled about them. Blessed Adrian the martyr was a senior officer in the time of Maximian. [Col. 1149A] Seeing how many bitter punishments the saints of God were enduring, he asked for what reward they were doing such things. When the twenty-three martyrs said that they endured martyrdom for the sake of the unfailing and indescribable joy of the heavenly kingdom, he immediately sprang forward, stood among them, and was enrolled among God’s confessors and athletes.

When Maximian heard Adrian’s name recited among the names of the saints, he ordered him, bound with iron, to be dragged with the other saints to prison. He was twenty-nine years old. When his wife, Natalia by name, a most Christian woman, heard this, she ran joyfully to the prison and, with many exhortations, urged him not to withdraw from sharing the martyrs’ fate either for the glory of any earthly dignity or through fear of the punishment that threatened him.

The emperor, enraged against Adrian, ordered him to be beaten so cruelly that his ribs were exposed and his entrails [Col. 1149B] could be seen. Again he was thrust into prison with the others. When they had been brought out a second time, their flesh almost consumed, it was ordered that their shins be broken with a great iron bar. After all their legs had been broken and their feet cut, Adrian’s hands were also cut off. Having thus been sent to Christ, Natalia sailed to Byzantium, where the bodies of the saints had been taken, and herself fell asleep in the Lord after several days.

**Fifth day before the Ides of September.**—The passion of Saints Dorotheus and Gorgonius, martyrs, at Nicomedia under the emperor Diocletian. They were masters of the offices performed within the palace and supervisors of the imperial bedchamber. As followers of the Christian faith, one day they saw a martyr being savagely torn by punishments and said: “Why, emperor, do you [Col. 1149C] persecute one whose worshippers we too are?” He summoned them before him and ordered them to be hung, lacerated with whips, drenched with salt and vinegar, then placed on a gridiron to be tortured, and finally strangled while suspended by a noose.

In the Sabine territory, thirty miles from Rome, the birthday of Saints Hyacinthus, Alexander, and Tiburtius, martyrs.

On the same day, Pope Sergius, who sat in Rome for thirteen years. He found a fragment of extraordinary size from Christ’s cross in the shrine of blessed Peter. He established that the *Agnus Dei* should be sung during the breaking of the Lord’s Body; and that on the feasts of the Lord’s Annunciation, the Dormition and Nativity of Saint Mary, and Saint Simeon’s feast—called *Hypapanti* in Greek—the litanies should [Col. 1149D] go out from Saint Adrian’s, and the people should meet at Saint Mary’s.

**Fourth day before the Ides of September.**—In Africa, the birthday of Saints Nemesianus, Felix, and Lucius, bishops.

Likewise, Felix, Litteus, Polianus, Victor, Jader, and Dativus. Under Decius [Gallienus] and Valerian, they were severely beaten with clubs for the faith of Christ, bound in fetters, and assigned to dig in the mines; thus they completed their martyrdom.

On the same day, at Chalcedon, Saints Sosthenes and Victor. While they were contending with blessed Euphemia for the name of Christ, they were thrust into prison. From there they were brought out and tied to a stake. Then [Col. 1150A] bears and a most savage lion were released against them. But when the beasts could not harm them in any way, the proconsul Priscus ordered them to be burned. Meanwhile, as they devoted themselves to prayer and gave one another the kiss of peace, they gave up their spirits.

**Third day before the Ides of September.**—The birthday of Saints Felix and Regula, his sister, martyrs. Since their feast is solemnly honored among us and the account of their passion is known to many, I do not think it necessary to add writings to what has already been written. It is enough to say that these martyrs, coming from the company of Maurice and his companions, traveled through the vast wilderness called Darona and reached the regions of Germany. They stopped at a certain place beside the river Lindimacus and devoted themselves with every work of piety to vigils and prayers. [Col. 1150B]

While these most holy brother and sister were engaged in this, messengers sent by the most impious Maximian arrived, so that they might either compel the saints of God to sacrifice to idols or not delay punishing them with various tortures. The blessed martyrs courageously resisted the sacrilegious demands and confessed that they were companions of Saints Maurice, Exuperius, Candidus, and Victor. They were bound to iron wheels heated white-hot and further tormented with unspeakable tortures. Blessed Regula was placed upon boiling pitch, and the executioner was also ordered to give her boiling lead to drink. Since they could not be separated from Christ by any severity of punishment, it was ordered that their heads be cut off. After this was done, the beheaded martyrs carried their severed heads in their [Col. 1150C] own hands and carried them fifty cubits from the place where they had been beheaded.

On the same day, on the Salarian Way, in the cemetery of Basilla, Saints Protus and Hyacinthus, martyrs, who were eunuchs of blessed Eugenia the virgin. After spending some time in Egypt in a monastery among servants of God, they returned to Rome with the most blessed virgin. Under the emperor Gallienus they were very severely beaten for the faith of Christ and then beheaded together. How blessed Eugenia, disguising herself as a man for God’s sake, led a most holy life; how she was detained by the prefect Nicetius and by prayer reduced an image of Diana to dust; and how, with a huge stone fastened to her shoulders, she was thrown into the Tiber and completed the struggle of her passion—the book of her Acts [Col. 1150D] explains sufficiently.

**Second day before the Ides of September.**—At the city of Ticinum, also called Pavia, Saints Syrus and Juventius [Hyventius], confessors. Sent there by blessed Hermagoras, bishop of Aquileia and disciple of blessed Mark the evangelist, they rested in peace after continuous and most urgent preaching and the working of many miracles.

**Ides of September.**—At Alexandria in Egypt, Philip the bishop and martyr. He was first a prefect, but afterward, summoned by divine grace, received the episcopate. Under Volusian and Gallienus, he was killed by the prefect Perennis and gained the palm of martyrdom.

[Col. 1151A] On the same day, Saint Anianus, priest and abbot of the monastery of Saint Romaric. He followed remarkable abstinence and the anachoretic life and led a life illustrious for miracles and virtues.

**Eighteenth day before the Kalends of October.**—At Rome, in the cemetery of Callistus, the birthday of Saint Cornelius the bishop. During the Decian persecution he was assigned to exile at Centumcellae. Later, brought before Decius, he could not be turned from the Catholic faith and was ordered to be beheaded. While he was being led away, he visited the wife of a soldier named Cerealis, who had lain paralyzed for five years; at Saint Cornelius’s prayer, she rose and was healed. Seeing this, many were baptized and were slain with blessed Cornelius, twenty-one in number, including Cerealis and his wife Salustia.

[Col. 1151B] On the same day, in Africa, blessed Cyprian the bishop and martyr. Under Valerian and Gallienus, with Aspasius acting as proconsul, he was sent into exile. Later recalled from exile, he was struck with a sword by Maximus the proconsul, who had succeeded Aspasius, because of his unconquerable steadfastness in the faith, and departed to the Lord. Crescentianus, Auctor [Victor], Rosula, and Generalis suffered with him. Envoys of the emperor Charlemagne, returning from the Persian king Aaron, brought his bones, together with the holy head of Saint Pantaleon and the limbs of the martyr Speratus, from the East. The bishop of Lyons placed these relics of the blessed martyrs, granted by the emperor, in his own city.

On the same day, the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. It was found by Helena [Col. 1151C] and divided through the middle in such a way that one cross was preserved at Jerusalem and the other was carried to Constantinople. After many years had passed, the Persian people, with their king Chosroes, devastated many Roman provinces and also invaded Jerusalem. Having taken away many distinguished ornaments from it, they carried off the Lord’s cross as well. Chosroes set it up in a silver tower and prepared for himself in that same tower a golden throne, on which he was accustomed to sit as though he were God’s associate.

Heraclius, therefore, the Roman emperor, undertook war against the Persians. After killing Chosroes, he brought back the venerable wood with great reverence. On that same day many blind people, paralytics, lepers, and demoniacs were healed, and even a dead person received life [Col. 1151D].

**Seventeenth day before the Kalends of October.**—The birthday of Saint Nicomedes the martyr. Because he buried the body of Saint Felicula the martyr and refused to sacrifice to idols, Count Flaccus ordered him to be beaten with leaded whips until he died. His body was thrown into the Tiber, but his deacon recovered it and buried it honorably.

On the same day, in the territory of Chalon [Cabillon], the birthday of Saint Valerian the martyr.

**Sixteenth day before the Kalends of October.**—In the city of Chalcedon, the birthday of Saint Euphemia. Under the emperor Diocletian she was handed over, with forty-nine others, to the proconsul Priscus. After imprisonment and the tortures [Col. 1152A] of wheels, after beatings and fires, after the weight of cornerstones, after axes and fiery frying pans, she was led into the theater and exposed to lions and beasts. Then, while the blessed virgin prayed, one of the beasts approached and sank its teeth into her holy body; thus the holy woman of God gave up her soul.

On the same day, at Rome, Saints Lucia and Geminianus. Blessed Lucia had served God in praiseworthy virginity for thirty-six years when she was accused by her son Euprepius and compelled to sacrifice to idols, under the emperor Diocletian and the judges Apophrasius and Megasius. Refusing to do so, after imprisonment and savage beatings she was thrown into a pot boiling with pitch and lead. She emerged unharmed, was loaded with iron and lead, and dragged through the streets [Col. 1152B] of the city. When she passed the house of a certain powerful man named Geminianus, that man, moved by a heavenly miracle—for a dove was seen to rest above his head—came to the place where the holy woman of God was being tortured. Asking for baptism, he was beheaded with her.

**Fifteenth day before the Kalends of October.**—In Britain, Socrates and Stephen.

At Noviodunum, Valerian, Macrinus, and Gordianus.

At Rome, the birthday of Saint Justin the priest, who was ordained by blessed Sixtus. Blessed Laurence washed his feet and commended himself to Justin’s prayers. The same Justin gave burial to the bodies of Saints Hippolytus, Concordia, Irenaeus, Abundius, and Cyrilla, the daughter of the emperor Decius. During the persecution under Decius, Gallus, and Volusian, he was especially distinguished for the glory of his confession.

Likewise at Rome, the martyrs Narcissus and Crescentio.

In the diocese of Tongeren, the birthday of Saint Landebert [Lambert] the bishop. When, inflamed with religious zeal, he rebuked the royal household, he was killed within the church’s house. His tomb is made illustrious by frequent manifestations of miracles.

**Fourteenth day before the Kalends of October.**—The birthday of Saint Methodius of Olympus in Lycia, later bishop of Tyre, who was crowned with martyrdom at Ebacis [Chalcis] under Diocletian.

At Vienne, Saint Ferreolus. When he held tribunitian authority, he was cruelly beaten for the faith of Christ and thrust into prison bound with chains. By God’s [Col. 1152D] command he was released from his bonds and brought out. Later, pursued by his enemies and taken to the territory of Brioude, he was beheaded.

**Thirteenth day before the Kalends of October.**—At Naples, a city of Campania, the birthday of Saint Januarius, bishop of Benevento; Sosius, deacon of Misenum; Festus, deacon; and Desiderius, lector. As they were being led to death, they saw among the others Proculus, deacon of Pozzuoli, and two laymen, Eutyches and Acutius, who asked why just men were ordered to be killed. When the judge realized that they were Christians, he ordered them to be beheaded with the others.

On the same day, in Palestine, the birthday of Saints Mark [Elijah], Paleus [Peleus], and Nilus, bishops, [Col. 1153A] who during Diocletian’s persecution were burned for Christ with many clerics.

At Niceria [Nuteria], Saints Felix and Constantia, martyrs, who suffered under Nero.

In the territory of the city of Langres, Saint Sigo, or Sequanus, the priest.

**Twelfth day before the Kalends of October.**—At Cyzicus, the birthday of Saint Fausta the virgin and Evilasius, under the emperor Maximian. Evilasius first ordered that her head be shaved and her hair cut off; then he had her suspended and tortured. He ordered little chests to be brought, and had her placed in them and cut in half as though she were a piece of wood. When the executioners could not accomplish this and the saws could not harm her, Evilasius, astonished, believed in Christ.

When the emperor learned this, [Col. 1153B] he ordered that Evilasius, suspended, be tortured more severely. He ordered Fausta to be brought naked from prison, her head drilled through, and keys driven into it; her face and entire body were also to be filled with nails. Afterwards a frying pan was heated, but it cooled while she sang psalms. During these events, summoned by a heavenly voice, they gave up their spirits.

**Eleventh day before the Kalends of October.**—The birthday of Saint Matthias the apostle and evangelist, whose passion is widely recounted.

**Tenth day before the Kalends of October.**—In Spain [Gaul], at the city of Sidunum [Sedunum], at the place of Acaunum [Agaunum], Saints Maurice and his companions, martyrs. They came from the East, departing from the city of Thebes, and under the emperor Maximian were slaughtered with their legion, numbering six thousand six hundred men, for the faith of Christ. They [Col. 1153C] had been summoned to Maximian’s aid, but when they refused to follow him in sacrilege, he ordered every tenth man to be slaughtered before their eyes, so that he might more easily bend the others afterward. When this decimation had been carried out twice by the executioners, and the survivors nevertheless remained firm in their resolve, all of them voluntarily presented their necks and were slaughtered in one identical massacre.

A fitting punishment struck Maximian. He was discovered plotting against his son-in-law Constantius, was strangled, and, afflicted with a most dreadful punishment, ended his impious life by a death he deserved.

**Ninth day before the Kalends of October.**—Sosius the deacon, concerning whom you will find an entry under the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October.

On the same day: the virgin Thecla, resting at Seleucia, who had been instructed at the city of Iconium by the blessed apostle Paul. When her mother saw that she was a Christian and rejecting marriage, she accused her before the judge. Thus the holy Thecla was brought in and thrown into a pyre; but when she made the sign of the cross, rain suddenly burst forth and extinguished the flames. Afterwards she was stripped and exposed again and again to lions and bears; protected from them by divine power, she was immersed in a pit full of water and serpents, from which divine grace nevertheless brought her out unharmed. Next she was bound to two exceedingly savage bulls, goaded with red-hot iron so that they might tear her apart. But when the ropes broke, the bulls scattered in every direction and left the martyr unharmed. Then the virgin was released. She strengthened Tryphaena, a devout woman who had also been present at her martyrdom, together with her entire household, in the faith of Christ [Col. 1154A]; she came to Seleucia and there rested in peace.

**VIII KAL. OCTOB.**—The Conception of Saint John the Baptist.

At Augustodunum: Saint Andochius the presbyter, Thyrsus the deacon, and Felix. Sent by Bishop Polycarp to teach Gaul, under the emperor Aurelian they were beaten with scourges, thrown into the fire, suspended with their hands turned backward, and finally struck on the necks with bars; thus they completed their martyrdom.

**VII KAL. OCTOB.**—The Nativity of the blessed Cleophas, to whom the Lord appeared on the road after his resurrection.

**VI KAL. OCTOB.**—The holy martyrs Cyprian the bishop and Justina the virgin. A certain scholar named Agladius [Col. 1154B], seeing the blessed Justina at Antioch, burned with desire for her and promised the magician Cyprian two talents of gold if he would inflame the virgin Justina with love for him. The magician Cyprian, summoning demons, began to work through them to seduce the holy woman of God. But when the demons were wholly unable to accomplish this and confessed that they were driven away from her by the sign of the Crucified One, Cyprian, scorning the devil’s power, asked Bishop Anthimus to instruct him in the Catholic mysteries. Not long afterwards he was ordained deacon, and then, increasing in powers and miracles, was elevated even to the dignity of bishop. As time passed, Bishop Cyprian and the virgin of Christ Justina were arrested and bound in chains. The bishop was suspended and torn with hooks; the holy woman of God was savagely beaten with raw sinews after receiving slaps [Col. 1154C]; then she was roasted in a frying pan with pitch, fat, and wax; finally both were beheaded with the sword. A certain Theognothus was also punished with them under the emperor Diocletian, by the judge Eutela(mi)us [Eutholmius].

**V KAL. OCTOB.**—At Aegeae: the nativity of the holy Cosmas and Damian, during the persecution of Diocletian, under the governor Lysias. They were natives of Arabia and practiced medicine; their brothers were named Anthimus [Antimius], Leontius, and Euprepius. Rejecting the worship of idols, they were bound hand and foot and tortured severely. Then, chained, they were plunged into the sea, from which they were delivered by an angel of God. Afterwards they were thrown into a blazing fire, which was extinguished while the saints prayed; then they were again suspended and tortured. Enduring this patiently [Col. 1154D], they were raised upon a cross and stoned, and afterwards attacked with arrows. But when they were harmed in no way, while many of those shooting and surrounding them were struck in return, the governor ordered them to be slaughtered with the sword.

**IV KAL. OCTOB.**—In Spain, at the city of Córdoba: Faustus, Januarius, and Martial. First tortured on the rack, then disfigured by having their eyebrows shaved and their ears and noses cut off, and by having their upper teeth knocked out, they finally completed their martyrdom through the ordeal of fire.

**III KAL. OCTOB.**—On Mount Garganus: the commemoration of the blessed archangel Michael, where a church consecrated in his name is maintained and became known in the following manner. [Col. 1155A] A certain very wealthy man named Garganus, from whose fate the mountain received its name, possessed an immense multitude of livestock. It happened that, when the herd was returning, one bull did not come home. Its owner searched for it through every byway and finally found it standing at the summit of the mountain, at the entrance of a certain cave. When he shot at it with an arrow, the arrow was violently turned backward and struck its owner. When the bishop learned of this, he proclaimed a three-day fast for the citizens and warned them to seek from God the reason for the man’s death. When the fast had been completed, Saint Michael appeared to the bishop and disclosed that this had been done by his will:

> “I have decided to inhabit this place and claim it as my own.”

He also said that it was not necessary for men to dedicate a church there, since it had been founded by him and, he said, consecrated by him as well. He merely ordered them to enter the place and frequent it with devout prayers. How, moreover, victory over the enemies was granted to the citizens through miracles shown by the holy archangel from heaven, and concerning the situation of that place and the multitude of miracles displayed there, you will find written in many books.

**II KAL. OCTOB.**—At Solodorum, a fortress of Gaul: the passion of the holy martyrs Victor and Ursus, of the Theban Legion. By order of Maximian, they were tortured with dreadful punishments by Hirtacus, then thrown into the fire, and finally put to death by the sword.

On the same day, at Bethlehem in Judea: the burial of Saint Jerome the presbyter. He was born in the town of Stridon, once situated on the boundary of Dalmatia and Pannonia [Col. 1155C], to Eusebius his father. At Rome, while still a boy, he received the Christian habit, and there from his earliest years he was educated in Greek and Latin literature. He also imitated the dress and conduct of the most approved monks. Ordained presbyter of the Roman Church by the judgment of all, he was deemed most worthy of the highest priesthood. But after he had been driven from Rome by the envy of his rivals, he went to Gregory, bishop of Constantinople, to study. From there he set out for Syria and, approaching the deserted regions, spent four years in a harsh solitude. Then, coming to the town of Bethlehem, he wisely withdrew into the Lord’s manger, intending to remain there like an animal. How many vigils and fasts he undertook there, and with what zeal he implanted the libraries of the Hebrews into Latin ears, is known to him to whom he offered his labors [Col. 1155D]. At last, after a life perfectly ordered and pleasing to God, he rested in peace at Bethlehem in the ninety-eighth year of his age, on the second day before the Kalends of October, in the twelfth year of the emperor Honorius. He completed his books over fifty-six years.

**OCTOBER.** The month of October has thirty-one days, but thirty lunar days.

**KAL. OCTOB.**—At Auxerre: the nativity of Saint Germanus the bishop. Because he had to refute the perfidy of the Pelagian heresy, he was sent to Britain by the judgment of all the Gallican bishops. While the blessed bishop was making the voyage in the middle of the sea, a hostile force stirred up a storm and brought great danger to the sailors [Col. 1156A]. But he rose, invoked the name of the Lord, and calmed the violence of the storms. Then, arriving in Britain, he suppressed the heresy that had arisen. He restored sight to the ten-year-blind daughter of a certain tribune; in the nearby little house where he was staying, he extinguished a raging fire; and he overcame the pain of his illness—for he was disabled by an injured foot—when a heavenly person visited him. At that time the Saxons and Picts brought war against the Britons. But when Germanus assumed the role of commander and fought with prayers rather than weapons, the enemies were put to flight. After many distinguished signs of his power, he came to Ravenna to plead for peace for the Armorican people. There he was honorably received by Valentinian, and after a few days he brought his present life to an end [Col. 1156B]. His body was carried back to his own city.

At the city of Tomis: the holy Priscus, Crescentius [Crescentis], and Evagrius.

At Reims: Saint Remedius, bishop and confessor, a man of outstanding virtue and holiness. He converted the Frankish people, who were devoted to idols, after first initiating their king. Among his other deeds, he raised a girl from the bonds of death. He completed approximately seventy years in the episcopate.

**VI NON. OCTOB.**—Eusebius the pope, who sat in the episcopal office for seven years and was buried on the Appian Way, in the cemetery of Callixtus. In his time the Lord’s cross was discovered. He found heretics in the City and reconciled them through the laying on of hands.

[Col. 1156C] At Nicomedia: the nativity of Saint Eleutherius the martyr. In the time of Diocletian, the palace happened to be consumed by fire. The emperor, falsely supposing that Christians had caused it, ordered all Christians to be gathered together; some were beheaded with the sword, others burned in the flames. The first among them, and the one who encouraged them all to martyrdom, was Leudegarius [Eleutherius]. Some were then thrown into the flames, others slaughtered with the sword, and very many were plunged into the sea. But the blessed Eleutherius, after being tortured for a long time with the most savage torments, was finally thrown into the flames and obtained the palm of martyrdom.

At Atrates [Arras], in the village of Syrricinius: the passion of Saint Leodegarius, bishop of Augustodunum.

[Col. 1156D] **V NON. OCTOB.**—The nativity of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, who was led to the faith by the apostle Paul, by whom he was also ordained the first bishop of Athens. Under the emperor Hadrian, after a most illustrious confession of faith and the gravest kinds of torture, he was crowned with martyrdom.

Among the ancient Saxons: the nativity of the holy presbyters Edili and Evaldori [the two Ewalds]. They came to Germany with Bishop Willibrord and went on to the Saxons. There, while preaching the word of God, they were killed by pagans. A light appearing at night over their bodies revealed what their merit had been.

**IV NON. OCTOB.**—At Corinth: Crispus and Gaius [Col. 1157A], whom the apostle Paul mentions in the First Epistle to the Corinthians (I Cor. V).

In Egypt: the holy martyrs Mark and Marcellian, brothers, and with them innumerable others of both sexes. Some of them were delivered to the flames, others drowned in the sea, some consumed by hunger, and certain others fastened to crosses; they merited heaven.

**III NON. OCTOB.**—In Sicily: Placidus and Eutychius, with thirty others.

In Gaul, at the city of Valence: Apollinaris the bishop, distinguished by miracles and martyrdom.

At Eumenia: Thraseas the bishop, who completed his martyrdom. He was one of the ancients who asserts that, as though he had received it by the tradition of his predecessors, he had learned that the Savior commanded the apostles not to depart from Jerusalem before the twelfth year [Col. 1157B].

**II NON. OCTOB.**—At Capua: the holy Marcellus, Castus, Aemilius, and Saturninus.

In Gaul, at the city of Agen: Faith [Fides], virgin and martyr, by whose example the blessed Caprasius was inspired to martyrdom.

On the same day: Sagaris the martyr and bishop of Laodicea, who was one of the disciples of the blessed apostle Paul.

**NON. OCTOB.**—At Rome, on the Appian Way: the nativity of Saint Mark the bishop and confessor. He sat in the episcopal office for two years, nine months, and thirty days. He established that the bishop of Ostia, who consecrates bishops, should use the pallium.

On the same day: the holy Julia, Sergius, and Bacchus, under the emperor Maximian. In his palace Sergius, the chief secretary, and Bacchus, the second secretary, were accused before the same emperor—or rather, most clearly discovered—to be worshipers of the true God, having abandoned the worship of idols. Since neither threats nor flatteries could draw them away from the steadfastness of faith, by the emperor’s order they were stripped of their military cloaks, dressed in women’s tunics, and dragged through the middle of the city with chains placed around their necks. Finally, by order of Maximian and under the command of Antiochus, they were crowned with martyrdom: Bacchus gave up his spirit while stretched out and beaten with raw scourges. Sergius, after many tortures, was struck with the sword. Christians took up their bodies and buried them honorably in one place. There the virgin Julia also rests beside the martyrs; she had suffered under the governor Martianus [Col. 1157D].

On the same day: the holy martyrs Marcellus and Apuleius. At first they followed Simon Magus, but when they saw the wonders that the Lord worked through the apostle Peter, they abandoned Simon, devoted themselves to the apostolic teaching, and, after the apostles’ passion, were themselves crowned with martyrdom.

**VIII ID. OCTOB.**—At Gortyna in Crete: the blessed Philip the bishop, a man of great virtues.

At Thessalonica: Saint Demetrius the martyr.

Likewise: the nativity of Reparata, virgin and martyr, who suffered at Caesarea in Palestine under the emperor Decius. After boiling lead had been applied and her breasts cut off, she was thrown into a blazing furnace. When the fire did not harm her at all, she was beheaded; a white dove was seen to fly from her neck.

**VII ID. OCTOB.**—Abraham the patriarch.

At Paris: the passion of Dionysius the bishop, Eleutherius the presbyter, and Rusticus the deacon. The blessed bishop, sent into Gaul by the Roman pontiff for the sake of pilgrimage, arrived at the city of Paris. There, while striving for several years to convert the people to the way of truth by miracles confirming the faith, he was arrested by the prefect together with Rusticus and Eleutherius and crowned with martyrdom.

At Cologne Agrippina: the nativity of Saint Gereon with three hundred nineteen others, who are said to have belonged to the legion of the blessed Mauritius. Scorning the deadly command of Maximian, they submitted their necks to the swords [Col. 1158B] for the true religion.

**VI ID. OCTOB.**—Lot the prophet.

In Crete: Pinytus the bishop, who left the memory of himself alive in writings published by him.

Likewise, at the city of Agrippina: the holy martyrs Mallosus and Victor.

In Britain: Paulinus, bishop of York. He was ordained bishop by the blessed Justus, whom Saint Augustine, the first pontiff of the English, consecrated. Paulinus converted the Northumbrian people—that is, the nation of the English living north of the River Humber—to the faith.

**V ID. OCTOB.**—At Tarsus, the metropolis of Cilicia: the nativity of the martyrs Tharacus the presbyter [Probus] and Andronicus. During the persecution of Diocletian, under the governor Maximus, they were punished with imprisonment, beaten with sinews, their testicles abraded, burned with flaming papyrus, subjected to the breaking of their jaws and the torture of their shins, and tormented by having vinegar and mustard poured into their nostrils. After burning stakes had been applied, after their fingers had been pierced with extremely sharp nails, and after their eyes had been pierced and their tongues cut out, they were thrown to bears and lions. But when none of the beasts harmed them, they were slaughtered with the sword and ordered to be thrown among the bodies of the slain. At night they were revealed to Christians as though by a splendid star sent down from heaven over the bodies of the saints; under the guidance of that same star they were committed to burial.

**IV ID. OCTOB.**—At Ravenna: Saint Edistus.

In Africa: four thousand nine hundred seventy-six holy confessors and martyrs who, during the Vandal persecution, were assigned by order of Hunneric, the Arian king, among the fiercest Moors. Among them were Cyrianus and Felix, outstanding priests of the Lord. Some, while being driven forward to run by the points of spears, and others, with their feet bound, being dragged through the roughest places, were torn apart by such savage punishment that they breathed out their spirits among the hands of those who dragged them.

At Rome: the nativity of Saint Bedistus [Edistus] the martyr.

In Syria: Eustatius [Eustachius] the presbyter, Eucharistus, Burrus, and Bonatus.

In Campania, at Patria: Fortunata.

**III ID. OCTOB.**—At Troas [Trohada]: Carpus, a disciple of the apostle Paul.

At Antioch: Theophilus, who held the episcopate of the Church as the sixth after the apostles, a most learned man. He established that a fast should be held on Saturday three times a year, according to the prophecy, concerning grain, wine, and oil.

In Spain: Faustus, Mark, and Adria [Januarius and Martial].

At Chalcedon: Marcellus.

At Alexandria: Saint Anastasius the bishop.

**II ID. OCTOB.**—The nativity of Saint Callixtus the pope, who suffered martyrdom under the emperor Alexander. After he had baptized the proconsul Palmachius and the senator Simplicius, together with all their households and many others, he was arrested by Alexander, tortured by hunger, beaten with clubs, and committed to prison. In that prison his presbyter Calepodius, who had long before suffered martyrdom, visited and consoled him. There he also healed a soldier named Privatus of ulcers and brought him into the Catholic faith [Col. 1159B]. Alexander, angered by this, ordered the blessed Callixtus to be thrown from the window of a house and, with a stone tied around his neck, plunged into a well; he ordered rubble to be heaped over him. His own people later lifted him out and committed him to burial in the cemetery of Calepodius.

At Córdoba: Saint Lupus and Aurelia.

At Lyon: the translation of Justus the bishop and confessor, who led an eremitical life and, in the prophetic spirit, foretold what would happen after him.

**ID. OCTOB.**—In Gaul, at Cologne Agrippina: the holy Moors from the soldiers of the sacred Theban Legion. Numbering fifty, they completed their martyrdom and were buried in the same city.

At Capua: Libulus and Saint Fortunata.

On the same day, at Lyon: Antiochus the bishop.

**XVII KAL. NOVEMB.**—In Asia: Cereas.

In Africa: two hundred seventy who were crowned together.

Likewise: the holy martyrs Martianus and Satyr(i)anus, with their two brothers, and Maxima the virgin. Under Geiseric, the Arian king, they were first torn apart with knotted clubs as far as the bones, then confined in the stocks and freed by divine power, immediately becoming unharmed. Maxima, the servant of Christ, was released and became the mother of many virgins. The others, by order of the most impious tyrant, had their feet tied behind their backs to running chariots; torn apart among thorny places, they died in the Lord [Col. 1159D].

[Note: Everything is taken from Walafrid Strabo.]

On the same day, among the Alemanni, who are also called Suebi, near the Rhaetian Alps: the burial, or passing, or birthday into eternal life of the most blessed Gallus the confessor is solemnly celebrated. He came from the island of Ireland, situated between Britain and Spain. Moved by divine love, he traveled as a pilgrim through Gaul with his master and abbot Columbanus and entered Alemannia. He came to a wilderness situated between the Rhaetian Alps and the shore of Lake Brigantinus. When Father Columbanus went on to Italy, Gallus was detained there by illness. When he had overcome it through the healing hand of God [Col. 1160A] and recovered his health, he desired to lead a solitary life. He cultivated the retreats of the wilderness by devoting himself entirely to God, yet without remaining idle.

When King Sigebert heard that he was living on royal possessions, he ordered a charter of security to be drawn up, so that the holy man might hold by authority the place where he lived. He also gave him weights of gold and silver and ordered Duke Cunzo, if the inhabitant of the solitude wished it, to provide him with assistance for building a cell. The athlete of God, therefore, intending to construct a spiritual building, devoted himself to frugality, prayers, and vigils. He recalled the people from the error of idolatry, smashed their images, and commended his preaching to his hearers through the effect of signs. Because the number of these signs is recorded and read everywhere in the book of his life and virtues, and is increased even today by the miracles formerly performed, we pass over them for the present [Col. 1160B]. We recall only this: divine mercy made the blessed Gallus an apostle to the Alemannian people. He found that nation enveloped in paganism and, having instructed it in the truth of the faith, led it from the darkness of ignorance to the sun of justice, which is Christ, as a skillful traveler on God’s road. He also found the place, previously inaccessible to human nature and occupied only by wild beasts, serpents, and demons; after driving out the enemies, he presented it as a dwelling place for the Godhead.

The greatest care must be taken, and fear must be felt, lest the tabernacle of God—which the holy man erected through divine revelation and many labors, and which by royal authority was set apart as God’s lot and allotted inheritance [Col. 1160C]—be attacked by any rashness of human presumption; lest human greed seize what has been cleansed from the rage of demons and the savagery of beasts. Finally, wherever the limbs of the deceased Gallus were carried by untamed horses, no human restlessness should dare to trouble him there.

**XVI KAL. NOVEMB.**—Martha, the sister of Lazarus, and Aristion, who was one of the seventy disciples.

Likewise: Heron, who governed the Church of Antioch after Saint Ignatius; this was also revealed to Ignatius himself as he went to his passion. Heron became an imitator of his master in both life and martyrdom, for he was Ignatius’s deacon.

[Col. 1160D] In Gaul, at the city of Orange: Florentius the bishop, renowned for many virtues, who rested in peace.

At Nicomedia: Alexander.

In Mauretania: Ninus, Victurius, Nobilitanus, Marianus, Lucius, Mittinus, and Crescentianus.

Likewise: the translation of the body of Saint Gallus and the dedication of his magnificent [Note: magnificent, that is, built at the greatest expense.] and most worthy basilica, constructed between the two mountains Cirrius and Walthrammesberch. It has the river Steinaha to the south and the river Nigraha to the north. The place is called the monastery of Saint Gallus after the blessed man’s name. There, as the Lord reveals the merits of his powers, the blind receive sight, the deaf are given hearing, the maimed are enabled to work, the mute rejoice in the loosening of their tongues, the lame have their steps directed, and the possessed are freed from evil spirits. Those confined to bed and the crippled are raised up after receiving health freely; toothache is restrained by the medicine of a beam, and the removal of other illnesses is also accomplished there.

**XV KAL. NOVEMB.**—Saint Luke the historian and evangelist. You will find an account of the conduct of his life, his professional calling, and the manner of his death in Paul’s Epistle, in the Acts of the Apostles, and in the preface to his Gospel.

At Rome: Tryphonia, the wife of the emperor Decius. After the killing of Callixtus and Laurence, and after her husband had been punished by God, she received baptismal water with her daughter Cyrilla, the daughter of Decius [Col. 1161B], and died the following day.

On the same day: Asclepiades of Antioch, bishop and martyr, under the emperor Decius.

**XIV KAL. NOVEMB.**—At Antioch in Syria: the nativity of Saint Beronicus, Pelagia, and fifty-nine others. Pelagia had first been a prostitute under pagan religious practice; afterwards, through the grace of God and the teaching of the holy bishop Nonnus, she was converted to the faith of Christ and baptized. She gave all her possessions to the poor and, on the Mount of Olives, leaving Antioch, built a small cell for herself at the place where the Lord ascended into heaven. In male dress and monastic discipline, she brought her present life to an end.

On the same day: the blessed martyrs Ptolemy [Tholomeus] and Lucius. After Ptolemy had been bound and imprisoned, and tortured by a centurion because of his confession of the divine name [Col. 1161C], he was brought before the judge Urbicius. The judge again questioned him about the worship of the gods. Ptolemy said to him:

> “Whoever denies what exists undoubtedly judges that what he denies is culpable.”

Immediately Urbicius ordered him to be led away. When a certain Christian named Lucius saw this, he said to the judge:

> “Why is this man, accused of no crime but only of professing Christianity, ordered to be led away to death?”

Urbicius said to him:

> “As I see, you too are a Christian?”

When Lucius confessed this, he too was ordered to be killed. A third man was also punished at the same time for the same reason. These martyrs suffered under Antoninus and were buried at Alexandria.

In Gaul, at the city of Agen: Caprasius the martyr [Col. 1161D]. Fleeing the persecution, he hid in a cave. But when he heard that the blessed virgin Faith was contending for Christ, he too was inspired and obtained the palm of martyrdom.

**XIII KAL. NOVEMB.**—At Nicomedia: the holy martyrs Dasius, Zot(i)cus, Gaius [Caius], with twelve thousand others.

Likewise: Simplicius, whose exemplary life was a cause of salvation for many, so that three thousand baptized persons were received into the bosom of Mother Church.

On the same day: our Father Hilarion, whose life full of virtues Jerome wrote. Having led a life entirely devoted to labor, when he recognized that his end was approaching and that nothing of a living man remained in him except consciousness [Col. 1162A], he said with open eyes:

> “Go forth, go forth, soul. What do you fear? What do you doubt? For nearly seventy years you have served Christ, and you fear death?”

With these words he breathed out his spirit.

On the same day: Saint Asterius the presbyter and Saint Callixtus. After he had buried the body of his father, having lifted it from the well, Alexander ordered him to be thrown from a bridge.

Likewise: the translation of the blessed Viator in the wilderness, companion of Saint Justus.

**XII KAL. NOVEMB.**—At Jerusalem: Mark, who was the first from the Gentiles to hold the episcopate there and completed his life by martyrdom.

Likewise: the blessed Salome, who, together with the other women [Col. 1162B], had been concerned with the Lord’s burial.

At Adrianople in Thrace: the holy Philip the bishop, Eusebius, Severus the presbyter, and Hermes the deacon. Because they opposed the churches being plundered by the wicked, they were crowned with martyrdom.

**XI KAL. NOVEMB.**—At Antioch in Syria: the nativity of Theodoretus [Theodorus] the presbyter. During the persecution of the impious Julian, he was cruelly tortured on the rack and with lamps. The soldiers who tortured him, terrified by an angelic apparition, fell face down and believed in Christ. The tyrant ordered them to be plunged into the sea. The blessed Theodoretus [Theodorus] said to them:

> “Go before me, brothers; I too, overcoming the enemy, will follow you to the Lord.”

Thus he was killed by the sword and completed his martyrdom. He also foretold by the prophetic spirit [Col. 1162C] the death of Julian in Persia.

In Spain: Servandus and Germanus. After scourging and a very long imprisonment, they completed a long journey laden with iron and finally completed their passion by having their heads cut off.

**X KAL. NOVEMB.**—At Venusia, a city of Apulia: the nativity of Saint Felix the bishop, Audactus [Audactes] and Januarius the presbyters, Fortunatus and Septimus the readers. In the time of Diocletian they departed through execution by the sword.

Likewise: Venantius the abbot, of whom it is written that, while still living on earth, he recognized that the solemn rites of the Mass were being completed in heaven. Once, when the Lord’s Prayer was being recited at Mass, he heard someone from a tomb answer the priest: “But deliver us from evil.”

**IX KAL. NOVEMB.**—At Nicomedia: the day of Severus and Dorotheus.

At Caesarea in Cappadocia: Longinus, concerning whom below.

**VIII KAL. NOVEMB.**—At Rome: the passion of Chrysanthus and Daria, who maintained perpetual chastity under the appearance of marriage. For Chrysanthus converted Daria from the error of paganism, and under the emperor Numerian, after many kinds of torture, they were thrown into a deep pit with his wife and sons and gave their souls back to God.

In Gaul, at the city of Soissons: Crispinus and Crispinianus. Under Maximian and Diocletian they were stretched upon the pulley, beaten with clubs, and stakes driven into their nails. In winter, with millstones hung around their necks, they were plunged into a river; they were thrown into molten lead and into boiling oil mixed with pitch and fat. But by divine deliverance they were rescued from all these torments. When their torturer Rictiovarus [Retiovapus] saw that no torture could harm them, he furiously threw himself into the fire. Maximian, hearing of the destruction of his subordinate, ordered them to be put to death by the sword.

On the same day, at the city of Périgueux: Saint Fronto. Ordained bishop by the blessed apostle Peter, he was sent with the presbyter Gregory to preach the Gospel. He converted a large part of the city’s people to faith in and confession of Christ. When his companion George died on the journey, Fronto placed the apostle Peter’s staff upon him and raised him from the dead; then he rested in peace [Col. 1163B].

Likewise, at Rome: the passion of forty-six soldiers who, baptized together by Pope Dionysius, were beheaded by order of the emperor Claudius. There, together with them, another one hundred twenty-one martyrs were also buried, among them the four named Theodosius, Lucius, Mark, and Parus [Peter].

Likewise: Boniface the pope, who established that neither a slave nor a person liable to civic service should be made a cleric.

**VII KAL. NOVEMB.**—In Africa: the holy martyrs Rogatianus the presbyter and Felicissimus, who suffered under Decius and Valerian.

On the same day: the holy bishops Vedastus and Amandus. Vedastus was serving as presbyter in the town of Toul. But after King Clovis had become the victor over the Alemanni, remembering the vow by which he had bound himself in the crisis of battle, he took the blessed Vedastus from Toul with him and hurried to Saint Remigius in the city of Reims for the grace of baptism.

The remainder is missing.

[Col. 1163]

**B. LETTER OF NOTKER BALBULUS, MONK OF SAINT GALL, TO RUODPERT.** He clears himself of the charge of disparagement.

(At Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum Novissimus*, vol. VI.)

[Col. 1163]

[Col. 1163C] To his brother Ruodpert, Notker, from exile.

You are scarcely known to me, and I wonder why you are already angry with me. One ought to maintain an unconquered spirit against anger, not be rashly stirred against anyone. It is written in the Gospel: “Whoever is angry with his brother without cause is liable to judgment” (Matthew V). In truth, by the faith that exists in love, I have never tried to damage your reputation, nor to criticize the foolishness of the brothers who are with you, as you threateningly charged through the presbyter Kazilin. Otherwise, if I diminished your glory, I would make myself inglorious. For I wish, through brotherhood, to reign together with you, if indeed you are reigning.

If you wish to believe me, I rejoice for your sake that you do not lend your ear rather to an evil report. But if you do, perhaps summon that impostor—I do not know who he is—who sowed the weeds. “He denied it,” you say, “the man whom you had accused before.” [Col. 1164C] And if he persists in lying and will not confess his falsehoods, the matter must now be handled by conjectures, since the deed is not admitted. The argument must be drawn from all the circumstances belonging to the person and the affair: from impulse of mind and reasoning, from the aspects of honor and utility. It is therefore difficult to distinguish an ambiguous matter without these points of inquiry. This is that rational status through which the *forus* [so the manuscript, for *forum*] resounds most loudly, and through which the fiercest battles and hostilities arise, with Cato prosecuting and Quintilian defending. By this method I too have decided to clear myself publicly of the accusation with which you charged me.

If, however, the choice is granted, and an unknown man can persuade an unknown man of anything, I trust that I shall be excused in your eyes. Meanwhile, refrain from anger. At any rate, you seem wise to me if you are a pursuer of virtue [Col. 1164D].

[Col. 1163]

**B. FORMULARIES OF NOTKER BALBULUS, MONK OF SAINT GALL**

(At Neugart, *Codex Diplomaticus Alemanniae*, vol. I, passim.)

[Col. 1163]

**I. WILLIHER’S TRANSFER.** (Year 855 or 860.)

[Col. 1163D]

I, Willihere, in the name of God, transfer to the monastery of Saint Gall, over which the venerable abbot Grimald is known to preside, one *hoba* in the forest adjoining Werimbretiscella [Note: Zell, a name borne by several villages in the Argengau.].

—Done publicly at Viskingun [Note: Fischen: one in the rural district of Lindau, another in Stiefenhof.], in the presence of those whose signatures are contained here. [Col. 1165A] Signature of Williger, the advocate. Signature of Heimo. + Signature of Sigifrid. + Signature of Egibert. + Signature of Ellinwart. + Signature of Ruadmunt. + Signature of Waldram. + Signature of Adalhelm. + Signature of Adalcoz. Therefore I, Notger [Notker], wrote and subscribed this in place of Irfing. I noted the day: the ninth day before the Kalends of October, the second weekday, in the twenty-first year [Note: Dominical letters F or GF, and therefore the date is in the year 835 or 840.] of King Louis, under Count Huodalrich [Note: Of the Argengau.].

**II. BEREFRID’S PRECARIA.** (Year 858.)

Therefore, by the favor of Christ’s mercy, it pleased me, Abbot Grimald, and the other brothers, with the consent also of our advocate Ruadbert, that Pereurid [Note: Goldastus presents Berefrid’s charter of transfer as no. 52, but the complete *precaria* as no. 72.] should possess under this *precaria*, in accordance with the transfer lawfully made by him, the properties that he transferred to Saint Gall. For that same Pereurid transferred everything that he owned in the district of Zurich, in a village named Pichilinchova [Note: Perhaps Büelhof, a name borne by three villages in the county of Kyburg.], except for one meadow between Parachstetin [Note: Now, I think, Bartstock, in the lordship of Grüningen in the territory of Zurich.] and Heremuntinchouun [Note: Hermikon on the River Glatt]. He transferred all the rest in its entirety to the aforesaid monastery, on this condition: that he himself should possess the same properties and pay an annual rent from them.

But if Perevrid himself had wished to redeem those properties, he was to do so for six denarii.

—Done publicly in the village of Pichilinchova, in the presence of those whose signatures are contained here. + Signature of Grimald the abbot. Signature of Hartmot the dean. Signature of Engilram the porter. Signature of Cozbert the provost. Signature of Selbo, and others. Therefore I, Notger [Notker], wrote and subscribed this. I noted the day: the second weekday, the fourth day before the Kalends of September, in the nineteenth year [Note: Dominical letter B.] of the reign of King Louis, under Count Kerolt [Col. 1165C] [Note: In Goldastus, erroneously Karotus; Keroltus governed the Zurich district.].

**III. HILTIBERT’S TRANSFER.** (Year 864.)

I, Hiltibert, transfer to the monastery of Saint Gall whatever property I possess by hereditary right in Zurichgau, in the place also called Huson [Note: Hausen, a village with a parish in the lordship of Knonau, in the Zurich district]. On this condition: that I go to that monastery itself and spend the remainder of my life there, and that all my property immediately revert to the same monastery, to be possessed forever; and that thirty-three yokes of land in Turbenthal [Note: Turbenthal, a notable village in Kyburg county] be granted by the monastery itself to Liutsinda and Engilsinda, the daughters of my daughter, at an annual rent of four denarii, so that they and their legitimate offspring may possess it forever.

I also wish it to be known to posterity that they, my granddaughters, later of their own accord returned those thirty-three yokes to the monastery through the hand of their father Eleland.

Done publicly at Rickenbach [Note: Rickenbach near the town of Wil, in the district of Saint Gall], in the presence of those whose marks are recorded here. The mark of Eleland and of his daughters, who, concerning the property that Hildebert acquired for them from the monastery itself, completed this sale and agreement. The marks of Abbot Grimald and of his advocate Amalung, and of the other witnesses: + Linco, + Adalbert, + Erchanbert, + Paldolt, + Hadabert, + Cozolt, + Winidhere, + Anzo, + Erchanbold, + Waldhere, + Pato, + Reginbold, + Wito, + Ruadho, + Lantpert, [Col. 1166B] + Adalbert, + Woffo, + Adabert, + Thancpert, + Reginker, + Pato, + Reginbert.

Therefore I, Notker, wrote and subscribed this document in the place of Provost Folchard. I recorded the day: Friday, the fourth day before the Nones of June, in the twenty-ninth year [Note: Epochal year 835, Dominical Letters BA] of the reign of Louis, under Count Adalbert.

### IV. LANDELOH’S TRANSFER (Year 870)

I, Landeloh [Note: Landeloh. P. Heregott lists him among the lords and nobles. Prolegomena IV, nos. 8 and 9, to the Genealogia diplomatica gentis Habsburgicae, discusses him at greater length. Ekkehard the Younger, On the Affairs of Saint Gall, chap. 1, says that Landeloh was the archbishop of Trier; the author of the related work, also called Minimus, relates in chapter 12 of the Life of Notker the Stammerer that he was bishop of Darien], in the name of almighty God, considering the salvation of my soul and of my ancestors, transfer to the monastery of Saint Gall, which the venerable Abbot Grimald is now known to govern, my basilica at Hoeng [Note: Hoeng, an hour’s distance below Zurich], my acquisition at Tellinghofen [Note: Daellicken in the prefecture of Regensdorf, in the Zurich district], and whatever I possess on this side of the Limmat [Note: The Limmat, the river that divides Zurich into the greater and lesser cities] in Zurichgau, except for my acquisition at Würenlos [Note: Würenlos, a parish in Baden county between Zurich and Baden].

I make this transfer on the condition that I possess these properties throughout my lifetime and pay an annual rent of one solidus. In addition, the administrators of that monastery shall, for as long as I live, grant me their property as a benefice: namely, the estate at Wurmspach [Note: Wurmspach on the right bank of Lake Zurich above Rapperswil, where there is now a convent of the Cistercian order]; two hides at Burg [Note: Burg in the lordship of Uznach in the same border region, or in the parish of Dürnten in the prefecture of Grüningen, in the Zurich district]; one at Wagen [Note: Wagen in the parish of Jona near Rapperswil]; one at Engstlingen [Note: Engstlingen, Engstringen, or Eystringen, between Hoeng and Weiningen]; one at Affoltern [Note: Affeltrangen in the parish of Hinwil, prefecture of Grüningen, or Affoltern in the parish of Regensdorf. The former is easier to understand from the etymology, the latter from the location]; and one at Regensdorf [Note: Regensdorf below Zurich].

And if my mother and my priest Willebold outlive me, then, while the other properties of the monastery return to their administrators, my mother shall have the one at Affoltern and pay one solidus in rent. Priest Willebold shall possess the hide at Engstringen, together with the basilica at Hoeng, throughout his life, at an annual rent of one solidus.

When they have died, the administrators of the monastery of Saint Gall shall claim for themselves everything in Zurichgau that was legally mine, except, as stated, my acquisition at Würenlos. This condition alone being observed: that these properties shall never again be granted to anyone as a benefice, and that the bondsmen found there at that time, whether within the estate or on the hides, shall revert to the monastery.

To prevent any doubt from arising concerning the rent mentioned above, I am to pay only one solidus both for my own properties and for the properties granted to me as a benefice by the aforesaid monastery. Likewise, my mother shall pay only one solidus for my possessions and for the aforesaid hide at Affoltern, and Willebold one.

If anyone should arise to oppose this charter, let him be compelled to pay three ounces of gold and five pounds of silver to the king’s treasury, and nevertheless let this transfer remain firm and stable, with the stipulation appended.

Done at Hoeng, in the presence of those whose marks are recorded here. The mark of Landeloh and of his advocate Oadalhard, who made this transfer, and of the other witnesses: + Ruochere, + Herbreht, Wolfhere, + Perichker, Landolt, Heitar, + Adalbreht, + Adalbern, + Otto, + Reginger, + Egino, + Wolfhere, + Wolfhart, + Ratker, + Hupreht, + Waning, + Cozhelm, + Adalhelm, + Oadal, + Undolf.

Therefore I, Notker, wrote and subscribed this document. I recorded the day: Wednesday, the fourth day before the Ides of February, in the thirtieth year [Note: Epochal year 840. Dominical Letter A] of Louis’s reign, under Count Rudolf [Col. 1167C] [Note: Rudolf, count of Zurichgau].

### V. WILLIBOLD’S TRANSFER (Year 873)

I, Willebold, providing for my old age and for the poverty that ordinarily accompanies it, transfer to the monastery of Saint Gall, which the venerable Abbot Hartmot [Note: Hartmot, dean of Saint Gall and acting in the abbot’s place until 13 June 872. “Abbot Grimald,” says Ratpert, On the Affairs of Saint Gall, chap. 9, “entrusting all the monastery’s business to Hartmot, himself freely attended the royal court”] now governs, my small estate at Uzwil [Note: Uzwil in Toggenburg county], namely twenty yokes of land.

This is on the condition that the little estate serve the guesthouse, and that I be received there in the house for guests, and that until the end of my life I receive food and clothing there like the first of their junior members: that is, every year one linen garment and another woollen one, and in the third year [Col. 1167D] a cloak, if the old one has become so worn, as well as shoes and [Col. 1168A] other expenses, just as the others in the monastery receive them.

I also wish that this little possession never be granted to anyone as a benefice. But if this should happen, so that the land is taken away from the hospice and I no longer receive provisions there, then I shall reclaim it for myself without anyone’s objection.

Done in the monastery itself, in the presence of those whose marks are recorded here. The mark of Engelram, the hospitaller [Note: The hospitaller alone among the monks of Saint Gall signed the charter, because the revenues from the bequest fell exclusively under his care]. The mark of Heitar, centurion, and of the other witnesses: + Wilhere, + Waldpert, + Hartman, + Richpert, + Thancpert, + Ruodpert.

Therefore I, Notker, wrote and subscribed this document in the place of Winidhari, monk. I recorded the day: Sunday, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the thirty-third year [Note: The thirty-third year of Louis the German, reckoned from the year 840, was still running in May of the year 873. Dominical Letter D] of the reign of Louis the Younger, under Adalbert, count of Durgau.

### VI. HUGPERT’S EXCHANGE (Year 882)

[Col. 1168B]

I, Hugpreht, providing for my poverty and my needs, transfer to the monastery of Saint Gall in Zurichgau, at the place called Eschicken [Note: Eschicken, a village in Kyburg county], belonging to the estate of Lindau [Note: Lindau, a village whose parish still includes Eschicken; it must not be confused with the imperial city of Lindau on Lake Constance, which Vadianus, in the cited passage, thought was meant here, followed by Ernst Tentzel, who, carried away by the heat of disputation, did not hesitate to assign the city of Lindau to Thurgau (History Vindicated, p. 216). See also p. 264. But from the location of the places and the name of Count Adalbert, I am convinced that this charter does not support the defenders of the Lindau charter], nine yokes of land, to be immediately brought under the monastery’s ownership.

In return I have received nine others in Thurgau, at the place called Elig [Note: Elig in Kyburg county], on the condition that I possess the land throughout my life at an annual rent of one denarius, and that my wife likewise possess it after me; and that after our death it be recalled into the monastery’s ownership.

Done at Zell [Note: Zell, in the same region, on the right bank of the Töss], on the Ides of February, in the second year of the empire of Charles II [Note: The writer calls Charles the Fat “the second,” because Charles the Bald, his uncle, had no jurisdiction over Alemannia], with Adalbert as count in Thurgau.

And these are the witnesses: Othere, Buozo, Zuozo, Maganloh, Cozolt, Echanolt, Eburhart, Rathere, Vodalhart, Hildibold, [Col. 1168C] Adalung, Richgowo.

I, Notker, wrote this at the command of another.

### VII. HUGPERT’S PRECARIOUS GRANT (Year 882)

I, Hartmot, by the grace of God abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall, together with my advocate Cozolt, received from a certain man named Hugpert, in Zurichgau, at the place called Eschicken, belonging to the estate of Lindau, nine yokes of land, to be immediately brought under the monastery’s ownership; and I gave nine other yokes in Thurgau, at the place called Elig.

This is on the condition that he possess the same land throughout his life at an annual rent of one denarius, and that his wife likewise possess it after him; and that after their death it be recalled into the monastery’s ownership.

Done at Zell, on the Ides of February, in the second year of the empire of Charles II [Col. 1168D], with Adalbert as count in Thurgau.

And these are the witnesses: [Col. 1169A] Othere, another Othere, Buozo, Adalram, Zuozo, Maganloh, Cozolt, Erchanolt, Richart, Eburhart, Rathere, Vodalhart, Gebehart, Hildibold, Adalung, Richgowo.

Therefore I, Notker, wrote this at the command of another.

### VIII. WOLFHARIUS’S PRECARIOUS GRANT (Year 904)

I, Salomon, by divine appointment bishop and abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall, have resolved, with the consent of those same brothers and through the hand of my advocate Wito, to restore to Wolfhere by this precarious grant the property that he transferred to us.

The same Wolfhere transferred to us whatever property he had in Ringgau, at the place called Farwangen [Note: I cannot find a place of this name in the Rhingau around the Rhine above Bregenz. There is, however, Farwangen in ancient Aargau and in the territory of Bern, near Lake Hallwil], and throughout the entire surrounding mark: vineyards, fields, meadows, private woods, [Col. 1169B] and use of the common lands, pastures and marshes, alpine meadows, waters and watercourses and their uses, as well as various buildings; and whatever he received in Thurgau, at the place called Uzwil [Note: Uzwil], and throughout all its boundaries, from powerful men and lawful heirs, or acquired by every sort of prudence and industry.

In return for these properties, he shall possess throughout his life, at an annual rent of one denarius, the village called Liubmann’s [Note: That is, Liubmanneswilare, as follows; today Lemenschweil or Loemenschweil], the little estate called the Smith Willebold’s, and another beside Roggwil [Note: Roggwil].

He shall also retain his own property until, according to the will of the administrators of that monastery and the mercy of God, it is joined to the same community.

After his death, or his renunciation of the world, his wife Hilddruda and his son Wolfthrige shall possess that little benefice at Liubmanneswilare, Willebold’s small estate, and the one at Roggwil only throughout their lives, at an annual rent of two denarii. After their death, all those properties shall return to the monastery.

He also received two little oratories, namely at Berg [Note: Berg] and Steinach [Note: Steinach. Each is in Thurgau], on the condition that he care for the celebration of Masses and psalmody and the provision of lights. The monastery dean shall give him annually three fattened pigs and four cartloads of grain—two of wheat and two of oats. All the things that he himself transferred from his own property shall, together with the oratories, after his death or his renunciation of the world, be converted to the benefit of the brothers.

He left one hide at Farwangen and his small slaves, together with various household goods, outside this transfer, for the sake of a certain close female relative of his.

If anyone should attempt to oppose or violate this precarious grant, let him be compelled to pay three ounces of gold and six pounds of silver to the royal treasury, and nevertheless let this precarious grant remain firm and stable.

Done at Hennau [Note: Hennau in Toggenburg county], publicly in the basilica, in the presence of those whose marks are recorded here. The mark of Bishop Salomon and of his advocate Wito. The mark of Folchard, dean; Otwin, sacristan; Beron, provost; Winidhari, porter; Engelbert, chamberlain. The mark of Wolfhari and of his advocate Othari, through whose hand he completed this transfer. The marks of Vodalrich, Eskerich, Richloz, Arolf, Immo, Wettin, Eolchard, Hadomar, Cozbert, Adalram, Wachar, Wolfhard, Ellenbald, Adalbert, Zulling, Ratpot, Hildibert, Adalbert, Buozo, and Willohelm.

Therefore I, Notker, an unworthy monk and hospitaller of Saint Gall, wrote this at the request of others. I recorded the day: Wednesday, the twelfth day before the Kalends of October [Note: Read “the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October,” which was a Wednesday in the year 904, the fifth year of the infant Louis; Dominical Letters AG], in the fifth year of the reign of . . . .

### IX. NANDOLF’S TRANSFER (Year 909)

In the name of almighty God. I, Nandolf, transfer to the monastery of Saint Gall, which the venerable Abbot Salomon is now known to govern, whatever property I appear to possess today in the mark of Cozzosowarro, in the village of Adelineswilare [Note: In the territory of Gossau I have found no place resembling this except Anweil or Andwil].

Done at Herinesowa. The mark of Nandolf himself, who made this transfer with his own hand. The marks of the other witnesses as well: Thiotpert, Puoto, Wolfhart, Winerat, Adalram, Waldo, another Wolfhart, Wito, Thietrich, Waldram, and Albgoz.

I, Notker, an unworthy monk, wrote and subscribed this document in the place of Provost Cozolt, who received this transfer with his own hand, in the presence of his advocate Amalung. I recorded the day: Wednesday, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August [Note: Dominical Letter A], in the seventeenth year [Note: Read tenth or thirteenth year] of the king, under Count Adalbert.

[Col. 1169]

## NOTKER, ON MUSIC

(From D. Gerbert, *Writers on Music*, vol. I.)

[Col. 1169]

### NOTICE

We present, following Canisius, *Ancient Readings*, vol. II, part III, p. 198, Basnage’s edition, Notker the Stammerer’s explanation of what each letter in the superscription of a chant signifies. The little German work on music by the same or another Notker—apparently Notker Labeo—is also included here, edited from a manuscript of Saint Gall dating from approximately the eleventh century, with a Latin translation added.

[Col. 1171] In the same Canisius, cited work, p. 199, the distinguished Father Jodocus Mezler, a professed monk of the monastery of Saint Gall and doctor of the Sacred Canons, testifies that Notker the Stammerer explained “to a certain friend the letters of the alphabet that a certain Roman had attached to particular little signs of antiphons [Note: We discussed him in *Church Music*, vol. I, p. 274]; he had been sent by Pope Adrian at Charlemagne’s request to restore to the churches of Gaul, which had strayed, the chant according to the ancient Gregorian manner.” In the same place Notker the Stammerer is said to have written one book *On Music and Symphonies*. I do not, however, think that this was the German work on music presented here; rather, as I have already noted, it seems to belong to another Notker, called the Third or Labeo, likewise a monk of Saint Gall. Schilter, volume I of the *Treasury of German Antiquities*, presents various works of his written in the old German language; I do not recall ever reading anywhere that such works were composed by the Stammerer.

## WHAT EACH LETTER IN THE SUPERSCRIPTION OF A CHANT SIGNIFIES

[Col. 1171A]

### NOTKER TO HIS BROTHER LAMBERT, GREETING

I have taken care, as far as I could and in accordance with your request, to explain what each letter in the superscription of a chant signifies.

A admonishes that the voice should be raised higher. B, according to the letters with which it is joined, indicates that the voice should be raised well and greatly, or lowered, or held; it “belgicates.” C certifies that the note should be sung quickly or rapidly. D demonstrates that it should be lowered. E declares that it should be sounded evenly. F demands that it be struck with a crash or a rasping sound. G genuinely rejoices that it should chatter gradually in the throat. H, just as it merely aspirates in writing, likewise resides in the notation. I signifies “lower” or “below,” and sometimes indicates gratitude in place of G. K, although it has no value among the Latins, is nevertheless used among us Alemanni in place of the Greek χ; it cries out *chlenige*, that is, “sound” or “ring.” L delights in raising. M recalls moderation, melody, restraint, and singing as though begging. N signifies notation, that is, recognition or marking. [Col. 1172A] O arranges the shape of itself in the mouth of the singer. P proclaims pressure or grasping. Q—why should it be sought among the meanings of the notes, when even in words it is written for no other purpose than that the following V should lose its force? R requests straightness or a scraping—not erasure, but curling. S whistles that one should climb upward or above. T testifies that one ought to draw out or hold. V, although it has lost its own force, like the very powerful Greek or Hebrew vau, makes the voice fly. X, although it begins Latin words by itself, nevertheless wishes one to wait. Y, among the Latins, sings no hymn. Z, although it too is purely Greek and therefore unnecessary to the Romans, must nevertheless, because of the aforementioned occupation of the letter R, be sought for other purposes. In its own language, seek *zitise*.

Whenever two, three, or more letters are placed in one position, their meaning can easily be understood from the explanation above, especially from what I said about B.

The Greek brothers greet you, reminding you to learn about the reckoning of the three-year intercalation, so that, with the biennial reckoning disregarded, you may be accurately informed without error concerning the value of Xerxes’ riches.

## ON THE EIGHT TONES

[Note: The German and Latin versions of the following texts are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1171]

### GERMAN TEXT

[Col. 1171C]

Let it be understood, therefore, that in chant there are seven changes of the voice, which Virgil calls *septem discrimina vocum*, “seven distinctions of voices,” while the eighth is of the same quality as the first. Thus in the lyre and in the psaltery there are always seven strings, and the seven are made equal. The organ also proceeds according to these principles. The alphabet does not go beyond the first seven letters: A, B, C, D, E, F, G.

Of these seven, four are, I mean, B, C, D, and E, in which every chant ends. Those of the first and second tones end on B; those of the third and fourth on C; those of the fifth and sixth on D; and those of the seventh and eighth on E.

Since a chant may descend from its ending as far as the fifth letter, and ascend as far as the ninth, so that it exceeds thirteen notes, as the antiphon *Cum fabricator mundi* does in the first tone, six of the alphabet’s letters, the first A, B, C, D, E, F, must be placed above, and the last three, E, F, G, below. Thus there are sixteen, just as the ancient musicians thought fifteen letters and fifteen strings sufficient. They wanted the cithara to have as many strings, extending from the highest to the lowest in a fourfold ratio. This is the greatest proportion and the greatest symphony, called *bis diapason*, “double diapason,” which is composed of the other symphonies. For a diatessaron and a diapente make a diapason; and just as a diatessaron and a diapente together make a diapason, so two diapasons make a double diapason. Thus four symphonies are found in one.

### LATIN TRANSLATION

[Col. 1172C]

It must therefore be understood that in chant there are only seven changes of the tones, which Virgil calls “seven distinctions of voices”; and the eighth is of the same quality as the first. For this reason there are always seven strings in the lyre and in the psaltery, and they are made equal. In these and other instruments the alphabet does not proceed beyond the first seven letters, A, B, C, D, E, F, G.

Of these seven, four are B, C, D, and E, in which every chant ends: that of the first and second tones ends in B; that of the third and fourth in C; that of the fifth and sixth in D; and that of the seventh and eighth in E.

If a chant wishes to descend from its conclusion down to the fifth letter, or [Col. 1172D] to ascend upward to the ninth, so that it exceeds thirteen notes, as happens in the antiphon *Cum fabricator mundi* in the first tone, then the first six letters of the aforesaid alphabet, A, B, C, D, E, F, must be placed above, and the last three, E, F, G, below. Thus there are sixteen, just as the ancient musicians thought fifteen letters and fifteen strings sufficient; [Col. 1173A] and they wanted the cithara to have the same number of strings, until the highest corresponded to the lowest in a fourfold ratio.

This is the greatest proportion and the greatest symphony, called *bis diapason*, and it consists of the other symphonies. For a diatessaron and a diapente produce a diapason; and just as a diatessaron and a diapente produce a diapason, so two diapasons constitute a double diapason. Therefore four symphonies are found in one.

## ON THE TETRACHORDS

[Note: The German and Latin versions of the following texts are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1173]

### GERMAN TEXT

In fifteen strings they counted four tetrachords; in eight strings, two disjunct tetrachords; in seven, two conjunct tetrachords. That means two separated and two joined tetrachords. But when one is added, all four are separated. The lowest is called the *graves*; the second, because all chants end in it, the *final*; the third, the *superiores*; and the fourth, the *excellentes*.

The fact that for sixteen strings in the lyre there are three times seven, and likewise that some instruments have three alphabets, was arranged for greater convenience, so that one might sing a complete chant while ascending with both hands, without difficulty and without needing to move the hand from the highest alphabet to the lowest. These three alphabets are therefore made alike, so that each contains a diapason, and also a diatessaron and a diapente. In the diatessaron there are three intervals: tone, tone, semitone. In the diapente there are four: tone, tone, semitone, tone.

### LATIN TRANSLATION

[Col. 1174A]

In fifteen strings they counted four tetrachords; [Col. 1174B] in eight strings, two disjunct ones; in seven, two conjunct ones. These are called two separate and two joined tetrachords. But if only one is added, then all four are separate. The lowest is called the *graves*, the second, because all chants end in it, the *final*, the third the *superiores*, and the fourth the *excellentes*.

The reason that, for sixteen strings in the lyre, there are three times seven, and that some instruments likewise have three alphabets, is greater ease: a complete chant can be formed by ascending without difficulty with both hands, and there is no need to move the hands above from the highest alphabet to the lowest. For this reason the three alphabets are necessarily alike, so that each contains a diapason, followed by a diatessaron and a diapente. In the diatessaron [Col. 1174C] there are three intervals: tone, tone, semitone; and in the diapente four: tone, tone, semitone, tone.

## ON THE EIGHT MODES

[Note: The German and Latin versions of the following texts are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1173]

### GERMAN TEXT

[Col. 1173C]

Whoever makes a lyre should measure it so that it does not become too loud because of excessive length, nor too weak because of insufficient length. The highest and lowest strings are, because of faulty measurement, the most unpleasant of all. Therefore the Phrygians and Dorians praised the middle, which lies between the two extremes.

The Dorians wanted to be somewhat nearer to the lowest than to the highest; the Phrygians wanted to be somewhat nearer to the highest than to the lowest. Music names these two modes after those peoples: the Dorian and Phrygian modes. Between them is the tone, which is their difference.

Above the Phrygian is the Lydian, whose difference is a tone. Above the Lydian, by one semitone, is the Mixolydian; and above that, by one tone, the hypermixolydian.
