Then there are three below the Dorian: one semitone lower is the hypolydian; one tone lower than that is the hypophrygian; and another tone lower is the hypodorian. This is the lowest; from it upward to the eighth is the hypermixolydian, the highest.

In these eight modes—namely, hypodorian, hypophrygian, hypolydian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, and hypermixolydian—we recognize eight species of the diapason symphony. Ascending from the lowest to the highest, we find these seven intervals: tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, semitone, tone.

The highest mode sounds at double the pitch of the lowest. Furthermore, when the mode is hypodorian, we begin to sing at the lowest point; when it is hypophrygian, we begin one tone higher; hypolydian, two tones higher; Dorian, one diatessaron higher; Phrygian, one diapente higher; and hypermixolydian, at the full diapason—twice as high—so that we cannot begin any higher.

But if the chant itself should rise farther from its starting point than to the eighth letter, the voice of a human being cannot reach a fourfold range. The fourfold range is therefore to be understood as follows: from the initial starting point in the hypodorian, which is B, or C, it rises by a double to B, or C, in the hypermixolydian; from there it rises again by a double to its eighth letter, which sounds double the former and four times the initial note.

You can then determine whether the chant rises farther from its starting point than to the eighth letter, as the antiphon mentioned above does. In that case it must not begin in the hypermixolydian, since in that mode no one can ascend above the eighth letter. Rather, on whatever letter one cannot ascend higher, one must descend from it to the same letter in the lower alphabet. From there, if the chant descends too far, it can immediately ascend again into the upper alphabet.

At the beginning, the singer has the power to intone as low or as high as desired. But once he has begun and proceeded, he has no power while singing to begin again either lower or higher, from double to single or from single to double, as can be understood from the monochord or the organ.

Whoever measures a pipe must avoid in it what must be avoided in a lyre. When the first pipes become too long, they are not sonorous and produce a hoarse tone, even though the others are sonorous. If they become too short, the lowest ones produce a thin tone, even though the first are sufficiently sonorous.

It is said of them that a pipe one ell long, measured from its mouth upward to the first letter, is too short, and one two ells long is too long; but those between these two, one and a half ells long, are suitable. Thus the eighth has, for half the diameter of one ell, a length of three quarters of an ell, and the fifteenth more than one third, which makes one third of an ell.

### LATIN TRANSLATION

[Col. 1174C]

Whoever makes a lyre should measure it so that, because of excessive extension, it is not too sonorous, nor, because of insufficient extension, less sonorous; for strings that are too high or too low are, because of faulty measurement, the most unpleasant of all. Therefore the Phrygians and Dorians praised the middle, which lies between those two extremes.

The Dorians preferred to approach the lowest tone somewhat more closely than the highest; the Phrygians, however, wanted to be somewhat nearer the highest than the lowest. Music names these two modes after those peoples: the Dorian and Phrygian modes. [Col. 1174D] Between them is the tone, which is the difference between the two.

Above the Phrygian is the Lydian, whose difference is a tone. Above the Lydian by one semitone is the Mixolydian, and above this by one tone the hypermixolydian. Next, three lie below the Dorian: the hypolydian is lower by one semitone; the hypophrygian is lower than that by one tone; and the hypodorian lower by yet another tone. This is the lowest, from which the eighth and highest, the hypermixolydian, is reached by ascending.

In these eight modes—namely, hypodorian, hypophrygian, hypolydian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, and hypermixolydian—we are shown eight species of the diapason symphony. In them we find, ascending [Col. 1176A] from the lowest to the highest, these seven intervals: tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, semitone, tone.

The highest mode sounds at double the pitch of the lowest. Moreover, when the mode is hypodorian, we begin to sing at the deepest pitch; when it is hypophrygian, we begin one tone higher; when hypolydian, two tones higher; when Dorian, one diatessaron higher; when Phrygian, one diapente higher; and when hypermixolydian, we sing the full diapason, that is, twice as high, so that we cannot begin any higher.

But if the chant itself should ascend from the place where it begins as high as it can, namely to the eighth letter, which sounds at double the pitch of the letter from which it began, the human voice cannot ordinarily reach a fourfold range. [Col. 1176B] The fourfold range is therefore to be understood as I have just explained: from the initial starting point in the hypodorian, which is B, or C, it rises by a double to B, or C, in the hypermixolydian; from there it rises again by a double to its eighth letter, which sounds double the former and four times the initial note.

You may then judge whether the chant should rise farther from its starting point than to the eighth letter, as the aforesaid antiphon does. In that case it must not begin in the hypermixolydian, since in that mode no one can ascend above the eighth letter. Rather, on whatever letter one cannot ascend higher, one must necessarily descend from that letter to the same letter of the lower alphabet. Thus, immediately afterward, if it has descended too far, it can ascend again into the upper alphabet. [Col. 1176C]

At the beginning, the singer has the power to intone as deeply or as highly as he wishes. But once he has begun and proceeded, he no longer has the power, while singing, to begin either lower or higher than from double to single or from single to double, as may be understood from the monochord or the organ.

Whoever measures a pipe must avoid what must be avoided in a lyre, for when the first [perhaps “strings”] become too long, they are not sonorous and produce a hoarse tone, even though the others are sonorous. But if they become too short, the lowest ones produce a very thin tone, even though the first are sufficiently sonorous. It is said of them that a pipe one ell long, measured from its mouth upward to the first letter, is too short, and one two ells long is too long; but those between the two, one and a half ells long, are suitable. [Col. 1176D] Thus the eighth has, for half the diameter of one ell, a length of three quarters of an ell, and the fifteenth more than one third, which makes one third of an ell.

## ON THE MEASUREMENT OF ORGAN PIPES

[Note: The German and Latin versions of the following texts are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1175]

### GERMAN TEXT

[Col. 1175D]

Having learned how all the pipes correspond to one another, do not hesitate now to learn their measurement as well. Make the first as long as was said above, as long as you wish, and as wide as you wish [Col. 1177A]; all of them must have the same width. Measure the others according to the first. First see how wide it is; this width is called the diameter. Then, for the length of the first pipe, leave an eighth of that width, and divide what remains downward from there to the tongue, which is called the plectrum, into nine equal parts. Give eight of those nine parts to the second pipe; this is its length upward from the tongue. Then, for the length of the second pipe, leave twice eight parts of the diameter, and again divide the remainder into nine; give eight of these nine parts to the third pipe; this is its length upward from the tongue.

Then take the first pipe, leave for its length one-third of the diameter, and divide what remains from there downward to the tongue into four parts; give three of the four to the fourth pipe [Col. 1177B]. This is its length, and here the diatessaron is found, with tone, tone, and semitone. Continue in the same manner, taking equal intervals upward from its tongue.

Take the first pipe again, leave for its length half its width, divide it into three parts, and give two of them to the fifth pipe. This is its length. Then take that same fifth pipe, leave for its length an eighth of the diameter, divide the remainder into four parts, and give three of them to the seventh pipe.

Next measure the eighth pipe by the first: in the first, leave as much as the diameter—that is, leave the entire width—and divide the remainder into two equal parts; give one of them to the eighth pipe. This is its length upward from the plectrum. Up to this point there is the diapente with tone, tone, semitone, and tone. Then give the same measurement to the remaining seven pipes that you gave, after the first, to the preceding seven [Col. 1177C].

Thus the first pipe has twice the length of the eighth, with one diameter above it; and likewise the eighth has twice the length of the fifteenth, with one diameter above it. But the first has four times the length of the fifteenth, and three diameters besides. If you wonder why there are three rather than two, understand the reason. If one diameter is left in the first pipe, and it is nevertheless twice the length of the eighth, which is its simple proportion, then its length before the diameter is extended becomes half that of the fifteenth. Consequently, the eighth must be twice the fifteenth, together with one diameter; and the first must necessarily be four times the fifteenth, together with two diameters, apart from the diameter of the first pipe.

If, however, the organ-builder wishes to make three full alphabets for fifteen or sixteen strings’ letters, he should measure the third according to the preceding two, just as he measured the second according to the first [Col. 1177D].

## Latin Interpretation

After you have learned how all the pipes answer to one another, do not now begrudge learning their measurement as well. Make the first as long as was said earlier, as long as you wish, and as wide as you wish [Col. 1178A]; all must have the same width. Measure the others according to the measurement of the first. First see how wide it is; that width is called the diameter. Then leave, as the length of the first pipe, an eighth part of that same width, and divide what remains from there downward to the lip, which is called the plectrum, into nine equal parts. Give eight of those nine parts to the second; this is its length upward from the lip.

Then leave, as the length of the second pipe, twice eight parts of the diameter, and divide the remainder again into nine parts; give eight of these nine parts to the third. This is its length upward from the lip. Then take the first pipe, leave as its length one-third of the diameter, and divide it from there downward to the lip into four parts [Col. 1178B]; give three of these to the fourth. This is its length, and here the diatessaron corresponds with a tone, a tone, and a semitone. Continue in the same equal manner upward from its lip.

Take the first pipe again, leave as its length half its width, divide it into three parts, and give two of them to the fifth. This is its length. Then take that same fifth pipe, leave as its length an eighth of the diameter, divide the remainder into four parts, and assign three of them to the seventh.

Then measure the eighth by the first: leave in the first as much as the diameter—that is, leave the entire width—and divide the remainder into two equal parts; give one to the eighth. This is its length upward from the plectrum. Up to this point there is the diapente with tone, tone, semitone, and tone [Col. 1178C].

Then assign the same measurement to the remaining seven that you assigned, after the first, to the preceding seven. Thus the first has twice the length of the eighth, with one diameter above it; and likewise the eighth has twice the length of the fifteenth, with one diameter above it. But the first has four times the length of the fifteenth, and three diameters in addition. If you wonder why there are three rather than two, understand its reason. If one diameter is left in the first, and it is nevertheless twice the eighth, which is its simple proportion, while its length before the diameter is extended becomes half the fifteenth, then the eighth is necessarily twice the fifteenth, together with one diameter; and the first is necessarily four times the fifteenth, together with two diameters, apart from the diameter of the first [Col. 1178D]. If the organ-builder wishes to make three complete alphabets for the letters of fifteen or sixteen strings, he should measure the third beside the first two, just as he measured the second beside the first.

# In the Year of the Lord 912. Hatto, Archbishop of Mainz

## Letter of Hatto and His Suffragans to Pope John IX

Concerning the death of Emperor Arnulf; his seven-year-old son Louis, hailed as king of Germany; and an archbishopric established among the Moravians.

*(In Labbé, General Councils, vol. IX, col. 496.)*

To the lord pope of the holy, apostolic, and universal Roman Church, Hatto, unworthy bishop of the Church of Mainz, together with all the suffragans attached to our insignificance, offers the due service of prayer and faithful obedience [Col. 1179A].

Let your holiness know that no brotherly community subject to the authority of the holy Roman Church appears more faithful, devoted, and obedient than we, who submit ourselves to your lordship and to the head of all the Churches with the full intention of our minds, rejoicing greatly in the Lord and in the gift of his grace: through your holiness and wisdom, the seat of that Church is being magnificently and most extensively enlarged in divine religion. For this we devote ourselves most earnestly to prayer, beseeching divine mercy to grant that you may always ascend to higher things and pursue and accomplish better things from day to day [Col. 1179B].

Furthermore, we inform your clemency that our elder, the Emperor Arnulf, has departed from the exile of this life [Note: [Col. 1179C] Emperor Arnulf, whose death is announced here, died on 20 November 899, during the pontificate of Stephen VI. Yet this letter was written not to him but to his successor John, as is easily understood from the complaint concerning the Moravian archbishopric, which this letter declares to have been instituted by John [Col. 1180C]. Why these bishops wrote only so late, they themselves explain in the letter. COSSART.]. But since, so long as we remain in this world, we are carried along amid uncertainties, not knowing where the souls of some people receive their dwelling after this light, we earnestly beg, as though prostrate at your feet, that by the authority of your power you release his soul from the bonds of sins, because “whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (Matthew 16).

After such a lord, ruler, and governor had been lost, the ship of the Church in our regions began to falter. For a short time it did not know whom it should choose as king. Since there was great fear that the united kingdom might be divided, it came about, as we believe, through divine inspiration, that the eldest son of our elder, although a mere child, was raised to kingship by the common counsel of the princes and the consent of the whole people [Col. 1179C–1180A]. Since the kings of the Franks have always come from one lineage, we preferred to preserve the ancient custom rather than establish ourselves through a new institution. But why this was done without your command and permission, your prudence, we do not doubt, understands.

No other cause is evident except that, because pagans stand between us and you, our journey to our holy mother, the Roman see, was obstructed, so that envoys from our insignificance could not be sent to your dignity. But since at last an opportunity and time have come when our letter could be presented to your sight, we ask that our common decision be strengthened by your lordship’s blessing [Col. 1180B].

Moreover, we inform your piety that our brothers and fellow bishops of Bavaria complained to us and groaned with deep sighs about how the Moravian peoples, rebels against Frankish authority, boast that they have separated themselves from their association and glory in having been elevated by your grant to a metropolitan of their own, although no metropolitan see had ever existed among them, but they had always remained attached to the province and diocese of the others.

They also lamented to us that, through the machinations of certain people, they had been marked with great infamy in your presence—namely, that they had entered into alliance and peace with pagans, and that those pagans, acting on their counsel, had committed so many wicked and unlawful deeds [Col. 1180C]. When the Bavarian bishops sought our counsel concerning all this, we replied that it was just always to cling to the support of one’s brothers [Col. 1181A], since the prophet says: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together” (Psalm 131). Those who withdraw themselves from the support of their brothers or prepare ambushes for their brothers do not dwell together.

Sympathizing with their sorrow, we do not wish to offer them counsel concerning such accusations before bringing the matter to your inquiry through our letter. We know that the carnal customarily persecute the spiritual, and that the malicious weaken and tear apart the well-disposed. Therefore all who persecute the priests of the Lord, secretly or openly, must take the greatest care lest what the Prophet said apply to them: “They devised wickedness in their heart; all day long they prepared battles; they sharpened their tongues like a serpent’s: the poison of asps is under their lips” (Psalm 139) [Col. 1181B]. And shortly afterward: “Coals shall fall upon them; you will cast them into the fire” (ibid.). And again: “The talkative man shall not prosper on earth; evil shall hunt down the unjust man to destruction” (ibid.).

Through Jeremiah the Lord says: “All are judged in blood; each one oppresses his neighbor. All prepare their hands for evil.” Outsiders ought not to become either accusers or judges of bishops. Hence it is written concerning Lot: “You entered as a stranger—will you also judge?” (Genesis 19). No servant, freedman, suspicious or disreputable person should be an accuser of bishops; enemies and all laymen should be rejected.

These brothers and fellow bishops of ours, the Bavarians, true worshipers of God and good shepherds, guard the flock entrusted to them with sleepless vigilance, lest the wolf’s rage seize any little sheep of the holy flock as its prey [Col. 1181C]. They stand as a wall for the house of Israel, lest any hostile force dissolve the Church’s stronghold. Whoever disturbs such men and attacks them with his malice will not escape the punishment to come, although he may escape the present, because it is written: “He who touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zechariah 2).

We have therefore sent all this in writing to you [Col. 1182A], who are the head of the whole holy Church spread throughout the world, and the consolation of all mourners, whatever sad things have befallen you in your members. For the most holy shepherds of Christ mentioned above, deviating in no matter from the Catholic faith but adorning it with holy works and ecclesiastical duties, complained to us and asked that we make these matters known to you; they also promised that, if life permitted, they would make the same things known to you themselves.

We therefore ask that your consolation restore their sorrow to joy, and that such members may always rejoice to cling to the supreme Head, which you are. But those Moravians, as has been reported to our ears, take as an occasion for their pride the fact that they say they receive a metropolitan from your grant [Col. 1182B] and, living apart, reject fellowship with the other bishops. If they continue to be inflated by this confidence, they will, as many think, rush as far as bloodshed.

As far as we dare, we admonish you that your authority, before this happens, should correct them and bring them down to the path of humility, so that at last they may recognize whose rule they ought to obey. We acknowledge ourselves obliged, if anything concerning the holy mother, the Roman Church, should slip away, to inform you of it, so that your power may lead it back to the line of rectitude.

If your admonition does not correct them, willingly or unwillingly they will submit their necks to the Frankish princes; and we believe that this can then be brought about well, without bloodshed and mutual slaughter on either side [Col. 1182C]. Again and again we repeat to the ears of your dignity that the Bavarian bishops and laymen are proved to be inferior to no people in Christian religion, and that the Franks have never accomplished anything worthy of mention, either in ecclesiastical matters or in military affairs, without their aid—not in deed or in reputation. Nor have the Bavarians without the Franks.

# In the Year of the Lord 913. Anastasius III, Roman Pontiff

## Historical Notice on Anastasius

*(In Mansi, Councils, vol. XVIII, p. 311.)*

Anastasius, a Roman by birth and son of Lucian, was substituted for Sergius, the usurper of the see, in the year of the Lord 910, during the time of the emperors Lambert and Leo. He sat for two years and as many months. According to Sigonius, book 6 of *On the Kingdom of Italy*, he adorned the Church of Pavia with many splendid ornaments, granting it the use of an umbrella, the right to ride a white horse, to have a cross carried before it on journeys, and to sit on the pontiff’s left at councils [Col. 1182D–1183A].

In his time Emperor Lambert, when he was thirty-two years old, was secretly killed while hunting by Hugh, Count of Milan; thereafter the full power of the kingdom fell to Berengar.

Leo, sixth of that name, Eastern emperor, suffering from dysentery, died in the twenty-sixth year of his reign. In addition, imitating Justinian, he issued 113 new constitutions concerning sacred and secular matters alike, excessively and rather ridiculously. One letter exists under his name in the library of the Holy Fathers, entitled *On the Truth of the Christian Faith*, in which he professes that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, in these words: “I am the Lord your God, your creator, light from light, the Word from the Father, from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds.”

I mention this so that you may understand that learned men of this period accepted orthodox doctrine; nevertheless, they protested that it had been placed in the Creed without the authority of an ecumenical council [Col. 1184A]. After Leo’s death, in the East his brother Alexander, a wicked man, succeeded to the empire together with Constantine, the young son of the Emperor Leo, in the twentieth year of Alexander’s age. After six months of rule, because of his contempt for God and the holy images, he died an infamous death, as the Curopalates and Arethas report, leaving the empire to Constantine alone.

Pope Anastasius, after sitting for two years and as many months, died in the year of our Redeemer 912. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter, as stated in his epitaph, which Baronius quotes from Manlius.

## Two Privileges of Pope Anastasius III

### I. Privilege for the Church of Vercelli (912)

*(Works of Atto, vol. I, preface, p. IX.)*

Anastasius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy Ragembert, bishop of the holy Church of Vercelli, for the days of his life alone [Col. 1183B].

If shepherds of sheep do not hesitate to endure sun and frost, day and night, in guarding their flock, and with watchful eyes look out lest any of the sheep perish by straying or be carried off, torn by the bites of wild beasts, how much labor and care ought we to show, who are shepherds of souls? We must be vigilant and must not cease to perform the office we have undertaken for guarding the Lord’s sheep, lest on the day of divine judgment we be tortured before the supreme Shepherd because of our negligence, since now we are judged higher than others in the honor of our office.

We grant to your holiness the pallium for celebrating the solemnities of Mass. We grant you its use, while the privileges of your Church remain intact, only on the holy and venerable day of the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ; on the feasts of the holy apostles; on the feast of Saint John; on the Assumption of blessed Mary, Mother of God; on the day of the Nativity of our Lord; on the solemnity of your Church; and also on the anniversary of your ordination, just as was done by our predecessor, the lord Gregory, bishop of this nourishing see [Col. 1183C].

Your fraternity must put on the pallium in the secretarium and then proceed to the solemn celebration of Mass, arrogating nothing more to yourself through rash presumption. Otherwise, while something is improperly seized in outward dress, even those things that could be done properly may be lost [Col. 1183D]. Since the honor of this garment must be preserved by the liveliness of modest conduct, we exhort you to make all your adornments accord with one another, so that, with God as author, you may rightly be conspicuous everywhere.

Thus let your life be a rule for your sons. If any strength has been placed in them, let them direct it according to you and look to you for imitation; by always contemplating you, let them advance, so that after God they may appear to possess the good that you have lived [Col. 1184B].

Therefore let neither prosperity, which flatters temporarily, lift up your heart, nor adversity cast it down; whatever happens, let it be overcome by the virtue of patience. Let hatred find no place with you, and let no indiscriminate favor find one either. Let the wicked recognize strictness in you; let evil insinuation not make the innocent guilty before you; let favor not excuse the harmful. Do not show yourself lenient toward offenders, lest you permit something that has not been punished to be committed. Let there be in you the sweetness of a good shepherd, and also the strictness truly belonging to a judge.

One task is to cherish those who live innocently; another is to restrain the restless from wickedness by striking them down. But sometimes the zeal of superiors, when correction seeks to be more severe under the appearance of the great, passes into cruelty [Col. 1184C]. Therefore restrain anger by judgment, and use disciplinary censure so that you may strike faults while never withdrawing from love of the persons whom you correct.

Show yourself merciful to the poor as virtue permits; let your defense assist the oppressed; let modest uprightness oppose those who demand what they wish; accept no person’s face against justice; despise no one who seeks what is just. Excel in preserving equity, so that neither the rich may persuade us to hear their cases outside the proper course because of their power, nor the poor, because of their humility, be made to despair of their own cause. Thus, by God’s mercy, may you be such as sacred reading commands, saying: “It is necessary for a bishop to be blameless” (1 Timothy 3:2).

You will be able to use all these things beneficially if you possess charity as your principal teacher, so that whoever follows you may not depart from the path [Col. 1184D]. Behold, dearest brother, among many other things, these are the duties of a priest . . . . . of the pallium. If you carefully preserve them, and show that what you have received outwardly you possess inwardly, may the Holy Trinity surround your reverence with the protection of its grace and direct us in the way of its fear, so that after the bitterness of this life we may reach eternal sweetness together.

Written by the hand of John, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of February, in the fifteenth indiction.

Fare well.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of February, through the hand of Theophylact, treasurer of the holy apostolic see, in the year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of the lord Anastasius, supreme pontiff . . . and one [year?] of Scili the Younger, P. P., in the most holy see of blessed Peter the apostle, indiction 15 [Col. 1185A].

### II. Privilege for the Church of Hamburg (912)

*(In Lappenberg, Hamburg Documents, I, 38.)*

+ Anastasius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Hogero, venerable archbishop of the Church of Hamburg, everlasting greeting.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those who flourish in pious religion with benevolent compassion and to grant the wishes of those who ask with joyful devotion. For by this we undoubtedly earn the greatest reward with God, when venerable places, suitably ordered, have through us been brought to a better condition.

Therefore, since you asked us to confirm the archbishopric of Hamburg in its entirety to you and your successors, as it was decreed by our predecessors Gregory and Nicholas of this apostolic see, we, inclined by your prayers, also grant and confirm it by apostolic authority, together with everything generally and specifically belonging to that aforesaid archbishopric: namely, everything that your predecessors acquired through their labors, as well as whatever has been or is being donated there by Christ’s faithful out of love for the eternal fatherland [Col. 1185B–1186A].

This includes those who in the present time have been converted to the faith of Christ through the prompting and protection of God’s grace—namely, bishops among all the peoples of the Swedes or Danes, Norwegians, Icelanders, Scridefinns, Greenlanders, and all the northern nations, as well as in those regions of the Slavs that extend from the River Peene to the River Eider—so that they remain under the authority of you and your successors, the archbishops of the Church of Hamburg, together with whatever, by divine favor, can be acquired by you from the error of unbelief, whether among people or in places, for the Christian religion.

We also send you the pallium and decree that you and your successors may use it perpetually and retain it inviolably. Furthermore, we have decreed that no archbishop, whether of Cologne or anyone else, may claim any authority for himself in your diocese [Col. 1186B], and so forth. We also permit your head to be adorned with the mitre, which is the distinguishing mark of the Romans.

If anyone attempts to oppose this privilege of our authority or in any way to violate it, let him be anathema; but whoever observes it piously shall receive grace and blessing from our Lord Jesus.

Given through the hand of Adrian, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of January, in the eighth indiction.

## Epitaph of Pope Anastasius III in the Basilica of Saint Peter

*(In Baronius, Annals, vol. X, col. 775.)*

The limbs of the poet Anastasius rest in a tomb,

but a small patch of earth never encloses his merit.

He ruled the apostolic see with gentle governance,

being third in succession among the pontiffs [Col. 1185C].

Going to Christ, he hopes that he can thereby

have all the bonds of sin mercifully loosed for him:

Ask God with devoted heart to grant rest

to all who come running from every side to the threshold of this temple [Col. 1186B–C].
